## Introduction


Gender disparities persist in how men and women divide paid work, housework and childcare responsibilities (Cotter et al., 2011; England, 2010; Kühhirt, 2012). Despite rising levels of education and labor force participation among women, they continue to perform a larger portion of housework and childcare compared to their male partners (Auspurg et al., 2017; Schulz, 2021). This gendered division of labor remains prevalent, even as traditional views on gender roles have declined in postindustrial economies (Grunow et al., 2018). While women have increasingly entered the workforce in the past decades, this shift has not been met with a corresponding increase in men's contribution to household tasks, particularly in childcare (Cotter et al., 2011; Kühhirt, 2012). Scholars have reviewed theoretical approaches to explain these continuing disparities (see Auspurg et al., 2017; Nitsche and Grunow, 2018). Understanding attitudes towards gender roles -contemporary and evolving beliefs about appropriate roles for women and men and gendered behavioral outcomes- is key for understanding the ongoing disparities of division of household labor (Auspurg et al., 2017; Düval, 2023; Pedulla and Thebaud; 2015; Schulz, 2021).

Against this background, in this paper we examine attitudes toward gendered division of work using original data from a multifactorial survey experiment conducted in Germany. Using the concept of gender ideology as an analytical heuristic tool (see Chatillion et al., 2018; Grunow et al., 2018), we propose a theoretical model to explore support for gendered divisions of work among couples. Our central question is how respondent evaluations vary based on specific arrangements of paid and unpaid work, which formulated according to contemporary gender ideology profiles that gender scholars previously identified through survey questions. We argue that this approach highlights a theoretical link between attitudes toward gendered division of paid and unpaid work and the current state of the art on gender ideologies. In light of the recent discussions of division of labor among couples, this strategy allows for a more nuanced interpretation of the results from our multifactorial survey experiment (cf. Auspurg et al., 2017; Düval, 2023; Pedulla and Thebaud; 2015; Schulz, 2021).

In addition, this strategy provides the necessary context for how participant evaluations of division reflect the contemporary gender ideologies. Our focus is on specific combinations of paid and unpaid work divisions that align with widely recognized typologies of gender ideologies, as gender scholars and sociologists recently identified (among others see Begall et al., 2023; Grunow et al., 2018; Knight and Brinton, 2017; Scarborough et al., 2019). Lastly, this strategy provides a theoretically grounded framework to better interpret

participants' evaluations of gendered divisions of paid and unpaid work among couples with children-an area where recent scholarship has not provided sufficient theoretical clarity (see Auspurg et al., 2017; Düval, 2023; Pedulla & Thebaud, 2015; Schulz, 2021).

In light of the ongoing reconfiguration of social structure such as increasing female labor force participation, rising homogamy rates among couples, higher immigration levels, as well as concurrent shifts in public childcare policies, we examine participants' attitudes with in relation to their gender and migration background (see Düval, 2023; Gambaro et al., 2023). Our analysis aims to deepen our understanding of the variation in gender role attitudes. Specifically, our main research question is how participants' gender determine their support across different combinations of division of paid and unpaid labor, each representing a distinct gender ideology profile. In addition, we incorporate migration background in to our analysis, investigating whether gender differences exist among native Germans (both Eastern and Western), Turkish and Dutch migrants toward gendered division of labor among men and women with children.


## Theoretical Framework



## Gender Ideology as a Heuristic Tool


In this study, we establish a theoretical link between participant evaluations of division of paid and unpaid work among couples and the specific typologies of gender ideology profiles. Gender ideologies are beliefs about gender roles and worth of men and women and encompass cultural and ideological understandings of men and women's roles in relation to both paid and unpaid work such as housework and childcare (Chatillon et al. 2018; Grunow et al. 2018). These ideologies shape individual beliefs about whether women's primary duty is to care for children and families and whether women's employment is secondary or optional.

Recent theorizing on gender ideologies has highlighted its multidimensional character, moving beyond a unidimensional concept that merely contrasts traditionalism and egalitarianism (among others, see Barth & Trübner, 2018; Begall et al., 2023; Grunow et al., 2018; Knight and Brinton, 2017; Scarborough et al., 2019). These studies rely on specific item questions in large-scale questionnaires, and generate latent classes based on maps of participant responses. Even thee studies rely on different surveys; and therefore on different items and use different labels for their latent classes (Kleinschrot, p. 391), they are largely in agreement about two findings: multidimensionality; the decline of traditionalism. This line of

research emphasizes that egalitarian development somehow continues but instead of all ideologies moving toward a liberal-egalitarian ideology, they identify a diversification of ideologies that adopt egalitarian tendencies to a certain extent or in some domains (Kleinschrot, 2024; Scarborough et al., 2019).

The multidimensionality of gender ideologies reflects the historical evolution of gendered division of labor between men and women. Despite substantial progress in women's educational attainment and labor force participation, women still tend to bear the larger burden of housework and childcare (Cotter et al., 2011; England, 2010; Kühhirt, 2012). The 'stalling' of the gender revolution in partnerships is often attributed to the fact that, while women's labor force participation has increased, men's involvement in household duties especially in childcare- has not kept pace (England, 2010; Sullivan, Gershuny and Robinson, 2018). There is an emphasis on existence of 'multiple equilibria,' in which alternative normative gender regimes coexist (Esping Andersen and Billari, 2015).

Faced with this historical reality, scholars of gender ideology emphasized the persistence of essentialist understanding of gender roles, which perpetuate the belief that 'fundamental innate differences exist between women and men' (Begall et al., 2023, p. 178), particularly in relation to childcare responsibilities. These essentialist beliefs suggest that women should primarily be responsible for childcare, especially in the early years after birth, leading to expectations that women should interrupt their professional careers to focus on caregiving (Hays, 1996; Shu et al., 2024).

Multidimensional gender ideologies are complex and they combine support for different combinations of paid-work, childcare and housework. Challenging the unidimensional understanding, scholars have drawn attention to the emergence of ambivalent gender ideologies. These combine varying degrees of gender egalitarian attitudes with traditional beliefs that view childcare primarily as a maternal responsibility (Grunow et al., 2018; Knight and Brinton, 2017; Scarborough et al., 2019). Ambivalent attitudes maintain the essentialist view about the gendered nature of skills and responsibilities, particularly the role of mothers as primary caregivers, even when supporting women's participation in paid work (Diabaté et al., 2023; Scarborough et al., 2019). Scarborough, Sin and Risman (2019, p. 184) further differentiate between pro-public and pro-private ambivalent gender ideologies: the former are more supportive of equality in the public sphere such as work and politics, whereas the latter express stronger support for equality in the private sphere of the home.

Research suggests that these beliefs may contribute to the persistent gendered divisions of paid unpaid work more generally. We use this theoretical framework as a heuristic tool to interpret respondent evaluations in a multifactorial survey experiment. Based on prior research, we identify two classical unidimensional and three multidimensional ambivalent gender ideology profiles for the German society (see Table 1 for an overview). The first is the egalitarian profile; also called choice egalitarianism (Begall et al., 2023; Knight & Brinton, 2017; Scarborough et al., 2019). In this profile, the couple share all paid and unpaid activities equally: both women and men work full or part-time and they share childcare and housework duties. At the other end of the unidimensional spectrum is the classical male-breadwinner model, i.e., the traditional profile, where men work full-time and women are stay home parents, who are primarily responsible for childcare and  housework (Knight & Brinton, 2017; Scarborough et al., 2019, also called traditional essentialism by Shu et al., 2024).

The first multidimensional gender ideology is the secondary earner profile, where men work full-time and women work part-time (Diabaté et al., 2023; Rosenfeld et al., 2004). This is a common practice in Germany, particularly in Western states, as sixty-six per cent of mothers have part-time jobs (Federal Statistics Office, 2022; Kleinschrot, 2024). Egalitarian familism is our second multidimensional profile. This profile combines the belief that women are active members of labor force with that of family and children are essential to women's identity and fulfillment (Knight and Brinton, 2017). Egalitarian familism emphasizes the responsibility of women as mothers, while supporting women's employment. Specifically, this ideology sees women and men as equals in their paid-work activity, but it perceives childcare as a maternal responsibility. Finally, we identify a profile, which we label as women's second shift, in which men and women participate equally in the labor force, but women also bear the sole responsibility for housework and childcare. We identify these profiles in congruence with the research on Germany that specify gender ideology profiles in this context (Barth and Trübner, 2018; Diabaté et al., 2023; Kleinschrot, 2024). According to our classification, egalitarian familsm and women's second shift differ from each other in terms of housework activity (see Table 1).


## Country-Level Characteristics and Policy Context


Our research builds on the seminal framework of Bolzendahl and Myers (2004), who identify exposure-based and interest-based factors to explain why women develop more

egalitarian gender role attitudes. In contrast, men often prefer traditional gender roles as these align with their own interests. However, social change also influence men, leading some to develop egalitarian attitudes (Düval, 2023, p. 3). Research indicates that men generally develop less egalitarian attitudes compared to women (Grunow et al., 2018; Khoudja and Fleischmann, 2018).

Exposure and interest framework necessitate paying closer attention to the specific country contexts and historical gender regimes, in which these attitudes unfold and develop into gender norms. Scholars emphasized the macro-level characteristics at the country level as a factor in the formation and spread of gender ideologies (Begall et al., 2023; EspingAndersen and Billari, 2015). Drawing on Risman's (2018) 'gender as a social structure' framework Begall, Grunow and Buchler (2023) highlight the interdependence of individual and macro-levels of social organization in their examination of multidimensionality of gender ideologies in advanced industrial economies. They argue that both individual and macro-level factors, as well as their cross-level interactions, shape the prevalence of specific gender ideology profiles in different contextual settings (Begall et al. 2023).

Economic well-being is often associated with greater gender equality, but it does not necessarily foster support for women's dual roles as caregivers and workers (Shu et al., 2024). Rising income levels might position women's employment as secondary or optional, reducing the pressure for women to join the workforce and making stay-at home motherhood a more politically acceptable choice for women (Begall et al., 2023, p. 184). The prevalence of 'male-breadwinner norms' in a society (Gonalons-Pons and Gangl, 2021) can further limit the spread of liberal egalitarian views while reinforcing ambivalent perspectives, previous scholars identified as 'flexible-egalitarianism' (Brinton and Lee, 2016; Knight and Brinton, 2017) or 'egalitarian essentialism' (Grunow et al., 2018). In German context, we observe this in the historical development of gender regimes between Federal and Democratic German Republics (Zoch, 2021; Sievers and Warner, 2023).

Work-family compatibility is another factor contributing to the multidimensionality of gender ideologies, as it affects the tension between caregiving and paid employment for women (Begall et al., 2023; Esping-Andersen and Billari, 2015). Social policies influence individual attitudes and preferences through feedback loops (Gangl and Ziefle, 2015). The availability of affordable, high-quality childcare can strengthen women's dual role in a society as it was the case for East Germany (Zoch, 2021). In contrast, the lack of such services may lead even egalitarian couples to adopt more essentialist division of paid and unpaid work (see

Grunow et al., 2012). Similarly, paid parental leave policies impact attitudes towards division of couple's labor after birth. Generous parental leave policies may encourage women to take longer breaks from their careers (Gangl and Ziefle, 2015), reinforcing familialist attitudes and reducing the expectation of equal responsibility for childcare between partners (Shu et al., 2024). The expansion of public childcare in Germany generated relatively increased support for maternal employment among mothers without a university degree (Zoch & Schober, 2018).

In light of these factors, we incorporate early childcare and education (ECEC) choices into our analysis of gender ideology profiles (Acar, Becker and Grunow, 2024; Klein and Becker, 2017). Publicly provided ECEC services alleviate parental childcare responsibilities, introducing a new dimension to the evaluation of gender ideology profiles, as parental childcare is a critical component in how partners divide paid and unpaid work. ECEC provision therefore, can influence individuals' attitudes toward gender roles and the ways in which they weigh the division of work. Previous studies on gender role attitudes using multifactorial survey experiments have often overlooked external childcare as a dimension (Auspurg et al., 2017; Düval, 2023; Schulz, 2021). We argue that the availability of ECEC is crucial for understanding the gendered division of labor, as it externalizes childcare duties beyond the household.


## Origin as a Determinant of Attitudes


In addition to gender, we argue that the origin of participants is an important factor in assessing their evaluations. In the German context, this is particularly relevant not only for migrant populations, but also for individuals from the former Eastern states of German Democratic Republic. Historically, migration to Germany began with the arrival of labor migrants in 1970s, and grew further with the resettlement of the ethnic German communities in the 1990s (Kogan, 2011). The twenty-first century brought new migration flows, including new labor migration and EU migration, primarily involving individuals from other European countries for employment opportunities. In the past decade, this period also saw the arrival of Syrian migrants fleeing civil war and other unregulated migration and asylum seekers from Middle-East and Central Asia (for an overview, see Olczyk et al., 2016). Today, thirty-five percent of the families in Germany have a migration background (BMFSFJ, 2017) originating from a wide variety of countries and regions. Therefore, the presence of large migrant community necessitates the examination of gender role attitudes among these communities.

Conceptually, we extend our 'exposure and interest framework' to migrants as well. On the one hand, regardless of their origin, women benefit from egalitarian relationships and more equal divisions of work with their partners. On the other hand, increasing educational attainment and greater access to tertiary education, and entry into the labor market expose women to ideas of gender equality and their dual role as caregiver and breadwinner (Bolzendahl & Myers, 2004; Shu, 2024). However, migrants may differ from the destination country' context in terms of their origin country's gender regimes and degree of gender equality. They may come from countries with gender regimes that reinforce essentialism about women's primary role as mothers and uphold male supremacy as a norm. This could lead women to embrace essentialist ideas their own gender role, while men may be more resistant to egalitarian changes. As these attitudes become entrenched as normative structures within social groups, pressure from the community may render norm-defying difficult.

Thus, country/region of origin plays a key role in determining individual attitudes about gender roles and norms. We analyze migration background by taking advantage of oversampling of participants with Turkish and Dutch origins in our dataset. These two groups are clearly distinct in their migration and adaptation histories in German society. Turkish migrants are largest and one of the historically oldest migrant group in Germany. Decades after their arrival, Turkish migrants still face disparities in educational attainment and tend to be relatively conservative in their familial arrangements. Turkish men are the most likely group to resist egalitarian division of labor and gender egalitarianism in general. Dutch migrants should be similar to West Germans in their gender role attitudes. The Netherlands is one of the most liberal countries in terms of gender and sexual revolution. It also has the highest attendance rates in early childcare and education (ECEC) among the OECD and EU member states, which makes Dutch society more acceptable toward maternal employment during children's young ages.

There is a recent interest in understanding the role of migration background in individuals' preferences of gendered division of work and gender roles (Blau et al., 2020; Fendel and Kosyakova, 2023; Gambaro et al., 2023; Marcen and Morales, 2019). In the US context, Marcen and Morales (2019) show that first and second generation migrant men who originate from countries with equalitarian gender norms tend to do more housework than those who come from traditionally oriented countries. Similarly, Blau et al. (2020) find that gender norms in the country of origin influence the allocation of unpaid work, that immigrant women do more housework than their native peers, whereas immigrant men contribute less

than native men do. They also show that traditional gender norms are stronger among migrant families (Blau et al., p. 946). Using German Family Demography Panel, Gambaro and colleagues (2023) find that male-breadwinner model of employment receive highest support among migrant respondents. They further also emphasize the heterogeneity of attitudes toward maternal employment among migrant populations in Germany, which largely vary by countries of origin and generation status (Gambaro et al., 2023, p. 356).

Finally, research indicates that East and West Germans have distinct attitudes about gender roles particularly about maternal employment, use of daycare for children, as well as the acceptable age for children to start daycare (Bozoyan and Schmiedberg, 2024; Kleinschrot, 2024; Lois, 2020; Zoch, 2021). Therefore, we further differentiate Germans from Eastern and Western states. While West Germans uniformly think that mothers of children up to their 12 th month should stop working, attendance in daycare few months after birth is rather acceptable for East Germans (Gambaro et al, 2023).

Employment policy of German Democratic Republic (GDR) heavily supported women's labor force participation (Lois, 2020). Women in East Germany was strongly socialized to a system, in which their employment even after childbearing was strongly supported. This does not mean however, that East German men were contributing to housework and childcare. In fact, the widespread availability of public child care services even for children under three years of old made this system function (Karl, 2011). Therefore, after unification the dual role of women deteriorated as the Federal German system was not as supportive of employment of mothers with young children. Nevertheless, the childcare provision continue to be extensive compared to Western states (Zoch, 2021). Finally, there are generational differences within Eastern Germany that those who grew up before reunification express more egalitarian views and are less similar to West German than those who grew up after (Ebner et al., 2020; Sievers Warner 2023).


## Empirical Predictions


We develop a series of hypotheses about group differences of attitudes toward division of work among vignette couples. We mainly hypothesize to find gender difference between men and women in their evaluations (Hypothesis 1). Specifically women would have higher interest in divisions of labor where they are relatively equal to men in terms of paid work, and they would have higher expectations of sharing housework and childcare responsibilities. For

men, on the other hand, would not be interested contributing to housework and childcare responsibilities as traditional arrangements are in their favor and studies indicate that they abstain contributing to household responsibilities.

We expect these gender differences to vary by country of origin, as well as between Eastern and Western Germans. We hypothesize migrants of Turkish origin to be more conservative than other groups in general, particularly in terms of men's involvement in housework and childcare activities (Hypothesis 2). Considering their relatively traditional familial arrangements, we expect Turkish men to be the most supporting less egalitarian arrangements.

For Dutch migrants, we anticipate respondents, particularly women, will be more favorable toward maternal employment (Hypothesis 3). In addition, they would express higher support for ECEC use, as the Netherlands has the highest rates of early childcare and education attendance for children under three years old among OECD and EU member states.

Among non-migrant native groups, we expect East Germans to be more supportive for maternal employment than the West Germans (Hypothesis 4). Even after three decades since unification East Germans and West Germans continue to differ in their gender role attitudes. Compared to West German women, however, East German women would be more accepting toward arrangements, in which men contribute little to unpaid activities of childcare and housework (Hypothesis 5). Although, in East Germany, women's dual role was widely accepted, formal gender equality was not as widespread as it was in West Germany.

In terms of ECEC, we expect use of half-day childcare to increase support for all gender ideology profiles due to its externalizing effect of childcare; however this would not generate any gender differences; as men and women would express equal support for it (Hypothesis 6). We expect gender differences in support for full-time childcare use (Hypothesis 7). Full-time childcare is less often preferred in the German context. Women would be less willing to support full-time external care, as children in our vignettes are two years old and younger, while men would be less sensitive to the age of the child, resulting in an increase in difference between men and women.


## Data and Methods


To address our hypotheses, we draw on original survey experiment data, which was part of a larger survey research conducted within the RISS (Reconfiguration and Internalization of Social Structure) Project in Germany (see Schäfer et al. 2024). RISS Survey is a large-N, register based, nationally representative sample from German population aged 18 or older (N=6,036). RISS Project team contacted potential participants who were selected for the nationally representative sample and provided them a web link and a personalized password to an online survey platform. Selection of sample through register data allows the findings to be generalizable and minimizes the external validity problem of our survey experiment. As part of the RISS Survey, we designed a factorial survey experiment addressing participant attitudes toward division of work among cohabiting/married heterosexual couples with children. Multifactorial survey experiments provide situational context of the issue at hand, and lower the desirability bias through avoiding loaded statements about gender relations (Düval, 2023). Scholars long used multifactorial survey experiments to measure attitudes and social norms (Jasso, 2006). Conjoint analysis based on vignettes better captures multidimensional preferences in participant attitudes (de la Cuesta et al., 2021). Respondents answer the RISS Survey in a self-completed module on their personalized devices, a preferred mode for multifactorial survey designs (Auspurg and Hinz, 2015).

In addition to main sample, the RISS Study oversampled participants of Turkish (N=2,493) and Dutch (N=909) origins in order to generate a comparative group of migrants. These oversamples are largest immigrant samples available for these two groups in the existing datasets that cover information about social structural backgrounds and ideological/political orientations (Schäfer et al. 2024). We draw these oversamples in order to facilitate comparisons between native German population and migrant populations. The field for the survey took place between November 2023 and January 2024. The overall response rate to the RISS survey is 31.5 %, which is relatively high for contemporary social science research.


## Experimental Design


For this study, we are using data from a multifactorial survey experiment that examines respondent attitudes toward hypothetical couples' division of household and employment responsibilities. The design contains hypothetical scenarios, called vignettes that describe

division of work among fictitious heterosexual couples. An introductory text describes the study and provides instructions for participants (see Figure A.1). In order to minimize the reading burden, we presented vignettes in a table form (see Figure A.2). Respondents evaluate whether they regard the share of the total division of work among couples as appropriate on a 7-point scale. For our experimental design, we manipulate six different attributes of couples, called dimensions, among their potential characteristics, or levels (Düval, 2023). These vignette dimensions are paid employment of the couple, their current (or last) hourly pay, age of their child, parental childcare, housework and child's time in daycare (see Figure A.3 for details of vignette dimensions and levels for each dimension).

These six dimensions represent a full factorial design. They have three to six levels and the complete set of scenarios adds up to 1458 combinations. Our sample is large enough to cover this vignette universe several times over; therefore, we use completely randomized samples to be selected from this universe (Auspurg and Hinz, 2015), instead of a sample of vignettes. That is, all combinations of vignettes appear for respondent evaluation. Each level within the dimensions appears with equal frequency across the randomly selected vignettes (See Appendix). As our question requires the evaluation of overall division of labor, there was no need to split vignette samples across participants.

The analysis sample consists of 32,406 evaluations from 6,485 participants. Every participant evaluated 5 randomly selected vignette couple in order to allow a more nuanced understanding of respondents' attitudes across different combinations and to provide a larger sample for analysis. In average number of observations is 4.9 per participant. Slightly less than half of the participants are women (48.7 percent). The sample consists of West Germans (47.4%), East Germans (13%), Turkish (31.4%) and Dutch migrants (8.3%). We provide further characteristics of the sample in Table 2. The average of dependent variable is 3.88 over a 7-point scale and it has relatively normal distribution (Figure A.4).


## Analytic Strategy


Our estimation strategy relies on analyzing the level of support participants express for a particular division of labor among vignette couples, which we formulate in light of uni- and multidimensional gender ideologies predetermined by the state of research. We investigate how participant evaluations vary by their gender and native/migrant background. To predict participant evaluations, we use linear regression models with cluster standard errors to

account for the hierarchical data structure. It is customary to use regression models with random intercepts as each respondent evaluates several vignettes (see Auspurg and Hinz, 2015). However, our design does not estimate all evaluations from a single participant simultaneously. If a participant does not encounter a vignette couple that corresponds to one of the preconstructed gender ideology profiles, they are not included in the analysis. We examine the vignette dimensions that correspond to our specific gender ideology. Therefore, the evaluations are nested in the participants, and our design do not necessitate random intercept models, but we use linear regression models with robust standard errors. We provide results from random intercept models in the Supplement.

We conduct all analyses using the software Stata 16. As the question to participants asks about overall level of division of work for the vignette couple, we have a single dependent variable to examine. The variable takes the value of 1 if the respondents think the division is not appropriate at all, and the value of 7 if they think the division is completely appropriate. Experimental design of multifactorial surveys and random assignment of vignettes to participants address the threats to validity and renders use of control variables unnecessary (Auspurg and Hinz, 2015).Nonetheless, we control for participant's education, occupation, age, presence of preschool children in the household and whether they live with a partner (Table 2).


## Findings



## Gender Differences in Support for Gender Ideology Profiles


Figure 1 presents evaluations of selected vignette dimensions by the gender of respondents, highlighting the level support for various categories compared to reference categories. These represent main effects of the vignette categories. In three dimensions, women express more negative evaluations than men: housework predominantly done by women, childcare predominantly done by women and children attending full-time daycare. These results suggest significant gender differences in attitudes toward division of housework and childcare responsibilities, and daycare attendance. There are no significant gender differences regarding employment categories. The single earner models-where either women work full-time, men do not, or vice versa-receive the lowest support from both men and women.

Next, we shift our focus to main findings, which explore the associations between specific arrangements of vignette dimensions and gender ideology profiles. Table 1 outlines the specific arrangements of paid and unpaid work among couples, which we constructed based on the gender ideology profiles. Figure 2 displays the level of support for these profiles by respondents' gender. Our findings reveal notable gender differences in attitudes toward the division of paid and unpaid work. In three out of five profiles, gender differences are statistically significant. Women are more likely to prefer egalitarian divisions, while men show higher support for secondary-earner and women's second shift models. Supporting the Bolzendahl and Myers framework (2004), women tend to express less interest in arrangements where they are responsible for all household activities, e.g., housework and childcare. Participants overwhelmingly support an egalitarian division, where couples share paid and unpaid work equally. This finding aligns with previous studies that show strong support for egalitarian arrangements.

Interestingly, the traditional and egalitarian familism profiles receive the secondhighest level of support, with nearly equal support from both men and women-despite their contrasting combinations of paid and unpaid work (see Table 1). For men, this support is unsurprising as both profiles maintain their breadwinner status while sharing housework responsibilities only in the egalitarian familism profile. For women, egalitarian familism may be acceptable because it involves equal employment levels (whether full-time or part-time) between partners, with women holding primary childcare but not the housework. Since children in the vignettes are two years old or younger, women may view this as an acceptable arrangement, thus expressing relatively high support. Egalitarian familism is, in fact, a good illustration of an ambivalent gender ideology, which combines support for maternal employment and women's primary responsibility for parental childcare.

It is more difficult to explain why women have almost equal support for the traditional profile. One potential explanation is the young age of children in the vignettes. Given children's young age, women may perceive the traditional division as a temporary and reasonable arrangement. Another explanation is that, while the traditional profile is not an egalitarian, it represents a familiar arrangement that does not require women to juggle both paid and unpaid work. Women's lower support for secondary earner and second shift profiles supports this explanation, as in these profiles they are responsible both paid and unpaid work. However, the decline of traditional views at the societal level challenges this reasoning, making  the 'temporary agreeableness' explanation more plausible. Further analysis suggest

that educational attainment plays a larger role in women's decision to support for traditional model, supporting the first explanation (results not shown).

To summarize, the levels of support for different gender ideology profiles align with our expectations: men are more likely to support less egalitarian arrangements, while women are more likely to support egalitarian ones. One surprising finding is the level of support for the traditional profile among women, which we attribute to its temporary and familiar nature.


## Gender Ideology Profiles by Gender & Migration Background


The factorial survey experiment allows us to examine whether there are gender and migration based differences in evaluation of these profiles. Figure 3 shows support for the two-unidimensional gender ideologies, egalitarian and traditional, by gender and migrant group. Once again, participants express highest support for egalitarian profile, where couple share all paid and unpaid activities over the traditional, male-breadwinner model. Within West German, Turkish and Dutch groups, there are also gender differences in support for egalitarian gender ideologies, though for Dutch this difference is not statistically significant. Women from these groups show higher support for egalitarian profiles than their male counterparts, whereas for East Germans, there are no gender differences.

There are no clear within group gender differences for traditional profile. The most surprising finding is that East German women are more supportive of traditional profile than West German women (see Table 3). Dutch women also express high level of support for traditional profile but both gender and group level differences are insignificant due to small sample size of the Dutch.

Between migrant groups, the Turkish show the lowest support for the egalitarian profile. Especially Turkish men are the most conservative group in all our findings, opposing joint responsibilities the most both in household and paid work (see Grunow et al., 2018). In sum, all gender and migrant groups unsurprisingly are supportive of an egalitarian division of labor than a traditional one. Moreover, although there are no gender-difference in support for traditional profile, West German and Turkish women express more support for egalitarian profile than their male peers do. Unlike recent work on gender role attitudes, our findings reveal a gender-based difference in support of an egalitarian division.

Next, we turn to the multidimensional profiles. Figure 4 shows the level of support for secondary earner, egalitarian familism and women's second shift profiles. For secondaryearner and second shift profiles, once again West German, Turkish and Dutch men (insignificant) express higher support than their female counterparts, indicating their preference for inegalitarian divisions of work. Even if the second-shift is the least supported profile, men still have higher preference for it than their female counterparts. Among East Germans, there are no gender differences in any three of the profiles.

For egalitarian familism, the only significant gender difference is among Dutch making Dutch women to express lowest level of support for this profile. Among women, East German and Turkish women express statistically highest support for egalitarian familism. For East Germans, this is not surprising considering their dual role as breadwinners and caretakers in the former Democratic Republic. For Turkish, this might be a reflection of their embrace of ambivalent views about gender roles. Looking across country of origin groups, Turkish men express highest support for the least egalitarian profiles of secondary earner and second-shift men. Compared to other men they have the highest level of support for them. Dutch men also express high levels of support for secondary earner and egalitarian familism profiles, yet the differences from other groups are not significant.

Overall, our hypothesis about Turkish group is supported as Turkish men are most supportive of least egalitarian models and Turkish women are supportive of ambivalent profiles (Hypothesis 2). Findings about Dutch group is less conclusive due the group's small sample size but there are indicators they are the most similar to West Germans than any others (Hypothesis 3). Dutch women's evaluations have lend support for our hypothesis that they are least supportive of egalitarian familism and second shift models. Given their support for traditional profile, Eastern Germans do not appear to be more supportive of maternal employment then Western Germans (Hypothesis 4), but their support for ambivalent egalitarian familism and women' support for second-shift profiles indicate that they are more accepting toward arrangements, in which men's contribution to the household activities (Hypothesis 5).

## Discussion


In this paper, we present results from an original factorial survey experiment conducted in Germany, which examines whether men and women from different origins have varying preferences regarding distribution of paid work, housework and childcare among fictitious couples with children. In doing so, we introduce a novel theoretical approach to better understand gender role attitudes by using gender ideology profiles as an heuristic tool for interpreting the results of our experiment. Specifically, we focus on particular combinations of paid and unpaid work divisions that align with well-established typologies of gender ideology, as recently identified by gender scholars (Begall et al., 2023; Grunow et al., 2018; Knight and Brinton, 2017; Scarborough et al., 2019). This strategy provides a

theoretically grounded framework for interpreting participants' evaluations of gendered divisions of work among couples with children. More importantly, this strategy establishes a theoretical link between gender ideology scholarship and the growing body of scholarly work that uses factorial experiments to study gender role attitudes (Auspurg et al., 2017; Düval, 2023; Pedulla & Thebaud, 2015; Schulz, 2021).

Our theoretical strategy proved successful, allowing us to answer our research questions more clearly. We examined whether men and women differ in their evaluations of specific gendered divisions of paid and unpaid work, which we constructed based on five gender ideology profiles. In three of the five profiles, we identified significant gender differences: women showed preferences for egalitarian arrangements, while men tended to support arrangements where they have limited contributions to housework and childcare. We also found relatively higher support for ambivalent ideologies, such as egalitarian familism, which combines support for maternal employment with the belief that women should primary be caregivers. In addition, we investigated whether these gender-based differences apply to different non-migrant native and migrant groups in Germany, taking into country the country's migration history and the distinct gender regimes under the Federal and Democratic Republics of Germany. In line with our expectations, we find significant differences in evaluations between participants from Western German and Eastern German, as well as Turkish migrants.

Our approach also differs from recent gender role attitude research in identifying gender-differences in participant evaluations. Previous research using survey methodology has consistently found small but systematic gender differences, with women generally holding more egalitarian gender role attitudes than men (Düval, 2023, p. 4). However, studies using multifactorial survey methods have not consistently identified significant gender differences (Auspurg et al., 2017; Carriero and Todesco, 2017; Düval, 2023; Pedulla and Thebaud; 2015; Schulz, 2021; Thebaud and Pedulla, 2016).

To explain the lack of gender differences in attitudes, Auspurg and colleagues (2017) suggest that although individuals may prefer equal divisions of labor between men and women, societal norms around traditional gender roles often prevent them from acting on these preferences. Similarly, Pedulla and Theabaud (2015) argue that when more egalitarian arrangements are available, both men and women tend to prefer them over traditional ones. Düval (2023, p. 13) claims that providing detailed contextual information about couple's

work-family dynamics in their vignette study reveals the 'conditionality of gender norms' and is essential when comparing gender role attitudes across different respondent groups.' (see Philippe, 2024). To summarize, these scholars argue that when participants are provided detailed context about the division of labor between men and women-context that survey item-questions cannot provide-they tend to express more egalitarian attitudes. According to this interpretation, although individual preferences lean toward egalitarian divisions, social norms and institutional arrangements continue to reinforce essentialist gender roles.

However, our findings suggest that providing detailed context does not necessarily lead men to express egalitarian views about the division of paid and unpaid work. As we show, despite receiving the least support from participants, the secondary-earner and women's second-shift profiles attracted higher support from men than from women. An indication that men are more likely to protect their breadwinner status. Moreover, support levels also varied by group, suggesting that historical and contextual factors play a significant role in shaping gender role attitudes. A notable example of this is the difference in support for the egalitarian familism profile between East German and West German women, which reflects the historical gender regimes in which these groups are socialized.

In conclusion, the key contribution of this study is its ability to link participants' evaluations of gendered divisions of labor with contemporary gender ideologies. Rather than focusing solely on individual attitudes, our analysis emphasizes how these attitudes align with current gender ideology profiles, which reflect wider societal level gender attitudes in specific contexts.

## Introduction


One of humanity’s greatest challenges – formalised in United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 12 (UN SDG12) – is transitioning to sustainable consumption and production to ensure strong economies while minimizing negative environmental impacts. Tourism performs poorly on sustainable consumption and production. In a year that is not affected by pandemic-related border closures, tourism activity contributes up to 8% to global greenhouse emissions (Lenzen et al., 2018). The aspiration for the tourism industry to grow into the future will further increase its burden on the environment unless new approaches can be developed and deployed to help transition the sector towards more sustainable operations.

Climate change mitigation cannot occur without significant behavioural change. In the tourism context, therefore, attention has shifted towards developing and empirically testing behavioural change interventions that can trigger more pro-environmental tourist behaviour. Any attempt of influencing behaviours is implicitly or explicitly guided by theory – a set of assumptions about what drives behaviour, in this case, environmentally sustainable behaviour. Over the past decade, research on environmentally significant tourist behaviour focused mainly on the association of cognitive constructs and pro-environmental behaviour, much in line with key theories of human behaviour, which assume that attitudes play a key role in driving behaviour.

Evidence is mounting, however, that attitudes may not in fact be as effective as is generally assumed. Targeting attitudes may, in fact, be the least promising approach, with changing defaults, changing infrastructure, and increasing pleasure conceptually more promising (Dolnicar, 2020). Similar conclusions were drawn by a recent systematic review of field studies testing a wide range of interventions deployed to trigger different types of environmentally sustainable tourist behaviour, including towel reuse, not wasting food, eating low emission foods, reducing water, or waiving daily room cleaning (Demeter et al., 2023).

The aim of the present critical review is to determine (1) whether indeed the current understanding of drivers of environmentally sustainable tourism behaviour is dominated by attitudes (research question #1), (2) whether indeed attitudes serve as the dominant construct targeted in studies that attempt to make tourists behave in more sustainable ways (research question #2). Based on the investigation of these two questions, (3) we develop a conceptual model that outlines the theoretical mechanisms by which attitudes are currently assumed to drive behaviour and behaviour change. From this model a set of hypotheses emerges; each postulates an alternative explanation for why attitudes may not be as influential as generally assumed. Those hypotheses are available for empirical testing in future to determine with certainty why attitudes often fail as target constructs in behavioural change interventions in sustainable tourism, and how strong the relative impact of each of the valid explanations is. As such, this critical review is conceptual and hypotheses-generating; it challenges the current understanding of drivers of environmentally significant tourist behaviour.

The scope of the review is limited to field studies testing – in real world contexts – the effectiveness of behavioural change interventions on making tourists behave in more environmentally sustainable ways. We include only field studies because self-reported sustainable tourist behaviour is known to be severely affected by social desirability bias – a bias caused by survey respondents answering survey questions in a way that projects a positive image of them.

Findings have far-reaching theoretical implications: (1) If the reasons for attitudes failing as the target construct in behavioural change interventions can be pinpointed, future studies targeting attitudes can be developed in a way that avoid those pitfalls. (2) If indeed the focus of researchers aiming to develop new behavioural change interventions has been on a limited set of theoretical constructs (attitudes), broadening research attention to constructs which have been neglected to date has the potential to lead to additional interventions that can make tourists behave in more sustainable ways. Practically, this opens opportunities for new tangible measures tourism businesses and destinations can put in place to influence behaviour and, in so doing, make tourism operations more environmentally sustainable and contribute to the collective goal of sustainable consumption and production.


## RESEARCH QUESTION #1 – Do attitudes dominate our theoretical understanding of why tourists behave in environmentally sustainable ways?


In tourism and hospitality research, one theory dominates our understanding of human behaviour: the theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen, 1985). A search for key behavioural theories shows that the theory of planned behaviour and its predecessor (the theory of reasoned action) are central to 433 articles published in the Clarivate category Hospitality, Tourism, Leisure and Sport since 1985, making this theory the most commonly used one within this field of research. Also heavily used are prospect theory (131 articles), social comparison theory (70 articles) and attribution theory (41 articles). Less popular as the basis of investigations in tourism and hospitality are value belief norm theory (also referred to as theory of environmentally significant behaviour; 17 articles), cognitive dissonance theory (15 articles) and the theory of normative conduct (16 articles).

The theory of planned behaviour posits that a behaviour results from a person having the intention to display that specific behaviour. The intention to display the behaviour, in turn, is influenced by the attitude towards the behaviour, the subjective norm associated with the behaviour and the perceived behavioural control over the behaviour. The overall attitude consists of the attitude towards trying the behaviour and failing and the attitude towards trying the behaviour and succeeding. Each of those attitudes, in turn, are formed by the sum of all outcomes of the behaviour weighted by the subjective probability a person attaches to each of those outcomes resulting from the behaviour. Many behavioural change interventions, which – either implicitly or explicitly – leverage the theory of planned behaviour, therefore attempt to modify attitudes. Theoretically, however, the theory of planned behaviour does not rely solely on attitudes as the catalysts of behavioural change; social norms and perceived behavioural control can also be targeted. Some of the criticisms of the theory relate to: intentions not translating to behaviour; people being treated as rational when they are not; the neglect of affect, anticipated affect, and emotions; and that the theory claims to contain all drivers of behaviour. According to Ajzen, most of these concerns are unnecessary because the theory acknowledges: that behavioural intentions mean that a person intends to try to behave in a certain way, but that – for many reasons – they may not be able to do so; that irrationality manifests in beliefs and subjective norms; that affect, anticipated affect and emotions are accounted for because they shape beliefs; and that the theory never assumed additional predictors could not be added to improve how well behaviour can be predicted (Ajzen, 2011).

Value belief norm theory (Stern, 2000) is another frequently used theory in tourism research that has been specifically developed to explain environmentally significant behaviour. Value belief norm theory underpins many investigations of pro-environmental behaviour in the tourism context, including that of adventure tourists, museum vacationers and cruise ship passengers. Personal norms emerge from these studies as having a strong association with people’s pro-environmental vacation behaviour, including using public transportation, water saving, switching off the light or air conditioning. According to this theory, pro-environmental behaviours are the result of personal values, the belief that something of importance is under threat, and the belief that personal actions can help alleviate the threat. In line with Ajzen’s (1985) notion that beliefs are precursors of behavioural intentions, which in turn affect behaviour, Stern and colleagues postulate a process in which environmental beliefs (such as potential negative consequences for valued objects, and perceived capability to mitigate threats) shape behavioural norms, which then shape a range of environmentally significant behaviours. Stern’s theory, if anything, relies even more on beliefs as the building blocks of attitudes than the theory of planned behaviour because attitudes are effectively the only mechanism by which behavioural change can be achieved. Values are stable across time; they form the basis of beliefs and the overall attitude towards the behaviour. This overall attitude then leads to a perceived personal norm which causes behaviour to occur or not to occur.

Social comparison theory (Festinger, 1954) posits that individuals assess their own abilities and viewpoints by contrasting them with those of others. Exposure to the beliefs and behaviours of others can result in a shift in norms and attitudes that, in turn, can lead to changes in behaviour. The outcome of the comparison process can vary based on a number of factors including the type of person being compared to (e.g. friend or stranger), the aspect being compared (e.g. income or social standing), and the direction of the comparison (whether it is upward, to someone who is considered superior, lateral, to someone on the same level, or downward to someone seen as inferior). Individuals may feel self-doubt when comparing themselves to others who are performing better or feel a sense of superiority when comparing themselves to those who are performing worse. Attitudes, therefore, play a central role in social comparison theory also, making it a key target for behavioural change interventions.

According to prospect theory (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979) people do not always make decisions based on rational thinking, but on the perceived value of potential gains and losses. The theory suggests that the way information is presented, or framed, can influence how individuals respond to it. People tend to be more sensitive to potential losses rather than potential gains, so the same information can produce different results depending on whether it is framed as a gain or a loss. While priming can indeed significantly influence behaviour, the impact of the message type (positive or negative) varies across experiments and requires further examination. Attitudes, therefore, play an important role in shaping how individuals perceive potential losses and gains in decision-making. Individuals’ attitudes towards a particular situation or object can impact their risk tolerance and the outcome of their decision.

Attribution theory (Heider, 1958) suggests that people evaluate the consequences of their behaviour by attributing the cause either internally (as being due to their own actions) or externally (to other factors). The theory holds that promoting internal attribution can lead to more environmentally friendly behaviour. Attitudes play a role in how people make attributions to causes of behaviours, effecting the way people interpret these events. If someone holds a positive attitude towards a person, they are more likely to attribute blame for environmentally unsustainable behaviour to external factors (such as lack of infrastructure) than to internal factors (such as a person’s lack of concern for the environment).

Cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger, 1957) posits that people strive to align their behaviour with their cognitions to reduce dissonance. If an individual sees themselves as environmentally friendly, they are likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviours. If their behaviour does not match their environmental attitudes, it can cause cognitive dissonance. To restore consonance, the person has the option of either altering their behaviour or changing their cognitions, including attitudes. Attitudes, therefore, play a central role in cognitive dissonance theory; altering attitudes that are not aligned with the desired behaviours or reminding people of consonant attitudes are the two primary paths to achieving behavioural change.

As can be seen from the brief review of key theories used in tourism and hospitality research to explain and change tourist behaviour, attitudes play a prominent role. Some theories differentiate between beliefs and attitudes, but they all have in common the assumption that tourists must notice, and process information provided to them for behavioural change to occur. We conclude, therefore, that attitudes do indeed dominate our current understanding of tourist behaviour.


## RESEARCH QUESTION #1 – Do attitudes dominate our attempts to entice tourists to behave in more environmentally sustainable ways?


The strictest test of the validity of a theory is to target key constructs postulated by that theory to influence behaviour and observe whether a behavioural change occurs as a result. Field experiments aim to achieve just that; they offer valuable insights into the effectiveness of attitudes as suitable targets for achieving behavioural change (Viglia and Dolnicar, 2020). A recent review analysed field experiments conducted in the context of sustainable tourism (Demeter et al., 2023); they aimed to reduce towel use, reduce plate waste, increase demand for low emission foods, reduce water use and entice tourists to voluntarily waive their daily routine hotel room clean. Studies included in this review used the following theoretical constructs as targets for enticing tourists to behave in more sustainable ways: attitudes, normative social influence, behavioural nudges, pleasure, and penalties. Attitudes emerged as the most frequently targeted construct.

For the present study we re-analysed the 47 articles included in Demeter et al. (2023) (references provided in Supplementary Materials) to identify the theories informing studies attempting to trigger environmentally sustainable tourist behaviour. Fourteen articles do not explicitly name the theory that guided intervention development; 17 articles reference theories without explaining how they informed intervention development. The 16 articles that explicitly state theories as the foundation of their work used the theory of planned behaviour (two studies), cognitive dissonance theory (two studies), the focus theory of normative conduct (three studies), attribution theory (one study) and value belief norms theory (one study; see Table I in Supplementary Materials).

At construct level, 74 of 146 interventions aimed at changing attitudes and 32 aimed at activating social norms (Demeter et al., 2023), suggesting that – implicitly or explicitly – sustainable tourism is understood to be highly influenced by attitudes and social norms, in line with the theory of planned behaviour. Half of all interventions targeted attitudes, making this (by far) the most dominant theoretical construct used in attempts to influence sustainable tourist behaviour (for a review of the 74 interventions targeting beliefs see Table II in Supplementary Materials). Behavioural change interventions targeting attitudes, however, result in a surprisingly low success rate of only 58% compared to changing defaults or choice architecture (82%) or increasing pleasure (100%) (Demeter et al., 2023) This success rate may drop further when accounting for publication bias.
