### Hypothesis #1 – Tourists do not notice messages attempting to change attitudes


The success of message interventions aimed at changing tourist behaviour depends on tourists being aware of the information; on tourists noticing the information. It is possible that message interventions often fail to capture the attention of tourists, for several reasons: tourists are exposed to many messages during their journeys, including general messages and messages providing them with information about the environmental implications of alternative behaviours and asking tourists to choose the most environmentally friendly options. Due to this information overload, tourists may not notice many messages aimed at making them behave in more sustainable ways. Examples of unsuccessful messages in the context of hotel towel reuse include: “Help to save the environment. Every day we clean a great number of towels, many of them are unused. Please help us to protect the environment. You can join us in this program to help save the environment by reusing your towel during your stay” (Bohner et al., 2014, p. 3); “Here at [hotel name], we have a number of efforts in place to care for our planet ranging from water and energy conservation, recycling and low-emission vehicles to eco-conscious options for resort guests” (Baca-Motes et al., 2013, p. 1073); and “Help save the environment. You can show your respect for nature and help save the environment by reusing your towels during your stay” (Goldstein et al., 2011, p. 449).

A distinctly different approach to targeting attitudes was taken in a Slovenian hotel study, where stickers were used to communicate with hotel guests (Dolnicar et al., 2016). Stickers were used because they could be interpreted easily by guests from different countries of origin and because they could be placed in the exact positions where the target behaviour occurred, such as next to light switches and next to the towel rail. This approach also proved ineffective in making hotel guests behave in more environmentally sustainable ways, excluding as a reason for the ineffectiveness of messages the possible reason that the message is not visible at the exact point at which the behaviour takes place.

The hypothesis that tourists do not pay attention to messages that aim to modify their attitudes or activate them, emerges as highly plausible. Lack of attention may well explain why attitude-based interventions have low success rates.


### Hypothesis #2 – Tourists are on holiday to relax; they are not willing to engage in cognitive processing


Another possible explanation may be that, while tourists notice the messages, they are unwilling to allocate cognitive resources to processing them because tourists aim to maximise their vacation enjoyment and cognitively processing messages is not an enjoyable task (Dolnicar, 2020). While increasing knowledge about the environment can increase a person’s attitudes and behaviours towards protecting the environment in the home context, increasing tourists’ environmental knowledge (cognition) does not consistently translate in pro-environmental behaviour on holiday. Providing information related to the carbon emissions generated while heating water for the shower did not reduce water use in a hotel (Günther et al., 2020, p. 6). The sign read: “Water heating is very energy and CO2 – intense: One second in the shower consumes more energy than a notebook PC in 1.5 hours. We compensate for your CO2 – emissions in the shower by supporting a myclimate-abatement project. Therefore, your shower today is climate-neutral.”

Providing information to tourists about the environmental implications of their behaviour is not always successful in changing behaviour because the information provided may be too vague. Adding more specific environmental information when changing the default from automatic daily room cleaning to room cleaning upon request only did not reduce the number of room cleans (Knežević et al., 2021, p. 7). The environmental information provided in addition to the default cleaning instructions and the pro-environmental call for action read as follows: “Please note that every time we clean a room we use 100 ml of chemicals, 35 l of water and 1.5 kWh of electricity, which is not good for the environment. You can make a difference and reduce the environmental burden of your stay by having your room cleaned upon request. Please help us make a difference to the environment.” Similarly, stickers on shower walls informing guests about the negative environmental impacts of long showers, along with the hostels commitment to offset these negative effects, did not reduce water use in a German youth hostel (Günther et al., 2020, p. 6). This study used the following message: “Water heating is very energy and CO2 – intense: One second in the shower consumes more energy than a notebook PC in 1.5 hours. We compensate for your CO2 – emissions in the shower by supporting a myclimate-abatement project. Therefore, your shower today is climate-neutral”.

These messages also have in common that they are generic; they do not provide clear action recommendations. Even including clear action recommendations did not improve effectiveness, as the following message illustrates (Leon and Arana, 2020, p. 2): “to take care of the environment and reduce the use of the precious water resource…:1) Place your towel in the bath/shower for daily washing if you want it to be changed (normal service). 2) Hang your towels on the towel rack if you decide to let them dry for reuse. The bed linen in this establishment are changed every 3 days. If you want to change your linen, place this sign on your bed… The replacement of towels and bedding has important impacts on the environment and water consumption”.


### Hypothesis #3 – Attempts to alter attitudes lead to reactance


Reactance is a negative psychological response that emerges when people experience a threat to or loss of their freedom. The perceived severity of the threat determines the extent of reactance. It is plausible that tourists who are asked to sacrifice their vacation enjoyment to protect the environment develop a reactance response. Tourists may perceive pro-environmental messages – including requests to conserve water or energy use, reduce waste or recycling – as limiting their freedom to act in a certain way or threatening their decision-making autonomy. Messages that tourists perceive as too prescriptive or overly controlling, may result in resistance to the messages and can lead to negative attitudes towards conservation efforts. Rather than objectively evaluating the message they may respond in reactance or pushback against the efforts of tourist operators to encourage pro-environmental behaviour.


### Hypothesis #4 – Attempts to alter attitudes do not influence habits


Another possible explanation for the unreliability of attitudes as behavioural change targets is that behaviours may, in fact, not be driven primarily by attitudes, but rather by other constructs, including habit. In situations where habits are strong, people evaluate counter-habitual information negatively. When Ajzen originally formulated the theory of planned behaviour, he noted that “a certain sequence of actions can become so habitual or routine that it is performed almost automatically […]” and that “Highly developed skills of this kind typically no longer require conscious formulation of a behavioral plan” (Ajzen, 1985, p. 11). Not surprisingly, therefore, Ajzen (2011) recommends that the automaticity that characterises habits warrants further exploration, acknowledging that habit formation is not accommodated within the theory of planned behaviour and indeed has the potential of expanding and enriching our explanations of human behaviour. As is the case with the theory of planned behaviour, value belief norm theory also omits constructs which may influence behaviour, including habits. As a result, it may prove to be unnecessarily limiting as tourism researchers work to develop interventions.

Despite the lack of a clear definition of strong, habitual pro-environmental behaviours that are also practiced during vacations, reducing food waste by eating up, waste separation, towel reuse proved to have a high transfer habit value from the home to the vacation context (MacInnes et al., 2022). Two-sided door hangers in hotel rooms with the following recycling instructions, for example failed to increase recycling behaviour (Grazzini et al., 2018, p. 1955): “By recycling we save over 12.5 million tonnes of paper and cardboard- the equivalent of 300 million trees every year in the UK alone. By recycling we save energy which results in less greenhouse gas emissions. If we use materials more than once, we will preserve our natural resources…Throw your waste into the specific bin (paper, plastic and/or glass).” In the same study, recycling effort was also not increased with the following message: “You can use the bins that you find in this room for recycling your waste. Recycling save the quality of our air, land and water resources. Recycling preserves the health of our environment. Recycling helps to reduce the pollution caused by waste. Recycling reduces the need for raw materials.” Asking hotel guests at check-in to sign the following commitment card was also ineffective: “I care about the environment at home and when I travel. As a friend to the earth, I will do my best to practice environmentally-friendly behaviour [save water and energy by re-using my towels] during my stay” (Baca-Motes et al. 2013, p. 1073).

When automatic processes are strong, normative activation and moral motivations are suppressed, and the individual defaults to habit-driven, automatic behaviour (MacInnes et al., 2022). These automatic behaviours are often performed without conscious awareness and are triggered by familiar environmental cues (Wood et al., 2002). Theories that ignore the role of unconscious factors in behaviour may not effectively change automatic behaviours that require little cognitive effort, such as towel reuse, reducing shower time, or reducing consumption of high-emission foods.


### Hypothesis #5 – Attempts to alter attitudes do not consider the effort required to perform the desired behaviours


Engaging in pro-environmental behaviours, such as selecting low-emission foods and drinks, using low-carbon transportation, or reducing air travel, can demand significant effort. When trying to change attitudes, the effort required to modify behaviour may be overlooked. Providing information on the carbon footprint of a bottle of wine in an Italian restaurant, for example, did not result in wine choices with lower carbon emissions (Soregaroli et al., 2021), possibly because it took too much effort to compare the labels. Similarly, providing different factual appeals including information about taste, nutrients, carbon footprint or distance of transportation at a hotel salad buffet showed that, while information about nutritional value and taste were effective in influencing food choice, the following environmental information was ineffective “Here you can find information about the environmental impact of our lettuce: For 100gr (1 portion) –Carbon footprint: 0.043 Kg per al KM ☺ The carbon footprint refers to the CO2 emission attributable to the transportation of lettuce” (Cozzio et al., 2021, p. 1308).


## Discussion


In recent years the focus of research into sustainable tourism has shifted towards developing and deploying interventions that encourage tourists to engage in more environmentally sustainable behaviours. This line of investigation is urgently needed to provide the tourism industry with tangible measures that can be deployed at destinations and businesses and that are proven to make tourist behaviour more sustainable and, as a result, can contribute to addressing global environmental challenges such as the UN SDG 12 of ensuring sustainable production and consumption. Despite the increasing interest, past studies fail to offer a general explanation or an overarching theory that guides effective intervention development in (sustainable) tourism.

The findings from this critical review challenge what appears to be the current dominant paradigm (our current collective understanding) of what drives (sustainable) tourist behaviour by analysing the limitations of the field’s predominant focus on cognitive constructs in general, and attitudes in specific. The analysis of failed attempts to leverage attitudes in order to entice tourists be behave in more sustainable ways leads to the identification of five possible explanation why attitudes have limited success in field experiments: tourists do not pay attention to message interventions; tourists are unwilling to cognitively process message interventions; tourists develop reactance in response to message interventions; attitude-based attempts to change behaviour ignore the role of habits; attitude-based attempts to change behaviour ignore the role of the effort associated with the desired pro-environmental behaviour. Each of these hypotheses, based on the field experiments conducted to date, appear to be highly plausible and are now available for empirical investigation.

Another important line of future investigation is the development and experimental testing of behavioural change interventions that do not rely on cognitive processing, such as increasing the enjoyment associated with the desired behaviour; reducing effort, targeting habits, emotional processing, or self-control; or altering the choice architecture tourists encounter (e.g., changing room cleaning defaults in a hotel from automatic daily room clean to no daily routine room clean with the choice of opting in, significantly reduced daily room clean requests; Knežević Cvelbar et al., 2021). The latter approach is commonly referred to as nudging (Thaler and Sunstein, 2021). Nudges are not habits but changing choice architecture can trigger system 1 thinking by influencing behaviour without restricting the freedom to choose alternative behavioural options. Nudges that trigger system 1 thinking have successfully reduced plate waste and the consumption of high emission foods (menu listing vegetarian and fish dishes, with meat dishes available upon request only or increasing the proportion of low-emission buffet options; for a review and references to these studies see Demeter et al., 2023). Nudges can help consumers avoid decision-making. This is typically achieved by changing default settings, such as the default room cleaning operations in a hotel from daily automatic cleaning to cleaning upon request only (Knežević et al., 2021).

Although habits and nudges both rely on automaticity of behaviours, empirical findings suggest that nudges are less effective than strong habits. For automatic behaviours that are enacted as habits (for example, food consumption or choice of transportation), new types of interventions are needed – interventions that either disrupt negative old habits or establish new positive ones. New habits can be created by triggering the brain’s reward centres through enjoyable experiences.

Extrinsic incentives, such as rewards, gifts or increased vacation enjoyment also have the potential to entice tourists to display the desired behaviours. Making the desired pro-environmental behaviour more enjoyable has proven successful in reducing plate waste of families by running a stamp collection game (Dolnicar et al., 2020). Similarly, sharing savings with hotel guests by giving them a drink voucher for each daily routine room clean they waive reduced room cleaning by 42% (Dolnicar et al., 2019b). Despite initial evidence of the potential of enjoyment-increasing interventions, only few practical measures developed to date have leveraged this mechanism.

Another construct that has largely been neglected is effort. One could argue that many interventions that involve modifying choice architecture leverage the fact that choosing the default option involves less effort than alternative behavioural options. It could also be argued that the theory of planned behaviour integrates aspects of effort in the construct of perceived behavioural control. Yet, effort has rarely been used as the target construct for behavioural interventions in its own right. Effort, therefore, represents a key construct that deserves increased research attention into the future.


## Conclusions


This study builds on several recent conceptual and empirical review papers that cast doubt on the effectiveness of attitudes as a leverage point to entice tourists to behave in more environmentally sustainable ways. The analysis of published field experiments in this area results in five possible theoretical explanations why attitudes frequently fail primary target of behavioural change interventions. Each explanation is based on existing knowledge and a hypothesis, which is now open for empirical investigation. Such empirical investigations represent a key future direction for research, as they will help pinpoint the relative strength of each reason, and, in so doing, guide the development of future attitude-based interventions. In addition, this study highlights several theoretical constructs which, to date, have been largely ignored, yet represent distinctly different theoretical pathways to achieving behaviour change. Future research leveraging these alternative theoretical constructs are urgently needed, especially given the high success rates achieved via these constructs in early studies. Pursuing these opportunities implies a theoretical reorientation from predominantly attitude-driven theories of human behaviour to alternative theories, such as habit theory or nudge theory. Attempting to leverage theory to develop effective interventions that lead to behavioural change directly links theory with important practical implications. Every behavioural intervention that is proven to be effective in a field experiment immediately delivers a tangible practical measure that tourism businesses and destinations can deploy to make their operations more environmentally sustainable. Harvesting the widest possible range of theories to develop new interventions, therefore, is highly desirable because it increases the likelihood of successful interventions emerging.

## Introduction


How do workers get attached to their jobs? People work for money, status and power, but only looking at extrinsic motivation does not carry us very far in understanding the full social meaning of work. Through their work people aim to find identity, direction and fulfilment (Budd, 2010), so for employers it does not suffice  to  only  offer  financial  gain  or  higher  status  as  rewards.  If  not  their  employees  run  the  risk  of alienating from their own labour. As such, a wilful workforce is (at least partially) dependent on identity regulation,  a  technique  of  government  through  which  organizations  steer,  build  and  process  the subjectivities of their workers (Adkins & Lury, 1999 Alvesson, 2010).

Eventually, work must be turned into a some kind of 'calling' (Weber, 2005) and therefore also the self of  the  worker  needs  to  be  culturally  (re)defined.  This  study  revisits  the  debate  on  workers'  identity construction by positing that organizational communication is a constitutive element within this form of managerial regulation. By depicting what they consider an 'ideal worker', firms and organizations actively contribute  to  shaping  the  professional  identities  of  their  employees  while  integrating  them  in  their organizational culture. The aim is to determine, on a discursive level, which repertoires organizations rely on to perform this identity regulation. In particular, the focus is on the case of multinational employers (N: 37), i.e. employment organizations that are active within multiple countries and recruit internationally, by analysing the employee testimonials (N:181) they post on their webpages.

Employee testimonials are personal narratives by current employees, published by organizations, that explain  why  they  value  working  for  the  organization,  what  drives  them  in  their  work  and  how  they experience  the  company  culture.  These  narratives  have  a  double  goal:  on  the  one  hand,  as  cultural

standards,  they  promote  a  type  of  professional  conduct,  expected  of  current  and  future  employees. Eventually these symbolic repertoires end up in people's 'cultural toolkits' (Swidler, 1986) on which they draw, to navigate their organizational lives. On the other hand, by using real employers, organizations attempt to humanize their organization. This allows them to tackle the problem of inauthenticity that is often attached to corporate branding (Maagaard, 2014), making the enterprise less impersonal and more attractive. Through a type of employee ventriloquism, the organization presents their ideal employees, making these testimonials a compelling site to analyze identity regulation as a managerial technique for both attraction and retention of employees.

This article aims to uncover the repertoires that multinational organizations rely on to produce the image of an ideal worker. We present the findings of a thematic content analysis, supported by quantitative and qualitative  coding,  of  employee  testimonial  collected  from  four  international  employment  sectors:  (1) energy, (2) technology, (3) finance and (4) governmental. The article starts with reopening the debate about alienation and work to continue with laying out how the ideal worker can enter as discursive vehicle to solve alienation by closing the gap between organizational and individual motivations. We finally end the theoretical part of the article by describing the historical changes in the way the ideal worker has been, over time, imagined and re-imagined. Subsequently we proceed to the empirical part by describing our case  selection  (multinational  employers),  our  data  (testimonials)  and  our  methodological  approach  (a combination of qualitative and quantitative thematic content analysis). Eventually we end the empirical part  with  describing  the  three  most  prevalent  types  of  ideal  workers  employed  by  the  multinational organisations in our sample: (1) the entrepreneur, (2) the trailblazer and (3) the cosmopolitan.


## The problem of alienation on the job


The argument that commitment to work can never fully be realized as long as the antagonism between self and work is not being transcended, dates back to at least early industrialization and has been the topic of much classical theorizing (e.g. Arendt 1998; Marx, 1988; Weber, 2005). Moreover, that this problem of alienation  through  work  is  more  than  a  philosophical  question  has  been  demonstrated  by  a  string  of empirical studies showing that unsatisfactory work is related to feelings of disassociation and distancing (for overview see Budd, 2011: 95). This problem can, however, be approach from drastically different angles.

The most classical way of interpreting the issue of alienation is through a Marxist perspective. Following a Hegelian  logic,  Marx  (1988)  saw  work  as  a  path  towards  self-realization.  By  working,  we  externalize ourselves as human beings and become objective realities to both others as well as ourselves. However, as Marx reasoned, in a capitalist economic system, surplus value is extracted from labour which is only possible when workers are systematically separated from control over production. Hence, the value of labour, he famously stated, is eventually hidden in commodities (Marx, 2013). Consequently, labour is reduced to a mere resource, making self-realization impossible. The argument has been reiterated many times both as a theoretical argument (cf. Arendt, 1998) as well as forming the basis for empirical research on labour exploitation (cf. Braverman, 1998; Buroway, 1979). Eventually, the solution to alienation is the reorganization  of  the  means  of  production  through  an  economic  and  political  empowerment  of  the worker.

However, the issue of alienation can also be approached from a very different angle by framing it as a practical  managerial  problem.  This  approach  focuses  on  regulating  organizational  productivity  by enhancing employee's motivation. As long as workers feel alienated from their work environment and professional tasks, they cannot fulfil their full potential as contributors to the organizational objectives. From this perspective, alienation is a problem of job satisfaction and psychological wellbeing. Solving this problem  became  one  of  the  core  tasks  of  modern  human  resource  management  and  Industrial  and

Organizational (I-O) psychology. Numerous managerial models, such as Schneider's (1987) AttractionSelection-Attrition model, Becker's (1964) emphasis on Human Capital or the Job Characteristic Theory of Hackman and Oldman (1975), were developed in an attempt to resolve alienation as a managerial problem  to  enhance    productivity,  competitiveness  and  efficiency.  These  models  were  built  on  the consensus - often implicitly infused by a Maslowian or essentialist concepts of self - that employees need to be intrinsically motivated to be fully productive. Hence, to eradicate alienation from the workforce, HR managers need to align people's personal needs with those of the organization. Or, to use a popular managerial idiom, optimize the Person-Organization (P-O) fit (Judge & Cable, 1997). This can be achieved through selecting  employees whose  intrinsic  motivation  and  values  already  fits  the  organization  or  by cultivating an attractive organizational culture conducive to a  'good morale'.

Although these perspectives propose very different roads towards solving the problem of alienation (i.e. rearranging  labour  relations  versus  managerial  intervention),  the  final  goal  remains  the  same:  a (re)unification of work and self. Yet, instead of a solution, this unification in itself can also be viewed as a problem, as a Foucauldian inspired approach reveals (see Alvesson & Willmott, 2002; Fleming, 2009; Rose 1989, Du Gay, 1996; Vallas & Cummins, 2015). The follow Foucault (1998) argument that power does not necessarily operates through subtraction, i.e. through punishment or rewards, but more often through enabling.  By  trying  to  unite  self  and  work,  organizations  actively  govern  employees  through enabling self-actualization and aligning it with company goals (i.e. conduct of conduct). In a similar vein Paul Du Gay (1996: 51) explained that ' 'job satisfaction' and 'motivation' are not phenomena that exist in some timeless, universal realm waiting to be discovered by, and deployed within, managerial discourse. Both the basic concepts and the practices that bestow upon them a material reality are products of changes in the imagination and organization of work.' Hence, the managerial gaze is directed towards processing subjectivities as a means of exercising power and organizing labour (Adkins & Lury, 1999). In other words, to unite self and work, and circumvent the Marxist problem of alienation, they engage in processes of 'identity regulation' (Alvesson and Willmots, 2002).


## Regulating identities through an ideal worker


Work identities emerge out of a kaleidoscopic arrangement of institutions, social positions and other cultural sources such as media, arts or entertainment. Much of our socialization into work takes place outside  of  the  workplace,  notably  through  family  upbringing  and  schooling.  Paul  Willis  (1977),  for example, shows this dynamic in his classical study on how working class 'lads' are being funnelled into a life of manual labour through cultural scripts of anti-intellectualism and masculinity. Bowles and Gintis (1977) even argued that schooling in capitalist society is only there to prepare a new generation of obedient and disciplined workers. Moreover, also popular culture is an important channel of identity formation, both directly - through career advice books or websites (Valles & Cummins,  2015, De Keere, 2014) and indirectly - through  novels, movies and television (Davis & Frink, 2014).

However, also managerial techniques play a substantial role in subjectification processes by directly and indirectly enabling workers' 'will to work'. The latter emerges by producing a subject that derives meaning out of work. Through managerial discourses on belonging, motivation and self-actualization, managers attempt to amend the 'dislocation' (Du Gay, 1996) between work and self. Hence, organizational power does  not  impede  self-formation  (i.e.  alienation  through  subtracting),  but  instead  produces  it  through defining possibilities and affirming ideals (i.e. regulation through enabling). This managerial unification of work  and  self,  however,  can  leave  the  worker  more  vulnerable  to  exploitation  as  strong  personal identification with work makes it harder to set boundaries and resist unfavourable working conditions (Cech, 2021). 'Through striving to fulfil their own needs and wishes at work,' as Nikolas Rose pointed out 'each employee will thus work for the advance of the enterprise; the more the individual fulfils him

or herself, the greater the benefit to the company.' (1989: 56).  As such, organizations can discursively regulate identities on multiple fronts (Alvesson and Willmott, 2002). Besides offering narratives on the self,  discursive  managerial control can work through setting a scene, cultivating organizational culture, declaring  mission  statement  and  acknowledging  industry  standards.  Additionally,  managers  can  also activate relational dynamics of belonging (and differentiation) as a way to bridge the gap between work and self  (Mears,  2015).  Finally,  organization's  activities  can  be  draped  in  positive  social  values,  allowing managerial discourse to tap into (already existing) moral identities of their employees. We argue here that these different aspects of identity regulation within organizations eventually converge in the image of an 'ideal worker'.

Yet, people are not born in work organizations, their life trajectories already bestow them with a certain set of dispositions, worldviews and self-conceptions (De Keere, 2020). The extent to which these a priori align with the organizational image of the ideal worker greatly varies. Previous research demonstrated that organizational gatekeepers more easily hire candidates that emit the right cultural signals and rely on (often classed) self-narratives that echo the organizational ideal (Rivera, 2016; Friedman & Laurison, 2019; De Keere 2020). Furthermore, as several studies have demonstrated, the ideal worker often also includes other extra-organizational societal markers such as race, gender, age or class, converging towards a white middle class model (Turco, 2010; Acker, 1990; Blair-Loy, 2009; Davies & Frink, 2014; Neely, 2020; Adkins & Lury, 1999). Hence, the image of the ideal worker also serves as a template for managerial decision-taking,  steering  recruitment,  retention  and  promotion  and  thus  operates  as  a  tool  of  both inclusion and exclusion.


## A changing ideal


The contours of the ideal white-collar worker are historically specific. Up until the 1980s, employment relations  in  most  industrialized  countries  were  characterized  by  long-term  commitment  and  intraorganizational  mobility  (Vosko  2009;  DiMaggio,  2001,  Neely  2020).  As  depicted  by  William  Whyte (1956) in his 'Organizational Man' - the ideal employee of that era - is a steadfast, loyal and risk-averse family  man  looking  for  lifelong  employment  and  a  career  within  the  company.  Through  a  historical analysis,  Davies  and  Frink  (2014)  point  out  how  this  ideal,  from  its  origin,  is  heavily  gendered  and racialized.  They  show  how  an  increasing  separation  between  work  and  private  life  under  Fordism, eventually  casted  the  white  middle-class  family  man  (with  a  stay-at-home  spouse)  as  the  only  eligible candidate for the ideal worker.

By  the  end  of  the  20   century,  several  political,  organizational  and  structural  changes  eroded  the th organizational man as an ideal. Firstly, the educational expansion meant a large influx of new class of higher educated young people collectively entering the labour market. As Pierre Bourdieu (1984) already observed  in  the  1960s,  this  group  is  marked  by  new  self-expressive  aspirations  and  a  disdain  for  old morality of duty and discipline, strongly contradicting with the ideal of the organizational man. Second, due to an organizational power shift, away from the manager and towards the shareholders and investors, the long-term relationship between employer and employees contract came under pressure (DiMaggio, 2001,  Vosko,  2009).  Instead  of  being  assessed  based  on  their  durability,  productivity  and  efficiency, organizations need to be primarily profitable and are seen as merely portfolios of activities which can be dropped, replaced or enhanced (DiMaggio, 2001: 21). Consequently, employment management became increasingly concerned with flexibility and inter-organizational mobility. Moreover, the 1980s witnessed the emergence of neoliberalism as a political program, which undermined the political power of labour union and minimized employment rights and benefits. As a result, the bargaining position of workers weakened, leading to what Boltanski and Chiapello (2005) called, a 'new spirit of capitalism', largely resting

on a 'project logic'. Instead of investing in developing specific skills through long-term commitments, the worker has to demonstrate their versatility and creativity by engaging in a range of different projects within multiple organizational settings.

This  new  employment  reality  impacted  the  description  of  the  ideal  worker,  taking  the  shape  of  an entrepreneurial and self-reliant homo economicus  (Du Gay, 1996; Rose, 1989). In this new discursive regime, drive and passion arouse as defining characteristics of the ideal worker, making them powerful moral imperatives within the professional realm (Cech, 2021; Neely & Roa, 2018, Author A). Moreover, unlike the organizational man, the loyalty of the entrepreneurial self lies in oneself only. The latter is inspired, flexible and focused on risk-taking and self-development. Neely (2020) aptly coined this cultural ideal the 'portfolio worker'. In order to survive within the neoliberal labour market, the contemporary employee  needs  to  work  on  their  own  authentic  'personal  brand'  rather  than  cultivating  long-term devotion toward one firm only (see also Vallas & Cummings, 2014).

In sum, whether you take a Marxist or managerial route to analyse our work lives, alienation arises as a persistent problem. In order to iron out the dislocation between self and work, organizations are forced to activate cultural processes of subject formation. Both the ideals of the 'organizational man' as well as the 'entrepreneurial self', have in the past been put to work as discursive tools of identity regulation to align the needs and aspirations of the worker with that of the organization.


## Towards an analysis


If identity regulation emerges as a managerial technique on a symbolic level, we should investigate the discursive conduits organizations have at their disposal to reach their workers. In this regards, employee testimonials emerge as prominent loci for the analysis, as they merge employee and employer together while being published by organizations themselves. Testimonials take many forms: from short interviews clips over  diary  entrances  through  longer  first-person  narratives  about  employee's  personal  and professional trajectory. In all cases, they eventually represent what kind of worker the organization deems ideal, thereby regulating the identities of both current and future workers.

Employee testimonials are not passive elements of organizational communication but play a performative role in organizational identity regulations by advertising a certain type of employee. People are attracted to organizations they perceive as having similar cultural attributes and values as themselves (Braddy et al., 2003). For instance, people accept substantial lower pay if they can work for a firm that advertises a strong cultural identity, aligning with their own personal dispositions (Calbe & Turban, 2003); this indicates that communicating an organizational identity directly taps into people's intrinsic motivations. We know that organizations that communicate on an individual or personal instead of on an institutional level appear more authentic and appealing (Van Hoy & Lievens, 2007; Maagaard, 2014). Moreover, there is also a potential selection effect at play. For example, Walker and colleagues (2009), demonstrated that Black respondents  were  more  drawn  to  companies  that  published  testimonials  of  employees  belonging  to minorities on their recruitment websites. Whites, on the other hand, even responded more negatively as the proportion of minority testimonials increased.

Our focus on employee testimonials allows us to empirically explore the question of which repertoires organisations are using in the 21  century to construct their ideal worker? So far, much of the writing on st organizational  control  and  work  identity  formation  was  based  either  on  theoretical  deduction  or investigating the perspective of the workers. Instead, by analysing employee testimonials, which always entail  organizational  ventriloquism,  we  shift  the  focus  towards  those  who  provide  the  discourses  that determine workers' identity. In addition, previous studies presented the ideal worker as rather generic; applicable to the labour market as a whole and equally valid in all employment sectors. By comparing employee testimonials from four different employment sectors - energy, tech, finance and governmental

- we take a first step in investigating the assumed universality of the entrepreneurial self while exploring the possibility of multiple ideal workers.

Furthermore,  analysing  current  employee  testimonials  offers  the  possibility  to  explore  whether  the discursive  construction  of  the  contemporary  ideal  worker  reflects  recent  changes  in  labour  market dynamics and managerial logics. Two important evolutions are being addressed through the selection of our case studies. First, between 1980 and 2010 the amount of labour migrants has more than doubled and by 2019 close to 5% of the global labour force is working in a host country (ILO, 2021), indicating an increasing  globalization  of  the  workforce.  On  top  of  that,  also  organizations  became  gradually  more international. According to the OECD (2018), by 2014, the share of global employment working for multinational enterprises has gone up to roughly 23%, which is a substantial part of the labour market. Hence, does this globalization of work translate into a new image of the ideal worker?

Second, the managerial logic changed over the last three decades. While the mid-20  century was marked th by a rising influence of shareholders, making profit maximization the prime managerial directive, we now witness a turn towards a diversification and even moralization of organizational objectives (Shamir, 2008). This  means  that  managers  are  increasingly  asked  to,  besides  still  considering  shareholders'  needs, prioritize issues such as sustainability, diversity, equity and good citizenship. A notable example is the fixed spot Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) attained on the agenda of any corporate board meeting as well as the increasing importance of the UN's Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) for investors (Preuss, Haunschild & Matten, 2009; Leins, 2020). Have also these dynamics also impacted the image of the ideal worker?

Thus, by analysing and comparing employee testimonials, we aim to empirically establish to what extent the dominant discursive elements of the ideal worker still fit the singular standard of the entrepreneurial self  or  whether  sectorial  differences  and  structural  changes  produce  variations  in  what  multinational organizations deem the desired employee.


## Findings



## Not for the love of money but for self-love


Before  we  delve  into  the  discursive  specificities  of  the  testimonials,  we  will  highlight  their  general similarities.  Despite  it  being  insensitive  to  nuance,  a  simple  word  count  highlights  relevant  patterns. Looking at the top-20 most used meaningful words (see Table 3), we immediately discern how central personal development is. The dominance of concepts such as career, opportunity, learning, experience and development indicates how the testimonials try to convey that working at their organization is a sure path towards personal growth. Hence, nearly all employees relied on a narrative that centred around their own  personal  trajectory  instead  of  only  describing  the  objectives  of  their  companies  or  extrinsic motivations.

Table 3 Word count

While references to self-development were ubiquitous, references to material benefits (money, salary, etc) were conspicuously absent. In total we could only identify three instances in which the employee would mention any sort of financial gain that comes from working at their organization. And even in these cases it would almost disappear in a long list of immaterial motivations: 'If you ask me why I would recommend Wells  Fargo  as  an  employer,  I  will  give  these  reasons:  great  culture,  amazing  recognition,  great

opportunities for career progression, training offerings, and competitive benefits and pay. And finally, a lot of fun at work.' (emphasis added, Cedrick Lorenzo, Project Manager). Instead, the testimonials seem to endorse the opposite view. As Luis Aranda, an artificial intelligence expert at OECD, states: 'The worst career advice that I've got is to follow the money. The best career advice is to follow your heart. When you follow your heart you make sure you find meaning in your job, in your everyday life.'


## Three repertoires


The performativity of organizational control lies in the ability to shape employee's identity so that their intrinsic  motivations  match  with  the  goals  of  the  organization.  By  presenting  employee  testimonials, organizations try to, indirectly, communicate which type of motivations they deem desirable. However, diverse set of intrinsic drives are imaginable. Our iterative coding eventually yielded 14 codes with high prevalence  and  validity  (see  Table  2).  Together  these  codes  make  out  the  discursive  universe  that multinational organizations produced to construct their ideal worker.

We observed that the trope of the entrepreneurial self alone does not fully cover the way the ideal workers are  represented  by  the  organizations  out  of  our  sample.  In  addition  to  notions  such  as  'risk-taking', 'working hard' and 'passion', we also discerned a strong interest for moral issues such as 'diversity', 'doing good for society' and 'sustainability'. Overall, the most dominant codes were 'belonging' and 'global firm', meaning that about one third of all employees would testify that they sensed a strong feeling of belonging at their organization and that they strongly appreciate the international experience it offers. Additionally,  working  out  of  passion  was  a  prominent  discursive  frame,  echoing  many  other  recent qualitative studies on the meaning of work in contemporary society (Cech, 2021; Neely & Roa, 2018, Author A).

However,  there  are  multiple  ways  we  can  combine  these  codes  into  separate  repertoires.  Seeing  the explorative nature of the study, the interpretation here is guided by a factor analysis of the codes. In this way, we let the covariance of the codes determine to what extent topics are being combined in a single narrative. A explorative factor analysis (with oblique rotation) of the codes eventually yields three factors. Since  the  components  do  not  correlate  significantly,  we  can  interpret  these  three  factors  as  separate repertoires.

Taking the factor loadings as guidelines, we distinguish three repertoires that each depict a different type of ideal worker. We coin the first type 'the entrepreneur' as it strongly resembles the entrepreneurial self (risk  taking,  hard-working,  pride)  while  adding  an  element  of  emotional  attachment  on  top  of  that (belonging, fun, passion). The second, in contrast, is much more outwardly directed. We labelled this ideal 'the trailblazer' as it encompasses strong believes in one's passion and the capacity to contribute to a  fast-changing,  sustainable  and  diverse  world.  The  last  repertoire,  finally,  centres  around  a  'the cosmopolitan', a global worker that is focused on helping the world to become a better place.  Although all codes appeared in all sectors, we still see that some repertoires are significantly more saliant than other in different employment fields. ## The entrepreneur


As yet pointed out, this repertoire strongly resembles the well-established entrepreneurial ideal and is by far the most popular within the tech sector. It is defined by the intersection between, on the one hand, economic drive, desire for success and risk-taking, and, on the other hand, the emphasis on authenticity, well-being and belonging (Fleming, 2009; Rose, 1989, Author A). At its core it pertains to the notion that meeting challenges, taking risks and working hard eventually lead, not just to economic gains but also to self-development. Lisa Milburn, a chief marketing communication officer, echoes this almost literally on the website of BMO: 'If you are ambitious and want to drive your career, there are lots of leaders in the bank ready to help. So many lessons … be self-aware of your strengths, areas of development and work on them.'

Thus, employees are constantly urged to take risks and undertake challenges head-on: 'If you see an opportunity, if you have the slightest doubt or 'what if' in your mind, just go for it.' (Sebastian Gabriel, designer  at  Google).  This  risk-taking  is  often  immediately  connected  to  psychological  benefits  and achieving  self-growth,  they  become  matters  of  well-being:  'What  I  love  about  my  role  is  that  it's challenging,  and  everything  moves  fast.  Being  honest  with  yourself  enables  you  to  be  aware  of  your weaknesses and improve them. It also means that you can keep your mind open to the opportunities ahead of you.' (Nur, Chemical Engineer, BP). Hence, the worker that is presented here is one that derives true happiness and self-discovery from following up on opportunities and working hard.

Yet, this working hard should not be stressful. If you really like would you are doing, as many employees explain,  then  you  should enjoy  it.  Hence  it  is  also  the  responsibility  of  the  company  that  you  can  be yourself, be productive and be happy. Anne-Jeanette from Capital describes it in the following way:

Capital  One really  values  associates  being  able  to  focus  and  be  innovative.  The  reality  is  that stresses are not conducive to innovation, creativity, learning and collaboration. And so I've seen a theme in our benefits of a commitment to say, 'Hey, we really do want to make life easier for you because we want you to enjoy working here and be able to focus when you're here.

Feelings of belonging and pride are symptomatic of a repertoire that harmonizes personal motives with those of the organization. This sort of employee-organization symbiosis is often quite literally stated; for instance, Shalini Nagarai, a Business Consultant for Wells Fargo, testifies: 'I was conscious that it also

contributed in a small way to Wells Fargo's growth and this gave me a sense of pride and achievement. In essence, you are growing along with the company.'


## The trailblazer


The trailblazer repertoire has been used equally by the employees from the four different sectors (see Figure 2). Seeing that the code for passion loads highly on both factor, it shares with the entrepreneurial repertoire an emphasis on passion. Hence, the ideal worker is one who, out of passion, can influence change. It is their personal drive for technological innovation and progress, as we for example find in tech sector, that leads all of us into a brave new world:

I have a lot of passion and love for the products we're building right now, so it tends to ooze out of my pores. I'm a daily, if not hourly, active user, so the team hears a lot of feedback and product ideas from me. I truly believe we're building a better, more connected world with the products we create. (Heidi Y, engineer, Facebook)

Employees are presented as passionate visionaries, set on changing the world. They are at the forefront of progress, ready to forge the future of humankind. 'Scientists across the energy sector are hard at work on new ideas just like that one - ideas that could change the world.' as Dhaval Bhandarie (chemical engineer) says on the website of Exxon 'Now, it's my turn to progress the scientific breakthroughs that came before me and run with them, expanding their revolutionary ideas into global realities.'

This repertoire depicts the contemporary worker as surrounded by a fast-changing and highly complex world  that they are personally responsible for. 'The  world  is rapidly evolving with complex, multidimensional challenges ahead of us. At a crossroads such as this, transformational and visionary leadership is key to fostering the changes the world needs.' (Natalia, Communication manager, BP). In this  way,  the  work  they  do  for  their  organization  propels  them  towards  the  cockpit  of  society,  codetermining its future.

Moreover,  this  futurist  vision  is  resolutely  green.  Many  employees  present  their  organization  as  an important vehicle to a cleaner, ecological and environmentally friendly future. 'I want to do what I can for the planet. I help Westpac Group find opportunities to be more sustainable in the way we build and operate our sites' (Manoj Bathela, an engineer at Westpac). Although sustainability is a common topic in the testimonials in all sectors - mentioned respectively in 4.2%, 8.5% and 10.3% of testimonials from the banking, tech, and governmental sector - it is most prevalent within the energy sector at 23 %. 'As a citizen of the planet, I am very interested in the role we can all play in tackling the climate challenge. BP's net zero pledge marked the beginning of real change in the industry.' (Natalia, communication manager, BP). The energy sector seems to mobilize employee testimonials for moral rebranding to tackle the stigma caused by their involvement in a series of natural disasters and promote their ecological responsibility. ## The cosmopolitan


The multinational organizations in this sample strongly advertise their global scope. About one third of the testimonials explicitly emphasized the international character of the organization, although people often work at local branches.  By mobilizing the cosmopolitan aspect of their organization, they deploy a repertoire hinting to a larger process of internationalisation of the corporate class (Bühlmann, David & Mach, 2013). These employers directly respond to this dynamic by actively deploying a cosmopolitan narrative, most notably in the supra-governmental sector. Organizations signal this cosmopolitanism in at least  two  ways:  employees'  trajectories  and  the  organization's  environment.  On  the  one  hand,  the employees from the testimonials present themselves as multicultural and international, by mentioning their international education or travel experiences. Sakina Soadatkadamova, an HR officer at OSCE born in Tajikistan, for example, explains how before getting this job she first studied in both Moscow and Berlin. Alternatively, their migration background is put forward. A testimonial by Mohsen Achour, a Conoco Philips engineer, really exemplifies this international life trajectory:

Having had all his college education in Stillwater and with re-joining ConocoPhillips in Bartlesville, Mohsen considers himself 'Tunisian by birth and Okie by choice.' 'Almost to the day, I've spent half of my life in Tunisia and half in Oklahoma,' he said, 'bouncing back and forth between the white sandy beaches of the Mediterranean and brown muddy country roads of Oklahoma.'

On the other hand, employees testify extensively about how working at their organization facilitates a cosmopolitan lifestyle. Through their jobs they acquire international experience on multiple fronts. First, it can give employees 'a real international flavour of travel' (John, General Supervisor, Saudi Aramco) or as Sabeen, a financial service provider at Goldman Sachs states:

I love to travel and experience different cultures - I've recently travelled to Bali, Singapore and Malaysia. This has been a great experience as I get to expand my network and learn about new places.

productivity, as she continues 'also I think that that makes you think about more original solutions, to be more open to new ideas.' Furthermore, the analysis revealed that ideal of a cosmopolitan worker coincides with a moral call to do good to society, with many employees making the case that their work allows them to contribute to society. Jennifer, an operation program manager at Apple, claims that she is not just doing this job for the money: 'Well,  here  it's always more  than  that,  whether  it's  the  environment  or  people's  experience  with  the product or something more. Consequently, 'doing the right thing', 'giving back to society' or 'helping our communities' are common idioms cosmopolitan workers use to express the way they value the ethical and social dimensions of their work. Hence, this repertoire does not only address the increasing globalization of work but simultaneously seems to incorporate the moral turn that has slowly been taking place in the corporate world (see above). The image of the ideal worker that is underlying this cosmopolitan repertoire is quite different than the more commonly known entrepreneurial self. The worker that is presented here is outwardly directed and has  a  societal  agenda,  which  almost  contrast  with  risk-taking  and  self-centred  employee  of  the entrepreneurial narrative. This incongruity can partly explain why they are both prevalent in different sectors (tech versus government).


## Conclusion


While analysing the problem of management during Taylorism, Harry Braverman came to the following conclusion:

The necessity for adjusting worker to work in its capitalist form, for overcoming natural resistance intensified by swiftly changing technology […], does not end with the 'scientific organization of labor', but becomes permanent feature of capitalist society' (1973, 43)

We come to agree with Braverman that this has become a permanent feature and have, in this artcile, argued that online communication figures prominently, in the post-Taylorist era, as a managerial technique to adjust the 'worker to work'. By diffusing what they deem the ideal worker, organizations contribute to the production of 'a will to work', enabling workers' ethos and regulating their identities. As such, workers align with the organization's goals and are controlled through a 'conduct of conduct'. We explored the transformation and multiplication of the discursive repertoires on the ideal worker, which multinational organizations  promote  through  employee  ventriloquism.  In  answering  our  research  questions,  we discovered  that  discursively  multinational  employment  organizations  rely  on  three  ideal  types:  the entrepreneur, the trailblazer and the cosmopolitan.

The entrepreneurial repertoire, most popular in the corporate sectors of tech and finance, centres on the employee's self, painting a better and more developed self for those who work hard and passionately take risks. As such, by seizing the moment, this ideal worker can foster self-growth while ensuring organizational productivity. A horizontal hierarchy, coupled with a stress on authenticity is the work environment that would foster this alignment. This dovetails seamlessly with many previous arguments on the neoliberal worker as a self-disciplining economic subject (Rose, 1989; Du Gay, 1996; Fleming, 2009).

The trailblazer  narrative  depicts  employees  as  drivers  of  change  who  can  meet  the  challenges  that  a constantly  changing  world  presents.  Their  passion  and  foresight  make  them  the  bearer  of  the  future. Through their participation, the world will be able to tackle its contemporary challenges: ranging from climate change to systemic inequality. It strongly resembles the ecomodernist discourses popular among corporate leaders such as Elon Musk or Bill Gates. At the same time, it mirrors the 'moral turn' in the corporate sector, moving away from maximalization of shareholders' return towards a stakeholder model, the latter manifests itself in increasing relevance of CSR and the ESG (Preuss, Haunschild & Matten, 2009; Leins, 2020). Trailblazing employees are presented as crucial partners in this change.

The cosmopolitan repertoire, most common among testimonials stemming from the supra-governmental sector, depicts workers as citizens of the world and their organizations as places where a cosmopolitan lifestyle can be fully enacted. This lifestyle, however, cannot take place at the expense of morality; we showed how working for a higher Good is quintessential to this repertoire. With an emphasis on 'doing the right thing', it also joins the corporate turn towards more social responsibility but at the same time this repertoire feeds more strongly into the globalization of the labour market.

Promoting cosmopolitanism, however, is less innocent as it initially appears. In a contemporary globalized society, being at ease in an international context can be an important status signal, fostering dynamics of exclusion (Calhoun, 2002). As Weenink (2008) argued, based on a study of international parenting, by pursuing the insignia of cosmopolitanism, many members of the middle class try to actively deal with the process of globalization. This cosmopolitan ethos becomes the core of a process of distinction, classifying people  based  on  their  level  of  internationality,  negotiated  through  international  degrees,  international internships, travels, global networks of friends or a multicultural attitude. Following Bourdieu's notion of capital  reconversion (1986), we can interpret the accumulation of these advantages as a cosmopolitan capital (Weenink, 2008; Bühlmann, David and Mach, 2013). Hence, job candidates that lack such capital or do not recognize themselves in this craving for a cosmopolitan lifestyle, might opt to not even apply to enter this occupational field leading to lack of inclusion and increasing homogeneity .

But also the other two repertoires carry the possibility of exclusion. As yet pointed out, the idea of the entrepreneurial self, based on risk-taking, drive and passion, is very much in geared towards white male middle class dispositions (e.g. Acker, 1990; Blair-Loy, 2003; Neely, 2020). An although we currently lack research on this, we can expect that the exaggerated belief in agency implied by the trailblazer ideals, leads to disidentification and self-exclusion for those who, through their life trajectory, lack such a strong sense of  entitlement.  We  know,  for  example,  that  even  subtle  agentic  wording  in  job  vacancy  texts  (e.g. leadership, competitive, dominant), which overall seen as more masculine, leads to women perceiving themselves as less suitable and expecting low sense of belongingness (Gaucher, Friesen and Kay, 2011). Hence, we can imagine that a repertoire depicting employees as  characterized by a self-confidence to change the world, could discourage many people to recognize themselves as potential employees. Yet, the extent to which self-exclusion occurs through the organizational backing of an ideal worker, is a question for further empirical research.

Finally, this study challenged the notion of the ideal worker as a universal template with a singular meaning, enforced equally on all workers (i.e. entrepreneur in the neoliberal market). Not only did we find that multiple and distinguishable ideals circulate, but also that the prevalence of these depend on employment contexts. However, seeing the explorative nature of this study, it falls beyond the scope of this article to explain why exactly entrepreneurialism was more prevalent among employee testimonials from the finance and tech sector, whereas the cosmopolitan repertoire was used most by the supranational governmental employers. Or why the trailblazer was equally embraced by all multinational organizations in our sample? These variations could be explained by organisational structures, types of output, historically grown field doxa's or varying levels of competition. It is up to future research to disentangle how certain repertoires

of identity regulation become more dominant in certain sectors than others. This is simultaneously a call for more meso-level research in uncovering the cultural foundations of our economic realities. In this case it means further dissecting the role of employment organisations and fields within the cultural construction of the meaning of work.

## The structure of commonality


Figure 2 depicts logically possible states of mutual awareness. Looking at it, we first of all have a rudimentary, or zero-order 6 State 1, corresponding to signs that neither Alpha nor Beta are aware of. As we move further, to the first order , there is State 2, where Alpha is aware of a certain sign, while Beta is not. If the sign under question are attributes Beta displays or his behaviors that Alpha, unknowingly for Beta, uses to reach some far-reaching conclusion about him, then Beta would be acting unwittingly, to use Goffman's wording, giving away some information on himself, while Alpha may percept him naïvely. State 3 reverses the relationships - Alpha acts unwittingly, while Beta perceives her actions naïvely. Finally, while aware of the sign themselves, the players may be unaware of each other's awareness, thus continuing to act unwittingly and perceive naïvely (State 4). A real-life example of signs belonging to the latter state may be nameless facial expressions, which we recognize when we see them in others, but cannot formulate what we recognize, and usually do not believe anyone else can recognize (what individuals usually refer to as 'intuition' or 'gut feelings' about others' thoughts or intentions).

This order's information asymmetry characteristic allows the more knowledgeable interaction participant to use information undiscernible to others to their strategic advantage. Alternatively, it can become a source of a moral obligation to warn these others, if, say, recognizing a sign is a part of professional training Alpha received - for example, say, Alpha is a doctor recognizing in Beta early symptoms of a disease invisible to non-experts. On this order, the degree of a sign's manipulability does not play a role, as, presumably, no one tries to manipulate it.

On the next, second order of awareness , we again find three possible states. Alpha may be aware of Beta's awareness of a sign, while Beta is unaware of her awareness (State 5), or vice versa (State 6), or both of them can be aware of the partner's awareness, without the partner being aware of his or her awareness being known about (State 7). Knowing that interaction partners recognize certain signs suggest players can influence their perceptions by using control moves. Learning that Alpha recognizes certain signs, and wishing to make certain impressions on her, Beta may try to find out if these signs are, theoretically, open to manipulation, and at what cost, then evaluating the available resources to manipulate them. Further, Beta is to estimate the prospective benefits of such manipulation imagining Alpha's likely reactions, and weigh these benefits against the costs.

An example can be the signifying properties of literary tastes. In the initial state of innocence, in which Beta believes that Alpha does not draw any association between reading and other personal attributes, his reading lists truly reflect his personal preferences. As soon as he finds himself at State 6, however, his reading (or at least contents of his bookshelves to which Alpha may have access) would probably reflect his self-presentational concerns. ## Careers of signs


So far, we have taken individuals seeking to locate themselves and others within the awareness structure. In this paragraph, we will trace trajectories of signs across it. We might hypothesize that, generally, an awareness of signals is likely to spread among those who feel that they can derive useful information from them, or who believe that they themselves serve the source of such information for others (Simmel, 1906: Goffman, 1969; Gibson, 2014). As soon as anybody announces the familiarity with a sign, others are likely to become at least theoretically aware that still others might also recognize this sign. This diffusing awareness is probably the central force in the evolution of any personal signal system as it creates pressure on any sign pushing it toward the upper part of figure 1. 27 Two themes related to this process are first, the natural selection of signals and their mutations, and second, processes, which sometimes block their evolution in the direction of common awareness.

## Concluding note


The main aim of this paper was to develop an approach to analyzing social signaling based on two principal variables Goffman pointed to in his pioneering work: degrees of manipulability and the position in the structure of mutual awareness. For that aim, I proposed a guide through the structure of mutual awareness, describing the moves each position in it dictates to individuals occupying it, their tactics aimed at locating themselves within this structure, and the trajectories of signs across it.

The most significant progress in this direction was made by interactionist sociology in the 1960s, namely, in Morris Friedell's (1969) analysis of the distribution of situation awareness, where he introduced the formal definition of common knowledge; in Goffman's studies of 'face' (1955; 1967; Pinker, 2007: 418-421); in Thomas Scheff's treatment of consensus (1967; 2005), and in Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss's work on the awareness of dying (1969).

Since then, however, relatively little has been done to develop this line of thinking. Some works originating from status construction theory analyze higher order status beliefs and the consequences of individuals believing that others believe certain attributes are associated with high social standing (Webster and Whitmeyer, 2002; Ridgeway 2014; Corell et al. 2017; Ridgeway, 2019). The cognitive sociology of culture explains the stability of cultural forms by their status as elements of commonly known 'focal points' (DiMaggio, 1997; Patterson, 2014). In the same vein, Luhmann's double contingency was used recently to account for the functions of university rankings (Esposito and Stark, 2019); one can also find the idea of pluralistic ignorance applied to sociological studies of norm enforcement (Willer et al., 2009). Eviatar Zerubavel's (2006) work on the 'elephants in the room' mechanisms of denial in everyday life that include various tactics of preventing common knowledge emergence - must be mentioned in this context. Most of these important research directions, however, have proceeded in an apparent isolation from one another as well as from earlier interactionist studies, and none have attempted a systematic mapping of the levels of mutual, or shared knowledge, between purely private (what someone thinks, with no awareness of what others think) and common knowledge. The most systematic treatment of this topic in sociology remains Goffman's Strategic Interaction (1969), his probably least known work.   Outside of sociology, this topic has been studied recently and fruitfully 3 in behavioral games theory (Nagel, 1995; Bosch-Demènech et al, 2002; Camerer, 2003), in which much experimental work was conducted to establish how many recursions individuals perform in strategic interaction.

## The Evolution of Environmental and Climate Concerns during Family Formation
