While the differences between women and men are significant, large differences also exist in the biography types within each gender. For both men and women, two groups are characterized by  stagnating  transition  states:  they  either  experience  a  long  waiting  period  in  the  asylum procedure (thus termed 'deferred transition') or a long and typically unsuccessful period of job search once the asylum procedure is finalized (groups 'lost in transition', see Figure 2). The men  'lost  in  transition'  are,  however,  more  likely  than  women  'lost  in  transition'  to nevertheless experience some spells of education. Men in this trajectory typically attend some sort of education in the first half of the observation period before going back to job search (or at very small shares into employment, Figure 2). Men in 'deferred transition', i.e. those with a disproportionally long time waiting for the result of the asylum procedure, switch into education rather in the second half of the observation period, and to a lesser extent into job search or employment.  Women  'deferred  in  transition',  if  at  all,  transit  into  job  search  (Figure  2). Accordingly,  both  male  and  female  'lost  in  transition'  groups  show  decreasing  entropies towards the end of the second year. Thereafter, entropy increases visibly for men and more moderately  for  women  (Figures  3  and  4).  For  the  biographies  in  the  'deferred  transition' groups, the entropy ranges at low levels in the first two years for women and for the first one and  a  half  years  for  men.  It  takes  up  speed  thereafter  for  both  groups,  which  I  cautiously interpret as an indicator for the delay in participation to slowly be coming to an end.

Women 'lost in transition' are slightly younger than the female average, show less educational attainment and are less likely to have job experience (see Tables A2 and A3 in the appendix). Men in this group are, in contrast, not selected by educational and job profiles and are instead older than the male average. They are furthermore more likely to have arrived with family members and have shorter travel durations than the male average. The opposite is the case for men in 'deferred transition'. These individuals report above-average travel durations (83 days vs the 51-days male sample average), less likely arrived with family and more likely reported traumatic experiences on the route. Just like women in this group, they also show a significantly lower  socioeconomic  profile  in  terms  of  education,  job  experience,  and  pre-migration socioeconomic status. Syrians are underrepresented in the 'deferred transition' trajectory type, while Afghans, Eritreans, Somalians and other nationalities are overrepresented (see Tables A2 and A3 in the appendix).

A third trajectory type is characterized by long periods of education for both men and women, thus referred to as 'long activation' group. With more than 15 months in education for both men and women, these biographies have much longer educational spells than other trajectories with education involved. Men and women, however, differ in the timing of the educational

spells. The proportion of male education spells rapidly grows after initial phases of inactivity during the asylum procedure and/or job search, while for women a delay can be observed for educational  activities  (see  Figure  2).  A  transition  into  the  job  market  happens  rarely  and exclusively  towards  the  end  of  the  observation  period.  Women  and  men  with  a  higher socioeconomic profile are overrepresented in the 'long activation' trajectory. They also report slightly  shorter  travel  durations  and  are  more  likely  to  have  arrived  with  family  members (Tables A2 and A3 in the appendix).

Another group of female biographies is characterized by a considerable share of educational activity, largely followed by job search. Remarkably, their course or training activities occur almost exclusively in the first half of the observation period. Also, their transition from asylum procedure into job search happens relatively quickly compared to the other groups, so I call this female trajectory 'early activation'. Syrians, and thus individuals with good asylum chances and primary access to integration measures, are overrepresented in this group (Tables A2 and A3 in the appendix). They furthermore have an above-average socioeconomic profile. For men, no such distinct group could be made out. Rather, men with short asylum procedures and early access to integration measures have a higher chance than other men to follow the long activation trajectory.

For men, I identify an additional group with comparatively long phases of inactivity during the asylum procedure and a rather hesitant subsequent participation in education and on the job market. After the asylum procedure, job search and education spells mix, seldomly resulting in paid labor. It seems that long asylum procedures delay their integration activities such that their entropy index is low in the beginning but strongly increases towards the beginning of the second year (Figure 4). I therefore label them the 'delayed activation' group. Biographies with a high proportion of gaps (including biographies that cannot be observed until the end of the threeyear window) also ended up in this group. Given the overall low importance of gaps (making up two percent of all person-month observations, see 4.2), I do not expect their presence in the 'delayed activation' group to bias the results. Syrians are underrepresented in this group. Men in this trajectory furthermore have a socioeconomic profile slightly below the male average.

A final group of male biographies is clearly marked by the dominance of employment (with an average length of 12 months, see Figure 4 and Table A1 in the appendix). Right after the end of  the  asylum  procedure,  marked  by  their  entry  into  job  search,  these  individuals  typically quickly proceed with courses or training and ultimately enter the labor market. I thus refer to this group of male biographies as the 'straight-line integration' trajectory. The average length

of educational spells remains below the male average of 10 months. This group also stays below the male sample's average length of the job search period of 11 months. Men in this group are on average younger and more educated than the male sample but show similar work experience patterns,  thus  representing  a  group  with  considerable  pre-migration  resources.  They  are furthermore less likely to have arrived with family members.

Finally, for women, the analysis revealed a type of biographies that shows more job activity than  the  other  trajectories,  labeled  as  'cautious  integration'  group.  Employment  spells  are, however, much less frequent than for the male 'straight-line' trajectory. The female 'cautious integration' trajectories are furthermore marked by above-average lengths of asylum procedure waiting periods. Also, once the asylum procedure is finalized, spells of education, job search, and paid work occur in mixed sequencing rather than composing an orchestrated biography with course participation succeeded by successful job search. The female 'cautious integration' biographies thus do not compare to the male 'straight-line integration' trajectory associated with  labor  market  integration.  Women  in  this  group  are  slightly  younger  than  the  female average and with a higher likelihood have pre-migration job experience (see Tables A2 and A3 in the appendix). They are furthermore less likely to have arrived with family and to indicate support networks at arrival. Syrians are underrepresented in this group.

Overall,  the  sequence  analysis  and  clustering  of  refugee  women  and  men  biographies  in Germany reveals quite distinct patterns over groups, suggesting a strong heterogeneity among them both in terms of pre-migration backgrounds and integration trajectories. Some trajectories are comparable across gender: both among women and men, there is each a group characterized by long and unsuccessful job search ('lost in transition'). While women in this group show disproportionally low socioeconomic profiles, men do not. Another type of male and female biographies is marked by extensive waiting periods in the asylum procedure without any other recorded activity and thus 'deferred in transition'. These patterns may to some extent be related to  their  legal  prospects  to  stay  and  to  participate  in  education  and  the  labor  market.  These individuals furthermore show significantly lower socioeconomic profiles than others and differ in terms of their travel characteristics. A third trajectory type is characterized by long education spells ('long activation' trajectory), but men and women differ in the timing of educational participation. Those who already show above-average educational attainment and qualifications are overrepresented in this group. Among women, an additional trajectory type shows short asylum waiting periods and very early education spells followed by unsuccessful job search ('early  activation'  trajectory).  Syrian  women  are  overrepresented  in  this  group,  and  their preferential treatment in asylum procedures as well as in the assignment to integration courses

could drive these patterns. For men, a fourth group evolved from the cluster analysis that shows long  waiting  phases  during  the  asylum  procedure,  delaying  their  participation  ('delayed activation' trajectory). Non-Syrians and individuals with a lower socioeconomic profile are particularly affected by this delay. Finally, for both men and women, one set of biographies is disproportionally dominated  by  labor market participation ('cautious integration' and 'straight-line  integration',  respectively).  This  trajectory  seems  more  promising  for  men, however, as job search is typically followed by course or training participation and subsequent employment. The female counterparts do not follow this straight-line path and furthermore still show much shorter periods of paid work.


## 1.4 Multivariate results


To test the statistical significance of the described correlations between refugees' individual determinants  and  their  integration  trajectories,  I  introduce  the  identified  gender-specific trajectories  as  outcome  variable  in  multinomial  logistic  regressions.  The  analyses  are  run separately by gender. Figures 5, 6, and 7 display the average marginal effects of individual determinants. Note that while the regression results are split into three figures, all determinants are tested simultaneously in one model. For the full models, refer to appendix Tables A4 and A5.

Firstly, the travel processes of refugees differ largely across groups. The multivariate analyses imply  that  the  integration  trajectories  after  arrival  to  some  extent  vary  significantly  with different  aspects  of  the  individual  migration  experiences.  Bear  in  mind,  however,  that  the underlying data is limited in capturing the manifold aspects of refuge migration processes, such as unpredicted events on the route, traumatic and existential experiences such as the loss of family  members  or  travel  partners,  financial  hardship,  physical  and  mental  challenges associated  with  irregular  migration  routes,  developments  in  the  home  country,  or  the uncertainty of the individual migration outcome and the mental stress associated with that.

The data nevertheless shows that for women and men, a longer travel duration increases the likelihood of a 'deferred transition' after arrival, i.e., a trajectory marked by lengthy states of waiting with little further activity (Figure 5). Lengthy journeys may thus strain an individual's resources to become active after arrival. The effect is rather small in size (with the likelihood of 'deferred transition' increasing by 1.2 percentage points (p.p.) per standard deviation for both  genders)  and  statistically  significant.  Those  who  stayed  in  a  transit  country  for  three months  or  more  are  in  contrast  less  likely  in  'deferred  transition'.  This  relationship  is statistically significant at the 95 percent level for women. Men who stayed in a transit country are furthermore 4.3 p.p. less likely to be in 'delayed activation'  (that is, experiencing long phases of inactivity and delayed integration activities). They are instead 3.7 p.p. more likely to follow a 'straight-line integration' trajectory after arrival which is marked by a quick transition from  course  participation  and  job  search  into  paid  labor.  I  cannot  determine  whether  this advantage is a matter of the stay itself (e.g., by accumulating work experience in the transit country, by advancing the planning of the onward travel or by generating social networks) or if this  simply  marks  a  selective  group:  women  and  men  who  temporarily  resided  in  another country may represent first movers or pioneer migrants, i.e. individuals who are among the first to  use  a  certain  route  to  reach  a  safe  destination  country,  followed  by  others  (e.g.  family members or friends) whose travel is marked by much less complications and a shorter duration. Such  'trail  blazers'  might  have  stayed  in  transit  countries  to  scout  the  route,  to  make  out smugglers and to gather financial resources and social networks (Lindstrom and Ramírez, 2010; Singer and Massey, 1998, Jokisch and Pribilisky, 2002). This group is presumably selective in terms  of  (unobserved)  characteristics  that  are  also  relevant  for  their  subsequent  integration trajectories (e.g. physical fitness, psychological strength, motivation, or skills such as the ability to form networks). Also, the stay in a third country can affect the asylum procedures of refugees because of the Dublin regulations (e.g. regarding the duration), which affects their activities and thus their integration trajectories in Germany. Finally, long journeys may cause financial hardship, resulting in stronger economic pressures upon arrival.

If men reported traumatic experiences, they are furthermore less likely to enter 'straight-line integration' or 'long activation' (i.e., a trajectory characterized by long educational spells), but these effects are not statistically different from zero. They are instead statistically more likely to  experience  a  'deferred  transition'.  For  women,  no  clear  picture  emerges:  integration outcomes for women do not seem to vary significantly by traumatic experiences on route. This finding is striking at first. However, the measurement of traumatic experiences in quantitative terms is limited, not only due to the associated stigma but also due to the inability to assess

extent and impact of these experiences. Also, recall that 34 percent of the men and 45 percent of the women denied answering to the respective item batteries (Table 2) 11 , and it is likely that this group substantially differs from the rest of the group in terms of journey experiences and intangible resource endowment. Given the high prevalence of violence and abuse women face on their routes towards safer destinations (IOM, 2017; Hourani et al., 2021), it may also be useless to make out differences between women who report traumatic experiences and those who do not, because few women will have made it through the journey without being affected. Also, women might after all possess effective coping strategies that they have developed over their life course in a world that is a dangerous place for a woman, even before embarking on risky journeys.

Finally, some individuals arrived with family members, while others did not. More than 90 percent of the women arrived with family, compared to 58 percent of the men. Interestingly, the family context particularly plays a role for the integration biographies of refugee men. For those men who arrived with family the likelihood to be 'lost in transition' (i.e., to experience long and unsuccessful job search periods after the asylum procedure is completed) increases by 5.5 p.p., while the probability to take the 'straight-line integration' trajectory drops by 7.2 p.p. They are at the same time less likely to be in 'delayed activation' and instead more likely to be in 'long activation' (Figure 5). This may reflect that having arrived with family members (and possibly sharing a life with them after arrival)  impedes or delays integration activities, e.g. because of care obligations or scarce financial and material resources. Another explanation is that the group of men who arrived with family members significantly differ from men who arrived  by  themselves  on  some  unobserved  characteristics,  relating  back  to  the  concept  of pioneer migrants. For women, no such significant differences between groups can be made out.

The analyses also unanimously show that integration trajectories vary by pre-migration capital. Individual resources, however, in parts play out differently for men and women. Before delving into human capital matters it is noteworthy that women tend to participate more actively at a higher age. The opposite is the case for men (Figure 6). A one-standard-deviation increase in men's age (equaling to ten years) decreases their likelihood for the 'straight-line trajectory' by 8.7 p.p. To be 'lost in transition' is 3.1 p.p. more likely. For women, the likelihood of being 'lost in transition' decreases by 2.7 p.p. with a one-standard-deviation increase (also ten years), while the likelihood of  'long activation'  increases  by  2.5  p.p.  This  may  reflect  the  true  or

associated disadvantages of young women who are either mothers for real or who are perceived as soon-to-be mothers (e.g. by potential employers or case workers), impeding or delaying their participation. 12 In contrast, older men are statistically more likely 'lost in transition' and less likely in the 'straight-line integration' trajectory. An age penalty is thus recorded for men, and an age premium for women.

Educational attainments matter in different ways for men and women. Women with longer educational experience are significantly less likely to end up 'lost in transition', a trend which cannot be confirmed for men. More educated women are furthermore significantly less likely in 'deferred transition' and are instead significantly more likely to be in 'early activation' (i.e., early educational participation typically followed by unsuccessful job search). A one-standard deviation increase in educational years (equaling to 5) is associated with a decreased likelihood of 5.6 p.p. to be 'lost in transition', of 3.1 p.p. to be in 'deferred transition' and an increased likelihood  of  6.7  p.p.  to  be  in  'early  activation'  (Figure  6).  The  likelihood  of  'cautious participation'  (i.e.,  a  mix  of  courses  or  training,  job  search,  and  paid  labor)  does  not significantly  vary  with  educational  attainment.  For  men,  years  of  education  are  a  strong predictor  for  the  likelihood  to  be  in  the  'straight-line  integration'  trajectory.  A  better educational attainment of men is furthermore associated with lower chances to be in 'delayed activation' or 'deferred transition'. A stronger educational background thus seems to translate more  directly  into  higher  labor  market  participation  chances  for  men,  while  for  educated women, chances increase to enter education quickly. The results furthermore align with the finding  by  Kosyakova  and  Brücker  (2020)  that  asylum-seekers  with  a  higher  educational background maneuver more quickly and more effectively through the bureaucracy at arrival, and the asylum procedure in particular.

Another human-capital related aspect determining integration trajectories is pre-migration work experience. For men, there is a straight-forward premium for those with work experience. The probability  of  men  to  take  the  'straight-line  integration'  trajectory  increases  with  work experience,  while  the  probability  of  a  'deferred  transition'  decreases  (Figure  7).  These relationships  are  statistically  different  from  zero  for  men  with  skilled  and  high-skilled  premigration  work  experience,  but  not  for  unskilled  workers.  Compared  to  men  without  job experience, the chances to enter the straight-line trajectory is 8.8 p.p. and 9.5 p.p. higher for

individuals with skilled and high-skilled job experience, respectively. Chances to be in 'long activation' increase with the skill level of previous work experience, but these estimates are not statistically different from zero.

For women, work experience also matters, but given the large share of women who has never worked (64 percent) and the overall smaller female sample estimators are more imprecise. The results  nevertheless suggest that women with pre-migration work experience are less likely 'lost in transition'. This relationship is statistically different from zero for skilled workers who are 9.0 p.p. less likely than women without job experience to be 'lost in transition (Figure 7). Also, the likelihood to be in 'early activation' or 'long activation' increases with skill level, albeit  not  being  statistically  significant.  Interestingly,  the  likelihood  to  take  the  'cautious integration' trajectory significantly decreases with skill level. Compared to women who never worked, those with high-skilled job experience have their chance decreased by 5.6 p.p. to be in the labor-market related trajectory and are instead more likely to be in the education-related trajectories. This goes in line with the results for educational attainment which suggested that a stronger  pre-migration  human  capital  endowment  of  women  directs  them  into  educational tracks rather than onto the labor market. A reason for this can be the type of pre-migration human capital they carry. Skilled refugee women in Germany tend to have knowledge-intensive job experience, often requiring good language skills and institutional knowledge or requiring country-specific qualifications  (such  as  in  the  education  sector).  To  capitalize  on  such  premigration capital, these skilled and high-skilled refugee women thus have to heavily invest in their host-country specific human capital (Kosyakova et al., 2023), explaining their low labor market attachment and their comparably high educational attachment.

Pre-migration German skills show a negative relationship with the likelihood to be 'lost in transition' for men but do not significantly alter integration trajectories of all others. Given the small share of men and women indicating German skills, the low variance of German skills between groups (Table 2) and a lack of information on the quality of these skills I deem the role of pre-migration German skills negligible.

The  self-assessed economic  status before migration represents the final indicator of socioeconomic background and only loosely relates to integration trajectory types. Likely, this indicator correlates with both educational attainment and pre-migration work experience and has  little  explanatory  power  to  add.  Note  that  analyses  without  pre-migration  status  as  a predictor do not alter the results for the other socioeconomic indicators (results available on request). Ultimately, I also included an indicator of existing social networks at arrival. Women

who indicate that family or friends were available for support at arrival are more likely in 'early activation', but also less likely in 'cautious integration', possibly because of lower economic pressure  (Figure  6).  For  men,  integration  trajectories  do  not  systematically  differ  by  social networks. The social network literature suggests that the underlying mechanisms can be genderspecific and highly complex (see Kim and Fernandez, 2023, for an overview). For example, the nature and quality of the networks could differ by gender, such that an assessment of the social capital  endowment  at  arrival  for  integration  trajectories  would  require  further  fine-grained investigation. Also, recall that newly acquired networks cannot be included in the analysis due to endogeneity issues (see 4.2).


## Discussion


In this article, I have firstly developed a typology of integration trajectories of refugee men and women in Germany. This departs from the main body of the empirical integration literature which usually studies the different life domain outcomes separately or in unidirectional relation to each other (e.g., the effect of language acquisition on job market outcomes), thereby forced to study outcomes in their chronological order. I argued that a biographical approach offers a more holistic perspective as it has space for several tantamount activities and states in whatever order. Applying sequence analysis (combined with cluster analysis) I grouped post-migration biographies into integration trajectory types. Subsequently, in multinomial regressions, I tested whether the individual resource endowment erodes with refugee migration or whether it has the power  to  determine  integration  trajectories  after  refugees'  arrival.  Importantly,  as  refugee journeys are typically risky and dangerous, I included journey characteristics as a potential set of factors in the analysis. I furthermore distinguished between male and female biographies such that gender-specific mechanisms can be identified. This is important not only because of general gender differences that may apply but also because refugee women and men who made it to Germany are both highly selected groups (Gundacker et al., 2024).

The identified clusters reveal that individual trajectories of refugee women and men after arrival can take very different shapes, confirming a strong heterogeneity among the refugee population both  in  terms  of  their  individual  backgrounds  and  their  integration  biographies.  Three integration  types  are  largely  comparable  across  gender.  For  both  women  and  men,  one trajectory is dominated by early and largely unsuccessful job search, such that these individuals seem 'lost in transition'. Women in this group have a particularly low socioeconomic profile. A second group of refugees is marked by disproportionally long waiting periods during the asylum procedure without any other activity,  hence  being  'deferred  in  transition'.  For  this

trajectory type, we see that men are more likely to take up activities towards the second half of the  3-year  period,  while  female  biographies  remain  'deferred'.  A  third  type  of  integration biographies is characterized by long educational spells, and individuals with an above-average socioeconomic background are overrepresented in this group.  Interestingly,  the  educational activity  of  women  in  this  trajectory  type  tends  to  occur  later  compared  to  their  male counterparts. For women, I additionally identify a fourth trajectory type characterized by very early education spells, typically succeeded by unsuccessful job search. For men, a fourth group shows comparatively long phases of inactivity during the asylum procedure and a rather hesitant subsequent activity mix of job search and education spells, seldomly resulting in paid labor. Non-Syrians and individuals with a lower socioeconomic profile are particularly affected by this  delay.  Finally,  one  set  of  biographies  is  disproportionally  dominated  by  labor  market participation  for  both  men  and  women.  Men  in  this  'straight-line  integration'  trajectory typically search for a job, take part in a course or training and subsequently enter employment. The corresponding female biographies are much less streamlined. They  show rather mixed patterns of education and job search and have much shorter periods of paid work.

In a second step, this study has assessed the role of pre-migration capital of refugee migrants for their integration patterns after arrival. The study unanimously showed that pre-migration capital does not (completely) erode with refugee migration. Rather, the individual integration trajectories  systematically  vary  with  socioeconomic  background.  Importantly,  the  way  a refugee journey unfolded also affects integration outcomes. Lengthy journeys seem to strain individual  resources  to  become  active  after  arrival.  Also,  traumatic  experiences  hamper integration  outcomes.  This  result  is  only  confirmed  for  men,  however.  I  relate  this  to  the methodological  difficulties  to  record  and  quantify  traumatizing  events  and  their  impacts. Furthermore, it can be argued that most women in one way or the other experienced violence and abuse on their way to Europe, such that it is somewhat pointless to distinguish between those who have and those who have not reported such incidents in the underlying survey.

Also, male but not female integration trajectories vary with the family context at arrival. Men who arrived without family members show a higher activity and quicker integration patterns compared to  their  male  counterparts  who  arrived  with  family.  This  could  indicate  that  the journey is more straining and riskier once family members (such as children, elderly or wives) come along, with negative consequences for the subsequent integration process. This finding could,  however,  also  reflect  the  selective  patterns  of  refugees  arriving  in  Germany.  Men arriving without family may represent a group of pioneer migrants who are better equipped regarding  some  unobservable  characteristics.  Upon  arrival,  they  may  furthermore  be  more

mobile and more flexible than family-bound individuals, facilitating their participation. Women also  represent  a  selected  group:  the  majority  of  women  arrives  with  family  members  in Germany,  and  care  obligations  mostly  lie  with  female  family  members,  such  that  female integration trajectories rather differ by other factors than the family context at arrival.  Overall, the  results  support  the  assumption  that  lengthy  and  risky  journeys  can  affect  the  available resources to an individual, at least for men. Given the particular selectivity of refugee women into Europe it requires additional research efforts to disentangle the effects of selection and resource depletion for refugee women in their integration trajectories after arrival, including the effects of the risky journey.

Once in Germany, can refugees still count on their resources or do qualifications and skills erode  with  refugee  migration?  The  multinomial  regression  models  strongly  suggest  an unbroken  importance  of  pre-migration  socioeconomic  capital  in  the  integration  patterns  of refugees after arrival. Refugees with a stronger socioeconomic background overall go through shorter  sequences  of  inactivity  and  maneuver  more  quickly  through  the  asylum  procedure, confirming  earlier  findings  (Kosyakova  and  Brücker,  2020).  A  stronger  educational  or employment background translates into more active trajectories for men, particularly in terms of labor market participation. Particularly skilled and high-skilled refugee men have a higher chance to enter the 'straight-line integration' trajectory into paid labor. More educated women or women with skilled or high-skilled work experience do not show an increased labor market attachment;  a  stronger  human  capital  background  rather  directs  them  into  education.  This finding supports the notion that the job experience of refugee women in Germany requires particular investments in their country-specific human capital for them to be able to capitalize on their pre-migration human capital (Kosyakova et al., 2023). Fueled by care obligations, this human capital devaluation delays or even prohibits their labor market entry. The discounting of foreign credentials and job experience thus particularly applies to women.

Delaying or never following up on women's skills and knowledge can erode these resources in the long run, increasing women's risks of precarious livelihoods and economic dependency. To facilitate women's participation in the country of refuge and to enhance their socioeconomic autonomy,  job  agents  should  assess  their  existing  skills  in  less  formalized  procedures  and identify suitable areas of study or training. Also, in light of the fact that most women live with a family to take care of, these human capital investments require a systematic support of the household to cover their financial and care needs in the meantime. Longer waiting periods can thereby have negative consequences. Also, the negative effects of straining refugee journeys require a sensitive approach, particularly given the effects post-migration stressors like material

and social conditions can have on refugees' wellbeing and participation (see Hynie, 2017, for an overview).

This article adds to the literature on the existence or erosion of human capital over the life course in the sociology of migration, with refugee migration representing a particular set of human  biographies.  The  analyses  imply  that  the  individual  resource  endowment  does  not completely  erode  with  refugee  migration.  The  study,  however,  also  revealed  the  continued research  gap  regarding  the  effects  of  the  journeys  that  refugees  take  to  seek  humanitarian protection (possibly deteriorating or adding to their individual resources) on their subsequent integration patterns upon arrival. The results in this article suggested that long and dangerous journeys  can  negatively  affect  the  participation  of  refugees,  but  these  effects  only  proved significant for men. Those women who managed to seek humanitarian protection in Europe already present a very selected  group of women, both in terms of individual resources and family composition at arrival. Studies on the integration of refugees which neglect migration contexts and selection outcomes may miss important aspects and draw invalid conclusions. The heterogeneous effects of refugee migration processes on post-migration biographies intersecting with the particular selection effects remain a research area with many unknowns that deserve further attention.

One important limitation to the analytical framework is that due to endogeneity issues, events or individual changes occurring during the analyzed biography period cannot be considered (e.g. a changed family composition, a legal status change or the acquisition of language skills). Furthermore, individual resources might have indeed been partially devalued by the refugee move but still to some extent affect integration trajectories after arrival. This partial erosion cannot be assessed in the chosen analytical framework. In sum, however, sequence analysis techniques offer an innovative way of describing and analyzing the heterogeneous biographies of refugee migrants, providing fine-grained insights into the various mechanisms that shape the integration trajectories of refugee women and men after their arrival.

## 1. Introduction


Climate change presents an existential threat to the world, and counteracting it necessitates political commitment from all states to promote high-level climate initiatives. The European Commission (EC) has adopted the Green Deal, a new growth strategy aiming to transform the European Union (EU) into a prosperous society with a competitive, resource-efficient economy that is decarbonized by 2050. This strategy ultimately seeks to uncouple economic growth from resource use [1]. The EU Green Deal incorporates a series of proposals to reduce emissions by 55% by 2030 compared to 1990 levels, in addition to binding the goal of climate neutrality to 2050.

The Fit for 55 package is designed to prepare the way for EU climate neutrality in 2050 [2] and has important  implications  for  EU  environmental  and  climate  policies. The  most  important  proposals include updating and expanding the emission trading system, increasing targets on energy efficiency and renewable energy use, increasing penetration of low-impact transport vehicles, taking measures

to prevent carbon leakage, making changes in taxation and fiscal policies, and taking actions to preserve and increase natural carbon stores such as forests and other ecosystems. It comes with potentially significant investment requirements and costs that urge pursuing the most cost-effective policies. A recent study found that several aspects could further improve the cost-effectiveness of current  EU  climate  policies  [3].  Among  the  changes  proposed  through  Fit  for  55,  it  is  worth highlighting the following.

First, the Energy Efficiency Directive has been recast, from which national energy efficiency targets have been established [4,5]. The Directives of the European Parliament and the Council 2018/2002 and COM/2021/558 require Member States to almost double their annual energy savings [6].

Second,  Directive  2018/2001  on  promoting  energy  use  from  renewable  sources  was  revised according to the EC proposal COM/2021/557. The revision sets a new target of 40% renewable energy  sources  (RES)  in  final  energy  consumption  by  2030.  This  target  requires  doubling  the penetration of RES in the European energy mix by 2030 [7].

Third, provided that the Effort Sharing Regulation 2018/842 consists of individual binding emission reduction  targets  for  EU  countries,  which  are  given  various  options  to  achieve  compliance  in  a supposedly flexible and cost-effective way [8], the Fit for 55 calls for increased emission reduction targets from -30% to -40% compared to 2005 by 2030.

Provided that climate policy instruments can be divided into command and control and policies based on market mechanisms [9], a policy impact analysis topic gaining momentum among scholars and policymakers is the coexistence of different policy tools heading toward similar goals. Within climate change policy options, policymakers increasingly combine multiple tools to achieve decarbonization targets [10]. Previous literature has noted that the combination of policy instruments that are part of EU climate policy can have significantly different effects in different European countries [11,12].

Despite  convergence  in  goals,  this  may  result  in  overlapping,  complementary,  or  eventually counterproductive outcomes [13]. In contrast, a recent study demonstrated that policies could diffuse as  a  result  of  an  interdependent  process  of  states  learning  from  and  emulating  each  other, coordinated  by  international  organizations  [14].  For  example,  another  study  suggested  that  the consequences of climate policy interactions can be costly in particular market conditions, making the interaction  of  carbon  pricing  policies  and  renewable  targets  hazardous  [15].  Because  global convergence on climate policy goals has become urgent, overlaps in climate policies characterized by institutional diversity may threaten the decarbonization path [16]. It is no wonder that there is a need  for  specific  analyses  to  support  the  scientific  community,  regulators,  and  policymakers  in understanding the implications of climate policies.

Starting  from  the  reference  scenario  (RSNECP),  which  is  the  scenario  foreseen  in  the  Italian Integrated Energy and Climate Plan 2030, updated according to the latest available statistical data and events affecting the energy system, we assessed the economic impact of the Fit for 55 package through a policy scenario (PSFF55). The PSFF55 includes recent economic updates, the pandemic effect on energy consumption, the hydrogen consumption predicted in the preliminary guidelines of the  Italian  hydrogen  strategy,  and  the  energy  measures  of  the  2021  National  Recovery  and Resilience Plan.

The research questions (RQs) were straightforward. RQ1 aims to understand in what sectors and the amount of investments required to comply with the Green Deal decarbonization targets boosted by the Fit for 55, RQ2 focuses on the socioeconomic consequences of meeting such targets, and RQ3  is  about  environmental  issues  in  terms  of  avoided  emissions  due  to  investments  in decarbonization.

To answer these questions, the research strategy was based on mixed methods research following the triangulation principle to enhance the validity of the findings and mitigate the presence of any research biases that typically emerge in scenario analyses.

Reliable information specific to investment strategies and prominent technologies was sourced from a  focus  group  of  experts  from  the  national  business  association.  This  source  enabled  the quantification of investment gaps. Meanwhile, to estimate the socioeconomic implications, we relied on the well-known economic analysis tool known as input-output analysis (IOA). This is a viable approach for analyzing the sectoral interdependencies that characterize the system, represented by the flows of goods and services within a general economic equilibrium context. The analyses were conducted using the Italian national symmetric input-output tables for 63 economic sectors.

The  remainder  of  the  document  is  organized  as  follows:  Section  Two  provides  the  background information,  outlines  the  analytical  approach  used  for  the  analyses,  and  defines  the  scenarios. Section Three presents the results, highlighting the effects on the economic system, the implications for  public  finance,  and  the  positive  externalities  resulting  from  reduced  emissions  and  energy savings. These results are then discussed in Section Four, which is followed by the conclusion.


## 2. Background


The decarbonization of economic systems is one of the most debated topics in the literature today, particularly after the global commitment to limit the global temperature rise to 1.5 °C [17].

With the aim of contextualizing the expected investments in technologies for the green transition, this section reviews the main drivers of decarbonization in light of recent European climate policies established  in  the  Green  Deal,  including  the  fit  for  55  package  that  aims  to  reduce  net  GHG

emissions by at least 55% by 2030 and set ambitious decarbonization targets to be achieved by 2050 [1]. Existing policies and legislation are being updated to accommodate this transition [18], along  with  the  design  of  efficient  carbon  markets  that  concurred  in  gradually  reducing  carbon emissions while preserving fair competition [19]. Indeed, finding an equilibrium between environmental and economic sustainability is challenging.

Based on data provided by the Italian business association in the scenarios and economic impact assessments  of  the  fit  for  55  objectives  2022  report  [20],  the  economic  analysis  in  this  paper presumes  that  overall  investments  will  heavily  occur  in  five  areas  that  represent  the  drivers  of decarbonization: energy efficiency, electrification of end-use consumption, green fuels, renewable energy, and carbon capture and storage.

Energy efficiency is key to mitigating climate change and achieving sustainable development [21]. It is not surprising that it is one of the pillars of energy policy [7], helping to ensure greater energy security  by  reducing  energy  demand and reducing external dependence [22] and promoting the transition  to  a  sustainable  energy  system  through  the  more  rational  use  of  energy.  The  civil, residential, and tertiary sectors are the main sectors for implementing energy efficiency measures. Similarly, the transportation sector is also expected to achieve significant results [23] as the industrial sector  [24,25].  Increased  electrification  is  also  expected,  for  example,  in  the  residential  [26,27], industrial [28], construction [29], and transportation [30] sectors.

Nevertheless, the increase in demand for electrical services is offset by improvements in average energy  efficiency  performance  and  stimulated  by  minimum  energy  performance  standards  [31], provided such products are designed for efficiency as well as by the development of markets for energy efficiency products [32]. The most obvious development is in the transportation sector, which is also given new business models. In the industrial sector, electrification will also increase due to technologies [33] supporting the new electricity market characterized by increasingly differentiated energy production.

Additionally, green fuels are likely to play a key role in decarbonization despite recent advancements in electrification [34,35].

Another important decarbonization lever is deploying renewable energy sources in the electricity system. There are well-known relationships between economic development and greenhouse gas emissions where renewable energies concur to smooth such a relation [36]. As is well known, the growth of renewables helps boost the transition to a low-emission economy [37]. That said, the process  of  phasing  out  from  fossil  fuels  in  a  cost-effective  manner  is  not  linear  and  involves considerably different efforts by European countries [38]. Industrial sectors are predicted to adopt carbon capture and storage technologies, with a substantial usage of these technologies in power

generation expected to significantly aid in decarbonizing the industry [39]. The EU views renewable hydrogen  as  a  crucial  element  for  attaining  carbon  neutrality  and  plans  to  foster  growth  in  the hydrogen sector [40]. In this regard, a recent study analyzed the challenges and opportunities of green and blue hydrogen production, which are crucial for a potential hydrogen society [41]. Given the diversity of these domains, decarbonizing the economy  requires synergies between technological development, political commitment, societal attitudes, and investment strategies [42].

Similarly,  given  that  multiple  factors  and  uncertainties  characterize  the  decarbonization  process, scenario  analyses  are  useful  for  asking  questions  characterized  by  medium-  and  long-term uncertainty [43].

In climate policy, scenarios are often used to support policymakers in designing effective policies [44] and to estimate whether planned technological developments are suitable for reducing CO2 emissions by a level consistent with the goals set [45].

Previous literature evaluated the economic implications of alternative energy policies for Europe's power sector [46], and forecasts show that ambitious emission reduction targets can be obtained cost-effectively if transmission and storage capacities are expanded adequately [47], considering that emission reductions in the energy supply sector are dominant up to 2030 [48]. While previous studies have delved into alternative scenarios regarding decarbonization, this paper contributes to the existing body of knowledge in more dimensions. First, we provide information on anticipated investments in key technologies for decarbonization. Such insights are instrumental in examining the potential evolution of strategic industries. Second, we investigate the possible effects of recent climate policies and crises, as mentioned in the  methodological section, on the Italian economy, which offers a template for potential replication in other nations. Third, helping in understanding how costs and goals outlined in the NECP might shift to align with supplementary requirements. This serves as a valuable resource for recalibrating current policies.

In this regard, the approach used in this paper allows for a detailed analysis of the potential impact of climate policies on the economy by focusing on the decarbonization drivers identified in this article. In particular, the paper provides concrete figures such as estimated investment needs, potential returns  and  avoided  costs,  making  the  results  more  actionable  for  stakeholders.  Finally,  by highlighting areas that require further investigation, such as the impact of the REPowerEU plan and potential  setbacks  resulting  from  the  implementation  of  high-level  policies,  the  paper  lays  the groundwork for future research.

Nevertheless,  it  is  worth  noting  that  this  paper  has  limitations;  for  example,  the  choice  of decarbonization  drivers could  vary based  on  different  perspectives,  countries  or  methodologies. Additionally, the expected investments are heavily predicated upon local legislation and incentives,

which might not be universally applicable. In addition, the significance of individual sectors to the economy could undergo shifts, altering the impact of these findings. Despite these challenges, the research method aligns with the primary aims of this paper.


## 3. Research method


Given the ambitious nature of the Fit for 55 targets, which will necessitate extraordinary investments, we can reasonably expect the impact of such investments to be felt across a wide range of sectors. To model the extent and manner in which these investments may affect the economy, we have chosen the input-output analysis (IOA) approach, which provides a valuable framework for analyzing policy  impacts  [49]  and  assessing  the  impacts  of  exogenous  demand  variations  on  prominent economic  variables  such  as  output,  value  added  (VA),  intermediate  inputs,  primary  inputs,  and employment.  Once  the  demand  variation  is  distributed  among  the  sectors,  IOA  facilitates  the calculation of the production required to meet the demand in each sector [50]. The demand was estimated based on data provided by documents and experts from the Italian business association; this estimated amount was then used as input for the IOA. The parameters for sectoral interdependence refer to data from 2019, the latest available from the national accounting system. These assumptions may limit the external validity of this study. Although IOA has been widely used for accounting studies, its application in evaluating the social, economic, and environmental impacts of future scenarios has increased, yielding significant policy implications [45,54].

That being said, RQ1, which focuses on the technologies and the investments required to comply with  the  Green  Deal  decarbonization  targets  as  reinforced  by  the  Fit  for  55,  was  addressed  by reviewing documents and interviewing experts from the national business association. RQ2, which explores the socioeconomic consequences of the investments identified in RQ1, was addressed using the IOA. RQ3, concerning the emissions avoided due to investments in decarbonization, was answered by simulating emissions based on our results.

Consequently, the scenario was set. Scenarios are frequently employed, given that they can aid in exploring  potential  future  alternative  pathways  to  handle  long-term  concerns  characterized  by unpredictability and complexity [43]. Scenario analysis is useful for projecting a wide range of topics, such as production, consumption, trade, prices, investments, and technology mixes [55].
