## 4. Discussions and Conclusions


Our research findings indicate that perceptions of a massive and socially biased prison population do not produce a significant weakening of trust in the CJS. However, these effects become salient and causally heterogeneous when taking into account the indigenous identity, migrant status, and political orientation of the respondents. Furthermore, our analysis of the causal heterogeneity by political orientation, demonstrated that the effects of the perception of mass incarceration vary significantly according to this variable, supporting our fourth hypothesis.

Regarding the heterogeneity by racial/ethnic categories, we observed that when migrants perceive a massive or a socially biased prison population, their trust in the CJS is strengthened, in comparison with non-migrants. Nonetheless, when these two dimensions of mass incarceration are perceived simultaneously, they have a detrimental effect, which contrasted with what we observed for non-migrants.

Moreover, when indigenous perceive a massive or a socially biased prison population, their trust in the CJS is slightly weakened, in comparison with non-indigenous. Nevertheless, when

they perceived both together, they showed a greater and positive effect than non-indigenous did, strengthened their trust.

To summarize, we observed important heterogeneity on the effects of the perceptions of mass incarceration on the trust in the CJS, by racial/ethnic variables. However, due to a severe lack of statistical power, our estimations in this regard, do not provide conclusive evidence.

These results converge with the literature reviewed. In the U.S., racial disparities on criminal justice contacts affect the perceptions of the justice system (Buckler et al., 2011; Muller & Schrage, 2014; Pettit & Gutierrez, 2018; Saperstein et al., 2014). In the same way that, as a consequence of mass incarceration Afro-Americans and Latinos, in the U.S., have an everincreasing distrust of the justice system, in Chile the migrant population, as a racialized and criminalized groups, showed similar patterns (Grau & Vergara, 2021; Dom´ ınguez, Grau, & Vergara, 2022).

Worthy of note that, apart from research carried out in Nigeria by Archibong and Obikili (2021), no other studies on this topic have been conducted outside the U.S.. It is also salient that Chilean society has historically been influenced by a 'race-blind' ideology, related to the notion of a homogeneous Mestizo population, even though, in practice, phenotype characteristics play a fundamental role in the dynamics of the social stratification (Torres, Salgado, Mackenna, & N´˜ nez, 2019). While the Chilean and Latin-American elites are predominantly u white, 'the colour of the prisons is that of the indigenous people (. . . ), as a sign of the history of colonial domination, which still continues until today' (Segato, 2007, p. 42). Therefore, our results contribute to the understanding of how justice systems interact with racial inequalities, producing heterogeneous effects, in a post-colonial context.

In this vein, evidence related to the discriminatory nature of the Chilean justice system has been recently published. These findings highlighted bias against poor (Grau & Vergara, 2021), migrants (Dom´ ınguez et al., 2022) and the Mapuche people (Grau & Vergara, 2021). Besides, the majority of the prison population is made up of socially marginalised individuals (Larroulet, 2016). Characteristics shared throughout the Latin-American region (M¨ uller, 2012).

Additionally, the effects of mass incarceration's perceptions are remarkably heterogeneous by political orientation. Whereas the massiveness of the prison population weakens the trust in the CJS among left-wingers, that is not the case among right-wing individuals. Along with it, in contrast of right-wingers, the leftist individuals experienced an increase in their CJS trust when perceived a massive but not socially biased prison population (Group C).

Besides, the effects of perceiving high social bias in the prison population are mostly homogeneous by political orientation, and nearly zero. Nonetheless, when the prison population is massive and socially biased, left-wingers seem to experience a diminution of their trust, contrasting with right-wing individuals.

As far as we can tell, our study is the first worldwide to address how the interaction between political orientation and mass incarceration affects perceptions of the legal system. Besides, this finding confirms that citizens' trust in justice institutions is based on their assessment of institutional performance, and on individual characteristics, such as political orientation (Bradford, Jackson, & Hough, 2017).

Likewise, studies on punitivism have observed that conservative and/or right-wing individuals tend to be more punitive than liberal and/or left-wing individuals (Kleck & Jackson, 2017; Manzano et al., 2022). Therefore, it is expected that individuals with different preferences

about punishment according to their political orientation would respond differently to mass incarceration.

To conclude, although our research has some methodological limitations, which inhibit the generalization of the results, it still contributes to the understanding of the macrosocial effects of punishment beyond the prison population. Specifically, our findings narrow the gap regarding the impacts on citizens' trust in the CJS.

## 1. Background


Degrowth speaks to the contradictions arising from the pursuit of capital accumulation, namely ecological overshoot and social shortfall. Despite mounting evidence that an absolute, global, and permanent decoupling of economic growth from all environmental pressures that is fast enough to avoid ecological collapse is highly unlikely (Vogel & Hickel, 2023), business practices and policy processes continue tinkering with market mechanisms rather than challenging systemic failures (Spash, 2024). But such approaches assume that the harms of capitalism are merely accidental and fixable rather than systemic and fundamental to the functioning of capitalism (Oksala, 2023). This is why a host of social movements continue challenging these historically specific social relations (Kothari et al., 2019). One recent perspective that challenges this orthodox logic in an attempt to disrupt the status quo is the heterodox concept of degrowth (for a review of the literature, see Kallis et al., 2018).

The landscape of degrowth has shifted since its emergence in the early 2000s. What primarily began as an informal social movement between French-speaking activists (Liegey and Nelson 2020), evolved into a formal scientific field dominated by English-publishing academics (Fitzpatrick, 2025). This is why many consider degrowth a multi-layered concept that combines both activism and academia (D'Alisa et al., 2014). In essence, people advocating for degrowth recognise that growth is an ideological, material, and social process that needs unpacking systematically (Schmelzer et al., 2022: 1-91), before alternative visions for sustainability that take biophysical reality serious can be developed and deployed (Barlow et al., 2022).

Our research emerges from a critical observation: the degrowth literature has expanded exponentially - from 3 texts in 2008 to 1715 in 2024 - yet we lack an overview of how this scholarship synthesises and advances knowledge. While previous research has investigated degrowth in relation to ecological economics (Hana č ek et al., 2020), organisational models (Hankammer et al., 2020), transition theory (Vandeventer et al., 2020), policy proposals (Fitzpatrick et al., 2022), value creation (Froese et al., 2023), monetary markets (Engler et al., 2024), and modelling studies (Laure et al., 2025), none of them have analysed how these literature reviews are conducted. This gap represents a potential blindspot in understanding how knowledge is created and understood in the rapidly evolving field.

Recent critics like Savin and van den Bergh (2024) have argued that degrowth scholarship is predominantly opinion-based and lacks rigorous analysis. This critique, however, reveals more about orthodox economic thinking than about degrowth's intellectual credibility (Parrique, 2024). By demanding quantitative models that inherently reproduce orthodox understandings of the economy, including the growth paradigm, mainstream orthodox approaches demonstrate precisely why degrowth is necessary: existing analytical frameworks cannot comprehend the depth, scale, and type of social change necessary to achieve environmental justice. Plus, how can one empirically study what does not yet exist? Inadvertently, these critics highlight the epistemological and ontological limitations of mainstream orthodox economics to conceptualise alternatives to capital-accumulating economies.

In response, our umbrella review maps the complex terrain of literature reviews within degrowth and post-growth, guided by two fundamental research questions: (1) What is the state and quality of evidence synthesis in degrowth and post-growth research? and (2) How do existing literature reviews contribute to our understanding of social-ecological transformation? Methodologically, we employ a rigorous and systematic approach that follows best practices in evidence synthesis such as the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence (CEE 2018), ROSES (Haddaway et al., 2018), and PRISMA (Page et al., 2019) reporting standards. This allows our analysis to go beyond simply cataloging existing research to providing a meta-level understanding of the intellectual genealogy behind degrowth research and its potential for social-ecological transformation. In other words, we can systematically analyse existing degrowth and post-growth literature reviews by tracking their philosophical presuppositions, theoretical frameworks, and methodological integrity.

The proliferation of degrowth research demands careful navigation. Our umbrella review offers researchers, policymakers, and activists a comprehensive map of existing knowledge, illuminating potential and pitfalls. By synthesising existing literature reviews, we provide a holistic view of degrowth as an emerging field of critical inquiry and practical imagination. In an era of heightened social and ecological contradictions, degrowth represents more than just an academic discourse. Rather it is an invitation to analyse and actualise the potential of human beings beyond the narrow that ongoing conversation, a systematic exploration of how scholars have begun to analyse and constraints of economic orthodoxy and its associated assumptions. This review is our contribution to actualise alternatives to the current growth paradigm.

Our study makes three principal contributions: (1) mapping the intellectual landscape of degrowth research, (2) critically evaluating the methodological approaches of existing degrowth and post-growth literature reviews, and (3) assessing the philosophical, theoretical and empirical evidence supporting degrowth's transformative potential. By doing so, we aim to provide a clear, comprehensive understanding of this important and rapidly evolving field of study.

## Introduction


Workers in large, dense metropolitan areas have higher wages than in smaller cities or rural areas. On average, the largest urban and highest-income areas, often dubbed 'Superstar' city-regions, have a higher share of college-educated workers than their respective national economies [7, 15, 8, 22]. But in addition, college educated workers in particular are paid more in bigger, denser cities than they are in smaller ones, giving them a large 'urban wage premium.'

Researchers agree that such urban wage premiums exist not only because the composition of the workforce is different in big cities compared to smaller ones, but also because similarly educated workers have higher incomes when they are in big, dense cities. Thus, there is something about 'bigness' which makes workers more productive. Larger cities make workers more productive by better matching workers with specific skills and aptitudes to the right task or firm, as there is a larger and more diverse set of employers and activities in big cities [18]. Relatedly, workers in big cities acquire more valuable experience across their careers, transiting through more jobs, learning new skills as they go along, and then bringing them to successive jobs, a phenomenon known as 'experience' or 'dynamic' effects [15].

The top plot of Figure 1 highlights these wage and salary income benefits of big cities. The figure shows a strong positive relationship between the size of a labor market ('ln(Population)') and the average hourly wage and salary income for workers. Yet, these benefits appear to accrue much more strongly to White workers, than their Black and Latinx counterparts [1, 9]. 1 This is evident in the bottom panel of Figure 1. White workers have a much stronger urban wage premium than all workers on average (i.e. a steeper slope). By contrast, Black and Latinx workers' wages are not only much lower, but hardly increase at all when they locate in larger cities, unlike their White counterparts. Consequently, there is substantially more Black-White and Latinx-White wage inequality within larger cities than in smaller cities. These disparities remain after controlling for a wide range of demographic characteristics [1, 3, 9]. 2

In the next section, we show that we show that racial inequality in the benefits of working in a big city is largely driven by experience effects. For White workers, our main estimates suggest that each additional year of work experience in a 'big' city (defined as U.S. labor markets which have over 6 million people, labelled with triangles in Figure 1) increases wages by 44 cents per hour more than each additional year of experience in a non big city. By contrast, each year of big city experience elevates Black and Latinx workers' wages by only about 21 and 10 cents an hour respectively. These results highlight how big city racial inequalities accumulate over workers' lifetimes to produce increasingly unequal outcomes as they build their careers.

## Estimating Rewards to Big City Work Experience by Race


Table 1 reports our main regression estimates. To generate the results we analyze panel data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (NLSY79) cohort. This survey follows an initial sample of 12,686 individuals from 1979 until the present, of which 7,589 are represented in our final sample (2,214 Black, 1,470 Latinx, and 3,905 White),

corresponding to 59,784 person-years. Respondents were between the ages of 14 and 22 when the survey began in 1979. They were interviewed every year from 1979 to 1994, and bi-annually thereafter. We focus on the years 1994 to 2018 (with income reported from the previous calendar year, so 1993 to 2017) when respondents were in their prime working years. Using the restricted access geocode files of the survey, we were able to match workers to either one of the big labor markets from Figure 1, or a non big city in each round of the survey. This allowed us to calculate their years of overall work experience ( All Experience ), and their years of Big City Experience as of each survey round. We then regressed their hourly incomes from wages and salaries ( Hourly Income -our dependent variable) on their years of overall and big city work experience, as well as worker, year, and labor market fixed effects (see the Materials and Methods section for how we identify 275 labor markets). When using panel data, a fixed effects approach is called for in order to control for characteristics of workers that do not change over time (including unobservable characteristics such as ability or effort, as well as observable characteristics such as education or sex), thus reducing potential omitted variable bias. Our fixed effects models also control for economy-wide shocks to wages in specific years, and workers' different propensities to move into higher wage labor markets. Additionally, each model includes a coefficient for In Big City . Whereas Big City Experience identifies the dynamic benefits of spending more time working in a big city, In Big City identifies the one time benefit of moving to a big city. 3 This captures the fact that the wage benefits of being located in a big city may be experienced statically at one point in time, rather than evolving over workers' careers. Interested readers can refer to the Online Appendix for descriptive statistics, including a graph of the bivariate relationships between experience and wages that closely matches our findings in Table 1.

We attempt to disentangle some of these channels and feedbacks by testing five possibilities. These can be seen in columns 3 to 7 of Table 1.

First, we consider whether the disparities in the benefits of big city work experience disappear when we account for the propensities of workers of different racial groups to work in different occupations. The bottom plot in Figure 1 shows that the urban wage premium is largely driven by the differences in the wages of White people, while there is very little variation in Black and Latinx workers' wages between big and small cities. The same is true for occupations. Other research shows that the urban wage premium is largely driven by workers in a select set of 'high skill' occupations [2]. The stronger returns to big city work experience for White workers might thus be due to their disproportionate likelihood of working in high skill occupations, regardless of skills and qualifications [32]. We control for this, by classifying workers into high-, mid-, and lowskill occupations [2, 4]. We also interact occupations with whether workers are currently

in a big city, since there are substantial differences in occupation-specific remuneration across big and small cities (the urban wage premium again). As shown in column 3, there is no great difference from the base model in column 2.

Second, and closely related to the above, we consider whether the disparities in the returns to big city experience may not solely be driven by disparities in workers' propensities to work in certain occupations, but instead, that there may be racial disparities in remuneration once workers sort into occupations. For example, it may be the case that upon sorting into a high skill occupation in a big city, Black and Latinx workers initial wage offers are simply much lower than those of White workers. Column 4 shows this effect to not change our main results in column 2.

Third and fourth, we look at a key possible channel of acquiring experience, which is job mobility or turnover. In the standard 'matching' model of agglomeration of workers and employers, high skill urban industries generate high levels of turnover as they rapidly hire and layoff workers, while workers concentrate together to facilitate successful job search through access to many possible specialized employers [21, 18]. Workers' faster wage growth in bigger cities may thus be due to job changes, rather than within-job wage growth, as workers capitalize previous experience into higher wages in their next job [31]. Thus, we examine differences in job mobility and the returns to high mobility. In the present context, we seek to know if there are differences in job mobility by race. Black and Latinx workers may for instance either switch jobs more frequently than White workers because of discrimination, or less frequently because of anticipated discrimination.

We sum the total number of jobs each respondent has had as of each year. We call this variable New Jobs as our inclusion of worker fixed effects means we capture how many new jobs a respondent has had since their last interview. As with occupations, we interact New Jobs with In Big City as there may be big/small city differences in remuneration for job mobility, as well as test a New Jobs * In Big City * Race interaction, as there may be racial differences in remuneration for job mobility that drive disparities in the value of Big City Experience . The results are reported in columns 5 and 6 of Table 1; again they do not alter the base results significantly.

Thus far, results for disparities in the returns to Big City Experience in columns 3-6 are essentially unchanged. This suggests that accounting for differences in occupational sorting/job mobility, as well as race-specific returns to working in certain occupations and for job mobility, does not explain why Black and Latinx workers benefit less from building a career in a big city. This does not mean that there are not differences in occupational sorting/job mobility, and race-specific remuneration therein, but rather, that these differences cannot explain inequality in the value of Big City Experience .

Finally, we consider whether disparate returns to building a career in a big city may be driven by disparities in the value of accumulating experience in high skill occupations (column 7). This provides some additional insight into the conclusions that can be drawn from the base model in column 2. Before continuing, it is worth noting that, as with All Experience and Big City Experience , Black and Latinx workers receive weaker returns to High Skill Experience than White workers. This is especially true for Black workers, whose hourly wages increase by about 40 cents an hour less than White workers for each additional year of experience in a high skill occupation. As noted previously, the urban wage premium is primarily driven by the much stronger returns workers enjoy from working in high skill occupations in bigger cities. However, as with the urban wage premium overall, this could result from one-time sorting (i.e. Black and Latinx workers are underrepresented in high skill occupations), racialized remuneration (i.e. Black and Latinx

workers get a smaller wage increases by moving into a high skill occupation) or dynamic effects that build over time. The latter would suggest that racial disparities in the value of Big City Experience may be driven by disparities in value of High Skill Experience . Here, the effect is important. The inclusion of High Skill Experience substantially decreases the disparities in Big City Experience . The coefficients decrease from -0.230 and -0.339 in column 2 to -0.143 and -0.239 in column 7 for Black-White and Latinx-White inequality respectively. This suggests that about one third of the disparities in Big City Experience can be explained by disparities in High Skill Experience . 5 Yet, even after accounting for differences in the benefits of High Skill Experience , the Big City Experience * Black and Big City Experience * Latinx coefficients are still negative and significant at the 10 percent and 5 percent levels. This suggests there is something about big cities, above and beyond the ways workers of different races deferentially sort into and gain experience in certain types of occupations, that generates inequality across workers' careers.

A counterfactual scenario where there were no differences in the benefits of High Skill Experience would also substantially change the interaction between All Experience and race. For Black workers there would no longer be a statistically significant difference from White workers while for Latinx workers there would be a slightly larger return to All Experience than for White workers (i.e. the interaction coefficient is positive). In other words, if not for their much weaker returns to Big City Experience and High Skill Experience , there would not be any racial disparities in the wage and salary income benefits that increase as individuals accumulate work experience over time. 6


## The Specific Role of Urban Size


We now ask what exactly it is about big cities that causes the disparities we observe in Table 1. Many interrelated features of cities come with increasing scale, and could create channels that increase inequality in labor markets. As a simple test of this, in Table 2, we consider how experience premiums vary across race in the labor markets with the 10 next largest values of different urban characteristics that are closely related to size. More specifically, we consider segregation using Black and Latinx isolation indices, population density, average rental prices, and average commute times. We also experimented with different ways of measuring segregation, cost-of-living, and commute times, which yielded similar results.

Before doing this, we first establish a baseline in column 1 by looking at returns to experience in the 10 next largest cities. This exercise sheds light on whether any of the relationships we observe with the other urban characteristics simply reflect the size of a city rather than the dimensions of labor markets that are found in the column headers. The coefficients for experience in the 10 next largest cities are generally insignificant (with the exception of Latinx workers, who do experience somewhat weaker returns to working in the 10 next largest cities than White workers). This finding implies that any racial differences we observe in columns 2-6 likely reflect labor market disparities induced by the characteristics in the column header per se, rather than through their relationships with population.

For segregation (columns 2 and 3) the results do not yield any statistically significant racial disparities, indicating this is not a channel through which urban scale creates uneven returns to experience.

Table 2: Mechanism Exploration: Endogenous Features of Urban Scale

We do not find significant racial disparities in the value of experience in dense and high commuting time cities either (with the exception that the coefficient for Latinx workers' experience in dense cities is negative and significant at the 10 percent level). However, Table 2 does yield another interesting result for dense and high commute cities. In both cases the coefficient for whether a White worker is currently in a dense or high commute labor market is relatively large, positive, and statistically significant. The same is true for expensive cities, and in all three cases there are no statistically significant differences for non-White workers. This is very different from what we observe in big cities, where the wage benefits are largely dynamic.

Our main finding in Table 2 is that there are also significant racial disparities in the benefits of working in expensive cities, larger in fact than the disparities for big cities.

Once again, these disparities increase over workers' careers. White workers are paid about 35 cents an hour more for each year they spend in an expensive city, relative to a city that is not big or expensive. By contrast, the coefficients for Black and Latinx workers imply that each year of experience in an expensive city is worth 16 and 30 cents less than experience in cities that are not big or expensive. This vast disparity is remarkable, and suggests that the size and cost-of-living of cities interact to favor White workers in leveraging skills and experience.


## Discussion: Deepening our Understanding of Racial Differences in the Economic Benefits of Urbanization


In this paper, we have documented that there are substantial racial disparities in the rewards that workers reap from career experience in big cities. But why would this be the case? One possibility is that the observed disparities are attributable to selection on characteristics of workers that we cannot observe here. Economists are often concerned with whether workers of different 'ability' levels sort into cities of different sizes [7, 14]. Imagine, for example, that low ability Black and Latinx and high ability White workers move to big cities, while high ability Black and Latinx and low ability White workers move to small cities. As noted, and in concert with the literature [13, 15], we included worker fixed effects to address selection on unobservable characteristics. It is conceivable that such worker fixed effects may not entirely capture this unobserved heterogeneity however if there is a great deal of mobility between cities combined with unobservable differences between the White and non-White populations who move to big versus small cities. In our view, there are several reasons to be reserved about this interpretation. First, 'ability' is neither a static nor innate feature of individuals; individual attributes that we commonly label as 'skill', 'effort' or 'motivation' can change over time and may be responses by an individual to their social and spatial contexts. As an example of this, consider that workers from marginalized groups may reduce their effort, or their investment in acquiring skills, if they believe they will face discrimination, reducing or negating the return to such efforts [20]. Along these lines, big cities in the U.S. typically have large inter-neighborhood disparities in exposure to environments that influence individuals' skills, effort, access to social networks and information, and hence motivation [12, 27]. Second, even if part of what we observe is due to racialized patterns of sorting according to unobservable individual characteristics across big and small cities, such spatial sorting would still be an integral dimension of the processes through which big cities end up fostering inequality [27]. Finally, mobility and migration are hardly the norm. Over the life span, most people live in the same cities in childhood and adulthood. Indeed, of the respondents in our sample, about two-thirds live in the same labor market at age 14 as at the start of our study in 1993, 7 and only about 10% ever move from a big to a small city or vice versa. We are thus observing processes that, in the vast majority of cases, occur over workers' lives differently in big versus small cities.

Another possibility is that there such finely grained differences in skills and experience that it is impractical to observe them, and that they are endogenous to race. These very subtle differences could, for example, be due to discrimination once in an occupation, or in moving from one job to another, within or across occupations. In this case, workers'

skills and experience somehow become qualitatively different across race, reflected in disparities in the accumulation of or fine-tuning of skills and experience. Alternatively, it could be that workers are remunerated differently for the skills and experience they possess and deploy, within or across jobs, but in ways that we are unable to observe from outside the immediate work context (disparities in valuation ). In this paper we have considered these possibilities to the extent that is possible with observational data, but it may be that through promotions, job mobility, network effects, or some other channel, Black and Latinx workers are not given the same opportunities to acquire and/or utilize skills and experience as White workers.

What might cause these disparities in the accumulation of skills and experience? Beyond the occupational structure of cities that we explored in this paper, it may be that the spatial structure of cities comes in to play here. A growing body of evidence suggests that there are ways in which the spatial structure of large, dense cities shapes patterns of residence, work and commuting in ways that establish barriers to non-White workers in accessing employment and other economic opportunities, as compared to White workers with the same observable skills and in the same occupations [19, 28, 9, 10]. Similar to other research [10] suggesting that Black-White commuting inequality is exacerbated by cities' overall population and high cost-of-living, we find that high cost-of-living appears to be a channel through which larger urban populations may contribute to experience inequalities in the labor market. The combination of a large population and high cost-ofliving may be particularly potent if it allocates workers within a city in ways that provide racially uneven access to labor market opportunities. Further research should follow up on this potential causal channel.

To conclude, race and the economy are intertwined in ways that are often subtle and difficult to detect. Yet, subtle initial differences can multiply up to impactful inequalities. Social scientists are increasingly unpacking these subtle forces, ranging from work on racial disparities in 'exposure' to different kinds of environments [27, 11, 16], to racial differences in the composition and mobilization of job referral networks [30, 29] to how social networks, lived experiences and the media shape the places where we choose to live [23], to name a few. Considerable recent research on work and wages has demonstrated that cities, and especially big cities, concentrate the relatively privileged population that works in high skill occupations. Research has also shown that there is a powerful urban opportunity machine through experience, and some important intergenerational advantages 'in the air' of some city-regions today [12, 15, 6, 2]. This picture is nuanced by the fact that these highly-skilled occupations are held by a minority of the population and that urban wage premiums and urban concentration of college-educated workers contribute to interpersonal and geographical income disparities that characterize the current age. In this paper, we have demonstrated that for many Black and Latinx workers, even locating in these big prosperous cities and working in high-skill occupations may simply not be enough to assure them equitable rewards.

## 1 Introduction


This is the sixth article in a series of papers analyzing urban travel trends and their variations among a range of socioeconomic groups for the U.S., using nationwide travel survey data since 1977 (Pucher, Henderickson, McNeil, 1981; Pucher & Williams, 1992; Pucher, Evans and Wenger, 1998; Pucher & Renne, 2003; Renne and Bennett, 2014). In this article, we examine the 2017 National Household Travel Survey (NHTS), which was first released in 2018 and then updated in 2019 and 2020 (Federal Highway Administration, 2020; WeStat, 2019). We focus on the interrelated variations in travel modes, trip frequency, trip distance, and vehicle ownership, and their differences across different income levels as well as home ownership, ethnicity, gender, age, and life-cycle classifications. We also compare these variations in the 2017 NHTS with its predecessors, the Nationwide Personal Transportation Surveys (NPTS) in 1969, 1977, 1983, 1990, and 1995; and the National Household Travel Surveys (NHTS) in 2001 and 2009 based on earlier studies in this series (Pucher, Henderickson, McNeil, 1981; Pucher and Williams, 1992; Pucher, Evans and Wenger, 1998; Pucher and Renne, 2003; Renne and Bennett, 2014).

The most noticeable trend in Americans' travel behavior over the past decade is the peak and decline in the popularity of private automobile travel (Tables 1-2). According to journey-towork data from the recent decennial census and the American Community Survey, the share of Americans taking private automobiles to work peaked in 2000 at 87.9%, then declined to 86.1% in 2009 and 85.3% in 2017 (see Table 1). The transit commuting share increased from 4.7% in 2000 to 5.1% in 2009 and remained at 5.0% in 2017.  Additionally, the share of Americans working from home has also increased, before the COVID-19 pandemic, from 3.3% in 2000 to 4.3% in 2009 and 5.2% in 2017 (see Table 1). The trends in all-purpose travel (i.e., both work-

and non-work-related) based on NPTS and NHTS data is similar (Table 2): the share of private automobile trips decreased from 86.4% in 2001 to 83.6% in 2009 and 82.6% in 2017. The share of transit trips increased from 1.6% to 2001 to 2.3% in 2009 and 2.9% in 2017.

Such trends in private automobile travel are reflected by changes in automobile ownership. The number of vehicles per licensed driver peaked in 2001 at 1.06, then dropped to 0.99 in 2009 and remained at 1.00 in 2017.  Similarly, vehicles per household peaked in 2001 at 1.89 and then dropped to 1.86 in 2009, although bounced back to 1.88 in 2017. Notably, the average household size also increased from 2.50 in 2009 to 2.55 in 2017 (McGuckin and Fucci, 2018; Pucher and Renne, 2003; Renne and Bennett, 2014). In other words, although the American economy has been emerging from the 2008 recession, private automobile ownership in 2017 did not bounce back to pre-recession levels. This trend is even more apparent among urban dwellers, who constitute an increasing share of the nation's total population during the first two decades of the 21 st century (United Nations, 2018). The percentage of urban households owning at least one automobile in 2017 was 91.3%, lower than the peak value in 2001 (91.7%); the rate

of urban households owning more than one automobile in 2017 wass 56.0%, which was 2.5 percentage points lower than the historical peak value in 2001 (58.5%).

Such trends can be attributed to many factors, including the expansion of transit-oriented developments (TOD) in urban America (Renne and Appleyard, 2019; Boarnet, Wang and Houston, 2017; Ewing and Cervero, 2010), intergenerational lifestyle changes (Garikapati et al., 2016; McDonald, 2015; Blumenberg et al, 2019), the increase of fuel price (Bastian, Borjesson and Eliasson, 2016; Stapleton, Sorrell and Schwanen, 2017), the rise of e-commerce and shared mobility (Brown, 2019; Cao, 2012; Dong, 2020; Le, Carrel and Shah, 2022), and increasing technologies that have enabled remote working (Aksoy et al., 2022; Su, McBride and Goulias, 2021). With the continuation of many of these factors, and recent changes due to the pandemic and the 'Great Resignation,' such as flexible work arrangements, it is an open and interesting question whether this trend in American urban travel will continue.

Nevertheless, such an aggregate trend may mask complex variations in travel patterns among different social and demographic sub-groups. Theoretical reasoning and empirical evidence support the fact that travel behavior differs by social and demographic profiles such as income, age, gender and ethnicity (Ben-Akiva and Lerman, 1985; de Dios Ortúzar and Willumsen, 2011; Pucher and Renne; 2003; Renne and Bennett, 2014). Vehicle ownership levels, trip frequencies, miles traveled and means of transport vary from one group to another, which is increasingly becoming a vital data issue for examining equity in travel. Examining such differences can help policy makers to better evaluate the effects of existing transportation infrastructure developments, to identify the sub-groups that deserves special attention for future transport plans, and to design more sustainable and equitable transport policies at local, state and federal levels. The following sections of this article introduces the 2017 NHTS, examines

variations in urban travel with respect to various socioeconomic factors, compares with earlier surveys and discusses the policy implications.


## 2 Data and methods


The 2017 NHTS is the most recent nationally representative travel survey in the United States. The data collection for this survey started in April 2016 and ended in April 2017 (Westat, 2019). The survey used an address-based sample and collected data from approximately 130,000 households and 275,000 persons; the study sample is nationally representative, although a few states and metropolitan areas were oversampled since the respective transportation planning agencies had purchased 'add-on' samples (McGuckin and Fucci, 2018; Westat, 2019). However, the NHTS provides weights for each household and each person in the study sample to adjust for such oversampling (Westat, 2019), and this article uses the respective weights to make the study sample nationally representative. Each participating household reported all trips by household members on a randomly assigned 24-hour 'travel day,' which could be either a weekday or a weekend day. The respondents then used a web-based survey interface to report their travel history on that 'travel day,' as well as other information, such as socio-demographic details, economic conditions, place of residence, and more (Westat, 2018). The full list of variables in the 2017 NHTS public sample is available at the NHTS website developed by the Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL, 2022).

The analyses in this article are based on the travel behavior data reported in the 'travel day' and adjusted for household-, personal- and trip-level weights provided by the 2017 NHTS. Since this study focuses on urban travel, the study sample is limited to residents in urban areas. Trips longer than 75 miles were excluded, which is consistent with the previous studies in this

series. The resulting sample includes 100,465 households and 202,907 individuals living in the urban area, as well as 712,198 urban trips. We start our analysis with examining the differences of urban travel with respect to trip purpose (e.g., work- and non-work-related) and geographical regions (e.g., New England, Pacific, and others); then we study the effect of economic factors (income, vehicle ownership, housing) on urban behaviors in the cities; finally, we examine the variations in urban travel by demographic factors (gender, ethnicity, age and life-cycle stage).

There are a few differences in the 2017 NHTS compared with earlier surveys (Westat, 2019). First, the 2017 NHTS differentiates 'round trips' from 'one-way' trips, while earlier surveys only recognized one-way trips. Thus, we split each round trips into two trips (and halved the distance) to make it comparable with earlier surveys. Second, the 2017 NHTS used an online mapping tool to estimate trip distances, which was different from the previous NHTS. To make the trip distance variables comparable with earlier surveys, the 2017 NHTS reports both the unadjusted (online mapping-tool derived) and adjusted (inflated by roughly 10% to be comparable with earlier NHTS) trip distances. In this article, we report both distances but mainly discuss the unadjusted ones. Additionally, a few categorical variables in the 2017 NHTS are defined differently from in earlier surveys, such as household income, trip purpose, and travel modes; we try our best to combine different categories in our analyses to make this study comparable with those based on earlier surveys, although a few variables still are not comparable across the different surveys. For detailed discussions on comparing the categorical variables of the 2017 NHTS with earlier NHTS/NPTS, see Westat (2019).


## 3 Results



## 3.1 Trip purpose and modal choice


As previously mentioned, the share of work- and non-work-related transit trips in the United States has steadily increased over the first 17 years of the 21 st century. In 2017, transit trips comprise 5% of the total commute trips (see Table 1), it is larger than the share of transit trips of total trips (2.9%, Table 2). Similarly, the share of transit trips for work-related travel is the highest, at 5.9%; specifically, the shares of bus trips and non-commuter-rail transit trips (i.e., subway, light rail, and streetcar) are 2.7% and 2.5%, respectively (Table 3). In other words, the shares of bus trips and subway/light rail/streetcar trips for work-related purposes are comparable. In contrast, most of the transit trips for shopping and services, social and recreational activities, and school and church purposes were made by bus. Additionally, 0.7% of total work-related trips were made by commuter rail, and the share of commuter rail trips for other purposes were much lower (0.1-0.2%, Table 3). Thus, the percentage of rail transit, including commuter rail, is highest for work-related trips.

Having that said, 82.6% of work-related trips were still made in private automobiles; solo drivers making up 66.3% of these and only 16.3% by carpools (see Table 3). In contrast, carpooling was the predominant mode for trips for the other three purposes (i.e. shopping and services, social and recreation, and school and church), which made up almost half of all trips. These carpooling trips for shopping and services, social and recreational activities, and school and church were typically made by family. In contrast, the low share of carpooling trips for work-related purposes implies that most family members could not carpool or chose not to carpool in their journeys to work. The percentage of non-motorized trips was the highest for social and recreational trips; almost one in every four of such trips (23.4%) was made by walking

or cycling. This is followed by school and church trips, 12.4% of which were non-motorized. The share of walking and cycling trips was lower for work- and shopping-related trips, at around 10%.

This subsection explores the impact of income on travel mode choice, as well as the variations of transit mode share across different city sizes. ## 3.3.4 Housing tenure and travel modes


The final economic factor that we examined is housing tenure, as shown in Table 13. Compared with the 2009 NHTS (Renne and Bennett, 2014), the shares of automobile trips for both owners and renters decreased in the 2017 NHTS. Specifically, the shares of automobile trips for owners and renters in 2009 were 86.1% and 72.2%, respectively, dropping to 84.7% and 71.0%, respectively, in 2017. These facts indicate that transportation network companies, such as Uber and Lyft have become particularly popular among urban residents, especially for renters.

## 3.4 Demographic factors and urban travel


Besides varying by economic conditions, urban travel patterns also vary by demographic factors, such as ethnicity, gender, age, and lifecycle factors. This section discusses the relationships between these demographic factors and various travel patterns.

As indicated in Table 14, non-Hispanic whites are the most auto-oriented ethnicity group, with 81.5% of their trips by automobile, followed by Hispanics with 80.2% of their trips by automobile. Within automobile trips, Hispanics are higher in carpooling, as 48.0% of their total trips were carpooling trips, while the number for non-Hispanic whites is only 41.3%. As the 'less auto-oriented groups,' including blacks and Asians also had the highest share of transit trips. Taking a closer look reveals that blacks were the highest in bus transit trips (5.8%), and Asians were the highest in rail transit trips (2.2%). Asians also had the highest share of non-motorized trips (17.7%), and Hispanics had the lowest share of non-motorized trips (13.1%). Although the share of non-motorized trips for the whites and blacks is comparable (around 14%), whites had a much higher share of cycling trips than blacks (1.3% vs. 0.5%, respectively). Finally, although the share of taxicab trips was comparable across different racial profiles, we do see that the share of taxicab trips was lowest among whites, at 0.5%, while other racial groups are all 0.7-0.8%.
