## 4 Conclusions and policy implications


The most noticeable takeaway of the 2017 NHTS is that although private automobiles continue to be the dominant travel mode for Americans, we saw a slight decline in the share of car trips after its peak in 2001, especially in urban areas. For the whole U.S., the share of automobile travel dropped from 86.4% in 2001 to 83.6% in 2009 and further to 82.6% in 2017 (Table 2). We saw a similar trend in automobile share in commute trips: which was 87.9% in the 2000 census, 86.1% in the 2009 ACS one-year estimate, and 85.3% in the 2017 ACS one-year estimate (Table 1). For urban America, the share of auto travel peaked at 85.9% in 2001, dropped to 81.9% in 2009, and further dropped to 79.7% in 2017 (Pucher and Renne, 2003; Renne and Bennett, 2014). A detailed look shows that the share of solo driving trips increased from 2001 to

2009 (37.3% to 38.6%) but decreased from 2009 to 2017 (38.6% to 37.1%), while the share of carpooling has consistently decreased from 48.6% in 2001 to 43.3% in 2009 and 42.6% in 2017. Although we can attribute the decrease from 2001 to 2009 to the economic recession, the continuation of this trend, based on 2017 data, may give us some cautious optimism that America's urban travel may experience a similar 'peak and drop' trend in automobile travel as other advanced economies ( Millard-Ball and Schipper, 2011; Wang and Akar, 2020). However, the dawn of ride-hailing between 2009 and 2017 could have had an impact on carpooling, in favor of trips using services like Uber and Lyft (Brown, 2019; Dong, 2020).

In addition, we see steady increases in the share of transit trips for urban travel. The share of total transit trips was 1.7% in 2001, increased to 2.8% in 2009, and further increased to 3.3% in 2017. Specifically, since the share of commuter rail trips remained relatively stable over time (0.1% in 2001, 0.2% in both 2009 and 2017), most of the increases come from the increasing share of bus transit trips as well as light rail/subway/streetcar trips (1.6% in 2001, 2.6% in 2009, and 3.1% in 2017). Perhaps the dawn of micromobility services between 2009 and 2017 made transit more appealing since last-mile connections became easier (Beak et al., 2021; Hong, Jiang and Lee, 2023). Although we are unable to further explore the temporal changes in specific shares (e.g., bus vs. rail) due to differences in the mode and income classifications between the 2017 NHTS and its predecessors, we see the increases in transit trip shares are consistent across housing ownership, ethnicity, and gender. Similarly, the share of non-motorized trips increased from 10.4% in 2001 to 12.9% in 2009 and 14.2% in 2017, with most of this increase coming from walking trips (9.2% in 2001, 11.8% in 2009, and 13.1% in 2017). In addition, we also see an increase in the share of taxicabs, which rose from 0.1% in 2001 to 0.2% in 2009 and 0.6% in 2017. Since the 2017 survey included ride-hailing trips (e.g., Uber/Lyft) as a part of 'taxi,' we

cannot precisely determine how much of the increase can be attributed to the rise of the ridehailing industry. Nonetheless, ride-hailing services provide a relatively affordable and flexible way to get around without taking private automobiles - especially for carless households in low-income neighborhoods (Brown, 2019; Dong, 2020).

Many different factors may be contributing to this general trend of 'peak and decline' for the share of automobile trips and the steady increases in transit, non-motorized, and taxicab trips in urban America. First, the continuous support from federal, state, and local sources to build transit infrastructure and encourage transit-oriented development has enabled urban residents to reduce car use and increase transit use (Spears, Boarnet and Houston, 2017; Lowe, 2013; Renne and Appleyard, 2019). Second, the past two decades have seen the rise and growth of the IT industry as well as other creative industries in urban neighborhoods and college towns with robust transit and non-motorized infrastructures; such 'urban clustering' of industrial growth not only causes growth in the populations of transit- and non-motorized-friendly communities but also brings about lifestyle changes in terms of living, traveling, and shopping (Alder and Florida, 2021; Blumenberg et al., 2019; Lee, 2020; Wang, 2019). Third, higher gasoline price reduces the frequency and distance of driving (Bastian, Borjesson and Eliasson, 2016; Stapleton, Sorrell and Schwanen, 2017); and the fuel price is likely to remain high in the near future due to political and policy reasons. Fourth, the rise of online retailers such as Amazon and Uber Eats has reduced the demand for shopping trips and evening dining trips due to convenience and often lower prices (Cao, 2012; Le, Carrel and Shah, 2022). Although we observe a decline in passenger travel by automobiles, we do see a steady increase in freight truck ton-miles over the last decade (Bureau of Transportation Statistics, 2020). Fifth, the rise of shared mobility - both ride-hailing, bike and scooter sharing - might also have helped attract urban residents to non-

automobile modes, since last-mile accessibility is easier. As discussed in the previous paragraph, we have seen the increase in taxicab trips for owners and renters, males and females, and across different ethnicities. It is very likely that ride-hailing services are the main mechanism of this universal rise, as they provide a more convenient and reasonably affordable way to travel (Brown, 2019; Dong, 2020). On the other hand, the prosperity of bike- and scooter-share programs across U.S. cities can help solve the first-mile/last-mile problem for potential transit takers, making transit more attractive than driving (Fukushige, Fitch and Handy, 2021; Martin and Xu, 2022). Sixth, working from home and flexible working schedules have been gaining popularity in American cities. As shown in Table 1, the share of Americans working from home increased from 3.3% in 2000 to 4.3% in 2009, and 5.2% in 2017, and post-covid American cities will see a further increases in the share of working-from-home arrangements (Li and Wang, 2022). Although it is still unclear whether people will make more trips to compensate for their reduced commute trips, it is worth noting that commute trips are more likely to be solo driving and long-distance trips, while non-commute trips are more likely to be transit and non-motorized trips of shorter distances (Boarnet, 2011; McDonald, 2015).

Most, if not all, of the six above-mentioned factors should continue into the near future: the transit system continues to expand, central city areas will still be IT-incubators with residents leading urban-oriented lifestyles, the fuel price may remain high, the online retail industry will keep prospering, shared mobility services will continue to be popular, and a few working-fromhome days per week very likely will become the new normal in a post-pandemic world. Thus, although it is still too early to tell whether such a 'peak-and-decline' trend in automobile travel will continue in urban America, the current trend provides an opportunity to encourage multimodalism in American cities. Further development of transit networks, more support of

transit-oriented development (from both public and private sectors), and ongoing expansion of non-motorized transport infrastructure could help American cities increase growth in becoming 'multimodal' in the future rather than reverting to a 'car-dominant' past. Such a 'multimodal' future will not only increase the environmental sustainability of American cities but also boost the economic and social sustainability of providing low-income urban residents with more convenient, flexible, and affordable ways to reach educational and economic opportunities (Chetty et al., 2022; Fan, Guthrie and Levinson, 2012).

Indeed, there are still many challenges for American cities to move toward multimodality and more equity in mobility. As this paper suggests, a general trend may mask the complex relationships between socioeconomic factors and travel pattens, and certain economic and demographic sub-groups face higher challengers than others. For instance, similar to earlier studies in this series using earlier NPTS/NHTS data, we see the lowest income group (household income less than $25,000), who were also more likely to be minorities and carless, were heavily reliant on transit - especially buses - to fulfill their mobility needs. Their daily trip frequencies and daily miles traveled were considerably lower than those of higher income groups, implying that their social activities and economic opportunities were also likely to be limited (Gobillon, Selod & Zenou, 2007; Klein, 2020). Such mobility challenges for the lowest income group were more severe in small- and mid-size cities, where the supply of transit is more limited than large cities. Moreover, the American population is rapidly aging, and more than 20% of the total population will be 65 and older by 2030. As previously discussed, most older adults heavily relied on driving and are not regular transit patrons, ride-hailing users, or cyclists. As they gradually reduce and even cease driving, providing senior-friendly, safe, and convenient alternative mobility options will be essential for maintaining their health and well-being

(Schouten et al., 2022; Loukaitou-Sideris, Wachs and Pinski, 2019). Also, the taxicab trips in the 2017 NHTS were more evenly distributed across socioeconomic groups compared with earlier surveys. Although such trends show the potential for ride-hailing to provide mobility options for those cannot afford cars or cannot drive cars, affordability issues for lower income people and acceptability issues for older adults may become barriers for equal access to TNCs (Brown et al., 2022; Leistner & Steiner, 2017). In sum, policymakers should consider the differences in travel patterns between higher-income vs. lower-income households, whites vs. non-whites, males vs. females, and young vs. old to ensure safe and convenient mobility options are provided equitably rather than catering to certain groups at the cost of others.

## Introduction


Modern  nation  states  have  long  sought  to  reduce  social  inequalities,  often  focusing  on expanding access to education as a key mechanism for fostering greater equality (Blanden & MacMillan 2016; Buchholz et al. 2016). Early in the 20th century, access to education and career  opportunities  were  largely  shaped by traditional  norms  and  structural barriers  (van Oertzen & Rietzschel 1997; Leopold, Skopek & Schulz 2018). The expansion of educational opportunities in the 1960s and 1970s marked a significant shift, as policies promoting greater access  began  to  challenge  entrenched  inequalities  in  education  (Schofer  &  Mayer  2005; Fernández  2013).  Gender-based  disparities  in  particular  came  under  increasing  scrutiny, leading to efforts aimed at reducing the barriers that had long limited women's educational and professional opportunities (Ronsijn 2014; Bailey & Graves 2016; Jackson & Holzman 2020). By the 1980s, these policies contributed to a reversal in educational gender inequality in many Western societies, with women increasingly surpassing men in higher upper secondary school and university graduation rates (DiPrete & Buchmann 2013; Becker 2014; Hadjar & Buchmann 2016).

Recent genetically sensitive studies have added new insights into how institutional and other forms of social change shape inequalities, highlighting that genetic effects become more pronounced as institutional and normative constraints on individual choices diminish (Herd et al.  2018,  Rimfeld  et  al.  2018;  Engzell  &  Tropf  2019;  Lahtinen  et  al.  2023).  Genetic  effects capture  the  association  between  specific  genetic  variants  and  an  outcome,  as  identified through large genome-wide association studies. In this literature, genetic effects serve as proxy indicators of equality of opportunity, reflecting the extent to which differences in individuals' ability to attain social positions like educational attainment are shaped by genetic variation rather than family background or ascribed characteristics such as gender or race (Branigan, McCallum & Freese 2013; Engzell & Tropf 2019, Baier et al. 2022).

A few studies have examined the effects of rapid social transformations following the collapse of the Soviet Union on equality of opportunity. Studies for Estonia (Rimfeld et al. 2018), Hungary (Ujma et al. 2022) and notably the former GDR (Fraemke et al. 2024) report increased  genetic  effects  on  individual's  educational  attainment  after  regime  change.  The authors argue that after the fall of the Soviet Union, political privilege-previously a key driver of  social  mobility  in  socialist  systems-was  replaced  by  more  meritocratic  structures.  As  a

result, genetic influences on educational attainment became more pronounced, suggesting a shift toward greater equality of opportunity. Herd et al. (2019) were the first to examine how the relationship between genetic influences and educational attainment changed in the United States over the second half of the 20th century, with a specific focus on gender inequalities. Historically, institutional barriers and gender norms restricted female labor force participation, reducing  incentives  for  women  to  pursue  higher  education.  As  a  result,  earlier  cohorts  of women showed a weaker association between genetic measures and educational attainment compared to men. Over time, social and normative changes gradually reduced these gender disparities. In the youngest cohorts, genetic effects on educational success now favor women, reflecting  broader  trends  of  higher  educational  attainment  among  females  (Buchmann, DiPrete  &  McDaniel  2008).  However,  there  is  still  little  evidence  on  how  the  interaction between genetic influences and educational attainment varies by gender outside the United States.

In this article, we adopt a genetically informed research strategy to examine how social transformations have affected gender inequality in educational attainment since the mid-20 th century. By examining the case of Germany, we contribute to research on social change and educational gender inequality in two key ways. First, we seek to replicate Herd et al.'s (2019) findings  for  the  United  States  within  the  German  context.  This  comparison  is  particularly relevant, as institutional differences between the two countries likely influenced the pace at which the gender gap in genetic influences on educational attainment eroded. Second, we extend  previous  research  by  analyzing  gender  differences  in  genetic  effects  on  education within  Germany,  both  during  and  after  its  division  into  the  socialist  German  Democratic Republic  (GDR)  in  the  East  and  the  liberal,  democratically  oriented  Federal  Republic  of Germany  (FRG)  in  the  West.  Historically,  (West)  Germany's  institutional  arrangements supporting traditional family structures, reduced incentives for female labor force participation, potentially limiting the perceived returns on prior educational investments for women (Orloff  1996;  Rosenfeld  et  al.  2004;  Mandel  &  Semnyonov  2006).  In  contrast,  the United States experienced earlier shifts toward female labor market participation and higher educational  attainment.  This  development  was  driven  by  a  weaker  welfare  system,  which provided fewer incentives for traditional family structures to persist (Esping-Andersen 1990; Hook & Paek 2020). Based on these institutional differences, we expect that gender disparities

in genetic effects on educational attainment may have eroded more slowly in Germany than in the United States.

Beyond  this  international  comparison,  the  division  of  Germany  presents  a  unique opportunity  to  examine  how  social  transformations  have  shaped  gender  inequality  in educational attainment over time, utilizing an institutional setting often described as a 'natural experiment'. We extend the evidence beyond the U.S. by comparing gender gaps in genetic effects on education within two distinct political systems. Each system followed its own path in shaping  post-war  educational  policies, social policy goals, and  normative  changes throughout the second half of the 20th century. Specifically, the GDR provides a unique case where  institutional  structures  actively  sought  to  reduce  class  and  gender  inequalities  in education and labor markets, contrasting sharply with the FRG. While social stratification and gender  parity  policies  in  the  GDR  aimed  to  reduce  educational  inequalities,  the  overall influence of genetic effects on educational attainment remained constrained by the regime's emphasis on political loyalty and prioritizing individuals from working-class background over individual merit (Bukodi & Goldthorpe 2010; Fraemke et al. 2024). Moreover, the GDR's focus on fostering educational participation primarily for economic development in industry and production, coupled with persistent gender inequalities in pedagogical concepts as well as paid and  unpaid  work,  suggest  that  gender  disparities  in  the  link  between  genetic  effects  and educational attainment likely persisted. This unique combination of progressive and restrictive policies makes the East-West comparison particularly valuable for understanding how different institutional contexts have shaped the relationship between genetic effects and educational attainment across genders.

Building on these contributions, we address the following research questions: (I) How have gender differences  in  genetic  effects  on  educational  attainment  evolved over  time  in Germany, and how do these trends compare to those in the United States? (II) How have institutional  differences  and  policy  changes  in  East  and  West  Germany  influenced  the gendered  associations  between  genetic  effects  and  educational  attainment  over  time?  To answer these questions, we rely on data from the Gene-SOEP which provides polygenic risk scores based on genetic data within the context of the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) study (Koellinger et al. 2023). The SOEP is Germanys largest and longest running panel study, started in 1984, covering around 20.000 household and surveys detailed educational and labor

market histories of participants. The Gene-SOEP provides the first genotyped sample that is representative  of  the  entire  German  population,  including  2,600  participants.  Crucially,  it covers the latest polygenic risk score for educational attainment (Okbay et al. 2022) which provides  the  basis  for  cohort  analyses  investigating  changes  in  the  gender  gap  of  genetic effects on educational attainment in East and West Germany. Specifically, it enables us to study birth cohorts from 1943 to 1992 thus covering the earliest cohorts attending school in newly divided Germany to cohorts ending their educational careers in a reunified Germany.


## Studying equality of opportunity: sociological and behavior genetics approaches


Assessing a society's equality of opportunity has a long sociological tradition, for instance by studying  intergenerational  social  mobility  (Ganzeboom,  Treiman  &  Ultee  1991;  van  de Werfhorst  &  Mijs  2010;  Blanden,  Doepke  &  Stuhler  2022).  Accordingly,  a  weaker  `social gradient` suggests that family background plays a smaller role, leaving less room for ascribed characteristics  based  on  inherited  social  positions  to  influence  attainment.  However,  this approach has come under scrutiny as the catch-all family measure of 'social background/origin'  is  a  broad  measure  that  may  be  genetically  confounded:  parental education is, at least partly, influenced by genetic effects, which are, at least partly, inherited by their children and contribute to their educational success (Freese 2008; Marks & 0'Connell 2023).  Hence,  this  broad  measure  of  'social  background/origin'  may  obscure  the  relative contribution  of  genetic  and  environmental  factors  to  status  attainment.  The  possibility  of genetic confounding seriously hampers an interpretation of these correlations as purely social pathways to inheriting privilege,  making  it  difficult  to  disentangle  the  influence  of  genetic inheritance from other factors. At the very least, they represent a combination of genetic and environmental effects. Hence, many genetically sensitive studies do suggest that intergenerational  correlations  in  educational  attainment  (e.g.,  Baier  et  al.  2022;  Eifler  & Riemann  2022;  Marks  &  O'Connell  2023),  as  well  as  attitudes  and  personality  traits  (e.g., Hatemi et al. 2010; Spörlein, Kristen & Schmidt 2024), are largely driven by genetic factors.

Genetically sensitive studies approach the question of equality of opportunity from a related  but  distinct  perspective:  first,  twin  studies  decompose  individual  differences  into genetic (i.e., heritability of an outcome) and environmental components (i.e., the shared and non-shared environment; Harden 2021a). In this framework, the extent to which educational

attainment is heritable (i.e., due to genetic differences) serves as an indicator of equality of opportunity. If the proportion of difference in a characteristic explained by genes increases, the proportion attributable to environmental factors - including shared family environment in which social background effects are subsumed -necessarily decreases. Engzell & Tropf (2019) demonstrate  that  genetic  endowment  mattered  more  in  societies  with  higher  equality  of opportunity (i.e., characterized by lower intergenerational correlation), while shared family environmental differences were less consequential. Moreover, these general patterns are also evident over time: as equality of opportunity increases, heritability estimates rise. In Norway for  example,  the  heritability  of  lifetime  income  doubled  over  the  20 th century,  while  the influence  of  shared  environmental  factors  vanished  (Isungset,  Baier  &  Lyngstad  2025). However, the same study also highlights persistent gender disparities: although heritability increased for both men and women across cohorts, women's genetic influence on lifetime income  still  lags  men's,  suggesting  persistent  environmental  barriers  to  full  equality  of opportunity.

The  second  approach  in  genetically  sensitive  studies  on  social  inequalities  directly genotypes  individuals  rather  than  trying  to  infer  genetic  contributions  through  family relationships.  These  genotyped  data  are  combined  with  results  from  large  genome-wide association  studies  (GWAS)  to  generate  polygenic  risk  scores  (Mills  &  Tropf  2020).  GWAS analyze genetic data from thousands to millions of individuals to estimate the correlations between genetic variants and various outcomes. For educational attainment, the latest GWAS identified around 4,000 genetic variants, each contributing a small influence on the likelihood of attaining higher education (Okbay et al. 2022). These identified genetic variants and their estimated correlations are used to construct polygenic risk scores (PRS), which serve as outof-sample predictors of genetic predisposition for educational attainment.

Research using PRS from genotyping individuals examines equality of opportunity by analyzing  how  the  association  between  genetic  predisposition  and  realized  educational attainment varies across social groups and contexts. Differences in this statistical relationship suggest that some groups face greater obstacles in realizing their genetic potential, following a similar logic to twin studies: the stronger the genetic influence on an outcome, the greater the equality of opportunity in its attainment. However, the term 'risk' is crucial, as PRS provide

a  probabilistic  estimate.  While  a  high  genetic  predisposition  for  education  increases  the likelihood of higher attainment, it does not determine the outcome.

The PRS-paradigm has been used to study changes in equality of opportunity following major societal transformations, particularly after the Fall of the Soviet Union. Because genetic influences  require  an  supportive  environment  to  manifest,  high  genetic  risk  for  high educational  attainment  may  remain  unrealized  when  social  and  familial  conditions  are restrictive (Kitcher 2001; Harden 2021b). Studies for Estonia (Rimfeld et al. 2018), Hungary (Ujma et al. 2022) and the former GDR (Fraemke et al. 2024) suggest that genetic effects were suppressed under Soviet-era policies restricting access to higher education based on political loyalty rather than ability (Filtzer 2013). Following the transformation to market economies in the early 1990s, he association between genetic effects, as measured by PRS, and educational attainment  strengthened,  indicating  that  the  removal  of  (social)  environmental  barriers allowed genetic effects to play a larger role, reflecting greater equality of opportunity.  This line of research therefore highlights so-called gene-environment interactions, where the social and institutional environment can either facilitate or suppress the impact of genes on behavior (Seabrook & Avison 2010; Knopik, Neiderhiser, DeFries & Plomin 2017; Mills & Tropf 2020). Accordingly,  the extent  to which  genetic  potential  is  realized depends  on  historical, institutional,  and  social  conditions,  making  PRS  a  valuable  tool  for  studying  the  interplay between genetics and social inequality.

Relatively little attention has been given to studying how genetic effects on specific outcomes vary across social groups, exemplifying gene-environment interactions. One notable exception is Herd et al.'s (2019) study on gender differences in educational attainment in the United  States  during  the  20 th century.  Their  findings  suggests  that  genetic  effects  on educational  attainment  were  initially  weaker  for  women,  likely  due  to  institutional  and normative barriers that limited access to education and career opportunities. These barriers limited the returns on educational investments, suppressing genetic effects in women. Over time, as structural constraints diminished and gender norms shifted, incentives for women to pursue higher education increased. Consequently, the association between women's genetic effects and educational attainment strengthened, gradually closing the gender gap in genetic effects.  By  the  2000s,  this  trend  had  completely  reversed,  with  women  born  in  the  1980s exhibiting stronger genetic effects on educational attainment than men. However, whether

and to what extent similar patterns exist in other contexts, particularly in the former Cold War partition and post-Soviet regions, remains largely unexplored.


## Gender inequality trends in educational attainment in East and West Germany


As in the United States, norms and structural constraints for female educational participation in Germany changed substantially over the course of the second half of the 20 th century. The German context, however, was characterized by its own historical idiosyncrasies, not least due to its separation into two ideologically distinct states post-WWII. In the following, we structure the discussion about gender inequality in genetic effects around historical periods characterized  by  marked  changes  in  structural  barriers  to  education,  normative  changes regarding gender roles as well as curricular and pedagogical changes within the school system.


## The 1950s:


The  GDR  differed  markedly  from  the  FRG  in  its  official  commitment  to  reducing  social inequality, particularly in education and the labor market. From its early years, the socialist government  implemented  large-scale  programs  designed  to  promote  social  mobility  and achieve parity in educational access. Therefore, access to higher education was not based on merit alone but was tightly regulated, particularly during the 1950s and 1960s, with strong emphasis  on  family  background  and  political  loyalty.  Students  could  qualify  for  university either through secondary level education (POS) or the combined vocational training and Abitur program (Berufsausbildung mit Abitur BmA). Despite the state's emphasis on equality and education, opportunities for higher education were deliberately limited in the so-called 'state of pheasants and workers'. The share of students obtaining the German high school diploma (Abitur) remained capped at about 10 percent per cohort, with an additional 5 % following the combined vocational track, which was subject to slightly less political oversights in admission. By the late 1950s, approximately 50 percent of university students came from working-class families  -  a  staggering  difference  in  equality  of  opportunity  compared  to  the  FRG  where corresponding  numbers  amount  to  less  than  10  percent  (Geißler  2014).  This  difference underscores the GDR's efforts to restructure social hierarchies by prioritizing university access for students from working-class families, while simultaneously maintaining strict control over educational pathways for each individual.

In  its  early  years,  the  GDR  prioritized  social  class  over  gender  in  education policies, leaving  decisions  about  higher  education  pathways  for  working-class  children  largely  to parents.  This  contributed  to  persistent  gender  gaps.  In  the  1950s,  gender  roles  remained traditional,  and  GDR's  support  for  families  and  women  -  especially  parental  leave  and childcare  policies  -  was  far  less  developed  than  by  the  mid-1970s  (Drasch  2012).  Thus, (working-class) parents may have been more inclined to invest in their sons' education, to foster  upward  mobility  and  labor  market  prospects.  This  male  preference  in  educational investment behavior appears to be common in resource-limited families (Powell & Steelman 1990).  Thus,  although  policies  promoted  greater  equality  of  opportunity  based  on  social background,  men  likely  benefited  more  due  to  persistent  gendered  norms.  We  therefore expect a male advantage in genetic effects on educational attainment in the 1950s - both in the GDR and the FRG.


## 1960s and 1970s:


Lower  birthrates  and  economic  demands  in  the  1960s  and  1970s  shifted  the  GDR's commitment from social to gender equality in education and the labor market contributing to near parity in female university enrollment in the mid-1970s - a milestone that West Germany did  not  achieve  until  the  2000s  (Geißler  2014).  Labor  market  participation  became  a  core element of GDR policies as the socialist government - unlike Western democracies such as the US  and  West  Germany  -  mandated  full  employment  for  both  men  and  women  as  a constitutional  obligation  (Article  24)  to  counter  labor  shortages  caused  by  technological underdevelopment  and  emigration  to  West  Germany.  Women  were  therefore  actively encouraged and supported to participate in the workforce. The introduction of supportive family policies, such as maternity and parental leave (1976), and increased provision of free public childcare, including after-school care and holiday programs for older children (Drasch 2012) enabled women to pursue higher education and careers comparable to men (Lane 1983; Rueschemeyer 1993; Miethe et al. 2015; Jessen 2022). By the late 1980s, female employment rates in the GDR were therefore among the highest in the world, nearly equal to those of men (Rosenfeld et al. 2004).

Apart from legal norms and institutional frameworks, in the GDR gender norms on work and family started to diverge from those in the FRG (Zoch 2021) or other Western societies such  as  the  US  (Goldin  1990;  Fernández  2013).  Rooted  in  the  ideal  of  the  'workers'  and

peasant state', the GDR propagated an image of working mothers as the norm, reinforcing this through education, media, or even children's literature and songs. Maternal employment and institutional  childcare,  even  when  of  low  quality,  were  portrayed  positively  and  widely accepted. Full-time work for women was not an exception, but a normative expectation. It was further  supported  by  policies  such  as  free  access  to  contraceptives  (since  1965)  and  legal abortion (since 1972), which granted women greater autonomy over their reproductive and professional lives. On the surface, societal norms towards the general role of women in society or female labor force participation specifically as well as the structural conditions discouraging gendered  labor  market  participation  provided  an  environment  where  investment  into educational  attainment  by  women  was  bound  to  reap  returns  as  high  as  those  of  men, presumably reducing the gender gap in genetic potential for educational attainment in sharp contrast to the FRG.

Despite  these  progressive  policies  and  ideological  commitments  to  gender  quality, gender disparities persisted  across societal, educational and labor market structures,  likely shaping  gender  differences  in  genetic  effects  on  educational  attainment.  Household  labor remained  gendered,  reinforced  by  policies  such  as  the  'household  day,'  granting  working mothers a monthly day off for domestic responsibilities, and financial incentives for married couples. These policies uphold traditional gender roles and shaped career trajectories, like educational  materials  and  societal  norms  that  steered  women  towards  teaching  or  carerelated professions (Ritter & Ritter 2016; Baader, Koch & Neumann 2023). Although women were expected to participate in the labor market alongside men, educational pathways often conveyed  conflicting  messages,  reinforcing  gendered  career  choices  that  required  lower educational investment. For example, the combined vocational track (BmA), which provided access to university education, was more commonly pursued by men, presumably due to its emphasis on technical and scientific fields (Correll 2004; Gambaro, Wilhelm & Schober 2023). Similarly, the advanced secondary education track (EOS; comparable to the Gymnasium in the FRG) emphasized science and technology from the 5 th  grade onwards, which may have further contributed to gendered educational sorting. And finally, one-quarter of EOS class slots were reserved for army officer candidates, effectively excluding women from this higher education pathway,  as  the  first  female  officer  in  the  GDR  was  not  appointed  until  the  mid-1980s (Waterkamp 1987).

While political loyalty was a key determinant of educational and career advancement in the GDR, it is unlikely that systematic gender-differences in loyalty played a major role, as parents of one gender were not inherently more or less aligned with the regime. However, other mechanisms may have favored boys over girls in accessing higher education and career opportunities. Political loyalty was often demonstrated through active membership in stateorganized youth groups such as the Thälmann Pioneers (ages 6-14) or the Free German Youth (FDJ, ages 14 and up). These organizations, structured hierarchically with a strong focus on discipline,  physical  training,  and  ties  to  the  National  People's  Army,  may  have  been  more appealing  to  boys,  reinforcing  their  pathways  into  leadership  roles  and  professions  with greater economic returns. Taken together, these structural barriers continued to channel men into fields with higher economic and professional returns while limiting women's access to certain  occupations,  thereby  reinforcing  traditional  gender  roles  and  stereotypes.  This dynamic likely constrained genetic effects on education for women.

In  the  FRG,  large-scale  policy  initiatives  to  reduce  gender  inequalities  were  either largely absent or driven by social movements (e.g., as a reaction to the counterculture of the late  1960s)  rather  than a  coordinated state agenda (Miethe et al. 2015). Hence, efforts to reduce gendered educational inequalities lagged the GDR, gaining momentum only after 1968. However, these effects remained short of achieving gender parity in - for example - university enrollment,  even  a  decade  after  reunification  (Geißler  2014).  While  norms  around  female higher education shifted post-1968, policies and gender ideologies remained rooted in the 'male breadwinner' model (Zoch 2021). Sparse parental leave policies (14 weeks compared to 12 months in the GDR in the mid-1970s), tax breaks for married couples and lack of public childcare rarely accommodated (full-time) employment (Rosenfeld et al. 2004; Drasch 2012). These constraints continued to push women toward family roles, likely suppressing genetic effects for women in the FRG during this period.

The  counterculture  of  the  late  1960s,  however,  initiated  substantial  social  changes, particularly  in  gender  roles  and  education.  One  vehicle  of  social  change  was  reforms  of pedagogical and didactical approaches such as a shift towards child-centered education and incorporating non-cognitive criteria in educational achievement (Noelle-Neumann & Petersen 2001; Phal 2022). Systematic gender differences in some aspects of non-cognitive skills (e.g., self-regulation, social competencies and classroom behavior) have been shown to contribute

to girl's higher success in education system (Weis, Heikmap & Trommsdorff; Ogden et al. 2023). This  normative  shift  and  evolving  education  system  increased  women's  opportunities  and incentives to pursue  higher education, gradually closing gender  gaps  in educational attainment. As a result, genetic effects on educational attainment for men and women in the FRG should have slowly converge during this period.


## 1980s and post-reunification:


With the  reunification  of  Germany  in  1990,  the  distinct  political  systems  merged  into  the Western model of the FRG. For West Germany, the trajectories of normative change in gender roles and its consequences for the educational systems in term of pedagogical approaches and curricular content remained essentially unchanged. However, in East Germany, the implementation of West Germany's tiered educational system (Hauptschule, Realschule and Gymnasium) was associated with substantial structural changes, restructuring pathways to higher secondary and tertiary education systematically. Hence previous avenues favoring boys, such as slots reserved for officer candidates, or the prioritization of MINT graduates coupled with gendered role expectations conveyed in schoolbooks (Ritter & Ritter 2016; Baader, Koch & Neumann 2023), were now largely blocked. Similarly, political loyalty to the GDR system as one criterion for access to higher education lost relevance, increasing the general relationship between genetic effects and educational attainment post-reunification (Fraemke et al. 2024), like in other post-Socialist countries (Rimfeld et al. 2018; Ujma et al. 2022).

Overall,  the  implementation  of  the  FRG's  educational  system  in  the  East  should therefore have led to similar patterns of gender differences in genetic effects on educational attainment  to  those  of  West  Germany.  In  the  West,  this  trajectory  was  already  on  a  path towards  erosion  of  gender  differences  in  genetic  effects  on  education  presumably  due  to ongoing normative change and improving labor market prospects.

## Data and Methods


We draw on the data from Gene-SOEP, a 2019 innovation sample from the German SocioEconomic  Panel  study  (SOEP;  Koellinger  et  al.  2023).  The  Gene-SOPE,  based  on  a  random sample of households, is currently the only German data source including both genotyped individuals as well as detailed information on demography, work and employment, health, educational,  attitudes and personality  as  well as  family-related  characteristics.  Overall,  the Gene-SOEP covers close to half of all information gathered for the Core SOEP (Goebel et al. 2019). From the original sample of 4,283 individuals, 2,598 individuals donated valid genetic samples (age range: 0-96) . Compared to characteristics of individuals sampled in the Core 4 SOEP, genotyped individuals in the Gene-SOEP tend to be socioeconomically somewhat better off (cf. Koellinger et al. 2023: Table 1).

The Gene-SOEP data provides 36 polygenic risk scores summarizing genetic associations among others for body mass index, life satisfaction, propensity to read, cognitive abilities and crucially for our study, educational attainment. Generating polygenic risk scores requires  two  distinct  tasks  to  be  performed.  First,  secondary  information  drawn  from independent large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) is gathered. GWAS rely on genotyped  data  from  thousands  to  millions  of  individuals  and  correlate  the  genetic information with individual's attributes and behavioral outcomes. Genetic variants (or more specifically single-nucleotide  polymorphisms  [SNPs])  whose  coefficients  are  statistically significantly related to the studied outcome are collected for the second task, an out-of-sample prediction of polygenic risk scores. In our case, a GWAS identified 3,952 SNPs - each with a

tiny effect - which together account for close to half of the genetic effects on differences in educational attainment (Okbay et al. 2022). Hence, polygenic risk scores cover by no means all genetic effects on the outcome for various reasons. Instead, GWAS tend to focus on common SNPs thereby missing the effects of rare variants (Young 2022). Moreover, polygenic risk scores do not solely capture genetic effects but can also be environmentally or socially confounded ('social  genetic  effects',  Burt  2024).  This  confounding  generates  indirect  genetic  effects whereby  individual  outcomes  are  influenced  by  behaviors  of  others  -  behaviors  which themselves possess a genetic component. Prior studies suggest that between a quarter to a third  of  genetic  effects  on  educational  attainment  captured  by  polygenic  risk  scores  are confounded in this way (Domingue & Fletcher 2020; Wang et al. 2021). Since our research design does not permit us to apply procedures to reduce social confounding (e.g., using a trio design which relies on data from the child as well as both parents), polygenic risk scores should be interpreted as an imperfect approximation of genetic effects.

From the original sample of 2,598 individuals with valid genetic samples, we restricted the sample to individuals with valid genetic information that passed quality control and those who provided valid information on all relevant measures. Our analytical sample thus consisted of 1,573 individuals of which 373 (24 percent) completed their educational attainment in the GDR or in East Germany after reunification. We classified individuals into GDR and FRG subsamples based on their place of residence in 1989. For those born after 1989, we relied on information on place of residence. Given the overall sample size, statistical power - especially for the GDR subsample - may be limited.

Our key dependent and independent variables were years of education (7 to 18 years) measuring  educational  attainment,  gender  (0=males  and  1=females),  and  the  biologically informed  measure  of  genetic  influences  on  education,  the  polygenic  risk  scores  (PRS;  for descriptive statistics see Table 1). For each individual i, PRS are formally defined as the sum of the number of alleles Xm for each SNP m weighted by their respective coefficient βm.

βm represents the association between SNPm and educational attainment from the most recent GWAS study (Ockbay et al. 2022). The number of alleles Xm can take the values 0 (no alleles inherited),  1  (one  allele  inherited  from  either  parent)  or  2  (one  allele  inherited  from  each parent;  Burt  2024).  When  standardized,  polygenic  risk  scores  summarize  an  individual's position in the risk distribution of the studied population. A polygenic risk score (EA-PRS) of 0 represents the average genetic predisposition for high educational attainment. In contrast, a score of 1 or -1 indicates that an individual's genetic predisposition is one standard deviation above  or  below  the  sample  average,  respectively.  It  is  important  to  emphasize  that  this measure summarizes risk and is therefore a probabilistic statement. Whether and to what extent this risk is manifested into higher or lower educational attainment is fundamentally a function of the social environment. The Gene-SOEP provides the educational attainment and other  polygenic  risk  scores  precalculated.  Moreover,  it  provides  the  first  20  principal components  of  genetic  ancestry,  a  common  set  of  measures  included  in  these  types  of analyses to account for population stratification (Mills, Barban & Tropf 2020). Note also that since GWAS are largely based on samples with European ancestry, it is common practice to restrict samples to this ancestry group because out-of-sample predictions for other ancestry groups tend to perform considerably worse (Lee et al. 2018).

To examine trends over time, we draw on birth years and constructed five synthetic birth cohorts on ten-year intervals covering the crucial period of the divided Germany: 19431952, 1953-1962, 1963-1972, 1973-1982 and 1983-1992. The lower limit of 1943 was chosen because children would typically enter school at age 6 which coincides with the foundation of the GDR and the FRG in 1949.

## Analytical approach


To examine gender differences in the genetic effects (EA-PRS) on educational attainment in East  and  West  Germany  over  time,  we  estimated  linear  regression  models.  These  models regressed years of education on gender, birth cohort, the EA-PRS and the first 20 principal components of  ancestry,  separately  for  the  GDR  and  FRG  samples.  We  estimate  stepwise regression models and included a two-way interaction between gender and the EA-PRS. To assess how gender effects evolved across cohorts, we extended the two-way interaction by

including a three-way interaction between gender, EA-PRS, and birth cohort. To facilitate the interpretation of these models, we will rely on marginal effects. Since the cohort boundaries are somewhat arbitrary and because of generally low statistical power, we present descriptive statistics  and  estimates  of  the  gender  difference  in  the  genetic  effect  on  educational attainment using ten-year moving windows. Given the low statistical power and that there is no alternative data source to study this and related research questions, the findings should be considered tentative, and our focus will be on effect sizes rather than statistical significance.

## Summary and Conclusion


This study examines changes in genetic effects on educational attainment in the context of rapid social and institutional transformations in Germany, with a particular focus on gender inequalities before and after reunification. Efforts to reduce social inequalities have frequently centered on educational reforms aimed at expanding access and fostering greater equality of opportunity. By applying a genetically sensitive framework and using the novel Gene-SOEP dataset, our study is among the first to investigate how institutional and normative changes have shaped gender differences in genetic effects on educational attainment outside the U.S. Specifically, we examine how the contrasting policy environments of East and West Germanywith the GDR's explicit focus on reducing class and gender inequalities versus the FRG's slower adaptation to gender equality in education-influenced the observed patterns. In replicating and extending the findings of Herd et al. (2019) for the United States, we offer insights into how policies environment and structural contexts modulate the interplay between genetic effects and social outcomes.

Our findings reveal three key insights: first, the results show a strong and consistent positive  relationship  between  genetic  effects  and  educational  attainment  irrespective  of region and subgroup. In the German case, a difference in polygenic risk scores of one standard deviation is associated with a one year difference in years of education. This finding aligns with a growing number of studies relying on polygenic risk scores from English-speaking countries (Belsky et al. 2018; Herd et al. 2019; Lahtinen et al. 2023) as well as selected (post-)Soviet societies (Rimfeld et al. 2018; Ujma et al. 2022).

Second,  our  findings  reveal  that  gender  differences  in  genetic  effects  on  education showed a considerable male advantage in post-war Germany which narrowed substantially over the cohorts studied until it resolves for birth cohorts since the mid-1980s. In comparing

our findings with those of Herd et al. (2019) for the United States, we observe broadly similar trends  in  the  erosion  of  gender  disparities  in  genetic  effects  on  educational  attainment. However,  the  temporal  trajectory  differed;  while  the  United  States  exhibited  a  more accelerated convergence, the FRG showed a delayed pattern by around a decade. This finding aligns with the expectation that the FRGs stronger and longer adherence to traditional family arrangements may have reduced female incentives for educational attainment and thereby suppressed genetic effects.

Third, our analyses do suggest contextual differences, but their influence was more pronounced for the FRG/USA relative to the FRG/GDR comparison. Overall, the patterns of gender differences in genetic effects are broadly similar between the FRG and GDR. Hence, we do not find convincing evidence that the GDRs policy focus on reducing social and gender inequality generated large and systematic differences to patterns in the FRG. This is a surprising finding,  given  the  GDR's  comprehensive  state-led  initiatives  and  propaganda  aimed  at promoting gender quality, such as universal childcare and full employment policies. However, the similarities in the erosion of gender gaps across both contexts suggest that broader societal factors - such as normative shifts - may have played a more decisive role than state policies alone.    In  addition,  it  is  important  to  consider  that  structural  inequalities  in  the  GDR educational  policies  may  have  additionally  constrained  genetic  effects.  Despite  formal commitments to equality, the GDR was marked by limited personal freedoms, restricted access to diverse educational and occupational pathways, and a rigid, state-controlled allocation of educational and professional opportunities - often to the advantage of men. These factors may  have  suppressed  the  extent  to  which  genetic  effects  could  influence  educational attainment, thereby muting the potential impact of gender-specific policies. This could explain why  the  GDR,  despite  its  focus  on  gender  equality,  did  not  exhibit  more  pronounced differences  compared  to  the  FRG,  where  individual  choice  played  a  larger  role  in  shaping educational trajectories.

It is important to reiterate that the limited statistical power of our dataset restricts the robustness  of  our  conclusions.  The  low  statistical  power  and  the  general  research  design cannot provide unambiguous evidence for one explanation (e.g., social policy) over another (e.g.,  institutionally  blocked  pathways  for  women)  and  should  therefore  be  considered descriptive.  We  tried  to  mitigate  this  issue  by  using  a  rolling  window  approach  but  any

attempts to statistically identify specific social drivers of the observed results are not feasible with the Gene-SOEP. Given the scope of historical idiosyncrasies happening over a relatively short time frame in formerly and ultimately unified social context, more in-depth studies could provide valuable insights for comparative  research. However,  identifying the precise mechanisms  underlying  these  shifts  will  remain  challenging  not  only  due  to  the  complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors but more fundamentally due to the lack of data enabling direct disentanglement of these influences. Fortunately, genetic data is fixed at birth so data collection efforts do not depend on historical luck to cover specific study periods but can be collected post facto. The Gene-SOEP represents an important step forward, and both this study and previous research highlight the potential of integrating a genetically informed perspective into comparative research. However, more large-scale and high-quality datasets outside  the  English-speaking  context  are  needed  to  leverage  the  potentially  of  genetically sensitive studies.

Within  the  broader  field  of  gender  inequality  and  comparative  research,  this  study emphasizes  the  importance  of  the  institutional  and  normative  context  in  shaping  genetic effects on educational attainment as one primary factor in shaping an individual's life chances and  trajectories.  Our  findings  underscore  the  value  of  integrating  a  genetically  sensitive perspective with historical and institutional analyses to illuminate the pathways through which broad social changes may influence educational outcomes. By examining gendered genetic effects on educational attainment, we offer a novel and more comprehensive perspective on the evolution of equality of opportunity.

## 1 Introduction


Gender equality is a fundamental value in contemporary societies, which expect all genders to be treated equally. This principle should ensure equal participation in the labor  market,  political  life,  and  private  relationships;  however,  numerous  gender disparities persist (Auspurg et al., 2017; Bernhard et al., 2021; Waitkus & Minkus, 2021). The #MeToo movement highlighted many of these inequalities, demanding greater equality, emancipation, and empowerment, and in doing so, politicized the concept of gender in several European countries. In particular, anti-gender and antifeminist actors mobilized against a socalled 'gender ideology,' influencing gender politics and debates both online and offline in various countries in the Global North (Graff & Korolczuk, 2022; Jackson et al., 2020; Kuhar & Paternotte, 2018; Wallaschek et al., 2022).

Social  media  is  a  key  channel  through  which  conflicts  over  gender  relations  are expressed (Barberá, 2020; Benkler et al., 2018; Ernst et al., 2017; Gentzkow & Shapiro, 2010). Although it has been blamed for creating filter bubbles and echo chambers that foster  polarization  and  fragment  public  discourse  (Pariser,  2011;  Sunstein,  2017), empirical  research  questions  the  persistence  and  impact  of  these  phenomena  on people's attitudes (Dubois & Blank, 2018; Fletcher et al., 2021).

Empirical  studies  indicate  that  the  rapid  spread  of  hate  speech -not  digital  echo chambers -is primarily responsible for the visibility of negativity on these platforms.

Frequent  social  media  users  tend  to  communicate  in  a  more  toxic  and  negative manner,  with  women,  minorities,  and  other  vulnerable  groups  being  especially targeted (Esposito & Breeze, 2022; Watson, 2024). In addition, this behavior influences other users' perceptions of social media content (Kim et al., 2021) and amplifies the overall visibility of hostile content. Moreover, negativity and resentment spread more quickly than positive or neutral content (Schöne et al., 2021; Tsugawa & Ohsaki, 2015), resulting in the fact that users are frequently exposed to such content (Bor & Petersen, 2022;  Guldemond  et  al.,  2022;  Karell  et  al.,  2023).  We  argue  that  this  continuous exposure to negative content not only shapes the overall discourse on social media but also influences how individuals view groups that are routinely portrayed in a hostile and derogatory manner.

Against this background, the present study poses two research questions. First, does social media use lead to more regressive views on gender issues? And second, is the intensity of social media use - that is, the amount of time spent on these platforms - associated with this relationship? To address these questions, we use a novel cross-sectional survey dataset from six European countries (France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Spain) in 2021. Our findings reveal a significant association between substantial time spent on social media platforms (Facebook, YouTube, Twitter 2 , Instagram) and regressive attitudes toward gender. Our results are corroborated by a wide range of robustness checks.

By  focusing  on  both  overall  social  media  use  and  usage  intensity,  our  study contributes  to  the  debate  on  the  influence  of  social  media  on  users'  attitudes  in European  societies.  Unlike  previous  research  that  mainly  examines  broad  usage categories (Fletcher et al., 2021; Kubin & von Sikorski, 2021; Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, 2022), we emphasize the distinct impact of the actual time spent on social media.


## 2 Literature Review



## Gender ideology and anti-gender beliefs


Research  shows  that  gender  equality  is  broadly  supported  in  Europe  and  North America,  and  this  support  has  increased  over  time  (Adams,  1997;  Bolzendahl  & Myers,  2004;  DiMaggio  et  al.,  1996;  Evans,  2003).  However,  scholars  also  note  an increasing politicization of gender issues and feminism. Norris and Inglehart (2019) argue that older age cohorts tend to be more conservative than younger groups, who are more likely to embrace progressive values regarding ethnic diversity, migrant tolerance, and gender equality. Consequently, older generations may feel threatened by cultural progress, turning to regressive views and supporting right-wing populist parties. This dynamic creates a generational value divide -a 'cultural backlash' that drives the rise of right-wing populism (for a more critical account see Schäfer, 2022).

Moreover,  empirical  evidence  suggests  that  support  for  feminist  positions  is influenced by a gender gap, as demonstrated by Elder et al. (2021) in the US. Their study shows that women tend to be more pro-feminist than men, and this gap widens with  increasing  education -more  educated  women  are  increasingly  pro-feminist, whereas men's views remain relatively unchanged. Although overall anti-feminist identification is low, younger individuals (both men and women) are more likely to identify  as  anti-feminist  compared  to  older  individuals  (see  also  Mathisen,  2025). Importantly, when it comes to specific policy issues related to feminist causes -such as  abortion  laws,  equal  pay,  universal  parental  leave,  and  increasing  women's political representation -a significant majority across feminists, anti-feminists, and those without a feminist label express support. The authors argue, therefore, that while gender-related issues are generally popular in the US, explicitly identifying as a feminist or anti-feminist remains more contentious.

The contestation of a feminist identity is also linked to the emergence of new actors who  bring  anti-feminist  and  anti-gender  issues  to  the  public  agenda.  In  various European countries, a transnational anti-gender movement has emerged (Kuhar & Paternotte, 2018), seeking to influence legislation and public discourse on issues such as abortion, gender-inclusive language, equal pay, and family policies both offline and online (Köttig et al., 2017; Off, 2023; Vida, 2022; Wallaschek et al., 2024).


## Social media use and attitudes toward gender issues


Scholars have demonstrated that some social media platforms provide unregulated spaces for discriminatory statements, hate speech, and misogynistic ideas (Frimer et al.,  2023;  Sydnor,  2018).  Hostile  content -such as toxic tweets and posts -spreads rapidly online, exposing many users to negativity and potentially fostering adverse beliefs and emotions (Frischlich et al., 2021; Guldemond et al., 2022; Schöne et al., 2021).

As  users  become  more  immersed  in  environments  where  negative  content  is prevalent, they are more likely to adopt similar behaviors. For example, individuals who experience incivility or trolling are prone to replicating such behavior, a pattern particularly common among frequent users (Frischlich et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). Additionally, the role of 'super users'--those who are highly active and influential on platforms like Twitter -further amplifies the reach and impact of hostile discourse (Hölig, 2018; Pew Research Center, 2021b).

Research  shows  that  online  hostility  mirrors,  and  sometimes  amplifies,  offline incivility (Bor & Petersen, 2022). For instance, YouTube users with existing racist or misogynistic  views  tend  to  consume  and  engage  with  radical  content,  driven  by recommendation  algorithms  and  subscription  patterns  (A.  Y.  Chen  et  al.,  2023; Hosseinmardi et al.,  2021).  Similarly,  on  fringe  digital  platforms  such  as  gab,  the spread of farright content has been linked to shifts in users' perceptions and even

participation in civil unrest (Karell et al., 2023). Such digital environments are further exploited by right-wing populist parties, fringe news websites, and political actors who use platforms such as Facebook and Twitter to spread their ideologies (Benkler et al., 2018; Ernst et al., 2017; Jacobs & Spierings, 2019).

Analyses reveal that among politicians, journalists, and users, women receive more hateful and misogynistic comments than their male counterparts (G. M. Chen et al., 2020; Döring & Mohseni, 2019; Esposito & Breeze, 2022; Gardiner, 2018). Moreover, Frimer  et  al.  (2023)  show  that  uncivil  tweets  by  US  politicians  garner  increased engagement (likes and retweets), further encouraging such behavior. By being more easily exposed to negative news on social media and consuming social media content on a high level, this creates a social environment in which negativity and hostility regarding other social groups can be shared and expressed more easily (Van Bavel et al., 2023).

While it is theoretically possible to assume that the radicalisation process on social media  occurs  in  both  partisan  directions,  potentially  leading  users  to  radical progressive  positions,  current  evidence  suggests  otherwise.  Previous  research suggests  that  extreme  negative  content  is  more  prevalent  among  high-frequency social  media  users,  spreads  more  quickly  and  efficiently  across  platforms,  and ultimately reaches  a wider  audience  than  radical  liberal-progressive  content. Therefore, we assume that a high frequency of social media use is associated with more regressive attitudes on gender issues.


## Different social media platforms


More and more critical voices have been raised about how social media shapes the public debate. In general, homophily seems to influence whether social media, offline personal networks, or both foster or constrain social conflicts (Asimovic et al., 2021; Van Bavel et al., 2021) .  For instance, scholars suggested that Twitter's architecture encourages the formation of homogeneous groups, and rather connects like-minded individuals that reinforce existing views than bridges partisan divides (Jakob et al., 2022). Settle  (2018) examines how users engage with Facebook groups focused on political content. She demonstrates that political interactions on Facebook are largely driven  by  negative  perceptions  of  out-groups  and  the  reinforcement  of  positive attitudes toward one's in -group, ultimately fostering communication and exchange among like-minded individuals. This is particularly strong for those Facebook users who use the platform to confirm their political interests and tend to one side of the political spectrum (Praet et al., 2022).

Studies on the 'platform effect' yield contrasting results. For example, Verbalyte and Eigmüller (2022) found that during the COVID-19 pandemic, Twitter and Instagram users were less critical of lockdown measures than Facebook users -a  divergence they  attribute  to  differences  in  user  composition  (elite  versus  ordinary  users). Similarly, Jakob et al. (2022) report that Facebook debates exhibit higher toxic outrage than  those  on  Twitter,  likely  because  the  blend  of  public  and  private  contexts  on Facebook  elicits  more  emotional,  personal  reactions.  Moreover,  while  Kligler-

Vilenchik  et  al.  (2020)  show  that  emotion-driven  conflicts  are  more  prevalent  on Twitter and Facebook than on WhatsApp, Yarchi et al. (2021) argue that Twitter's heterophilic user structure fosters heated interactions among diverse social groups, potentially sparking broader societal conflicts.

Research  on  political  and  social  conflicts  often  focuses  on  social  media  alone, overlooking legacy media's influence. Feezell et al. (2021) demonstrate that 'non -algorithmic  news  consumption'via  newspapers,  magazines,  TV,  and  radio -neither  increases  partisan  conflicts  nor  predicts  higher  levels  of  partisanship,  as traditional news has not grown more partisan over time(but see Muise et al., 2022). Nonetheless, Boxell et al. (2017) state that in the US, older cohorts with lower internet usage experienced the largest rise in partisan views; even as social media use among adults increased from 50% in 2011 to 72% in 2021 (Pew Research Center, 2021a), and in Europe from 36% in 2011 to 59% in 2023 (Eurostat, 2024).

In summary, while the literature points in various directions regarding social media's influence, we assume that different platforms may exert distinct effects on gender attitudes.


## 3 Data and Methods



## Data


We use the ValCon Survey, a survey conducted in six European countries (France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Spain) in April and May 2021. The survey data was collected by the public opinion research company IPSOS and is based on an online access panel. The target population for this panel is all residents in Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Spain, and France between the ages of 18 and 65 with internet access. From this online access panel, 2,000 respondents per country were recruited, applying quotas for age, gender, and education (in total 12,000 individuals for six countries). The data  is openly available in the GESIS research data repository (Díez-Medrano et al., 2024).

The ValCon Survey includes various items on people's value orientation, main socio -demographic  characteristics,  political  participation  variables,  and  a  wide  array  of variables on  social media use. Respondents have been asked how often they use various traditional media sources such as TV, radio, newspapers (offline or online) as well as the four main social media platforms Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, Instagram in the last month, ranging from 'never used this source' to 'every day' (with the option to say 'don't know'). 3 In this quota sample almost half the respondents are male, the average age is 49 years, and the mode for education is middle education (a

more detailed description of the dataset and a table with summary statistics can be found in the appendix.).


## Variables


The central outcome of our analysis is attitudes toward gender issues. Since support for  gender  equality  and  attitudes  toward  gender  issues  are  latent  constructs  that should  thus  not  be  measured  using  solely  one  instrument,  in  the  following estimations  we  use  three  different  indicators.  Following  previous  studies  that distinguish  between  women-related issues  and  LGBTQI-related issues  (Kantola & Lombardo, 2017) as well as being able to consider the recent politicization of feminism (Elder et al., 2021), we use three outcomes to examine whether and to what extent social media use is associated with attitudes toward gender issues. The questionnaire administered  included  three  questions  on  the  agreement  with  the  following statements: 'Most feminists just hate men'; 'Women should be treated equally to men in the labor market' as well as 'Lesbian, gay, transgender and bisexual people should have the same rights as the rest of the population'. All three variables were measured using a four-point Likert scale excluding a middle category. In order to account for that, we recorded 'don't know' as the middle category to end up with a fivepoint scale. Robustness checks excluding the 'don't know' were carried out as well  (see  section  'Further  Robustness  Analysis'). Additionally,  we  run  a  factor analysis and all three items load on one factor (results not shown).

The central independent variable in our study is the use of social media, with the data providing  information  on  respondents'  engagement  with  different  social  media platforms.  In  addition,  information  is  available  on  the  consumption  of  traditional media, including TV, radio and newspapers, which serves as an additional control group in the following analysis. The questionnaire first asked respondents to select the media sources they had used in the past month. If they indicated that they had engaged with any of the listed (social or traditional) media sources at least once, or if they selected "don't know," they were prompted with a follow-up filter question. This question  inquired  about  the  average  time  they  spent  actively  using  these  media sources each day. The response options included: "less than half an hour," "more than half an hour but less than an hour," "more than 1 hour but less than 2 hours," "more than 2 but less than 5 hours," and "5 hours or more," along with the option to answer "don't know". 4

For  each  platform,  including  TV  and  radio,  we  construct  two  dummies:  One indicating whether the platform was used at least once in the past month (ever = 1), or whether they either did not use the platform in the last month or never used the platform (never = 0), and another indicating the intensity use. High-intensity use is defined as two or more hours per day (> 2h = 1), while low-intensity use is defined as

less  than  two  hours  per  day  (<  2h  =  0).  Sensitivity  checks  were  performed  with alternative time thresholds.

We include several control variables. Specifically, we control for age (in categories), gender,  paid  employment,  educational  attainment  (based  on  ISCED),  urban-rural divide  (self-assessed  measure),  and  self-assessed  financial  situation.  All  models include country fixed effects.


## Sample


For the subsequent analysis, we pool the countries and use the full dataset of 12,000 respondents. Since we coded 'don't know' as a meaningful category, we do not have any missing in the outcome variables. However, excluding those responses that have missing  values  on  the  independent  variables  leaves  us  with  an  overall  sample  of 11,318. The sample sizes for the different platforms vary, also with regard to which central independent variables are used (never vs ever user and high vs low intensity, see above). For a descriptive overview of the sample characteristics by frequency of usage and the individual plattform, see Tables A.1-A.4 in the Appendix.


## Method


We present the results in three steps. First, we present a descriptive analysis. The aim is  twofold:  to  provide  a  detailed  description  of  the  univariate  distribution  of  the outcome variables and to assess the degree of variation in attitudes towards gender issues based on the frequency of social media use among users.

We then use a multivariate analysis to examine whether attitudes towards gender issues  differ  by  overall  use  of  social  media  and  by  intensity  of  use,  while  also employing controls. More specifically, we use linear probability models (LPM) to test the association between social media use and attitudes towards gender issues. By including a simple dummy in the OLS, we first compare the attitudes of social media users with those who do not use social media. Secondly, we compare high and low intensity social media users. In addition, we compare social media users with those who use traditional media ("TV\_Radio"). The latter comparison helps us to see if the association  between  social  media  and  gender  attitudes  is  systematically  different from that between gender attitudes and traditional media use, a media source that has been found to not foster regressive attitudes (see above). We ran separate LPMs for each platform, each including a dummy for the platform and the controls. We do this for all three outcomes. In total, the main analysis in this paper consists of thirty models  (3  different  outcomes  [feminism,  labor  market  equality,  LGBT  rights]  x  5 media  platforms  [YouTube,  Twitter,  Facebook,  Instagram,  and  Radio  &  TV]  x  2 different types of use [never v ever, low v high frequency]). The results are presented as  graphs  showing  only  the  associations  between  social  media  platforms  and outcomes,  thus  reducing  each  model  to  the  association  of  the  central  dependent variable. Full tables with control variables can be found in the appendix.

Third, to test the robustness of our results, we perform several sensitivity checks, including using different thresholds for time spent on social media, reverse causality checks, sample selectivity checks, and several smaller sensitivity analyses.
