## Multivariate Analysis: Testing for reverse Causality


Reverse causality is a concern in our findings. It may be that high-intensity social media users are already skeptical of gender equality, and that social media merely serves as a digital meeting place for like-minded individuals, rather than social media use causing less progressive gender attitudes. Indeed, previous work suggests that distrust  in  political  institutions  as  well  as  voting  for  a  populist  party  indicate discontent and may drive individuals to a higher social media use (Lorenz-Spreen et al., 2022).

To address these concerns, we  reran our analysis by including additional independent  variables  that  are  likely  to  serve  as  confounders -variables  that influence both social media use and attitudes toward gender, potentially distorting the  association  between social media and gender issues and leading to erroneous coefficients. We included trust in government as an additional control in the analysis. Our  findings  indicate  that  social  media  usage  remains  a  significant  predictor  of gender attitudes (see Figure 7). This reinforces our conclusion that there is something unique about intense social media use that negatively impacts progressive attitudes on gender, regardless of prior political orientations. To further support this argument, we also ran models that included a dummy variable for voting intention toward a right-wing populist party, as well as a variable representing political interest -both of which may already be related to a critical mindset on gender issues. Neither of these variables altered our main findings (see Figure A.1 and Figure A.2).


## Further Robustness Analysis


To ensure the robustness of our results, we conducted several additional sensitivity tests.

First, we aimed to ensure that our findings were not influenced by sample selectivity. Tables A.1-A.4 in the Appendix demonstrate that our treatment group (social media users) and control group differ significantly on several covariates. To address this issue, we reran our analysis using propensity score matching (PSM) instead of simple OLS,  which  allowed  us  to  construct  a  more  appropriate  control  group.  Using  a matching  technique  like  PSM  is  a  valuable  robustness  analysis  because  it  helps mitigate the effects of confounding variables, thereby providing a clearer comparison between the treatment and control groups. However, similar to traditional regression techniques, a limitation of PSM is that it can only account for observable confounders. Despite this limitation, the results (Figure A.3) show only marginal deviations from the OLS models, further supporting our main findings. Second, we reran our result discarding respondents who answered 'don't know' on the three gender equality items (on equal treatment, LGBT rights, hateful feminists). In the main analysis, the 'don't  know' category is utilized as  the  middle  category of  the  four-point  Likert scale.  Overall,  the  results,  shown  in  Figure  A.4,  resemble  the  main  results  of  this paper. However, results have become more pronounced, i.e. we find more significant results. This is to be expected, since including 'don't know' introduces ambiguity. While one can assume that some of those who selected 'don't know' might not have

done so if a middle category were available, there might also be a significant number of respondents who in fact have no clear expressed opinion on gender equality issues.

Third, given the overall significant association between high-intensity social media use and regressive gender attitudes, we pooled social media usage across platforms to test whether the patterns for ever versus never users and high versus low-intensity users hold. Indeed, the same pattern emerges as high-intensity use is associated with more regressive views on gender issues (Figure A.5).

Fourth,  we  run  ordered  logit  models  given  the  nature  of  our  (ordinal)  outcome variable. Results largely replicate our main models (Figure A.6).


## 5 Conclusion


This article examined the relationship between social media use and attitudes toward gender-related  issues.  Our  findings  indicate  that  intense  social  media  use  is associated with regressive views on these topics.  In particular, it is not the use of social media per se, but rather the intensity of use, in terms of the amount of time spent on these platforms, that is most associated with such opinions.. Across all three outcomes  examined -support  for  equal  treatment  in  the  labor  market,  positive perceptions  of  feminists,  and  support  for  LGBT  rights -those  spending  over  two hours  per  day  on  social  media  were  significantly  less  supportive.  In  contrast, consuming  traditional  media  (TV  and  radio)  either  increases  support  for  gender

equality  or  has  no  significant  effect.  The  results  were  corroborated  by  a  range  of robustness checks, including tests for reverse causality, sample selectivity, different usage time thresholds, and other validity assessments. Thus, our results demonstrate that extensive social media use negatively shapes attitudes toward gender issues.

We argue that the spread and exposure to negativity and hostility on social media is most effective  among  users  who  spend  substantial  time  on  these  platforms.  Such high-intensity  users  are  more  likely  to  encounter  this  content,  which  shapes  their attitudes toward gender issues. Furthermore, these users may create an alternative media environment by connecting with like-minded individuals -following specific Facebook pages, Twitter or Instagram accounts, or subscribing to particular YouTube channels -which can result in less diverse content regarding gender-related issues. Although previous studies have indicated that only a small YouTube user group is exposed  to  harmful  content  and  that  recommendation  algorithms  may  not  be  as influential  as  assumed  in  promoting  extremist  videos  (A.  Y.  Chen  et  al.,  2023; Hosseinmardi et al., 2021), our results underline that the total digital consumption time is a crucial factor in shaping people's attitudes. A factor that has hardly been considered in previous research.

Nonetheless, our study has several limitations. First, the non-probabilistic sample is based on an online access panel, yielding an internet-savvy group (Dutwin & Buskirk, 2022;  Lehdonvirta  et  al.,  2021).  Second,  drawing  causal  conclusions  from  crosssectional  survey  data  remains  challenging  (Gattig  &  Minkus,  2021).  While  our

robustness checks support the conclusion that intense social media use is associated with regressive attitudes toward gender equality, future research could benefit from for example employing panel data to better assess intra-individual changes in social media use and the corresponding shifts in gender-related attitudes.

In  conclusion,  our  study  demonstrates  that  high-intensity  social  media  use  is  a significant driver of regressive views on gender-related issues. We are the first to show the crucial role of consumption time in the association between general social media use and gender attitudes. Our findings highlight the crucial role that extended social media use and exposure to social media content can play in shaping attitudes.

## INTRODUCTION


A considerable amount of contemporary cultural and political debate in the United States is over the interpretation and recognition of 'rights,' or that to which Americans are morally and legally entitled as human beings (in the case of human rights) or citizens (Hoffman 2012; Mencken and Froese 2019; Gran 2021). Research seeking to explore how and why differences of interpretation or understanding of these 'rights', such as 'freedom of speech' or 'freedom of religion,' among Americans has consistently identified cultural framing and group centrism as salient factors. Cultural scripts, or 'frames,' often act in an iterative process in which ostensibly clear and enumerated civic rights are contextualized not by their legal precedent, but by grouporiented understandings of whether a specific 'right' should or should not be supported based upon who is believed to benefit from it (Nelson and Kinder 1996). In other words, the framing of a right as more beneficial to in-group members are likely to be prioritized, while those that tend to be more important to out-groups are likely to be deemphasized. Further, Americans' subjective understanding of both the definition and application of civic rights serve more often as symbolic assertions of group values and beliefs than objective knowledge of how enumerated rights are applied and maintained in daily life (Djupe et al. 2014).  Put more simply, citizens' support or opposition to protections and rights outlined in the Constitution are heavily influenced by group loyalty and cultural narratives. Among the leading factors shaping how Americans evaluate what they consider to be rights or which rights they prioritize -specifically those framed as issues concerning individual liberty or minority protection-including political partisanship and educational attainment, is religion (Breskaya et al. 2018; Djupe et al. 2014; Ellison et al. 2021; Lewis 2017; Mayrl 2018).

Traditionally, scholars have argued that religion operates to provide a cohesive theological narrative undergirding group support for rights such as freedom of religion or freedom of speech. Yet beyond traditional measures of religious identity, commitment, theological conservatism, or political ideology, recent scholarship has identified a 'public dimension of religious commitment' (Stewart et al. 2018:33) that operates differently from indicators of private religious behavior or belief. This dimension seems oriented around 'social order' or 'public life' in a way that conflates sectarian Protestant ideals about in-group loyalty, hierarchies, and traditionalist morals with American history, identity, and policy (Gorski and Perry 2022). Though different labels such as 'public religious expression' (Stewart et al. 2018) and 'tribal civil religion' (Williams and Fuist 2013) have been used, the more common term that now seems to transcend disciplines is 'Christian nationalism' (Al-Kire et al. 2021, 2022; Armaly et al. 2022; Braunstein 2021; Corcoran et al. 2021; McDaniel et al. 2011). Put simply, Christian nationalism is a social and cultural framework which seeks to marry a heavily constrained vision of Christianity to American civic life and polity such that conservative, predominantly white Evangelicalism establishes and maintains a position of explicit privilege in American society.

Within the burgeoning research on Christian nationalist ideology, scholars have consistently found the construct to be associated with insistence on certain kinds of 'liberty' such as religious liberty, gun rights, libertarian economic policies, or liberty to expose oneself to COVID-19 (Adler et al. 2021; Perry et al. 2021; Perry, Schnabel, et al. 2022; Whitehead et al. 2018) while minimizing the liberty of others and an emphasis on formal means of social control (Armaly et al. 2022; Davis 2018; Davis and Perry 2021; Perry, Whitehead, et al. 2022). Indeed, Christian nationalism itself reflects this contradiction in that its adherents would insist that the government cannot 'limit the free exercise of' Christians; yet it is powerfully associated with Islamophobia, anti-Semitism, and anti-atheist sentiment' (Whitehead and Perry 2020). Similarly,

it seeks to elevate and institutionalize Christian identity above others, while sacralizing the founding documents that clearly forbid Congress from passing laws 'respecting an establishment of religion' (Gorski and Perry 2022).

In an effort to elucidate these apparent contradictions, we draw on recent, nationally representative data to examine the association between Christian nationalist ideology and various rights and protections outlined in the Constitutions which Americans affirm. Specifically, we evaluate Americans' identification of the 'most important' among seven options drawn from the American Bill of Rights, which include (1) freedom of speech, (2) freedom of the press, (3) freedom of religion, (4) the right to a speedy and fair trial, (5) the right to keep and bear arms, 6) rights not outlined as going to the federal government go to the states, and (7) protection against unlawful searches or seizures. Building on insights from research on Christian nationalism and desires for more stringent social control among Americans, we anticipate Christian nationalist ideology would be associated Americans' support for the rights most closely associated with historical majority groups, especially those rights framed as necessary for the maintenance of traditional power structures including the freedom of religion and the right to bear arms. Further, we would expect Christian nationalism to be negatively associated with protections for vulnerable groups perceived as threats such as crime suspects. Finally, we would anticipate Christian nationalism to deprioritize rights that provide opportunities to criticize or overturn power and which may upset social order including the freedom of the press or the view that voting is a fundamental right and not a civic privilege. In light of prior literature demonstrating the salience of Christian nationalist ideology above and beyond measures of social and political conservatism, we would expect these relationships to hold even when subjected to an extensive battery of sociopolitical and demographic control measures.


## BACKGROUND AND EXPECTATIONS



## Politics, Religion, and 'Rights' in the United States


Sociologists and political scientists interested in the understanding and application of rights outlined and protected by the Constitution among the general population find that there are myriad sociopolitical influences at play. Research on how Americans evaluate 'rights' often shows that persons who are more politically and theologically conservative are likelier to favor more circumscribed definitions of 'rights' while prioritizing rights that maximize the liberty of the in-group, including the liberty of the in-group to defend itself from cultural, economic, or political threats (see review in Davis and Perry 2021). As political theorist Corey Robin (2016:8) explains, this tendency is fundamental to the conflict between conservatism and liberalism.

Though it is often claimed that the left stands for equality while the right stands for freedom, this notion misstates the disagreement between right and left. Historically, the conservative has favored liberty for the higher orders and constraint for the lower orders. What the conservative sees and dislikes in equality, in other words, is not a threat to freedom but its extension. For in that extension, he sees the loss of his own freedom.

Political conservatism, in part, can thus be understood as a movement to maximize in-group liberty and control threats to that liberty. So too can conservative religion often function as broad marker of ethno-cultural identity, justifier of the social status quo, and foundation for beliefs about cultural or moral 'purity' (Adler et al. 2021; Rawls 1972). It is consequently a key mechanism for identifying and distinguishing outsiders and constraining privileges, rights, and protections available to them. Unsurprisingly then, Schwadel and Garneau (2019) find evidence that affiliation with evangelical denominations, and a literalist interpretation of the Bible is

associated with lesser willingness to allow full freedom of speech to marginalized out-groups. Similarly, Eisenstein and colleagues (2017) demonstrate that, while evangelical Protestants have increased in political tolerance toward stigmatized groups since the 1980s, they remain consistently less willing to extend free speech than are mainline Protestant or Catholic respondents net of salient political and social indicators of intolerance.

Far from simply acting as a marker of which rights Americans are more inclined to restrict , however, sociologists and political scientists have demonstrated that religion also helps us understand which rights Americans support . Gun ownership (Mencken and Froese 2019; Stroope and Tom 2017; Yamane 2016), expansive police powers and desires for more stringent social control (Thompson and Froese 2016; see also Baker and Booth 2016), and support for broadly defined 'freedoms' associated with conservative or libertarian ideologies (Braunstein and Taylor 2017; Marti 2020) are all frequently couched within a religious framework in political and social discourse. Lewis (2017) describes the recent decades as a 'rights turn' among conservative religious groups who now articulate their political agenda to preserve their cultural influence while marginalizing others in terms of 'religious liberty' or 'religious freedom' (see also Mayrl 2018; Mayrl and Venny 2021). Furthermore, Braunstein and Taylor's (2017) research indicates that religio-political appeals undergird claims that some conscribed set of rights are god-ordained even among the irreligious, suggesting that rhetorical strategies sacralizing some freedoms over others may be more important for understanding American political beliefs than religious belonging or practice per se. Such studies highlight the need for research outlining the sustained and transformative role of religious influences in American civic life (Adler et al. 2021; Delehanty et al. 2019; Stewart et al. 2018; Williams and Fuist 2013).


## Christian Nationalism, Civic Belonging, and Rights


In what is now both an expansive and growing literature exploring the role of Christian nationalism in American politics, evidence shows that as a person more intimately intertwines 'Christian' identity with being 'truly American,' their concept of who is deserving of protection and privileges within society becomes more constrained. Specifically, Gorski and Perry (2022) contend that Christian nationalism provides cultural narratives in the form of a 'deep story' which simultaneously mythologizes the role of Christianity in the founding of America and in the framing of national institutions and traditions. This story, they contend, acts as a framework through which Christian nationalists understand the past and examine the present such that legacies of social and structural stratification are often obfuscated, and efforts highlight and critique these injustices are resisted (Perry, Whitehead, and Davis 2019; Perry and Whitehead 2019; Perry et al. 2022). In effect, then, the cultural framework of Christian nationalism constructs a narrow view of what it means to be a 'real' or 'true' American. As one might expect, this framework tends to be most salient among Americans who are less educated, white, Southern, and evangelical (Whitehead and Perry 2020).  And while Christian nationalism is commonly associated with political and social positions that are popular among conservatives and Republicans, scholars have consistently found that Christian nationalism's influence remains salient even when controlling for respondents' political ideology. In sum, these studies indicate that Christian nationalism operates both in concert with and independently from political ideology to inform Americans' social and political attitudes, and is often a factor in both what aspects of American civic life Americans support, as well as those which they oppose.

As a consequence of this narrower sense of civic belonging, Christian nationalism tends to elevate attitudes that are more closely aligned with the maintenance of a more 'traditionalist' image of social order both formally and symbolically (Davis 2018; Whitehead and Perry 2019;

Perry and Whitehead 2022). Davis (2018), for example, finds that Christian nationalists are likelier to emphasize the use of strict or even lethal means of formal control for 'criminals' and 'troublemakers.' Similarly, Whitehead, Schnabel, and Perry (2018) argue that Christian nationalism's conflation of a subset of civic rights with 'God's plan' for America inclines adherents, above and beyond sociodemographic and political identities, to oppose the expansion of firearms legislation. This research also demonstrates that this framework is associated with prioritizing expansive freedoms among those culturally framed as more authentically American, and particularly opposing infringements of abstract notions of liberty in the form of Covid-19 restrictions (Perry, Whitehead, and Grubbs 2021; Perry and Whitehead 2020; Adler et al. 2021). Finally, Christian nationalism is also associated with approval for rights and practices that are believed to support cultural and social hierarchies including protection of gun rights (Du Mez 2020; Marti 2020), supporting government funding of border security and expansive criminal justice institutions (Davis 2019), and voting for candidates whom they feel are committed to combating the decline of Christian hegemony by supporting 'religious freedom' (Perry, Schnabel, et al. 2022). 1

At the same time, however, white Christian nationalism is strongly associated with efforts to constrain the liberties of perceived outsiders. As a necessary component of Christian nationalism's framework constructing an image of 'real Americans,' it also implicitly and explicitly identifies those groups that are less entitled to the rights and privileges of American society. Prior research demonstrates that Christian nationalism predicts greater opposition to same-sex marriage, and reigning in access to abortion services for women (Whitehead and Perry 2015, 2020). Similarly, Cravens (2022) finds that Californians who report higher levels of Christian nationalist beliefs are less supportive of political leaders who identify as LGBT+, arguing that adherence to this ideology supports hetero and cisnormative conceptions of who is fit for leadership positions in America. Supporting this connection between beliefs that America is a 'Christian nation,' and adherence to more stringent sexual norms, Perry and Whitehead (2022) show that Christian nationalists are significantly more inclined to support bans on pornography across multiple sources of data.

Beyond influencing attitudes towards sexual morality, Christian nationalism's commitment to social order often inclines adherents to express desires for a more constrained vision of access to the political process. Civic engagement, particularly voting rights, has become increasingly framed as a 'privilege' among republican voters and political representatives (Gomez and Doherty 2021). Supporting this understanding are beliefs that voting in the United States is 'too easy,' and that this allows for 'rampant voter fraud' which are significantly more common among Americans who subscribe to Christian nationalism compared to other cross sections of the population (Perry, Whitehead, et al 2022). This suggests that commitment to social order articulated within Christian nationalist mythos implicitly views broader access to civic influence as a threat. Further, Davis and Perry (2021) find that among five historically marginalized groups Christian nationalism's emphasis on social order writ large is associated with preferences for more constrained speech for all groups. Yet, the implicit understanding that

racists and militarists may be strategic allies along political and cultural lines leads Christian nationalists to prioritize their speech over communists, atheists, and homosexuals (see also Dahab and Omori 2019).

Taken together, research exploring Christian nationalism within the American political economy indicates that it simultaneously foments support for more 'traditionalist' visions of America, while providing a framework to deemphasize the rights and privileges of perceived outsiders. In light of this, we explore the potential association between Christian nationalism and identification of specific rights outlined in the Constitution as the 'most important.' We outline our expectations of these relationships and our plan for formal analyses in the following sections.


## Expectations


Given Christian nationalism's association with prioritization of social order, links to election conspiracy theory and beliefs that voting is 'too easy' in the United States, as well as resistance to restrictions on 'individual liberties,' we expect Christian nationalism to be significantly tied to which rights respondents deem 'most important' from the Bill of Rights.

Specifically, we expect that adults who more strongly adhere to Christian nationalist ideology will be less likely to support rights associated with liberal democracy including the freedom of the press-whom Trump framed as the 'true enemy of the people' (Wagner 2018)and protections for free speech. However, given both the unique position of 'freedom of speech' as particularly sacred in broad American culture and discourse, as well as an emergent debate among Americans on the meaning of 'free speech,' we expect this relationship to be more complex. Specifically, recent movements among those on the political left attempting to levy social and economic consequences against speech they deem hateful or vitriolic has sparked a counter movement from the political right against 'wokeism' and 'cancel culture' (New York Times 2022).

We would also expect the cultural framework of Christian nationalism to manifest itself in disregard for rights which might protect vulnerable populations who are more easily presented as threats (e.g., those suspected of criminal activity) and thus stifle efforts to maintain social order and hierarchy. Such rights include the right to a speedy and fair trial and protections against unlawful search and seizure. And because voting represents a pathway by which citizens can peaceably overthrow those in power, we also anticipate Christian nationalism would be negatively associated with defining voting as a 'right' as opposed to a 'privilege' that those in power can curtail or revoke. Finally, we expect Christian nationalism to bolster support for civil liberties which might be framed as bastions of a more traditional social order oriented about structure and individual liberties including the right to bear arms, freedom of religion, and an emphasis on states' rights. 2

## Data


Data for this study come from the Public Discourse and Ethics Survey (hereafter PDES) (Author DATE). There are eight waves of the PDES. For our analysis, we use data from two PDES waves: Wave 1, collected in August 2019 (for most controls) and Wave 8, collected in August 2021 (for Christian nationalism and views about rights). Survey waves were designed by the authors and the survey instrument was fielded by YouGov, an international research data and

analytics company. YouGov recruits a panel of respondents through websites and banner ads. 3 These respondents are not paid directly but are entered into lotteries for monetary prizes. In order to draw a nationally representative sample, YouGov employs a method called 'matching.' Drawing a random sample from the American Community Survey, YouGov then matches a respondent in the opt-in panel who is the closest to the Census respondent based on key sociodemographic factors. Because of the specific recruitment and sampling design used by YouGov, the company does not publish traditional response rates. However, YouGov develops sampling weights to ensure the survey sample aligns with nationally representative norms for age, gender, race, education, and census region. Results from the PDES Wave 1 compare favorably with results from the 2018 General Social Survey on demographic factors such as age, gender, race, marital status, region, educational attainment, and evangelical affiliation (see Appendix Table A1). The resulting original survey sample included 2,519 Americans that were matched and weighted. After sample attrition and listwise deletion of a modest number of cases with missing data our final analytic sample consists of 1,137 cases. Looking at a comparison of demographics from the Wave 1 PDES and the analytical sample after attrition and listwise deletion (Appendix Table A1) reveals only minor differences, suggesting that attrition and missing cases were not patterned, but random. ## Outcomes: Americans' Views on Rights


The outcomes for this study come from two measures used in Wave 8 of the PDES. For the first, we provided Americans with a list of 7 rights outlined in the Bill of Rights. These are: (1) freedom of speech, (2) freedom of the press, (3) freedom of religion, (4) the right to a speedy and fair trial, (5) the right to keep and bear arms, (6) rights not outlined as going to the federal government go to the states, and (7) no unlawful searches or seizures. We then asked Americans to choose among these which they believed to be 'the most important right.' Because this variable indicates a single priority among rights outlined in the Constitution, and not an ordinal ranking of these rights, dichotomization of responses into a series of dummy variables is most appropriate (Long and Freese 2014). As a result, our analyses include seven dichotomous dependent variables where a value of (1) indicates respondents identification of a right as 'most important,' while a value of (0) indicates that a respondent believes some other listed right is most important. We then estimate binary logistic regression models estimating Christian nationalism's association with the likelihood that Americans believe \_\_\_\_\_ is the most important right vs. all the others.

Because initial bivariate analyses indicated these outcomes fell predictably along patterned lines, we also created another binary outcome separating respondents who prioritized rights that were consistently selected by ideological and partisan conservatives and those who chose rights that were not. Specifically, respondents who indicated the 'most important right' was freedom of religion, the right to keep and bear arms, or states' rights were coded 1, while all others who selected freedom of speech, freedom of the press, right to a speedy and fair trial, or no unlawful searches or seizures were coded 0.

For the last outcome, we use a single question from Wave 8 of the PDES in which we ask Americans simply whether they believe voting is a 'privilege' or a 'right.' We code responses such that those who believe voting is a right = 1, privilege = 0. We estimate binary logistic regression models to estimate Christian nationalism's association with viewing voting as a right (something that shall not be infringed) rather than a privilege (something that can be limited or taken away entirely).


## Christian Nationalism


While 'Christian nationalism' has been measured in various ways (e.g., Al-Kire et al. 2021, 2022; Corcoran et al. 2021; McDaniel et al. 2011), the Christian nationalism scale used by Whitehead and Perry (2020) has become the standard across disciplines like sociology, social psychology, and political science (Al-Kire et al. 2021, 2022; Davis 2018; Armaly et al. 2022). We use a slightly extended version adopted by Gorski and Perry (2022).

The Whitehead and Perry (2020) scale includes six level-of-agreement questions with the statements: 'The federal government should advocate Christian values,' 'The federal government should declare the United States a Christian nation,' 'The federal government should enforce strict separation of church and state (reverse coded),' The federal government should allow religious symbols in public spaces,' 'The federal government should allow prayer in public schools,' and 'The success of the United States is part of God's plan.' Gorski and Perry's (2022) scale adds an additional statement: 'I consider founding documents like the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution to be divinely inspired.' Responses range from 0 = Strongly disagree to 4 = Strongly agree. Following previous research, we combine these measures into an additive scale ranging from 0 to 28, with higher scores indicating greater adherence to Christian nationalism (Cronbach's alpha = .91). The Christian nationalism measures used in these analyses appear on Wave 8 of the PDES. The average score is 13.1 (SD = 8) indicating most Americans hold views on Christian nationalism slightly below the median.


## Control Variables


In light of previous research on Americans' views of rights, we expect our outcomes to be highly correlated with political and religious characteristics. All controls come from Wave 1 of the PDES. For conservative political ideology we use an ordinal measure ranging from very liberal = 1 to very conservative = 5. Religion controls include religious tradition and frequency of service attendance. Affiliation with a religious tradition is measured with six categories: Evangelical Protestant (reference), Liberal Protestant, Catholic, Other Christian, Other Religion, and Seculars (including atheists, agnostics, and the unaffiliated).  Religious service attendance is 4 measured from 1 = never to 6 = several times a week.

Sociodemographic controls from Wave 1 include variables for race, gender, family income, and region as well as a range for age and educational attainment.  These categories are shown as binary indicators for race (white = reference, Black, Hispanic, Other race), gender (male = 1), household income (less than $30,000 per year = reference, $30,000-59,999, $60,00099,999, $100,000-199,999, $200,000 or more, did not report income), and region (Southern

residence = 1). Age is measured in years from 20 to 82. And educational attainment ranges from 1 to 6 representing having completed less than a high school diploma to a postdoctoral degree.

Table 1 presents descriptive statistics for all variables along with zero-order correlations between variables and Christian nationalism. Bivariate findings affirm that prioritizing particular rights falls consistently along predictable lines. Americans who score higher on Christian nationalism are more likely to believe that gun rights (r = .29, p < .001), religion (r = .25, p < .001), or states' rights (r = .11; p < .001) are the 'most important right,' while selecting freedom of the press (r = -.28, p < .001), free speech (r = -.16, p < .001), right to a speedy and fair trial (r = -.09, p < .01), or protection from unlawful searches and seizures (r = -.16, p < .001) are negatively associated with Christian nationalism. Unsurprisingly, Christian nationalism is positively associated with selecting 'conservative rights' (gun rights, religion, and states' rights) as the most important (r = .46, p < .001). Christian nationalism is also negatively associated with believing that voting is a right rather than privilege (r = -.30, p < .001). Given that these patterns are so intuitively associated with political ideology and racial identity, we turn to multivariate analyses.

## DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS


Americans often express profound disagreement as to what opportunities and resources should be considered 'rights' versus privileges in society, as well as whether some enumerated rights are more important than others. Building on research associates Christian nationalist beliefs with support for formal means of social control (Davis 2018), desires to constrain freedom of speech for marginalized groups (Davis and Perry 2021), and beliefs that emphasize in-group liberty and out-group control (Davis 2019; Perry, Whitehead and Grubbs 2021 Whitehead, Schnabel and Perry 2021), we anticipated that Christian nationalism would prioritize rights historically linked to ideas of "liberty' by dominant majorities while deprioritizing rights that grant protections and subversive liberties to those outside of structural positions power. Our findings largely confirm our hypotheses. Christian nationalism was among the strongest predictors that Americans would prioritize 'conservative rights' (freedom of religion, gun rights, states' rights) either separately or together, while deprioritizing rights like freedom of speech (past a certain threshold), the press, right to speedy and fair trial, and protection from unlawful

searches or seizures. Lastly Christian nationalism was also the strongest predictor Americans view voting as a 'privilege' rather than a 'right.'

Our findings extend research on Americans' understandings of 'rights' as well as research investigating Christian nationalism in several important ways. First and foremost, the data clearly and consistently indicate that Americans' divergent views on whether to prioritize certain rights over others, or even to define certain civic activities as 'rights,' are not solely determined by political ideology, but also by beliefs that center 'Christianity' within America's deep story and future. Indeed, Christian nationalism was often a stronger predictor than conservative political ideology in its influence. In terms of religious factors shaping Americans' views about civil rights, Christian nationalism was almost always more substantively important than religious tradition and most often contributed more substantively than religious service attendance. Why is this the case? As work on 'public religious expression' has argued, Christian nationalism represents a fundamentally different religious dynamic than personal religious identity or religiosity that is ultimately related to broader social order and power (Delehanty et al. 2019; Perry and Whitehead 2022; Stewart et al. 2018). In line with prior research from Whitehead and Perry (2020) we also found that indicators of personal religiosity exhibit opposite directional associations to Christian nationalism when both are included in the model. This suggests that while religious commitment is often associated with conservative or reactionary political views, it is likely Christian nationalist ideology that accounts for that association. Once we hold that influence constant, our results indicate that religious commitment can exhibit a more liberalizing tendency.

Why does Christian nationalism relate to 'rights' in a way that political ideology does not? Christian nationalism is fundamentally about American cultural membership and who rightfully deserves access to citizenship and civic participation. To those Americans who subscribe to Christian nationalism, 'rights' are intended to protect 'our' liberties, not those of deviants, usurpers, outsiders, or those who are 'unworthy' (Perry, Whitehead, et al. 2022). Yet Christian nationalism is also clearly different from 'conservative' political ideology in that both remain powerfully significant predictors of emphasizing various rights. Though Christian nationalism is certainly a form of conservatism, it is possible that Christian nationalism captures a more explicit, reactionary 'us vs. them' dynamic in American politics compared to the singleitem measure of political ideology on its own. 10

An issue that is worth mentioning is that the associations were generally consistent across racial identity and gender. In contrast with numerous other studies (e.g., Armaly et al. 2022; Gorski and Perry 2022; Perry, Cobb, et al. 2022; Perry and Whitehead 2019), supplementary analyses showed black and white Americans did not diverge sharply in their patterns of association between Christian nationalism and political attitudes. And only Hispanics showed minor slope differences from whites. Meanwhile, the associations for men and women were largely the same except that Christian nationalist men were slightly more likely to prioritize 'conservative' rights than their women counterparts. Though enough research has shown that Christian nationalism's influence is often racialized and gendered, it is also common that various

outcomes in such studies did not necessarily yield the same patterns. In this case, the issue may be due to smaller samples of racial minorities in the samples reducing the possibility of statistically significant interaction effects. Alternatively, the reason may also simply be that Christian nationalism's influence on how Americans prioritize and deprioritize various 'rights' is more uniform in its tendency to elevate the rights that bolster in-group liberty and deprioritize 'subversive' protections and rights. To our knowledge, research looking at Christian nationalism and the rights of gender or sexual minorities has never found a moderating effect of race or gender, and thus, we may simply be witnessing a similar pattern here (Whitehead and Perry 2015, 2019, 2020).

Some data limitations should be acknowledged in order to chart a path for future research. First, the key variables come from Wave 8 of the PDES, making the analysis crosssectional. As such we are unable to establish temporal precedent and strong causal claims must be made with caution. It is conceivable that Americans who hold certain views on fundamental rights are more inclined to favor political theologies like Christian nationalism that justify their prioritization (e.g., religious liberty). Though we would argue that our assumed causal ordering (Christian nationalism influencing the prioritization of certain rights over others) is more plausible and has more precedent in research, we acknowledge the possibility of bidirectional relationships.

Second, and as previously acknowledged, the structure of the dependent variables listed here do not allow us to explore the nuanced dimensions of why respondents believe their 'most important' right should be prioritized. Individuals' understanding of civic rights are often more heavily influenced by cultural interpretations and frames situated within a complex array of personal memories and in-group out-group sentiments, rather than legal definitions and precedent (Chong 1993; Chong and Druckman 2007). Survey data, and especially that which is cross-sectional, is often ill-equipped to fully capture this nuance, and to explore contextual or cultural frames with appropriately rich data. We therefore urge future research to explore the relationships between religious and national identities with attitudes towards fundamental rights in more qualitative ways. Future studies would also ideally make use of temporal and experimental methods to order to establish causal direction more definitively. Finally, future studies could inquire about other 'rights' issues that currently divide Americans, such as abortion rights, health care, welfare, privacy, and education. Though we have focused on more fundamental rights (voting, free speech, and religious liberty), many other opportunities and 'entitlements' would be worth examining.

Our findings have particular relevance amidst the current political discussions about gun rights following numerous mass shootings, transgender rights, the fall of Roe, and increasing voter restrictions throughout the country. We have shown that Christian nationalist ideology seems to incline Americans toward authoritarian and anti-democratic views of 'rights' that prioritize in-group liberty, such as freedom of religion (ours, not theirs, see Perry, Schnabel, et al. 2022), gun rights, and states' rights. It also tends to deprioritize the rights and protections that either facilitate criticism of government leaders (free speech, free press, and voting rights) or limit the governments' ability to suppress problem populations (right to speedy and fair trial, protection from unlawful searches and seizures). Given these patterns, we would expect Christian nationalism's role in contemporary debates over abortion, guns, and voter access to favor the liberty of historical majority groups (whites, conservative Christians, cisgender persons, and men) and to limit the rights of racial, religious, sexual, and gender minorities.

## 1 Introduction


People with disabilities are employed at far lower rates than people without disabilities. When recessions occur, they typically experience a sharper decline in employment, and during economic recoveries, their employment typically recovers more slowly. Recent analyses, however, have indicated that the covid recession and recovery were different: that employment among people with disabilities declined only proportionately when covid hit and recovered faster than it did among people without disabilities (Ne'eman & Maestas, 2023). This good news raises questions about the extent to which people with different types of disabilities experienced the narrowing in the employment gap.

People with intellectual disabilities have historically been especially stigmatized, though attitudes toward people with intellectual disabilities have improved since people with intellectual disabilities moved out of institutions and into the community with the closure in the last part of the 20 th century of many state institutions where they had been segregated (Dell'Armo & Tassé, 2021).

The Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) of 2014 (Public Law 113-128) amended the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 to call for maximizing opportunities for subminimum wage earners to achieve competitive integrated employment at least at minimum wage. Segregated vocational services reduce the potential for future positive outcomes toward competitive integrated employment, and integrated vocational service models incorporating strategies such as supported and customized employment lead to improved outcomes in economics, quality of life, and mental health (Taylor et al., 2023).

Under Section 14(c) of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, an employer may nevertheless pay below federal minimum wage to people with disabilities if the employer holds a 14(c) certificate from the US Department of Labor.

Recent reports by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) have identified structural and policy barriers to transitioning to competitive integrated employment (Government Accountability Office, 2021) and have recommended increasing timely oversight over 14(c) programs (Government Accountability Office, 2023). Almost all people in 14(c) programs have an intellectual/developmental disability (Government Accountability Office, 2023).

The US Commission on Civil Rights has recommended that 14(c) be repealed (US Commission on Civil Rights, 2000). Fifteen states have enacted legislation since 2015 to phase out subminimum wage and 14(c) (Christensen, 2024). It has recently been reported that the US Department of Labor has submitted a rule for review by the White House Office of Management and Budget to tighten reporting and enforcement of 14(c) programs and possibly phase them out altogether (Alemany & Beard, 2024).

Subminimum wage programs have been extremely controversial. Their promoters typically argue that they provide productive work and socialization for people who could not otherwise work. Their detractors typically decry the segregation experienced by people employed at subminimum wage in 14(c) programs and note that people typically work for years in 14(c) without an opportunity to transition to competitive integrated employment (possibly with support) notwithstanding WIOA's expectation of such a goal.

## 2 Materials and Methods


All analyses used R 4.2.1 (R Core Team, 2024), with code and data at https://github.com/acobolew/disability-employment


## 2.1 American Community Survey Employment Data


I downloaded employment data, by type of disability (or lack of disability) and state (including DC and Puerto Rico) from the American Community Survey via the US Census API, from the year of the 2010 decennial census through the most recent data available (2023). I calculated employment rate, by year, disability type, and state, as the number of people employed divided by the sum of people employed, unemployed, and not in labor force. For each disability type, I calculated employment ratio as employment rate divided by employment rate for people with no disability. For every derived quantity I also calculated standard errors using the margin-of-errors for a derived quantity as recommended by the Census Bureau and implemented in R package tidycensus (Walker & Herman, 2024). Due to low response rate, the Census Bureau did not publish data on the target variables for 2020.


## 2.2 Department of Labor 14(c) Subminimum Wage Data


For data on 14(c) Community Rehabilitation Programs I downloaded all data directly available from the US Department of Labor Wage and Hour Division website, with availability starting October 2021. To access data from before this date I also downloaded all unique data releases from archive.org. The URLs are at https://github.com/acobolew/disability-employment, as are Excel files containing the downloaded data. Number of programs was available starting in January 2010, and number of people employed at subminimum wage was available starting in October 2015. (Because there were periods when the Department of Labor processed applications particularly slowly, I calculated number of programs as the sum of current and pending.) Department of Labor data includes the jurisdictions included in the ACS as well as Guam. To calculate per-capita rate of people paid subminimum wage I divided the number of such people by census population estimates (which excluded Guam). Because census population estimates by state were available only through 2023, I also used 2023 estimates in 2024. ## 3 Results



## 3.1 American Community Survey Employment Data


From 2010 to 2023, employment rose in every disability classification: hearing, vision, cognitive, ambulatory, self-care, and independent living (Fig. 1A). Furthermore, the long-term trend since 2010 in the employment gap (quantified in Fig. 1B as the employment ratio: employment rate among people with a given disability type divided by employment rate among people with no disability) was that the gap narrowed (employment ratio grew) before the pandemic for people with vision, cognitive, and independent living disabilities, and somewhat for people with hearing disabilities, though the gap widened before the pandemic for people with self-care disabilities. Since the pandemic, the employment gap narrowed for every disability category with the possible exception of self-care disabilities.

The largest rise in employment ratio was for people with cognitive disabilities. From 2010 to 2023, employment among people without disabilities rose from 72.8% to 79.4%, while employment among people with cognitive disabilities rose from 23.4% to 40.6%. The employment ratio for people with cognitive disabilities thus rose from 0.32 to 0.51.

Applying the 2010 versus 2023 rates of employment among people with cognitive disabilities to the 2023 estimate of the number of people with cognitive disabilities in the US, the narrowing in the employment gap amounts to 1.8 million people.

Most, though not all, of the narrowing in the employment gap occurred in 2021 and 2022.

## 4 Discussion


For all disability types in the ACS classification, employment ratio improved, with the possible exception of people with self-care disabilities. The post-pandemic improvement was especially large and accelerating for people with cognitive disabilities, for whom employment gap increased somewhat immediately after the 2014 passage of WIOA before accelerating and increasing dramatically post-pandemic. In particular, the employment ratio for people with cognitive disabilities thus rose from 0.32 to 0.51.

An employment ratio over 0.5 for people with cognitive disabilities is historic. It means that, for the first time in the data record, people with cognitive disabilities are employed at more than half the rate of people with no disability.

The biggest co-variation state-by-state by far is that states with the most subminimum wage jobs per capita saw the largest per-capita decrease in such jobs. Viewed across almost a decade, no state increased subminimum wage jobs.

Over this long term, number of people paid subminimum wage fell even in states that, more recently, increased the number of people paid subminimum wage. For example, in Missouri the number of people per 100k population paid subminimum wages in 14(c) CRP programs fell from about 130 in 2015 down to about 25 in 2021 before rebounding and then plateauing around 55.

These patterns suggest that WIOA's promotion of competitive integrated employment, by itself, may have been modestly successful, but that the post-pandemic labor market may have created significant opportunities for competitive integrated employment of all people with disabilities, but especially for people with cognitive disabilities-over and above increased employment among people without disabilities. As labor market conditions shift, it will be important to consolidate these gains and use successful work placement settings as a model for future initiatives to promote competitive integrated employment.

For example, the Rehabilitation Services Administration (RSA) has awarded five-year grants for the federal fiscal year 2022 Disability Innovation Fund demonstration project to provide 14 state vocational rehabilitation agencies with funding to implement Subminimum Wage to Competitive Integrated Employment (SWTCIE) Innovative Model Demonstration projects, informed by a systematic review of the evidence base (Luhur et al., 2023). RSA and the model demonstration projects should consider engaging in a mid-point review to ensure they are taking advantage of the opportunities provided by the post-pandemic rise in employment ratio for people with cognitive disabilities. Taking advantage of these opportunities is especially important to ensure that transition to competitive integrated employment is successful.

Gains in overall disability employment post-pandemic have been concentrated in teleworkable, essential, and non-frontline occupations (Ne'eman & Maestas, 2023), and people with cognitive/mental health impairments (as well as mobility impairments) were most likely to telework during the pandemic (Ameri et al., 2023). It is worth growing the evidence base on the extent to which people who might otherwise be employed in sheltered workshops could benefit from telework options and accommodations.

While there remains a large employment gap for persons with cognitive disabilities, it has narrowed dramatically post-pandemic. Research to inform public policy and hiring and retention practices by all employers should take advantage of this. The country has invested in employerfocused research and training centers (Center for Disability-Inclusive Employment Policy Research, Grant #90RTEM0006-01-00, Funded by National Institutes on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research, n.d.; Employer Practices Leading to Successful Employment Outcomes Among People with Disabilities, Grant #90RTEM0008-01-00, Funded by National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research, n.d.), and the long range plan of the National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research continues a focus on building the evidence base for employers to successfully hire, retain, and promote people with disabilities (National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research, 2024). ## Reproducibility: A key measure of how scientific a field is 212

This macroscopic perspective derived from an analysis of the ways thousands of 213 archaeologists communicate their research has produced a complex picture of archaeology 214 as a science. In the context of a broad spectrum of other research areas, archaeologists 215 behave like social scientists. ## Introduction


High voter turnout is commonly seen as a sign of democratic health, as it is indicative of an active and engaged citizenry. Many scholars also believe that more widespread electoral participation is the most effective way to equalize voting rates across different segments of society (Tingsten 1937; Lijphart 1997).

In the past decades, many countries have therefore strived to increase turnout by making voting more convenient and less costly for their citizens, for instance by introducing expanded opportunities for early in-person voting, or ballot submission by mail or proxy. The central idea behind these convenience reforms is that lower barriers to voting will lead to a larger and more socially representative electorate (Gronke et al. 2008). But do these policies actually have the desired effect? Whereas most scholars seem to agree that the enactment of various convenience reforms is likely to raise overall turnout, the alleged equalizing impact of these reforms has been subject to debate (Alvarez and Nagler 2000; Southwell and Burchett 2000; Berinsky 2005; Gerber et al. 2013).

Drawing on Campbell's (1960) classic distinction between 'core' and 'peripheral' voters, Berinsky (2005) claims that reforms designed to make voting more convenient will actually decrease, rather than increase, the social representativeness of the electorate. The reason for this, he argues, is that easy voting procedures provide a means for more resourceful and engaged citizens ('core' voters) to insure against different idiosyncratic shocks that can hamper the propensity of election day voting. That is, 'sometimes even the most engaged and interested citizens will fail to cast their vote on the election day because they are sick, the weather is bad, they have missed the registration deadline, they have moved or they are called out of town unexpectedly on business' (Berinsky 2005, 477). A key feature of various convenience voting procedures is that they can be used to offset the impact of haphazard events such as these. However, according to Berinsky (2005), available empirical evidence indicates that it is primarily 'core' voters who will take advantage of this opportunity. And since 'core' voters tend to have higher incomes and education levels than 'peripheral' voters (cf., Bhatti et al. 2019a), reforms aimed at making voting more convenient may therefore actually exacerbate the socioeconomic bias in the composition of the electorate.

This conclusion, is however, questioned in a quasi-experimental study by Gerber et al. (2013). By analyzing the staggered implementation of all-mail elections in the state of Washington, the authors find that the reform increased participation more 'among registrants who rarely vote than among registrants who often vote' (Gerber et al. 2013, 92).

In this study, we seek to shed new light on this important debate using Swedish data to examine the extent to which different socioeconomic groups take advantage of the opportunity of early voting when faced with the risk of not being able to vote on election day. More precisely, we focus on the uncertainty associated with expecting a child around the time of the election, and analyze whether 'core' voters are more likely to react to this uncertainty by voting in advance than are 'peripheral' voters.

In so doing, we advance the existing literature in at least two regards. First, to our knowl-

edge, we are the first to provide a direct empirical test of the theoretical mechanism proposed by (Berinsky 2005). Second, unlike many previous studies, such as that of Gerber et al. (2013), our study is situated in a context where postal voting (in advance) is used as a complement, rather than as a substitute, to traditional election day voting.

Our main findings are as follows. First, in line with previous studies on the impact of childbirth on turnout (cf., Bhatti et al. 2019b; Cools 2022; Kam et al. 2022), we find that receiving a child close to the election day reduces turnout. Second, and more importantly, this effect is mainly due to lower turnout among parents that have a looser attachment to the electorate. Specifically, 'core' voter-measured either as having a higher education, or as being more likely to vote in 'low salience' elections-are considerably more likely to compensate for childbirth by casting an early vote. We thus find support for the theoretical mechanism hypothesized by Berinsky (2005).

Although our analysis studies one type of obstacle to election-day voting, namely having a baby on or close to election day, we argue that the results can be generalized to other similar events that voters' cannot control but know of in advance, such as having to work on election day, planned healthcare procedures, or childcare responsibilities. Our results indicate that such barriers give rise to a 'double inequality' as 'peripheral' voters are not only less likely to vote, but also less likely to circumvent obstacles to voting on election day by casting an early vote.


## Institutional setting and empirical design


The choice of situating our study in Sweden is not only motivated by access to high quality administrative data, but also by how voting in Swedish elections is carried out. First, elections are held on Sundays to reduce the cost of voting for the majority of citizens who work on weekdays. Second, voters have the possibility to cast an in-person early vote as early as 18 days before the election day in any polling station intended for early voting. Sweden thus has one of Europe's most generous possibilities to vote early (Lindskog 2020). If early voting decreases voting inequality, then we should see it in Sweden, more than in other democratic countries.

Voter turnout in Sweden has been high for the past couple of decades. The 2002 elections saw the lowest turnout rates since the 1950s at just above 80 percent, and around 30 percent of those were early votes (see Table 1). In the 2010 election, the year under study in this paper, the turnout rate was slightly above 82 percent, and almost 40 percent of the voters cast an early vote.


## Childbirth as an exogenously given shock to voting costs


To examine how the propensity to cast an early vote is affected by a voter's inability to cast a vote on election day, we must identify voters who face such an obstacle. Importantly, the event (obstacle) that we study cannot be related to voters' underlying propensity to turnout to vote. For instance, if less educated individuals are more likely to work (long shifts) on election day,

One such exogenous event is childbirth. We consider the closeness of the day of birth to the election day as randomly assigned, and unrelated to other practical voting costs across voter groups. Parents are in practice unable to affect the timing of the birth: childbirth occurring on or close to the election day can therefore be considered a random 'negative shock' to the ability to cast an on-election day vote. 1 We use this random variation to examine how the turnout gap between lower and higher educated voters is affected by births that happen close to the election day.


## Individual-level turnout data


In this study, we employ individual-level voter turnout data from the 2010 general elections in Sweden. These data stem from digitized election voter rolls in Sweden and covers about 95 percent of the total electorate (Lindgren et al. 2019). The voter rolls contain information on whether each citizen voted or not in the three elections held on election day (national, county, and municipality). For those who voted, there is information on whether they voted on election day, or whether they cast an early vote. The register data also include information on all citizens' birthdays, as well as links between parents and their children. The use of register data has a large advantage over survey data, as people tend to overreport participation in surveys, and survey data rarely produces large enough subsamples of respondents who voted early, to adequately address differences within this group (Stein and Vonnahme 2010).

For each parent, we construct a measure of the distance, in days, between the day of childbirth and the election day in 2010. Using this measure, we group births in seven-days intervals, where the week before the election day-between the election day and six days before the election day-is referred to as the election week . 2 We categorize births in weekly intervals to avoid overly large variation in turnout rates between different days, as the estimates would

## Empirical methods and descriptive statistics


For our empirical analysis, we construct a turnout variable equal to 1 if the parent participated in the election, 0 otherwise; for those who voted we construct a variable indicating whether they cast an early or an election-day vote. Matching the data on the timing of births relative to the election week with the turnout data allows us to estimate separate turnout rates for each group of births, from -12 to 12 weeks after the election day. We estimate these rates separately for 'core' and 'peripheral' voters.

To separate between 'core' and 'peripheral' voters we use two strategies: First, we distinguish between lower and higher educated parents (Bhatti et al. 2019a), using a dummy variable indicating whether the parents' highest attained education level is above a high school diploma, or not. In Sweden the positive association between level of education and voter turnout is of average strength compared to other advanced industrial democracies (Gallego 2010). Second, following Campbell's (1960) suggestion that 'peripheral' voters tend not to vote in less salient second-order elections, we distinguish between parents who did or did not vote in the European Parliament (EP) elections (Reif and Schmitt 1980) in the preceding year (2009). Thus, we can compare the turnout gap between 'core' and 'peripheral' voters for those who gave birth on the election week to the same gap for those who gave birth on other weeks.

Consequently, the existing turnout gap between these groups widens further by the inequality in early voting among voters who face obstacles to voting on election day. One issue remains: can we be certain that the gap really widens due to the difference in early voting pick-up rates? What would the gap have been in the absence of early voting possibilities? If instead on-election day voting among 'peripheral' voters is more negatively affected by election week childbirth, then we cannot rule out that early voting possibilities actually help to narrow the gap that would otherwise have been even wider.
