## 4.5 Robustness checks


The main results are tested for robustness using a somewhat different selecƟon of families from the data by selecƟng only selected children whose parents have two or more known siblings (are from families of at least three children), so that all parents in the analyses are at risk for having at least 2 sibling deaths. This results in the selecƟon of 199,060 children (a reducƟon of 18,249 children or about 8 percent). Results can be found in the Supplementary Material (Table S4) and are almost idenƟcal to the analyses presented here. Next, I include sibling mortality as a proporƟon of the number of children in the family of origin of the parents. Results are in Table S5. Effects are somewhat stronger in this single indicator of childhood mortality among the siblings of the parents, but results are similar: increased mortality for children whose mothers and fathers came from a high-childhood-mortality family, with stronger effects for mothers than fathers, and effects that persist over Ɵme. These models are not chosen as the main model as they are less intuiƟve in their interpretaƟon and the proporƟon of child deaths depends on the number of siblings that mothers and fathers have.


## 5. Conclusion and discussion


Child  mortality  was  distributed  unequally  between  families,  and  this  inequality  persisted  between generaƟons in historical the Netherlands. Analyses based on full populaƟon family reconsƟtuƟon data (LINKS) for a province in the Netherlands, Zeeland, 1835-1919 show that both socioeconomic status and parents' families' level of child mortality contribute to the risk of child death before age 5. Children of mothers and fathers who experienced a larger number of sibling child deaths had an increased risk of death before their own fiŌh birthday. Importantly, intergeneraƟonal persistence of child mortality is not driven by social class of parents or grandparents. InequaliƟes accumulate, as low-SES families of which both parents originated from high mortality families had the highest level of mortality.

Like earlier authors, I show that there is a social gradient in child mortality in the period studied. Higher socioeconomic status groups had lower child mortality than unskilled and lower-skilled workers. Effects are largely similar over Ɵme, except for lower skilled workers, among whom mortality becomes even higher than among unskilled workers in the last two periods studied here. In historical the Netherlands, social  mobility  was  low  (Knigge  2016)  so  that  low  SES  across  generaƟons  could  contribute  to  the intergeneraƟonal  persistence  of  child  mortality.  Yet,  high  risk  of  child  death  is  not  explained  by socioeconomic  characterisƟcs  of  the  family  in  which  a  child  grows  up,  nor  their  grandparents' socioeconomic status.

However, there is a correlaƟon between grandparental socioeconomic status and grandchild hazard of mortality before age 5, even aŌer controlling for socioeconomic status of the household in which the child grows up,  using occupaƟon of the father. Grandparental effects on grandchildren, for example social  status  aƩainment  of  grandchildren,  have  in  the  past  been  interpreted  as  a  broad  effect  of grandparental resources and social networks on grandchildren (Mare and Song 2023; Knigge 2016). Such studies  have  shown  that  socioeconomic  factors  affect  social  status  aƩainment  not  just  over  one generaƟon - father to child - but also over several generaƟons of relaƟves - grandfather to grandchild (Dribe and Helgertz 2016). Such effects persist even if grandparents and children never met nor if the compeƟƟon over grandparental resources is larger, so that such residual effects of socioeconomic status can point to imprecisely measured socioeconomic status effects that work through resources of the family of origin of the child (Helgertz and Dribe 2022). If only the occupaƟon of the father is included, unexplained variance because of measurement error could be captured by grandparental measurements  of  social  status  (Engzell,  Mood,  and  Jonsson  2020).  Similarly,  the  contribuƟon  of grandparents' social  status  to  grandchild  survival,  aŌer  considering  the  socioeconomic  status  of  the

parents, may be related to imprecise measurements of parents' SES. Yet, grandparents could also have contributed resources, knowledge and help in Ɵmes of need. Further research should establish what drives this relaƟonship.

Over Ɵme, child mortality declined strongly in the Netherlands. IntergeneraƟonal transmission effects are  found  even  when  child  mortality  had  declined  strongly,  parƟcularly  for  women.  For  mothers  to children, effects remained largely similar over Ɵme, with increased mortality parƟcularly for children of mothers originaƟng from families where several child deaths occurred among their siblings. This finding implies that even among women with the strongest disadvantage - in terms of both a low socioeconomic status  and  elevated  mortality  in  their  household  of  origin  -  the  absolute  risk  of  losing  their  young children decreased over Ɵme. Yet, compared to other families in the populaƟon, these women and their children  remained  at  the  strongest  disadvantage  over  Ɵme.  For  fathers,  the  magnitude  of  the intergeneraƟonal effect declined when child mortality rates decreased, parƟcularly for more average experiences of sibling mortality (e.g. loss of one or two siblings in childhood).

It  is  unclear  why  the  intergeneraƟonal persistence  of child  mortality  is  stronger  from  mother  to her children than from father to his children. Commonly, studies invesƟgaƟng persistence of social status find the opposite: a stronger intergeneraƟonal persistence from father to son or daughter than from mother  to  son  or  daughter  (Dribe  and  Helgertz  2016),  although  some  work  has  shown  a  stronger influence  of  maternal economic parƟcipaƟon on her daughter's than sons' status aƩainment (BreaMarƟnez 2023). In this work, a higher hazard raƟo of mortality is observed for children whose mothers came from high-mortality households than for children whose fathers originated from high mortality households.  A  possible  reason  is  the  larger  role  for  women  in  caretaking  of  children  in  this  period (Janssens 1997), and possibly, girls learned child-care pracƟces such as unsuitable feeding pracƟces in the household of origin and used these for their own children (Das Gupta 1990). The possible help of grandmothers,  for  example  aŌer  childbirth  or  when  children  were  sick,  could  be  gendered,  and  a previous literature has established that in some contexts the help of a mother's own mother could make a  crucial  difference  for  child  survival  in  historical  Europe  (Sear  and  Mace  2008).  In  families  where grandmothers raised their children in unfavorable condiƟons, indicated by her own high child loss, they may neither have had the health nor knowledge to assist their daughters and daughters in law with the care of their grandchildren - and instead, their outdated knowledge or own need of help may have been a burden on their daughters and daughters in law.

Studying  the  Ɵme-trend  in  intergeneraƟonal  persistence  of  high  mortality  shows  the  long-term development in equality of opportunity. Over Ɵme, high mortality in the families of origin of the mother and father show a persistent correlaƟon to the mortality hazard of young children, despite sibling child deaths becoming less common. Thus, intergeneraƟonal persistence of high child mortality is a clear marker of inequality in historical the Netherlands. To study such intergeneraƟonal inequaliƟes in other contexts, such as contemporarily developed socieƟes, it is essenƟal to study mortality over a broader age range as mortality at young ages contemporarily tends to be mercifully low. In children's health, however, broader paƩerns of intergeneraƟonal persistence may sƟll be a key indicator of inequality in the standard of living.

There are some drawbacks to this study. First, the staƟsƟcal analysis relied on data originaƟng from linked indexes of civil cerƟficates. Individuals are not conƟnuously observed in registers, as they would with, for example, a church or state populaƟon register. Although earlier work has shown that for this area and  period  the  resulƟng  life  course  and  family  reconstrucƟons  generally  reflect  the  result  from conƟnuous populaƟon register data (van den Berg et al. 2021), important characterisƟcs of individuals and  their  families  are  not  included  in  these  linked  vital  event  data,  including  religion,  migraƟon movements,  and  household  income.  Second,  families  across  Zeeland  have  been  included,  so  that

regional migrants - who moved for marriage or work opportuniƟes, but not over long distances - can be tracked. SpaƟal and geographic differences in inequality in child deaths over Ɵme were not included in this work. The local condiƟons for children to grow up in could have been quite different between places  of  residence,  given  that  Zeeland  consists  of  islands  with  somewhat  different  economic opportuniƟes and physical limitaƟons such as access to safe drinking water. Together, the reasons for accumulaƟon  of  high  child  mortality  across  generaƟons  beyond  poverty  and  socioeconomic  status remain therefore somewhat of a black box. Yet, as was argued previously, the overall accumulaƟon of inequaliƟes in the likelihood of early child death across Ɵme is an important indicator of families' relaƟve standard of being and inequality in opportunity in socieƟes.

In a previous study of intergeneraƟonal persistence in child mortality, Lu and Vogl (Lu and Vogl 2023) argue  that  studying  the  topic  of  child  concentraƟon  in  mortality  is  important  to  study  inequality  in bereavement. I argue here that it is important to study intergeneraƟonal persistence as an indicator of inequality in mortality itself. Some families are more likely to experience child mortality and to have poor health. This phenomenon should not solely be invesƟgated from a socioeconomic perspecƟve (the social gradient  in  mortality)  or  in  relaƟon  to  other  social  and  socioeconomic  indicators  but  is  worthy  of aƩenƟon and a measurement of inequality in the living standard and the distribuƟon of mortality in itself.  Addressing  the  trend  in  intergeneraƟonal  persistence  in  mortality,  and  differences  between contexts, serves as a measurement of inequality between places and over Ɵme.

In conclusion, intergeneraƟonal persistence of (high) mortality, as shown in this work, highlights the lack of opportunity for children to achieve a long life already at the Ɵme of their birth, given in which family they were born. IntergeneraƟonal persistence in young age mortality is of pressing importance as it eradicates opportuniƟes for individuals to live a long and healthy life before their lives have even fully started. This paper shows evidence that there was inequality of opportunity in young-age survival which persisted over Ɵme in 19 th and early 20 th century the Netherlands. Whether this trend conƟnued later in the 20 th and 21 st century and whether it generalizes to mortality at older ages or health of children are important avenues for future research.

## Introduction


The Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka is an island situated in the Indian Ocean, just off the southernmost tip of India. Sri Lanka has a long democratic tradition dating back to its independence from Britain in 1948, and currently has a parliamentary democracy with an executive president. In 2009, the government defeated the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), a separatist terrorist organization, ending a 26-year civil war and ushering in a new era of economic growth.

Despite ending a protectionist economic regime in 1977, Sri Lanka remains a strongly socialist state and provides free state sponsored education and healthcare to all its citizens. 1 Sri Lanka boasts an overall adult literacy rate of 98.5% and a female literacy rate of 90.7%. 2 However, the nation still struggles with gender equality in the workplace, with an adult female labor force participation rate of only 36.4% in 2019. 3 Sri Lanka's relationship with gender equality is thus complex - for example, the nation elected the world's first female prime minister in 1960, yet women only made up 5.3% of the Sri Lankan parliament in 2020. 4

<!-- image -->

An estimated 47.1% of Sri Lanka's employed population is engaged in the service sector. 5 It is also estimated that 57.4% of Sri Lanka's employed population works in the informal sector. 6 Such a distribution of employment skewed in favor of the informal sector presents a challenge for the enforcement of labor laws.

Given its relatively poor results in Sub-Index A, and the country's even more disappointing performance in Sub-Index B, Sri Lanka places in the 'Emerging' band for the GCPI with a total score of 3.42.


## Key Care Policies


The Labor Code of Sri Lanka consists of chapters that cover different sectors of the labor force, and cumulatively aim to cover all workers in formal employment. Among these chapters, the Shop and Office Employees Act regulates the remuneration and working conditions of all employees working in shops or offices, while the Establishment Code regulates the employment conditions of public sector servants in particular. Domestic workers, as privately employed individuals working outside of shops or offices, are not able to access the protections provided by either of these laws.

Buttressing these two major laws are more specific laws - the Factories Ordinance that governs the rights of factory workers, and the Maternity Benefits Ordinance which regulates maternity leave. The Maternity Benefits Ordinance is the baseline legislation that applies to all females engaged in a trade for pay, but excluding those employed on a casual basis or within shops and offices. Both the Shop and Office Employees Act and the Establishment Code contain sections on maternity benefit provisions for the workers they apply to. Though the Maternity Benefits Ordinance does not explicitly exclude domestic workers, it is only intended to apply to workers employed in a 'trade.' This ambiguity means that the law could exclude domestic workers since a 'trade' refers to a commercial undertaking happening outside of a private household. 7

Sri Lanka's social welfare schemes provide comprehensive welfare to most workers in formal employment. Welfare benefits are accrued via two main methods -the Employee's Provident Fund through which the government and employers contribute towards employee pensions, and the

Employees Trust Fund which provides death, injury, and other benefits to member employees. Sri Lanka also provides free healthcare to all its citizens, which has ensured that the entire poorest 40% of the population spends less than USD4 per month on average, or less than 2.5% of their total household expenditures, on health-related matters. 8


## Key Actors


The Department of Labor (DOL) in Sri Lanka is tasked with implementing labor legislations passed by the Sri Lankan Government. The DOL enforces laws regarding workplace safety and employee rights, but also works to resolve industrial disputes. Following recent incidents of violence against domestic workers, the State Minister of Labor announced that new regulations would be introduced to better regulate domestic service. 9

The Ministry of Women and Child Development is mainly engaged in improving the socioeconomic opportunities of women, improving education for children, and protecting both women and children from abuse. 10

The Domestic Workers' Union (DWU) has historically been engaged in protests against incidents of violence against domestic workers. The DWU has demanded the formalization of domestic work, and the introduction of a formal complaint mechanism whereby domestic workers can report misdemeanors by their employers. 11


## Recent Care Policy Developments


Prior to 2018, the duration of maternity leave that a Sri Lankan working woman was entitled to was dependent on how many living children she already had. If she had fewer than two living children at the time of childbirth, then she would be afforded 12 weeks of paid maternity leave. But, as part of the government's population planning measures, if the woman already had two or more children, she would

only be afforded 6 weeks of paid leave. This idiosyncrasy was removed from law in 2018, and now all mothers whose labor results in a live baby are entitled to 12 weeks of paid leave. Parallel amendments to the Shop and Office Employees Act also introduced mandatory nursing breaks per 9-hour work period for all mothers nursing children under the age of one.

Aside from this development, Sri Lanka's care policies for family caregivers have largely remained stagnant. In 2006, a Public Administration Circular granted male state employees 3 days of paternity leave upon the birth of their child. However, subsequent momentum stalled: paternity leave was not extended to the private sector, nor was the duration of state sector paternity leave subsequently increased. In the 2019 budget, a proposal for the state to partially fund maternity leave benefit payments in the private sector through tax deductions was included. However, the follow-up actions to gazette and implement the proposal were not taken.


## Key Events


On July 15th 2021, a 16-year-old girl who was employed as a domestic worker died of severe burn injuries. The girl had been employed at a prominent Sri Lankan Member of Parliament's residence. Subsequent investigations showed that the underage domestic worker had been a victim of long-term sexual assault. At the time of writing this report, investigations have not yet revealed whether the death was a suicide or a manslaughter by her employers. The event highlighted the prevalence of underage domestic work in Sri Lanka, and the dangers associated with unregulated domestic service.

Sri Lankan legislators are in the process of amending laws in response to this tragic event. Firstly, the State Minister for Women and Child Development stated that a Cabinet paper is being prepared to raise the minimum age of employment to 18. 12 Secondly, the Labor Commissioner of Sri Lanka announced that the government's list of hazardous jobs is to be expanded to include domestic service. 13

This measure would outlaw anyone under the age of 18 from being employed in domestic service. Thirdly, the Sri Lankan government announced that it intends to introduce a system for the registration of domestic workers. 14 Finally, the Minister of Labor also announced that the nation's social protection schemes (the Employees' Provident Fund and Employees' Trust Fund) would soon be amended to include domestic workers. 15

<!-- image -->

With an overall score of 3.73 for Sub-Index A, Sri Lanka's protections for family caregivers fall within the 'Emerging' index band of the GCPI. Sri Lanka performs well in providing new mothers with generous breastfeeding breaks, and state healthcare services for mothers are some of the best in South Asia. However, Sri Lankan laws remain outdated in that they have limited recognition of non-female family caregivers, and all maternity leave costs must be borne by the employer rather than being state-subsidized.


## A1Pregnancy and Maternity Leave Coverage (3.61/10)


Sri Lanka guarantees maternity leave to workers in the private sector through the Shop and Office Employees Act and the Maternity Benefits Ordinance. Workers in the state sector are offered maternity benefits through Section XII of the Establishment Code. All categories of employees are guaranteed 84 days (12 weeks) of fully paid maternity leave. This fulfills Sri Lanka's obligations under the ILO's C103 convention, but falls short of the 18-week recommended maternity leave set out by R191, the ILO's most recent set of recommendations around maternity protection. A four-week compulsory maternity leave is mandated by the Maternity and Benefits Ordinance and the Establishment Code - however, the Shop and Office Employees Act makes no mention of compulsory postnatal maternity leave. Notably, adoptive mothers in both the public and private sectors have no access to maternity leave protections, as all relevant laws guarantee leave to the mother only in the event of her 'pregnancy' and the 'birth' of her child.


## A2Protections during Pregnancy and Maternity Leave (3.60/10)


Depending on which sector she works in, an eligible female employee is guaranteed a maximum of 100% of her wages during her maternity leave, and a minimum of six-sevenths of her normal wages. However, all maternity leave remuneration costs must be borne by the employer, and are not subsidized by the government. Sri Lanka's model of free state sector healthcare ensures that all mothers are afforded generous prenatal and postnatal care. The Sri Lanka Every Newborn Action Plan (SLENAP), launched in 2017, outlines the government's plans for medical interventions at every stage of maternity. Sri Lanka's maternal healthcare is also strengthened by a strong network of Public Health Midwives (PHMs) who facilitate home deliveries and post-natal check-ups for each mother. However, employment protections to shield female employees from discrimination due to their pregnancy or marital status are inadequate. Under the Maternity Benefits Ordinance, a woman is protected from dismissal for three months commencing from the date of her confinement (childbirth). This Act however only applies to employees in the private sector, and the Establishment Code (which applies to employees in the state sector) does not explicitly prevent employees from dismissal due to pregnancy. Nevertheless, the Establishment Code mandates that maternity leave should not inhibit a female employee's promotion prospects.


## A3Paternity Leave Policies (2.21/10)


Sri Lanka continues to take a traditional approach to paternity leave. Fathers in the public sector are afforded paternity leave of just 3 consecutive days. However, new fathers working in the private sector and adoptive fathers are not guaranteed paternity leave.


## A4DependentCareLeave Policies (7.33/10)


Sri Lankan law does not explicitly guarantee dependent care leave, however, the Shop and Office Employees Act does guarantee seven days of 'Casual leave' every year to each employee. Such leave is fully remunerated and can be used for any purpose, including the care of dependents. Casual leave is granted in addition to the minimum of 14 days of annual holiday leave granted to all employees.


## A5Flexible Work Arrangements (0.50/10)


The Employment of Women, Children, and Young Persons Act limits the number of night-time work shifts that a female employee can be allocated in a month. While this gendered policy may allow female workers with familial responsibilities to be able to see to their duties at home, it fails to accord the same protections to male workers with similar caregiving responsibilities. Sri Lankan labor laws have also not been adapted to account for modern developments in working arrangements such as telecommuting and flexitime.


## A6Mother-Friendly Workplace Policies (5.13/10)


Sri Lankan laws perform well in providing mothers with nursing support in the workplace. Section 12B of the Maternity Benefits Ordinance mandates two nursing intervals in a period of nine hours of work for working mothers. The Ordinance also mandates that employers of a significant number of women in any trade should establish and maintain childcare centers (known in Sri Lanka as crèches) for the children of their employees, provided that these children are under five years of age. However, workplaces are not explicitly required to conduct risk assessments on the working conditions for pregnant employees. The Shop and Office Act and Maternity Benefits Ordinance protect a pregnant woman from engaging in "any such work as may be injurious to her or her child" for three months preceding her confinement. However, parallel legislations do not exist for women in the state sector, and even existing legislations do not protect women during the whole period of their pregnancy.

<!-- image -->


## B1 Coverage under National Labor Laws (0.50/10)


Despite the widespread prevalence of domestic workers in many Sri Lankan households, domestic workers are excluded from almost all of Sri Lanka's labor laws. The only dedicated law for domestic workers is the Domestic Servants Ordinance No. 28 of 1871 - an outdated law which fails to set out any protections of domestic worker rights. Most other workers have their labor rights guaranteed through the Shop and Office Employees Act, which regulates leave, working conditions and remuneration. As

domestic workers do not work in a shop or an office, they are automatically omitted from the protections contained within this Act. The only contemporary labor law which extends its protections to domestic workers is the Industrial Disputes Act. Through this Act, contract disputes between domestic workers and their employees can be addressed. In the past, domestic workers have been able to seek legal redress through this Act, such as in the case of Wijedeera v. Babyhamy, 16 where the courts affirmed the ability of a domestic worker to sue her employer for wrongful termination.


## B2Fair Employment Process (0.00/10)


As domestic workers are effectively not covered under national labor laws, there are no regulations for their contractual agreements, or recruitment and employment processes. While these regulations are mandated in the Shop and Office Employees Act, they do not apply to domestic workers. In general, Sri Lankan domestic workers are recruited via word of mouth. 17 Though private employment agencies for domestic workers do exist, there are no regulations that govern how they may place domestic workers in private homes. Ironically, as Sri Lanka is a large country of origin of migrant domestic workers for the Middle East and Southeast Asian markets, Sri Lanka's Bureau of Foreign Employment Act has extensive regulations on the placement of its native-born domestic workers overseas by private employment agencies.


## B3 Decent Working and Living Conditions (0.29/10)


As domestic workers are excluded from the Shop and Office Employees Act, normal working hours and overtime pay rates are not defined for domestic workers. Domestic workers are also excluded from the regulations on working conditions set out by the Factories Ordinance and the Shop and Office Employees Act. This omission is particularly concerning for live-in domestic workers, whose working conditions overlap with their living conditions. Domestic workers are also not afforded any mandatory annual leave allowances, or daily rest periods. Further, there is no minimum wage for domestic workers in Sri Lanka. For a minimum wage to be set for an industry in Sri Lanka, a Wage Board must

first be established for the trade. 18 As there is no Wage Board for domestic workers, there are almost no legal protections for the remuneration of these employees. The National Minimum Wage Act of 2016 sets a minimum monthly wage of LKR10,000 (~USD50) and a minimum daily wage of LKR400 (~USD2) for all workers - yet explicitly excludes domestic workers from the definition of 'worker,' thus denying them a fair minimum wage. 19


## B4Labor Rights (7.22/10)


All workers in Sri Lanka are afforded the rights to freedom of association and collective bargaining. In addition, the Domestic Workers Union that represents domestic workers is semi-active. However, there are few legislative provisions to ensure that domestic workers have access to formal complaint mechanisms. Section 31B of the Industrial Disputes Act entitles domestic workers to make complaints regarding the termination of their services and poor conditions of work. 20 However, there are no provisions by which the household premises of a domestic worker's employer can be subject to on-site labor inspections.


## B5Protections for Forced/Under-age Domestic Workers (7.58/10)


In Sri Lanka, the minimum age of employment is 16. However, Sri Lanka provides special protections to workers under the age of 18. Section 2 of the (Amended) Employment of Women, Children and Young Persons Act states that "No person shall employ a child in such a manner as to prevent that child from attending school in accordance with provisions of any written law." Therefore, domestic workers under the age of 18 should technically still be able to attend school. Victims of forced labor are also entitled to government support through the National Anti-Human Trafficking Task Force (NAHTTF). 21


## Public Sector Leave


Though Sri Lanka offers public servants a generous leave allocation, various structural factors and social stigma often prevent female state employees from using all their maternity leave. Female state employees are entitled to 84 days of paid leave, 84 days of half-pay leave, and an additional 84 days of unpaid leave. However, most female employees choose to utilize only the first phase of their eligible leave - the 84 days of full-pay leave. Female employees in the state health and education sectors reported a scarcity of replacement employees as a major motivating factor behind this decision. Thus, female state employees report an obligation to return to work after taking their first phase of maternity leave, as opposed to availing their full leave package. 22


## Childcare centers


Though there is a requirement for employers with a significant number of women employees to provide their female employees with childcare centers, there is a lack of data on how many employers comply with this law. Additionally, the term 'significant number of women' has not been clarified, and remains vague enough to avoid legal enforcement. On average, working Sri Lankan women tend to rely on immediate or extended family for childcare support as opposed to formal childcare centers.


## Forced Labor


Though Sri Lanka appears to actively attempt to combat forced labor and child trafficking, the effectiveness of existing government measures is questionable. NGOs report that government investigators did not have adequate facilities or human resources to carry out investigations - investigators lacked transportation facilities, and the Sri Lankan Police lacked facilities to record evidence. 23 Furthermore, while the labor inspectorate is able to inspect factories for forced labor violations, there are no legal provisions for inspections of private households that employ domestic workers. 24 Thus, it is doubtful that the protections contained in the Employment of Women and Children Act can be fully enforced in the context of domestic workers.

Introduction


The number of people in prisons in England and Wales is at an all-time high. As of 1 March 2024, the prison population stood at 88,133: 5% higher than 12 months ago (83,990; Ministry of Justice, 2024). The prison population is projected to grow even further to between 94,600 and 105,800 by 2028 (Ministry of Justice, 2024b). At the same time, the number of prison staff has shrunk. A recent report by the Prison Reform Trust revealed that, compared to 2010, there are 10% fewer frontline prison staff in England and Wales (Prison Reform Trust, 2023). Staff turnover and retention remain ongoing issues, particularly for new employees. In 2023, over half (54%) of the 2,978 prison officers who left the service had been in the role for less than three years, and almost one third (31%) had been in the role for less than a year (HMPPS, 2024). The impact of staffing shortages on prison operations is far-reaching, from a lack of access to work and rehabilitative services for those incarcerated (The Guardian, 2023), to impacts on staff safety and wellbeing (Clements & Kinman, 2020). In what is already a demanding and challenging job, staffing shortages risk tipping the prison sector to breaking point.

Research has explored how different aspects of the work environment impact on correctional staff. One area of enquiry has centered around the influence of procedural justice, or the extent to which employees perceive their workplace as fair. Studies have shown that prison officer perceptions of fair treatment influence important workplace outcomes, such as job satisfaction, job stress, and organizational commitment (Lambert et al., 2007; Lambert, Boateng, et al., 2023; Taxman & Gordon, 2009). A meta-analysis focusing on criminal justice organizations found that procedural justice was a strong predictor of turnover intent (Matz et al., 2014). Furthermore, when prison staff experience procedural justice, studies have shown they are more likely to engage in organizational citizenship behavior (Lambert & Hogan, 2013).

Organizational citizenship behavior can be defined as voluntary contributions from employees that go above and beyond their formal job requirements. Within the wider organizational literature, procedural justice has been consistently associated with organizational citizenship behavior (e.g., Colquitt et al., 2013; Tepper & Taylor, 2003). When employees feel they are treated fairly by their organization, they are more willing to go above and beyond what is required of them at work. Only a couple of studies have linked procedural justice to organizational citizenship behavior among prison officers (Lambert & Hogan, 2013; Nelson & Appel, 2022). In one study, Nelson and Appel (2022) explored the impact of procedural justice on two types of citizenship behavior: individual-targeted citizenship behavior (e.g., willingness to help fellow prison officers) and organization-targeted citizenship behavior (e.g., taking action to improve the organization). They found that procedural justice was most strongly related to organization-targeted citizenship behavior.

Our study extends this line of research in several ways. First, we explore the relationship between two different forms of procedural justice (supervisory procedural justice and organizational justice) and organization-targeted citizenship behavior. Second, we explore the additional influence of officers’ mental wellbeing. Previous research has shown that perceptions of procedural justice are associated with emotional states and mental wellbeing, with procedural justice eliciting positive emotions and procedural injustice eliciting negative emotions (Colquitt et al., 2013). Emotional states have also been shown to mediate the relationship between procedural justice and workplace outcomes, such as compliance with policies (Murphy & Tyler, 2008; Wu et al., 2017) and organizational citizenship behavior (Colquitt et al., 2013). However, no research has explored the link between mental wellbeing and organizational citizenship behavior among prison officers. To test this relationship, we draw on a sample of new prison officers in England and Wales who were recruited via the Unlocked Graduates Leadership Development Programme (Unlocked Graduates, 2022). Understanding how the concepts of procedural justice, mental wellbeing and organizational citizenship behavior relate to each other in a sample of prison officers new to the job will be particularly valuable for addressing the issues of staff turnover and retention.

The paper proceeds as follows. First, we describe the concept of procedural justice and its importance within organizations. We then discuss organizational citizenship behavior and outline the extant research connecting procedural justice with this type of behavior. We then introduce mental wellbeing as a potential mediator of this relationship, before presenting the conceptual map that guides our analyses.


Procedural Justice Within Organizations


Procedural justice theory (PJT) is premised on the idea that people pay close attention to the fairness of the processes through which those with power interact with them (Tyler, 2006). PJT suggests that individuals care not only about the outcomes of decisions made by authority figures, but also about the way those decisions are made (Lind & Tyler, 1988). Most of the extant research on procedural justice has been outward facing, showing that the fairness through which authority figures treat people (usually members of the public) has important effects on a range of socially desirable behaviors, including compliance with the law and cooperation with authorities (Bolger & Walters, 2019; Tyler, 2006; Walters & Bolger, 2019). Within correctional institutions, prison officer use of procedural justice has been linked to lower rates of misconduct amongst people in custody, lower rates of institutional rule-breaking, and lower rates of reoffending after release (Barkworth & Murphy, 2021; Beijersbergen et al., 2015, 2016; Reisig & Mesko, 2009).

A related line of research explores procedural justice within criminal justice organizations (i.e., the extent to which employees feel they are treated fairly and equitably by their organization; Trinkner et al., 2016). A growing body of research has shown that procedurally fair and respectful treatment experienced by criminal justice employees (e.g., police officers, prison officers) influences important workplace outcomes, such as trust in the administration, job satisfaction, organizational commitment, and turnover intent (Donner et al., 2015; Lambert et al., 2007; Lambert, Boateng, et al., 2023; Matz et al., 2014; Taxman & Gordon, 2009; Trinkner et al., 2016). Further, studies have shown that perceptions of procedural justice enhance employees’ self-legitimacy (Akoensi & Tankebe, 2020; Bradford & Quinton, 2014), and increases compliance with organizational rules and policies (Bradford et al., 2014).

########### Organizational Citizenship Behavior

An outcome of procedural justice within organizations that has received less scholarly attention is organizational citizenship behavior, or the act of going ‘above and beyond’ formal, compensated job requirements (Bateman & Organ, 1983). According to Lambert and Hogan (2013), organizational citizenship behavior comprises three key elements: (1) the behavior must be discretionary and based on personal choice (i.e., not required as part of the role); (2) the behavior must benefit the organization, not the individual; and (3) the behavior must not lead to a guaranteed reward or other form of compensation. Examples of organizational citizenship behavior include helping colleagues, participating in activities that are not mandatory or part of the role, and taking action to improve processes within the organization. Research has shown that when employees experience procedural justice within their organization, they are more willing to go above and beyond their formal job requirements to carry out these discretionary actions (Colquitt et al., 2013; Tepper & Taylor, 2003).

Very little research has explored the relationship between procedural justice and organizational citizenship behavior among prison officers. One study using survey data from a private prison in the US found that procedural justice was significantly associated with organizational citizenship behavior (defined as volunteering to help others and to take on additional work; Lambert & Hogan, 2013). Another study conducted in Israeli prisons explored the impact of procedural justice on two types of citizenship behavior: individual-targeted (defined as participants’ willingness to assist fellow prison offers) and organization-targeted (defined as participants’ willingness to take action to improve the organization; Nelson & Appel, 2022). The authors conceptualized organization-targeted citizenship behavior as benefitting the organization directly, and individual-targeted citizenship behavior as having more indirect benefits (Nelson & Appel, 2022). Procedural justice was measured at the commander-level (e.g., “the commander treats all the officers in the shift equally”) and at the organization-level (e.g., “the organization respects officers’ rights”).

The authors found that commander procedural justice was significantly associated with both forms of citizenship behavior (Nelson & Appel, 2022). Organization procedural justice, on the other hand, was only significantly associated with organization-targeted citizenship behavior, and it was found to mediate the relationship between commander procedural justice and organization-targeted citizenship behavior. In a follow-up experiment, commander procedural justice significantly enhanced organization- but not individual-targeted citizenship behavior (Nelson & Appel, 2022). Taken together, these findings suggest that procedural justice is most strongly related to citizenship behaviors related to the organization (as opposed to the individual).

Nelson and Appel (2022) explained these findings using social exchange theory: a paradigm that describes how different kinds of resources can be exchanged in a way that fosters high-quality relationships within organizations (Colquitt et al., 2013). Social exchange theory hinges on the concept of reciprocity. Cropanzano et al. (2017) defined social exchange theory in broad terms as comprising three steps which can take a positive or a negative form. In the positive or desirable condition (1) an initiator provides some kind of benefit towards the recipient, (2) a positive social exchange relationship occurs, (3) the recipient provides some kind of benefit toward the initiator in return. A negative relationship follows the same process but with the initiator harming the recipient at the outset and a negative or undesirable reciprocal relationship forming (Cropanzano et al., 2017).

In other words, social exchange theory suggests that supportive behaviors or fair treatment by an organization or supervisor is a resource that leads employees to reciprocate through positive work behaviors and attitudes (Cropanzano & Mitchell, 2005). In explaining the findings of Nelson and Appel (2022), the authors posited that helping the organization directly is a more deliberate form of reciprocation for procedural justice, which explains the stronger effects of procedural justice on organization-targeted citizenship behavior. Helping colleagues, on the other hand, may only have indirect benefits for the organization. In the current study, consistent with the social exchange perspective, we measure organization-targeted citizenship behavior, viewing it as an exchangeable resource given by prison officers in response to fair treatment.


Connecting Procedural Justice, Mental Wellbeing and Organizational Outcomes


In attempting to explain the relationship between procedural justice and positive workplace behaviors, scholars have considered mental wellbeing as a possible mediator. First, in relation to social exchange theory, Colquitt and colleagues (2013, p. 204) highlighted the relevance of affect, and particularly state affect (“feelings at a particular point in time”) in understanding the exchanges between authorities and employees. According to appraisal theories (e.g., affective events theory; Weiss & Cropanzano, 1996), procedural justice ‘triggers’ individuals to consider whether an ‘event’ is harmful or beneficial to their goals; procedural injustice is perceived by individuals as harmful, resulting in negative or unpleasant affect, whereas procedural justice is perceived as beneficial, resulting in positive affect (Lazarus, 1991; Weiss et al., 1999). Affect, in turn, is hypothesized to mediate the relationship between procedural justice and behavioral outcomes, such as task performance and organizational citizenship behavior (Colquitt et al., 2013).

Second, the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model was developed to explain the way in which workplace conditions impact on a range of work outcomes, with a specific focus on factors relating to mental wellbeing, such as stress and burnout (Bakker & Demerouti, 2007). According to the JD-R, workplace attributes such as shift work, workload and time pressure and job resources, such as supervisor support, participation, and job control influence mental wellbeing. When job demands are excessive, and when there are inadequate job resources, stress and disengagement arise (Demerouti et al., 2001). Research has positioned organizational justice and supervisory procedural justice as important job resources that can impact upon employees’ psychological well-being (Boyd et al., 2011; Clements & Kinman, 2020; Kinnunen et al., 2011).

Third, and more broadly, Prilleltensky’s theory of Wellness as Fairness (2012, p. 9) argues that the relationship between justice and wellbeing permeates all facets of life in that justice supports “fair and equitable access to the objective and subjective components of well-being at the personal, interpersonal, organizational, and community levels”. Here, objective wellbeing consists of more concrete measures such as income and education level, and subjective wellbeing is about evaluations and experiences. Prilleltensky (2012, p.10-13) goes on to explain that “different conditions of justice predispose different conditions of wellness” and, that optimal conditions of justice allow people and organizations to “thrive”. Prilleltensky explains that this process can work within organizations but also across levels of society from the individual to the organization, community and so on.

There is empirical support for the theorized links between procedural justice, mental wellbeing, and workplace behaviors. First, studies have shown that perceptions of procedural justice in the workplace are associated with positive emotions, and perceptions of procedural injustice with negative emotions (Colquitt et al., 2013). For example, in a national sample of 2366 American employees Murphy and Tyler (2008) found a significant relationship between procedural justice and positive emotions (happiness). Another study using a sample of police officers in Taiwan found that procedural justice was negatively associated with negative emotions, such as anger and frustration (Wu et al., 2017). Research with prison officers has shown that perceptions of procedural injustice are associated with higher levels of job stress and burnout (Elechi et al., 2020; Lambert et al., 2007; Lambert, Boateng, et al., 2023).

In turn, studies have shown that positive and negative emotions influence a range of desirable and undesirable outcomes in the workplace. In Murphy and Tyler’s (2008) study, happiness was associated with workplace compliance behavior. Further, the positive emotion of happiness mediated the relationship between procedural justice and compliance (i.e., there was an indirect relationship between procedural justice and compliance behavior through happiness). Similarly, Wu et al (2017) found that negative emotions mediated the effect of procedural justice on compliance with policies: procedural justice was associated with less anger/frustration, which, in turn, was associated with more compliance with policies. Among prison officers, job stress and burnout have been shown to be related to negative workplace outcomes, such as turnover intent and a lack of commitment to the organization (Griffin et al., 2020; Lai, 2017; Lambert, Solinas-Saunders, et al., 2023).

In terms of organizational citizenship behavior, a meta-analytic review of the wider organizational literature found that both positive and negative state affect were related to organizational citizenship behavior, and there was a significant indirect effect of procedural justice on organizational citizenship behavior through affect (Colquitt et al., 2013). In other words, procedural justice led to more positive affect, which, in turn, increased organizational citizenship behavior (procedural injustice had the opposite effect, leading to more negative affect and less organizational citizenship behavior).

No research that we know of has explored the link between prison officer wellbeing and organizational citizenship behavior. Based on theoretical accounts and research conducted with other types of employees, we would expect that greater levels of mental wellbeing would be associated with more willingness to engage in organizational citizenship behavior among prison officers, and that mental wellbeing would mediate the association between procedural justice and organizational citizenship behavior.

########### The Current Study

This study explores whether procedural justice (supervisory procedural justice and organizational justice) facilitates organizational citizenship behavior directly, as well as indirectly through mental wellbeing (see Figure 1). We draw on a sample of new prison officers recruited through the Unlocked Graduates Leadership Development Programme. We make three specific hypotheses:

H1: Procedural justice will be positively associated with mental wellbeing.

H2: Mental wellbeing will be positively associated with organizational citizenship behavior.

H3: Mental wellbeing will mediate the association between procedural justice and organizational citizenship behavior.

########### Materials and Methods

########### Participants

Participants are band 3 prison officers in England and Wales, recruited via the Unlocked Graduates’ Leadership Development Programme (2021, 2022 and 2023 cohorts). Unlocked Graduates is a registered charity based in England and Wales, with a stated mission “to develop outstanding leaders to break cycles of reoffending in prison and throughout society” (Unlocked Graduates, 2024). The Unlocked Graduates Programme was one of the key recommendations to emerge from the Coates’ Review of prison education in England and Wales (Coates, 2016): a report that argued that education needs to be put at the heart of the prison service to improve the rehabilitation of people in custody. Unlocked Graduates introduce the realities of the prison officer role to top graduates, 90% of whom have never previously considered a career in the prison service before hearing about the program (Unlocked Graduates, 2024). Since 2017, Unlocked Graduates has recruited and placed nearly 900 graduates to work on the frontline of 38 prisons across England and Wales, attracting more than 40 applications for every place on the programme (Unlocked Graduates, 2024). The two-year Leadership Development Programme developed by Unlocked Graduates blends theory with practice-based learning, the delivery of a master’s degree and a focus on accelerating the impact and leadership potential of prison officers in frontline operational roles (also see Fenn et al., 2024).

A total of 232 prison officers completed the online survey (55 from 2021; 83 from 2022; and 94 from 2023), representing a response rate of 77%. Three quarters of the sample were female (75.4%, n=175) and the majority identified as White (75.9%, n=176). A smaller percentage identified as being from ethnic minority backgrounds (21.6%, n=50). Compared to the overall prison workforce in England and Wales, the current sample includes a greater proportion of female police officers (75.4% compared to 31.6% of all band 3-5 prison officers; HMPPS, 2023) and a greater proportion of officers from ethnic minority backgrounds (21.6% compared to 12.6% of all band 3-5 prison officers; HMPPS, 2023). This is not surprising given the emphasis Unlocked Graduates place on attracting and recruiting a more diverse pool of officers to work in operational roles in the prison service.

########### Constructs and Measurement Model

The analysis involved two exogenous variables, one mediating variable, and one endogenous variable. Variables for analysis were generated via Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA). Table 1 presents the items used to construct the factors, descriptive statistics, factor loadings and the Cronbach’s alpha of each factor. The first exogenous variable – supervisory procedural justice – was constructed with five items reflecting the extent to which participants felt their line managers were supportive and treated them fairly and respectfully (e.g., “My line manager treats me with respect”). The second exogenous variables – organizational justice – consisted of three items reflecting the extent to which participants felt their organization was procedurally just (e.g., “In my establishment, my opinions are valued and taken into account”). For both exogenous variables, participants responded on a five-point Likert scale from ‘strongly disagree’ to ‘strongly agree’.

The mediating variable – mental wellbeing – was measured using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (SWEMWBS; Stewart-Brown et al., 2009) which is a seven-item scale capturing the emotional, cognitive, functional and social components of mental wellbeing. The seven items are positively worded (e.g. “I’ve been feeling optimistic about the future, “I’ve been feeling relaxed”) and participants are asked to respond on a five-point Likert scale from ‘none of the time’ to ‘all of the time’. The scale captures participants mental wellbeing over the last two weeks. Previous studies have shown the scale to have good internal reliability (α = 0.84; Ng Fat et al., 2017).

The endogenous variable – organizational citizenship behavior – was constructed with three items which reflected participants’ confidence in taking action to improve the organization (organization-targeted citizenship behavior). The three organizational citizenship behaviors measured were: starting something new in prison, influencing other staff in their prison, and influencing system change in their prison. Participants responded on a three-point Likert scale: 1=not confident, 2=fairly confident, 3=completely confident.

To assess the scaling properties and empirical distinctiveness of our variables, we used CFA using the R package lavaan. All observed indicators were set to ordinal, and the model was estimated using diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS) with robust standard errors. Model fit statistics showed the measurement model was a good fit for the data, with high CFI and TLI values and a low RMSEA value: 𝛘2 = 261.18, df = 129, p <.001; CFI = 0.981; TLI = 0.978; RMSEA = 0.067.

########### Discussion

Organizational citizenship behavior is defined as discretionary actions that employees take which benefit the organization. For prison officers, these types of behaviors could play a vital role in improving practice within prisons and facilitating more positive outcomes for people in custody. Previous research has found that a key determinant of whether prison officers are willing to engage in organizational citizenship behavior is procedural justice: officers who feel treated fairly by their commanders and organization are more willing to go above and beyond their formal job requirements (Nelson & Appel, 2022). Our study extended this work to investigate the influence of mental wellbeing as a mediator of this relationship. Drawing on a sample of newly employed prison officers on the Unlocked Graduates Leadership Development Programme, our study yielded two key findings. First, we found a significant direct association between supervisory procedural justice and organizational citizenship behavior. Second, we found the association between organizational justice and organizational citizenship behavior was fully mediated by mental wellbeing. We will discuss each of these findings in turn.

First, our study found that officers who felt they were treated fairly and respectfully by their supervisors were more confident in carrying out organizational citizenship behaviors. This finding is consistent with the prior work of Nelson and Appel (2022) who found, across two studies, a significant direct relationship between commander procedural justice and organization-targeted citizenship behavior (as well as an indirect relationship through organizational justice). It is also consistent with research in other types of professions (Colquitt et al., 2013; Tepper & Taylor, 2003). The association between procedural justice and organizational citizenship behavior has been explained in prior studies using social exchange theory (Cropanzano & Mitchell, 2005): the idea that experiences of fairness foster reciprocal actions on the part of employees (Colquitt et al., 2013). Organizational citizenship behaviors are viewed as an exchangeable resource, given by employees to organizations in response to fair treatment. Our findings fit with this perspective – fair treatment by supervisors was “exchanged” for behaviors that benefit the organization – and suggest the way supervisors treat their subordinates has important implications for how prison establishments can foster discretionary actions among prison officers new to the service.

Our second key finding was that organizational justice had an indirect effect on organizational citizenship behavior through mental wellbeing. Unlike supervisory procedural justice, there was no direct effect of organizational justice on organizational citizenship behavior. Although at odds with social exchange theory, affect has been put forward by scholars as a mechanism to explain the exchanges between authorities and employees (Colquitt et al., 2013). According to this perspective, employees interpret procedural justice as beneficial to their goals, resulting in positive affect; procedural injustice, on the other hand, is perceived by employees as harmful, resulting in negative or unpleasant affect (Colquitt et al., 2013; Lazarus, 1991). Affect, in turn, is thought to influence important workplace behaviors, such as task performance and organizational citizenship behavior (Colquitt et al., 2013). Our findings support this basic premise: organizational justice was associated with better mental wellbeing and mental wellbeing, in turn, was associated with greater organizational citizenship behavior.

Our findings also align with the Job Demands-Resource (JD-R) model and Prilleltensky’s (2012) theory of Wellness as Fairness where “different conditions of justice predispose different conditions of wellness”. According to Prilleltensky, optimal conditions of justice allow people and organizations to “thrive”. The flow-on effects of organizational justice to mental wellbeing and organizational citizenship behavior may indicate that participants’ experiences of justice are creating the optimal conditions for individuals to not only feel well in themselves, but that allow them to go above and beyond their formal role requirements. We found that supervisory procedural justice had a weaker association with mental wellbeing than organizational justice (see Table 2), and the association between supervisory procedural justice and mental wellbeing was non-significant in the full SEM after controlling for organizational justice. It seems that fairness in supervisory relationships may be less important for determining how individuals feel (i.e., their affect) than fairness experienced from the wider organization.

Limitations

Before we conclude, we should note there were several limitations to the current study. First, the data came from a cross-sectional survey. This methodology naturally precludes us from making causal inferences; future research should adopt longitudinal designs to test the proposed causal pathways more rigorously. Second, we were limited by the measures available in the dataset. Our measure of organizational citizenship behavior differed from previous research by asking respondents to rate their confidence in carrying out certain actions, as opposed to their willingness to do so or measuring their actual behavior. Confidence in carrying out organizational citizenship behaviors may not necessarily translate to actual behavior and may instead relate more to participants’ self-efficacy in their role, as opposed to their willingness to go above and beyond their role requirements.

The final limitation has to do with our sample. We used a sample of new prison officers who were part of the Unlocked Graduates Leadership Development Programme. Officers who join this programme are likely to be highly motivated individuals who may be more likely to engage in organizational citizenship behaviors than officers who join by the usual route. Unlocked select officers who demonstrate a “sense of possibility” during the recruitment process: a belief in the capacity of people and systems to change for the better.  Candidates are assessed for their leadership skills, decision-making, resilience and self-awareness, and the ability to develop each of these attributes to a high standard. During their time on the program, Unlocked participants are encouraged to be “radical disruptors” (Unlocked Graduates, 2024:3) and are assessed on their ability to critically reflect on leadership styles; to assess and apply change management models to address challenges within a prison context; and to formulate an applied research project including evidence-based recommendations to promote system change. These extend beyond the eligibility requirements of officers joining the prison service through mainstream entry routes.

########### Conclusion

This study highlights the role of procedural justice in fostering organizational citizenship behavior among newly recruited prison officers. Our findings suggest that both supervisory and organizational justice encourage behaviors that go beyond formal job requirements, albeit through differing mechanisms. Supervisory procedural justice was directly associated with organizational citizenship behavior, suggesting that supportive and respectful treatment from line managers fosters positive, reciprocal actions by employees. Conversely, organizational justice influenced organizational citizenship behavior indirectly through mental wellbeing, highlighting the broader organizational culture's role in fostering both the psychological health of staff and their willingness to go beyond formal role requirements.

The practical implications of these findings are particularly relevant to addressing the challenges faced by the prison service, including high rates of officer turnover, gaps in the provision of effective line management and more widely, the need for cultural and systemic improvements within prisons. By prioritizing procedural justice at both supervisor and organizational levels, correctional institutions can create an environment that not only supports staff wellbeing but also motivates them to take initiative in improving prison practices and systems. Our study suggests that a focus on fairness and wellness may bolster the capacity of new officers to thrive in their roles and engage in more positive discretionary actions, ultimately contributing to more humane prison environments and better outcomes for people in their care.
