## Evolution of data protection



## Right to privacy (1890)


In the early 20th century, the concept of privacy began to gain more attention in legal circles in the United States. One of the first cases to recognize a "right to privacy" was the 1890 case of Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis v. The Commonwealth of Massachusetts. Warren and Brandeis, both lawyers, wrote an influential article in the Harvard Law Review in 1890 titled "The Right to Privacy," which argued that a new legal right of privacy should be recognized in the United States («The Right to Privacy (Article)», 2022).

In the case of Warren and Brandeis v. The Commonwealth of Massachusetts, the Supreme Court of Massachusetts recognized a "right to privacy" as a common-law tort in which individuals have the right to control the use of their own name and likeness. The court ruled that Warren and Brandeis had a right  to  prevent  the  unauthorized  publication  of  their  photographs  in  a  newspaper  without  their consent.

This case was important because it was one of the first to recognize the importance of protecting an individual's right to control their own personal information and reputation. It set a precedent for future cases involving privacy and the right to control the use of one's name and likeness.

This case was also important because it was one of the first to recognize the privacy rights of individuals who were not public figures. Prior to this case, privacy rights were largely limited to protecting the privacy of public figures, such as celebrities and politicians. This case established that privacy rights also extend to private individuals who are not in the public eye  (Glancy, 1979).

The Warren and Brandeis case was the first to recognize the concept of privacy as a legal right in the United States, and it set an important precedent for future privacy cases in the country.


## The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)


The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a seminal document adopted by the United Nations in 1948 that sets out the fundamental human rights to which all individuals are entitled. Article

12 of the UDHR specifically addresses the right to privacy, stating that "No one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to attacks upon his honor and  reputation.  Everyone  has  the  right  to  the  protection  of  the  law  against  such  interference  or attacks."

The inclusion of Article 12 in the UDHR was a significant step forward in the recognition of privacy as a fundamental human right. It established the right to privacy as a universal principle that applies to all individuals, regardless of their nationality or location (Woods, 2019).

In  the decades following the adoption of the UDHR, several international treaties and conventions have been adopted that further strengthen the protection of privacy. For example, the International Covenant on (ICCPR) adopted in 1966, which includes Article 17, which provides additional protection against arbitrary or unlawful interference with an individual's privacy, family, home, or correspondence («International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights», 2023).


## The hessian data protection law (1970)


In the aftermath of World War II and the fall of the Nazi regime, the German government set out to rebuild the country and establish a new democratic system based on the rule of law. This included a strong emphasis on protecting individual rights and freedoms, including the right to privacy.

The historical experiences of Nazi-era surveillance and repression were still fresh in the minds of the German people, and many feared that a return to a surveillance state could happen again. This fear was further exacerbated by the existence of the Stasi, the secret police of East Germany, which was known for  its  extensive  surveillance  of  citizens  and  human  rights  abuses.  In  response  to  this,  the Federal Republic of Germany placed a strong emphasis on protecting individual rights, including the right to privacy (Freude & Freude, 2018).

In 1970, the state of Hessen enacted the first data protection law in the world, which was signed into law by Governor Oswald. He referred to George Orwell's novel "1984" and declared that the Hessian data protection law was intended to prevent the surveillance state forecasted by Orwell.

This was followed by the Federal Data Protection Act, passed by the Bundestag and Bundesrat in 1977. This law established the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information and provided a legal framework for the protection of personal data.

In 1983,  the  German  Constitutional  Court  recognized  an  implied  right to information  selfdetermination, which emanated from the express rights to dignity and personality. The court's decision

was based on the fundamental right of informational self-determination, which was derived from the German Constitution.

As a result of these laws and court decisions, data protection has become a fundamental principle in Germany, and the country has become a leader in data protection law. However, the legacy of the Stasi state has had a lasting impact on the population, and the government has had to work to regain trust and ensure that individuals' rights are protected.


## The Patriot Act and its impact on data protection


The terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, had a profound impact on the United States, including on the country's approach to data protection. One of the most significant responses to the attacks was the passage of the USA PATRIOT Act (Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism Act) in 2001 («Patriot Act», 2022).

The PATRIOT Act greatly expanded the government's surveillance powers, giving law enforcement and intelligence  agencies  unprecedented  access  to  personal  information.  Section  215  of  the  act,  for example, allows the FBI to obtain "any tangible things" relevant to a terrorism investigation, including personal records such as library records, bank records, and business records.

Section  802  of  the  PATRIOT  Act  also  expands  the  definition  of  domestic  terrorism,  enabling  law enforcement agencies to investigate individuals and groups that they suspect of being involved in terrorist activities. This has raised concerns about the potential for abuse of these powers and the impact on civil liberties, including privacy (Warwick, 2014).

Critics of the PATRIOT Act argue that the broad definition of terrorism and the expanded surveillance powers granted to law enforcement agencies threaten civil liberties and privacy. They also argue that the act does not include sufficient safeguards to protect against abuses of power.

On the other hand, supporters of the PATRIOT Act argue that the act is necessary to protect national security and that the expanded surveillance powers are necessary to prevent terrorist attacks. They also argue that the act includes sufficient safeguards to protect against abuses of power.

The Patriot Act has been a subject of ongoing debate and controversy since its passage. It has been renewed several  times,  but  some  of  its  provisions  have  been  expired,  and  it  has  been  amended. However, it continues to shape the way the US government and law enforcement agencies collect, use and share data.


## Technological determinism and historical events


Technological determinism and historical events have played a significant role in the evolution of data privacy legislation. The scientific and technological advancements of the industrial era allowed for the creation of new technologies that had a social impact on the way personal data was collected and used.  The  rise  of  photography,  video,  and  audio  recording,  for  example,  created  new  ways  for individuals to create and share personal data.

The events of World War II and its aftermath also had a significant impact on the development of data privacy  laws.  The  atrocities  committed  during  the  war,  including  the  Holocaust,  led  to  a  greater awareness of the potential misuse of personal information. This led to a push for greater protections for personal data, particularly in democratic societies.

Overall, the evolution of data privacy legislation has been shaped by both technological determinism and historical events. The development of new technologies and societal experiences, such as those experienced during World War II, have played a major role in shaping the laws and regulations that protect personal data today.


## European approach to data protection through GDPR


The process of constructing the problem of data protection in the EU involved several actors and stakeholders,  including  policymakers,  experts,  industry  representatives,  and  civil  society  groups. Several comparative studies were conducted to assess the effectiveness of existing data protection frameworks and to identify areas for improvement. This process was characterized by several debates and controversies, as different actors argued for different approaches to data protection and sought to influence the direction of policy ( Proposal for a REGULATION OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL on the Protection of Individuals with Regard to the Processing of Personal Data and on  the  Free  Movement  of  Such  Data  (General  Data  Protection  Regulation) ,  2012).  But  one  report compressed all the debate at European level and lead to the legislative reformulation acceptation by the European Commission.


## Context of emergency for GDPR


The context in which the problem of data protection emerged was one of rapid technological change and the growing importance of data in the economy. As data became a more valuable resource, private companies sought to collect and use it to drive business growth and innovation. At the same time, concerns about privacy, security, and the potential negative impacts of data collection and use on

individuals and society more broadly began to rise. The GDPR was seen to address these concerns and ensure that data protection in the EU kept pace with technological change.


## Public Cases that influenced Policy Change


Prior  to  2010,  significant  events  occurred  that  served  to  underscore  the  need  for  improved  data protection regulation in the EU.

In  2005,  it  was  revealed  that  the  United  States  National Security  Agency had conducted extensive surveillance of internet and telephone communication without judicial oversight, causing outrage and leading to the implementation of laws and regulations, including the USA Freedom Act, to address such abuses of power (Eff, 2011).

In 2006, the UK government proposed a national identification card system that would necessitate all citizens to provide personal data, including biometric information, for storage in a centralized database (Sullivan, 2007). This proposal was met with significant concern and opposition, ultimately leading to the abandonment of the project.

The Google Street View data collection scandal occurred in 2010 when it was discovered that Google's Street  View  cars,  which  were  collecting  images  and  mapping  data  for  the  company's  Street  View feature,  had  also  been  collecting  data  from  unsecured  wireless  networks  as  they  drove  through neighborhoods.  This  data  included  personal  information  such  as  emails,  passwords,  and  medical records (Burdon & McKillop, 2013).


## Structure and enforcement of the GDPR


The GDPR operates at multiple levels to effectively protect personal data and ensure compliance with data protection rules. At the international level, data transfers to countries outside the EU are subject to strict restrictions, and third countries must be deemed to have an "adequate level of protection" by the European Commission for data to be transferred to them. To facilitate data transfers within the EU, the GDPR establishes a framework for the free flow of personal data between Member States.

At the EU level, the GDPR establishes a European Data Protection Board (EDPB) to provide consistency in the actions of the different national supervisory authorities and to issue guidelines and opinions on data  protection  matters.  The  EDPB  also  plays  a  role  in  cooperation  and  consistency  proceedings between national supervisory authorities.

At  the  national  level,  the  regulation  establishes  independent  supervisory  authorities,  such  as  the National Commission for Data Protection in Portugal, to oversee the implementation and enforcement

of the GDPR in each Member State. These authorities are responsible for monitoring compliance with the  GDPR,  handling  complaints  from  data  subjects,  and  imposing  sanctions  on  organizations  that violate data protection rules.

The GDPR also creates a designated data protection officer (DPO) role at the organizational level, responsible  for  monitoring  compliance  with  the  GDPR  and  serving  as  a  point  of  contact  for  data subjects. DPOs are required in certain types of organizations, such as those that carry out large-scale processing of special categories of data or that engage in profiling activities with significant effects on data subjects.

Finally, the GDPR places a strong emphasis on the rights of data subjects, including the right to give informed consent, the right to access and rectify personal data, the right to object to profiling and certain  other  processing  activities,  and  the  right  to  have  personal  data  erased  under  certain circumstances. These rights are intended to empower individuals to control how their personal data is used and to hold organizations accountable for their handling of personal data.


## Risk-based Approach to Data Protection: The Role of Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) in the GDPR


Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) are a key tool for organizations to ensure compliance with the GDPR. A DPIA is a process that organizations must follow to identify and assess the potential data protection risks of a particular project or activity, and to put in place measures to mitigate those risks. DPIAs are required in situations where a project is likely to result in a considerable risk to the rights and  freedoms  of  individuals,  such  as  when  new  technologies  are  being  introduced  or  when  large amounts of sensitive personal data are being processed.

To conduct a DPIA, an organization must first identify the scope and objectives of the project, as well as the types of personal data that will be processed. It must then assess the potential risks to data protection, considering the nature of the data, the context in which it is being processed, and the impact on individuals. Based on this assessment, the organization must then determine the measures that are necessary to mitigate any identified risks and must document the DPIA process and its results.

The  GDPR  requires  organizations  to  consult  with  the  relevant  data  protection  authority  before conducting a DPIA in certain situations, such as when the processing of personal data is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. In addition, organizations must keep records of their DPIAs and make them available to the data protection authority upon request.


## GDPR Brussels effect


The Brussels Effect refers to the EU regulatory capacity and propensity to exercise global regulatory authority, meaning that it has the institutional structures and resources necessary to produce and enforce regulations effectively (Bradford, 2012, p. 10). The Brussels Effect is more likely to occur when the market of an importing country is larger than the market of an exporting country and the exporting country is more dependent on access to the market of the importing country. Being a regulatory power is  a  conscious  choice  made  by  the  EU  rather  than  something  that  is  inherent  in  its  market  size (Bradford, 2012, p. 12). The EU must also have the regulatory capacity to translate its market power into tangible regulatory influence (Bradford, 2012, p. 16). The EU's efforts to create a harmonized regulatory scheme for artificial intelligence and other industries are driven by export-oriented EU firms seeking consistent and predictable regulatory frameworks. The EU's ability to export its standards to third countries ensures the competitiveness of European firms and enables the EU to defend its social preferences without compromising the competitiveness of its industries (Bradford, 2012, p. 40).

The  heavy  investment  in  enforcement  of  the  legislation  through  European  board  level,  national authorities, and Data Protection Officers (DPOs) has created a ground-breaking approach that has truly created a Brussels effect on other countries like Brazil, Canada, South Korea, Israel, Nigeria, along many others ( 16 Countries with GDPR-like Data Privacy Laws , 2022).

One of the key impacts of the GDPR has been the alignment of regulations in other countries with those of the EU. Many countries have adopted similar regulations to ensure compliance with GDPR and maintain access to the EU market. This has led to an increased focus on data privacy and security globally,  as  companies  operating  in  non-EU  countries  have  had  to  adapt  to  the  new  regulatory framework.

Another impact of the GDPR has been a change in the behavior of the private  sector  in terms  of regulatory  compliance.  The  race  to  the  bottom,  where  companies  would  seek  to  minimize  their compliance costs by operating in countries with weaker regulations, has been replaced with a focus on meeting the higher standards set by the EU. This has led to an overall improvement in the protection of personal data and a reduction in the risk of data breaches (Rustad & Koenig, 2019).

The Brussels Effect of GDPR has been significant, with the EU's regulatory power and enforcement capabilities  driving  changes  in  privacy  regulations  around  the  world.  This  has  led  to  increased protection of personal data and a shift in the private sector's approach to regulatory compliance.


## United States approach to data protection and CCPA



## Piecemeal approach to data privacy regulation


The  United  States  has  taken  a  different  approach  to  data  privacy  regulation  compared  to  other countries,  such  as  those  in  the  European  Union.  Instead  of  implementing  a  broad,  omnibus  data processing regulation, the United States has enacted a patchwork of sector-, situation-, and harmspecific data privacy laws. These laws are intended to address specific issues and concerns related to personal data, rather than providing a comprehensive framework for data protection (Determann, 2019).

This  approach can be traced back to the early 1970s, when Congress and state legislatures began enacting laws to address specific issues related to data privacy. Examples include the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) which regulates the use of personal health information, and the  Children's  Online  Privacy  Protection  Act  (COPPA)  which  protects  the  personal  information  of children under 13.

The United States also have Federal Trade Commission (FTC) which has the power to enforce privacy and data security laws against companies that fail to protect consumer data, this includes the ability to fine companies for non-compliance.

This piecemeal approach to data privacy regulation in the United States has been criticized for its lack of consistency and for creating confusion among companies and individuals. However, it also allows for flexibility and the ability to adapt to new technologies and societal concerns as they arise.


## California Consumer Privacy Act set a precedent for comprehensive data privacy legislation in the United States


California set a precedent for comprehensive data privacy legislation in the United States and has long been considered a leader in protecting individual privacy rights, thanks in part to the inclusion of the right to privacy in the California State Constitution through a 1972 ballot initiative. In 2003, California also implemented the first state data breach notification system in the country (Baik, 2020).

The  California Consumer  Privacy  Act  (CCPA)  is  an extension  of this rights-based approach, acknowledging that California law has not kept pace with new technologies. The political climate in California enabled the passage of the CCPA, while other states may not have the political will to pass similar legislation. The initial version of the CCPA was first introduced in February 2017 but was moved to the inactive file in September 2017 due to opposition from large tech companies. However, a ballot

initiative introduced in October 2017 by a real estate developer prompted the passage of the CCPA in June 2018.

The CCPA grants Californians specific rights related to their personal data, including the right to know what data is collected about them, the right to request deletion of their data, the right to decline the sale  of  their  data,  the  right  to  access  their  data,  and  the  right  to  not  be  discriminated  against  for exercising these rights. It also defines personal information as "information that identifies, relates to, describes, is reasonably capable of being associated with, or could reasonably be linked, directly or indirectly, with a particular consumer or household."

Despite some limitations, such as the lack of a private right of action for violations, the CCPA has set a precedent  for  comprehensive  data  privacy  legislation  in  the  United  States  and  has  been  widely adopted by companies operating in California.

## Structure and enforcement of the CCPA


The California  Consumer Privacy  Act  (CCPA)  is  a  legislation  passed  in  California  in  2018  that  gives California residents certain rights over their personal information that is collected and processed by businesses. The CCPA is enforced by the California attorney general, and private rights of action for data breaches are allowed under certain conditions.

## Structure:

The CCPA is divided into several sections that cover different aspects of the law. Some of the main sections include:

Definition of terms: The CCPA includes definitions for key terms such as "personal information" and "business" that are used throughout the law.

Consumer  rights:  The  CCPA  establishes  the  rights  of  California  residents  to  know  what  personal information is being collected about them, to request that it be deleted, and to opt-out of the sale of their personal information.

Business obligations: The CCPA sets out the obligations of businesses that collect personal information, including providing notice to California residents about their rights under the CCPA, and making certain disclosures about their data collection and sharing practices.

## Enforcement:

The  CCPA  establishes  the  enforcement  mechanisms  for  the  law,  including  penalties  for  noncompliance, and the role of the California attorney general in enforcing the law.

Additionally, private rights of action are allowed under certain conditions, such as when a business fails to implement and maintain reasonable security measures and a data breach occurs as a result. The aggrieved person can file a lawsuit in that case.

The CCPA has also set up a 30-day cure period for businesses in case of a violation, which means that the business will be given a chance to correct the violation before any action is taken against it.


## Social movement versus corporativism


The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) was not only a response to technological advancements, but also a product of a growing social movement against corporativism and the abuse of personal data by  large  companies.  This  movement,  led  by  consumer  advocacy  groups  and  privacy  activists,  put pressure on lawmakers to act and protect the rights of individuals in the digital age.

One of the key players in this movement was real estate developer Alistair Mactaggart, who sponsored the ballot initiative that ultimately led to the passage of the CCPA. Mactaggart had become increasingly concerned about the lack of regulation around the collection and use of personal data by companies, and saw the need for a comprehensive law that would give individuals more control over their own data (Wakabayashi, 2018).

The CCPA is also seen as a response to a growing public awareness and concern about the ways in which companies collect, use, and share personal data. This awareness was fueled in part by highprofile data breaches, such as the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which brought to light the extent to which companies were collecting and using personal data without consent.

The CCPA was also influenced by a growing sense of distrust towards large tech companies and their role in society. The tech industry, dominated by a few large corporations, has been accused of having too much power and influence over the political process and the economy, and of prioritizing profit over the privacy and well-being of individuals.

In this context, the CCPA can be seen as a step towards pushing back against corporativism and giving individuals more control over their own personal data. The law was a response to a growing social movement that called for more regulation around data privacy and represents a step towards a more rights-based approach to data protection in the United States.

## Cultural harmonization for analytical purposes


The main difference between China and the EU in terms of data protection is the approach to personal data processing. In China, data protection primarily focuses on the individual as a consumer, while in the EU, it is focused on the individual as a "data subject" with a set of rights to protect their personal information. Additionally, the EU places a greater emphasis on the protection of individual rights and privacy, while in China, the focus is more on the economic and commercial aspects of data protection.

The protection of the right to privacy may be better under current Chinese law, although the concept of privacy is perceived differently in China than in Europe. In China, the right to privacy is protected in basic Chinese law at both the constitutional and civil law level, and it is ultimately connected to the right to dignity. However, the protection of privacy in China is more limited than in Europe as the Chinese government has a more active role in monitoring and controlling citizens' personal data, and there are fewer legal safeguards in place to protect individual privacy rights (Hert & Papakonstantinou, 2015) .

The Chinese political system is a one-party socialist republic, with the Communist Party of China (CPC) being  the  sole  legal  political  party  in  the  country.  The  CPC  is  led  by  a  General  Secretary  and  the President, who holds the title of Chairman of the Central Military Commission. The President, as the head of state, is the highest-ranking official in the country, and is also the commander-in-chief of the military. The government is made up of several branches, including the National People's Congress (NPC), the State Council, and the judiciary («Politics of China», 2023).

The Chinese productive system is a combination of state-owned and private enterprises. The stateowned enterprises (SOEs) have traditionally played a major role in the economy, particularly in key

industries such as energy, telecommunications, and transportation. The government also maintains significant control over the banking sector, and foreign investment is often subject to government approval.  In  recent  years,  there  has  been  a  push  to  increase  private  sector  participation  in  the economy, and the government has implemented several reforms to promote entrepreneurship and innovation. However, the CPC still maintains significant control over the economy and the government continues to play a central role in guiding economic development (Ran, 2018).


## Cybersecurity scandals


One of the most notable incidents that contributed to the need for the PIPL was the Alipay, China's largest third-party payment platform, announced that it had discovered a data leak that occurred in January  2014,  which  resulted  in  the  exposure  of  sensitive  personal  information.  The  leaked  data reportedly included transaction information from before 2010. The company stated that it is taking steps to address the situation and prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future. It is not clear how many users were affected by the data leak.

In March 2019, it was reported that the personal data of 364 million Chinese users of the popular social messaging networks QQ and WeChat had been leaked online. The data included sensitive information such as Chinese citizen ID numbers, user images, addresses, GPS location data, and personal messages. The incident was not confirmed by the companies until it was made public. It is unclear how the data was obtained or who was responsible for the leak. The companies likely took steps to mitigate the issue and prevent similar incidents from happening in the future.

In October 2018, Hong Kong-based Cathay Pacific Airways announced that it had suffered a significant data  breach.  The  company's  internal  system,  which  stored  the  personal  data  of  over  9.4  million passengers, was breached by attackers. The suspicious activity within the system was initially noticed in March of that year. Upon investigation, security experts discovered that hackers had accessed client data, which included personal data, membership information, customer service remarks, and historical travel information. Additionally, the hackers were able to gain access to 403 credit card numbers, some of which included CVV information.

After the incident was discovered, the company informed the affected parties, urged them to request new credit cards, and informed them about its efforts to improve system security.

These high-profile incidents and data breaches have contributed to the need for stronger regulations and  laws  to  protect  personal  information  in  China  and  have  played  a  significant  role  in  the development and implementation of the Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) in the country.


## Agenda Setting of PIPL


The PIPL was enacted by the Standing Committee of China's National People's Congress (SC -NPC) on 20 August 2021. The law's implementation date is set for 1 November 2021. The PIPL is a culmination of over a decade of incremental legislative reform in China, aimed at protecting the rights and interests of personal information and promoting the reasonable use of personal information. The first draft of the PIPL was released in October 2020 and was revised in a succession of drafts. The final law consists of 74 sections, with half of them having non-trivial amendments since the first draft. The PIPL is part of China's near-complete cyber-security laws and is based on the Constitution of China, but citizens cannot sue to enforce constitutional rights directly (Calzada, 2022) . 'More than most data privacy laws, this law also has to be considered as part of China's cybersecurity protections, because there are many ways in which the data export, data localization, extraterritorial, retaliatory and 'platform' provisions can be utilized to further the PRC's foreign policy objectives.' (Greenleaf, 2021, p. 6).

The Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) in China was enacted in part as a response to several high-profile cyber security incidents and data breaches that occurred in the country in recent years. These incidents not only resulted in the loss of personal information of millions of individuals, but also raised concerns about the ability of Chinese companies and organizations to protect personal data and the lack of effective regulations in place to address such issues.


## Structure and enforcement of the PIPL


The  PIPL  is  divided  into  six  chapters:  General  Provisions,  Collection,  Use,  Provision,  Security Management and Supervision and Enforcement. The law also includes provisions for cross-border data transfer and personal information security breaches.

Under the PIPL, businesses must obtain explicit consent from individuals before collecting, using or providing their personal information. The law also requires businesses to disclose their data collection, use and provision policies, and to provide individuals with the right to access and correct their personal information.

The  PIPL  also  includes  provisions  for  security  management,  requiring  businesses  to  implement necessary technical and organizational measures to protect personal information. In the event of a security breach, businesses are required to report the incident to the relevant authorities and take measures to mitigate the impact on individuals.

Enforcement of the PIPL is carried out by the relevant government agencies, including the Cyberspace Administration of China and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. Violations of the

PIPL can result in fines, penalties, and even revocation of business licenses. Individuals also have the right to file civil lawsuits against businesses for compensation for damages resulting from violations of the PIPL.


## Data sovereignty and internal social control


One key aspect of the PIPL is its focus on international data sovereignty, which aims to protect the personal  information  of  Chinese  citizens  from  foreign  companies  and  countries.  The  law  requires foreign companies that collect, use, or store personal information of Chinese citizens to comply with the PIPL and establish a representative office in China. It also places restrictions on the cross-border transfer  of  personal  information  and  requires  companies  to  obtain  approval  from  the  Chinese government  before  transferring  personal  information  abroad (Greenleaf,  2021). The  Chinese government has control over the collection, storage, and use of personal data within its borders. This contrasts with the EU, where personal data is protected by a comprehensive data protection regime that places strong emphasis on the rights of the individual data subject.

Another key aspect aims to ensure that companies and organizations use personal information in a responsible and ethical manner. The law requires companies and organizations to obtain consent from individuals  before  collecting  their  personal  information  and  to  provide  clear  and  transparent information about their data practices. It also gives individuals the right to access, rectify, and delete their personal information and establishes a complaint and redress mechanism for individuals who believe their rights have been violated.

Finally,  the  PIPL  also  has  a  strong  focus  on  internal  social  control,  which  means  that  the  Chinese government  can  use  personal  data  for  the  purpose  of  maintaining  social  stability  and  security. However, the law is not clear on how the government can use personal data for these purposes, which raises concerns about potential misuse of personal data.

## Introduction


Times of crises and uncertainty are often associated with both lower fertility preferences and a decline in births (Skirbekk, 2022; Sobotka et al., 2011). As crises become more frequent and fertility levels remain low or ultra-low, promoting fertility resilience is likely to increase in importance (Lutz, 2024; Salonen et al., 2024). Therefore, understanding how people respond to different types of crises and how these experiences shape their fertility preferences is crucial. Some crises may lead to postponement or reduction in fertility preferences, while others may accelerate childbearing (Lee et al., 2023; Skirbekk, 2022). Identifying the factors that drive these different responses can provide insights into the mechanisms behind fertility resilience and support policies aimed at mitigating the negative demographic effects of crises.

Here, we examine how two recent major crises - the COVID-19 pandemic and Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - were associated with self-reported changes in fertility preferences of adults in Finland, a high-income European welfare state. We utilize both quantitative and qualitative data from a representative Family Barometer survey conducted in Finland in August 2022 (Sorsa et al., 2022). For each crisis, respondents were asked whether the crisis changed their fertility preferences. Those who reported any change where further asked how their preferences changed and offered the possibility to elaborate in open-ended questions.

Our study contributes to the fertility literature in the following ways. First, we expand the prior research documenting the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on fertility preferences in high-income countries with data from Finland, which has experienced prolonged fertility decline since 2011, with a short-lived exception in 2020 and 2021. Second, we provide insights into how an ongoing war and increased military threat from neighboring countries affect fertility preferences. To our knowledge, no studies have yet examined how the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine shaped fertility preferences in

Finland or other countries bordering the conflict zones. Third, we employ a mixed-methods approach, analyzing both survey data and textual answers to gain a more nuanced understanding of how these two recent crises shape fertility preferences. By analyzing openended survey responses, we can explore in a more nuanced way the cognitive, emotional, and social processes that inform individuals' decisions and concerns about childbearing in times of uncertainty. Fourth, unlike many previous studies that focus primarily on women, our study examines the fertility preferences of both men and women, which yields a better understanding of gender-specific dynamics in fertility decision-making.


## Theoretical Background


In contemporary high-income countries, people are likely to delay or reduce their fertility choices during uncertain times, or in some cases, forgo childbearing if circumstances remain unfavorable (Skirbekk, 2022; Sobotka et al., 2011). However, certain types of crises can also increase fertility preferences (Lee et al., 2023; Skirbekk, 2022). The theoretical rationale for these two opposite effects is grounded in the life history theory as applied to evolutionary demography: resource scarcity and societal crises may either suppress childbearing ('waiting for better times') or, on the contrary, accelerate fertility ('the right time may never come, better hurry') (see, for example, Sear et al., 2016).

On the one hand, lack of security and protection is a strong signal to avoid having a child. For instance, in many countries, fertility preferences (here used as an umbrella term for fertility ideals, desires, and intentions) declined during the pandemic, with many people delaying or abandoning their plans to have children or wishing to have fewer children than before (e.g., Golovina et al., 2023; Kahn et al., 2021; Lindberg et al., 2020; Luppi et al., 2020).  Economic instability, limited access to healthcare, concerns about health risks, and increased psychological distress were key factors driving the decline in fertility preferences

during that crisis (e.g., Flynn et al., 2021; Kahn et al., 2021; Malicka et al., 2021; Micelli et al., 2020; Sienicka et al., 2021). The increased childcare responsibilities for mothers during quarantines were also associated with reduced fertility desires (Golovina et al., 2023).

On the other hand, existential crises may highlight the importance and value of reproduction. Thus, armed conflicts or terrorist attacks may increase fertility preferences (Khawaja & Randall, 2006; Rodgers et al., 2005). This prediction is in line with the terror management theory, which notes that when people are reminded of their mortality, their family values and desire for children often increase (Greenberg et al., 1997, 2014; Mathews & Sear, 2008). Childbearing can both symbolically and literally defy death, providing biological continuity and the transmission of cultural values to future generations. For instance, during and after the World War II, fertility increased in Western countries (van Bavel & Reher, 2013). Following the Oklahoma City bombing in April 1995, there was a consistent and significant increase in births in the Oklahoma region (Rodgers et al., 2005). Likewise, high fertility in Gaza during the 1990s has been attributed to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict (Khawaja & Randall, 2006).

Previous Research on COVID-19 and Russia's Full-Scale Invasion of Ukraine on Fertility Preferences

The COVID-19 pandemic let to delayed fertility plans in high-income countries (for review, see Safdari-Dehcheshmeh et al., 2023). At the onset of the pandemic, approximately every second woman who was trying to conceive reported delaying or abandoning their fertility plans (Flynn et al., 2021; Kahn et al., 2021; Micelli et al., 2020). However, by the middle of the pandemic, in the summer of 2021, the impact on fertility preferences had weakened, with only about one in five women reporting changes in their childbearing plans (Lindberg et al., 2021). It is important to note that short-term fertility intentions (e.g.,

concrete plans to have a child soon) were more affected than long-term fertility desires (a general wish for children) or long-term intentions (planning to have a child ever) (BuberEnnser et al., 2023; Lazzari et al., 2023; Malicka et al., 2021). Additionally, several studies indicate that a small proportion of people reported increased fertility preferences (Lazzari et al., 2023; Lindberg et al., 2021; Micelli et al., 2020) or expressed a desire to accelerate childbearing due to the pandemic (Flynn et al., 2021; Lindberg et al., 2021; Naya et al., 2021). In fact, after a decline in birth rates in late 2020 and early 2021, many Western countries witnessed an increase during 2021 (Sobotka et al., 2024). In Finland, as described above, the total fertility rate rose in 2021, followed by a decrease in 2022.

In contrast to the extensive research on the COVID-19 pandemic, there is comparatively less work examining the impact of Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine on fertility preferences. According to a qualitative study comprising 16 focus-groups interviews with individuals from eastern regions of Ukraine, which have been most affected by the armed conflict since 2014, factors such as displacement, ongoing violence, and economic insecurity have intensified feelings of uncertainty regarding the desire to have more than one child (Perelli-Harris et al., 2024; Perelli-Harris & Hilevych, 2023). Participants also expressed concerns about depopulation of some regions of Ukraine, attributing this decline primarily to the reluctance of young people to have larger families and the emigration of young, economically active individuals. Interestingly, while depopulation and economic challenges were major concerns, the high death rates related to the COVID-19 pandemic in Ukraine were not as frequently mentioned as a reason for postponing or limiting childbearing (Perelli-Harris & Hilevych, 2023).

Fertility preferences are also shaped by a range of individual characteristics. Age is a critical factor in family planning, as both fertility desires and intentions tend to decline with increasing age (Gray et al., 2013; Heiland et al., 2008; Kuhnt et al., 2017). The number of

children also plays a key role in shaping fertility preferences (Gray et al., 2013; Kuhnt et al., 2017). During the COVID-19 pandemic in Poland, people who were childless or had only one child were more likely to reduce their fertility desires whereas those with two or more children were inclined to increase them (Golovina et al. 2023). Additionally, COVID-19 related stress had greater impact on fertility desires than the actual exposure to the disease (Marcinkowska et al., 2024). Socio-economic variables, particularly education, are linked to both fertility desires and intentions, while employment and financial situations strongly influence short-term fertility intentions (Gray et al., 2013; Heiland et al., 2008; Kuhnt et al., 2017). In several countries the economic instability brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine have lowered fertility preferences (e.g., Kahn et al., 2021; Perelli-Harris et al., 2024). Additionally, partnership status affects short-term fertility intentions, as individuals often adjust their plans after separation or repartnering. However, partnership dynamics have less impact on general fertility desires. (Gray et al., 2013; Hagewen & Morgan, 2005; Heiland et al., 2008; Kuhnt et al., 2017).


## The Finnish Context


Finland is a high-income Nordic country known for its strong social welfare system and high standards of living, consistently ranking among the top countries in gender equality as well as global quality of life and happiness indices. Despite these advantages, Finland has been experiencing a sharp fertility decline, with the total fertility rate falling from 1.87 in 2010 to all-time low of 1.26 in 2023 (Official Statistics of Finland, OSF, 2024). The tempoadjusted total fertility rate has also decreased in Finland over the last decade, suggesting that a postponement of childbearing to later ages does not fully explain the fertility decline and that cohort fertility will also decrease (Hellstrand et al., 2020). Decreasing first births explain about 75% of the current fertility decline in Finland (Hellstrand et al., 2020).

The Family Barometer survey was collected in August 2022. This was 2.5 years since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, which reached Finland in early March 2020, and half a year since Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Both crises represented a large societal shock for the entire Finnish population, although the war did not affect young adults directly.


## The COVID-19 Pandemic in Finland 2020-22


As the COVID-19 virus spread from Italy to the rest of Europe, Finland imposed a six-week lockdown as a first measure, from March 16 to May 13, 2020. This limited public gatherings, closed several educational institutions, and encouraged remote work. Early childhood education and primary schools stayed open, except for a brief closure of schools in spring 2020, while secondary education operated remotely until spring 2021. Restrictions on large social gatherings and recommendations for remote work continued through 2020 and parts of 2021, with face masks recommended indoors from August 2020. All restrictions were lifted by autumn 2021, one year before the data of survey collection.

At the onset of the pandemic, Finland reported fewer psychological stressors due to the pandemic, higher trust, and greater resilience compared to other countries (Blackburn et al., 2022). Restrictions helped prevent excess mortality and prevent stress on the health care system during the first two pandemic waves, but excess deaths occurred in 2021 and 2022 after restrictions were lifted, predominantly among the elderly population. The virus did not affect the health of young adults to a larger extent, but social restrictions and remote work were linked to worsened mental health, especially among young women (Kiviruusu et al., 2024). The mental impact on adults aged 18-34 varied based on factors like remote work opportunities, livelihood, and views on vaccinations and masks. By the time of our survey,

despite the pandemic causing many deaths, media coverage had shifted, and most young adults were no longer directly affected or preoccupied with it.

The pandemic's demographic effects were mixed. Partnership formation and dissolution rates remained stable, as was the case in the other Nordic countries (Norlén et al., 2022). Birth rates, which had been rising since late 2019, continued to rise into 2020 and 2021. Especially the first pandemic Spring of 2020 led to a spike in births in February 2021, which cannot be explained by underlying fertility trends (Nisén et al., 2022).  Then birth rates in Finland resumed their decline after 2021, with the 2020-21 'baby bump' now appearing as an exception, similar to that observed in the other Nordic countries (with the exception of Sweden) (Ohlsson Wijk & Andersson, 2024).


## The Effects of Russian 2022 Invasion of Ukraine on Finland


If the pandemic had preceded to the background by August, 2022 when the survey data was collected, the psychological impact of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine was more immediate. Finns share a strong collective memory of being attacked by the Soviet Union in 1939 and the ensuing Winter War (1939-1940) and Continuation War (1941-1944), which older generations recall from their childhood. Finland successfully retained its independence, though around 95,000 Finnish soldiers died, and Finland had to cede territories to the Soviet Union. After World War II, the main concern in Finnish foreign policy was balancing between open pressure from the Soviet Union and maintaining sovereignty as a European democracy (e.g., Tarkka, 2013). Finland was militarily neutral and maintained politically friendly relations with the Soviet Union until its demise in 1991, although the Eastern neighbor was persistently, if quietly, perceived as Finland's primary potential enemy. Finland maintained mandatory military conscription for all males and high levels of military and disaster preparedness into the 21 st century - a fact that proved advantageous during the

COVID-19 pandemic. Finland held observer status in NATO since 1994 and, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, swiftly applied for membership in 2022, officially becoming a NATO member in April 2023.

The mental and psychological effects of Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 on Finns have been sparsely studied. A representative survey conducted in March 2022 (N=1,000) found that 82% of Finns aged 18-70 supported sanctions against Russia, and onethird had personally donated money or goods to aid Ukraine (STT, 2023). Around 10% expressed they were favorable to Russia. Many were concerned about the economic impacts, with half of the respondents worried about their personal finances. Men were more likely than women to support providing military aid to Ukraine, with 48% of men and 27% of women in favor (STT, 2023).

Media reports and anecdotal evidence suggest that the war deeply affected many Finns. In the early months, elderly people recalled childhood memories of bombings, reported nightmares, and expressed fears of a full-scale European or nuclear war (Malminen, 2022). Members of Finland's reserve forces, both men and women, were particularly affected, and for the first time in decades young adults perceived the possibility of war as a reality (Malminen, 2022; Rosvall, 2022).


## The Present Study


We investigate whether men and women in Finland changed their fertility preferences in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Given that fertility is known to be influenced by natural disasters and societal shocks (Sear et al. 2016; Lee et al., 2023; Skirbekk, 2022), we anticipated that Finns of reproductive age would report changes in their fertility preferences following these two major crises. Based on previous research in demography and the social sciences, we hypothesized that Finns would be more

likely to report a decrease in their fertility preferences due to the pandemic, given that it involved economic uncertainty and psychological distress typically associated with lower fertility and fertility desires. In contrast, we expected that the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 would be associated with increasing fertility preferences, because of the strong association with mortality and existential threat, according to the terror management theory (Greenberg et al., 1997, 2014). We also examine how different socio-demographic factors are related to the likelihood of changing fertility preferences due to these crises. Based on the previous literature, we expected that especially age, partnership status, and own economic situation will be related to changes in fertility preferences during these two crises, in general so that those with more resources have less reduced fertility preferences. Finally, using qualitative data from open-ended questions, we aim to identify the key reasons behind these changes in fertility preferences due to the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.


## Methods



## Data and Sample


We used cross-sectional data from the Family Barometer survey in 2022, conducted by the Population Research Institute at Väestöliitto, the Family Federation of Finland, examining various topics related to family life and childbearing in Finland (Sorsa et al., 2022). The survey was conducted in August 2022 as online survey by KANTAR TNS Gallup Oyj using their panel of respondents consisting of approximately 50 000 households representing the Finnish population aged 20 to 59 years, among whom respondents were recruited during the time of the survey. The sample size for the online survey was predetermined at 3000+ respondents, and the data collection was finished once the sample size was reached. Respondents with children were overrepresented in the sample, but this was

taken into account in the data weights. The data weights included age, gender, having children in the household, region of residence, and education.

The total sample comprised 3398 respondents aged 20-59 years. We excluded respondents with low probability of childbearing due to age (older than 45 years), resulting in n = 2009. Among them, 1960 respondents had complete data on all the variables of interest, which formed the analytical sample for this study.


## Measures


Changes in fertility preferences were assessed in relation to both the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Fertility preferences during the pandemic were measured by asking about the desired number of children and the timing of having a child. The specific questions were: 'Have your wishes regarding the number of children changed due to the COVID-19 pandemic?' (1 = no, 2 = yes, increased, 3 = yes, decreased, 4 = I don't know / prefer not to answer); and 'Has the COVID-19 pandemic influenced the timing of when you had or plan to have (more) children?' (1 = no, 2 = yes, sooner, 3 = yes, later or never, 4 = other / I don't know / prefer not to answer). These questions were followed by open-ended prompts inviting participants to elaborate on their responses: 'You indicated that your preferences regarding the number of children have changed due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Would you like to provide more details? Please write your answer here…' and 'You indicated that the pandemic has influenced when you had or plan to have (more) children. Would you like to provide more details? Please write your answer here…'.

Response alternatives regarding timing and number of children were correlated, so that those who decreased their fertility desires were also more likely to postpone having children to later times or renounce childbearing (r = 0.43, p < 0.001), and those who increased their fertility desires were also planning to have children sooner (r = 0.49, p <

0.001). Therefore, we created a combined variable indicating changes in fertility preferences due to the COVID-19 pandemic in the following way: 1 = indicated no change in either of the question, 2 = increase in the desired number of children or planning to have them sooner, 3 = decrease in the desired number of children or planning to have them later or never, and 4 = I don't know/I don't want to answer. For the purpose of data homogeneity, the few groups of respondents who reported a decrease in the desired number of children but planned to have them sooner (n = 7) and those who reported an increase in the desired number of children but planned them later or never (n=15) were not included in the final analyses.

Fertility preferences in response to the war in Ukraine were assessed with the following question: 'Has the war in Ukraine, which started this year, and the changed security situation affected your plans to have children?' (1 = no, 2 = yes, increased, 3 = yes, decreased, 4 = other / I don't know / prefer not to answer). Participants were then invited to elaborate on their responses with the prompt: 'You indicated that the war in Ukraine and the altered security situation have impacted your plans for having children. Would you like to provide more details? Please write your answer here…'.

Socio-demographic characteristics included the following: age (used as a continuous variable), sex (0 = male, 1 = female), partnership status (0 = single, widowed, divorced, or separated, 1 = cohabiting, 2 = married or being in a registered partnership), number of children (coded as 0, 1, 2, 3+), education (1 = basic, 2 = secondary, 3 = lower tertiary, 4 = upper tertiary), personal income (1 = low [<20000 €], 2 = middle [20001-40000 €], 3 = high [>40000 €]), employment (1 = employed, 2 = unemployed, 3 = not working, i.e., being a student/on maternity or paternity leave/retired/conscripts), house ownership (0 = renting a house, 1 = owning a house where living), and region of residence (1= Metropolitan area, 2 = Uusimaa and Southern Finland, 3 = Western Finland, 4 = Northern and Eastern Finland).


## Statistical Analysis


Quantitative analysis. To examine associations between the socio-demographic characteristics and changes in fertility preferences, we fitted multivariable multinominal logistic regression models for changes in fertility preferences due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine (no change in fertility preferences was used as a reference category). Separate models were built for each of the two outcomes, and the models included age, gender, partnership status, number of children, education, employment status, house ownership, and region of residence as predictors, all mutually adjusted. All the models also included weights. Statistical analyses were conducted in Stata 18.0 (StataCorp, 2023).

Qualitative analysis. To analyse the responses from the open-ended questions, we used a mixed inductive-deductive coding approach to ensure systematic and reliable coding of responses (Boyatzis, 1998; Terry et al., 2017). This method allowed us to ground the analysis in pre-existing theories, such as the Traits-Desires-Intentions-Behaviour model (Miller, 1994), the Second Demographic Transition theory (Lesthaeghe, 2010; Zaidi & Morgan, 2017), and other relevant literature (e.g., Gietel-Basten et al., 2022; Hashemzadeh et al., 2021; Morgan & King, 2001; Raybould et al., 2023; Schleutker, 2014). A comprehensive list of 45 codes was developed prior to analysis based on the existing literature, aligning the current coding scheme with existing theoretical frameworks. Each code was accompanied by a label and precise definition to guide the coding process (see Appendix 1 for details).

Two independent and qualified judges were trained in the coding procedure, including familiarization with the codebook and the opportunity to clarify any questions or uncertainties. They initially coded a training sample to ensure consistency and establish interrater reliability (see Appendix 2 for details on the training sample).

The judges then coded responses to all three questions using the codebook. They were allowed to add new codes if they addressed previously uncovered themes, resulting in three

additional codes - 'infertility treatment', 'patriotism', and 'overall bad situation in the world'.

The judges subsequently coded all open-ended answers, and interrater reliability was assessed both collectively for all responses and separately for each question to ensure high degree of agreement. The Cohen's kappa coefficient, based on McHugh's (2012) guideline, classified interrater reliability as strong (0.80-0.90, 82-100% of the data considered to be reliable), moderate (0.60-0.79, 35-63%), weak (<0.60), minimal (<0.40), or none (<0.21).

The Cohen's kappa coefficient for the question related to changes in the desired number of children was 0.91 ( p <0.001), and for the question related to timing of childbearing was 0.87 ( p < 0.001), indicating a strong level of agreement between the judges. The Cohen's kappa coefficient for the question related to war was 0.87 ( p < 0.001), indicating a strong level of agreement between the judges.
