## Conclusion


Based on a modeling strategy that enables us to estimate differences across ages, survey years, and generations, we do not find meaningful differences in support for legal abortion in the United States across generations, especially relative to the differences across ages and survey years. Although numerous studies and polling reports indicate noteworthy generational differences, our findings cast doubts on their conclusions. Again, none of these studies incorporated an analysis approach that enabled its authors to uniquely identify each of these differences. We are skeptical of claims that generational replacement, in and of itself, will move abortion opinion in a liberal direction. Instead, we find larger differences across ages and survey years.

A remaining question is what to make of, and how to proceed with, our finding of minimal differences across generations? A somewhat premature answer would be to conclude that generation or cohort theories are simply uninformative in terms of abortion attitudes-and that existing studies and polling reports have unquestionably confounded generation effects with period effects and age effects. A more appropriate takeaway is that the generation classification scheme that pervades contemporary discussion in the United States does not provide meaningful insight into abortion attitudes. Incorporating conventional cut-points and the common nomenclature (Silent Generation, Baby Boomers, Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z), we largely sidestepped whether this scheme makes empirical or theoretical sense. A possible contributor to our relatively weak generation effects is the somewhat arbitrary and ambiguous construction of the generations in this most widely adopted classification scheme (see Cohen 2021). Cohorts demarcated via theorizing about epochal events pertaining to abortion rights specifically may produce more sizable generation effects. Also, our modeling approach lends itself to a data-driven definition of a cohort: we can vary the definition of a 'generation,' and compare the explanatory power of the different definitions. This type of analysis may reveal meaningful differences in the attitudes across alternatively defined generations. In future work, guided both by consideration of major abortion-related events and exploratory data analysis, researchers should consider the relative ability of alternative definitions to account for abortion attitudes. But using the popular definitions, we find that differences in abortion attitudes across generations are small.

## INTRODUCTION


Studies exploring the social antecedents of pornography use among adolescents have consistently found that youth who view pornography more frequently often report experiencing weak or troubled family relationships (Ma & Shek, 2013; Mesch, 2009; Mesch & Maman, 2009; Peter & Valkenburg, 2016; Shek & Ma, 2012a, 2012b, 2014; Wolak, Mitchell, & Finkelhor, 2007; Ybarra & Mitchell, 2005). While some scholars argue that weaker or troubled family ties might encourage pornography use by leaving the door open for unwanted exposure from friends or forms of 'deviant' sexual exploration due to loss of social control (Ma & Shek, 2013; Mesch, 2009; Shek & Ma, 2012a, 2012b, 2014; Weber, Quiring, & Daschmann, 2012), others suggest part of the appeal of pornography use might be as a coping strategy to escape family problems, feel comfort or a sense of control, intimacy, and so on (Baltazar et al., 2010; Cortoni & Marshall, 2001; Grubbs et al., 2019; Ybarra & Mitchell, 2005).

This study aims to make two key contributions to the literature on the social antecedents of sexual behavior, and particularly pornography use and masturbation. First, it tests whether weak or troubled family relations growing up may be predictive of adult pornography use and masturbation. Research has connected young adult pornography consumption to use patterns that present themselves during adolescence (Rasmussen & Bierman, 2016, 2018). Building on the literature cited above, it was theorized that a pattern of adult pornography use and masturbation may have initially been promoted, at least in part, by troubled relational experiences earlier on in life. That is to say, young people dealing with distant parental relationships, an unloving home atmosphere, or otherwise traumatic family relationships might have initially sought out masturbation and/or pornography use as a coping strategy (see Leonard, 2010 for preliminary theorizing and analyses), which then may have carried on into adulthood.

Second, this study builds on recent research suggesting measures of pornography viewing are often a proxy for the practice of solo-masturbation (e.g., Perry, 2019a, 2020; Prause, 2019), and thus, findings regarding participants' regular 'use' of pornography as a coping strategy may really be telling researchers more about why people masturbate (while often using pornography to facilitate that behavior). Thus, a theoretical model is proposed in which troubled family background predicts more regular masturbation as an adult, which then mediates any association between family troubles and adult pornography use.

Lastly, and supplemental to the above contributions, this study also tests whether either association is moderated by age and gender. It was anticipated that any predictive power that troubled family background has on adult sexual behavior would be limited primarily to younger adults who are simply less removed from their family backgrounds compared to older adults; and it was expected that troubled family background would be more strongly associated with women's sexual behavior, since men's pornography use and solo-masturbation are more common and widely-accepted, and thus, less variable.


## BACKGROUND AND EXPECTATIONS



## Pornography Use and Family Relations During Adolescence


In their review of two-decades of research on adolescents and pornography use, Peter and Valkenburg (2016) identify 'weak or troubled family relations' as among the four most consistent predictors of pornography use (along with being male, sensation seeking, and being at a more advanced pubertal stage). In a relatively early study examining exposure to Internet pornography in a sample of American youth, Ybarra and Mitchell (2005) found that participants who intentionally sought out explicit sexual material showed lower levels of emotional bonding with their caregiver and were more likely to have experienced coercive discipline from their

caregiver. Similarly, Wolak et al. (2007) reported that at the bivariate level American youth who scored higher on parent-child conflict were nearly twice as likely to intentionally seek out pornography as to have no exposure. In studies of Israeli adolescents, Mesch (2009; see also Mesch & Maman, 2009) found that participants who reported lower commitment to their parents and family were more likely to use the Internet to search for X-rated material. And in a series of collaborative articles on adolescents in Hong Kong, Shek and Ma (2012a, 2012b, 2014; Ma & Shek, 2013) found pornography use associated with lower family functioning, and specifically 'mutuality' or experiencing mutual love, support, and concern among family members.

One explanation presented for this persistent (and cross-national) connection between weak or troubled family relations and adolescent pornography use is through social control theory. Mesch (2009), for example, argues that adolescents who are less connected to their parents, either emotionally or practically, will either miss out on the socialization that would develop more self-control against such behaviors as pornography use, or would naturally invite deviant influences (see also Ma & Shek, 2013; Sevcikova et al., 2014; Shek and Ma 2012a, 2012b, 2014). This theory would be consistent with other findings suggesting adolescents who score higher on 'social control' scales (with questions asking about how close family members and friends would feel about them viewing pornography) are less likely to view pornography (e.g., Hardy, Steelman, Coyne, & Ridge, 2013). Others, however, propose that patterned pornography use may be a response to conflict in the relationship, either as a form of rebellion against overbearing parents (Weber et al., 2012; Wolak et al., 2007; Ybarra & Mitchell, 2005) or as a means of coping with loneliness, or distant and hurtful relationships (Grubbs et al., 2019).

While few studies have observed trajectories of pornography use over time, Rasmussen and Bierman (2016, 2018) observed in a panel study of Americans during their adolescent and

young adult years that more regular pornography use earlier on was robustly predictive of higher pornography use as a young adult, suggesting patterns of sexual behavior persist over time. To the extent that some adolescents initially develop a practice of masturbating to pornography, at least in part, as a response to distant or strained parent or family relationships, it is proposed that this patterned behavior may carry on and predict such sexual behavior as an adult. Stated more formally, it would be expected that:

- H1: Reporting more troubled family relationships growing up will be positively associated with masturbation practice as an adult.
- H2: Reporting more troubled family relationships growing up will be positively associated with pornography use as an adult.

However, consistent with emerging research, it is also theorized that the pornography use that received almost exclusive focus in previous studies cited above might reflect an underlying coping strategy in solo-masturbation. This idea is outlined further below.


## Research Disentangling Pornography Use and Masturbation


While viewing pornography and solo-masturbation are often functionally related, and masturbation is almost certainly implied in discussions of individual pornography 'use,' it is pornography that has received the overwhelming amount of attention in sex scholarship. Yet previous studies have reported that the most frequently cited reason for viewing pornography is for sexual stimulation and/or to obtain sexual release (Baltazar et al., 2010; Bridges & Morokoff, 2011; Grubbs et al., 2019; Paul & Shim, 2008), suggesting that an expectation of masturbating is often the primary motivating factor behind seeking out pornography in the first place. Recent empirical findings have also challenged the dominant assumption that watching pornography is the most consequential action in view when solo-masturbation is involved. In a recent fMRI study, Gola et al. (2017) found that the correlation between ventral striatal cue-reactivity and

pornography use was no different from its correlation with masturbation frequency, suggesting the two might be confounded. And in a more recent study using electroencephalography, Prause (2017) found that masturbation was actually a more important factor influencing EEG patterns compared to visual sexual stimuli (VSS), prompting her to more recently (2019) conclude, 'Given the very high covariance between VSS viewing and masturbation, any study that does not account for masturbation…cannot be understood as a study of 'pornography' effects.'

Most recently, Perry (2020) tested whether the oft-cited relationship between pornography use and relational happiness was primarily being influenced by solo-masturbation. He found that while pornography use was initially negatively associated with relational happiness in multivariate models, once masturbation was accounted for the coefficient for pornography use was not only rendered non-significant, but reversed signs and became positively associated with relational happiness with some differences by gender. Consequently, Perry (2019a; see also Prause, 2019) suggests a revised masturbation-pornography path model in which a desire to engage in solo-masturbation precedes pornography use and is in fact the more central sexual behavior to consider. Building on this emerging line of research, it is proposed:

H3: Any association between more troubled family relationships growing up and adult pornography use will be mediated (rendered completely non-significant) by accounting for masturbation practice in multivariate models.


## Potential Moderating Effects of Age and Gender


Research on how family experiences in childhood influence adult outcomes indicates that any influence of such experiences tends to diminish over time as persons mature and find themselves in different social contexts (Harris, 2009; Pinker, 2002). Because it is theorized that experiencing weaker or troubled family relationships growing up may promote a pattern of masturbation and pornography use that persists into adulthood, it is reasonable to expect that

these associations would be stronger for younger adults who are simply less removed from their family background than older adults. Conversely, it is expected that as adults age, any influence their family background might have on their sexual behavior would be attenuated. Thus, it is anticipated that:

H4: Any association between more troubled family relationships growing up and adult pornography use and masturbation will be stronger for younger adults compared to older adults.

It is also hypothesized that the association between troubled family background and adult masturbation and pornography use may differ somewhat by gender. Research suggests solomasturbation and pornography use are more widely accepted for men compared to women, and these behaviors are also less variable among men than women (Leitenberg, Detzer, & Srebnik, 1993; Peterson & Hyde, 2010, 2011; Regnerus, Price, & Gordon, 2017; Robbins et al., 2011). Statistically, this means that the predictive power of troubled family background on adult masturbation and pornography use may ultimately be weaker for men than for women, since men would already be more inclined to engage in both sexual behaviors. Based on this assumption, the final hypothesis states:

H5: Any association between more troubled family relationships growing up and adult pornography use and masturbation will be stronger for women compared to men.


## METHODS



## Participants


Data for this study come from the 2014 Relationships in America Survey, which was originally distributed to a national probability sample of 15,738 adults between the ages of 18 and 60 years old in January and February 2014. Data collection was sponsored by the Austin Institute for the Study of Family and Culture and also conducted by Knowledge Networks/GfK using the Knowledge Panel strategy described above for the 2012 NFSS. The main survey

completion rate for the RIA survey instrument was 62 percent. Cases in the RIA sample were assigned a weight based on the sampling design and their probability of being selected (WEIGHT2 in the data set), ensuring a sample that was representative of American adults ages 18-60. This sample weight was used in all analyses. The analytical sample for the RIA is 12,932 adults who provided information for all variables used in the analyses. For more information about sampling and data collection procedures, see Litschi et al. (2014).


## Measures


Masturbation and pornography use. The key outcome variables for this study are participants' practice of masturbation and intentional pornography use. To measure masturbation practice, participants were first asked if they have ever masturbated (Yes or No). Those who answered that they had ever masturbated were then asked, 'When did you last masturbate?' Responses ranged from 1 = today to 9 = over a year ago. Responses to both questions were combined and recoded such that those who had never masturbated were coded 0 and then most recent masturbation (1 to 9) was reverse-coded such that higher numbers indicated more recent masturbation. This resulted in a masturbation practice measure ranging from 0 = never masturbated to 9 = masturbated today. While this question technically does not inquire about frequency, the operative assumption is that-on average-persons who reported masturbating as recently as 'today,' or 'yesterday,' or '2-4 days ago,' will tend to masturbate more consistently than someone who reports last masturbating 'over a year ago.' As Regnerus et al. (2017) point out in their identical use of this masturbation measure, the framing of this question helps to avoid certain drawbacks of 'average pattern' questions that ask respondents how often they engage in a certain activity, such as recall bias and under-reporting due to either regressing to the mean or social desirability bias (see also Chang & Krosnick, 2003).

As with masturbation, the RIA also measured pornography viewing frequency in terms of participants' last time intentionally viewing it. The RIA asks: 'When did you last intentionally look at pornography?' Participants could answer 1 = today to 10 = I've never intentionally looked at pornography. These responses were reverse-coded so that higher numbers indicate that the participant viewed pornography more recently, and thus, is likely to be a more frequent consumer of pornography. Parallel analyses of this measure of pornography use with more traditional 'frequency' measures in other surveys suggests high continuity and thus support the validity of this measure (see Regnerus, Gordon, & Price, 2016).

Because of the nature of the dependent variables, ordinary least squares (OLS) regression is used as the model estimation strategy.

Troubled family background. The RIA includes five measures indicating the degree to which participants experienced (subjectively) significant family troubles growing up that are combined to construct a scale.  The RIA asks participants their level of agreement with the 2 following five statements: (1) While growing up, my father and I had a warm, close relationship. (2) While growing up, my mother and I had a warm, close relationship. (3) We had a loving atmosphere in our family. (4) There are matters from my family experience that I am still having trouble with. And (5) There are matters from my family experience that negatively affect my ability to form close relationships. Response options ranged from 1 = strongly agree to 5 strongly disagree, and each were coded in such a way to where higher scores indicated more significant family troubles. All five measures were then combined into a scale set to zero with scores ranging from 0 to 20. The alpha for the scale was .80 indicating reasonable internal consistency.

Controls. The analyses include a variety of control variables in order to mitigate the potential for spuriousness. Because both pornography use and masturbation may simply serve as substitutes for a lack of sexual activity, analyses included controls for sexual frequency and satisfaction (see Perry, 2020). Participants were asked how often they had intercourse 'within the past 2 weeks,' for which they could provide any number. They were also asked about their sexual satisfaction. Specifically, participants were asked 'Are you content with the amount of sex you are having?' They could answer 'Yes' (reference), 'No, I'd prefer more' (= 1), or 'No, I'd prefer less' (= 1).

Both masturbation and pornography use could also serve as coping behaviors for someone who was currently experiencing symptoms of depression (Perry, 2018a, 2019b; Stein et al., 2001). Thus, the analysis controlled for current depressive symptoms using a scale created from five questions asking about how many times in the past twelve months participants had been 'bothered by things that usually don't bother you;' 'you could not shake off the blues, even with help from your family and your friends;' 'you felt depressed,' and 'you enjoyed life (reverse-coded).' Participants could answer 1 = never or rarely to 4 = most or all of the time. Participants were also asked 'How happy or unhappy are you with your life these days?' Responses ranged from 1 = very happy to 5 = very unhappy. All five questions were standardized into Z-scores and summed to create a 'depressive symptoms scale' with an alpha score of .80.

Lastly, analyses included a number of sociodemographic controls. Age was divided into 4 broad categories in order to make interactions with troubled family background more intuitive.

Categories included 18-29, 30-44, 45-59, and 60+.  Dummy variables were included for gender 3 (male = 1, female = 0), marital status (marred = 1, not married = 0), and race (white = reference, Black = 1, Hispanic = 1, other race = 1). In order to account for contextual and subcultural factors that might influence masturbation and/or pornography use (MacInnis & Hodson, 2015; Perry, 2018b, 2019b; Perry & Whitehead, 2020; Whitehead & Perry, 2018), dummy variables were also included for whether participants live in the South (South = 1, other = 0) and whether they are evangelical Protestant (evangelical = 1, other religion = 0). Respondents were also asked about their number of living biological children, which ranged from 0 to 12. Educational attainment was measured with a four-value scale ranging from 1 = less than high school to 4 = bachelor degree and beyond. Household income was measured as a continuous measure with values from 1 = less than $5,000 per year to 19 = $175,000 per year. Religiosity was measured with a summative scale from two questions about respondents' frequency of religious service attendance (1 = never to 8 = more than once a week) and importance of religious faith in their lives (1 = not important at all to 5 = more important than anything else). These measures were both standardized into Z-scores and summed to create a religiosity scale with an alpha score .79. For descriptive statistics of all variables in the analyses, see Table 1.


## Plan of Analysis


The analysis proceeds as follows. Table 2 provides zero-order correlation coefficients of all variables included in multivariate models in order to observe key bivariate associations. Table 3 presents OLS regression models predicting masturbation practice. Model 1 excludes pornography use in order to establish a net association between troubled family background and

adult masturbation practice before taking pornography use into account. Model 2 introduces pornography use in order to test whether accounting for pornography use (as a potential mediator) significantly alters the predictive power of troubled family background. Models 3 and 4 include interaction terms between troubled family background and age and gender, respectively, in order to discern whether any observed association between troubled family background and adult masturbation is moderated by whether participants are younger or older, male or female.

Table 4 is identical to Table 3 except that pornography use and masturbation are reversed. Model 1 excludes masturbation to establish a net association between troubled family background and pornography use before taking masturbation practice into account. Model 2 introduces masturbation practice. And Models 3 and 4 introduce the age and gender interaction terms, respectively. All models present unstandardized beta coefficients ( b ), standard errors (SE) and unstandardized betas (β) in order to draw observations about substantive significance as well as statistical significance.


## RESULTS


Zero-order correlations presented in Table 2 indicate that reporting a more troubled family background is positively associated with more recent masturbation (r = .07, p < .001) and pornography use (r = .04, p < .001). This would initially appear to support the first two hypotheses (H1 and H2). Yet while these associations are each statistically significant beyond .001, each correlation is substantively quite weak. Plotting the bivariate mean scores for both masturbation and pornography use across values of troubled family background (not shown) indicates that mean scores for masturbation increase at a somewhat stable (though shallow) rate

across scores on the troubled family background scale, while scores for pornography use fluctuate a good deal and do not increase substantively.

Turing to the multivariate models, Model 1 in Table 3 indicates that reporting a more troubled family experience growing up is positively associated with more recent masturbation among adult participants (b = .03; p < .001; β = .05). In terms of substantive significance, troubled family background is not remotely close to the strongest predictor of adult masturbation, yet it is a stronger predictor than other significant predictors such as current depressive symptoms and household income. Model 2 introduces pornography viewing into the regression equation and though pornography use is powerfully associated with masturbation (b = .56; p < .000; β = .56) and increases the adjusted R 2 tremendously (from .267 to 476), the influence of troubled family background is virtually unaffected (b = .03; p < .001; β = .04). The only notable change is that the standardized coefficient decreases slightly from .046 to .037, though now it is a substantively stronger predictor of masturbation practice than sex frequency, preferring less sex, being male, identifying as neither white nor black, the number of living biological children, household income, and southern residence. The fact that the association between troubled family background and masturbation does not change substantively even with pornography use included supports the idea that pornography use does not mediate any relationship between troubled family background and masturbation, because an intent to masturbate likely comes first in the causal order between masturbation and pornography use. The first hypothesis (H1) thus receives strong support.

Model 3 introduces the interaction term for troubled family background × age, and the term is negative and statistically significant (b = .03; p < .01; β = -.10). This indicates that as age increases across the four categories, the positive association between troubled family background

and masturbation practice decreases. This affirms the fourth hypothesis (H4). Figure 1, Panel A illustrates this trend. As young adults aged 18-29 report higher scores on the troubled family background scale, their predicted masturbation practice increases. As the age groups increase, this trend shallows and then reverses to the point where adults age 60 and above actually decline in their likelihood of masturbating across values of the troubled family background scale.

Lastly, Model 4 introduces the interaction term for male × troubled family background, which is negative and statistically significant. In this case, this sign indicates that as troubled family background scores increase, the distance between men and women in their likelihood of masturbating more recently diminishes. That is, women's masturbation practice is more strongly associated with reporting a troubled family background compared to men, which affirms the fifth hypothesis (H5). Panel B in Figure 1 illustrates this trend fairly clearly. At lower levels of troubled family background, men and women show quite distinct scores on the masturbation practice measure and both increase in their masturbation score as troubled family background scores increase. However, as the trendlines indicate, women's masturbation scores increase at a faster rate to where they are less distinguishable from men at the highest levels of troubled family background. Thus, while troubled family background is associated with more recent masturbation for both men and women even after accounting for depressive symptoms, sex frequency and satisfaction, and even pornography use, this net association is particularly strong among women.

Table 4 presents OLS regression models predicting pornography use with the same format as in Table 3. In Model 1, results show that reporting a more troubled family background is only a marginally significant predictor of more recent pornography viewing (b = .01; p = .055; β = .02) and this association is quite weak in terms of substantive significance. Model 2

introduces the masturbation practice measure and this dramatically increases the variance explained (adjusted R 2 increases from .325 to .517) and completely washes out any association between troubled family background and adult pornography use. The persistence of the association between troubled family background and masturbation and the disappearance of the marginal association between troubled family background and pornography use once masturbation is accounted for strongly suggests that masturbation practice mediates any relationship between troubled family background and pornography use, as predicted in the third hypothesis (H3).

Models 3 and 4 introduce the interaction terms for age and gender respectively and both are non-significant. Thus, while troubled family background and adult masturbation remain associated in full models (almost exclusively for younger adults, and especially among women), it is observed that any association between troubled family background and pornography use, for either men or women, is completely mediated through masturbation.


## DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS


While numerous studies have found that adolescents who report weaker or troubled family backgrounds tend to view pornography more often, no research has examined whether troubled family backgrounds might also be predictive of adult pornography use and masturbation, suggesting that a pattern of either behavior might have developed initially in connection to the family troubles and persisted into adulthood. Building on emerging research suggesting masturbation practice may be the primary factor at play in analyses of pornography use, this study used a large, representative data set to test whether experiencing a more troubled family background growing up would predict more recent (and reasonably more frequent) masturbation and pornography use, and whether masturbation would fully mediate any

association between troubled family background and adult pornography use. The analyses also sought to test for the potential moderating effects of age and gender.

Findings have affirmed that higher scores on the scale of troubled family background is associated with more recent masturbation even after accounting for sex frequency and satisfaction, depressive symptoms, pornography use, and a hose of sociodemographic and ideological factors. Moreover, this association was limited almost exclusively to young adults (age 18-29) and was particularly strong for women. The marginal association between troubled family background and adult pornography use, however, was washed out by taking masturbation into account, suggesting that masturbation mediates any association between troubled family background and pornography use.

Because the analyses sought to hold constant potential mental health, relational, and sexual factors that could account for participants' masturbation practice, it is argued that the observed relationship between experiencing significant relational troubles growing up and adult masturbation reflects the habituation of a practice that developed earlier on. That is to say, young people who experience significant relational troubles at home might develop a habit of masturbation (and possibly viewing pornography to facilitate masturbation) that eventually carries on into adulthood.

But what are the precise mechanisms through which these factors are connected? Following scholars who connect weak or troubled family relations with adolescent pornography use through social control theory (Ma & Shek, 2013; Mesch, 2009; Sevcikova et al., 2014; Shek and Ma 2012a, 2012b, 2014), it could be that participants who reported troubled family backgrounds experienced less parental control which allowed for more exposure and experimentation with sexual behaviors like masturbation and pornography use that might have

been discouraged under situations with greater social control. Conversely, it could be that troubling family experiences reported by participants reflected a relatively extreme, coercive parental control, and thus, masturbation (with pornography) was a response to the greater restrictions preventing sexual intercourse (Weber et al., 2012; Whitehead & Perry, 2018; Wolak et al., 2007; Ybarra & Mitchell, 2005). Following another line of research, however, that connects masturbation and pornography use with depressive symptoms and coping strategies (Stein et al., 2001), it could be that participants with more troubled family backgrounds initially looked to masturbation as a coping strategy, providing comfort, reducing anxiety, affording a sense of control, and so on (Baltazar et al., 2010; Cortoni & Marshall, 2001; Grubbs et al., 2019; Ybarra & Mitchell, 2005). In this case, a practice of masturbation could simply have been carried on into young adulthood as a chosen means of dealing with daily stress.  This last explanation 4 could have also played a role in combination with either of the previous two.

Although the data do not make it possible to definitively identify the precise mechanisms linking troubled family background and masturbation practice, because two of the statements in the troubled family background scale specify, 'There are matters from my family experience that I am still having trouble with,' and 'There are matters from my family experience that negatively affect my ability to form close relationships,' this would suggest that participants who more strongly affirm these statements are experiencing persistent emotional trauma that currently affects their relationships, and thus, the connection with masturbation might have originally been one of coping (providing feelings of intimacy, safety, and comfort) that persists into adulthood.

The findings regarding the moderating influences of age and gender also nuance our understanding of how troubled family backgrounds might be linked with adult masturbation practice. To the extent that adolescents experienced significant family troubles that promoted regularly engaging in private sexual experiences that persisted into adulthood, this would naturally be more observable among young adults who have likely had less time to process through earlier hurts, but are also at a life stage in which sexual energy is at its peak.

Less intuitive, perhaps, is the finding that troubled family background is more strongly associated with adult masturbation for women than for men. It was theorized that this would likely be because men are already masturbating more frequently than women, and thus, their practice would not be as variable or affected by troubled family backgrounds compared to women. Related to the issue of the variability of sexual experience, it could also be that the trajectory of women's sexual experiences tend to be slightly more malleable than men's based on previous emotional and relational experiences (Ogas & Gaddam, 2011). Panel data along with qualitative interviews would be ideal to disentangle the precise connections between family background, gender, and sexual experience through the life course.

In addition to some of data limitations already addressed, several others should be acknowledged. First, while the troubled family background measure is asking about participants' past experiences and thus provides greater potential for establishing causal ordering with adult masturbation and/or pornography use, the data are still cross-sectional and the possibility cannot be ruled out that young participants may have been masturbating or viewing pornography before they experienced family difficulties and simply carried on those habits into adulthood. Although this is somewhat unlikely, given the data, it is also plausible that individuals who masturbate more are just more likely to recall their family backgrounds as troubled (i.e., recall bias). Yet,

neither of the previous possibilities would account for why participants who report more recent masturbation as adults also reported troubled family backgrounds, since the two factors would have no mechanism linking them. Nevertheless, actual longitudinal data that could track the introduction of both masturbation and family troubles in peoples' lives over time would be necessary to definitively establish temporal precedence. Another limitation, addressed in the methods section, that the measures do not strictly measure masturbation or pornography viewing frequency but how recently someone did either. As argued earlier, these measures mitigate several limitations of 'frequency' measures (e.g., recall bias and social desirability bias) and have proven to be quite consistent with frequency measures in other surveys (e.g., Regnerus et al., 2016). Nevertheless, readers should keep in mind that the argument regarding frequency of masturbation and pornography use is contingent on the likelihood that persons who masturbated or viewed pornography more recently are also likely to do so more frequently.

These limitations notwithstanding, this study has extended our understanding of the social antecedents of private sexual behaviors like masturbation and pornography use. Adult masturbation, particularly among younger adults and especially so among women, seems to be in some way connected to experiencing weaker or troubled family relationships growing up. While a number of legitimate mechanisms potentially connecting these two factors need to be further adjudicated, it was theorized that adolescents experiencing significant family trouble may develop a masturbation habit as a coping strategy to feel control and comfort, relieve stress, etc., and this habit may simply persist into young adulthood. Furthermore, this study has provided further support for the emerging body of research suggesting that solo-masturbation is the more central behavior to focus on, rather than pornography use, with the latter accompanying and/or proceeding from the former.

## 1. Introduction


Following the 'normative turn' in innovation policy in addressing urgent societal challenges (Schlaile et al. 2017; Uyarra et al., 2019), 'directionality' has become a key concept. The notion of 'directionality' is not only employed in the innovation policy discourse, but also in sustainability transitions research, where it is related  to the normative direction of transformative change processes.  While inherently related, the ways the concept of directionality are used in these literature streams suggests the need for distinguishing between 'systemic directionality' and 'giving direction', as they seem to hold different meanings.

On  the  one  hand,  conceptualizations  stemming  primarily  from  research  on  sustainability transitions  range  from  (interacting)  transitions  in  socio-technical  systems  in  a  certain  direction (Andersson et al., 2021; Schot & Kanger, 2018), the direction of socio-technical pathways in transitions (Foxon et al., 2013; Pel et al., 2020; Rosenbloom, 2017; Rosenbloom et al., 2018, 2019; Stirling, 2008, 2011), or normative visions of desirable futures guiding the direction of transformative change (Kemp & Loorbach, 2006; Loorbach, 2010; Smith et al., 2005). Directionality in transitions is seen as a feature of systemic,  evolutionary  processes  of  transformative  change,  in  which  cumulative  choices  and processes in a certain direction can limit or open up development pathways in which transitions unfold (Pel et al. 2020; Røpke, 2012; Rosenbloom et al., 2019; Stirling, 2011). Such emergent pathways or directions in transitions are increasingly seen as normative and political (Elzen et al. 2011; Kok & Klerkx,  2023;  Rosenbloom  et  al.,  2018),  and  highlight  the  temporal,  process-oriented  nature  of directionality (Pel et al. 2020).

On the other hand, using the same term, directionality in the innovation policy field is advocated as a crucial component of innovation policies, contributing to addressing societal challenges (Diercks et al., 2019; Grillitsch et al., 2019; Janssen et al., 2021; Lindner et al., 2016; Schot & Steinmueller, 2018; Weber & Rohracher, 2012). This changes the focus from the direction of broad societal change processes to the specific direction given by public policies (i.e. policy direction) and policy actors, who may  guide,  block  or  accelerate  innovation  processes.  For  example,  how  policy  actors  formulate expectations and policies shapes the selection environment and guides the search in innovation systems (Bergek et al., 2008; Hausknost & Haas, 2019; Hekkert et al., 2020; Yap & Truffer, 2019). Particularly in the transformative innovation policy (TIP) and mission-oriented innovation policy (MIP) literatures, directionality  in  innovation  policies  has  been  a  topic  of  recent  discussions,  sparking  empirical investigation (e.g. Andersson & Hellsmark, 2024; Borrás & Schwaag Serger, 2022; Grillitsch et al., 2019; Hirschmann et al., 2022; Parks, 2022), and also criticism (e.g. Cappellano et al. 2022; Sanström & Alm, 2022) on the effectiveness of directional policies in light of societal challenges. For example, it  matters  how  societal  demands,  policy  goals,  sectors,  and  solutions  are  defined  and  by  whom (Andersson  &  Hellsmark,  2024;  Boon  &  Edler,  2018),  and  which  pathways  are  taken  through  the

problem-solution space (Wanzenböck et al. 2020), for the potential of innovation policies to deliver transformative change (Ghosh et al. 2021).

Despite  having  a  different  focus,  we  argue  giving  direction  and  systemic  directionality  are inherently related and interdependent. Systemic progression in a certain direction may be reflected in a diversity  of  potential  desirable  futures  and  possible  development  pathways,  which  can,  in  turn, materialize in public policies and current decision-making in different ways, such as the formulation of long-term policy goals and missions advocated for by certain actors. As such, specific directions in public policies (related to the view of the innovation policy field on directionality) may be nested in systemic evolution of a diversity of possible societal development trajectories (related to the view of the sustainability transitions field on directionality). We advocate an understanding of directionality that captures this nested, interdependent relationship between  giving direction and systemic directionality, through  seeing  it as: 'a political  process  of  negotiating  normative  policy  directions, which influences and is influenced by the pathways that emerge and materialize in transitions.'

Our view on directionality builds on previous conceptualizations in both literature streams that have emphasized the political character of the concept (e.g., Hausknost & Haas, 2019; Kok & Klerkx, 2023; Pel et al. 2020; Stirling, 2011), have discussed the governance of directionality (Könnöla et al. 2021; Lindner et al., 2016; Pel et al., 2020; Salas Gironés et al., 2020), the outcomes of directionality (Andersson et al.,  2021;  Ghosh et  al.  2021),  and  how  directionality  is  brought  into  policy  practice (Andersson & Hellsmark, 2024; Bergek et al., 2023; Boon & Edler, 2018; Grillitsch et al., 2019; Parks, 2022).  However,  we  foreground  and  deepen  the  political  dimensions  of  directionality  and  giving direction,  through  engaging  with  political  questions  and  insights  from  political  theory,  which  has received relatively little attention in the context of directionality.

We take a political-theoretical view of policy and policymaking as a starting point, in which the ontological distinction between policies and politics is challenged. Along this view, policies are not to be seen as neutral, but as a negotiated outcome influenced by different actors in different positions of power, both in and beyond the public policy sphere (Durnova et al., 2016; Fischer & Forester, 1993; Fischer & Newig, 2016; Majone, 1989). Particularly those policy issues related to complex societal challenges tend to be politically contested, and policymaking around such issues rarely happens in a political vacuum (Wanzenböck et al., 2020). Consequently, a broad range of actors are affected by the resulting direction, and can win or lose depending on which direction prevails. We, therefore, consider any policy direction taken as the outcome of a political decision-making process and an outcome of prioritization.

Moreover,  considering  the  relevance  of  viewing  directionality  through  the  lens  of  political policy processes, there has been surprisingly little attention to integrating relevant policy process theory to  better  understand  directionality,  exceptions  aside.  To  close  these  gaps  in  existing  literature,  we present the following research question: How can the politics of directionality be conceptualized using policy process frameworks? We employ an integrative literature review (Paré et al., 2015), which aims

to integrate insights from different academic fields for the generation of new theoretical insight. By answering this question, the article provides a relevant contribution to understanding innovation policy as  subject  to  political  negotiations  and  decisionmaking  processes;  a  view  which  has  remained underdeveloped in the innovation policy field (Ghosh et al. 2021; Haddad et al., 2022; Kern & Rogge, 2018; Kok & Klerkx, 2023; Parks, 2022; Salas Gironés et al., 2020; Wanzenböck et al., 2020).

We start by introducing the questions who gives which direction, where, how, when and why, inspired  by  Lasswell  (1936),  as  analytical  structuring  device  for  understanding  the  politics  of directionality. Through analysing questions that relate to 'giving direction', such as ' how is direction given?' , as well as questions relating to 'systemic directionality', such as ' when do directions change?', our  first  aim  is  to  contribute  to  bridging  the  gap  in  understanding  of  directionality  between  the innovation  policy  and  sustainability  transitions  fields.  We  then  draw  on  various  prominent  policy process  frameworks  from  the  field  of  policy  studies,  with  the  aim  to  harvest  relevant  conceptual contributions and new insights from political science conceptualizing the politics of directionality. As an outcome we present a conceptual framework of the politics of directionality, integrating insights from policy process frameworks, with important implications for the innovation policy field.

The remaining chapters of this article are organized as follows: section 2 presents state-of-theart insights from existing literature about the political dimensions of directionality, through discussing the  questions  of who  gives  which  direction,  where,  how,  when  and  why. Section  3  outlines  the methodology, data collection and analytical steps of the integrative literature review, and introduces the policy  process  frameworks used in the analysis.  Relevant conceptual contributions from the policy process  frameworks  in  light  of  existing  literature  on  the  politics  of  directionality  are  discussed  in Chapter 4.  Chapter  5  concludes  with  presenting  the  conceptual  framework,  critical  methodological reflection,  an  empirical  research  agenda,  and  relevant  implications  for  the  field  and  practice  of innovation policy.


## 2. The politics of directionality


How this article discusses specific political aspects of directionality is inspired by a classic definition of politics by Harold D. Lasswell (1936): 'who gets what, where, when, how and why' . In the context of the politics of directionality, the statement can be reformulated as: 'who gives which direction, where, how, when and why' . These questions present a clear, understandable way to study politics, specifically the politics of directionality, which is why they have been employed as an analytical structuring device for this study. 1

We cover questions from a perspective of 'giving direction' (i.e. who gives direction, which direction is given, how is direction given and where is direction given) and 'systemic directionality' (i.e.  when  do  directions  change  and  why  do  some  directions  prevail  over  others).  While  discussed separately for analytical clarity, the questions and their insights are considered in relation to each other. For example, who gives direction has important implications for which direction is given and why

certain  directions  prevail  over  others.  Hereafter,  each  of  the  six  questions  will  be  introduced  and discussed in light of existing literature from the fields of innovation policy and sustainability transitions, giving an entry point for how to engage with a political understanding of directionality, and highlighting current gaps that emerge when viewing directionality from a political perspective.


## 2.1 Who gives direction?


Who  is  involved  in  processes  of  directionality  points  to  the  relevance  of  power,  power  relations, participation and inclusion, as it matters 'who is giving direction' (Kok & Klerkx, 2023; Parks, 2022; Salas Gironés et al., 2020; Stirling, 2008). Who gives direction has ramifications for which directions are recognized and reflected in policy goals, and whether short-term activities by actors giving direction will  contribute  to  or  hinder  progress  towards  these  goals.  As  the  debate  on  'just  sustainability transitions'  highlights,  these  matters  have  important  implications  for  the  democratic  legitimacy  of policy (Bennett et al., 2019; Hendriks, 2009; Swilling, 2019), which is why, as Stirling argues, more attention should be paid to diversity in directionality (Stirling, 2011). Similarly, broad inclusion is often advocated, such that societal engagement is a major source for direction-setting (Könnölä et al., 2021; Lindner et al., 2016; Schot & Steinmueller, 2018). This implies for instance the involvement of nonstate actors (Kuhlmann & Rip, 2018) and citizens (Trischler et al., 2022).

However, despite the will and effort for democratic participation in processes of directionality, relevant  decision-making  might  happen  outside  of  open  debate.  Instead,  having  relevant  resources, access to significant policy actors, interest and skills to influence policy formulation, or bring about new collaborations, such as policy entrepreneurs (Salas Gironés et al., 2020), institutional entrepreneurs (Grillitsch et al., 2019), regulatory agencies (te Kulve et al., 2018) or intermediaries (Hirschmann et al. 2022), may be crucial for providing directionality. This implies 'who gives direction' is a matter of power, and power relations between actors with varying capacities to mobilize resources and institutions to achieve their goals, and who may win or lose as a consequence (Avelino, 2017).  Regarding 'who gives direction', more attention is yet to be paid to how these actors are embedded in broader networks of  actors  involved  in  decision-making  processes,  how  their  directing  activities  influence  power (im)balances within those networks, and to which normative ends these activities are directed (Kok & Klerkx, 2023).


## 2.2 Which direction is given?


Important for understanding which normative direction is given, is the political nature of the directions themselves. Which direction is given through policy has important ramifications for whether specific societal  needs  and  challenges  adequately  addressed  (Boon  &  Edler,  2018),  and  whether  legitimate development pathways are selected or reinforced as a consequence (Rosenbloom, 2017; Rosenbloom et al., 2019). These issues matter for evaluating the transformative potential (Haddad & Bergek, 2023), and the outcomes (Andersson et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2021) of innovation policies.

However, little attention has been given to the character of directions beyond technological dimensions, as recognized by Andersson et al. (2021) and Hausknost & Haas (2019). For example, choosing between two alternative technologies for decarbonizing the energy system is connected to different pathways towards carbon neutrality, affects different sets of actors, and may prioritize different values. Moreover, Pel et al. (2020) suggest directionality is characterized by a multiplicity of competing socio-technical configurations, and diverse forms of normative appraisal and assumptions. Therefore, deciding  on  a  particular  solution  likely  has  ramifications  for  innovation  and  societal  development beyond technology selection.

We view a policy direction as a discourse related to a ' direction towards…' a particular solution, a  related  view  about  the  problem  this  solution  aims  to  solve,  and  political,  ideological  values  that underly such problem frames and advocated solutions related to particular envisioned futures. In policy formulation, this relates to how goals, sectors and solution pathways are defined, demarcating which directions can materialize (Andersson & Hellsmark, 2024). Through viewing directions as a discourse, the  normativity  of  directionality  and  the  political  ideologies  underlying  different  directions  can  be highlighted, providing a more political view to current understandings of directionality. Importantly, discourses do not only manifest in policy texts, but are enacted through the social practices and actor relations related to a particular direction (Fairclough, 2013). Through power, certain directions become dominant and reinforced by institutional structures (Schmidt, 2011).


## 2.3 Where is direction given?


Spaces where direction is given have been described along many forms and dimensions. Many of the models in innovation studies consider markets as the main, and apolitical, selection environment for innovation  (Hausknost  &  Haas,  2019).  Others  such  as  Andersson  et  al.  (2021),  show  that  from  a systemic perspective, the space in which directions develop can be broadend to spatial, socio-technical, and temporal dimensions. In a similar way, Røpke (2012) shows different conditions at the regime and landscape level are important for influencing the direction of (ICT) innovations.

From the perspective of policy formulation, the way goals, sectors, and solution pathways are defined form a defining space in which directionality unfolds (Andersson & Hellsmark, 2024), which can materialize differently across different geographical scales and policy domains (Grillitsch et al., 2019). From a political point of view, spaces of policymaking, decision-making, and broader political arenas are relevant sites of directionality, which are linked in relevant ways to transition dynamics (Edmondson et al.,  2019;  Markard  et  al.,  2016;  Normann,  2015,  2017).  Furthermore,  demand-side innovation policy, sector-specific policies and challenge-oriented policies provide relevant spaces in which societal needs and demands are articulated (Boon & Edler, 2018). Lastly, the concept of an 'arena' has been introduced to describe the space where actors come together to formulate and govern societal  missions  (Janssen  et  al.,  2023;  Wesseling  &  Meijerhof,  2023),  develop  a  shared  problem perception,  vision  and  agenda  among  frontrunners  in  a  transition  (Loorbach,  2010),  or  where

institutions,  technologies,  visions  and  practices  come  together  in  a  cognitive  space  (Jørgensen  & Sørensen, 2002). Considering these relevant contributions regarding 'where direction is given', this article more explicitly pays attention to the political nature of sites of directionality. In line with this gap, Hausknost & Haas (2019) suggest to (re)politicize the space where direction is given, through shifting the boundaries of the selection environment in which solutions are sought, from markets to a space marked by planetary boundaries.


## 2.4 How is direction given?


From a political point of view, the governance approaches by which direction is given matter for the prevailing direction, that is, the outcome (Ghosh et al. 2021; Andersson et al. 2021). Pluralistic,  bottomup approaches of experimentation and participatory governance are often advocated for to align the interests of broad stakeholder groups, create shared expectations and coordinated action (Grillitsch et al. 2019; Könnölä et al., 2021; Kuhlmann & Rip, 2018; Schot & Steinmueller, 2018). In contrast, giving direction through mission-driven governance has often been connected to a more top-down approach, in which the mission dictates the direction of change, with a role for policy to tilt the playing field in favor of the mission and related actors (Kattel & Mazzucato, 2018; Mazzucato, 2018). However, this dichotomy  may  more  be  nuanced,  as  suggested  by  Boon  &  Edler  (2018,  p.445):  ' Directional policymaking cannot be a completely top-down, administrative exercise, but it will not organically grow bottom-up  either.  (…)  The  state  has  a  special  role  in  this  space,  because  there  is  a  need  for  a coordinating role (go beyond sectors), an inspiring role (go beyond incremental innovations), and a strategic role (go beyond easy solutions).'

Regardless  of  differing  governance  approaches,  the  quote  above  illustrates  how  a  large responsibility is placed on the state and public policy actors to shape the direction of innovation and sustainability transitions (Bergek et al., 2023; Laatsit et al., 2022). For example, directionality requires policymakers to stimulate innovation in societally desirable directions (Ghosh et al., 2021; Könnölä et al., 2021; Weber & Rohracher, 2012), while also destabilizing regimes and phasing out activities that hinder transformative change towards sustainability (Ghosh et al., 2021; Kivimaa & Kern, 2016; Røpke, 2012). This requires finding a converging pathway through the problem-solution space (Wanzenböck et al., 2020), resolving conflicting actor interests, developing shared visions, promoting institutional entrepreneurs, developing new governance capabilities (Grillitsch et al., 2019), handling conflicting policy  goals  identifying  realistic  pathways,  mobilizing  relevant  policy  domains  and  accessing intervention points (Bergek et al., 2023). These are no easy tasks, and this may imply demands beyond the scope of STI or sectoral policies (Laatsit et al. 2022, Boon & Edler, 2018).


## 2.5 When do directions change?


Systemic dynamics of directionality inherently point to the relevance of temporality in the emergence, development, and outcomes of negotiating different directions over time. Such processes have been relatively  well  covered  in  existing  literature,  examining  relevant  positive  and  negative  feedback

mechanisms (Edmondson et al., 2019), which create dynamics of openness for change in direction, and subsequent closing down and lock-in (Foxon et al., 2013; Pel et al., 2020; Rosenbloom, 2017; Stirling, 2008).

From a political point of view, an important aspect of when directions change is to gain insight into  when,  and  by  whom,  moments  of  openness  and  closing  are  influenced.  During  moments  of openness, political choices can impact the pace and direction of change (Foxon et al., 2013; Pel et al., 2020; Rosenbloom et al., 2018; Stirling, 2011). Critical moments are so-called  branching points', when ' political choices determine whether and in which direction the pathway is followed (Foxon et al., 2013, Rosenbloom et al. 2018).

At the same time, directionality is characterized by path dependency, meaning early sequences of  choices  can  set  in  motion  self-reinforcing  courses  of  development  that limit  the  possibilities  for change in direction (Rosenbloom et al., 2019; Stirling, 2008). While it is an accumulating sequence of choices that shape the outcomes of directionality, the particular policy choices influence the ways in which self-reinforcing patterns of development can be enacted (Rosenbloom et al., 2019).


## 2.6 Why do some directions prevail over others?


Why certain directions prevail over others can be seen as an outcome of the aforementioned aspects of directionality. For instance, temporal dynamics related to path dependency (when) can influence the composition of the group of actors involved in the negotiation and decision-making processes (who), and spaces where directionality takes place (where). In this sense, directions more closely related to current perspectives regarding societal challenges and their desired solutions will likely prevail over those that are more divergent. As the diversity of possible directions closes down, a path dependency is formed for a particular transition pathway as a consequence of cumulative choices favoring a certain direction over others (Rosenbloom, 2017; Rosenbloom et al., 2019).

Importantly,  as  the  literature  on  critical  discourse  highlights  (e.g.,  Fairclough,  2010,  2013; Howarth & Griggs, 2015; Sum & Jessop, 2015), which direction prevails and has historically prevailed, is  also  a  question  of  power,  and  thus  is  related  to  ' who  gives  direction' . Power  in  relation  to directionality can be seen as a productive means to promote certain understandings, meaning and value to a direction, implying some directions are recognized and formalized, while others are excluded or marginalized.


## 3. Review approach


Within the scope of literature reviews with distinct approaches and purposes, this study most closely aligns with an integrative literature review, which aims to assess, synthesize, and integrate literature on a research topic from different fields, enabling new theoretical frameworks and perspectives to emerge (Paré  et  al.,  2015;  Snyder,  2019;  Torraco,  2005,  2016).  We  use  questions  about  the  politics  of directionality ( who gives which direction, where, how, when and why) as an analytical tool to review policy process frameworks, enabling new perspectives on the politics of directionality to emerge. Our

aim is not to present an all-encompassing overview of the policy process field, but rather to translate their insights for the study of the directionality, understood in terms of a political negotiation process, providing relevant insights for the field of innovation policy.


## Policy process literature


Within  policy  studies  and  political  science,  this  review  focuses  specifically  on  policy  process frameworks. 2 While  recognizing  the  relevance  of  other  policy  studies  literature,  policy  process frameworks  give  a  particularly  suitable  starting  point  for  analysing  the  politics  of  directionality. Specifically, they have a theoretical focus on mechanisms of policy stability and change, which are crucual elements to directionality because of its dynamic and temporal nature. Furthermore, literature on policy process frameworks is developed in active research communities, who continuously advance knowledge regarding the policy  process  frameworks  based  on  new  insights,  critically  discuss  their advantages, limitations, and future research avenues, while maintaining consistancy in the interpretation of core concepts.

Within the scope of literature concerning policy process frameworks, a specific selection of relevant frameworks was made through evaluation of the following selection and inclusion criteria, which were formulated prior to the analysis (not in order of relevance). The framework:

- · Engages  with  complex  policy  dynamics  of  stability  and  change:  the  framework  gives insight into the policy process with attention to complex dynamics of policy stability and change, beyond policy stage heuristics and short-term policy cycles.
- · Engages  with  policy  processes  broadly:  the  framework  addresses  political  negotiation processes  within  spheres  of  decision-making,  while  linking  to  sites  of  broader  political debate.
- · Is well-known and theoretically mature: the framework has been developed and empirically employed across diverse geographical, temporal and (policy) field-specfic contexts for a long period of time (i.e., at least more than ten years).
- · Has an active research community: the framework shows continuous effort to challenge, revise and enhance theoretical conceptions based on recent contributions and publications.

As a second step, a screening took place within the field of policy process studies, to identify policy process frameworks (n=16), which could potentially fit the evaluation criteria. The following policy process frameworks were selected after evaluation: Multiple Streams Framework (MSF), Punctuated Equilibrium Theory (PET), Policy Feedback Theory (PFT), Advocacy Coalition Framework (ACF) and the Narrative Policy Framework (NPF).
