## 4.1 Who gives direction?


The question of ' who gives direction' points to the relevance of which actors are included in processes of negotiation and decision-making in directionality (Könnölä et al., 2021; Kuhlmann & Rip, 2018; Schot & Steinmueller, 2018), and who is able to influence decision-making processes (Grillitsch et al., 2019; Hirschmann et al., 2022; Salas Gironés et al., 2020). Policy process frameworks can build on existing  insights  regarding  who  gives  direction  in  terms  of  policy  actors  and  their  configurations, through the concepts of policy subsystems, policy monopolies and policy entrepreneurs.

The policy process frameworks present the variety of actors involved in the policy process as a ' policy subsystem ' (PET, ACF, NPF), or a 'policy community' (MSF). A policy subsystem is seen as a  network of actors  which is  issue-bound and particular to a  geographical area, making  it a  useful concept for contextualizing 'who gives direction', as well as 'where is direction given' (see chapter 4.3). The concept of a policy subsystem thus shows actor involvement in giving direction goes beyond

policy  domains  and  across  sectors  to  include  any  actor  involved  with  a  particular  policy  issue. Moreover, the policy subsystem concept includes actors from within, and beyond the public policy sphere, such as policymakers at any level of government, private sector actors, and representatives from NGOs, media, and research organizations (ACF, NPF).

However, PET and MSF emphasize that important decisions in policy subsystems or policy communities are predominantly made by a limited group of actors, consisting, for example, of policy experts, political party advisors, academics, consultants, bureaucrats and lobbyists (Green-Pedersen & Princen, 2016; Herweg, 2016). This implies the frameworks differ in how they see the level of influence policy actors have on decisions within a policy subsystem. In fact, PET suggests policy subsystems can become monopolies of influential actors with a single interest, who may prevent groups outside the dominant policy subsystem from engaging in significant decision-making (Baumgartner et al., 2018; Givel,  2010).  Given  policy  monopolies  are  supported  by  a  strong  policy  image  and  institutional structure,  who  gives  direction  may  be  subject  to  path  dependencies.  For  example  decision-making structures, state capacities, interest group formation and broader membership in the political community are shaped by how policy processes have historically developed (PFT).

Consequently, most policy issues are treated outside of wider political debate and discussion (PET),  indicating  that  the  call  for  broadening  participation  in  direction-setting  related  to  societal challenges  may  prove more  challenging  than  existing  literature  on  directionality  literature  suggests (e.g., Könnölä et al., 2021; Kuhlmann & Rip, 2018; Lindner et al., 2016; Schot & Steinmueller, 2018). Importantly, deeper engagement with participation beyond open calls for broadening inclusion is crucial because of the political nature of directionality in the context of sustainability transitions, and the need for democratic legitimacy in direction-setting (Boon & Edler, 2018; Elzen et al., 2011; Kuhlmann & Rip, 2018; Schot & Steinmueller, 2018).

Furthermore, who gives direction is also a matter of who has relevant resources, capabilities, power, and political support for initiating policy change, as empirically shown by e.g., Salas Gironés et al. (2020) and Hirschmann et al. (2022). The MSF has introduced the concept of ' policy entrepreneur' (Kingdon,  1984,  2011),  and  later  notions  of  a  'problem  broker'  (Knaggård,  2015)  and  'political entrepreneur' (Herweg et al., 2015, 2018), as actors that can institute policy change. Attention is brought to specific problems by 'problem brokers', who frame conditions as public problems and work to make policymakers accept these frames (Knaggård, 2015). Policy entrepreneurs attach problems to solutions and adapt them to find broad support among members of the policy community (Herweg et al., 2018). Once the problem and potential solution have been brought to the agenda, policy makers with a relevant formal leadership position, that is, 'political entrepreneurs', can seek a majority for the proposal after which a decision can be made (Herweg et al., 2018). Salas Gironés et al. (2020) have applied the policy concept of policy entrepreneurs in the context of directionality in innovation policy, and have found it points to the relevance of early-stage direction-setting by policy entrepreneurs.


## 4.2 Which direction is given?


Characterizing which direction results as an outcome of negotiating different policy directions beyond technological dimensions has  been a  relevant  gap  in  the  literature  (Andersson  et  al.,  2021).  Policy process literature contains relevant concepts for understanding the normativity of directions that emerge beyond technological dimensions, relating to which values, norms, and ideas may be represented in policies and policy discourse.

The ' belief system ', 'a set of basic values, causal assumptions and problem perceptions', provides individuals with meaning and sensemaking (ACF, NPF) (Sabatier & Jenkins-Smith, 1993, p. 25). It consists of three layers: the 'deep core beliefs', related to fundamental normative values and political  ideology,  the  'policy  core  beliefs',  containing  empirical  assessments  of  the  causes  of  the problem, normative value priorities and preferred solutions, and the secondary beliefs, regarding the seriousness of the problem, or the design of a specific policy instrument (Sabatier & Jenkins-Smith, 1999).  The  different  layers  of  the  belief  system  provide  a  new  way  of  understanding  the  political characteristics  of  directions  beyond  alternative  technologies.  Importantly,  the  concept  of  the  belief system is relevant to understanding how directions are materialized in the form of public policies. ACF and NPF analysts consider policies as the translations of a belief system as manifested in goals, rules, incentives, taxes, and other policy instruments. Public policies are thereby never neutral but reflect the narratives, beliefs, political values, problem frames and preferred solutions of the actor coalition that prevailed in the policy debate.

Additionally, the notion of a ' policy image' (PET) can be helpful to understand the stability of such policy belief systems. Policy images related to political values, emotive appeals and empirical information, which can be used to reproduce a frame around a particular policy problem (Baumgartner et al., 2018; Baumgartner & Jones, 1993). As long as subsystem politics remain stable, the assumptions related to a particular policy problem are taken for granted, and the policy image hereby contributes to feedback processes reinforcing the stability of existing policy monopolies (Baumgartner et al., 2018; Princen, 2013).

Both concepts of a 'policy image' and a 'belief system' thus point to the relevance of normative and  ideological  values  that  guide  which  direction  is  given  through  policy,  addressing  the  gap  of characterizing directions beyond specific (technological) solutions.


## 4.3 Where is direction given?


From  a  systemic  perspective,  relevant  dimensions  within  which  directionality  unfolds  are  spatial, temporal, and socio-technical dimensions (Andersson et al., 2021), and regime and landscape levels (Røpke, 2012). Within these dimensions, spaces of policymaking, decision-making, and political arenas are relevant sites of directionality, about which policy process literature has insights to offer.

The policy process frameworks suggest negotiation of directions might take place both within arenas of policymaking, such as policy subsystems (PET, ACF, NPF), and in spaces of macropolitics

(PET, PFT). Both are relevant for directionality, as directions, problem frames and solution pathways may be discussed in broader political arenas, as well as having their ramifications for policy formulation and  objectives. As  such,  there  are inherent linkages  between  systemic  dimensions  in  which directionality  unfolds  and  the  decision-making  processes  that  take  place  within  sites  of  political negotiation.  Additionally,  past  policies  may  shape  the  ' policyscape '  in  which  current  policies  are formulated and debated, implying broader political spaces and policy subsystems are further connected through the ways in which past policies shape the context in which directionality is given (PFT).

Furthermore, the MSF distinguishes three main spaces of policymaking and politics, and how they can be connected during specific moments in time called 'windows of opportunity' (Kingdon, 1984) (also see chapter 4.5). The problem stream is where changes in societal indicators, feedback from previous policies or focusing events are framed into problems. As problem frames are an important part of directions, the problem stream can be seen as a space where directions first emerge. In the policy stream , multiple policy solutions to the policy issues are generated by the policy community, which are gradually reduced through discussion, modification, and recombination of different ideas. Here, directions are shaped further through the identification of a diversity of policy solutions. In the political stream ,  negotiation processes around the legitimacy of directions occur, and may be influenced by (changes in) 'national mood', the degree of interest group mobilization, and changes in ideological preferences related to political cycles (Herweg et al., 2018). The MSF hereby provides more specific insight into the spaces where direction is given, and how directions are negotiated through agendasetting and decision-making processes.

Lastly, the concept of the ' policy venue' may be important as space for directionality, as this is where (narrative) debates regarding specific policy issues between opposing coalitions of actors play out (ACF, NPF). Policy venues may take form in formal institutions, such as parliaments, or informal ones, such as (social) media platforms (NPF, PET). The concept of policy venues hereby provide a more political understanding of spaces such as 'mission arenas' (Janssen et al., 2023; Wesseling & Meijerhof, 2023), where direction is given.


## 4.4 How is direction given?


Giving direction can imply different actor roles and governance strategies with regards to navigating the challenging combination of stimulating transformative innovations and the phase-out of undesirable activities in light of relevant societal transitions (Kivimaa & Kern, 2016; Røpke, 2012). Policy process literature offers additional insights regarding the question of navigating policy conflict and the process of negotiating different policy directions.

Firstly, the concept of ' softening up' gives a relevant idea of how direction is given through discussing, altering, and recombining alternative solutions, filtering out many policy alternatives along the way (MSF). In this way, many directions advocated by diverse actors may be 'closed-down' during

the policy process (Stirling, 2008), highlighting the political nature of negotiating different directions beyond selecting technologies through market mechanisms (Hausknost & Haas, 2019).

Furthermore, existing literature points to the various challenges related to the governance of directionality,  for  example  in  bridging  normative  values  between  diverse  stakeholders  in  seeking consensus  (Grillitsch  et  al.,  2019),  or  coordinating  conflicting  policy  goals  (Bergek  et  al.  2023), potentially promting policy conflict . The ACF and the NPF give relevant insight into the dynamics of policy conflict, indicating that the level of conflict (i.e., the extent to which actor coalitions perceive the objectives or actions of opponents as a threat), depends on which strategies they employ to influence the policy process. For instance, if an actor coalition perceives themselves as losing a policy debate, they  are  more  inclined  to  used  strategies  related  to  expanding  conflict  (NPF),  exaggeration  of maliciousness  of  the  opponent,  growing  mistrust  and  obstruction  of  policy  solutions  (ACF). Overcoming  policy  conflict  is  easier  when  coalitions  converge  on  policy  beliefs,  or  negotiated agreement is facilitated by mutual interaction, broad representation, commitment, and trust (ACF).

Lastly, how direction is given by different actors may vary over time, and between spaces of policymaking and macropolitics (PET, MSF). In a policy subsystem with a dominant monopoly of actors, and a widely accepted policy image, there may be lower levels of contestation and conflict, compared to periods when a policy issue enters the macropolitical arena, and political mobilization and societal debate take place (PET). Likewise, in the policy stream interaction is characterized by arguing and  linking  problem  frames  with  proposed  solutions,  while  in  the  political  stream,  bargaining  and powering for political support  dominate  (MSF).  These  insights  are  relevant  for  understanding  how directions may be differently negotiated through closed politics of soliciting, or open societal debate.


## 4.5 When do directions change?


Existing literature on directionality has pointed to the relevance of feedback mechanisms and pathways with moments of openness related to when directions change (Foxon et al., 2013; Pel et al., 2020; Rosenbloom, 2017; Stirling, 2008). Policy process theory can be of additional value to understanding directional change through insights on policy dynamics and -change.

Punctuated  equilibrium  theory  (PET)  sees  policy  change  to  be  related  to  short  lurches  of potentially major deviations from past policies. Such major policy change stems from built-up friction in the form of unaddressed issues and external shocks (Baumgartner & Jones, 1993). When pressures for change are sufficient, policy issues move from the policy subsystems onto the macropolitical and governmental agenda, potentially leading to major policy change led by previously uninvolved political actors (Baumgartner et al., 2018). A new equilibrium is established as new institutions are put in place by  a  new,  or  newly  altered  policy  community,  and  public  and  political  involvement  recede (Baumgartner et al., 2018).

The  Advocacy  Coalition  Framework  (ACF)  identifies  four  conceptual  avenues  for policy change including: (1) events external to the subsystem, such as crises (2) internal events, such as policy

failures  or  scandals,  (3)  policy  learning  through  gradual  altering  of  concepts  and  assumptions  of subsystem  participants,  or  (4)  negotiated  agreement  among  previously  warring  coalitions  (JenkinsSmith et al., 2018, pp. 145-146). Any of these paths can contribute to major policy change, though they should be considered more as a necessary, but not sufficient source of major policy change (JenkinsSmith et al., 2018).

Furthermore, policy narratives also affect the likelihood of policy change (NPF) (Shanahan et al., 2011; Shanahan, Jones, McBeth, et al., 2018). The relative strength, stability, and cohesion of these policy narratives provide the 'coalitional glue' that binds coalition actors. This glue provides focus and purpose within an advocacy coalition, making it more likely that a coalition is successful in realizing their preferred policy outcomes (NPF) (Shanahan et al., 2011, 2018).

Lastly, the idea of critical branching points as moments where choices can be made to change direction may align with ' windows of opportunity' (MSF). Such a window presents a period where a condition in society is seen as a problem, a potential solution is 'coupled' to this problem, and has political  support  from  policymakers,  providing  the  necessary  conditions  for  agenda-change  and subsequent decision-making (MSF).


## 4.6 Why do some directions prevail over others?


Explanations of why certain directions prevail over others can arguably be seen as a combination of path  dependency of  existing  directions,  as  well  as  a  question  of power to  promote  certain understandings,  meaning  and  value  to  a  direction,  implying  some  directions  are  recognized  and formalized,  while  others  are  excluded  or  marginalized.  Ideas,  values,  and  envisioned  solutions  to societal challenges that are more closely aligned with current directions will likely prevail over those that are more divergent.

Similarly, policy dynamics are characterized by feedback mechanisms and path dependency, characterizing policy processes mostly with stability and lock-in effects, rather than dynamic policy change (PFT, PET). Policy Feedback Theory (PFT) extensively studies path dependencies in policy processes, which can add to these existing insights.

PFT suggests past policies are important in shaping current policies and politics, making current directions  and  direction-setting  dependent  on  past  choices  and  pathways.  This  policy  process framework suggests a plurality of self-reinforcing feedback mechanisms, such as feedbacks related to economic  returns,  expansion  of  state  capacities  in  existing  domains,  sociopolitical,  fiscal, informational, and interpretive feedbacks. Consquently path dependencies result in terms of agendasetting, offering frames for interpretation, imposing resource restrictions and commitments, configuring governing capacity and institutionalizing standard operating procedures. Additionally, policy outcomes shape politics through shaping the social, economic and political conditions in which individuals and groups take part in the policy process and the goals they pursue (Mettler & Sorelle, 2018; Pierson, 1993).

Furthermore, policy process theory also sheds light on why certain directions may prevail due to  particular problem recognition .  Limited  periods  and  serial  processing  of  information  affect  the recognition and attention to certain problems and their related solutions over others (PET, MSF, ACF). Additionally,  problems  have  become  more  contested,  while  the  relevance  of  traditional  ideologies guiding policymaking has decreased (Herweg et al., 2015, 2018). This implies that choosing between solutions is ever more difficult for policymakers, making them more receptive to lobbying and public opinion. As a result, policy processes are characterized by ambiguity (MSF) and non-linearity (PET). Under  these  conditions,  values,  belief  systems  (ACF)  and  policy  narratives  (NPF)  are  central  for sensemaking and legitimizing which directions are relevant.

Lastly,  legitimization  of  certain  directions  is  related  to  power,  as  power  legitimizes  certain problem understandings, meaning and value of a direction, while others are excluded or marginalized. Such power can stem from resources ,  like  formal  authority to make policy decisions, influence on public opinion, access to relevant information and networks, ability to mobility support, time, financial resources, and skills related to leadership, negotiating and persistency (MSF, ACF).


## 5. Discussion and conclusion


This study started from the concept of directionality, which is understood in the innovation policy literature mainly through actors 'giving direction', and contributing to transformative change , and in the sustainability transitions literature as 'systemic directionality' a feature of transformative change needed in the face of urgent societal challenges. Regardless of these somewhat different meanings, both perspectives point to the relevance of a process-oriented and political understanding of directionality. We have therefore proposed a view of directionality as ' a political process of negotiating normative policy directions, which influences and is influenced by, the pathways that emerge and materialize in transitions'. Departing from such a political understanding of directionality, we addressed the question how can the politics of directionality be conceptualized using policy process theory ?


## Conceptualizing the politics of directionality


In answer to the research aim and question, we present a conceptual framework for analyzing the politics of directionality through the lens of policy process frameworks in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Conceptual Framework ¶

The framework above summarizes and builds on the insights presented in chapters 2.1-2.6 and 4.1-4.6, showing the nested relationship between the political process of giving direction (in terms of who, where and how direction is given) resulting in negotiated policy directions ( what ), and systemic directionality in terms of emerging and prevailing directions ( why ), as well as dynamics of stability or change in the direction of pathways ( when ).

The  questions who  gives  direction,  how  is  direction  given, and where  is  direction  given represent  political  decision-making  processes  of  giving  direction,  related  to  actors  who  may  steer, accelerate or block policy directions. These questions are most relevant for understanding and engaging with policy subsystem politics and policy processes, and potentially speak most to the innovation policy community.

Firstly,  policy  process  frameworks highlight the importance of critically reflecting on actor involvement ( who ), democratization and legitimation processes of giving direction, because the spaces where important  decision-making  processes  around negotiatin  policy  direction  takes  place,  may  be limited in its openness towards actor influence outside of the dominant policy subsystem, and closed to open  public  debate  (PET).  This  highlights  important  challenges  for  the  call  from  diverse  authors regarding the need for more democratic engagement in processes of directionality (e.g. Könnölä et al., 2021; Kuhlmann & Rip, 2018; Lindner et al., 2016; Schot & Steinmueller, 2018; Trischler et al., 2022).

Furthermore, it matters how policy problems and solutions are recognized and prioritized, and how policy conflict is addressed, for the resulting policy direction ( what ). Policy process frameworks provide insight into policy conflict and how to overcome it, contributing to understanding and resolving challenges around how direction is given, as indicated in recent literature (e.g. Bergek et al., 2023, Grillitsch et al., 2019). Importantly, Grillitsch et al. (2019) suggest the inability to resolve conflicting normative interests  can  result  in  vague  policy  formulation  and  lack  of  direction  needed  in  light  of addressing societal challenges. Overcoming policy conflict can be enabled through converging policy beliefs, or negotiated agreement between coalitions through mutual interaction, broad representation, commitment, and trust (ACF; NPF). Policy process literature hereby indicates that in giving direction, there is  a  need  to  be  reflexive  about  the  underlying  beliefs  and  values  of  actor  coalitions  trying  to coordinate and find relevant policy solutions, and to foster conditions of trust and commitment between them.

Thridly, the concepts of ' belief systems' and ' policy images' give a complementary, political understanding  of which  direction  is  given beyond  technological  trajectories,  which  addresses  an important gap pointed out by Andersson et al. (2021). Both concepts show that public policies are never neutral but reflect political values, problem frames, beliefs and preferred solutions of actors who were successful  in  influencing  policy  debates  and  reiterating  dominant  policy  images.  Policy  process literature affirms policy directions ( what ) involve ideological values, policy images and beliefs around which problem-solution constellation is 'the right direction'.

Lastly, negotiated policy directions resulting from the political process of giving direction have relevant implications for why some directions prevail over others and when directions change. These questions  are  relevant  for  analyzing  directionality  from  a  more  long-term  perspective  of  evolving societal  development  and  emerging  pathways  (systemic  directionality).  Such  questions  are  more systemic in nature, and might therefore be more relevant among sustainability transition scholars. Policy process frameworks highlight policy directions and politics are subject to similar structural dynamics of positive and negative feedbacks as relevant in transitions, which may create opportunities for change or lock-in of policy directions (PET, PFT). This is in line with existing contributings in the sustainability transitions  literature,  which  have  shown  how  policy  mixes  co-evolve  with  socio-technical  systems (Edmondson et al., 2019), and how cumulative choices a certain direction guides systemic directionality of transitions over time (Rosenbloom et al., 2018). In particular, Rosenbloom et al. (2019) have pointed out the need for viewing the 'branching points' at which directions change as political, for which policy process literature has relevant insights to offer, related to different conceptualizations of policy change (all frameworks) and 'windows of opportunity' (MSF). Finally, why some directions prevail over others may be informed by insights from policy process literature related to power and influence on problem recognition and agenda-setting (MSF, PET, ACF), and relevant resources to legitimize problem frames and solutions, and influence decision-making (MSF, ACF, NPF).


## Limitations and methodological discussion


The previous discussion shows policy process literature has relevant insights to offer with regards to the politics of directionality. However, the policy process frameworks were not written with this explicit purpose in mind, which implies there are limitations to this study to consider.

Firstly, no single framework offers a silver bullet for understanding the politics of directionality. For instance, Punctuated Equilibrium Theory (PET) and Policy Feedback Theory (PFT), have strong temporal characteristics, focusing on feedback mechanisms, policy change and path dependency. As such, these frameworks are more relevant for understanding when directions change or why some are more persistent than others, compared to questions such as who gives direction, or how is direction given.  For  the  latter  questions,  the  Multiple  Streams  Framework  (MSF),  the  Advocacy  Coalition Framework  (ACF),  and  the  Narrative  Policy  Framework  (NPF)  offer  more  relevant  insights,  for instance, around navigating and understanding policy conflict among different actor coalitions.

Secondly,  the  policy  process  frameworks  studied  in  this  article  comprise  large  research communities and bodies of literature in and of themselves. Through the integrative review approach used in this article, much of their depth and nuance is lost in the need for a concise understanding of their core concepts and their potential use for conceptualizing the politics of directionality. While it was not the purpose of this review to be all-encompassing in presenting the policy process frameworks, other methods would be more suitable when aiming for a complete picture of one or more policy process framework(s).

Lastly, as also discussed by Kern & Rogge, (2018), policy process frameworks differ in their ontological and epistemological foundations and assumptions. Some have a more positivist history and application, (e.g. the ACF), while others have more post-positivist, constructivist characteristics (e.g. MSF or NPF). It is important to be aware of such differences when applying them in new contexts such as innovation policy or sustainability transitions. Regarding the politics of directionality, arguably a more interpretive and constructive understanding of policy reality is fitting, as this involves a political view of policymaking characterized by sensemaking processes and argumentation, rather than a causal chain  of  events.  Nonetheless,  it  would  lack  the  necessary  nuance  in  understanding  any  of  the frameworks  as  fully  positivist,  or  fully  constructivist.  A  telling  example  is  the  Narrative  Policy Framework, which holds a constructivist ontology, while employing quantitative methods, traditionally related to a more positivist epistemology (Jones & Radaelli, 2015).


## Promising avenues for future research


This paper has proposed a conceptual distinction between  'giving direction' and 'systemic directionality', to clarify the different understandings of directionality that exist in the innovation policy and sustainability transitions communities. While this article has made a first step towards bridging the gap between these different conceptual understandings, more explicit discussion and reflexivity around the  intended  meaning  is  necessary  when  engaging  with  this  concept.  Furthermore,  this  article  has foregrounded the inherently political nature of  directionality,  through  presenting  and  employing  an relevant  questions  about  the  politics  of  directionality.  Future  research  could  develop  an  empirical knowledge base on the politics of directionality through mobilizing the conceptual framework presented in this article.

Such empirical analysis could firstly be focused on the historical processes of when directions change and why certain directions have prevailed over others . Important insights could be gained in more specifically identifying and analyzing periods of openness to directional change and moments where existing pathways were reinforced, through mobilizing 'branching points' (Foxon et al., 2013; Rosenbloom et al., 2018) or 'windows of opportunity' (MSF). Literature on policy change can help to better understand the conditions under which directions change and how they can be fostered in light of relevant societal challenges.

Secondly, this study points to the relevance of an actor-centered approach when it comes to studying directionality in an innovation policy context. It matters who gives direction , and how direction is given for which actors are involved and excluded from relevant decision-making processes regarding different possible directions, their power relations and the resulting direction that is given (Avelino, 2017). Furthermore, enriching current empirical insights into practical challenges that come with how direction is given related to navigating diverging interests, values, identifying pathways, formulating strategies  and  stimulating  coordinated  action  (Bergek  et  al.,  2023;  Grillitsch  et  al.,  2019)  will undoubtedly render relevant learning opportunities for innovation policy practitioners and academics.

Interesting would be to explore sectoral and geographical differences in this regard, with the aim of generating more geographically and domain-specific insights on giving direction.

Lastly, empirical attention is needed to which direction is given through policy, as an outcome of  political  processes  related  to  directionality.  Such  empirical  investigation  should  centralize  the normative values underlying different directions and stimulate reflexive discussion on their desirability considering societal challenges, e.g. how they might align or create tensions with the pursuit for just sustainability transitions. Important to consider here is the relative power position of and strategies used to promote certain directions, as this has important implications for the legitimacy of directions, related to problems recognition, and which solutions and accompanying visions of desirable futures are to be stimulated through public policies.


## Implications for innovation policy


The  politics  of  directionality  as  conceptualized  in  this  article  have  important  implications  for  the innovation policy community. Arguably, both in academic literature and policy practice - three policy directions  have  materialized,  related  to  market-failures,  system-failures,  and  transformative  change paradigms (Diercks et al., 2019; Schot & Steinmueller, 2018; Weber & Rohracher, 2012). Each of these rationales represents a distinct normative direction ( what ), involves specific actors ( who ), in a specific policy subsystem ( where ), who influence the policy discourse over time ( when ). These policy directions now co-exist in parallel, for example through the co-existance of policy instruments related to growthbased R&D  incentives and university-industry-government relations, with policies fostering experimentation and upscaling for transformative change. In light of our conceptual framework, two conclusions can be drawn about present-day innovation policies.

First, past innovation policies and instruments are not as 'neutral' as the more recent call for more 'directionality' to innovation policy suggests implicitly. Even those science and R&D policies that have been understood as generic policies  to stimulate innovation  'horizontally' instead of favoring particular technologies or industries, have political consequences in terms of the kinds of innovations, industries  and  firms  that  benefit  from  such  policies  (Rodrik,  2009).  For  example,  manufacturing industries profit more from R&D subsidies compared to services, and larger firms more than smaller firms, due to lower involvement of services and smaller firms in R&D activities eligible for subsidies (Frenken, 2017). As such, innovation policy, like any other type of policy, knows winners and losers, and  is subject  to  ongoing  struggles  between  actor  groups  for influence  on  decision-making, prioritization,  and  policy  outcomes.  Resulting  policies  and  instruments  can  therefore  be  seen  as translations of prevailing actors' beliefs and ideologies, challenging the assumption that innovation policy has been 'non-directional' before, and now requires 'more direction'.

Second,  the  policy  directions  related  to  addressing  market-failures,  system-failures  and transformative change contain alternative political values, which have relevant ramifications for which direction is currently given through innovation policies. While economic growth and neoliberalism have

historically underpinned market-failure policies, catching-up, job creation and stimulating universityindustry-government relations underpinned system-oriented innovation policies. Alternatively, transformative  approaches  aim  to  support  social  and  ecological  sustainability  transitions,  hereby addressing urgent societal challenges. The normative and ideological values they represent (economic versus sustainability) have however been historically at odds with one another, making their coexistence challenging, if not conflicting. Current innovation policy can therefore give rise to policy conflict, or political compromise inhibiting transformative action towards sustainability (Grillitsch et al., 2019). Contributing more to transformative change in the direction of sustainability transitions will require prioritizing values such as environmental sustainability, democracy, human rights and social justice in innovation policy and phasing-out growth-aiming rationales. This involves being reflexive and explicit about the values underlying current innovation policy instruments, challenging existing power relations in relevant policy subsystems, and overcoming policy conflict through converging policy beliefs, broad representation, and fostering commitment and trust among actors involved.


## Conclusion


The aim of is paper has been to study the politics of directionality through the lens of policy process frameworks, harvesting important conceptual insights for understanding who gives which direction, where, how, when and why . Policy process literature has been thoroughly reviewed using an integrative review approach to meet this aim, which has resulted in a conceptual framework that mobilizes relevant concepts and ideas from policy process frameworks, advancing the conceptualization of the politics of directionality. Importantly, this study has begun to engage with directionality and giving direction as fundamentally political processes, for which political theory has relevant insights to offer.

For innovation policy scholars and practitioners, it is important to engage meaningfully with the politics of  current  innovation policy rationales and their implications in the context of  pressing societal challenges. It implies that the call for 'more directionality' may be challenged, as this rests on the flawed assumption that innovation policy has been neutral or 'non-directional' before. From the perspective of policy processes, innovation policy rationales and instruments contain their own political values and ideologies and should therefore be treated as political. Overcoming the differences between them will undoubtedly raise difficult questions of prioritization, require reflexivity and challenging existing belief systems, policy images, practices, and power relations. Additionally, all (policy) actors involved will face the challenges of navigating new conflicts that come with the political and complex character of the problems challenge-oriented innovation policy aims to address.

## 1. Introduction


Visitation estimates are critical for informing a wide range of questions about how to effectively manage public lands - from quantifying the economic contributions of outdoor recreation (BEA 2023, NPS 2023), to the impacts of diminished air quality (Keiser et al. 2018) and events like oil spills and wildfires on park and beach usage (Tourangeau et al. 2017, Gellman et al. 2022). As a result, most developed countries spend considerable resources developing sampling designs and counting visitors on public lands (NPS 2023, Schägner et al 2017, English et al. 2020, Tourism and Research Institute 2023). While these programs produce incredibly valuable data, the logistical challenges and expense of counting visitors using on-the-ground methods means monitoring programs rarely produce consistent and comprehensive estimates, leading to pleas for more and better data, from management agencies (Wilkins et al. 2024), academics (Eagles 2014, Loomis 2000), and politicians (US Congress 2023).

One approach to overcoming data limitations and estimating visitation at many locations has been to build predictive models of visitation. Models typically rely on the functional relationship between empirical visitation estimates and factors such as site characteristics, weather conditions, and nearby populations (Barnett-Itzhaki et al. 2023, de Castro 2015). More recent research has begun evaluating whether predictive visitation models benefit from the addition of

predictors derived from widely available digital mobility datasets (Merrill et al. 2020, Wood et al. 2020). Digital mobility data are locations of visitors derived from geolocated content shared on social media platforms and cellular device locations, among other sources (Winder et al. 2025). To date, the limited evidence suggests that digital mobility data are informative predictors of visitation (Wood et al. 2013, Sessions et al. 2016, Heikinheimo et al. 2017, Tenkanen et al. 2017, Fisher et al. 2018, Tsai et al. 2023). Models incorporating a mix of functional variables and digital mobility data sources provide one effective approach for estimation at individual sites and across land management units, when compared against on-the-ground visitation data (Tsai et al., 2023, Winder et al. 2025). Furthermore, the best-performing visitation models are ones that incorporate predictors from multiple mobility data sources (Wood et al. 2020, White et al. 2023, Winder et al. 2025).

Studies have suggested that it may be feasible to construct generalizable visitation models that can be applied in estimation over large spatial and temporal scales, but this hasn't been tested. No study to date has evaluated alternative approaches for estimating recreation use at a national scale, across units managed by different entities. Consequently, we do not know which digital mobility data sources, or what combination of sources, are most useful for developing more general predictive visitation models. Furthermore, it is unclear how visitation models should be parameterized and applied in practice and the accuracy of the visitation estimates derived from models is not fully known.

In this study, we constructed national-scale models of monthly visitation to individual recreation units managed by three U.S. federal agencies using on-the-ground visitation data and multiple predictors including five types of digital mobility data. We address three applied research questions (RQ): 1) what is the relative contribution of different types of digital mobility data to the performance of models that estimate visitation, 2) how transferable are the models among the three federal agencies, and 3) can the models be used to estimate visitation for new locations or unstudied time periods? This research is motivated by the practical application of using models built with digital mobility data for monitoring visitation to public lands and waters. We evaluate predictive models using cross-validation routines that correspond to potential applied uses of these models.


## 2. Data



## Study area and timeframe


We studied public lands managed by the U.S. National Park Service (NPS), Forest Service (USFS), and Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), during 2018 and 2019 (Figure 1). The NPS units were 38 of the 50 most visited units in 2018 and 2019, excluding NPS parkways and units with road network issues, special events (e.g., large festivals) that altered recreation characteristics, and extended closures during the study years (as in Tsai et al. 2023). We included the 49 USFS units sampled under the USFS National Visitor Use Monitoring (NVUM) Program in federal fiscal years 2018 and 2019, and three USFS units sampled in federal fiscal

year 2020 (to cover calendar years 2018 and 2019). Finally, we included seven USFWS national wildlife refuges with on-the-ground visitation data collected by refuge staff.

To obtain the digital mobility data, we first defined the geographic areas of interest. For the NPS units, we used the administrative boundaries from the DataStore at the NPS website (https://irma.nps.gov/DataStore/, as used in Tsai et al (2023)). We used the administrative boundaries of the USFS units

(https://data.fs.usda.gov/geodata/edw/edw\_resources/meta/S\_USA.AdministrativeForest.xml) to define the polygons for the cellular device location data. These administrative boundaries included private inholdings surrounded fully by USFS land and sometimes populated areas immediately adjacent to USFS lands. We used a more refined layer of USFS land ownership (https://data.fs.usda.gov/geodata/edw/edw\_resources/meta/S\_USA.BasicOwnership.xml) to define the USFS polygons of interest for which social media data was obtained. We used the FWS National Realty Boundaries from the FWS Cadastral Database (https://ecos.fws.gov/ServCat/Reference/Profile/121225) to define the FWS polygons.

## Cellular device location and social media data


We sourced a commercial cellular device location-derived visitation dataset from AirSage Inc., which provided aggregated estimates of population-level, daily visitation during 2018 and 2019 to our defined points of interest (geographic units described above) based on their panel of cellular device locations and their proprietary processes. These daily estimates were summed to generate monthly visit estimates. For the NPS, the AirSage data is what was used in Tsai et al. (2023). For the USFS and USFWS, we purchased equivalent retrospective AirSage data for our study period.

For every geographic unit we gathered data from three geolocated social media platforms (AllTrails, Flickr, and Twitter) and the geolocated community science platform eBird. Flickr images were retrieved by querying the Flickr application programming interface (API) in January 2023. Twitter posts were downloaded in real-time from Twitter's 'statuses/filter' streaming API between January 2018 and December 2022 (before the platform was renamed X). eBird checklists (Sullivan et al., 2009) were requested from the eBird administrators and received in January 2023. We used a spatial join to identify all AllTrails locations (downloaded from the AllTrails website in January 2023) within the boundaries of the units, then counted the number of trip reports for each location based on information displayed on the AllTrails website in January 2023.

Following the collection of the raw social media data, we quantified the number of users each day who shared posts on social media and the community science platform who were present within the boundaries of each unit. Then, for each data source, we calculated the number of user-days (unique users in a given location on a given day; Wood et al. 2013) for each unit and summed these into monthly totals of user-days per data source per unit.


## Unit visitation data


Monthly park visitation to NPS units was retrieved from the NPS Stats database (https://irma.nps.gov/STATS/) recreational visit series and are those described in Tsai et al (2023). For USFS Forests, monthly visitation estimates were created with data from the NVUM Program, which generates unit-level recreation estimates that cover a 12-month period corresponding to U.S. federal fiscal years (October through September). Each unit receives a visitation estimate once every five federal fiscal years. We converted these annual estimates into monthly figures by adapting the 'all-forest information' downscaling approach for NVUM data described by White et al. (2007). Because the federal fiscal year spans two calendar years and a subset of USFS units are sampled in each fiscal year, we were able to use USFS units representing a diverse array of types and settings to cover the 24 months of our study. In total, our analysis included data from 52 forests and the number of forests represented in any single month was 25 (Jan 2018 - Sept 2018), 24 (Oct 2018 - Sept 2019), and three (Oct 2019 - Dec 2019). For USFWS wildlife refuges we acquired data on refuge visits from individual refuge managers whom we contacted as part of a related project and are those described in Winder et al (2025). We vetted the methods reported by the refuge managers and selected refuges with robust visitor estimation techniques.


## Covariates


We collected six covariates that have been found to be useful for visitation modeling in past studies. A correlation matrix for the covariates can be found in the Appendix (Figure A1).


## Region


To capture variation in visitation due to differences in recreational behavior across the U.S., we assigned each unit to one of eight regions (Pacific Northwest, Pacific Southwest, Inter-Mountain, Great Plains, North Central, South Central, Northeast, and Southeast; Figure 1). These regions are based on the subregions developed for the USFS Resources Planning Act (RPA) Assessment which capture broad ecological and socioeconomic patterns across the U.S. For the assignment, we intersected a shapefile of the regional boundaries with the centroids of each unit. Eight unit centroids were located in oceanic waters where the regions are not defined, and so were assigned to the nearest region manually.


## Population within unit boundaries


We defined the AirSage data of interest using the administrative boundaries for the USFS forests; these boundaries include some privately-owned lands within (i.e., inholdings surrounded by USFS land) and on the periphery of USFS land that can contain populated areas. To control for the AirSage data that could be attributed to the daily activities of people living within the administrative boundary that are unrelated to recreating on USFS land, we estimated the population living within the unit boundaries (administrative boundaries for the USFS, standard unit boundaries for the NPS and FWS). To do this, we intersected a shapefile of the unit boundaries with a rasterized map of estimated population at a 30 meter cell resolution (EPA 2024), then summed the population estimates for each intersected cell within a unit.


## Population within 30 miles


To quantify the impact of nearby population density, we estimated the population living within a 30-mile distance of the unit boundaries (ownership boundaries for the USFS, standard unit boundaries for the NPS and FWS). We intersected the 30-m resolution population raster with the geometries of the units after applying a 30-mile buffer, and summed the population estimates for all cells that intersected the buffered boundaries.


## Temperature


To capture the effect of climate and weather on visitation, we included temperature in the model. We used mean monthly temperature from the ERA5-Land dataset which is provided at a 0.1 degree latitude by 0.1 degree longitude resolution. We intersected the geometries of the units with the centroids of the rasterized temperature map, then averaged across all intersected cells within a unit by month. Some units were small enough to not intersect with any temperature cell centroid, in which case we used the data from the cell with the closest centroid to the unit.


## Month and Year


To capture seasonality in recreation behavior we included categorical variables indicating the year (2018 or 2019) and the month of the year.

It was calculated for models with every possible combination of predictors and then averaged across all formulations. Since our model is a mixed model with unit-level random effect groupings, we quantified the relative contribution of each variable to two different measures of model fit: marginal and conditional R 2 (Nakagawa and Schielzeth 2013).


## Model transferability across agencies, locations, times


We created three cross-validation (CV) routines to simulate potential applications for predictive visitation models to address RQ2 and RQ3 (Table 1). Each CV represents, sequentially, a conceivably 'easier' task for model prediction. These tests are useful for understanding the visitation prediction accuracy of models in ways managers and researchers may want to apply them.

Table 1 : Scenarios in which managers or researchers may want to apply visitation models, and the descriptions of the cross-validation routines we used to evaluate prediction accuracy of each. For each scenario, we performed the CV routine on eight distinct models representing four variations of inputs to the base model (Table 2).

Across-agency transfer : One use may be to fit a visitation model on one agency's data and use that to predict visitation to a different agency's units. To simulate this, we fit our base model (Eq. 1) on the NPS observations then used that model to predict the visitation series for the USFS and USFWS. We opted to use the NPS as the initial agency because the NPS monitoring data is the most extensive within our analysis. This method simulates a potential use-case in which a

practitioner transferred a model fit on one observational series to prediction for units managed by a different agency, which might lack as robust of a visitor monitoring program. We created scatter plots of observed vs. predicted values for each of the two predicted agencies (USFS, USFWS). We also calculated goodness-of-fit metrics including the coefficient of determination (R 2 , calculated by squaring Pearson's correlation between predicted and observed values), root mean square error (RMSE), and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE).

Across-units transfer : Another use may be to predict visitation to unmonitored units in the same agency. We created visitation models using a subset of units and then used those models to predict visitation for the other units. This application reflected the situation where an agency has an existing on-site visitation monitoring system that is implemented at some agency units and a model could be used to predict visitation at unmonitored units. We simulate this use by creating a repeated k-fold cross validation where folds are whole units across all agencies. We used a 10-fold cross validation, repeating a random draw of an average of 9.7 units in each fold, 100 times, and created the same goodness-of-fit metrics as above based on the predictions on the held-out folds.

Across-time transfer : Lastly, visitation models may be used as part of a hybrid monitoring approach in which some on-site visitor counting is done in every unit, but only intermittently. This use-case is analogous to the USFS recreation monitoring system, where on-site monitoring happens every fifth year but there may be a desire to create visitation for unmonitored times, or a case of using a model to fill in months missing from visitation series due to staffing or equipment failure. We simulated this application by using the same 10-fold cross validation process described in the across-unit test, except here the folds are random sets of an average of 155.8 months across all units.

To judge the individual and combined mobility data sources' efficacy for these three applications, we performed each CV routine on four variations of inputs to the base model (Eq.1, Table 2):

- 1. Covariates - a model with just the covariates, not including mobility data sources.
- 2. Individual mobility data source- models with the standard covariates in Eq. 1 and one mobility data source, with each individual source in a separate model.
- 3. All Sources - a model with all the standard covariates and all mobility sources together (our base model).
- 4. Social media - a model with all the covariates plus the social media mobility data.

For each variation we produced common fit metrics for both estimated visits and log-transformed visits. These CVs help us answer RQ2 and RQ3 for potential uses of visitation models, while the variation in the inputs to the models (1-4 above) help us answer RQ1 in a prediction setting as opposed to using in-sample results in the dominance analysis.

## 5. Discussion


Being able to measure public land visitation over time, across diverse landscapes, remotely and continuously, would revolutionize our view of the human use of and impacts on natural areas (Merrill et al 2020, Wood et al. 2013). Visitation models integrating digital mobility data, constantly recorded traces of people's movement and choices, move this lofty goal closer to being operationally feasible. As researchers in multiple fields of natural and social sciences, along with natural resource managers, take advantage of this growing source of large-scale social information, visitation data series and other inferences created based on such models must be critically assessed in terms of bias and accuracy for common intended uses. Misestimating visitation could lead to false signals and over-confidence in the derived data series for important uses, such as in natural resource damage assessment cases (Tourangeau 2012) or in official reporting to decision makers weighing the expenditure of public resources

(NPS 2023). A critical assessment, such as the one presented here, not only informs appropriate uses of models that integrate digital mobility data, but also provides direction for future research and development.

Consistent with other studies (Tsai et al. 2022, Winder et al. 2025), we found that digital mobility data are generally well-related to observed visitation patterns for public lands. However, we showed this relationship can be quite poor for some individual units even when agency-wide correlations are good. Relationships vary considerably across different types of digital mobility data, units, and agencies. This is in keeping with previous work, which has found high site-to-site variability in the relationship between mobility data sources and on-site visitation, as well as model performance (Wood et al. 2020, Winder et al. 2025, Tsai et al. 2022).

Predictive performance of models varied widely across sites, but was improved with the inclusion of some observational visitation data from the units of interest. To see the practical implications for visitation estimation, we can compare the accuracy of visitation models with and without on-the-ground data in the units of interest included in the construction of the models. The best performing model in the across-time transfer (includes some on-site data from each site) predicted monthly visits with a MAPE of 30.5% (visit terms). This same All Sources model had an 85% MAPE when applied to predicting visits at new locations (without on-site data), which is substantially worse. These results spotlight the challenges of building models of visitation across diverse geographies and unit types, while building evidence for the currently most-promising uses given the present limitations. These uses of visitation models driven by mobility data might include imputation of missing values, real-time forecasting, or as a complement to on-the-ground methods in a hybrid visitation modeling approach. While we did not explore it here, understanding how much on-the-ground data may be needed for a given level of desired accuracy in a hybrid approach is a natural direction of future research.

We found that mobility-data-based-models fit on one agency's visitation data were generally poor and biased predictors of another agency's observed visitation. The differences we found across agencies points to differences in how the mobility data sources represent use across these agencies' lands. It may also point out fundamental biases in the agencies' count systems and statistical methods to create monthly visitation totals. In other words, they may not be counting and reporting in a way to create comparable metrics on the same visitation scale (Legget et al. 2017). The same logic holds for the differences we found between units within an agency. The models we created cannot tell us where the differences are coming from, but future studies are warranted on that topic.

While we quantitatively assessed the bias and accuracy of the mobility data driven models, information for assessing the accuracy of the traditional methods of visitor use quantification and resultant data series is rare (King and McGregor 2012). Knowing which on-the-ground series are more reliable and unbiased could improve our ability to disentangle the differences we found across agencies and units in our models. There is a need to harmonize and standardize the on-the-ground visitation series creation and reporting across a diverse set of natural lands (e.g., parks, beaches, forests). One potential direction for research aimed at

reducing the deviations is to better match the spatial definitions of the areas of interest for the mobility data (i.e., the geofence) and the areas that the traditional counting methods are capturing. This spatial definition is not always clear for on-the-ground visitation data series and similarly the choice of geofence can cause large discrepancies in mobility datasets if it mistakenly captures the use of nearby high-use infrastructure such as roads. Without more formally documented and widely available visitation observations, general predictive models built on mobility data will struggle to improve in usefulness. This means there is a need to potentially conduct more, not less, traditional visitation quantification methods to improve on the novel approaches.

The potential for commercial cellular device location data as a mobility data source to fill a wide array of research and management needs has been touted in peer-reviewed literature (Merrill et al. 2020), popular media (Vincent 2021), and legislation (U.S. Congress 2023). The quantity of cellular device location data, its spatial resolution, and near real-time availability all suggest its potential superiority-compared to other forms of digital mobility data-for modeling visitation. We did find cellular device location data to be the most useful individual digital mobility data source (in most cases), but not substantially so. Our models that incorporated multiple digital mobility data sources were still more accurate than models based solely on cellular device location data, or any other individual source. Additionally, the marginal contribution of adding the cellular device data to a model already using a set of combined social media sources was small. Our findings provide some evidence that if researchers or managers can only incorporate one type of digital mobility data in their statistical visitation model, cellular location data may be the best choice. However, there are many commercial cellular device location data vendors with varying location data panels and processing pipelines available, and we only evaluated one of these (AirSage). More research is needed to confirm that this finding holds across different vendors, settings, and in future years given continuing changes in the input data from cellular devices and the algorithms used by the sellers of cellular location data.

We did not address temporal stability of the models in this study, as we were only able to combine two years of overlapping data across all geographies. While we did not find significant year effects between those two years, the mobility data sources are undeniably changing over time with differences in smartphone application popularity, privacy settings and use, resulting in changes in the panel makeups in the cellular device products (Mashhadi et al. 2022, Keegan 2021). These instabilities have implications for predictive models, as the temporal changes in mobility data sources lead to differences in relationships with on-site visitation estimates (Winder et al. 2025). Future research is needed to quantify the impact of temporal instability on predictive performance of models using mobility data sources, and create and test combined (on-the-ground counts and mobility data) approaches to handle the changes in practical applications.

The commercial cell data performed similarly to the individual social media sources and evidence suggests it should be treated as a promising member of a group of potential visitation predictors, but it does not fully bridge the more challenging gap in our understanding of differences in visitation across units. Combining multiple sources of people's behavior and

choices improved the models compared to those based on individual sources, in most cases. For example, we found evidence that activity-specific mobility sources, such as AllTrails, may perform well in settings where the captured activity represents a good portion of the variation in visitation to those locations (e.g., USFS). Overall, models using multiple sources of mobility data were better than those based on single sources. As the sources of available mobility data evolve over time, there may be a place for ensemble modeling systems with common ground-collected benchmarks (Mendes-Moreira 2017).

## Introduction


Humans face major environmental challenges, including climate change, biodiversity loss, deforestation, and plastic pollution (MacLeod et al., 2021; Richardson et al., 2023). These challenges began to be widely recognized from the 1960s to the 1980s through seminal work in environmentalism, including 'Silent Spring' (Carson, 1962) and 'The Limits to Growth' (Meadows et al., 1972).

The  mainstream  response has been further advancing scientific knowledge  and technology (McKenzie, 2021; Stein et al., 2024). As consequence, educational curricula

have  incorporated  environmental  science.  Elementary  and  middle  school  curricula  in most  countries  now  include  environmental  science  (OECD,  2009;  UNESCO,  2019). Higher  education  has  also  mainstreamed  environmental  research,  aiming  to  produce much higher numbers of STEM graduates (Kelly and Knowles, 2016), and producing vast scientific knowledge about the environment (Glavovic et al., 2022). These educational changes  may  partly  explain  the  high  awareness  of  environmental  challenges  among people (UNESCO, 2019; UNDP, 2021).

However, environmental challenges have worsened over the past several decades and are projected to continue this trajectory (United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, 2021). This suggests a need to explore alternative approaches. One alternative approach,  termed  the  'cultural  approach,'  has  gained  attention  in  both  academia  and policymaking  (Reid  et  al.,  2021;  Komatsu  et  al.,  2023;  Rappleye  et  al.,  2024a). This approach posits that environmental challenges are rooted in a dominant worldview that emphasizes human independence from and superiority over nature (White, 1967; Naess, 1973; Haraway, 2016a; Silova, 2021). The cultural approach does not assume that modern science and technology alone can resolve environmental challenges. The reason is that it views modern science and technology as largely based on the same dominant worldview that gave rise to these challenges (see the next section). Instead, the proposed Cultural Approach  proposes  a  shift  towards  a  worldview  that  emphasizes  interdependence between humans and nature and rejects human superiority over nature. After decades of skepticism and non-engagement, this approach is finally gaining mainstream recognition. Indeed, the United Nations now acknowledges the failure of the dominant concept of education and calls for its reorientation (United Nations, 2021). International organizations like the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) have emphasized the need to promote a sense of interdependence between humans and nature through education (UNESCO, 2016, 2020; White et al., 2023, 2024). This shift is, in  part,  due  to  accumulating empirical evidence  supporting the cultural approach. For example,  psychological  studies  have  found  that  individuals  with  a  stronger  sense  of interdependence are more likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviors (Frantz and Mayer,  2014;  Restall  and  Conrad,  2015).  Environmental  studies  have  reported  that societies  with  prevalent  senses  of  interdependence  tend  to  have  lower  environmental impacts (Komatsu et al., 2019, 2020, 2021). More evidence is detailed below.

Meanwhile, education scholars and practitioners are now exploring and experimenting

with methods to promote a sense of interdependence among students. Studies suggest that incorporating direct sensory experiences in learning (e.g., smelling herbs, tilling soil and sowing seeds, and listening to sounds of wildlife) can broaden students' self-concepts and promote  a  sense  of  interdependence  (Beery  and  Jørgensen,  2018;  Inoue  et  al.,  2018; Pirchio et al., 2021). Encouraging students to take the perspective of natural elements (e.g., fish and rocks) is also suggested as effective (Gordon and Ross, 2003; Barrable, 2019).  Several  scholars  suggest  that  learning  Indigenous  stories,  myths  and  bodily practices (e.g., yoga and meditation) can foster a sense of interdependence (Korteweg et al., 2010; Farrelly, 2019; Tsevreni, 2024). These stories often embody a deep-rooted sense of interdependence with nature.

While  these  explorations  are  promising,  most  remain  in  experimental  phases,  raising questions about their large-scale applicability in formal education (modern classrooms). Our intended contribution in this piece is to address these concerns by examining the case of Japanese formal education. Japan began incorporating Indigenous animistic stories into its  elementary language curriculum over a half century ago, and today these animistic stories constitute a major pillar of the elementary school curriculum. The intent is twofold: by presenting Japan's case, this paper aims to (i) inspire those seeking to integrate similar methods into formal education settings, and (ii) promote, on a worldwide scale, greater  sensitivity  to  how  the  underlying  meanings  and  messages  found  in  language curriculum and textbooks connect (or fail to connect) to environmental concerns.

To accomplish this, the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a simplified theoretical discussion and schematic understanding of the relationship between interdependence and the environment, laying the groundwork for this study. Section 3 elaborates  on  how  elementary,  compulsory  education  in  Japan,  initially  focused  on independence as a result of the imported  Western models, began emphasizing interdependence by incorporating Indigenous animistic stories from the 1960s onwards. Section 4 showcases examples of these stories and explores their use in teaching. Section 5  concludes  by  summarizing  the  implications  of  including  Indigenous  stories  in elementary language textbooks.


## Theoretical and conceptual lens: interdependence and environmental challenges


This  section  explores  the  relationship  between  worldviews  and  the  environment, foregrounding  European  history.  The  aim  is not to be exhaustive  but  to work schematically,  to  highlight  (i)  the  historical  marginalization  of  the  interdependent

worldview,  (ii)  the  persistence  of  this  marginalization,  and  (iii)  the  environmental implications that arise from marginalization. This conceptualization lays the framework for the sections that follow.


## Marginalization of interdependence: source


Before the Middle Ages,  a  worldview  centered  on  interdependence  was  predominant, even in the West. In this worldview, an individualized self did not hold primacy; instead, the focus was on the relationship with others, including nature, as primary reality (Figure 1a). Neither the self nor others are assumed to exist in isolation, as represented by the overlapping area between the self and others in  Figure 1a. This perspective informed premodern ceremonies like land blessings, ubiquitous globally before the Middle Ages and  still  observed  in  non-Western  countries,  including  Japan  (Baron,  2012).  These ceremonies assume that humans need nature's approval to construct buildings on land (Komatsu and Rappleye, 2017a). The interdependence worldview assumes that construction takes place in the overlapping area between humans and nature (Figure 1a).

Figure 1. Historical shifts in the dominant worldview in the West. The interdependent worldview (a) was first replaced by one emphasizing independence (b), and later by a worldview incorporating both independence and superiority (c).

However, the ascendancy of Christianity gradually replaced the interdependent worldview with an independent one. Christian doctrines, particularly in interpretations of Paul the Apostle, St. Augustine, Martin Luther, and John Calvin, underscored the primacy

of  one's  relationship  with  God,  creating  a  gap  between  oneself  and  others,  including nature (Figure 1b). Max Weber (1904) recognized this process and elaborated its impacts on the modern world. In Protestantism, God 'has decided the fate of every individual and regulated  the  tiniest  details  of  the  cosmos  from  eternity,'  leading  to  'a  feeling  of unprecedented inner loneliness of the single individual' (Weber, 1904, p. 60). The primary concern in the Protestant radicalization of Christianity, therefore, became the 'exclusive trust in God' (Weber, 1904, p. 62), rather than interactions with others. This development is one of the primary origins of strong individualism in the West, where Christianity came to dominate.

During  this gradual process of domination  spanning  two  millennia,  Christianity simultaneously  introduced  the  concept  of  human  superiority  over  nature.  In  JudeoChristian texts, humans are granted 'dominion' over nature and are believed to be capable of understanding God's intentions (via the Bible), which places them far above nature (Figure 1c). This hierarchical perspective devalued non-human entities, treating them as mechanistic and devoid of intrinsic worth (Descartes, 1637). Indeed, Descartes argued that 'if there were such machines having the organs and outward shape of a monkey or any other irrational animal, we would have no means of knowing that they were not of exactly  the  same  nature  as  these  animals'  (Descartes,  1637,  p.  46).  This  hierarchical perspective also led Francis Bacon to view 'man as the minister… of nature' (Bacon, 1620, p. 8). Bacon asserted that 'the empire of man over things is [should be] founded on the arts and sciences alone, for nature is only to be commanded by obeying her' (Bacon, 1620, p. 49). This theological-turned-social shift marginalized direct engagement with nature. The impacts of this are evident in phenomena like witch hunts, where individuals perceived as linked to nature - usually females who opposed the Church Fathers - faced persecution  (Stengers,  2012;  Komatsu  and  Rappleye,  2017a).  We  term  this  strong individualism and superiority over nature an 'independent' worldview.


## Marginalization of interdependence: persistence


While the power of Christianity waned with the rise of Enlightenment thought in Europe, the independent worldview persisted. One significant reason for this persistence is that Enlightenment thinkers inherited the independent worldview from Christianity. Modern science is dedicated to deciphering the scientific laws governing elements in the world, akin  to  Christianity's  quest  to  understand  God's  intentions  (Komatsu  and  Rappleye, 2017a). Indeed, pioneers of modern science, such as Galileo and Newton, studied nature to decipher God's intentions (Burtt, 1924/2003). Notably, scientists primarily focused on

their vertical relationship with scientific laws, relegating their relationship with nature to a secondary role. This helps explain the historical dominance of physics over biology. Nature was served merely as material for uncovering scientific laws. Modern technology, when viewed as the application of modern science to manage the world, reflects a variant of Francis Bacon's thought.

The independent worldview has deeply influenced modern education, which has placed a strong emphasis on science and technology (Komatsu and Rappleye, 2017b). Even if contemporary educators view themselves as wholly secular and disavow any Christian legacy in their practices, the major motifs of modern liberal education trace their lineage to this Christian-Enlightenment cultural complex: individuals, freedom, knowledge, texts, cognition (Siedentop, 2017; Dewey, 1930). Student-centered pedagogy is an illustrative example. Although it takes multiple forms and can be mixed with other values, studentcentered pedagogy is fundamentally characterized by the assumption that students act as independent experimenters (Komatsu and Rappleye, 2017c; Komatsu et al., 2021). Under this  approach,  students  design  their  individual  projects  and  derive  learning  from  the outcomes. The foundational principles of student-centered pedagogy can be traced back to Rousseau, who posited that humans are born as individuals but become susceptible to corruption through interactions with others (Komatsu and Rappleye, 2017c). Rousseau's analogy likening a child to 'a sapling… sown in the midst of the highway, bent hither and thither  and  soon  crushed  by  the  passers-by'  (Rousseau,  1763,  p.  5),  underscores  his advocacy for minimizing interactions with others. It is evident that Rousseau strongly championed the independent worldview.

Until  very  recently, student-centered  pedagogy  was  heralded  as  the  panacea  for environmental  challenges,  particularly  by  influential  international bodies  such  as UNESCO, the OECD, and the World Bank (Komatsu et al., 2020, 2021; Rappleye and Komatsu,  2024).  However,  there  has  been  a  notable  shift  in  the  stance  of  these organizations in recent years, a development we address below.


## Environmental implications


Criticism of the independent worldview emerged among scholars in the 1960s and 1970s, coinciding with a growing awareness of serious global environmental challenges. While mainstream  scholars  advocated  for  increased  reliance  on  science  and  technology  to address these  challenges,  a  group  of  critical  humanities  scholars  argued  for  a  shift  in worldview  (White,  1967;  Naess,  1974).  They  contended  that  the  dominance  of  the

independent worldview was a primary contributor to environmental challenges. White (1967) particularly scrutinized the entrenched Christian notion of human independence from  and  superiority  over  nature,  warning  that  continued  reliance  on  science  and technology could exacerbate environmental issues. Instead, he advocated for a restoration of the interdependent worldview. Works in the 1980s-1990s elaborated these basic ideas, some expanding on feminist critiques (Plumwood, 1993), on critiquing the ChristianEnlightenment notions of self (Mathews, 1991), and on showing the vast implications for education (Bowers, 1995).

Initially, these arguments, drawn from the humanities, lacked strong empirical evidence, limiting societal and educational impact. However, contemporary research, built out of newly available global datasets on society, education and ecological footprint, has since provided substantial empirical support. The earliest of these studies primarily focused on individual-level pro-environmental behaviors, revealing a positive correlation with the interdependent worldview (Frantz and Mayer, 2014; Restall and Conrad, 2015; Komatsu et  al.,  2022a).  Subsequent research then expanded to the societal level, demonstrating correlations between the interdependent worldview and pro-environmental behaviors, as well as tangible environmental impacts like ecological footprint (Komatsu et al., 2019, 2020,  2021).  Our  own  analyses  indicate  that  students  tend  not  to  engage  with  proenvironmental behaviors in countries with strong individualism where the independent self is dominant (Figure 2a, r = -0.557 with a bootstrapping 95% confidence interval of [-0.701, -0.386], n = 59). The data on pro-environmental behaviors are derived from the OECD's Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2018, which measured whether students engaged in five pro-environmental behaviors, including reducing energy use, choosing ethical/environmental products, participating in environmental activities, boycotting  products  for  ethical/environmental  reasons  and  signing  online  petitions (OECD, 2022). Similarly, the ecological  footprint tends to be high for  countries with strong individualism (Figure 2b, r = 0.584 with a bootstrapping 95% confidence interval of [0.380, 0.759], n = 52). Taken together, these findings confirm the earlier critiques and underscore the importance of cultivating the interdependent worldview through education to enhance environmental sustainability. They also suggest that modern education may be contributing to, rather than resolving, environmental challenges by reinforcing notions of human independence from and superiority over nature.
