As environmental challenges intensify, a significant shift in educational perspectives has emerged within international organizations. The United Nations (2021) and UNESCO (2020)  now  recognize  the  need  to  reform  mainstream  education,  acknowledging  the importance  of  the  interdependent  worldview.  Similarly,  the  OECD  considers  the interdependent worldview, labelled as an eco-centric worldview, as crucial for achieving environmental  sustainability  (White  et  al.,  2023,  2024). These  shifts  mark  significant departures  from  the  previously  upheld  independent  worldview  by  UNESCO  and  the OECD.

While some may argue that addressing environmental crises does not inherently require a reconsideration of worldview, we challenge the effectiveness of maintaining concepts like human independence and superiority. Environmental stewardship, often touted as a solution while preserving these concepts, assumes human independence and superiority. Environmental stewardship requires rational, scientific understanding of nature, which provides the basis for human intervention to guide nature back to recovery (Taylor, 2020). Environmental  stewardship  is  thus  a  variant  of  Francis  Bacon's  idea  of  'man  as  the

minister…  of nature' (Bacon, 1620, p. 8). 1 Empirical evidence questions the effectiveness  of  environmental  stewardship  approaches.  Psychological  studies  have revealed that individuals with a strong sense of independence and superiority are less likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviors (Frantz and Mayer, 2014; Restall and Conrad, 2015; Komatsu et al., 2022a).


## The case of Japan: shift from independence to interdependence in Japan


This section explores the historical shift in the Japanese elementary curriculum, from an emphasis on independence to interdependence. Central to this shift is the inclusion of Indigenous  animistic  stories  in  language  textbooks. 2 Unlike  scientific  frameworks, animism  attributes  agency  to  all  beings,  highlighting  their  mutual  influence  and interconnectedness. In some animistic narratives, humans and other beings are depicted as interchangeable, representing different expressions of a shared, fundamental life force that sustains the world.

To explore the integration of these Indigenous animistic stories, we analysed language textbooks for Grades 4-6 published by three major Japanese publishers: Mitsumura Tosho, Tokyo Shoseki, and Kyoiku Shuppan. Mitsumura Tosho holds the largest market share at 60-70%, while Tokyo Shoseki and Kyoiku Shuppan hold approximately 20% and 10%, respectively. One of the two stories analysed in detail in the following section appears in textbooks  from  all  three  publishers,  while  the  other  is  included  in  the  textbooks  of Mitsumura Tosho and Tokyo Shoseki. Consequently, these stories are read by at least nine out of ten elementary students in Japan.


## The Meiji period and the rise of the independent worldview


Modern education in Japan began during the Meiji period after the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate in 1867. Based on imported Western models of society, the Meiji government prioritized the production of individuals with an independent worldview as a key measure to develop a strong nation. In education, the elementary school model was imported from the  United  States  (Duke,  2008),  and American  teachers  and  texts  were  central  to  the earliest modern teacher training institutions (Lincicome, 1995). Learning from Western advisors,  particularly  Germans,  the  government  recognized  that  the  strength  of  these countries  lay  in  their  tradition  of  Christianity,  which  produced  individuals  connected primarily to God  (Fukushima, 2009; Rappleye, 2018). Despite the decline of Christianity's direct influence recognized  across  Europe,  the  Meiji  leaders  were convinced - by their German tutors - the system represented by Figures 1b and 1c enabled people to unite for common goals, such as national defense.

The  problem,  however,  was  that  premodern  (Tokugawa)  Japan  was  fragmented  into approximately 300 small domains called hans, where people identified more with their local region than with Japan as a whole. This fragmentation posed a significant challenge in responding to the rising threats from Western powers. Moreover, the education in these domains was largely based on Buddhist temples (terakoya), a system that had no 'vertical' access and taught interdependence (see, for example, Rappleye et al., 2024b).

In  this  context,  the  Meiji  government  implemented  policies  aimed  at  fostering  an independent  worldview  and  weakening  interdependence  among  communities.  These policies included creating new administrative districts that ignored traditional boundaries and banning local holidays and festivals (Makihara, 2008). Education - of a new kind played a pivotal role in advancing these efforts (Yamada, 2014; Rappleye and Komatsu, 2020). Unlike the Tokugawa period, where most teachers were local community members or Buddhist monks, teachers in the Meiji period were selected by local governments. The educational content shifted focus from fostering community membership to developing individual identity within the 'nation' of Japan. In alignment with this change, early Meiji elementary  textbooks,  particularly  those  for  moral  education  (shushin),  emphasized independence and individual achievement (Mita, 2012; Rappleye and Komatsu, 2016). Subsequently,  textbooks  began  to  emphasize  loyalty  to  the  emperor,  connecting individuals to the emperor rather than to their local communities. This mirrors the rise of individualism in the West, albeit with Japan using the emperor instead of Christianity

(Mita, 2012). 3


## Post-war Japan and the continued emphasis on independence


Japan emerged as a superpower in the Far East in the early 20th century but was defeated in  the  Asia-Pacific  War  (Second  World  War)  in  1945.  However,  this  defeat  did  not diminish Japan's emphasis on independence; rather, it reinforced this orientation. Japan interpreted its loss as a result of an insufficient commitment to an independent worldview. This interpretation is clearly articulated in the Guideline for New Education published in 1946 by the Ministry of Education, Science, Sports and Culture (MEXT), a document under strong supervision from the United States  (Aoyagi, 2021).  Some scholars  even argue it was written by the United States, wherein the US military took up the role once played by the German advisors in Meiji (Shibata 2004). The guideline posits that the reckless  war  was  initiated  by  the  fascist  government,  but  it  also  emphasizes  that  the populace  failed  to  prevent  this  due  to  'a  lack  of  rationality  and  scientific  thinking.' Consequently, the guideline underscores the importance of an independent worldview and 'critical  thinking  skills.'  From  this  perspective,  it  critiques  pre-war  textbooks  for including 'myths such as deities creating the land, mountains, rivers, plants, and trees.' This emphasis on independence is also reflected in the Fundamental Law of Education implemented in 1947, which highlights the need for an 'independent mindset' (MEXT, 1947).

In response to this interpretation of the war loss, post-war textbooks strongly emphasized science and rationality. Conceptually, Japan began to replace the transcendental figure of the emperor with science and rationality (or an idealization of the United States, which was perceived to possess high levels of science and rationality, Osawa, 2008). With the abolition  of  the  moral  education  subject  (shushin)  after  the  war,  language  textbooks assumed the primary role of promoting the independent worldview. Post-war elementary language textbooks included numerous biographies of scientists and engineers, such as Galileo Galilei, Louis Pasteur, and Thomas Edison (Ikuta, 2012). These biographies often depicted nature as a threat to humans, to be overcome through the application of science and technology (Ikuta, 2005). In addition to scientists and engineers, textbooks featured biographies  of  individuals  who  contributed  to  the  development  of  modern  states,

including  Abraham  Lincoln  and  Fukuzawa  Yukichi.  Fukuzawa  Yukichi,  a  Meiji-era thinker who advocated for the modernization of Japan, is a complex figure with many ambivalences  about  the  place  of  Japan  in  the  world,  but  his  biographies  in  official textbooks consistently emphasize his orientation towards independence and scientific and rational thinking (Ikuta, 2005, 2013).

Post-war textbooks, up until the early 1960s, rarely highlighted interdependence between humans and nature. Animistic stories were carefully avoided, likely because animism was viewed as antithetical to scientific, rational thinking. Prominent educational psychologists of the post-war period often argued that animism characterized 'a way of thinking for those intellectually underdeveloped, such as children and savages' (Hatano and Takizawa, 1963,  p.  161).  They  expressed  concern  that  'children  in  rural  areas  have  fewer opportunities to overcome animism due to their limited access to civilization' (p. 167) and argued that 'erasing all superstitions from this world would facilitate the enhancement of children's scientific spirit' (p. 178).


## Incorporation of animistic stories and the shift towards interdependence


However,  starting  in  the  1960s,  elementary  language  textbooks  began  incorporating Indigenous animistic stories. This shift coincided with growing awareness of environmental  problems,  prompting  a  re-evaluation  of  the  prevailing  independent worldview and human relationships with nature. The most critical environmental issue at that time was Minamata Disease, first reported in the 1950s in Minamata, a city in western Japan.  A  chemical  factory  had  discharged  mercury-laden  wastewater  into  the  sea, assuming  the  toxins  would  dissipate  harmlessly  in  the  water,  consistent  with  the independent worldview that posits humans as separate from nature. However, mercury accumulated in fish through the food web, causing neurological disease in people who consumed the contaminated fish. After prolonged debate throughout the 1950s and 1960s, the  government  finally  acknowledged  in  the  late  1960s  that  the  chemical  factory's wastewater was the cause of Minamata Disease. Environmental challenges like Minamata Disease, coupled with the influence of global environmental movements (Avenell, 2017), highlighted the reality that humans cannot exist independently of nature, despite advances in science and technology.

In response to these environmental concerns, elementary language textbooks began to modify  their  content.  One  such  Indigenous  animistic  story,  'The  Fox  Named  Gon,' appeared in a textbook from one publisher in the late 1950s and subsequently spread to

textbooks from other publishers in the 1960s and beyond.   Other stories like 'Granpa 4 Daizo and a Duck,' 'A White Hat,' 'Wild Pear,' and 'The Life of Ocean,' some of which will be discussed in the next section, were also included. The inclusion of Indigenous animistic  stories  appears  to  have  been  a  grassroots  movement.  There  was  no  central authority designing language textbooks in Japan; rather, publishers monitored each other's offerings to find ways to enhance their appeal. This mutual learning process was the main driver  behind  the  widespread  inclusion  of  Indigenous  animistic  stories  in  Japanese textbooks. 5

Simultaneously,  the  number  of  biographies  of  scientists  and  engineers  in  textbooks declined significantly in the 1970s and 1980s. While a few biographies remained in the 1980s and beyond, they often focused on figures highlighting the negative aspects of science and technology, such as Rachel Carson and Tanaka Shozo (Ikuta, 2013; Sakai, 2013). Tanaka Shozo was a politician and social activist known for his tireless efforts to address the environmental damage caused by industrial pollution during the Meiji period. These changes in language textbooks seemingly influenced the guidelines for teaching materials, which are typically updated once a decade. The guidelines from the late 1980s emphasized that teaching materials should help students 'respect life and others' and 'love nature and be moved by its beauty' (MEXT, 1989). The most recent guidelines have gone further,  underscoring  the  importance  of  Indigenous  stories  and  myths,  suggesting  that animism has become fully mainstreamed (MEXT, 2017, p. 52-53).

In concluding  this section, we  emphasize  how  quickly  textbooks  responded  to environmental  issues.  Changes  in  textbooks  preceded  shifts  in  intellectual  discourse.

Thinkers began advocating for reconsidering the dominant worldview in the late 1970s. One prominent figure, sociologist Maki Yusuke (1977) argued that environmental and social  problems  could  be  addressed  by  changing  the  dominant  worldview,  viewing animism  as  a  crucial  resource  for  this  shift.  Similarly,  philosopher  Ohmori  Shozo (1985/1994) contended that animism is not irrational and can be a key resource for solving environmental problems. He posited that both animism and science organize experiences, with animism doing so directly without dualism, while science employs dualism. Later thinkers identified philosophical similarities among animism, Mahayana Buddhism, and Shintoism 6 , proposing  their  use  in  fostering  environmental  sustainability  (Umehara, 1989; Nakazawa, 1996) 7 . These thinkers played a crucial role in highlighting missing elements in contemporary society and suggesting future directions. It is noteworthy that elementary language textbooks pointed in this direction even before these intellectuals did.


## Indigenous animistic stories: textbook examples


To illustrate the historical transition described above, this section introduces two specific stories to illustrate their content and teaching methods. One story focuses on rejecting human superiority,  while  the  other  emphasizes  interdependence  between  humans  and nature.


## Rejection of human superiority


The story 'Granpa Daizo and a Goose' (Daizo Jiisanto Gan) has been included in Grade 5 textbooks since 1980 and emphasizes rejecting human superiority. This long narrative spans approximately five thousand Japanese characters, equivalent to about two thousand English words, and is typically taught over seven sessions. The instructional approach

highlights the protagonist's emotional and attitudinal changes, encouraging students to identify and  discuss  these transformations.  Teachers  facilitate a facilitative role, prioritizing student-led discussions rather than imparting  their own  perspectives. Interestingly, this instructional method is itself grounded in the principle of interdependence, eschewing the role of authoritative judgment reminiscent of Christianity (Figure 1b) in favor of fostering collaborative and interdependent learning environments (Figure 1a). 8

A brief synopsis of 'Granpa Daizo and a Goose' unfolds as follows: Daizo, an aged and seasoned hunter, endeavors to capture a flock of geese that visit his region every winter. Despite his best efforts, his traps have consistently failed due to the cunning leadership of the geese. Frustrated by his repeated failures, Daizo devises a more sophisticated trap, cunningly utilizing the innate instincts of the geese: where one flies, the others will follow. His  strategy  involves  his  domesticated  goose,  trained  to  return  upon  his  signal.  He introduces his goose to the flock. However, just before he signals his goose to fly into the trap, a falcon attacks the flock. While most geese manage to evade the predator, Daizo's trained goose fails to escape and is targeted by the falcon. Unexpectedly, the leader of the geese returns to rescue Daizo's goose. The leader manages to expel the falcon in a fierce battle but is injured in the process. Recognizing he cannot escape from Granpa Daizo, who has been watching intently, the goose leader gazes at Daizo with dignity. Moved by the leader's noble demeanor and act of compassion for the trained goose, Daizo finds himself unable to carry out his initial intention to shoot him. Instead, Daizo brings the injured leader home and provides care until his recovery, which occurs with the arrival of spring. Upon the leader's restoration to full health, Daizo releases him, honoring his valor with the words, 'You are a hero. I don't want to hunt you unfairly. Come back again this winter. We should fight with dignity.'

Teachers typically guide students to reflect on Daizo's attitudinal changes (Ueno, 1990; Tanaka,  1996).  Initially  frustrated  by  the  leader's  interference  with  his  traps,  Daizo eventually develops reverence for the goose, recognizing its intellect and dignity. This story  underscores  that  animals  can  possess  intellect  and  dignity  akin  to  humans, promoting students' rejection of human superiority over nature. Subsequently, teachers guide students to contemplate Daizo's final words (e.g., Nishihara, 2002). Students easily

grasp the meaning of Daizo's statement, 'I don't want to hunt you unfairly,' implying that shooting the injured leader would be unjust. The phrase 'We should fight with dignity' is left  open  ended,  prompting  deeper  discussion.  Discussions  often  explore  potential approaches Daizo might adopt in the upcoming winter, probing the nuances of respecting the  dignity  of  the  leader  (e.g.,  Edupedia,  2024).  Through  these  dialogues,  students cultivate a deeper appreciation for a desirable relationship between humans and nature.


## Interdependence


As a story emphasizing interdependence, we introduce 'the Life of the Ocean' (Umino Inochi). This story has been included in Grade 6 textbooks since 1996. Despite being shorter than 'Granpa Daizo and a Goose,' it presents a more intricate storyline. Japanese educators often regard learning this narrative as the culmination of elementary school education,  as  it  is  positioned  towards  the  end  of  the  6th-grade  curriculum  (Saga Prefectural Education Center, 2011; Mitsumura Tosho, 2024). The narrative is typically taught over eight sessions, using a similar instructional approach to 'Granpa Daizo and a Goose,' with a focus on the protagonist's emotional and attitudinal changes. Through peer discussions, students refine their interpretations and deepen their understanding.

Below is a synopsis of 'The Life of Ocean.' The protagonist is a young fisherman who practices free diving, hailing from a family with a long history of coastal living. His father, a  renowned  free  diver,  always  attributed  his  success  to  the  blessings  of  the  ocean, maintaining a humble demeanor. Tragically, the protagonist's father is killed by a giant fish when the protagonist is on the cusp of adolescence. Under the tutelage of another fisherman,  the  protagonist  learns  the  art  of  free-diving  fishing,  emphasizing  the importance  of  only  harvesting  the  necessary  number  of  fish.  When  the  protagonist encounters  the  same  giant  fish  responsible  for  his  father's  demise,  he  initially  seeks retribution. However, he experiences a transformative moment when he is moved by the fish's serene presence, reminiscent of his father's humility, ultimately choosing to forego revenge.

The crux of this narrative lies in the protagonist's pivotal decision, prompting students to explore  the  underlying  motivations.  Various  interpretations  have  been  offered  by educators and scholars, detailed in academic and popular literature (Yamamoto, 2005; Tomiyasu, 2011). However, all interpretations converge on the protagonist's realization of interdependence  in  the  story's  culmination.  One  interpretation  posits  that  the protagonist  initially  views  killing  the  giant  fish  as  a  rite  of  passage  to  becoming  a

proficient  fisherman.  However,  the  fish's  tranquil  demeanor  evokes  memories  of  his father's  reverence  for  the  ocean's  blessings,  leading  him  to  reject  vengeance  as  it contradicts  his  father's  ethos.  Notably,  seeking  revenge  is  only  possible  when  the protagonist holds an independent, rather than an interdependent, worldview (Figure 1c). In  the  interdependent  worldview,  the  protagonist  is  part  of  the  ocean,  and  vice  versa, making  seeking  revenge  theoretically  impossible  (Figure  1a).  Another  interpretation posits that the protagonist recognizes that his father's death in the ocean does not warrant retribution,  as  humans  receive  the  blessings  of  nature  throughout  their  lives  and  thus should return to the ocean upon death. Both interpretations assume that the protagonist develops a deep recognition of the interdependence between fishermen's livelihood and the ocean . 9

Importantly, students learn 'The Life of the Ocean' in Grade 6 after studying 'Granpa Daizo  and  a  Goose'  in  Grade  5.  This  sequence  is  theoretically  appropriate:  the  first challenges the notion of human superiority, and the second emphasizes interdependence. This order is the opposite of the historical progression shown in Figure 1. Historically, interdependence  was  first  replaced  by  independence,  followed  by  the  introduction  of human superiority. The Japanese language curriculum thus guides students to trace the history from the present to the past.


## Conclusions: implications of Japan's case


Elementary language textbooks in Japan began including Indigenous animistic stories in the 1960s while reducing the number of biographies of scientists and engineers. This case demonstrates a successful attempt to transform education to emphasize interdependence. Interestingly,  this  transformation  was  conducted  through  a  bottom-up  approach.  One publisher first  included  an  Indigenous  animistic  story,  and  others  followed  suit  in  the 1960s,  a  time  when  the  importance  of  animism  and  interdependence  was  not  widely

recognized in either domestic or international academic research circles. Education policy now acknowledges that Indigenous thoughts have been significant resources for language education over the past decade. Those seeking to scale up education for interdependence in formal schooling settings may find inspiration in Japan's approach. 10

Some readers may question whether this educational shift has really transformed people's worldviews and reduced environmental impacts. While it is impossible to prove causality, significant change in both worldviews and environmental impacts have been observed in Japan over the past several decades. People's worldviews began to shift in the 1970s after the  inclusion  of  'The  Fox  Named  Gon'  in  language  textbooks. A  longitudinal  survey examining people's views on human-nature relationships asks respondents, 'What kind of relationships should humans have with nature to live happily?' Respondents choose one of three options: (1) humans should conquer nature, (2) humans should use nature, and (3) humans should align with nature. Since the late 1960s, the number of respondents choosing  the  first  option  has  decreased,  while  those  choosing  the  third  option  have

Interestingly, these shifts in worldview may partly explain the popularity of Studio Ghibli (Miyazaki Hayao and Takahata Isao) animation works in the 1980s, such as 'Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind' (1984) and 'My Neighbor Totoro' (1988). The themes of these animations, which question the relationship between humans and nature, were already present  in  the  Indigenous  animistic  stories  included  in  language  textbooks. This  prior exposure may have conditioned audiences to be more receptive to the messages in Studio Ghibli's works (Yoneyama, 2021). For instance, 'Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind' portrays a post-apocalyptic Earth where a toxic fungus forest and giant insects, initially seen  as  threats,  are  revealed  to  purify  the  polluted  land. 11 This  theme  of  humans benefiting from nature despite their initial antagonism mirrors the Indigenous animistic stories in textbooks. Studio Ghibli has continued producing works on this theme (e.g., 'Pom Poko' and 'Princess Mononoke'). Notably, Studio Ghibli's influence has come full circle, with the current Grade 6 textbook including an essay by Takahata Isao, one of the Studio's founders and the director of 'Pom Poko' (Mitsumura Tosho, 2023). The story of Pom Poko is about forest creatures that 'shape shift' into humans, thus blurring the lines between human and animal, in their attempts to combat deforestation.

The  changes  in  people's  worldviews  may  have  contributed  to  a  decline  in  Japan's environmental impacts since the 1990s. The Ecological Footprint peaked in 1996 at 5.6 gha per capita and has since declined, reaching an estimated 4.0 gha per capita in 2022, a 29%  reduction  (Global  Footprint  Network,  2024).  Similarly,  Material  Consumption peaked in 1991 at 13.6 tons per capita and decreased to 10.8 tons per capita in 2022, a 21% reduction (OECD, 2024). Despite these declines and a stagnant economy, subjective well-being in Japan has remained stable (Komatsu et al., 2022b; Komatsu and Rappleye, 2024a).

These changes suggest that emphasizing interdependence has been a crucial component of Japan's approach to environmental sustainability. While Japan's case is not presented

as a perfect model, it offers valuable insights 12 . The educational approach effective in Japan may not be directly applicable in other contexts, but the global success of Studio Ghibli's works indicates a potential for wider applicability. However, careful consideration of specific contexts is essential for achieving desired educational outcomes. The next step for education in high-income countries should focus on mainstreaming educational approaches that address worldview shifts, building on the existing foundation of scientific and environmental literacy.

From a more academic, theoretical perspective, the integration of these stories suggests how one country is already 'reclaiming animism' (Stengers, 2012), via education and curricular  change.  However,  given  that  animism  was  linked  to  State  Shinto,  it  is  still viewed within domestically Japan as somewhat dangerous and thus remains undertheorized  (Takayama,  2023).  Still,  it  is  useful  for  educational  researchers  and curriculum specialists to contemplate how stories in textbooks foster certain worldviews, and how those might need to be changed in the face of the environmental challenge. Given the narrative character of human understandings of the world, school curricula have a crucial  role  to  play  in  the  re-storying  of  the  world  (Haraway,  2016a)  away  from  an unsustainable independent worldview.

## 1 Relation to the Literature


A vast and growing literature studies agency problems lurking behind politician-bureaucratic interactions. With respect to credit taking or blaming, three broad possibilities are studied. One, blame or credit can indeed be shifted and is one of the motives for delegation. 12 Principals can strategically prevent themselves from being blamed for policy failures by just letting bureaucrats do the actual work (Fox and Jordan 2011; Almendares 2012; Bartling and Fischbacher 2012; Tamada and Tsai 2018). Two, principals can willfully delegate potentially unpopular decisions to agents to prevent negative impacts of reputation concerns in decisionmaking, and prevent learning about the principal's type (Pei 2018). Three, politicians may take the blame to actively enhance their reputations as competent and high type leaders (Miller and Reeves 2022). We contribute to this literature by formally studying blaming and crediting as communication -the ability and credibility of the principal to communicate to the interested audience-and its potential effect on agent's effort. 13

The literature on the study of effort extraction by the principal in these interactions has examined how intermediaries can provide information about the performance of reputationconcerned agents (Ekmekci 2011; Pei 2016). Here, publicizing information about performance may make an agent's reputation more sensitive to performance, thereby increasing incentives to exert effort. We contribute to this literature by focusing on two different key aspects that are relatively understudied. One involves the third party in our case being uninformed about who was actually responsible for the policy outcome. The other is that the principal in our approach also cares about their reputation.

Closest in spirit to our paper is Glazer and Segendorff (2005), who analyze team production with a leader and subordinate, where the public is uncertain about the individual production

of each actor. We distinguish ourselves in two ways. One, in Glazer and Segendorff (2005) there is a probability that an untruthful credit claim is discovered and the leader then incurs a cost for lying. We assume that credit claiming is purely cheap talk and does not directly affect payoffs. Two, we endogenize incentives to exert effort, whereas the outcome is exogenously determined in Glazer and Segendorff (2005). 14

While the kind of politician-bureaucrat interactions we have described are all pervasive, a note on the scope conditions for our approach is necessary. In our setup, the principal is typically an elected representative with a greater ability to communicate to the outside world than the agent. The agent is the bureaucrat who delivers the policies that the principal wishes to execute. In this context, the bureaucrat (or the agency at large) we refer to is part of a hierarchical setup. That said, the bureaucrat is a professional with sufficient insulation from the principal. Three elements of well-established public bureaucracies would seem fundamental for understanding the structure in which bureaucrats operate and how politician behavior might be conditioned: (1) bureaucrats are a diverse lot and may vary greatly in their abilities; 15 (2) removing most public sector bureaucrats is generally difficult, so shirking by reducing effort can be a viable option (Horn 1995); 16 and (3) bureaucratic effort and successful policy choices should be positively related (Carpenter 2001; Decarolis et al. 2020). The politician has reputation concerns, and the bureaucrat prefers public approval for its own sake or for instrumental reasons like career advancement, the availability of outside job opportunities or reduce the severity of political oversight that the bureaucrat finds distasteful. 17 Therefore, our results are stronger in contexts where the policy outcome is salient and observable.


## 2 The Model


We consider a setting with a politician P (she), bureaucrat B (he), and non-strategic public that observes the politician-bureaucrat interaction. As in the leading example, we think of the Dutch Prime Minister as the politician, and the head of the Dutch tax agency-or the agency as a whole-as the bureaucrat. The public comprises the voter or any interested organization that cares about who bears responsibility for the political outcome but is uncertain about it. The game consists of two periods of effort and policy outcomes in which the politician can publicly communicate via cheap talk in between.

There is uncertainty about the bureaucrat's talent t B ∈ { L, H } and the politician's talent t P ∈ { L, H } , which are either low or high. These values are independently drawn in the beginning of the game and remain constant throughout. The prior probabilities that the bureaucrat and politician have high talent equal Pr( t B = H ) = β 0 ∈ (0 , 1) and Pr( t P = H ) = γ 0 ∈ (0 , 1). That is, the bureaucrat and politician start with an initial reputation β 0 and γ 0 , respectively, after which they interact. Notably, as in models with symmetric learning (Holmstr¨m 1999), the politician, o bureaucrat, and public are all unaware of the politician's and bureaucrat's talent level but share a common prior.

In the first period, either the bureaucrat or the politician is responsible for the policy outcome. Both possibilities are determined by Nature and are equally probable. This is represented by r 1 = B (Bureaucrat responsible) and r 1 = P (Politician responsible). The politician and bureaucrat observe who is responsible but not the public. This assumption is made to capture the policy-making process being complex and not always easily understandable to outside observers, while those inside an organization are better able who will be responsible for what. To illustrate the mechanism as sharply as possible, we assume that either actor is responsible (but not both or neither).

If the politician is responsible for the outcome, we assume that the policy succeeds with probability p H if she is of high talent, and with probability p L otherwise. In the other case,

the bureaucrat is responsible and chooses whether to exert effort at a cost of c ∈ (0 , p L ). If the bureaucrat shirks ( e B 1 = 0), the policy outcome always fails, while if the bureaucrat exerts effort ( e B 1 = 1), the policy succeeds with probability p L or p H depending on the bureaucrat's talent t . The bureaucrat's effort choice is private and not observed by the politician and public. We assume that p L = 1 -∆ 2 and p H = 1+∆ 2 so that, conditional on effort, highly talented bureaucrats and politicians are more likely to produce good outcomes. The parameter ∆ ∈ (0 , 1) measures the difference between the probability of success of a highly and lowly talented player. Subsequently, the policy x 1 either succeeds ( x 1 = s = 1) or fails ( x 1 = f = 0).

After the policy outcome, the politician observes whether it is a success or failure and can comment about who was responsible. Conditional on knowing who was responsible and on knowing the policy outcome, the politician sends a cheap talk message m ∈ { m ,m ,m ϕ B P } , where m ϕ is interpreted as silence, m B as the bureaucrat being responsible, and m P pointing toward the politician being responsible. This message is then observed by all players.

Once the politician has commented following the policy outcome, there is another stage in which a second policy outcome is produced. For simplicity, it is known that the bureaucrat will be responsible for the second-period policy outcome and can make an effort choice. 18 This outcome is generated in the same way as in the first period, where the bureaucrat's effort choice is private. That is, if the bureaucrat shirks ( e B 2 = 0) then the policy is a failure, and if the bureaucrat exerts effort ( e B 2 = 1), the policy succeeds with probability p ′ L = 1 -∆ ′ 2 or p ′ H = 1+∆ ′ 2 depending on the bureaucrat's talent, with ∆ ′ ∈ (0 , ∆]. 19 That is, the policy outcome may be generated differently by bureaucrats in the second period compared to the first. This could be because the second-period policy is less informative about the responsible party's talent because it is a different project that is less able to be controlled.

Finally, the game ends and payoffs are realized. The politician cares about policy outcomes and her reputation at the end of the interaction. For example, the politician is only re-elected if her reputation is good enough. The value from a good reputation follows a threshold-form, where the politician obtains a payoff of 1 if her reputation exceeds the threshold of 1 2 , and a payoff of 0 if it is below the threshold.

- 1. A first-period effort level for the bureaucrat e B 1 ∈ { 0 1 , } .
- 2. A communication strategy for the politician, where π m r , x ( | 1 1 ) is the probability of message m ∈ { m ,m ,m ϕ B P } given a first-period policy outcome x 1 ∈ { f, s } and a first-period responsible actor r 1 ∈ { B,P } .

We require that these strategies are sequentially rational given the beliefs about the bureaucrat's and politician's talent, which in turn are determined by Bayes' rule wherever possible. Beliefs about the politician's and bureaucrat's talent play a central role in the analysis, and we discuss them in some detail.

Before delving into the analysis, we acknowledge that some model aspects are stylized. This approach helps in clarifying the role of blaming and crediting for incentives to exert effort over time. Given this, different aspects of the model may benefit from more explanation.

First, politicians and bureaucrats do not disagree about policies. This simplifying assumption serves to isolate the role of blaming and crediting on effort for a single policy. Politicianbureaucrat alignment may add a layer to the analysis (Bendor and Meirowitz 2004; Forand, Ujhelyi and Ting 2023; Spenkuch, Teso and Xu 2023).

Second, politicians and bureaucrats strongly care about their reputations. Again, this is to emphasize how blaming and crediting work. Presumably, players care about being blamed, shifting blame, and giving or receiving credit because it affects their reputation for competence. By making strong assumptions about reputation-based preferences, we remove other channels through which bureaucrats could be incentivized. 21

Third, reputation concerns take a threshold form. For exposition, we assume that this threshold is 1 2 . This is without loss of generality; a different threshold would only shift equilibrium conditions without substantively changing the core results. A more salient generalization would be reputation payoffs of a different form. For example, reputation payoffs could be strictly increasing in β and/or γ . We discuss this after presenting the main results. We assume a threshold form for tractability and to sharpen the results.

Fourth, we assume that players do not know whether they have high or low talent (Holmstr¨m o 1999), and the politician does not observe the bureaucrat's effort. This reduces the number of the politician's information sets to only knowing who was responsible and the policy outcome. In turn, this helps us to focus on blame and credit, which are messages about responsibility, and not directly about types or effort.

We take three steps to study the effect of blame and credit on policy outcomes. First, we study the implications of a politician who does not provide information ( uninformative equilibria ) about who was responsible for the outcome. Equivalently, it is similar to a situation in which politicians always claim responsibility for the outcome, as the concept of ministerial responsibility prescribes in the Netherlands. This is always a possible equilibrium strategy and serves as a benchmark for subsequent analyses. Second, we analyze politicians who are fully transparent about the responsibility for policy outcomes. When politicians are responsible for the policy outcome, they say that they are, and when bureaucrats are responsible, politicians blame them for failures or give them credit for successes. We show that such equilibria may not always exist. Then, we study politician-optimal equilibria in which, depending on the politician's and bureaucrat's initial reputation, the politician may selectively reveal information about who was responsible to illicit effort. These equilibria analyze the case where politicians can optimally choose when and how to communicate about responsibility. Formally, these equilibria maximize the politician's payoff from an ex ante perspective.

## 6 Comparative Statics and Robustness


Our main results illustrate the importance of a politician's and bureaucrat's initial reputations in determining equilibrium outcomes. How do the results rely on other parameters? We consider the effect of ∆ and ∆ , which is the informativeness of policy outcomes conditional ′ on effort, and the player's reputational payoffs.

Effect of ∆ and ∆ ′ . By changing ∆, the public learns more about whether the politician and bureaucrat are of high or low talent. This is because an actor with high talent succeeds with probability p H = 1+∆ 2 conditional on effort, and the one with low talent succeeds with probability p L = 1 -∆ 2 . Thus, the greater is ∆, the wider is the range of bureaucrat's initial reputation β 0 for which he exerts effort. This implies that a more informative outcome reduces the need for the politician to make claims about responsibility. At the same time, blame and credit can shift beliefs more, which may also increase the potential for communication to affect a bureaucrat's effort choice. Similarly, by increasing ∆ , there is a greater ′ scope for second-period effort to be feasible because the second-period outcome is more informative about the bureaucrat's talent. This also means that the politicians faces fewer constraints if it wants to incentivize the bureaucrat in the first period while still ensuring effort in the second period.

Politician's reputation payoff functions. We use a stark payoff function for the politician's reputation concerns. That is, the politician's payoff is constant below some threshold, and constant above it, with a sharp discontinuity at the threshold. This is important because

the politician's ability to communicate relies on her indifference between two messages. This indifference possibility breaks down if, for example, the politician's reputation concern is a strictly increasing function of γ 2 . However, it is possible to retain the possibility of indifference for other reputation payoff functions, if effort choices were made differently. That is, if the bureaucrat's effort choice was made from a continuous set, then it may occur that the politician is indifferent between two messages. This is possible as long as the message which induces a better politician reputation also has a lower bureaucratic effort level, while the other message leads to a lower politician reputation and higher bureaucratic effort level.

Bureaucrat reputation payoff functions. In the main model, the bureaucrat's reputation payoff follows a threshold form. The bureaucrat's reputation payoff, however, does not need to be so stark. It can also be increasing in the bureaucrat's reputation. The key aspect is that revealing information about who was responsible spreads out posteriors. This will be helpful for the bureaucrat, as credit and blame are informative about the bureaucrat's talent. Qualitatively, results will be similar because reputational updating is stronger when beliefs are closer to 1 / 2. In Appendix B.2, we formally study a version of the model in which the bureaucrat's reputation payoff is linearly increasing in β . As in the main model, for some values of β 0 , the bureaucrat exerts effort if the politician revealed information about responsibility, increasing effort relative to politician silence. As before, the bureaucrat is willing to exert effort for an intermediate range of reputations. A key difference now is that the cost of effort plays a stronger role. The possibility of effort extraction via cheap talk is attenuated if effort is more costly.


## 7 Discussion and Conclusion


When asking experts or voters what makes good political leaders, words like honesty, integrity, trustworthiness, and character are typical responses. Indeed, voters are shown to hold politicians in higher esteem if they sometimes take the blame (Miller and Reeves 2022). Nonetheless, politician blaming of bureaucratic underlings when something goes awry is not

uncommon. Interpretations of such accusations have typically been to view the politician as not embodying such characteristics but rather trying to avoid responsibility. If apt, this description suggests that being a good leader is not key for political selection and that voters and their surrogates are either insincere in saying what they care about or are easily misled.

Alternatively, we provide a rationale for blaming and credit claiming that is more consistent with positive leadership. Broadly, our analysis contrasts with previous work by studying the battle for credit as strategic communication. Assuming that politicians want to get policy right and that more bureaucratic effort raises the probability of success, the ability to blame and give credit may in some cases be advantageous to politicians. Specifically, in our model a politician's ability to criticize can increase the likelihood of effort-induced good policy. Given that the public is observing, the politician's comments may spur a bureaucrat to work harder despite the bureaucrat otherwise being protected from being fired. The threat of blame alone may spur the reputation-sensitive bureaucrat on, as such criticism plays an informational role for a judgmental public. Politicians may not always be avoiding accountability but instead providing the public with an ability to update about bureaucrats that, in turn, can potentially produce better policy outcomes.

We also contend that politicians are strategically balancing the acts of being fully transparent about attribution and being silent about it. We show that a politician can strategically keep quiet to protect the bureaucrat and accrue future effort. Contrary to this, under some conditions, transparency might be good to incentivize bureaucrats to exert effort. In fact, we show that a politician can incentivize the bureaucrats to exert effort by truthfully acknowledging that bureaucrat was responsible for failure or success.

We acknowledge that aspects of our modeling approach are stylized and that this approach certainly masks some empirical realities. One, politicians and bureaucrats may have concerns that are not purely reputational. Two, determining who is actually responsible poses

considerable challenges. In fact, in the aforementioned Dutch child care benefits scandal, the bureaucrats contended that they were merely implementing the law passed by the legislature, whereas the politicians countered by stating that the law was incorrectly implemented. That said, the modeling approach we have followed has advantages too. One, our strategy allows us to isolate and understand the politician-bureaucrat battle for credit that we observe in many settings. Two, we conceptualize blaming and crediting purely as communication, which allows us to study incentives for agent effort, providing conditions under which such communication can be credible.

Finally, our study of the battle for credit has implications for institutional design. In the interaction between the politician and the bureaucrat several questions arise. Should politicians always transparently attribute responsibility? Should politicians remain silent? Should they do a mix of both? Our analysis shows that politicians can strategically evaluate these options because they are concerned about bureaucrat's effort, subsequent policy outcomes, and their own careers. How should this be thought of from an institutional perspective? There are ongoing debates about what a minister is actually responsible for, and whether a political failure should lead to a forced resignation. For instance, the constitutional Dutch advisory board ( Raad van State ) stated:

'Who can be held accountable for all this? Is it the involved minister or is it other people? What about the responsibility of civil service and competence? Does Parliament have sufficient control? In the core, these questions are about the workings of ministerial responsibility.' 26

In the Dutch context, ministerial responsibility refers to the head of a ministry ultimately

being formally responsible for policy outcomes. 27 In isolation, this may be normatively desirable. However, a politician's frequent interactions with the bureaucrat muddies the waters due to the agency problems underlying this interaction, and our analysis highlights this aspect. In this context, our analysis contrasts with the near exclusively negative view of politician blaming by bringing to the fore politicians strategically using silence and crediting/blaming to motivate their agents via communicating to the public.

Given that blaming may be a product not just of efforts to elude responsibility but to induce bureaucratic effort, it is not unsurprising that it is a common phenomenon. We show that blame can serve a function that is analogous to the principal's ability to adjust an individual's wages and hire or fire as in principal-agent approaches in the theory of the firm. In turn, this recognition directs attention toward other considerations, such as whether politicians should be routinely condemned for criticizing their underlings. Our findings indicate that allowing a policy-motivated politician to blame her underlings might lead to positive outcomes under certain conditions. Dissuading politicians from doing so, for example by fostering norms where politicians criticizing the bureaucracy are sanctioned by negative responses by voters, may induce less bureaucratic effort in the aggregate and the wrong choice being made more frequently. This contrasts with claims, dating back to Fiorina (1977, 1982)'s canonical works, viewing the ability to blame the bureaucracy as exclusively negative and indicating that blaming should be condemned.

## 2 Material and relational wealth


Material wealth inequality-defined as differential access to resources between individuals or groups-has persisted over human history [25-27], and pervaded multiple cultural and ecological settings [7, 28], often with major impacts on life outcomes. Most consistently, individuals with privileged access to material resources are often healthier [2931], and have greater reproductive success [especially men; e.g., 32-36]. The ubiquity of material wealth inequality, and the importance of being wealthy, beg questions as to how inequality has emerged to become a fundamental characteristic of human social organisation.

Focus has primarily been on the macro-level ecological processes and structural features that cause material wealth inequality to emerge. Anthropologists, in particular, focus on the environmental conditions that allow individuals differential access to material resources [37]. Specifi-

density and patchiness [40], storage [41] and institutions 2 for inter-generational transmission [9] can produce payoff 3 structures for individuals that encourage the privatization 4 of resources [42-44], thereby giving rise to inequality [8]. 5 When such dynamics are coupled with an analysis of micro6 level factors, we can learn about who becomes rich and 7 why. Individuals with embodied wealth [e.g., skill, knowl8 edge, strength, health; 45] may increase their production or 9 control of resources. These effects may be direct, through 10 simply grabbing wealth by threatening harm, but often op11 erate through informal social influence, whereby an indi12 vidual's perceived ability and willingness to provide ben13 efits improves their status within a community, at times 14 strengthening hierarchical structures [46-48]. Akin to this, 15 leadership roles often accompany expectations of making 16 decisions in the best interest of a group [49], and in turn 17 greater access to the material goods that are available to 18 their group [50]. The rich will find such ties advantageous [especially when disadvantaged groups are large; 54]. These preferences can amount to social networks becoming structured by wealth homophily [21, 55]. Furthermore, homophily can become self-reinforcing insofar as wealthy individualswith greater access to valued material, social and informational resources-become increasingly valuable as partners [24, 56]. The resulting wealth gap can be bolstered by preferences for, or assortment by, personal characteristics that signpost shared norms [e.g., religion; 57], or by perceived badges of status [e.g., discrimination based on gender or ethnicity that can further entrench poverty traps; 18, 5860]. Such preferential assortment by wealth can inhibit upward mobility, prevent learning, and create clustering and separation in networks based on relative wealth [61]. Individuals who are less wealthy can only mobilise the resources that their similarly impoverished friends have access to, which are likely less valuable and diverse in comparison to wealthier counterparts [62, 63]. Given this, homophily based on preferential assortment by wealth may be a leading factor in creating and sustaining wealth inequality, and will leave a signature on the networks of some communities.

In some contexts, wealthier individuals may be motivated to form asymmetrical patron-client relationships [64-68], or be well-positioned to broker relationships between other group members [69-72]. This is because they are either in a position to extract resources from others, and/or have disproportionate control over resources that other group members lack. In such situations, the non-wealthy may try to gain access to resources through social relationships, wage labour, or co-working ties, and we might expect to see ties typical of patron-client relations, such as labour being sent from the poor to the wealthy and food (or other benefits) from the wealthy to the poor. The realisation of such relationships nevertheless rests upon the decisions of wealthier group members, who may prefer to retain their isolation given their economic independence [73]. The extent to which wealthier individuals might be allowed to occupy network positions that allow them to maximize personal gains, and go unchecked by other group members, could depend on the strength of relationships among the non-wealthy and their ability to mount challenges to the status quo [74, 75].

There are, however, constraints on the wealthy protecting their privilege. This is particularly the case when there is a high premium on coordinating group activities, such as managing subsistence tasks [e.g., foraging, livestock management; 65, 76], reducing costly intra-group conflict [23], succeeding in inter-group conflicts [77], or managing risk [42]-linking back again to macro-level features in the environmental and institutional context. Our network-based approach advances an empirical framework for understanding the meso-level processes that structure relational wealth. By going beyond simple correlations between different centrality metrics calculated on a network, we depart from existing approaches to the emergence of material wealth inequality. Instead, we consider the structure of different forms of relational wealth, and how such structure is connected to material wealth. ## (d) Concluding remarks


In the absence of any clear wealth homophily, there is as yet little evidence of emerging cleavages in relational and material wealth that can exacerbate wealth inequality, as so widely reported in the literature. Despite the opportunities for highly unequal cash windfalls that are contingent on sharp differences in tree ownership (cloves and other), there appear to be few pathways whereby wealth inequality will become entrenched or socially divisive in Mitini. This is not necessarily true of Pemba more generally, given that we selected a village for study that had no ties of remittance with relatives in Oman or other foreign lands. However, in Mitini we suggest-albeit through inference and ethnographic knowledge-that it is the unpredictability of cash income that drives everyone to buffer their fortunes with relational wealth, and benefit from the strong prescriptions for interdependence among neighbours, as prescribed by Islam. Perhaps the only emerging cracks in the fabric are that men are clearly carefully selecting co-workers based on reciprocity rather than genealogical relationship or distance, and that a small clique may be emerging among households with Nguvu Zetu members that share a positive orientation towards development. These patterns may take on a new significance in the future. Examining this patterning will allow us to understand how persistent inequality emerges between regions, groups and populations [103], and might indicate where and how development interventions can most effectively reduce inequality [20].

More generally, bridging individual-level and macro-level structural factors, core meso-level forces-such as social networks-provide a platform for gaining a deeper understanding of mechanisms leading to material wealth inequality. We suggest that the type of study presented here, that attempts to disaggregate theoretically-relevant features of relational wealth and how they are related to material wealth, will allow exploration of how individual-level processes aggregate up to form the norms and conventions that, in turn, feed back into individual differences in access to material resources.

## 1. Introduction


In 2020 (quite recently), the implementation of Project 5-100 ended in Russia. Three years have passed, but the results are still under heated discussion. Opinions are extremely contradictory: some note positive changes in the number of publications of Russian universities, others complain about the lack of institutional changes and emergent effects, as well as the unresolved problem of the gap in funding with the world's leading benchmarks. However, everyone agrees on one point: the main declared goal of the project was not achieved, five Russian universities did not enter top 100 of global university rankings. The successor of the project was the Priority-2030 program, which formally moved away from the ranking race. On the other hand, in Priority-2030 some indicators are inherited from Project 5-100, which, in turn, were designed for promotion in global university  rankings  (even  though  they  have  changed  a  bit).  Therefore,  the  issue  of  rankings traditionally occupies an important place in Russian academic discourse.

Despite significant differences, there is a strong relationship between global university rankings and research evaluation. The emergence of global rankings is closely related to the neoliberal paradigm  of  higher  education,  within  which,  since  the  end  of  the  last  century,  the  so-called excellence initiatives have  emerged. By excellence initiatives, we understand a special type of political initiatives aimed at increasing the global competitiveness of the national higher education system and identifying an elite group of national universities. The appearance of the first rankings is closely connected with the excellence initiatives in East Asia (primarily in China). In turn, the emergence of the  first Academic Ranking of  World  Universities  (ARWU) triggered  a  wave  of excellence initiatives in Europe.

However, the rankings only focus on what they measure, which may not be enough to evaluate a system  as  complex  as  a  university  and  divert  attention  from  the  really  important  factors.  Are indicators of university rankings socially significant? Should society be focused on getting a group

of national universities into the top 20 (50, 100, 200, etc.) world rankings? In my opinion, the question  sounds  even  broader,  whether  universities  are  just  commercial  enterprises  for  the production of knowledge, or whether they still have to fulfill a social mission (as understood, for example, by Bernal (1939) and Draper (1964)). Besides, it remains an open question whether we can call the practice of using university rankings in research assessment responsible in terms of basic  documents  in  research  assessment  ( San  Francisco  Declaration  on  Research  Evaluation (DORA) Leiden Manifesto , , Hong Kong Principles for Researcher Evaluation , etc.).

The goal of this academic article is to provide a thorough understanding of how global university rankings are interpreted and understood in Russia. This will be achieved through a rigorous and comprehensive review of the Russian-language academic literature, which will help shed light on the  various  perspectives  and  viewpoints  emerging  from  Russia  regarding  the  utilization  and interpretation of global university rankings. The selection of Russian literature for this study was purposeful  and  strategic.  The  focus  on  Russian  literature  aligns  with  the  objectives  of  Project 5top100 flagship excellence initiative (2013-2020) which was heavily influenced by university rankings. In fact, the project derived its name from the goal of having five Russian universities ranked within the top 100 globally by the year 2020. Besides, that part of the Russian academic discourse that is more or less closed to the international readership will be analyzed. We also highlight the problem from the point of view of global trends.

The article is organized as follows. In the next section, we provide the necessary background for the problems under consideration. The methodology is described in Section 3. Section 4 provides a brief current snapshot of the global perspective based on the key statements about responsible research  assessment.  Finally,  Section  5  provides  a  systematic  review  of  the  Russian-language literature on the problem. In the concluding section, we conceptualize the main findings of the paper with implications for further research and practice.


## 2. Background



## 2.1. The Emergence of Global University Rankings


The emergence and wide distribution of rankings at the beginning of the 21st century was due to a number of premises. Foremost, one should note here that globalization has penetrated all public spheres,  including  higher  education.  Globalization  in  higher  education  was  expressed  in  the growing trend of student and academic mobility between countries (in Europe, this was greatly facilitated by the Bologna system). Accordingly, students and faculty needed a transparent tool for comparison and decision-making. However, the competitive situation for universities has changed. For the first time, many universities concluded that they must consider international competitors and need a reliable international benchmarking tool. Thus, the initial intent of rankings was a marketing and benchmarking tool.

How  did  rankings  become  part  of  political  discourse  and  national  strategies?  The  neoliberal paradigm of higher education plays a direct role here, which is characterized by the marketization, industrialization, and commercialization of higher education in a global context (Yuhan 2022). The  university  is  turning  into  an  enterprise  to  produce  knowledge,  more  specifically,  human resources  and  knowledge  assets  (intellectual  property  and  publications).  Under  conditions  of knowledge  capitalism (D.  M.  Kochetkov  and  Kochetkova  2021),  effective  accumulation  of intellectual  resources  (including  talent  acquisition)  has  become  a  priority  for  university,  the national system of higher education, and the state as a whole.

The neoliberal paradigm, together with shifts in the global landscape of  higher education (the desire  to  move  away  from  the  unipolar  system),  has  resulted  in  the  emergence  of  excellence initiatives. The first such initiative appeared in China ( Project 211 ).  Achieving the goal of the initiatives (Project 211 was followed by Project 985 (Project 211 and 985 2020)). The aim of these

policy initiatives was achieving 'world class' -for Chinese universities, and this task required a benchmarking tool. Not surprisingly, the first global university ranking, the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU), was released in China by Shanghai Jiao Tong University in 2003. In turn, the release of the Shanghai ranking provoked a wave of excellence initiatives in Europe (Hazelkorn and Mihut 2021). Therefore, these two phenomena are closely related.

Hazelkorn and Mihut (2021) listed 25 global university rankings. In the framework of this study, we will not dwell on each of them in detail. Based on the scope of this study, we focused on the emergence of the Big Three (ARWU, THE, and QS), Leiden Ranking as well as rankings that use an innovative  set of metrics, U-Multirank  and  the  Three  University  Missions.  Besides, Webometrics was added to this list because it is distinguished from other rankings by its special focus . 1

ARWU came out against the background of ongoing excellence initiatives in China (Projects 211 and 985), so its main task was to digitize the concept of 'world class university'. The ranking is -characterized by a stable methodology that exclusively uses verifiable data. The ranking is also distinguished by the presence of 'luxury' indicators, such as the number of employees - Nobel and Fields Prize winners.

The  first QS  World  University  Rankings were  jointly  published  by  the  British  company, Quacquarelli Symonds , and Times Higher Education magazine. The entry threshold compared to ARWU has been lowered because of the abandonment of luxury indicators. At the same time, 50% of  the  final  index  depended  on  reputation  surveys.  The  QS  ranking  came  under  fire  from  the academic community from the very beginning. Therefore, in 2010 the Times Higher Education magazine released an updated Times Higher Education World University Rankings ;  thus, there was a 'divorce' of QS and THE. It is noteworthy that THE initially swi tched to Web of Science publication data, but in 2014, there was a return to cooperation with Elsevier. Compared to the joint  QS-THE rating, the changes affected overweighting of subjective reputation surveys and skewness of publication metrics towards hard sciences (Miguel Antonio Lim 2018). Besides, the indicator of industry income was added. To the best of our knowledge, THE is the only Big Four ranking that highlights university's innovative activities. Nevertheless, the modest weight of this indicator of 2.5% is surprising: is it really that the university devotes only 1/40 of its activities to innovation and knowledge transfer? Of course, the answer to this question largely depends on the particular university, but it's still surprising.

The Leiden Ranking is  compiled by the Centre for Science and Technology Studies of Leiden University (Netherlands). It has several significant differences from those previously described. First, it is purely a bibliometric ranking; thus, this ranking is relatively transparent compared to other rankings  . The second difference is the absence of a composite index as such. As a result, 2 the Leiden Ranking is more of a benchmarking tool. The third difference is the calculation of values in the two versions: size-dependent and size-independent. The second option allows a user to level the scale effect. The ranking methodology is constantly evolving. In particular, the ranking included open access and gender indicators quite recently.

U-Multirank was developed by international consortium in 2009 as an alternative to ARWU and THE-QS. In 2011, the European Commission decided to fund the implementation of U-Multirank. The ranking methodology stabilized in 2013. It is based on a very wide range of indicators, among which we would especially like to note the presence of a group of indicators that characterize regional engagement. Like the Leiden Ranking, it is rather a benchmarking tool: the user can compare universities in any of the areas, by country, region, or subject area.

The Three University Missions is the youngest ranking in the list. It is issued by Moscow State University (Russia). In 2021, the ranking covered 1650 universities from 97 countries; thus, the Three  University  Missions  is  one  of  the  most  comprehensive  global  university  rankings.  The ranking is  based  on  the  university's  assessment  of  three  key  missions:  education,  science,  and community engagement. Reputation surveys were excluded; however, data from the university's public records are used.

The Webometrics ranking by Cybermetrics Lab (Spain) is released twice a year. It should be noted that this is by far the most global ranking in terms of enrollment (the latest edition includes 11998 universities). Half of the composite index depends on the number of external links to the university website; the other half depends on publications and citations. A small number of indicators (three) and content distinguish this ranking from the others.

Thus, we can classify university rankings in at least two ways: (1) the calculation of a composite index, and (2) the use of reputation surveys (Fig. 1).

Most  ranking  providers  also  calculate  industry  or  subject  rankings  (only  Webometrics  is  an exception). We believe that subject rankings are more useful than institutional rankings, because an 'average' university may not excel in all subject areas, but it may well excel in one or two.
