In Table 2 and Appendix Table A1 we use as control group those treated at grade 10 (or this group combined with the never treated). However, for some of the specific treatment effect parameters given by grade of separation ( 𝑔 ) and event time ( 𝑒 ) reported in Table A1, we could choose alternative control groups of later treated. When estimating the effect of separation at grade 4 on test scores in grade 4, we might use all not-yet treated as control group, that is, those treated in grades 6, 8 and 10. This would be in accordance with the suggestions in Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021). An alternative might be to only use those treated at grade 6 because this control group may be expected to be more similar to the treatment group in terms of observables and unobservables, making the common trend assumption more likely to hold. Estimates for all possible choices of control groups of not-yet treated for each parameter are shown in Appendix Table A2.  The results are robust to the choice of control group. If we compare with the estimates using 𝑔 = 10 as control group (see column 1 in Table A1, and columns 1, 7 and 10 in Table A2), the alternative control groups tend to reduce the estimated effects at event time 0 and 2 for treatment group 𝑔 = 4 , but to increase the estimate for event time 0 for treatment group 𝑔 = 6 . However, these differences are not statistically significant, and again we find that pre-trends are not statistically different between treatment groups and control groups of later treated. 15 In sum, this gives a strong indication of robust results regardless of control group.


## 6.1.3 Robustness check: Results applying the Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) approach


As an additional robustness check we have applied the CSA approach. The CSA method and our results using this method are discussed in detail in Appendix B. Here we only briefly discuss the results. The main conclusion is that the results we obtain using the CSA approach are very similar to our main results reported in Table 2. There are no significant differences.

In the CSA approach, each 𝐴𝑇𝑇(𝑔,𝑡) parameter is estimated separately using all observations for not-yet treated individuals as control group. For instance, for those experiencing separation at grade 4 ( 𝑔 = 4 ) we estimate the effect on test scores in grade 4 ( 𝑡 = 4 ) using all other treatment groups ( 𝑔 ∈ {6,8,10} ) (and possibly the group of never treated) as control group; the effects in grades 6 and 8 are estimated using smaller control groups, omitting group 6, and groups 6 and 8, respectively. When aggregating the 𝐴𝑇𝑇(𝑔,𝑡) estimates to average effects by event time, the size of each treatment group is used as weights. Both the varying control groups and the aggregation procedure may give rise to different results than our stacked regression estimates.

Our CSA point estimates for effects at event time 0 are almost the same as the main results in Table 2. When we use later treated as control group, our CSA point estimates for event time 2 and 4 are a little smaller than in Table 2 (column 1), but when we include never treated in the control group our CSA point estimates are approx. the same for event time 2 and a little larger for event time 4 compared to Table 2 (column 3). Allowing pre-treatment covariates to affect counterfactual test score trends tend to reduce our CSA estimates, but the reduction is very small.

Differential pre-trends are estimated in a rather different way in the CSA approach, so they are difficult to compare to the pre-trend estimates in Table 2, but again there are no significant differential pre-trends when we use later treated as control groups, whereas including never treated in the control group again results in significant negative trends for the treatment groups compared to the control groups from event time -6 to -4.


## 6.1.4 Mechanisms and heterogeneity in effects


To investigate at what levels of test scores parental union dissolution has important effects, we now present results of applying distribution DID regressions with later treated as control group; see the discussion in Section 4.1.3. Figure 3 shows on the y-axis the effect of parental union dissolution on the probability of scoring below the test score level indicated on the x-axis. The model corresponds to that in the first column of Table 2, except for the dependent variable. Each graph in Figure 3 shows results for a given event time. At negative event times (the two upper graphs), the results indicate no significant effect of separation at any point in the distribution of test scores. For nonnegative event times (the three lower graphs), the results indicate that it is the middle of the test score distribution that accounts for the negative effect of parental union dissolution on children's test scores. Because the outcome variable is normalized with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, it is roughly the middle 50-60 percent of the distribution that carries the effect, indicating that the test scores of both high and low ability pupils are on average unaffected by parents ending their union. 16 Possible mechanisms may be that high-ability students are likely to be more resilient, and that low school performance may tend to be related to poor home environments that may on average not be worsened much by parental separation; see the discussion in Section 2.

We also investigate heterogeneity in terms of gender which might result from gender differences in resilience. Appendix Table A3 shows results from estimating the model of column 2 in Table 2 separately for boys and girls. Point estimates indicate larger negative effects of separation for girls, but these gender differences are not statistically significant.

As discussed in Section 2, some mechanisms behind negative effects of parental separation may be related to parental resources including income and educational level. It is therefore interesting to explore potential effect heterogeneity in these dimensions. Appendix Tables A4 and A5 show results for models estimated separately for long and short levels of parental education, and for high and low levels of income (measured at child age 5). Differences are not statistically significant, and there is no clear pattern in the size of the point estimates. One exception is that effects tend to larger for those with high paternal income. This might be explained by children losing more economic resources if fathers have a high income before separation because they will often live mainly with the mother after separation.


## 6.2 Immediate Effect of Parental Separation: RDD Regressions


To study the immediate effect of parental separation on test scores, we rely on a an RDD analysis, where the running variable R is the difference between the date of sitting the test and the date when parents move apart.  We control for grade of test and grade of separation. We use the rdrobust command of Calonico et al. (2017) with automatic bandwidth selection. Table 4 shows results for models with triangular or uniform kernel, and with polynomials of order 1 or 2 in the running variable, reporting both conventional and bias-corrected estimates. We find a significant effect at the threshold (where the date of separation equals the test date) of between -0.03 and -0.05 SD. The automatically selected bandwidth varies between 105 and 177 weeks.

Corresponding to the models in Table 4, Figure 4 plots the weekly-binned average test scores (adjusted for grade of test and grade of separation) across the running variable ( 𝑅 ) with an imposed cutoff at the time when separation date equals test date, and with a fitted linear or quadratic curve on each side of the cutoff. As seen from the figure, there is evidence of a discrete decline in test scores at R = 0. The discontinuity is fuzzy which may be explained by the considerable

heterogeneity in dissolution processes and by the fact that test scores are determined by many other factors than parental dissolution.

At the bottom of Table 4 we report p-values of the McCrary (2008) test for indications of parents manipulating the timing of separation relative to the date of the test. There is no statistically detectable evidence of manipulation. As a balancing test, Table A6 in the Appendix reports results from RDD regressions for parental and child characteristics. There is no evidence of a discontinuity in covariates occurring at the cutoff. In total, we find some indications of an immediate decline in test scores following parental separation. The basic RDD estimates in the first row of Table 4 are numerically smaller than the long-term effects from the DID models, but still substantial.


## 7. CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION


We find that parental union dissolution has both immediate and longer term negative effects on children's test scores in the range 3.0-6.5% of a standard deviation. Effect sizes are relatively large and driven by children in the middle of the test score distribution. Our estimation strategy using dynamic DID models, taking account of individual fixed effects, as well as RDD models, overcome important difficulties in estimating effects of parental separation. Thus, there exists not only selection into families that experience union dissolution, but also selection into timing of separation, and effects may be dynamic, which may lead to confounding issues in more traditional approaches to estimating the effect of union dissolution on children. The results corroborate previous work using sibling-fixed effects models by Laird et al. (2020), who also found close-to-immediate impact on school leaving GPA of parental union dissolution, and expand on them by highlighting the potential dynamic effect of union dissolution on children's educational achievement.

In this study, we have extensively demonstrated that parental union dissolution has substantial and likely dynamic negative effects on children's learning. Initial parameter estimates are of an absolute size similar to the effect of small classrooms in the STAR experiment (Krueger 1999), the effect of

an increase in teacher-quality of 0.5 of a standard deviation (Rockoff 2004), or the average effect of offering high-dosage tutoring (Fryer and Howard-Noveck 2020), and the dynamic effects estimates hint at even larger learning losses as time from union dissolution increase. More than 30% of Danish children can expect their parents to dissolve their union before the children leave primary school. For most of these children, the parental break up occurs before they even start school, at a time where parental influence and investments likely are even more important for skill development (Cunha and Heckman 2007) than at the margin that we have considered in this study. Insofar as the initial and dynamic nature of the effect of parental union dissolution on children's learning extends backwards similarly, the learning loss that is occurring due to parental union dissolution are likely substantially higher than what we have identified.

The findings of this study raise the question of how to address the disparities in children's skill formation caused by parental union dissolution. Forcing parents to remain in a relationship is both at odds with central tenets of modern ethics and family policies but would also require the assumption that parents' relationship would not degenerate to a state as harmful for children's learning as it would be if the parents dissolved their union. Previous work studying the first modern divorce reforms has generally found no effect on educational attainment in the very first birth cohorts whose parents were affected by the reform change (Gruber 2004; Piketty 2003), perhaps because the divorcing marriages were bad, so children would be as well off with their parents being divorced (see also Clark et al. 2015). More recently and considering a setting where divorce is much less of a rare event and more normatively accepted, work from Denmark (Fallesen 2021), the Netherlands (Kabátek 2019), and South Korea (Lee 2013) all corroborate that forcing divorcing couples to have a mandatory separation or 'cooling-off' period causes about 10 percent of couples to reconsider their decision. If the home environment does not deteriorate further after such a change of heart, it might be a viable intervention to avoid 'unnecessary' union dissolution, where parents change their minds if given time to reconsider.

This still leaves us with a substantial group of children of parents who would separate anyway. For this group, it is hard to envision a policy targeting their domestic situation that may help mitigate their loss of human capital due to their parents' union dissolution. This shifts the focus to what can be done in the school-environment. Teachers are often some of the first to know about changes to children's domestic situation. Increased intensity of schooling through remedial programs or scholastic focused after-school care could perhaps offset the loss to learning due to the parental union dissolution. Non-academic investments improving child well-being might also have positive effects on academic achievement.

Lastly, we have shown that the children whose test scores decrease the most following their parents' union dissolution likely are the children found in the middle of the skill distribution. This is a group often ignored by educational policy and interventions, which instead often and with good reason considers how to increase performance among those in the lowest part of the distribution, and how to ensure that high performance students continue to be challenged and progress in the classroom. Yet, when it comes to parental union dissolution, it appears to be this middle group that experience most, if not all, of the negative consequences of parental union dissolution. This further means that for this group, the effect is likely much higher than the average effect that we estimate in our main analysis.

## Introduction


The Philippines is an archipelagic Southeast Asian country in the Western Pacific Ocean. Since its post-war decolonization in 1946, the Philippines has been a unitary presidential republic with a bicameral legislature. It also experienced an interlude of dictatorial rule under the Marcos regime from 1965 until the 1986 People Power Revolution. A newly industrialized economy, the Philippines is transitioning from an agriculture-based economy to one centered around services and manufacturing. The Philippines has ratified 38 ILO conventions, of which 30 are in force. These include C143, C156, C183, and C189 -key conventions relating to carework.

The Philippines had an overall GCPI score of 7.23 (out of 10) placing it in the higher end of the 'Maturing' Index Band - on par with some of the highest performing countries in the GCPI and ahead of fellow lower-middle-income countries. Its strong performance was buoyed by its high levels of protection for domestic workers in Sub-Index B and strong maternity leave provisions in Sub-Index A, but is penalized by inadequate dependent care leave and flexible work arrangements.

With a progressive women's rights environment, the Philippines is the top Asian country in performance for closing the gender gap and is the only Asian country in the top 20 of the World Economic Forum's

Global Gender Gap Report 2020. 1 Among many recent women-focused laws, the Philippines also passed a Magna Carta of Women (Republic Act No. 9710) in 2009 seeking to eliminate gender discrimination. 2 Nevertheless, the active and dynamic women's movement in the Philippines has been hampered by deep-seated patriarchal gender norms and high incidences of domestic violence. 3 Women's labor force participation rate for the Philippines in 2020 fell to 42.62%.

A 2020 survey found that 1.4 million Filipinos were working locally as domestic workers, or kasambahay . Of this number, about a million were in live-out arrangements, and about 4% or 49,000 were child domestic workers. 4 As an occupation that is dominated by poorer women and rural-urban migrants, domestic work is often denigrated and discriminated against. 5 The Philippines is also a major country of origin for migrant domestic workers. Of the 1.7 million Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in 2020, a majority were women and 827,540 were engaged in domestic work. 6 In 2021, 8.9% of the Philippines' GDP (equivalent to USD34.9 billion) was derived from the remittances of OFWs.


## Key Care Policies


The Labor Code of the Philippines is the primary labor legislation - providing regulatory protections around working hours, annual leave, employment and working conditions, and maternity and gender protections. Domestic workers are notably excluded from Title I and II of Book III of the Code which relates to regulations on normal working hours and employment terms. A separate law, the Domestic Workers Act (Republic Act 10361) or the Batas Kasambahay supplements the Labor Code in providing protections for domestic workers in the Philippines.

The 105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law (Republic Act No. 11210) is a key law which governs maternity leave provisions and protections. Other key laws relating to carework protections include: the Magna Carta of Women (Republic Act No. 9710), the Paternity Leave Act of 1996 (Republic Act 8187), the Expanded Breastfeeding Promotion Act of 2009 (Republic Act 10028), the Solo Parents' Welfare Act of 2000 (Republic Act 8972), the Telecommuting Act (Republic Act No. 11165), the Night Workers Act (Republic Act No. 10151), the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Act (Republic Act No. 11058), and the Social Security Law (Republic Act 8282).

The Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act (Republic Act No. 9208) and Special Protection of Children Against Child Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act (Republic Act No. 9231) are also relevant for protections for forced-labor and under-age domestic workers.


## Recent Care Policy Developments



## Maternity and Family Protections


In 2009, two key laws, the Magna Carta of Women and the Expanded Breastfeeding Promotion Act, were passed with the aim of gender mainstreaming and supporting gender protections in the workplace. In 2019, the '105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law,' was signed into law, extending paid maternity leave from 60 days to 105 days following long-term advocacy by the women's movement. 7 The law also grants an extension of fifteen days for solo mothers.

The Telecommuting Act was also introduced in 2019 during the COVID-19 pandemic, providing flexiwork arrangements if sought by employers, although only for a three-year period. 8 Efforts are currently underway to make this provision a permanent statutory arrangement. 9

The Senate Bill No. 1411 was passed in December 2021, amending the Solo Parents Welfare Act of 2000 and extending coverage to OFWs - thus the

left-behind spouses of OFWs are now also eligible for extended parental leave and parental benefits. 10


## Domestic Worker Developments


In 2012, the Philippines was the second country to ratify C189, the ILO Domestic Workers Convention - a result of prolonged advocacy by local civil society groups and the Department of Labor and Employment. 11 C189 itself was also the result of international advocacy by the Philippines alongside several Latin American countries - all significant countries of origin for migrant domestic workers. 12 The Philippines subsequently passed the Domestic Workers Act in 2013, building on popular civil society and political momentum from its earlier ratification of C189. 13


## Key Actors


Key government agencies include the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) , the Philippine Commission on Women (PCW) , DOLE's Bureau of Workers with Special Concern , and the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) . In addition to its advocacy and regulatory work, DOLE also conducts labor inspection programs and operates labor advisory and reporting hotlines. The PCW, formerly known as the National Commission on the Role of Filipino Women (NCRFW), was expanded and restructured in 2009 with the passing of the Magna Carta of Women. It works primarily on gender mainstreaming and monitoring implementations of gender protections.

Prominent civil society organizations and unions advocating for domestic workers include Visayan Forum Foundation Inc. (VF), SUMAPI (or the Association and Linkage of Domestic Workers in the Philippines), and the United Domestic Workers of the Philippines .

## Sub-Index A:



## Protections for Family Caregivers


The Philippines' performance in Sub-Index A was buoyed by recent legislative progress on maternity leave provisions which increased benefits and comprehensive coverage for a wider range of working mothers. However, inadequate provisions for dependency leave and flexible work arrangements presented a significant shortfall in its performance. Overall, the Philippines scored 5.88 (out of 10) for Sub-Index A.


## A1Pregnancy and Maternity Leave Coverage (8.75/10)


All categories of working women - including those in the informal economy - are guaranteed maternity leave. This is however conditional upon payment of 3 months of Social Security contributions. The duration of maternity leave is 135 days for non-solo mothers, and 150 days for single or solo mothers. While maternity leave can be extended in cases of complications, there is no extended maternity leave in cases of simultaneous multiple births. These provisions are also available for adoptive mothers.


## A2Protections during Pregnancy and Maternity Leave (9.25/10)


Eligible working women are entitled to receive their full salary for the first 105 days of maternity leave only. The remaining 30 days are unpaid. These benefits are paid through social security. Those who are not eligible for wage replacement - like 'indigent women' may access cash benefits through the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) or the National Health Insurance Program. Working women are also protected from dismissal from work during and after their maternity leave on grounds relating to their pregnancy. However, there are inadequate protections against job discrimination of workers with family caregiving responsibilities not relating to pregnancy.


## A3Paternity Leave Policies (7.93/10)


Only married men are guaranteed paternity leave, and only for their cohabiting spouse's first four pregnancies. The seven-day paternity leave benefit also extends to married working men in the informal sector. In cases of the death, sickness, or hospitalization of the mother where the mother cannot care for the child, the father is entitled to leave of a duration equal to the unexpired portion of the postnatal maternity leave. Mothers are also allowed to allocate seven days out of their own maternity leave benefits to their partner's paternity leave allocation, whether or not they are married to the father of their child.


## A4DependentCareLeave Policies (1.25/10)


There are no statutory provisions for dependent care or childcare leave, except for solo parents who are eligible for 7 days of childcare leave.


## A5Flexible Work Arrangements (1.25/10)


Where there are provisions of flexitime and telecommuting, these are conditional upon the voluntary provision of these benefits by employers and may not be requested by employees. Only solo parents may request flexible working schedules. There are some protections to ensure that women do not need to engage in nightwork but no similar provisions to adapt shiftwork assignments for male and female workers with family responsibilities.


## A6Mother-Friendly Workplace Policies (6.88/10)


Nursing breaks for working mothers are mandated, and may be counted and compensated as working time. Facilities for nursing must also be provided by employers. While employees are empowered to assess, report, and eliminate workplace risks, there is no specific mention of safety provisions for pregnant women. There is also no specific mention that a pregnant or nursing woman is exempt from performing work that has been determined to be prejudicial to the health of the mother or the child.


## Best Practices


The Philippines leads in a number of key best practices when it comes to its caregiver protections. These include its provision of additional support and extended parental leave benefits for single and solo parents regardless of marital status under the Solo Parents' Welfare Act; and the provision that in cases of the death, sickness, or hospitalization of the mother where the mother can no longer care for her child, the father is entitled to leave of a duration equal to the unexpired portion of the postnatal maternity leave. Another best practice is the explicit extension of coverage of most caregiver protections to workers in the informal sector.

## Sub-Index B:



## Protections for Domestic Workers


Comprehensive regulatory protections for locally employed domestic workers contributed to the Philippines' strong performance of 8.58 (out of 10) in Sub-Index B. The country's dedicated protections against the abuse of domestic workers with specialized provisions from the Department of Social Welfare and Development to rescue and rehabilitate victims, is particularly noteworthy. Nevertheless, there are still key areas for improvement, particularly when it comes to the regulations regarding the working hours and rest periods of domestic workers, and the living conditions of live-in domestic workers.


## B1Coverage under National Labor Laws (10.00/10)


All categories of domestic workers are covered under the Labor Code of the Philippines (with the exception of Article II of Book III relating to working hours regulations) and the Domestic Workers Act or the Batas Kasambahay .


## B2Fair Employment Process (7.90/10)


Written contracts in the native language of the domestic worker are a requirement under Philippine law, and these contracts must provide for key terms of employment. However, information such as the method of calculation of the worker's wages, their daily rest period, and the duration of their period of probation are not required to be in contracts. The recruitment and placement of domestic workers are regulated, and the deduction of workers' wages as part of their recruitment and placement fees is prohibited. There are however no measures to prohibit employment discrimination on the basis of medical testing results.


## B3Decent Working and Living Conditions (5.49/10)


Regulations around domestic workers' working hours and environment are inadequate. There are no regulations on their normal working hours or limits to standby hours of work. There are also no requirements for the accurate recording of hours worked or for compensatory rest days to be provided if a domestic worker is asked to work on their rest day. Paid annual leave is also only five days. There are however provisions for daily rest, weekly rest, and requirements for a safe and healthy working environment.

The minimum wage for domestic workers is below the national minimum wages for non-agricultural workers, and there is no overtime compensation rate. There are however regulations on workers' forms of payment, the periodicity of their pay, and the payment of outstanding wages upon termination of their employment. Domestic workers are also eligible for most social security protections.

There are however no measures to allow live-in domestic workers to choose whether or not to live in their employer's household, and there are no explicit guarantees of access to sanitary facilities nor accomodations with privacy for these live-in workers.


## B4Labor Rights and Protections (10.00/10)


Domestic workers may form their own unions of their own choosing and engage in collective bargaining. Domestic workers' access to complaint mechanisms and dispute resolution mechanisms are also provided under the law.


## B5Protections for Forced/Under-age Domestic Workers (9.50/10)


The illegal extraction of forced labor from domestic workers is a punishable penal offense. Victims of such forced labor are protected and have access to remedies and rehabilitation. The minimum age for domestic workers is 15. Nevertheless, domestic workers under 18 are guaranteed access to compulsory education, and are protected from excessively demanding work and night work.


## B6Protections for Migrant Domestic Workers ( - /10)


The Philippines was not scored for B6 as it does not host a significant workforce of foreign domestic workers within its borders. 14 Instead, the Philippines is a major source of migrant domestic workers for other countries.


## Policy-Practice Gap



## Obstacles to Uptake of Parental Leave


The uptake of paternity leave in the Philippines has been hindered by traditionalist gender roles that encourage Filipino fathers to refrain from childcare labor. This is reflected in the limited paternal involvement in childrearing and the low women's labor force participation rate in the two-and-a-half decades since the introduction of the paternity leave policy in 1996. 15 16

The high degree of informality in the labor market and the requirements for contribution in the Social Security System also present dual obstacles to the uptake of parental leave. Despite the extension of coverage of maternity leave to working women in the informal sector, a large majority of informal workers, and even 25% of mothers in the public sector, and 45% of mothers in the private sector, do not receive maternity benefits. 17


## Gaps in Domestic Workers Protections


Despite nearly a decade having elapsed since the passage of the Domestic Workers Kasambahay Act in 2013, its implementation continues to be hampered by poor rights awareness among local domestic workers and the difficulties around the labor inspection of private homes due to the need for warrants. 18 In addition, a 2020 survey by the National Wages and Productivity Commission found startling and prevalent gaps between the protections afforded by the Act and the reality on the ground: 4% or 49,000 of the 1.4 million domestic workers in the Philippines are minors, only 2.5% have written employment contracts, 83% lack social security coverage, 36% of live-in domestic workers do not take their weekly rest days, and the average wage of surveyed domestic workers falls short of the stipulated minimum wage. 19 These statistics highlight how the Philippines has much room for improvement in its implementation and enforcement of domestic worker protections, despite its relatively strong performance in Sub-Index B.

## 1  Introduction


The definition for workplace surveillance in this paper is an employer's enactment “to monitor, record and track employee performance, behaviours and personal characteristics in real time” (Ball 2010: 87). Sewell and Barker (2006) denoted surveillance as either coercive or caring with coercive surveillance referring to negative, intrusive efforts while caring surveillance aims to protect employees and help them grow within an organisation. Therefore, workplace surveillance is a necessity for the success of a capitalist society and has intensified greatly since the pandemic (Manokha 2020; Vitak & Zimmer 2023). Foucault (1977) attempted to explain how workplace surveillance functions, with his metaphoric panopticon, where the supervisor could be watching, ensuring that employees are working. Accordingly, it is not surprising that a wide majority of employees reported negative attitudes towards being surveilled intensively, and some even took part in resistance acts (Clawson & Clawson 2017). While it is not the only cause for deviant behaviours in the workplace, it is no doubt one of the contributors that negatively impacts organisations financially (Baharom et al. 2017). The problem is most of the literature around this topic has only focused on traditional and remote workers. There is a new type of worker that scholars are gradually becoming interested in, the Digital Nomad (Hannonen 2020). Unlike traditional workers, these workers can travel globally while doing their work remotely (Herman & Paris 2020). This article will therefore fill in this gap of surveillance literature to see how Digital Nomads interact with workplace surveillance and resistance.

Research question: How does the Digital Nomad lifestyle interact with workplace surveillance and resistance acts?

2.1  Workplace Surveillance and Capitalism

Workplace surveillance has always been a pressing issue for society with the first notable examples originating in the 20th century. Ford introduced their “5 Dollar Day scheme” in the 1900s, promoting a healthy lifestyle for factory workers” (Loizides & Sonnad 2004). Their sociology department would make surprise visits on these workers, collecting “information on every one of the employees on living conditions and lifestyles” (Ford Motor Company, as cited in Manokha 2020a: 548). This scheme was shut down shortly after, due to opposition from workers who found it too intrusive (Manokha 2020). This idea that intensive and intrusive surveillance has negative impacts upon employees remains prevalent in the 21st century.

The advancement of technology has resulted in the increasing amounts of interest in workplace surveillance (Ball 2022). It has intensified greatly as employers are now able to carry out: “personal data gathering, Internet and email monitoring, location tracking, biometrics and covert surveillance” (Ball 2010: 87). Empirical studies on employee attitudes suggest mixed responses to whether this is a positive or negative practice. Allen et al. (2007) carried out 154 interviews on employees from different organisations and the majority felt positive towards surveillance, arguing it as a necessity to ensure workers are being productive. Similarly, Kizilglu (2018) surveyed 218 employees in Turkey and found that there was no relationship between workplace surveillance and employee stress. On the other hand, there are studies that highlight negative attitudes, such as Lockwood (2018) finding that Employees were concerned about being watched in their workplace, feeling issues of trust, creativity and demotivation. Similarly, Siegel et al. (2022) carried out a meta-analysis finding that electronic monitoring decreases job satisfaction while increasing stress. They also did not find a relationship between increased productivity and monitoring thus contrasting Allen et al. (2007) findings. One issue with studies on workplace surveillance is that it is experienced on such a subjective, individual level in different forms, so it is hard to conclude outright that it causes positive or negative effects in workplaces. However, it can be argued that workplace surveillance can cause negative effects, especially with the more intensive forms.

Being that there is a relationship between productivity and workplace surveillance, a discussion of capitalism and its role in workplace surveillance is important. In a capitalist society, employees are exploited for their labour to produce commodities that owners sell to gain a profit (Marx et al. 2008). What maintains this continuous production of commodities by employees is the constant threat of unemployment (Patnaik 2019). Surveillance allows employers to ensure that employees are doing their job under the threat of unemployment, thus making it a necessity for the success of a capitalist society (Manokha 2020a). This gives reason for why some individuals, such as the participants in Allen et al. (2007) believe that monitoring in the workplace will maintain productivity. Employers need to ensure that their workers are being productive, which workplace surveillance can help achieve.

2.2  Resistance in the Workplace

There are two types of resistance behaviours that can stem from intensive workplace surveillance: production deviance and resistance to surveillance. Lawrence and Robinson (2007) said that resistance is the act of going against power structures in their workplaces. Production deviance can include “working slow intentionally, avails excessive breaks [8], gossiping on non-work topics with coworkers during official working hours, late arrival at workplace and leave office early, day dreaming while on job [8], and involved in cyber loafing” (Baharom et al. 2017: 3). These behaviours that resist power structures are a massive problem for companies and can cost them millions in lost revenue (Baharom et al. 2017). Employees carry out deviant behaviours when they feel dissatisfied in their workplace and start to develop negative attitudes (Kalemci et al. 2019). One of the factors that develops employee negative attitudes is the experience of intensive and invasive surveillance in workplaces. This can result in resistance to surveillance actions with employees turning off devices on purpose or covering their cameras on laptops (Clawson & Clawson 2017). A case study illustrates this where employees resisted the installation of new CCTV cameras in a power station because they felt their managers did not trust them. (Mason et al. 2002). There was also another case study where employees refused to use the new management system, “Casemix” in a hospital because the information it collected was deemed too invasive (Johnson et al. 2014). Overall, it appears there is a relationship between intensive surveillance and resistance acts in traditional workplaces. However, there is no research on Digital Nomads and resistance acts in their virtual workplaces, so it is necessary to research this and compare it with traditional workers.

2.3 Foucault's Hegemony and other Theoretical Assumptions

The most popular and hegemonic surveillance theory that addresses workplace surveillance is Foucault’s panopticon theory (Haggerty 2006). Despite the various critiques and extensions of this theory, it still manages to remain relevant in surveillance studies (Manokha 2020a). Foucault, who based his theory from Jeremy Bentham’s prison design, aimed to explain how surveillance is a disciplinary tool that functions in enclosed environments such as the prison (Foucault 1977). The work setting is one of the “enclosure” examples that Foucault discussed when addressing the factory as a panoptic tool (Foucault 1977). For a panopticon to achieve its goal of conformity and docility, the surveillance must be visible yet unverifiable (Foucault 1977). This makes the bodies of the surveilled subjects ‘docile’ because there is now the possibility that they are being watched (Foucault 1977). Hence this explains how and why individuals self-regulate their behaviour, which in a workplace enclosure environment would be attributes of productivity. Despite the panopticon’s hegemony in surveillance studies, it has been critiqued for not considering the technological advancements in society (Haggerty 2006). This has resulted in other scholars Lyon and Manokha extending or interpreting his unfinished work.

Lyon discussed the idea of an “electronic panopticon” where the conditions of the panopticon are applied to modern surveillance methods (Lyon 1993). Despite this, Lyon never explains in his literature how the conditions are applied to contemporary society and instead argues that an electronic panopticon is only partially applicable to workplace surveillance (Lyon 1994). Yet, 26 years later, Manokha (2020a) believed that the panopticon theory is even more useful in the modern age when addressing workplace surveillance due to technological advancements. He claimed that new surveillance technology fully meets the requirements of the panopticon: “(1) the omnipresence of the inspector, ensured by his total invisibility; (2) the universal visibility of objects of surveillance; and (3) the assumption of constant observation by the watched” (ibid: 547). This idea is based on new surveillance technologies being able to run in the background, so it is unknown if the employee is being watched, making them docile to the supervisor.

A second theory, aiming to explain the motivations for workplace surveillance is Sewell and Barker (2006) and their theory on coercive and caring surveillance. Coercive surveillance aims to monitor workers, observing productivity whereas caring surveillance aims to monitor workers for beneficial reasons (Allen et al 2007). Panopticon surveillance could be grouped together with coercive surveillance since they are both concerned with employee productivity and regulating behaviour. Caring surveillance would receive positive responses from employees since it is done to benefit instead of discipline them (Allen et al 2007). In Allen et al. (2007), 58% of research participants saw surveillance as coercive, being a necessity for tracking productivity. Coercive surveillance efforts are more intensive and invasive and there is evidence that this type of surveillance can increase actions of resistance (Anteby & Chan 2018). Hence, this theory is useful for categorising whether surveillance efforts are done for positive or negative purposes.

When addressing empirical research, references to the panopticon are more common than other surveillance theories. Firstly, Johnson et al. (2014) found that the panoptic “CaseMix” software resulted in resistance measures from employees because they found it too invasive (Johnson et al. 2014). Additionally, Ramasundaram et al. (2022) found that employees in an office were uncomfortable that they were being surveilled constantly and felt a lack of trust. Furthermore, there was a decrease in productivity from employees due to being constantly watched (Ramasundaram et al. 2022). Perhaps panoptic surveillance is partially flawed since employees have resisted it, which goes against the objective of achieving docility. Nevertheless, regardless of its effects, panoptic surveillance does achieve its goal partially since employees are aware that they could be getting watched.

But evidence has shown that it does not achieve self-regulation and is instead met with resistance. It would be interesting to see if it is possible to apply these surveillance theories to the Digital Nomad workplace.

2.4  Technological Advancements, the Pandemic and Digital Nomads

Many scholars have argued that workplace surveillance has intensified greatly since the start of the pandemic due to employees working from home (Kalischko & Riedl, 2021; Masoodi et al. 2021; Ball 2021). The closest literature that can be applied to Digital Nomads and workplace surveillance would be the emerging research on remote employees and their surveillance experiences. This gives reason for why it is important to research Digital Nomads, they are remote workers but travel around instead of staying in one place (Hannonen 2020). During the Covid-19 pandemic, there was an increased demand for monitoring software from companies and this software had a panoptic nature, running in the background (Ball 2021; Kalischko & Riedl 2021). Surveillance during the pandemic became more intrusive as it extended into the privacy of an employee’s own home (Manokha 2020b). Vitak and Zimmer (2023) carried out a survey on 645 traditional US workers during the pandemic and found increased usage of surveillance tools, increased job stress and decreased satisfaction from employees. Therefore, this extends the narrative that surveillance in the workplace on traditional workers has become more intensive, especially since the pandemic. Capitalism plays a role here with employers having to ensure employee productivity.

While this literature review has discussed traditional worker’s experiences of surveillance and resistance, Digital Nomads live a different lifestyle from these workers. They are defined as a “mobile knowledge worker equipped with digital technologies to work anytime, anywhere” (Müller as cited in Hannonen 2020: 4). In broad terms, a Digital Nomad is a worker who is on the move while doing their work remotely. There is a steady growing amount of sociological interest with examples of Goffman’s dramaturgy theory and Bauman’s liquid society idea being applied to Digital Nomads (Nina 2020; Herman & Paris 2020). Yet, due to the lack of literature, it is unknown if Digital Nomads experience the same levels of surveillance as remote and traditional workers. It is also unknown if they take part in resistance acts in their workplaces. They live a very different lifestyle to the traditional employee and many chose to become a Digital Nomad because they felt unsatisfied with their traditional lifestyle (Reichenberger 2018). They opted to escape a lifestyle with less balance so they could have a more balanced lifestyle between work and leisure (Fabiola 2020). Unlike traditional tourists, Digital Nomads believe their experiences with culture are more authentic because they spend a longer time residing in foreign countries (Thompson 2019). Research from Fabiola (2020) has shown that they tend to have a better balance between work and leisure and live a more fulfilling life. After conducting 50 semi-structured interviews, Fabiola reported that Digital Nomads wanted to escape their traditional lifestyle to seek happiness and freedom (Fabiola 2020). Similarly, participants from the 22 interviews from Reichenberger (2018) reported feelings of freedom and location independence. This new type of worker is fascinating because their lifestyle is different from traditional workers where they are less constrained to traditional structures. Therefore, it is necessary to include them within the research of workplace surveillance and resistance to introduce new findings in surveillance and resistance studies.


## 3  Methodology


The research consisted of 5 semi-structured interviews, 4 on Zoom and 1 by email. Semi-structured interviews were identified as the most suitable method for this research. Qualitative methods allow the researcher to get closer with the participants and gain a deeper understanding of how social phenomenon is constructed (Aspers & Corte 2019; Cleland 2017). It is important to seek out Digital Nomads and learn about their experiences and attitudes towards workplace surveillance and resistance acts in the workplace.

Digital Nomads were recruited using the online snowball sampling method on social media platforms: Facebook, Reddit, LinkedIn and Discord. Posts were made reaching out to Digital Nomads that were interested in partaking in a study on workplace surveillance and resistance. It was hard to obtain participants especially when there was no financial incentive for them.

Nevertheless, interviews were arranged, corresponding with the timezones of the 5 Participants.  An information sheet and consent form was given to them to uphold ethical practice. A topic guide was used, containing around 14 questions and ideas to be used as a prompt. Question topics ranged from asking about their backstory, motivations to become a Digital Nomad to experiences and opinions of workplace surveillance and resistance acts. For example: “How would you say that your lifestyle is different to the lifestyle of the traditional worker?”, “Do you feel like you are being surveyed in your workplace?” and “Could you tell me a memorable time that you felt surveyed?”.

The interviews lasted from 20 to 35 minutes and were recorded on Zoom then transcribed manually.  Thematic analysis was carried out to analyse the transcripts where 101 coded statements were identified between 10 codes. Then 3 themes emerged from finding patterns between the transcripts and codes. Step-by-step guidance from Braun and Clark (2006) ensured that thematic analysis was carried out rigorously.

The 5 participants' nationalities were Brazilian, American, Italian and Colombian. Job sectors ranged from the travel industry, tutoring, local government and technology. The countries they explored between themselves were on a global scale: europe, central america, north america, southeast asia and western asia. While not working remotely they enjoyed leisure activities such as hiking, sunbathing, food tours, embracing new culture, snorkelling, scuba diving.


## 4  Results & Discussion


Three themes emerged from the empirical data: shift from traditional restraints, perks of elite workers and panopticon’s future. These themes were constructed with the purpose to further explain the relationship between the Digital Nomad lifestyle, surveillance and resistance.

4.1  Shift from Traditional Restraints

The Digital Nomad lifestyle differs from the traditional worker lifestyle but they first started out as a traditional worker, feeling a desire to escape from traditional structures:

[P1] ‘‘...and had to start dealing with being alone in the living room, just doing my work by myself the entire day and it was so boring and like no, I hate this!’’

This feeling is similar to findings from Reichenberger (2018) where Digital Nomads were unsatisfied with their lifestyle. Whether it was commuting to work or working remotely from their homes, they realised that it was time for a drastic lifestyle change:

[P5] ‘‘I'm one of those who are not comfortable staying in one place; I crave changes of scenery and location’’

Therefore, the nature of remote work allows for Digital Nomads to fulfil this craving of escapism, granting them the freedom they desire. Taking on the role as a Digital Nomad, has allowed them to have the agency to travel, free from restraints that traditional workers are tied to:

[P2] ‘‘Part of the reason Digital Nomad is so attractive to me is because of the freedom it provides me’’

This idea of freedom and agency has already been established by some scholars, arguing that Digital Nomads experience “freedom from an office to travel the world” (Thompson 2019: 27). Alongside freedom is this heightened sense of exploration when exploring new areas and culture. Digital Nomads have the ability to do leisure activities that traditional workers are restricted:

[P5] ‘‘I go trekking, snorkeling and scuba diving, walking around historical sites, taking pictures, eating exotic foods, hanging out in karaoke bars and trying local beers’’

One of the benefits of this lifestyle appears to be the limitless leisure activities that Digital Nomads can partake in. While their lifestyle is different from the traditional worker, participants also stressed how they do share a normal work-life with the traditional worker:

[P3] ‘‘There's a lot of preparation to be put into travel, but then it's exciting and adventurous although we are technically working the same as if we were at home but then when we stopped working at the end of the work day, we are just exploring a different place instead of a walk in the hometown’’

This participant suggested that their identity as a Digital Nomad does not make a difference to their working lifestyle; they are working as if they were working remotely from home but then acting out the role of Digital Nomad outside of work hours. Therefore, there is a feeling of normality in their lifestyle as they are no different from remote workers when discussing work life:

[P1] ‘‘The more you try to organise your schedule the better, so I try to have the same as I used to have when I used to work in an office. I have a job that is 9-5 full time… so monday to friday I need to work…’’

However, they still need to be flexible in their time management skills where they may be working hours that are unsociable or against social norms:

[P1] ‘‘So if I’m in Europe it happens like late in the afternoon, 2 or 3pm depending where I am’’

Participant responses demonstrated how their lifestyle has changed and what made it more exciting. They experienced a shift from their previous lifestyle where they were constrained by the traditional worker structure. They are able to partake in exciting activities in their leisure time which traditional workers do not experience.

4.2  Perks of Elite Workers

Engaging in these leisure activities is only one part of this lifestyle; they still have to work. Digital Nomads are professional, elite workers as shown from their work experience, high education and lucrative professions. While one of the benefits is the possibilities of the wide range of leisures activities, there is another benefit of this elite worker, they do not experience high levels of surveillance in their workplaces.

[P4] ‘‘I don’t think so… I’m so lucky that I don’t have that sort of thing, control in my work’’

The only notable example of surveillance was from one participant who had to track their hours for their employer:

[P1] ‘‘We have a tracking platform for hours but it is not because they are actually tracking everything that I am doing… they wanna measure how many hours I’m spending in each project so they can budget better’’

This type of surveillance relates to the theory of caring surveillance, where surveillance is done for the purpose of helping employees (Allen et al. 2007). This example here had the purpose of helping the company improve, instead of disciplining the worker. But when asked about sentiments of intrusive surveillance, participants showed signs of resistance and were slightly insulted by the idea of intensive surveillance in their workplace.

[P1] ‘‘I am not giving my time, I am giving my work, I'm delivering the projects with quality, that's what they are paying me for…In my principles I wouldn’t work for a company that would make me stay on the computer that is paying me for my hours’’

They believe that intensive surveillance is coercive, done to ensure that employees are constantly working, because employers are fearful that they are not. The main reason that Digital Nomads in this study did not experience intensive surveillance is that they found jobs that reward capitalist attributes such as productivity and efficiency. They certainly know their worth in the job market:

[P2] ‘‘This is something I've been building up skills for, for years and it's also stupid to not take advantage of it and enjoy life while you have it’’

Nevertheless, it cannot be claimed that all Digital Nomads do not experience workplace surveillance as this is something that differs in each individual organisation. There are still some Digital Nomads who could be prone to face more intensive surveillance:

[P5] ‘‘They tend to be employees, and are looking for ways to conceal their location from an employer that doesn’t permit international travel by their remote workers’’

Taking part in production deviance acts such as browsing on the internet is an activity that Digital Nomad workers also take part in. Despite the first part of this study suggesting that Digital Nomads do not carry out much resistance acts, one participant claimed that Digital Nomads are probably lying:

[P2] ‘‘Oh I absolutely do… my phone’s right here… I feel like a Digital Nomad who says they don’t is probably lying’’

Another participant made a similar point, that they feel they need to prove themselves:

[P5] ‘‘I suspect that part of this is that DNs feel the need to prove themselves more than those in traditional roles’’

This does highlight one of the limitations with asking participants directly if they take part in actions that they may not want to admit, particularly towards a researcher. Especially when considering the idea that Digital Nomads are skilled workers and take pride in their lifestyle; they do not want to have negative connotations attributed towards a community they are representing for research purposes. Nevertheless, resistance acts is something that is more common when the worker is being paid for their time, not their skills:

[P3] ‘‘When you are forced to be at work 9-5 regardless of what's left to do its way more likely that you will found other distract yourself’’

Findings from this research illustrate the idea from Manokha (2020), that workplace surveillance is a necessity for the success of a capitalist society. Digital Nomads have been established as elite workers who are productive and sought after, so companies that hire them do not need to monitor them intensively because of their worth in the job market. When surveilled, participants experienced what Sewell and Barker (2006) would call caring surveillance. This is also done for capitalist purposes but is more positive and less intensive. Other types of employees do not hold the same value as these elite Digital Nomads, so they are surveilled more intensively because their employers are fearful that they are not working, limiting profit for the company. Previous scholars such as Ball (2021) have illustrated many examples of intrusive surveillance on remote and traditional workers because employers are trying to check if they are working. This was shown to produce the opposite effects: negative sentiments, production deviance or resistance to surveillance. Overall, Digital Nomads in this study are elite workers, having a better workplace culture with surveillance only existing for caring purposes. Some may take part in resistance acts but they are not actively resisting their companies because they make up for lost time with efficiency and high productivity.

4.3  Theme 3: Panopticon’s Future

As it has been established, Digital Nomads in this study did not experience extensive surveillance so it is difficult to discuss Foucault’s panopticon. However, participants did recall more intensive examples of workplace surveillance from friends and employees that were both traditional workers and Digital Nomads. Participant 3 recollected an example from a student who was trying to pass an exam for a job during the pandemic.

[P3] ‘‘The exam was 9 hours long and they couldn’t leave the room where they were because of surveillance for the whole 9 hours, so they were recommended to wear an adult pad if they needed to go to the bathroom which to me is absolutely unacceptable’’

This student was watched through a webcam and was not allowed to leave their room in their own home. This example illustrates Foucault’s panopticon perfectly where this individual has been made “docile” within the restraints of their own room. While the supervisor may not have been watching for the whole 9 hours, there is no guarantee of this, so the supervisor's gaze is visible but unverifiable (Foucault 1977). This does suggest that Foucault’s panopticon theory can still be applied in the modern era, thus extending the thesis from Manokha (2020) that panoptic surveillance has intensified in the digital society.

Similarly, Participant 1 spoke about a Digital Nomad peer who did experience intensive surveillance in their workplace:

[P1] ‘‘But I’ve heard from another Digital Nomad friend who had a tracking system that was the same requiring to stay in front of the screen for a while and they found ways to trick the system’’

This also illustrates electronic panoptic surveillance where activity is being watched but it is unverifiable when they are being watched by a supervisor. Interestingly, participant 1 claimed that they “found ways to trick the system”, thus highlighting that intrusive surveillance will be fought back with resistance measures. It is evident that Foucault's theory is still useful as a metaphor when discussing workplace surveillance, especially when it is intrusive and intensive. But in this example, the Digital Nomad was not “docile” and instead chose to resist the surveillance. This relates with research showing workers resisting panoptic surveillance such as the casemix case study from Johnson et al. (2014).

5  Implications for Future Research

One of the major limitations of this study was the small sample size. In an ideal situation, it would have been great to have received more responses and to have carried out more interviews. Therefore, is it difficult to conclude that the majority of Digital Nomads do not experience surveillance from just 5 interview participants. This small sample provided an insight into how Digital Nomads interact with surveillance and resistance in workplaces but the research should not stop here. Other surveillance scholars need to start including Digital Nomads within their research. There is a vast amount of research on workplace surveillance on traditional and remote workers, but there is none on Digital Nomads except from this study. Scholars should not just repeat what has already been established, they need to branch out and research surveillance on Digital Nomads in their future research. There is already a small, yet insightful amount of literature on Digital Nomads and their lifestyle which surveillance scholars need to add towards. I urge future researchers to seek these Nomads that have experienced workplace surveillance and see how it interacts with this paper's idea of the elite worker status of the Digital Nomads.


## 6  Conclusion


This research has contributed to the ongoing work on workplace surveillance and resistance by incorporating the Digital Nomad lifestyle towards it. The interviews found that Digital Nomads experienced limited surveillance due to their status as an elite worker that produces results. This status allows them to take part in leisure activities that traditional workers are constrained from. It also allows them to seek employment in companies that do not carry out intensive, coercive surveillance. The only notable example of surveillance identified was caring surveillance, which was not even met with resistance since its purpose is to benefit the employee. This differs from literature demonstrating that surveillance has intensified since the Covid-19 pandemic for traditional workers. Therefore, the high status of the Digital Nomad is significant for understanding why participants in this study did not recall intensive surveillance. Secondly, resistance acts were carried out by Digital Nomads but they were not actively resisting their company. Instead, common resistance examples were acts of productivity deviance such as going on the internet, which was reported to not affect productivity. This has been shown to differ from current literature which showed resistance to be an issue in traditional workplaces resulting in less productivity and other negative effects for organisations. Thirdly, participants were not applicable under Foucault’s panopticon theory being that they did not experience the same style of surveillance. However, evidence from this study adds to the belief that it is still a great theory for traditional workers that experience intensive surveillance. Further research should aim to increase the sample size to investigate how Digital Nomads have experienced intensive surveillance. A funded study could help achieve this, where participants are more likely to share their experiences if they receive a financial incentive.

## Curbing the Spread of H5N1: A Survey of the Current Policy Landscape


One potential policy mechanism available to curb the public health threats posed by H5N1 is the expansion of compensation programs that incentivize early H5N1 reporting. Presently, the federal government -- via the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) -- pays poultry farmers for chickens, turkeys, and other avian livestock culled (killed) in order to prevent H5N1 spread on farms with documented cases of the disease (Jacobs 2024). Farms are not compensated for poultry that become sick and die from H5N1 infection. Correspondingly, the USDA's poultry compensation programs incentivize farmers to vigilantly test and monitor for signs of H5N1 infection.

Policies requiring or incentivizing testing of poultry and bovine livestock offers another potential pathway toward combating the spread of H5N1. The USDA's "Defend the Flock" initiative (APHIS 2024a) provides farmers with guidelines for how to ensure that their flocks are compliant with National Poultry Improvement Plan biosecurity standards (including the disinfection of farm equipment, engaging in state-overseen audits to determine preparedness for infectious disease outbreaks). While NPIP is technically voluntary, compliance not only reduces the likelihood that flocks get sick with infectious diseases like H5N1, but is necessary in order to ship poultry products across state lines (APHIS 2024b).

Similarly, in the wake of documented spread of H5N1 to bovine livestock, the USDA issued new guidance in 2024 requiring cow farmers to participate in a similar testing regimen (USDA 2024). In order to move lactating cattle across state lines, farmers must subject milk samples to rigorous testing from state accredited veterinarians, unless those animals are sent directly to slaughter (in which case farmers must provide evidence that their livestock have been inspected by veterinarians).

One final set of mechanisms by which governments can control the spread of H5N1 is through policies that promote animal and human vaccination (Bernstein et al., 2022 and Nolen 2023).

Regarding the former, vaccines for H5N1 in poultry populations have existed since the early-2000s (Parry 2005). Similar vaccines are also currently being developed for bovine livestock populations (Cohen 2024).

However, while H5N1 vaccines have been demonstrated to be both safe and effective at curbing the spread of avian influenza, poultry raised in the US are not required to be vaccinated against H5N1. Concerns about international trade may help explain why vaccination is not mandated in farm settings; i.e., because vaccinated poultry may be less likely to exhibit influenza symptoms, thereby "masking" infection. Because, as noted above, rigorous testing for H5N1 is not technically required at US farms, international trade partners may be wary of doing business with farms that vaccinate their poultry. Correspondingly, efforts to encourage or mandate widespread vaccination may be most effective if paired with policy efforts to require more-stringent testing for H5N1 on poultry farms.

Additionally, pharmaceutical manufacturers are presently developing vaccines designed to prevent H5N1 infection in humans (Garg 2024). While efforts to bolster federal funding for the development of "universal flu" vaccines (which can protect humans from infections with many strains of influenza) have been introduced in Congress, bills providing for this funding are (as of this writing) stalled in legislative committees (HR 6184; S 3215).

Even in the absence of enhanced federal funding for vaccines that could protect humans from H5N1, pharmaceutical manufacturers - in partnership with the Department of Health and Human Services are working to mass produce existing influenza vaccines that might offer partial protection against the currently-circulating strain, with plans to pursue updated vaccine development (Schnirring 2024). Once prepared for public use, states could enact legislation requiring those who work on farms -- and may thereby come into regular contact with infected animals -- to receive these vaccines as a condition of employment.


## Hypotheses


Given the relative dearth of public opinion polling about a potential H5N1 pandemic, the extent to which the public expresses concern about the issue and/or supports policy solutions aimed at mitigating the likelihood of human transmission is a relatively open question. While the renewed salience of H5N1 attributable to its spread to the commercial milk industry could - in theory - raise cause for concern and/or ameliorative action, experiences with the COVID-19 pandemic suggest that the salience or objective risks posed by a pressing a public health threat alone may be insufficient to inspire mitigating action (Cilton et al., 2020; Gadarian et al., 2022).

Thus, we ask the following set of inter-related research questions:

RQ1: How many Americans believe that (a) the H5N1 pandemic is likely to pose a public health threat to humans, (b) are concerned about its effects on human life conditional on being transmissible between humans, (c) believe that raw milk is generally unsafe to drink, and (d) are willing to support empowering federal and state governments to take a wide range of policy actions to reduce the spread of H5N1; including support for expanding culling repayment programs that incentivize testing, livestock testing and vaccination programs, and/or research and development into human vaccination?

Additionally, we suspect that those who hold negative attitudes toward scientific experts - views which tend to be particularly on the ideological right (Oliver & Rahn 2016; Motta 2018; Merkley 2020) - should be more likely to reject warnings from public health agencies like the CDC (see: Motta et al., 2022) regarding the public health risks borne by H5N1 transmission and raw milk consumption.

Correspondingly, we expect to observe both partisan asymmetries (H2) and asymmetries on the basis of attitudes toward the scientific community (H3) in both H5N1 risk perceptions and policy attitudes.

Specifically, we propose that:

H1: Self-identified Republicans (compared to Democrats and Independents) will be significantly less likely to (a) believe the H5N1 pandemic is likely to pose a public health threat to humans, (b) express concerned about its effects on human life conditional on being transmissible between humans, (c) believe that raw milk is generally unsafe to drink, and (d) support empowering federal and state governments to take a wide range of policy actions to reduce the spread of H5N1; including support for expanding culling repayment programs that incentivize testing, livestock testing and vaccination programs, and/or research and development into human vaccination.

And …

H2: People who hold more negative attitudes toward scientific experts will be significantly less likely to (a) believe the H5N1 pandemic is likely to pose a public health threat to humans, (b) express concerned about its effects on human life conditional on being transmissible between humans, (c) believe that raw milk is generally unsafe to drink, and (d) support empowering federal and state governments to take a wide range of policy actions to reduce the spread of H5N1; including support for expanding culling repayment programs that incentivize testing, livestock testing and vaccination programs, and/or research and development into human vaccination.


## Analytical Strategy.


We assessed the prevalence of H5N1 risk perceptions and policy support (RQ1) by calculating the weighted mean proportion of our sample endorsing each of the available response options listed in Table 1. We then constructed a series of ordered logistic regression models (for all categorical outcome variables listed in Table 1) and logistic regression models (for all dichotomous outcome variables listed in Table 1) that regress each outcome on measures of (H1) partisan identity and (H2) anti-intellectual attitudes, plus a series of standard demographic controls (described in the Measures section).


## Data & Methods


Data.

Data for this study will come from the second wave of a nationally representative and longitudinal study of N W1 = 1,400 US adults fielded in August 2024. We recruited respondents to participate in Wave 1 via YouGov, which used propensity score matching methods to draw a nationally representative sample from its large online opt-in panel sampling service. To account for any remaining deviations that may occur by chance between our sample and the US adult population, YouGov calculated post-stratification weights on the basis of: respondents' gender, racial, and ethnic identity; educational attainment; household income; Census region; and political party.

As we detail below (see: Table 1), many of the items measuring H5N1 concern and policy attitudes (the primary outcome variables in our study) are featured only on its second wave, conducted in July - August 2024, which had a final N W2 = 831 respondents (attrition rate = 41%). Incentives for participation were 'back loaded' (i.e., comparatively more generous in Wave 2 than Wave 1, relative to the time burden associated with each survey) in order to encourage high recontact rates. We provide asymmetric attrition in the manuscript's Supplemental Materials (Table S1), where we note that our recontacted subsample in Wave 2 was somewhat holder and less racially diverse than our Wave 1 sample.

We account for asymmetric attrition in two ways. First, we apply post-stratification weights that re-calibrate the weights designed in Wave 1 to account for non-response across survey waves. Second, we condition on all demographic factors that produced asymmetric attrition levels in our models; i.e., to account for and identify reporting differences on the study's primary outcome variables among members of groups more likely to 'drop out' in the study's second wave who did complete both waves.


## Measures.


The primary outcome variables in our study are a series of polychotomous indicators of respondents' public health risk perceptions associated with H5N1, perceptions that raw milk is safe to drink, and opposition to policies that aim to reduce the public health risks of H5N1. Full question wording and available response options used to measure each of these concepts are presented in full in Table 1, along with additional information about how we coded each variable in our analysis.

All multivariate models employed in this study control for respondents' anti-intellectual attitudes (H1), and dichotomous indicators of whether respondents self-identify as Democrats or Republicans (H2; with Independents and other partisans serving as an omitted reference group) . Additional information about the specific questions, response options, and coding decisions used to measure these concepts is also available in Table 1.

Additionally, all models control for dichotomous indicators of respondents' racial identity (taking on a value of 1 if respondents self-identify as White and non-Hispanic, 0 otherwise), gender identity (taking on a value of 1 if respondents self-identify as women, 0 otherwise), and educational attainment (taking on a value of 1 if respondents completed a 4-year college degree, 0 otherwise).

## Results


Descriptive Analyses.

We begin our analysis by taking stock of the degree to which the American public expresses concern about the infectious disease risks posed by H5N1, and support for policies aimed at preventing those risks. Table 1 presents weighted population estimates for all outcome variables featured in this study.

There, we find that relatively few Americans express the highest observed levels of concern about the public health risks of H5N1 (27%). This may be due in part to the small minority (15%) of respondents in our survey who felt that it was 'very likely' that H5N1 might come to be spread between people.

Low levels of concern about H5N1 are mirrored by high levels of misinformation acceptance about raw milk safety. We find that a minority of Americans (43%) believe that raw milk is unsafe to drink. The remainder either express uncertainty about its safety (30%) or believe that it is safe to drink (26%).

We believe that high levels of misinformation about raw milk safety is a particularly important finding, as a lack of public concern about H5N1 - coupled with misinformed beliefs about raw milk safety may imply that people are more likely to consume or support the sale of products that could endanger public health. Indeed, we find that a minority (32%) either somewhat or strongly support federal policies banning the sale of raw milk across the states. And, as we document later, misinformation about raw milk appears to be strongly associated with opposition to federal bans on raw milk sales.

However, the American public appears to hold more positive attitudes toward regulatory policies that might influence the public health risks posed by avian influenza. As Table 1 demonstrates, we find that outright majorities of the American public support policies regulating farmers' incentives to test for avian flu and to raise infected livestock. We further document widespread support for vaccinating chickens that could potentially become infected with H5N1.

## Multivariate Analyses.

To this point, we have shown that the American public expresses relatively low levels of concern about the public health risks borne by H5N1. They also accept misinformation about the safety of raw milk, and oppose federal bans on its sale. However, Americans are generally supportive of regulatory policies aimed at curbing the spread of H5N1.

Next, we offer a series of multivariate analyses that aim to explore why Americans feel this way about H5N1. In line with our pre-registered analysis plan, Table 2 regresses each of the H5N1 risk and raw milk misinformation indicators described earlier on a series of potential socio-political and demographic correlates. The results provide support for our pre-registered theoretical expectations.

Consistent with our pre-registered theoretical expectations, we find that people who hold higher levels of anti-intellectual attitude endorsement are significantly less likely to express concern about H5N1 public health risks ( β = 1.11, p < 0.05), and are less likely to view raw milk consumption as safe or to express uncertainty about its safety ( β = -1.12, p < 0.05). We detect no significant effects of anti-intellectualism on views about the possibility of H5N1 transmission between humans.

Similarly, and again in line with our theoretical expectations, we find that strong identification with the Republican Party is associated with a lack of concern about the public health risks of H5N1 ( β = 0.50; although we note that this effect only approaches conventional levels of two-tailed significance at the p < 0.10 level), and views that the virus is not likely to spread to humans ( β = 0.70, p < 0.05). Interestingly, we detect partisan asymmetries in views about raw milk safety only among Independents ( β = 0.61, p < 0.05) and Independents who lean toward the GOP ( β = 0.95); both of whom are more likely to accept scientific consensus about its health risks. This pattern of results suggests that widespread misinformation endorsement may not be colored by political partisanship in any obvious way.

It is important to note that, in addition to their statistical significance, these effects are also substantively large. For example, anti-intellectual attitude endorsement is associated with a 35 percentage point increase in the predicted probability that people view raw milk as either safe or express uncertainty about its safety; from 45% at the lowest observed levels of anti-intellectualism to 70% at the highest.
