## 5.1.4.2 Other robustness checks


The ability of Synthetic Spain to correctly reproduce financial wellbeing in real Spain without the IMV depends on the choice of units in the donor pool and the choice of predictors of the outcome variables. If removing a donor country or predictor leads to a good pre-treatment fit but to different results post-intervention, my results could be driven by a post-intervention shock to a donor country or a predictor variable so that, in the absence of the IMV, Spain would not have trended as Synthetic Spain. This is a nonnegligible possibility in my analysis since I study the Covid-19 crisis period.

To test for the assumption that results are not driven by the choice of control countries or predictors, I conduct 'leave-one-out' tests. The tests consist in taking out from the sample each  of  the  control  countries  and  predictors  one  at  a  time  (Gilchrist et  al. ,  2022).  If  the exclusion of control units or predictors leads to estimates before and after the intervention that are close to those using all donor pool countries or all predictors, then results can be considered robust (Abadie, 2021; McClelland and Mucciolo, 2022). The 'leave-one-out' test for predictors has no impact on the direction and (in)significance of the effects found. In the 'leave-one-out'  test  for  countries,  the  exclusion  of  Romania  in  the  poverty  rate  and  gap analyses and of the Netherlands in the perceived financial situation, do affect the direction

and size of the estimates (See Appendix 9.2 for graphs). This is expected as these are the countries  that  are  given  large  weights  in  my  analysis.  However,  the  insignificance  of  the 'leave-one-out' estimates are the same as when all countries are used. Moreover, the pretreatment fit when excluding these countries is worsened significantly implying the difference in estimates is not driven by a shock to the excluded countries, which would confound my results when including this country, but rather by the fact that Synthetic Spain cannot be accurately constructed without those countries.

The validity of my SCM results also rests on the assumption that the only treatment effect found happened after the IMV intervention. If an effect is found before the intervention, this would call the model's predictive power into question, implying my post-intervention results could  be  biased.  I  thus  need  to  check  that  there  are  no  unusually  large  and  statistically significant treatment effects before 2021 when the treatment was not implemented relative to  the  effect  found  for  2021  (Pang,  Liu  and  Xu,  2021).  I  perform  a  time  placebo  test  by reassigning the treatment status to each other year in the pre-intervention period. I also test for  the  statistical  significance  of  these  results.  No  placebo  intervention  yields  any  effect, except for a few results having effects larger than those found for 2021 and having a relatively good pre-treatment fit, but which turned out to be insignificant (See Appendix 9.3 for graphs).

From the SCM and RASCM analyses, I conclude that the IMV had no statistically significant effect on households' real and perceived financial situation. However, it might be that the results are insignificant because I am not accounting for the full effect of the IMV. First, I use the whole of 2020 as a pre-intervention period. This allowed me to account for the Covid-19 effect  in  the  creation  of  the  synthetic  control,  which  is  important  to  accurately  construct Synthetic Spain to mimic as closely as possible real Spain. However, it means I might be losing some of the shorter-term effects of the IMV between June and December 2020. To solve for this potential underestimation of the IMV effect, I would need monthly data that includes June-December 2020 in the post-intervention period.

Second, I only study one post-intervention period (i.e. 2021). This might be too little time to be able to see any effect of the IMV on national financial wellbeing outcomes, especially considering  the  lagged  rollout  of  the  policy.  If,  as  of  December  2021,  only  0.82  million individuals had benefited from the IMV out of the 2,3 million the government hoped to reach, by  December  2022,  the  IMV  had  reached  1.54  million  individuals  (La  Moncloa,  2021; Ministerio de Inclusion, Seguridad Social y Migraciones, 2022a). To analyse the full impact of the IMV, I would need data that goes beyond 2021.

In the next section, I perform the same analysis but using monthly data between December 2019 and December 2022, which allows me to have 31 post-intervention points as well as to analyse the effect of the IMV during its first few months of implementation whilst accounting for the Covid-19 shock. Since monthly income data from surveys is not available, I can only conduct this monthly analysis for the subjective financial wellbeing measure.

## 6 DISCUSSION


Both the SCM and RASCM yearly analyses show that, in 2021, the IMV had no statistically significant effect on objective measures of households' financial wellbeing (i.e. poverty rate, poverty gap, mean income). However, the more nuanced monthly analysis, which accounts for the initial IMV effect from its introduction in June 2020 and allows me to study its effect after 2021, reveals that the IMV helped households feel less pessimistic about the evolution of  their  finances  during  the  Covid-19  and  cost-of-living  crises.  Between  June  2020  and December 2022, the IMV increased the balance between those saying their financial situation improved and those saying it deteriorated by a magnitude of between 10.1 (SCM) and 14.6 (RASCM) points.

While the research approach does not enable me to determine the mechanisms behind the results obtained, I offer a few conjectures. In terms of the insignificant results obtained on objective financial wellbeing measures in 2021, it seems that, as explained in Section 2, a

combination of low levels of adequacy, low take-up and work disincentives might have been at play. In future research, I assess the work disincentives hypothesis since I study the labour supply effects of the IMV on beneficiaries themselves.

The issue of non-take-up appears to be particularly relevant, especially for explaining the insignificant results on the poverty gap and mean income. Estimates of non-take-up lie at 57% in Spain for the IMV (Marc et al. , 2022). The government (Ministerio de Inclusion, Seguridad Social y Migraciones, 2022b), AIReF (2022) and academics Ayala, Jurado and Perez (2022) have identified several reasons for non-take-up: potential beneficiaries (i) lack information about the existence of the policy; (ii) believe they would not qualify it; (iii) are put off by the complexity of the application process; or (iv) do not find it worth applying given the amount they would receive, especially when they have other support means.

The  high  non-take-up  of  the  IMV  in  2021  might  also  be  due  to  the  slow  processing  of applications by the administration. As of December 2021, the administration had received 1.5 million submissions, most of them issued in the first three months. The limited administrative capacity meant that during the first few months, the average application processing time was 150 days. Over 40% of applications took more than three months to be resolved. However, the situation has since improved and towards the end of 2021, 80% of applications were now being resolved within 3 months, including a majority being resolved within 1 month (AIReF, 2022).

Another factor explaining the insignificant results obtained on objective financial wellbeing measures might be the strategic behaviour of some regions. The introduction of the IMV appears to have incentivised regions to decrease the generosity and coverage of their regional schemes to make savings in their regional budgets. Thus, despite some households receiving the national IMV, current regional MISs beneficiaries might have seen their disposable income decrease, meaning overall national financial wellbeing remains unchanged. According to the State  Association  of  Directors  and  Managers  of  Social  Services  (Asociacion  Estatal  de Directoras y Gerentes en Servicios Sociales, 2022), evidence suggests that at least five out of seventeen regions, namely Castilla-La-Mancha, Aragón, Extremadura, Madrid and Castilla y León, have reduced the budget allocated to regional MISs by almost 50% in 2021. A further thirteen regions have decreased the amounts of their regional MISs and twelve regions have decreased their coverage. There were 150,000 less beneficiaries of regional MISs in 2021 compared to 2020 despite the Covid-19 crisis (Ministerio de Derechos Sociales y Agenda 2030, 2022). It is key for the central government to better coordinate the integration of the national IMV with the existent regional MISs.

In terms of the significant IMV effect on subjective financial wellbeing, this might be due to various reasons. On the one hand, it might be that the subjective financial wellbeing effect reflects  improvements  in  objective  financial  wellbeing  after  2021.  The  more  extensive monthly analysis could be capturing better the lagged rollout of the policy or the effect of the

initiatives  that  the  government  implemented  from  2022  to  improve  the  IMV's  take-up, amounts, coverage and to address potential labour supply disincentives. If this is the case, once income data for 2022 becomes available, I should see that the IMV improved objective financial wellbeing indicators.

On the other hand, if this effect of the IMV on objective financial wellbeing after 2021 does not materialise, it will reflect a mismatch between the financial status of households and how they perceive their situation. The mismatch could mean that there is an 'anticipation effect' of the policy by which poor households that have already started an application process but whose application has not been processed, feel their financial situation has improved even though their material conditions remain unchanged. This could fit in a context where there were bottlenecks in the administrative processing of IMV applications. More broadly, the mismatch could also reflect a 'placebo effect' by which households perceive the IMV as a safety net they could access in case of need, thus providing a sense of financial security and reducing uncertainty in a context of economic crisis.

Finally,  the  mismatch  could  also  be  due  to  positive  'spillover  effects'.  The  government's introduction of the policy during the Covid-19 crisis could have signalled adverse economic conditions to the population, which in turn made them feel like they are not doing as bad relative to others, namely the target population of the IMV. Individuals adapt the subjective assessment  of  their  living  conditions  to  their  expectations  about  the  current  economic conditions and the financial situation of those around them. Such a finding would add new evidence to 'adaptation theory' but also corroborate findings of the 'signalling literature' on the importance of governments' announcement and introduction of policies compared to their actual implementation. It would also add to the 'spillover theory', disproving previous findings that non-recipients become envious and consider that their financial situation has deteriorated given the perceived material gains of others, instead shining a light on a more empathetic view of social relations.


## 7 CONCLUSION


In this paper, I used the case study of Spain and a Synthetic Control Method to examine how MISs affect households' financial wellbeing and whether this effect differs across objective material conditions and households' perceptions. The results show that, while the policy had no statistically significant effect on objective financial wellbeing measures (i.e. the poverty rate,  the  poverty  gap  and  mean  income)  in  2021,  it  did  considerably  improve  subjective financial wellbeing between June 2020 and December 2022, as it helped households feel less pessimistic about the evolution of their finances during the Covid-19 and cost-of-living crises. Between June 2020 and December 2022, the IMV increased the balance between those saying their financial situation improved and those saying it deteriorated by a magnitude of between 10.1 and 14.6 points. Spain's new MIS acted as a lifeline in times of economic uncertainty. Two main questions remain that I will be able test once data becomes available: (i) whether

the policy effect on households' perceptions will be sustained over time after December 2022 and (ii) whether it reflects improvements in objective measures beyond 2021.

I  have tried to explain the results putting forward several hypotheses that will need to be tested in future research. The insignificant effects of the Spanish minimum income scheme on objective measures in 2021 might be due to the policy's small reach given low levels of take-up, to its low amounts as well as to labour supply reactions of the target population and to the strategic behaviour of regions, which might have offset any positive effect of the policy on national-level financial wellbeing. The relatively large and significant effect of the Spanish MIS on households' perceived financial improvements might reflect the lagged rollout of the policy  and  the  impact  of  the  government's  initiatives  to  improve  the  policy's  adequacy, coverage, take-up and compatibility with work from 2022. These significant results might also reflect disparities between objective and subjective wellbeing, which could be explained by anticipation  effects  among  IMV  applicants,  placebo  effects  among  potential  beneficiaries and/or positive spillover effects among non-recipients.

The findings of this paper are relevant to Spanish policymakers as they provide an overview of the achievements and limitations of this new national-level MIS, which has come to be seen as a turning point in the fight against poverty in the country. More generally, the results add empirical causal evidence to the debate on the effects of MISs on financial wellbeing and on the different design elements that make these policies successful. The paper also highlights the importance for practitioners to consider subjective measures of financial wellbeing when assessing  income  support  schemes.  Subjective  financial  wellbeing  indicators  can  reveal important information we might otherwise overlook. In addition, while income data from surveys is available with a two-year lag, some subjective financial wellbeing measures like the one  used  in  this  paper  can  be  accessed  with  only  a  couple  of  months'  delay,  meaning subjective  indicators  can  also  be  particularly  relevant  if  we  are  interested  in  the  timely monitoring of minimum income schemes.

## INTRODUCTION


There is no doubt that emerging technologies will continue to have an impact both positively and negatively on society as they continue to develop. We can attribute this to the fact that they continue to transform the world in which we live. This is in the same way that most changes in our everyday lives have done so. It is impossible for us to predict how this is going to turn out in the long run. The question of how it can be made to work is still open. This means that people will need to think about how they can customize it to suit their needs and lifestyles. In addition, they will need to think about the way they live their everyday lives. According to the author, the changes are a good thing for most people, since he is an optimist. The author, however, believes that there may be some instances where extensive human intervention is required, and in those situations, dealing with them may prove to be challenging.

It is well known that people have biases, and these biases can be passed along to emerging technologies that they program.  In the future, emerging technologies may even be able to learn biases from data sets without realizing it. There are many reasons why  employers  should  not  use  emerging  technologies  when  it  comes  to  recruiting candidates for jobs. There's no doubt that that's not going to be an issue in the distant future.  There  are  plenty  of  companies  today  that  use  emerging  technologies  to  sort through the application process for jobs, but a software program could potentially throw out resumes that do not match its biases.

Researchers  have  highlighted  that  while  emerging  technologies  are  great  for processing transactions quickly and accurately, they fall short in many areas that require complex thoughts or emotions in order to accomplish those tasks. As a result of the lack of  emotional  intelligence  that  is  possessed  by  emerging  technologies,  it  becomes  a problem for them to compete with people. As an example, consider chatbots. Due to the lack of emotional intelligence, they are unable to provide a positive customer service experience in the majority of cases. When a human touch is required or a complex and creative solution to a problem is required, they tend to fall short.

With the advent of emerging technologies, machines are capable of understanding and achieving specific goals. One of the emerging technologies is the use of deep learning in machine learning. There are two types of machine learning: the first involves machines automatically learning from existing data without the assistance of human  beings.  Using  deep  learning,  computers  are  now  capable  of  absorbing  huge amounts of unstructured data, such as text, images, and audio files, without a problem. As a result of the advancement of emerging technologies, it is possible to improve the welfare of people, to contribute to sustainable economic growth around the globe, to increase productivity and innovation, and to address key global challenges in a positive and sustainable manner. There are many sectors in which it is being deployed, including production, finance, and transportation, as well as healthcare and security. Emerging technologies are both benefits and challenges for our economies and societies, especially in regards to economic shifts and inequalities, competition, changes in the labor market, and implications for democracy and human rights.

The concept of emerging technologies is much more about the process and the ability to think and analyze data in a more powerful way than it is about any particular format  or  function.  Although  emerging  technologies  conjure  up  images  of  highfunctioning, human-like robots taking over the world, they are not intended to replace humans. There are numerous success stories that demonstrate the value of emerging technologies. Adding machine learning and cognitive interactions to traditional business processes and applications can significantly improve user experience and productivity.

It is important to note, however, that there are some obstacles. There are several reasons why few companies have deployed emerging technologies at scale. It is often computationally expensive to carry out emerging technologies projects if they do not use cloud computing. As well as being complex to build, they require a high level of expertise, which is in high demand but in short supply. It will be easier to minimize these  difficulties  if  you  are  aware  of  when  and  where  to  incorporate  emerging technologies, as well as when to turn to a third party for assistance. The promise of emerging technologies is often not realized by many companies because they fail to capitalize on the full potential of machine learning and other emerging technologies. This  has  been  investigated  by  the  author  in  an  attempt  to  determine  the  cause. Interestingly,  it  appears  that  the  problem  lies  primarily  with  people.  Inefficient workflows  can  prevent  companies  from  gaining  the  full  benefits  of  emerging technologies. In order to build machine learning models for emerging technologies, data scientists  may  experience  challenges  in  obtaining  the  resources  and  data  they  need. Collaborating with their teammates may prove challenging for them. They must also manage  many  different  open  source  tools,  while  application  developers  must  often entirely recode models that data scientists develop before they can incorporate them into their  applications.  As  a  result  of  the  growing  number  of  open  source  emerging technologies tools, IT departments are spending more time supporting the data science teams  by  continually  updating  their  work  environments.  As  a  result  of  the  lack  of standardization across data science teams, this issue is compounded. It is also possible that  senior  leaders  will  not  be  able  to  see  the  full  potential  of  the  investments  their organizations  are  making  in  emerging  technologies. ## What are Emerging Technologies


An emerging technology is generally understood to refer to a technology that has not yet reached its full potential. Either in terms of their development, their practical application, or both. New technologies are included in this category, but older technologies may also find new  applications  in  this  area. Developing  new  technologies  involves  the  practical implementation of ideas that lead to the introduction of new products or services as well as an  improvement  in  how  existing  products  and  services  are  provided  as  a  result  of  the introduction of new technologies.

The  perception  of  new  technologies  as  capable  of  transforming  existing conditions  is  that  they  have  the  potential  to  do  so.  The  characteristics  of  emerging technologies include radical novelty (in applications as well as origins), rapid growth, coherence,  notable  impact,  and  uncertainty  and  ambiguity.  Different  scientists  have defined emerging technologies differently, but there is one element that is common to all  of  them:  a  focus  on  newness,  improvement,  and  dissemination  of  ideas  and technologies that are emerging. Emerging technologies are those that exhibit a degree of coherence over time and have the potential to have a significant impact on a wide range  of  socioeconomic  domains.  As  a  result  of  affecting  the  pattern  of  interaction between actors and institutions as well as the composition of actors and institutions, the socioeconomic domain(s) have a significant impact on the broader domain(s). While this technology will have the greatest impact in the future, its application during the emerging phase is somewhat clear. The ambiguity arises from the fact that it is likely to have the greatest impact in the future.

A  wide  range  of  emerging  technologies  exists,  such  as  drone  technology, educational  technology,  machine  learning,  self-driving  cars,  nanotechnology,  genetic engineering,  robotics,  and  artificial  intelligence.  Developing  emerging  technologies involves  the  design,  development,  and  implementation  of  new  products,  processes, services, technologies, art works, and business models that innovators are able to offer to markets, government agencies, and society as a whole in order to make it more efficient.

Several industries have changed the way in which they operate their day-to-day operations  as  a  result  of  the  emergence  of  emerging  technology  within  the  last  few decades,  as  well  as  the  way  in  which  they  perform  and  conduct  their  day-to-day operations. Throughout the past few decades, the introduction of emerging technologies has played a significant role in the transformation of the research and manufacturing sectors. During a relatively short period of time, however, the finance and healthcare sectors were transformed by technology in a way that was unprecedented. Throughout history, it has been proven that emerging technologies and related technologies have had a positive impact on how the global IT sector performs as a whole and how it operates as a whole. It is important to note that there is a branch of computer science known as emerging technology. We aim to transform computers into intelligent machines that would not  be  possible  without  the  direct  intervention  of  a  human  being  in  order  to achieve the goal. There will be a time in the future when emerging technology and machine learning will be used to create systems that mimic human behavior. These systems will provide solutions to complex and difficult problems, and create simulations

that will ultimately become emerging technologies at the level of humanity in response to  these  problems.  This  will  be  made  possible  through  the  use  of  computer-based training and advanced algorithms.

There is the possibility that different systems evolving towards similar goals may lead to the development of new technological fields. The convergence of technologies has resulted in previously separate technologies, such as voice (and telephony features), data (and productivity applications), and video, sharing resources and interacting with each other. Convergent technologies represent fields that were previously distinct but are now becoming more interconnected and working towards similar  goals  through  the  use  of technical innovations. A lot of emerging technologies are developed as a result of the engineering process that is often used to solve technical or scientific problems. Emerging technologies are technical innovations that represent the development of a field in order to achieve  a  competitive  advantage.  While  there  is  no  doubt  that  several  emerging  and converging technologies will have an impact on society in the near future, there exists a wide range of opinions regarding their impact, status, and economic viability.

Traditionally,  human  thought  is  analyzed  in  accordance  with  certain  principles, which are incorporated into individual codes of conduct. In light of emerging technologies, a computer is now capable of thinking logically and solving problems in much the same way as a rational individual.  As a result, the solution to a given problem often differs greatly from the solution in practice, and technology relies on this logical reasoning in order to function properly. It is evident, however, that society as a whole will be significantly affected by the development  of  emerging  technologies  in  the  long  run.  In  addition,  it  is  important  to determine  how  the  application  will  be  implemented,  in  addition  to  addressing  ethical concerns, legal constraints, and ensuring transparency. We  should have a better understanding of how these technological advancements affect the broader public due to their potential impact. Technology advancements have the potential to transform society and to become one of mankind's most important inventions.

The nature of emerging technologies is multifaceted. Emerging technologies are difficult to define, and there are many divergent perspectives on the subject. There is a wide range of  potential  hazards  associated  with  emerging  technologies.  There  are  a variety of dangers  associated  with  advancing  technologies,  depending  on  their sophistication and type. There is a substantial difference between the danger posed by a self-aware computer program and the danger posed by a simple emerging technology or automation system. Business benefits from emerging technologies far outweigh their disadvantages.  It  is  expected  that  there  will  be  more  commercial  applications  of emerging  technologies  in  the  near  future.  More  and  more  companies  are  adopting emerging technologies, resulting in a shift in social norms.

## 1. Introduction


Many young people take their lives every year, as suicide belongs to the leading causes of death among 15-29-year-olds worldwide (World Health Organisation, 2021). People who live(d) in state  care,  often  due  to  previous  child  abuse  or  neglect  (Department  for  Education,  2021; Statistisches Bundesamt, 2021b), have an elevated risk of suicidal ideation, behavior and dying by suicide (see Evans et al., 2017; Vinnerljung et al., 2006).

Suicidal thoughts and behavior among people with care experience can occur from a young age. Taussig et al. (2014) found high rates among care-experienced children aged 9-11, which they reported as five times higher compared to findings from the same age group in the general American population (King et al., 2001; cited in Taussig et al., 2014). During adolescence, teenagers with care experience show higher rates of suicidal ideation (25% compared to 11%) and behavior (4% compared to 1%) than peers without care experience (Evans et al., 2017). In California, about 25% of older adolescents (16-17 years old) in foster care attempted suicide at some time during their life (Okpych & Courtney, 2018). Particularly during the late teen years between 17 and 19 years, an increase in suicides can be seen in England generally (Rodway et al., 2016), similar to 18-19-year-olds in Germany (Statista, 2022). This increase is particularly critical as many young people leave care when they turn 18, sometimes even younger, with fewer resources and support available than their peers who usually leave their parental home in their mid-20s (Sievers et al., 2014; Stein, 2012). A recent study showed that about two-fifth of 314 care leavers in Northern Ireland were reported to be at medium to high risk of suicide, with one-fifth  of  care  leavers  having  attempted  suicide  within  the  previous  year  before  data collection (Kelly et al., 2022). In adulthood, a Swedish study showed that care-experienced adults were four to five times more likely to be hospitalized due to a suicide attempt than the general population (Vinnerljung et al., 2006).

These studies demonstrate an unusually high risk of suicide among people with care experience from different countries. However, cross-national comparative studies are missing on the risk of suicide, particularly suicidal ideation, among people with care experience and those in the transition from care to adulthood. Therefore, it remains unclear how far different countries show similarities  and  differences  in  the  occurrence  of  suicidal  thoughts  among  people  with  care experience. Research on this topic from England and Germany is scarce, especially focusing on young  adults  who  have  left  the  care  system.  However,  a  cross-national  comparison  with differences in the care system can help identify how different approaches in care may influence suicidal ideation among care-experienced people.

The two care systems in England and Germany show some similarities and differences. While the English care system and social work focus on child protection and risk aversion (Evans & Kessl, 2016), the care system in Germany belongs to legal child-rearing support within the conservative  welfare  state  (Köngeter  et  al.,  2008).  In  Germany,  care  functions  as  child protection and a support service for families and young people, with non-consensual adoption being  uncommon,  which  may  also  explain  the  different  numbers  of  young  people  in  care (Boddy et al., 2009; Gupta, 2016). With a general population of about 56,500,000 in England (Office  for  National  Statistics,  2022),  almost  81,000  children  were  looked  after  by  local authorities by March 2021 (143/100,000 citizens). Foster care is the most dominant type of care in  England,  with  56%  of  looked-after  young  people  living  in  non-relative  foster  care (80/100,000) compared to 14% (20/100,000) in residential care (Department for Education, 2021). Of 83,200,000 citizens in Germany (Statistisches Bundesamt, 2021a), 158,000 young people  were  in  care  by  December  2020  (190/100,000  citizens).  In  contrast  to  England, residential care for young people is more dominant in Germany, with 51% of all young people in care (97/100,000) living in a residential care facility, compared to 28% in non-relative foster care  (54/100,000)  (Statistisches  Bundesamt,  2021b).  Unlike  in  Germany,  residential  care  in England has been considered a last resort and used as a marginal service (Gupta, 2016). In England, the support for care leavers is mandated legally by providing a personal advisor, a pathway plan and advice until age 21 and beyond if in education or training (Butterworth et al., 2017). Similarly, support for young adults leaving care is available until age 21 in Germany and, if in education or training, also beyond, but it was not compulsory to be granted. Thus, access to support for care leavers differed from one local authority to another on the likelihood of a young person receiving ongoing support (Ehlke et al., 2021). In 2021, the reform 'Kinderund Jugendstärkungsgesetz' (Act to Strengthen Children and Youth) strengthened the legal obligation for support in early adulthood. While some similarities exist in the provision of care, the two systems show differences, especially in the care types and legal support in the transition from care.

In England and Germany, the risk of suicide among care-experienced people, especially young adults leaving care, has received little attention. However, due to the vulnerability of people with care experience, a comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon is vital for suicide prevention.  Cross-national  research  with  both  countries  helps  to  explore  similarities  and differences  in  the  occurrence  of  suicidal  ideation  between  the  two  care  systems  and  their influences on the risk of suicide.

The presented study focuses on the following research question: What is the occurrence of suicidal ideation among care-experienced young adults in England and Germany? With the combination  of  quantitative  and  qualitative  data,  this  question  goes  beyond  prevalence  by exploring times and forms of the occurrence of suicidal ideation in greater depth.  Not only knowing  how  common  suicidal  ideation  is  among  people  with  care  experience  but  also understanding  what  suicidal  ideation  means  and  in  what  forms  it  occurs  is  crucial  for practitioners to identify a person at risk. Given the opportunities a cross-national study can provide, I examine the range of suicidal ideation among people with care experience in two European countries. The study follows a mixed-methods design to provide broad and in-depth information on suicidal ideation among young adults with care experience. States of suicidal ideation  and  times  at  which  such  thoughts  occur  among  people  with  care  experience  are identified. The data presented here contribute to a better understanding of what suicidal ideation means for people with care experience and will help to align professional support.


## 2. Methods


A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining an online survey and semi-structured interviews.  Mixed  methods  were  chosen  to  both  broaden  and  deepen  our  understanding  of suicidal ideation among people with care experience, reflecting on the time during care and recently in early adulthood. The data was collected between July 2020 and June 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants aged between 18 and 40 were required to have been in foster or residential care on or after their 16 th birthday  in  England or Germany. They were recruited  from  various  sources,  including  relevant  organizations  such  as  local  authorities, residential or foster care providers, care-experienced peer networks and advocacy groups, and social media. Participants provided informed consent for each part of the study and received written information about the study before commencing the survey or interviews and a list of support services. The study received ethical approval from the university's Research Ethics Committee.


## 2.1. Survey:


For the survey, 45 people with experience in foster and/or residential care completed the online questionnaire, with 29 from Germany and 16 from England. With an age range from 18 to 40 years,  the  average  age  was  25.7.  On  average,  participants  came  into  care  at  age  11.4.  The

majority of survey participants were female (78%). Further sample characteristics are reported in Appendix 1.

The online questionnaire consisted of 72 items and was available in English and German (see Appendix 2). Apart from questions collecting information on, among other things, demographic data and care experience, four questions measured suicidal ideation from low to high severity based on interview questions by Paykel et al. (1974), also known as the Paykel Suicide Scale (PSS,  excluding  the  fifth  question  about  suicide  attempts).  The  PSS  differentiates  between passive suicidal thoughts (item 1: 'Have you ever felt that life was not worth living?' and 2: 'Have you ever wished you were dead?') and active suicidal thoughts (item 3: Have you ever thought of taking your life?' and 4: 'Have you ever reached the point where you seriously considered  taking  your  life,  or  perhaps  made  plans  how  you  would  go  about  doing  it?') (Ashrafioun  et  al.,  2016;  Fonseca-Pedrero  et  al.,  2019;  Van  Orden  et  al.,  2015).  Different timescales are considered by distinguishing between lifetime occurrence of suicidal thoughts, last occurrence (last month, last 12 months, earlier) informed by Dennis et al. (2009), and a care-related  occurrence  (only  while  in  care,  while  in  care  and  after  leaving  care,  only  after leaving care). Questions about when the suicidal thoughts appeared first followed, including their age and changes at the time. Open-ended questions asked about what participants consider as causes of their suicidal thoughts, coping strategies, and the role of their care experience and the care system for suicide prevention.

The survey data were analyzed with SPSS 25. Descriptive analyses were conducted. ShapiroWilk tests indicated that the variables presented here were not normally distributed. MannWhitney tests for two independent groups for non-parametric distributions were undertaken to explore whether the differences between groups were significant. Data from the open-ended questions were analyzed with NVivo 13 and Excel to show frequency distributions across the different themes.


## 2.2. Interviews:


Thirteen young adults aged between 18 and 30 were interviewed, with seven from England and six from Germany. All interview participants experienced suicidal thoughts at some point in their past, which was a necessary inclusion criterion for the interviews. The interview sample consisted of nine females, including one transgender female, and four males. All participants from Germany had German nationality, including one with double citizenship. Four participants from England identified as 'White' or 'White British' and three as 'Asian British', 'Mixed' and 'Iranian/Middle Eastern'. Interviewed participants entered care between the ages of 1 to 17 and

spent accordingly the same range of lengths in care (1-17 years). While all participants from Germany entered care during their adolescence and were in residential care only, the English sample showed a greater variety, with the majority having lived with foster families either only or at least at some point during their time in care. The number of care placement changes was higher among the English sample, with 1-48 changes compared to 0-2 changes in the German sample.

The  13  semi-structured  interviews  took  place  in  one-to-one  remote  settings,  with  an introductory call in advance and an additional debriefing call a few days after the interview. All participants were fully informed about the study's aim to find out about their experiences of suicidal  ideation.  They  received  a  reimbursement  of  £/€15.  The  interviews  were  either  in English  or  German,  transcribed  in  their  original  language  (see  the  transcription  guide  in Appendix 3) and anonymized (D1-6 for interviewees from Germany and E1-7 from England). The  interviews  were  analyzed  with  the  framework  method  by  Ritchie  &  Spencer  (1994). Framework analysis is a systematic analytical approach for qualitative data, suitable for semistructured interviews in applied health, social and policy research to understand, explain and theorize social behavior. It applies five constitutive steps: familiarisation, identifying a thematic framework, indexing, charting, and mapping and interpretation (Gale et al., 2013; Parkinson et al., 2016; Ritchie & Spencer, 1994). A thematic framework was identified with a joint index in English. The thematic framework was applied to all transcripts in NVivo. Framework matrices were used to create  charts  by  theme,  one  for  England  and  one  for  Germany,  to  facilitate  a comparison between the two groups and summarised in Excel. Analytical memos supported the final interpretation process to identify patterns and make comparisons of responses. This paper focuses on one theme identified as the experiences of suicidal ideation to answer the research question.

## 3.2. Interview findings


The  findings  from  the  interviews  provide  an  overview  demonstrating  the  range  of  suicidal ideation reported by the participants. This range covered the following topics: first suicidal ideation, passive and active suicidal ideation, self-harm, ambivalent attitude towards life and death, and suicidal ideation as continuous background noise.

The interview sample described the age of their first suicidal thoughts ranging from 8 to 18 years.  Seven  participants  reported  having  been  between  the  ages  of  11  and  13  when  they experienced suicidal thoughts for the first time. One young woman from Germany mentioned the beginning of her puberty as the time for her suicidal ideation to occur for the first time. In both groups, the first suicidal thoughts occurred before entering the care system, during the time in the care system or after leaving care.

The interviews clarified the difference between passive and active suicidal ideation as part of the range of suicidal thoughts. The severity of such cognitions can vary from 'life is not worth living' (D5), 'I should just die' (E4), or 'hoping to not have to […] exist […] for much longer' (E7),  up  to  serious  suicide  plans.  One  young  woman  from  England  described  her  passive suicidal thoughts:

And I was having um like, like suicidal ideation, like kind of 'Oh, it would be great if I could just disappear.' (E1)

A young man from Germany described his passive suicidal thoughts first occurred in residential care:

' For me it's easier when I'm not here.' So not here from [the residential home], but here, eh, on earth and [not?] underground [six feet under]. These (-) these thoughts then came up at some point. They also started to creep up on me, um, and then (-) first (-)  I  started  to  self-harm.  Um,  and  only  then  did  it  develop,  um,  with  the  suicidal thoughts too (-) but it was also very, very gradual. It didn't happen all of a sudden, it went on for weeks, maybe even a few months, until it manifested itself. (D4)

As the young man mentioned, several other participants from both countries also reported selfharm as part of the suicidal experience or a coping strategy, varying from cutting to misusing medication. A young woman from Germany also reported starting with self-harming practices before having suicidal thoughts. She described that residential care workers ignored her selfharming practices while in care, a time when she did not have suicidal ideation. Her suicidal thoughts occurred first when she moved out to live alone in a supported flat by the same care provider, where she was sexually assaulted and attempted suicide. She reflected that her selfharming behavior had two functions: one was a coping strategy, and the other was a cry for help, help that she did not receive from the residential care workers.

Trajectories from passive suicidal thoughts from a young age that developed into active suicidal thoughts later in life were identified in the interviews. A young woman from England reflected on her experienced trajectory from passive to active suicidal thoughts. In her quote below, she mentioned  the  time  of  transition,  particularly  from  care  to  university,  and  having  several problems coming up at once as triggering the change in the severity of her suicidal thoughts, which initially started when she experienced abuse before entering foster care.

S omewhere around 11 or 12, I started internalizing everything […] I was like have thoughts like 'Oh, it must be my fault. […] I should just die.' […] They weren't that

serious to begin with […] And then got to self-blame and lots of kind of 'Maybe I should just (.) not be here then.' […] And I think the older I got up more and more I stopped thinking it was other people and more it was me. […] I think, probably the first time I had a serious blank I would have made a plan and I might do this, um, I was (-) probably my first year at uni actually. It got just worse and whether the first time I had a plan wouldn't have been until I was (.) yeah, at uni. (E4)

As  another  characteristic  of  the  range  of  suicidal  ideation,  several  participants  reported  an ambivalence between suicidal and life-affirming thoughts and behavior. A young man from Germany whose first severe active suicidal thoughts were triggered by a drug overdose in the year after leaving the care system described the ambivalence between active suicidal thoughts as an escape from painful problems and fear of taking this action.

Suicidal thoughts, you don't look forward to it, it's a reaction. Something that at least caused me a lot of fear. I was (-) afraid of taking this way out. […] it's a way out, because if you're no longer alive, you no longer have any problems. So if you look at it soberly. […] you want to live, and you're very afraid of no longer (-) being there, and then you lose what you have. (D3)

Professionals need to consider the possible ambivalence between life and death when working with young people with care experience and conducting a risk assessment as a challenge to identify a suicidal person. This ambivalence includes the fear of death or planning one's future while simultaneously having the wish to die by putting oneself into life-threatening situations, as a young woman from England described as follows:

It was confusing because I've always had two sides to me. […] So, I had this like whole destructive side and like suicidal side that I was planning my future at the same time. So, it was just (.) a really weird kinda dynamic that I had in my head, which was really confusing to the professionals as well because I'd be in hospital talking to them about the courses I have applied to and the work experience I want to do but, you know, I'm sitting  there  because I did that to myself and I'm putting myself in danger, and I'm jeopardizing all the things that I'm planning. (E7)

Some experienced suicidal ideation as something re-occurring or chronic, as one participant described  a constant  ' background  noise ' (E5).  Some  mentioned  having  such  thoughts regularly or consistently being hidden in the background until they received psychotherapeutic treatment and finally coped with the triggering experiences they had undergone. One young

woman  from  Germany  described  that  her  acceptance  of  chronic  depressive  and  suicidal experiences helps her cope:

Of course, there are still dark days when, for example, I harm myself or something, which hasn't been the case for a long time […] it's really been reduced. And I think it also has a lot to do with acceptance, simply understanding that this will accompany me throughout my life and that there will always be one or two dark days a year. (D6)

According  to  the  open-ended  survey  questions  above,  the  interviews  provide  various perspectives  on  how  participants'  care  experience  influenced  their  suicidal  ideation.  Those ranged from contributing to their occurrence up to receiving much-appreciated support to help the young person cope with their suicidal thoughts.

There are many similarities between the reports by participants from both countries that covered the  difference  between  passive  and  active  suicidal  thoughts,  connections  to  self-harming practices, continuous suicidal ideation, and the ambivalent attitudes between the wish to die and  to  live.  Participants  from  both  countries  reported  a  range  of  ages  when  participants experienced  suicidal  thoughts  for  the  first  time.  Furthermore,  in  several  interviews,  the connection  between  participants'  care  experience  and  times  of  suicidal  ideation  became apparent.  For  instance,  suicidal  thoughts  started  with  experienced  abuse  as  a  child  before coming into care, occurred during their time in care or at times of transition from care, when previous  suicidal  thoughts  intensified  for  some.  To  summarise,  the  reports  demonstrate  the broad range and complexity of suicidal ideation, with overall similarities between reports from the two countries.


## 4. Discussion


The results show that care-related experiences can play a unique role in the occurrence of this risk and contribute to a better understanding of suicidal ideation in the context of care. The survey findings align with previous research results that many people with care experience have suicidal ideation (Evans et al., 2017; Pilowsky and Wu, 2006). While not everyone would act on suicidal ideation, the risk of doing so and, thus, dying by suicide increases with the presence of these thoughts. These findings underline the importance of this topic for everyone working with people with care experience.

The findings show that suicidal ideation shows a variety of occurrences. Knowing the range of suicidal ideation is essential for professionals involved with people with care experience to understand this phenomenon better and help them identify people at risk.

First, suicidal ideation among people with care experience can occur from a young age. Similar to the findings of the study by Taussig et al. (2014), the pre-adolescent age at which many participants  reported  having  experienced  their  first  suicidal  ideation  highlights  the  need  for early suicide prevention tailored to children in care. However, others experienced their first suicidal thoughts during adolescence or adulthood. While many care-experienced people start facing suicidal thoughts from a very young age, suicidal ideation can first occur at different ages, from pre-adolescence to adulthood. Therefore, suicide prevention requires a long-term perspective and continuous awareness across all ages. However, early preventive steps would help reduce the risk of suicide from a young age and in the future.

Second,  suicidal  thoughts  can  re-occur  and  deteriorate  at  different  times.  Early  suicide prevention is even more critical when looking at possible trajectories of suicidal ideation up to early adulthood. Emerging adulthood appears to be a vulnerable time for suicidal ideation to occur increasingly or more severely. The occurrence of suicidal thoughts seems to stay at least similar  high  in  early  adulthood  as  during  adolescence,  as  the  study  by  Evans  et  al.  (2017) estimated. The findings identified critical times that suggest that the risk of suicidal ideation and behavior may even increase in early adulthood. With many changes at age 18, when young people usually leave care in both countries, the findings support Boeninger and Conger's (2012) report that this risk is likely to increase during emergent adulthood. As shown, the risk of suicide may even escalate in early adulthood during the transition from care and when services cease supporting  young  people.  These  times  with  a  higher  risk  for  suicidal  ideation  among  careexperienced young adults need to be considered for suicide prevention. Thus, suicide prevention for people with care experience needs to start from a young age and continue until adulthood, as  suggested  above.  This  would  help  counteract  the  further  trajectory  of  suicidal  ideation, especially by raising awareness for emergent adults.

Third,  suicidal  ideation  occurs  in  different  forms,  ranging  from  passive  to  active  suicidal thoughts and sometimes chronic experiences. Continuous, possibly chronic suicidal ideation has been found in the context of emotion dysregulation and as a risk factor for future suicide attempts  and  hospitalizations  among  young  people  (Wolff  et  al.,  2018).  Considering  that suicidal thoughts can re-occur or be experienced chronically contributes to a realistic view of different trajectories of suicidal ideation and recovery. Acknowledging the possible

ambivalence between suicidal ideation and the will to live, which may challenge practitioners, helps  address  this  sensitive  topic,  especially  as  signs  of  suicidal  ideation  may  not  often  be explicit.

According to van Orden et al. (2015), who also used the PSS (Paykel et al., 1974), the severity of suicidal ideation can be differentiated between passive and active suicidal thoughts, which were also identified in the interview data. Passive suicidal thoughts, on the one hand, were found in statements such as feeling life was not worth living, the wish to disappear from the world or not to exist any longer. Active suicidal thoughts, on the other hand, were identified as serious suicidal thoughts or plans of taking one's life (Paykel et al., 1974; Van Orden et al., 2015). Specific times can trigger the occurrence of active suicidal ideation, such as the transition from care to adulthood.

Any suicidal ideation needs to be taken seriously. Passive suicidal thoughts from a young age can further develop into active suicidal thoughts with an increased risk of acting on them and, thus, dying by suicide. Particularly, the previous or simultaneous occurrence of self-harming behavior is critical for the risk of suicide. Several participants reported self-harming practices, such  as  trajectories  from  non-suicidal  self-harming  to  later  experiencing  suicidal  ideation. Higher pain tolerance due to non-suicidal self-harm may contribute to the increased risk that young people may act on suicidal ideation and, hence, the risk of suicide (Joiner et al., 2012). As Wadman et al. (2017) reported that non-suicidal self-harm is considered highly prevalent among care-experienced young people, the risk of attempting or dying by suicide increases in combination with active suicidal ideation.

With  this  knowledge,  the  refrained  support  reported  by  one  young  woman  appears  highly critical who described that residential care workers ignored her self-harming practices while in care,  and  she  attempted  suicide  when  she  lived  alone  in  semi-independent  accommodation. Ignoring self-harming behavior appears highly risky and negligent regarding suicide prevention by those supposed to act as the corporate parent. Harvey et al. (2015) highlighted that young people, especially in the transitions from places and institutions like leaving care, can trigger self-harming behavior as a coping strategy to deal with their emotions. While the transition from care to early adulthood is a critical time at which suicidal ideation can occur, and its severity  can  increase,  the  risk  of  suicide  is  heightened  if  a  person  engages  in  self-harming behavior.  Therefore,  practitioners  must  take  self-harming  behavior  seriously  as  the  young person might develop suicidal thoughts at some point, especially during or after transitions.

Finally, while a few differences appeared, such as in care types, the risk and range of suicidal ideation  are  similar  between  the  samples  from  England  and  Germany.  Thus,  the  findings indicate that the hitherto empirical knowledge about suicidal ideation among care-experienced people  is  likely  to  apply  cross-nationally,  as  several  studies  looking  at  different  countries reported similar trends (Berlin et al., 2011; Evans et al., 2017; Katz et al., 2011; Vinnerljung et al., 2006).

Among other things, the open-ended survey results on respondents' reflections on their care experience and their wishes for change indicate how far the care systems and their structures, independent from the country, can influence the well-being of care-experienced people and contribute to suicide prevention. The more negative evaluations of the influence of their care experience  on  their  attitudes  towards  life  by  survey  respondents  from  England  may  be, hypothetically, due to different approaches in care and care-related experiences that contributed to  instability  in  care  and  relationships.  These  considerations  will  be  discussed  in  a  separate publication focussing on interpersonal factors.

The mixed-methods approach contributes to a better comprehensive understanding of suicidal ideation among people with care experience in England and Germany, which has received only little attention so far, considering early adulthood and in-depth investigations. Challenges of finding adult participants who have left care, generally known as a hard-to-reach group with limitations to actualizing large randomized samples (see Mezey et al., 2015), were, among other things, the structural barriers during the pandemic. Those included the only possibility to collect data remotely and the digital divide that excluded some care leavers from participating in online activities,  such  as  this  survey  (see  Partnership  for  Young  London  et  al.,  2020).  While  the number  of  survey  participants  does  not  allow  a  conclusion  on  general  prevalence,  the combination of quantitative and qualitative methods provides broad and in-depth insights into this underresearched topic.

For practical implications, the findings underline the need to strengthen suicide prevention in social work and the (leaving) care systems across different countries. Assessments and suicide prevention need to be incorporated into the care system, starting from older childhood/preadolescence  and  continuing  up  to  adulthood.  For  instance,  practitioners  need  to  take  selfharming  behavior  as  a  risk  factor  for  suicide  seriously  and  acknowledge  the  ambivalence between life-affirming attitudes and suicidal thoughts. Therefore, everyone working with young people in care and care leavers requires a solid understanding of suicide prevention to better

identify critical times and young people at risk, provide adequate support and avoid stigmatizing practices.


## 5. Conclusion


The range of suicidal ideation, possibly occurring from a very young age but re-occurring or maintaining up to adulthood, highlights that suicide prevention needs to start early and cannot end  when  young  people  leave  care  when  turning  18.  A  long-term  perspective  with  an understanding of the variety of suicidal thoughts is essential if suicide prevention for people with care experience across different ages is taken seriously, as this study shows. The findings provide new insights into the range of suicidal ideation among people with care experience, with many similarities found among samples from England and Germany. They further offer novel  perspectives  on  this  underresearched  topic  and  contribute  to  a  better  comprehensive understanding of this important matter by combining quantitative and qualitative information. Overall, this innovative study highlights the importance for greater awareness of the risk of suicide when working with people with care experience, independent of national borders and care systems.

This extended knowledge about the range of suicidal ideation among young people with care experience is essential for policymakers and practitioners to plan and implement tailored suicide prevention strategies for care-experienced people. Therefore, a stronger awareness of the risk of suicide with a better understanding of suicidal thoughts among people with care experience is vital for suicide prevention within the (leaving) care systems.

## Introduction


Machine Translation (MT) began in the second half of the last century. It went through several phases of development, with different approaches to machine translation that led to the gradual improvement in machine translation output. The introduction of Example-Based Machine Translation  (EBMT) and Statistical Machine Translation (SMT), followed by Neural Machine Translation (NMT) paved the way towards better MT output.

Several aspects of MT between Arabic and English have been investigated. For instance, some  studies  examined  error  typology,  others  conducted  comparisons  between  several  MT engines, and other studies analysed the progress of MT output through time (Adly & Al Ansary, 2009; Al-mahasees, 2022; Hadla, Hailat, & Al-Kabi, 2014; Hijazi, 2013; Jabak, 2019). However, Machine Translation Quality Assessment (MTQA) of legal texts from Arabic into English has not been studied before to the best knowledge of the researcher. Hence, the present study aims to explore this aspect of legal discourse and machine translation.

The significance of the study arises from the fact that the introduction of a corpus-based approach to MT is assumed to raise the percentage of accuracy of MT output since previously translated corpora are used as a reference. In addition, the study sheds light on the accuracy of MT output of legislative texts and its compliance with the features of legal discourse. To achieve the objective of the study, the research questions are as follows:

- 1What are the types of errors found in the MT output of legal texts?
- 2Does MT's output of legal texts maintain features of legal discourse?

The paper is divided into four parts. The first part presents a review of the literature; it gives a brief overview of features of legal discourse, machine translation, and previous related studies on MT quality assessment with an indication of to research gap. The second part outlines the  study  data  and  method  of  analysis.  The  third  part  presents  an  analysis  of  the  study  data. Finally, a discussion of the study findings in light of previous literature is addressed.


## Literature Review


This section is divided into three parts. The first part discusses the features of English legal discourse such as lexical features, and syntactic features. The second part addresses the history and development of MT. It also tackles different approaches to MT quality assessment. Finally, the last part reviews relevant studies on MT quality assessment. The suggested contribution of the present study in light of previous studies is highlighted as a conclusion to this section.


## Legal Discourse


Legal  discourse,  also  known  as  'legalese',  is  a  specialized  type  of  language  that  has distinctive features. Lexical features of English legal discourse include archaic adverbs such as hereby,  thereof,  said,  hereunder,  aforesaid ,  etc.  Due  to  the  influence  of  Latin  and  French  on English legal discourse, several legal terms are borrowed from these two languages such as bona fide, ipso facto , etc. In addition, the use of the quantifier ' any' is also found in legal texts; e.g., 'any interest and penalties' (Alfarahaty, 2014; Hijazi, 2013).

Several  syntactic  features  are  recognized  in  English  legal  discourse.  Nominalization  is when a noun is used to replace a verb. The purpose of using such a feature is to not indicate the tense, person, modality, agent, etc.  In addition, the passive voice is very common in some legal

texts such as statutes and laws. Wh-forms are usually deleted, and nouns are followed immediately by  the  past  participle  forms  as  in  ' the  notices  given '.  Another  syntactic  feature  that  is  highly detected in legal texts is the use of conditional clauses and restrictive connectors; for instance, provided that, notwithstanding, subject to, and others. The use of pronouns and demonstratives in legal discourse is avoided. Rather, words like said, such, and the same are used. Pronouns and demonstratives can also be avoided through the repetition of nouns. Furthermore, legal texts are characterized by long, complex sentences that contribute to clarifying the meaning and avoiding ambiguity and multiple interpretations (Alfarahaty, 2014; Hijazi, 2013).

One of the essential aspects of legal discourse is the use of models. The most frequently used models in legal discourse are shall, may, and must (Alfarahaty, 2014; Hijazi, 2013). Modals in legal discourse tend to have meanings different than general English. They are used to express obligation, prohibition and permission rather than futurity (Foley, 2002).


## Machine Translation


The history of MT dates back to the 1950s. There are more than 20 approaches to machine translation  that  led  to  the  fast  development  of  MT  such  as  Rule-Based  Machine  Translation (RBMT),  Corpus-Based  Machine  Translation  (CBMT),  Data-Driven  Machine  Translation (DDMT), Example-Based Machine Translation (EBMT), Statistical Machine Translation (SMT), and Neural Machine Translation (NMT). Rule-Based Machine Translation (RBMT) is considered the first technique used in machine translation (Hutchins, 2000). RBMT is made of a collection of rules and lexical items in the form of dictionaries (Alqudsi, Omar, & Shaker; 2012). On the other hand,  Corpus-Based  Machine  Translation  (CBMT)  is  a  technique  that  is  based  on  the  use  of parallel  corpora  (Sin-wai,  2016).    Statistical  Machine  Translation  is  based  on  statistics  and probability techniques and is used by the most well-known machine translation engines globally; Google Translate,  and  Microsoft Bing (Sin-wai, 2016). However, Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is the most recent development in MT which proved to give better results compared to previous MT approaches. It is 'an integration of neural language models into traditional statistical machine translation systems' (Almahasees, 2022, p. 23).

Arabic  is  considered  one  of  the  few  languages  that  has  been  first  researched  with  the introduction of MT in the USA in the 1950s (Sin-wai, 2016). Almahasees (2022) claimed that several reasons contributed to this fact such as cultural communication, and global commerce. The first Arabic machine translation company, Sakhr, was founded in 1982. Almahasees (2022) listed several issues that face machine translation of Arabic such as relatively free word order, complex morphology, subject embedding, diacritics, and punctuation.

Nevertheless,  the  speed  of  translation  provided  by  MT  engines  does  not  guarantee  the quality of the output (Adly & Al Ansary, 2009; Al-mahasees, 2022; Hadla et al, 2014; Hijazi, 2013;  Jabak,  2019).  Hence,  researchers  in  translation  technology  proposed  two  approaches  to assess the quality of MT output; i.e., human and automatic machine translation quality assessment (Castillho,  Doherty,  Gaspari,  &  Moorkens;  2018).  Human  evaluation  of  machine  translation includes declarative evaluation which covers fidelity and intelligibility . Fidelity explores the extent to which the target text contains the information found in the source text. Intelligibility evaluates the  well-formation  of  sentences  in  the  target  text.  However,  human  evaluation  of  machine translation can be slow, expensive, and inconsistent (Way, 2018). Hence, automatic evaluation of machine translation is seen as an alternative due to its speed and objectiveness; yet, it is considered

less  comprehensive  since  it  does  not  indicate  the  category  of  errors.  Nevertheless,  several automatic MTE metrics were proposed to compare the MT output with a reference translation (Castillho, et al, 2018).


## Previous Studies


Several studies investigated the quality of Google Translate in translating between Arabic and English. Some researchers conducted a manual qualitative Translation Quality Assessment (TQA). Other studies followed an automatic evaluation by using certain software. The following review of the literature is divided into two parts. The first part discusses studies on the quality of MT output of legal texts in different language pairs; while the second part presents a summary of some studies that analyzed the quality of machine translation between English and Arabic.

Hijazi (2013) assessed Google Translate's performance in the translation of 14 legal texts from English into Arabic. Errors were classified into two categories: lexical and syntactic. Each category was further subdivided into subcategories. Lexical errors included polysemy, homonymy, legal  doublets,  and  legal  adverbs.  On  the  other  hand,  syntactic  errors  included  morphology, concord, and modality. The study concluded that the system did not succeed in providing a feasible and precise legal translation. Nevertheless, the researcher's overall assessment showed that Google Translate provided a gist translation that can assist readers in understanding the subject matter of the text in general. Another study that tackled legal translation with a different language pair is Killman's (2013) study. Killman (2013) examined the accuracy of Google Translate output of vocabulary items in legal texts from Spanish into English.  The results of the data analysis showed that  almost  70%  of  legal  terms  were  translated  correctly.  A  point  to  be  taken  is  that  the aforementioned studies were based on SMT architecture. The only study, as far as the researcher knows, that evaluated the MT output of legal texts after the introduction of NBMT is Wisemann (2019). The study compared the NMT output of two systems; i.e., Deepl Translator and MetaCat. The researcher followed a manual human evaluation approach and the study data consisted of Italian legal documents translated into German. Several error categories were detected such as ellipsis, mistranslation, translation of synonyms with the same word, terminology inconsistency, etc. In general, both NMT systems produced fluent translation; however, the results of the study showed that Deepl Translator performed better than MetaCat.

Al-Mahasees  (2022)  conducted  a  comparative  study  on  three  MT  systems:  Google Translate, Microsoft Bing, and Sakhr. Several texts were translated from English to Arabic and vice versa. The results revealed that Google Translate presented the best output of UN and WHO texts in terms of accuracy and fluency. However, in performance in translating literary texts from English into Arabic; Microsoft Bing achieved better.

Izwaini (2006) analyzed the performance of three MT systems; i.e., Google, Sakhr and Systran. He evaluated the problems faced in sentence translation. The study results showed that the output of the three MT engines was distorted and lacked cohesion and coherence.  Al-Sukhni, Al-Kabi  and  Al-smadi  (2016)  compared  the  translation  of  Google  Translate  and  Microsoft Translator of chapters from the Holy Quran into English. The output was assessed automatically by  using  ATEC.  The  study  indicated  that  machine  translation  when  compared  to  human translation, was ineffective in providing an accurate translation of Quranic texts.

Jabak  (2019)  assessed  the  quality  and  accuracy  of  Google  Translate  Arabic-English translations.  The  error  analysis  showed  that  Google  Translate  output  contained  lexical  and

syntactic errors. Lexical errors were the highest leading to faulty, inaccurate translations. The study concluded  that  the  Google  MT  system  cannot  be  used  separately  without  any  human  posttranslation interference.

Hadla, Hailat, and Al-Kabi (2014) compared Google Translate and Babylon MT systems. The study data included more than 1000 sentences distributed among the four sentence functions: declarative,  interrogative,  imperative,  and  exclamatory.  BLUE  was  used  for  the  automatic evaluation  of  the  data.  The  results  showed  that  Google  Translate  provided  a  more  precise translation.  A  similar  study  conducted  by  Adly  and  Al  Ansary  (2009)  explored  the  difference between three MT systems: Google Translate, Babylon, and Tarjim. They followed an automatic evaluation approach. The three MT systems failed to grasp the semantic cohesion and style of Arabic.

In  conclusion,  the  previous  review  of  the  literature  indicates  that  regardless  of  the accelerating  advancements  in  MT,  the  MT  output  still  contains  several  errors  from  different categories.  MTQA,  whether  manual  or  automatic,  highlighted  a  variety  of  error  typologies; nevertheless, some MT systems provided better performance such as Google Translate and Deepl Translator. Previous work failed to address the NMT of legal texts as a very limited number of studies evaluated the quality of specialized translation. Furthermore, to the best of the researcher's knowledge,  machine  translation  of  legal  texts  from  Arabic  to  English  has  never  been  studied before. Hence, the present study aims to evaluate the quality of NMT of legal texts from Arabic to English.  The  selected  MT  system  is  Google  Translate  since  previous  literature  indicated  its superiority over other MT systems.

Omission varies from the deletion of a word to the deletion of a whole clause. Al-Mahasees (2022) defines omission as 'the deletion of an item that should appear in a well-formed and meaningful sentence' (p. 83).  The omission was the least detected category of errors. ## Discussion


The research's main aim is to evaluate the quality of MT output of legal texts from Arabic to English. Two research questions were proposed.

- 1. What are the types of errors found in the MT output of legal texts?
- 2. Does MT's output of legal texts maintain features of legal discourse?

The findings of the study showed that Google Translate provided a good translation; nevertheless, several error types were found.

To  answer  the  first  question,  errors  were  classified  and  calculated.  The  data  analysis revealed four error types: lexical, syntactic, register-related and omission. 512 errors out of 10389 words were found in the data constituting 5% of the data. Significantly, the data analysis indicated that lexical errors constituted almost half of the errors. Lexical errors were the highest in the study data, which is consistent with Jabak's (2019) study. the least reported error type was omission with only 8 cases.

As for the second question, the data analysis indicated that legal discourse errors came second in the study sample. The inaccurate use of modals can be attributed to the differences between Arabic and English. Verbs in Arabic can carry modality, but English verbs require other helping verbs to express modality. The same can be applied to archaic terms. The prepositional phrases  in  Arabic  were  translated  instead  of  using  archaic  adverbs  due  to  their  different morphology in English.

Hence, it can be implied from the findings of the study that Google Translate failed in presenting a legal document that follows the norms of English, which comes in great agreement with Hijazi's (2013) study. In contradiction with Killman's (2013) study, legal terms in the present study were poorly translated. Al-Sukhni et al. (2016) reported that Google Translate could not translate  Islamic  texts  efficiently;  supporting  the  findings  of  the  present  study  that  Google Translate,  when  compared  to  human  translation,  could  not  provide  an  accurate  specialized translation; i.e., legal translation.


## Conclusion


The present research objective is to study the quality of Neural Machine Translation of legal texts from Arabic into English. The researcher followed a manual evaluation to assess the quality  of  NMT  output.  The  study's  contribution  is  twofold:  the  evaluation  of  the  NMT architecture of Google Translate in general; and the diagnosis of legal discourse features of English NMT output in specific. The results indicated that the introduction of NMT to Google Translate has  not  succeeded  in  solving  common  issues  related  to  errors  in  MT  output.  Though  Google Translate provided a comprehensible output, lexical and syntactic errors were seen in the data. The paper also suggested that Google Translate failed in translating several factors of legal discourse.

## BACKGROUND


In recent years, lifespan inequality has become an important indicator of population health, alongside more established longevity measures. Uncovering the statistical properties of lifespan inequality measures can provide novel insights on the study of mortality developments.


## METHODS


We revisit the e † measure of lifespan inequality, introduced in Vaupel and Canudas-Romo (2003). We note that, conditioning on surviving at least until age a , e † ( a ) is equal to the covariance between the conditional lifespan random variable T a and its transformation through its own cumulative hazard function (hence generalizing a result first noted in Schmertmann, 2020). We then derive an upper bound for e † ( a ). Leveraging this result, we introduce the 'Average Uneven Mortality' (AUM) index, a novel relative mortality index that can be used to analyze mortality patterns. We discuss some general features of the index, including its relationship with a constant ('even') force of mortality, and we study how it changes over time.


## RESULTS


The use of the AUM index is illustrated through an application to observed period and cohort death rates as well as to period life-table death rates from the Human Mortality Database. We explore the behavior of the index across age and over time, and we study its relationship with life expectancy. The AUM index at birth declined over time until the 1950s, when it reverted its trend. The index generally increases over age and reduces with increasing values of life expectancy, with differences between the period and cohort perspectives.


## CONTRIBUTION


We elaborate on Vaupel and Canudas-Romo's e † measure, deriving its upper bound. We exploit this result to introduce a novel mortality indicator, which enlarges the toolbox of available methods for the study of mortality dynamics. We also develop some new routines to compute e † ( a ) and σ T a from death rates, and show that they have higher precision when compared to conventional and available functions, particularly for calculations involving older ages.
