## Introduction


The  impact  of  genes  on  socioeconomic  outcomes  is  a  central  focus  of  research  on  social inequalities (Guo & Stearns, 2002; Krapohl et al., 2014; Lin, 2020). We argue that this impact should  also  be  at  the  centre  of  the  debate  surrounding  equality  of  opportunity.  Traditional approaches  to  equality of opportunity  consider  that  inequalities produced by differences in genetic endowments are fair (Rawls 1971; Breen and Jonsson 2005; Conley and Fletcher 2017). In this study, however, we take the stand of the luck egalitarian perspective, and argue that since individuals do not have control over the genes they are born with (Roemer 1998; Cohen 2008; Arneson 2018; Harden 2021), differences in  socioeconomic outcomes due to genetic endowments should be considered unjust. Our study aims to advance our understanding of the role of genes in explaining social inequalities by examining whether their relationship with socioeconomic  outcomes  is  moderated  by  societal  characteristics.  To  estimate  interactions between genes and the environment, natural experiments, which induce exogenous variation in the environment, need to be employed (Schmitz and Conley 2015).

When examining why people differ in their socioeconomic outcomes, the literature has traditionally distinguished between two components: heritability and environmental factors. The first speaks to the variance in socioeconomic outcomes that is attributable to the genetic endowments of a person, whereas the second has to do with the context in which a person grows up. This strict dichotomy has been questioned by more recent research that suggests that there is an ongoing interaction between the genes and the environment where a person lives. This has opened the door to the exploration of the gene-environment interactions (GxE) (ScarrSalapatek 1971; Rowe et al. 1999; Guo and Stearns 2002; Ayorech et al. 2017; Ronda et al. 2022; Ghirardi and Bernardi 2023).

An important realization of the GxE research has been that people growing up in more and less disadvantaged contexts are unequally likely to develop the potential associated with

their genetic configurations (Scarr-Salapatek 1971; Rowe et al. 1999; Turkheimer et al. 2015). However,  a  constraint  of  this  literature  is  that  it  shows  a  narrow  understanding  of  the environment, usually associated with the family in which an individual is raised. Some recent studies suggested that the impact of genetic predispositions on socioeconomic outcomes might also depend on the broader societal, economic, and cultural contexts (Colodro-Conde et al. 2015; Engzell and Tropf 2019; Lin 2020; Lahtinen et al. 2023).

We expand this research avenue by focusing on a very specific societal change, namely the Education Act of 1944 in England, which increased the compulsory schooling of children by one year and ensured free secondary education for all students up to age 15. We implement a regression discontinuity design (RDD) to exploit the cut-off produced by the reform and use ELSA  data,  which  combines  genetic  information  on  individuals'  predisposition  towards education,  namely  the  polygenic  index  for  educational  attainment  (PGI),  with  measures  of individuals' socioeconomic outcomes across three dimensions: education, income, and wealth.

Results show evidence of a reduction in the association between genes on socioeconomic outcomes due to the Education Act of 1944 in  England. This can be explained either by  a compositional  change  towards  a  more  heterogeneous  selection  of  individuals  attaining education (Martschenko et al. 2019), or by the saturation of educational levels, as suggested by the maximally maintained inequality theory (Raftery and Hout 1993; Lin 2020). Moreover, the Education  Act  of  1944  was  especially  beneficial  for  individuals  with  a  lower  genetic predisposition towards education, as compared to  their better-endowed counterparts. At the same time, our findings show that the relationship between family SES and socioeconomic outcomes remained unaffected by the reform.

We  interpret  the  finding  of  a  decrease  in  the  role  of  the  PGI  of  education  for socioeconomic outcomes as evidence of an increase in equality of opportunity in England after the Education Act of 1944, viewed through the lens of luck egalitarianism: By reducing the

association between genes and socioeconomic outcomes, it enabled individuals with a lower genetic predisposition towards education to stay longer in school. Our interpretation contrasts with that of Lahtinen et al. (2024). These authors found an increase in the association between genes and education after an educational reform, which in their case affected tracking, and interpreted  this  as  an  overall  improvement  of  equality  of  opportunity.  However,  only  fair equality of opportunity, grounded on the notion that individuals with the same abilities should have similar socioeconomic outcomes (Rawls 1971; Breen and Jonsson 2005), was improved.

From the perspective of luck egalitarian equality of opportunity, factors beyond someone's control that impact socioeconomic outcomes are considered as unjust (Roemer 1998; Arneson 2018;).  For  instance,  Cohen  (2008:  18)  described  the  luck  egalitarian  view  of  equality  of opportunity as follows: 'inequalities are just if and only if they reflect patterns of choice, and of failures to choose, on the part of the people among whom the inequality prevails.' This view can  be  applied  to  genetic  endowments.  An  individual  has  no  choice  over  the  genetic endowments she or he is born with. Therefore, from the luck egalitarian perspective, it is unjust if  genetic endowments affect life chances, a point explicitly made by Harden (2021)  in her influential book on The Genetic Lottery .

Thus, we interpret the reduction in the role of the PGI of education for socioeconomic outcomes after reform as an increase equality of opportunity from the perspective of the luck egalitarian approach. At the same time, the association between family SES and socioeconomic outcomes was not changed by the reform,  underscoring  that  the  reform  did  not  reduce  all sources of inequality in socioeconomic outcomes.

The main empirical contribution of the present study is to examine whether the effects of genetic endowments on socioeconomic outcomes are weaker or stronger once there is a macrosocietal  change  such  as  an  educational  reform  that  increases  compulsory  schooling  and abolishes school fees at the secondary level. We expand previous research in three ways: (I.)

Differently from previous studies relying on twin models (Colodro-Conde et al. 2015), we use direct genetic measures, namely polygenic indices; (ii.) Instead of exploring the evolution of the  role  of  genes  over  cohorts  (Lahtinen  et  al.  2023),  we  exploit  a  natural  experiment,  the Education Act of 1944 in England, which allows us to disentangle the moderating effect of an educational  reform  that  increased  education  from  other  societal  and  cultural  changes;  (iii.) While Barcellos et al. (2018) examine a similar question for health outcomes, we account for three different measures of socioeconomic outcomes, namely education, income, and wealth. The main theoretical contribution of our study is that we provide a deeper insight into the role of genes for equality of opportunity by incorporating the luck egalitarian perspective.


## Theoretical Background


Interactions Between Genes and the Environment in Affecting Socioeconomic Outcomes Understanding  the  extent to which  their genetic endowments  matter  for  individuals' socioeconomic outcomes has recently become one of the crucial questions in social science research (Conley 2016). Although most studies agree that genes matter, there are differences in the magnitudes of their role based on several environmental factors (Branigan et al., 2013). This has sparked the emergence of the gene-environment interaction (GxE) literature.

The  first  approach  to  the  idea  that  the  importance  of  genetic  factors  on  educational outcomes could depend on the specific context was Scarr-Salapatek (1971). This study showed that the increase in educational opportunity across time boosted the dependence of educational outcomes on genes. Similarly, Rowe et al. (1999) found that among U.S. twins and siblings, those coming from high socioeconomic backgrounds were more influenced by their genetic predispositions. This idea is now widely known as the Scarr-Rowe hypothesis.

Later  attempts  to  test  this  hypothesis  showed  mixed  support,  as  pointed  out  in  the comprehensive review by Ghirardi & Bernardi (2023). A meta-analysis by Tucker-Drob and

Bates (2016) concluded that there were large cross-national differences in how much genes mattered  and  for  whom.  For  instance,  Guo  &  Stearns  (2002)  found  that,  among  the  U.S. population, the heritability was suppressed in disadvantaged families. Ronda et al. (2022) also found that children from deprived contexts in Denmark were less likely to develop their genetic potential. However, other studies found that the role of genetic factors was actually stronger among low-SES (i.e., Asbury et al., 2005 in the UK; or Lin, 2020 in the U.S.). For instance, Ayorech et al. (2017) showed that individuals born in disadvantaged families could experience upward mobility when they had a positive genetic predisposition to do so. Finally, some studies found no moderation effects (i.e., Conley et al., 2015; Isungset et al., 2022; Sluis et al., 2008).

How the Societal Context May Moderate the Relationship Between Genes and Socioeconomic Outcomes

Most of the existing research examining GxE interactions focused on whether the relationship between the genetic endowments and socioeconomic outcomes varied regarding the specific micro-context of the individual during childhood. This means that an individual's environment was generally understood in terms of the socioeconomic background of the family, migration status,  or  gender.  This  can  be  considered  as  a  narrow  (or  atomistic)  approach  to  the environment. However, some researchers expanded this understanding of the environment to include  broader  societal  characteristics,  such  as  gender,  cohort,  and  life  course  differences (Herd et al., 2019).

The first study to do so was Heath et al. (1985). The authors used a Norwegian twin panel and compared the influence of genetic factors before and after several societal and educational changes were implemented after the Second World War. They found that there was more room for  genetic  influences  after World War II. A more recent paper by Engzell  & Tropf (2019) explored whether what they  called 'the balance of  nature and nurture' was different when

intergenerational mobility was higher at the societal level. They found that, in contexts with higher intergenerational mobility, the proportion of the variance explained by genetic factors remained mostly constant, whereas the family environment was less explicative of the total variance in educational attainment.

However,  a  constraint  of  these  studies  was  that  they  did  not  include  direct  genetic measures but relied on the shared genetic configurations by twins. There are several limitations linked to these designs. First, as Liu (2018) explains in detail, these models require very strong and sometimes unrealistic assumptions. Second, family studies limit the potential exploration of the mechanisms underlying genetic influences (Engzell & Tropf, 2019). Finally, the use of genome-wide association study (GWAS) allows a higher accuracy in interpreting how much of the educational attainment is due to genetic factors (Lee et al., 2018).

Therefore, instead of relying on clusters of genetically related individuals such as twins or  siblings,  more  recent  research  has  used  direct  measures  of  genetic  influences. A  good example  is  Lin  (2020),  who  hypothesized  that  the  importance  of  genes  for  educational outcomes  was  dependent  on  the  historical  context.  Lin  (2020)  compared  the  association between the polygenic index for education and the educational attainment of individuals from different cohorts (1920-1959) in the United States and found partial evidence of the fact that when societies become more equal, the association between genes and educational attainment increased. Rimfeld et al. (2018) took a similar approach but focused on a different societal change,  the  end  of  the  Soviet  Union  in  Estonia.  Their  results  showed  that  the  end  of  the communist  regime  led  to  an  increase  in  the  percentage  of  variance  explained  by  genetic components.

In  a  similar  line,  Lahtinen  et  al.  (2023)  explored  how  secular  changes  that  increased educational  opportunities  impacted  the  balance  between  environment  and  heritability  in Finland. This study compared cohorts across time (from 1925 to 1989), with the underlying

assumption that, since the educational system expanded widely during those decades, it was more likely that the variation in education attributed to the environment decreased. Their results showed  a  curvilinear  pattern  in  the  association  between  the  PGI  for  education  and  final educational  attainment.  Relatedly,  Herd  et  al.  (2019)  examined  whether  the  realization  of women's genetic endowments increased as the structure of opportunities for women expanded. They found  that  with  the  expansion  of  women's  education  over  the  1970s  and  1980s,  the relationship between women's genetic endowments and their educational attainment became stronger.

While using direct measures of genetic endowments represents an improvement over analyses involving siblings or twins, a key limitation persists in this body of literature: It relies on broad observations of societal  trends over  time  instead of specific societal changes. By focusing on overarching historical trends rather than specific societal shifts, these studies were not able to isolate the impact of a specific macro-level change on the relationship between genes and socioeconomic outcomes.

Therefore, most research so far does not identify a causal effect of the environment on the  association  between  genes  and  socioeconomic  outcomes.  Schmitz  and  Conley  (2017) argued that 'current GxE studies are often unable to support causal inference because they use endogenous  measures  of  the  environment  or  fail  to  adequately  address  the  nonrandom distribution  of  genes  across  environments,  confounding  estimates.'  (p.  10).  To  isolate  the causal effect of the GxE interactions, researchers need to employ quasi-natural experimental designs based on exogenous environmental shocks.

There are two main examples of this practice. First, the recent work by Lahtinen et al. (2024), which examined whether an educational reform which postponed tracking from age 11 to  16  in  Finland  increased  the  association  between  the  polygenic  index  of  education  and educational attainment. The study found some partial evidence that the reform increased the

strength of the association between PGI and educational attainment for those exposed to the reform. This effect was concentrated among men and individuals from lower SES backgrounds.

Second, Barcellos et al. (2018) examined whether the association between genes and health was moderated by an educational policy that increased schooling by one year in England, Scotland and Wales in 1972. This study found that the association between genes and health outcomes was lower for those who were exposed to the reform. Moreover, the positive effect of  additional  schooling  was  especially  concentrated  among  those  with  a  higher  genetic predisposition to health problems.

Our  present  study  aims  to  expand  this  literature  by  asking  whether  the  association between genes and socioeconomic outcomes varies when there is an educational reform that increases the length of compulsory schooling and abolishes school fees at the secondary level. Reforms in  the  length  of  compulsory  schooling  involve  a  substantial  increase  in  access  to educational opportunities, aiming to boost educational attainment levels and  to improve the overall educational environment (Shavit and Westerbeek 1998; Araki 2020). This shift provides an ideal scenario for examining the extent to which genetic factors contribute to socioeconomic outcomes in the context of enlarged environmental opportunities.

There  are  two  studies  which  have  examined  the  impact  of  increased  compulsory schooling on the relationship between genetic endowments and life outcomes. First, ColodroConde  et  al.  (2015)  examined  whether  the  relative  role  of  genetic  differences  and  shared environment in explaining educational attainment varied as a result of the 1970 educational reform in Spain. The authors used a genetically informed twin design, with the underlying logic that if genetic factors matter more than environmental factors, monozygotic twins will resemble more between them than dizygotic twins. Their results showed that the role of genetic factors increased in the post-reform cohorts. However, as mentioned above, an important limitation of

this study was that it lacked a direct examination of the genetic configuration and relied on the shared genes between twins.

In  a  recent  working  paper,  Ahlskog  et  al.  (2024)  studied  the  impact  of  a  Swedish educational reform that extended compulsory schooling by two years. Despite conducting over 100 tests across various PGIs, outcomes, and subpopulations, the authors found only partial effects of the reform (i.e., out of the 20 outcomes they study, the reform only had a significant impact  on  4  of  them).  Their  results  reveal  a  negative  interaction  between  the  PGI  for educational attainment  and the reform on  the  likelihood of obtaining  at  least  a junior high school degree, observed only among females. They interpret this as evidence that the reform primarily benefited individuals at the lower end of the educational distribution.

Our study builds on this literature by examining how an educational reform that increased compulsory schooling in England and guaranteed universal access to free secondary education (the Education Act of 1944) moderated the relationship between genetic endowments and three dimensions of socioeconomic outcomes: education, income, and wealth.


## Hypotheses


Our  first  set  of  hypotheses  concerns  how  an  educational  reform  increasing  the  length  of compulsory  schooling  may  change  the  relationship  between  genes  and  socioeconomic outcomes.  If,  as  suggested  by  some  of  the  previous  studies  (Colodro-Conde  et  al.  2015; Lahtinen et al. 2024), an increase in compulsory schooling implies that students have more chances to develop their genetic endowments, we would expect that the association between genetic configurations and socioeconomic outcomes will increase following a rise in the length of compulsory schooling (Hypothesis 1a).

A competing possibility is that, in the context of the educational reform increasing the length of compulsory schooling, the selectivity of the education system is lower, which implies

that it is more likely that individuals with a lower genetic predisposition towards education will stay in school, and the salience of the genotype for education will be reduced (Martschenko et al. 2019). This compositional change towards more genetic heterogeneity would imply that the association between genetic configurations and socioeconomic outcomes will be reduced after an  educational  reform  which  lengthens  compulsory  schooling (Hypothesis  1b). A  further reason, why this hypothesis may be true, is that lower levels of education can be saturated for children with a high genetic predisposition for education, so that the reform may only increase education among those with a low genetic predisposition towards education (Raftery and Hout 1993; Lin 2020).

The  second  set  of  hypotheses  refers  to  how  an  educational  reform  may  affect  the association between family SES and socioeconomic outcomes, a topic which has already been studied by previous research (Sturgis and Buscha 2015; Grätz 2022). This research was usually motivated by the idea that primarily students from socioeconomically disadvantaged families profited from an increase in educational opportunities due to a reform in the minimum school leaving  age.  Following  this  logic, the  association  between  family  SES  and  socioeconomic outcomes will decrease in the presence of an increase in the length of compulsory schooling (Hypothesis 2a). This intuition is further supported by the maximally maintained inequality hypothesis, which posits that the expansion of higher education seeks to reduce the association between family SES and educational attainment by broadening opportunities for  everyone. However, it could also be that children from socioeconomically advantaged families, who have not achieved a high level of education before the reform, profited most  from a reform that increased the minimum school leaving age. If this process was dominant, we would expect the association between family SES and socioeconomic outcomes to increase in the presence of an educational reform increasing the length of compulsory schooling (Hypothesis 2b).

Finally,  we  can  also  develop  hypotheses  on  how  the  relationship  between  genes  and family SES changes jointly because of the Education Act of 1944. One possibility is that the most advantaged individuals, namely the individuals with high genetic predisposition towards education from high SES families, benefit the most from the reform. This would mean that the association between genetic predispositions and family SES would be boosted in the context of an increase in the length of compulsory schooling (Hypothesis 3a). Alternatively, the Education Act of 1944 might offer more opportunities to individuals with varying genetic predispositions and from different SES backgrounds, who otherwise would have struggled to develop their potential fully. In this scenario, the reform increasing the length of compulsory schooling would diminish  the  association  between  genes  and  SES  in  determining  socioeconomic  outcomes (Hypothesis 3b).


## The 1944 Educational Act in England


We exploit the Education Act of 1944 in England to isolate the moderating effect produced by a change in the length of compulsory schooling and the implementation of universal access to free secondary education on the relationship between genetic predispositions and socioeconomic outcomes. The Education Act of 1944, commonly referred to as the Butler Act, was the beginning of a transformative era in the education system of post-war Britain (GalindoRueda, 2003). Its primary aim was to ensure universal access to free secondary education for all  British  children up  to the age of 15 . As a  consequence, from April 1947, the minimum i school leaving age increased by one year from 14 to 15 (Del Bono and Galindo-Rueda 2004). The first cohort fully affected by this reform was the 1934 cohort (Sabates and Duckworth 2010). It is important to notice that secondary education was made accessible to all schools funded and managed by Local Education Authorities, which also applied to grammar schools.

In terms of impact, the reform was responsible for an increase in two million students between the end of the Second World War and the 1970s. Oreopoulos (2006) suggested that the percentage of 14-year-olds leaving school fell from 57% to less than 10%. In the long term, the reform had a positive effect on schooling and earnings (Clark & Cummins, 2020; Harmon & Walker, 1995; Oreopoulos, 2006). However, research found null results when looking at other outcomes such as mortality rates (Clark & Royer, 2013) or children's health (Lindeboom et al. 2009).

A common inquiry when examining reforms impacting the minimum school leaving age is to establish who gained the most from the change. Harmon & Walker (1995) asserted that the  Butler Act  boosted  particularly  the  participation  in  post-compulsory  education  among individuals who would have otherwise exited the system at age 14. Also according to GalindoRueda (2003),  the  increase  in  children's  school  participation  favoured  mainly  those  at  the bottom of the educational distribution, because of the types of schools that were opened.

Furthermore, it is important to emphasize that while the goal of raising the  minimum school  leaving  age  may  have  been  to  guarantee  greater  access  to  education  for  children, particularly those from disadvantaged families, expanding access to education can also lead to unintended effects, such  as increased heterogeneity in polygenic  indices and further compositional changes. These shifts, in turn, may influence the relationship between genetic predispositions and socioeconomic outcomes, even if this was not an intended objective of the reform.

## Main Findings


Individuals  with  a  higher  genetic  predisposition  for  education  and  those  from  higher socioeconomic backgrounds tend to achieve more years of education, as well as greater income and  wealth. This  pattern  is  evident  in  the  baseline  models  shown  in Table A2 ,  before  any interaction  effects  are  considered.  The  coefficient  of  the  PGI  for  educational  attainment  is consistently higher for years education than for income or wealth, which aligns with the fact that we are specifically using the PGI for educational attainment, as PGIs for income or wealth are not available in our data. Moreover, this result is  consistent with prior evidence showing that  the  PGI  for  educational  attainment  is  associated  with  a  wide  range  of  socioeconomic outcomes  on  top  of  educational  attainment  (Belsky  et  al.  2018).  The  main  effect  of  the educational  reform  remains  positive  and  statistically  significant  for  educational  attainment,

consistent with Table 1 . However, when additional covariates are included, the reform's effect on income and wealth loses statistical significance. This aligns with previous research that has found educational reforms to have a limited impact on earnings (Meghir and Palme 2005).

This gives support to the idea that increasing the length of compulsory schooling by one year and implementing universal free secondary education reduces the relation between genes and socioeconomic outcomes.

Robustness Checks and Sensitivity Analyses

We re-run the analyses using the bandwidth selection suggested by the algorithm developed by Calonico et al. (2020). Table A3 in the Supplementary Materials shows that these findings are completely consistent with the main results: There is a positive association between the PGI for  education  and  socioeconomic outcomes, but this association is significantly smaller  for

those who experienced the reform.  In all cases, and as expected given the reduction in the sample size, the resulting estimates for these models are smaller in magnitude than the ones from the main analyses.

We implement a series of placebo tests using arbitrary cut-offs to examine whether the discontinuities in the associations between the PGI for education and socioeconomic outcomes also occur at other thresholds (3 and 5 years before and after the original cutoff). These results ( Table A4 ) show that there are no significant differences in the associations between the PGI for education and  socioeconomic  outcomes  when  the  cut-off  is  established at other discretionary thresholds. Therefore, we can be assured that the observed effect of the reform is not spurious or random. If they were so, we would have observed similar effects using these arbitrary cut-offs.

Table A5 presents the results stratified by gender. The negative interaction term between the PGI and the reform, observed in the main results, is only present for men when we look at years of education, for both genders in terms of income, and exclusively for women regarding wealth. Interestingly, the interaction between PGI and SES indicates that high-SES women benefit the most from a high PGI (as compared to low SES). In the case of men's income, we also observe a significant three-way interaction between PGI, SES, and the reform. Figure A4 illustrates  this  relationship,  suggesting  that  among  men,  those  from  lower  socioeconomic backgrounds exhibit particularly low income in the absence of the reform. However, the reform appears to have an equalizing effect, resulting in more similar income levels among individuals with varying PGI and family SES.

Given the age range of our sample (over 50 years old), it would be possible that  our results are affected by selection due to mortality. For instance, if individuals with higher PGIs live longer, they might be overrepresented in the oldest cohorts including in our analysis. We partially account for this in our optimal bandwidth results. To be reassured, we plot the average

PGI by cohort in Figure A5 , which shows that, although with some fluctuation over time, there are no statistically significant differences among the eldest and youngest cohorts in their PGIs.

We also follow Domingue et al. (2017) and apply inverse probability weighting (IPW) to account  for  mortality  selection  before  the  genetic  data  was  collected  from  the  ELSA participants. The results are presented in Table A6 , which details the variables used to compute the weights, primarily related to the participants' health in the first wave. Our findings show that for education and income, the estimates remain consistent with our main results. However, for wealth, we find that the interaction between the PGI and the reform is no longer statistically significant after applying IPW, although the relationship still shows the expected direction and magnitude. This outcome can be interpreted in several ways. First, since the coefficient for wealth was already smaller, the stricter model specifications required for IPW might explain the loss of statistical significance. Second, from a theoretical perspective, higher mortality risks could limit the time available for individuals to accumulate wealth, leading to more pronounced differences in wealth across mortality risk categories. In contrast, income and education are less sensitive to mortality risk-income reflects shorter-term earnings, and education is usually a fixed characteristic after a certain age-meaning that selection on mortality has a smaller effect on them.

Our main findings are also robust to a binary specification of the outcome variable in the case of education, namely attaining tertiary education or not, instead of the original years of education. These results are presented in Table A7 as average marginal effects (AMEs). The average marginal effect of PGI on the probability of obtaining a tertiary education degree for those exposed to the reform is 5.6%, compared to 7.8% for those not exposed to the reform. This is consistent with the idea that the reform diminished the relative importance of PGI for the respondents' educational attainment in the long term.

Interpreting  interaction  results  requires  consideration  of  whether  the  sample  size  is sufficient  to  detect  an  effect.  To  address  this,  we  conducted  a  series  of  power  analyses  to determine if our data is adequately powered to observe interactions. In the absence of previous literature to guide effect size choice, we used Cohen's d classification, calculating power for effect sizes of 0.5 and 0.3. The results, detailed in Table A8 , consistently show power levels above 0.8, indicating that the data should be sufficiently powered to detect the interactions of interest across all models, including the three-way interactions.

We account for the possibility of a non-linear relationship between the PGI for education and the reform for income and wealth vi . In Table A9 , we introduce an interaction term between the squared value of the PGI for education and the reform. Our findings reveal a quadratic relationship between the PGI for education and income, indicating that while the association between the PGI for education and income is generally positive, the relationship weakens at higher levels of the PGI. Moreover, the negative and significant interaction term between the square of the PGI and the reform suggests that after the reform, this weakening effect is even more  pronounced.  In  other  words,  the  educational  reform  reduces  the  strength  of  the relationship between the PGI for education and income, especially at higher levels of PGI. We do not find, however, any evidence of a non-linear relationship for wealth.

Although in all our models we include controls for time trends, it is also possible that the time trends were non-linear. Thus, we replicate our main models with additional controls for quadratic and cubic time trends. These results, presented in Table A10 , demonstrate that our primary findings remain robust, even after incorporating non-linear time trends.

Finally, we extend our analysis by including the 1933 cohort among the treated groups. While this cohort was initially excluded because the reform's implementation was only partial in  that  year,  a  substantial  proportion  of  students  were  nonetheless  affected  by  the  reform, making their inclusion an important consideration. The results, shown in Table A11 , reveal that

even  with  this  conservative  definition  of  the  treated  group-which  may  encompass  some individuals  who  were  not  fully  exposed  to  the  reform-the  findings  remain  robust  and consistent with our main results.


## Discussion and Conclusion


Determining how genes contribute to socioeconomic outcomes alongside the environment has become one of the central challenges for the literature on equality of opportunity. In this study, we  have  provided  evidence  on  how  the  relationship  between  genes  and  socioeconomic outcomes varies in the context of an educational reform that increased the minimum school leaving age by one year and abolished school fees at the secondary school level in England.

There  are  two  central  findings.  First,  the  reform  led  to  a  decrease  in  the  association between  genes  and  socioeconomic  outcomes.  This  is  reflected  by  the  negative  interaction between PGI and the reform for all three outcomes (education, income, and wealth). Second, there is an absence of a significant interaction between SES and the educational reform, which suggests  that  the  association  between  family  SES  and  the  socioeconomic  outcomes  of education, income, and wealth did not diminish following the reform.

In terms of the explanation of these results, there are two main avenues we consider. First, we  follow  Lin  (2020),  who  interpreted  similar  findings  using  the  maximally  maintained inequality (MMI) hypothesis (Raftery and Hout 1993). The MMI framework states that with the  educational  expansion,  a  particular  level  of  education  gets  saturated  (i.e.,  all  high-SES children attain that level of education), and therefore, the relative advantage of achieving that educational level decreases. Therefore, we could expect to see more inequality at later, not saturated,  levels  of  education.  For  the  specific  case  of  our  results,  and  in  the words  of  Lin (2020) 'if the effect of genes is regarded as meritocratic ability, when levels of education are saturated, genetic influence might also decline.' (p. 15). Our findings regarding the reduced

role of genes are consistent with the MMI hypothesis. However, the absence of any change in the association between family SES and socioeconomic outcomes before and after the reform contradicts the MMI hypothesis, which predicts that the association between family SES and these outcomes would decrease when educational opportunities are expanded for all.

Another potential explanation for our PGI results is that there has been a compositional change in the population who continued in the educational system post-reform, given the lower selectivity  of  the  system.  This  means  that  whereas  in  the  pre-reform  era,  the  group  of individuals could be more selected in terms of their genetic propensity for education, more diverse students can now access later educational levels. This would introduce heterogeneity in the level of the PGI for education in the post-reform cohorts, which could reduce the intensity of its association with final educational outcomes. To test this idea further, we computed the variance of the PGI for education for cohorts exposed and not exposed to the reform. Among the cohorts not exposed to the reform (born 1922-1932), the variance of the PGI for education is 0.907, while for the exposed cohorts (born 1934-1944), the variance of the PGI for education increases to 1.056. We conducted an F-test to compare the variances of these two groups and found the difference to be statistically significant. This suggests that the decline in the relevance of PGIs post-reform may be due to increased heterogeneity in the distribution of the PGI for education, driven by broader access to education. Given that support for the MMI hypothesis is only partial, we are more inclined to explain our results in terms of a compositional change, where shifts in the population's characteristics provide a better explanation for the observed patterns.

In the case of wealth and income, the post-reform cohorts exhibit a very small effect size of  the  PGI  for  years  of  education-0.026  for  income  and  0.073  for  wealth-especially  in contrast to the effect size for education, which is 0.386. We believe these smaller effect sizes align with theories of diminishing returns to education: Expanding access to education provides

greater opportunities for individuals with lower genetic predispositions, but it also reduces the long-term influence of these genetic predispositions on income and wealth. This occurs because educational attainment becomes more uniformly distributed across the population, diminishing its role in driving the variability in long-term socioeconomic outcomes. Additionally, the PGI for education used in our analysis is directly tied to educational attainment, but its connection to income and wealth is more indirect, which may further explain the smaller observed effects. Finally,  while  genetic  configurations  and  education  are  measured  at  the  individual  level, income  and  wealth  are  family-level  measures.  This  introduces  the  potential  influence  of assortative mating, which could impact income and wealth outcomes but cannot be accounted for in our analysis due to data limitations.

Our findings regarding the lack of change in the role of family SES following the reform align with previous studies that report similar results in the context of educational reforms that raised  the  minimum school  leaving age and impacted the intergenerational transmission of education  (Grätz  2022;  Espadafor  and  García-Sierra  2024). A  possible  explanation  for  this finding  is  that  the  intergenerational  transmission  of  education  is  primarily  influenced  by external factors, rather than those within the school system. As Grätz (2023) points out, this aligns with classical sociological research highlighting the family's role in the persistence of educational inequalities across generations, regardless of reforms aimed at improving access or opportunity within the school system (Coleman et al. 1966; Jencks et al. 2014). This finding also emphasizes that the interplay between genetic and environmental influences should not be viewed as a zero-sum game, where a decrease in the role of genes automatically translates into an increase in the role of family SES.

The observed decrease in the role of the PGI for education after the reform is consistent with  some  studies,  while  contradicting  others.  First,  our  findings  diverge  from  those  of Colodro-Conde  et  al.  (2015)  who  observed  an  increase  in  the  heritability  of  educational

attainment following the 1970 educational reform in Spain. Several differences between their study and ours may account for these diverging outcomes. First, they employed twin models rather  than  direct  measures  of  genetic  propensities.  Second,  their  results  suggest  that  the benefits  of  the  Spanish  reform  primarily  fell  on  those  already  inclined  towards  primary education (namely men). However, the Education Act of 1944 in England notably favoured individuals who were less predisposed to remain in education. According to Galindo-Rueda (2003), these individuals were students positioned at the lower end of the distribution in a series of ability tests taken.

Second, our findings are also at odds with those of Lahtinen et al. (2024), who found that the association between genetic endowments and education strengthened (among men) after an educational reform in Finland. An important difference between their study and ours has to do with the  character of  the  reform  exploited: The Finnish comprehensive reform school they examine postponed tracking from age 11 to age 16, whereas the 1944 education act in England increased the minimum school leaving age from 14 to 15 years old. We know from previous literature that the reforms suppressing early tracking are especially beneficial for high-ability children from low-SES (van de Werfhorst 2018), whereas the effects of the Education Act in 1944 in England was concentrated among low-ability children (Galindo-Rueda 2003).

Third, our findings align with Barcellos et al. (2018), who  found a decreasing association between the PGI of BMI on health outcomes after the 1972 educational reform in England. The congruency between these and our findings is relevant for two reasons. First, this study also focuses on the English case (although it used a later educational reform). Second, it is, to the best of our knowledge, the most similar study to ours in terms of design, since it exploits a school leaving age educational reform, accounts for PGIs, and implements an RDD.

Fourth, our results are also partially in line with some papers exploiting variation across cohorts, instead of reforms. For instance, Okbay  et al. (2016) showed  that the explanatory

power of the PGI for educational attainment for educational attainment decreased over birth cohorts in Sweden, which the authors suggested could be related to the increase in compulsory education  in  the  1950s  and  1960s.  Conley  &  Domingue  (2016),  also  found  a  declining association  between  the  PGI  for  educational  attainment  and  educational  attainment  across cohorts in the U.S. for most of the educational transitions.

Likewise, Lahtinen et al. (2023) found that the association between PGI and education decreased in the latest cohorts they observe in Finland, which are precisely the ones exposed to  the  comprehensive  school  reform.  Finally,  although  the  study  by  Lin  (2020)  showed  a positive relationship between PGI for educational attainment and education for most of the cohorts, the exception from this was the last set of cohorts included in the analyses, which overlap with the more universalised access to education in the United States.

Another interpretation of our results is that, among individuals with higher PGIs, the reform does not significantly affect their socioeconomic outcomes. However, among those with lower PGIs, the reform is especially beneficial. This finding is consistent with Barcellos et al. (2018), who find that the most vulnerable group, i.e., those with a higher genetic predisposition to obesity, benefit the most from the educational reform. Our results also confirm the findings by Galindo-Rueda (2003) and Harmon & Walker (1995) about the local average treatment effect  of  the  Education  Act  of  1944  in  England,  which  was  particularly  beneficial  for individuals at the lower end of the ability distribution. Moreover, our results align with Ahlskog et al. (2024), who find that the Swedish reform which increased compulsory schooling also benefited those with lower PGI for education, although only among women in their case.

Two final findings should also be discussed. First, the association between the PGI for educational attainment and education does not vary at different levels of SES in our results, apart from a small positive interaction effect in the case of education. Therefore, for income and wealth, our findings are in line with some previous studies showing null GxE interaction

effects (Conley et al., 2015; Isungset et al., 2022; Sluis et al., 2008). In the case of education, our results provide partial support to the idea that genes expression is more likely in high-SES contexts,  as  suggested  by  the  Scarr-Rowe  hypothesis vii (Scarr-Salapatek  1971;  Rowe  et  al. 1999; Turkheimer et al. 2015). Second, this positive effect of PGI among high-SES individuals does not consistently vary before and after the Education Act of 1944 in England, as shown by the null findings of the three-way interaction (except for males in the case of income).

The substantive interpretation of  our findings speaks to the literature on equality of opportunity. Lahtinen et al. (2024) claim that, because the impact of genes on socioeconomic outcomes increases after the reform in their analyses, 'the reform was successful in achieving its  central  goal  of  increasing  socioeconomic  equality  in  the  educational  system'  (pg.  203). However, we argue that this statement is only true from a liberal understanding of equality of opportunity, which is based on the premise that individuals with the same abilities should enjoy similar socioeconomic outcomes (Rawls 1971; Breen and Jonsson 2005).

However,  according  to  the  competing  luck  egalitarian  approach,  any  factor  that  is beyond an individual's control and affects their socioeconomic outcomes should be considered unfair (Roemer 1998; Arneson 2018; Harden 2021). Thus, since individuals do not have control over their genes, the fact that these become more important in determining their socioeconomic outcomes after an educational reform does not mean that more equality of opportunity was achieved.

Integrating this perspective, we argue that our results should be understood as evidence of  the  fact  that  the  Education Act  of  1944  in  England  increased  the  levels  of  equality  of opportunity from a luck egalitarian perspective: By reducing the association between genes and socioeconomic outcomes, it enabled individuals with less predisposition towards education to  stay  in  school.  Moreover,  the  fact  that  the  reform  was  especially  beneficial  for  those individuals  with  lower  genetic  propensities  towards  education  corroborates  its  equalizing

effect. However, it is important to note that during the same period, the reform did not lead to a reduction in the association between family SES and socioeconomic outcomes.

Our findings particularly align with the institutional luck egalitarianism framework. As Tan (2014) explains, inequalities can be categorized into two types: Natural inequalities that do  not  result  in  institutional  disadvantages,  and  those  where  institutions  transform  natural differences into unjust inequalities. We argue that differences in genetic predisposition towards education fall into  the  latter  category,  as  the  traits  captured  by  PGIs  reflect  institutional  or structural decisions to reward certain traits. From this perspective, the decline in the influence of  the  PGI  for  educational  attainment  following  the  Education  Act  of  1944  reflects  an improvement in the luck egalitarian equality of opportunity.

When interpreting these results, it is essential to recognize that they apply specifically to  compliers-individuals  whose  decision  to  remain  in  school  until  age  15  was  directly influenced by the reform. Thus, our findings represent the Local Average Treatment Effect, estimated through the RDD, which captures the reform's impact on this subgroup. Importantly, this approach assumes that the effect is not confounded by factors such as parental migration or local grammar school policies, as these factors do not systematically vary at the policy cutoff. We believe that focusing on compliers in this study is particularly relevant because both previous literature (Galindo-Rueda 2003) and our findings suggest that the individuals most affected by the reform-those who benefited the most-were those with lower predispositions toward education. Without the reform, these individuals would probably not have remained in education beyond the age of 14.

A limitation of our study is that, for reasons of data availability, we cannot account for parental genes. Therefore, the estimate we are assigning to children's genes can partially belong to their parents' genetic configurations, which have been previously noted to explain around one-third  of  the  association  between  children's  PGI  for  education  and  their  educational

outcomes (Liu 2018). Moreover, while fairly comprehensive, our measure of parental SES is imperfect, as it relies on recall questions answered by ELSA respondents aged 50 and older. This could partially explain the absence of a GxSES interaction in some of our results.

It is also relevant to acknowledge that the PGI for education only accounts for a part of the total heritability of traits (Lahtinen et al. 2024). Similarly, it has been argued that GWASbased studies underestimate the contribution of genes since they only rely on genetic variants which have a large enough association with phenotype to be detected in samples of limited size (Harden 2021). Therefore, this could affect the accuracy of the results, making our estimates conservative measures of the true role of genetic endowments. At the same time, Okbay et al. (2022) concluded that PGI's predictive power is not only the product of direct genetic effects but also of gene-environment correlations at the level of the family. This problem, which is common to most of  the  research  using  PGIs,  implies  that  the  estimates  obtained  could  be overestimating the impact of genes, which is why we interpret the results as indicating the changes in the association between the PGI for education and socioeconomic outcomes due to the Education  Act  of  1944  (similar  to  the  association  between  family  SES  and  the socioeconomic  outcomes,  which  also  does  not  represent  the  causal  effect  of  family  SES). Finally, the PGI for educational attainment has been shown to correlate with a wide range of traits, including those directly related to education, such as learning aptitude, as well as traits influenced by environmental factors, such as interviewers' perceptions (Boardman et al. 2024). Therefore, a direct equivalence between PGIs and students' inherent ability should be avoided when interpreting these results.

On a more general note, it is important to recognize that the predictive power of PGI measures may fluctuate over time, influenced by societal and educational changes that alter which traits are valued in different periods. Therefore, their predictive power may diminish when  applied  to  different  historical  periods.  However,  in  our  RDD  analysis,  this  is  less

concerning since the causal effect of the  Education Act of 1944 is estimated locally at the discontinuity, comparing individuals who are very close to each other in time.

This study has an empirical and a theoretical contribution. In empirical terms, we expand previous literature examining the associations between genes and socioeconomic outcomes by accounting for a major societal change such as an educational reform increasing the minimum school leaving age in England. While past studies have tackled this question using twin models, integrating  genetic measures  enables  a  more  direct  assessment  of  the role of genes. Additionally,  we  build  upon  prior  research  that  examines  environmental  changes  in  the significance of genes over cohorts by exploiting a natural experiment that allows us to isolate their impact from other societal and cultural factors. Furthermore, we expand previous studies by considering three distinct indicators of socioeconomic outcomes.

In terms of the theoretical contribution, we expand the literature on the moderating role of the educational reforms in the relationship between genes and socioeconomic outcomes by offering a more nuanced understanding of equality of opportunity, one that integrates the luck egalitarian perspective from political philosophy.

The findings from this study emphasize that to understand the contribution of genes on socioeconomic outcomes, it is important to consider the broad societal context in which those individuals live.  Inequalities,  therefore,  should  be  understood  as  the  product  of  an  intricate interaction among genetics and micro- and macro-environmental factors.

## 1. Introduction


Protest  stickers, as a form  of  communicative  street art  (Chaffe,  1993;  Clough,  2011;  Hundertmark,  2003; Lewisohn, 2008; Riggle, 2010) are ubiquitous ephemeral objects that can be viewed,  if we  choose  to  'see' them,  mainly  in  urban  areas,  especially  cities  where pedestrianisation is high. Locations such as streetscapes around retail space, the periphery of train and bus stations, and university campuses are all fertile hunting grounds. (Gerbaudo, 2014; Velikonja, 2021). The messages that the stickers convey are decoded or interpreted by the viewer (Hansen and Flynn, 2015; Tedford, 2021; Collins, 2022; Bodden and Awcock, 2024).This individualised interaction with  and  reading  of  the  message  is  reliant  on  the  text, images, culture and symbols being popular in mainstream discourse, for understanding to be internalised and will  already  be  part  of  the  everyday  lexicon  of  ordinary language of the viewer. Of course, we all possess differing linguistic  and  cultural  vocabularies,  so  the  more  subtle the message, the greater the possibility for alienation or reinforcement of ingroup and outgroup bias (Nouri et al, 2017).

This pervasiveness of protest stickering draws on both a cultural and historical dimension of communication. Cave drawings, artefact symbology, paintings recording people, places and events could all be classed as the precursors to the protest sticker (Chaffe, 1993). Somewhat later in the advent of image making, decalcomania (the etymology of the modern 'decal') was invented in the 1800's (McCormick, 2010).  More  contemporary  iterations  of  this  material media  can  still  trace  their  lineage  to  over  one  hundred years ago with the advent of the silent agitators produced by the Industrial Workers of the World which were used to mobilise awareness against poor employment practices and encourage unionisation (Tedford, 2019). Today, protest  stickers  that  seek  to  advance  non  mainstream political  agenda  span  the  political  spectrum  espousing their support for multiple political domains including left wing, anarchist and single issue causes (LASIC); extreme right  wing ideology (XRW); environmental activism (EA) and international conflicts (INTER).

## 2. Theoretical framework


I situate  my  work  on  protest  stickers  within  cultural criminology  and  edgework,  albeit  from  a  disembodied stance.  Lyng's  (1990)  seminal  writings  about  edgework recognised some individuals freely commit illegal acts in pursuit  of  their  interests.  This  concept  was  developed by Ferrell (1998) investigating illegal street art practices, specifically graffiti. In the UK, fly posting, which includes stickering, on any available surface without the permission of the owner, is a criminal offence. Specific laws, namely, the Town and Country Planning Act 1990, The Highways Act  1980  and  the  Anti-Social  Behaviour,  Crime  and Policing  Act  2014  are  all  relevant  in  this  regard.  My disembodied perspective aligns with my fieldwork being undertaken after the stickers had been displayed, without the stickerist being present. Whilst gendered criticisms of edgework being male dominated, such as that posited by Newmahr (2011) are relevant, applying such criticisms to this work without being able to know the gender of the stickerist, would be problematic. I further expand on my cultural criminological situatedness in my methodological section below.

Evaluation and meaning making of protest stickers is an individual construct. When faced with the sticker material, any text included, symbols, pictures and images displayed and  even  online  references  for  further  exploration  (the signifiers) of  the  message  conveyed  (the  signified),  a plethora of information is visible (Sebeok, 2001). Let us explore just one element: a raised fist for instance, which could signify solidarity. To others the fist may represent defiance or even disobedience. How such elements are interpreted  has  often  relied  on  semiotics  to  provide  an explanation. Ferdinand de Saussure and Charles Sanders Peirce  are,  amongst  others,  credited  with  significantly contributing to the study of modern semiotics (Yakin and Totu, 2014). Contemporary works by academics such as Jaworski and Thurlow (2010), Visgo (2010), Reershemius (2019) and Cosmeleata (2022), to cite just a few, have all used  the  semiotic  framework  to  offer  explanations  on protest  stickers.  In  contrast  to  this  approach,  Umberto (1978)  questions  the  sole  use  of  semiotics  to  interpret stickers.  For  instance,  issues  relating  to  interpretative

G

S

variability, cultural and contextual dependency as well as ideological bias from the interpreter have all been raised as limitations of semiotics.

What  additional  approaches  allow  for  protest  sticker evaluation? Rather than viewing stickers as acquiescent, the  interaction  with  stickers  by  the  viewer,  to  construe meaning  can  be  multifaceted  in  response  with  no  set method  of meaning-making. Geographies of protest stickers (Awcock,  2021);  political  stickers  as  a  form of  protest  (Awcock  and  Rosenberg  2023);  and  active subjectivity of sticker meaning-making  (Bodden  and Awcock,  2024)  are  such  alternative  approaches.  The celebrated sticker artist Shepard Fairey (2010, p.9) states  'the  more  I  put  up  stickers,  the  more  I  thought about  how  they  created  interactions  and  how  these differed from the interactions people typically have with urban environments'. In addition, Betancourt  (2010, p.283) states stickers 'introduce elements that promote reflection, reaction, or offer passers-by a space in which to engage with ubiquitous urban advertisements'. This is not to suggest that every sticker has such active processes of engagement. Clough (2011, p.9) identifies that 'people coexist  with  stickers  every  day,  but  most  were  totally unaware  of  their  existence'.  In  support  of  this,  Invader (2019,  p.9)  discusses  sticker  awareness  and  recognises that 'only about one in a thousand might notice them'.

For those  that are aware  of  protest  stickers, what theoretical  framework  would  lend  the  most  value  for analysis? I believe that a conflation of semiotics and the active subjectivity of viewing stickers in action, would offer a rounded approach. Semiotic analysis can be undertaken in isolation and without active subjectivity however active subjectivity  needs  to  coexist  with  semiotics.  Therefore, I  posit  that  the  conflated  lens  of  semiotics  and  active subjectivity  is  my  theoretical  framework  of  choice  for protest sticker analysis.


## 3. Methodology


In this section I try to provide a thick description (Geertz, 1973) of my endeavours or, as I have since come to, quite literally and figuratively term it, a rich picture of my work. The  ethnographic  fieldwork  I  undertook  to  gather  my primary data occurred between January 2022 and June 2024 around the publicly accessible areas of the Clifton campus  of  the  University  of  Bristol  which  is  located  in the  southwest of England. I undertook once fortnightly tours  of  a  quarter  mile  radius  spanning  outwards  from a central building known  as  Senate  House,  visually documenting, by photographing using my mobile phone camera,  new  findings  of  protest  stickers  with  date  and location.  Once  saved  I  would  add  a  quick  footnote  to each picture offering my initial interpretation of political doctrine that I believed the sticker promoted, along with any other pertinent information. I undertook this process usually  commencing  at  0800  hours  so  consistency  of both my geographical movements and daylight during the darker winter months was achieved. Each tour lasted one hour. During the thirty months undertaking the fieldwork I  committed sixty five hours to the research. I began to notice which stickers were no longer present and which had  started  to  weather.  I  also  became  aware  of  those stickers that had been partially removed or defaced. What I was not aware of were any stickers that were placed and removed in between my fortnightly tours. I will return to this later.

I  utilised  the  consistent  morning approach to try and remain as unobtrusive as possible (Webb et al, 1966; Kellehear, 1993). However, data gatherings were not always achieved on the first sighting of a new sticker. Occasionally I had to loiter close to the new find, pretending to be interacting with  my  phone  or  simply  sitting  on  a  nearby  bench  or wall drinking my coffee to try not to arouse curiosity of others who were transiting through the locality. Most of the  time  this  patient  approach  paid  off  although  there were a few occasions when my days' commitments were fast approaching and I undertook the best discreet shot I could obtain whilst walking slowly past the new offering. Where  this  occurred  and  the  text  was  not  entirely  in focus, I added an additional footnote to the saved picture replicating the text in case of any future ambiguity during subsequent analysis.

The sites of data were attached to the exterior of buildings, street furniture and areas of buildings that allowed public access at the university campus, which is integrated into

G

S

the  local  community.  The  street  furniture  consisted  of litter  bins,  lampposts, street signs, postboxes and utility structures. The external areas of buildings examined were those accessible to the public and were either building or periphery walls. The areas of buildings that allowed public access  were  cafes  and  entrance  spaces.  I  recorded  235 protest stickers and these were categorised into one of the four political domains of LASIC, XRW, EA and INTER. In  terms of data, I have categorised 143 as LASIC; 7 as XRW; 54 as EA, and 31 as INTER. By photographically recording each fluid moment in time, the context of each protest sticker is archived for future semiotic and active subjectivity analysis. This approach captures the essence of  the  moment  to  enable  the  process  of  analysis  to  be undertaken (Reershemius, 2019).

I am conscious that my field research of protest stickers, and  my  role  documenting  such,  will  be  subjective  and formed from my own perspective. Within the established methodologies  of  cultural  criminological  and  edgework fieldwork, such subjective accounts can be both critical and reflexive whilst still providing a fervent narrative. This has been encapsulated by Weber (1978, p.4) and his concept of criminological verstehen detailing 'interpretative understanding and sympathetic participation'. My establishing of a rapport with each of the protest stickers will  assist  with  my  understanding  and  analysis  of  the criminal  act  of  displaying  each  sticker.  Or,  put  another way  and  to  quote  Geertz  (1973,  p.5)  'my  analysis  of  it to  be  therefore  not  an  experimental  science  in  search of  law  but  an  interpretative  one  in  search  of  meaning'. My objectivity is achieved by my careful and consistent data gathering whilst my emotional attachment, semiotic interpretation and analysis is, as per my research design, purely subjective.

My  shift  in  status  from  a  casual  observer  of  protest stickers  to  a  primary  data  collector  in  January  2022 was centred around one incident. On spotting three far right stickers, two on a lamppost and one on a litter bin, without applying a critical lens, I set about removing them as  quickly  as  I  could  and  depositing  them  in  the  same litter bin that was displaying. This was the first time I had removed any sticker. The stickers were #IOTBW, 88 and

Hundred Handers. It was only later when reflecting on the finds that I began to think deeply on my actions. I did not photograph them in situ before removal. I felt annoyed that  such  stickers,  and  by  extension,  stickerists  were  in my locale.  It  was  then  that  I  began  to  understand  that my own bias to these political stickers had served to be rash in my actions and by doing so I had lost an important moment of visual ethnographic data collection. As Becker (1967,  p.239)  states  'the  question  is  not  whether  we should  take  sides,  since  we  inevitably  will,  but  rather whose  side  are  we  on.'  I  had  displayed  my  ideological bias, a fact recognised in my theoretical framework and cautioned against by Umberto (1978). Side stepping any ethical arguments, I had taken the position of not giving the XRW a voice and as a researcher, to deny the empirical evidence invalidates the very ethos of my undertakings.

From  this  point  on  I  decided  to  be  non  judgemental  in my  recording  actions  of  political  stickers  and  resolved to transfer this non judgementality from recording to subsequent analysis, albeit tempered with my interpretation of each sticker, in keeping with my methodological approach of cultural criminological verstehen.  In  the  following  section  I  document  one protest  sticker  from  each  of  the  four  political  domains already outlined above.

However, before I get to this stage, I also acknowledge that my choosing of which sticker to present in this work would also be inherently subjective. So, to overcome this bias  and  introduce  an  element  of  objectivity,  I  assigned each  of  the  stickers  in  the  LASIC,  XRE,  EA  and  INTER political domains a number, corresponding to the amount of  data  in  each  category.  I  then  used  an  online  random number generator to select one number from each of the recorded  domains  to  choose  which  sticker  to  present. The numbers generated were LASIC 107, XRE 6, EA 19 and  INTER  21.  This  random  sampling  approach  of  the complete population of protest stickers I had collected is a recognised rigorous method of enquiry (Brown, 2023). As my collected data is comparatively small, this process was manageable, cost effective and not too time consuming. I  do  recognise  that  my  complete  population  of  protest stickers may not fully represent what was actually present

## 4. Ethical considerations


As an independent researcher, I am not currently attached academically  to  any  university.  I  undertake  this  work from a cultural criminological practitioner perspective to inform the academic study of cultural criminology. Whilst I am bound by my professional association's ethical code of  conduct,  I  have  no  corresponding  formal  academic obligations. Although that may seem to hark back to the founding days of the Chicago School of Criminology, the reality is, recalling such necessities of ethical conformity from  both  my  under  and  postgraduate  studies,  it  is crucial, maybe even more so without recourse to formal structures of academia, that I include my ethical position in this work.

Undertaking this fieldwork necessitated that I was involved  with  criminality.  This  criminality  though  had already been undertaken and I was neither present nor partook in the law breaking. I undertook the fieldwork in a post criminal ethnographic capacity.

Therefore,  to  guide  all  elements  of  my  research  from inception  to  completion,  I  was  both  cognisant  of  and compliant with the British Society of Criminology's statement of Ethics and used it as a frame of reference to  guide  my  complete  approach.  This  dovetailed  into my professional  association's  ethical  code  of  conduct.  I abided by both.

Additionally, when I consider academics that have already published  in  this  area  (for  example  see  Awcock,  2021; Awcock and Rosenberg, 2023; and Bodden and Awcock, 2024),  they  were  all  attached  to  academic  settings  so would all have needed ethical clearance for their work. As my work is of a similar nature to theirs, I believe that my ethical stance is within acceptable parameters.

## 5.2 Extreme Right Wing - XRW


This  category  covers  a  loose  grouping  of  those  that  do not  represent  a  single  body  who  are  often  fragmented although espouse a similar ideology to further their cause.

The main text on this sticker in figure 2 is in Italian, 'Me Ne Frego', which translates as 'I don't give a damn' although this translation has been disputed and there are multiple other,  even  vulgar,  possibilities  (Salemi,  2005).  There  is other  text  on  the  helmet,  just  below  the  symbol.  Both of  these  texts  are  in  different  types,  fonts  and  sizes. This  text  on  the  helmet  states  'ATP'  and  is  an  English acronym for Albanian Third Position. The symbol on the helmet is of three vertical lines which represent multiple interpretations  of  politics  and  identity  with  the  oblique line  providing  unity  of  associated  meaning  (ATP,  2023). The  third  position  came  to  signify  neo-fascist  political movements  in  many  European  countries  during  the twentieth century. The image is of a skull wearing a helmet with a knife clenched between the teeth. Intriguingly, the swastika on the knife's handle is in the original Hindu or Buddhist left facing design as opposed to the right facing design which has been appropriated by far right ideology. The image is solely in black and white and these colours are used mainly by far right groups, although not always (for instance Atomwaffen Division and Pepe the Frog are two  examples  of  right  wing  groups  who  use  additional colours).  Additionally  some  Islamist  Extremist  Terrorist Groups also use just black and white in their propaganda, for instance Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL) and Ansar Al-Islam.
