They  are  rarely  attained  a  habilitation  or  took  on  a  deputy professorship  before  being  awarded  a  full  professorship  in  Germany.  It  remains  unclear whether this cluster primarily consists of returnees to Germany or immigrants from abroad. Nonetheless, this trend aligns with the current global tendency for universities to increasingly cater  to  an  international  clientele,  both  in  terms  of  students  and  staff  (Redden  2015). This reaffirms that international capital seems to be of importance in the German academic field.


## German career paths to professorship in international comparison


As the German academic system is characterized by a comparably steep hierarchy with the full professorship  on  the  top,  the Endurance  Career trajectory  is  probably  very  distinct  in international comparison (Kreckel 2015). As described in the introduction, until the beginning of  the  millennium,  the  only  path  to  university  professorship  was  via  habilitation.  The introduction of junior professorships with an optional tenure-track in 2002 and tenure-track professorships in 2016 was supposed to open alternative pathways to a professorship. However, the number of junior and tenure-track professors remains low in Germany. In 2022, only 1,147 former junior professors without tenure-track and 942 junior professors with tenure track or tenure-track  professors,  had  attained  a  position  as  full  professor  (Statistisches  Bundesamt (Destatis) 2023). This includes all types of universities and schools of higher education and the arts and sums up to only 5.4% of all prior qualifications for tenured professors in 2022. Thus, it  must be concluded that these novel paths have not (yet) become a true alternative to the prolonged postdoctoral phase including gaining the habilitation as a second degree. However, the introduction of 'habilitation-equivalent accomplishments'-which is a term that has no fixed legal set of criteria but can be defined by the institution that appoints the professorappears  to  have  opened  manyfold  paths  that  are  especially  reflected  in  the  shorter  career trajectories within the heterogeneous Unconventional and International Careers .

Beyond tradition: Successful career paths to full professorship

The increasing importance of international mobility is evident across many countries within the academic sector. As the pathway to a full professorship becomes more competitive, both international and interinstitutional mobility are becoming crucial (Brechelmacher et al. 2015; Kwiek and Antonowicz 2015). The fact that the International Career cluster comprised the relatively highest proportion of men, underscores that international mobility as a competitive edge  bears  the  danger  of  increasing  gender  inequality  in  the  competition  for  secure  and independent positions in science. It is not unlikely that the larger proportion of men in this international mobility cluster is related to family obligations. As one interviewee in a study by Øyslebø Sørensen and Korsnes Kristensen (2022) described the situation: 'My contract now is for  one  more year. I really want to continue in academia as long as possible. But I have a daughter that is in school, and a husband with a permanent position here. The focus on mobility is really strong, so I guess it would be possible for me to get a position somewhere, but when your family is here and they don't want to go elsewhere, it is hard.'. The critical phase for deciding to have children ends earlier for women than for men, simply based on the menopause as a biological determinant (Dratva et al. 2009). However, this family formation falls into the most important career stage, between 30 and 40 years. According to Havighurst's model of developmental tasks, middle adulthood is the stage during which individuals establish their career and their family (Havighurst 1956). As Nagy, Froidevaux, and Hirschi (2019, p. 237), put  it  'This  settling  down  period  ordinarily  begins  at  around  age  30  and  ends  at  40-45, constituting  one  of  the  most  crucial  steps  in  adult  development.'. The  observation  that  the unconventional career cluster, with the shortest trajectory to full professorship also contains the  relatively  largest  proportion  of  women  could  be  interpreted  as  an  indication  that  those pathways that diverge the most from the traditional endurance career represent an important opportunity especially for women.

## Limitations and further research


When interpreting the results, several limitations have to be discussed. First, the conclusions that  can  be  drawn from  the current study's  findings are limited by the sample, which only included success participants in being appointed a professorship. Our sample does not cover careers of those who strived towards but did not achieve a full professorship. This positive selectivity is partially visible in the 'non-significance' of the scientific productivity indicators in our sample. Moreover, the respondents' educational trajectories were not recorded, which is why no statements can be made about the extent to which they were already pursuing a (non)academic career before their doctorate. Similarly, the dataset does not provide information on times of unemployment. As we excluded professors who have reported gaps in their careers, we  cannot  rule  out  additional  academic  career  pathways.  We  therefore  encourage  further research on the specific selection biases in career surveys.


## Conclusion


Our study explores the multifaceted career trajectories toward achieving a full professorship within the German academic system, highlighting the interplay of traditional and emerging career trajectories over the past two decades. Our study adds to the current body of literature about academic careers by revealing four distinct patterns of academic careers to a successful appointment as a full professor and providing insides into the determinants of the predominant career  clusters.  The  analysis  underscores  the  significance  of  international  experience  and diverse professional backgrounds, particularly in facilitating career paths that tend to attract a higher  proportion  of  women.  Our  paper,  therefore,  contributes  to  the  ongoing  dialogue  on academic  career  progression,  providing  valuable  perspectives  on  the  dynamics  of  career development in the context of recent policy changes and global trends.

## 1. Introduction


Political	efficacy	is	among	the	strongest	predictors	of	political	participation	(e.g.,	Lane 1965;	Nie	et	al.	1996;	Verba	et	al.	1995;	Verba	et	al.	2005;	Beaumont,	2011;	Marx	and Nguyen	2016,	2018).	Traditionally,	research	differentiates	between	two	dimensions	of political	 efficacy:	 internal	 political	 efficacy,	 i.e.,	 perceptions	 of	 one's	 own	 ability	 to understand	politics	and	to	become	politically	involved	(Lane	1965;	Campbell	et	al.	1960; Rico	et	al.	2020;	Marx	and	Nguyen	2016,	2018),	on	the	one	hand,	and	external	political efficacy,	i.e.,	the	belief	in	opportunities	to	influence	politics	and	in	the	system's	reaction or	responsiveness	to	citizens'	demands	(Lane	1965;	Campbell	et	al.	1960;	Davis	and	Hitt 2017;	Merolla	et	al	2024;	Davis	2014;	Karp	and	Banducci	2007),	on	the	other.

A	standard	assessment	of	political	efficacy	in	surveys	refers	to	'people	like	me'. The	'people	like	me'	stimulus	is	particularly	prominent	with	regard	to	survey	questions on	external	efficacy.	Some	examples	illustrate	this:	two	items	to	assess	external	efficacy in	the	renowned	American	National	Election	Survey	reads	'People	like	me	don't	have	any say	about	what	the	government	does.'	and	'Public	officials	don't	care	much	what	people like	me	think'	(same	or	similar	formulations	in	ANES	1952-2020);	and	an	exemplary	item in	 the	 established	 European	 Social	 Survey	 is	 'And	 how	 much	 would	 you	 say	 that	 the political	system	in	[country]	allows	people	like	you	to	have	an	influence	on	politics?'	(ESS waves	7-11). 	These	formulations	to	assess	external	efficacy	imply	that	there	might	be 1 differences	between	the	group	that	I	belong	to	and	one	or	more	other	groups	-	but	the way	the	survey	questions	are	phrased	does	not	reveal	which	group	they	refer	to.	As	they leave	this	question	open	for	each	respondent	to	decide	individually,	researchers	have	no clue	whatsoever	which	group	identities	individuals	have	in	mind	when	they	respond	to such	questions	-	which	severely	constrains	the	reliability,	validity,	and	comparability	of responses	(for	a	similar	argument	see	Phoenix	and	Chan	2024).

In	this	paper,	we	theoretically	argue	and	empirically	show	that	individuals	clearly distinguish	 between	 internal, general external , and group-related	 external political efficacy	 (for	 easier	 readability,	 we	 mostly	 refer	 to	 these	 forms	 as	 external	 and	 group efficacy,	respectively,	in	the	remainder	of	the	article).	More	concretely,	we	suggest	that people	 are	 aware	 of	 differences	 in	 opportunities	 to	 influence	 politics	 and	 system responsiveness	between	different	societal	groups,	and	thus	differentiate	between	how

the	system	reacts	to	people's needs	and	demands in	general ,	and	the	responsiveness	of the	political	system	to	a	concrete group that	they	belong	to.	In	other	words,	we	expect	that external	efficacy	has	a	general	and	a	group-related	dimension.	In	this	paper,	we	examine whether	differentiating	between	a	general	version	of	external	efficacy	items	and	a	grouprelated	 version	 that	 explicitly	 refers	 to	 respondents	 (family)	 background	 in	 terms	 of education,	income	or	migration	status	helps	to	better	understand	the	dimensionality	of political	efficacy.	However,	and	more	generally,	we	propose	that	group-related	external political	efficacy	is	relevant	for	other	categories	as	well,	i.e.	gender,	sexual	orientation,	age groups,	rurality,	or	religion.	Moreover,	we	argue	that	the	'people	like	me'	stimulus	works very	differently	for	people	from	a	privileged	background	compared	to	individuals	from	a less	 privileged	 background,	 both	 in	 socio-structural	 and	 political	 terms.	 While	 people belonging	to	more	advantaged	groups	are	expected	to	report	higher	group-related	than general	 external	 efficacy,	 those	 belonging	 to	 more	 disadvantaged	 groups	 should	 have lower	group-related	than	general	external	efficacy.

Based	on	these	considerations,	this	article	addresses	four	questions:	(1)	Can	we empirically	differentiate	three	dimensions	of	political	efficacy?	(2)	If	so,	how	do	the	three dimensions	 of	 political	 efficacy	 vary	 across	 societal	 subgroups	 (e.g.,	 by	 economic, educational, or migration background)? (3) How are individuals' background characteristics	related	to	their	political	efficacy	in	the	three	dimensions?	Lastly,	we	are interested	in	whether	and	which	individuals	differentiate	between	external	and	group efficacy:	(4)	what	are	constellations	of	the	three	dimensions	of	political	efficacy	within individuals,	and	how	large	are	the	groups	that	differentiate	between	external	and	group efficacy?

To	address	these	questions	empirically,	we	developed	novel	items	to	differentiate between	external	and	group	efficacy	that	build	on	existing	measures.	More	specificallty, while	 we	 kept	 the	 items	 as	 similar	 as	 possible	 to	 established	 instruments	 to	 assess external	efficacy,	we	replaced	the	-	too	vague	-	prompt	of	'people	like	me'	with	a	stimulus that	explicitly	frames	efficacy	beliefs	in	the	context	of	particular	group	memberships,	i.e., regarding	economic,	educational,	and	migration	backgrounds,	and	ask	respondents	to answer	items	for	both	system	efficacy	in	general	(without	any	group	reference)	and	items for	group	efficacy	(using	a	group	reference).	We	implement	the	new	items	in	two	large-N register-based	surveys,	one	fielded	among	adults	and	one	among	adolescents	in	Germany in	winter	2023/24.

The	results	show	clear	evidence	of	three	distinct	dimensions	of	political	efficacy, generally	supporting	our	argument.	In	both	surveys,	confirmatory	factor	analyses	confirm that	three-dimensional	models	fit	the	data	best.	This	confirms	that	political	efficacy	is most	adequately	conceived	of	as	having	three	dimensions:	internal,	general	external,	and group-related	external	political	efficacy.	Furthermore,	the	three	efficacy	dimensions	show varying	distributions	and	systematic	differences	between	societal	subgroups.	In	general, individuals	 with	 more	 disadvantaged	 background	 characteristics	 (having	 a	 migration background,	 less	 money,	 lower	 education)	 tend	 to	 have	 lower	 group	 (and	 internal) political	 efficacy	 than	 their	 more	 advantaged	 likes.	 Importantly,	 there	 are	 relevant segments	in	both	our	youth	and	our	adult	samples	which	combine	high	or	low	group efficacy	with	the	opposite	level	of	external	efficacy.	The	contrast	between	external	and group	efficacy	is	more	pronounced	with	regard	to	migration	background	than	with	regard to	economic	and	educational	background.	Finally,	our	results	highlight	the	importance	of explicitly	mentioning	the	group(s)	of	reference	that	the	researcher	is	interested	in.

By	 analysing	 the	 dimensionality	 of	 political	 efficacy	 among	 both	 adults	 and adolescents,	 we	 contribute	 to	 different	 literatures:	 First,	 we	 theoretically	 argue	 and empirically	 show	 that	 political	 efficacy	 encompasses	 not	 only	 internal	 and	 external efficacy,	but	that	it	is	important	to	additionally	conceptualize,	measure,	and	consider	a third	 dimension,	 namely	 group-related	 external	 efficacy;	 this	 is	 of	 importance	 to	 any scholar	in	political	behaviour	and	in	particular	to	those	interested	in	political	inequality. Second,	we	also	speak	to	studies	on	political	responsiveness	by	showing	that	(certain) individuals	seem	to	internalize	unequal	responsiveness	in	their	political	efficacy	beliefs. Third,	by	studying	adolescents	in	addition	to	adults,	we	contribute	to	studies	on	political socialization,	showing	that	there	are	clear	patterns	in	the	three	dimensions	of	political efficacy	already	among	those	whose	political	efficacy	is	still	developing	(Bacovsky	and Fitzgerald	2023).

## 2. Conceptual	Considerations

Political	 efficacy	 belongs	 to	 the	 oldest	 and	 most-established	 concepts	 for	 explaining political	engagement	(see	Lane,1965;	Campbell	et	al.	1960;	Campbell	and	Converse	1972; Verba	and	Nie	1972;	for	more	recent	literature	see	e.g.,	Beaumont	2011;	Lee	2010,	Marx and	 Nguyen	 2016;	 Wolak	 2018;	 Rico	 et	 al.	 2020;	 Leininger	 et	 al.	 2023;	 Wolak	 2018; Alaminos-Fernández	 et	 al.	 2024).	 Typically,	 the	 literature	 distinguishes	 between	 two

dimensions,	internal	and	external	efficacy	beliefs.	Internal	political	efficacy	refers	to	the belief	that	oneself	is	politically	effective,	i.e.,	able	to	understand	politics	and	to	become	successfully	-	politically	involved	(Lane	1965;	Campbell	et	al.	1960).	External	efficacy	is defined	as	the	belief	that	the	state	and	its	elites	are	responsive	to	citizens'	demands	(Lane 1965;	Campbell	et	al.	1960).

However,	 there	 is	 a	 lot	 of	 research	 showing	 that	 governments	 are	 not	 equally responsive	to	all	members	of	society.	Instead,	the	interests	of	disadvantaged	groups	most	 importantly:	 citizens	 with	 a	 migration	 background,	 with	 lower	 income,	 or	 with lower	 education	 -	 often	 are	 less	 well	 represented	 in	 political	 processes	 and	 policy outcomes	(see	review	by	Elkjær	and	Klitgaard	2024;	Gilens	2012;	Elsässer	et	al.	2021). Moreover,	that	individuals	from	less-advantaged	backgrounds	consistently	report	lower external	 efficacy	 might	 very	 well	 result	 from	 their	 evaluation	 of	 state	 authorities' responsiveness	being	influenced	by	the	'people	like	me'	stimulus.

We	 argue	 that	 individuals'	 awareness	 of	 group-related	 differences	 in	 system responsiveness		impacts	their	political	efficacy	beliefs.	More	concretely,	we	suggest	that citizens	are	able	to	differentiate	between	how	well	the	government	reacts	to	demands	of citizens	in	general,	versus	how	well	government	reacts	to	the	demands	of	citizens	who belong	to	a	certain	group.	While	the	former	defines	citizens' general	external	efficacy ,	the latter	defines	their group-related	external	efficacy .	 To	 illustrate,	 consider	 the	 following example:	an	individual	with	a	migration	background	may	believe	that	she	understands politics	and	feels	able	to	make	her	voice	heard	in	politics	(internal	efficacy);	she	may	also believe	 that	 the	 political	 system	 in	 general	 responds	 to	 citizens'	 demands	 (general external	efficacy);	but	she	may	be	well	aware	that	her	particular	group	is	discriminated against	in	politics,	resulting	in	lower	group	efficacy.	In	other	words,	we	propose	that	to adequately	understand	and	measure	political	efficacy,	we	need	to	distinguish	not	only between	internal	and	external	efficacy,	but	add	a	group-related	dimension	of	external efficacy.	 The	 group	 dimension	 occupies	 an	 intermediate	 and	 somewhat	 transverse position	between	internal	and	external	efficacy:	it	refers	to	external	efficacy	and	thus	asks for	a	perspective	on	the	political	system's	responsiveness,	but	relates	this	concept	to	a particular	group	that	the	individual	belongs	to.

So	far,	group-related	differences	have	found	relatively	little	attention	in	political efficacy	research	(exception:	Phoenix	&	Chang	2024),	but	are	prominent	in	areas	such	as studies	on	relative	deprivation	(Jetten	et	al.	2001;	Smith	and	Ortiz	2001;	Smith	et	al.	2012; Tropp	&	Wright,	1999)	and	social	movement	research	(e.g.,	Lubell	et	al.	2007,	Seligson

1980;	van	Zomeren	et	al.	2008,	Lee	2010;	McAdam	et	al.	2001).	Overall,	this	research shows	that	there	are	group-related	differences	in	the	perception	of	 discrimination	 by authorities	(see	also	Diehl	et	al.	2021). That	group-related	differences	in	political	efficacy have	 so	 far	 been	 relatively	 ignored	 in	 political	 science	 is	 all	 the	 more	 surprising	 as assessments	 of	 political	 efficacy	 -	 in	 particular	 of	 external	 efficacy	 -	 often	 include	 a 'people	like	me'	stimulus:	they	ask	respondents	to	think	of	other	people	who	are	similar to	themselves	when	making	their	assessment	of	how	well	the	government	reacts	to	their needs.

This	 measurement	is	problematic.	Having	numerous	potentially	group-defining characteristics	-	gender,	country	of	origin,	education,	economic	status,	to	mention	a	few -	individuals	belong	to	different	groups.	The	group	that	they	identify	with	the	most	may depend	on	the	context:	in	some	situations,	they	may	identify	more	with	the	group	of	their own	gender,	in	other	situations	more	with	the	group	of	parents,	in	others	more	with	the group	of	craftsmen	or	university	graduates,	and	in	yet	other	contexts	more	with	other people	from	their	country	of	birth,	with	their	religion	or	their	political	preferences.	Thus, the	 question	 arises	 as	 to which of	 the	 multiple	 possible	 social	 identities	 comes	 to	 an individual's	mind	and	guides	their	responses	when	asked	about	'people	like	me'.	As	the 'people	like	me'	stimulus	is	too	vague	to	make	people	think	of	a	concrete	group	that	they belong	to,	completely	different	groups	may	be	salient	to	respondents	when	answering	the respective	question(s).

Self-categorization	theory	argues	that	the	salience	of	group	membership	depends on	the	relative	accessibility	of	the	category,	which	in	turn	depends,	among	other	things, on	the	individual's	in-group	identification	and	the	frequency	and	recency	of	activation (Oakes	 et	 al.	 1991,	 p.	 126)	 or	 media	 reporting	 (McAdam	 et	 al.	 2001).	 As	 the	 item formulation	'people	like	me'	does	not	explicitly	activate	a	group	salience,	the	salience may	depend	on	the	last	contact	person	of	the	respondent	or	a	salient	political	issue	that day	or	a	conflict	with	another	person	at	work	or	the	content	of	media	the	person	has consumed	before	answering	the	survey	-	or	even	the	previous	survey	questions,	which can	activate	certain	group	identities.	In	other	words,	the	'people	like	me'	stimulus	is	too vague	 and	 leaves	 unclear	 which	 group(s)	 respondents	 are	 supposed	 to	 think	 of.	 In consequence,	answers	may	not	be	comparable	across	subgroups	of	populations.	Although items	 using	 the	 'people	 like	 me'	 stimulus	 seems	 to	 imply	 that	 there	 are	 differences between	groups	with	regard	to	their	external	efficacy,	the	formulation	is	too	vague	to adequately	measure	group	efficacy.

We	argue	that	to	adequately	capture	the	three-dimensional	structure	of	political efficacy,	measures	of	external	efficacy	should	explicitly	differentiate	between	items	that assess	general	external	efficacy	and	those	that	assess	external	efficacy	related	to	one	or several	concretely	mentioned	groups.	In	this	paper,	we	focus	on	groups	that	are	relevant in	 much	 political	 science	 research,	 in	 particular	 in	 research	 on	 political	 inequality: individuals	from	low	(versus	high)	educated	backgrounds,	individuals	from	poor	(versus rich)	 families,	 and	 individuals	 with	 (versus	 without)	 migration	 background	 (see	 e.g. Schaub	2021;	Jungkunz	und	Marx	2021;	Macdonald	2020;	Marinova	and	Anduiza	2020; Auspurg	et	al.	2019;	Thijssen	et	al.	2019).	These	groups	often	experience	deprivation and/or	discrimination	-	which	is	why	we	expect	to	find	a	particularly	large	association with	on	their	efficacy	beliefs. 2

Although	 efficacy	 beliefs	 have	 been	 'one	 of	 the	 most	 continuously	 examined constructs'	(Morrell	2003:	589;	Chamberlain	2012:	117),	there	is	still	no	consensus	on	its measurement'	(Schneider	et	al.	2014:	208;	see	also	Xena	2015;	Scotto	et	al.	2021).	More than	 three	 decades	 ago,	 Gecas	 (1989:	 297)	 described	 the	 measurement	 of	 efficacy	 as 'primitive'	and	contended	that	'instrument	development	has	not	been	very	extensive'. Nothing	significantly	has	changed	since	then.	In	particular	with	regard	to	political	efficacy, Frank	 et	 al	 claim	 that	 'high	 ratios	 of	 unreliability	 warrant	 the	 search	 for	 superior indicators	for	political	efficacy'	(Frank	et	al.	2014:	216).	We	do	not	want	to	add	to	this cacophony	of	voices	on	how	to	measure	efficacy	correctly.	We	actually	propose	that	the exact	wording	of	items	may	not	be	so	relevant.	However,	we	want	to	caution	researchers to	 use	 items	 including	 stimuli	 such	 as	 'people	 like	 me'	 because	 it	 remains	 so	 utterly unclear	what	the	reference	group	of	respondents	answering	to	such	items	is.	By	contrast, we	 recommend	 to	 take	 the	 group-related	 of	 political	 efficacy	 beliefs	 seriously	 and formulate	items	which	clearly	indicate	the	reference	group.

## 3. Research	design	and	empirical	contribution

We	test	the	proposed	three-dimensionality	of	efficacy	beliefs	in	two	different	large-N, register-based	surveys	in	Germany:	one	focusing	on	adults,	and	one	focusing	on	15-	to	18year-olds	-	an	age	at	which	political	efficacy	still	develops	(Condon	&	Holleque	2013). Both	surveys	are	representative	of	the	population	and	include	over	4,000	respondents each.

From	 a	 comparative	 perspective,	 citizens	 in	 Germany	 have	 average	 levels	 of political	efficacy,	both	with	regard	to	their	internal	and	external	efficacy.	With	regard	to political	 responsiveness,	 Elkjær	 and	 Klitgaard	 (2024)	 find	 in	 their	 systematic	 review barely	any	differences	in	political	responsiveness	across	established	democracies.	Thus, Germany	can	be	considered	a	typical	case,	and	our	findings	are	unlikely	to	be	driven	by German	peculiarities	or	to	only	apply	to	countries	with	a	similar	political	or	economic system.	 That	 is,	 the	 results	 of	 our	 study	 will	 be	 informative	 and	 relevant	 for	 many democracies	beyond	the	particular	case	of	Germany.

## The	surveys

Both	surveys	were	conducted	as	part	of	the	DFG-funded	research	group Reconfiguration and	Internalization	of	Social	Structure (RISS).	In	the	adult	survey,	the RISS	Internalization Survey (RISS-IS),	 we	 surveyed	 a	 representative	 sample	 of	 adults	 in	 Germany. In	 the adolescent	 survey,	 the RISS	 Youth	 to	 Adulthood	 Panel (RISS-YAP),	 we	 surveyed	 a representative	sample	of	adolescents	aged	between	15	and	18	years	old	(Schäfer	et	al. 2025).	In	this	age	group,	political	efficacy	still	develops	as	these	young	individuals	have comparatively	little	personal	experiences	in	politics	and	concerning	the	responsiveness of	political	elites	and	governments	(Condon	and	Holleque	2013;	Bacovsky	and	Fitzgerald 2023).	At	the	same	time,	though,	adolescents	become	increasingly	aware	of	and	interested in social and	 political phenomena,	 including	 educational,	 economic,	 and	 political inequalities,	 which	 may	 foster	 the	 development	 of	 their	 political	 efficacy.	 Accordingly, adolescents	have	repeatedly	been	shown	to	have	a	sense	of	(both	internal	and	external) political efficacy, which varies by their families' socioeconomic and migration backgrounds	(Condon	&	Holleque	2013;	Jungkunz	&	Marx	2024;	Akee	et	al.	2020;	Shore &	Tosun	2019)	and	which	may	change	following	their	first	elections	(Leininger	et	al.	2022; Garritzmann	 et	 al.	 2025).	 We	 thus	 believe	 that	 it	 is	 highly	 interesting	 and	 extremely relevant	to	study	the	dimensionality	of	political	efficacy	not	only	among	adults,	but	also among	adolescents	-	not	least	because	they	will	be	tomorrow's	voters.

Both	surveys	were	fielded	between	November	9 th ,	 2023	and	February	1 st ,	 2024 (here	and	following	see	Schäfer	et	al.	2025).	Respondents	were	invited	to	participate	in the	 online	 survey	 by	 a	 letter	 mailed	 to	 their	 home	 addresses,	 which	 included	 an unconditional	 5€	 incentive.	 Respondents	 who	 had	 not	 yet	 responded	 received	 a	 first reminder	3	weeks	after	the	initial	invitation,	and	those	who	still	not	responded	received a	second	reminder	5	weeks	after	the	initial	invitation.	The	surveys	had	the	topic	'Living together	in	Germany',	and	focused	on	assessing	the	educational,	economic,	and	migration backgrounds	of	respondents	and	their	parents,	their	opinions	on	a	number	of	different cultural	and	political	topics,	and	their	identification	with	different	groups.	While	the	youth survey	 was	 similar	 to	 the	 adult	 survey,	 some	 questions	 were	 adapted	 to	 the	 younger target	 groups	 and	 it	 had	 a	 special	 focus	 on	 education	 and	 political	 participation.	 The response	rates	were	35	percent	in	the	adult	survey	and	44	percent	in	the	youth	survey.

## Variable	operationalization

Measuring	the	three	dimensions	of	political	efficacy

To	measure	the	three	dimensions	of	political	efficacy,	we	systematically	collected items	 that	 had	 been	 included	 in	 previous	 surveys	 to	 measure	 internal	 and	 external efficacy,	discussed	them	in	light	of	our	theoretical	argument,	and	developed	new	scales that	 allow	 us	 to	 differentiate	 between	 internal,	 external,	 and	 group-related	 external efficacy. 	 In	 the	 youth	 survey	 RISS-YAP,	 we	 use	 four	 items	 per	 dimension	 of	 political 3 efficacy.	 To	 assess internal	 political	 efficacy ,	 we	 rely	 on	 items	 that	 have	 been	 used	 in previous	 surveys.	 To	 differentiate	 between	 external	 and	 group	 efficacy,	 we	 first	 ask respondents	about	their	perceptions	of	political	responsiveness	in	general,	using	four items	that	have	been	used	previously	or	adapted	by	removing	any	group	stimulus;	these are	 our	 items	 for general	 external	 political	 efficacy (see	 Table	 1).	 Finally,	 to	 measure group-related	 external	 efficacy ,	 we	 gave	 respondents	 a	 short	 introductory	 statement: 'Now,	we	are	interested	what	you	think	about	the	political	system	in	Germany, this	time regarding	your	family	background .'	We	had	referred	to	family	background	already	earlier in	 the	 survey,	 and	 as	 family	 background	 is	 still	 a	 rather	 vague	 notion,	 had	 added	 an explanation	 there. 	 Nevertheless,	 to	 ensure	 that	 think	 of	 these	 same	 aspects	 of	 social 4

stratification	when	responding	to	the	group	efficacy	items,	we	added	a	brief	reminder:	' As a	reminder,	'family	background'	means	that	families	in	Germany	are	very	different,	e.g.	in terms	 of	 their	 origin,	 their	 educational	 qualifications	 and	 the	 money	 they	 have	 at	 their disposal .'	The	items	assessing	group	efficacy	were	formulated	identical	to	those	assessing external	efficacy,	but	replace	the	general	'people'	with	the	group	reference	'people	with my	family	background'.	Table	1	presents	the	exact	items	used	for	each	dimension.

Among	the	adults	in	the	RISS-IS,	the	same	considerations	apply.	However,	we	could only	allocate	less	survey	space	and	time	to	assessments	of	political	efficacy	-	which	is	a challenge	well-known	to	any	survey	researcher.	Thus,	based	on	our	quantitative	pre-test among	youth,	we	developed	short	scales	that	measure	each	dimension	of	political	efficacy with	two	items. 	To	adapt	to	the	adult	sample,	the	items	only	refer	to	their	background 5 (not	their	family	background)	because	most	adults	have	achieved	their	final	educational qualification	 and	 have	 an	 economic	 situation	 independent	 from	 their	 parents,	 and	 we wanted	them	to	think	of	their	own	background.

However,	when	being asked	about	their	political	efficacy,	respondents	had	answered	a	number	of	questions regarding	 their	 educational,	 economic,	 and	 migration	 background,	 which	 may	 have increased	the	salience	of	these	aspects	of	social	stratification	in	their	minds. ## Measuring	educational,	economic,	and	migration	background

To	measure educational family background among	adolescents	in	RISS-YAP,	we use	 information	 on	 parents'	 highest	 educational	 certificate.	 We	 differentiate	 between individuals	of	whom	at	least	one	parent	has	a	university	degree	versus	individuals	of whom	no	parent	has	a	university	degree.	Among	adults	in	RISS-IS,	we	use	information	on respondents'	own	highest	educational	certificate.	Again,	we	differentiate	between	those who	have	a	university	degree	versus	those	who	do	not	have	a	university	degree.

With	regard	to economic	background ,	we	use	information	on	the	financial	situation of	the	family	in	RISS-YAP.	Adolescents	were	asked:	'Some	families	have	a	lot	of	money	at their	disposal,	others	have	only	little.	How	is	the	situation	in	your	family?'	with	answer options	on	a	7-point	Likert	scale	ranging	from	'very	little	money'	to	'a	lot	of	money'.	As in	other	such	questions,	the	most	frequently	mentioned	answers	are	the	middle	category (22	percent)	and	the	one	above	(29	percent);	we	thus	differentiate	between	those	on	the lower	half	including	the	middle	category	and	those	on	the	upper	half	on	this	scale;	this results	in	two	approximately	equally	sized	groups	of	33	percent	of	respondents	whose parents	have	rather	little	money	and	44	percent	of	respondents	with	rather	more	money; around	23	percent	of	adolescents	did	not	provide	an	answer	for	this	question.	Among	the adults	in	RISS-IS,	we	use	information	on	the	household's	net	income	and,	if	people	lived by	 themselves,	 on	 their	 personal	 net	 income	 to	 generate	 a	 categorical	 indicator differentiating	between	those	with	little	money	(35	percent)	and	those	with	more	money (35	percent).	To	avoid	losing	23	percent	of	adolescents	and	30	percent	of	adults	in	the two	samples,	we	in	addition	included	a	category	for	individuals	with	missing	information on	their	economic	situation	in	both	datasets. 6

With	regard	to migration	background ,	we	distinguish	between	natives	(respondent and	parents	born	in	Germany),	individuals	with	own	migration	background	(respondent born	in	other	country)	and	individuals	whose	parents	have	a	migration	background	in both	surveys.

## Further	control	variables

Furthermore,	our	models	include	gender	and	age	as	control	variables	that	could be	 associated	 with	 political	 efficacy.	 Gender	 is	 known	 to	 be	 associated	 with	 political efficacy	as	males	typically	have	higher	levels,	in	particular	of	internal	political	efficacy (Pflanzelt	&	Spieß,	2019;	Oser	et	al.	2023;	Fraile	&	Marinova,	2024).	Among	adolescents in	 RISS-YAP,	 we	 differentiate	 between	 males,	 females,	 and	 those	 indicating	 'diverse'; whereas	among	adults	in	RISS-IS,	we	differentiate	between	males	and	females	(based	on their	gender	assigned	at	birth).	Age	is	an	additional	important	control	variable	as	more experience	with	politics	as	people	grow	older	might	result	in	more	crystallized	political efficacy	beliefs	(Bacovsky	and	Fitzgerald	2023)	-	however,	as	this	effect	might	go	in	both directions	(some	adults	may	have	higher,	others	lower	political	efficacy),	we	do	not	expect to	find	an	overall	effect	of	age.	The	distribution	of	these	variables	in	the	two	samples	can be	found	in	Appendix	1,	Tables	A1	and	A2.

## Analytical	approaches

To	 empirically	 investigate	 whether	 political	 efficacy	 encompasses	 two	 dimensions	 internal	 and	 external,	 as	 is	 the	 standard	 in	 political	 behavior	 research	 -	 or	 three dimensions	-	adding	group	efficacy,	as	we	argue	in	this	paper	-	we	conduct confirmatory factor	 analyses . This	 method	 is	 based	 on	 structural	 equation	 models,	 assuming	 that respondents'	answers	on	each	of	the	items	are	driven	by	one	or	several	underlying	latent variable(s),	 i.e.,	 the	 dimensions	 of	 political	 efficacy.	 More	 specifically,	 the	 researcher specifies	the	number	of	latent	variables,	and	tests	how	well	the	models	perform	by	using different	 goodness-of-fit	 indicators	 (more	 details	 below).	 To	 test	 the	 reliability	 of	 the scales,	we	in	addition	report	Cronbach's	alpha	scores	for	the	full	samples	as	well	as	for subsamples	defined	by	the	economic,	educational,	and	migration	background.

Subsequently,	we	graphically	illustrate	the	distribution	of	the	three	domains	of political	 efficacy,	 both	 in	 the	 full	 samples	 and	 for	 different	 societal	 groups.	 We	 then analyze	 the	 association	 of	 individuals'	 background	 characteristics	 with	 their	 internal, external,	and	group	political	efficacy	by	estimating	linear	regression	models.	Finally,	we investigate	 constellations	 of	 political	 efficacy	 dimensions	 within	 individuals	 in	 our samples	by	differentiating	between	above	versus	below	average	levels	of	political	efficacy on	 each	 dimension.	 We	 are	 interested	 in	 particular	 in	 groups	 with	 opposing	 levels	 of

external	and	group	efficacy,	i.e.,	high	(low)	general	external,	but	low	(high)	group	efficacy, and	whom	these	groups	are	composed	of.

To	 test	 whether	 political	 efficacy	 consists	 of	 three	 dimensions,	 we	 perform confirmatory	factor	analysis .	 As	explained	in	our	theoretical	section,	we	assume	that political	efficacy	consists	of	internal,	external,	and	group	political	efficacy.	We	assessed these	dimensions	with	12	items	among	the	youth	respondents	and	6	items	among	the adult	 respondents	 of	 our	 surveys.	 Using	 confirmatory	 factor	 analyses	 (estimated	 as structural	 equation	 models,	 using	 Stata/SE18.0),	 we	 model	 political	 efficacy	 as	 unidimensional	(assuming	that	there	is	just	one	underlying	dimension,	i.e.,	latent	variable, driving	responses	to	our	items),	as	two-dimensional	(differentiating	between	internal	and external	efficacy,	as	has	been	the	standard	in	the	large	majority	of	studies	so	far),	and	as three-dimensional	(differentiating	between	internal,	external	and	group	efficacy,	as	we suggest	to	be	more	adequate).	We	then	compare	different	goodness-of-fit	indicators	to see	which	model	fits	the	data	best,	i.e.,	which	models	finds	the	most	empirical	support.

Since	 not	 all	 individuals	 answered	 all	 of	 the	 items	 to	 assess	 the	 different dimensions	of	efficacy,	we	estimate	full-information	maximum	likelihood	models.	This method	makes	use	of	all	given	information	without	listwise	deletion	of	cases,	and	without imputing	values	(and	thus	avoids	assumptions	associated	with	imputation).	Nevertheless, we	 had	 to	 exclude	 observations	 from	 the	 analyses	 if	 respondents	 did	 not	 provide meaningful	answers	to	all	items	capturing	at	least	one	dimension	of	political	efficacy	(i.e., they	did	not	respond	or	answered	'don't	know').	This	applies	to	783	adolescents	in	RISSYAP,	and	to	965	adults	in	RISS-IS. 7 8 , The	final	confirmatory	factor	analyses	thus	are	run on	a	sample	of	3,914	adolescents	(RISS-YAP)	and	4,933	adults	(RISS-IS).	In	each	model, we	allow	the	errors	of	items	assessing	external	and	group	efficacy	to	covary	with	each

other's	 pendant	 -	 this	 is	 because	 the	 items	 assessing	 group	 efficacy	 are	 formulated identical	to	those	assessing	external	efficacy,	only	adding	the	emphasis	'people	with	my (family)	 background'	(see	above).	Such	similar	wording	can	by	design	lead	to	similar answer	patterns,	which	then	result	in	covariation	between	the	errors	of	respective	items.

To	assess	the	performance	of	the	different	models,	we	follow	standard	procedures and	report	the	following	goodness-of-fit	indicators:	the	Chi-square	value	and	degrees	of freedom	(df),	the	Comparative	Fit	Index	(CFI),	the	Tucker-Lewis	Index	(TLI),	as	well	as the	Root	Mean	Squared	Error	of	Approximation	(RMSEA)	(e.g.,	Hu	and	Bentler	1999;	Nye 2023).	Models	with	a	better	fit	have	a	smaller	Chi-square	value,	a	value	closer	to	1	for	the CFI	 and	 the	 TLI,	 and	 a	 value	 below	 0.5	 and	 closer	 to	 0	 for	 the	 RMSEA	 (ibid).	 As	 the correlation	between	items	assessing	external	and	group	efficacy	is	very	high	in	the	RISSIS	survey	(adults)	and	each	dimension	is	measured	with	two	items	only,	the	model	testing a	 three-dimensional	 structure	 required	 constraining	 the	 covariance	 between	 the	 two latent	variables	'external	efficacy'	and	'group	efficacy'.	We	here	report	the	performance of	a	model	that	constrains	this	covariance	to	be	0.9;	however,	using	alternative	covariance constraints	does	not	alter	the	main	results	(see	Appendix	2	table	A3).	Table	2	displays	the goodness-of-fit	indicators	of	the	different	models	that	test	the	dimensionality	of	political efficacy	in	the	adolescent	and	the	adult	samples.

Table 2: Goodness-of-Fit indicators of Confirmatory Factor Analyses

The	 results	 of	 the	 confirmatory	 factor	 analyses	 are	 very	 clear:	 a	 model	 that assumes	a	three-dimensional	structure	of	political	efficacy	performs	the	best;	this	holds among	 both	 the	 adolescents	 and	 the	 adults.	 More	 specifically,	 the	 three-dimensional models	 have	 the	 lowest	 Chi-square	 value	 and	 are	 the	 only	 models	 that	 reaches	 the thresholds	for	good	fit	as	measured	by	the	CFI	(higher	than	.95),	the	TLI	(higher	than	.95) and	 the	 RMSEA	 (below	 .05).	 This	 strongly	 supports	 our	 core	 argument	 that	 political efficacy	 consists	 not	 only	 of	 internal	 and	 external	 efficacy,	 but	 also	 of	 a	 group-related version	of	external	efficacy.	Importantly,	also,	we	observe	a	three-dimensional	structure of	political	efficacy	not	only	among	adolescents	after	explicitly	prompting	them	to	think about	their	family's	economic,	educational,	and	migration	background,	but	also	among adults	who	did	not	receive	a	similarly	detailed	description	of	the	groups	of	reference	and only	answered	two	items	per	dimension.	While	this	is	good	news	for	researchers	working with	surveys	(that	typically	do	not	want	to	allocate	much	space	for	measuring	political efficacy),	the	convergence	issue	of	the	three-dimensional	models	among	adults	suggests that	a	more	explicit	explanation	of	the	groups	of	reference	is	required,	and	/	or	that	ideally respondents	should	answer	three	items	per	dimension.

To	test	the	reliability	of	our	scales,	we	analyze Cronbach's	alpha .	This	indicator ranges	from	0	to	1,	with	higher	scores	on	Cronbach's	alpha	showing	a	higher	inter-item reliability.	In	general,	values	over	.8	are	regarded	as	providing	evidence	of	high	reliability. As	shown	in	the	second	column	of	Table	3,	each	single	scale	shows	a	high	reliability: Cronbach's	alpha	is.	.88	for	the	internal	efficacy	scale,	.86	for	the	external	efficacy	scale, and	 .87	 for	 the	 group	 efficacy	 scale	 among	 adolescents.	 Among	 adults,	 the	 respective values	are	.71	for	the	internal	and	general	efficacy	scale,	and	.74	for	group	efficacy.	As adults	 only	 answer	 two	 items	 per	 scale,	 these	 lower	 reliability	 scores	 among	 adults compared	to	youth	are	not	surprising.

Since	 we	 are	 making	 an	 argument	 about	 group-related	 measures	 of	 political efficacy,	we	next	analyze	how	reliable	our	scales	are	among	different	groups.	As	described above,	in	RISS-YAP	we	focus	on	groups	to	which	membership	is	determined	(mostly)	by birth,	i.e.,	which	are	based	on	the	ascriptive	characteristic	of	migration	background,	and parental	 (educational	 and	 income)	 background.	 By	 contrast,	 in	 the	 adult	 sample education	and	income	are	indicators	of	stratification.	The	results	of	these	analyses	are displayed	 in	 columns	 three	 to	 nine	 of	 Table	 3.	 Accordingly,	 in	 particular	 the	 scales composed	of	four	items,	as	used	in	the	RISS-YAP	among	adolescents,	are	highly	reliable:

they	achieve	alpha	scores	above	.84	for	each	single	subgroup	of	respondents.	Among	the adults	in	RISS-IS,	where	each	dimension	of	political	efficacy	was	assessed	with	two	items only,	the	scale	reliability	is	-	as	expectable	-	lower,	but	still	adequate,	with	alpha	scores between	.66	and	.75	in	the	different	subsamples.

## How	are	the	three	dimensions	of	political	efficacy	distributed?

Next,	we	look	at	the	distributions	of	political	efficacy	overall	as	well	as	in	the	different subgroups	in	both	samples.	To	do	so,	we	construct	indices	of	internal,	external,	and	group efficacy	by	generating	additive	means:	we	add	the	answers	given	for	each	item	in	a	scale and	divide	by	the	number	of	items.	The	indices	range	from	1	(very	low	political	efficacy) to	5	(very	high	political	efficacy).

With	 regard	 to	 adolescents,	 Figure	 3	 shows	 clear	 differences	 between	 the distributions	of	internal,	external,	and	group	political	efficacy:	although	there	are	peaks at	the	intermediate	category	for	all	three	dimensions	of	political	efficacy,	this	is	the	most pronounced	for	external	efficacy.	Interestingly,	adolescents	seem	to	have	higher	group than	external	efficacy,	as	a	higher	share	of	individuals	have	medium	to	high	group	political efficacy.

We	 believe	 that	 the	 lack	 of	 an	 explicit explanation	of	the	concrete	background	aspects	that	we	wanted	adults	to	think	of	when responding	 to	 our	 group	 efficacy	 items	 accounts	 for	 a	 large	 share	 of	 that	 difference between	adolescents	and	adults;	in	addition,	the	lower	number	of	items	might	contribute.

Next,	 we	 turn	 to	 variation	 in	 these	 distributions	 between	 different	 societal subgroups.	 As	 before,	 we	 focus	 on	 groups	 identified	 by	 migration,	 economic,	 and educational	background	as	important	characteristics	of	social	stratification.	We	start	by discussing	 differences	 by	 subgroups	 among	 adolescents,	 illustrated	 in Figure  5 , and subsequently	turn	to	the	adults.

Among	adolescents	in	RISS-YAP,	differences	in	the	distribution	of	political	efficacy by	societal	subgroups	are	pronounced.	Regardless	of	which	background	characteristic	we look	 at,	 adolescents	 belonging	 to	 the	 advantaged	 group	 (who	 have	 no	 migration background,	 whose	 parents	 have	 a	 university	 degree,	 or	 whose	 parents	 have	 a	 lot	 of money)	have	high internal	political	efficacy much	more	often	than	those	belonging	to	a disadvantaged	group	(who	have	a	migration	background,	whose	parents	do	not	have	a university	degree,	or	whose	parents	have	little	money). 	With	regard	to 9 external	political efficacy ,	 individuals	 belonging	 to	 disadvantaged	 groups	 tend	 to	 evaluate	 the	 systems' responsiveness	more	negatively	than	those	belonging	to	an	advantaged	group.	However, contrasts	are	much	starker	for group-related	political efficacy:	Adolescents	belonging	to an	advantaged	group	much	more	often	indicate	high	group	efficacy	than	those	belonging to	a	disadvantaged	group,	whereas	the	latter	much	more	often	indicate	low	group	efficacy than	 the	 former.	 That	 is,	 adolescents	 from	 more	 advantaged	 backgrounds	 more	 often think	that	the	political	system	in	general	gives	them	-	i.e.,	the	group	of	people	without	a migration background, with highly educated parents, or with richer parents -opportunities	to	participate	in	politics	and	reacts	to	their	demands,	whereas	individuals from	more	disadvantaged	backgrounds	more	often	believe	that	their	group	-	i.e.,	people with	a	migration	background,	with	less	educated	parents,	or	with	poorer	parents	-	does not	have	such	opportunities	and	are	less	heard.	As	these	diverging	patterns	show,	both individuals from	 advantaged	 and	 those	 from	 disadvantaged	 backgrounds	 clearly differentiate	between	external	and	group-related	political	efficacy.

Among	 the	 adults	 in	 RISS-IS,	 as	 illustrated	 in	 Figure	 6,	 differences	 between individuals	belonging	to	advantaged	versus	disadvantaged	groups	are	less	pronounced than	among	adolescents,	but	still	clearly	observable. Overall, the distributions of internal, external, and group efficacy differ systematically	 between	 individuals	 belonging	 to	 advantaged	 and	 those	 belonging	 to disadvantaged	groups,	and	they	differ	in	line	with	our	theoretical	expectations. Next,	we	turn	from	descriptive	illustrations	of	differences	between	societal subgroups to empirical analyses, investigating how strongly the background characteristics	are	associated	with	the	three	dimensions	of	political	efficacy.

## What	predicts	the	different	dimensions	of	political	efficacy?

To	better	understand	how	individuals'	background	characteristics	-	in	particular:	their economic,	educational,	and	migration	background	-	relate	to	the	different	dimensions	of political	 efficacy,	 we	 now	 estimate	 linear	 regression	 models	 that	 include	 all	 of	 these variables.	Although	all	analyses	are	strictly	speaking	correlational,	the	core	background characteristics	are	assigned	to	adolescents	mostly	by	birth.	Thus,	it	is	highly	unlikely	and unplausible	 that	 there	 would	 be	 reverse	 causality,	 i.e.,	 that	 political	 efficacy	 would influence	 group	 membership.	While	this	argument	does	not	similarly	holds	for	adults (who	influenced	their	educational	and	economic	background,	and	potentially	also	their migration	 background	 themselves),	 it	 is	 highly	 unlikely	 even	 among	 adults	 that	 their external	 or	 group	 political	 efficacy	 causally	 influenced	 their	 choice	 of	 educational	 or occupational	careers	or	their	decision	to	migrate.

We	further include	the	other	dimensions	of	political	efficacy	to	assess	interdependencies.	We	also estimated	 models	 that	 in	 addition	 control	 for	 political	 interest	 and	 satisfaction	 with democracy,	 which	 are	 other	 important	 political	 predispositions.	 Although	 political interest	 is	 strongly	 positively	 related	 to	 internal	 efficacy	 (~.6),	 and	 satisfaction	 with democracy	is	positively	related	to	both	group-	(~.08)	and	external	(~.23)	efficacy,	the coefficients	on	the	background	characteristics	do	not	differ	much	between	the	models reported	 in	 the	 main	 section	 and	 models	 including	 these	 variables. Figure	7	and	Figure	8	show	the	results	of	the	analyses	for	the adolescents	and	the	adults,	respectively,	by	plotting	the	point	estimates	as	well	as	their 95	percent	Confidence	Intervals.

The	results	for	migration	background	mainly	confirm	the	impressions	from	the previous	section:	Individuals	with	a	migration	background	have	lower	internal	political efficacy	than	individuals	without	a	migration	background;	the	respective	coefficients	is more	strongly	negative	for	those	who	migrated	to	Germany	(1 st generation	migrants)	than for	 those	 whose	 parents	 migrated.	 Both	 1 st and	 2 nd generation	 migrants	 have	 higher external	political	efficacy	than	natives;	for	2 nd generation	migrants,	however,	this	only holds	when	controlling	for	their	group-	and	internal	efficacy.	The	coefficients	are	larger for	1 st generation	migrants,	suggesting	that	those	who	migrated	themselves	perceive	the political	system	in	Germany	as	offering	in	general	many	opportunities	of	influence	for citizens	and	as	considering	citizens'	opinions	in	policy-making	-	and	that	they	are	more likely	to	have	this	impression	than	natives.	With	regard	to	group	efficacy,	we	see	negative coefficients for both	 1 st and	 2 nd generation	 migrants,	 suggesting	 that	 they	 have significantly	 lower	 group-related	 political	 efficacy	 than	 natives.	 Individuals	 with	 a migration	background	clearly	differentiate	between	external	and	group-related	political efficacy,	 and	 are	 acutely	 aware	 of	 the	 lower	 levels	 of	 political	 representation	 of	 and responsiveness	to	their	group.	Importantly,	these	patterns	hold	for	both	adolescents	in RISS-YAP	and	adults	in	RISS-IS,	although	coefficients	are	often	a	bit	smaller	among	adults than	among	adolescents.

Before	proceeding,	it	is	worth	to	take	a	look	at	the	coefficients	on	the	other	political efficacy	 dimensions.	 Among	 adolescents,	 group-related	 political	 efficacy	 is	 positively related	to	internal	efficacy,	and	-	with	a	much	larger	coefficient	-	also	to	external	efficacy; among	adults,	the	coefficient	on	external	efficacy	is	similarly	large,	but	the	coefficient	on internal	efficacy	is	statistically	insignificant.	That	is,	individuals	with	higher	group-related political	 efficacy	 tend	 to	 also	 have	 higher	 external	 political	 efficacy.	 As	 shown	 and discussed	above	(in	particular	Figure	1	and	Figure	2),	the	strong	correlation	of	external and	group	efficacy	is	expectable	since	they	both	refer	to	beliefs	with	regard	to	the	political system	 and	 are	 assessed	 with	 highly	 similar	 question	 wording.	 Internal	 efficacy,	 in contrast,	is	less	correlated	with	the	other	two	dimensions	-	which	is	not	surprising,	since it	 refers	 to	 individuals'	 beliefs	 in	 their	 own	 abilities.	 In	 line	 with	 this,	 coefficients	 of internal	 efficacy	 on	 external	 and	 group	 efficacy	 are	 either	 statistically	 insignificant	 or comparatively	small.

Overall,	 these	 analyses	 reiterate	 -	 with	 more	 empirical	 rigor	 -	 that	 individuals from	disadvantaged	backgrounds	tend	to	have	lower	levels	of	internal	and	-	importantly -	 lower	 group-related	 political	 efficacy.	 This	 is	 fully	 in	 line	 with	 our	 expectations.	 In particular	 the	 observation	 that	 individuals	 with	 a	 migration	 background	 may	 have

opposing	external	and	group-related	political	efficacy	speaks	in	favor	of	our	argument	and highlights	the	relevance	of	distinguishing	between	these	dimensions	of	political	efficacy.

## Patterns	in	the	dimensions	of	political	efficacy	within	individuals

So	far,	 we	have	looked	at	each	dimension	of	political	efficacy	separately.	While	highly informative,	this	does	not	answer	how	the	three	dimensions	of	political	efficacy	look	like within	individuals,	i.e.,	which	constellations	of	the	dimensions	we	see	empirically	within individuals.	We	are	particularly	interested	in	people	who	differentiate	between	external and	group	efficacy,	and	how	large	this	group	is.	To	scrutinize	this,	we	distinguish	between individuals	with	high	(above	average)	and	low	(below	average)	scores	on	each	dimension of	political	efficacy,	and	generate	a	categorical	variable	for	each	possible	constellation	of internal,	group-,	and	external	political	efficacy.	Figure	9	shows	the	sizes	of	the	different groups	in	percent.

The	patterns	illustrated	in	the	figure	yield	several	interesting	insights.	A	first	quick look	already	reveals	that	the	overall	patterns	in	political	efficacy	constellations	are	highly similar	 among	 adolescents	 and	 adults.	 For	 example,	 the	 three	 largest	 groups	 are individuals	with	high	political	efficacy	on	all	three	dimensions;	with	high	internal,	but	low group	and	external	efficacy;	and	with	low	political	efficacy	on	all	dimensions	(although the	exact	shares	differ	somewhat	between	the	different	samples).

The	 most	 interesting	 groups	 from	 a	 theoretical	 perspective	 are	 composed	 of individuals	 with	 opposing	 group	 and	 external	 efficacy.	 Around	 30	 percent	 of	 the adolescents	in	the	 RISS-YAP,	and	around	22	percent	of	the	adults	in	the	RISS-IS	have opposing	group-related	and	external	efficacy.	In	more	detail,	these	are	individuals	with high	internal	and	group,	but	low	external	political	efficacy;	high	internal	and	external,	but low	group	efficacy;	low	internal	and	group,	but	high	external	efficacy;	and	low	internal and	external,	but	high	group	efficacy.	Each	of	these	single	groups	accounts	for	between	6 and	9.5	percent	among	adolescents	and	4	to	8	percent	among	adults;	and	while	these	are the	 four	 smallest	 groups	 in	 terms	 of	 their	 political	 efficacy	 constellations,	 they	 jointly account	for	a	sizeable	share	of	over	one	fifth	among	adults	and	almost	a	third	among adolescents.

Individuals	 with	 either	 high	 or	 low	 political	 efficacy	 on	 all	 three	 dimensions account	for	46	percent	of	the	sample	among	adults,	and	40	percent	among	adolescents.	In both	samples,	the	largest	group	is	composed	of	individuals	with	high	political	efficacy	on

all	 dimensions	 -	 which	 is	 somewhat	 relieving	 since	 political	 efficacy	 is	 such	 a	 strong predictor	of	political	participation.

For	 them,	 a	 two-dimensional conception	and	assessment	of	political	efficacy	is	inadequate	and	results	in	imprecise measures.

An	 almost	 automatic	 follow-up	 question	 thus	 is:	 Who	 are	 these	 people	 who differentiate	between	external	and	group	efficacy?	To	answer	this,	we	treat	these	groups separately	as	dependent	variables	and	estimate	linear	regressions	with	the	background characteristics	(economic,	educational,	and	migration	background)	as	core	predictors	of belonging	to	each	of	these	groups.	We	in	addition	include	individuals'	gender	and	year	of birth	as	controls.	Again,	we	replicated	these	models	further	adding	political	interest	and satisfaction	 with	 democracy	as	control	variables.	This	barely	alters	the	results	for	the background	 characteristics,	 as	 shown	 in	 Appendix	 4.	 We	 in	 addition	 estimated	 these models	 for	 groups	 of	 individuals	 with	 either	 high	 or	 low	 political	 efficacy	 on	 all dimensions.	 As	 we	 are	 not	 theoretically	 interested	 in	 these	 groups	 in	 this	 paper,	 but consider	these	groups	as	relevant	-	among	other	aspects,	because	of	their	size	-	we	report results	for	interested	readers	in	Appendix	5.

First,	we	focus	on	individuals	with	high	internal	efficacy	and	contrasting	external and	 group	 efficacy. Figure  10 illustrates	 the	 corresponding	 results.	 In	 both	 samples, migration	background	emerges	as	the	most	important	background	characteristic	in	this regard:	Individuals	with	a	migration	background	(both	1 st and	2 nd generation)	are	much more	likely	to	have	high	internal	and	external,	but	low	group	efficacy	than	those	without a	migration	background,	and	conversely,	they	are	much	less	likely	to	have	high	internal and	group,	but	low	external	political	efficacy.

For	migration	background, the	patterns	are	similar	to	Figure	10:	Individuals	with	a	migration	background	are	more likely	to	be	in	the	group	with	(low	internal	and)	low	group,	but	high	external	efficacy,	and less	likely	to	be	in	the	group	with	(low	internal	and)	low	external,	but	high	group	efficacy. Having	a	better	educational	or	economic	background,	in	contrast,	is	not	associated	with belonging	to	any	of	these	groups.	Among	adults,	though,	those	with	a	university	degree	or with	more	money	are	less	likely	to	belong	to	these	groups	with	low	internal	and	opposing group	and	external	efficacy.	One	reason	for	this	is	that	these	individuals	are	less	likely	to have	 low	 internal	 efficacy.	 An	 interesting	 additional	 observation	 in Figure  11 is	 that women	are	more	likely	to	be	in	both	of	these	groups	-	which	is	likely	due	to	the	lower level	of	internal	efficacy	among	women	(see	discussion	above).

Overall,	the	analyses	of	within-individual	constellations	of	political	efficacy	beliefs have	two	main	take-aways:	over	one	fifth	of	adults	and	almost	one	third	of	adolescents	in our	surveys	have	opposing	external	and	group	political	efficacy.	In	particular	migration background	plays	a	role	in	this	regard,	but	economic	and	educational	background	also matter.	 Specifically,	 individuals	 with	 disadvantaged	 backgrounds	 are	 more	 likely	 to belong	 to	 the	 group	 with	 have	 high	 external	 and	 low	 group-related	 political	 efficacy, whereas	 individuals	 with	 advantaged	 background	 characteristics	 are	 more	 likely	 to belong	to	a	group	with	high	group	and	low	external	political	efficacy.	That	is,	many	people are	aware	of	their	worse	resp.	better	representation	in	politics	-	and	researchers	better acknowledge	their	differentiated	perspectives	on	political	responsiveness.

## 5. Conclusion


Political	efficacy	is	a	core	predictor	of	political	participation,	and	usually	conceived	of	as having	 an	 internal	 and	 an	 external	 component:	 the	 belief	 in	 one's	 own	 ability	 to understand	politics	and	meaningfully	participate,	on	the	one	hand,	and	the	belief	in	the

political	system's	responsiveness,	on	the	other.	However,	political	responsiveness	is	far from	equal	for	different	subgroups	in	society.	In	this	paper,	we	theoretically	argued	that people	 are	 aware	 of	 such	 differences	 and	 that	 political	 efficacy	 thus	 consists	 of	 three dimensions:	internal, general external and group-related	external	efficacy .	 Furthermore, we	argued	that	standard	items	to	assess	external	efficacy,	which	typically	use	the	stimulus 'people	like	me',	are	too	vague	to	specify	which	group	respondents	should	think	of	when answering	the	items,	thus	resulting	in	imprecise	measures	of	external	political	efficacy. We	thus	developed	a	new	format	to	assess	these	different	dimensions	of	political	efficacy, which	differentiates	between	general	and	group-specific	item	formulations,	and,	in	the youth	sample,	also	adds	an	introductory	statement	that	explicitly	mentions	the	groups	of reference.	We	fielded	our	new	measures	in	two	large-N,	register	based	surveys	among adolescents	and	adults	in	Germany.	The	results	support	our	core	claims:	Among	both adolescents	and	adults,	a	three-dimensional	model	of	political	efficacy	fits	the	data	best. The	three	dimensions	of	political	efficacy	have	different	distributions,	which	in	addition vary	by	societal	subgroups.	Furthermore,	individuals	background	characteristics	show different	associations	with	the	three	dimensions.	Finally,	analyses	of	constellations	of	the three	dimensions	of	political	efficacy	within	individuals	reveal	that	a	sizeable	share	of individuals	-	between	one	fifth	and	one	third	of	the	population	-	have	opposing	external and	 group	 efficacy.	 This	 highlights	 the	 importance	 of	 differentiating	 between	 these dimensions	of	political	efficacy	both	theoretically	and	empirically.

That	 said,	 differences	 in	 our	 assessment	 of	 the	 three	 dimensions	 of	 political efficacy	in	the	adult	survey	(RISS-IS)	and	the	adolescent	survey	(RISS-YAP)	-	particularly, the	lack	of	an	explanation	of	the	reference	groups	in	RISS-IS	-	can	teach	us	an	important lesson:	Although	our	main	results	hold	in	both	samples,	differences	between	external	and group-related	external	political	efficacy	are	less	pronounced	among	adults	than	among adolescents.	This	is	surprising,	since	adolescents,	due	to	their	younger	age,	have	had	less personal	experience	with	and	in	politics,	which	should	result	in	less	crystallized	political efficacy	(i.e.,	more	similar	group-related	and	general	external	political	efficacy).	Thus,	we believe	 that	 the	 lack	 of	 an	 explanation	 of	 what	 'my	 background'	 means	 blurred	 the difference	between	external	and	group	efficacy:	People	hold	so	many	multiple	identities and	potential	group	memberships,	ranging	from	class,	education,	migration	to	gender, sexual	 orientation,	 age,	 religious	 belonging	 etc.	 Without	 specifying	 which	 of	 these respondents	should	think	of,	respondents	may	think	of	completely	different	aspects	of

their	identities,	namely	those	that	had	recently	been	activated	in	real	life,	either	through personal	experiences	or	media	reporting.

To	 prevent	 such	 a	 blurring	 between	 the	 external	 and	 the	 group	 efficacy dimensions,	 we	 urge	 that	 the	 conceptually	 and	 empirically	 meaningful	 distinction requires	the	precise	activation	of	the	group	memberships	which	are	of	interest	for	the respective	 researchers.	 That	 is,	 survey	 items	 must	 indicate	 the	 group	 dimension	 by formulating	concrete	items	such	as	'people	of	my	gender',	'my	migration	background', 'my	age	group',	etc.	Now,	some	would	accuse	such	formulations	of	activating	artificial group	identities.	We	do	not	think	that	this	is	correct.	If	people	do	not	feel	that	they	belong to	a	certain	gender,	migration	or	age	group,	they	will	not	differ	in	their	answers	on	group specific	efficacy	items	compared	to	external	efficacy	items.	However,	this	is	a	claim	which needs	 further	 testing	 in	 the	 future.	 With	 this	 paper	 we	 mainly	 wanted	 to	 raise	 the awareness	 that	 item	 formulations	 with	 stimuli	 such	 as	 'people	 like	 me'	 or	 'my background'	are	unlucky	as	they	blur	the	boundary	between	internal,	external	and	group efficacy.	However,	if	researchers	are	not	interested	in	the	-	as	we	think	-	highly	relevant dimension	of	group	efficacy,	but	only	care	about	the	traditional	concepts	of	internal	and external	 efficacy,	 they	 are	 well	 advised	 to	 use	 items	 without	 connotations	 to	 some abstract	groups	such	as	'people	like	me'.
