Lastly, we want to provide a potential explanation for the lower relative performance of text features based on CrisisWatch reports as opposed to taxed features based on BBC data. As CW texts have a special focus on developments regarding the conflict situation in a specific country, the features extracted from the reports might only capture latent information that is already covered by conflict history. Consequently, in a conflict intensity prediction task, they may not be able to complement features measuring conflict trends and history as well as in other settings. Features extracted from broader corpora of texts, such as the BBC Monitoring articles might offer complementary information. Although not all of the many articles might be specifically talking about conflict-related events, they might cover different dimensions relevant to conflict predictions.

Overall, text features seem to capture ongoing conflict dynamics and appear to have the potential to complement traditional input features for prediction models. However, on a global level with conflict history available, we have shown that few features can supplement conflict trends as predictors. Our results and the findings by Mueller and Rauh (2022a) point in the direction that text features could add more to predictions of conflict onset in cases where there is no conflict history (the so-called hard case problem) instead of global-level conflict intensity. Although further

research is needed to systematically identify the conditions and cases in which text features can improve existing conflict prediction models, this paper is a first attempt to provide an overview of the potential benefits of using text features for crisis early warning models. Other interesting areas of further research might be to extend this evaluation to a more granular level, meaning to move beyond the country-month level. In general, it is advisable to use a high-quality newspaper corpus. The challenges associated with constructing such a newspaper corpus, however, are plenty, especially concerning country coverage and the challenge of constructing a diverse corpus consisting not only of articles from one international newspaper agency.


## Conclusion


Conflict prediction continues to be a challenging task. However, the potential benefits of anticipating the next conflict or crisis continue to motivate researchers to improve upon existing approaches. Particularly the multifaceted and dynamic nature of conflicts, coupled with challenges related to data, human behavior, and the importance of contextual factors, contributes to the ongoing difficulty in accurately predicting when and how conflicts will arise.

However, with recent advancements in computational performance and wider and easier access to new data sources through the internet, researchers have been able to improve the predictive performance of models. Applying natural language processing (NLP) methods to large corpora of text documents stands out as one promising direction to improve upon these efforts even more. Particularly, conflict reports and newspaper articles could be helpful in this regard, as they include relevant information about current and future dynamics of conflict in a country.

Therefore, in this article, we examined strategies to extract features from text data for out-of-sample conflict prediction using different NLP techniques, providing an overview of the most popular NLP approaches and presenting a comparative assessment of their benefits for crisis-early-warning models. We do so by applying topic models, dictionary approaches, a document scaling method, and transformer models to two text corpora (CrisisWatch reports and BBC Monitoring news articles) and investigate how well these features can help predict conflict intensity. While text features alone cannot reach the same predictive performance as using conflict trends or other structural data, some of them, particularly transformer models, reach acceptable levels of performance, considering these predictions are based on text data alone. We find that the integration of NLP methods for conflict prediction underscores the potential of leveraging textual data to enhance the accuracy and depth of forecasting models. Although NLP is not a silver bullet, our findings reveal that incorporating NLP tools can offer valuable insights and can complement and depending on the context even supplement alternative approaches. This is underlined by our results, showing that including text features in the prediction models improves their performance, even if only marginally. We sought to identify the most effective NLP approach based on the nature of text sources and the availability of other structural variables. Our assessment of various NLP methods on distinct corpora, encompassing general newspaper articles and expert-authored CrisisWatch reports, emphasizes the need for a tailored approach that aligns with the specific characteristics of the data at hand. Furthermore, increased model complexity and computational cost does not always translate into better performance and depending on the context, applying a simpler NLP approach may save computing time at no expense of performance. With no single NLP approach outperforming the others, our results underline the importance of continuously investigating new approaches and their applicability to conflict prediction.

Crucially, our research sheds light on the complementarity of NLP features with traditional structural variables like socio-economic indicators, conflict history, and political indicators. The synergy between these approaches reinforces the idea that a holistic understanding of conflict prediction requires the integration of a diverse set of data sources and modeling approaches. Given the importance of improving conflict prediction models, we hope that this study can serve as an initial step toward assessing the efficacy of different NLP methods. While we evaluated how well models fare at predicting conflict intensity, future research looking at how different text features could help predict outbreaks or escalations of violence, in line with findings by Mueller and Rauh (2022a), could prove beneficial.

Finally, natural language processing, and machine learning more generally, are fast-developing research areas that have seen an immense boost in popularity in recent years. Particularly the new Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) model family is evolving rapidly, with impressive results in many different areas. However, currently, there is no straightforward or intuitive way to apply these generative models for prediction tasks on tabular data. While they may be helpful in prediction adjacent tasks (see e.g. Parolin et al., 2022), their usefulness for generating features for conflict prediction is limited for now. Moving forward, continued assessment in different contexts will be essential to evaluate future approaches and improve the accuracy of conflict prediction.

## Introduction


Among policy makers, practitioners, and researchers there is a great need to understand which educational programs are effective and under which conditions. Assessing program effectiveness can, however, be complicated due to insufficient commitment to research of stakeholders, a lack of research funding or improper designs for evaluation. As a solution, researchers propose using aggregate school-level datasets to carry out program evaluation in valid, nonintrusive, and cost-effective ways (Jacob et al., 2014; Hallberg et al., 2018; Stuart, 2007). A number of within-study comparisons demonstrate that quasi-experimental designs can produce valid estimates that are similar to experimental designs when the comparison group is carefully selected and the pre-intervention trend is adequately modeled (e.g., Hallberg et al., 2020; Jacob et al., 2016; Sims et al., 2022; St. Clair et al., 2016). Multiple studies have therefore employed aggregate datasets to assess program or policy effectiveness on the school and state level, for instance on the No Child Left Behind Act (Dee & Jacob, 2011, Wong et al., 2015).

In the US context quasi-experimental designs with aggregate data are frequently used as schools are compelled to collect data on student achievement. However, applications of such designs to evaluate educational programs are less common outside the US. This lack of research is unfortunate for two reasons. First, it remains unclear to what extent quasiexperimental designs with aggregate school-level datasets are also applicable in other national contexts. Second, it limits understanding how program effectiveness may vary between national contexts (Reynolds et al., 2014).

In this study, we present the evaluation of the efficacy of an extended school week in the Netherlands, using a quasi-experimental design, leveraging unique school-level registry data and synthetic control analysis. The intervention is part of the National Program Rotterdam South ( Nationaal Programma Rotterdam Zuid : NPRZ), a unique program in its

scope, long-term orientation and involvement of various stakeholders (Custers et al., 2023; Dol et al., 2019). The extended school week aims to improve educational outcomes among disadvantaged students in 30 primary schools (NPRZ, 2012). During the extra hours, children engage in both curricular and extracurricular activities.

The intervention is strongly inspired by the Harlem Children's Zone (HCZ), a program that has substantially increased test scores (Dobbie & Fryer, 2011, 2015). Evaluating the HCZ adoption in the Netherlands provides an interesting case because the Dutch educational landscape is considered 'policy-dense' with many stakeholders (Ladd & Fiske, 2011; Waslander et al., 2016), meaning implementation of interventions might be complicated (Custers, 2023). Our study discusses to what extent educational concepts such as the HCZ can be successfully transferred to other contexts (Kerr & Dyson, 2014). In addition, since in practice the NPRZ intervention predominantly operates as an after-school program, we also consider how our findings relate to the literature on these programs.

In the current paper, our goal is to estimate the causal impact of the NPRZ intervention on educational achievement. For this, we use register data from the system of social statistical datasets (SSD), a unique system from Statistics Netherlands that combines register data from educational, tax, and other administrative authorities (Bakker et al., 2014). Based on these registers, we construct a longitudinal dataset including 22 intervention schools and relevant control schools drawn from the nationwide registry data, in principle including all schools in the Netherlands, for 5 pre-intervention and 9 post-intervention years. The causal effect of interest is the post-intervention improvement in educational outcomes for the 22 intervention schools.

To estimate the causal effect of the NPRZ intervention, we perform a quasiexperimental synthetic control analysis (Abadie, 2021), which attempts to estimate the postintervention counterfactual ('what would the study outcomes have been in absence of the

intervention') for each school. The method achieves this by creating a weighted combination of control schools for each intervention school. In contrast to the comparative interrupted time series (CITS) method commonly used in educational policy research, synthetic controls enable the estimation of intervention effects for individual schools, which is particularly useful in our study because schools have some autonomy in how they implement the program (Kruiter et al., 2020), meaning that effects might differ between schools. Synthetic controls have not been applied much in educational research with some exceptions (e.g., Betts et al., 2024; Bifulco et al., 2017; Klasik, 2013). Our paper therefore adds to the education literature, demonstrating how this method can be used for program evaluation.

The present paper is structured as follows: First, we contextualize our study by discussing the HCZ and relevant findings from similar after-school programs. Second, we describe the setup and context of the NPRZ intervention, including relevant characteristics of the Dutch education system and potential issues with the intervention. Third, we describe the register data and the resulting longitudinal dataset, after which we explain our methodological approach. Finally, we present the results and end with a brief discussion.


## Findings from the HCZ and after-school programs



## Harlem Children's Zone


The HCZ is an educational and social service organization that creates educational opportunities for students in central Harlem (Hanson, 2013). The philosophy behind the program is to create a 'pipeline' or 'conveyor belt' through which children from disadvantaged families are supported by high-quality services from birth to college. The HCZ is internationally known for its 'doubly holistic' approach, as it focuses both on the student's school career (within-school) as well as the family and community context (outside-ofschool) (Kerr & Dyson, 2014). The program was created in 1997 with a 24-block area and

has since then step-wise expanded to a 97-block area. In 2004 and 2005 the Promise Academy was launched, which enrolls a new kindergarten and sixth-grade cohort each year until becoming a full K-12 charter school (Dobbie & Fryer, 2011).

The HCZ is widely regarded as a pioneering and effective program (Hanson, 2013; Kerr & Dyson, 2014). Dobbie and Fryer (2011) evaluated the impact of attending the Promise Academy by comparing students who are admitted after a lottery (winners) to students who were rejected (losers). They estimate that students who enroll in Promise Academy middle school gain about 0.2 standard deviations in mathematics each year, while students who enroll in Promise Academy elementary school gain approximately 0.2 standard deviations in both math and English Language Arts (ELA) per year. In a later study, Dobbie and Fryer (2015) find that six years after admission in the Promise Academy middle school lottery winners score almost 0.3 standard deviations higher on an index of academic achievement than lottery losers. However, lottery winners are not doing better on educational attainment, including high school graduation and college enrollment, than lottery losers. In addition, Whitehurst and Croft (2010) compare the Promise Academy to other charter schools in New York City (NYC) and find that its performance of standardized math tests is somewhat higher than the average charter school whereas the score on ELA is below average. On the other hand, the Promise Academy still has better results than traditional schools with similar demographics.

Dobbie and Fryer (2015) argue that the Promise Academy is effective because it largely adheres to the five characteristics of effective charter schools that they identify in another paper: frequent teacher feedback, the use of data to guide instruction, high-dosage tutoring, increased instructional time, and high expectations (Dobbie & Fryer, 2013). Some data seem to support this observation. For instance, in the 2010/2011 school year Promise Academy middle schoolers spent 46% more time in school than NYC public school students

and the level of teacher attrition was very high in the first years of operation, indicating many low-performing teachers were either fired or let go (Dobbie & Fryer, 2015, p.99). Regarding the latter, Yeh (2013, p.8) suggests that teacher attrition might explain the HCZ results just as well as the attraction of high-qualified teachers. Highly dedicated teachers are willing to work long hours and endure conditions that often cause less-dedicated teachers to quit. However, teachers who cannot maintain the exhausting pace of long hours and high expectations either quit or are fired. Students do therefore not only profit from their new hard-working teachers, but they are also less exposed to less-dedicated teachers.

An important question is to what extent the HCZ model is transferable to other contexts such as the NPRZ (Hanson, 2013; Kerr & Dyson, 2014). We discuss two aspects here: the possibility of attracting high-quality teachers and how the program is governed. First, high-quality teachers are believed to play a central role in the HCZ's success (Dobbie & Fryer, 2011). Yeh (2013, p.16), however, argues that it is practically unattainable, if not logically impossible, to hire such teachers in other settings:

The KIPP [Knowledge is Power Program] and HCZ approaches work by recruiting highly dedicated teachers, creating a work environment that only the top half of all teachers can survive, and constantly recruiting additional teachers across the nation in a wide-ranging attempt to fill the empty teaching slots. The consequence, however, is that this process inevitably pulls the best teachers from across the country, leaving an insufficient number of those teachers to implement the same approach in every school nationwide.

Attracting high-quality teachers has also been a challenge for the NPRZ within a context of teacher shortages in the Netherlands. The teacher shortage is especially severe among schools

with a high share of minority and/or poor students (Inspectorate of Education, 2019), and is therefore also experienced within the NPRZ schools (NPRZ, 2023).

Second, the 'pipeline' vision by the HCZ requires the central coordination of their services within the Harlem area. The HCZ is run by an overarching organization that has the power and mandate to steer and alter services. The full integration of schools with numerous support services is considered one of the core strengths of the HCZ (see Hanson, 2013). However, this also means that the concept of the HCZ cannot be easily copied to the Dutch urban context. This would require building a 'new' infrastructure in Rotterdam South, but such an infrastructure with schools and related services already exists. The HCZ model is therefore incorporated into the existing infrastructure, which leads to several challenges such as common goal setting and dealing with school autonomy.


## After-school programs


To further contextualize the NPRZ program, we also discuss findings from after-school programs, for three reasons. First, even though the NPRZ intervention is based on the HCZ, in its current form it operates more like an extended school week or after-school program than the HCZ 'pipeline' model. Second, the intervention addresses Dutch primary school students (sixth grade), whereas findings from the HCZ largely concern middle and high school students. Third, the HCZ evaluation includes two Promise Academies with specific programs, whereas after-school program studies often include many schools and centers. Our analysis is closer to the latter, focusing on intervention effects in many schools. We mainly discuss studies on the 21st Century Community Learning Centers (21st CCLC) because, overall, this program has many similar characteristics to the NPRZ intervention, including a mix of academic and enrichment activities, serving primarily minority and/or poor students,

collaboration with local organizations, and taking place within the school (James-Burdumy et al., 2007).

Results from the 21st CCLC regarding academic outcomes have been mixed. JamesBurdumy et al. (2007) find no effects for elementary students in 26 centers two years after implementation of the program. They attribute these findings to problems in coordination between regular school staff and after-school program staff, a potential lack of participation, and the fragmentation of after-school activities in which relatively little time was focused on academic learning. Jenner and Jenner (2007), on the other hand, show that in Louisiana participation in after-school programs led to higher test scores on reading and language, especially for at-risk students who had higher attendance. In line with these findings, Holstead and King (2011) demonstrate that at-risk students in Indiana improved their reading and math scores after attending 60 or more days in the 21st CCLC. They only studied centers that were rated as high quality, meaning there was a strong focus on academic learning, a close link with regular school activities, qualified staff, and good coordination with stakeholders. Finally, Leos-Urbel (2015) analyzed 29 after-school programs in NYC that served both elementary and middle school students. The results indicate that a more supportive environment relates to increased test scores for elementary school participants. Structured interactions between staff and participants are associated with improvements in reading scores for middle school students. Interestingly, purposeful engagement - measured as whether students are challenged, take responsibility and are collaborative - had a negative association with academic outcomes. Leos-Urbel (2015) suggests that activities that aim to push students to a higher level might not have been implemented in a productive way.

The outcomes of these studies are in line with meta-analyses about what makes afterschool programs effective. Durlak et al. (2010) included 20 and 25 studies that investigated achievement test scores and school grades, respectively. They conclude that programs with

stronger SAFE (Sequenced, Active, Focused, Explicit) features are considerably more effective in raising academic performance. This means that learning should be broken down into smaller steps and that material is provided in a sequenced and ordered way, youth should be activated after receiving instruction, time and attention need to be focused on specific tasks, and the learning objectives should be clear. This aligns with a broader notion in the literature that the amount of instructional time is not necessarily decisive, but rather how this time is spent and the quality of the services delivered (e.g. Bohnert et al., 2010; Roth et al., 2010). In a recent review, Kraft and Novicoff (2024) point out that it matters when and how much time is added. The returns become marginal as the school day gets longer. For instance, extending an already long school day from 7 to 8 hours is unlikely to have the same benefit as increasing a short school day from 5 to 6 hours (Kraft & Novicoff, 2024, p. 29).

In summary, findings from after-school programs are mixed, with seemingly strong dependence of program effectiveness on implementation details as well as intended outcomes.


## The NPRZ Children's Zone


The NPRZ is one of the largest urban policies in Dutch history that targets a specific area. It aims to improve socioeconomic conditions in Rotterdam South, an area with over 200,000 residents that is historically one of the poorest districts in the Netherlands. Through a collaboration between multiple stakeholders, including the national government, local authorities, educational institutions, housing corporations, and employers, investments are made in three domains: Education, employment, and housing. The program started in 2011 and will operate for 20 years.


## The extended school week


The HCZ was the main source of inspiration for the educational component, which resulted from a visit of public administrators to the HCZ (NPRZ, 2012). The initial ambition was to replicate a Children's Zone (NPRZ CZ) in seven neighborhoods in Rotterdam South, an area that includes 30 primary schools. About one third of all Rotterdam South residents live in this specific area. The main reason the area was selected for the NPRZ CZ is that disadvantage is more concentrated here than in the whole of Rotterdam South and Rotterdam (Municipality of Rotterdam, 2011). This selection was supported with statistics on schooling levels, dropouts, age distribution, single parent households, housing values, and income levels. However, other research has argued that the NPRZ CZ resembles other disadvantaged areas in Rotterdam and the Netherlands (Custers, 2023; Custers et al., 2023). Schools in the NPRZ CZ do not substantially differ from many schools outside the NPRZ CZ in terms of a wide range of observable statistics, including migration background, students' socioeconomic status, and school achievement. The existence of similar schools outside the intervention area therefore facilitates our quasi-experimental analysis approach.

The educational component has two main goals: 1) to achieve better test scores and educational results within the Children's Zone and 2) to steer students to studies in care, engineering, and port-related work to increase their labor market opportunities. Our study focuses on the first goal. Multiple interventions have been introduced to replicate the HCZ pipeline model, such as more investment in preschooling, neighborhood care teams, professionalization of teachers and school management, and an extended school week (NPRZ, 2012, 2015). The extended school week has, however, been the main priority of the educational component (Kruiter et al., 2020). Although the other interventions are relevant, most of them operate in other parts of the city as well. Our discussion here therefore focuses on the design and implementation of the extended school week.

With the extended school week schools provide six to ten hours of extra schooling per week. Since 2019 it is mandatory for schools to administer ten hours, while before most schools offered six hours (Kruiter et al., 2020). Almost all schools started with the extended school week in the school year 2013/2014, although the degree and intensity of implementation has differed between schools. In the first year the extended school week operated for all students in sixth grade. In the following years, the intervention was gradually extended to lower grades until it applied in all grades up to kindergarten.

Interestingly, the NPRZ does not provide a clear rationale for how the extra hours are expected to contribute to higher academic performance. It is generally assumed that longer school days will lead to better academic outcomes, but how this will be achieved is not explained. This lack of theoretical substantiation relates to the design of the intervention where schools have considerable autonomy to fill in the extra hours, which resulted from early discussion on intervention (Custers, 2023). The NPRZ board compels the schools to provide ten hours and in return, they can largely choose how they spend these hours (Kruiter et al., 2020). This relates to the high degree of independence regarding curricula that schools have in the Dutch education system (Dol et al., 2019; Waslander et al., 2016). Furthermore, it has also been mentioned that a more informal goal of the extended school week is to 'keep children off the street' (Kruiter et al., 2020).

Schools thus have leeway in how they execute the extra hours. The main components are language, mathematics, study skills, English, career orientation, culture, and sports. Almost all schools have a mix of cognitive learning activities and activities for leisure or broader development (Kruiter et al., 2020; Sardes & DSP-group, 2023). The content and organization differs between and within schools. For instance, a school might reserve some days for learning after school, whereas on other days they might program playful activities during breaks. Another school might prefer that activities mostly take place after school,

without adjusting the regular program too much. At the start of the intervention, many schools were unable to provide the extra hours due to staffing problems. In most schools external providers therefore take care of the extended school time. Schools receive funding to hire these organizations and can choose accordingly which services and people match their curriculum.


## Program issues


Here we discuss some relevant issues that have emerged since the program's introduction.  A 1 first issue is that the goal of the extended school time has shifted over time. In the first years the NPRZ strongly emphasized that the goal of the Children's Zone is to increase academic performance among students. In this period many interventions are explicitly framed as contributing to academic performance, which in turn should lead to better school careers and successful futures (NPRZ, 2012, 2015). The emphasis on academic achievement is also reflected in the choice of indicators for program monitoring, which includes indicators such as average test scores and the percentage of graduates in different track levels (e.g., NPRZ, 2015).

However, in more recent years a broader formulation of the intervention appears. The current focus is not only on educational results, but also on enrichment and socioemotional development (Sardes & DSP-group, 2023; NPRZ, 2023). Moreover, a qualitative evaluation of the intervention in four primary schools mentions that enrichment is their highest priority (Sardes & DSP-group, 2023). Enrichment comprises a broad range of activities such as discovering talents and visiting places outside the neighborhood. The change in goal orientation can be considered a risk for program effectiveness in academic performance,

given that other studies stress the need for consistent and clearly defined goals (e.g. Durlak et al., 2010).

A second issue is that during the course of the program a national teacher crisis has developed, meaning there is a general lack of qualified teachers in primary education (Inspectorate of Education, 2019). This teacher shortage is especially high in the NPRZ CZ (NPRZ, 2023), because schools with a high share of minority and/or poor students are the least popular places to work among teachers (Inspectorate of Education, 2019). Research from the US also shows that schools with these demographics tend to attract teachers that are less experienced and less effective in teaching, which might further decrease the quality of instruction (Steele et al., 2015). In addition, it has been suggested that some teachers left the NPRZ CZ schools because of the combination of staffing issues and the problems associated with the coordination of the extended school time (Kruiter et al., 2020). It is thus difficult to organize effective teaching because qualified staff that can be employed for both the curricular and extracurricular activities is scarce. Since it has been argued that high-quality teachers are the basis for success in the HCZ (Dobbie & Fryer, 2011), a lack thereof in the NPRZ CZ might undermine the effectiveness of the extended school week.

Third, in most schools external providers take care of the extra hours, because schools already have staffing problems for regular classes. However, in some cases the coordination has been challenging. For instance, when something goes wrong with enlisting for the extra hours, parents address the school director and staff while the external providers are actually responsible (Kruiter et al., 2020, p. 13). Yet, over the years the coordination has become better due to the experience that both schools and external providers have gained (Sardes & DSP-group, 2023). However, the quality of staff from external providers remains an issue (Sardes & DSP-group, 2023; Kruiter et al., 2020). External providers often work with freelancers who have less educational training and pedagogical skills than regular teachers.

Their level of instruction is therefore generally lower and some lack experience in working with disadvantaged students.

Finally, the degree of participation in the hours after school varies between schools and students. The NPRZ has stated that participation in the extended school week is mandatory, but in practice schools have their own guidelines on whether students should participate. In some schools the after hours are optional, in other schools all students should be present. This has also created some frustration among parents, who complain that children have more freedom at other schools in the neighborhood (Kruiter et al., 2020, p. 13). The lack of participation in some schools can be considered problematic, since other studies show that participation is an essential prerequisite for effectiveness (e.g., Holstead & King, 2011; Jenner & Jenner, 2007).


## The Dutch education system


We provide a brief overview of the Dutch education system to provide more context on how we measure educational achievement (see also Jacobs et al., 2023). A crucial transition in the school career is from primary to secondary school, after sixth grade, which occurs around age twelve. Based on a track recommendation by the teacher, students are allocated to four tracks in secondary education: practical education (PRO), pre-vocational education with four levels (VMBO), senior general secondary education (HAVO), and pre-university education (VWO). The track allocation system has changed over time due to policy changes. Prior to 2014, primary school students first took a standardized national exit exam (a high-stakes test) followed by the teacher's track recommendation. From 2014 and onwards, teachers provide a preliminary recommendation which can be revised based on exam results. This change grants teachers more autonomy in determining the final track recommendation, which ultimately decides the track students will follow in secondary school.

Another policy change introduced in 2014 is that schools can choose between different providers of the high-stakes test (Jacobs et al., 2023). In earlier years Cito was the provider of the high-stakes test, but after the policy change multiple schools switched to alternative tests (e.g., IEP or Route-8). In the academic year 2017/2018 the Cito-test was still used in approximately 55% of all primary schools, whereas before 2014/2015 this was over 80%. Schools that scored low on the Cito switched more often to other test providers (Swart et al., 2019), including a substantial part of our intervention schools. These changes have some implications that will be discussed below.


## Limitations and assumptions


A first limitation is the lack of precise data on the implementation and participation of the extended school week. Ideally, such data is available to better understand why interventions are effective (or not) (Durlak et al., 2010). However, because no rigorous evaluation of the NPRZ CZ was planned, such data have not been centrally collected. Instead, we conduct a post hoc evaluation using school-level data (Jacob et al., 2014; Hallberg et al., 2018).

Second, for the outcome variables we use track recommendations and Cito scores. Track recommendations are a more subjective measure that are potentially prone to teacher bias. The teacher determines the track recommendation based on the student's learning potential, ability, and performance on the high-stakes test. Class and ethnic stereotypes may thereby influence the teacher's judgment (Batruch et al., 2023). The track recommendation is thus a different outcome than standardized test scores. In our analysis, we do control for variables that affect teacher bias, such as class and ethnic measures, hence diminishing possible unobservable influences since we assume the level of bias is similar between synthetic control and intervention schools.

Standardized high-stakes tests such as Cito are more suited for objectively assessing academic performance. Valid Cito scores are, however, only available for a selection of intervention schools that continued to use the test after the test market was liberalized in 2014. We thus have high-stakes test data for a selection of schools, but for other schools the test data are not comparable between years.

Third, a standard assumption in fully experimental studies is that control units do not receive any intervention, but this is unrealistic in school-based studies (Durlak, 1985). In the Netherlands, disadvantaged schools with a high share of minority and/or poor students receive extra resources from both the national government and municipalities (Driessen & Dekkers, 2008; Ladd & Fiske, 2011). Municipal subsidies are frequently used to support preschool education for 2-4 year olds. National funds are allocated to schools who decide how they spend these resources, for instance through hiring more teachers and supportive staff or organizing extracurricular activities. This implies that we are not comparing our intervention group to a control group with no intervention, but rather to a control group with other interventions. Yet, we emphasize that our intervention schools are also entitled to these national and municipal subsidies. The NPRZ CZ was thereby designed to provide more than the 'regular' schemes for disadvantaged schools. In summary, we assume that we are estimating the effect of the extended school week on top of other interventions happening in both the control schools as well as intervention schools.


## Data and methods


In this section, we explain how the data was collected and how different variables were operationalized, as well as how these are entered into the analysis to produce an estimate of the impact of the NPRZ intervention on educational achievement. The data come from the Social Statistical Database (SSD), combining various administrative sources in the

Netherlands, including the population register, education institutions, and tax authorities (Bakker et al., 2014). Statistics Netherlands enables access to researchers to use anonymized individual-level data for academic studies, provided they comply with stringent legal and ethical guidelines. Statistics Netherlands reviews research output to ensure privacy protection.

All data processing and analysis methods described in this section are implemented using the R programming language. The code for this study -  including the operationalization of the relevant variables and the analysis implementation - is publicly at van Kesteren et al. (2024) although it is not possible to share the empirical data following Statistics Netherlands policies.

Conceptually, the synthetic control method can be seen as a generalization of matching: In the special case when there is a single unit in the donor pool, with weight = 1, we can consider the method to be equivalent to one-to-one matching. To compute the weights , the synthetic control method minimizes the distance between the intervention school and the synthetic control school in the years before the intervention took place ( ). There are many possible operationalizations of this distance: What should be minimized exactly and how? Two of the most important choices are (a) which covariates to account for in order to control for potential confounding, similar to matching methods, and (b) how strongly to emphasize the fit of the synthetic control school to the pre-intervention outcome (educational attainment) in the intervention school. We will discuss the former choice in the next section, and outline our strategy for the latter choice here.

A specific advantage of our study is the large number of schools (>5,000) that can be incorporated in the donor pool for each intervention school. However, the standard synthetic control method of Abadie et al. (2010) cannot be applied to such large donor pools due to computational limitations. To solve this issue, we take the penalized synthetic control approach proposed by Abadie and l'Hour (2021), as developed and implemented in the R package pensynth (Van Kesteren, 2024). The penalized synthetic control method allows for smoothly interpolating between the synthetic control method and one-to-one matching by using a penalty parameter . In this way, the method benefits from the advantages of both methods: It does not require a single exact match to exist in the donor pool, but it does prefer

donor schools which are as similar as possible to the intervention school, improving upon the standard synthetic control method.

Specifically, in our implementation for each intervention school we choose to produce a synthetic control school which (a) minimizes the squared error to our chosen preintervention covariates, while (b) tuning the penalty parameter of the procedure to best approximate pre-intervention educational attainment. This procedure creates an acceptable fit while avoiding overfitting of the pre-intervention outcomes which has a detrimental effect on the estimation of the counterfactual in the post-intervention period (see, e.g., Ben-Michael et al., 2021).

In the next sections, we describe the control and outcome variables we have used to estimate the counterfactuals, after which we relate these variables to our analytic strategy.


## Outcome variables: Educational achievement


The first dependent variable is the track recommendation, based on the International Standard Level of Education ( ISLED ) (SSD file: INSCHRWPOTAB). Track recommendations were categorized into four groups, which were subsequently converted into ISLED scores (Schröder & Ganzeboom, 2014). The assigned scores are: lower pre-vocational education (LPV) (PRO/VMBO basis-kader, ISLED = 29.34), upper pre-vocational education (UPV) (VMBO gemengd-theoretisch, ISLED = 45.27), senior general secondary education (SGS) (HAVO, ISLED = 62.3), and pre-university education (VWO, ISLED = 71.92). In cases of dual track recommendations, the average of two ISLED scores was taken. For instance, a LPV/UPV recommendation received a score (29.34+45.27)/2 = 37.31. The second dependent variable is the Cito score , indicating the performance on the high-stakes test in the final grade of primary school. The Cito test consists of different subjects such as mathematics and language. The performance on different parts of the test results in a standardized score

between 501 and 550. The test is usually administered on multiple consecutive days somewhere in January or February. Both dependent variables are calculated as the average score at the school level (see also Table 1).


## Control variables


We identified several control variables relevant to educational achievement to adjust for potential confounding in our synthetic control analysis. First, parental education is determined based on the highest registered level of education (SSD file: HOOGSTEOPLTAB). Specifically, we consider both the share of lower educated mothers and lower educated fathers (below vocational level MBO-2). Next, standardized household income is calculated based on percentiles from the national income distribution (SSD files: IHI/INHATAB). The average percentile score for each school is used to represent household income levels.

Furthermore, we take school size into account, which is measured by the number of students enrolled in sixth grade (SSD file: INSCHRWPOTAB). The available data only allows for the calculation of school size, not individual class sizes. Some schools have multiple sixth grade classes. School retention refers to the number of years students remain enrolled in the same school (SSD file: INSCHRWPOTAB). The retention rate is determined by averaging the number of years students spend at a particular school. If students spend more than eight years at the same school, indicating grade retention in the final year, then their number of years at school is capped at eight years. The last school property is the school denomination , indicating the ideological and religious 'pillar' under which the school is registered (SSD file: INSCHRWPOTAB). We discuss specifics of this variable in the next section.

Finally, children's ethnicity is classified according to Dutch state definitions, which consider a child to have a migration background if either the child or one of their parents was born abroad (SSD file: GBAPERSOONTAB). We consider the share of native Dutch , Surinamese , Turkish , Moroccan , and Antillean/Aruban students. We also include the share of students living in a single parent household (SSD file: GBAHUISHOUDENSBUS). An overview can be found in Table 1.

## Analysis choices in covariates and outcomes


Here, we further explain the choices made in operationalizing our control covariates and the outcomes. First, we include socioeconomic and demographic variables that relate to both the intervention assignment and the outcomes. Schools with a high proportion of disadvantaged

students are often prioritized for interventions, since educational outcomes tend to be lower among disadvantaged and minority students. This pattern is also evident in the NPRZ, where schools were chosen based on neighborhood disadvantage. In addition to the socioeconomic factors of parental education and income, we incorporate five ethnic groups. These groups were selected because of their relative size, which significantly impacts outcomes at the school level, and due to notable differences in educational outcomes among them (e.g., Custers et al., 2023). Additionally, single parent households are often considered as an indicator of disadvantage, which is predictive of educational achievement (De Lange et al., 2014). Finally, while retention rate and school size did not play a direct role in selecting intervention schools, prior studies suggest these factors may affect educational outcomes (e.g., Custers et al., 2023; Leithwood & Jantzi, 2009).

Another explicit choice is that we restrict the donor pool for each intervention school to schools with the same denomination, leading to an exact match of the intervention school and the synthetic control school in terms of this variable. Schools in the Netherlands are historically organized around ideological and religious 'pillars', meaning that schools with the same denomination are more likely to share similar views and pedagogical philosophies (Dronkers, 1995). Although religion has become less important in school choice, schools are still organized in boards based on denomination. These boards have considerable autonomy, for instance in the appointment of teachers (Karsten, 1994). Restricting the donor pool to schools with the same denomination therefore increases the likelihood that potential donor and intervention schools share similar school philosophies, policies, and practices, thereby controlling for the confounding effects of these factors.

For the track recommendation outcome, we used all available years in the SSD set of datasets, namely 2009-2022. For the Cito outcome variable, we had to restrict the analysis to

2010-2017 due to privacy restrictions, missing data handling, and schools abandoning the Cito test.


## Missing data


In parental education there is a considerable amount of missing data on a per-student level (cf. Custers, 2023), particularly in earlier years. Thus, we compute this variable only for the last two pre-intervention years (2012 and 2013). However, missing data in these years is still large. For example, in 2013 the percentage of missings on the mother's and father's level of education are 26.7% and 47.2% for the intervention schools, respectively. In our main analysis, we make the assumption that there are no systematic differences in the missing data between the intervention and donor pool schools; accordingly, we compute the share of lower educated fathers and mothers in a school as proportions of the valid observations. To investigate whether the missing data might have a substantial influence on the results, we include the school-level proportion of missing values in parental education as a variable in the robustness checks (Online Appendix). This does not lead to different conclusions than presented here in the paper.

The outcome variables (ISLED score and Cito score) only receive a valid score after meeting two conditions. First, for each school in each year, there should be at least 10 valid observations (student results) per school. This prevents individual student scores from having a substantial influence on the school mean. Second, schools should have at least 75% valid scores on the outcome variable. If these conditions are not met for a particular school-year combination, the outcome is considered missing. Subsequently, we specify that schools need a minimum of two valid scores in both the pre- and post-intervention period, otherwise they are excluded from the analysis. The remaining missing values were imputed using predictive mean matching as implemented in the mice package (Van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn,

2011). Note that single imputation generally produces unbiased model estimates, but often leads to underestimation of uncertainty in the parameters; however, since we only produce point estimates of , this has only a minor impact on our results.

## Conclusion and discussion


This study investigated to what extent an adoption from the Harlem Children's Zone in the Dutch urban context has been effective in improving educational outcomes in disadvantaged primary schools. The main intervention involves extending the school week with six to ten hours, including both curricular and extracurricular activities. The results indicate that the program has had little effect on either track recommendations or standardized test scores. There is some variation between schools in the size and direction of the effects, but overall the evidence shows limited impact of the program. These findings are corroborated by additional robustness checks. In the remainder of this article we provide some tentative explanations and discuss the implications of our findings.

Multiple explanations can be provided for the limited effectiveness of the program, including the degree of participation, the quality of support staff, goal setting in relation to chosen activities, and teacher shortages (see also Custers, 2023; Custers et al., 2023). Starting with the former two, other studies highlight how program effectiveness depends upon the quality of staff and participation (e.g., Jenner & Jenner, 2007; Holstead & King, 2011). Successful programs often employ staff that received extensive training and are experienced in working with disadvantaged youth. Additionally, participation is often high throughout the program with students attending on a daily or weekly basis. The NPRZ CZ appears to be lacking these features. It is generally acknowledged that many of the staff hired for the extra hours miss the necessary pedagogical skills (Kruiter et al., 2020). Moreover, there are differences between schools in participation. Although the program bureau states that participation in the extended school week is mandatory for all students, schools seem to be flexible in how they comply with this obligation.

An explanation that has received less attention so far is the change in goal setting. The focus within the educational component of the NPRZ has undergone a rather unnoticed

transformation during the program's course. At the start the main goal was to improve academic achievement (NPRZ, 2012), but in recent years the goal has been articulated more broadly, now also explicitly including 'enrichment' and socioemotional development (NPRZ, 2023). The reasons for this change remain somewhat unclear. One possibility is that the NPRZ has responded to the growing criticism in Dutch educational discourse concerning the emphasis on academic achievement. There have been several critiques on the dominant achievement culture (e.g., Elffers, 2023), which is believed to crowd out other aspects of education. However, the need for clear and consistent goals of educational interventions is frequently stressed in the literature, so that instruction and activities can be structured according to these goals (Durlak et al., 2010). In the case of the NPRZ, the goals have been rather inconsistent over time and moreover, the activities within the extra hours are not clearly aligned with the initial goal of boosting academic achievement.  Schools had 3 considerable autonomy in choosing activities for the extra hours and many schools opted for a broad mix of activities (Kruiter et al., 2020). This laissez-faire approach might have resulted in that a relatively low share of activities has been dedicated to instruction and focused learning, which are considered crucial to produce substantial effects on academic achievement (Kraft & Novicoff, 2024). 4

Furthermore, our study illustrates the complexities of transferring a concept such as the HCZ to other contexts (cf. Kerr & Dyson, 2014). Some of the central elements of the HCZ, including hiring high-qualified teachers and a central governing structure, are difficult to realize in other settings. In the Netherlands a national teacher crisis has developed simultaneously with the implementation of the NPRZ (Inspectorate of Education, 2019),

which has made it nearly impossible for schools in the NPRZ CZ to attract good teachers especially in the absence of other incentives. In addition, the HCZ has built its own infrastructure with a small number of schools and many affiliated services, whereas the NPRZ is incorporated into the existing infrastructure of multiple schools and welfare services. Implementing such a program across thirty schools with various boards and stakeholders has been complicated (Dol et al., 2019). The NPRZ CZ should therefore not be viewed as a copy of the HCZ, since the HCZ has merely served as an inspiration.

Finally, we discuss some limitations of our study. First, we can only offer tentative explanations as to why the NPRZ CZ seems ineffective in affecting educational outcomes. Since we have no data on the actual implementation of the program, it cannot be directly tested to what extent aspects such as the quality of staff, the types of activities or the level of participation are associated with program outcomes. Second, although we estimated effects for individual schools, thereby showing variation in program effectiveness, we lack further insight into the heterogeneity of the program's effects. It is possible that the effects vary between subgroups, for instance based on class or ethnicity, or even at the student level. Thus, the program could still have worked for some students, but we were unable to detect these effects.

To conclude, this study showed which factors and processes are likely to influence program effectiveness, and we have contributed empirical evidence for the lack of overall effectiveness on the NPRZ program's educational achievement goals.. We have also demonstrated the applicability of quasi-experimental designs with school-level data outside the US context. We estimated causal effects for individual schools by combining Dutch register data from various sources with synthetic control analysis. We think our study could therefore be a showcase of how such designs can be applied in other settings for educational evaluation research.

## Background


Research  must  be  conducted  transparently  and  should  be  reproducible  to  the  extent  possible.  This emerging consensus is endorsed by funders, required by journals, and supported by researchers across disciplines in the social sciences and beyond [1]. While not without skeptics, the transparency agenda has been widely accepted in quantitative research. Among qualitative researchers, however, transparent research methods and data sharing have been adopted more hesitantly [2-4].

Some of the reservations voiced by qualitative researchers stem from fundamentally different views of the research process and the epistemologies underlying their work [5]. More broadly, though, skepticism about 'qualitative transparency' is rooted in a justified unease with applying concepts developed for quantitative  research  to  qualitative  work.  There  is  a  rich  tradition  in  qualitative  research  of conceptualizing analogous markers of good research, for example, for reliability [6], generalizability [7], or sample size calculations [8]. These works do justice to the distinctive characteristics of qualitative research,  yet  simultaneously  appeal  to  the  same  overarching  goals  and  principles  of  (social)  science research. This paper works within this tradition, seeking to adapt transparent workflows to the practices and epistemologies of qualitative researchers.

In  this  paper,  we  seek  to  advance  our  understanding  of  transparent  qualitative  research  based  on  a unique  collaboration  between  a  group  of  qualitative  public  health  researchers  at  the  Guttmacher Institute  and  qualitative  methods  and  curation  specialists  at  the  Qualitative  Data  Repository.  The research group engaged in in-depth consultation throughout the entire planning, data collection, and analysis process of a study investigating sensitive topics in reproductive health. This paper presents one key outcome of this process: a detailed checklist for collecting and documenting steps in the planning and implementation of qualitative studies [9]. We describe the philosophical, structural, sociological and organizational goals of this checklist and how they deviate from the goals of existing qualitative research checklists.

Given its origin, we believe this checklist will be particularly relevant for highly structured qualitative research,  such  as  projects  based  mainly  on  focus  groups  and  semi-structured  interviews.  It  will  also improve other research that includes significant amounts of pre-planned and plannable activities and/or team-based  efforts.  On  the  other  end  of  the  spectrum,  we  would  expect  it  to  apply  much  less  to immersive, participant research such as many ethnographies [although ethnographers may indeed be concerned with transparency, see 10, and 11 for contrasting perspectives].

We begin by briefly summarizing the state of the discussion surrounding transparency in qualitative research.  A  second  section  discusses  the  role  of  checklists  in  research  and,  more  specifically,  in supporting research transparency. Finally, we introduce, justify and describe a qualitative transparency checklist and describe its relationship to existing transparency guidelines. We end with an account of using the checklist in practice.


## Defining and understanding key terms: Reproducibility vs. Transparency


One  of  the  key  goals  of  the  'transparency  movement'  in  the  social  sciences  is  the  promotion  of reproducible research practices, i.e., ensuring that applying the same analysis procedures to the same data  produces  the  same  results  [12].  A  closer  look  at  some  of  the  foundational  texts  advocating  for reproducible  research,  however,  shows  that  reproducibility  is  not  a  goal  in  itself.  It  is,  instead,  a convenient way for quantitative research to be evaluable and accountable : the ability to investigate, e.g., the statistical code underlying an analysis is an ideal way to follow every analytic step and to detect flawed procedures. In an early statement calling for reproducibility in political science research, King [13] bases its importance on the fact that it ensures 'that sufficient information exists with which to understand,  evaluate,  and  build  upon  a  prior  work.'  Similarly,  David  Donoho  (one  of  the  original proponents  of  reproducible  research  in  the  1990s)  and  co-authors  argue  that  a  key  advantage  of reproducibility is its ability to make the shortcomings of research and its underlying procedures visible:

'[I]f everyone on a research team knows that everything they do is going to someday be published for reproducibility, they'll behave differently from day one. Striving for reproducibility imposes a discipline that leads to better work.'  [14]

Qualitative  researchers  have  rightly  been  skeptical  about  the  applicability  of  reproducibility  to qualitative research. The same text, for example, will inevitably be interpreted somewhat differently by different researchers; different researchers will pick up on different key topics in an interview; and with coding tasks, inter-coder reliability over 90% can be difficult to achieve, especially when coding more complex texts such as interview transcripts [see the extended discussion in 15]. While reproducibility in the literal sense is neither achievable nor desirable for most qualitative research, we believe that making qualitative research as understandable, evaluable, and accountable as possible is both [16]. This move is in line with a significant literature that seeks to establish criteria for evaluating qualitative research on its own terms [see, e.g., 17 on credibility, 7 on generalization, 18]. We describe research that aims to fulfill these goals as 'transparent research' and thus define research transparency as making the materials and procedures underlying research available to the extent that is possible and responsible. Transparent research is an ideal, and transparency is best understood on a continuum: research can be more or less transparent and, all things being equal, we should strive to move our practices towards the transparent end of that continuum. By providing practical guidance for more open, transparent qualitative research, we add to a growing literature on openness in qualitative research, including on such topics as pre-registration [19],  authorship  [20],  consent  for  sharing  data  [21-23],  and  de-identifying  and  sharing  sensitive qualitative data [24, 25].


## Aspects of Transparency


In order to make progress on advancing tools for qualitative research transparent, we adopt a three-part classification of different aspects of research transparency as suggested in the ethics guidelines of the American Political Science Associations:

'Data access: Researchers making evidence-based knowledge claims should reference the data they  used  to  make  those  claims.  If  these  are  data  they  themselves  generated  or  collected, researchers should provide access to those data or explain why they cannot.

Production transparency: Researchers providing access to data they themselves generated or collected should offer a full account of the procedures used to collect or generate the data.

Analytic Transparency: Researchers making evidence-based knowledge claims should provide a full account of how they draw their analytic conclusions from the data, i.e., clearly explicate the links connecting data to conclusions.'  [26]

We  refer  to  these  categories  throughout  this  paper  and  introduce  a  'Transparency  Checklist  for Qualitative Research,' that will help researchers plan for, collect, and organize transparency-related information throughout the research process. Production and analytic transparency are closely related to  reporting guidelines for qualitative research such as COREQ [27] and SRQR [28], but the detail we believe can and should be reported significantly exceeds that typically expected by reporting guidelines: where reporting guidelines envision including brief details on each list item, we recommend including entire  documents.  This  allows  readers,  evaluators,  and  not  least  authors  themselves,  to  retrace  and

understand the entire research process. Pre-registration checklists tend to include more details, but are mostly limited to capturing decisions made prior to conducting a study (and deviations from those initial decisions). Data management checklists, which share with our list an emphasis on documentation and sharing,  focus principally on data and their collection, leaving analytic decisions unexplored.


## ¤Benefits of Transparency


More  transparent  research  offers  significant  benefits  to  the  scientific  community.  We  will  briefly summarize  the  most  salient  benefits  of  transparent  research,  as  described  in  a  large  and  growing literature,  especially  as  they  apply  to  qualitative  research.  At  its  most  fundamental  level,  research transparency is a requirement for rigorous research: 'Following the reason-based rules that guide the type  of  social  inquiry  in  which  a  scholar  is  engaging-i.e.,  conducting  rigorous  research-allows  the scholar to generate knowledge claims that will be considered valid by their research community.' [29] Only  when  others  can  observe  and  verify  that  and  how  these  rules  have  been  followed  is  research trustworthy. By opening up research processes to more scrutiny - from comparing the analysis in an article to preregistered hypotheses to inspecting details of shared data - transparency also ensures that science is more effectively self-correcting and thus further enhances the reliability of science [30]. More transparent  science  also  allows  for  better  science  training.  By  making  workflows  visible  and  data available, more transparent research allows researchers-in-training to better understand the logic of published  research  and  learn  from  it  [31,  32].  Finally,  more  transparent  research  also  improves knowledge accumulation. Shared data allows for secondary analysis and re-use of data; shared protocols and  questionnaires  allow  for  running  similar  studies  in  different  contexts;  high-quality  procedural documentation (especially when combined with documentation of obstacles encountered) can inform and improve similar future studies [5, 33-35].


## Transparency in Qualitative Research: Slow Progress amidst Concerns


The slower adoption of transparent research practices has been due, in significant part, to questions about their suitability for qualitative social scientists, driven principally by three broad sets of concerns: 1)  Is  transparent  research appropriate for  qualitative  methods  given  its  epistemological  bases?  2)  Is transparent research ethical given the close interaction between researcher and participants and the sensitive topics frequently addressed during these interactions? 3) Is transparent research pragmatically feasible given the lack of accepted approaches, or will it create an undue burden on researchers?

Researchers,  particularly  those  working  in  interpretivist  traditions,  have  argued  that  the  role researchers  themselves  play  in  qualitative  research  makes  it  impossible  to  separate  the  original researcher(s) from underlying data. In the words of Feldman and Shaw [3], '[a] researcher's situatedness in these research processes, therefore, means that they are implicated in the generation of data, whether through ethnographic encounters, participant observation, or in-depth, open-ended interviews, that usually take place over an extended period of time.'

Ethical issues loom large in debates about qualitative transparency. In a thoughtful discussion of various ethical concerns in sharing qualitative data, Tsai et al. [4] describe various ways in which transcripts from qualitative interviews or focus groups may be particularly difficult -- if not impossible -- to de-identify and warn that the mere act of requesting permission for data sharing from participants may deter their participation in the research.

Finally, qualitative researchers have warned that even if possible, qualitative transparency could put an undue burden on researchers. Hall [36], writing about the opportunity costs of data sharing, argues that 'the steepest trade-offs arise from requirements for the deposit of qualitative data - not only because it is more difficult to provide and prepare such data for deposit but because the gains to doing so are more meagre.'

Moreover, even for a researcher willing to spend the requisite time on making their qualitative work transparent,  there  are  no  clear  guidelines  of  what  such  transparency  would  even  entail  beyond  the sharing of underlying data, leaving them to fend for themselves. The checklist we introduce in this paper can be read as a guide that supports qualitative researchers in considering and deciding on making key documents  and  parts  of  their  workflows  transparent  while  being  mindful  of  epistemic  and  ethical responsibilities as well as pragmatic limits to researchers' time.


## Methods: Developing a Transparency Checklist


Initially developed in aviation, checklists have been popularized through their successful application in medicine [37] and are now used in domains as diverse as product manufacturing, software development, and healthcare [38]. Researchers are also drawing on checklists for reporting [see the collection of almost 500 such guidelines on 39], peer review [e.g., 40], and, most recently, the transparency of (quantitative) studies [41] .

Checklists fulfill different functions in different domains. In aviation and medicine, for example, their role of avoiding error in high-stress situations is of particular importance [38]. In comparison, research checklists  more  typically  focus  on  standardizing  methodologies  and  providing  a  framework  for improving analysis or reporting. In this, they may be more similar to checklists for software design [42] or building constructions [37].

Research-oriented checklists have proliferated over the last 30 years. They appear most frequently in the form  of  reporting  guidelines  as  captured  by  the  EQUATOR  Network  [39].  Guidelines  have  had  a tremendous  impact  on  publishing.  Using  Google  Scholar  citation  counts,  the  PRISMA  metric  for systematic reviews has been cited almost 90,000 times. The CONSORT (randomized trials) and COREQ (qualitative research) guidelines have each been cited more than 10,000 times. Reporting guidelines were originally intended to help writers include the most relevant information in manuscripts. Some such guidelines have taken on a second life, however, as de-facto reviewer checklists. This use, in particular, has been met with resistance, in particular among qualitative researchers, who are worried that the standardized application of checklists in assessing qualitative research will impose methodological and epistemological assumptions on a diverse set of methodological traditions and will prioritize mechanical 'box-checking' over careful understanding of qualitative work [43, 44].

We began constructing the transparency checklist from several existing documents: the two most widely used  reporting  guidelines  for  qualitative  research,  COREQ  [27]  and  SRQR  [28];  the  Qualitative  Data Management  Checklist  from  the  Qualitative  Data  Repository  [45];  as  well  as  the  recently  published preregistration template for qualitative studies [46]. We diverge from these checklists in some important ways:

Philosophically , we  seek  to  return  to  the  checklists  as  a  return  for  (principally  internal)  process improvement rather than external process control. The goal of research checklists in general, and for qualitative research in particular, must be to support researchers in conducting the best research and not to rigidly commit them to a given template.

Structurally, we see a checklist for transparent qualitative research resembling both the complex building plans described by Gawande (ch. 3) as well as the simple steps of a surgical or aviation checklist, which need to be usable under time pressure. Our checklist, therefore, highlights not just the 'checking of boxes' but views the notes associated with every item as equally important as the presence of those items.

Sociologically ,  we  believe  that  a  key  component for the success of a checklist is its ability to increase communication within a team. This feature is frequently highlighted in discussions of medical checklists [37] but has found little attention in discussing and promoting reporting guidelines for research.

Organizationally, the  checklist  serves  as  an  inventory  for  the  significant  amount  of  documents  and documentation produced in the course of a complex qualitative research project. It allows a research team  to  keep  track  of  the  existence  and  whereabouts  of  each  document  and  make  early,  informed decisions about which of these documents will be shared externally.


## Results: Developing and Using the Checklist


Striving for increased transparency in qualitative analyses at a public health research organization

The Guttmacher Institute has used qualitative inquiry as a systematic approach to understanding the social and cognitive processes that drive people's sexual and reproductive health (SRH) behaviors and outcomes for decades [47-50]. The Qualitative Transparency checklist was developed as a part of a larger initiative at the Guttmacher Institute to begin incorporating reproducible practices into its quantitative workflows and publicly sharing the  data and code that underlie its quantitative analyses. Expectations for transparency in qualitative work are much less established, however [51], so the Guttmacher Institute sought guidance through a collaboration with experts from the Qualitative Data Repository (QDR) when seeking to expand this initiative to their qualitative work.

QDR assisted the Guttmacher Institute in its conceptual translation of computational reproducibility in quantitative research to qualitative transparency by providing concrete examples  and guidance such as ethical data sharing practices, templates for informed consent documents that enable data sharing and detailed data management plans. Qualitative researchers at the Guttmacher Institute then created the checklist to translate these practices and general guidance into actionable workflows.


## Developing the Transparency Checklist


Checklists may aim to aid in the achievement of abstract concepts such as transparency, but they also exist to concretely improve practice. They are therefore ideally developed within existing practice so that they are directly responsive to the specific needs of that practice. Below we describe how the phases

of applied qualitative public health research engendered the development of the items on the Qualitative Transparency Checklist.

At  Guttmacher,  like  many  public  health  agencies,  researchers  work  in  teams;  the  initial  set  of  staff members involved in project design and development may not be the same as the people who implement the work  and  analyze the data. Therefore, maintaining documentation  of the project goals, methodological underpinning and justification, and changes to this overarching narrative is not only essential to working transparently, but it is also crucial to produce and maintain as teams work, to ensure continued alignment among researchers.

Similarly, documentation of the specific steps, tools and processes used in qualitative data collection, management and analysis  provides  a  trail  that  leads  from  raw  data  to  findings,  interpretation,  and conclusions. Therefore, the checklist includes an overview of methods, including: selection criteria for data  collection,  plus  approach,  sample  size,  any  documentation  of  refusal/nonresponse,  credibility strategies, recruitment and data collection setting. It suggests noting interviewer and analyst identities and training,  as  well  as  the  inclusion  of  positionality  or  subjectivity  statements  in  which  these  staff reflect on how their identities may have influenced their approaches and conclusions.

Data in all of its formats is included as items on the checklist: original recordings of interviews and focus group  discussions,  unedited  transcripts,  cleaned  and  edited  transcripts,  and  field  notes.  Documents related to data production, such as guidance about how verbatim transcripts are edited and de-identified, are also included.

Analytic products such as the initial, interim and final versions of the coding schemes that researchers use to tag their data into categories used for building their observations about patterns and themes from the 'bottom up,' by organizing the data into increasingly more abstract units of information [52] are present  in  this  section.  Analytic  memos  (which  may  be  used  for  summarizing  information  for  each respondent in a systematic format) are also included.

A detailed analytic plan articulating how the data will be examined is an item in this section of the checklist. Queries and reports produced by analytic software for instance, showing all the data coded in a certain way, perhaps divided by metadata on the respondents like demographic information that are called for in the analytic plan would also be included. Spreadsheets, referred to as 'matrices,' which help organize the data and assist in the identification of emerging themes by uncovering which themes are salient to most respondents and which may represent outlying experiences are present, and exposing patterns and connections within and between respondents and between groups of codes [53] are an item in  this  section.  The  summaries the researchers produce to synthesize and illustrate their findings in preparation for writing are also included, in addition to manuscript drafts before and after peer review.

Our initial drafts of the Transparency Checklist drew on the range of existing guidance and checklists for reporting  and  documenting  qualitative  research  described  above.  We  found  these  lists  to  be  useful starting points, as they covered disparate but overlapping aspects of qualitative design, data collection and reporting. However, these resources are generally outward-focused, aimed at demonstrating to an outside audience that certain standards had been followed and appropriately recorded. Additionally, even taken together, they covered most, but not all, stages of the research life-cycle; they were not sufficient to guide in the creation of a transparent qualitative research project from start to finish.

To understand how our draft checklist might address gaps left by other resources and serve as an aid to improving our qualitative practice, we carried out a mapping exercise using four sources, the COREQ (Consolidated  criteria  for  Reporting  Qualitative  research)  guidelines  [27],  the  SRQR  (Standards  for Reporting  Qualitative  Research)  [28],  the  DMP  (Data  Management  Plan)  Checklist  [45],  and  the  COS Qualitative Preregistration Template [46]. The items from each of these were isolated and mapped to the items in the draft of the Transparency Checklist. We used this process to assess the comprehensiveness of the Transparency Checklist. After adding any missing items, it became apparent that the checklist covers novel areas such as pilot materials, transcript cleaning guidelines, including de-identification criteria, analytic memos, coding query or node reports, matrices and bullet points that were not covered in other qualitative reporting checklists. It also identifies crucial items for inclusion in a data repository, such as transcripts and respondent demographic information that were not present in existing checklists because they were outside of the scope of those tools. Based on this, we added a column to indicate whether each item is intended for inclusion in a public repository or as an internal document meant to aid in achieving transparency within data production and analytic practice. Finally, we added columns to indicate which aspect of transparency each item was meant to address and a brief description of each item. A summary of the checklist can be found in table 1.
