## Opportunities for upscaling private investment in nature in Europe


From our interviews with 25 elite biodiversity finance experts across Europe we identified two key themes regarding the opportunities for upscaling private investment: 1) macroeconomic and political factors driving potential increases in both supply and demand of projects for private finance, and 2) various sources of innovation and specialised experience that emerge as these markets develop.


### Large-scale economic and political changes opening opportunities for private investment


In our sample, the intensification of rhetoric and efforts to upscale private investment in conservation were fundamentally perceived to be driven by increasing public awareness and demand for policies addressing biodiversity loss, coupled with a lack of trust that governments possessed the capacity or political capital required to directly address the problem through increasing public spending on biodiversity conservation. “So we can continue to think and expect that governments will solve our problems, but they don't. They have consistently proven in the last 50 years of my existence here on earth, they don't... so you need to focus on private markets, and you need to make that work (P2)”.

In this context, our interviews pointed to a range of potential drivers incentivising increased demand for investments in conservation. These included the traditional motivations of corporate social responsibility and marketing29, organisational net zero and nature-positive commitments46, as well as the voluntary and policy drivers outlined above such as TNFD and CRSD. We note that interviewees did not substantiate the exact mechanisms through which they thought these supportive policies and initiatives were to drive demand for conservation investment47. Interviewees highlighted interactions between these different mechanisms, with voluntary corporate initiatives often seen as a necessary precursor to the adoption of supporting policies in legislation. Risk management was another key driver28,48, with companies’ dependencies on nature especially in corporate supply chains perceived as an increasingly powerful lever for making biodiversity loss material to companies and therefore drive demand for nature-related investments. An increasing number of commodification mechanisms and policies were seen to be creating opportunities to derive cashflows from biodiversity improvements (e.g. new and increasingly established nature markets such as England’s Biodiversity Net Gain), increasing investability.

On the supply side, interviewees noted the increasing regulation and economic pressures on farming, which they believed appear to drive an interest of land managers to diversify their income streams and participate in environmental markets. Additionally, interviewees and focus group participants noted interactions between consolidated land ownership and participation in environmental markets, with landholders or organisations with large non-operational landholdings looking to use these markets as opportunities to generate revenues through land ownership, but in ways that also delivered environmental benefits.


### Opportunities arising from innovation and experience


Alongside large-scale ‘push-pull’ factors, various forms of innovation and the development of experience within the biodiversity finance sector were perceived as key enablers of further upscaling. Technological innovation including advancements in near real-time biodiversity monitoring (interviewees mentioned images taken through smartphones and standardised sampling protocols, bioacoustics, eDNA, and remote sensing) were seen as central49. Interviewees believed it would enable demand by increasing buyers’ ability to obtain evidence that their contributions to biodiversity improvements mattered. They did not point out that high-resolution monitoring is insufficient to prove causal impact without credible counterfactuals50–53.

Other non-technological forms of innovation were also found to be critical. Interviewees alluded to new markets and asset classes taking a long time to develop and reach maturity, and there was a sense of ‘learning by doing’, leading to the generation of new financial innovations and logistical or legal innovations to enable these new investment classes. These included fund aggregation9, and new types of governance structures such as innovative contract designs including ecological conditionalities, and insurance to attempt to ensure the delivery of the biodiversity enhancement underpinning the investments54. Alongside these new structures, another key element was the development of skilled practitioners with combinations of conservation and finance expertise able to effectively broker between the two disciplines55.


## Challenges to upscaling investment and its ecological and social benefits


Upscaling private investment in nature faces myriad challenges. In our interviews the overarching themes were the lack of highly profitable investment opportunities, and inherent mismatches between the perceived realities of risks and uncertainties of doing conservation in practice and the level of risk that private investors are willing to bear. Put simply, conservation is subject to many categories of risk38, and for investments in conservation to deliver risk-adjusted returns that are competitive with other options available to investors, the cashflows from private investments need to be either sufficiently high to justify the risks31,33, or the risks need to be mitigated (e.g. derisking via blended finance). Otherwise, as one interviewee stated: “they have easier ways of making money (P20)”. One recent paper demonstrated for a biodiversity-related private equity firm, investments which were nominally delivering biodiversity improvements had a mean target internal rate of return of 14.7% (and blended finance deals subject to derisking had a mean of 11.9%)33. This corroborated evidence from our interviews highlighting the very high returns required to justify the risks of investment, and a fundamental lack of mechanisms that can deliver sufficiently high revenues. “I would consider us very risk-tolerant investors, very, in the grand scheme of things. And we're looking at things that others would definitely not look at. But even for us, so many of the projects we see are just... It's not clear where the revenues are going to come from. (P17)”.

We identified three subthemes relating to risk in our interviews: risks relating to politics and regulation, risks stemming from the mismatch between the complexity of ecology and the needs of investors, and risks stemming from social perceptions and inequities.


### Political and regulatory risk


Interviewees noted that the ecological success of mechanisms for attracting private investment into conservation would require political will and substantial investment in ensuring high-quality governance, just as public-sector-led conservation investment would56. They noted therefore that the development of market-based approaches for conservation financing are not a substitute for genuine political will for addressing biodiversity loss; the ecological outcomes of either state-led or private-led investments in conservation outcomes hinge on that same political will31,56, thus both are subject to political risks. Inconsistent political will to address biodiversity loss translates into widespread regulatory uncertainty, which acts as one of the key barriers to both supply and demand for conservation outcomes and therefore to the certainty of cashflows generated through such investments. On the demand side, investors seek a high degree of confidence that there will be a market for the biodiversity benefits generated so that they can sell commodified biodiversity increases to generate cashflows, but the looming threat of governments weakening or removing legislation that is the driver of this demand was a major driver of risk (especially in compliance markets). On the supply side, this same regulatory uncertainty was perceived as a large barrier to initiating the enrolment of land managers into delivering conservation land management, leading to undersupply.


### Mismatches between finance and ecology


Some conventional critiques around the commodification of nature appeared in our interview dataset of interviews (e.g. relating to non-fungibility, unsuitability for some types of biodiversity, emphasis on carbon over biodiversity, risks of greenwashing)57–63. Beyond these concerns, there were still risks hindering the upscaling of investment. A main barrier to investment cited by investors was the cost of monitoring, and the lack of ecologically-realistic metrics to evidence increases in biodiversity55. Therefore, investors often use proxies for signalling the biodiversity value of the investment, which might be some form of sustainability certification in the case of agriculture or forestry-related funds35, or biodiversity or carbon metrics aligned with offset certification schemes or national legislation. However, periodic impact evaluations demonstrate that many of the proxies on which they rely are highly imperfect, and often overstate the contributions of these investments to enhancing nature16,39,40,59,64,65. The lack of accepted metrics is a barrier, as interviewees noted, because even well-intentioned purchasing of biodiversity or carbon outcomes using a commodification mechanism or key performance indicators, may present a reputational risk if subjected to public criticism. Participants and focus groups highlighted that carbon credits were by far the main well-developed bankable revenue streams to date, presenting challenges as the kinds of projects and ecologies optimising for carbon were misaligned with those optimising for biodiversity.

Additionally, interviewees noted both spatial and temporal mismatches between conservation and the needs of investors. Temporally, conservation was perceived as requiring large up-front investments for uncertain long-term payoffs11, which was a challenge both because of uncertainties regarding the long-term potential revenues from the investment, and because enrolling in selling biodiversity-related outcomes meant land managers would have to forgo their existing revenue streams in the short run, reducing their incentives to enrol. One interviewee noted that this alone meant such projects were likely better matched to receiving non-commercial, long-term public investment. Spatially, interviewees noted that areas of high biodiversity value tend to be located in areas of low human pressure and weak institutions, highlighting that these are the very places where institutions are likely too weak to give investors confidence66, although this was in the context of European investments in the global South.


### Risks from social perceptions and inequities


Interviewees and focus groups noted that those best positioned to take advantage of the opportunities created by upscaling private investment opportunities were institutions with rights over key limiting factors such as land, or prior experience of social and environmental management for large land-based projects such as businesses with large non-operational estates; therefore interviewees acknowledged that expanding biodiversity-related investment opportunities have the potential to exacerbate pre-existing inequities. Social engagement at project sites for project developers throughout our interview sample was consistently mentioned as something that was a ‘nice-to-have’, but resource shortages frequently meant these activities were deprioritised beyond just satisfying the basic requirements of legislation or accreditation schemes. Additionally, interviewees recognised these inequities may pose a reputational risk to the credibility of these markets themselves through public opinion, especially in the context of blended finance, in cases where public funding backed by taxpayers would be used to derisk investments for financial institutions67.


## The role of public policy


The role of public policy was emphasised by all interviewees. A diversity of views were represented, from perceptions of government as the stifler of market innovation and real action to address biodiversity loss, to government’s emphasis on scaling up private investment being a ‘symbolic instrument’42 designed to impose minimal disruption and ultimately legitimise prevailing unsustainable business practices, through to cautious optimism about the attempts of public policy to internalise biodiversity into business and investment decisions contingent on high-quality governance and enforcement. We identified two core themes: recognising biodiversity finance as just one small part of the conservation puzzle, and identifying that public policy is the key to the entirety of biodiversity finance. Public policy presented as the creator of these private investment opportunities yet also their major threat.


### Private biodiversity finance as just one piece of the puzzle


Interviewees frequently caveated their expectations around upscaling biodiversity finance by situating it as just one piece of the public policy landscape required to address biodiversity loss. They reiterated the public good nature of biodiversity and the challenge in commodifying most types of biodiversity, and therefore highlighted that public investment remained essential. They recognised opportunities for improving the effectiveness of public investment, including through results-based budgeting. Interviewees emphasised the importance of governments strengthening regulations to prevent biodiversity loss, even arguing that this would help create more opportunities for investors as profitable innovation would be required to overcome constraints created through direct regulation of ecological harms68,69.

Interviews identified a swathe of policies that could be enacted to both address biodiversity loss and facilitate the development of private investment opportunities, including improved data transparency on land management activities70, changes in taxation regimes, financial regulation and supervision71, and investment in biodiversity-related state capacity and skills72 (Table S1 Supporting information).


### Public policy as the great enabler and its own worst enemy


Public policy was perceived as the dominant driver of opportunities for investing in nature. Through the creation of biodiversity-related markets public institutions were framed as the mediators of the outcomes of private finance through the design of well-designed commodification mechanisms that would be aligned with delivering positive outcomes coupled with effective enforcement. Additionally, public funding was seen as necessary to catalyse market opportunities through direct subsidies for projects attempting to enter nascent nature markets and derisking of investments in these same projects. These perspectives challenge the view that there is a dichotomy between public and private biodiversity finance – substantial public investment in creating, governing, and stimulating demand for the markets that public policy itself created was perceived as fundamentally essential.

Given the overwhelming role of public policy, effective governance and well-coordinated regulations were viewed as critical. However, interviewees and focus groups highlighted fundamental tensions between different public policies that appear to both stimulate private investment opportunities and suppress them. One key tension related to the need for access to land to implement projects for nature markets, and public policy as a major barrier to land acquisition or enrolment. Nature investment requires the enrolment of land, yet in some jurisdictions restrictions on using public money to purchase land meant that nature investment projects that included land acquisition as part of their conservation management were unable to access public funding or support, preventing projects from proceeding9. Additionally, agricultural subsidies were perceived as a major barrier to enrolling land in conservation management. In providing land managers with stable public-policy-derived incomes, enrolment in nature projects must deliver a business case that exceeds the opportunity cost, which spans not just the revenues from subsidies but also the long-term stability of those payments. Subsidies were perceived to be internalised into land prices, increasing the value of land, reducing the viability of privately-funded conservation management. On one hand public policy aims to create and scale nature markets; on the other through the subsidy system governments invest in its main competition for land.

A second key tension identified was between the derisking being demanded from governments to help address the uncertainties facing investors, and governments as one of the key causes of these uncertainties. Political and regulatory uncertainty increases risk for investors, as does the uncertainty of how well these markets will be enforced in practice and therefore whether investors will end up investing in something that is later exposed as being noncompliant, highlighting the importance of consistent and long-term policy signals and regulatory certainty for upscaling markets.

Lastly, a critical sub-theme was poor coordination between different sources of finance (i.e. non-return seeking grants and subsidies and private finance opportunities) that leads to competition between existing sources of funding, with projects having a preference for non-return-seeking grants9. A lack of coordination can lead to projects, which were strong candidates for return-seeking finance ending up funded by direct grants, drawing potential supply out of markets. This highlights the need for better coordination at landscape scales between funding sources to direct different kinds of financing into different projects based on the ecological characteristics of the projects and their suitability for funding through existing market-based funding mechanisms.


## Conclusion


Conservation remains overwhelming publicly-funded, and prevailing policy frameworks and political discourse in Europe highlight the biodiversity funding gap and emphasise the need to upscale private investment in conservation and restoration to address this gap. However, this framing underappreciates the degree to which public policy is the critical enabler of private investment, through creating the commodification mechanisms that underpin markets, regulation to prevent enrolment of poor projects, and then even stimulating demand through derisking and blended finance to bring nature investment projects up to the high risk-adjusted rewards required to attract mainstream private investment. Therefore, whilst these markets have arisen as a ‘second-best’ solution to better direct public regulation and investment in biodiversity-related public goods, their success remains contingent on similar political will, and substantial public investment. It remains an open question whether solving the nature finance gap through the expansion of public policy-derived private investment opportunities or direct public policy and public investment is the more cost-effective solution to achieving biodiversity funding goals. This work highlights many avenues for future research, including some that to our knowledge remain unaddressed in the literature such as empirical explorations of the interactions between agricultural subsidies and nature markets, the appropriate role of derisking in nature markets to maximise value to society, and how to coordinate across different funding streams to direct the right kinds of capital into the right places to deliver on overarching biodiversity goals.

## 1. Introduction


Systematic similarities in socioeconomic outcomes between family members come from two broad types of sources: environmental and genetic. It is well established that genetics play a role in educational attainment, and to some extent for economic outcomes such as income and wealth. However, the role of genetic influences in the attainment of occupation-based measures of  class  positions  has  not  been  systematically  tested  in  neither  sociological  stratification research  nor  behavioral  genetics,  and  the  research  on  genetic  influences  on  occupational prestige and status attainment (hereafter colloquially referred to as 'status') is very limited.

Both additive genetics and environmental influences shared by siblings explain a substantial share of the variation in educational outcomes (Baier, Lang, et al., 2022; Branigan et al., 2013; Engzell  &  Tropf,  2019;  Heath  et  al.,  1985;  Lichtenstein  et  al.,  1992).  For  wealth,  shared environmental influences appear to play a more important role than genetics (Black et al., 2020; Fagereng  et  al.,  2021),  while  for  income  and  earnings,  genetic  influences  are  of  a  similar magnitude as those found for education (Erola et al., 2022; Hyytinen et al., 2019) though some studies also find that the home environment plays an important role (Bowles & Gintis, 2002). Class and status are central to sociological theories of social mobility and are arguably the most important link between educational attainment and economic outcomes. Despite this, we know very little about the extent to which they are influenced by genetics. This is especially true for conceptualizations of class. A better understanding of the role of genetics in class and status attainment may have important theoretical implications. Not only would it provide valuable insight  into  the  extent  to  which  attainment  works  through  environmental,  genetic  and/or idiosyncratic pathways, it would help establish whether genetic influences should be accounted for as potential confounding factors in a large and important field of study in sociology. Such understandings are also  relevant  to  discussions  on  equality  of  opportunity.  Providing  more equal opportunities is  an  important  goal  regardless  of  whether  opportunities  are  limited  by

heritable or socially transmitted factors, and understanding why inequalities persist is important for assessing what policies might reduce them (Harden, 2021).

Two research literatures have largely existed in parallel, despite being concerned with different aspects of the same broad question; what factors influence socioeconomic outcomes? The first is the sociological literature on occupation-based class and status attainment. This rich research tradition has produced many important empirical and theoretical contributions to understanding social stratification (Erikson & Goldthorpe, 1992; Ganzeboom et al., 1992; Treiman, 1970; Wright, 2005). Characteristic of this research tradition is the use of theoretically informed, occupation-based,  categorical  class  schemes  or  metric  status  scales  to  study  attainment (Wright,  2000),  and  a  strong  theoretical  focus  on  explanations  related  to  social  family background  characteristics,  such  as  parents'  class  and  status,  parents'  education,  the  home environment etc. The other literature links genetics to socioeconomic outcomes. This research, originating in behavior genetics and psychology, is focused on conventional indicators of social advantages and disadvantages, such as education, income, and wealth. Using twin and family designs  and,  more  recently,  measured  genotype  data,  researchers  have  produced  important findings on the role of genetics for socioeconomic outcomes. However, with a few notable exceptions (Akimova et al., 2023; Belsky et al., 2018; Lichtenstein et al., 1992; Liu, 2019; Nicolaou  &  Shane,  2010),  this  literature  has  not  used  occupation-based  measures  of socioeconomic status, and no prior studies have used sociological, categorical conceptualizations of class in addition to status measures in a genetically informed research design.

There are several reasons why these research traditions have not interacted. The sociological research tradition on class and status attainment is based on a set of theories and theoretical traditions attempting to explain how social hierarchies are structured in terms of social classes, status  or  prestige,  and  how  social  origins  affect  individuals'  chances  of  attaining  different

positions. Partly because of the bleak history of the field of genetics, these theoretical traditions have almost exclusively focused on social origins-related (or shared environmental) factors in explaining attainment, and have not extensively investigated the possibility of genetics playing a role (Freese, 2008). Behavioral geneticists, on the other hand, have only to a small extent been concerned with status attainment, and hardly with sociological theories or operationalizations of class.

Our study is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to estimate the proportion of variance in class attainment that is attributable to genetic factors - i.e., the heritability of class - based on the definitions and theoretical conceptualizations that are central to the sociological enterprise. We estimate a range of behavioral genetic models on class and status attainment data for more than 5000 Norwegian twin pairs, using the classical twin design (CTD), with adaptations for categorical outcomes. This allows us to decompose the variation in class and status outcomes into components that can be attributed to additive genetics, environmental influences shared by twins, including their social origins, and environmental influences not shared by twins.


## 2. Sociological theories of class and status attainment


Although  there  are  several  theories  of  class  and  status  attainment  that  offer  distinct conceptualizations, existing sociological theories largely highlight the role of family background or shared environments as crucial in  explaining  social  stratification.  The  NeoWeberian theories formulated by Goldthorpe and colleagues (for instance Breen, 2005; Bukodi & Goldthorpe, 2022; Erikson et al., 2005; Erikson & Goldthorpe, 1992; Goldthorpe, 1996, 2000) focus on rational action and relative positions, closure, opportunity hoarding, and on how  educational  attainment,  an  important  factor  for  class  attainment,  is  affected  both  by primary and secondary effects (i.e., effect of family background on individual performance and

ability, and on attainment, net of performance and ability, respectively). Other theories, such as Bourdieu's conceptualization of class (Andersen & Hansen, 2012; Bourdieu, 1984; Hansen, 2011; Lareau, 1987; Lareau & Weininger, 2003), focuses on other mechanisms, such as the role of different forms of capital in social reproduction, and how families from a higher-class background  socialize  their  children  within  the  dominant  culture  and  facilitate  educational attainment,  which  passes  on  advantages .  Although  various  traditions  mention  different 1 mechanisms of attainment, they all emphasize the relevance of status and class in structuring life chances and opportunities (Chan & Goldthorpe, 2007; Oesch & Vigna, 2023; Treiman, 2004; Wright, 2005). In this sense, we see  class and status  as important markers of social inequality that are relevant for chances and outcomes across the life course, which is one of the reasons why studying the forces behind its attainment is essential.

The potential role of genetics has been explicitly recognized in relation to primary effects on educational  achievement  (Goldthorpe,  1996;  Jackson  et  al.,  2007;  Van  De  Werfhorst  & Hofstede, 2007), whereby genetic factors are mentioned as one of the potential links between class backgrounds and educational performance. However, beyond mentioning that genetics could play a role in primary effects, most sociological theories of class and status attainment have  not  extensively  engaged  with  research  on  the  genetic  heritability  of  traits  beyond academic performance, and empirical studies employing these theories usually do not explicitly model the potential role of genetics (Freese, 2008). In recent work updating and re-formulating their theoretical framework, Bukodi and Goldthorpe (2022) do not mention the potential role of genetics at all. Based on sociological theories in the field, we should expect factors related to  social  family  background, captured by shared environmental influences (C) to explain a substantial share of the variation in class and status outcomes, and additive genetics (A) to matter relatively little. Based on the developing genetic literature that finds strong genetic links to many other socioeconomic outcomes, however, we argue that besides the family background

and hence the C-component, a genetic or A-factor might also be relevant to class and status attainment.

We  aim  to  assess  genetic  and  environmental  variance  components  for  a  wide  range  of sociological research traditions concerned with occupation-based measures of class and status. Our aim is to provide overall estimates of the heritability of these indicators to determine the magnitude  of  the  genetic  component.  The  operationalizations  we  include  match  different theoretical understandings of what 'class' and 'status' is and what processes are important to their attainment . In our main results, we focus our attention on three indicators of class or 2 occupation-based status; the Erikson-Goldthorpe-Portocarero scheme (EGP; a Neo-Weberian classification; Erikson et al., 1979), the Socio-Economic Index of occupational status (ISEI; Ganzeboom et al., 1992) and the Standard International Occupational Prestige Score (SIOPS; Treiman,  1977).  The  latter  two  represent  gradational  conceptualizations.  In  supplementary analyses,  we  additionally  include  schemes  based  on  conceptualizations  from  two  other theoretical traditions. To represent a Bourdieu-inspired classification, we use the Oslo Register Data Class Scheme (ORDC; Hansen et al., 2009), while we employ the Oesch class scheme (Oesch,  2006)  to  analyze  a  classification  based  on  a  horizontal  work  logic.  We  were unfortunately not able to include the neo-Marxist scheme developed by Wright (2015), due to data limitations.

Including a variety of operationalizations allows us to provide estimates that are robust, to assess whether they are sensitive to the specific empirical operationalization of class and status, and to recognize the heterogeneity of approaches within sociological research. Each of these operationalizations and their central theoretical assumptions are elaborated upon in Section A of the Online Appendix. An important concern is that existing twin modeling approaches are suitable  for  continuous, ordinal  or  binary  outcomes,  while  classes  are  theorized  as  discrete groups that are not strictly hierarchically ordered. While classes in the EGP scheme are not

intended to be treated as an ordinal scale, previous research has shown that there is a clear hierarchy in the structure of the scheme (Breen & Whelan, 1985; Smallenbroek et al., 2022).

Recognizing the limitations of the twin-based methodology in the face of categorical outcomes, we have therefore chosen a two-pronged modeling strategy. We treat the 7-class EGP scheme as ordinally ordered in our main analyses, allowing us to use a modified classical twin model designed  to  analyze  ordinal  outcomes.  However,  we  also  provide  supplementary  analyses based on binary analyses where we use this scheme in line with its theoretical foundations, as categorical classes. The results from these two approaches are compatible.


## 3. Bringing in genetics: The heritability of class and status


Heritability is a complex concept. Its interpretation is far from trivial, and may be estimated using a number of techniques (Barry et al., 2023). The conventional heritability measure is typically  obtained  from  classical  twin  studies,  and  does  not  include  non-additive  genetic effects, and can be considered a narrow-sense heritability. Extended pedigree designs allow researchers to also include non-additive effects in a broader concept of heritability. Definitions involving data on measured genotypes, such as the variance explained by additive effects of individual genetic variants, h²snp, or estimates from  genome  relatedness  matrix-based approaches, such as GCTA, return markedly lower estimates. This complicates comparisons across designs and data types. The definition used in this paper, is the conventional heritability from twin studies, previously used in a number of related contributions (Branigan et al., 2013). Heritability measures signal how much variation in the outcome can be explained by additive genetics in a given population that has experienced a particular social structure . Thus, any comparison of such measures must be sensitive to differences in social structures.

While heritability coefficients of many medical as well as psychological traits and behaviors have been estimated previously, the study of genetic factors in outcomes of prime importance to  social  scientists  (especially  beyond  educational  outcomes)  is  somewhat  more  recent (Johnson  et  al.,  2009).  It  is  important  to  recognize  that  part  of  the  reason  for  the  stalled investigation of heritability of social traits stems from early genetics research using biological factors  to  legitimize  inequality  and  discrimination  (Akimova  et  al.,  2023).  We  explicitly distance ourselves from such accounts and are instead interested in providing a probabilistic exploration of whether class and status attainment might in part be related to genetics. The goal is to inform theory-building and policies that might level the playing field between children from  different  origins.  Exploring  heritability  estimates  is  relevant  to  better  understand  the sources of inequalities in society and to assess whether genetics could operate as a confounding factor when studying social background effects.

When discussing whether class or status is heritable, heritability does not mean that there are specific genes or combinations of genes that directly or deterministically cause people to attain different positions. There is no 'lower middle-class gene', 'white collar gene' or 'secondary school  teacher  gene'.  Instead,  individual-level  traits  that  affect  people's  opportunities, advantages and disadvantages in education and labor markets, or lead people to hold different preferences or make different choices, may in part be affected by their genetics in complex ways. Genetics may be relevant for attainment through several of the mechanisms described by the abovementioned theories, such as by affecting educational attainment (Branigan et al., 2013), through factors affecting abilities and test performance (Baier, Lang, et al., 2022), by influencing cultural tastes and cultural consumption (Jæger & Møllegaard, 2022), and more. It is important to note here that many of the mechanisms through which genetics operate might be environmental, but in part stem from initial genetic variation. Genetics may also be relevant for  class  and  status  attainment  through  mechanisms  that  these  theories  do  not  emphasize,

including job preferences, dispositions and personality traits (Keller et al., 1992; Vukasović & Bratko, 2015), mental health (Gatt et al., 2014), physical health (Steenstrup et al., 2013) and other physical characteristics (Zempo et al., 2017). Even physical appearance might affect labor market outcomes and thus class and status attainment (Mobius & Rosenblat, 2006), including racialized phenotypical traits that may  make  individuals victims of racial or ethnic discrimination. As the latter example illustrates, the observation that genetics may matter for socioeconomic outcomes at the population level does not imply that inequalities are inevitable, immutable, or fair. The relationship between genetics and socioeconomic outcomes is always contextual, and depends heavily on what traits are rewarded and penalized in a given society, at a given point in time (Harden, 2021; Herd et al., 2019). The handful of previous studies using continuous, occupation-based measures of socioeconomic status show support for the notion that  heritable  traits  are  relevant  in  the  attainment  of  such  positions  (Akimova  et  al.,  2023; Belsky et al., 2018; Lichtenstein et al., 1992; Liu, 2019).

In sum, we expect to find that class and status attainment is at least to some extent influenced by genetics. But how much? Different methods and contexts will provide different answers. Pedigree-based estimates of the heritability of education are frequently found somewhere in the range of 20 to 60 %, depending on the data source and context. Recent evidence from Norway suggests a relatively high heritability component (Baier, Eilertsen, et al., 2022). But heritable characteristics may affect people's class and status attainment through other pathways besides education, which might produce a higher heritability of such outcomes than what is commonly found for education. On the other hand, post-educational socioeconomic outcomes may have a lower heritability  (Black et al., 2020; Fagereng et al., 2021), possibly because children from upper-class families may use their family resources to find other ways to succeed in the labor market, if they do not succeed in education. We also add that individual choices, idiosyncrasies, randomness and path dependency in education and the labor market may lead

very similar people to end up in different positions, leading to the potential of a relatively high E-component.


## 4. The Classical Twin Design (CTD)


To assess the role of genetic and environmental factors in class and status attainment, we apply a  classical  twin  design.  Twins  are  not  only  related,  but  also  largely  exposed  to  the  same environmental circumstances in their families of origin, including the parents' class and status. The  CTD  decomposes  the  variability  in  an  outcome  into  three  components:  a  component measuring variation related to additive genetic factors (the A-component, or the heritability), a part that is  due to  shared environments (the C-component) and variation that is specific to individuals,  i.e.  the  non-shared  environment  (the  E-component).  The  E-component  also incorporates any measurement error. Decomposing the variation in these three components is done by estimating so-called ACE-models, which allow us to give an approximation of the heritability of class and status. The CTD has nevertheless been subject to extensive debate and criticism, related to its underlying assumptions and its potential underas well as overestimation of genetic versus shared environmental components.

First, the models assume additive influences of genes and environments, implying that they operate  independently  of  each  other.  However,  genes  and  the  environment  could  both  be interacting and be correlated, which can lead to an overestimation of heritability (Plomin et al., 1977). The CTD also assumes that different genes do not interact with each other, which is not a given, and could lead to an overestimation of heritability (Zuk et al., 2012).

More  importantly,  the  no  assortative  mating  assumption  (NAM)  requires  that  there  is  no genetic assortative mating among parents of twins with regards to traits that are relevant to the outcome. In our case, this implies that there is homogamy in class and status or traits that may

affect  attainment.  The  result  of  violations  of  this  assumption  is  that  estimates  of  shared environmental  influences  (C)  are  biased  upwards,  exaggerating  the  importance  of  home environments  and  between-family  differences.  We  know  there  is  strong  homogamy  in socioeconomic outcomes (Horwitz et al., 2023), and we also know genetics explain a nontrivial  proportion  of  several  socioeconomic  outcomes.  Hence,  this  assumption  is  clearly violated  in  most  circumstances,  as  indicated  also  by  studies  from  the  Norwegian  context (Torvik et al., 2022). Wolfram and Morris (2023) found that a substantial share of the large C component commonly found in CTD studies of educational attainment could be attributed to assortative mating, suggesting that twin studies might underestimate genetic heritability and overestimate  the  role  of  the  shared  environment.  To  hence  consider  the  role  of  assortative mating, we conduct sensitivity analyses where the no assortative mating assumption is relaxed (see further).

The  equal  environments  assumption  (EEA)  stipulates  that  monozygotic  twins  experience environments that are equally similar as the environments of dizygotic twins (Hettema et al., 1995). This assumption may be violated in different ways, which may lead monozygotic twins to make more similar educational and labor market choices (Erikson & Goldthorpe, 2002). Several tests of the EEA have found that it holds reasonably well, that violations do not produce large biases, and that violations of the EEA and NAM tend to cancel each other out (Barnes et al.,  2014;  Conley  et  al.,  2013;  Derks  et  al.,  2006;  Felson,  2014;  Kendler  et  al.,  1993; Mönkediek,  2021).  Meanwhile,  several  studies  have  identified  relevant  violations  of  this assumption or criticized tests of it (examples include Burt & Simons, 2014; Fosse et al., 2015; Pam et al., 1996; Richardson & Norgate, 2005).

Some reassurance can be found in studies that apply methods that rely on different assumptions. CTD studies, multiple children of twins-studies, studies of twins reared apart, adoption studies, and  studies  exploiting  quasi-experimental  variation  mostly  reach  compatible  conclusions

regarding educational outcomes, which are strongly related to class and status (Baier, Eilertsen, et al., 2022; Baier, Lang, et al., 2022; Black et al., 2020; Bouchard et al., 1990; Branigan et al., 2013; Engzell & Tropf, 2019; Herd et al., 2019; Lichtenstein et al., 1992; Lindahl, 2011). In recent years, measured genotype data has also been used to estimate heritability coefficients in socioeconomic  and  other  phenotypes   In  a  recent  working  paper  on  occupational  status, . Akimova et al. (2023) found that genomic measures of genetic inheritance explained up to 9% of individual differences and 40% of the intergenerational transmission. Estimates from such data have benefits compared to estimates from pedigree data, but also come with their own weaknesses (Friedman et al., 2021). Importantly, most large-scale genomic data sources only include the most common genetic variants (SNPs) and not all genetic variation. This is likely a reason for the generally lower heritability estimates from genomic data, compared to CTDs. Genomic methods often provide a lower-bound estimate of heritability and may lack power to pick up all genetic signals (Young, 2019).

As a result,  we  believe  the  CTD  provides  an  intuitive  and  useful,  albeit  imperfect,  tool  to provide  heritability  estimates  from  pedigree  data.  As  this  is  the  first  study  assessing  the heritability of class and status attainment, it is preferable to provide a first estimate that includes all genetic variation. Our results can in turn serve as a benchmark for future studies relying on genomic or extended family data.


## 5. Data and methods



## 5.1. Data


Two separate data sources are used to answer our central research questions. Data from the Norwegian Twin Register (NTR) are used to identify twin pairs and hence obtain heritability estimates. The NTR includes a total of 40418 twins born in the years 1895-1960 and 1967-

1979, who are above 18 years of age and who have consented to being included in the registry (Nilsen et al., 2013). For 39738 individual twins, information is available on zygosity, which makes them eligible for CTDs. Zygosity indicates whether twins are monozygotic (identical) and hence share 100 percent of their genetic material, or dizygotic (fraternal), which implies that siblings are (on average) 50 percent genetically similar. In our study, we restrict the sample to same-sex twins born between 1941 and 1979. This is because we have data on occupations from between 2003 and 2021, which for the oldest individuals would render the occupation at age 62 (the earliest age of old-age retirement).

The second data source is administrative register data, which can be linked to the NTR through a unique personal identification number. The register data include individual-level information on  annual  earnings,  education  levels,  employment  status,  company  identifiers  and,  most importantly for our purposes, occupational codes (based on ISCO-88). After data harmonization, the observed occupation (between the ages of 30 and 62) closest to the age of 50 is used, so that class positions and status are sufficiently established. Based on this, 6904 twin pairs (13808 individuals) are retained. However, as not all these pairs have information on the occupation of both twins, the analytical sample is around 5000 twin pairs (the exact number of valid observations varies over different operationalizations and analyses, from 4814 to 5226 twin pairs in the main analyses, see Table B1 in Online Appendix). To address concerns about the representativeness of the twin sample, which is based on twins consenting to include information on their zygosity, descriptive statistics for both twins and the full population, both between 1941 and 1979, are displayed in Table 1. The statistics indicate that overall, the twin sample is similar to the full population (see also Nilsen et al., 2013), although women and older individuals are somewhat overrepresented.

## 5.2. Variables


We construct several class schemes based on the indicators available in our register data

The Erikson-Goldthorpe-Portocarero scheme (EGP) is an 11-class scheme (see Figure A1 in the Online Appendix) based on neo-Weberian theory emphasizing the labor contract, rational action, primary and secondary effects in education, and closure and opportunity hoarding by the upper classes (Breen, 2005; Erikson et al., 1979; Erikson & Goldthorpe, 1992). It is based on  ISCO-88  codes,  but  also  utilizes  variables  that  indicate  whether  individuals  are  selfemployed  and  the  number  of  employees  that  work  in  the  company  of  the  self-employed. Unfortunately, the class of 'Farmers and other self-employed workers in primary production' cannot be constructed, as no information is available on the type of work (occupational codes) for those who are self-employed. In the ordinal analyses we further collapsed this scheme to seven classes, as this version is more clearly hierarchically ordered, which makes it easier to use in twin models based on ordinal variables. Specifically, we distinguish between (1) the Service  Class  I,  (2)  Service  Class  II,  (3)  Routine  non-manual  employees  higher  grade,  (4) Routine non-manual employees lower grade, (5) Lower grade technicians and supervisors of manual  workers,  (6)  Skilled  manual  workers  and  (7)  Unskilled  manual  workers.  The  selfemployed are excluded from these analyses, as they cannot be ordered in the class hierarchy. Treating these classes as ordinal groups is not ideal, since they are conceptualized as discrete. However, treating the classes as categorical produces very similar results. This is shown in section E in the Online Appendix, where we also include the self-employed.

Second,  The  Standard  International  Occupational  Prestige  Score  (SIOPS)  is  a  gradational measure of occupational prestige that was developed using international surveys asking people to assign prestige scores to different occupations (Ganzeboom et al., 1992; Treiman, 1970).

Third, the International Socio-Economic Index of Occupational Status (ISEI) index (Ganzeboom et al., 1992) is a continuous, occupation-based measure of socioeconomic status developed using data from 16 countries on educational attainment, occupations and income for males.  The  index  is  designed  to  maximize  occupations  as  an  intervening  variable  between education and income.

Both of these continuous measures, SIOPS and ISEI, are  associated with the 'status attainment' tradition in sociology, and have commonly been used in comparative studies of occupational status attainment and mobility. Their application to our data is purely based on occupational codes, and assigns a predetermined score to each occupation. Since they are metric scales, no groups are omitted, but the scores are only assigned to employees.

Last, we compare our heritability estimates to indicators more often used in genetics research as benchmarks to evaluate the results. Specifically, twin analyses are performed on the years of education and the income rank (calculated within year, age and sex; 1-100), both measured as close as possible to the age of 50, to serve as a point of comparison. In addition, analyses are performed  on  two  additional  class schemes  (ORDC  and  Oesch),  for  which  the measurements and theoretical justifications are elaborated upon in the Online Appendix.


## 5.3. Modelling strategy


The models for SIOPS and ISEI as well as for education and income rank are estimated using a CTD with a metric outcome, but for the EGP class scheme we conduct ordinal analyses where we assume a hierarchical ordering of the categories. These models are all estimated using the umx package, which sets up threshold matrices for ordinal and binary variables and models them as thresholds of latent variables (Bates et al., 2019). All our models for the class and

status outcomes control for the age at which occupation is measured, expressed as the deviation from the ideal age of 50 years.

We also conduct additional analyses to gain more insight into the sensitivity of the results to differences between modeling strategies, assumptions and operationalizations. Specifically, we conduct (a) models for two additional class schemes that belong to different traditions, namely the Oslo Register Data Class Scheme (ORDC) and Oesch scheme, (b) models that correct for assortative mating, (c) binary (multi-categorical) analyses that estimate ACE coefficients for each class in every class scheme relative to all other classes (i.e., analyzing membership in each class as a dichotomous outcome), and (d) metric and ordinal analyses separately for women and  men  as  well  as  for  the  1941-1960  and  1961-1979  cohorts  to  shed  light  on  subgroup differences.

In addition, to provide a more descriptive overview, we also calculated the correlations between the class and status positions of twins for both monozygotic and dizygotic twin pairs. These estimates, together with the heritability obtained from the Falconer's Formula are shown in Table B1 in Online Appendix (not discussed here). In addition, phenotypic as well as genetic correlations  between  the  schemes  used  in  the  main  analyses  are  displayed  in  Section  B  in Online Appendix. We also provide unstandardized variance estimates for A, C and E in the metric and ordinal models in the Online Appendix (see Table B4) to gauge absolute variances.


## 6. Results



## 6.1. Main analyses


Estimates and 95% confidence intervals for the A-, C- and E-components of the analyses for metric and ordinal outcomes are displayed in Table 2 (see Table B4 in Online Appendix for unstandardized results). First, the results for the analysis of the SIOPS scale indicate that about

34 percent of the variability is due to genetic differences (A), 14 percent is accounted for by shared environments (C), and 52 percent is attributable to unshared environmental influences and measurement error (E). This suggests that both environmental and genetic factors play an important  role  and  that  quite  a  high  share  of  variation  in  occupational  prestige  attainment relates to genetics. Very similar results are obtained for the ISEI score, but the share of variance due to genetic differences is slightly larger (37 percent), while the share related to the unshared environment is slightly lower (0.49).

Turning to  the  ordinal  model  using  a  seven-class  version  of  the  EGP  scheme,  we  observe considerably higher estimates of heritability. For the EGP scheme, almost half of the variance is attributable to genetics (47 percent), 9 percent is accounted for by the shared environment and  44  percent  is  related  to  nonshared  influences  and  measurement  error.  Results  from additional bivariate twin models highlight that the schemes correlate very strongly with each other both phenotypically (around 0.85-0.90) as well as genetically (around 0.90-0.95) (see Table  B2  and  B3  in  Section  B  in  Online  Appendix).  Nevertheless,  despite  these  high correlations, the differences in heritability estimates could partly be due to different sample sizes and modeling strategies. All in all, these estimates seem to point to the conclusion that roughly 35-45 percent of the variation in class and status attainment is attributable to genetic differences, while shared environments account for 10-15 percent of this variation, and 45-50 percent is due to nonshared environmental factors.

We can compare this to indicators more often used in genetic research, such as income and education in order to get a sense of how comparable the estimates are to the heritability of our class and status measures. For years of education we find an A-component of 0.35, which is comparable to the heritability found for the metric scales. However, the shared environment explains a substantially larger share of the variance for education, as demonstrated by a Ccomponent  of  roughly  38  percent,  which  is  in  line  with  estimates  from  previous  research

(Branigan et al., 2013). For income, the heritability is also very similar (40 percent), but the Ccomponent is smaller than for the metric  status  measures  (7  percent).  The  phenotypic  and genotypic correlations displayed in Online Appendix, obtained from additional bivariate twin models, highlight that both education and income correlate strongly with the different class and status scores on a phenotypic (rp = 0.50-0.55) and especially genetic level (rg = 0.65-0.80). While  this  highlights  that  similar  genes  might  contribute  to  variability  in  the  different socioeconomic  outcomes,  the  genetic  overlap  between  education,  income,  class  and  status measures is not perfect (although Akimova et al, 2023 found much higher genetic correlations).

## 6.2. Sensitivity analyses


As a first  step,  we  conduct  analyses  on  two  additional  class  schemes.  One  inspired  by  the theories of Bourdieu (ORDC), and the other based on a horizontal work logic differentiation (Oesch). The results of twin models conducted on four-class ordinal versions of these schemes, as well as a four-class version of the EGP scheme as a point of comparison are displayed in section C of the Online Appendix. First, for the Oesch scheme, the variability attributable to genetics is estimated to 43 percent, while the shared and nonshared environment account for 15 and 42 percent of the variability, respectively. Second, the results indicate that for the ORDC scheme, heritability is estimated to be around 41 percent. The C-component is considerably higher than for the other schemes as it is estimated to be 23 percent. The four-class version of EGP has a slightly higher A-component (51 percent) than the seven-class version. All in all, analyses on these additional class schemes show a heritability of around 40-50 percent, which is slightly higher than the estimates from the metric measures.

Second, we conduct additional analyses that consider heightened genetic similarity between dizygotic  twins  due  to  assortative  mating  among  parents.  Specifically,  based  on  previous research on educational attainment (Baier, Lang, et al., 2022; Torvik et al., 2022), we estimate both  models  that  assume  that  dizygotic  twins  are  60  and  70  percent  genetically  similar, respectively, due to assortative mating. The results are displayed in section D in the Online Appendix. As expected, the heritability estimates become considerably larger when correcting for assortative mating, which highlights that a violation of the assumption of assortative mating will underestimate heritability. Specifically, heritability estimates increase to roughly 45 to 50 percent for the metric measures and to 50 to 60 percent for the ordinal class measures. For all measures, the shared environmental components become considerably smaller when taking into account assortative mating, even approaching zero.

Third, we estimate binary, or categorical ACE models for each class compared to all other classes in each of the full class schemes and average this across all classes to obtain an average estimate, for which the results are displayed in section E in the Online Appendix. This strategy is truer to the intended use of the original class schemes, as it does not force us to collapse and hierarchically order classes. However, the estimates for each of the classes separately is noisy, as we are dealing with limited sample sizes. No confidence intervals are displayed, as they are not  available  when  manually  averaging  over  the  class-specific  estimates.  In  general,  most heritability estimates based on full class schemes are somewhat lower and point to roughly 3540 percent of the variability in class attainment being accounted for by genetic differences, around  10-15  percent by shared environments  and  roughly  50  percent  by  unshared environments or measurement error. This might suggest that using ordinal four-class versions of the class schemes could be too crude and lead to an overestimation of heritability coefficients (as also evidenced by the higher A for the EGP four-class versus seven-class version). Note

that even when including the inactive (those with missing class schemes) as a separate category, the results remain very similar.

Last, we study subgroup differences to assess whether the heritability varies across with sex and whether there are cohort-based gene x environment interactions. First, comparing men and women (see Tables F1-F4), we find that for SIOPS, the A-component is larger for women, but for  all  other  class  schemes  or  status  measures,  heritability  is  somewhat  larger  for  men. However, the differences are rather small and the confidence intervals overlap, meaning that these differences are not statistically significant. For education, however, there is substantially and significantly larger heritability estimate for men than for women, which is in line with previous research (Silventoinen et al., 2004).

Turning to the differences across the two broad cohorts (see Tables F5-F8), it is evident that individuals  from  older  cohorts  have  consistently  larger  heritability  estimates  than  younger generations and this is outside of the confidence intervals for most of the class schemes and status measures. Younger generations appear to be, to a much larger degree, influenced by the shared environment, as indicated by the higher C-components. As more of the twin sample is part  of  the  older  cohort,  they  could  partly  be  driving  the  heritability  estimates  in  the  main analysis. However, part of the reason for higher A-estimates in the older cohort could be related to our age of measurement, which is often around or above 50 for the older generation (given that occupational data is available from 2003), but between 30 to 50 for the younger generation. For the latter this could mean that occupational status is for some individuals not established enough. Especially given the very small differences in estimates for education and income between cohorts, where there was less dispersion in the age of measurement due to more data availability, this could be an important explanation.


## 7. Discussion and conclusions


In general, sociological theories heavily emphasize social origins as important for class and status attainment. Drawing on the sociological and behavioral genetic literatures, we argue that sociologists should also examine how much of the variation in class and status attainment is related  to  genetic  differences.  Understanding  the  sources  of  variation  in  class  and  status attainment, is important for both theory building, policy development, and to inform future studies of family background effects.

Our results suggest that class and status attainment is neither purely a result of social origins, nor genetic origins. In the egalitarian context of Norway, additive genetics overall account for around  35-45  %  of  the  variation  in  class  and  status  outcomes  among  twins,  while  shared environments (including, but not limited to, social origins) account for around 10-15 % of this variation. The largest source of variation is related to the unshared environment (or unexplained variance),  which  encompasses  both  measurement  error,  and  numerous  factors  that  make identical twins different, including different experiences, random chance, individual choices, and  human  agency.  These  results  are  largely  consistent  across  operationalizations  and modeling  strategies,  despite  important  differences  in  the  theoretical  foundations  of  the schemes. Our analyses provide a benchmark of the heritability of class and status attainment that further studies can build on, and illustrate that genetic differences are important - in one way or another - when analyzing and explaining class and status attainment.

The literature on the heritability of social outcomes is large, and contains relevant comparison points to our results. From twin and pedigree studies a classical reference is Lichtenstein et al., (1992) who, using data on twins both reared apart and together, found that - at least for men genetic effects was a more important source of familial resemblance in socioeconomic status. Liu (2019) found that genetics explained 30% to 40% of variance in SES-related measures

(including a measure of occupational status) using data from the United States and GREML methods, which akin to twin models estimate genetic contributions to variance on the basis of degrees of relatedness. Akimova et al. (2023) used measured genotypes and found a heritability of sociologically  informed  occupational  status  measures  between  0.10  and  0.15.  The discrepancy between Liu's, Akimova et al's, and our results allude to the 'missing heritability' phenomenon, where estimates from measured genotype methods are generally lower than twin estimates. It could be tempting, then, for some social scientists to argue that the discrepancy is evidence  for  a  general  inflation  of  twin  estimates,  and  that  genetics  play  a  small  role  for occupational status-related outcomes. Even though that is conceivable, it is also likely that their estimates derived from measured genotypes are too low, due to the many complexities involved in  estimating  effects  of  individual  genetic  variants  (cf.  Turkheimer  (2012)  for  a  critical discussion). All in all, our results tie well into the extant literature, and complement them by adding class measures.

The results from this study will be sensitive to context. On the one hand, social origins might matter more and genetics less in less egalitarian contexts than Norway, as genetics are argued to be relatively more important in countries with more social mobility (Engzell & Tropf, 2019). However, we encourage others to attempt to replicate our findings in other contexts and across different  environments  and  social  groups,  and  to  use  other  analytic  designs  that  are  less sensitive to the abovementioned modeling assumptions. If similar results are found in other contexts and with alternative methods, the theoretical implications of this are, in our view, that sociological theories of class and status attainment should incorporate the important role of both environments and genetics. Ignoring or downplaying the role of genetics in theorizing on class and status attainment may lead researchers to overlook an important source of variation (Freese, 2008).

It is important to stress that we reject any argument that because socioeconomic outcomes are shown to have a high heritability, social inequalities are somehow  'natural' or  'fair'.  Both social and genetic origins represent sources of unequal opportunities that may be addressed by policy. Regardless of whether systematic differences in class and status outcomes are primarily due to social or genetic origins, the vast inequalities in rewards that are seen today between different social strata are nowhere close to egalitarian ideals of fairness (Swift, 2004). Some people may be born with traits that make them particularly suited for specific types of jobs. Others may be born with traits that severely hamper their opportunities in the labor market. That does not mean that such traits necessarily must be heavily rewarded or penalized (Harden,

2021; Swift, 2004).
