## Key facets of online monitoring activism



## (1) Knowledge as a core practice: OMA as networks of connective knowledge sharing


Knowledge-sharing, always central to activists (Casas-Cortés et al., 2008), emerges as a critical compound of their relationship with other online monitoring activists. Knowledgesharing among online monitoring activists is primarily necessitated by the affordances of digital activism, that is, the abundance and additivity of information online. OM activists, therefore, often specialized in thematic or local sub-groups of the COVID-19 protests they observed. Still, as they are outnumbered and their adversaries are well connected with each

other, monitoring activism must be a socially shared practice, even if it is not coordinated firmly.

'We've exchanged information relatively often and also because not everyone is in all Telegram groups [...] and we've given each other information about people behind the scenes [...] without being asked'

- '[…] when I had a question, for instance: Do you know these people? […]'
- '[...] hints were given like here, beware, they are planning something in your region, or I have received information here.'

While OM activists do not usually gather for coordinated efforts as other activists have previously done (Hatakka, 2020), they share information with each other ad-hoc where needed. Localized and specialized expertise thereby gets transferred within a loose network of like-minded without the formation of a collective activist identity. The reach of leverageable social control extends and transcends local and special-interest boundaries, with the mere availability of socially shared activists' expertise benefitting both the individual and the loose collective of activists.

As OM activists spin a web of transparency about their adversaries, knowledge is not merely a tool but at the core of the practice. Those caught in the web lose control over what is known about them. At the same time, OM activists gain potential and leverage for social control by collecting and adding knowledge about their adversaries. This knowledge accumulation puts them, as explained below, in an empowered and enjoyable position as arbiters of knowledge about their adversaries. However, it is also a practical necessity to make informed decisions about who or what to expose.


## (2) OMA as corrective action: Dissatisfaction with institutional performance


The perceived necessity of OMA in the face of insufficient institutional awareness and action requires more attention and emerges as a second core theme of OMA. Again, OMA as corrective action is multi-faceted, reflecting practical implications for the distinct activist action of OMA, identity constructive elements, and a particular normative standpoint on surveillance culture. 6

In our case, OMA operates in an ambiguous relationship with the state. For what Brayne, Lageson & Levy (2023) describe as 'surveillance deputies' state and civilian interests converge and hence they are willing to participate in denunciation behavior more or less facilitated and institutionalized by the state. However, this is not the case for OM activists. Their activism, albeit in some instances it can entail informing law enforcement, is not about becoming an accessory to the reporting and punishment of criminal behavior. Yet, they are also not necessarily to be understood as a form of counterpower (Feenstra & CaseroRipollés, 2014) against state institutionalized interests. Instead, OM activists hope to draw attention to a perceived lack of institutional reach and liberal democratic resistance to far-right mobilizing efforts. Direct reporting of illegal content or criminal behavior is scarce in their practice and seen as not particularly fruitful in the face of institutional incompetence and overburdening.

'As I said, I'm trying to be fair to the police here, but […] I also saw that the police were leaking information to the demonstrators (COVID-19 protestors). There was an incident recently where a police officer hugged a female demonstrator who was also playing a leading role during the demonstration, and of course, that's scary.'

'I've been doing this for three years now, so I know how people think there [police], what they actually do, and I'm now also relatively legally fit to say whether it's worth reporting it or not. [...] It's got better, no question. But sometimes there are still no professionals there.'

On the surface level, they, therefore, do not compete with or contest the liberal democratic normative order and its institutions of media, politics, and law enforcement but claim a more active and vital role within the public as monitorial arbiters of information, filling a gap in democracy's introspection afforded by monitorial civic duty. Analogous to Hatakka's (2020) findings on civic monitoring of the Finnish radical right on Facebook, the primary self-reported objective for the online monitoring activists here was to expose extremists' beliefs. On a deeper level, however, the discontent with the state sparking their monitoring and reporting action reveals the normative standpoint on what a state ought to do, for instance that law enforcement should take a greater interest in actively monitoring the protest spheres online, that grounds OMA in surveillance culture,

'In principle, we pave the way for these officials. Of course, I think they have relatively few opportunities to actively scan so many telegram channels in their time. They also have a lot of bureaucratic things to do. And we prepare everything by basically already starting the investigations.'

OMA leverages and extends the scope of the transparency imperative (Han, 2022) in digital information society to a surveillance imperative : Because everything is available as information, it must be collected. This imperative reflects a normatively weighty and contradictory demand for far-reaching institutional and social control closer to the digital panopticon on the pessimistic spectrum of interpretations of surveillance culture. State control is seen as incompetent, overburdened, and at times complicit in the unfavorable growth of farright threats. It is precisely the inactivity of the state vis-à-vis the availability of information that encourages OMA. Still, OM activists try to coax institutions into action where legislative

frameworks are ambiguous, not reaching, or where they remain unresponsive. OM activists, therefore, employ tried and tested attention mechanisms. Notably, traditional media power, that is facilitating critical media reporting, is seen as a powerful tool to leverage social control and to increases pressure on politicians and coax them into action.

'I've already leaked things to several media outlets on my own initiative, some of which are things that I don't publish myself or don't do anything about. If I come across something really interesting, I pass it on to the media, and if they say no, it's not interesting, then I just do it myself. So, really tricky things, I would always do this route because I think it's more effective because they have the better reach, and of course, I have a completely dubious Twitter profile, so a dubious name.'

'What we did a few times in the beginning was to send local politicians a little more information. But after a reasonable amount of time, we simply stopped doing that due to a lack of feedback.'

'[…] it's about the threshold is simply getting higher for them [politicians]. Shall we get involved with XY in [city/location]? Or could that be tricky for us?'


## (3) The ethical normative framework of OMA


In their normative ethical orientation, OM activists navigate multi-faceted tensions and contradictions. The activists cultivate a liminal identity of protecting the normative order of liberal democracy against a far-right threat while always risking to breach norms themselves. Activists see their role as filling a gap left by, in their eyes, democratic institutions' inadequate defense against far-right threats. On the one hand, they fulfil the role of active citizenship in monitory democracy, but on the other, they also reinforce the transparency imperative and the wish for far-reaching security and control inherent to surveillance culture. The transparency afforded by their adversaries' online connective action and mobilizing efforts legitimizes their surveillance and demands surveillance.

'They're all public channels for me, so I don't have any concerns about that now.' 'I don't publish anything from private channels.'

'[...] As long as the groups are public, why should that be punishable? Taking a public posting from a public group and putting it somewhere else publicly...'

'[…] There is no right to Nazi propaganda, and that's why I have no moral scruples at all.'

Despite their reinforcing of the transparency imperative, OM activists must evade surveillance themselves. The risk of counter-surveillance forms a boundary for their actions. Maintaining anonymity limits their ability to expose adversaries as they must refrain from actions that can, for instance, entail being subjected to criminal investigations and the risk of being exposed by that (e.g., GDPR violations). A right for anonymity in an otherwise transparent surveillance society is hence invoked selectively based on the threat/no-threat perception of the OM activists:

'If, in our opinion, they were clearly anti-constitutional or went against the established consensus in society. If swastika flags are posted there or swastikas made from coronavirus syringes, or if anti-Semitic and racist comments are made there. Yes, we dragged that out into the open […] how else is society supposed to realize that rightwingers think they are safe again and publish such things publicly or partially publicly?'

What is for them a mere practical need of evading retaliative action and the concrete threat of far-right actors, something that they have actual experiences with, however, also reflects the liminal identity of OM activists in a digital society in which being subjected to surveillance is an otherwise normal expectancy and where anonymity is fragile, unexpected yet necessitated by surveillance culture. In other words, online monitoring activists reinforce

and subvert the transparency imperative of contemporary digital surveillance society simultaneously.

'There are a lot of people on Twitter who don't want to be public with their work. Women who are simply afraid of being hit on […] so if you work with clear names, you have to reckon with the fact that you'll be 'hunted' so to speak.'

'It's about threats to life or destruction of cars, denunciation in the workplace, and things like that here, which is unfortunately a subculture, a culture that has emerged. And I can understand when people say: No, I want to remain absolutely anonymous because I'm simply afraid for my children, my job, and I don't know what.'

'There's always a kind of wanted notice. Who is that? Who is doing it? Who is behind it? I don't necessarily advertise it to the world. I don't boast about what a cool Twitter account I have. That's not the case. That's not useful.'

Finally, surveillance practices bear an element of enjoyment. Most prominently on surface-level, OM activists can find joy in digging deep into their adversaries' communicative structures, exposing them, making fun of them and filling in for a perceived lack of institutional surveillance - reflecting the established fun/pastime activity dimension in Lyon's (2017) surveillance culture. Importantly, however, the enjoyment of surveillance practices is not to be found merely by infiltrating and exposing the other or feeling empowered as the surveillant by that. It is also found in the reflexive practice of what one could call surveillance without exposition in the context of OMA. In Žižek's (2017) terms surplus-enjoyment, that is pleasure 'gained by the very form (procedure) of pursuing the goal' (p. 9), is gained throughout the process of OMA as the surveillant decides who or what is not worth or legitimate monitoring and/or exposing. To know yet to choose not to act for moral reasons or because the potentially monitored is not considered worth monitoring can be a pleasurable

experience of power for online monitoring activists. Moreover, accumulating localized and specialized knowledge, even if it is never used, has a rewarding aspect.


## Conclusion


In this study, we offer two main contributions. Firstly, by conceptualizing online monitoring activism as the continued systematic collection, processing, and publishing of information on adversary observable others online, we define OMA and make the phenomenon operationalizable for future research. Secondly, we situate OMA within the framework of digital activism and surveillance culture and critically discuss the normative implications of OMA, drawing attention to their contentious practices and activist identity that oscillates between virtuous citizenship and vigilantism, reinforcing the imperative of surveillance in the digital society.

OMA is a practice of civic monitoring (Hatakka, 2020, p. 1322; Feenstra & CaseroRipollés, 2014, p. 2451) enacted not necessarily as a form of counterpower but as counteractivism. Thereby, OMA comprises a specific form of individual digital activism that is not directly affiliated with organized protest movements or social movements yet contributes to their existence by furnishing essential information. This information serves a dual purpose: it can contribute to awareness-raising and consciousness-building efforts and inform organized activists' or institutions' actions. This form of activism aims to disrupt, if not prevent, opposing social movements by making strategic use of the power of visibility but also of institutionalized power within an ambivalent framework of general belief in the normative institutionalized order and vigilante self-empowerment facilitated by a perceived disparity of far-right mobilization and institutionalized regulative power and control prohibiting that online. OM activists neither necessarily compete with institutionalized monitoring of threats to liberal democratic society nor employ themselves as their surveillance deputies (Brayne et

al., 2023) but, although aware of legislative and regulatory constraints, aim to coax them into action.

The goal of leveraging social control, also at times by proxy of state control, grounds the practice of OMA firmly in surveillance culture. Hence, OMA is facilitated by and, at the same time, reinforces surveillance culture. Online monitoring activists thereby invoke a surveillance imperative with far-reaching normative implications: Because everything is available as information, it must be collected and consequently leveraged for social control. Simultaneously, they subvert the surveillance imperative by elevating anonymity to an unexpected, rare, and necessary good that is selectively granted. Within this paradigm of general transparency, the surveillant takes an empowered position. Partially removed from the surveillance imperative by its own contradictions, the surveillant gains power and surplusenjoyment by deciding on and directing the gaze of transparency, that is, by ruling over who will be made transparent and who will not.

Our observations on OMA certainly expand the existing framework of civic monitoring practices and counter-action (Feenstra & Casero-Ripollés, 2014; Meyer & Staggenborg, 1996), but they do not exclude existing or other forms of civic monitory action. For instance, in our study, the scrutinization and exposure of adversaries' communication was directed at the disruption of far-right movements. However, contexts are conceivable in which OMA is directed against progressive movements or institutionalized power. The whistleblower and watchdog function of civic monitoring can become more salient in OM activists infiltrating, for instance, political party chat groups or parliamentary communication channels of other sorts. Due to the specific relative openness of Telegram as a platform, the infiltration aspect was not as salient in our study. Still, it could entail significantly more effort and risk in other cases.

That the OMA studied here was bound to Twitter/X likely stems from activists' desire to spread awareness about their observed to larger audience and elite target groups. OMA is, however, not necessarily bound to any one platform and we should continue to observe whether the practice emerges elsewhere. Platform rules and regulations might inform possible adaptations of OMA. While the practice of OMA as a form of digital counterprotest will likely prevail, the counter-activists we interviewed here were just in the earliest stages of forming a loosely coordinated countermovement (in van Haperen et al.'s 2023 words, a 'swarm') whose action repertoire was bound to the expressive activity of the primary movement, the coronavirus protests. However, if these surveillance practices are normalized as expected in surveillance culture, they will transcend the particular phenomenon and increasingly transfer into the everyday action repertoire of digital activism.

Expanding the present research to diverse other contexts should thus be an objective of future, more generalizable, research. Further, the digital/technical background and gender of activists could play a role in OMA. Therefore, a further promising direction can be to analyze the socio-genesis of online monitoring activists in more depth and with larger samples if they are accessible. As OMA will likely be an emergent civic monitoring practice observed in manifold online contexts, broader theoretical reflections of the activists' role as intermediaries between divergent online (counter-)publics could be an interesting novel perspective. With an expansion of contexts in OMA research, one should also pay attention to the localized nature of OMA. Despite the digitality of the practice, physical space could profoundly influence the genesis of OMA and should be explicitly studied. Finally, we call for more normative work on OMA and its contentious practices in digital society and surveillance culture. While the normative positionality of OMA seems clear yet contradictive, it is imperative for scholars and policymakers to critically engage with the question of whether and to what extent more control and by whom is actually wishful for liberal democracy. In other words, we should

further study the surveillance imperative at the core of online monitoring activism before judging its merit.

## 1. Introduction



## 1.1 Korean Peninsula and its Demilitarized Zone


The  Korean  peninsula  has  long  been  re-shaped  by  internal  conflicts  and  the  influence  of  larger neighbouring  countries  (Park,  2006).  In  1945,  Japanese  colonization  was  ended  by  their  defeat.  The victorious armies of the Soviet Union and USA then occupied Korea, north and south of the 38th parallel (Kim, 2021). The cold war then rapidly arose between these former allies, led to their occupation resulting the client countries of the North and South Korea. In 1950, North Korea invaded South Korea, and after 3 years of brutal fighting that killed about 3 million people that involved both Korean armies and the great powers of the cold war (Park, 2010). The war halted in a stalemate in 1953 with Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) established between the countries. The DMZ is about 4 km wide, and it extends for 250 km across the Korean peninsula. In South Korea, a Civilian Control Zone (CCZ) extends a further 5-20 km south from the DMZ (figure 1).

At the end of the Korean war, South Korea was a poor country. In 2024, South Korea is Asia's fourthlargest economy and the world's thirteenth-largest by GDP (Yoo, 2023). This transformation, known as the 'Miracle of the Han River' (Doucette & Pak, 2019), was fuelled by government-led economic programs, often termed 'authoritarian developmentalism' (Song, 2020). Military rule ended in the late 1980s, and in  the  1990s,  South  Korea  was  regarded  as  being  a  highly  developed  country  with  very  high  human development (Kwak & Ryoo, 2024).  South Korea's state-driven model spurred not only economic growth but also changes in political, social,  and  cultural  domains  (Wang  &  Kim  2015).  Key  industries  such  as electronics, automotive, mining, and tourism, while driving growth, have also generated environmental problems (Oh & Jin, 2016). South Korea has rapidly urbanized, with rural areas being depopulated. It has also fostered a highly competitive education system and job market. However, these changes have also led to increased consumerism, materialism, and associated stress on citizens (Jang et al., 2022).

At the end of the Korean War, North Korea was impoverished and heavily reliant on Soviet aid. Today, it remains one of the world's most isolated nations. North Korea has been ruled by three generations of the Kim family, and they have maintained an economic focus on heavy industry, agriculture, and military expansion (Oh & Park, 2023). The country has developed urban areas, however, many rural regions remain poor, with persistent food insecurity (Cha, 2014). There has never been a peace treaty between North and South Korea, and their relations have oscillated between periods of conflict and reproachment, while the social, cultural, and economic differences between North and South Korea have grown (Kim, 2018).

In  the  seventy  years  since  the  DMZ's  creation,  limited  human  activity  has  allowed  diverse  species  of animals  and  plants  to  flourish  within  the  DMZ.  Abandoned  paddy  fields  have  evolved  into  wetlands, creating naturally restored terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems. Today, the DMZ serves as a habitat for thousands of species that move through this borderland (Brady, 2021; Kim, 2019). However, in some places, landmines, vegetation removal for surveillance, and wildfires limit this movement (Kim & Lee, 2024). This resurgence of nature has transformed the DMZ into a space for unique geopolitical ideas,

merging ecotourism with security tourism (Chun et al., 2022). South Korea's post-developmental policies promote initiatives such as 'green growth' (Kim & Thurbon, 2015), 'green détente' (Na, 2022), and 'NetZero'  (Joo  et  al.,  2023).  Additionally,  the  DMZ  is  being  reimagined  with  'Eco-Peace-Oriented'  goals, combining ecology and peace-building (Shin, 2021). Despite numerous scientific and political efforts to establish the DMZ as a biosphere reserve or peace park, these initiatives have not yet succeeded (BentonShort, 2020; Brady, 2008, 2021).

Sustained peace and preserved nature in the DMZ are critical, and the Korean peninsula needs new and actionable visions for the future. These visions should aim to enhance the benefits of geopolitical and economic developments, improving the well-being of people and nature.

## 1.2 DMZ Open Festival and EcoPeace Forum


Since  1972,  when  Imjingak,  the  Bridge  of  Freedom  over  the  Imjin  River,  was  established,  Gyeonggi Province has developed various facilities in this area, which serves as the closest passage to North Korea in the metropolitan region. Starting with the establishment of Peace Nuri Park in 2005, the province has hosted  various  DMZ-related  events.  In  2019,  an  integrated  festival  titled  "Let's  DMZ"  was  initiated, combining exhibitions, concerts, marathons, and academic conferences, in the pursuit of inter-Korean exchange. Towards the end of 2022, the DMZ OPEN Festival was launched, highlighting the history and nature of the DMZ since the Three Kingdoms dynasty (Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla) in the Korean Peninsula. The festival aims to present the value of peace and ecology through the means of arts, music, sports, and scholarship. The term "DMZ Open" signifies the physical space, genre, and inclusivity of experts and the general public. Exhibitions, music concerts, and marathons in and around the Korean DMZ are held from May to November to provide a comprehensive experience to citizens, making the DMZ more accessible as a space for healing and creation (Shim et al. 2023).

The EcoPeace Forum is an academic forum that started in 2023 as part of the DMZ Open Festival, following the predecessor DMZ for a few decades. The 2023 EcoPeace Forum held on 19-22 September 2023 aimed to understand diverse values of ecology and peace by providing a venue for global and national experts, together with relevant officials, practitioners and citizens working and living in border areas, to openly discuss futures of the DMZ. The Visioning Workshop, for this reason, was expected to play a role in cocreating  new  discourses  on  plausible  and  desirable  futures  of  the  DMZ.  The  visioning  was  therefore designed to develop a set of pluralistic and positive visions of how nature in the DMZ could be conserved, how people and nature could intersect, and how culture could be recalled and re-created in and through the DMZ of the Korean peninsula. The workshop was organized and conducted with the expectation that it will contribute to enhancing understanding of the diverse ecological, cultural and social values of the DMZ and the conservation of nature and the well-being of humanity nationally, and globally.


## 1.3 Visioning Living in Harmony with Nature in 2050


Futures approaches, such as scenario and vision development, can help people think systematically and constructively about the future, especially when the future is uncertainty and contested (Cork et al., 2023; Lazurko et al., 2023). They are especially helpful in studying the complex dynamics between human and natural systems (Hichert et al., 2021, Kuiper et al. 2024). Futures studies in biodiversity science argue that actively developing ideas, images and/or stories about can help identify achievable visions, pathways and actions towards desirable futures (Durán et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2023).

The '2050 vision of living in harmony with nature' of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) has long been a collective goal in biodiversity conservation, but this policy-framework driven vision has not been elaborated or explored sufficiently to envision or imagine what the future will look like. The CBD's newly approved Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework encapsulates diverse ways countries and cultures perceive nature, including anthropogenic and environmental drivers that the CBD parties consider are essential to tackle to improve the state of nature and its benefits to people (CBD 2022). The Nature Futures Framework, a new scenario modelling framework, developed by the Intergovernmental Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), positions three complementary and intertwined value perspectives on nature, which can be used to develop desirable futures for nature and people (IPBES, 2023; Pereira et al., 2020). As the CBD and IPBES collaborate closely with their member states on policy and scientific assessments respectively in the domain of biodiversity and human wellbeing, they were optimal  for  developing  ecologically  diverse  and  harmonious  visions  for  the  future  of  Korea.  Further, employing the Seeds of Good Anthropocene (SOGA) approach enables the futures visions to be built based on locally relevant and existing practices while considering global ideals or initiatives that are in line with Korean initiatives (Hamann et al., 2020; Raudsepp-Hearne et al., 2020). Hence, the integrative use of policy (CBD KMGBF), scientific (IPBES NFF) and data (SoGA) frameworks and approaches optimized the imagination of nature- and people-positive and realizable futures.

The Visioning Workshop at the 2023 DMZ Open Festival's Ecopeace Forum brought together research institutes, government agencies, civil society organizations, and citizen networks as catalysing agents to inspire societal transformations through co-learning, co-designing, and co-creating small to large scale initiatives that can develop nature- and people-positive future visions. ## 2. Methods


The visioning process entailed an in-person workshop along with pre- and post-workshop activities, which we describe in this section (Figure 3). The process started from conceptualizing and scoping the workshop to align with, and to inform, the aims and the purpose of the Ecopeace Forum iteratively with Gyeonggi Province as the coordinating agency of the DMZ Open Festival. The workshop programme was designed building on previous experiences around the globe and adapted for Korean context and culture.

## 2.1 Pre-workshop preparation


As  the  visioning  had  'living  in  harmony  with  nature'  at  its  centre,  the  organizing  committee  of  the Ecopeace Forum and a subset of the visioning workshop facilitation team sought out participants that were  interested  in  positive  societal  changes  or  were  working  in  related  occupations.  A  call  was disseminated to recruit participants broadly across sectors, regions and disciplines, and also across the networks and institutions known to have well-suited stakeholders. Prospective participants were asked to complete a short application form that elicited their motivations for participating in the workshop, factors that could play a key role in creating a co-existence paradigm for nature and people in the DMZ, and seeds for the visioning exercises. As the recruitment resulted in the number of participants expected for  the  workshop  and  all  applicants  had  demonstrated  proven  potential  for  their  contribution,  all applicants, in a total of 23 were invited to the visioning workshop. This participant group was joined by nine facilitators, four artists, and four writers, making it altogether 40 individuals in the workshop.

Next, building on the ideas and suggestions from the applicants on potential attributes to nature and people co-existence paradigm in the DMZ, the workshop facilitation team who were familiar with the visioning processes and environmental status in Korean society further identified seeds to build the seed bank for the workshop. Seeds are existing initiatives that are not yet mainstreamed but have potential to contribute to sustainability (Bennett et al., 2016). This required thinking broadly across the country and

societal domains on what has been working well in improving environmental awareness and practices by the citizens on a daily basis, at the community level, and also at the systems level (e.g., policies). Some of the regional and global initiatives (e.g., degrowth) that are being implemented in small scales were also considered to allow cross-scale connections and interactions. These seeds were then matured by the facilitation team, imagining the conditions/status of the seeds if they were mainstreamed in Korea in 2050 'Living  in  Harmony  with  Nature'  (see  SM  I).  These  matured  seeds  were  foundational  to  the  visioning process.


## 2.2 Workshop process and methods


The one-and-a-half-day visioning workshop started with the introduction of the visioning process and various frameworks and key concepts. Through a facilitated exercise, participants formed four groups that shared similar perspectives on their relationship with nature, and thus similar locations in the NFF triangle. Groups were then led to the wall of seeds that included the matured condition of seeds positioned in the NFF triangle in accordance with their relative position and composition of nature value perspectives. Each group chose three seeds covering different themes or societal domains that were also in line with their group's position in the NFF triangle (Figure 4a).

The four groups separately developed visions through a series of exercises. First, each group identified the first-  and second-order implications of each of the matured seeds to create three Future Wheels (Glenn  2009)  (Figure  4b).  In  doing  so,  groups  considered  implications  from  Science,  Technological, Economic,  Environmental,  Political,  and  Values  domains  ( STEEP-V )  (An  et  al.  2020).  Each  group  then 'clashed' the three Future Wheels (of three seeds) to identify synergies and conflicts across the wheels as a step toward their integration into a single vision (Figure 4c). Facilitators then used a range of questions from the VERGE framework to enrich the visions by encouraging participants to describe the prevailing: 1)  worldviews,  paradigms,  social  values  and  attitudes;  2)  family  structures,  business  models,  and governance  structures;  3)  information  technology,  urban  design  and  language;  4)  manufacturing, efficiency, and rule-making; 5) patterns of consumption, modes of exchange, consumer preferences and marketing; 6) conflict, rules and norms; and 7) people and nature relationships (Lum, 2014).

The participants then synthesized and presented their group's vision in plenary. As participants were encouraged to be creative in their performances, presentations took the form of news reporting, theatre, and music and dancing. The workshop concluded with participants reflecting on the visioning process, comparing and contrasting the visions and sharing the lessons learned.

## 2.3 Post-workshop processing


After the workshop, the facilitator team developed full narratives (see SM II), illustrations (see section 3.1) and storylines for the four visions based on the products of the workshop. The narratives were drafted based on notes from the rich discussion of facilitated exercises at the workshop, which then were written in the form of synthetic and inspirational storylines by the facilitation team while the artists finished the illustrations depicting the future states and key concepts of the four visions for the DMZ in 2050. These narratives were disseminated to the workshop participants for review comments and edits, and a subgroup of these participants contributed to the revision and translation of the four future visions.

Once the full narratives were drafted and refined, the four visions were compared and contrasted using a range of socio-economic-ecological domains sensible for Korea's sectoral structure and development for internal  consistency  and  refinement  (Table  2).  The  visions  were  also  developed  into  11  seeds-based

illustrative stories in manga style with visuals by the human-commanded ChatGPT to help communicate and were disseminated along with the narratives across stakeholders in the Ecopeace Forum (Peterson, 2024). It is expected that the stakeholder participants who contributed to the visions' development will be key ambassadors and catalysts for mobilizing changes in their networks to initiate and enable necessary transformations to realize co-developed visions.


## 3. Results



## 3.1 Stakeholder composition and their aspirations


Visioning  workshop  participants  are  crucial  contributors  as  their  ideas,  values  and  norms  shape  the discourse and the resulting visions. By the nature of DMZ Open Festival, the recruitment of participants was open and publicized through a broad range of mediums including governments, research institutes, civil  society organizations, academia, and citizen networks. In this workshop, many of the participants worked  in  nature  conservation  but  had  diverse  professional  backgrounds  including  the  academia, research  institutions,  international  organizations,  activism,  startup/entrepreneurship,  education,  law, press, and arts (see SM III). Their academic fields were varied and included ecology, statistics, sociology, spatial planning, urban architecture and health, while their age ranged from college students to elderly post-retirement,  with  the  majority  in  their  20s  to  50s.  This  provided  an  opportunity  to  exchange perspectives  across  disciplinary  practices  and  generations,  understanding  historical,  cultural,  and relational values of nature broadly in the Korean context and hope for a harmonious coexisting future.

The key motives for participation were to gain inspiration, with specific goals varying by profession. They included, for example, designing an educational programme that involves principles of the Nature Futures Framework, giving better consulting, drawing on various creatures living in DMZ, and researching how coexistence proceeds in DMZ compared to other urbanized places. Some applicants were in search of a vision of life, wanting to contribute to the world in a meaningful way. Values that applicants showed were sustainability,  recovering  social  cohesion,  living  without  damaging  the  environment,  finding  balance between technical innovations and conservation, and listening to people and the ecosystem on the front lines of crisis. Critical reflections that applicants had were on the social development that caused the climate crisis, and the lack of citizen awareness about the importance of biodiversity to humanity, leading to slow progress or suspension of nature preservation efforts.

## 3.2 Korea's seeds of good Anthropocene


As  the  foundational  elements  for  the  visions,  the  seeds  of  the  SoGA  concept  were  collected  in  their initial/present state on ideals, practices, institutions and/or technologies that currently exist in Korea as well as those that are being promoted globally to allow for local to global fertilization (e.g. zero waste village in Korea, circular economy ideal). These seeds were collected from the workshop participants as well as facilitators that cover societal domains including environment, economy, technology, agriculture, energy, business, tourism, climate, and traditions (Table 1, see SM I for the full list).

As a result of the nature value perspective sharing exercise in the NFF triangle, three of the four vision groups self-clustered at each distinct value perspective at the NFF vertices, while one group was located between the Nature for Nature and Nature as Culture value perspectives, combining the two. Each group chose three matured seeds that were mapped near the value perspective that the group chose in the NFF triangle  space  (see  coloured  and  clustered  seeds  in  Figure  6).  The  subsequent  exercises  (e.g.  Future Wheels, STEEP, VERGE) of visioning of the future built upon these chosen seeds, imagining the future where small sustainable initiatives of today were successfully scaled up and practiced in Korean society. The Nature for Nature vision group chose 30% of the world protected for conservation, return of tiger and other  large  mammals,  and  zero  pollution  village,  focusing  on  nature's  restoration  and  resilience supporting human wellbeing. The Nature for Society vision group chose nature-based climate solutions, healthy food and wellbeing with low pollution, and low-growth economic  model, rooted on environmentally  friendly  societal  development  towards  climate  mitigation  and  human  wellbeing.  The Nature  as  Culture  vision  group  chose  the  revival  of  guardian  spirit  in  DMZ,  nature's  benefit  from ecotourism, and mainstreamed ecological knowledge, which had a strong preservation of culture from history as well as innovations of today applied, optimized for nature's conservation and co-creation of new culture. Finally, the vision group combining Nature for Nature and Nature as Culture chose the seeds that most people live in big ecological archaeologies, 100% renewable energy-run villages, and elephants in the DMZ, which had a mix of returning to the past with highly nature-bounded human settlement across country. Hence the four visions reflected dominantly the nature values that the vision is positioned closely with some reflection of other nature values that allow more realistic, diverse and nuanced representation of nature's values.

The  Nature  as  Culture  (NC) vision describes the multifaceted  and  intertwined aspects of nature and culture, focusing on three main areas: the  integration  of  ecological knowledge into mainstream education, benefits of ecotourism for nature and inspirational  branding  of  the DMZ  by  reviving  its  guardian spirits. It envisages the DMZ as a space for coexistence between  humans  and  nature that is underpinned by biodiversity, and  where  the historical  preservation  of  the DMZ serves as a metaphor for returning  to  nature  through  embracing  culture  and  arts.  This  vision  is  built  upon  a  model  of  selfgovernance  that  is  unique  to  the  DMZ,  where  the  occupations  of  residents  reflect  the  needs  and preservation of the region. This autonomy grants new political power to the DMZ, offering an alternative to traditional political divisions. At the institutional level, strategies are put in place for the utilization and management of the DMZ, including urban planning, transportation systems and biodiversity monitoring. This  autonomy also enables financial  resources  to  be  secured  for  implementation  of  these  strategies through  mechanisms  such  as  DMZ  taxes  and  environmental,  social,  and  governance  (ESG)  branding. Ecologically positive contributions to the DMZ are incentivised through eco-point and ecological welfare point  systems  and  programmes  that  recognize  different  specialities  and  therefore  contributions  to ecological resilience in the region. People are highly connected to the DMZ and its nature and explore ways to increase familiarity with it through innovative means such as the DMZ cloud and Metaverse. Society envisions the DMZ space as a hub for cultural exploration and storytelling, creating new narratives beyond political boundaries. This deep-seated connection between nature and culture is fostered from an early age by integrating ecological knowledge into mainstream education and reorganizing curricula to emphasize ecology. Specialized institutions like 'ecology higher education' are established, and ecological education is incentivised through scholarships and field trips. Education is a crucial tool for fostering a deeper  understanding  of  human-nature  relationships  and  promoting  sustainability.  Ecotourism  is promoted  within  the  DMZ  through  branding  that  restores  and  reawakens  traditional  stories  of  the spiritual guardians of nature. This expands awareness and understanding of the unique nature of the DMZ embracing  academic,  economic,  ecological  and  social  dimensions  of  ecotourism.  Ecotourism  leads  to ecological  conservation  efforts,  stimulating  humanistic  appreciation  for  wildlife  and  alleviating  social stress through leisure and educational activities, and creating green jobs. Ultimately, people advocate for

approaches that prioritize the preservation of the relationship between humans and nature, fostering sustainable development through ecotourism and institutional innovation.

'문화로서의 자연(NC)' 비전은 자연과 문화, 그리고 그 상호 연관성의 다각적인 측면에 집중한다. 특히 브랜딩을 통한 DMZ 수호령의 부활, 주류 교육 내 생태지식의 통합, 생태관광이 자연에 주는 혜택 이라는 세 가지  주요  영역에  초점을  맞추고  있다.  이  비전은  비무장지대를  인간과  자연이  공존하는  공간으로 상상하는데 있어서 문화와 예술의 통합을 통해 비무장지대의 역사적 보존과 자연으로의 회귀를 은유적으로 상징한다. 이 비전은 주민들이 지역보존의 기여에 필요한 직업을 기반으로 형성된 DMZ 만의 독특한 주민자치 구조를 바탕으로 한다.이러한 자치권은 비무장지대에 새로운 정치적 힘을 부여하여 기존의 전통적인 정치적 분열에 대한 대안을 제시한다. 제도적 차원에서는 도시 계획, 교통 시스템, 생물 다양성 모니터링 등 DMZ의 활용과 관리를 위한 전략이 마련된다. DMZ 세금과 ESG 브랜딩 등의 방식을 통해 미래의 DMZ를 위한 재원 확보의 중요성을 강조한다. 이 비전은 DMZ 브랜딩을 통해 자연의 정신적 수호자 역할을 되살린다. 생태적 기여를 장려하고 지역의 특수성을 인정하기 위한 에코 포인트 시스템과 생태 복지 포인트 개발을 중심으로 제도적 논의가 이루어 진다. 또한  DMZ 클라우드 및 메타버스와 같은 혁신적인 수단을 통해 DMZ 공간에 대한 친숙도를 높이고, 문화 탐험과 스토리텔링의 허브로서 DMZ 공간이  정치적  경계  너머  새로운  내러티브를  만들어  낸다.생태를  강조하는  커리큘럼  개편,  '생태 고등학교'와 같은 전문 기관 설립, 장학금과 현장학습을 통한 생태 교육 장려 등 생태 지식을 주류 교육에 통합한다. 교육은 인간과 자연의 관계에 대한 깊은 이해를 돕고 지속가능성을 증진하는 데 중요한 도구이기 때문이다. 이 비전은 다양한 분야의 연구를 통해 DMZ에 대한 인식과 이해를 넓히면서 생태관광을 학문적, 경제적, 생태적, 사회적 측면에서 탐구한다. 생태관광은 생태 보전 노력과 인간의 야생동물에 대한 존중 강화,  여가  및  교육  활동을  통한  사회적  스트레스  완화,  그리고  친환경  일자리를  창출로  이어진다. 궁극적으로 사람들은 생태관광과 제도적 혁신을 통해 지속 가능한 개발을 촉진하며, 인간과 자연의 관계 보존에 우 선순 위를 두 는 접근 방식을 지지한다.

In the Nature for Society vision, the DMZ is a space of opportunity for nature and human's symbiotic coexistence. This vision adopts a holistic approach to sustainability, environmental restoration, healthy food  production  and economic resilience with social equity, cultural preservation and human wellbeing for generations  to  come.  This  is enriched  by  its  historical  and political significance and supported through strict regulations and institutional safeguards  to  prevent  overdevelopment  and  environmental  degradation.  The  vision  focuses  on

environmental restoration, healthy food production and a shift towards a low-growth economic model, all of which enable the creation of thriving communities in harmony with nature. At the core of the vision is the Natural Environment Restoration Project, which focuses on increasing carbon sinks through forest greening and land restoration. This not only mitigates climate change but also restores ecosystems and conserves biodiversity. These restoration efforts, coupled with ecotourism, revitalize local communities and strengthen the relationship between humans and nature. The vision emphasizes the importance of healthy soils in underpinning human wellbeing, highlighting the importance of eco-friendly agriculture and smart farming. Preserving soil health and producing safe food contribute to human wellbeing while eliminating pollution and ensuring food security. The biodiversity of plant genetic resources is secured by cultivating  diverse  native  plants  adapted to the ecosystem in a semi-wild state on farms in the DMZ. Consumer  choices  change  towards  sustainable  consumption,  including  the  expansion  of  veganism, reduced food waste and a circular economy, further supporting healthier and more sustainable food systems.  In  parallel,  there  is  a  paradigm  shift  towards  a  low-growth  economic  model  that  prioritises quality  of  life  over  endless  consumption  and  development.  By  emphasizing  leisure  time,  efficient communication, and a society where processes are valued over results, a foundation is established for a more balanced and sustainable approach to economic growth. The governance and institutional reforms and  democratic  processes  are  put  in  place  to  address  human-nature  conflicts  and  promote  inclusive decision-making. Community values and individual rights and freedoms are appreciated and respected. Advanced information technology connects people and nature, fostering symbiotic rather than exploitive relationships. Through ICT-assisted smart farms, eco-friendly agriculture and ecotourism, rural communities thrive while preserving natural heritage and fostering a deeper connection with nature. This vision of smart, eco-friendly and sustainable communities builds on the ideal of 'healthy rurality' as a local identity.

'사회를 위한 자연' 비전에서 DMZ는 자연과 인간이 공존할 수 있는 새로운 기회의 공간이다. 이 비전은 지속가능성, 환경 복원, 건 강한 식 량 생 산 , 경제적 회복력, 사회적 형 평 성, 문화 보존, 다 음 세대를 위한 인간 복지에 대한 총체 적인 접근 방식을 채택 한다. 난 개발과 훼손 을 막 는 철저 한 규 제와 제도적 안전장치 아 래 보존되며 역사적, 정치적 중요성도 풍 부하 게 갖 추고 있다. 이 비전은 환경 복원, 건 강한 식 량 생 산 , 저 성장 경제 모 델 로의 전환에 중점을 두 고 자연과 조화를 이루며 번 영하는 지역사회를 형성한다. 자연 환경복원 프 젝 로 트는 산림 녹 화 및 토지 복원을 통해 탄소 흡 수원을 늘 리는 것 을 목표 로 한다. 이를 통해 기 후변 화를 완화할 뿐아 니라 생태계를 복원하고 생물 다양성을 보존한다. 생태관광과 결 합된 복원 노력은 지역 사회에 활력을 불 넣 어 고 인간과 자연 사이의 관계를 강화한다. 비 옥 한 토양과 웰빙 을 강조하며 친환경 농 업과 스마트 농 업의 중요성을 강조하는데 토양을 건 강하  보존하고 안전한 식 게 품 을 생 산 하는 것 은 오염 을 제 거 하고 식 량 안보를 보장하는 동시에 인류의 복지에도 기여한다. DMZ의 농 가에서 해 당 생태계에 적 한 다양한 재래 응 종 식물을 반야생상태로 육성하여 식물유전자원의 생물다양성을 확보한다. 소 비자 선택 이 채 식의 확대, 음 식물 쓰 레기 감소 순 , 환 경제 등 지속 가능한 소 비로 변 함 화 에 따 라 더욱 건 강하고 지속 가능한 식 품 시스템이 형성되고 지지된다. 동시에, 패 러다 은 무한한 임 소 비와 개발보다 삶 의 질 을 우 시하는 선 저 성장 경제 모 델 로 전환된다. 여가 시간, 효율 적인 소 통, 결 과보다 과정을 중시하는 사회를 강조 으로  보다 함 써 균 형 있고 지속 가능한 경제 성장의 토대가 마련된다. 거 넌 버 스 및 제도 개혁과 민주적 절 차를 통해 인간과 자연의 갈 등을 해 결 하고 포용적 의사 결 정을 도모한다. 공동 체 의 가치, 개인의 권리와 자유가 인정되고 존중된다. 첨 단 정보 및 기술은 인간과 자연을 연 결 하여 착취 가 아닌 공생의 관계를 돕는다.  C I T 를 활용한 스마트 팜 , 친환경 농 업, 생태관광을 통해 농촌 지역사회는 자연 유 산 을 보존하고

자연과 더 깊은  관계를  형성하며 번 영을 누 린다.  현 명 하고  친환경적이며  지속  가능한  지역사회에 대한비전은 지역정 체 성으로서 ' 건 강한 농촌 ' 이라는 이상을 현 실 화 한다.

In the Nature for Nature vision, the DMZ has transformed into a beacon of hope, a space for ecological-peace. The entire DMZ is recognized as the world's first ecological legal entity, prioritizing the rights of all living species in the DMZ. This metamorphosis was achieved through three environmental goals: recovery of large mammals, 30% expansion of protected  areas  globally,  and  zero  pollution villages. Multinational consensus around conservation  is  achieved  through  effective articulation and communication of the shared goals and benefits of large mammal conservation facilitated by the 'Northeast Asia International Cooperation for Tiger Conservation' multilateral organisation of. Asian black bears have been successfully restored in both Koreas and now  travel unrestricted through  the  DMZ's  ecological corridor.  In  the  early  stages  of  identifying priority sites for conservation in the northeast Asian region, the DMZ was selected as a core conservation zone, prompting the establishment and expansion of protected areas that now form a regional network of interconnected ecological  corridors.  The  expansion  of  global  protected  areas  was  complemented  by  comprehensive policies  that  protect  and  restore  endangered  species  with  nature  granted  legal  rights  equivalent  to humans. This comprehensive conservation effort transformed the DMZ and surrounding areas, which became the cornerstone of an environment-friendly socio-economic system for local communities. These positive  changes  from  the  restoration  of  the  DMZ's  environment,  with  cleaner  air,  water,  and  soil, contribute to the eradication of diseases and health problems. There is a resurgence of practices such as eco-friendly  agriculture  and  foraging  and  people  now  contribute  to,  rather  than  exploit,  nature.  The communities in the DMZ thrive on revitalized economies. Economic opportunities, such as ecotourism, attract  eco-friendly  investment  groups  and  boost  sustainable  trade  activities  related  to  biodiversity, climate  change,  and  pollution.  Robust  research  and  development  of  new  technologies  support  the creation of pollution-free villages and low-carbon infrastructure. Settlements for local residents consider population density, energy efficiency, and climate resilience. Infrastructure uses natural materials that blend well with the surrounding landscape. The expansion of protected areas safeguards the health and

integrity  of  the  entire  DMZ's  social-ecological  system.  With  no  pollution,  restored  habitats  and  vast protected areas, benefits to nature and people are manifold. Once endangered species, such as tigers, have  rebuilt  resilient  ecosystems.  Healthier  villagers  mean  healthcare  costs  are  significantly  reduced, while nature-based economies have emerged that contribute to the revitalization of local communities and  a  flourishing  local  eco-culture.  These  gains  have  made  the  DMZ  the  centre  for  domestic  and international  exchanges  on  ecology  and  peace.  The  DMZ  has  emerged  as  a  testament  to  the transformative power of nature-centred human stewardship, where the intricate dance between people and nature now creates a harmonious symphony at the heart of the Korean peninsula.

' 자연을 위한 자연  비전의 비무장지대는 ' 희망 의 등대이자 생태 평 화의 공간으로 변 모한다. DMZ 전 체 가 세계 최 초의 생태 법 격 인 으로 인정 받 으며 DMZ에 사는 모 든 생물들에 게 권리가 주어진다. 이러한 변 화는 대형 포유류의 회복, 전 세계 보호구역 30% 확대, 무공해 마을이라는 세 가지 환경 목표 를 기반으로 이루어진다. '동 북아 아 시  호 랑 이  보전을  위한 국 제 협 력'은  대형  포유류  보전의  공동 목표 와 혜택 을 효 과적으로 표 현하고 소 함 통 으로  보전에 대한 다 써 국 적 공 감 대 형성을 촉진한다. 남북 한에서 복원된 반 가 달 슴곰 이  비무장지대  생태통로를  통해  이동한다.  보전을  위해  우 선순 위  지역을 선 정하는  초기 단계에서 비무장지대를 핵 심 보전 지역으로 선 정하여 보호구역의 설립과 확장을 촉진하고 상호 연 결 된 생태 통로의 지역 네 워크 트 를 구 축 한다. 전 세계 보호지역의 확대는 자연에 게 인간과 동등한 법 적 권리를 부여하여 멸종 위기에 처 한 종 을 보호하고 복원하는 포 괄 적인 정 책 으로 보완된다. 이러한 포 괄 적인 보전 노력은 비무장지대와 주 변 지역을 변 화시 고, 이는 지역 사회를 위한 환경 친화적 사회경제 시스템의 키 초 이 된다. 석 깨끗 한 공기, 물, 토양 등 DMZ 환경 복원을 통한 긍 정적인 변 화는 질병 과 건 강 문제를 감소 키 시 고 병 원비를 절감 하는데 기여한다. 친환경 농 업과 채 집과 같은 관 행 이 다시 부활하고 사람들은 자연을 착취 하기 보다는 보호한다. 비무장지대의 지역사회는 활성화된 경제와 함께번 창한다. 생태관광과 같은 경제적 기회는 친환경 투 자 그 룹 의 유치를 이 끌 고 생물다양성 및 탄소 와 관련된 지속 가능한 무역 활동을 촉진한다. 신기술에 대한 활발한 연구와 개발은 무공해 마을과 저탄소 인 프 라 구 축 을 지원한다. 지역 주민 정 착 은 인구 밀 도, 에너지 효율 성, 기 후 회복력을 고려하여 이루어진다. 인 프 라는 주 변 경관과 잘 어우러지는 자연 소 재를 사용한다. 보호구역의 확장은 DMZ의 사회 생태 시스템 전 -체 의 탄 력성과 회복력을 유지한다.보호 지역이 넓어지고 서식지가 복원되면서 오염 이 줄 고 이로 인해 자연과 사람에 게 돌아 가는 혜택 은 다양해진다. 호 랑 이와 같이 한때 멸종 위기 종 었던 이 주요 동물 종 들로 생태계가 복원된다. 자연을 기반으로 한 경제가 활성화되면서 지역 커 뮤 니티에 생태문화가 번 성한다. 이러한 성과를 바탕으로 한 의 비무장지대는 생태와 국 평 화에 대한 국 제적 교류의 중심지가 된다. 비무장지대는 자연 중심의 인간 관리로 변 혁의 동인으로 부상한다. 이제 한반도의 중심에서, 사람과 자연 사이의 복 잡 한 춤 사위는 조화로운 교 향곡 을 만들어내는 중이다.

In  this  Nature  for  Nature  and Nature as Culture infused future, Korea had undergone a remarkable transformation into a harmonious and ecologically conscious society. The  once-divided DMZ  now stands as a symbol of environmental rejuvenation, where endangered species like the Fairy psitta and elephants roam freely in the DMZ. The air is filled with  the  sounds  of birds and animals, and the lush forests intertwine with the urban  landscape,  creating a serene and balanced environment. The government has embraced a holistic approach to conservation, expanding protected  areas  along  the  border  and  actively  restoring  ecosystems.  Ecovillages  cover  the landscape  across  the  country,  where  people  live  in  harmony  with  nature,  embracing  the  benefits  of biodiversity and sustainable practices. Carbon-zero villages powered by renewable energy is the norm, and payments for ecosystem services ensure the well-being of the environment and local communities. This  preference  for  decentralized  living  spreads  within  cities  and  creates  smaller,  nature-friendly communities. Architectural innovations, such as wildlife migration corridors, prevent the collision of urban life with the natural world. The laughter of people echoes through calm and green cityscapes, where the movement of heat and energy is optimized, making the cities sustainable and pleasant places to live. Lifelong environmental education throughout the country and field trips to the DMZ promote a deep connection with nature, reducing stress, anxiety, depression and violence in society. Education fosters citizens' ecological senses and contributes to a populace that values time, happiness and a low-growth economy. The demand for green jobs and the expansion of renewable energy industries reduces youth unemployment and increase volunteerism  in  older  generations  that  live  longer  and  healthier.  In  this transformed  society,  economic  sustainability  is  intertwined  with  ecological  preservation.  A  circular economy has been established that utilizes technology to prevent ecosystem destruction and promote efficient energy consumption. The carbon neutrality card symbolizes responsible citizenship, encouraging public services to reduce carbon emissions and moderate competition in the private sector. Decisionmaking power has shifted beyond government and institutions to the grassroots level. Citizens actively engage in conservation efforts, demanding more from their government and supporting businesses that align  with  their  ecological  values.  The  transformation  takes  place  to  create  a  caring  society  with diminished inequality as mutual understanding and selflessness replace fierce competition in society. Korea has become a society where citizens' voices are heard, and politicians and businesses adapt to the changing preferences and demands. People live more like nature, embracing symbiotic relationships and

activating grassroots democracy. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and robots are used as tools for enhancing quality  of  life,  reducing  labour  deficit  and  minimizing  social  conflict.  In  this  future  Korea,  the  journey towards a sustainable and harmonious coexistence with nature is a reality built on ecological awareness, compassion, and a shared commitment to the well-being of the planet and its inhabitants.

자연을 위한, 그리고 문화로서의 자연 비전에서 미래의 한 국 은 괄목 할 만한 변 화를 겪 으며 조화와 생태를 생각하는  사회로 변 모한다.  한때  분단되 었던 비무장지대는  이제 멸종 위기 인 종 팔색 조와  코 끼 리가 자유 롭게 돌아 다니는 환경 회복의 상징으로 자리 잡았 다. 울 창한 숲 이 도시 경관이 어우러 져 새와 동물의 소 리와  고요 함 이 균 형 잡힌 환경을  조성한다.  정부는 국 경을 따 라  보호구역을  확대하고  생태계를 적극적으로 복원하는 등 보존에 대한 총체 적인 접근 방식을 채택 한다. 생태마을은 사람들이 자연과 조화를 이루며 살 아 가는 전 국 적인 풍 경으로, 사람들은 생물 다양성과 지속 가능한 삶 의 혜택 을 누 린다.  재생 에너지로 구동되는 탄소 제로 마을이 일반적이며, 생태계 서비스에 대한 지 불 을 통해 환경과 지역사회의 안 을 보장한다. 이러한 도시 내 분 녕 산 형 생활이 확 산 되어 자연 친화적인 소규 모 커 뮤 니티가 형성된다. 야생동물이 도시생태통로와 같은 혁신적 건축 을 통해 인간과의 공존이 가능해진다. 열과 에너지의 이동이 최 적화된 조용하고 푸른 도시에 사람들의 웃음 소 리가 울 려 퍼 진다. 도시는 지속 가능하고 쾌 적한 삶 의 터전이  된다.  전 국 에서 실행 되는 평 생환경교육과  비무장지대  현장학습은  자연과의  깊은  유대 감 을 증진하여 사회에서의 스트레스, 불 안, 우 울 증 및 폭 력을 감소 킨 시 다. 교육은 시민들의 생태적 감 각을 키워 시간, 행 복, 저 성장 경제에 가치를 두 는 시민상이 형성된다. 친환경 일자리에 대한 수요와 재생 에너지 산 업의 확장은 청년 실 업 을 률 낮 추고, 더 건 강하고 오 래 사는 노인 세대의 자원 봉 사 증가로 연 결 된다. 이 렇게 변 화된 사회에서 경제의 지속 가능성은 생태 보존과 밀접 게 하  연관되어 있다. 기술을 활용하여 생태계의 파괴 를 방지하고 효율 적인 에너지 소 비를 촉진하는 순 환 경제가 안정적으로 자리 잡 는다. 탄소 중립 카 드는 책임 있는 시민의식을 상징하는데, 이는 공공 서비스가 탄소 배 출을 줄 이고 민간 부문의 경 을 완화하도 쟁 록 장려한다. 사회 권력은 정부와 기관을 넘 어 풀뿌 리 수 준까 지 이동한다. 시민들은 정부에 더많 은 것 을 요구하고 생태적 가치에 부합하는 기업을 지지하면서 환경보호 노력에 적극적으로 참 여한다. 이러한 변 화는 상호 이해와 이타심이 사회의 치열한 경 쟁 을 대 체 하면서 불평 등이 줄 든 배 어 려의 사회를 만드는 데 기여한다. 한 국 은 시민의 목소 리가 들리고 시민의 선 호와 요구에 부 응 하는 변 혁적 정치와 기업의 사회가 된다. 사람들은 공생관계를 포용하고 활성화된 풀뿌 리 민주주의 사회에서, 자연과 더 닮 은 삶 을 살 간다. 인공지능과 로 아 봇 은 인간의 삶 의 질 을 높이고 노동력 부 족 을 줄 이며 사회적 갈 등을 최소 화하는 도구로 이용된다. 이러한 미래 대한민 국 에서, 자연과 지속 가능하고 조화로운 공존을 향 한 여정은 생태적 인식과 연민, 지구와 그 안에 사는 다양한 생 명 들의 안 녕 을 위한 공동의 헌 신을 바탕으로 실 현된다.


## 4. Discussion



## 4.1 Comparison of four Korean Nature Future visions


These four visions imagine the Korean peninsula in which existing local initiatives mainstream and scale up to contribute to an ecological, sustainable, peaceful and thriving DMZ. The visions share a number of features related to these overall goals, yet they are also designed to explore different nature values. Despite these predefined commonalities and differences, distinctive features emerged that are unique to Korean society (Table 1).

The theme that is recurring the most among the four visions is a strong call for rewilding, with the DMZ as  a  focal  zone  for  restoring  natural  ecosystems  and  anchoring  mitigation  and  adaptation  to  climate change in the Korean peninsula. Similarly, all four visions also recognize biodiversity as an important value of  the  DMZ.  They  describe  the  DMZ  as  a  space  where  humans  and  many  non-human  species  live  in symbiosis, and where the ecological connections between species can be illustrated idealistically and realistically.  Striking  a  balance  between  ecological  preservation  and  socio-economic  needs  of  local communities remains a persistent challenge in biosphere reserves such as the DMZ. The zoning approach of the UNESCO's Man and Biosphere (MAB) program may align well with the nature's value perspectives of the Nature Futures Framework in this complex context (Park & Yeom, 2023). The strategic allocation of core, buffer and transition zones, together with community engagement strategies, can foster a more sustainable and equitable relationship between humans and nature within the DMZ (Moon, 2021).

Local communities are recognized for their essential role in stewarding and benefiting from the DMZ's ecological state and resources. There is unanimous agreement across the visions that the future of the DMZ should aim to enhance local livelihoods and well-being, underscoring the importance of community engagement in conservation efforts and decision-making processes despite continued urbanization and rural depopulation. Furthermore, each vision acknowledges the DMZ's unique capacity as a significant educational and restorative space (Kim et al., 2005), enhancing ecological literacy and social cohesion through history. All visions emphasize the long-shared history of conflict in the DMZ with potential as an involuntary park for fostering deeper connections between human and the natural world. Developing sustainable  ecotourism  and  educational  programs  with  hospitable  engagement  of  local  communities avoid the imposition of repeated conflicts and hardships (Lee & Maeng, 2012). Promoting traditional ecological  practices  over  chemical  pest  control  and  encouraging  lifestyle  shifts  among  residents  with profound spatial and historical connections to the area are seen as key to fostering a just transition.

Differences in  nature  values  among  the  visions  produced  differences  in  approaches  to  human-nature interactions, economic models, governance systems, autonomy of citizens, and the use of technology and education (Lee, 2015). The "Nature as Culture" and "Nature for Society" visions integrate human activities with ecological stewardship via different modes of communities, interactions with nature, and tourism. In contrast, the "Nature for Nature" vision spares space for nature to reduce human pressure and allows key ecological processes to take place at large spatial extents. The 'Nature for Nature-Nature as Culture' vision integrates nature all around the country with most people living in archology.

The motivation for economic transformation varies among the visions, with 'Nature for Nature', 'Nature for  Society',  and  'Nature  for  Nature-Nature  as  Culture'  envisioning  a  low-growth  model  focused  on quality of life and enhanced livelihood respectively (Kim, 2014). All four visions support a variety of smaller scale, community-oriented, and fair-profit-based businesses, that are to varying degrees connected to government,  cities  and  large  corporations  for  balanced  and  equitable  futures  (Aghion  et  al.,  2022). Governance and autonomy within the DMZ vary among the visions, from autonomous ministry for the governance of the DMZ ('Nature as Culture'), grassroot and local community driven system ('Nature for Nature-Nature as Culture'), to collaborative multi-stakeholder governance that involves both national

governments and international bodies ('Nature for Nature'). These variations present a variety of options that are possible in the future governance of the DMZ.

Technology and education are integrated into the visions with varying beliefs about the role of innovation and  traditional knowledge  in  achieving  ecological  and  societal goals. All visions embrace  new technological solutions for ecological monitoring and sustainable living, but how technology is used and who owns and controls it are varied. While local knowledge and experience-based ecological education contribute  to  learning  and  living  in  harmony  with  nature,  the  use  of  smart  technology  and  AI  is  also highlighted in enabling enhanced monitoring and management of nature and its benefits to people.

There are limitations that are shared in the visions. The most notable one is the lack of consideration of the  current  geopolitical  situation  in  the  DMZ  and  the  visions  offer  only  few  suggestions  on  how  to overcome this issue in the future. Taking this political context into account will be key if the DMZ is to become a space for reimagining the relationship between nature, people and culture in the context of peaceful co-existence of the Korean peninsula. While these geopolitical challenges post many constrains in  visioning  preferable  futures,  they  are  not  just  DMZ-specific  issue,  however,  but  a  shared  and interconnected challenge with disruptive economic and political changes and tensions of the world.
