## 6. Conclusion and discussion


The increasing popularity of Mobile Instant Messenger Services (MIMS) such as WhatsApp so far has gone hand in hand with our limited empirical knowledge about these online social networks, as most of our knowledge about online networks is based on Twitter (X) and Facebook. In this study, we propose to remedy this situation by applying the research strategy of data donation among a probability-based sample of the Dutch general population. Through data donation, research participants can provide researchers with existing digital traces that platforms and other entities collect about them. To our knowledge, our study is the first data donation study in a probability sample.

Given the lack of empirical knowledge about MIMS networks, we focused on a key feature of network topology, namely the distribution of the number of connections (i.e., degree ), both at the population level and in terms of determinants of individual-level variance. Moreover, we studied the distribution of group membership , as the prominence of group-based communication is a characteristic feature of WhatsApp. The results can be summarized as follows.

First, we find that the distribution of connections is heavy-tailed, as to be expected in a large network. However, in contrast to what is commonly claimed in the network science literature, we do not find evidence for a power-law distribution. Instead, we find that a log-normal distribution fits the data best. Interestingly, this finding is in line with earlier research claiming that large social networks, including online social networks, tend not to conform to the supposed empirical regularity of power law degree distributions in large complex networks (Corten, 2012; Jackson & Rogers, 2007). Our study thereby contributes to the ongoing debate on the universality of the celebrated power law degree distribution (e.g., Broido & Clauset, 2019; Voitalov et al., 2019). At the same time, however, we are not aware of an established theoretical foundation for the log-normal degree distribution, even though log-normal fits are commonly found in empirical data (Barabási, 2016; Broido & Clauset, 2019). Our findings thus once more underline the need for such theoretical foundations, that is, a plausible model of the emergence of large social networks that generates such distributions.

Second, we find that also the individual-to-groups degree distribution (that is, the number of group memberships per individual) has a heavy-tailed distribution. In this case, the empirical distribution appears to follow an exponential distribution. To our knowledge, our study is the first to demonstrate the heavy-tailed nature of the degree distribution of the individual-to-group network. We thereby contribute to the still relatively scarce empirical literature on the topology of two-mode networks (Mitrović & Tadić, 2012; Shang et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2008), and provide further evidence that can be used to theoretically model such networks (Guillaume & Latapy, 2006; Vasques Filho & O'Neale, 2018). More substantively, our findings reconfirm the dominance of groups in MIMSs: not only do users in our data on average participate in more than 50 groups, the heavy-tailed nature of the distribution also suggests that some users are extremely well-connected to groups, and may thus be able to very quickly transfer information between groups. As compared to the influence of such 'hubs' in one-mode networks (Albert & Barabási, 1999, 1999), one could argue that in two-mode networks, such influence is further amplified as with each connected group, users potentially reach many other users at the same time. However, such claims warrant further investigation as such 'amplification' may be dampened by overlap between the groups to which a user is connected, which we could not assess with

our data. Nevertheless, the large variance in degree, both for individual-to-individual and individual-to-group connections, highlights the usefulness of examining individual-level predictors of this variance.

Turning to the explanation of individual-level variance, we find that for the number of connections, our findings are to a large extent in line with the literature on extended social networks (Hofstra et al., 2021; Lubbers et al., 2019). That is, we find that younger users, women, those with higher incomes, and those with more education have more connections, consistent with the logics of choice and constraint articulated in this literature. These results also resonate with the general notion that online social networks are, to a large extent, reflections of interactions in face-to-face ('offline') networks (Dunbar, 2016; Dunbar et al., 2015; Hofstra et al., 2017). However, not all findings from the literature on extended networks can be reproduced: in particular, we find no significant associations with having a partner, children, or a migration background.

In our analysis of the antecedents of the number of group memberships, we tested whether the same individual traits that are expected to predict individual contacts, also predict group membership. Find that this is the case for some, but not all these traits: indeed, younger and higher educated respondents participate in more groups, but although the associations with the remaining predictors are consistently in the same direction as for individual contacts (and consistent with expectations), none of them are statistically significant. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that the explained variance in the model for group membership is higher than that in the model for individual connections, even though only age and education are statistically significant predictors of group membership.

Clearly, our study also has a number of limitations. First, even though we started with a large panel sample, our eventual sample is relatively small due to high drop-out rates at various points in the data collection procedure. This indicates that the data donation approach has its limitations, because even though our procedure is specifically designed to protect participants' privacy and the participants are to a large extent experienced panel respondents, not all respondents are willing to donate data. However, the methodology of data donation is still in its infancy, and as a consequence, some of the drop-out in the procedure is likely caused by technical issues or imperfections in the communicative aspects of the procedure. Indeed, we saw that the share of respondents willing to donate is considerably larger than the proportion that eventually donated. In the end, the response rate in our study is on par with the response in other data donation studies, which indicates that there is still considerable room for improvement in the methodology of data

donation. As a consequence of the relatively small sample, some of the non-significant findings in our analyses may be attributed to a lack of statistical power.

Second, we observed considerable selectivity in response, in that conditional on being a WhatsApp user, younger people and people with more education are more likely to donate. While we see little reason to expect that this would bias our regression results, our descriptive results are likely to be affected by this selectivity. That is, because we know from our regression results that younger and more educated people also tend to have more connections and group memberships, it is likely that the shapes of our observed degree distributions are somewhat biased towards those with higher degrees. However, this does not necessarily undermine our conclusion that these distributions are not power-law distributions, as the inclusion of more nodes with relatively low degrees (which would render the distributions more representative) would shift these distributions even further away from power law distributions. Nevertheless, addressing these biases in order to achieve a more accurate estimation of the degree distributions in the population should be a priority of future research.

Third, the meaning of the connections captured by our method is open to interpretation. The list of contacts in the DDP provided by WhatsApp contains all contacts that are included in the user's phone's contacts, and who are WhatsApp users themselves. Thus, on the one hand, we miss contacts who the user did not store in their contact list but with whom they nevertheless interacted. Note that this also implies that alters with whom the user interacted in groups are also not necessarily included. On the other hand, the DDP includes contacts who are present in the contact list but with whom the user never actually chatted (although they could have, since they are both WhatsApp users). While these biases thus work in opposite directions, we have no reliable way of assessing their relative strength. Similarly, the list of groups in the DDP simply contains all groups of which the user is a member at the time of the data request, regardless of whether the user (or any other member of the group) still actively participates in the group. This means that the list is likely to contain many 'dormant' groups that are no longer active but for which the user did not take the effort to actively delete or leave them. Clearly, the extent to which this is the case may differ between individuals.

The seriousness of this selectivity will crucially depend on the nature of more specific research questions on mobile instant messenger networks. Research that focuses on questions that relate directly to activity in such networks (for example, if we were to compare activity in face-to-face friendship networks to online networks) will probably require a better assessment of which connections are actively used and which are dormant. However, for research more interested in the potential offered by connections

(for example, the potential of mobile instant messenger networks to spread misinformation), these biases may be less consequential, as even connections that were infrequently used in the past may still be used to spread information in the future.

Nevertheless, future research should invest in better assessing the nature of connections, groups, and group memberships. While the data available through DDPs by themselves offer little information for that purpose, the method of data donation, conceptually, provides the possibility to gather additional information as respondents can be prompted to answer additional questions based on the data that are being donated. In this sense, data donation methods have an advantage over digital traces data collected via 'unobtrusive' methods such as scraping or API access, as these provide little opportunity to interact with research subjects with the purpose of collecting additional data.

Another avenue for further research involves the study of the content of actual chat messages via data donation. While the collection of chat messages is conceptually possible, it is faced with considerable practical and ethical challenges. First, due to the nature of the platform, the WhatsApp DDP does not contain chat messages (as these data are not stored by the data provider in the first place). The smartphone app allows for exporting individual chat conversations, but only one at a time, which implies that collecting large numbers of chat conversations is prohibitively time-consuming (for respondents) in this manner. Second, due to privacy concerns, collecting raw chat data is problematic, as they contain not only data about the respondent but also about conversation partners. Consequently, chat conversations will have to be processed and anonymized on the respondent's device before donation, which, depending on the measures of interest, may require considerable computation power. Nevertheless, we believe that our study demonstrates that data donation provides a valuable and feasible method for the empirical study of online platforms that were thus far almost inaccessible to researchers.

## Introduction


The advances during the last few decades of research have revealed that Neanderthals colonized a vast territory that stretched from Spain to Siberia (Krause et al., 2007; Mafessoni et al., 2020; Vernot et al., 2021). The earliest Neanderthals likely arrived in Asia shortly before marine isotope stage (MIS) 6 (190-130 ka) (Slon et al., 2017; Jacobs et al., 2019). Following MIS 6, we see a new, and genetically distinct, connection between European and Siberian Neanderthals dated between 110-70 ka during MIS 5; first documented in the genetic similarities between the Mezmaiskaya and Chagyrskaya fossils (Mafessoni et al., 2020), this genetic evidence of a second movement of Neanderthals east now is confirmed by ancient DNA from sediments at several caves in Europe and Siberia (Vernot et al., 2021). Archaeologically, this genetic connection is accompanied by a number of sites in the Russian Plain, the Caucasus, and Siberia that share morphological characteristics in their stone tool assemblages belonging to the Middle Palaeolithic (Kolobova et al., 2020).

Ancient human populations in Eurasia have consistently been structured by geographic changes. During the penultimate (MIS 12) and antepenultimate (MIS 6) glacial periods, continental ice sheets reached down to the Dnieper basin, almost completely separating Europe from Asia (Batchelor et al., 2019). The earlier of the two may have contributed to the separation of Neanderthals (in the west) and their closely related Denisovan cousins, in eastern Asia (Goñi, 2020). The MIS 6 glacial expansion likely separated Siberian Neanderthals from European Neanderthals until glaciers retreated, reopening the connection between the Russian and West Siberian plains. It is unclear if the two populations came into contact during the succeeding warm interglacial (MIS 5e) or not, because there are too few sites (for example, as demonstrated by the ROCEEH Out of Africa Database, Kandel et al., 2023). The next connection between the European and Siberian Neanderthals is documented solely through genetic evidence that suggests a dispersal of Neanderthals east at the end of MIS 5e and during the next cooling phase (MIS 5d-a, 110-70 ka) (Vernot et al., 2021; Skov et al., 2022). The colder phase that follows, MIS 4, is believed to have transformed the open Eurasian landscapes into a cold desert, with populations retreating into mountain refugia, where they persisted until the next warm phase, MIS 3. Broadly, the archaeological record of MIS 3 is characterized by an increased diversification and regionalization of stone tool assemblages (Ruebens, 2013), as well as by sparse, fragmented populations (Bocquet-Appel and Degioanni, 2013) occupying smaller and smaller territories (Henry et al., 2017).

Despite the genetic evidence for multiple long-distance dispersals by Neanderthals across Eurasia, we still have limited knowledge about the possible routes they would have taken to get to Siberia and the behavioral adaptations required for that journey. Archaeologists often use least-cost paths (LCP) to model past movements (Howey, 2011; Herzog, 2020). However, traditional LCP analyses make the assumption that the entire landscape is perfectly known in advance and that travelers will always choose the easiest and shortest route between two points (Howey, 2011). This is not realistic for modeling movement in unknown environments. Here, we use an agent-based least cost path (AB-LCP) approach to more realistically model mobility decisions when a traveler can only use information about their local surroundings (Gravel-Miguel and Wren, 2018) and, importantly, when they do not have a specific destination they must reach. This methodology is similar to step selection models used to model animal movement and to investigate the peopling of Australia (Salles et al., 2024), but has yet to be applied to Neanderthals. Our model improves on traditional LCP analyses and simplifies the step selection methodology to reconstruct ancient migrations with as few assumptions as possible.

Here, we created paleogeographically realistic agent-based least cost path model to simulate dispersal of Neanderthal populations between MIS 6 and MIS 3. Using cost surfaces derived from elevation, climate, hydrological, and glacier data, we explore possible paths that Neanderthals may have taken across Eurasia when dispersing out of the Caucasus Mountains.


## Materials and methods



### Agent-based least cost path model


We simulate agent-based cost-minimizing Lévy walks of mobile agents (ODD protocol of model available in SI). The model is based on Gravel-Miguel and Wren’s agent-based least-cost path model (Gravel-Miguel and Wren, 2018). This model was coded in NetLogo 6.3.0 (Wilensky, 1999) and is available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/H5BJK.

Agents traverse a landscape defined by a 1km-resolution raster of cost values (described below). To start, agents are placed on a random raster square in the Caucasus Mountains. At each tick of the model, the agent evaluates its local landscape by assessing all eight adjacent squares in a 360-degree radius and faces the square with the lowest cost value. From there, the agent makes a number of steps determined by a Lévy walk probability equation (Tsallis, 1997; Raichlen et al., 2014; Davies et al., 2018). At each step of the Lévy walk, the agent evaluates the squares within a 100-degree radius and again moves to the adjacent square with the lowest cost value; during the Lévy walk, the agent does not consider the squares behind itself to keep the agent moving in roughly the same direction for the entirety of the Lévy walk.

To simulate colonization behaviors, we allowed agents to move farther if they found themselves in “new territory,” meaning they had not previously occupied most of the surrounding grid squares (Kelly, 2003). This is accomplished by allowing agents to assess if they have previously occupied any raster squares within a 5km radius, which approximates the average distance across which humans can see.

We run the model on cost rasters corresponding to MIS 6 through 3 (available at http://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/AH2MK), a time span which bookends the estimated date of divergence of the Neanderthal populations represented by individuals at Mezmaiskaya (Caucasus) and Chagyrskaya (Altai) and the occupation dates of Chagyrskaya (Kolobova et al., 2020; Mafessoni et al., 2020; Vernot et al., 2021). We varied the starting location of the agents, including areas north and south of the Caucasus Mountains (SI Fig 2). These areas are derived from the locations of Middle Paleolithic sites in the region (see SI Table 5). Each iteration of the model is run for a total of 400,000 Lévy walks, which results in approximately 830,000 individual steps (SD = 392,309.7) on average across all modeled scenarios. We intentionally kept model runs short because we were interested in exploring the possibility of distinct long-distance dispersal routes (Kolobova et al., 2020), instead of simply calculating when general eastward population advance would eventually reach the Altai.

For each combination of isotope stage (MIS) and starting location in the Caucasus, we ran the model five times (see SI Table 4) to test for the potential of rapid long distance dispersals under our simple model assumptions. We identified multiple successful routes (see below) from this set of 110 total model runs.


### Building cost surfaces


The 1 km resolution cost rasters for this study were built using data from digital elevation models (Tozer et al., 2019), paleoclimate data on annual precipitation (Leonardi et al., 2022), Pleistocene glacier extents (Batchelor et al., 2019), extents of modern rivers, lakes, and oceans (Lehner and Grill, 2013; Messager et al., 2016; Flanders Marine Institute, 2018), and paleogeographic data on Pleistocene glacier lake outbursts. Importantly, we do not include any information on the location of Middle Paleolithic sites when constructing our cost rasters, so agents do not consider them when moving.

We used slope-dependent cost functions to estimate energy expenditure by a walking individual via Llobera and Sluckin’s walker cost function (Llobera and Sluckin, 2007; Herzog, 2020). The slope-based costs were used as a base map to which other costs were added. We increased the base cost of desert areas that received less than 250 mm of annual precipitation (Li et al., 2019) to allow short movements across these regions (Field and Lahr, 2005; Field et al., 2007). We increase the cost for the cells by the amount equivalent to an increase from a slope of 0 degrees to a slope of 15 degrees (Fábrega-Álvarez et al., 2011; Güimil-Fariña and Parcero-Oubiña, 2015; Canosa-Betés, 2016), which is equivalent to a 74% increase in cost.  We used glacier extent data from Batchelor et al. (2019) to create glacial barriers. Similarly, we used modern lake and ocean data to define some of our water barriers. For rivers, we used average long-term water discard estimates to approximate river width (Moody and Troutman, 2002; Frasson et al., 2019). Rivers with a width greater than a kilometer are considered barriers. Rivers with width less than a kilometer were crossable, but given a 74%-increased cost (Fábrega-Álvarez et al., 2011; Güimil-Fariña and Parcero-Oubiña, 2015; Canosa-Betés, 2016).

In addition to modern lakes and rivers, we simulated paleohydrology using the Lake Flood function in QGIS (Conrad et al., 2015). We reviewed the literature for estimated Middle Pleistocene lake and sea levels (SI Table 7) and used these values to flood the DEM based on estimated conditions for each marine isotope stage and substage (SI Table 8). A full description of cost raster development can be found in the SI. All derived rasters used for creating the cost rasters and the cost rasters themselves can be found at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/H5BJK.


### Analysis of routes


Model outputs a series of XY coordinates documenting each step agents take in the model. We produced maps of paths taken for each climate scenario for both starting points (SI Fig 3-10) by calculating the relative frequency with which agents occupied a given set of XY coordinates across all runs of each modeled scenario. We also identified successful individual runs by creating a 500 km buffer around the archaeological sites in the Altai and determining which paths had steps that fell within that buffer. We calculated the Euclidean distance between the last set of coordinates for each model run and the 500 km buffer zone. To look at linear movements, we calculated movement path angles and identified portions of the path where angle does not change for at least 5 steps in a row. For estimating arrival times, we counted the number of steps, represented as XY coordinates, taken to reach the Altai during each of the successful model runs. We divided this number by the average annual distance traveled for hunter-gatherer populations occupying similar climates (SI Table 9) (Binford, 2001; Marwick et al., 2016). For analyzing areas of redundant movement, we considered all model runs that moved beyond the Caucasus region, namely those during MIS 3, MIS 4, MIS 5a, MIS 5c, and MIS 5e. We calculated the frequency of agent occupation for each set of XY coordinates to identify those within 1 standard deviation of the mean occupation frequency.


## Results



### Route and timing of successful dispersals


We defined success as reaching a point within 500 km of the Altai site cluster. This is based on ethnographically-derived data demonstrating that mobile populations can move about 500 km within one year. Only three out of 110 runs were successful, all tracing an arc through the Urals and southern Siberia before reaching the Altai (see Fig. 1). Two of the successful runs take place in MIS 5e and one during MIS 3. Additionally, two other unsuccessful runs reach within 1000 km of the Altai during MIS 5e and MIS 5c.

### Effect of starting point


Because sites on both sides of the Caucasus are thought to have been part of a larger glacial refugium, we tested dispersal patterns that started both north and south of the mountain range. In our model, no successful runs used a southern route through the Caspian corridor (Ghasidian et al., 2023), and several of the routes starting south of the Caucasus turned north. One of the successful runs during MIS 5e started from the southern side of the Caucasus Mountains, but only reached the Altai site cluster after turning north and following the arc described above.


### Effect of paleogeography


Many of the previous calculations of least cost paths have ignored the major changes in landscape that followed the climatic changes associated with the end of the Last Interglacial. In particular, the re-routing of the hydrological network from the Kara Sea to the Aral Sea, currently estimated during MIS 5a (Panin et al., 2020) could have affected landscape connectivity. We therefore tested the effect of lake damming and water level rise in the hydrological network to reconstruct possible paleorivers and paleolakes in a systematic way. Given that following river valleys appears to be a characteristic of successful runs, paleolake flooding would be expected to create additional pathways for movement along new river conduits (Kelly, 2003). Contrary to expectation, our study shows that these simulated water bodies acted as barriers rather than conduits for dispersal eastward. For example, Caspian Sea transgressions prevent movement out of the Caucasus Mountains during cooler periods. This may be a limitation of our method for reconstructing the paleohydrological network. Future work should be done to refine these reconstructions for fully understanding their impact on dispersal.


### Estimated arrival times


We estimate how long it takes the agents to reach the Altai by counting the number of movements they make. In each of the successful dispersals, it takes between 925,000 to 1 million steps before arriving by the Altai site cluster (Table 1). This translates to approximately 1 million kilometers of movement. Using ethnographic data (Binford, 2001) about how far hunter-gatherer populations move within a year (SI Table 9), we estimate that Neanderthals could have arrived in the Altai within 2000 years of initial movement out of the Caucasus Mountains. Estimates of Neanderthal energetics suggest that Neanderthals would have moved less per year compared to modern humans (Macdonald et al., 2009), so it is possible that Neanderthal dispersals would have taken slightly longer than 2000 years. However, the model still suggests dispersal could have occurred relatively quickly. Such a dispersal may have left relatively few vestiges along the route, as Neanderthals would have spent relatively little time in any one location.

### Areas of redundant movement


Across the model runs that make it out of the Caucasus Mountain region, agents frequently traverse river valleys in the Eastern European Plain like those of the Volga and Kama (see SI Fig 1). Agents also frequently move in the Irtysh River valley near the northern Kazakhstan border; this is the area that typically funnels agents into the Altai region. There is frequent movement in the Turgai depression from the northern Kazakhstan border into the Turgan Lowlands, corresponding with the location of Middle Paleolithic surface deposits in Kazakhstan (Artyukhova, 1980, 2013; Osipova et al., 2020). Agents also frequently move around the Caspian Sea basin during regression periods, so these sites would be underwater today.


## Discussion and conclusions


Our results suggest that Neanderthals could have quickly dispersed from the Caucasus Mountains to the Altai Mountains via a northern route during MIS 3 and MIS 5e. Consistent eastward movement out of Western Eurasia occurs across most modeled scenarios even though agents have no goal destination and can freely pick a direction of movement. This suggests that Neanderthal dispersal to the Altai is an inevitable outcome of local movement decisions defined by geography.

The results of our analysis correspond with archaeological evidence from Chagryskaya and Okladnikov Caves that demonstrates that the Altai was occupied by Neanderthals by at least 59,000 years ago, firmly within MIS 3 (Kolobova et al., 2020; Skov et al., 2022). Genetic evidence also suggests a rapid expansion of Neanderthals from Europe around 100 - 115 ka (Vernot et al., 2021; Skov et al., 2022), which is at the end of the Last Interglacial or MIS 5e. The close correspondence of our modeled routes with the archaeological and genetic record highlights the unique strength of using agent-based least-cost path modeling to explore Neanderthal long-distance movements.

Most modeled routes that disperse out of Western Eurasia do so by moving north through the Ural Mountains. Current archaeological evidence limits occupation there to the later stages of MIS 3 (Pavlov et al., 2004; Shirokov et al., 2005; Svendsen et al., 2010; Kotov et al., 2020), yet our model suggests Neanderthals would have been able to move into this region during the warm MIS 5 substages and even during MIS 4. Future fieldwork there may reveal older occupations.

While previous research suggested that dispersal might have been facilitated by changes in hydrology during the colder periods, our study shows that dispersal likely occurred during the warmer periods, even when accounting for these geographic changes. Dispersal during warmer periods matches expectations based on reconstructions of Neanderthal niche space that show an increase in habitat suitability in the northern parts of Eastern Europe and Central Asia during warmer marine isotope stages (Yaworsky et al., 2024).

Neanderthals taking a northern route into Central Asia may have been expanding into Denisovan territories. Recent studies reconstructing the distribution of Denisovans suggest this species could have occupied much of the Eurasian Steppe, particularly between the Urals and the Altai, during MIS 5e and MIS 3 (Ruan et al., 2023). The timing and locations of our modeled routes would therefore allow for inter-species encounters, which is consistent with the genetic evidence for multiple interbreeding events between Neanderthals and Denisovans (Slon et al., 2018). The potential for overlapping ranges also suggests that some of the Middle Paleolithic sites we know from southern Siberia may be Denisovan sites or even sites occupied by mixed groups, as suggested by the first-generation Denisova 11 hybrid individual (Slon et al., 2018), dated to approximately 90 ka. The archaeology of this region will likely provide important insights into the genetic and cultural consequences of these inter-species interactions.

Another area of interest is the Turgai Valley of Kazakhstan to the north of the Aral Sea. This region is visited four times during simulations under MIS 5e, MIS 5c, and MIS 4 conditions. Here, a large number of Mousterian occupations are documented in surface assemblages (Artyukhova, 1980, 2013; Osipova et al., 2020) despite a lack of stratified sites (Iovita et al., 2020). Future research in this region could provide important data on Neanderthal dispersals.

Despite good agreement between our model and archaeological data, a final test of the model requires more sites with a clear Neanderthal association. Some of our modeled routes bring agents close to Obi Rakhmat, Teshik-Tash, and Anghilak  – the sole sites in Central Asia with Neanderthal remains (Glantz et al., 2003, 2008; Krause et al., 2007). Agents always enter the southern parts of Central Asia from the north, contradicting previous modeling that suggests Neanderthals reached Obi Rakhmat and Teshik-Tash by dispersing along the Southern Caspian Corridor (Ghasidian et al., 2023). Our model offers no southern route. It is possible that research will prove the existence of a southern dispersal route for Neanderthals. Archaeological research continues to identify sites with Middle Paleolithic assemblages in Iran (e.g. Ghasidian et al., 2017; Vahdati Nasab et al., 2019, 2024; Heydari et al., 2021; Heydari-Guran et al., 2021; Shoaee et al., 2021, 2023; Bazgir et al., 2022; Sadraei et al., 2023; Hashemi et al., 2024), including some with hominin fossils (Trinkaus et al., 2008; Zanolli et al., 2019). As we learn more about the Middle Paleolithic of this region and adjacent areas, like Turkmenistan and Afghanistan, we may learn more about the Neanderthal range as it expanded during the Late Pleistocene, although southeastern range expansions may be unrelated to northeastern ones. Future iterations of our model could seed Neanderthal populations out of locations further south than the Caucasus, such as the Iranian Plateau or Iraq to test if a different origin point would result in southern routes across Eurasia.

It is important to note that this model is a simplification of a real-world process. For example, our model does not account for every external factor that may have affected how Neanderthals were able to move within this landscape. Factors such as access to resources (e.g. Vahdati et al., 2019), distance to water sources (e.g. Breeze et al., 2016; Hussain and Floss, 2016; Shoaee et al., 2023), annual or seasonal weather patterns and climate change (e.g. Beeton et al., 2014; Timmermann and Friedrich, 2016; Glantz et al., 2018), vegetation preferences (e.g. Zeller et al., 2023), and others (Rockman and Steele, 2003) may have played important roles in dictating daily movement decisions of dispersing Neanderthals. Future use of this model will incorporate these diverse factors for developing new cost rasters; this will allow us to identify new possible dispersal routes and test hypotheses about what factors structure movement.

The results of the agent-based least cost path model demonstrate that rapid dispersal of Neanderthals from Eastern Europe to the Altai via a northern route would have been possible during multiple time periods after the retreat of the MIS 6 glaciers. Moreover, traversing the Eurasian steppe was facilitated by river valleys that would have directed random daily foraging movements, leading to eastward expansion. These results demonstrate a remarkable east-west geographic connectivity of northern Eurasia via river corridors. This highlights the strength of this methodological approach to generate specific archaeologically-testable hypotheses for pathways humans would have taken within vast landscapes. Where ecological niche and species distribution modeling allow us to define large areas suitable for habitation, an AB-LCP approach  mimics ethnographic expectations of wayfinding in unknown landscapes (Kelly, 2003), leading to the discovery of possible movement paths that made successful long distance treks into new areas possible.

## Introduction


In the present educational landscape, research has become one of the pivotal indicators of academics, institutions, and  country  performance (Cerado &  Naanep,  2023;  Hue  et  al., 2022; Jameel & Ahmad, 2020). Research Engagements offer substantial academic benefits, such  as enriching knowledge, fostering personal and professional growth, and boosting career advancement (Alhassan  &  Ali,  2020;  Khairiah  et  al.,  2024  &  Novita  et  al.,  2023).  At  the institutional level, research is a pivotal determinant of national and international ranking (Ibrahim & Fadhli, 2021). Institutions with solid academic research engagement and cultures contribute to higher  research  outputs  that  enhance  their  rankings  in  global  university  assessments, attract substantial  funding,  and  strengthen  institutional missions  (Vidal  &  Ferreira,  2020).  Besides individual benefits, Research Engagement (RE) is paramount in elevating Research productivity (RP),  determining a  country's international standing, and  bolstering innovation capabilities in higher education (Barrot, 2017; Henry et al., 2020; Jameel & Ahmad, 2020; Nguyen, 2015; Sukoco et al., 2023).

Despite the Indonesian government's efforts and investment to improve research through regulations, funding,  and  mentoring programs,  research  performance in  Indonesia  still needs global recognition (Ibrahim & Fadhli, 2021). Indonesia's research outputs have surpassed countries like Malaysia and Singapore. However, the quality and global impact remain insufficient; no one of the universities in Indonesia succeeded in the 100 lists of QS world-ranking universities in the last three years, while institutions like the National University of Singapore (NUS) have secured the  eighth position, Nanyang  Technological University ranks  fifteen, and  Universiti Malaysia holds position sixty. This discrepancy highlights a critical issue: the need to enhance research engagement and  research  productivity in   Indonesia  across all  educational sectors,  especially private  universities whose  research  productivity  was  not  outstanding  compared  with  public universities (Huda et al., 2020).

One  of  the  areas  requiring  attention in  research  productivity is  English  as  a  Foreign Language,  a  field  within  Arts  and  humanities,  which  consistently  shows  lower  publication outcomes than other fields of study like natural science, technological engineering, and life science medicine (Haqiyah, et al., 2021). English Education Departments are notably absent from the top ten  departments  with  the  highest  research  productivity  at  the  national  level.  The  leading departments nationally include Informatics (S1) with a score of 3799, Management (S1) with 2868, and Electrical Engineering (S1) with 1787, underscoring the dominance of science, technology, and management fields in research outputs.

Studies  on  RE  and  RP  in  the  EFL  context  within  Higher  Education  have  addressed significant concerns on a global scale. Further, Kutlay (2013) continued this line of inquiry in Turkey, offering further insights into how English teachers engage with research in different institutional contexts.

## Literature Review


## Research Engagement

Research Engagement (RE) encompasses active involvement in conducting and interacting with research (Heng et al., 2020). Borg affirmed that RE refers to engaging in research (for example, by conducting it) and engaging with research, for example, by reading and using it (Borg, 2010). Similarly, RE  includes reading and  systematically using  research for  professional development (Anwaruddin & Pervin, 2013). Eam (2015) referred to RE as activities related to research, such as proposing funding, carrying out research, developing the framework, method, and procedure of the study, reviewing the  literature, publishing articles, disseminating research, data analysis, writing research, giving research reports to stakeholders and the public, as well as integrating research in teaching. In addition, Bai (2018) highlighted activities that counted as research, including compiling books or dictionaries, translating texts, synthesizing literature, reflecting on teaching practices, and conducting principled inquiries. Moreover, Yousefi et al. (2019) conceptualized RE-encompassing activities such as publishing journal articles, presenting papers at conferences, authored books, and participating in research projects. Further, this involvement extends beyond researching to generating ideas, leading projects, writing reports, and disseminating research  (Heng et al., 2020).

The conceptualization of activities related to research provided by Eam (2015); Bai (2018) Yousefi et al.(2019), and Heng  et al.(2020) covered a wide range of activities, emphasizing the multifaceted nature of  RE.  However, these definitions only partially capture the scope of  RE  in Indonesia. Through its detailed metrics for assessing RP,  the Sinta Database implies that RE  in Indonesia includes additional activities such as conducting community service, registering intellectual property rights, developing technological prototypes, supervising a thesis, becoming an editor in a journal, reviewing research outputs in a journal, networking which is crucial for academic assessment and  recognition in  the  local  context. This  highlights the  need  for  an  expanded and  localized understanding of RE that reflects Indonesia's unique educational environment and expectations, going beyond the definitions provided by previous scholars.

## Research Productivity

Research  Engagement  and  research  productivity are  closely  intertwined, as  RP  is  the tangible outcome of scientific academics' involvement in various research-related activities called publications (Yousefi et al., 2019). They are commonly measured through quantifiable indicators covering published books or book chapters, disseminated findings, reviewed articles, and achieved research funding, including grants and commercialization income (Heng et al., 2020; Akbaritabar et al., 2021).  Further, the  dimension of excellence in academics' research profiles is evaluated through bibliometric methodologies such as the count of citations, rates of citations, the h-index, and other metrics (Agarwal et al., 2016). In the Indonesian context, RP for academics can be the measurable output in research activities stated in individual metrics of RP in the Sinta database. Sinta  is the  integrated information system that records  and  manages academics' research and community  service  in  Indonesia,  including  scientific  publications,  researchers,  and  research institutions (Ibrahim & Fadhli, 2021; Ahmadi, 2019). The current study utilized the academics' overall score in the Sinta database as the basis for level categorization.

## Methods


The researchers employed descriptive quantitative research to gain and analyze numerical information  that intends  to describe,  explain,  predict,  or control  the  phenomenon  under investigation through quantitative measures that do not manipulate variables (Creswell & Creswell, 2018). In alignment with this research's objectives, using descriptive quantitative data, including measures  such  as  mean  and  percentages,  facilitates  a  comprehensive  understanding  of  the characteristics  of the  studied  phenomenon.  It  is  comprehensively suitable  for  achieving  the intended goal by describing, highlighting, and underscoring the  RP and RE of EFL academics in East Java's private universities.


## Participants


The study involved 30 SI EEDs that covered 288 EFL Academics in private universities in East Java, Indonesia, recorded in the Sinta databases. It was intended to investigate the SI English Education Department based on their overall Sinta scores. Further, to achieve the second and third objectives of the study, 165 respondents from a total population of  288 were involved in the online survey.  Purposive  sampling  was  employed  to  select  participants  based  on  specific  criteria: respondents had  to be  active lecturers, teach in S1  English Education programs, and  possess a National Lecturer Identification Number. This method ensured that the sample was representative of the population relevant to the study. The minimum sample size of 100-200 respondents is often considered adequate for descriptive quantitative studies if the population is minor. It provides a sufficient margin for error and enhances the generalizability of the results (Memon et al., 2020); Researchers referred to Slovin's formula to calculate the sample size; a confidence level of 95% was applied, providing a margin of error and enhancing the generalizability of the findings. The sampling strategy employed was purposive sampling. It is a non-probability method for choosing individuals or  cases  with specific characteristics or  experiences relevant to  the research aims. Although this sample may not accurately reflect the broader population, the selected participants can offer substantial insights into the investigated research question (Turner, 2019).


## Research Instruments


Researchers collected data from the Sinta Database regarding the universities' names, SI EED, EFL numbers, and average overall scores to achieve the first aim. The consistency of this data was verified by cross-referencing it with other databases, such as Google Scholar, Scopus, and "PDDIKTI" to ensure accuracy. Additionally, the researchers utilized a closed-ended online survey to determine EFL academics' RE consisting of 23 statements in part 1 with a 5-option Likert scale: Always,  Often,  Sometimes, Rarely,  and  Never.  Part 2  of  this survey  aimed to  underscore the motivations behind EFL academics' involvement in or with research, covering 15 statements with a five-option Likert scale: Agree, Agree, Slightly Agree, Disagree, and Strongly Disagree. This survey slightly differed from previous studies, which mostly adopted Borg's. This current survey was aligned with the activities related to research based on academics' scoring metrics in the Sinta database. Before distributing it, a pilot study was conducted on 37 respondents to ensure validity and  reliability. The  Cronbach's alpha coefficient result demonstrated good  internal consistency higher than 0,7. The result indicated that the items were valid and reliable (Ghazali, 2016).

## The Motivation for EFL Academics' Engagement  in /with Research

The finding indicated that the highest score of EFL academics' research motivation was to enhance professional development (89.45%), followed by contributing to disciplinary knowledge (88.24%) and academics' awareness that research was part of their job besides teaching (87.27%). A significant number also research out of love for it (85.94%) and to solve classroom problems (84.24%). Lower motivations include researching for government ranking improvement (75.27%), obtaining professional allowances (75.40%), and institutional obligations (77.09%). These results indicate that while intrinsic motivations and  job-related duties are motivating drivers, external incentives like promotions and allowances are less effective in encouraging research engagement. ## Discussion


The findings reported that 1) the research productivity level among 30 EEDs  at private universities in East Java, Indonesia, was mainly low. 2) EFL academics are intensively engaged in activities related to research, including writing, citing, conducting, and reading research. However, publishing research in recognized international journals indexed by Scopus or Web of Science, publishing in accredited national publications (Sinta Tiers one and two), and proposing intellectual property rights  received less  scrutiny. 3)  EFL  academics' research drives  were  primarily for professional advancement, knowledge addition, and recognition that research is a component of their  job  alongside  teaching  and  community  services.  However,  promotions,  governmental positions, and professional allowances were less motivating.

The  first finding showed  that most EEDs  achieved low  levels of research productivity based  on  the  overall  score  in  the  Sinta  Database.  4  out  of  30  EEDs  achieved  high  research productivity. In addition, 10 EEDs fell into the moderate productivity category. Most EEDs, 16 out of 30 EEDs, have low research productivity. The EEDs achieved high levels of RP, including EED  at  Universitas Islam  Balitar, Universitas Muhamadiyah  Surabaya, Universitas Nahdlatul Ulama Surabaya, and Universitas Ronggolawe. Remarkably, a small institution like the EED of Universitas Islam Balitar has surpassed more prominent universities despite its faculty members. This finding suggests that a solid commitment to research excellence, self-driving forces, and a strategic focus on research activities can significantly enhance RP. These results underscore the importance of  institutions in  boosting the  internal motivation of  their academics by  offering appreciation and rewards as well as a research mentoring system (Arsyad et al., 2019; Chen, 2015 & Tien et al., 2019)

Moreover,  the  EED  in  Universitas  Islam  Balitar  performed  high  RP  with  only  six academics.  However,  the  EED  at  Universitas  Muhammadiyah  Malang,  with  twenty-three academics, and Universitas Islam Malang, with sixteen academics, suggest improvement in their RP. This result emphasizes the crucial role of individual commitment and active participation in research,  whatever  the  institution's condition  (Novita  et  al.,  2023).  In  addition,  EEDs  like Universitas Islam Majapahit Mojokerto, Universitas Bhineka  PGRI  Tulungagung,  Universitas Islam  Jember Universitas Katolik Widya Mandala Surabaya  demonstrate potential for growth through enhanced  institutional support, faculty development initiatives, and  fostering a  robust

The second finding highlighted that EFL  academics at private universities in East Java, Indonesia, primarily engaged in activities such as writing and citing researchers' works, conducting research regularly, and reading research outputs. These  lower  engagement  levels  suggest  challenges  in achieving high-impact publications and securing intellectual property rights, which may require additional support and resources. The lower engagement in international publications, especially publishing in journals indexed by Scopus and WoS, or events in Tier 1 or Tier 2 of accredited national journals was in the same vein as previous researchers who have admitted that academics have many challenges in publishing research in those prestigious journals (Arsyad et al., 2019; Teixeira da Silva, 2021; Kardiyanto, et al., 2021).

The  challenges  stem  from  exceptionally  high  standards  and  rigorous  peer-review processes; articles submitted to these databases frequently require extensive revisions, increasing the time and effort needed to meet the journals' stringent criteria (Paltridge & Starfield, 2023). The competition  for  publishing  in  Scopus  and  WoS  journals  is  intense,  and  researchers  often experience rejection, which can be discouraging (Asif et al., 2020). This result highlights the need for  institutional and  governmental funding  support,  especially for  academics  from  small  or developed universities to publish research in reputable journals (Arsyad et al., 2019; &Pho & Tran, 2016). It implies the need for future research to know the factors contributing to the challenges in publishing research in  reputable journals indexed  by  Scopus  or  Wos  and  accredited national journals Tier  1  and    Tier 2.  Furthermore, IPR  engagement  is  low,  possibly  due  to  a  lack  of awareness or limited knowledge about the process. Increasing socialization and understanding of IPR can encourage its pursuit. Institutions should prioritize legal reforms and training programs to protect intellectual property and enhance RP (Judijanto et al., 2024). Further research is needed to understand why IPR engagement is low among EFL academics.

The  last  finding  underscores  that  the  top  reasons  for  EFL  academics' engagement  in research  are  for  professional  development,  contributing  to  disciplinary  knowledge,  and  the awareness of academics that research is part of their job, not only teaching. These highlighted a solid commitment to personal growth, academic contribution, and professional responsibilities. Conversely, the three most minor motivating factors are researching for promotion, increasing the government's international rank, and getting an honorary or professional allowance. This result indicates that while intrinsic motivations and job-related duties are significant drivers, external incentives like promotions and allowances are less effective in encouraging research engagement. ## Conclusion


The investigation of EFL academics' RP  in private universities in East Java, Indonesia, revealed that over  half of  EEDs  at  private universities in  East  Java, Indonesia,  achieved  low research productivity. Only four EEDs belong to High levels, such as EED at Universitas Islam Balitar,  Universitas  Muhammadiyah  Surabaya,  Universitas  Nahdlatul  Ulama  Surabaya,  and Universitas  Muhamadiyah  Ronggolawe.  In addition,  EFL academics  showed  engagement intensely in research activities, such as writing and citing research, conducting research regularly, and reading research outputs; however, they were less involved themselves in activities such as publishing research in recognized international journals indexed in Scopus and WoS, publishing in accredited national Tier 1 and 2, and proposing intellectual property rights. Furthermore, the primary motivations behind their research engagement were intrinsic, focusing on professional development, knowledge  contributions, and  the  awareness  that  research  is  an  academic duty besides teaching. At the same time, promotion, increasing government rank, and career incentives are less motivating. The implications of these results highlight the need for targeted funding and mentorship  to  support  publication  in  reputable  international journals,  promote  technological development,  and  encourage  the  pursuit  of  intellectual property  rights  to  enhance  research productivity.

## De-escalation in situ


While there is an extensive literature on de-escalation in a variety of disciplines (in policing and psychiatric nursing in particular), much of it provides theoretically motivated normative procedures, rather than a naturalistic examination of real cases of de-escalation. Two exceptions stand out. The first is the literature on negotiation in hostage situations and other crises (Donohue and Ramesh 1992; William A. Donohue, Ramesh, and Borchgrevink 1991a; Donohue and Taylor 2007; Hammer 2001; Rogan 2009, 2011; Rogan and Hammer 1994, 1995; Rogan and Hammer 2002; Taylor and Donald 2004). The second is the emerging literature on de-escalation that has begun to grow out of the microsociological study of violence (Collins 2019), and its emphasis on avoiding selection on the dependent variable. Much of this literature has focused on protest or crowd-like situations (Bramsen 2018; Nassauer 2015, 2018; Weenink, Dhattiwala, and van der Duin 2022). I discuss each of these in turn below.


## Crisis Negotiation


Before diving deeper into the literature in this area, it is worth bearing the range of possible outcomes of hostage/crisis negotiations in mind. One of the best conceptual mappings is that put together by Blair, Martaindale and Nichols (2014), reporting on active-shooter events in the US between 2000 and 2012, reproduced as fig. 2 below.

Crisis negotiations, of course, cover far more situations than active shootings-hostage-takings, barricade events, and suicide attempts are all handled in similar ways by police negotiating teams, and as a result have similar interactional features. A few features in particular stand out. In the

This is in line with FBI statistics on hostage and barricade situations, which indicated that suicides and attempted suicides accounted for more than a third of crisis negotiation incidents to which police responded (cited in Rogan 2009:35), while by one set of accounts, nearly 80% of school shooters had a history of suicide attempts (Newman et al. 2004:244). Police tactical responses are also common, and until the negotiation crises in 1972, represented the dominant response to hostage and barricade situations (Rogan and Hammer 2002). But other scenarios also exist, including situations where the attacker leaves, situations where victims subdue the attacker (violently or non-violently), and situations where the police subdue the attacker without shooting them. The present study falls into one of the low-frequency categories, representing a case where one of the would-be victims of the threatened school shootings convinces the attacker to surrender.

The hostage negotiation literature, like the role of professional hostage negotiator, grew partly as a response to failures of confrontational approaches to crisis situations during the Attica Uprising of 1971 and the Munich Olympic Games in 1972. In both high profile incidents, tactical responses to hostage takers led to the deaths of hostages, law enforcement personnel, and hostage-takers, and later high profile negotiation failures like the 1993 negotiations with the Branch Davidian group in Waco, TX, served to underscore the need for these investigations. While early work drew primarily from practitioner experience, social scientists using recordings from FBI negotiation teams began to produce more rigorously researched naturalistic studies of negotiation in the early 1990s (Rogan

and Hammer 2002:230, 234).

Work by William Donohue and colleagues (William A. Donohue et al. 1991b) set the agenda for the next 2 decades worth of work in the area, highlighting several characteristics that distinguished what they called 'crisis bargaining' from other forms of negotiation-the prominence of coercive challenges and strategies, a lack of complete information for both parties, high stakes, high emotional arousal, a sense of urgency, a preponderance of 'face' or identity issues, a narrow focus on a limited set of alternative outcomes, and relatively little negotiation about implementation, monitoring, or contingencies. In the face of these distinctive challenges, they highlighted three aspects of crisis bargaining communication. The first was relationally oriented communication, focused on building trust, a sense of closeness or immediacy, informality, and the handling of situational control. The second, related to the 'content' of communication, included negotiating demands, exploring feelings, and integrating information. The third, aspect, that of strategic consideration, related to tasks of adjusting positions, gaining compliance, and developing proposed courses of action. All three aspects served as part of a main goal of nudging the interaction from a crisis bargaining mode-'you do this or I'll hurt you'-to one of normative bargaining-'you do this and I'll do that.' Finally, Donohue et al provided an overview of a practitioner-created phase model of negotiations, tracing negotiations through the tasks of intelligence gathering, establishing communication, clarifying problems and developing a relationship, problem solving, and resolution. Perhaps more important than these theoretical frames, however, was the use of transcript extracts from an actual hostage negotiation to ground the discussion of phases, a move that laid the groundwork for a generation of studies that tested and modified these hypotheses based on transcripts and recordings of negotiations, mostly collected by FBI negotiators (William A. Donohue et al. 1991b).

One of the early results of the new generation was the finding that while phase models provided reasonable descriptions of the simulated situations created to train negotiators, real negotiations rarely followed a consistent sequence of tasks. Instead, problems related to maintaining communication channels, keeping the attention of impaired hostage-takers, and changing negotiators shed light on the ways in which large-scale tasks frequently had to be repeated or re-sequenced (Holmes 1992; Holmes 1997; Holmes and Sykes 1993).

Decoupled from a rigid phase model, investigations of communicative action proved more useful. Donohue, Rogan and Borchgrevnik (William A. Donohue et al. 1991a) found that language that communicated spatial immediacy-using words like 'these' instead of 'those', 'here' instead of 'there', words specifying nearness or contact ('adjoin', 'meet', 'touch') rather than distance or displacement ('away', 'remove') correlated well with cooperative moments in negotiation, while their opposites correlated with more competitive negotiation phases (William A. Donohue et al. 1991a).
