## Conclusion


There is a point of irony in the story that can easily elude its casual reader. After the turning point of the conversation, one of Tuff's chief projects was to convince Hill that things didn't have to turn out for the worse-that he could receive mental health care at a hospital rather than a violent death or certain imprisonment. In this respect, the hopeful world Tuff and Hill envisioned surpasses our own. Despite his mental health issues, his apparent suicidality, his apology, and his willing surrender, Hill was ultimately retrieved from his submissive position on the floor at gunpoint, interrogated, jailed, and sentenced to serve 20 years in prison (Anon 2014). While crisis negotiation as a path to nonviolent resolution has entered the police repertoire, an ongoing stream

of police shootings serves as a reminder that confrontational approaches to policing remain the norm. Meeting violence with violence is a deeply ingrained habit, but one which cases like that of Tuff and Hill give us resources to combat. Of course, Hill's tentative approach was markedly different from that of many other mass shooters whose clandestine methods and focus on tactics of surprise make crisis negotiation an inappropriate framework. Nonetheless, there are lessons that this and other cases of negotiated surrender offer that have wider applicability in the study of violence.

Previous cases have demonstrated that an approach that focuses on bargaining, negotiation, and deliberation over outcomes, while preferable to a confrontational approach to threats of violence, is often insufficient. Attention to issues of relational rapport and identity repair are crucial, as is a contextually sensitive approach to challenging the assumptions expressed by people in crisis. This study highlights the central importance of emotional dynamics to the study of violent situations. Emotional dominance of the situation creates the space for those seeking non-violent solutions to open deliberations about outcomes, build relational rapport, and offer aggressors opportunities for identity repair. In violent situations particularly, the field of tension and fear that accompanies confrontation affords an opportunity. Attackers who can be confronted, isolated from sources of immediate emotional support, and sufficiently contained to prevent casualties are likely to suffer emotional exhaustion, creating openings for negotiated, non-violent solutions.

Directing attention toward the emotional dynamics of violent situations offers more hope for an answer to the fundamental questions of nonviolence than most previous paradigms. If we are wise, we will use the insights it offers to build a less-violent world.

## I Introduction


Are  movement  parties  successful  transmitters  of  movements'  policy  demands into institutions and legislature of a country? In other words, do they succeed in representing their associated social movements  at  the  institutional level? Movement  parties,  as  originally  defined  by  Kitschelt  (2006:  280),  are  parties

formed  by  political  activists  originating  from  social  movements  and  trying  to apply  social  movements' modes  of  organisation  and  strategic  practice  to  the arena of party competition. They are thus actors of a hybrid nature: with one foot in  the  party  system  and  the  other  one  in  the  social  movement  world  (Mosca 2019: 357). Due to this hybrid nature, the agenda of movement parties is often suspected to directly reflect the political demands of the movements from which the movement party developed or with which it is closely associated. However, since  political  parties  follow  different  dynamics  than  movements,  due  to  their partially different roles in politics, often movement parties part ways with their associated movements with time, and their policy demands start to differ -if not in  kind  than  at  least  in  intensity.  Often,  the  movements  increasingly  become critical of the movement party and its officials as well as of the party s slow or ' diverted progress in achieving policy demands (e.g. Fridays for Future 's criticism of the German Greens).

In  this  article,  to  evaluate  the  policy  influence  of  movement  parties  and determine the pathways through which they are able to achieve it, we look at the actual  outcomes  of  policy  demands -from  their  formation  at  the  movements ' level to their incorporation into the party's agenda and to their adoption, or lack thereof,  in  the  institutions.  On  concrete  policy  examples,  we  examine  whether they  survive  institutional  settings  and  whether  they  transform  and  undergo significant  changes  on  the  way.  Through  this  study,  we  contribute  to  the literature on democratic representation and coalition governance in general, and representation by movement parties in particular.

Instead of focusing on movement parties' success or failure in elections and on the effect that their presence in government at a certain point in time has on their performance in the subsequent elections, we assess policy success of such parties: do they manage to foster the adoption of the key policies for the party and  its  associated  social  movement?  At  the  same  time,  we  also  investigate  if parliament or government membership of a movement party has any effects on the  success  of  its  policy  agenda  and  its  consistency  and  continuity  with  the associated  social  movement.  We  are  thus  providing  empirical  evidence  on  the movement parties' policy -making and adding both the to the recent research on the  importance  of  electoral  priorities  (party  programmes)  on  actual  policy

outputs  (Brouard et  al .  2018,  Guinaudeau  and  Guinaudeau  2023),  and  on  the responsiveness of movement parties to the policy priorities of social movements within  institutional  constraints  (della  Porta  et  al.  2017,  Mosca  and  Tronconi 2019).

We  determine  what kinds of survival of policy demands  by  social movements occur and propose a  possible typology of movement parties' policy influence.  To  this  end,  we  analyse  four  cases  of  movement  parties  and  their affiliated social movements  in Germany (the Greens and Alternative for Germany) and Italy (Five Star Movement and the Greens). The following section presents  the  literature  that  informed  our  theoretical  expectations,  and  our research  design  and  country  cases.  The  third  section  describes  our  analytical framework and data collection, while the fourth section presents our findings on the types of policy success that movement parties are able to achieve within the institutions and the constraints on this policy influence. In the final section, we close with the conclusions on the role of the movement parties as transmitters of social movements' demands to the core institutional system and the implications for democratic representation and public policy research.


## II Movement Parties and Policy Process


Is  policy  success  of  a  social  movement  dependent  on  its  movement  party's electoral performance? How does being part of a government coalition affect the ability of the movement party to push forward its policy agenda? Are there other ways  towards  policy  influence  and  policy  success  that  social  movements  and movement parties  might  benefit  from?  How  effectively  can  a  movement  party serve as an intermediary between the social movements and the policy-making process  in the institutions? To  answer  these  questions,  we  implement  a comparative  design  with  two  parties  in  each  of  the  two  country  cases.  Our research expectation was that policy influence of a social movement/movement party might depend on the performance of the movement party in elections and in parliament  or  government  (its  ability  to  have  an  important  role  in  a government  coalition,  for  example).  We  selected  cases  of  both  electorally

successful  and  rather  unsuccessful  parties  in  Germany  and  Italy  to  allow  for testing of this hypothesis.

Although it has been widely acknowledged in public policy research that policy  change  is  slow  and  cumbersome  (Lindblom  1959),  political  parties  are constrained  in  their  policy  impact  due  to  political-economic  interdependence (Lehner and Schubert 1984), and policy implementation is slow due to the gap between  party  rhetoric  and  action  (Lutz  2021),  recent  literature  on  electoral priorities  and  party  manifestos  impact  on  policy  agenda-setting  calls  for  a renewed  attention  towards  their  importance  for  policy  decisions,  underlining that  there  are  both  incentives  for  parties  to  enact  electoral  promises  and considerable  institutional  or  coalitional constraints  that  can  hinder  party's mandate  responsiveness  (Brouard et  al . 2018,  Guinaudeau  and  Guinaudeau 2023; Martin and Vanberg 2015). We follow the latter strand in the expectation that,  under  certain  conditions, parties  are  more or  less  able  to  deliver  on  their election programmes, and we specifically investigate this capacity for movement parties (Kitschelt 2006), which claim to be more responsive to the policy needs of  their  electorate  than  established  parties.  At  the  same  time,  we  take  into consideration  possible  complex  trade-offs  that  movement  parties  can  face  as they  balance  the  different  goals  competitive  political  parties  pursue -voteseeking, policy-seeking, and office-seeking (Strøm 1990) -and what that means for policy influence of these parties and their representation of social movements. For example, office-seeking behaviour might result in diluting policy positions to secure legislative power, which brings to the fore the dual nature of a movement party: that of a representative of a social movement and of a party competing in the elections.

For the purpose of our analysis, we find it useful to consider the policy cycle  stages  (Wilson  2008),  as  it  allows  to  assess  the  influence  of  not  only  the parties that are part of the government but also of those in opposition with very limited parliamentary representation, but are associated with prominent social movements. The stage-model helps open up the black box of the policy-making process  (Biard  2017),  showcasing  how  actors  can  intervene  at  the  different points, e.g. agenda-setting  or  decision-making  stage,  possessing  sometimes

vastly different resources and employing diverse strategies to influence policymaking.  For  example,  it  was  previously  argued  that  populist  parties  in  the opposition can and are highly influential especially at the agenda-setting stage (Schain 2006). Although radical right populist parties reach the highest level of influence on public policies when they are part of government (see Minkenberg 2001, Zaslove 2004, Lutz 2019, Hayes and Dudek 2020), at least some influence capacity  of  populist  parties  on  public  policies  regardless  of  their  access  to government  has  been  established  by  most  scholars  in  the  policy  analysis literature (Biard 2017: 22; Schain 2006; Caiani and Kröll 2017). We believe this also to be the case for movement  parties  of  non-radical  right  populism orientation.  In  this  paper,  we  posit  that  also  movement  parties  of  elusive ideology, 'eclectic populism', such as M5S (Mosca and Tronconi 2019), and of the left, such as for instance the Green parties, have policy impact not only (and not primarily) through government positions and direct policy-making, but through their  influence  on  agenda-setting  and  pressure  on  the  established  parties.  We also expect, based on the differentiation of our cases, that the movement parties' influence on public policies takes both implicit and explicit forms.


## Country Cases


Our country cases Germany  and  Italy are well-established Western European  democracies,  characterized  by  multi-party  systems.  Although  they show some notable differences,  such  as  low government  stability  and  (in  part connected to this) high numbers of political parties in Italy, but not in Germany, they  are  still  rather  similar:  both  made  their  first  steps  towards  a  democratic governance after fascist experiences and World War II; both are parliamentary democracies  with  a  weak  Head  of  State;  both  are  federal  countries  (although with  different  intensities);  both  lived  through  alternating  times  of  left  and/or right-wing extremism; both are founding members of the European Union, etc . Both  Italy  and  Germany  have  recently  seen  several  notable  social  movements gain  popularity  (representing  agendas  as  different  as  ecological  and  climate topics, migration, doubts about democracy and facts, etc .), indicating a malfunctioning transmission belt between the citizens' agenda and the existing political system. In other words, the emergence, persistence, and intensification

of social movements can be a sign of a (partial) failure of political representation, which in Italy and Germany, known as Partitocrazia or as Parteienstaat ,  means predominantly a failure of political parties. Therefore, in these settings the study of movement  parties is especially beneficial, as they connect the social movements, with the state institutions of policy-making.

Our  comparative  design  has  several  dimensions. As  party cases, we selected the Greens in both countries and the Movimento Cinque Stelle (Five Star Movement, M5S) for Italy and the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) for Germany. These  parties  differ  in  their  time  of  foundation  and  their  associated  social movements. The Greens in both Italy  and  Germany  are  among  the  pioneers of movement  parties  and  originated  in  the  1980s  as  a  result  of  the  New  Social Movements of the 1960s-1970s, notably the environmentalist, anti-nuclear and anti-war movements. The AfD and the M5S, on the other hand, are more recent examples of movement parties, with the AfD founded in 2013 on the wave of the opposition to the EU's handling of the financial  crisis,  and  the  M5S founded in 2009, originating from the Five Star Civic Lists. Therefore, different 'generations' of movement parties are addressed.

The Five Star Movement (M5S) party in Italy is not only closely aligned with a social movement, but grew directly out of one: the blog started by Beppe Grillo and Gianroberto Casaleggio in 2005, followed by local meetup groups and 'V -Day' demonstrations, led to the official foundation of a M5S party by the same two  leaders  in  2009.  Although  sharing  similar  organizational  practices  and principles as the early Green parties in Europe (ideals of grassroot democracy, assembly-based organisation, rejection of hierarchy and professional politicians as leaders etc.), the M5S is a different phenomenon of a movement party as its success is a product of the digital revolution of the 2000s and of the reaction to the  Great  Recession  in  Europe  between  2009-2013  (Campus  et  al.  2021; della Porta  et  al.  2017).  In  addition,  it  acted  as  the  voice  and  hub  of  the  already existing  protest  movements  in  Italy  (e.g. NoTAP,  No  Tav,  No  Gronda,  No  Dal Molin ),  becoming a 'movement of the movements' (Casaleggio and Grillo 2011; Biancalana  2020;  Campus  et  al.  2021),  rather  than  representing  one  social movement.

The AfD did not originate from a social movement per se. It was formed in 2013 by a professor of economics and former members of the established party CDU, as a reaction to the handling of the Euro-crisis by the German government, particularly to Angela Merkel's 'no alternative' framing of the decision (Decker 2022). However, with time, the AfD shifted its focus from mobilizing against the EU monetary policies towards radical right positions and campaigned for stricter migration  policies  and  securing  the  state  borders,  as  well  as,  recently,  against governmental anti-Covid regulations (Lehmann and Zehnter 2022). Born out of frustration and disappointment with the mainstream establishment and policies, the  party  was  envisioned  as  a  'true  alternative'  to  the  established  parties. Throughout the AfD transformation-to-the-far-right process, protest movements such  as Pegida,  Identitäre  Bewegung, and Querdenken became  known  as  the party's followers and supporters. Although formally rejecting any links with the movements, especially  with Pegida ,  the  AfD  party  members  were  nevertheless seen  at  some  of  the  rallies,  thereby  endorsing  them,  and  some  of  the  party leaders  even  called Pegida protesters  the  AfD's  'natural  political  allies' (BBC 2015; Amann et al. 2018; Chambers 2018).

The  question  of  the longue durée also  becomes  important  with  regard  to the  relation  between  the  movement  party  and  the  core  party  system.  Younger parties  are  often  challenger  parties,  while  older  parties  might  already  have become part of the political game in the institutional arena. De Vries and Hobolt (2020) define challenger parties as those that have never held national office and attempt  to  break  the  status  quo  and  fight  the  political  mainstream,  whereas dominant parties already have government experience.  Therefore, a party that becomes part of the national government is no longer considered a challenger party. In addition, younger parties might lack the necessary party apparatus that helps in planning political processes, while older parties can rely on a professional party organization. Having one party of each kind in both countries, we control for this.

Indeed, while the German Greens at the time of their foundation have called themselves an 'antiparty' party and an alternative to traditional political actors, they  have  now  been  fully  integrated  into  the  political  system  and  do  not

challenge it dramatically (Bukow 2016: 112). The same can be said of the Italian Greens, which have also gone through a major process of institutionalization and incorporation within the Italian political system, and have departed from their 'movement'  component  through  a  substantial  separation  from  the  grassroots environmentalist movements and initiatives (Biorcio 2016: 186-194). The Green parties  promoted the ideas of the  New Social Movements on the structure and organization of a party as a challenge to the notion of traditional political parties (Rihoux 2016: 209-300). However, nowadays only several of those distinguishing,  ideal-typical  features  have  remained -prominently,  the  dual leadership of the party for both the German and Italian Greens, and the women's quota on positions and mandates, especially in the case of the German Greens.

The  M5S  and  the  AfD  are  also  on  their  way  towards  integration  into  the respective political systems, but still claim to be radically anti-establishment and to  represent  an  alternative  to  'corrupt  traditional  politics'.  In  contrast  to  the Green parties, the AfD and M5S in their current agendas still retain the proposals of introducing more elements of direct democracy as well as the need to fight the establishment  and  the  traditional  political  'caste'  that  is  held  responsible  for  a country's problems (Mosca and Tronconi 2019 ; Pirro 2018; AfD 2021).

The  second  variation,  which  our  research  design  captures,  refers  to ideology.  The  Greens  in  Germany  and  Italy  have  a  clear  centre-left/left-wing ideology focused on environmental politics, while the AfD and the M5S represent the relatively new phenomenon of a populist party, with the AfD clearly falling into the right-wing populist camp and the M5S remaining at least ambiguous in their  ideology.    The  M5S,  initially  conceived  as a  post-ideological  party,  openly rejected the left-right axis in politics (Casaleggio and Grillo 2011; Campus et al. 2021:  137)  and  attracted  voters  of  both  centre-right  and  centre-left  views (Romei 2017). Over the course of their stay in power, the party shifted between and  combined  left-wing  and  right-wing  policies,  made  alliances  in  government with actors from the left and the right alike ( Lega and Partito Democratico ), and overall exhibited an 'eclectic' type of populism (Mosca and Tronconi 2019).

A  further  differentiation  concerns  the  electoral  results  of  the  movement parties. Some of them are more successful in the elections than others. We have

specifically chosen  two  examples  of  (relatively)  electorally successful and (relatively) unsuccessful movement parties as our case studies, one per country. Inclusion  of  both  electorally  successful  and  unsuccessful  parties  in  our  cases helps  us  evaluate  whether  and  how  policy  success  depends  on  the  movement parties'  electoral  performance.  Despite  initial  policy  successes  and  favourable context  in  the  1980s,  the  Italian  Greens  ( Federazione  dei  Verdi, FdV)  have negatively impacted their own popularity after joining the centre-left coalition in the 1990s because this decreased their autonomous political role (outside of the coalition) and cost them the ability to widen their electoral base. In addition, the FdV lost the role of the sole representative of the environmentalist initiatives in institutional settings, having parted ways with many environmental movements and associations (Biorcio 2016: 182-183). Consistently fluctuating between 0.5% and  3%  in  the  general  parliamentary  elections,  they  have  not  yet  managed  to regain  momentum  or  perform  well  electorally,  although  their  performance slightly  improved  in  the  2022  elections  (12  seats  with  the  Left  Alliance,  in comparison to zero seats in the 2018 elections).

Bündnis 90/Die Grünen in  Germany, on the other hand, reaching their best result of 14.8% in the federal election 2021, entered the coalition government as a major  electoral success. Already  before, they were  part of the federal government coalition from 1998 to 2005, were discussed as a partner in the later Merkel governments, and have been regularly and frequently part of Land level governments  for  nearly  40  years.  The  prime  minister  of  the Land of  Baden Württemberg also belongs to the Green party. The German Greens have arrived in the heart of the German political system, both with regard to parliament and government  representation.  More  recently,  the  German  Greens  have  benefited from the spread of the Global Climate Protests, the Fridays for Future movement, which superseded the old environmentalist movements, and the importance of climate issues for the political agenda. In fact, while the Greens by the mid-2010s were no longer resembling a 'movement party' and became an incorporated part of  the  established  political  system  (Bukow  2016:  134),  the  rise  of  the  FFF movement made a rekindling of the Green party's image as a movement party with tighter linkages to activists and movement groups possible.

The  new  anti-establishment  movement  parties  in  our  analysis -the  AfD and the M5S -also offer us the differentiation in their electoral outcomes: there is the 'success' story of the M5S and the 'failure' story of the AfD (again, these are relative success and failure, and both might change in the near future, as both the M5S decline and the latest AfD results in the 2024 Land elections show). In 2013, the M5S party entered the Italian parliament after a huge success in their firstever national elections, but remained in opposition, despite having received the highest number  of votes (25.6%). The real challenge for it as an antiestablishment  actor  was  its  success  in  the  2018  elections  (32.7%)  and  the decisions to form a government coalition as a major partner, first with the rightwing  populist Lega , and  then,  in  2019,  with Partito  Democratico. The  latter decision  was  especially  unpopular  with  the  core  members  of  the  party,  thus marking an important turning point for the M5S: the very nature of the protest movement  as the rejection of the political class and of the traditional establishment  actors  was  swept  away  by  the  M5S  joining  the  system  it  had campaigned  against  (Corbetta  2018).  These  actions,  together  with  the  2021 adoption of a new party statute with a clear hierarchy and with Grillo stepping aside from the political leadership and becoming instead the 'Guarantor' of the Movement, finally instituted the M5S as a fully-fledged political party. However, forming alliances with various established parties from the different ends of the political  spectrum  undermined the support for the M5S, and pulling out of the 'national  unity  government'  in  July  2022  was  also  an  unpopular  move  for  the majority of Italians, which led to a spiral loss of M5S  popularity after four years ' in power, resulting in only 15% votes in the 2022 elections.

Finally, the AfD case did not have the opportunity  of getting into government  as  of  yet.  It  serves  as  as  an  example  of  the  anti-establishment movement  party  preserving  its  anti-establishment  rhetoric  and  position  after entering the parliament in 2017 with 12.6% of the votes and becoming part of the  core  political  system.  From  the  early  days,  the  AfD  members  perceived themselves as a 'non party party' with a different organisational structure and -ideals  of  direct  democracy  (similar  to  the  Italian  M5S):  party  speaker  Bernd Lucke in numerous speeches accused the establishment and positioned the AfD as an anti-elitist party, an alternative to a system where the opposition parties

were  no  longer  a  true  opposition  to  the  parties  in  government  (Berbuir et al. 2015:  163-164).  Although  their  performance  in  the  2021  federal  elections (10.4%) was not much lower than that of the Greens, the AfD was and is far away from  forming  agreements  with  other  parties  to  become  part  of  a  governing coalition, partially due to their previously proclaimed programme.  Major political  parties  have  agreed  to  reject  cooperation  with  the  AfD  in  federal  or Land -level coalitions and even abstain (if feasible) from single-policy cooperation at the local level.

With this comparative design and differentiation of cases, we show how the movement  party  serves  as  the  intermediary  that  puts  the  social  movements' demands  on  the  agenda  of  the  institutions  and  strives  to  influence  their adoption. We determine what conditions and what constraints make this process more or less successful.


## III Analytical Framework and Data Collection


To assess the success of the movement parties in transmitting the policy demands  of  the  social  movements  into  the  institutional  arena  and  influencing policy-making  in  Italy  and  Germany,  we  adopt  a  structured  approach  and examine the similarities and differences in how policy success was achieved by the selected movement parties and what kind of success it was. In doing this, we consider the movement parties' characteristics and their relationship with their associated social movements, their alliances with other parties and the effect of those,  and  finally,  the  role  of  other  actors  in  the  political  arena  for  the  policy impact of the movement parties.

Our starting point for analysis is the interest in the intermediary role of the  movement  party  in  transferring  the  social  movement's  demands  into  the policy-making  arena  and,  ultimately,  transforming  them  into  state  policies.  In other  words,  we  are  interested  in  tracking  how  the  policy  issues  originating through social  movements survive  the  process of shaping  a  movement  party's agenda and the policy cycle stages in the institutions, when the movement party becomes part of the parliament or government. In this regard, we expect several possibilities: the policy issues may not survive this process at all (thereby, dying

or disappearing from the agenda). They may survive in a weak form, changing in the  scope of  the  demands or intensity of the movement requirements. Or they may  survive  strongly,  fully  reflecting  the  movement's  demands  and  shaping corresponding  state  policies.  From  this  angle,  we  analyse  several  key  policy issues that our four chosen movement parties were concerned with and brought to  the  policy-making  arena,  and  examine  what  happened  with  these  issues  on their journey from a movement's agenda to the state institutions.

To  carry  out  this  analysis  and  build  a  comprehensive  picture  of  the movement → movement  party → institutions  journey  of  selected  policy  issues, we rely on a variety of sources for movements, parties, government coalitions, and  national  ministries.  We  combine  written  documents  (party  programmes, dossiers, election manifestos, coalition agreements) and website material (blog posts of the movements, press releases, draft legislature), as well as secondary sources.  For  example,  for  the  AfD  policy  agenda,  we  examine  their  2017  and 2021 election manifestos. For the movement phase of the M5S, we refer to the blog posts on Beppe Grillo's blog, which came to be known as the official organ of the movement,  where  all important decisions and  policy demands  were disseminated to the public (Mosca and Tronconi 2019). For the party phase of the  M5S,  we  analyse  their  election  manifestos  for  national  and  European elections. Likewise, the Fridays for Future website provides written documents of the  movement's  demands  and  policy  agenda,  while  election  manifesto  of Die Grünen serve  as  an  important  source  for  analyzing party  policy  agenda.  In  this fashion, we examine the demands and agenda in all our selected cases. For the outcomes  of  policy-making  process,  we  consult  ministerial  and  parliamentary websites  and  news  reports.  We  identify  what  contributed  to  the  survival  of selected policy issues, what was the role of the movement party in their success or failure, and present the resulting patterns in the next section.


## IV Varieties of policy success


We arrive  at  a  typology  of  movement  parties' paths  to  policy  influence,  which take  into  account  cooperation  with  their  associated  social  movements  on  core policy  issues  and  outline  the  mechanisms  through  which  the  policy  demand

arrived at the institutions, and in some cases, at policy adoption. We concentrate on the policy  demands, which can largely be defined as successful  and analyse what made them possible.


## Type 1. Policy influence through explicit agenda-setting by the movement party and influence on voter issue priorities


We  identify  the  first  type  of  policy  success  in  our  list  as  a  success  which  is achieved while being closely aligned with the movement, by influencing explicitly the  agenda-setting  process  in  the  political  system  and  issue  priorities  of  the voters.

We  observe  this  type  of  success, for example,  in the case of the abandonment  of  Italy's  nuclear  programme  in  the  1980s  possibly  the  most significant and lasting result of the Italian Green party's initiatives. Despite being generally  perceived  as  one  of  the  less  successful  and  politically  relatively marginal Green parties in Europe, along with the other Green parties of Southern Europe (Biorcio 2016), Federazione dei Verdi (Italian Greens, currently named -Europa Verde/Verdi) was able to achieve important policy results during their time in parliament and in government coalitions. Particularly with respect to the Italian nuclear power questions, the movement party was perfectly aligned with the  environmentalist movement, which demanded to put a stop to the nuclear programme and construction of new nuclear power stations in Italy. Since 1974, environmental  associations,  such  as Italia Nostra and  the World Wide Fund for Nature -Italy ,  campaigned against nuclear power plants, which, according to a national  energy  plan,  were  to  be  expanded  to  a  total  of  twenty  nuclear  power plants (Standish 2009: 951).

The newly established Green party (known as the Green Lists at the time) took over  this  policy  issue  from  the  larger  Italian  environmentalist  movement and included the goal of stopping the nuclear programme in its party agenda: in the programmatic manifesto of 1987, it asked for the 'definitive renunciation of nuclear energy' and pledged to organize national referenda against the development of the nuclear programme during the electoral campaign (Europa Verde/Verdi 2021). Even though the Greens took just 2,5% of the votes in the

1987 general election, the environmentalist movement and the Greens were very successful in influencing state policy: three referenda against the development of the nuclear programme were held in November 1987 and were approved by the majority  of  the  voters,  resulting  in  the  cutting  of  government  support  to  the nuclear industry, termination of work on the power plants under construction, and  early  closure  of  the  functioning  power  plants  in  1990  (World  Nuclear Association  (WNA)  2022).  Furthermore  and  specifically,  a  1987  motion  of  the Greens was approved in the parliament, leading to the five-year moratorium on new  nuclear  constructions  (Europa  Verde/Verdi  2021).  However,  this  policy adoption  success  was  influenced  to  a  large  degree  by  the  1986  Chernobyl nuclear disaster, swinging public opinion against nuclear power (Standish 2009). In  addition,  due  to  this  accident,  the  major  parties  in  the  parliament  in  this period (e.g. the Socialist party and the Communist party), previously supporting nuclear power, chose to back the anti-nuclear referendum campaign, while the largest  party  in  the  parliament,  the  Christian  Democrats,  also  did  not  wish  to object and delegated the decision to its voters in the referendum (Hardenberg 2011). Thus, through influencing issue priorities of the electorate and setting the agenda, the Greens were able to co-opt other political parties in the establishment  and  impact  the  end  result  of  the  policy-making  process.  The Greens  maintained  their  influential  role in this question  and  anti-nuclear position throughout the years, with their leader Pecoraro Scanio as the Minister for  Environment  (2006-2008)  blocking  the  re-introduction  of  nuclear  power plants in the country (Standish 2009).

The Berlusconi government pushed for resuming nuclear production and reopening nuclear power plants in Italy and passed bills to that purpose in 2009, but the 2011 Fukushima nuclear accident forced the government to put a oneyear moratorium on its nuclear expansion plans. The FdV, despite having left the government and the parliament after unsuccessful election, in 2011 campaigned extensively and mobilized the population across the country to say no to nuclear power (Europa Verde/Verdi 2021). A referendum held in June 2011 resulted in the definitive rejection of the revitalization of nuclear power production and the cancellation of all  legislative  and regulatory measures that were introduced by the government to that intent previously (94% of the votes, with 55% turnout)

(WNA 2022). In this  case,  neither  being  in  government  nor  in  parliament,  the Greens  were  able  to  contribute  to  and  influence  the  policy  agenda  on  nuclear power, although again in the favourable context of public opinion turning against nuclear energy after Fukushima, and with the help of a populist anti-corruption party Italia dei Valori, which initiated and petitioned for the referendum against nuclear  power  (World  Nuclear  News  2011).  This  case  demonstrates  the  high impact the Greens had on the agenda-setting stage of the policy cycle, due to the importance  of  the  issues  raised  for  the  population  and  their  close  association with a popular social movement, and the consequences thereof for the success of their policy demands, first with and then even without parliament or government participation from the Greens' side.

## Type  2. Policy influence through implicit agenda-setting  impact  and influence on issue priorities

When the agenda-setting influence of a movement party is not as clearly visible through institutional channels, there still is an option of exerting implicit policy influence and achieving policy demands of a movement/party in this way. Even  without  parliamentary  representation  or  as  a  minor  opposition  group,  a party can shape policy through its effect on public debate. Given that all other parties  in  Germany  refuse  to  collaborate  with  the  AfD  and  the  AfD  officially denies  connections  to  right-wing  protest  movements,  it  stands  as  a  strong example  of  possible  implicit  policy  achievements.  The  demand  for  stricter migration  policies  represents  a  policy  success  story  for  a  party  that  has  only been in opposition at the federal level, but has nonetheless managed to influence the  agenda-setting  and  policy  formulation  stages  of  the  policy  process  by  its electoral breakthrough, close alignment with significantly-sized protest movements, and the co-optation reaction by the established parties.

A demand for stricter migration policies was raised in both the Identitäre Bewegung and Pegida movements. Identitäre Bewegung (in 2013/14) demanded a change in immigration policy to 'prevent a swap out of the population' and was -opposed to unregulated mass migration and 'parallel societies', es pecially Islamic

ones  (BPB  2023).  The Pegida movement,  as  its  name  suggests  (translated  as 'patriotic Europeans against the islamisation of the occident'), demanded an end to the 'islamisation' of Germany and stricter legislation (Zuwanderungsgesetz) to limit  'uncontrolled  quantitative  immigration' through  imposing  the  duty  of integration rather than assimilation (Pfahl-Traughber 2015). The AfD had a very similar  approach  to  migration  policies  and  incorporated  similar  proposals  in their election programmes of 2017 and 2021. For example, multiculturalism and migration were viewed as threats to social peace and the integrity of the nation as a cultural union (AfD 2017: 92). More deportation is deemed necessary (AfD 2021:  90),  as  the  AfD  claims  that  migration  is  connected  to  crime  and  terror attacks, separatism of Islamic communities, etc. (91), and opposes 'uncontrolled, predominantly  illegal  immigration  of  unqualified  people'  ( AfD  2017:  123), whereas highly qualified skilled workers' migration should be heavily regulated and  limited  (122-125).  The  AfD  also  advocates  harsher  penalties  and  more deterrence  against  illegal  migration  (AfD  2021:  93-94).  Considering  Angela Merkel's well -known welcome policy for Syrian refugees in 2015, it might seem that these policy demands  were  not  successful  in influencing legislation. However, in fact some were successful to a degree.

After the refugee crisis of 2015, asylum policies in Germany took a right turn. This was prior to the entrance of the AfD to the Bundestag in  2017, but at the height of the popularity of Pegida protesters and against the background of soaring popularity of the AfD in the polls after 2015 (Forschungsgruppe Wahlen 2017).  Adopted  measures,  such  as Asylpaket  I and II , and  the  Law  for  the improved  enforcement  of  the  duty  to  leave  the  country,  tightened  German migration policy (Mediendienst Integration 2022).  After the AfD success in the 2017 elections, a second law for the improved enforcement of the duty to leave the country was adopted in 2019, introducing even stricter rules, less freedoms and harsher penalties for immigrants, as well as easier deportations (Deutscher Bundestag  2019).  At  the  same  time,  some  legislation  easing  the  integration process into the German labour market was adopted, following the tendency to favour controlled skilled migration with good integration chances (Flüchtlingsrat Berlin 2023). Thus, though the most radical demands by Pegida or the AfD might not have made it into laws, a gradual tightening of the migration legislation has

occurred  exactly  as  the  AfD  and  Pegida  demonstrated  an  increase  in  support after 2015.

This  is  a  notable  survival  of  the  policy  demand  by  a  movement  and movement party  in  the  institutions,  given  that  at  the  time  of  many  legislation changes, the AfD has not yet entered the Bundestag. However, the agenda-setting power of the movements and the party and their growing popularity, expressed among other things by an electoral breakthrough of the AfD, meant a changing political  dynamic  around migration policy and put pressure on the established parties to seek ways to undermine their support by adopting measures of similar character.


## Type 3. Policy Success through direct policy-making or by governing


A policy success can be achieved by movement parties at a different stage of the policy  cycle,  when  they  manage  to  secure  a  major  role  in  government  or government coalition. In this case, the party has many more resources to achieve its policy  goals  directly  through  participating  in  policy-making,  therefore  it participates  not  only  in  the  agenda-setting  stage,  but  also  in  the  solutionformulation  and  decision-making  stages.  When  a  party  has  the  majority  in parliament,  it  is  more  likely  to  be  able  to  push  through  its  preferred  policy solutions,  and  depending  on  its  importance  within  the  governing  coalition,  it does  not  always  have  to  give  much  consideration  to  the  preferences  of  other parties. However, the sustained influence of such policy success depends on how well  the  movement party is able to secure its position in power, or, if it is not able to do so in the next elections, on whether the policy adopted had sufficient support from coalition partners or other political parties that might take over the governmental position. With this regard, we differentiate the policy outcomes of this  pathway  between  durable  and  non-durable  and  proceed  first  with  an example  of  so  far  a  durable  success  story,  specifically  with  one  of  the  key demands of the FFF movement and the Green party regarding the expansion of renewable energy in Germany.

Although  no  official  direct  cooperation  exists  between  the  movement

Fridays for Future Germany and the Greens, neither in terms of organization nor in  the  formulation  of  the  party  election  programme,  membership  levels  of  the Green  party  rose  significantly  by  67%  between  2018  and  2022  (Statistisches Bundesamt 2024), in large  part due  to  the popularity  of  the Fridays for Future agenda  and  demonstrations,  which  energized  younger  generations  to  become more politically engaged, leading some to formally join the party, and increased the  party's  voter  base. Furthermore, Fridays for Future influenced  the  political discourse in Germany, making climate action a top issue in elections and political debates. In the 2021 national elections, the Greens placed third with 14.8% of the  vote  and  formed  a  coalition  with  the  Social  Democrats  (SPD)  and  Liberals (FDP). In November, they published a Coalition Agreement detailing, inter alia , plans  for  environmental  protection  and  energy  (SPD et  al. 2021).  One  month earlier,  Fridays  for  Future  published  its  demands  for  the  new  government, urging  action  in  the  first  100  days  to  meet  the  Paris  Agreement's  1.5-degree target  (Fridays  for  Future  2021;  Hackenbruch  2021).  Via  the  analysis  of  these documents and the  Greens'  election  manifesto  (Alliance  90/The  Greens  2021) , partly shaped by years of Fridays for Future protests, we illustrate how a policy demand  of  the  movement  successfully  made  its  way  from  a  movement  to  the party and then to the state legislation.

One of the key demands by the FFF in their 100Days document was 'The removal  of  all  (political)  brakes  on  the  expansion  of  solar  and  wind  energy' (Fridays for Future 2021). Interestingly, the Greens' proposals to that end are in fact more specific than that of FFF, namely they would like: for solar energy -to see the photovoltaics both on roofs and on the ground, to 'improv[e] the political and  legal  frameworks'  and  'mak[e]  construction  easier';  for  wind  energy  to 'speed  up  the  approval  process',  'reduc[e]  bureaucratic  hurdles'  and  'create clear framework  conditions' ( Alliance 90/The  Greens 2021: 22-23). The Coalition Agreement in this respect promises specifically:

'We  will  significantly accelerate  planning  and  approval  procedures.  [...]  We  are committed  to  effectively  relieving  the  regulatory  authorities  by  using  external project  teams.  The  start  of  the  legal  approval  periods  is  to  be ensured  by  clear requirements  for  the  application  documents . A  clarification  of  the  implementation deadlines for approvals should also be made.' ( SPD et al. 2021: 56) (our translation)

This  demonstrates  that,  in  comparison  with  the  FFF  demands  and  the Greens'  proposals,  the  coalition  agreement  suggests  even  more  detailed  and specific measures, and implies that the three political parties were able to reach an  easy  agreement  on  the  topic.  From  this,  we  can  conclude  that  the  policy demand for the removal of obstacles for the expansion of solar and wind energy strongly  survived  when  brought  to  the  institutional  settings,  namely  into  the government coalition plan. Moreover, the German parliament effectively passed the Easter Package in 2022 and Solar Package I in 2024 to significantly boost the development of renewable energy in Germany. For instance, the EEG amendment of 2023, included in the Easter Package, establishes a legal priority for  renewable  energy,  increases  compensation  for  solar  panels,  and  enhances financial involvement of local governments in wind energy projects (Bundesregierung 2023).

Apart from the FFF protests that amplified the importance of environmental  issues  for  a  growing  portion  of  the  electorate,  a  plausible explanation  for  this  strong  survival  of  the  policy  demand  lies  also  in  its  easy implementation, requiring just the removal of the (political) brakes on renewable energy. Indeed, it is easier to achieve a change in policy if the state just needs to adjust its regulations, rather than when new capacities have to be built (Majone 1997; Genschel and Jachtenfuchs 2016). On the other hand, in the existing political and social climate at the time, it would have been difficult for the  coalition  to  argue  why  these  obstacles  for  the  expansion  of  renewable energies  should  not  be  removed.  Thus,  through  a  close  alignment  of  the movement  and  movement  party's  agendas,  together  with  the  agenda -setting power  of  the  Fridays  for  Future  protests,  which  increased  the  salience  of  the issue in the country, and durable policy success was achieved by the Greens in via direct participation in the solution-formulation and decision-making processes.

Similarly,  the Five Star Movement in  Italy  was  able  to  directly  influence policies through governing, i.e. being a major partner in a government coalition. However, in the next example, we demonstrate that this type of policy impact is not  always  sustained  in  the  long  term,  if  the  right  conditions  are  not  met.

Introduction  of  the  universal  basic  income  ( reddito  di  cittadinanza/ RdC),  or citizenship income by the M5S was in fact considered the most prominent policy success of the party. The policy proposal itself developed during the party-phase of the M5S in 2013 (M5S 2013), although already as a social movement, the M5S' policy orientation towards more welfare expansion and a strong role of the state in the economy was clear and already present in the 2009 electoral programme, adopted at the time of the party's official foundation just as it was transformed from  being  a  social  movement.  The  2009  programme  eventually  became  the 2013 Elections manifesto without any major changes (Mosca and Tronconi 2019; M5S 2013). In his 'Tsunami tour' in 2013, Grillo often stated that 'no one will be left behind', hinting at the idea of the guaranteed minimum income (Mosca 2015: 159). Continuity with the movement's economic policy manifested in the senate M5S  group 's  2013  proposal for  the  universal  basic  income  of  780  Euros  per month for all people below the poverty threshold (Senato 2013). Moreover, two national  demonstrations  'Five  Star  Marches',  organized  in  2015  and  2017  in order  to  attract  public  attention  to  this  policy  proposal  and  to  give  it  more visibility ,  confirmed  the  policy's  alignment  with  the  movement  preferences  as well (della Porta et al. 2017; Mosca 2019: 364).

The M5S managed to introduce this ambitious proposal as a state policy early during their first government term (Conte I government) in January 2019 (voted  in  parliament  in  March  2019).  The  success  of  the  policy  proposal  was largely due to the high relevance of it for the party itself, the support from the social  movement  base,  and  the  significant  role  of  the  M5S  in  the  coalition government  with  the Lega . In fact, approval  of the RdC measure  was  a requirement on the M5S '  behal f  for  forming  the  coalition government  with  the Lega (Fischer and Giuliani 2023: 227). Being the majority party in the coalition, the M5S played a crucial role in garnering support for the  RdC proposal within the  parliament.  Moreover,  to  maintain  public  support  for  the  measure,  it continued to communicate with its base and the wider public, emphasizing the importance  of  the  RdC  as  a  means  of  addressing  economic  inequality  and providing assistance to those in need.  Partially, the RdC measure was meant to offset the stagnation and economic decline in Southern Italy, disproportionately affected  by  the  2011  Eurocrisis  state  budget  cuts  (Mayr  2023),  and  the  large

electoral base of the M5S in the Southern regions was one of the main reasons to keep this policy measure as a priority.

However, the success of this policy demand proved out short-lived, as no allies  of  the  policy  on  the  political  scene  were  insured  by  the  party  long-term. The  2022  national  elections  in  Italy  were  won  by  the  centre-right  coalition, which  included  the Lega party  and  had  campaigned  for  the  abolition  of  the citizens' income  measure  entirely.  With  the  new  government's drastically different outlook on economic policies, this policy did not survive the M5S  exit ' from  the  government  and  loss  of  any  influence  on  the  government  coalition. Whilst still in the coalition with the M5S, the Lega had to agree to measures that were problematic for the party's ideology, especially so with the RdC, because a universal basic income would benefit the poorer Southern regions of Italy at the expense  of,  in  the  Lega's  belief,  more  deserving  hard -working  people  of  the Northern  regions  (Fischer  and  Giuliani  2023).  Thus,  the  labour  market  and welfare  policy  preferences  of  the  M5S  and  Lega  widely  differed  from  the  very beginning,  and  the Lega only  unwillingly  accepted  the  policy  proposal  of  the majority  coalition  partner,  often  in  return  for  the  M5S  agreement  to  other reforms fit  to Lega 's  preferences (e.g.  on  migration).  Once  the  M5S  was  out  of government and the Meloni government was in, no supporters of a citizenship income policy remained in government. In the end, this measure was cancelled in the  2023  budget  and  substituted  by  two  alternative  anti-poverty  subsidies suggested by the Meloni government from 2024, which prioritized employment and integration into the labor market over unconditional income support.

This  development  shows  that  success  by  governing,  in  other  words, implementing one's key policy priorities while relying only on one's decisive role in  the  current  government formation, is not a recipe for a long-term sustained influence  on  the  policy  field.  On  the  contrary,  the  necessity  of  like-minded coalition partners for the durability of this policy impact path becomes clear in light  of  the  short-lived  M5SLega coalition,  their  highly  conflictual  coalition politics, and subsequent policy change by the centre-right coalition.


## Type 4. Policy demand success at the movement-to-movement party stage, but no policy adoption by institutions


In  this  last  type  of  policy  impact  by  movement  parties,  we  turn  the  attention towards  partially  successful  policy  cases,  specifically  to  the  instances  of  the policy  demand  travelling  from  the  social  movement  to  the  movement  party agenda, but not making it into the state institutions or legislation in the end. The reasons  for  not  pursuing  its  policy  demands  can  vary  from  the  absence  of political will by the party leaders, lack of allies in the parliament, to simply the role  change for the movement party -i.e. losing  its  protest-against-the-system character  and  becoming  an  actor  within  the  establishment  itself,  prioritising office-seeking over policy-seeking goals (Strøm 1990).

The first example of this type concerns the policy demand of the Fridays for Future movement in Germany for independent control of climate protection. One of their key demands was the ' Introduction of a mechanism to check all laws and infrastructure projects for compatibility with the CO2 budget' (Fridays for Future 2021), where the FFF pushed for a 1.5 degree target compliant budget for Germany (Hackenbruch 2021). In their 2021 electoral program, the Greens also advocated for  systematically  'incorporat[ing]  climate  protection'  into  the  legal system.  They  proposed  a  'CO2  brake'  to  make  climate  protection  a  cross -sectoral  task  by  reviewing  laws  for  climate  impact,  ensuring  alignment  with national  climate  targets,  and  promoting  climate-friendly  alternatives  (Alliance 90/The Greens 2021: 20-21). However, the Greens did not explicitly commit to the  1.5-degree  target  (18-19).  In  fact,  the  measures  proposed  by  them  were shown  to  only  limit  global  warming  to  1.75  degrees  (Kuhnehenn et al. 2021), already  demonstrating  insufficient  alignment  with  the  goals  of  the Fridays for Future movement. In turn, the Coalition Agreement omitted any reference to a CO2 budget and only proposed making climate protection a cross-sectoral task by  requiring  relevant  departments  to  review  their  bills'  climate  impact  and alignment  with  national  targets,  providing  appropriate  justification  (climate check) (SPD et al. 2021: 55).

Therefore, despite the mention of a 'climate check', the coalition actually did not commit to any specific targets or budget measures nor to an independent

control of the legislation and infrastructure projects for compliance with the CO2 budget.  Thus,  the  goal  of 'systematically  incorporat ing  climate  protection  into the legal system'  by the Greens did not pass the coalition negotiations successfully  and  has  only  partially  reflected  the  policy  demand  of  the  FFF movement  at  the  party  agenda  stage.  This  is  not  entirely  surprising,  since achieving and agreeing on a 1,5 degree compliant CO2 budget is not an easy task in  the  first  place,  requires  a  lot  of  state  resources  and  political  will,  and,  in  a coalition  government  context,  it  is  harder  to  achieve  progress  on  this  goal compared  with  the  example  of  removing  obstacles  for  the  renewable  energy expansion.

The second example of this type of weak policy success is provided by the M5S party in Italy and  a set of their proposals for having a smaller and 'clean parliament' in Italy. At the movement stage, Beppe Grillo advocated in favour of this  concept  and  even  created  lists  of  parliamentarians  with  previous  criminal convictions, which they would have liked to see removed from office. A popular initiative (citizens' petition) for this goal was started: 'clean parliament' was one of the key demands of the V-Day public demonstration in September 2007, which made the Movement enter the national arena for  the  first  time  (Campus et al. 2021: 146-147). With this event, the M5S managed to gather 450,000 signatures for their three legislative initiatives for a 'clean parliament' (Biorcio 2014: 40). This  topic  was  kept  in  the  movement  party's  agenda  after  the  party's  official foundation. The M5S argued against corruption, for 'zero cost politics', meaning -that politics should not become a person's career or a way to make money. They have implemented these ideas within the party and prohibited those who had a criminal record to run for public office. Furthermore, Grillo introduced the rule of limiting the terms of office for MPs to two, without any possibility to run again (Beppe Grillo's blog 2011).

While the 2018 election campaign goal of the M5S to reduce the Italian parliament by one third has been successful through the introduction of relevant legislation and a referendum vote on this in 2020 (BBC 2019), their proposals of a 'clean parliament' with no criminal convictions and the rule on the two -terms limit  for  MPs  only  remained  at  the  party  level  and  have  not  been  introduced

further into state institutions. With regards to the latter though, already in 2019 the party representatives, including Di Maio, sought to bypass or abolish the twoterm limit for MPs, concerned that enforcing it would force many  of their own experienced  MPs  and  councilors  to  resign,  causing  the  party  to  lose  valuable political experience (Reuters 2019).

Hence, the M5S successfully implemented many of its proposed measures at the party level and influenced the adoption of some new laws aimed at fighting corruption  and  "changing  politics."  However,  the  success  of  these  initiatives often relied on having the right coalition partner. For example, the constitutional reform  was  introduced  only  in  the  coalition  with  the  PD,  not  with  the Lega . Additionally, some measures rooted in the movement's early ideals of transparency and the frequent rotation of representatives were later abandoned by  the  party,  as  the  practicalities  of  parliamentary  experience  rendered  these limits inconvenient for their MPs.

Therefore, these cases demonstrate that despite an initial success of the policy  demand  of  a  movement in  making  it  to  the  movement  party's  agenda , becoming an establishment actor comes with certain sacrifices, as party leaders renege on some proposals for the coalition's, party's , or personal careers' sake. This  puts  in  question  to  what  extent  a  movement  party  can  be  considered  as representing its associated social movement(s)  and  protecting the policy demands of the movement s participants. If becoming part of the establishment ' leads to reconsideration of the party's priorities and preferences for policies, can the  movement  parties  claim  to  be  much  different  from  other  political  parties, which  they  often  criticize  for  making  politics  a  profession  and  neglecting  the needs  of  the  population?  Movements  like  the Fridays  for  Future  Germany , or several minor movements in Italy that supported the M5S at its initial stages in election campaigns can be and are quite critical of the political representation of their  interests  by  the  German  Greens  and  the  M5S.  This  invites  for  further research  into  the  coherence  of  the  promises  and  actual  policy  impact  and achievements by the movement parties to assess their capacity for representation of citizens upon entering state institutions.


## V Conclusions


This article analysed the ability of the movement parties to transmit the policy demands of the social movements they are associated with into state institutions legislation. A capacity to do that speaks to the democratic representation of the citizens  by  the  movement  parties.  We  were  interested  in  the  varieties  of pathways  through  which  movement  parties  can  channel  policy  demands  and achieve  policy  impact  and  identified  several  of  them  with  empirical  evidence from the four selected parties.

In this article, we  set  out  a  preliminary  typology  of  policy  impact pathways. Regardless of a movement  party being in government or in opposition, there are ways to influence policy-making or to fail doing so despite having  good  electoral  results.  In  fact,  electoral  success  is  not  automatically translated  to  policy  impact  success.  Instead,  intervening  at  the  agenda-setting stage of the policy cycle is particularly important. Via implicit agenda-setting and influencing voter priorities, paying attention to the demands of social movements and pushing them onto the agenda, parties can achieve significant impact, regardless of the ideological leaning of the party. Explicit agenda-setting, when  the  movement  party  is  in  a  government  coalition,  for  example,  is  also helped by closer alignment with prominent social movements, as other coalition partners become more receptive towards corresponding policy proposals. Issue priorities  and  alignment  with  the  movement  are  key  to  the  policy  success. Moreover, older generations of movement parties can benefit from aligning their policy  agenda  with  recent  social  movements  and  revitalize  their  role  in  the country's  political  system. In  addition,  we  confirmed  that  it  is  easier  to  exert policy influence in a coalition setting, when  the  policy change  demands adjustment in regulations rather than resource redistribution.

Our evidence suggests that when a party engages in direct policy-making from  a  position  of  power  within  a  coalition,  it  may  initially  achieve  more prominent  and  impactful  policy  outcomes.  However,  if  these  results  are  not grounded  in  genuine  consensus  with  coalition  partners  or  other allies in parliament,  they  are  vulnerable  to  reversal  when  a  new  governing  coalition assumes power. This underlines the importance of forming government

coalitions  with  parties  that  agree  at  least  on  the  principle  and  direction  of  the most  important  policy  issues  (if  not  on  the  extent  of  them).  Implications  for public policy and coalition governance research are that ideologically heterogenous coalitions are risky not just for stability of the coalition, but also for policy durability.

Results of this analysis also imply  that political  representation of issues important  for  citizens  by  movement  parties  is  not  only  possible,  but  often beneficial for the policy influence of the party in the institutions, as success can be  achieved  without  a  majority  role  or  even  without  significant  parliamentary representation by the party. High prioritization of a policy issue by citizens might instead  lead  to  the  cooptation  of  a  movement  party's  policy  demand  by  other major  political  parties,  concerned  with  preserving  office  or  votes  in  the  next elections.

Our  results  confirm  our  expectation,  that  for  movement  parties  as  well election  programmes  predict  they  legislative  policy  priorities  (Brouard et  al. 2018), but several policy cases demonstrate a weakening of the links between a social movement and a movement party as the latter becomes an establishment actor or enters the government. Although at first sharing similar policy demands with the associated social movement  and  partially advocating for them, movement parties  might  significantly  change  their  policy  preferences,  as  they enter  the  establishment  and  start  prioritizing  their  office-seeking  role  of  a political party (Strøm 1990) over the policy-seeking goal of the social movements.  These  cases  support  the  hypothesis  that  movement  parties,  once they  enter  the  political  arena,  begin  to  operate  under  dynamics  distinct  from those of social movements (Mosca 2019). The findings show that they diverge from their original policy goals, either due to institutional or coalition constraints -consistent with insights from the literature on mandate responsiveness  and  democratic  representation  (Guinaudeau  and  Guinaudeau 2023) -or  driven  by  their  own  political  expediency.  This  puts  into  question whether  a  movement  party  can  better  represent  citizens  involved  in  social movements  or  experiencing  grievances  from  the  political  status  quo  than  the established parties do, as it becomes more integrated into the political system.

However, the  insight  that  moderate  to  low  electoral  success  of  political parties  does  not  preclude  significant  policy  influence  of  those  parties  on  state policies is especially important in the context of the emerging movement parties and  their  connection  with  social  movements -it appears  that  even  if  the movement is only able to secure little representation through a movement party (or sometimes, by choice, through other established parties) in parliament, this political representation can help achieve important policy goals for the movement, at least while the issue salience remains high.

## Introduction


Young children and older adults are at elevated risk of experiencing severe complications from infection with Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV). In adult populations aged 65 and older (the subject of the present research), infection with RSV is estimated to result in as many as 160,000 hospitalizations and 10,000 deaths in a typical year (Havers et al., 2023).

Adult RSV vaccines were approved and made available for public use for adults aged 60 or older in Fall 2023. While these vaccines substantially reduce the likelihood that older adults will experience severe complications from RSV infection (Falsey et al., 2023), less than 1 in 5 US adults over the age of 60 opted to receive the vaccine by the end of the 2023 calendar year (CDC 2024a). These figures differ sharply from the share of Americans aged 60 or older who received an updated COVID-19 shot in 2023 (approximately 37%; CDC 2024b), and the approximately 69% who received their annual flu shot during the same timespan (CDC 2024c).

Promoting RSV vaccine uptake through strategic health communication messaging could help reduce the hospitalization and mortality burdens borne by those most at risk of severe complications from RSV infection. Yet, to date, few have considered what effective RSV vaccine promotion messages might look like. We remedy this shortcoming by applying what we refer to as reversal narrative messaging to a novel communication framework for RSV vaccine promotion.

Reversal Narratives (RN) are a class of strategic health communication messages that make an effort to describe (a) a message source or target (i.e., the subject of a message) as holding opinions or exhibiting behaviors at odds with evidence-based medicine, which they then (b) came to update in response to some stimulus or stimuli (e.g., a negative health outcome), in order to (c) encourage those who share the message source/target's initial position to change their attitudes and behaviors as well. For example, popular press stories (e.g., Farmer 2021) about COVID-19 vaccine skeptics who experienced hospitalization as a result of infection with the virus -- and who subsequently urge others to avoid meeting a similar fate by opting to receive the vaccine -- could be fashioned into RN messages promoting vaccine uptake.

The idea that skeptics who "see the light" can be effective health communicators is grounded in social psychological research on source credibility and trust. People are more likely to accept (and act on) messages sourced by individuals they trust (Chaiken 1980; Pornpitakpan 2004; Ismagilova et al., 2020). Reversal narratives establish trust by employing what we might colloquially refer to as the "I was like you" heuristic; i.e., by identifying common ground between the (current) attitudes/behaviors of a message's audience, and the (past) attitudes/behaviors of the messenger. Correspondingly, people holding views at odds with the evidence-based medicine should become more likely to embrace scientific evidence upon being exposed to reversal narrative messages.

Although past research on the persuasive power of RNs in vaccine communication contexts is limited, previous work offers suggestive evidence that they may be effective at changing health attitudes and behaviors. For example, in a naturally occurring quasi-experiment, Stecula and colleagues (2022) find that when prominent daytime talk show host Dr. Mehmet Oz-- who had previously given a platform to vaccine skeptical voices on his show -- devoted an episode of his program toward combating MMR vaccine hesitancy in the wake of the 2019 Rockland Measles Outbreak, regular viewers who knew the least about vaccine science came to hold significantly more positive views toward MMR vaccination. Relatedly, a survey-based randomized controlled trial embedded in a convenience sample of US adults (Borah et al., 2022) found that exposure to narrative messaging emphasizing the regret an unvaccinated person experienced upon being hospitalized with COVID-19 was associated with increased vaccination intentions relative to a message providing statistics about the benefits of vaccine uptake.

While past work raises the possibility that reversal narratives can indeed be effective at changing vaccine-related attitudes and behaviors, there is much researchers still do not know about their effectiveness. For example, vaccine-related reversal narratives may take one of several forms; including both the regret some may experience as a result of not vaccinating, as well as efforts to rationalize why one updated their previously held beliefs in response to new information. Additionally, whether or not findings derived from research on highly-salient public health problems like the COVID-19 pandemic and recent Measles outbreaks might generalize to less-salient issues -- e.g., vaccination against RSV; where the risks of not vaccinating may appear less obvious -- remains an open question. More generally, the accumulation of RCT evidence pointing in favor of the reversal narrative approach, in its many potential forms, can help further underscore its viability as a persuasive health communication tactic.


## Expectations & Analytical Strategy


We suspect that exposure to both forms of RN messaging will be associated with increased intentions to receive an RSV vaccine among eligible sub-populations (i.e., those aged 60 or older) in the Fall 2024 vaccination cycle. We test H1a-d this expectation by (a) presenting weighted mean comparisons of vaccine uptake across experimental conditions, and (b) constructing multivariate linear probability models that regress dichotomous indicators of vaccine acceptance (see Table 3 for a full list) on dichotomous indicators of experimental treatment assignment (with assignment to the study's control condition serving as an analytic baseline; see Experimental Design). We apply survey weights in the estimation of both sets of models.

In the event that formal balance tests listed in Table 2 document demographic asymmetries in treatment assignment as a result of random chance, we had planned to amend these models to control for any demographic variables distributed unequally across groups; as indicated in our pre-analysis plan. As we note in Table 1, however, we documented no evidence of demographic imbalance across conditions.


## Experimental Design


In this study, we test the effectiveness of two different forms of RN messaging.

The first form of RN messaging is what we refer to as the Regret-Based Reversal Narrative ("Regret," for short). Regret-Based RN Messages aim to inspire vaccine acceptance by highlighting the personal stories of those who feel as if their prior vaccine-related (in)action caused them to experience some type of health-related misfortune.

Similar to the previously-mentioned study conducted by Borah and colleagues (2022), we present experimental subjects with a text-based narrative message -- taking the form of a short newspaper story -- detailing the experiences of a person who (a) refused to receive a RSV vaccine, (b) became seriously sick as a result of failing to get the vaccine, and (c) expressed regret about their decision to not vaccinate, in order to (d) highlight the benefits of receiving an RSV vaccine. The treatment materials were adapted from a real news story about an unvaccinated man who died from complications related to a severe case of COVID-19, and featured lightly modified quotations from his experience in order to better suit the story to our experimental design (and focus on RSV). Experimental treatment text is provided in full in Table 1.

The second form of RN messaging we test is what we refer to as the Rationalization-Based Reversal Narrative ("Rationalizing," for short). Rationalizing RN messages aim to provide audiences with information about why individuals opted to change their mind about their previous vaccine-skeptical stances.

Inspired by the program studied in Stecula and colleagues' (2022) research, this approach -- structured analogously to the first (and again summarized in Table 1) -- also made an effort to present a story about someone who previously held vaccine-skeptical views about the RSV vaccine. This time, though, the messenger walks the reader through how their analysis of both the potential risks of RSV and scientific evidence about the benefits of RSV vaccination led them to change their mind. Like the Regret message, the Rationalizing message also concludes with an appeal for respondents to vaccinate against RSV.

Respondents in our representative state and national samples (see: Data) were randomly assigned to read either the Regret RN message, Rationalizing RN message, or to receive no message at all (the study's control group). To increase compliance with the study's intent to treat (ITT) design, we informed respondents that they would be required to answer questions about what they just read later on in this study, and (if assigned to read either RN message) required them to spend at least 15 seconds on the page including the treatment materials.

## Data & Measures



## Data


We assess the effectiveness of two different forms of RN messaging in a series of RCTs embedded in a representative survey of Rhode Island - a state among the nation's leaders in elective adult vaccine uptake (N = 800), as well as in a nationally representative sample of the US adult population (N = 1,000). Given the focus of this RCT on RSV vaccination, both the RI (N = 50) and national (N = 300) surveys will included of the adult population aged 60 or older. We conducted both surveys in partnership with the Rhode Island Department of Health, and limited our analysis to just those respondents aged 60 or older (N = 504 in the national sample; N = 202 in the Rhode Island sample).

One major benefit of our approach is that it allows us to assess the effectiveness of RN messaging in both a "hard test" case study where we may be less likely to observe experimental treatment effects -i.e., in a state that is among the national leaders in RSV vaccine uptake -- and to assess its scalability into a national messaging strategy. Documenting evidence of RN messaging effectiveness in both contexts would provide strong evidence in favor of its efficacy; even in locations where vaccine uptake is relatively (albeit insufficiently) high.

We will conduct both surveys in partnership with YouGov, which will use propensity score matching methods to recruit state (RR = 87%) and nationally representative (RR = 88%) samples of each population under investigation. To account for any remaining deviations between the US and RI publics that may occur as a result of random sampling error, YouGov calculated post-stratification weights that adjusted for respondents age, racial identification, gender identification, educational attainment, household income, and political partisanship. We apply these survey weights throughout our analyses. For reference, Table 2 summarizes the basic demographic composition of each sample.
