## 5. Discussion


Our results give insights on leveraging LLMs for stance detection in applied social science research. On the one hand, results speak to the potential of LLMs for stance detection and hint toward best practices in applications. On the other hand, results show potential limitations and biases with zero-shot prompting specifically.

First, we evaluated a number of LLMs, which crucially differed in size between 8B (8 billion parameters) and 70B (70 billion parameters) models. The much larger 70B model outperformed the smaller models, which is unsurprising. However, what is interesting is the magnitude of the difference in performance, keeping in mind that at upper ends of performance level for machine learning models in general, performance gains are usually not linearly scaling with model complexity. 70B models show increased performance across all implemented prompt chains, but some 8B models almost approached their performance for the best performing prompt chains. Given that larger models come with much higher inference costs and are much more challenging to deploy, this suggests that smaller models may be worth applying in applied research contexts, if a well performing application method can be found.

Second, we evaluated a number of differently constructed prompt chains. Results show that of the two most performant prompt chains ( sis shown in Figure 6, and is2 displayed in Figure 8, in our evaluation), one is relatively short in comparison and both contain a summary step. In a summary step, we prompted the LLM to summarize the input text with regard to the statement to evaluate against first, before classification. Going forward, these results suggest that a lower number of components within a prompt chain, if feasible, is preferable and that complex classification tasks can be improved by leveraging summarization capabilities of models.

Third, when it comes to limitations and biases to be aware of in applying LLMs for stance detection, entity masking (thus masking the entity for which the stance is evaluated by substitution with a generic string) should be considered. In our evaluations, entity masking did not lead to statistically detectable differences in performance across evaluation runs. These results should not be considered evidence for absence of bias, as we tested for impacts on performance, not bias. Rather, taking a precautionary approach, given that evidence strongly suggests that applications of LLMs always need to consider subtle and not so subtle biases (Dai et al. 2024; Prakash and Lee 2023), our results support the application of entity masking, given that performance penalties seem minimal.

Fourth, our results show that performance depends to an extent on specific statements stances are evaluated against. In our case, zero-shot prompting performed particularly well in relation to predicting stances toward reducing air traffic, and to a lesser extent, reducing parking spaces and lowering speed limits to decrease emissions. This variability may be attributed to the inherent differences in stances on these issues or to the linguistic complexities involved in detecting them. A similar pattern was observed during the manual annotation process, though it was most pronounced in the case of parking space reduction, which exhibited relatively low agreement among human annotators. Overall, using LLMs for stance detection is thus very likely not statement-agnostic and researchers should be careful with assuming that evaluation results in different contexts may apply to their specific research domains.

Lastly, we want to put our results in the context of the overall challenge of annotating realworld data. The annotation of stances on real-world data presents a significant challenge not only for statistical models, but also for human annotators, as qualitative researchers have

known for decades (and as the IAA scores reported in this article show). The performance of automated stance detection approaches therefore also should not be judged against unrealistic expectations. Properly annotating or classifying stances is hard because ambiguities and nuances in language, such as sarcasm or irony, can make it challenging to accurately capture stances, as mediated through a written medium, but also because of the real-world complexity of stances held by humans, which might not always neatly confirm to the categories we want to classify them into.

We also want to mention one last limitation of our study, which is the context supplied to annotators and LLM classification. We annotated stances within newspaper paragraphs, mostly due to considerations of computational efficiency in data processing (as the stance detection model was part of a larger processing pipeline) and to be able to create a test set of similarly sized, comparable units. However, the larger context of the overall article a paragraph is part of is lost in this approach and likely could have improved performance for human annotators as well as for the statistical models.


## 6. Conclusion


Many months into what can only be described as a hype around LLMs, many researchers across different fields of the social sciences are finding out that their application is no panacea for substantially complex research problems. Rather, utilising these general-purpose language models to specific tasks in empirical research brings with it new challenges alongside marginal benefits. Our analysis of employing and evaluating LLMs in an applied social science research context for stance detection is very much in line with this.

Stance detection is a complex process, both for humans and statistical models. In this study, we evaluated one-shot stance classifications with LLMs towards five distinct statements. Our results warrant cautious optimism regarding the application of LLMs for stance detection in applied empirical social science contexts. Given evaluation metrics obtained, applied researchers should experiment with, but not blindly utilize them. In many ways, this is the overall conclusion of our study: LLMs are general purpose models, which need high quality, context-sensitive evaluations, if applied in specific contexts. As in many areas of social science methodology, progress requires translation of theoretical models into application and continuous testing and re-testing of tools, gathering evidence on performance and bias across diverse application contexts. We look forward to seeing more studies in this vein.

## Introduction


In recent years, English educational researchers have gained much attention for linguistic features of learners' oral performance (Hsieh & Wang, 2019). Analyzing oral characteristics across different  proficiency  levels  enabled  researchers  to  investigate  the  progression  of  speaking proficiency as it evolved (Gu & Hsieh, 2019). Researchers employed various teaching methods and strategies to examine the impact on learners' oral proficiency (Wulan Wuryantari et al., 2019; Tiu et al., 2023). Project-Based Learning (PBL), as a highly communicative teaching method, was widely employed to incorporate to develop EFL learners' oral proficiency (Sirisrimangkorn, 2021; Firdaus & Septiady, 2023). PBL offers students ample opportunities to improve their oral fluency, accuracy, and  the  overall quality of  their work  throughout  the  different stages of  the  project (Thakur  et  al.,  2019).  Participation in  PBL  within  authentic learning  environments has  been demonstrated to enhance students' language skills, content knowledge, and cognitive abilities (Sari & Tridinanti, 2021; Hairuddin & Irmawati, 2024).

The previous studies reveal that PBL could enhance learners' various features of speaking proficiency (Bataineh et al., 2020; Zubaidi & Suharto, 2024). Kristianto and Harendita (2022) reported that students perceived PBL as an effective learning method to enhance their vocabulary, grammar, and fluency. Zubaidi and  Suharto's study (2024)  indicated that PBL  could improve students' speaking  skills in  pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary,  fluency,  and  understanding. However,  these studies on  oral  performance within  PBL  focus  primarily on  five overarching conceptual  categories  commonly  scrutinized  in  empirical  research:  fluency,  pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary,  and  content. These  studies used  human ratings to  assess students' oral features.  Only  one  study  examined  the  changes  in  EFL  learners'  oral  features  after  PBL implementation based on objective measurement of complexity, accuracy, and fluency (Spring, 2020).  Limited studies  investigated different proficiency learners' complexity,  accuracy,  and fluency.

This study aimed to examine the changes in complexity, accuracy, and  fluency among learners of different proficiency levels in a PBL context and to identify the linguistic features in their oral performance. Two research questions are addressed in this study.

- 1. What  are  the  changes  in  different proficiency  learners'  complexity,  accuracy,  and fluency before and after using PBL?
- 2. What are the linguistic features of different proficiency learners' complexity, accuracy, and fluency in a PBL context?


## Literature Review


PBL, rooted in social constructivism, is a student-centered pedagogical approach where students collaborate in groups and engage in social interactions to address problems (Torres & Rodríguez,  2017).  PBL  creates opportunities for  students to  tackle real-world issues,  linking learning to personal experiences by establishing connections beyond the classroom. It shifts from a teacher-centered  to a student-centered  method,  providing  English  learners  with more opportunities to use the target language in real communicative situations.

PBL  has  been  extensively  utilized  to  enhance  students'  oral  proficiency  in  English language  education (Mohamad & Tamer, 2021; Imbaquingo & Cárdenas, 2023). Researchers employed various instruments to evaluate the impact of PBL on students' speaking proficiency. Several studies utilized speaking tests to examine the influence of PBL on oral features such as fluency,  accuracy,  vocabulary,  pronunciation,  and  grammar  (Zare-Behtash  &  Sarlak,  2017).

## Research Design


This study utilized a one-group pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design. This research design is advantageous when a random assignment of participants to groups or the inclusion of a control group is not feasible (Abbuhl et al., 2013). By employing this design, the study aimed to compare and  describe the  linguistic features of  oral  performance among  learners of  different proficiency levels before and after implementing PBL.

## Participants


A homogeneous group of 45 Chinese college students from an  oral English class at  a polytechnic was selected for this study. The participants, aged from 17 to 21, consisted of 2 males and 43 females. They were divided into three subgroups based on their oral performance in the pretest. Two instructors evaluated the participants' complexity, accuracy, and fluency using a fivepoint scale modified by Nitta and Nakatsuhara (2014). According to the distribution of mean scores in the pretest, the learners were categorized into high (N=15), medium (N=15), and low (N=15) proficiency groups. These learners participated in the study to investigate the various changes and characteristics of complexity, accuracy, and fluency in a PBL context.


## Data Collection


Data collection for this study spanned 12 weeks and included six primary project-based activities: topic discussion, plan report, scaffolding activities, project development, presentation, and evaluation. The initial data collection instruments were oral pretests and posttests. The pretest was  administered  before  implementing PBL,  and  the  posttest  was  conducted  afterward.  A descriptive task from the second phase of the IELTS Speaking Test was employed in the study. This phase was selected because its format and content closely matched the course instruction. The pretest and posttest covered five similar topics. During the tests, participants received a task card prompting them to discuss a specific topic and were given two minutes to take notes and prepare.

The second instrument involved transcriptions of students' oral performances in both the pretest and posttest, converting their spoken language into written form (Bailey, 2008). These transcriptions enabled  the  researchers to  analyze  learners' complexity, accuracy,  and  fluency within  the  PBL  context.  Despite  being  a  time-consuming process,  transcribing oral  language allowed for more detailed detection of  specific aspects of learners' oral performance, such as syntactic complexity, syntactic accuracy, and self-repairs.


## Data Analysis


In this study, complexity was assessed through syntactic and lexical measures. Syntactic complexity was determined by the average number of words per AS-unit (Norris & Ortega, 2009). Lexical complexity was evaluated using the type-token ratio (TTR) (Daller et al., 2003). Accuracy was  measured  by  syntactic  accuracy  and  pronunciation  accuracy.  Syntactic  accuracy  was calculated based on  the proportion of error-free AS-units (Michel, 2017),  while pronunciation accuracy was  determined by  the  percentage of  correctly pronounced words,  facilitated by  the IFlytek Voice Input app known for its high accuracy in converting spoken words into text (Liu et al., 2019). Fluency analysis focused on speech rate, measured in syllables per minute (Yousefi, 2016), and self-repairs, assessed by the rate of corrected syllables per minute (Skehan, 2003).

Following  data  collection  and  analysis,  one-way  ANOVA tests  were  employed  to determine whether statistically significant improvements were observed among learners of varying proficiency levels. Post hoc comparisons using the Tukey HSD  test were conducted to explore further differences between high, medium, and low-proficiency learners.

The complexity, accuracy, and fluency of oral transcripts were meticulously analyzed using specific coding protocols. Dependent clauses were enclosed in brackets [...] following Foster et al. (2000). Grammatical errors were indicated by underlining. Self-repairs, such as repetitions, selfcorrections, false starts, and reconstructions, were denoted with {...}. Reconstructed or restarted words  or  phrases  were  annotated  with  an  em  dash  (-)  at  the  end.  The  primary  researcher

## Discussion


This study examined the changes and linguistic features of different proficiency learners' complexity, accuracy, and fluency in the PBL context. The findings of this study reveal different changes  and  linguistic  features  in  complexity,  accuracy,  and  fluency  among  the  different proficiency learners after they participated in PBL. As for complexity, PBL significantly enhances syntactic complexity across different proficiency levels. High proficiency learners demonstrated the use of various dependent clauses, including noun and adverbial clauses, and complex AS-units with  nested  dependent  clauses.  Medium  proficiency  learners  employed  dependent  clauses predominantly in  noun and  adverbial forms related to time and  reason, while low  proficiency learners also  utilized these  clauses, mainly focusing on  noun  and  adverbial structures. These findings are consistent with the Torres and Rodríguez' s study (2017) in which PBL could improve students' oral production. In PBL activities, learners are asked to explore, negotiate, interpret, and create in an attempt to construct solutions (Lee, 2015). Both learners and teachers focus on the process of learning which involves developing language and content knowledge or completing the actual  project  work  (Park  &  Hiver,  2017).  In  such  a  PBL  context,  learners  with  different proficiency levels increased their syntactic complexity.

Significant  differences  in  lexical  complexity  were  observed  between  high  and  low proficiency learners following PBL.  High proficiency learners could acquire a  more extensive vocabulary  and  construct  more  complex  sentences,  likely  facilitated by  their  engagement  in information search and project material exploration. PBL supports vocabulary development and enhances oral production (Torres & Rodríguez, 2017), offering students opportunities to analyze, evaluate, and  discuss real-world problems within a classroom setting, thereby deepening their knowledge through project design and construction (Aminah & Maulida, 2021). However, low proficiency learners, constrained by limited linguistic resources, tend to express content using a narrower vocabulary. As learners progress from lower to higher levels of oral proficiency, they typically employ more precise and specific vocabulary, reflecting their development in spoken language  skills (Wang  &  Zhou,  2023).  These  findings  resonate with  Ellis's (2005)  research, suggesting that higher-proficiency learners possess a larger repertoire of linguistic chunks and use them more fluently than their lower-proficiency counterparts.

In terms  of  accuracy,  high  proficiency  learners  demonstrated  significantly  greater pronunciation accuracy compared to low proficiency learners in the PBL context. These findings are  consistent  with  Iwashit's  (2006)  research,  which  found  that  higher  proficiency  learners

generally produce more  accurate speech  than  those at  lower  proficiency levels. PBL  offers a practical context for language practice and allows learners to integrate pronunciation skills into their project activities, which facilitates the retention and application of correct pronunciation in relevant contexts. High proficiency learners, who often possess strong autonomous learning skills, could self-correct their pronunciation errors, leading to significant improvements in pronunciation accuracy within the PBL framework.

However,  no  significant differences were  observed in  syntactic accuracy among  high, medium, and low proficiency learners. Analysis of oral transcripts revealed ongoing grammatical errors across all proficiency levels. High proficiency learners commonly made errors related to past tense usage, while medium proficiency learners struggled with errors involving past tense, plural forms, third person singular, and personal pronouns. Additionally, low proficiency learners exhibited errors primarily in sentence structures. This lack of improvement in accuracy can be attributed to the communicative nature of PBL, which prioritizes real-world communication over explicit grammar instruction (Spring, 2020).  Teachers  in  PBL  settings typically do  not  focus directly on teaching grammar rules, which may explain why there was no noticeable enhancement in oral accuracy across college learners with varying proficiency levels over time.

Regarding fluency, significant differences in self-repairs were found between high and low proficiency learners. High  proficiency learners showed a  notable decrease in  repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections following their participation in PBL, contrasting with the ongoing selfrepair tendencies observed in low proficiency learners. More proficient speakers tend to engage more actively in speaking activities within the PBL environment, as noted by Akpur (2021), who highlights a direct link between proficiency levels and class participation. In PBL settings, higher proficiency learners typically demonstrate greater involvement in group discussions and willingly respond  to  teacher  prompts,  enhancing  their  oral  fluency  through  increased  interaction  and practice. As a result, the impact of PBL on fluency is particularly evident when comparing learners with high and low proficiency levels.

However, no significant differences were found in speech rate among learners of different proficiency levels. All three subgroups showed similar increases in speech rate after engaging in PBL activities. PBL creates a supportive and interactive environment where students collaborate on various project-based tasks, such as group discussions, interviews, field trips, and role-plays, all  conducted  in  English.  As  group  members adjust  to  engaging  with  each  other,  consistent communication helps learners feel less anxious when  speaking (Avsheniuk et al.,  2023). This supportive PBL environment contributes to enhanced oral fluency as students feel more relaxed and motivated to communicate in English (Torres & Rodríguez, 2017; Widiyati & Pangesti, 2022). Consequently, learners across various proficiency levels experienced comparable improvements in speech rate within the PBL context, where speaking English became a natural and integral part of their collaborative project work.


## Conclusions


This study aimed to examine how PBL influenced the complexity, accuracy, and fluency of learners across different proficiency levels. Significant enhancements in syntactic complexity were  noted  across  varying  proficiency  levels.  High  and  low  proficiency  learners  differed significantly in lexical complexity, pronunciation accuracy, and self-repairs. However, no notable differences  were  found  in  syntactic  accuracy  and  speech  rate  among  learners  of  different proficiency levels. Successful teaching and learning are now synonymous with the use of technology in ESL classrooms. ESL teachers in Malaysia have additional options and resources to improve teaching and learning, ultimately improving the experience gained by the students. The performance of pupils in Malaysian schools, as well as their overall fluency in English, has been the focus of multiple initiatives spearheaded by the Ministry of Education. The Malaysian Education Blueprint 2013-2025 emphasises the teacher's responsibility to incorporate ICT into teaching and learning process as it relates to globalised learning (Bakar, 2020). The Malaysian government prioritises Information and Communication Technology (ICT) innovation to enhance teaching and learning processes. Based on the Malaysian Education Blueprint, the Frog Virtual Learning Environment (Frog VLE) is one of the methods proposed to meet the educational needs of Malaysian students (Mai & Muruges 2018). ## Reading skills in primary ESL classrooms


Reading comprehension is a multifaceted and taxing cognitive process that takes place through  active  interaction  between  the  reader  and  the  text  (Choi  &  Zhang  2021).  Reading comprehension  often  becomes  arduous  for  pupils  with  poor  reading  ability  since  they  do  not acquire the necessary knowledge, vocabulary and skill to understand the text. Reading impacts learners'  development  through  the  acquisition  of  phonics,  vocabulary,  and  sentence  structures which  lead to comprehension  of  the reading material. Reading  comprehension  requires understanding at the word level and actively engaging with the reading content to create a mental representation of the text. The study conducted by Abdullah and Yunus (2019) revealed that pupils face difficulties in deriving and understanding information from texts due to their lack of schemata and vocabulary, which ultimately leads to poor reading skills. Lim, Eng, Mohamed and Ismail (2018) also supported that reading comprehension becomes challenging, and disadvantageous for pupils with poor reading ability. However, to become successful users of a second language, there is a great need to improve reading skills. Pupils will be able to learn and read with comprehension provided with the right aid, technique, media and teaching strategies (Putri & Tiarina, 2021)

The issues faced by ESL learners during reading class can be improved with the integration of  technology.  This  generation  of  ESL  learners  is  more  exposed  to  technology  and  has  more interest in learning with the introduction of technology in the classroom. Learners interact with text  effectively  with  the  help  of  technology  in  the  reading  classroom  and  proper  classroom strategies (Ariffin & Razali, 2019). Pupils gradually have the potential to understand the reading processes and the interaction needed with the text when the learning processes are eased with the integration of technology. The use of technology in reading classes has significantly improved pupils'  learning  experience,  supported  comprehension  of  the  text  and  developed  reading  skills (Bani-Hamad & Abdullah, 2019; Samat & Aziz, 2020). Reading activities can be supported by an array  of  social  media  platforms  such  as  TikTok,  Facebook,  YouTube,  Instagram,  Twitter  and Whatsapp. The integration of multimedia and social media enabled pupils to extract information that  eases  the  understanding  of  reading  the  text  through  the  multimedia  elements  of  graphics, audio, video and animation (Hasin & Nasir, 2021). The inclusion of Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) further spurred the changes in language teaching that benefits teachers and pupils by transforming and elevating the learning processes in classrooms. ## Pupils' Perceptions of the Use of Technology in the Classroom


Technology  has  been  widely  used  in  teaching  and  learning  for  the  benefit  of  pupils. Technological  applications  assist  pupils  in  having  visual  representation,  using  graphics  and simulations  to  form  connections  and  supply  contextual  information  on  the  reading  texts. Technologies provide opportunities for pupils to learn based on their individual learning needs and various learning styles, which progressively motivate pupils to learn. Akhmedov and Shuhkrat (2020) exemplified that technology complemented with teaching strategies and suitable materials impacts learners of various learning styles to benefit from the advancement and integration of technology  through  the use  of  visuals,  graphics,  animations,  audio,  videos  and  other  forms  of media.  Pupils  become  more  enthusiastic  about  language  learning  with  the  integration  of technology. This is also supported by Yee and Zainuddin's (2018) research signifying that utilising E-books increased pupils' engagement and motivation which helped pupils' comprehension by listening attentively and participating in discussions. Advanced learners can explore more depth regarding a topic, whereas intermediate and starters can learn more efficiently. The changes in the

teaching  methods  address  pupils  of  different  backgrounds  and  cultures.  Ultimately,  language learning becomes a space for learning opportunities of different forms of meaning-making where the textual equips to the visual, audio, spatial and behavioural aspects. Integrating technology goes beyond building knowledge, grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation but also supports learners in becoming  an  effective  communicators,  and  developing  critical  thinking  skills  and  soft  skills (Yunus, 2018).

Additionally, students welcome the use of technology positively. A supportive learning environment is established with the inclusion of technology as the emphasis will shift to making learning  more  personalised  and  relevant  for  the  varsity  learners  while  encouraging  student engagement  (Elmahdi,  Al-Hattami,  &  Fawzi,  2018;  Ovbiagbonhia,  Kollöffel,  &  Brok,  2019). Active participation in learning can be influenced with the help of technology through engaging class contents and fun activities, enabling students to communicate and socialise with peers. A technology-integrated environment is more integral for language learning rather than environments where students from universities work on tasks alone and receive negative feedback from teachers, which inhibits learning  (Ghory & Ghafory, 2021). A study conducted by Baba and Affendi (2020) also found that Malaysian students had better reading habits and an overall positive attitude  towards  reading  when  exposed  to  digital  materials  as  opposed  to  printed  texts  due  to students' preference for technology and accessibility. This was also evident in Pandian, Baboo and Yi (2020) study where Malaysian students were self-confident and aware of their digital media skills. Likewise, a study carried out by Azmuddin, Nor and Hamat (2020) showed that Malaysian students' learning  progresses  effectively  with  the  addition  of  technology  in  the  learning environment. The results of a study by Halim, Hashim and Yunus (2020) conceded that primary school pupils have higher motivation, interest, and positive perceptions towards learning English because online quiz games like Kahoot! and Quizizz provides elements of excitement, fun, and enjoyment while promoting healthy competition between individuals which makes learning more interesting.

There is a need for additional studies to assess the efficacy of technology in the teaching of languages to students in elementary schools, particularly with regard to the improvement of language abilities from the perspective of learners  (Fithriani, Dewi, Daulay, Salmiah & Fransiska, 2019;  Dalim,  Sunar,  &  Billinghurst  2020).  There  exists  a  necessity  to  account  for  learners' perspectives when implementing technology in the reading classroom, as this could reveal insights about their acceptance of technology. Hoi (2020) emphasised that there is relatively little empirical evidence  has  been  offered  to  understand  the  acceptability  of  technology  among  learners, particularly in the context of a developing country. There is not enough research investigating pupils' perceptions, especially primary school pupils towards the implementation of technology in language  classrooms.  In  this  study,  the  research  gap  is  addressed  by  examining  learners' perspectives, particularly primary school pupils' perspectives towards the integration of technology in the reading classroom. The success or failure of the integration of technology is contingent  on  the  degree  to  which  ESL  learners  are  prepared  to  embrace  technology  as  an educational tool (Moorthy, Yee, T'ing, & Kumaran, 2019).

## Introduction


In recent decades, the topic of socio-political polarization in general and attitudinal polarization in particular has received ample scholarly attention in the US in light of the highly divided party politics  (Abramowitz  &  Saunders,  2005;  Baldassarri  &  Park,  2020;  DiMaggio,  Evans,  & Bryson,  1996;  Lelkes,  2016).  In  contrast,  attitudinal  polarization  in  Europe  has  received relatively little attention (Nuesser, Johnston, & Bodet, 2014), even though polarization is often discussed as  a  potential  risk  for  social  cohesion  in  light  of  seemingly  polarized  debates  on immigration, cultural diversity, EU integration, gender and sexual identities, and environmental protection. However, should we be concerned about attitudinal polarization in Europe?

Attitudinal polarization captures how the attitudes of the general population toward one or many political issues are divided. The concept is most commonly studied in three forms: disagreement,  issue  alignment,  and  sorting  (Baldassarri  &  Gelman,  2008;  DiMaggio  et  al., 1996;  Lelkes,  2016). Disagreement indicates  whether  the  population  is  grouped  into  two opposing  camps  based  on  individual  attitudes  toward  a  particular  political  issue. Issue alignment provides an insight into the degree of ideological cross-cuttingness by describing whether individuals' positions on one political issue are predictive of positions on other issues. Sorting refers to the degree to which individuals' positions on a specific issue are connected with their political identities such as party or ideological affiliations. Whereas disagreement, issue alignment, and sorting capture different aspects of attitudinal polarization, studying all three forms of it is necessary to get a full picture of the structure of public opinion (Park, 2018) and thus, the critical state of political polarization.

Empirical  evidence  on  the  state  of  attitudinal  polarization  in  Europe  is  remarkably scarce making it difficult to assess differences in levels of polarization. Existing studies tend to focus on polarization within individual countries such as Britain (Adams, Green, & Milazzo,

2012a, 2012b; Cohen & Cohen, 2019; Perrett, 2021), Germany (Munzert & Bauer, 2013; Teney & Rupieper, 2021), and the Netherlands (Adams, De Vries, & Leiter, 2012). Moreover, they address  different  forms  of  attitudinal  polarization  and  use  different  measurements  for disagreement, issue alignment, and sorting. Finally, the issues and specific instruments used to investigate  attitudinal  polarization  also  vary  across  studies,  with  some  focusing  solely  on economic matters (e.g. Adams, Green, et al., 2012a) and others examining a combination of economic  and  cultural  issues  (e.g.  Munzert  &  Bauer,  2013).  These  methodological  and conceptual differences make it difficult to assess how polarized Europe is as a whole.

To  study  the  state  of  attitudinal  polarization  across  Europe,  we  ask  three  research questions: (1) Which issue dimensions are more or less polarizing across Europ e? (2) Which EU countries demonstrate higher or lower levels of attitudinal polarization? (3) Do different types of attitudinal polarization co-occur, and if so, how?

Addressing these three research questions results in two key contributions to European polarization research. First, we provide a broader descriptive picture of the level of polarization in Europe, by comparing levels of disagreement, issue alignment, and sorting across twentyone EU member states using the European Value Study 2017 (EVS, 2022). The cross-nationally harmonized  instruments  of  this  data  allow  us  to  capture  different  patterns  of  attitudinal polarization within separate European countries and identify the differences between countries and across  European  regions.  Second,  we  draw  on  the  dominant  framework  for  examining attitudinal divides in Europe, the cleavage theory (e.g. Bornschier, 2010; Deegan-Krause, 2007; Ford & Jennings, 2020; Kriesi, 2010), to select attitudes toward five divisive issues: social inequality, immigration, EU integration, gender and sexuality, and environment. We then link claims  from  the  cleavage  literature  about  the  divisiveness  of  these  attitudes  to  the  central concepts of the polarization literature to compare levels of polarization between issues.


## Attitudinal Polarization: state of research


In sociology, the concept of attitudinal and other forms of polarization dates back to the works of Ross (1921, p. 415) and reappears in other seminal works of the twentieth century, such as Blau (1977), Deutsch (1973) and Galtung (1966) thereafter (see Bauer, 2019 for a review). Importantly,  these  early  writings  already  distinguish  analytically  between  unidimensional forms of polarization, capturing the now prominent concept of opinion disagreement and its multidimensional forms, such as issue alignment (Blau, 1977; Ross, 1921, p. 164).

Contemporary polarization research focuses on different types of socio-political divides that  have  the  potential  to  result  in  political  conflict  or  volatility  (DiMaggio  et  al.,  1996). Attitudinal  polarization   captures  the  divides  within  the  general  population  based  on  the 1 attitudes  toward one or several relevant socio-political issues (Adams, Green, et al., 2012a; Baldassarri  &  Gelman,  2008;  DiMaggio  et  al.,  1996;  Lelkes,  2016).  In  its  extreme  form, polarization  refers  to  a  society  divided  into  two  camps  of  equal  sizes,  each  taking  extreme positions on one or many politically relevant issues.

Different studies emphasize different characteristics of a divided society as crucial for attitudinal polarization (for an overview, see Bauer, 2019; Hetherington, 2009; Lelkes, 2016). Esteban  and  Ray  (2008),  for  instance,  highlight  the  importance  of  comparable  sizes  of  the groups (i.e. 50-50 in the most extreme case) and the distance between their positions (i.e. both on the respective extremes of the axis) for a polarized society. Fiorina and Levendusky (2006), however,  emphasize  that  polarization  is  a process of  disappearing  political  center  as  the population increasingly shifts toward the extremes.

Polarization, hence, can be conceptualized as a state or as a trend (DiMaggio et al., 1996; Lelkes, 2016). Studies on polarization as a trend explore whether attitudes in a given society are becoming more  or  less  opposed  over  time  (Baldassarri  &  Gelman,  2008).  Though  this

## How polarized is Europe?

approach  to  attitudinal  polarization  has  many  advantages,  it  also  comes  with  high  datademands, which are at present only met by a small number of surveys. Ideally, one would need to measure many comparable attitude items repeatedly, over a long period in a large number of countries. Polarization as a state, in contrast, refers to the extent to which attitudes are divided relative to a given threshold. This approach is easier to address with existing comparative data sets for a broad set of attitudes and many countries. In this paper, we, therefore, study the state of  polarization  across  countries  and  issue  dimensions.  By  drawing  on  a  diverse  range  of populations with distinct institutional contexts and histories, these comparisons can give us a better sense of the variation and range in the levels of attitudinal polarization, and provide a reference point for future research.

The three main types of attitudinal polarization are public opinion disagreement, issue alignment, and sorting (Baldassarri & Gelman, 2008; DiMaggio et al., 1996; Fiorina & Abrams, 2008;  Lelkes,  2016).  Though  the  question  of  which  of  the  three  types  captures  the  'real' attitudinal polarization has been extensively discussed in the US-centered studies (Hetherington,  2009;  Lelkes,  2016),  more  recent  research  suggests  that  a combination of disagreement, issue alignment, and sorting is needed for a society to be polarized. This research argues that if a society scores high on one type of attitudinal polarization, this does not imply that social and political cohesion is necessarily under threat (Park, 2018). 2

In what follows, we discuss which aspects of polarization the three types capture and provide an overview of European polarization research.


## Disagreement


Public opinion disagreement is also referred to as ideological divergence (Lelkes, 2016), policy extremity (Adams, Green, et al., 2012a) or simply polarization (DiMaggio et al., 1996). Studies on disagreement analyze how attitudes toward some issue are distributed among the population, with  the  extreme  form  of  polarization  looking  like  a  bimodal  distribution  with  individuals clustered  at  the  opposite  poles.  In  contrast,  if  most  observations  are  grouped  together,  the distribution is unimodal, and such a society features consensus rather than disagreement over an issue (DiMaggio et al., 1996; Fiorina & Abrams, 2008; Fiorina & Levendusky, 2006).

Empirical evidence on the levels of disagreement in Europe is scarce and demonstrates relatively low overall levels of disagreement among the general population, nowhere close to bimodal  distributions  (Lux,  Mau,  &  Jacobi,  2022).  For  Britain,  Adams  et  al.  (2012a)  used standard deviations and proportions of respondents at the extreme ends of scales to show the relatively low levels of disagreement over economic issues (i.e. redistribution, social services, nationalization  of  industry,  and  inflation).  Perrett  (2021),  using  variance  as  a  measure  for disagreement, found that cultural attitudes of authoritarianism-libertarianism (i.e. hierarchy and sameness) featured even less disagreement than economic attitudes.

In Germany, the levels of disagreement, measured with van der Eijk's (2001) index of agreement, over immigration and EU were found to be generally higher than over economic and environmental issues, though disagreement over immigration declined the most over time (Teney & Rupieper, 2021). Similarly, Adams et al. (2012) demonstrated that euthanasia and nuclear  power  in  the  Netherlands  caused  more  disagreement,  measured  with  standard deviations, than social inequality. Overall, empirical evidence remains patchy on which issues cause more disagreement in which European countries.

## Issue alignment


Issue alignment, also known as issue constraint (Baldassarri & Gelman, 2008) or ideological consistency (Lelkes, 2016), focuses on similarities in attitudes held by individuals. It captures to what extent attitudes toward certain issues constrain individuals to hold certain positions on other attitudes, i.e. whether one's position on one dimension (e.g. support for abortion) can predict their position toward other issue dimensions (e.g. support for more restrictive migration policies)  (Abramowitz & Saunders, 2005;  Baldassarri  &  Gelman,  2008;  Munzert  &  Bauer, 2013). A high level of issue alignment suggests that attitudes toward different issues form a single  dividing  line,  which  promotes  contrasting  identities  in  the  opposing  groups  and, therefore, poses a risk for social cohesion (Baldassarri & Gelman, 2008).

In  fact,  the  findings  cannot  even  be  compared  because  the  studies  analyze  different  sets  of attitudes and categorize them, using different logics. For instance, Perrett (2021) uncovered a rather  strong  average  degree  of  alignment  between  authoritarian-libertarianism  and  welfare state  attitudes  in  Britain,  with  average  correlations  cores  between  attitudes  toward  the  two dimensions being around 0.5. However, economic left-right attitudes only had a low degree of alignment  with  authoritarianism-libertarianism  (correlations  around  0.1)  and  with  welfare attitudes (correlations around -0.01).

In  the  Netherlands,  the  strongest  alignment  was  observed  between  attitudes  toward income differences and euthanasia (i.e. average correlation around 0.4) (Adams, De Vries, et al., 2012). In Germany, the strongest average alignment between 1980 and 2010 was between attitudes  towards  immigration,  homosexuality,  and  gender  roles  (all  still  relatively  low

## Sorting


Sorting captures consistency between issue attitudes and political identities, i.e. party choice or affiliation  with  particular  ideologies  such  as  liberalism  versus  conservatism  (Baldassarri  & Gelman,  2008;  Lelkes,  2016).  From  this  perspective,  individuals  sort  themselves  into  the 'correct' party following elite cues, so that supporters of each party exhibit similar attitudes toward  particular  issues,  while  there  is  a  gap  in  attitudes  between  supporters  of  opposing political  parties  (Fiorina  &  Levendusky,  2006;  Hetherington,  2009).  Sorting  is  typically measured  via  correlations  between  attitudes  toward  particular  issues  and  party  identity  or ideological self-placement.

In Britain, Adams, Green, et al. (2012a) demonstrated that sorting over economic issues between Labor and Conservative voters was the highest for attitudes toward nationalization. According to Perret (2021), sorting between  Labor and Conservative voters in Britain over economic  left-right  attitudes  was  higher  than  over  welfare  state  and  the  cultural  issues  of authoritarianism-libertarianism, as sorting over the latter was virtually negligible between 1986 and 2018.

In the Netherlands, Adams et al.  (2012) found the gap between the voters of two major parties at the time, CDA (Christian party) and PvdA (labor party) to be the biggest for left-right economic attitudes followed by attitudes toward nuclear power. Though sorting over nuclear power,  left-right  and  income  inequality  attitudes  decreased  substantially  between  1986  and

1998, sorting over euthanasia remained stable over time and by 1998 became the most dividing issue.

In one of the few cross-national comparisons addressing partisan sorting, Noël, Thérien, and Bucher (2021) found Western democracies to show the strongest correlations between leftright self-placement and political attitudes such as confidence in armed forces, churches, major companies, and attitudes toward income equality. Attitudes toward homosexuality and abortion, however,  were  comparatively  less  related  to  left-right  self-placement.  Focusing  on  Europe, Freire (2015) showed that attitudes toward immigration, socio-economic values, religion and social liberalism were more related to left-right voting than attitudes toward law and order, and environmental attitudes. Studies on sorting in Europe, therefore, also do not offer a consistent picture on which issues are more or less dividing, and, even less so, in which countries.


## Polarization and cleavages


Whereas studies on attitudinal polarization frequently demonstrate variations in the degree of polarization between different issue dimensions, they typically lack a theoretical framework that explains which dimensions are most polarized. The literature on changing cleavages in Europe has addressed this question, even if from a different perspective (e.g. Ford & Jennings, 2020; Kriesi, 2010;  Lipset & Rokkan, 1967), and offers some theoretical ideas that can be applied to attitudinal polarization research.

Cleavages stand for institutionalized political conflicts between two social groups (i.e. the structural component) with conflicting political preferences (i.e. the normative component) that lead to voting for opposing political parties (i.e. the behavioral component) (Bartolini & Mair, 1990; Lipset & Rokkan, 1967). The normative component of cleavages is analytically

## Pless, Khoudja, and Grunow, 2023

close to polarization as disagreement and issue alignment because it too captures differences in political views among the population. The behavioral component connects attitudes to voting and, hence, is close to polarization as sorting.

One of the key aims of cleavage research is to identify issue dimensions that produce societal divides and hence create an attitudinal basis for long-lasting political conflicts (Ford & Jennings,  2020).  Central  to  the  old  class  cleavage  are  the  issues  of  social  inequality  and redistribution (i.e. the desired extent of state involvement into the economy to reduce social inequality) (Brooks, Nieuwbeerta, & Manza, 2006; Lipset & Rokkan, 1967). Because of the weakening link between class and voting in the second half of the twentieth century, some social  scientists  expected  social  inequality  to  become  less  dividing  (Clark  &  Lipset,  1991), while others claimed that these issues were rather overshadowed by the cultural issues (Kriesi, 2010; Van der Waal, Achterberg, & Houtman, 2007).

Cultural issues moved center-stage of Western political agendas as a result of sociopolitical  transformations  of  the  1960s  that  allowed  younger  birth  cohorts  to  shift  from materialist value orientations (i.e. class-based economic considerations) to postmaterialist  ones 3 (i.e.  primarily  environmental  concerns  and  gender  relations).  Over  the  past  decades,  the environmental domain grew to include environmental pollution and climate change, whereas the family and gender domain grew to encompass sexuality and procreation, sexual identity, gender roles and divisions of paid and unpaid work (Dolezal, 2010).

In the 1980s-1990s, globalization and European integration intensified public debates on immigration, cultural diversity, and national identity (Bornschier, 2010; Kriesi et al., 2006). Political parties of the radical right then politicized these issues, framing them as a threat to national cultural homogeneity of different European countries (Bornschier, 2010; Häusermann & Kriesi, 2015). At present, attitudes toward EU integration and immigration are considered

## How polarized is Europe?

key dimensions of the new cultural cleavage and, therefore, are expected to show the highest levels of polarization (Kriesi et al., 2006).

Whereas the concepts of attitudinal polarization and cleavages both serve to analyze societal divides, the two respective strands of literature hardly interact directly. However, combining the two perspectives enables us to look inside the black box of cleavages by capturing the structure of public opinion on different issues for the whole population, not only selected cleavage groups. Specifically, our paper seeks to fill the gaps of European polarization research by showing which issue dimensions (i.e. old or new) are more and less polarizing across Europ e, which EU countries demonstrate higher or lower attitudinal polarization, and whether and how different types of attitudinal polarization go together .


## Data and measurement


The  data  for  the  analysis  come  from  the  European  Value  Study  2017  for  twenty-one  EU countries. The sample consists of countries from all geographical regions of Europe, both old and new democracies, with and without Communist experience. For analytical purposes, we refer to the geographical clusters within Europe: North (i.e. Denmark, Finland, and Sweden), West (i.e. Austria, France, Germany, the Netherlands, and the UK), South (i.e. Italy, Portugal, and  Spain),  and  East  (i.e.  Bulgaria,  Croatia,  Czech  Republic,  Estonia,  Hungary,  Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia). At the time of the survey, the UK was formally still a member of the EU even though the Brexit referendum had already happened. The individuallevel sample in use amounts to 32,999 observations with an average of 1,571 observations per country.

Based on the cleavage theory, we select items from the following five key attitudinal dimensions: social inequality, immigration, EU-integration, gender relations and sexuality, and environment. All responses are coded from leftist attitudes (i.e.  support  for  social  equality, immigration, EU, environmental protection, and progressive stances on sexuality) to rightist attitudes opposing these positions. ## Disagreement


Public opinion disagreement is also referred to as ideological divergence (Lelkes, 2016), policy extremity (Adams, Green, et al., 2012a) or simply polarization (DiMaggio et al., 1996). Studies on disagreement analyze how attitudes toward some issue are distributed among the population, with  the  extreme  form  of  polarization  looking  like  a  bimodal  distribution  with  individuals clustered  at  the  opposite  poles.  In  contrast,  if  most  observations  are  grouped  together,  the distribution is unimodal, and such a society features consensus rather than disagreement over an issue (DiMaggio et al., 1996; Fiorina & Abrams, 2008; Fiorina & Levendusky, 2006).

Empirical evidence on the levels of disagreement in Europe is scarce and demonstrates relatively low overall levels of disagreement among the general population, nowhere close to bimodal  distributions  (Lux,  Mau,  &  Jacobi,  2022).  For  Britain,  Adams  et  al.  (2012a)  used standard deviations and proportions of respondents at the extreme ends of scales to show the relatively low levels of disagreement over economic issues (i.e. redistribution, social services, nationalization  of  industry,  and  inflation).  Perrett  (2021),  using  variance  as  a  measure  for disagreement, found that cultural attitudes of authoritarianism-libertarianism (i.e. hierarchy and sameness) featured even less disagreement than economic attitudes.

In Germany, the levels of disagreement, measured with van der Eijk's (2001) index of agreement, over immigration and EU were found to be generally higher than over economic and environmental issues, though disagreement over immigration declined the most over time (Teney & Rupieper, 2021). Similarly, Adams et al. (2012) demonstrated that euthanasia and nuclear  power  in  the  Netherlands  caused  more  disagreement,  measured  with  standard deviations, than social inequality. Overall, empirical evidence remains patchy on which issues cause more disagreement in which European countries.

## Conclusion


Should we be concerned about attitudinal polarization in Europe? To address this question, we provided a descriptive comparison of levels of disagreement, issue alignment, and sorting across twenty-one EU member states. In doing so, we have captured different patterns of attitudinal polarization within separate European countries and identified differences between countries and regions. Furthermore, we drew on the cleavage literature to identify attitudes towards the five potentially most divisive issues: social inequality, immigration, EU integration, gender and sexuality, and environment. We linked claims from the cleavage

## How polarized is Europe?

literature about the divisiveness of these attitudes to the central concepts of the polarization literature and compared levels of polarization between issues.

In response to our first research question regarding the more and less dividing issue dimensions in Europe, we conclude that immigration is only slightly more dividing than other issue dimensions across the three types of attitudinal polarization, contrary to what could be expected from the new cultural cleavage literature. In fact, immigration only stands out in terms of issue alignment, while absolute levels of disagreement over it are far from polarizing. However, low within-country disagreement reflects pro-immigration consensus in some countries and anti-immigration consensus in others, suggesting potential for polarization on this issue between (rather than within) countries. Importantly, EU integration, which is often considered to be at the center of the new cleavage in Europe together with immigration (e.g. Kriesi et al., 2006), appears to be the least polarizing dimension, with the UK as the only exception. The polarizing power of EU integration there is hardly surprising given that UKbased respondents were surveyed after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

Moreover, our results indicate that social inequality has not lost its polarizing power (Van der Waal et al., 2007). Compared to other issue dimensions, social inequality shows the highest levels of disagreement, especially in Eastern and Southern Europe, and relatively high levels of sorting, especially in the North and West. However, because this dimension is also almost unrelated to all other (i.e. 'cultural') dimensions, our findings support the notion of a two-dimensional ideological space in Europe, made up of a cultural and an economic dimension (Bornschier, 2010).

Responding to the second and third research questions on the more and less polarized countries of Europe and the co-occurrence of the three types of polarization, we have observed a geographical divide between the North-West and South-East of Europe. On the

## Pless, Khoudja, and Grunow, 2023

one hand, countries of Southern and Eastern Europe demonstrate higher levels of average disagreement but lower levels of average issue alignment and sorting. Attitudes toward different issues might cause high levels of disagreement there but the resulting divides are cross-cutting, thus leaving room for political alliances to form in spite of disagreement (Park, 2018). Countries of Western and Northern Europe, on the other hand, show lower average disagreement but higher average alignment and sorting. Under these conditions, political alliances between opponents may be possible because overall levels of disagreement are rather low. In sum, the three types of attitudinal polarization do not peak jointly, as countries that score high on disagreement are likely to score low on issue alignment and sorting. It could, therefore, be concluded that a polarization of public opinion is currently not a serious threat for the social cohesion within European countries.

Our findings, however, point to a different type of threat to social cohesion, in the form of between -country attitudinal disparities inside the EU. In fact, a strong within -country consensus on certain issues might be more problematic for the future of the EU than high within-country disagreement. This is especially the case where within-country consensus is high on the political pole that goes against current EU values. For example, countries that demonstrate a right-wing consensus on immigration (i.e. Czech Republic) or sexuality (i.e. Romania) might hinder the respective debates and policy development on the EU level. In addition, we found evidence of geographical North-West versus South-East divides that might deepen in the future, should they become politicized on the EU level.

Given the limited existing research on attitudinal polarization in Europe, the main goal of this study was to paint a broad picture of how divided Europe currently is and to open a conversation on polarization not just in specific countries of Europe but in the region as a whole. Such a research design has several limitations that should be addressed in further studies. First, because of the magnitude of our research questions, we could not study

## How polarized is Europe?

attitudinal polarization between particular social groups. Introducing socio-structural variables (e.g. gender, class, education, religion) into the analysis would paint a more detailed picture of polarization and closer connect the literatures on polarization and cleavages, where social structure plays a crucial role.

The second limitation stems from the use of left-right self-identification as a proxy for political identity to construct the sorting scores. As discussed in the measurement section, the EVS dataset does not offer an alternative variable that would better capture political identity without substantially reducing the number of observations. Though we performed robustness checks with a variable that measures left-right positions of the parties preferred by the respondents, this variable does not solve the issue that the left-right political continuum is a context-dependent black box of various political attitudes. In different countries, these attitudes may be influenced by only economic or only cultural concerns, or both types of concerns jointly (Freire, 2015; Hooghe, Marks, & Wilson, 2002; Knutsen, 1997). To account for the multidimensionality of European political arenas, future studies would benefit from using a multidimensional variable to measure political identities (e.g. more nuanced ideological affiliations).

Finally, focusing on the state of attitudinal polarization across Europe in a comparative perspective did not allow us to investigate the time trends in the respective forms of polarization. Introducing the time dimension would thus be the next logical step. Studying the trends in disagreement, issue alignment, and sorting over an extended period of time will demonstrate how the patterns of polarization evolve, i.e. how issue dimensions become more or less dividing, countries shift toward disagreement or consensus, and political identities become more or less tied to certain issues. This dynamic picture of Europe will shed light on the direction in which Europe and its member states are heading, i.e. whether we grow together or further apart?

## Pless, Khoudja, and Grunow, 2023

To summarize, we have found relatively low overall levels of polarization across Europe though with some country and dimensional variation. In particular, the rates of disagreement are nowhere close to bimodal distributions, sorting is virtually inexistent in Eastern Europe, and levels of issue alignment are generally low. Furthermore, the three types of polarization never appear simultaneously in any of the examined countries, suggesting that there is much room for cross-cutting alliances within the countries. But while the findings show that polarization within individual countries in Europe is not a significant risk, polarization between countries may pose a greater threat to the cohesion of the European Union in the future.

## Introduction


The COVID-19 pandemic has left an indelible mark in the United States. The pandemic has resulted in over 6.9 million hospitalizations and caused over 1.1 million deaths, impacting countless more whose lives have been forever altered by the loss of a loved one or who themselves are still dealing with the consequences of long COVID (CDC 2024). The reality, however, is that the pandemic could have been far worse. Estimates suggest that COVID-19 vaccines saved over 2 million lives and hundreds of billions in health care costs. By quickly mobilizing to develop, test, and deliver vaccines to the American public, we helped to avert what could have been an even more devastating public health crisis.

Of course, COVID-19 vaccine uptake has not been universal in the United States or equal across the country. The most recent federal data available (from May 2023), finds that only 69.5% of Americans completed their primary COVID-19 vaccine series, with only 17% receiving an additional booster dose, due in large part to pervasive vaccine hesitancy among some segments of the US population (CDC 2024). Research suggests that this undervaccination has resulted in at least 232,000 additional deaths in the United States that could have been avoided (Jia et al., 2023).

Critically, with COVID-19 now endemic and likely to circulate globally alongside other respiratory viruses like influenza moving forward, vaccination remains crucial to protecting the public from COVID's most deadly consequences (Jung et al., 2024; Marks, Woodcock, & Califf 2022). This includes both primary series vaccination for individuals who have thus far refused to vaccinate, as well as the vast majority of Americans who vaccinated during the peak of the pandemic but have since elected not to pursue additional vaccine doses suggested by the CDC. With the protection afforded by vaccines waning over time and the threat of new variants of COVID-19 that could evade current immunity ever-looming, identifying strategies to improve uptake of annual COVID-19 vaccines remains vital.


## Study Context


Our work assesses the effectiveness of three novel risk communication strategies on annual COVID-19 vaccine uptake behaviors via Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) embedded in four public opinion surveys. Specifically, we assess how efforts to (a) normalize the idea that the spread of COVID-19 is endemic (Normalization Messaging; 'NORM'), (b) emphasize the health risks associated with endemic COVID (Normalization + Risk Messaging, or 'N+R'), and (c) denormalize the spread of COVID-19 as presenting a constantly changing public health threat (De-Normalization Messaging, or 'DENORM') might impact Americans' vaccine attitudes and behaviors (see Experimental Design for additional information).

We developed these messages (see: Experimental Design for additional information) in consultation with the Department of Health in a highly vaccinated US State interested in identifying health communication strategies for improving vaccine uptake (Rhode Island). Therefore, we began our analysis by assessing the impact of our vaccine promotion efforts in two representative surveys of the Rhode Island adult population. Rhode Island is a national leader in elective vaccine uptake against COVID-19 and seasonal flu, and has some of the strongest vaccine mandate laws in the country. It therefore offers a "hard test" of the effectiveness of our vaccine promotion messaging, as comparatively greater numbers of vaccinated state residents in the state implies that we have fewer opportunities to detect intended behavioral change in vaccine uptake intentions among partially or fully unvaccinated subpopulations.

Correspondingly, we suspect that detecting positive effects of our vaccine promotion messages in a 'hard test' case like Rhode Island should imply broader effectiveness across the US. To assess this possibility, we also tested our vaccine promotion messages in two nationally representative surveys, conducted during the same timeframe.

In both the state and nationally representative surveys, we are primarily interested in studying Americans who are either under-vaccinated - i.e., those who are yet to receive a COVID-19 'booster' vaccine - or who are fully unvaccinated against COVID-19 - i.e., those who have yet to complete their primary COVID-19 vaccination series. These subpopulations are presumably less likely than those who keep 'up to date' on COVID-19 vaccination to intend to receive future annual COVID-19 vaccines. Correspondingly, they represent a critical population to reach with vaccine promotion efforts (i.e., because they are less likely to vaccinate), and theoretically should exhibit greater capacity to be influenced by our experimental treatments. Thus, while we offer tests of our theoretical expectations at population level throughout our analyses, we are primarily interested in offering sub-population specific tests across unvaccinated and 'non-boosted' subpopulations.

Study Context: A 'Hard Case.' Vaccine Promotion Messaging in a Highly Vaccinated US State

Rhode Island offers a 'hard case' for detecting experimental treatment effects of vaccine promotion efforts, as many Rhode Islanders have demonstrated being amenable to COVID-19 vaccination. Over 25% of the adult population in Rhode Island had already received an updated COVID-19 vaccine at the time of this study in Fall 2023 (ranked 7th in the U.S; CDC 2024).

More generally, the Rhode Island adult population has consistently been among the top two most highly vaccinated against seasonal influenza since 2010; boasting vaccine uptake levels in excess of 60% in the 2022-2023 flu season (CDC 2023). Moreover, Rhode Island is just one of two US states that requires school-aged children to receive Hepatitis A & B, rotavirus, Hib, pneumococcal, and seasonal flu vaccines - in addition to polio, DTap, and MMR vaccines required in all US states - prior to entering public school, and is just one of four states that requires HPV vaccination for teenagers.

Comparatively high levels of vaccine uptake in Rhode Island may be due to a wide range of factors including political differences as well as intensive efforts at health promotion in the state as compared to the rest of the country. From a political perspective, Rhode Island is particularly liberal, voting to send a Democrat to the White House in 20 of the past 24 presidential elections, including continuous Democratic presidential votes since 1988. While the state has a long history of electing candidates for governor from both parties, its politically liberal voting affinities in national elections could help to explain why Rhode Islanders boast some of the highest vaccination rates in the nation . There is growing evidence that Republicans are less trusting of scientific consensus (Gauchat 2012; Motta 2018, 2024; Merkley 2020; Merkley & Loewen 2021), which in turn shapes their views toward vaccine safety and efficacy (Motta 2021). Correspondingly, self-identified Republicans and more-conservative places in the US t have lower levels of vaccine uptake than Democratic ones (e.g., Callaghan et al., 2022; Gadarian et al., 2023). Equally important, with the majority of anti-vaccine rhetoric coming from conservative political leaders and media outlets, a particularly liberal state like Rhode Island is less likely to be influenced by this anti-vaccine rhetoric.

Of course, politics alone cannot fully explain Rhode Islanders proclivity towards vaccination. The strong emphasis on vaccination as seen through childhood vaccine mandates and the vaccine promotion efforts of the Rhode Island Department of Health also prove impactful.

Political differences between Rhode Island and more conservative states, coupled with expansive existing vaccine promotion efforts in the state, could influence the effectiveness of our vaccine promotion messaging efforts in one of two ways. On the one hand, higher levels of annual COVID-19 vaccine uptake in Rhode Island could imply muted treatment effects in the Ocean State. If this is the case, our efforts to promote annual COVID-19 vaccine uptake may be comparatively more effective when implemented nationwide, as there is simply greater opportunity to detect treatment effects in the American public.

On the other hand, differences in political and public health culture may imply that Rhode Islanders including unvaccinated sub-populations in the state - are comparatively more receptive to vaccination and vaccine promotion efforts. For example, if unvaccinated Rhode Islanders are comparatively more politically liberal, exposed to messaging about the importance of vaccination, and/or aware about their ability to access free annual COVID-19 vaccines, the ability to 'scale up' our vaccine promotion efforts might be comparatively more difficult in nationally representative samples without these characteristics. If this view is correct, we might expect to only observe treatment effects in US states that resemble Rhode Island with respect to their levels of elective vaccine uptake (which may 'stand in' for the many political and public health differences that contribute to asymmetric receptivity across states).

Given these conflicting expectations, we ask:

RQ1: Do experimental treatment results we might observe in Rhode Island replicate in nationally representative samples of the US adult population?

Empirical Expectations: Responsiveness to Differences in Message Content

We expect that efforts to normalize the seasonal health risks borne by endemic COVID-19 ('NORM') might encourage annual vaccine uptake by reminding Americans about the usefulness of yearly vaccination efforts (Dai et al., 2021; Milkman et al., 2021; Reñosa et al., 2021). That is, because COVID-19 is always with us, making an effort to vaccinate every year represents a safe and effective way to protect oneself and others from getting sick. ( H1a )

At the same time, however, we recognize that emphasizing persistent health risks could induce a sense of helplessness; thereby decreasing vaccine compliance ( H1b ). Consistent with this view, past research (Witte 1996; Skinner & Zimmer-Gembeck 2011; Smith 2022) suggests that people who feel as if a threat is beyond eradication or outside of their control subsequently feel less , not more, inclined to do something about it. Our RCTs aim to adjudicate between these two competing possibilities.

Normalization plus risk messages ('N+R') offer an alternative approach to promoting vaccine uptake by appending information about individual health risks of getting sick with COVID-19 to messages that describe the virus' spread as endemic and seasonal. Our expectations regarding normalization plus risk messaging ('N+R') are much clearer than those of normalization messages alone. Messages emphasizing individual health risks of getting sick with COVID-19 have been shown to increase intentions to vaccinate against the disease (Ashworth et al., 2021; Motta et al., 2021). Because N+R messages augment normalization messaging by emphasizing the risks to one's personal health borne by COVID-19 infection, we expect that these messages increase intentions to vaccinate on a yearly basis ( H2 ).

Finally, recognizing the possibility that normalization messages might 'backfire' (H1b) by instilling a sense of helplessness about one's own ability to overcome endemic infectious disease threats, we suspect that efforts to describe the COVID-19 virus as a constantly-changing threat (DENORM) will bolster annual vaccination intentions ( H3 ). Conceptually, highlighting the virus' unpredictable nature might cause some people to experience anxiety, which has been shown to (a) increase people's tendencies to abandon previously-held beliefs, and (b) increase openness to the advice of medical and scientific experts aimed at curbing infectious disease threats (Albertson & Gadarian 2014, 2015; see also: Brader 2005, Marcus, MacKuen, & Neuman 2011).

If these theoretical mechanisms are correct, we might expect that DENORM message exposure might engender self-efficacious beliefs in their abilities to take action to prevent themselves and others from getting sick. We therefore ask whether individuals exposed to the DENORM condition, compared to the NORM condition, may feel comparatively more efficacious in their ability to overcome COVID-19 health threats through preventative action ( RQ2 ).


## Methods


Data. Data for this study are derived from four randomized controlled trials embedded in large,representative, cross-sectional public opinion surveys before and following the availability of updated COVID-19 vaccines. We collected these data in partnership with YouGov's online sampling service. YouGov ensures national and state-level representativeness in the data they collect by first drawing a random sample of hypothetical survey respondents from nationally representative US Census data, and then using propensity score matching techniques to identify members of their large, online, opt-in panel who most-closely resemble those individuals identified in the Census data, and invite those individuals to participate in the survey.

To account for any remaining deviations between the sample and Rhode Island adult population, YouGov calculated post-stratification weights that adjust for respondents' gender, age, race, educational attainment, and 2020 presidential vote choice. We apply survey weights in all analyses presented in this paper.

Experimental trials 1 and 2 were conducted in June 2023, and randomly exposed a state-representative cross-section of individuals in Rhode Island (Trial 1, N = 800) and a nationally representative cross-section of US adults (Trial 2, N = 1,000), to messages that normalize COVID-19 as endemic (NORM, N = 202RI, 257Ntl), or emphasize the personal health risks - specifically, the possibility of developing COVID-19 symptoms lasting longer than four weeks ('Long COVID') - posed by endemic COVID-19 (N+R, 194RI, 252Ntl); vs. an over-assigned control group (N = 404 RI , 491Ntl ).

Trials 3 and 4 were conducted in October 2023, and randomly exposed a state-representative cross-section of Rhode Islanders (Trial 3, N = 800) and a nationally representative cross-section of US adults (Trial 4, N = 1,200) and with messages that either 'de-normalize' (DENORM, N = 200RI , 306Ntl ) constantly-changing viral threats posed by endemic COVID-19, or the NORM message (N = 214RI , 299Ntl ) featured in Trials 1 and 2 (vs. a control group; N = 386 RI , 595Ntl ).

Note that, as all four trials were embedded in surveys that also featured observational analytical components, we over-assigned respondents to a study-wide control group such that approximately 50% of each sample was assigned to view no interventional materials.

After consenting to participate in our study, respondents were randomly assigned to read one of the interventional materials discussed above. In order to increase compliance with our intent to treat (ITT) design, we required respondents to spend at least 7 seconds on the page containing the short passage prior to advancing on with the survey. ## Measures .

Outcome Variable: Annual COVID-19 Vaccine Uptake Intentions. One of the primary outcome variables in our analyses is an ordinal measure of respondents' intentions to receive an annual COVID-19 vaccine in Fall 2023. In all trials, respondents were asked 'How likely would you be to receive an annual COVID-19 additional booster vaccine if recommended to do so by public health experts?'. Participants could respond that they were either 'very likely,' 'somewhat likely,' 'not too likely,' or 'not likely at all' to do so. We dichotomized intended uptake measures, such that a score of 1 corresponded to being 'very likely' to receive the vaccine, with all options expressing greater levels of uncertainty scored as 0.

Explanatory Variable: Experimental Treatment Assignment. The primary explanatory variable in our analyses are dichotomous indicators of experimental condition assignment, which take on a value of 1 if respondents were assigned to one of the experimental conditions summarized in Figure 1; 0 otherwise. Note that we treat control condition assignment as an analytic baseline in all multivariate models.

Moderating Variables: Previous COVID-19 Vaccine Uptake Behavior. As we are primarily interested in studying vaccine treatment effects in un-/under-vaccinated subpopulations, we asked respondents in all trials: 'Have you been vaccinated against COVID-19 previously?' Respondents indicating that they had received a full initial vaccine sequence (e.g., two doses of mRNA vaccines from companies like Pfizer & Moderna; a single shot Johnson & Johnson vaccine) and at least one 'booster' shot are treated as the reference category. We classify respondents as under-vaccinated if they received some or all of an initial vaccine sequence, but no 'booster' vaccine, and as fully un-vaccinated if they have not received any COVID-19 vaccines at all. We fashioned responses into a nominal variable taking on values of 1 and 2 (respectively) to describe under- and unvaccinated people across samples, and 0 for the reference group.

## Estimation Strategy.

We estimate experimental treatment effects (H1-H3) by constructing a series of linear probability regression models (LPMs) that regress our dichotomous annual COVID-19 vaccination intentions on each indicator of experimental treatment group assignment, across each experimental trial and interacted with our nominal vaccine status indicator. Parameter estimates from these models provide a sense of the degree to which assignment to each treatment condition is associated with increased vaccine uptake for each group; relative to the control condition, and controlling for assignment to each study's other experimental condition. For ease of interpretation, we extract predicted probabilities from significant interaction terms across each model that hold all other covariates at their observed sample means.

## Experimental Treatment Effects in a Highly Vaccinated State

We begin our analysis by assessing the effectiveness of exposure to our experimental treatments on annual COVID-19 vaccination intentions in the Rhode Island adult population, across Studies 1 and 2 (i.e., Trials 1 and 3). Across both studies, we detect no significant 'main effects' of exposure to our experimental treatments.
