Following the administration of Study 1 - in which we failed to detect significant effects of NORM message exposure on annual COVID-19 vaccine uptake intentions - we added a series of questions to Study 2 that allowed us to test whether or not exposure to directly test whether or not NORM messages may 'backfire' by engendering feelings of helplessness about one's ability to take action to protect themselves from getting sick with COVID-19. We measure respondents' beliefs in their abilities to overcome the infectious disease threats posed by COVID-19 by asking them to choose which of two statements, across two pairs of statements, 'comes closest to your views about the endemic health risks posed by COVID-19, even if neither is exactly right.' The first set of statements asked respondents whether 'Avoiding getting sick with COVID-19' is either 'mostly something that I can control' or 'mostly something that I cannot control.' The second asked respondents whether 'Taking action to avoid getting sick with COVID-19' is either 'worthwhile' or 'not worthwhile.' From these questions, we fashioned a dichotomous self efficacy indicator taking on a value of 1 if respondents endorsed both the 'worthwhile' and 'control' options, and 0 otherwise.

Consistent with this view, average levels of reported self efficacy across both questions are indeed lower in the NORM condition (weighted M = 0.57, 95% CI = 0.49, 66) vs. the study's control group (M = 0.60 , 95% CI = 0.53, 0.66). However, as demonstrated by the overlapping confidence intervals across (weighted) mean estimates, these differences fail to attain either even one-tailed significance. While we are therefore open to the possibility that depressed feelings of self-efficacy might motivate public resistance to NORM messaging in Rhode Island, we are reluctant to make that conclusion on the basis of the present data, and welcome future research on this question.

## A 'Scaled Up' National Vaccine Promotion Strategy

Next, we assess whether or not the experimental treatment effects that we observed in Rhode Island - a state with high levels of vaccine uptake - might translate into effective vaccine promotion strategies nationwide. Because Rhode Island represents a 'hard test' of our experimental stimulus materials - given high levels of vaccine uptake in the Ocean State - we expected to find a similar (and perhaps even larger) pattern of effects at the national level.

Surprisingly, though, the results presented in Columns 3-4 in Table 1 suggest that we failed to detect an analogous pattern of effects among un- and under-vaccinated Americans in our nationally representative samples (p > 0.10 in all cases). In other words, both the N+R and DENORM conditions, which proved impactful in Rhode Island, had no statistically discernible effect in nationally representative samples.

Post hoc tests reveal, however, some important socio-demographic differences between unvaccinated Rhode Islanders (i.e., the group for whom we detect significant treatment effects in our state-level analyses) and the American public more generally. Table 2 summarizes some notable differences between unvaccinated respondents across samples by presenting (weighted) mean estimates - and corresponding significance tests - of a wide range of socio-demographic factors that could potentially influence vaccine uptake across samples. For example, unvaccinated Rhode Islanders are significantly less likely (by factors of 22 and 14 percentage points, across Studies 1 and 2, respectively) to self-identify as Republicans. Given the strong link between partisan self-identification with the Republican Party and COVID-19 vaccine resistance identified in previous research (e.g., Callaghan et al., 2022; Gadarian et al., 2023), failure to replicate state-level experimental treatment effects in the national sample could result from partisan asymmetries across samples.

Likewise, comparatively higher levels of access to health insurance - which has been shown to be correlated with increased likelihood of receiving a COVID-19 vaccine (Nguyen et al., 2021; Ku 2022) - in the Rhode Island sample could imply that unvaccinated Americans have less access to vaccines and preventive care. Moreover, unvaccinated respondents who are less inclined to take action to protect themselves and others from COVID-19 (perhaps owing to lower concern about its public health risks) may yield similar effects (Lam et al., 2021; Latkin et al., 2021).
