## It is far riskier to receive $10 million from a firm

tomorrow than to receive in 20 years.

This is what schools around the world effectively have been teaching over half a century, as predicted by Markowitz (1952) asset risk and the agency theory of Jensen and Meckling (1976), since the present value of benefits (PVB) of the former is far greater than that of the latter. Nie (2023) argues that asset holding risk approaches zero as any one of the three orthogonal dimensions approaches zero (see, Appendix B), suggesting that the literature misses the holding time length of asset risk, which is indispensable dimension of the asset holding risk bound with untradability. In  this  spirit,  this  study  examines  if  the  inside  debt  risk  is  cumulative  over  maturity:  the  risk approaches zero as maturity approaches zero. I expect that this longitudinal risk (LR), captured as debt micro-risk premium over maturity as Nie (2024a), reflects a manager's skin in the game. I obtain LR for option grants and stockholdings over the (in)visible time lengths of untradability as in Nie (2024b). My analyses are twofold. First, I analyze whether LR captures the inside debt risk that motivates a manager's risk-shifting incentives in M&As. Second, I investigate if the inside debt risk approaches zero when maturity (which negatively reflects the CEO age) approaches zero.

The literature finds the relationship between the age and the risk attitudes nonmonotonic (e.g., Barsky et al., 1997), positive (e.g., Yim, 2013; Serfling, 2014), or negative (e.g., Glenn, 1974). To control for the noisy effects, I employ dummy orthogonalization to examine how the inside debt impacts this causal relationship. I expect that the inside debt reduces the effect of age (a negative proxy of maturity) on a manager's conservatism if the risk moves towards zero when maturity

moves towards zero. In this study, the risk premium is obtained as in excess of the central bank's short-term rate as Nie (2024a) that addresses a conventional misconception about the risk-free rate.

The choices of merges and acquisitions (M&As) may be associated with different risks (e.g., Elnahas  and  Kim,  2017)  and  managerial  risk  tolerance.  Managerial  conservatism  plays  an important role in M&A choice of targets and method of payment, and the immediate and longterm price effects related to M&A announcements (e.g., Hirshleifer and Thakor, 1992; Milidonis and Stathopoulos, 2014). Using yearly data on US acquirers from 2003 to 2021, I investigate if the LR metric raises, as if the inside debt reduces the effect of age on, a manager's conservatism.

I present my analysis in three steps. In the first step, I examine how the LR and inside debt ratios affect firm acquisitiveness. I observe that the LR ratio decreases, as if the inside debt ratio increases the effect of age on, firm acquisitiveness. As debt-like holdings motivate the executives to align their interests with those of debtholders and thus avoid risky actions, I investigate how the inside debt influences the effect of age on acquirer proportion of cash payment and target of safer firms (i.e., public firms and firms of lower leverage). A Heckman analysis indicates that the LR ratio  positively  affects,  as  if  the  inside  debt  negatively  impacts  the  effect  of  age  on,  acquirer proportion of cash payment and choice of safer firms. This implies that the LR ratio captures the inside  debt  risk  that  approaches  zero  as  maturity  approaches  zero.  A  one-standard-deviation increase  in  the  age  on  the  top  decile  of  inside  debt  ratio  decreases  the  relative  probability  of acquirer target of a public firm by 7.0% and a firm of lower leverage by 10.4%. The results are not weakened by the inclusion of a number of variables such as market capitalization, cash flow risk, CDS spread, hubris, expected tenure, bond volatility, and stock volatility.

Next, in the second step, I exploit a quasi-experiment to interpret the causal effect of inside debt on a manager's conservatism: an experiment of the adoption of a state antitakeover law prior the

M&A bid in the bid year (henceforth, ANTI). The ANTI reduces credit spread (e.g., Francis et al., 2010) and thus induces an exogenous decrease in the risk that motivates a manager's conservatism. I exploit the ANTI announcement that shocks the risk exogenously. I study how the ANTI shock impacts  the  effect  of  inside  debt  on  the  likelihood  of  acquirer  target  of  safer  firms.  Using  a difference-in-differences approach, I show that, in line with my final sample results, the ANTI leads to a less positive impact of the LR ratio, as if a less negative impact of the inside debt on the effect of age, on the treatment group's conservatism, relative to the change in the control group. This evidence supports that the LR ratio captures the inside debt risk that approaches  zero as maturity approaches zero. With the ANTI, a one-standard-deviation increase in the age on the top decile of inside debt leverage reduces the relative probability of choice of a public target by 7.1% and target of a firm of lower leverage by 8.7%. I also rule out change in firm risk, captured as the micro-risk of firm debt, as an alternative explanation to the observed change in the inside debt risk.

The ANTI experiment establishes that the LR ratio captures the inside debt micro-risk, which shifts towards zero as maturity shifts towards zero. To obtain additional evidence, I also exploit information on the selected group of instruments that are found to be important determinants of inside debt (e.g., Sundaram and Yermack, 2007; Anantharaman, Fang and Gong, 2014; Cassell et al., 2012). In the third step, I analyze if the inside debt through maturity impacts acquirer restructure of CEO compensation package and adjustment of firm risks and firm leverage from the year prior to M&A bid to the year following M&A deals. I document that the LR ratio positively affects, as if the inside debt reduces the effect of age on, a manager's conservatism. This implies that the risk moves  towards  zero  as  maturity  moves  towards  zero,  regardless  of  the  PVB.  This  causal relationship is similarly revealed in acquirer adjustment of firm risks and leverage. A one-standard-

deviation increase in the age on the top decile of inside debt leverage leads to a 7.7% increase in firm risk from the year prior to M&A bid to the year following the deal.

asset  risk  that  is  not  cumulative  over  time  length. ## 3. The Main Hypothesis


The literature supports that large inside debt holdings might cause firm executives to manage their firms conservatively, preserving liquidity and avoiding risk in a pattern that appeals to the firm's other lenders (e.g., Jensen and Meckling, 1976). Wei and Yermack (2011) argue that the inside debt is one measure that is associated with conservative firm policies. Eisdorfer, Giaccotto, and White (2015) find that the pension plans of top executives are related with agency problems and negatively affect future firm performances. Cassell et al. (2012) argue that the inside debt exposes the executives to default risk similar to that is faced by the outside creditors, since such claims are generally unsecured and unfunded firm liabilities.

M&A choices are motivated by the objective to maximize the CEO's expected utility, especially when  they  have  financial  capital  that  is  attached  to  the  existence  of  the  firm,  their  corporate decisions may not be value creating for shareholders (e.g., Tufano, 1996: May, 1995; Smith and Stulz, 1985). I expect that the LR ratio captures the inside debt risk, which approaches zero as maturity approaches zero. 4 Therefore, the main testable hypothesis is:

H1 The LR ratio positively impacts, as if the inside debt negatively influences the effect of age (which negatively captures maturity) on, managerial risk-shifting incentives in M&As.

Before proceeding to test the prediction, I describe the data and sample.

## 5.2 Endogeneity Checks


The previous results, while consistent with the hypothesis, still subject to endogeneity concerns. One could doubt whether the executives who prefer inside debt because their age is negatively associated with their conservative behavior. If this is the case, my analysis captures a spurious relationship between the inside debt and the causal relationship between the age and managerial risk-shifting  incentives.  I  address  this  issue  with  a  two-pronged  approach.  First,  I  employ  an experiment of the ANTI to analyze how the inside debt impacts this causal relationship. As an additional test, I perform an instrumental variable analysis.


## 5.2.1 A Quasi-experiment


I expect that the ANTI negatively affects conservatism with a decrease in inside debt risk since the adoption of a state antitakeover law reduces firm bond spread (e.g., Francis et al., 2010). 10 Using the ANTI as an experiment, I now consider an exogenous shock on inside debt risk that affects conservatism. The ANTI impacts the market upon the announcement of the law adoption, an impact that is likely to be exogenous because the LR and inside debt metrics, like all other controls, are all lagged by one year. This also implies that the ANTI impact is likely to be strong.

I have no reason to believe that managers would go forward with M&As only if their inside debt risks are negatively affected by the ANTI. Thus, the ANTI effectively generates a randomized experiment that exogenously shocks LR, which leads to my identification strategy.

I  use a diff-in-diff approach, using the ANTI as a natural experiment to examine the causal effect of an exogenous change in the inside debt risk on the causal relationship between the age and  acquirer  target  of  safer  firms.  Treatment  acquirers  are  those  with  the  ANTI  and  control acquirers are the remaining ones. I consider that the ANTI window captures the effect (ex ante) of reduced inside debt risk as opposed to that of realized risk.

I conduct the standard diff-in-diff regressions in this analysis. Since I include both the industry and year fixed effects, the coefficients of D10.InsLev × Log(Age) × ANTI captures the change in treatment group (acquirers with the ANTI) relative to that in the control group (i.e., diff-in-diff estimate). The results reported in Table 4 observe that, with the ANTI than that without, the LR ratio reduces, as if the inside debt positively impacts the effect of age on, a manager's conservatism. The effect of the ANTI is significant both economically and statistically. A one-standard-deviation increase  in  the  age  on  the  top  decile  of  inside  debt  leverage  raises  the  relative  probability  of acquirer target of a public firm by 7.1% and target of a firm of lower leverage by 8.7%. 11 Overall, the results support a causal effect of the ANTI on the inside debt risk that approaches zero as maturity approaches zero.

Next, I execute the following placebo tests. A decrease in managerial conservatism, as reflected by acquirer choice of safer targets, may be driven by lower firm risks associated with the ANTI. I compute firm risk as the micro-risk of firm debt in Nie (2024a).

To address the concern that the decrease in managerial conservatism is affected by the decrease in firm risks that are associated with the ANTI, I study the difference in firm risks of the treatment acquirers relative to the difference among the control acquirers (Panel B). I find little change in firm risks for the treatment firms. More importantly, the difference in the change in firm risks between  the  treatment  and  the  control  acquirers  is  essentially  zero  both  statistically  and economically. Thus, I find that a decrease in managerial risk-shifting incentives in M&As is not due to a negative effect of the ANTI on firm risks. To sum up, the evidence supports the identifying strategy for using the ANTI as an exogenous shock that reduces the inside debt risk.

Overall, the results confirm the identifying assumption that the treatment and the control firms are  comparable  in  the  announcement  year  either  or  not  experience  the  ANTI.  Therefore,  the decrease in managerial risk-shifting incentives in the treatment acquirers is due to a decrease in the inside debt risk that accumulates over maturity. This evidence indicates that LR captures the inside debt risk, which approaches zero when maturity approaches zero.

Next, I complement the previous analysis with an instrumental variable approach. I repeat the specifications in Table 3 Panel B using the selected group of variables as instruments for the LR inside debt metrics. ## 6. Conclusion


This study tests if previous studies miss the indispensable dimension of holding time length of managerial risk that is bound with untradability. I measure this longitudinal risk as risk premium over the time length of untradability. To examine if my LR ratio captures the inside debt risk that represents a manager's skin in the game, I exploit a dummy orthogonalization methodology to analyze if the risk approaches zero as maturity approaches zero. In particular, I examine if the inside debt negatively affects the effect of age on managerial risk-shifting incentives in M&As.

Using  yearly  data  on  US  acquirers  from  2003  to  2021,  I  observe  that  the  LR  ratio,  which negatively affects firm M&A engagement, positively impacts managerial risk-shifting incentives in acquirer proportion of cash payment, target of safer firms, restructure of compensation packages towards an optimal level of LR ratio, and adjustment of firm risks and firm leverage. The results support that the LR ratio positively influences, as if the inside debt negatively affects the effect of age on, managerial conservatism. Similarly, I document that the LR ratio negatively impacts, as if

the inside deb positively affects the effect of age on, a manager's conservatism in acquirer price effects for the announcement window. The evidence supports that the LR ratio captures the inside debt risk, which shifts towards zero as maturity shifts towards zero.

A natural experiment of the ANTI that exogenously shocks the inside debt risk provides an opportunity to test if the LR ratio captures the risk and if the inside debt reduces the effect of age on conservatism. Among otherwise comparable M&As, I observe a significant decrease in the effect of LR ratio, as if an increase in the impact of inside debt on the effect of age, on a manager's risk shifting incentives, for M&As with the ANTI relative to the change for control M&As. An instrumental variable analysis complements and confirms the experiment's evidence.

The findings indicate that the LR ratio, captured as risk premium over the asset holding time length, represents the inside debt risk that approaches zero as maturity approaches zero. My results are consistent with the argument of Nie (2023) that asset holding risk approaches zero as any one of  the  three  orthogonal  dimensions  of  asset  risk  approaches  zero.  The  evidence  challenges Markowitz (1952) asset risk, revealing that agency and contracting theories incorrectly calibrate asset risk (e.g., Jensen and Meckling, 1976; Holmstrom, 1979). For regulators and policy makers, this study sheds new light regarding on executive compensation.

## Introduction


English has become the lingua franca globally across various professional fields, including medicine. The demand for proficiency in English, particularly in English for Specific Purposes (ESP), such as English for medicine, has heightened, especially in non-native English-speaking countries. In China, the drive for educational reforms has strongly emphasized enhancing English language proficiency among college students, particularly those in specialized fields like medicine (Yu & Liu, 2018; Chen, 2024). The emphasis on English for medicine reflects academic needs and responds to the increasing requirements for medical professionals to engage with international research, clinical practices, and communication (Li & Wang, 2024; Zhang, 2024).

In the medical field, English is growing in importance, and students often face challenges in achieving proficiency, which may be influenced by their motivation and motivational behaviors to learn the language. The L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS), proposed by Dörnyei (2005, 2009), provides a comprehensive framework to understand the motivational dynamics of second language acquisition. This model, which includes components such as the Ideal L2 Self (IL2S), the Ought-to L2 Self (OL2S), and the Second Language Learning Experience (SLLE), has been widely studied across various contexts.

When examining the predictors of success in medical English courses, it is essential to consider how these motivational factors interact with traditional measures of language proficiency, such as college entrance English scores. The present study explores the relationship between L2 motivation and motivational learning behaviors among college students enrolled in an English for medicine course at a university in Zhejiang, China. Specifically, it aims to examine how different components of the L2MSS--namely, the Ideal L2 Self (IL2S), the Ought-to L2 Self (OL2S), and the  Second  Language  Learning  Experience  (SLLE)  relate  to  students'  Motivational  Learning Behaviors (MLB). The study also investigates the influence of college entrance English scores as a  potential  predictor  of  these  behaviors.  The  significance  of  this  study  lies  in  two  aspects:  it contributes to the theoretical understanding of L2MSS by exploring its components within the English  for  medicine  classroom  in  China,  extending  the  application  of  L2MSS  to  a  specific educational and  cultural  setting.  Pedagogically,  this  study  offers  guidelines  for  the  teachers  to make the best use of the specific motivational factors related to learners' performance to arouse, enhance, and maintain students' motivation in learning English by creating teaching activities to foster intrinsic motivation and a positive learning environment. Therefore, the research objectives of this study are:

- (1) To investigate the relationships between college entrance English scores, L2 motivation, IL2S, OL2S, SLLE, and MLB of medical students in the medical English course.
- (2) To determine how IL2S, OL2S and SLLE influences the motivational learning behaviors of these students respectively.
- (3)  To  identify  the  strongest  predictors  of  MLB  among  medical  students  in  medical  English courses, considering college English entrance scores, L2 motivation, IL2S, OL2S, and SLLE.
- To achieve these research objectives, the study poses five research questions:
- (1) What is the relationship between college entrance English scores, L2 motivation, IL2S, OL2S, SLLE, and MLB of students in the medical English course?
- (2) How does the Ideal L2 Self impact motivational learning behavior among these students?
- (3) How does the Ought-to L2 Self impact their motivational learning behavior?
- (4) How does the Second Language Learning Experience influence their motivational learning

## Literature Review Language Motivation


The study of L2 motivation, particularly within English for Specific Purposes (ESP), has been extensively studied in recent years, with the focus mainly on understanding how different motivational  components  would  impact  language  learning  outcomes.  One  of  the  central frameworks used in this area is Dörnyei's (2005) L2 Motivational Self System, which includes the Ideal  L2  Self,  the  Ought-to  L2  Self,  and  the  Second  Language  Learning  Experience  as  key elements influencing language learning behavior and language achievements. The Ideal L2 Self represents the learner's aspirations and desires to become proficient in the target language, which strongly predicts motivated learning behaviors in western and Chinese contexts (Csizér & Kormos, 2009; Liu, 2013; Liu & Zhang, 2013; Papi &Teimouri, 2012, 2014; Papi & Abdollahzadeh, 2011; Papi et al., 2018; Takahashi & Im, 2020). Dogomeo (2023) illustrated that learners who maintain a clear vision of their Ideal L2 Self are more likely to sustain their motivation throughout their language-learning journey. This element is particularly relevant in medical English as students often link language proficiency to their future profession, motivating them to succeed.

On the other hand, the Ought-to Self, which represents the perceived external pressures and expectations  from  society  or  significant  others,  also  plays  a  critical  role  in  shaping  one's motivation. Although the Ought-to Self can motivate learners, its impact on learning behaviors is often distinct from that of the Ideal L2 Self. Research suggests that while the Ideal L2 Self tends to  foster  positive  and  proactive  learning  behaviors,  the  Ought-to  Self  may  result  in  a  more avoidance-oriented motivation, where learners engage in tasks primarily to avoid failure rather than to achieve success (Taguchi et al., 2009; Yue et al., 2022; Dörnyei & Chan, 2013; Kamaruddin et al., 2017).

Besides personal factors, the Second Language Learning Experience (SLLE) also plays a vital role in influencing motivation. This SLLE encompasses the social, academic, and institutional settings where language learning occurs. 'Motivation is responsible for why people decide to do something, how long they are willing to sustain the activity, and how hard they are going to pursue it.' This  quote  by  Dörnyei  and  Skehan  (2003)  emphasized  the  critical  role  of  motivation  in language learning, indicating that a positive SLLE can significantly enhance learners' commitment and effort in mastering a second language. Studies have shown that when learners view that they were in a supportive and favorable environment for learning, they are more willing to display motivated learning behaviors and achieve better language outcomes (Henry, 2014). Similarly, the classroom setting is vital in molding students' motivation. Research emphasizes that fostering a positive and interactive classroom atmosphere can significantly boost students' participation and motivation (Yang, S, 2023; Vibulphol, 2016).

Recent  developments  in  the  study  of  second  language  motivation  in  China  reflect  an

## Motivational Learning Behaviors


Motivational learning behaviors in English classrooms, mainly through the lens of the L2 Motivational  Self  System  (L2MSS)  theory,  emphasize  the  interplay  between  learners'  selfperceptions, goals, and the learning environment. L2MSS posits that the ideal self, the ought-to self, and the learning experience influence motivation, collectively shaping learners' engagement and persistence in language learning.

The psychosocial environment of the classroom significantly impacts students' motivation and commitment to learning English. Gelete (2023), Nottingham and Henning (2014), and Iraj et al. (2021) all highlighted that a supportive classroom atmosphere and favorable feedback enhance students'  motivation  because  the  learning  process  predominantly  occurs  within  this  context. Integrating enjoyable and engaging teaching methods, such as flipped classrooms and communicative  teaching  activities,  has  further  enhanced  learners'  motivation  and  academic performance in the Chinese context (Ying & Ayub, 2022).

Moreover,  teachers'  application  of  motivational  strategies  plays  a  vital  role  in  shaping students' learning behaviors. Zhang (2023), as well as Yang and Wyatt (2021), emphasized that motivational techniques not only make the classroom more engaging but also facilitate effective teaching and learning. Similarly, using transformational leadership in classrooms, as noted by Ying and Ayub (2022), can stimulate students' interest and set motivational goals, thereby enhancing their engagement.

In  addition  to  the  classroom  environment  and  teaching  strategies,  the  role  of  learner autonomy and external factors cannot be overlooked. Soviyah's (2022) study indicated that while students  may  exhibit  a  high  level  of  autonomy  in  their  learning,  their  engagement  in  outsideclassroom activities remains moderate. This study suggests that fostering a sense of responsibility in learners is essential for enhancing their motivation.


## Motivational Learning Behaviors in English for Medicine Classroom


Motivational learning behaviors are crucial in the medical English classroom. Alzabidi and Khadawardi (2022) and Sak (2020) found that the IL2S significantly affects students' willingness to communicate (WTC) in speaking classes, indicating that when students visualize themselves as competent speakers in their specific fields. Studies in China have shown that students who possess a strong Ideal L2 Self are more likely to engage in proactive learning behaviors and demonstrate higher levels of motivation (Wang, 2023).  This study also aligns with findings that highlight the instrumental motivations of Chinese medical students, who often regard good English proficiency

As  for  OL2S,  in  the  context  of  medical  education  in  China,  these pressures often derive from academic requirements, social expectations, and the competitive nature of the medical field (Mayers, 2023). Research indicates that students who perceive strong external expectations are motivated to learn English, although this motivation may not be as robust as that driven by intrinsic aspirations (Metakides, 2023; Ahmadishokouh, 2024).

Additionally, the quality of the Second Language Learning Experience (SLLE) plays a critical role; positive and engaging learning experiences significantly enhance  students' commitment to learning (Dewaele, 2020; Dörnyei &  Ryan, 2015). Effective teaching methodologies, such as interactive and student-centered approaches, have been shown to enhance students' motivation by creating engaging and supportive learning environments (Dai, 2023; Wang & Liu, 2023).

In summary, although the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS) has been widely studied in general English and ESP contexts, research specifically addressing its application in medical English classrooms is rare. There remains a significant gap in the literature regarding how these motivational factors influence students' learning behaviors in ESP contexts, particularly in English for medicine courses in China (Xu et al., 2024; Hotak et al., 2024). Besides, though motivational factors such as L2 motivation, IL2S, OL2S, and SLLE are recognized as significant, their relative predictive power in explaining motivational learning behaviors among medical students has not been adequately explored. A quantitative analysis is needed to identify the strongest predictors within these students in English for medicine class.


## Method


In order to answer the research questions above, the present study adopted a quantitative approach.  The  setting  was  a  local  university  in  Zhejiang  province  of  China,  which  has implemented English for medicine classes for first-year and second-year medical students. This course is conclusory for medical students, and it is a bridge course connecting general college English to academic medical English. In this class, the instructor mainly adopted a communicationoriented teaching approach and motivational strategies to ensure the students are highly involved in the classroom. Meanwhile, students have a wide range of English exposure opportunities, such as talks, seminars, TV shows, video clips, and radio.

The relationship between L2M, IL2S, OL2S, SLLE, and motivational learning behaviors was presented using a survey and data analysis  of the research data. This section will present further discussions by referring to relevant studies based on the five research questions.


## RQ1: What is the relationship between college entrance English scores, L2 motivation, IL2S, OL2S, SLLE, and motivational learning behavior of students in the medical English course?


The results indicate the strong correlations of L2M and SLLE with MLB, suggesting that both a robust L2 Motivational Self System and positive language learning experiences are critical drivers of motivational learning behaviors in this context. The IL2S is moderately correlated with motivational behavior, indicating its importance but suggesting that it may not be as critical as L2M and SLLE in this sample. Moreover, the limited impact of OL2S can be noted. The weaker and non-significant correlation of OL2S with MLB suggests that external pressures or obligations play a less significant role in motivating students than internal motivations and experiences.

The findings regarding the strong  correlations between the L2M and SLLE with MLB highlight  the  importance  of  intrinsic  factors  in  language  learning.  The  L2MSS  framework,  in particular,  suggests  that  learners'  motivation  is  deeply  related  to  their  self-perceptions  and experiences in language learning. Moreover, the moderate correlation of the IL2S with motivational behavior indicates its relevance but also suggests that it may not be as critical as L2M and SLLE. Papi and Teimouri (2012) highlight that strong attitudes to the IL2S can significantly predict motivation. However, they  also  note  that  this  self-image  must  be  supplemented  by  positive  learning  experiences  to engage learners fully. Thus, in this study, it could be found that while the Ideal L2 Self plays a role in  medical  English  class,  the  combination  of  self-perception  and  experiential  factors  drives motivation more robustly.

The limited impact of the OL2S is particularly significant. The weaker and non-significant correlation of OL2S with MLB suggests that external pressures or obligations are less effective in motivating students than intrinsic motivations and positive experiences. This finding echoes the work of Dörnyei and Chan (2013), who argued that motivation is more effectively fostered through personal relevance and internalized goals rather than external expectations. This perspective is also echoed by Kamaruddin et al. (2017), who identified intrinsic motivation as a significant factor influencing  language  learning,  further  supporting  the  notion  that  internal  drives  are  more influential than external obligations.

These  findings  highlight  the  importance  of  developing  strong  internal  motivation  and cultivating supportive learning settings to increase students' effort and participation in medical English classes.

## RQ3: How does the Ought-to L2 Self impact their motivational learning behavior?


The Ought-to L2 Self (OL2S) exerts a modest influence on motivational learning behavior among  medical  students  studying  English,  as  evidenced  by  various  studies  that  explore  the dynamics of language learning motivation. While external expectations associated with the OL2S can  contribute  to  students'  commitment  to  learning,  the  effect  is  limited  compared  to  other motivational  constructs,  particularly  the  Ideal  L2  Self  (IL2S).  This  distinction  is  crucial,  as  it highlights the varying degrees of influence that different components of the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS) have on learners' engagement and persistence in language learning. Research indicates that while the OL2S, which encompasses the pressures and expectations from others (such as family, teachers, or society), can motivate students to some extent, it often lacks the depth and sustainability of motivation derived from the IL2S. For instance, Takahashi and Im (2020) found that the relationship between OL2S and motivated learning behavior is weaker than that of IL2S, which is more closely linked to intrinsic motivation and personal aspirations.

Moreover, studies have shown that the IL2S is a stronger predictor of language learning outcomes than the OL2S, echoing this study's findings. For example, Alzabidi and Khadawardi (2022) emphasized that the IL2S not only arouses interest but also sustains it as students invest time and effort to achieve their language learning goals. This aligns with the findings of Bóbkina et al. (2021), who reported that higher levels of motivation associated with the IL2S corresponded to more excellent proficiency in the language, while the OL2S was more prevalent among students with  lower  proficiency  and  limited  learning  experiences.  Such  evidence  suggests  that  while external pressures can motivate students, they do not foster the same level of commitment and engagement as the internalized aspirations represented by the IL2S.

Furthermore, the modest influence of the OL2S can be attributed to its nature, which often focuses on avoiding negative outcomes rather than pursuing positive goals, which has the same results as the study of Wisnuwardhani(2022). Dörnyei and Chan (2013) highlighted that the OL2S is primarily concerned with fulfilling obligations and meeting expectations, which may not inspire the same enthusiasm and dedication as pursuing an Ideal L2 Self.

In this study, medical and professional programs often have rigorous language requirements. Students might be motivated to learn English simply to pass exams or meet these requirements (OL2S) in the Chinese context, but not explicitly demonstrated as intended efforts and commitment in language learning behaviors.

## RQ5: What are the strongest predictors of motivational learning behavior in medical English courses among medical students, considering college English entrance scores, L2 motivation, IL2S, OL2S, and SLLE?


Firstly,  L2  motivation  was  found  to  be  a  significant  positive  predictor  of  Motivational Learning Behavior, indicating that students with a strong motivational self-system are more likely to engage in behaviors supporting their language learning. This aligns with previous research that highlights the central role of L2M in motivating students to put forth effort in language learning contexts (Dörnyei,  2005).  Moreover,  it  aligns  with  Dörnyei's  foundational  work,  which emphasizes the central role of the L2M in motivating students to exert effort in language learning contexts (Papi & Teimouri, 2012; 2014), and English for medicine is no exception.

Secondly, the Second Language Learning Experience (SLLE) also emerged as a significant positive predictor, suggesting that students with positive experiences learning a second language are more likely to engage in motivated learning behaviors. Educational psychology literature has

supported the importance of positive learning experiences in enhancing motivation and learning outcomes (Ushioda, 2008). Moreover, the interplay between teacher motivational practices and student motivation has been shown to enhance the effectiveness of the L2M framework. Papi and Abdollahzadeh (2011) demonstrated that teachers' motivational strategies significantly influenced students' motivated behavior, reinforcing the idea that a supportive educational environment can amplify the effects of the L2M on student engagement. This is further supported by findings from (Wang  et  al.,  2023),  which  suggested  that  the  L2M  framework  can  be  effectively  applied  to understand  the  motivations  of  learners  in  various  contexts,  including  the  influence  of  selfperception on language learning.

This  relationship  is  particularly  important  in  ESP  contexts,  where  students  often  have specific professional goals tied to their language learning. The findings of Yang and Wyatt (2021) highlighted  that  teachers'  beliefs  about  their  motivational  practices  directly  impact  student motivation in ESP settings. Their study emphasized the need for teachers to adopt motivational strategies that resonate with their students' specific needs and aspirations, thereby enhancing their engagement and learning outcomes. This aligns with the notion that teacher support can play a pivotal role in sustaining motivation in specialized fields like medicine, where students may feel pressure  to  achieve  proficiency.  For  example,  by  addressing  students'  anxiety  and  fostering  a supportive classroom environment, teachers can help students develop a clearer vision of their ideal L2 self, which is essential for motivation in ESP contexts.

Thirdly, the Ideal L2 Self (IL2S) showed a marginally significant favorable influence on Motivational Learning Behavior in this study. This finding suggests that students with a clear and motivating vision of their future L2 self are more likely to exhibit motivated learning behaviors. However, this effect was just above the conventional threshold for statistical significance. The role of the ideal self in motivation has been extensively discussed in L2 motivation theory (Dörnyei, 2009). This finding suggests that students' visions of their future selves as proficient language users can enhance their motivation to engage in language learning activities. However, the degree of this influence may vary depending on contextual factors and the specific nature of the ESP environment.

In the context of ESP, particularly in fields such as medicine, the IL2S can be a powerful motivator.  As  indicated  in  Alzabidi  and  Khadawardi's  (2022)  study,  when  students  visualize themselves  as  competent  speakers  in  their  specific  fields,  they  are  more  likely  to  participate actively in language learning. This aligns with the notion that motivation is a crucial factor in language acquisition, especially in specialized contexts where students may feel the pressure to achieve proficiency for professional purposes.

Moreover, Sak (2020) explored the relationship between the IL2S and WTC (Willing ness To Communicate), noting that the construct does not uniformly correlate with communication settings inside and outside the classroom. This suggests that while the IL2S can motivate students to  engage  in  language  learning,  its  effectiveness  may  be  influenced  by  the  specific  classroom dynamics and the opportunities for the practical application of language skills. In medical English education, students may be more motivated to communicate in scenarios that closely resemble their future professional interactions, enhancing their learning experiences' relevance. The reason why IL2S was a weak predictor in this study may lie in the lack of authentic communicative activities related to their professions.

Ought-to L2 Self (OL2S) did not significantly predict Motivational Learning Behavior, suggesting that external obligations or expectations, such as perceived duties or responsibilities,

do  not  powerfully  drive  motivated  learning  behavior  among  these  students.  This  finding  is consistent with some studies that found the ought-to self to be less influential in language learning motivation than the ideal self (Papi, 2010).

Finally, the College Entrance English Score also did not significantly impact Motivational Learning  Behavior,  showing  that  past  academic  performance  in  English  does  not  necessarily predict current motivation to engage in language learning behaviors. This finding may suggest that students' self-concepts and learning experiences more influence motivation in the current learning context than past achievements.

In  conclusion,  the  L2M,  SLLE,  and  IL2S  are  significant  predictors  of  Motivational Learning  Behavior,  and  their  effectiveness  can  be  enhanced  through  targeted  pedagogical strategies  and  communicative  teaching  approaches  that  align  with  the  specific  needs  and aspirations of students in ESP classrooms, such as English for Medicine. In ESP contexts, where students  often  have  specific  professional  goals,  fostering  a  strong  IL2S  can  be  particularly beneficial. By helping students develop a clear vision of their future selves as competent language users, educators can significantly enhance the motivation and engagement of students in language learning.


## Conclusion


This study aimed to examine how different components of the L2MSS--namely, the Ideal L2 Self (IL2S), the Ought-to L2 Self (OL2S), and the Second Language Learning Experience (SLLE) relate to students' Motivational Learning Behaviors (MLB). The study also investigated the influence of college entrance English scores as a potential predictor of these behaviors. It is found that there are strong correlations of L2M and SLLE with MLB, suggesting that both a robust L2 Motivational Self System and positive language learning experiences are critical drivers of motivational  learning  behaviors  in  this  context.  The  IL2S  is  moderately  correlated  with motivational behavior, indicating its importance but suggesting that it may not be as critical as L2M and SLLE in this sample. Moreover, the limited impact of OL2S on MLB suggests that external pressures or obligations play a less significant role in motivating students than internal motivations and experiences.

Moreover,  the  L2  Motivational  Self  System  is  an  important  factor  in  predicting motivational learning behavior. The results showed that the components of the L2 Motivational Self System play an important role in improving medical students' classroom engagement and learning effort in medical English courses, emphasizing the importance of L2 motivation, positive L2  learning  experience,  and  the  Ideal  L2  self  in  promoting  students'  motivational  learning behavior. The results also showed that the L2 learning experience significantly impacts medical learning behavior, indicating that improving  students' language learning experience can effectively  enhance  their  motivation  and  participation.  Additionally,  while  the  Ideal  L2  Self showed potential as a motivator, enhancing students' vision of the future as proficient English speakers through interventions may significantly increase their engagement and effort in language learning. Last but not least, it is found that although external expectations (OL2S) can promote students' learning engagement to a certain extent, but their effect is limited. Finally, the College Entrance English Score did not significantly impact Motivational Learning Behavior, showing that past academic performance in English does not necessarily predict current motivation to engage in language learning behaviors.

## Implications


This  empirical  study  contributes  to  the  broader  understanding  of  language  learning motivation, particularly in specialized educational contexts such as medical English classrooms. These  findings  provide  valuable  insights  into  the  factors  that  influence  motivational  learning behavior among students, particularly emphasizing the roles of internal motivation and positive learning  experiences.  Medical  English  educators  and  policymakers  should  focus  on  fostering strong motivational self-systems and creating positive learning environments to enhance student engagement in language learning.

Additionally, given the relatively weak influence of OL2S on MLB, educators and program designers might focus on strengthening students' IL2S, which could be more effective in fostering long-term  commitment  and  motivation  in  English  language  learning.  Interventions  that  help students align their personal goals with their professional aspirations in the medical field, rather than merely responding to external pressures, may yield better motivational outcomes.

Future research could explore the potential mediating effects of other motivational factors, such as the teaching approaches and activities, to further elucidate the mechanisms through which IL2S influences MLB. Also, the current study was conducted with a relatively small sample of 80 students in a single university in Zhejiang, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Further  research  could  extend  the  geographical  scope  to  represent  the  broader  population  of medical students in different regions or countries.

## 1 Introduction


On October 3, 2020, a group of climate activists from Elokapina, the Finnish branch of Extinction Rebellion, blocked traffic in Helsinki with a livestreamed sit-in protest. The police pepper sprayed a group of 10-15 protesters who refused to comply with dispersal orders. The unexpected and unprecedented use of force by the police was subjected to intense scrutiny after footage of it spread online. In June 2023, the officer in charge was convicted of negligent breach of duty (Yle News 2023). This event, which remains the most violent action taken against climate protesters in Finland, marked the beginning of a series of repressive activities by the Finnish government against Elokapina, which include police investigations that froze movement funds and approximately 800 charges filed as of late 2022 (Kilpel¨inen 2022). a

In the context of climate activism, it is increasingly common to find in liberal democracies instances of repression, broadly defined as the violation of civil liberties and human rights by state actors with the intent of deterring dissent and political participation (Davenport 2007; Earl and Braithwaite 2022). Beyond Finland, climate movements have faced a wide range of repression (e.g., physical violence, legal prosecution, monitoring and infiltration) in democratic countries including Austria, Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, the U.K., and the U.S. (Wahlstr¨m and o de Moor 2017; Nosek 2020; Stephens Griffin 2021; Gobby et al. 2022; Gulliver et al. 2023; Forst 2024). These patterns are expected to worsen as states increase efforts to criminalize activism (Gordon 2024).

Climate movements impact political agendas, climate policy outcomes, and public views of environmental problems (Huxster 2022; Johnson and Agnone 2022). Climate activism also allows participants, especially youth, to express their political agency on an issue that is otherwise making them feel increasingly anxious, depressed, and hopeless (Pickard, Bowman and Arya 2022; Clayton 2020; Hickman et al. 2021). Beyond obstructing climate policy, state attempts to suppress climate action through repression of climate movements therefore have the danger of adversely shaping political participation, political efficacy beliefs, and democratic representation (Bernardi et al. 2023). In a recent report, the United Nations' Special Rapporteur on Environmental Defenders raised these issues as major threats to human rights and democracy (Forst 2024). It is therefore critical for us to understand how climate activists and movements sustain their existence over time in response to continued state repression. What is their understanding of the available tools? How do they use them to overcome potential demobilization and other chilling effects following repression?

Recent observations indicate climate movements are increasingly using social media as technological tools to leverage the networked aspects of social movement formation, mobi-

lization, and organization (Kavada and Specht 2022), substantiating expectations from the social movements literature that social media has the potential to be a central component of protest mobilization (Earl and Kimport 2011; Cammaerts 2015; Jackson, Bailey and Welles 2020). In this literature, a number of studies have started to consider social media platforms explicitly in terms of how they shape social movements' responses to repression, focusing primarily on how these platforms provide low cost mobilization through information cascades conducive to large scale mobilization during or immediately following repression (SteinertThrelkeld et al. 2015; Odaba¸ s and Reynolds-Stenson 2018; Pan and Siegel 2020). Across these cases, social media platforms' features resulted in rapid and wide information spread, leading to heightened backlash mobilization.

The literature, however, has yet to explicitly consider how social media platforms have affordances - a set of enabled actions that emerges from how users perceive features of the technology (Evans et al. 2017) - that can sustain stable participation in the long term outside of heightened mobilization periods, which is critical to a movement's existence over time (Tilly 1993). This is a wholly different mobilization process from backlash mobilization, requiring not only inducing initial commitment but also retaining a stable group of dissidents between periods of heightened activity (Taylor 1989).

With this in mind, we study how social media platforms sustain movements facing repression by looking at how Finnish climate activists participated in climate activism and engaged with each other on Twitter in the 16 months following the October 2020 pepper spraying incident. Drawing on in-depth interviews with climate activists from Elokapina, which inform our statistical analysis of individual-level and movement-level participation dynamics over time, we argue that social media platforms sustain movements because the highly visible information cascades they enable raises the cost of inaction when movements are faced with publicized instances of repression. Following an audience cost logic (Fearon 1994), because social media platforms are widely understood to afford information amplification at a low cost (Fox and McEwan 2019), by using social media to communicate with its members and the public, social movements create a strong audience expectation for sustained engagement, making any kind of withdrawal from the established baseline highly salient to supporters, detractors, and the general public.

In the context of repression, where a movement is expected to respond and rally against the threat, inaction will then be understood by all audiences as evidence of a chilling effect. In turn, following the same information amplification mechanism identified in prior research, we should expect this chilling effect to lead to cascading demobilization as movement members receive information about one another's nonparticipation (Partheym¨ller and Schmitt-Beck u 2012; Demirel-Pegg 2017). In other words, social media's ability to drive cascading participa-

tory tendencies in either direction - resulting from its amplifying and performative aspects - makes each individual's participation in social media space more worthwhile, and consequently more costly when it is lost. As social movement actors tend to be cognizant of collective mobilization mechanisms (Everett 1992), the anticipated audience cost of inaction should compel them to act despite repression increasing dissenting costs.

Our argument speaks directly to key concepts from the affordances literature (Ronzhyn, Cardenal and Batlle Rubio 2023), which argues that affordances, technological or otherwise, not only enable but can solicit action from users as the existence of an affordance necessarily defines the set of actions understood to be possible, and in turn what it means to use or not to use what is afforded (Dings 2018; Withagen et al. 2012). An illustrative nontechnological example of this is the case of how social movements inadvertently created an obvious metric of movement failure when large protest sizes - a phenomenon that affords demonstrations of movement legitimacy - became evidence of movement success such that any time a protest is not large, it is considered to have failed (Everett 1992). In our case, once activists started using social media to amplify the movement, it became a necessity to continue doing so, as any interruption to this pattern is immediately noticeable and can lead to a cascading chilling effect that activists want to avoid. By accounting for how climate activists perceive, use, and form institutionalized understandings about social media, we extend our current understanding of how social media shapes the repression-dissent nexus: more than a cost reduction mechanism, it is a double-edged sword that can compel action following an audience cost logic.

The Elokapina case (July 2020-February 2022) has a number of nice properties for our study. First, Finnish Twitter is an open space for elite political contestations (Nelimarkka et al. 2020; Christensen and ˚ sa Bengtsson 2011), including public political debates and onA line activism, meaning that actions in this digital space should be understood as meaningful political behavior. There is also no known form of online repression or censorship, so how activists respond to repression on social media will not be constrained by direct government intervention. Next, as the first physically violent and highest profile incident of a series of continuing repressive actions taken toward climate activists in Finland, the pepper spraying event can be understood as a large and unexpected shock to a previously stable system. Finally, more than the pepper spraying event, our observation period also includes continued repression by the Finnish government and a number of pre-planned campaigns run by Elokapina, making it suitable for our study of how movements behave when facing long term repression.

The remainder of this paper proceeds as follows. In section two, we highlight important concepts from the social movements in social media literature. In section three, we outline

findings from our interviews. Notably, we find activists to be highly cognizant and ostensibly responsive toward social media's impact on the networked aspects of movement mobilization. In section four, we describe our data collection and processing. Next, we present a set of statistical analyses informed by our interviews. In section five, we assess the potential chilling effects of repression. Across Twitter activity and expressed identities in terms of Twitter bios, we find no evidence of chilling effects. Instead, activists remained stable except for elevated engagement in response to important external events. In section six, we explore how activists' retweeting patterns reflect their understanding of information cascades on social media. We show that activists' retweeting exhibited sustained patterns of network centralization despite the natural tendency for these patterns to decay, which we believe is a key factor in a movement being sustained longer term post-repression. We conclude by discussing our empirical findings in the context of social media affordances and social movement sustenance.


## 2 Social Media and Networked Social Movement Behavior


Climate movements are increasingly turning to social media platforms as technological tools to leverage the networked aspects of social movement formation, mobilization, and organization (Kavada and Specht 2022). The literature on social movements in social media has identified a number of important reasons driving this pattern.

First, when considering whether to dissent, especially when faced with possible repression, individuals' choices to participate or not are influenced by their social networks (Siegel 2011). Through their social ties to each other, they are exposed to planned actions such as recruitment (Snow, Zurcher Jr and Ekland-Olson 1980), and also to organic information about shared grievances and identities (Van Stekelenburg and Klandermans 2013). The tendency for social information to spread through networks in a cascading fashion (Watts 2002), where individuals make decisions based on information from their peers and, by doing so, amplify the information to their own networks, opens the possibility of large scale coordinated mobilization or demobilization in the short term (Lohmann 1994; Demirel-Pegg 2017). Social networks also factor into the longer term sustenance of social movements outside of critical periods. During periods of movement abeyance (Taylor and Crossley 2022), social networks serve to maintain activist communities that can be revived or triggered to form a new movement (Rohman 2019). Similar to the possibility of cascading demobilization, however, depending on what is shared, these networks can also lead to declined participation (Chen and Gorski 2015; Tang and Chung 2022).

As technology platforms based on social networks, social media facilitates network-based

mobilization (Tufekci 2017; Larson et al. 2019). Social media is a means of public and direct communication that reduces the cost of broadcasting and information-seeking for both individuals and social movement organizations (Margetts et al. 2015; Bennett and Segerberg 2013). In this capacity, it provides important pathways to participation, as potential dissidents can be motivated by others through their social ties (Jost et al. 2018). This kind of public and social information leads to coordination among the larger group, potentially generating cascades that motivate further participation (Gonz´lez-Bail´n et al. 2011). a o

According to studies that explicitly consider social media's role in how movements respond to repression, social media's informational functions reduce the cost of organizing and the risk of participation, which are understood to be the primary mechanisms through which movements converge on backfire mobilization against repression. For example, Odaba¸ s and Reynolds-Stenson (2018) looked at how these platforms' capacity to reach new participants decreases the cost of recruitment following repressive events. As information about repression of protesters reaches previously uninformed audiences on social media, especially as alternative to other information channels, backlash mobilization will be more likely as individuals become increasingly aggrieved. Steinert-Threlkeld et al. (2015) find that increased coordination through social media decreases the perceived risk of being repressed when participating in offline protests, as a larger number of participants reduces the risk for any one individual to experience repression. Pan and Siegel (2020) find evidence of a similar mechanism in the context of backlash mobilization online, where low cost participation diffused risk among a large group and led to greater backlash against the repressive regime.

While these existing studies have explored social media's role in short term mobilization, they have yet to consider its relationship with how movements are sustained over time when facing continued repression. Importantly, as long term sustenance follows a different logic from short term mobilization (Taylor 1989), it is not immediately clear how the logic of low cost information spreading extends to keeping activists engaged over time in the face of continued low-level repression. A recent study of movements in Indonesia found that social media can maintain movement continuity during abeyance by facilitating continued social interactions between activists, which strengthens important communities (Rohman 2019). However, it does not explicitly consider how social media interacts with the existence of continued repression, where the combination of the chilling effect and the natural decay of activist involvement can easily lead to movement failure.

In our study, we explore how social media contributes to a movement sustaining itself after critical periods while continuing to face repression. Because our focus is on the mechanisms underlying this pattern, we begin by directly asking activists how they perceive government repression and the role of social media in their activism. It has been shown

that activists tend to understand the logic of mobilization mechanisms (Everett 1992), and specific to technology, activists are cognizant of relevant features of different information technology platforms and consciously make use of them in their advocacy efforts (Kow et al. 2016; Rohlinger and Corrigall-Brown 2018).


## 3 Climate Activists' Views on Social Media and Repression


To inform our theoretical understanding and analysis of social media in the context of sustained climate activism and repression, we conducted an exploratory survey with 43 climate activists from Elokapina recruited through its internal messaging system. These activists had a wide range of prior experience with climate or environmental protests. All but six had some form of prior experience, and some had participated in more than twenty protests. We followed our survey with in-depth, semi-structured interviews with eight survey respondents, all but one of whom had prior protest experience. The surveys and interviews took place during December 2021-January 2022.

Our survey and interviews broadly covered the respondents' activism both online and offline, including their involvement with Elokapina and other climate movement organizations, social media use, protest and repression experiences, including those with the October 2020 protest, and views on policing in Finland. In our semi-structured interviews, we additionally delved into the activists' motivations for participating in Elokapina and the role of social media in climate activism. Participant recruitment was coordinated by a contact person within Elokapina who posted our recruitment materials to Elokapina's internal messaging system with a link to the survey. Individuals opted into the survey after reading the study information and consent form. We recruited respondents for further interviews with a message at the end of our survey and then followed up with willing individuals. Additional details about the implementation of our survey and interviews, including a discussion of ethical considerations, are in Appendix S1.

In the following paragraphs, we present the main findings from our survey and interviews, and discuss how they inform our subsequent statistical analysis. We begin by detailing how activists describe government repression of climate activism and how they see it impacting political participation and the climate movement. Then, we discuss how activists view the relationship between activism and social media. Notable survey results are summarized in Figure 1. ## 3.1 How Activists View Repression's Impact on the Movement


The interview and survey findings directly corroborate our understanding that the use of pepper spray in October 2020 was an unprecedented and exceptionally severe instance of repression in Finland. Several interviewees [ a,d,e,g ] described the incident as shocking and unexpected, and most had not previously experienced equivalent use of force by the Finnish police. Similarly, 82% of survey respondents had no prior experiences of police repression. The incident was formative for activists, as it brought forth new information about the risks of climate activism in Finland. Interviewees [ c,d,e ] stated that while they were initially shocked, they now expect repressive policing as a matter of routine during Elokapina protests.

The incident commenced a series of repressive actions the Finnish government has taken against Elokapina. From our interviews, it is evident that Elokapina activists are cognizant of the heightened tension between them and the government, as they frequently referenced repressive actions that have occurred since October 2020. Interviewees [ a,d ] outright stated that the Finnish police has been targeting Elokapina. In terms of specific events, some interviewees [ b,c,d,e ] mentioned police investigations conducted in 2021, when climate activists proclaimed support for civil disobedience. 1 Others [ a,d,e,h ] described hostile interactions between activists and police during protests, such as the police did not intervening when climate activists faced threatening behavior from counter-protesters [ b ] . Speaking about these incidents, most activists recognized state repression can make movement participants feel unsafe or discouraged [ a,b,c,d,f,g ] .

These interactions potentially have a chilling effect, but the interviewees also offered evidence that repression does not necessarily deter their participation. First, interviewees [ a,c,d,e, ] maintained that the risks associated with protesting, such as altercations with the police and the potential legal repercussions, are insignificant compared to the cost of not urgently pushing for climate policies. These activists appear to have high political efficacy, with 94% of the survey respondents stating that protesting and civil disobedience increase citizens' capability to shape social and political outcomes.

Second, the activists noted the importance of social ties in preventing them from withdrawing. Specifically, interviewees [ a,c,f,g ] emphasized solidarity within the Elokapina community as key to sustaining their motivation to participate. Most interviewees [ a,b,c,d,f,h ] mentioned being motivated by seeing others from their social networks participate in climate activism. One interviewee [ f ] explicitly stated that their belief that others will continue to participate helped them overcome their fears of police repression. Other interviewees [ c,d ] , despite recognizing there was some dropout, pointed to the consistent number of protesters to support their belief that the pepper spraying incident did not deter participation but in fact mobilized the movement.

On the whole, our findings demonstrate that activists are attuned to movement mobilization and demobilization mechanisms, corroborating prior social movement research (Everett 1992). They recognized both the challenges repression poses to the movement through potential chilling effects on participation, and the role social ties have in overcoming these effects.


## 3.2 How Activists Understand Social Media's Role in Activism


To see how social media affordances (i.e., the actions users understand platforms to offer) impact how the movement sustains itself in response to repression, we need to understand how activists view the role of social media in climate activism and how it relates to coordinating collective behavior. From our interviews, we identified two general trends in Elokapina activists' understanding of social media and how it relates to collective behavior.

First, Elokapina activists appear to be cognizant of the audience demands - expectations from both within and outside the movement - surrounding social media communication. We find that they view the consistent use of social media communication as a necessity for the movement and have dedicated organizational resources to make it a part of their advocacy strategy. When asked about how they view social media, all interviewees explicitly stated that social media platforms are crucial for coordinating movement activity, such as through outwardly-facing communication that reaches new audiences or spreads information. Activists [ b,c,d ] specifically discussed the movement's dependency on public social media

platforms, with some [ c,d,e ] noting that Elokapina formally allocates organizational and human resources to social media communication tasks, including developing formal training protocols [ c ] . Importantly, activists acknowledged that sustaining communication on social media is critical because it is a part of the movement's appearances. One interviewee [ c ] discussed at length the need for movement members to prioritize the visuals of communication - impact and consistency - and, along with another [ d ] , revealed that message presentation is in fact part of Elokapina's social media training.

Second, activists' understanding of how information spreads and is amplified on social media appears to inform how they view information cascades on social media as a critical component of the movement's success. One interviewee [ c ] explicitly talked about how information cascades on social media lead to successful mass mobilization. They pointed to mechanisms at both the organizational level - Elokapina announcing the number of people planning to attend a protest on their public social media accounts to mobilize additional participation - and the personal level - activists publicizing their planned protest participation on social media encourages peer participation. Another activist [ d ] discussed how 'filter bubbles' make social media effective for spreading information among like-minded users, and stated that it is important for Elokapina to consider this aspect of social media communication.

These two trends - activists understanding the audience demands surrounding social media communication and recognizing how information cascades determine movement success - are important in the context of our study on how movements sustain themselves through repression by overcoming potential demobilization. From our interviews, we find that activists are cognizant of how social media platforms can drive movement success or failure by facilitating cascading mobilization dynamics, specifically that information spreading through social media networks can generate cascading effects on participation in either direction. Because the movement is normally expected to be active on social media, inaction when facing repressive events is likely to be perceived as a chilling effect. And because perceived chilling effects have the potential to lead to cascading demobilization, activists are compelled to act to preempt the anticipated high cost of inaction. 2

The result is that the movement remains active through repression events because engaged actors see the alternative as even more costly. Further, as activists are cognizant of the mechanisms that underlie mobilizing cascades and appear to internalize behaviors that lead to movement-amplifying cascades as a part of their social media activism - which has

been observed on climate activist Twitter elsewhere (Xia, Chen and Kivel¨ 2021) - we expect a them to be particularly vigilant in maintaining this type of cascade-reinforcing behavior when facing the risk of cascading demobilization. Specifically, there should be continued resource coordination (planned or unplanned) that gives the movement the most visible display of strength and coherence. In the context of Twitter, which is driven primarily by public endorsements through retweets, we expect this to manifest as recurring centralized patterns in retweeting behavior as activists converge on retweeting the same messages.

There is a performative aspect to social media communication, which is accentuated on public platforms such as Twitter that afford information cascades. In the context of social movements, it is an affordance that sustains movements through repression because it elevates the cost of inaction. Building on our interview findings, we study activists' online behavior with an eye toward the performative aspects of online communication amidst repression. First, we explore how activists respond to repression in the short and long term, specifically examining whether repression has chilling or mobilizing effects. Second, we examine the networked aspects of online behavior, as our interviews suggest that activists' understanding of social media affordances would lead to coordinated behavior that sustains mobilization cascades, which we measure as tendencies for centralization in the retweet network.


## 4 Data and Measurement: Finnish Climate Movement on Twitter


Our data, comprising climate-related Tweets from 15,115 users over an 82-week span, allows us to observe the real-time online behavior of 1,190 climate activists throughout repressive events. Our approach is based on examining first, whether and how temporal variation in individual- and system-level outcomes on Twitter maps onto major offline events, and second, how climate activists differ in their response compared to the non-activist public, which serves as a baseline that captures both the effect of major events in Finnish climate politics and general temporal dynamic over time. These variations allow us to speak to our theoretical expectations and examine the effects of repression on activists' online behavior while accounting for other changes in the Twitter networks. We describe our data in this section, including data collection and how we identify activists online. Specific methods used for subsequent analyses are included in their respective sections.


## 4.1 Data collection


We collected climate-related tweets using Twitter's publicly available application programming interface (API). Specifically, we used the filter/statuses v1.1 endpoint, which allows us

to collect, in real-time, all tweets that satisfy a predefined set of keywords. 3 In total, our data collection spans an 82-week period from July 18, 2020 to February 11, 2022. From this raw data, we extracted all 501,486 Finnish retweets and 176,627 original statuses (i.e., original tweets with or without mentions to another user). 4

Elokapina organized a total of three protest campaigns throughout our observation period. The first and most significant instance of repression that we identified occurred during the first campaign, in the beginning of week twelve. Based on our interviews, continued episodes of repression have occurred since this initial and formative event. Figure 2 shows the weekly activity (2-week moving average) for the observation period. The first substantial peak aligns with the pepper spray incident, when average daily activity in the week following the event reached just under 4,500, which is more than four times the baseline activity level. The two subsequent Elokapina campaigns in 2021 both induced even larger increases in the daily volume of climate-related tweets than the 2020 campaign. Our data collection ends right before the Russian invasion into Ukraine in late February 2022, which right-bounds our data because of its large impact on Finnish Twitter activity (Xia et al. 2024).

## 4.2 Identifying climate activists on Twitter


A key task in our study is identifying climate activists within our overall set of Twitter users. Because we want to study the effect of repression on individual and group behavior, we focus on users who were already part of the climate movement before the pepper-spraying event.

To identify activists, we use Twitter bios, self-reported profile descriptions encoding important textual information (including emojis) that represent social identities and political alignments held by the account owner (Pathak, Madani and Joseph 2021; Essig and DellaPosta 2024). We began by extracting all 21,168 unique bios observed from all 15,115 users who appeared at least once during the pre-pepper spray period. We observe more bios than users, as some users changed their bios. Next, we used a two-stage labelling procedure to identify activists based on these bios.

First, based on external knowledge and additional qualitative reading of Finnish climate tweets, we identified a set of words that are likely to be used by climate activists to indicate their identity as such. Our list includes keywords related to climate issues (e.g., climate, green, nature) and activism (e.g., activist, XR). 5 Using these keywords, we filtered the 21,168 bios for manual labeling. This first-stage keyword filter matched 6,419 unique bios from 4,506 users. Second, we manually labelled these bios as belonging to climate activists, climate skeptics, or non-activists. Users who changed their bios during our period of investigation were given a separate label for each observed bio. Any user with at least one bio matching the activist criteria were labelled as an activist. Our manual labeling criteria is described in Table 1. We detail our procedure (e.g., labeling agreement) in Appendix S2. We obtained 1,190 climate-positive activists and 34 climate-negative activists. The remaining users and those not passing the first-stage filter add up to 13,891 non-activists. In all subsequent analyses, due to the low number of skeptics, we only distinguish between activists and everyone else.

## 5 Chilling and Mobilizing Effects on Activists' Online Behavior


To see how climate activists respond to government repression in their social media behavior, we begin by exploring their short and long term post-repression activity for evidence of chilling and mobilizing effects. In our interviews, we found evidence for both effects, as while most of our interviewees indicated they remain motivated to participate despite increased concerns, they also recognized that repression can be a deterrent for continued participation. Building on our interviews, we study the behavioral consequences of repression in more detail by focusing on observable behavior on Twitter. We measure changes in climate activists' online behavior by looking at the volume of participants and their activity as a broad measure of mobilization or demobilization. In Appendix S5, we show that our results here are robust to measuring online behavior as expressions of movement affiliation in Twitter bios.

For this analysis, we used a day-level time series of all observable Twitter activity (i.e., tweets, retweets, and replies). To study this time series, we used the Bayesian Estimator of Abrupt change, Seasonal change, and Trend (BEAST) model. The model, originally developed for ecology (Zhao et al. 2019) and recently used to study social media engagement (Reuning, Whitesell and Hannah 2022), simultaneously estimates the temporal trends and cyclical patterns that make up an observed time series, and the changepoints in both of these dynamic processes that best fit the observed data. By decomposing the observed time series into two separate dynamic processes, it allows us to focus only on the temporal trend and its changepoints while effectively denoising periodic patterns not relevant to our study, such as the weekly cycle on Twitter where activity tends to be lower on weekends.

We examined the volume of tweets for climate activists, mapping detected changepoints onto repressive events (e.g., the pepper-spraying incident) and mobilizing events (e.g., large climate protests). By taking an exploratory approach to studying the entire time series, we are able to learn about both the short term and long term responses to repression. First, detected changepoints in activity trends allow us to see how changes in Twitter activity correspond to offline events. Second, we are able to examine trends in disaggregated intervals as indicated by estimated changepoints, which allows us to compare short and long term responses to the pre-repression period. We also examine non-activists activity patterns as a baseline of how Finnish climate Twitter generally responds to offline events. The specifications of our analysis, including fitting details, are described in Appendix S4.
