The observed short term mobilization during these campaigns are both sudden and brief, as the level of activity spikes then shortly returns to the pre-repression baseline of approximately 150 events a day. Notably, instead of exhibiting signs of a chilling effect, this baseline activity persists between short term spikes even after the onset of continued government repression.

While climate activists and non-activists are similarly responsive to larger events, we also identify changepoints that differentiate climate activists from our non-activist public. These changes correspond with smaller offline events - a climate protest in September 2020 and the publication of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Climate Report in 2021 - that mobilized activists but did not lead to appreciable change among the non-activists. Importantly, these findings demonstrate that the online behavior of climate activists differs from that of our non-activist control group.

Overall, we find that offline events, including the pepper spray incident and large scale protests produce rapid, considerable increases in the daily volume of tweets for both climate activists. Activists having a heightened response to the pepper spray incident, instead of becoming chilled, corroborates prior studies that demonstrate the tendency for backlash mobilization (Steinert-Threlkeld et al. 2015; Pan and Siegel 2020). Additionally, we also show that activists' online activity levels are sustained in the longer term despite continued repression, as short term mobilizations are always followed by a restabilization back to the remarkably stable pre-repression baseline through our entire 82-week period.

This indicates that climate activists on the whole are not responsive to the potential chilling effects of repression. Although some activists we interviewed describe feeling a heightened sense of concern following repression, the pepper spraying incident did not demobilize the movement at large. Importantly, we find a long term sustenance of online activity despite state repression both in terms of large shocks and continued repression.


## 6 Network Centralization in Activist Communication on Social Media


What explains the sustained social media behavior of climate activists? Based on our interviews, we argue that activists are cognizant of the need to maintain movement participation so as to avoid cascading demobilization. We examine this in terms of activists' ingroup behavior on social media which we expect to exhibit a persistent pattern that serves to sustain the performative function of the movement's social media presence. This should occur because of training from Elokapina and also the activists' general understanding of information cascades on social media, both of which we uncovered during our interviews, and can be planned or unplanned. Specifically, we expect that, due to activists' understanding of the importance for the movement to demonstrate its strength and coherence on social media, they will converge on retweeting the same messages and hence reinforcing movement mobilizing cascades. This will result in a centralization effect in the observed retweet network.

To study the tendency for performative ingroup centralization, we consider the collection of all retweets as a networked system because it allows us to observe emergent networked behavior. We focus on retweets as they are generally understood as indicators of public endorsement (Metaxas et al. 2015), which is suitable given our aim to examine performative behavior on social media. We study the dynamics of these retweet networks over time by comparing the behavior of activists against non-activists.


## 6.1 Exponential Random Graph Models for Retweet Networks


To examine the structural features of the climate communication networks at the systemlevel, specifically network centralization, we constructed weekly networks using retweet data, and analyzed them using exponential random graph models (ERGM). The ERGM is a statistical model that allows for inference on generative features that underlie tie formation in a network (e.g., dyad homophily, receiver popularity) by considering the entirety of observed ties and non-ties as a draw from a multivariate distribution (Cranmer and Desmarais 2010).

In an ERGM specification, model terms are statistics computed over the observed system, which in our case is the weekly retweet network. These statistics are usually raw or weighted counts of local network configurations that should be observable if the hypothesized factors

Importantly, while these local configurations often exist at the node or dyad levels like in a dyad-level logistic regression model, these local configurations can additionally be specified to include as many nodes as necessary to capture the conceptualized generative feature. In its simplest formulation, network centralization in a directed retweet network - where a directed edge from i to k means i retweeted k - is specified as an 'in two star' comprising three nodes (i.e., i → k, j → k ). This configuration captures the tendency for retweets (i.e., from i and from j ) to be directed toward the same node k instead of spreading to another node k ′ in the network, with the process being one of preferential attachment based on k having a higher retweet count than k ′ .

In our models, to capture network centralization among activists, we use the geometrically weighted in-degree (gwidegree) model term. The gwidegree term follows the same preferential attachment logic as the in two star, but extends it by downweighting the effect of multiple incoming ties instead of letting the effect of preferential tie formation increase linearly with the in-degree of the receiver. Specifically, each additional in-degree will add less to the popularity of the receiver such that the difference between having ten and nine incoming ties, for example, is smaller than the difference between having one and no incoming tie. This extension greatly improves model fit, generally decreasing the tendency for ERGM estimation problems (Snijders et al. 2006). It is important to note that the term is formally specified as the opposite of preferential attachment (Snijders et al. 2006), meaning that a negative coefficient estimate on this term will capture lower centralization (Levy 2016). We therefore refer to this term as the degree equality term.


## 6.1.1 Network construction and ERGM specification


For our network analysis, we focus on the subset of users who consistently interacted with others about the climate issue. In our main set of models, we included users who retweeted other users in at least 6 out of the 11 weeks for which we have observations before the pepper-spraying incident. We additionally explored the importance of consistency by fitting models using definitions of consistency ranging from 3 to 9 weeks. We also included 34

important public figures in Finnish climate politics who were on Finnish climate Twitter but were not consistently retweeting others. Users in this group, fully presented in Appendix S6, include, for example, then-Prime Minister Sanna Marin. When specifying our ERGMs, we modeled other users retweeting these 34 users but did not model their outgoing retweets, which captures a more realistic picture of the retweet network while preserving the inclusion criteria for our network data.

For our full networks constructed using the 6-week consistency threshold, this yielded weekly networks of 230 activists - users who meet our activist criteria in at least one prepepper-spraying week - and 728 non-activists. Ties in this network are based on retweets, where a directed tie indicates the sending user retweeted the receiving user at least once during the week. In total, we have 81 networks, 11 before the pepper-spraying event and 70 after.

In our ERGM specification, we include the gwidegree term, the degree equality term which we use to study network centralization, separately for activists and non-activists. This allows us to study network centralization among activists while having a comparison baseline of how centralization dynamics generally play out in Finnish climate Twitter. As noted, the gwidegree term adds downweighting to the preferential attachment effect. In our ERGM specification, we use the highest level of downweighting, which in effect conditions retweeting tendency based on whether receivers have existing retweets. Different levels of downweighting tend to yield substantively similar findings, and this particular specification facilitates a straightforward interpretation - the coefficient captures degree equality by modeling the tendency for retweets to be sent to nodes without existing retweets as opposed to those that do (Schmid, Chen and Desmarais 2022). At the system level, this means the network will be less centralized.

In addition to the degree equality term, we include the following terms in each of our weekly models. First, we include a set of actor- and dyad-level terms to account for baseline activity and homophily. Next, to account for confounding through clustering, which is another commonly observed behavioural tendency in networks, we include the geometricallyweighted edgewise shared partner term (gwesp) for activists and non-activists, which allows our two gwidegree terms to properly recover activist and non-activist network centralization effects (Levy 2016). 7 Finally, we include a lagged dependent variable (i.e., whether i retweeted j in the previous period) to account for past endorsement patterns.

In our analysis, we fit separate models for each of our weekly networks so we can examine

dynamic changes in the system using the statistical process monitoring approach we describe below. To confirm these networks are complex systems with important interdependencies that cannot be modeled with a dyad-independent model like the logistic regression, we compared fit statistics between our network models with logistic regressions that omit four network terms. Deviance tests (i.e., difference in deviance compared against a chi-squared distribution with 4 degrees of freedom) between the two models across all 81 periods indicate a statistically significant improvement in fit when including the network terms. A similar examination using the BIC shows improvements ranging between 272-3988 for the 81 periods. Additional details of our ERGM specification and estimation are in Appendix S6.


## 6.1.2 Detecting change in generative features of networks

Specifically, we fit the ERGM for each weekly network to obtain the time series of the coefficient estimate for the degree equality term (i.e., gwidegree), then compared the coefficients post-pepper spray (weeks 12-82) to pre-pepper spray (2-11). ## 6.2 Results


Our main finding is presented in the left panel of Figure 4, which shows the comparison of network centralization for activists and non-activists across our entire observation period (i.e., preand post-pepper spray, as indicated by the vertical gray line). First, note that the degree equality term for activists and non-activists across all periods are negative and statistically significantly different from zero. This means that both groups exhibit network centralization, which is expected as it is a fundamental feature of social networks such as retweet networks (Bild et al. 2015; Overbey et al. 2013). Our focus is on differences between temporal changes in this tendency.

Here, we see that the general Finnish non-activist climate Twitter exhibits signs of decay in network centralization, as the degree equality increased over time. Starting in December 2020, which is approximately two months after the pepper spraying event, the network centralization among the non-activists becomes significantly lower compared to the prepepper spraying period (i.e., increasing above the EWMA monitoring bounds indicated by the dashed lines). This kind of decay in network centralization has recently been found to be a feature of Twitter networks (Atwal, Murphy and Garibay 2021), whereby an aging effect means retweets to the oldest accounts are less subject to preferential attachment. This is particularly relevant for our analysis, as our networks are built using the same set of users who were active since the beginning of our 81-week observation period, so the centralization

decay should be understood to be the normal state of progression for networks like this.

Strikingly, however, this pattern does not hold for the climate activist subnetwork, as degree equality for climate activists remained reasonably stable throughout our pre- and post-pepper spray periods. While there is a slight upward trend in the degree equality term that plateaus, it is well within the EWMA monitoring bounds, which indicates that the post-pepper spray period is statistically indistinguishable from the pre-period. This means that, as we hypothesized following our interviews, climate activists' Twitter behavior exhibits emergent properties (i.e., non-decay of network centralization) that sustains long term participation despite continued police repression.

We additionally explored how variation in activists' consistency influence our findings by fitting models for climate activists with consistency thresholds set to the range of 3 to 9 weeks. Our results are shown in the right panel of Figure 4. First, with the exception of the most relaxed threshold of 3 weeks, our findings about sustained network centralization hold across different thresholds. Further, more than just a robustness check, this examination speaks directly to our argument about activist behavior because consistency captures a combination of investment in the movement's social media activism and awareness of Twitter's affordances. We find a clear pattern that subsets of increasingly consistent activists exhibit increasingly stronger adherence to retweet centralization. This supports our argument that the longer term sustenance of movements is driven by activists' understanding of social media affordances, as those more connected to the movement are more compelled to engage in movement sustaining actions.


## 7 Discussion and Conclusion


Our analyses of activists' online participation and retweet network dynamics show that the climate movement is remarkably consistent in maintaining its established pre-repression baseline social media engagement, apart from short term increases when mobilizing against police repression and heightened activity during major climate events. Activists persist in this pattern of sustained online participation even with unexpected police brutality and continued episodes of repression aggravating their concerns regarding participation. Our findings show a lack of long term chilling effects on the volume of direct online participation and public expression of movement affiliation, and a persistent pattern of ingroup centralization in terms of endorsement of messages within the movement.

These sustained patterns of 1) activity after backlash mobilization at pre-repression levels and 2) retweet network centralization corroborate findings from our interviews, where we uncovered a mechanism that addresses how movements sustain themselves through continued

repression beyond immediate short term responses. Activists are cognizant of the importance of performative online participation to movement success, especially when facing repression, because social media can generate cascading effects on participation in either direction. This compels continued participation, especially in terms of behavior that reinforces movement sustaining cascades, which manifests as network centralization in the context of retweet networks.

Our findings speak directly to the social movements literature on social media's role in the repression-dissent nexus. Previous studies in this area have examined either social media's role in short term backlash mobilization because they reduce the costs of organizing and participating immediately following repression (Pan and Siegel 2020; Odaba¸ s and ReynoldsStenson 2018; Steinert-Threlkeld et al. 2015), or how they maintain longer term activist communities during periods of post-movement abeyance by persisting as communication structures (Rohman 2019; Tang and Chung 2022). While these factors are ostensibly at play in our case, we extend this literature by showing that social media platforms can also, through a social informational mechanism that compels action, sustain movements during continued repression.

Further, our study establishes important and previously unexplored connections between the affordances literature and the social movements literature. While prior studies have extensively pointed to the ease of information spreading through social media as a cost reduction feature, we identified a social informational mechanism that requires activists to understand the potential longer term audience costs associated with this feature. In doing so, we engage the affordances literature, which emphasizes the importance of looking beyond technology features in themselves to instead also consider how they are understood by their users. Social media's affordance of sustaining movements through repression, then, is the result of an emergent process that involves the interaction between technology features and how users perceive them. We also extend the existing affordances literature, which has thus far only focused on individuals, by highlighting the possibility for it to be a group phenomenon. Here, the costliness of activist inaction stems from activists' shared understanding of the possibility of cascading demobilization, which is another type of emergent process involving positive feedback among like-minded actors. In all, our study adds to the growing number of studies highlighting the importance of engaging with the affordances literature (e.g. Odaba¸ s and Reynolds-Stenson 2018; Earl and Kimport 2011) by offering an approach that considers the effects of social media beyond its cost-reducing capacities, centering activists' perception and understanding of social media platforms as attributes that direct their use.

## I NTRODUCTION


Debt has always been part of American life. As one delegate at  a  state  constitutional  convention said in 1877, 'I recognize that this is a debt-ridden land . . . .'  Among the early settlers, a 1 fifth  were  indentured  servants  who  agreed  to  work  to  repay their debt upon arrival.  In the beginning, debts tended to be 2 relatively small and owed locally, acting as a sort of social glue. 3 Refined gentlemen earned most of their income through loans, not labor.  Even the military was impacted. The 1776 Articles of 4 War had a provision governing how a soldier's debts would be

resolved if they died while in service.  The 1878 Articles of War 5 provided that no soldier could be arrested for debt unless it was contracted before enlistment and was for a certain amount.  To 6 this day, military courts-martials can prosecute a servicemember for a 'dishonorable' failure to pay a debt. 7

Debtors' prisons, too, have always been part of America. As the name implies, these were jails used to punish the financially misfortunate. At the time of the American Revolution, only two states offered any constitutional protections to debtors.  Today, 8 forty-one states have constitutional provisions explicitly banning imprisonment for debt in whole or in part.  This Article 9 seeks to connect those dots, tracing the issue of imprisonment for debt through the constitutions of the states.

This  Article  proceeds  in  four  Parts.  Part  I  provides  an overview of debtors' prisons in early America. The American system  of  debt  imprisonment  is  modeled  off  of  the  English system. The common law allowed creditors to bring suits for debts that resulted in imprisonment before any court adjudicated the matter. Thousands were imprisoned in debtors' prisons  in  early  America  and  living  conditions  for  prisoners were abysmal. Because the federal government took a handsoff approach to this problem, progress on the issue was up to the states.

Part  II looks  at  constitutional  developments  during  the Revolutionary  Era  through  the  Era  of  Good  Feelings  (1776 through  1825).  Among  the  original  thirteen  states,  only  two states offered any protections for debtors facing imprisonment in  their  founding  charters-or  less  than  one-sixth.  By  1825,

## A. Legal Structure of Debtors' Prisons


Debtors'  prisons  can  be  seen  throughout  the  history  of Western  civilization  in  some  form  or  another.  The  Twelve Tables, the oldest codification of Roman law we have, permitted its usage in 451 B.C. and is the first known codification of debt imprisonment. 11 Roman  debtors  could  be  imprisoned  after thirty days of failure to pay their debts, and further punished with  death  or  being  sold  into  slavery. 12 If a debtor  was delinquent with multiple creditors, the creditors could dissect his body and split it up amongst them. 13 This continued until a creditor savagely beat the son of an imprisoned debtor after the son refused the sexual advances of the creditor. 14 This caused such a public outcry that the Roman Senate felt compelled to end debt imprisonment altogether in 326 B.C., as well as release all confined debtors. 15 Ancient Greece, as well, permitted debt slavery, until Solon of Athens forbade it. 16

In the sixteenth century, New Spain's landholding aristocracy enslaved native peoples, but by the seventeenth century, the Spanish Crown renounced slavery. 17 So the aristocrats shifted

## A. Constitutional Protections for Debtors: First Steps


In  1776,  coinciding  with  the  Declaration  of  Independence, most of the original colonies passed their own state constitutions. 153 Like the federal government, the states largely neglected  to  provide  constitutional  protections  to  debtors,  or were  outrightly  hostile  towards  them.  South  Carolina,  for example, barred debtors from public office in its first constitution-a disability the state would hold onto for nearly 100 years. 154 Though the states hewed to the federal constitution in  many  respects-three  branches  of  government,  bicameral legislatures, bills of rights, and so forth-imprisonment for debt is one area in which the states would eventually chart their own path.

With  the  Revolution,  every  state  except  Connecticut  and Rhode Island adopted constitutions-rather than continuing to

rely on  royal  charters. 155 Both  Pennsylvania 156 and  North Carolina 157 adopted declarations of rights with language against debtors' prisons. Pennsylvania's was ratified first, on September  28,  1776.  Section  28  of  the  Pennsylvania's  first Constitution read:

The person of a debtor, where there is not a strong presumption of fraud, shall not be continued in prison,  after  delivering  Up,  bona  fide,  all  his estate real and  personal,  for the use of his creditors,  in  such  manner  as  shall  be  hereafter regulated by law. All prisoners shall be bailable by sufficient sureties, unless for capital offences, when  the proof is evident, or presumption great. 158

Two parts of this constitutional provision bear note--as they crop up again and again around the country. First, there is an exception for fraud. Debtors who hid property, 'gave away' property to friends and family, or else acted dishonestly, could still  find  themselves  behind  bars.  Second,  the  debtor  had  to 'deliver  up,'  or  surrender,  all  of  their  real  and  personal property  to  their  creditor  to  stay  out  of  jail.  This  serves  to streamline the collection process for the creditor by still holding out  the  threat  of  imprisonment  for  obstinate  or  slow-footed debtors. Notwithstanding these deficiencies, it was still a huge step forward in a society where incarcerating debtors was the norm.

Before  Pennsylvania  adopted  this  provision,  it  dealt  with debtor-inmates through 'frequent interpositions of the legislature  in  behalf  of  particular  persons,'  which  were  'too often dependent upon favor or prejudice' of the people seeking

## A. Constitutional Developments: Exponential Growth


As this  Section  will  illustrate,  the  debtors'  prison  abolition movement took off in the middle of the nineteenth century. Not only did more states join the Union with protections for debtors in  their  constitutions,  but  states  also  started  adding  stronger protections,  and  states  that  had  previously  shunned  debtors changed course. The progress was aided by the readmission of southern states after the Civil War, whose post-war constitutions were drafted by a much more diverse coalition of voices, which resulted in more help for debtors, among other things. 301


## 1. The Jacksonian Era


In  this  period,  there  was  a  flurry  of  constitution-making, much of it protecting debtors. During the Jacksonian Era (18251849), many state constitutional conventions were called, often

in  response  to  public  debt  crises  over  the  years. 302 Fittingly, many of these conventions also responded to the private debt crisis of using incarceration to punish insolvency. 303

After  Missouri  joined  the  Union  in  1821,  the  United  States entered  the  longest  drought  of  new  membership  up  to  that point in its history: fifteen years. 304 Arkansas ended the fifteen years  of  stagnation  with  an  1836  constitution  that  barred imprisonment for non-fraudulent debtors who offered up their estates to creditors. 305 In this way, it reflected the same scope of protection as the fairly recent constitutions of Alabama, Illinois, Mississippi,  and  Indiana,  as  well  as  the  1790  Pennsylvania Constitution. 306 It would also kick off a nearly thirty-year chain of states joining the Union with constitutional protections for debtors.

## C. Modest Federal Progress


By the latter half of the nineteenth century, people in power were starting to take notice of the movement against debtors' prisons. Famed Senator Daniel Webster said when it comes to imprisonment for small debts, 'I am decidedly against it.' 403 The  Governor  of  South  Carolina  spoke  at  the  state's  1868 convention  to  encourage  the  body  to  end  imprisonment  for debt. 404 The issue became potent enough that President Andrew Jackson felt compelled to voice his support for it in his first State of the Union  message  to  Congress.  He  called  upon  the legislature to examine whether the present debtor laws 'may not,  consistently  with  the  public  interest,  be  extended  to  the release of the debt where the conduct of the debtor is wholly

exempt from the imputation of fraud.' 405 He believed that '[a] more liberal policy than that which now prevails in reference to this unfortunate class of citizens is certainly due to them, and would prove beneficial to the country.' 406 The present system of imprisonment  only  served  'to  dispirit  the  debtor,'  causing them to 'sink[] into a state of apathy, and become[] a useless drone  in  society  or  a  vicious  member  of  it,  if  not  a  feeling witness of the rigor and inhumanity of his country.' 407

Two years later, after Congress passed a weak act, 408 Jackson renewed his plea in another State of the Union message. He was still  making the same complaints as the last time: he said the law had not been adequate to provide 'relief to this unfortunate class  of  our  fellow  citizens.' 409 He  once  again  insisted  that imprisonment should be limited to fraudulent concealment of property, not for people who simply could not afford to pay off their debts. 410

Notwithstanding Jackson's entreaties, the federal government's actions remained tepid on the matter of debtors' prisons. Throughout the nineteenth century, no national party platform in a presidential election mentioned the issue. 411

## A. Constitutional Developments: Abolitionists Triumph, then Fade Away


After the dust settled on the Civil War and Reconstruction sputtered out, not only was the Southern rebellion vanquished, so too was the intellectual case for debtors' prisons. Never again would a state join the Union without constitutional protections for debtors after West Virginia did in 1863. 419

Post-Civil  War,  the  next  state  to  adopt  a  constitution  was Nebraska  in  1875. 420 It  protected  debtors  except  for  fraud. 421 Colorado  joined  in  1876  and  revived  the  requirement  that debtors surrender their property to creditors, a feature no state had in its inaugural constitution since Arkansas in 1836. 422

Following Nebraska and Colorado was the 'Class of 1889,' when four new states joined at once, which was the most in one year since 1776. 423 The states were North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana, and Washington. 424 Each  state  protected  debtors  in some form. North Dakota and Montana both excepted fraud and required debtors to surrender their property to creditors 425 -the  last  states  to  retain  that  colonial-era  policy. Washington only allowed imprisonment for absconding debtors, 426 a first, and South Dakota banned imprisonment for all contractual debt. 427 Closing out the century, Idaho,

## Homeworking and Division of Domestic Work: the Role of Gender Role Attitudes in Germany


Olga Leshchenko  and Heejung Chung § 


## 1 Introduction


Homeworking (i.e., telecommuting) is generally perceived to allow workers  to better balance work and private demands by providing more time for leisure and family (Noonan and Glass 2012). This is done through the reduction of commuting costs, through enhancing the flexibility and permeability of boundaries between work and family (Clark 2000; Halford 2006), and through the increase of work autonomy (Allen, Golden, and Shockley 2015). There is some evidence of homeworking reducing workfamily  conflict  for  parents  (Kelly,  Moen,  and  Tranby  2011).  However,  other  studies  show  that homeworking can increase work-family conflict, particularly for women (Hjálmsdóttir and Bjarnadóttir 2021; Yucel and Chung 2023). This is because homeworking reinforces the gendered division of labour (Chung 2020; Lyttelton, Zang, and Musick 2022) increasing the amount of time women spend on both paid and unpaid work (Hilbrecht et al., 2008; Lott, 2019; Sullivan and Lewis, 2001; Chung and Booker 2023). In fact, scholars argue that flexible working has the potential to exacerbate gender inequality for this very reason (Chung 2022; Chung and van der Lippe 2020).

Previous studies have shown the importance of Gender Role Attitude (GRA) in predicting the division of childcare and housework among heterosexual couples or in explaining levels of work-life conflict (Nitsche and Grunow, 2018; Schober, 2013). More recently, studies have noted the variation in the  gendered  work-family  outcomes  of  flexible  working  in  different  gender  normative  contexts (Kurowska  2020;  Lott  2015).  Similarly,  studies  have  shown  how  GRA  moderates  the  association between homeworking and work-family conflict (Yucel and Chung 2023), with an assumption that GRAs shape how individuals use homeworking to carry out more paid or unpaid labour. What is less known is how GRA might moderate the association between homeworking and the division of domestic work. A better comprehension of the role of GRA is necessary for a more fine-tuned understanding of what the wider  spread  of  homeworking  we  observe  can  mean  for  gender  equality  (Chung  et  al.  2021). Homeworking  may  not  exacerbate  gender  inequality,  as  once  expected  in  certain  pockets  of  the population, where gender performance is not restricted by social norms. What is more, if GRA shape flexible working outcomes, this can, on the one hand, provide us with yet another justification of the need to tackle gender biases in social roles in today's societies, and on the other, work on the policy solutions to ensure that flexible working can bring about better gender equality outcomes.

Our paper also explores the role of GRA during the COVID-19 pandemic period when there was the expansion of homeworking, alongside the rise in childcare and housework demands. Previous studies have shown that during this time there were signs of men contributing more to domestic work (Craig and

Churchill 2021; Steinmetz et al. 2022) potentially due to the widespread use of homeworking (Chung 2022;  Lyttelton,  Zang,  and  Musick  2022)  and  with  it  a  reduction  in  the  stigmatised  views  against homeworkers. This may have enabled workers, especially egalitarian men, to use homeworking for care and housework purposes (see also, Rudman and Mescher, 2013). At the same time, there was evidence for  the  re-traditionalization  of  roles  during  the  pandemic  period,  with  women  performing  even  more domestic work than before (Allmendinger 2020) as couples fell back on traditional gender roles.

We explore the role of GRA in shaping the association between homeworking and the division of domestic work, using the German Family Panel data (Brüderl et al. 2022) from 2008 to 2021 (waves 1-13), and applying hybrid models separating the between effects and within individual changes. This article contributes to the research on the outcomes of homeworking in two ways. First, given the long period covered in our data, we are able to estimate the effect of homeworking over 13-years' time and control for the role of the COVID-19 pandemic in shaping the division of housework and childcare when homeworking.  Second,  we  explore  the  role  of  gender  and  gender  role  attitudes  in  this  relationship. Enabling a more precise look at the potential heterogeneity across pockets of population with regards to how flexibility is used at work (Clark, 2010), as well as how gender norms shape performance of gender within the household, we enable a better understanding of what an expansion of homeworking can mean for gender inequality patterns in the future.


## 2 Theory



## 2.1 Homeworking and division of domestic work


Flexible working arrangements (Kelly, Moen, and Tranby 2011) can be based on location of work (i.e., homeworking, working from home, telecommuting) and scheduling of work (i.e., schedule control, flexitime  with  hours  count).  Here  we  focus  on  the  flexibility  in  the  location  of  work,  the  use  of opportunity to work from home always or regularly (Noonan and Glass 2012). Homeworking is actively promoted as a resource to provide a better work-life balance, particularly, for employees with children (Chung 2022). However, empirical evidence shows that homeworking can increase rather than decrease work-family  conflict  (Allen,  Golden,  and  Shockley  2015;  Yucel  and  Chung  2023).  This  is  largely because homeworking can blur the boundaries between work and private sphere, leading to increase in housework or paid work, or both, largely depending on one's gender - and the roles attributed to them by social norms (Chung and van der Lippe 2020; Clark 2000; Kurowska 2020).

Domestic work is housework and childcare that individuals perform to maintain family and home (Coltrane 2000). Housework activities include cooking, cleaning, buying groceries and laundry, which

are labelled as routine tasks and considered less enjoyable as non-routine tasks, i.e., taking care of the garden, repairs and bills (Coltrane 2000). Research on the unequal division of housework and childcare (e.g., Chung and Booker 2023; Petts, Carlson, and Pepin 2021) mainly focuses on routine tasks.

How partners divide domestic work can be explained by several theories. According to the time availability  perspective  (Huber  and  Spitze  1981),  a  partner  with  more  time  available  will  do  more domestic work relative to the partner who has less time. Relative resources theory argues that the partner with more resources, especially with the potential to gain more market income, would carry out a smaller share  of  the  domestic  work  (Becker  1991).  For  example,  those  with  higher  market  income,  higher education  would  do  less  domestic  work.  These  perspectives  are  gender  neutral,  i.e.,  assume  that regardless of gender,  an individual with more time available or fewer resources will carry out more domestic work. The 'doing gender' approach argues that gender norms shape who does more housework because  men  and  women  are  socialized  to  perform  different  roles  in  society,  namely,  men  as  the breadwinners and women as the homemakers or caregivers (West and Zimmerman 1987). In line with this perspective, societal gender norms define how housework is distributed. In most countries, women spend  more  time  on  housework  compared  to  men  (Eurofound  2022),  but  in  countries  with  more egalitarian gender norms (i.e., Denmark, Norway), the gap between men and women is smaller (Kan, Sullivan, and Gershuny 2011).

Homeworking can shape how heterosexual couples divide household responsibilities (Sullivan and  Lewis  2001).  The  new  opportunities  for  flexibility  model  (Huws  et  al.,  1996)  argues  that homeworking can allow gender roles to converge, where women can take a larger role in 'breadwinning' and men in domestic tasks. This is because homeworking provides workers with more time and flexibility to shape work around their family and personal demands. In other words, (long hours) working in the office may have prevented men from taking a larger role in the household, but with homeworking men are able to save commuting time and have flexibility at work to better engage in domestic work (Carlson, Petts, and Pepin 2021). On the other hand, the flexibility and permeability that homeworking provides have been shown to improve labour market participation of women with care responsibilities (Chung and van  der  Horst  2018;  Lyttelton,  Zang,  and  Musick  2022).  Therefore,  homeworking  can  provide  an opportunity for couples to break the patterns of traditional gender roles if they wish to do so. On the contrary, the exploitation model (Haddon and Silverstone 1993) sees homeworking as a tool to better exploit women's labour by enabling women to take more part in paid employment, namely work longer hours, without disrupting the unequal division of domestic work within the household (Chung and van der Lippe 2020). Similarly, men may adhere to their gender role and use the blurred boundaries between

work and home to do more paid work rather than engage more in unpaid domestic work (Chung 2022; Glass and Noonan 2016).

Combining the theories of division of domestic work and homeworking models, we can either expect that homeworking will enhance gender equality in the division of domestic labour by giving the opportunity  for  men  to  engage  in  the  household  chores,  relieving  their  female  partners'  load. Alternatively,  it  might  exacerbate  gender  inequality,  where  women  do  much  more  housework  when homeworking, with potential negative career consequence due to this (Chung 2020), and where men enact the masculine role and do more paid work yet even less housework when homeworking (Marsh and  Musson  2008).  According  to  the  gender-deviance  neutralization  theory  (Bittman  et  al.  2003), unemployed and economically dependent men who could potentially contribute more to housework, still do less than their partner, and potentially even less than employed men, to compensate for the deviation from their role as male-breadwinners. Men's masculine identities may also be threatened when working flexibly, as flexible working, especially for care purposes, is seen as feminine in addition to deviating away  from  the  ideal  worker  norm  (Borgkvist  et  al.  2021;  Rudman  and  Mescher  2013).  Since homeworking was not (and is not) normalized for the male worker, men may end up doing less unpaid work, even when it is possible to do more, to compensate for the deviation from the norm.

In sum, we come to the two competing hypotheses:

Hypothesis 1a : Homeworking (WFH) is associated with a higher contribution to domestic work for both men and women.

Hypothesis 1b: WFH is associated with a higher contribution to domestic work for women, but not for men.


## 2.2 The role of gender role attitudes


Gender role attitudes (GRA) are views held by individuals regarding the roles men and women should play in society (van der Horst 2014). The way men and women will distribute domestic duties when  homeworking  relates  to  their  beliefs  about  gender  roles  (Kan  et  al.,  2011;  Schober,  2013). Psychological  research  on  the  relationship  between  attitudes  and  behaviour  also  suggests  that individuals' behaviour is in line with their attitudes (Cooper and Croyle 1984) and that people act in accordance with their identity (Cast 2003). Empirical research supports this assumption and shows that egalitarian men are more likely to contribute to housework and childcare (Greenstein 1996; Grunow and Baur 2014), while women who viewed family as their primary sphere would do more housework (Nitsche

and Grunow 2018; Schober 2013) and women with egalitarian attitudes participate more in paid work (Cunningham 2008).

Gender role attitudes are multi-dimensional in that different beliefs about men's and women's roles do not necessarily align in the traditional - egalitarian spectrum for all individuals (Knight and Brinton, 2017). Based on the existing studies, we  see that  the beliefs around mother's employment, primacy of family or work for women, men's role in the family, and finally  beliefs around couple's income generation roles can all constitute as different attitudinal dimensions. Attitudital ambivalence can be found, namely that individuals can hold egalitarian views on some dimensions and traditional ones on the other (Sjober, 2010). In this respect, it is important to distinguish between different types of GRAs when exploring how  GRAs can moderate the association between homeworking and the division of housework. Given the focus of our study, the most relevant GRAs are the perception of women's role with regards to family and work, and men's role in the household.

How couples view the gender roles can especially  matter when  homeworking. Border theory (Clark, 2000) argues that flexibility and permeability in the work-family boundary will result  in the expansion of the sphere an individual identifies more with. This is why we expect that workers with different GRAs will have different priorities with regards to how they use their additional resources of time and energy saved from not having to commute into work, and flexibility of boundaries between work  and  family  when  homeworking.  Previous  qualitative  evidence  shows  that  couples  with  more egalitarian GRAs used flexibility in their work to divide domestic chores equally, whereas women with traditional  GRAs  viewed  flexibility  as  an  opportunity  to  do  more  housework  and  childcare  chores (Sullivan  and  Smithson  2007).  Similarly,  Yucel  and  Chung  (2023)  demonstrate  that  homeworking increased work-to-family interferences among women with egalitarian GRA while it increased familyto-work  interference  among  women  with  traditional  GRA.  GRA  did  not  play  a  role  for  men  in  this relationship. This finding is in line with the expectation that women with traditional views will identify more as a homemaker, and expand the domestic work, while women with egalitarian views will focus more on the expansion of paid work when homeworking.

Based on these previous studies, we expect that it is especially women who believe that their primary focus is the family and that men should not do household chores (i.e., traditional GRAs) will be increasing their share of domestic work when homeworking, whereas this will not be the case for women with egalitarian GRAs. On the other hand, men with egalitarian GRAs will be those who will use the newly obtained flexibility in their work to try to be more involved in housework and childcare, whereas men with traditional GRAs are unlikely to do so. Considering the multi-dimensions of GRAs, we expect that  for  men,  particularly  the  attitudes  towards  men's  role  in  the  household  will  matter.  For  women,

attitudes around women's role in the work and family might be important, as they shape women's beliefs around work roles, but also attitudes towards men's role in the household will matter since they shape women's responsibilities in the domestic sphere.

Therefore, we hypothesize:

Hypothesis 2a WFH is associated with a higher contribution to domestic work among women with traditional GRA compared to women with egalitarian GRA.

Hypothesis 2b WFH is associated with a lower contribution to domestic work among men with traditional GRA compared to men with egalitarian GRA.


## 2.3 The COVID-19 context


The pandemic period provides us with a unique opportunity to look at the association between homeworking and division of housework among couples. From March until July 2020 and from about December 2020 to May 2021, Germany, like many countries, entered a strict lockdown to contain the spread of the COVID-19 virus. Schools, day-care, restaurants, and nonessential retail were closed, and many  employees  were  either  furloughed  or  had  to  work  from  home.  The  sudden  expansion  of homeworking, and the fact that it has been imposed by the government as a way to reduce the spread of the virus, has been shown to have reduced stigmatised views against homeworkers (Abendroth et al. 2022). This may have enabled parents, especially fathers, to use flexible working to be more involved in housework and childcare without the fear of repercussion on their careers (Chung 2022). What is more, due to school closures, not only was there more housework and childcare to be carried out, there was more of an understanding that workers, especially parents, had to address both care and work demands during the lockdown periods (Chung et al. 2021; Petts, Carlson, and Pepin 2021; Zoch, Bächmann, and Vicari 2022).

The research on the consequences of COVID-19 initially proposed and found evidence for two opposing hypotheses: 1) the re-traditionalization hypothesis (Allmendinger 2020) that the pandemic will bring back the traditional unequal division of household chores (Çoban 2022; Nagy et al. 2023; Wojnicka and Kubisa 2023), and 2) the equalizing hypothesis (Craig and Churchill 2021; Steinmetz et al. 2022) that changes in the working hours, income, time and location of work will provide space for both partners to engage more equally in the domestic work. Until now, the studies showed evidence for both, depending on the country and circumstances, the male partner contribution either relatively increased or decreased (Hipp and Bünning 2021; Zamberlan, Gioachin, and Gritti 2022).

Taking this into account, we can expect two opposing outcomes with regards to homeworking and division of labour during the pandemic. On the one hand, we can expect an even stronger moderation of GRA during the periods of COVID-19. In such a time of crisis, and with the increased demand for domestic work, workers with a more traditional GRA may have reverted more to their assumed gender roles  with  a  clearer  division  of  responsibilities,  where  men  fully  take  on  the  breadwinning  role  and women the caregiving roles. Similarly, those with a more egalitarian GRA may have welcomed this new opportunity provided by the pandemic to enact their ideal division of labour (Milkie et al., 2002) to divide the increased domestic work more equally. This may have especially changed behaviours of egalitarian men, who may have previously been cautious of doing so due to stigmatised views around their flexible working (Rudman and Mescher, 2013). On the other hand, we could potentially expect that GRAs do not matter as much with regards to division of housework and childcare during the COVID-19 lockdown periods. Regardless of one's GRA, working parents were presented with unprecedented high demands of  housework and childcare during the pandemic.  Therefore,  homeworking parents may have had to spend time on housework and childcare. Between men and women, we can expect to see more changes in men in this case, as we expect that women would have already used homeworking to be more involved in housework and childcare.

Thus, we hypothesize:

Hypothesis 3a: WFH is associated with a higher contribution to domestic work for both men and women during COVID-19.

Hypothesis 3b WFH is associated with a higher contribution to domestic work among women with traditional GRA compared to women with egalitarian GRA during the COVID-19.

Hypothesis 3c WFH is associated with a lower contribution to domestic work among men with traditional GRA compared to men with egalitarian GRA during the COVID-19.


## 3 Data and Methods


To analyse how GRA moderate the relationship between homeworking and the distribution of domestic work, we use data from the German Family Panel (pairfam), release 14.0 (Brüderl et al. 2023). Pairfam includes extensive information on gender role attitudes, working arrangements, and the relative distribution  of  household tasks. Pairfam data has been collected yearly since 2008. We use  the prepandemic waves 1-12 conducted from 2008/9 to 2019/20 and the pandemic wave 13 collected between November 2020 and April 2021. Moreover, part of the wave 12 sample was conducted in 2020 when the first lockdown begun. We include those cases and create a control variable to indicate which cases were

affected by the lockdown measures and the homeworking expansion. The analytical sample comprises heterosexual couples with children under the age of 18 due to the low number of cases among same-sex couples. The sample consists of 13745 total observations with 948 men and 1169 women participating in at least three waves during the observed period (unbalanced panel).

We assess the overall and gendered effect of homeworking by pooling men and women in the same models. To explore the role of the GRA, we build separate models for men and women. We apply hybrid models (Allison 2009) to explore the within individual change in the homeworking status and how  it  affected  the  relative  division  of  housework  and  childcare  and  the  between  variation  among different groups. The operationalization of the variables is presented below with more information in the appendix Table 1.
