## 5 Discussion and Conclusion


Homeworking has been introduced as a policy that can enable workers to have a better work-life balance  by  saving  their  commuting  costs  and  providing  more  work  autonomy  (Allen,  Golden,  and Shockley 2015; Noonan and Glass 2012), contributing to gender equality both at home and in the labour market (Council of the European Union 2019). While some research supports the idea of homeworking benefiting workers, for instance, helping workers relieve tensions between work and family life (Huws and et al. 1996), others argue that it may enable the exploitation of individuals, especially women, where homeworking enables them to carry out more of both paid and unpaid work (Chung 2022; Haddon and Silverstone 1993). The use of homeworking might be gendered with women traditionally devoting their spare time to the household chores in addition to paid work, while men might be able to focus only on the later (Kurowska 2020), exacerbating the unequal division of labour across gender (Chung and van der Lippe 2020). Previous studies (Hilbrecht et al. 2008; Lott 2019; Lyttelton, Zang, and Musick 2022; Sullivan  and  Lewis  2001;  Chung  and  Booker  2023;  Wang  and  Cheng  2023)  have  explored  this assumption  and  analysed  whether  homeworking  changes  the  relative  distribution  of  housework  and childcare among heterosexual couples. We contribute to this debate by looking at a longer time frame and looking at both between and within individual changes, including the COVID-19 pandemic which provides  a  unique  period  where  homeworking  was  normalised,  yet  the  childcare  facilities  were suspended. What is more, we contribute to the debate by examining how the gender role attitudes of

individuals may shape the use of homeworking with regards to their engagement in domestic work across gender. Thus, we expected that women with egalitarian GRAs would not necessarily increase their share of domestic work when homeworking, whereas traditional women might use the flexibility of their work to 'do gender'. Similarly, we expected egalitarian men would be the ones to use homeworking as a way to engage more in domestic work, whereas traditional men would not. These assumptions have been tested using data from the German Family Panel in the span from 2008 to 2021.

At first glance, homeworking did not make any difference to the division of housework among heterosexual couples, although homeworkers contributed more to childcare. There are differences across gender and whether we examine within or between individuals. Compared to women who worked on site, women who were homeworking carried out a larger share of childcare. However, gaining access to homeworking did not change women's contribution to childcare. On the other hand, when men gained access to homeworking (within individual change) they seem to contribute more to childcare. On an even closer  inspection,  as  expected,  gender  role  attitudes  mattered.  Men  with  egalitarian  GRAs  generally contributed  more  to  housework  and  childcare  compared  to  men  with  traditional  GRAs,  and  when egalitarian men gained access to homeworking their contribution to childcare increased even further. Homeworking  did  not  change  traditional  men's  childcare  contributions.  Similarly,  women  with traditional GRA did a larger share of housework and childcare compared to egalitarian women. When women with traditional GRA gained access to homeworking they increased their share in childcare even further. This pattern was not observed for women with egalitarian GRAs. The type of GRA mattered. For both men and women, the perception of men's contribution to housework mattered, whereas the attitudes towards women's role in family and career did not matter. Furthermore, we investigated whether gender  role  attitudes  mattered  in  the  COVID-19  pandemic  and  the  expansion  of  homeworking.  The findings are similar to the ones observed in the longer time span for women yet not for men. During the pandemic, men who gained access to homeworking increased their contribution to childcare regardless of their GRAs, indicating that homeworking could potentially help support gender equality at home as homeworking became more normalised and possibly its use for care purposes was less stigmatised.

The study  has  some  limitations.  The  division  of  housework  and  childcare  is  not  an  absolute measure, but rather a perception of the individual and their share within the couple in very broad terms. Future studies could potentially use time use data and other sources to have more precise measures of the division of housework and childcare carried out by couples. Couple's division of mental load (Dean, Churchill, and Ruppanner 2022) would also be important to explore, with regards to how homeworking can help division of labour. Similarly, the intensity of different homeworking settings must be considered as those who are homeworking daily might differ in their household practices compared to those who are

homeworking only occasionally. The homeworking variable used in our study measures a combination of use and access, and previous studies have shown the importance of access in explaining work-family outcomes  in  addition  to  use  (Chung  and  van  der  Horst  2018).  Regardless,  future  studies  should distinguish  between  workers'  access  to  and  use  of  homeworking,  in  addition  to  the  frequency  of homeworking to better understand the dynamics of home and hybrid working on the division of labour within couples. Additionally, it is important to consider the role of organizations, i.e., supervisors, in providing access to homeworking (Hennekam, Kelland, and Dumazert 2023). Moreover, studies need to account for the changes in the gender role attitudes over the life course and particularly how people adapt their values due to different critical events, such as childbirth or COVID-19 (Vandecasteele et al. 2022).

Despite these limitations, this study has provided important contributions to the on-going debate around whether the expansion of homeworking practices can result in a more  egalitarian division of labour  within  households.  Unlike  the  fears  of  previous  studies  (Chung  2022;  Hilbrecht  et  al.  2008; Lyttelton,  Zang,  and  Musick  2022;  Sullivan  and  Lewis  2001),  the  results  of  this  study  suggest  that homeworking  has  the  potential  to  contribute  to  a  more  equal  division  of  labour  in  the  household. However, this largely depends on individuals' and in a way society's views on gender roles. Conservative attitudes towards the role of men and women might reproduce a more unequal distribution of labour particularly when homeworking. In other words, if we want homeworking to pave the way to gender equality, we need to ensure that the gender normative context in which it is introduced changes. For instance,  ensuring  that  all  individuals,  regardless  of  their  gender,  are  treated  equally,  starting  from intentional interventions in early education to eliminate gender biases, would be useful. Guaranteeing that fathers take up the parental leave especially for over two months periods independently without the mothers being at home (Bünning 2015), could also help change society and individual's perceptions of gender roles. Thus, the expansion of homeworking can pave a way for greater gender equality if we are able to provide the right contexts for this to happen.

## INTRODUCTION


As a social species, the propensity of humans to come together and support one another is sometimes cited as one of our characterising and evolutionarily advantageous traits. 1 4 -Since our earliest civilisations, we have organised ourselves into systems that allow the exchange of practical and psychosocial resources.  Theorists 5 from a range of disciplines, including psychology, social epidemiology and anthropology have built frameworks to  explain  how  and  why  coming  together  benefits our  lives,  our  society,  and  our health. 6 10 -For  example, theorist Robert Putnam proposed that civic participation is a key aspect of social capital, and suggested that its decline has deteriorated the quality of American society.  In fact, some researchers have argued that social 6 resources are fundamental, yet often overlooked, determinants of health. 11 Some of this discourse has focused on community groups, including arts groups, 12 sports clubs, 13,14 or voluntary organization, 15 17 -and investigated how membership of such associations benefits individuals and communities, as well as wider society.

Yet,  research  into  the  patterns  and  predictors  of  community  engagement  has  suggested  there  is  a  social gradient in accessing these spaces. 18 22 -At present, much of our understanding of community engagement and group membership comes from analysis of countries such as the Western, Global North countries such as the UK 18,19,23 -25 , the US, 26,27 and Europe 28 , although there is also evidence from China 29 and Latin America 30 . These typically  find  that  individual-level  socioeconomic  factors,  such  as  income,  education  and  employment  are associated with membership rates. Practically, this may reflect how individuals in higher social positions are able to meet the costs of membership fees, transportation or equipment. Additionally, motives to engage with communities may be transmitted through educational, occupational, or familial systems, as forms of cultural capital. 19,31 As  a  result,  membership  may  be  more  prevalent  amongst  individuals,  as  well  as  families, communities  and  societies  with  greater  resources.  However,  because  most  of  this  research  has  been conducted in countries with similar demographic and economic structures, it is still not entirely clear whether this social gradient persists across diverse demographic and cultural settings. One Global South analysis of 20 Sub-Saharan African countries found a similar social patterning of community group membership, suggesting this challenge is not geographically isolated. 17 But research taking a global perspective is missing.

In addition, the potential role of country-level socioeconomic factors in predicting membership rates are at present underexplored. This is important because community participation involves individuals interacting with their communities and wider society, and so is likely to reflect the structure and nature of the wider socioeconomic context. However, these country-level predictors may be complex. On the one hand, higher income countries with greater infrastructure may offer more opportunities for community group formation, like venues and local funding. For example, one investigation into the predictors of volunteering in 55 countries across the world found that country wealth and educational levels, as well as indicators of social values and democracy and religiosity, predicted volunteering rates. 32 On the other hand, groups can emerge organically within communities even in the absence of formal infrastructure, through collective efforts of individuals. 33 The 20-country Sub-Saharan African analysis described above found that membership rates were also high in less  advantaged  social  groups,  and  less  wealthy  countries. 17 Accordingly,  there  is  a  need  to  extend  these analyses  by  exploring  how  country-level  socioeconomic  factors  may  influence  a person's engagement  in community activities, and how these country-level factors may interplay with individual-level factors to predict membership rates across the world.

In this light, for the present analysis we used data from 50 countries across seven geographical regions in the World Values Survey (WVS), 34 to map individual- and country-level socioeconomic predictors of community organization  memberships. We examined associations between community organization membership and individual  income,  educational  level,  and  employment  status,  as  well  as  four  country-level  socioeconomic factors:  country-level  wealth  (GDP  per  capita),  income  inequality  (Gini  coefficient),  educational  quality (compulsory educational years) and employment (unemployment rate).


## METHODS



## Data


Data from Wave 7 of the WVS (2017-2022) were analysed. The WVS is a repeated cross-sectional survey conducted in over 90 countries, exploring global differences in people's values, attitudes, behaviours, and subjective wellbeing. We selected Wave 7 as it is the most recent wave that includes questions on community organization  membership.  In  this  wave,  geographic  coverage  was  expanded  to  include  countries  such  as Greece, Myanmar, Nicaragua, and Tajikistan for the first time, and a total of over 129,000 respondents from 78 countries or territories were interviewed. Each of these countries used nationwide random probability sampling, and there was a minimum sample size of 1,200. Samples were representative of all people aged 18 and above living in private households in each country. National research teams obtained as many Primary Sampling Units (PSU) as possible to ensure that the sample is representative of the population of each country, with a maximum of 10 respondents per PSU. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews conducted at respondents' homes or residence s, with responses recorded via paper questionnaires or CAPI (Computer Assisted Personal Interview). 34,35

This study analysed data from the latest (6.0) version of the Wave 7 data release, which comprised data for 66 countries  or  territories. 34 Of  those  included  in  the  data  release  (N=97,220),  86,796  individuals  from  64 countries  or  territories  answered  the  questions  on  community  organization  membership,  and  81,765 completed measures of individual socio-demographic variables. Sixteen countries did not include questions on the country-level predictors we planned to include, providing a final analytical sample of 64,065 participants from  50  countries  across  seven  geographical  regions.  These  countries  were  diverse  geographically  and economically:  Argentina,  Armenia,  Australia,  Bangladesh,  Bolivia,  Brazil,  Canada,  Chile,  China,  Colombia, Cyprus, Czechia, Ecuador, Egypt, Ethiopia, Germany, Great Britain, Greece, Guatemala, India, Indonesia, Iraq, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Kyrgyzstan, Lebanon, Malaysia, Mexico, Mongolia, Morocco, Myanmar, Netherlands, Nicaragua, Pakistan, Peru, Philippines, Romania, Russia, Serbia, South Korea, Tajikistan, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, Ukraine, United States, Uruguay, Vietnam, and Zimbabwe.


## Measures


Community organization membership was measured as self-reported active and inactive membership across the following activities: sports or recreational organization (e.g. football/baseball/rugby team); art, music, or educational organization; political party; environmental organization; professional association; humanitarian or charitable organization; consumer organization; selfhelp or mutual aid groups; women's groups ;  or any other organization. Religious or labour group organization were excluded as these can require specific beliefs or types of employment, meaning they are not open to everybody. Each respondent's number of memberships was summed to generate a total membership score which ranged from zero to 10. We included both active and inactive membership in our main analyses, but sensitivity analyses focused on active memberships only.

Three individual-level socioeconomic predictors were used: (1) perceived household income; (2) educational level;  and  (3)  employment.  For  perceived  household  income,  participants  were  asked  to  position  their household on a 10-point scale that represents the highest and lowest income groups in their country, taking all wages, salaries, pensions, and other incomes into account. This measure has the strength of providing more insight about the value of a specific salary within a particular country context and enabling comparisons of income position between countries with very different socioeconomic structures. To ensure comparability across countries, education was measured using the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED), as endorsed by the United Nations (UN) and UNESCO. 36 Four categories were used; none or primary education only,  secondary  education,  post-secondary  education,  and  degree  or  above.  Employment  status  was measured as a three-category variable indicating whether participants were employed or self-employed, not in labour force, or unemployed.

Four country-level socioeconomic predictors were considered: (1) compulsory education duration (in years) measured by the World Bank in 2018; (2) unemployment rate (% of total labour force) measured by the World Bank in 2019; (3) Gini income inequality index measured by the World Bank in 2012-2019; and (4) GDP per capita measured by the World Bank in 2019 (transformed into log to ensure a normal distribution; countries with zero GDP per capita were omitted). 34

The analyses were adjusted for age (a continuous variable, top coded at the 95th percentile; ranges from 18 to 89); gender (female vs male), respondent's immigration status (native born vs immigrant), marital status (married or living together as married, divorced/separated/widowed, single), and household size (a continuous variable ranges from 1 to 10).


## Analysis


To  explore  the  associations  between  individual-level  and  country-level  socioeconomic  predictors  and community organization membership, we used multilevel  models (MLM). We fitted a two-level model to account for the nested structure of the WVS data, as individuals living in the same country might be more similar to each other than to those living in another country. In the model, we allowed for the estimation of a random slope for education, perceived household income and employment status as we assumed that the relationship between these socioeconomic predictors and community organization membership varied across countries. Two sensitivity analyses were conducted. First, we redefined the outcome variable and explored the total number of active membership organizations (N=43,010). Second, we ran multilevel logistic regression modelling to examine the associations between socioeconomic predictors and membership in each type of community  organization.  In  these  models,  we  were  only  able  to  estimate  random  slopes  for  perceived household income for the models to converge.

We used coefficients and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) to present the associations between individual- and country-level factors and community organization membership, except for the sensitivity analysis that used multilevel logistic regression modelling. When fitting the MLM, we applied an 'individual -level ' weight (level 1) to adjust some sociodemographic characteristics in the sample population to the distribution of the target population. This was calculated based on the marginal distribution of age, gender, education and religion. 34,37 We  also  applied  a  'country level'  weight  (level  2)  using -the  population  scaled  weight  to  transform  each country's sample size to 1000, so that all countries contributed equally to the combined analysis, while also ensuring the sample size for each country was in proportion to the population size of the region covered by the sample. 37 Both weights were provided in the WVS. Missing data were handled using listwise deletion (16% of participants did not have complete individual-level data). The risk of multicollinearity was minimal (mean VIF=1.70).


## RESULTS



## Descriptive analyses


In our analytical sample, 52.7% of respondents were female and the average age was 42.8 years (standard deviation [SD]=16.5). The minority (3.90%) had immigrated to their current country of residence, 58.4% were employed, 22.8% had a degree or above educational qualification. The mean of respondents reported their position on the subjective 10-step income scale was 4.95 (SD=2.08). A breakdown of distribution between average number of organization memberships and age, gender, education, employment status and perceived household income by country is presented in Figs. S1-S5.


## Prevalence and patterns of memberships across the globe


When looking at the full sample (a sample with data on community organization memberships), participants were members of, on average, 1.58 community organizations (SD=2.52). Across 64 countries or territories, the highest average number of memberships were seen in Kenya (4.33 community organization memberships) followed by Colombia (3.56) and Mongolia (3.54). Lowest rates were reported in Greece (0.50), Russia (0.35), and Egypt (0.24) (Fig. 1; Table S1). A similar demographic distribution was also observed in our analytical sample (Table S2). The average number of active organization memberships was positively correlated with the total number of organization memberships, indicating that countries with a greater number of memberships also tend to have more individuals actively involved in these organizations. However, there are exceptions. For instance, in our analytical sample living in Morocco, the average number of total organization memberships was  2.44,  but  only  0.35  of  these  were  active.  A  similar  pattern  was  observed  in  Malaysia,  where  3.29 memberships with 0.56 active memberships, and in Zimbabwe, where the averages were 2.32 memberships and 0.38 active memberships.


## Individual-level socioeconomic factors


When compared with respondents with no or primary education, those with post-secondary education and degree or above had 0.26 (95%CI=0.07, 0.45) and 0.49 (95%CI=0.29, 0.69) more community organization memberships, respectively  (Fig.  2;  Table  S3).  Most  countries  show  an  educational  gradient  in  community memberships,  especially  for  participants  with  a  degree  or  above  (Figs.  S6a-S6c).  However,  this  trend  is reversed  in  Thailand,  where  individuals  with  no  or  primary  education  instead  had  more  organization memberships than those with a degree or above (Fig. S6c). There was also a positive correlation between perceived household income and organization membership, in which a unit increase in perceived household income was associated with 0.06 more memberships (Fig2; Table S3). This pattern was most prevalent in India, Pakistan and Canada, and was reversed in Thailand, Iraq, and Bangladesh (Fig. S7). No significant association at  a  multi-national  level  was  found  for  employment  status,  although  some  countries  showed  individual associations. For instance, employed individuals living in Thailand, Malaysia and India had more organization memberships than those who were unemployed. However, the trend is reversed for those living in Colombia, Tajikistan and the US where unemployed individuals had more organization memberships. On the other hand, those who were not in labour force living in Mongolia, Colombia and Great Britain had more organization memberships  than  those  who  were  unemployed,  whereas  those  who  were  not  in  labour  force  living  in Tajikistan, the US and Nicaragua had less memberships than unemployed individuals (Fig. 2; Table S3; Figs. S8a & 8b).


## Country-level socioeconomic factors


When exploring  country-level  factors,  memberships  were  negatively  associated  with  unemployment  rate (coef=-0.06,  95%CI=-0.11,  -0.00)  but  positively  associated  with  Gini  income  inequality  index  (coef=0.07, 95%CI=0.03, 0.11) (Fig. 2; Table S3). These associations are shown in more detail in Fig. 3, with the predicted probability of organization memberships from the MLM plotted according to each country-level predictor. No associations were found for GDP per capital and compulsory education years.


## Sensitivity analyses


The sensitivity analysis on socioeconomic predictors of active membership shows a similar trend to the main analysis: individuals with post-secondary education, those with a degree or above, people with higher income, those living in countries with lower unemployment rate or people living in countries with a higher Gini income inequality index had more active memberships (Fig. S9). However, we also found that individuals who were employed or self-employed also had more active memberships in community organizations than unemployed individuals, which was not observed in the main analysis.

When exploring each community organization, we found some variations in a socioeconomic gradient across community organizations. For instance, a stronger educational gradient was observed particularly for sports or recreational organization, arts, music or educational organization, professional organization, and charitable or humanitarian organization memberships (Table S4). Compulsory education was negatively associated with the odds of being in a political party membership and the odds of being in a self-help/mutual aid group. With the  exception  of membership  of  self-help/mutual  aid  group,  political party, and  other  community organizations, perceived household income was positively correlated with the odds of membership. Unlike all other  organizations,  no  individual  socioeconomic  factors  were  observed  for  self-help/mutual  aid  group membership.


## DISCUSSION


Using  data  from  over  64,000  individuals  across  seven  geographical  regions,  we  demonstrate  ubiquitous engagement  with  community  groups  across  every  region  of  the  world.  But  we  also  find  intriguing  and important differences in individual- and country-level socioeconomic predictors of community organization membership  and  unique  insight  on  how  compositional  and  contextual  factors  may  promote  or  prevent membership rates. Across 64 nations, we found the highest membership rates in Kenya, where the average respondent was a member of 4.33 community groups, and the lowest rates in Egypt, where the average rate was  0.24.  Countries  with  a  greater  number  of  memberships  also  tend  to  have  more  individuals  actively involved  in  these  organizations.  But  there  are  exceptions;  for  instance,  of  the  analytical  sample  living  in Morocco, Malaysia and Zimbabwe, the average number of organization memberships was over 2.3 but the average number of active memberships was less than 0.6.  In our analytical sample from 50 nations, a social gradient  in  membership  rate  was  observed  and  individual  educational  level  emerged  as  a  particularly important and consistent socioeconomic predictor of group involvement, although some differences across activity-type were also seen. At a country level, higher income inequality and lower unemployment rates were also associated with a higher group membership rate.

For the individual-level predictors, educational level appeared to be the most consistent and important factor in  influencing  community  organization  membership  across  countries  and  activities.  Firstly,  educational environments such as schools, colleges or universities are places where ideas are introduced and exchanged. As a result, they may foster pro-social attitudes, or environmental, political, or social justice related values that motivate membership. 38 Secondly, school environments may valorise creative, community-oriented or selfexpressionist attitudes, and therefore could influence individuals with higher levels of education to seek out community groups. 17,39 Thirdly, skills and knowledge that are typically acquired in educational systems may be required for some community group activities. This could include literacy, or creative or sports skills. This skill accumulation can be framed as forms of capital, and may extend to the social skills, customs or knowledge that allow individuals with higher levels of education to feel more comfortable or welcome in community group  settings.  Finally,  many  social  theories  frame  education  as  an  aspect  of  cultural  capital,  and  see community groups as a way for individuals  with  higher educational  levels  to  demonstrate  or  affirm  their cultural  capital  or  social  position. 19,20,40 This  may  extend  to  social  roles,  whereby  community  organization memberships,  particularly  professional  organizations,  may  enable  members  to  demonstrate  their  status. Indeed, it is notable that individuals across all nations reported membership of groups that they did not actively participate in currently. This affirms previous research on capital, suggesting that membership alone can be a way  for  individuals  to  project  an  image  of  themselves  as  active,  knowledgeable,  or  community-oriented individuals, and bolster their social identity. 41

Although individual-level education is an important factor of community organization memberships, countrylevel  education  (measured  by  compulsory  education  years)  is  not.  This  suggests  that  joining  community organizations may not depend on the length of mandatory education in a country, but rather on whether individuals have equal opportunities to pursue higher education or build cultural and social capital. In fact, apart from Thailand where the trend is reversed, participants with a university degree or higher tend to have more memberships than those with only primary or no education, regardless of whether attaining a university degree is more or less common within their country. That said, there is exception for political party and selfhelp/mutual aid group memberships, where compulsory education was negatively associated with the odds of being in these organizations. One explanation is that in countries with fewer compulsory education years, people may have actively joined these organizations to support their country 's socio-political development.

Income  was  another  significant  and  consistent  individual-level  predictor  of  community  organization membership. With the exception of membership of self-help/mutual aid group, political  party,  and  other community  organizations,  individuals  who  perceived  their  household  income  to  be  higher  had  higher membership rates. This is most prevalent in countries such as India, Pakistan and Canada. This association may, again, reflect resource accumulation, whereby household level financial resources, or the perception of affluence,  encourages  people  to  invest  into  community  organizations.  This  might  involve  purchasing equipment or membership fees, but also could act at a community level. In addition to resource accumulation, the resource theory developed in the volunteering literature may also explain this observation. The theory suggests that employed and wealthy individuals have more financial and psychosocial resources to engage with voluntary associations, and volunteer their time, but also their interest and care. 32 This is reflected in our main analysis, as well as in the sensitivity analysis where employed or self-employed individuals have a greater number of active memberships than those who were unemployed.

Whilst individual income was associated with community organization memberships, we did not find evidence that  this  extended  to  country-level  wealth.  There  was  no  association  between  GDP  per  capita  and organizational memberships. However, a positive correlation was observed between memberships and Gini income  inequality  index.  One  interpretation  is  that  countries  with  greater  income  inequality  have  less developed infrastructures, and as a result, community organizations serve as proxies for formal provisions. 42 -44 This might be particularly relevant to educational, labour, and professional community groups. Alternatively, in high income countries (which often have lower income inequality), community organizations are generally funded  though  membership  fees, 45 while  in  lower  income  countries  (which  often  have  higher  income inequality)  community  organizations  may  be  less  about  leisure  and  more  about  essential  collective cooperation, or the distribution of basic, essential resources and social groups are systems of reciprocity. 15 The  correlation  between  higher  Gini  income  inequality  and  higher  membership  rates  could  also  reflect differences  in  values  and  cultural  norms.  High-income,  western,  Global  North  countries  with  low-income inequality  such  as  the  UK,  are  often  described  as  highly  individualist. 46 In  these  settings,  community engagement  relates  more  to  leisure  and  is  accordingly  more  associated  with  individual  socioeconomic resources. By contrast, countries in the Global South typically have more collectivist cultures 46,47 which may encourage community engagement. Although cultural values are complex and require more detailed research, this could explain the exceptionally high rates of memberships we observed in countries such as Kenya and Colombia.  Overall,  these  unexpected  findings  invite  us  to  consider  not  only  how  engagement  rate  in community groups differs across countries, but also how the potential health and social benefits of community engagement might vary in different social and cultural contexts.

We  also  observed  a  correlation  between  country-level  employment  rates  and  community  organization membership, but no  correlation  between  individual  employment  status  and  membership,  suggesting  this effect occurs at a country-level but not at an individual-level. Specifically, as unemployment rate increased, the average number of group memberships per person was seen to decrease. There could be two explanations for this. First, employment status is less relevant in predicting community organization memberships because these memberships may reflect one's cultural and economic capital, which are influenced by education and income. Second, at a country-level, labour forces generate country-wide resources, services and infrastructures  that  could  support  community  group  formation. 17 High  unemployment  rates  can  occur alongside fewer social, cultural, and economic opportunities, such as those resulting from lower state funding and poorer social leisure and community infrastructures. As a result, fewer people engage in these activities.

Our findings reveal a clear socioeconomic gradient in community group membership across various countries and cultural settings. Such gradient is in parallel with the socioeconomic gradient in health, whereby people with higher socioeconomic position enjoy better health. As such, our results can be interpreted in two ways. First,  community  engagement  could  be  considered an  'asset' more  frequently  accessed  by  those  from privileged  backgrounds.  Second,  community  engagement  can  be  seen  as  a  modifying  health  behaviour. Indeed,  epidemiological  studies  have  suggested  that  community  engagement,  including  arts  and  cultural participation, 12,26,48,49 volunteering 50 53 -or  leisure  activities  more  generally 54,55 are  beneficial  to  health. Mechanistically,  this  has  been  proposed  to  act  through  a  range  of  social,  psychological,  biological  and behavioural processes, such as the establishment of psychosocial support networks, changes to inflammatory systems  or  habit  formation.   In  particular,  participation  in  groups  or  in  communities  can  facilitate  social 7 connections, build social capital and develop social identities, which have been shown to help improve health and wellbeing. 11 All of these can help contribute to community wellbeing, collective happiness, social cohesion and societal harmony. In this light, we might consider how socioeconomic barriers to community participation could exacerbate health and social inequalities by preventing those most in need from accessing community spaces. 56 Yet,  because  this  work has  largely  examined socioeconomic patterning in wealthy countries, our understanding  of  role  of  these  socioeconomic  barriers  in  exacerbating  health  inequalities  is  limited  to resource-rich  contexts.  Therefore,  our  demonstration  that  lower  educational  levels  and  lower  perceived income are persistent barriers to community organization membership across countries could be relevant to understanding  global  health  inequalities.  Further  still,  the  roles  of  both  individual-level  and  country-level socioeconomic factors in predicting membership highlights how compositional and contextual factors may compound and further entrench socioeconomic barriers to the benefiting effects of community engagement on individual and societal wellbeing.

One of the key strengths of this analysis is the use of a large dataset of representative samples from over 50 countries, which allowed us to examine how diverse socioeconomic and geographic contexts may influence community engagement. The richness of the WVS dataset permitted us to examine associations between individual- and country-level socioeconomic factors and membership rates. Our analyses also accounted for the nested structure of the WVS data and allowed for the associations between individual socioeconomic predictors and membership to vary across countries. However, because the WVS data were only available cross-sectionally, we were limited in drawing causality, and this represents a significant limitation of the study. In  addition,  measurement error may have arisen from the use of subjective measures, such as perceived income, in the analysis. We also lacked data on the country heterogeneity in high-level infrastructure and policy, which may affect individual-level predictors of organizational membership. Nevertheless, our findings are  important  in  understanding  how  socioeconomic  factors  promote  or  inhibit  participation  and  could contribute to the reduction of global social and health inequalities.

In  addition, we acknowledge important challenges around undertaking global epidemiological research on complex social exposures. The definition or interpretation of concepts such as community groups will naturally vary by country. While the data collection for WVS is designed by social scientists representing each country involved, the necessity of using the same question cross-nationally could mean other forms of community engagement  may  have  been  missed  or  individuals  may  have  under-reported  related  activities  that  they perceived to fall outside the definition of community groups. This is particularly a challenge for countries where close community activity may be more interwoven into daily life rather than constituting separate 'leisure' behaviours. As  such,  it  is  important  to  acknowledge  our  analysis  presents  just  part  of  the  overall picture of global patterns of membership enrolment to community activities. We support efforts to further decolonise global epidemiological research through expanding the tools, approaches and lenses used.


## CONCLUSIONS


This analysis has demonstrated associations between individual-level and country-level socioeconomic factors and community group memberships across seven geographical regions in the World Values Survey. Owing to the globality of the dataset, we were able to generate range of novel findings and offer insight on the role of country-level  factors  in  predicting  community  group  membership  rates.  By  using  a  large-scale  dataset  of representative  samples  from  50  different  countries,  we  demonstrated  associations  between  community organization membership and individual-level income, education, employment, but showed that individual educational level was the most consistent across different countries and type of group.  Gini coefficient and employment  rates  were  also  positively  associated  with  community  organization  membership,  suggesting country-level  resources  and  infrastructure  may  influence  participation.  Overall,  we  show  that  there  are socioeconomic  barriers  to  community  organizations  that  persist  across  different  socioeconomic  and geographical contexts. We therefore highlight community groups, and the targeting of these socioeconomic barriers, as a possible focus for efforts to reduce global health and social inequalities.

## 1 Introduction


The  COVID-19 pandemic has  had  far  reaching  consequences  for  individuals,  including  an impact on their well-being (e.g., Bähr et al. 2022; Wanberg et al. 2021). However, the literature in this domain has mostly focused on individual-level explanations and suffers from a lack of causal  identification.  Our  study  contributes  to  this  field  by  analyzing  household-related inequalities  in  changes  in  subjective  well-being  with  a  special  focus  on  gender  differences. Complementing previous studies, we primarily examine the impact of the spread of the COVID19 disease, reflected by incidence rates, on well-being based on prospective household panel data and a causal identification strategy. We argue that analyzing changes in subjective wellbeing (operationalized as overall life satisfaction), is important because, based on sociological theory, a satisfied life constitutes the overall outcome all individuals strive for (Lindenberg 1996). Additionally, as many prior findings on the COVID-19 pandemic rely on (convenience) samples initiated during the crisis or simple pre- and post-COVID-19 comparisons, we argue that sociological COVID-19 research will benefit from the application of high-quality data in combination with a causal identification strategy that differentiates aspects of the pandemic, such as analyzing the impact of incidence rates while holding countries' containment policies constant.

Prior research investigating the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on subjective well-being based on prospective panel data and using a before-and-after comparison has shown negative short-term  effects  on  subjective  well-being  measured  with  the  standard  single-item  life satisfaction  question  (e.g.,  Bähr  et  al.  2022;  Wanberg  et  al.  2021).  These  studies  have demonstrated a negative effect, which has appeared to intensify over the course of the pandemic (e.g., Entringer and Kröger 2021). Additionally, one study found that the overall effect of the COVID-19  pandemic  varies  by  district-level  incidence  rates  in  Germany,  indicating  that individuals in districts with higher incidence rates experienced the largest decline in subjective

well-being (Bittmann 2022). Furthermore, the initial literature on subjective well-being has indicated  that  women's  and  in  particular  mothers'  well-being  has  declined  most  strongly (Huebener  et  al.  2021;  Zoch,  Bächmann,  and  Vicari  2021a).  Some  potential  explanations include that women experienced higher levels of COVID-19-related anxiety and psychological distress (Metin et al. 2022), more COVID-19 infections (Connor et al. 2020) and higher risk of job loss during the initial phase of the COVID-19 pandemic than men (Möhring et al. 2021).

However,  even  though  the  body  of  research  investigating  the  effects  of  the  COVID-19 pandemic on life satisfaction is large, several blind spots remain. In this paper, we contribute to the literature by investigating how household characteristics lead to heterogenous effects of incidence rates on life satisfaction. Specifically, we investigate how household composition and household affluence moderate the effect of incidence rates. First, we investigate differences in household  composition.  To  this  end,  we  analyze  the  heterogeneous  effect  of  high  rates  of COVID-19  on  changes  in  subjective  well-being  among  individuals  from  households  with children aged 15 or younger, with care duties of older individuals in the same or a different household, and in various household types (i.e., single- vs. multi-person household). These household characteristics refer to individuals' social relations. Therefore, these factors should have  shaped  the  effect  of  the  COVID-19  pandemic  on  individuals'  subjective  well-being through affectional and emotional channels (see, for instance, Cohn et al. 2009; Ormel et al. 1999). Second, we investigate whether differences in household affluence affected COVID-19related changes in life satisfaction. To this end, we analyze whether the quality of housing (i.e., whether individuals live in deprived homes or not), level of net income, or household financial situation (i.e.,  net  incomes  and  savings) might buffer or amplify the negative consequences associated with high incidence rates during the initial COVID-19 shock in 2020.

Third  and  finally, we  are  interested in gendered  effects of the pandemic,  as  the aforementioned research shows that men and women are differently affected by the pandemic.

For  example,  women  with  children  may  be  more  strongly  affected  by  pandemic-induced

burdens compared to men with children, as childcare is typically provided by women and this burden intensified during the pandemic due to, for example, school closures.

We employ a causal identification strategy that uses representative household panel data from Germany (Panel Labor Market and Social Security; PASS) and administrative data on incidence rates at the district level (RKI 2021). Based on these data, we employ a differencein-difference  (DiD)  design  that  exploits  the  timing  of  interview  responses  (i.e.,  interviews before and after the first societal lockdown) and whether an individual lives in a district with high incidence rates (i.e.,  above  the  median)  at  the  time  of  the  interview  in  2020.  In  using temporal and regional variation (i.e., comparing different individuals from the same district according to the incidence level), we identify the impact of high incidence rates on subjective well-being changes independent of the initial overall shock of the COVID-19 pandemic due to lockdown measures.


## 2 Theoretical considerations and empirical findings



## 2.1 Theoretical  background:  Social production function  theory  and  the  relevance  of incidence rates for individuals' subjective wellbeing


According to social production function theory  (Lindenberg 1989, 1996; Ormel et al. 1997 1999), all rational actors (i.e., homo socio-oeconomicus (Lindenberg 1990)) strive to achieve high  levels  of  happiness  in  their  lives  by  reaching  goals  within  a  given  set  of  means  and restrictions  (Lindenberg  1996;  Ormel  et  al.  1999).  Within  this  framework,  two  universal goals-physical and social well-being-produce the overall outcome subjective well-being. Through their maximization of five instrumental goals, individuals are able to achieve high levels of physical and social well-being. Physical well-being can be maximized by high levels of stimulation or activation (i.e., an optimal level of arousal) and comfort (i.e., the absence of physiological  needs  and  a  pleasant  and  safe  environment).  Social  well-being  is  maximized through status (i.e., control over scarce resources), behavioral confirmation (i.e., approval for 'doing the right things'), and affection (i.e., positive inputs from caring others).

Maximization strategies always rely on resources such as money, education, social class, employment, social relations, health and physical activities. Empirical research widely supports the  role  of  such  resources  in  the  production  of  happiness  and  the  hierarchical  structure  of resources,  instrumental  goals  and  well-being  outcomes.  For  instance,  research  provides evidence for the importance of health and money in maximizing subjective well-being, thereby providing support for the proposed hierarchical structure, where subjective well-being is the overall outcome (e.g., Easterlin 2001; Steverink et al. 1998; Wolbring et al. 2013).

Within this  proposed  theoretical  heuristic,  high  COVID-19  incidence  rates  pose  risks  to individuals' social production functions because they limit the means that are necessary for the maximization  of  happiness.  This  is  because,  on  the  one  hand,  COVID-19  incidence  rates influence  individuals'  perceptions  of  health-related  risks.  On  the  other  hand,  COVID-19 incidence rates determine the expected duration and type of policy interventions associated with key resources that are important for individuals' life satisfaction, such as employment or social contacts.

To illustrate the two different pathways linking COVID-19 incidence rates to individuals' well-being, we provide four stylized examples. First, COVID-19 incidence rates may reduce individuals'  means  for  reaching  their  instrumental  goal  of  comfort  simply  because  people become  ill  or  experience  a  reduction  in  vitality  through  pain.  Second,  self-isolation  or quarantine measures due to contact with infected individuals (more likely during high incidence phases) may reduce access to the activities and social relations that would stimulate and produce arousal in the absence of the COVID-19 pandemic. Third, high incidence rates (in particular, during the prevaccine phase of the pandemic) are a clear indicator of high utilization of hospitals and may therefore represent a warning signal to citizens about hospital congestion, which may reduce the perception of sufficient medical care in case of illness. Official statistics indicate that planned surgeries and noncritical medical interventions were postponed until low COVID-19 incidence  phases  (e.g.,  Destatis  2021a).  Fourth,  research  indicates  that  the  spread  of  the

coronavirus leads to a decrease in social trust (Collischon and Patzina 2022). Thus, high rates may signal that fellow citizens are not complying with mandatory COVID-19 distancing rules, which  may  lead  to  perceptions  of  high  infection  risks  and  an  unsafe  environment.  Such insecurities may cause mental distress due to fear of infection, harming mental health (e.g., Bhattachariee and Acharya 2020), which in turn may be detrimental to happiness (Ormel et al. 1997). Therefore, we expect that higher COVID-19 incidence rates have been accompanied by more pronounced decreases in individual life satisfaction, even when excluding the effects of lockdown measures.


## 2.2 Heterogeneous effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on life satisfaction


Thus  far,  we  have  proposed  a  theoretical  heuristic  that  explains  why  higher  COVID-19 incidence rates may affect individuals' subjective well-being.  In the following sections, we elaborate  on  why  differences  in  household  composition  and  affluence  may  have  led  to inequality in subjective well-being changes during the first phase of the COVID-19 pandemic based on incidence rates. Moreover, we discuss the potential role of gender differences in the effects of the focal household dimensions.


## 2.2.1 Household composition


Heterogeneity in subjective well-being changes may occur because of differences in household composition. In this study, we focus on three types of households that may lead to individuallevel differences in subjective well-being changes. First, we differentiate between single- and multi-person  households.  Second,  we  argue  that  individuals  from  households  with  young children react differently than individuals from households with older or no children. Third, we expect that individuals from households that perform caregiving duties for older individuals have been more strongly affected by the COVID-19 pandemic than individuals from households without such caregiving duties.

A simple explanation for why subjective well-being changes among individuals in singleperson  households  may  differ  from  well-being  changes  among  individuals  in  multi-person households  may  be  that  incidence  rates  cause  higher  levels  of  anxiety  and  fear  among individuals who live alone. This might be obvious, as individuals who live alone face greater challenges  in  organizing  their  own  care  in  the  event  of  a  COVID-19  infection.  Moreover, individuals from single-person households receive less emotional support in times of quarantine and in adapting to new situations. Thus, COVID-19 research highlights the intervening role of loneliness  in  explaining  decreases  in  mental  health  during  societal  isolation  and  distancing measures (e.g., Lee et al. 2020). A counterargument, however, might be that during times of quarantine and lockdown, conflicts within multi-person households are likely to emerge, which have a negative effect on subjective well-being (Humphreys et al. 2020). Indeed, some evidence suggests that family conflicts increased during the COVID-19 pandemic (Barboza et al. 2021). In addition, individuals in multi-person households face higher risk of infection and, thus, might react  more  strongly  to  higher  incidence  rates  compared  to  individuals  in  single-person households. Therefore, it is not entirely clear whether the effect of loneliness outweighs the potential negative effects of conflicts and higher infection risks in multi-person households or whether higher COVID-19 incidence rates cause higher emotional distress in single- or multiperson households.

Regarding minor children in the household, however, evidence from the first months of the COVID-19  pandemic  in  2020  indicates  that  individuals  with  young  children  (age<15) experienced  a  decrease  in  life  satisfaction  greater  than  that  of  individuals  with  older  or  no children (e.g., Huebener et al. 2021). This effect may have occurred because during the initial phase of the COVID-19 pandemic, it was unclear how severe the disease was for children. This uncertainty, in combination with higher incidence rates, likely triggered parents' fear that young children were at risk and induced distress, which led to their decreased subjective well-being. Research provides evidence for such a claim and shows that having children under age 10 led

to greater distress and anxiety during the COVID-19 pandemic (Rosen et al. 2020). Moreover, school and day care closures shifted care and teaching responsibilities to parents. Thus, higher incidence rates and expected extensions of school and childcare closures presented parents with a stressful situation, entailing long periods of balancing their work and childcare (Achterberg et al. 2021)-a circumstance that is likely detrimental to subjective well-being.

Similar to  individuals  with  childcare  responsibilities,  life  satisfaction  is  likely  to  decline more  for  those  with  private  caregiving  responsibilities.  In  most  cases,  people  who  require nursing are older and have a chronic disease and/or other health issues (e.g., Destatis 2020, OECD 2022). These circumstances expose the individuals in need of care to higher risk of death from COVID-19 (e.g., Ou et al. 2020). Consequently, private caregivers might have had higher fears  of  personal  infection  because  they  did  not  want  to  transmit  COVID-19  disease  to  the individuals  they  cared  for.  Moreover,  high  rates  of  hospitalization  and  hospital  congestion because of high incidence rates may increase worries among caregivers regarding sufficient health  care  possibilities.  Data  on  hospitalization  rates  demonstrate  such  worries,  as  the hospitalization rates of chronically ill individuals during high incidence phases were lower than in  prepandemic  years  (e.g.,  Blecker  et  al.  2021).  Moreover,  policy-makers  also  actively suggested postponing scheduled nonessential surgeries to ensure medical coverage for COVID19 cases (German government 2021). Additionally, if personal care did not take place within an individual's household, the care arrangement could have been in jeopardy in the event of prolonged social closures or the caregiving individual's quarantine. Thus, among individuals with caregiving responsibilities (in terms of childcare or other care duties), high incidence rates should have caused higher mental distress and anxiety, which would have been detrimental to subjective well-being.


## 2.2.2 Household affluence


Heterogeneity in subjective well-being changes may occur because of differences in household affluence. In this study, we focus on two dimensions of affluence that may lead to individuallevel differences in subjective well-being changes. First, we argue that the financial situation of households influences subjective well-being changes. Second, we argue that housing quality, or more precisely housing-related material deprivation, should lead to individual differences in changes in subjective well-being.

As one part  of  a  household's  affluence,  financial  resources  may  be  an  important  buffer against the adverse effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. For instance, households with higher financial  resources  than  households  with  poor  financial  resources  have  greater  means  to purchase high-quality food or meals from delivery services or other platforms, which enable individuals  to  maintain  or  even  increase  healthy  behaviors  during  lockdown  or  quarantine. Additionally, households with greater financial resources possess greater means to purchase health-protecting  equipment  or  medication.  Thus,  individuals  from  households  with  greater financial resources should have been able to maintain high levels of living during the pandemic by  finding  ways  to  pursue  a  healthy  lifestyle.  Moreover,  households  with  greater  financial resources  may  have  been  better  able  to  compensate  for  individual  income  shocks  due  to unemployment, which was particularly high during the outbreak of the pandemic (e.g., Béland et  al.  2020).  Consequently, higher incidence rates and the resulting longer periods of social distancing may have affected the means of producing life satisfaction to a lesser extent in such households  than  in  households  with  fewer  financial  resources.  As  a  result,  members  of financially well-equipped households should have experienced fewer negative changes in life satisfaction than those living in nonaffluent households.

Another important household characteristic that may have influenced subjective well-being changes during the COVID-19 pandemic is housing-related material deprivation (e.g., having

limited space or damp walls). During the COVID-19 pandemic, housing deprivation affected individuals' potential to recover from the illness, making them more likely to suffer longer from COVID-19  and  its  side  effects  (Ayala  et  al.  2021).  Moreover,  housing  deprivation  should increase the risk of infection because deprivation often leads to overcrowding (Ayala et al. 2021).  Overcrowding  appears  to  have  been  particularly  important  during  the  COVID-19 pandemic; as empirical research indicates, crowding has a negative effect on psychological distress (i.e., negative emotions such as feeling nervous, restless or worthless), which might be more detrimental in the case of illness, quarantine or prolonged periods of societal lockdowns (Pierse  et  al.  2016).  Consequently,  as  mental  health  constitutes  an  important  resource  for achieving  high  happiness  levels,  household  deprivation  may  have  amplified  declines  in individual-level subjective well-being during the initial phase of the COVID-19 pandemic.


## 2.2.3 Gender differences


COVID-19 research on the early phase of the pandemic has indicated gender differences in many  domains.  For  instance,  studies  have  indicated  higher  COVID-19  infection  risks  for women than men, which might be explained by  occupational  segregation  in  labor  markets (Connor et al. 2020). Additionally, women were more likely to lose their jobs (Möhring et al. 2021)  and  to  take  over  caregiving  responsibilities  during  school  and  institutional  childcare closures (Zoch, Bächmann, and Vicari 2021b), thus increasing their stress levels during phases of high incidence rates. Moreover, women's and, in particular, mothers' well-being declined most strongly during the initial phase of the COVID-19 pandemic (Huebener et al. 2021; Zoch et  al.  2021a).  A  meta-analysis  of  gender-related  differences  in  COVID-19-related  fears  has revealed that women experience higher levels of COVID-19-related anxiety and psychological distress than men (Metin et al. 2022). The potential mechanism by which women reacted more strongly  to  COVID-19  incidence  rates  may  have  been  differences  in  risk  preferences  or COVID-19-related risk perceptions (Niño et al. 2021). Because higher incidence rates reflect

both individual health-related risks and the expected consequences of political interventions, such as school and childcare closures, we also assume that there were gendered differences in the negative changes in subjective well-being during the initial phase of the pandemic, to the disadvantage of women.

In addition, we  also expect that there were gendered effects of household-level characteristics  on  subjective  well-being  changes.  For  instance,  if  we  take  into  account  that women, compared to men, had on average higher COVID-19-related risk perceptions, they should have had worse subjective well-being changes when living in single-person households because  they  had  less  social  support,  which  could  have  buffered  their  COVID-19-related anxieties  or  fears.  Additionally,  women,  in  comparison  to  men  in  multi-person  households, could on average have reacted more strongly to the COVID-19 pandemic because these women had been socialized into the role of a caregiver who feels responsible for others' health in their household (Umberson 1992). Consequently, the  effects  of caregiving  duties,  which  emerge through the presence of either young children or older individuals in need of care, should have been more severe on women than on men.

Regarding household affluence, we might expect adverse effects on men. Research indicates that men's breadwinner role within their household contributes to gender differences in life satisfaction, thereby suggesting that having the role of the primary wage-earner contributes to men's life satisfaction (Salinas-Jiménez et al. 2012). As the COVID-19 pandemic has posed a threat to such roles, compared to women, men could have reacted with stronger subjective wellbeing decreases. However, in terms of housing deprivation, it remains unclear whether men or women suffer more from deprivation or whether there might be no difference between the two.


## 3 Methods, measures and data



## 3.1 Data


We use data from the Panel Labour Market and Social Security (PASS) (Trappmann et al. 2019),  a  large-scale  panel  study  of  German  households.  The  panel  has  been  surveying approximately 10,000 households and approximately 15,000 individuals since 2006. The PASS consists of a representative general population sample as well as a sample of welfare benefit recipients,  thus  allowing  an  investigation  of  fine-grained  heterogeneities  due  to  its  large statistical power. In our main analysis, we restrict the sample to the years 2019 and 2020 to have no confounding events that could affect our estimation but use the data from 2015 onwards to investigate trends in life satisfaction and for robustness checks.

The PASS data set constitutes an ideal source for the evaluation of the effects of the COVID19 pandemic on subjective well-being for two reasons. First, these data allow us to investigate pre-COVID trends. Second, the data collection for the 2020 survey wave started in February of that year. This is important because this data feature enables us to compare responses both prior to and after the outbreak of the pandemic within the 2020 survey year. Our analytical strategy thus exploits this key feature of the data.

As we are interested in the effect of incidence rates on life satisfaction, we link data on district-level incidence rates to the survey data. The Robert Koch Institute (RKI 2021) collected data on the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic, facilitating the creation of 7-dayrolling averages of cases per 100,000 inhabitants at the district level in Germany.

Our observation period comprises the key lockdown events in Germany and the entire first wave of the spread of the coronavirus. Specifically, we use interviews from February to May to (i) ensure a roughly balanced time frame before and after the onset of the pandemic and (ii) to ensure that the policy framework remains comparable in all districts, as the German-wide lockdown  in  2020  lasted  until  May.  In  Germany,  on  10  March,  the  federal  government suggested cancelling large events, and then, on 13 March 2020, German state governments

announced school closures. On 22 March 2020, the first country-wide lockdown started. The entire  duration  of  the  first  lockdown  was  seven  weeks.  The  first  peak  of  the  disease (approximately 6,000 cases a day) in Germany was at the end of March/beginning of April (Dong et al. 2020).


## 3.2 Measures


To measure individuals'  subjective  well-being,  we  use  individuals'  life  satisfaction.  We derive this measure from answers to the following question: 'How satisfied are you with your life, all things considered?' Respondents could rate their satisfaction on a scale ranging from 0 to 10. Individuals' answers thus reflect their cognitive component of well-being and indicate their evaluation of life in terms of their predefined goals (Diener 1984), which aligns with social production theory.

The main independent variable of interest is a treatment indicator that assigns individuals the value 1 if an individual answers the PASS survey after 22 March and lives in a district with an above-median incidence rate.

The data also contain detailed information on the household and individual characteristics that we use to investigate heterogeneities. Specifically, the PASS contains data on whether a child under the age of 15 lives in a household, on whether individuals are caregivers for other adults,  such  as  their  parents,  on  household  savings  (in  categories),  on  individuals'  incomes (OECD-equivalent household incomes) and on gender. Furthermore, the PASS collects data on household deprivation, which we use to construct a binary indicator. This indicator takes the value 1 if a household does not have a separate toilet, a balcony, a bathroom in the flat, sufficient rooms, or cannot replace old furniture-all due to financial reasons. We also have information on education, age and gender, which we use as covariates in some analyses. Table 1 lists the sample descriptive statistics for our baseline estimation by survey year.
