## 5 Discussion, limitations and suggestions for future research


If  educational practitioners and policy makers are to monitor their efforts, they need  useful measurement  instruments  to  do  so.  Developing  reliable  and  valid  scales  that  allow  such monitoring in education for sustainable development is challenging due to the complexity of the notion of quality in this context. With the current study, we took important steps on the path toward operationalizing quality education for sustainability teaching (QUEST) as perceived by students through development of the QUEST-Q measurement instrument. The aim was in the first place to explore the feasibility of taking on the challenge to make QUEST measurable from a  comprehensive student perspective, and secondly, to gain further insight in what QUEST entails from an empirical perspective to better understand its theoretical groundings.

## Contributions of the QUEST-Q to existing research

Regarding  the  first  aim,  the  QUEST-Q  makes  two  distinct  and  important  contributions  to existing monitoring instruments. First, the monitoring tool (the QUEST-Q)  takes a comprehensive perspective addressing all aspects of quality education in line with the QUEST framework. No instrument has previously done so. Second, the QUEST-Q assesses students' learning rather than teachers' teaching, which is also a novel and important contribution to existing measurement instruments in sustainability and quality education research.

Previous instruments looked into specific components of QUEST, such as student participation (Torsdottir, Sinnes, Olsson, & Wals, 2023), or teachers' beliefs regarding their holistic and pluralistic educational approach (Sinakou, Donche, Boeve-de Pauw, & Van Petegem, 2021). We contribute to the field of research and practice with the development of a set of measurement instruments that jointly form the QUEST-Q, providing tools for assessing students' experiences with their school's QUEST implementation efforts at a comprehensive level, i.e., including the what , how where and with whom , of the teaching-learning process.

Additionally, existing measurement instruments take a teacher perspective (see e.g. Malandrakis et al., 2019; Sass et al., 2022; Sinakou et al., 2021). The current study contributes to the field by adding a student perspective on QUEST implementation at their whole school, rather than in specific school subjects by specific teachers. Instead, QUEST-Q is developed in a  way  that  enables  evaluation  of  quality  education  across  all  school  subjects.Thus,  we  are adding a measurement instrument fit to assess QUEST at the student level. By tapping into how students  perceive  their  learning  experiences  rather  than  into  the  teachers'  self-perceived teaching approaches (e.g. Malandrakis et al., 2019; Sass et al., 2022) we are adding a novel perspective  on  measurement  of  the  learning-teaching  process.  This is an emphasized perspective in research (Treviño & Carrasco, in press).

For each of the constructs within the QUEST framework ( why , what , how , where and with whom ) we propose valid and reliable instruments that show excellent psychometric qualities. Means  and  standard  deviations  found  for  scale  and  item  scores  in  this  study,  indicate  the absence of floor and ceiling effects, as well as the discriminant power of the scales.

In sum, earlier instruments tend to focus on one particular component of quality in sustainability teaching, e.g., sustainability competencies as learning outcomes, and are designed to assess the teachers'  perspective.  The  current  study  contributes  to  the  field  by  1)  taking  a  student perspective on 2) their whole school's comprehensive and holistic QUEST implementation, which was the first aim of this study.

In the following section, we zoom in on our second aim, i.e., further developing theoretic insight in QUEST from a student perspective.

## Theoretical validation and development of QUEST

Psychometric data, as obtained in this study, can tell us how constructs are related to each other according to how respondents (in this study secondary students) reply to them (deVellis, 2017).

When finding models that best fit the data, modification indices suggest addition of covariances between subconstructs. These covariances provide insight in the theoretic associations between QUEST (sub)components. Regarding the second aim of this study, i.e. a further development of  the  QUEST  framework,  covariances  support  the  theoretic  claims  that  the  constructs  are closely related in the respondents' (i.e., the students') minds. We here discuss the theoretic implications of covariances between the subconstructs that were included in the QUEST-Q scales. Still, as we opted for the least complex model for reasons of parsimony, the absence of covariances in the QUEST-Q models does not mean there is no theoretic connectivity within the subcomponents of the QUEST framework.

Regarding our second aim, the current study's findings largely confirm expectations from a theoretic point of view regarding the interrelated framework of QUEST as outlined by Sass et al. (under review). As suggested by the dotted lines in Figure 1, QUEST (sub)constructs are theoretically assumed to be closely linked to each other. We now return to this notion and look more deeply into empiric evidence for this assumption.

The holistic knowledge model included statistically significant ( p = 0.000) covariances between subconstruct  knowledge  about  sustainability  problems  in  general  and  1)  knowledge  of  the different sustainability dimensions of problems (p<0.05), and 2) knowledge about norms and values related to sustainability problems and possible solutions ( p = 0.000). This confirms the holistic  nature  of  the  knowledge  QUEST  component  as  suggested  by  theoretic  work  (e.g., Mogensen & Schanck, 2010; Sass et al., under review).

The sustainability competencies model included statistically significant ( p = 0.000) covariances between  communication  items  (2  and  3)  and  between  subconstructs  future  thinking  and communication. Items 2 and 3 both referred to an active listener's attitude toward partners' explication  of  values  that  underly  preferences  for  certain  solutions  (item  2)  and  respectful negotiation of values that guide choices for a specific societal solution (item 3). From a theoretic

perspective, this makes sense, as these can be considered important conditions for effective decision-making, collaboration and joint action. Also, the association between subconstructs future thinking and communication can be explained theoretically. Communication of a desired (i.e., sustainable) future is paramount if we, the current generations, want to find answers for this global problem through collective action. Finally, the future thinking subscale showed the strongest  factor  loading  in  this  sustainability  competencies  scale.  This  is  in  line  with  the emphasis policy makers put on providing acceptable living conditions for all current and future generations  through  programs  such  as  the  United  Nations  2030  Agenda  for  Sustainable Development  (United  Nations,  2015)  and  the  European  Union's  Green  Deal  (European Commission, 2019).

An action-oriented approach as perceived by students, turned out to be the most complex of all the  models  explored  in  the  current  study.  In  view  of  indications  that  an  orientation  toward action, i.e., learning by doing (Van Poeck, Östman, & Öhman, 2019), affects all components of action competence (Sass et al., 2023; Sinakou et al., 2019; Varela-Losada et al., 2016), the students' perspective on the learning by doing subconstruct in this model draws our attention. The high factor loading of the action-taking subcomponent here, underscores earlier theoretical assumptions (Sinakou et al., 2019; Varela-Losada et al., 2016) and evidence-based confirmation (Sass  et  al.,  2023).  Furthermore,  covariances  between  subconstructs  reflecting  and  learning from mistakes are also in line with earlier evidence (van Harskamp, Knippels, Boeve-de Pauw, & van Joolingen, 2023). This indicates the salience of creating safe educational environments in  which  mistakes  are  not  sanctioned  without  delay,  so  students  experience  the  value  of mistakes in their learning process.

In sum, the covariances found in this study underscore the interrelated character of the different QUEST dimensions in the scales and the interconnectedness between the what how where and , , with  whom in  quality  education  for  sustainability  (Figure  1).  This  study  shows  that  a

comprehensive perspective on quality education for sustainability is important, as previously theoretically  argued  by  Sass  et  al.,  (under  review).  Our  results  highlight  the  importance  of implementing, and thereafter monitoring, all aspects of the what, how, where and with whom of  sustainability  education.  Even  though,  in  certain  contexts  and  situations,  it  might  be necessary to focus on one or other of these dimensions from a practical perspective, the results of this study show that it is important not to lose sight of the comprehensive perspective due to the  interconnectedness  of  all  aspects  of  QUEST.  Thus,  we  achieved  our  second  aim  by furthering theory development regarding quality education in the Anthropocene.

## Limitations and suggestions for future research

Results  regarding  the  student  perspectives  on sustainability  competencies scale  showed interesting results for subscale critical thinking item CT\_4. Its factor loading (.450) was the lowest in this subscale. Judging from a closer look at the items in this scale, this might indicate that  critical  thinking  possibly  consists  of  different  aspects,  i.e.,  critical  scrutiny  of  different perspectives on the one hand (represented by items CT1 to 3), and of the accuracy of certain sources that claim to offer factual knowledge (represented only by item CT4) on the other hand. Due to theoretical considerations,  this  item  was  deemed too  pertinent  to  be  deleted.  Future studies  may  want  to  broaden  this  scale  with  additional  items  delving  into  critical  thinking related to so-called fake news. Furthermore, the covariance between students' perspectives on future thinking and communication as taught and learned at their school, are in line with the United Nations' (2015) emphasis on the need for partnership when looking for solutions to sustainability conundrums.

The student perspectives on a pluralistic approach scale was the only one that did not include any  covariances  between  items,  nor  subconstructs.  The  low  factor  loading  of  subconstruct democratic  dialogue  is  puzzling,  as  pluralism  and  democratic  educational  approaches  are theoretically thought to be related (Mogensen & Schnack, 2010; Öhman & Östman, 2019).

Further research is needed to find out if democratic dialogue should be interpreted as related to a participative approach rather than as in line with a respectful communication in a context typically defined by conflicting interests and opinions.

Finally, we need to acknowledge that the data used in this study, were collected within a specific sample of students in higher secondary education, enrolled in academic tracks. While this was part  of  the  design  of  the  current  study,  further  work  on  the  applicability  of  the  QUEST-Q instrument set is needed across other target groups, in larger samples across entire schools, and in different cultural-educational contexts.

## Implications for how to use the QUEST-Q

The  QUEST-Q  is  intended  to  serve  as  a  research  instrument  and  a  monitoring  tool  for researchers as well as educational practitioners and policy makers. Furthermore, users may opt for using all five QUEST-Q scales to stay true to the comprehensive and holistic character of QUEST. This would allow looking into the associations between the different scales. Still, this comprehensive element also makes for a lengthy questionnaire. For students of a younger age, it may be too demanding to administer all five scales in one session.

Alternatively, each of the five scales can be used as a separate monitoring instrument, as they were validated per scale (i.e. students' experiences with a teaching-learning process that focuses on 1) holistic knowledge , 2) sustainability competencies , through 3) a pluralistic approach , 4) an action-oriented  approach ,  and  in  collaboration  with  5) partners within  and  beyond  the school).

In conclusion, the insights gained and questions raised by this study may inspire future research into, policy for, and monitoring of QUEST implementation. Researchers, policy makers and practitioners now have access to a novel set of scales to support their efforts for QUEST. In the

end, all of us are equally charged with the ambitious aim to support educational efforts in quality education for sustainability.

## Introduction


Although online distance learning opportunities have developed over the past few years, their widespread adoption in all areas of education worldwide has increased significantly since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. The abrupt and rapid shift from face-to-face to online learning environments,  called  as  emergency  remote  teaching  (ERT),  posed  significant  challenges  for educators across various disciplines. Faculty members with no prior online teaching experience were given minimal preparation time - typically only one week - to transition their face-to-face courses to an online format (Marasi et al., 2020). In this period of global and local disruption of traditional teaching routines, educators' satisfaction with navigating this unfamiliar environment is  likely  to  profoundly  impact  the  teaching  process  and  the  well-being  of  both  instructors  and students.

Instructor  satisfaction  with  online  teaching  is  defined  as  the  perception  that  the  online teaching process is efficient, effective, and personally beneficial (Bolliger et al., 2014). It is also considered  a  strong  predictor  of  the  success  of  any  online  education  program,  impacting instructors,  students,  and  program  outcomes  (Stickney  et  al.,  2019).  The  Online  Learning Consortium (2021) emphasizes that quality online education is built upon five pillars, and faculty satisfaction is one of them.

Due to its specific characteristics and requirements, online language teaching poses several challenges.  Lack  of  face-to-face  interaction  and  sometimes  real-time  communication  may negatively affect language education's communicative and interactive essence. (Matiso & Makena, 2022). Therefore, teachers in online education need a distinct set of skills from instructors trained for traditional, face-to-face classrooms and those needed by online educators in other disciplines (Moorhouse et al.,2021). Although it is generally assumed that effective online teaching goes hand in  hand  with  basic  ICT  competence,  it  requires  much  more  to  address  broader  pedagogical concerns. According to Bennett and Marsh (2002), these include recognizing key differences and similarities  between  face-to-face  and  online  learning  environments,  as  well  as  developing strategies to support online learning, such as helping students take advantage of both independent and collaborative learning opportunities.

The  TPACK  framework  emphasizes  the  importance  of  teachers  having  a  balanced understanding of how technology, pedagogy, and content intersect in educational contexts. It is particularly relevant to emergency distance learning, as it can help teachers create engaging online activities, assess student learning, and maintain continuity of quality education. Therefore, there may be a significant connection between language teachers' TPACK and their level of satisfaction with teaching online.

Instructors with strong TPACK can experience greater satisfaction with online teaching by enhancing  student  engagement,  supporting  interactive  language  practice,  delivering  timely feedback, addressing diverse learning styles, offering authentic language resources and multimedia materials, and effectively resolving technical issues, among other factors. (Quyang & Scharber, 2018; Major & McDonald, 2021).

Although the TPACK levels of language educators in various contexts have been widely studied, to the researcher's knowledge, there is a lack of specific studies examining the direct relationship between (TPACK) and instructors' satisfaction with online teaching. Therefore, this

paper  aims  to  present  findings  from  a  more  extensive  study,  specifically  focusing  on  the relationship between instructors' TPACK and their satisfaction with teaching online.

This study aims to contribute to this growing area of research by exploring the relationship between language teachers' TPACK and satisfaction with teaching online. Adequate TPACK may enable  English  instructors  to  effectively  utilize  online  platforms,  digital  tools,  and  resources, thereby creating engaging and interactive online learning environments and ensuring the continuity and quality of language teaching across various modalities (Antari et al.,2023; Darsih et al.,2023). To our knowledge, no study has yet investigated the relationship between these two variables. Therefore, this study is expected to significantly contribute to the literature by demonstrating how possessing adequate TPACK enhances online language teaching.


## Literature Review


The context of online education during the pandemic differs significantly from that of prepandemic  studies,  given  the  unique  challenges  and  circumstances  of  the  Emergency  Remote Teaching (ERT) period. As previous studies do not adequately capture the specific conditions and demands of teaching in this unprecedented context, the literature review on online education in this study will focus exclusively on research conducted during or in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Several studies have explored teachers' and faculty members' experiences and perceptions during  the  Emergency  Remote Teaching  (ERT)  process  and  identified  key  factors  influencing online teaching satisfaction. A major theme was the need for adequate ICT competence. Many educators felt unprepared for the use of online teaching strategies and digital tools, highlighting the need for additional training (Trust & Whalen, 2020). Related to this, computing self-efficacy and online teaching efficacy were found to be positively correlated with higher satisfaction among Chinese teachers (Chen et al., 2023; Du et al., 2023).

Challenges such as unreliable internet connections, high costs, and power outages were also found to contribute significantly to dissatisfaction with online education (Pete & Soko, 2021; Ontha  et  al.,  2020).  Similarly,  university  teachers  reported  high  levels  of  stress  and  low  job satisfaction due to inadequate IT infrastructure, lack of student engagement, and difficulties with online  assessments  (Ali  et  al.,  2021).  Teachers  also  reported  an  increase  in  workload  and demotivation due to the additional effort required for online lesson preparation (Ontha et al., 2020).

Institutional support, interaction during online classes, and self-efficacy in both computer use, and online teaching were critical factors in increasing satisfaction with online teaching (Pham & Nghiem, 2022). In addition, studies have shown that technology pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK)  and  work  engagement  were  positively  associated  with  instructor  self-efficacy, satisfaction  with  teaching,  and  future  intent  to  continue  teaching  online  (Huang  et  al.,  2022). Nevertheless, some studies have found an improvement in satisfaction over time. For example, teachers  with  access  to  improved  digital  tools,  such  as  Microsoft  Teams,  reported  greater satisfaction due to improved interaction and usability (Durak & Cankaya, 2020).

Several studies have investigated language teachers' experiences of teaching online during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the findings are broadly consistent with the research from other teaching  disciplines  outlined  above.  The  technical  and  infrastructural  challenges  faced  by educators are a recurring theme. For instance, Talidong (2020) found that although Filipino English language  teachers  acknowledged  the  benefits  of  online  learning,  they  experienced  significant challenges,  including  poor  internet  connections,  technical  difficulties  and  conference  tool

overload. Similarly, a study by Hazaea et al. (2021) found that in low-tech Arab countries, such as Yemen and Libya, online teaching was severely disrupted due to a lack of technical infrastructure.

Language teachers' ICT competence also emerged as a critical issue. Vietnamese vocational English teachers, for example, reported that their positive attitudes towards online teaching were tempered by difficulties related to their digital skills and online classroom management (Tue & Hanh, 2021). This view is repeated in the Turkish EFL context, where teachers expressed the need for more training on how to use digital tools effectively and how to adapt communicative language teaching  methods  to  distance  learning  (Tumen Akyildiz,  2020b;  Turegun  Coban  &  Kuyumcu Vardar, 2021).

The  increased  workload  associated  with  ERT  was  also  highlighted  in  some  studies. Vietnamese English teachers identified heavy workloads, together with students' varying levels of technological competence and the need for technical support, as key challenges (Tue & Hanh, 2021).  Similarly, Turkish  EFL  teachers  (Turegun  Coban  &  Kuyumcu Vardar,  2021)  found  the process of adapting to online teaching challenging, with technical issues adding to the workload.

Despite  these  challenges,  the  teachers  identified  some  positive  aspects  of  ERT..  For example, Turegun Coban and Kuyumcu Vardar (2021) found that Turkish EFL student teachers and their instructors appreciated certain features of distance education, such as the flexibility of time and space, the affordability of online education, and the opportunity to share a wide range of resources. In addition, the ability to review recorded lessons was also highlighted as a benefit, which, in certain contexts, could enhance learning outcomes.

Regarding  pedagogical  adaptation,  using  digital  platforms  was  an  important  part  of facilitating online teaching. Linh et al. (2021) reported that Vietnamese tertiary English teachers preferred platforms like Gmail, Google Classroom, Zoom, and Google Meet, mainly because of their  practicality  and  alignment  with  teachers'  digital  competencies.  These  platforms  helped teachers  to  manage  their  online  classrooms  more  effectively  by  enabling  the  delivery  of  live lessons.

In view of all that has been mentioned so far, it can be inferred that teachers' ability to integrate technology into their teaching is essential for the successful implementation of remote instruction. The studies reviewed suggest a strong need for continuing training in digital literacy and online pedagogy to equip language teachers better to teach remotely in future crises.


## Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK)


The  TPACK  framework  was  introduced  to  provide  a  theoretical  basis  for  integrating technology into teaching. It highlights that educational technologies arise from the intersection of pedagogical, content, and technological knowledge (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Previous studies of technology use in education have focused primarily on teachers' technological knowledge, but it is  now recognized that this alone is insufficient. Teachers need to integrate their technological knowledge with content and pedagogical knowledge, a concept known as TPACK (Voogt et al., 2016). This framework shows how these three areas of knowledge interplay can lead to effective, discipline-based teaching using educational technologies (Harris et al., 2009).

As shown in Figure 1, the TPACK framework emphasizes integrating content, pedagogy, and technology to support effective teaching with technology. Content knowledge (CK) refers to a teacher's understanding of their subject, whereas pedagogical knowledge (PK) includes skills related  to  teaching  methodology,  lesson  planning,  and  classroom  management  (Koehler  et  al., 2013; Shulman, 1986). The intersection of CK and PK, known as pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), is '…the blending of content and pedagogy into an understanding of how particular aspects of  subject  matter  are  organized,  adapted,  and  represented  for  instruction'  (Mishra  &  Koehler, 2006, p.1021).

Technological  knowledge  (TK)  includes  the  ability  to  use  hardware,  software,  and communication tools, but goes beyond technical skills to understanding of how these technologies enhance learning (Voogt et al., 2016; Compton, 2009). Technological content knowledge (TCK) focuses on the relationship between technology and content and supports teachers in selecting appropriate technologies to represent subject matter (Cox & Graham, 2009; Koehler et al., 2013).

Technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK) is defined as 'knowledge of the existence, components,  of  various  technologies  as  they  are  used  in  teaching  and  learning  settings,  and conversely, knowing how teaching and capabilities might change as the result of using particular technologies' (Mishra & Koehler, 2006, p.1028). It refers to understanding how technology can support teaching and learning in pedagogically sound ways, regardless of specific content (Angeli et al., 2016). It fosters creativity by enabling teachers to adapt non-educational technologies for educational purposes (Mishra & Koehler, 2006).

Technological  pedagogical  content  knowledge  (TPACK)  emerges  from  the  complex interplay  between  CK,  PK,  and  TK.  It  goes  beyond  the  individual  elements  to  provide  a comprehensive framework for teaching with technology (Harris et al., 2009) and forms the core knowledge required to effectively integrate technology into the classroom. Mishra et al. (2009) describe how the TPACK framework provides a fresh perspective on educational technology, as in the following:

How does  the  TPACK  framework  offer  a  new  way  of  thinking  about  educational technology?  First,  by  stressing  how  technology  interacts  with  pedagogy  and  content, innovations are not necessarily relevant for teaching. Instead, emphasis is put on evaluating

## Previous Studies on Language Teachers' TPACK


Several studies have examined language teachers' TPACK levels, often through self-report questionnaires.  Teachers  generally  reported  being  satisfied  with  their  TPACK  competencies, particularly  in  content  knowledge  (CK),  but  highlighted  weaker  competencies  in  technologyrelated areas such as technological knowledge (TK), technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK) and technological content knowledge (TCK) (Cheng, 2017; Atar et al., 2019; Wu & Wang, 2015; Chai et al., 2013).  Similarly, in Wu and Wang's study (2015), English language teachers reported their need for further development in TK.

The  effectiveness  of  TPACK  in  improving  language  learning  outcomes  has  been highlighted in several studies. A TPACK-based online writing course improved Taiwanese nursing students' writing skills (Tai et al., 2015), while TPACK-led reading instruction improved Jordanian EFL students' reading performance (Abu-Hardan et al., 2019). Teacher training using the TPACK model  also  significantly  enhanced  the  CALL  proficiency  of  Taiwanese  English  teachers  (Tai, 2015).

Lastly, research into developing TPACK  among language teachers shows that telecollaboration, Web 2.0 tool integration, and digital storytelling positively influenced TPACK development (Bueno-Alastuey et al., 2018; Bustamante, 2020; Sancar Tokmak & Yanpar-Yelken, 2015). This section presents the summary of the existing literature on online language teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic and TPACK in language teaching. The following section provides details about the methodology of the study.


## Methodology



## Research Design


Given  the  study's  aims,  a  mixed  methods  approach  was  adopted,  integrating  both quantitative and qualitative techniques. The reason for this is that reliance on either quantitative or qualitative methods alone does not adequately respond to the requirements of the main approaches used  in  the  social  and  human  sciences  (Creswell,  2003). As  Malina  et  al.  (2011)  point  out, combining these two approaches allows researchers to delve into more complex dimensions and relationships within the human and social world, resulting in stronger research findings than either method could achieve on its own.


## Participants


This  study  used  a  convenience  sample  of  205  EFL  instructors  from  12  different  state universities in Turkey for the quantitative phase, selecting participants based on accessibility and willingness  (Teddlie  &  Yu,  2007).  For  the  qualitative  phase,  semi-structured  interviews  were conducted  with  16  EFL  instructors  who  were  also  selected  using  convenience  sampling.  The

interviewees were selected from among the survey respondents who had volunteered for further participation.


## Data Collection Instruments


This study collected data using a background questionnaire, the TPACK-EFL survey, the OFSS survey and semi-structured interviews . The TPACK-EFL survey, which was developed and validated by Baser et al. (2016), was used for the assessment of EFL educators' perceived level of technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK). The survey consists of 39 items grouped into seven factors according to the TPACK framework.

The Online Faculty Satisfaction Survey (OFSS), developed by Bolliger and Wasilik (2009), was used to measure satisfaction with online teaching. The OFSS consists of 28 items grouped into three factors: student-related, teacher-related, and institution-related. Two items in the OFSS survey are specifically related to general satisfaction with online teaching.

The qualitative phase involved using semi-structured interviews with 10 questions. These questions are based on a literature review (Durdu & Dag, 2017; Ritter, 2012; Donmez, 2016) and the researcher's own ideas and experience. Two experts in the field of language education, one of whom  has  conducted  research  on  ERT,  validated  the  content  of  the  interview  questions  and suggested minor revisions. After piloting, further adjustments were made, and two questions were removed. The final interview format consisted of 10 questions. As stated earlier, this paper presents findings  from  a  more  extensive  study. Therefore,  in  line  with  the  objectives  of  this  study,  the responses to one of the questions served as the qualitative data set for the research

## Discussion


This paper aimed to explore the relationship between EFL instructors' perceived TPACK levels and their satisfaction with teaching online in an emergency remote teaching context. Data were collected using quantitative and qualitative methods and analyzed using correlational and content analysis techniques. The findings indicated a statistically significant but weak relationship between instructors'  TPACK and their satisfaction with teaching online. Although participants acknowledged the importance of TPACK for effective online teaching, factors such as low student participation, lack of motivation, and problems with internet connection had a negative impact on their satisfaction with teaching online. Thus, while having a sufficient level of TPACK is essential, it alone is not enough to ensure satisfaction in online teaching.

Although  previous  studies  have  explored  aspects  of  TPACK  and  online  teaching,  the relationship between TPACK and satisfaction with online teaching has received limited attention. This study thus contributes uniquely by demonstrating that TPACK can, to some extent, predict satisfaction with online teaching. This finding supports Huang et al.'s (2022) study, which found out  TPACK  and  work  engagement  were  positively  associated  with  instructor  self-efficacy, satisfaction with teaching, and future intent to continue teaching online. It is also in line with the previous  research  that  showed  computing  self-efficacy  and  online  teaching  efficacy  were positively correlated with higher satisfaction among Chinese teachers (Chen et al., 2023; Du et al., 2023)

It  was also revealed that having sufficient TPACK, while important, is not sufficient to ensure satisfaction due to negative factors such as low student motivation and participation, as well as problems with internet connection.  These findings are consistent with previous research that identified these challenges as barriers to effective online teaching (Pete & Soko, Talidong, 2020; Ali  et  al.,2021).  In  summary,  those  with  inadequate  TPACK  faced  greater  difficulties  during emergency remote teaching, while those with sufficient TPACK were still hindered by external issues, limiting their ability to fully apply their knowledge.


## Conclusion


The findings of this study hold significant implications for future online teaching and the integration of TPACK in online language education. The findings demonstrated that TPACK can somewhat  predict  satisfaction  with  online  teaching.  However,  it  also  highlighted  that,  while crucial, possessing adequate TPACK alone is insufficient for achieving satisfaction in teaching online.  This  suggests  the  need  to  raise  TPACK  awareness  among  educators  teaching  online, regardless  of  their  subject  area.  Specifically,  for  online  language  teachers,  ongoing  in-service training should focus on developing the four language skills using interactive and collaborative tools. This approach could help address the lack of student motivation, identified as one of the major  challenges  in  online  education.  Moreover,  it  is  essential  to  standardize  regulations  for managing online education, particularly concerning student attendance, to prevent inconsistent practices. Implementing clear rules regarding attendance is necessary for more effective online learning.

International development cooperation is understood as one of the essential strategies for achieving United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs) (Helgason 2016; OECD 2023; United Nations 2019). As such, international development cooperation fundamentally depends on the way that particular projects are envisioned, planned, designed and implemented. Crucially, all these aspects are shaped by their underpinning knowledge systems (Cummings et al. 2018; Mosse 2014; Powell and Cummings 2019). Such knowledge systems comprise the way relevant actors understand the world in which international development projects are nested, and, consequently, which types of knowledge and resulting interventions in social-ecological dynamics they prioritize and embark on (Powell 2006; Whitfield 2015).

In addition, knowledge serves not only implicitly as the basis of international development cooperation design, but also as an explicit element that gets actively transferred and

<!-- image -->

shaped among actors within project implementation (Mosse 2014; Ojala and Hooli 2022; Shepherd 2010) e.g. in the form of training, workshops and awareness raising campaigns, particularly as transfer and dissemination of knowledge have become the core of many international development projects (Janus et al. 2015; Molina-Maturano et al. 2020; Taylor and Bhasme 2018; Thuijsman et al. 2022).

Thus, it is vital to map and better understand where such knowledge originates from, how it is created, distributed, and utilized. The overarching aim of this paper is to build on the system thinking and sustainability science perspective that is enabling us to reflect on and to unravel the complex mechanisms that are shaping and are being shaped by the diversity of knowledge entering the international development cooperation. To this end, we use the Czech development cooperation (CDC) as a case study to critically analyse its knowledge system, comprising diverse types of knowledge and the actors that engage with them (Apetrei et al. 2021). Furthermore, we identify learning points on how to facilitate knowledge representation and cross-fertilization in the CDC knowledge system to contribute to long-term outcomes of implementation of UN SDGs.

In the development studies perspective, the role of knowledge  in  development  cooperation  started  to  be questioned in the early 2000s after the release of the World Bank's influential report Knowledge for Development (World Bank 1999). In the report, the World Bank understands the unequal distribution of (mostly technical) knowledge as one of the key impediments of development and promotes knowledge transfers from the Global North to Global South as a major development tool. However, according to Evers et al. (2009) this approach keeps maintaining the asymmetric relationship between the 'developed' and 'developing' and, as suggested by McFarlane (2006), it prioritizes technocratic and unilinear flows of knowledge from one place to another. This is especially problematic as these approaches hardly pay attention to the local specifics (Bruckmeier and Tovey 2008). Recently, a  similar discussion emerged regarding the agenda of the UN SDGs, especially in relation to what Cummings et al. (2018) calls techno-scientific-economic discourse, where top-down scientific and technical knowledge are represented as means for achieving economic growth and development. Another issue is the lack of emphasis on participation in fulfilling the SDGs hence undermining the agency of local people (Lepore et al. 2021). Another strand of development research relates to decolonial approaches to knowledge, urging the acknowledgment and leveraging of Indigenous and local knowledge (Brokensha et al. 1980; Chilisa 2017; Narayanaswamy 2013; Scoones and Thompson 1994). At the same time, this invisibility of non-scientific knowledge leads to epistemic injustices that are further sealing the superiority of scientific and expert

<!-- image -->

knowledge over the knowledge existing on the ground (Boogaard 2021; Latulippe and Klenk 2020). On top of that, decolonial approaches highlight the danger of fortification of existing power relations and imbalances that determine whose values and knowledge are prioritized over another (Chambers 2014; Mosse 2014; Pottier 2003).

As a response for tackling the superiority of the external, primarily scientific knowledge and top-down approaches, there is a long-standing tradition of participatory approaches to  design  and  implementation of development projects (Amauchi et al. 2022; Chambers 1994; Keahey 2021; Rahnema 1990) followed by the recent surge of knowledge co-production and transdisciplinarity in the development practice (Hainzer et al. 2022; Vincent 2022; Wittmayer and Schäpke 2014). However, despite the critique above and the relatively extensive body of research on the role of knowledge in acceptance of new, mostly agricultural, approaches and practices in development (e.g., Bouwman et al. 2019; Girard 2015; Glover et al. 2019; Hermans et al. 2021, 2023), reflection on the complex functioning of the overall knowledge systems in international development cooperation has been limited so far (Jacobi et al. 2017).

The framing of knowledge through decoloniality and epistemic injustice present in development studies can be expanded by the perspective of sustainability science . In particular, the field of systems thinking and leverage points within sustainability science (Meadows 1999; Abson et al. 2017) provides a valuable framework to systematise and structure the analysis of inherently fluid, qualitative and dynamic phenomena such as knowledge systems (Fischer and Riechers 2019). In this respect, within the framing of systems thinking, systems can be framed as specific and tangible objects (e.g., a food system) or as less tangible phenomena (e.g., a knowledge system), with a recognition that they are nested, interconnected, and often shape each other (Davelaar 2021; Leventon et al. 2021). As such, systems are defined as being composed of entities and their flows (e.g., actors, materials, resources, power, knowledge).

There are multiple types of rationale for studying knowledge systems from a qualitative systems thinking perspective. For instance, Apetrei et al. (2021), argue that people operate in specific knowledge systems representing a formative force to our way of knowing, related to individuals, groups or a culture, and that are usually associated with a geographical context. Furthermore, knowledge systems tend to be understood as networks (formal, informal or a mixture of both) (Cornell et al. 2013) in which knowledge is produced, reproduced, exchanged, and used in the process of knowledge translation into practice and actions (Tàbara and Chabay 2013). At the same time, as pointed out by Gorddard et al. (2016), knowledge systems determine agency (i.e., the ability to act based on reasoned choices), and thus underpin decision-making processes.

Importantly, what knowledge systems are understood as legitimate is influenced by particular decision contexts. Thus, sustainability science urges us to embrace the notion of pluralism (Leventon et al. 2022) and knowledge cross-fertilisation (Tengö et al. 2014), i.e. bringing together diverse knowledge systems in search for their complementarities and synergies to be able to actively act upon them. For instance, Chillisa (2017) calls for fundamental re-thinking of how knowledge existing in African countries is being represented and included in existing modes of knowledge production that are influential for the planning and implementation of development projects. In this respect, knowledge cross-fertilisation is a vital formative force for reshaping the existing superiorities of some knowledge systems, hence strengthening the agency of often marginalized voices (Caniglia et al. 2021).

Hence, we argue that sustainability science and its perspective on the functioning of knowledge systems through systems thinking (Apetrei et al. 2021; Cornell et al. 2013; Mazzocchi 2020; Tàbara and Chabay 2013) can provide valuable insights in the role of different types of knowledge in international development cooperation projects that aim to create change for sustainability. To this end, we apply system theory and utilize system properties (paradigms, design, structures, and resources) (Abson et al. 2017; Meadows 1999) as an analytical tool to map the knowledge existing amongst CDC actors, in order to provide a broader reflection of how knowledge is being framed by development actors in Eastern Europe. For the purpose of this study, we define the CDC knowledge system as comprising both the knowledge existing amongst CDC actors, and the knowledge existing amongst actors in Zambia. In addition, we classify which interventions are available to change the respective components of the knowledge system to enable knowledge cross-fertilization (Tengö et al. 2014), especially among CDC actors and target communities of development projects. Finally, we propose a set of learning points that are relevant across different types of development actors. In order to reach these goals, we set two research questions:

- 1. What are the system properties in the CDC knowledge system (materials, processes, design, and paradigms)?
- 2. What are the overlooked system properties inhibiting knowledge flows within the CDC knowledge system and associated interventions to tackle them?

## Systems thinking as an analytical framework


## Conceptual background: systems thinking


When characterising systems, we can refer to their system properties. Meadows (1999) refers to these as 12 leverage points, or system properties that can be altered in order to change the system. These can roughly be put into four categories (Abson et al. 2017): (1) materials; (2) processes; (3) design; and (4) paradigms. Working with these characteristics can help with defining and understanding systems. Furthermore, it is also a useful heuristic framework for considering how interventions aimed at changing the system in focus may work, while remaining reflexive about the social construction of those system boundaries and the implications therein (Lam et al. 2020; Leventon et al. 2021, 2023; Matamanda et al. 2020).

These leverage points can also serve as a way to question how we are intervening with systems; which system property we are targeting with an intervention to create change (e.g. Dorninger et al. 2020; Nabong et al. 2022). Here, interventions are defined as activities that create change by engaging with these system properties. Also, the interventions vary with the system being changed, e.g. interventions in food production systems will be different to those in policy systems. In Meadows' original essay, she outlines that engaging with these deeper system properties (paradigms and design) creates more fundamental transformation because the other properties are nested within and thus change too. Whereas changing only materials addresses merely a shallow leverage point, this creates very little immediate change to the overall nature of the system in question (though shallow interventions can create impacts to deeper leverage points over time-see e.g., Manlosa et al. 2019). Significantly, deeper leverage points are less tangible and visible, and therefore are often overlooked (Abson et al. 2017). We thus frame overlooked systems characteristics as those that are not often targeted by interventions that are seeking to create change.

## Analytical framework: applying systems thinking to the CDC knowledge system in Zambia

We define the CDC knowledge system as a complex web of relations and dynamics among diverse knowledge actors acting and interacting across scales and geographies. We thus understand systems as socially constructed objects with boundaries (Cilliers 2001; Preiser et al. 2018). Knowledge actors include individuals and organisations who hold knowledge that can potentially contribute to development outcomes. These include development cooperation organisations, local communities, government organisations, civil society-simply saying anyone who has a role in shaping, or is influenced by, development cooperation. The system is characterised by the actors recognising multiple forms of knowledge (including e.g. scientific, local and Indigenous knowledge) as 'materials' within the system, without our own systems framing giving particular weight or importance to any specific form of knowledge. We thus define the CDC knowledge system in a way that allows for diverse framings

of knowledge. Within this system, we operationalise system properties to form an analytical framework (see Table 1) to answer research questions stated in the introduction.

In our analytical framework the paradigms set the perspective for what happens within the CDC knowledge system-what knowledge entities are included, what processes and dynamics are understood as legitimate and what should be the cornerstone of the policies and strategies for development. This entails considering, for example, whose knowledge counts, even where it represents a radically different way of understanding the world that may not feel comfortable or even valid to the way we are trained (Bohensky and Maru 2011; Hernandez 2022). Despite their limited tangibility and highest level of abstraction, the paradigms fundamentally underpin the entire CDC knowledge system. We understand the paradigms as cross-scale-for example, the agenda of UN SDGs determines the overall agenda of donors and the development organizations but also the thinking of development actors as individuals (i.e. their understanding of what is development and how to achieve it).

Design of  the  CDC  knowledge system encompasses diverse concepts of development practice (e.g., behavioural change, integrated agriculture, market-system development) and approaches to development practice (e.g., evidencebased and place-based projects) that shape the planning and implementation of specific projects. These are often in conjunction with policies and strategies existing on national and sub-national levels in both Czech Republic and Zambia, and indeed shaped by broader development practices and paradigms. Practically, the design translates into what knowledge is to be (co)produced, how and with what purpose.

Materials of the CDC knowledge system are represented by the knowledge held by different actors present in the system-the actors' knowledge . The dynamics and relations across the actors' knowledge can be understood as processes existing within the CDC knowledge system. However, we understand materials and processes as inseparable since the delineation between what is happening among different types of actors' knowledge and within them would lead to oversimplifications and reduction.

Importantly, we understand all properties of the CDC knowledge system as dynamic and evolving over time.

To achieve diversity of participants in the sample and to mitigate possible bias, part of the research participants involved were also approached with the help of other Czech NGO(s)/academic institutions active in the Western province of Zambia, as well as by using the snowball technique.

This phase was focused on what actors' knowledge (and particular knowledge entities) are important for planning and implementation of development projects, and what paradigms are essential in shaping the CDC knowledge system. To this end, questions asked during the interviews were aimed at understanding what knowledge is used for planning and implementation of development projects and where does it originate from, as well as on the perceptions of the construct of development itself and the understanding of the conception of successful projects.

The purpose of the second phase of knowledge mapping in the Western province of Zambia was twofold. First, the interviews with key stakeholders and transect walks aimed to understand the processes of how different actors' knowledge from outside of Zambia proliferates into the practice of governmental bodies, especially extension officers who provide services in target communities, and to understand the design and paradigms that are significant for their work. Furthermore, the interviews with key stakeholders were focused on the identification of overlooked system properties

## Data analysis


The majority of the interviews and focus groups carried out in the first two phases of the research process were recorded. All the recordings were transcribed verbatim, aiming to capture all nuances. We used MAXQDA software for thematic analysis using the combination of inductive and deductive coding strategies in order to answer the two research questions (see below). This approach allowed for identification and interpretation of linkages and patterns emerging in the dataset (Ribbs 2007). Since we do not consider the prevalence of themes across the data set as crucial, we preferably evaluate the importance of the occurring theme in respect to research questions. Below, we provide an overview of specific analytical steps applied to answer the two research questions (RQ) stated in the introduction.

<!-- image -->

## RQ1: What are the system properties in the CDC

knowledge system (materials, processes, design, and paradigms)? To answer the RQ1, we depart from the need to first diagnose and map the system in order to get a grasp on the dynamics and flows within it. First, the data from the interviews, focus groups and transect walks generated during the first two research phases were inductively coded to unravel the diverse themes related to knowledge in general, its production, flows and exchanges within the CDC projects. Secondly, we used the system properties as operationalized in our analytical framework as deductive categories for the inductively identified themes. By this approach, we were able to identify paradigms and design that frame the materials and processes of the CDC knowledge system. Additionally, the materials and processes of the CDC knowledge system were analysed through a composition of a diagram (see section 'Materials and processes of CDC knowledge system', Fig. 2) displaying the dynamics and complexities that exist across actors' knowledge(s) and that simultaneously shape them.

RQ2: What are the overlooked system properties inhibiting knowledge flows within the CDC knowledge system and associated interventions to tackle them? Answering RQ1, as well as responding to the conceptual background introduced in section 'Conceptual background: systems thinking', set the premise that materials and processes are primarily context-specific and practical manifestation of the key system properties that exists at the level of paradigms and design of related knowledge systems. While the materials and processes were visible to CDC actors in Czech Republic and Zambia, the paradigms and design were often overlooked hence creating some of the major barriers to knowledge cross-fertilization in international development cooperation. Therefore, in order to answer RQ2, we examined specifically the themes under the specific categories of system paradigms and design that were identified by the research participants in Czech Republic and Zambia as: (1) often overlooked and/or insufficiently targeted by the diverse actors, hence potentially hindering the materials and processes of the CDC knowledge system; and (2) specific interventions proposed in order to tackle the overlooked system properties to shift the CDC knowledge system towards a higher level of knowledge cross-fertilisation.

The workshop implemented in the Phase 3 was used for the validation of the research results. The key points of the reflection were used for proposing a set of interventions that are essential for pushing the CDC system towards higher levels of knowledge cross-fertilization. These were used to refine the results presented here and inform the recommendations that we make in the discussion section.

## Paradigms of CDC knowledge system

The  paradigms  of  the  CDC  knowledge  are  inherently derived from the paradigms set by the development agenda on a global level where UN SDGs represent an umbrella for all Czech development cooperation activities. In the CDC knowledge system, SDGs materialize in the notion of a successful project (i.e., how do actors perceive and understand the desired outcomes of the development project). This is composed of three partially interrelated dimensions that exist, in the view of CDC actors, in a hierarchical order. To this end, the overarching aim of the CDC is centred around the achievement of sustainable livelihoods, that stems from the long-term change in target communities and resulting resilience, and that stretches beyond mere

In this sense, the precondition of reaching sustainable livelihoods is formed by project sustainability, i.e.  the continuation of the activities after the end of the project. It expects the taking over of the activities by engaged communities/other actors after the end of the funding period, therefore it depends on higher involvement of target communities and on an emphasis on more hands-on aspects of such trainings. For instance, this can be done by more active engagement of the target communities and through creating space for integrating their knowledge into development of their projects as well as by strengthening capacities of local extension officers and other governmental representatives. Finally, the last dimension of the paradigm of a successful project refers to development pragmatism , i.e. the fulfilment of outcomes and related indicators set during the

<!-- image -->

preparatory phase of the project. Unlike the previous two dimensions, the development pragmatism purely depends on single direction flow of the knowledge of CDC actors, and it practically does not require significant presence of knowledge of CDC project participants nor local governmental bodies and any active knowledge exchange. Although CDC actors communicate reaching their ideal priority to be sustainable livelihoods, it is hard to materialize in reality. Thus, the practice is rather guided by the development pragmatism which is closely tied to the design of CDC knowledge system.

## Design of CDC knowledge system

The paradigm of a successful project underpins the design of the CDC knowledge system. This is often embedded in those that are promoted by UN agencies but also other donors (e.g., GIZ, SIDA, USAID) and large development NGOs (e.g., Oxfam, CARE international). In this respect, the design is framed by CDC actors as the concepts and approaches for fulfilling the paradigm of a successful project. To this end, CDC actors suggest that the projects should be built on an equal approach, mutual respect and partnership as well as on cooperation of various types of actors across sectors . From the perspectives of CDC actors, all of these designs are expected to be built on mutual learning, capacity building at the institutional and community levels, and on close cooperation with the governmental authorities in the implementing country at both national and regional levels. Further, they set the ground for the design of placebased and evidence-based projects that nest the projects in the specific context, and are built on a user-friendly approach as well as emphasize the community ownership of the implemented project. Such place-based and evidence-based projects are preconditions for bringing in innovations, such as market-systems development, behavioural change, or integrated agriculture. At the same time, the design is subjected to national policies and strategies in both Zambia and Czech Republic, and to internal guidelines of CDC actors. These are met through aligning the design described above with the respective policies but also with the element of visibility and regionality of the development projects, that is required especially on the side of Czech development cooperation strategy.

At first sight, the design of the CDC knowledge system appears to be a perfect base for knowledge cross-fertilization. However, as shown in Fig. 2 and explained below, these approaches used in projects are often rather proclamatory and mirror the actual practice of CDC actors only partially. The knowledge of CDC project participants is very rarely mentioned by CDC actors in respect to planning and implementation of development projects and it is therefore more likely on the margins of the CDC knowledge system.

## Materials and processes of CDC knowledge system

The materials and processes are represented by knowledge(s) of diverse actors ranging from project participants, communities, local government to CDC project implementers, and interactions across them. The materials interact with each other within development projects via diverse workshops, training, establishment of demonstration sites and other activities. Since the knowledge materials and processes are formative to each other and inseparable, we explore them simultaneously and display them in Fig. 2, as rendered by different types of knowledge holders (see Table 2 for description of actors' knowledge).

The top part of Fig. 2 explains how the knowledge material of CDC actors is created. As such, it is shaped by constant interaction between the knowledge of local context and expert knowledge and experiences existing within a particular CDC organisation. Furthermore, the knowledge of CDC actors is underlined by knowledge of international development cooperation actors, knowledge of universities and research institutes, and knowledge of global agencies. These three types of actors' knowledge are influential to knowledge of CDC actors in respect to inspiration on what types of approaches and methods are suitable for specific development projects as well as to acquiring specific baseline data. Additionally, there is also knowledge of other CDC actors , that is often transmitted to knowledge of CDC actors through mostly informal networking and sharing of lessons learnt through implementation of various development projects. Moreover, the knowledge of CDC actors is in complex interaction with actors' knowledge in Zambia, especially knowledge of extension officers and knowledge of NGOs based in Western province. Both are informing knowledge of CDC actors about local context and conditions. Simultaneously, they are also exposed to new approaches and innovations brought in by development interventions carried out by CDC actors.

However, the knowledge of extension officers and knowledge of NGOs based in Western province do not exist in exclusive  interaction  with  knowledge  of  CDC  actors. Instead, both are in close relationship with each other and both of them are informed by the knowledge of government bodies (e.g., ministry of agriculture) and vice versa. Finally, there is also knowledge of Zambian universities and research institutes , that directly and indirectly feeds into other actors' knowledge in Zambia. First, it creates a base for knowledge of government bodies and at the same time is driven by their demand. Second, it is also interacting with knowledge of extension officers, especially in terms of trainings and additional education, and with knowledge of NGOs based in Western province by informing it on various data and evidence generated. In some specific and rare cases, it also contributes to the knowledge of CDC actors.

Finally, the bottom part of Fig. 2 describes the knowledge of CDC project participants . It comprises two types of actors' knowledge: knowledge of lead farmers/volunteers and knowledge existing in target communities . These two are in assumed interaction, i.e. interaction that is expected on the side of CDC actors. However, this interaction is constrained by various issues stemming from a specific position of lead farmers/volunteers in their communities, where they are sometimes perceived as people with special treatment and as someone who is too hard to trust. Therefore, the reliance of CDC actors on the lead farmers/volunteers might bring new power relations within communities and as such inhibit the expected knowledge transfer. Moreover, the knowledge of CDC project participants is underpinned by knowledge of traditional leaders that is safeguarding the traditional knowledge existing within the communities. However, from the perspective of CDC actors, such knowledge is often perceived as backwards hence understood as a potential disabler for new innovations brought to the communities under the development projects.

Although the interaction between the knowledge of CDC actors and knowledge of CDC project participants is predominantly single directional through implementation of development projects, there is also a flow of knowledge that goes the opposite direction. Firstly, the knowledge of CDC actors is being formed by various assessments carried out in target communities that are incremental, especially for knowledge of local context. Secondly, the processes related to monitoring and evaluation should represent a structured way for getting feedback from the target communities and for providing insights into the functionality of the development projects. Both, the assessments and monitoring and evaluation are one of the key formative forces of the knowledge of CDC actors. However, these two processes are often of technocratic character and bring in only limited feedbacks from the target communities that would reflect more profoundly on how the projects impact them and their knowledge. Importantly, there is also a process of observing and learning that happens to a limited extent across knowledge of CDC project participants, knowledge of CDC actors but also knowledge of extension officers and knowledge of NGOs based in Western province of Zambia. To this end, it is apparent that although the design of CDC knowledge claims the importance of presence of knowledge of CDC project participants, it is mostly of demonstrative character. Hence, this situation does not necessarily ensure that this type of actors' knowledge is considered when planning development projects.
