This finding is surprising in more than one way. Given the outsized role that social inequality plays in sociology, one would have good reason to expect the field of SVE to engage with this topic more extensively. But the finding is even more surprising if one considers how SVE, and its intellectual agenda, was established: One of the key founding moments of SVE as a more coherent, self-proclaimed research field was the publication of a review article by Michèle Lamont in 2012, which had a major impact on the formation of SVE as an institutionalized field. Being a cultural sociologist with a long-standing interest in social inequality, Lamont envisioned a sociological research program on (e)valuation that would be in close conversation with research on social inequality (Lamont 2012). In fact, in a subsequent publication, Lamont and  colleagues  even  explicitly  conceptualized  evaluation  as  a  cultural  process  that  can contribute  to  the  (re-)production  of  social  inequality  and  called  for  more  research  on  this pathway to inequality (Lamont, Beljean, and Clair 2014). It is surprising to note that these intellectual impulses have not been taken up more widely.

However, drawing such a conclusion may be premature. Because, if we understand SVE not as  an  institutionalized  field  but  as  a  general  concern  with  practices  and  processes  of (e)valuation, our focus must not be confined to key journals and publications. Indeed, as we are going to show next, if we define SVE more broadly, social inequality can be considered a more central point of interest of scholarship concerned with (e)valuation.


## Social inequality and (e)valuation beyond the institutionalized field of SVE


The  field  of  SVE  emerged  in  the  course  of  the  last  decade  and  is  thus  a  rather  recent development. But sociological interest in (e)valuation certainly did not start with the formation of SVE: Sociologists have long been concerned with various aspects of (e)valuation. In fact, one  could  argue  that  questions  about  practices  and  processes  of  (e)valuation  have  already featured  prominently  in  the  works  of  several  thinkers  who  are  now  considered  part  of  the sociological  canon,  such  as  Harold  Garfinkel,  Michel  Foucault,  Erving  Goffman,  Pierre Bourdieu, and Judith Butler.

The works of these and other scholars continue to inspire a great deal of sociological research that touches on processes of (e)valuation in one way or another. However, a large part of this current scholarship does not sail under the official flag of SVE. Hence, by considering only contributions to SVE in a narrow sense, we would miss a major part of existing sociological research on (e)valuation. To obtain a fuller picture it is therefore indispensable to broaden our definition of SVE and consider a wider body of scholarship.

In the following, we will point to several lines of sociological research that are concerned with processes of (e)valuation but have evolved largely independently of SVE in a narrow sense. They  reveal  that  the  relationship  of  (e)valuation  and  social  inequality  is  a  key  concern  of various well-established lines of inquiry within sociology. However, as Lamont (2012) pointed out already, the bulk of this scholarship is scattered across different substantive subfields of the discipline and therefore only weakly integrated. Thus, in this chapter, we draw connections between several lines of research that  are not usually in conversation with each other. We organize our discussion around four key concepts that are drawn from the sociological canon and that have been productive in generating research on the relationship of social inequality and (e)valuation.


## Classification


A  first concept  that has generated  research on  social inequality and  (e)valuation is classification. The concept is central in the works of two of the abovementioned canonized sociologists:  Bourdieu  and  Foucault.  For  pragmatic  reasons,  we  focus  here  on  Foucault's understanding  of  classification.  Foucault  (1965,  1973)  saw  classification  as  a  process  that

disciplines and normalizes individuals and populations, thus representing both a technique of power and a procedure of knowledge (cf. Hacking 2002). In his historical studies, Foucault identified two effects of classification that are contradictory only at first sight: Classification has homogenizing effects by indicating membership to a normalized social body, and it has individualizing effects by making it possible to measure deviations and differences between individual cases. In this way, classification routinely plays a role in the (re-)production of social inequality in a variety of fields. For example, employed as a scientific technology it allows entrepreneurs to evaluate the productivity of workers and calculate their wages accordingly. Or employed  as  a  'fundamental  principle  of  the  prison'  (Foucault  1991,  268)  it  enables  the criminal justice system to establish the degree of perversion of delinquents and the term of imprisonment.

It  is  testament  to  the  productivity  of  Foucault's  notion  of  classification  that  quite  different literatures  draw  on  it.  For  example,  one  line  of  research  is  concerned  with  statistical classification as a means  of  control  and  governance.  This  literature  emphasizes  that classification  is  not  only  a  technical  instrument  for  determining  unemployment  rates  or defining poverty, but a means of distinguishing, and thus creating, social groups (Desrosières 1998; Savage 2010). Thus, by implication, statistical categories have far-reaching consequences on how inequality is made visible and addressed via political means (Farley 2011).  A  second  literature  is  concerned  with  the  recent  advent  of  data  infrastructures  and predictive algorithms. Such technologies routinely rely on classification, which scholars have shown to reinforce discrimination, influence the distribution of resources, and determine life chances (Bowker and Star 1999; Healy and Fourcade 2017; Diaz-Bone 2019). This is the case, for  example,  when  insurance  tariffs  are  calculated  in  ways  that  punish  the  poor,  or  when medical treatment is oriented by big data analysis of patient behavior. Lastly, a third body of literature  that  sheds  light  on  the  relationship  of  classification  and  social  inequality  is criminological research. For example, studies find that the proliferation of criminal background check laws in the United States is driven by increases in the share of African-American citizens holding a criminal record (McElhattan 2022). Meanwhile, ethnographic research shows how racial  classifications  in  prison  are  negotiated  between  prison  administration,  correctional officers,  and  inmates  (Goodman  2008;  cf.  Walker  2016).  These  studies  illustrate  how discriminatory processes and inter- and intra-group violence rely on racial classifications.


## Consecration


A second concept that has been productive in generating insights into the relation between social  inequality  and  (e)valuation  is  consecration.  Understood  as  an  authoritative  symbolic recognition of social distinction, consecration can be divided into three analytically distinct steps (cf. Accominotti 2021, 1) Individuals or groups receive accolades from third parties; 2) this results in a distinction between those who are chosen and those who are not; and 3) this distinction  becomes  a  social  fact  recognized  by  all  -  a  'socially  guaranteed  difference' (Bourdieu  1997,  25).  In  doing  so,  acts  of  consecration  produce  first  and  foremost status disparities,  but  indirectly,  they  also  contribute  to  the  (re-)production  of material inequities. Bourdieu derived the concept of consecration from religious acts of ordination, but it is in fact the state, not religion, that he sees as the primary authority of consecration in modern societies. For the state enjoys a monopoly of legitimate symbolic violence which gives it the authority to legalize,  ratify,  and  legitimize  differences  (e.g.,  borders),  relations  (e.g.,  contracts),  and temporalities (e.g., school vacations).

Bourdieu has highlighted many examples that illustrate the consecratory authority of the state. One example that is important for the study of inequality are national censuses. Censuses not only create social groups through processes of classification, but transform those classifications into official and almost natural entities of representation through the symbolic authority of the state  (Bourdieu  1997,  243-245).  The  state  also  plays  a  crucial  role  because  it  ensures  the recognition of other authorities of consecration. For example, educational certificates issued by  schools  and  universities  shape  their  holders'  opportunities  in  life  (cf.  R.  Collins  1979). Currently,  the  concept  of  consecration  is  frequently  used  in  research  on  fields  of  cultural production. For example, research on the film industry shows that directors and their films are more  likely to be consecrated retrospectively if they had received contemporaneous professional  recognition  (Allen  and  Lincoln  2004)  and  less  likely  to  receive  contemporary recognition if they are located on the periphery of their field (Cattani, Ferriani, and Allison 2014). Other studies have examined the consecratory effects of prizes in the literary field. For example,  Childress,  Rawlings,  and  Moeran  (2017)  show  how  publishers'  nominations  of authors for the prestigious Booker Prize position authors and novels within a literary field, but it is the political agenda and deliberations of the award jury that eventually determine which of those writers and their products are awarded the Prize and thus get consecrated. Lastly, the relationship of consecration and inequality has also been examined in research on academic

fields.  Here,  scholars  have  conceptualized  rankings  as  consecratory  authorities  that  propel power  shifts  by  favoring  certain  academic  milieus,  paradigms,  and  strategies  over  others (Hamann and Schmidt-Wellenburg 2020), or found that symbolic recognition follows patterns of  cumulative  advantage (Merton 1968) and disadvantages women systematically (Rossiter 1993).


## Stigmatization


A third concept that offers insights into the relation of (e)valuation and social inequality is stigmatization.  Goffman  (1963)  has  described  stigmatization  as  a  process  through  which negative attributes like inferiority or dangerousness are ascribed to individuals or groups. The ascribed labels or valuations become associated with dispositions that discredit the targets of stigmatization. Building on Goffman's groundwork, contemporary research has identified four interrelated process components of stigmatization (Link and Phelan 2001: 1) the distinction and labelling of differences; 2) cultural beliefs that link differences with negative attributions or stereotypes; 3) the establishment of distinct categories that separate 'us' from 'them'; and 4) and the experience of status loss and discrimination by stigmatized groups that lead to durable inequality.  Stigmatization  occurs  when  these  components  co-occur  in  power  situations  that allow them to unfold (Link and Phelan 2001).

Social psychological research typically focuses on the effects of stigmatization on an individual level such as harm to one's social identity (cf. Major and O'Brien 2005). In contrast, current sociological research attends to the broader cultural, structural, and historical foundations of stigmatization (cf. Link and Phelan 2001; Pescosolido and Martin 2015; Tyler and Slater 2018), for  example, by examining how different forms of stigma shape social inequality faced by different groups (cf. Tyler 2020). Two broad bodies of literature are concerned with relations between stigmatization and social inequality. The first examines how stigmatization is related to determinants of social inequality like race, class, gender, sexuality, and health. For example, research has pointed to shaming narratives that see the roots of poverty in personal flaws and 'bad choices' (O'Hara 2020). Other studies have shown how stigma management constrains male sex workers' sexual risk disclosure (Padilla et al. 2008) and how residents who have experienced  upward  mobility  relate  to  the  territorial  stigma  of  their  former  neighborhoods (Born  2022).  The  second  body  of  literature  compares  responses  to  stigmatization  across stigmatized groups  and  societies. Among  the  responses  are  resignation,  understating,

confrontation,  legal  action,  and  social  movements  (Lamont  et  al.  2016),  as  well  as  the development of autonomous 'socialities' that allow for different sources of subjective value (Skeggs 2011).


## Homophily


As a fourth concept, research has established insights into the relation between social inequality and  (e)valuation  via  the  concept  of  homophily.  Homophily  describes  the  tendency  of individuals to associate with others who are like them with respect to key social attributes such as social class or age (McPherson, Smith-Lovin, and Cook 2001). This principle of association is based on processes of value attribution and is thus closely tied to processes of valuation. But existing sociological scholarship has shown  more  interest  in how  homophily  affects individuals' evaluation of others. This perspective has gained prominence in sociology through the  work  of  Bourdieu  (1984),  who  theorized  that  individuals'  habitual  dispositions,  for example, their values or aesthetic orientations, are a product of their position in social space (e.g., classes) and lead them to react more favorably to others who display dispositions similar to their own. According to Bourdieu, these dispositions give rise to systematic inequalities of social participation, recognition, and distinction on the basis of taste-based judgments. 8

Homophily effects have been documented for a variety of empirical contexts. One such context is education. For example, Bourdieu and Passeron (1979) suggest that university teachers' class background and habitus lead them to perceive middle-class students to be more gifted than working-class  students,  and  thus  evaluate  them  more  favorably.  Secondly,  scholarship  on homophily in  academic  contexts  shows  that  peers  respond  more  favorably  to  work  that  is similar to their own (Lamont 2009). Especially when the evaluation of knowledge claims is based  on  the  speaker's  inferred  identity  such  as  race,  ethnicity,  or  gender,  identity-based epistemic judgments can contribute to the reproduction of social inequality (Bacevic 2021). A third context for which homophily has been studied extensively is hiring. This literature shows, for example, that recruiters in elite professional service firms favor candidates they deem not only competent but also culturally similar to themselves (Rivera 2012; De Keere 2022). A fourth  important  context  for  the  study  of  homophily  are  cultural  fields,  where  homophily

explains both preferences in cultural consumption and the emergence of cultural niches (Mark 2003) and intermediaries' preference for cultural products (Childress and Nault 2019). As this overview shows, the majority of research on homophily as a pathway to social inequality puts the  analytical  focus  on  gatekeeping  or  intermediaries.  In  such  contexts,  homophily  is particularly  likely  to  produce  inequities  when  unequal  representation  of  social  groups  as gatekeepers and consumers interacts with evaluative agents' homophily (cf. De Laat and Stuart 2022).


## Integrating Research on Social Inequality and (E)Valuation?


Over the past decade, SVE has developed into a flourishing and highly productive field of research. But core contributions to the field have paid only little attention to the topic of social inequality: Reviewing several key publications closely associated with the field, we find that only few studies relate practices and processes of (e)valuation to the production and persistence of social inequality. However, we come to a widely different conclusion if we broaden our definition of SVE. If we understand the concern with (e)valuation as a more general research perspective, we find that there are in fact various strands of sociological scholarship that offer insights  into  how  social  inequality  is  connected  to  (e)valuation,  including  research  on classification, stigmatization, consecration, and homophily. Yet, to date, these lines of research have remained largely disconnected from each other despite sharing similar questions.

In conclusion, we would like to invite scholars to remedy this situation and develop a more systematic  research  program  on  the  relationship  of  (e)valuation  and  social  inequality.  The advantages of such a research program would include the theoretical integration of research findings and the development of a unified and coherent research agenda on (e)valuation and social inequality. The development of such an agenda is beyond the scope of this chapter, but we  believe  that  one  possible  framework  of  integration  could  be  derived  from  mainstream stratification and inequality research. This framework draws scholars' attention to the interplay of determinants , mechanisms (or processes ) and consequences of social inequality (cf. Solga, Berger,  and  Powell  2009).  Future  scholarship  could  use  this  framework  to  expand  our knowledge in the following three ways:

First, more research is needed to understand how (e)valuation contributes to the emergence of social  differences  -  for  example,  gender,  class,  or  race  -  and  the  transformation  of  those

differences  into determinants of  social  inequality.  With  the  concept  of  classification,  we highlighted  one  possible  heuristic  to  address  this  issue.  Second,  scholars  could  study (e)valuation  as  a mechanism or process that  contributes  to  the  (re-)production  of  social inequality. While it is fairly well established to think of (e)valuative processes as pathways to social inequality (cf. Lamont, Beljean, and Clair 2014), less is known about the micro-social processes through which structural social inequalities shape the outcome of situated practices of (e)valuation. Concepts like homophily or consecration represent analytical tools that can help penetrate both these issues. Third, different dimensions of social inequality, for example, income inequality, educational inequality, or health disparities, differ in their consequences . More research is needed to understand how these consequences are perceived and (e)valuated, for example, as legitimate or problematic. Concepts like stigmatization or discrimination offer possible  starting  points  for  doing  so.  Because  processes  of  (e)valuation  are  pivotal  to  the functioning of markets and the distribution of rewards in modern capitalist societies, advancing sociological scholarship on the relationship between (e)valuation and social inequality is more critical than ever.

## Introduction


Pakistan, located in South Asia, is the world's fifth most populous country. An Islamic federal republic with a multi-party parliamentary system of governance, Pakistan was established after the 1947 partition of British India. It comprises four provinces and one federal territory. With a rapid population boom since its establishment, Pakistan's sustained economic growth has not translated into per capita economic gains for its people and it remains a predominantly agricultural economy.

Pakistan has ratified 36 ILO conventions, of which 31 are in force, but these do not include C183, C156, C189, or C143 - the key conventions related to carework.

A significant proportion of Pakistan's population is employed in the informal sector, and nearly a quarter live below the poverty line. 1 The female labor force participation rate is 21%, 2 the lowest in South Asia. Staunch social conservatism hinders many women from completing their education or working outside the home. 3

Domestic work is a significant segment of Pakistan's informal sector with over 5 million people employed in this sector, 60% of whom are women. 4 There are

also significant incidences of child labor in the domestic work sector.

As a result of its lack of comprehensive national legislation for unpaid family caregivers or paid domestic workers, Pakistan scores poorly on the GCPI, with a score of 2.73 (out of 10) - thus placing it in the lower end of the 'Emerging' Index Band of the GCPI. However, its largest province, Punjab, introduced a Domestic Workers Act in 2019, demonstrating that it is possible for Pakistan as a whole to offer more legal protections to domestic workers across the country.


## Key Care Policies


The Pakistan Maternity Benefits Ordinance 1968 grants women workers 12 weeks of maternity leave, fully paid by employers at the rate of their last paid wages, provided they have worked at that establishment for at least four months. Certain sectors of the economy have their own, more targeted, legislation providing slightly different coverage levels and eligibility criteria. For instance, the Mines Maternity Benefits Act 1981 states women workers in the mines must be employed for at least six months before they are eligible for maternity leave, 5 while the Civil Servants Act 1973 allows for 13 weeks of maternity leave.

The Punjab Domestic Workers Act 2019 is the first attempt within Pakistan to define and recognise domestic work, and to regulate it. 6 Aside from this, national labor laws only apply to domestic workers in small part. For example, the Provincial Employees Social Security Ordinance 1965 requires employers to provide healthcare to full-time domestic workers.

## Domestic Worker Protections


The passing of the Punjab Domestic Workers Act 2019 was a huge step towards recognising and affording rights to the millions of domestic workers in the province of Punjab. ## Maternity and Paternity Protections


In January 2020, the Senate approved the Maternity and Paternity Leave Bill 2018, 7 which would grant working women six months maternity leave for their first birth and 30 days of paternity leave for working fathers (up to three times during their employment). It would also allow women 180 days leave upon their first birth, 120 days on their second, and 90 days on their third. However, this Bill is yet to be approved by the National Assembly. Outside of the legislature, public attitudes in Pakistan are changing and there is growing support for more progressive care policies as underscored by the Pakistan Cricket Board's (PCB) decision to grant one-year maternity leave and one-month paternity leave. 8 Given the popularity of cricket in the country, the PCB's decision will hopefully prompt other organizations and companies to introduce similar family-friendly policies.

Numerous international NGOs and bodies are pushing for better caregiver and careworker rights in Pakistan, alongside local governmental and non-governmental actors.

She also successfully passed a bill in the Islamabad Capital Territory declaring domestic work hazardous and thereby illegal for children. 10

The 2015 formation of the Domestic Workers Union, the first trade union of its kind in the country, was an important step in recognizing domestic workers as workers under the law. 11 It is credited with training scores of domestic workers, increasing their skills and knowledge to empower them to access better wages and rights in their workplace.

## Coverage (4.26/10)

All women workers in Pakistan are guaranteed 12 weeks of maternity leave, with the condition that they had been employed in that establishment for at least four months prior to delivery and that they be married (as extramarital sex is outlawed). 13 Six weeks of leave after childbirth is compulsory, and women may decide whether to take the other 6 weeks of leave before or after childbirth. leave legislation exists only in the small capital territory of Islamabad, with up to 30 days of paternity leave guaranteed. ## B1Coverage under National Labor Laws (5.00/10)

While there is no national legislation to recognize domestic workers as employees or offer them any protections, Pakistan's largest province of Punjab introduced the Punjab Domestic Workers Act in 2019, laying out detailed protections for those employed as domestic workers in the province. ## B2Fair Employment Process (1.46/10)

While there is no national legislation protecting them, domestic workers in the Punjab are required to be informed of the terms of their employment. However, there are no further detailed specifications regarding the exact information that a contract must contain. There is no legislation to ensure domestic workers are given information about their living conditions or any detailed information about their wages. The legal requirement is only that the employment contract must state the amount of the monthly wage; details about overtime or standby pay are not required. While there is largely no regulation of the recruitment and employment process, the Punjab Domestic Workers Act includes private employment agencies in its definition of employers, and hence these agencies are governed by the provisions of the Labor Code in Punjab province. 16

## B3Decent Working and Living Conditions (3.05/10)

There is no centralized, national piece of legislation that guarantees the right to decent working and living conditions for all domestic workers in Pakistan. However, in the Punjab Act, domestic workers are protected from being required to work for more than eight hours a day. The Act also grants domestic workers the right to standby pay and to a safe and healthy working environment. Furthermore, the Act mandates that domestic workers be allowed at least one day off per week, eight sick days, and 10 festival holidays per year. Two provinces (Punjab and Sindh) also include domestic workers in their minimum wage legislation. In general, as citizens, domestic workers are eligible for social security benefits. However, as informal employees, they are not covered by the Employees Old Age Benefits Institution, and so do not receive any old age benefits. 17 There is also no detailed legislation to regulate the living conditions of live-in domestic workers.

## B4Labor Rights and Protections (5.00/10)

Domestic workers are allowed to unionize as per their constitutional right. In the Punjab, there are also dispute resolution mechanisms they can access. In the Punjab, places of employment can be inspected and employers fined if they are not granting domestic workers their rights. The first Domestic Workers Trade Union was registered in 2015, and has been involved in raising awareness and projects such as drafting model employment contracts for domestic workers.

## B5Protections for Forced/Under-age Domestic Workers (5.35/10)

The Pakistan Constitution bars forced or bonded labor. The minimum age for work in the country is 14, but the Punjab Act mandates that those under 18 only do domestic work that is part-time and not hazardous. Despite this, however, hundreds of thousands of children continue to be exploited across the country for their cheap labor, with their abuse hidden behind the closed doors of private homes. 18 Even though Pakistan ratified the Convention of the Rights of the Child in 1990, there are still no countrywide protections for children under 18 to protect them from economic exploitation or hazardous work.

## Policy-Practice Gap


The policy-practice gaps in Pakistan are stark. Despite policy provisions guaranteed under the law, the pace of implementation of these policies has been slow: for example, workplace daycares have not been built 19 and the Dispute Resolution Committee for domestic workers has not been established either. 20 Beyond this infrastructural gap, the policy-practice gap has also been aggravated by poor rights awareness and limited enforcement of existing policy protections.


## Lack of Rights Awareness


Manyworkers in Pakistan are unaware of their rights and protections under existing labor laws. A 2019 survey of 25 domestic workers found that none of them knew about labor laws in Pakistan, and only two had basic knowledge of the minimum wage. 21 This lack of rights awareness is the result of illiteracy and poor access to information, thus impoverishing the effectiveness of existing labor protections. Rampant poverty further compounds the challenges of reporting workplace abuses, as domestic workers often see no alternative but to accept the dismal conditions they are offered. Finally, the long-held public perception of domestic work as 'women's work' or a private matter also exacerbates domestic workers' invisibility within Pakistan society. 22


## Lack of Enforcement


At present, laws are routinely flouted due to the lack of stringent enforcement. With only 337 labor inspectors in the entire country, many labor violations go unnoticed or reported. 23 Furthermore, the continuing failure to establish a Dispute Resolution Committee for domestic workers further limits their avenues for recourse or reporting.

This treaty is, on the one hand, described as the dawn of a new Middle East, while as a dangerous setback for peace on the other hand [1]. The signing of the Accords is based on the short-term interests exchange between the Arab states, in the context of the American Presidential Election and the global COVID-19 pandemic. Under such a complex background, although the signing of the Accords can promote the realization of common interests, it may also trigger new conflicts. For example, the Accords will not necessarily lead to the normalization of Arab-Israeli relations. Some external, internal, and other factors are contributing to the signing of this peace treaty. The external factor is mainly the intervention from the US. In addition to  supporting  Israel  and  its  Arab  Allies  by  reducing  bilateral  conflicts,  America's  purpose  of promoting the signing of the Accords can be summarized as curbing and disturbing: suppressing Iran, containing and disconcerting China, and restricting Russia. Other factors, like the outbreak of the COVID-19, the dictatorship of Arab leaders, and the personal political pursuit of the leaders from other regions, contributed to the signing of the Accords as well. The paper combines the theories of Classical Realism [2, 3], Neo-realism [4], and Constructivism [5] to explore the factor(s) contributing to the signature of the Abraham Accords, which officially represents the normalization of relations between Israel with United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.

Classical realism theory shows that the relationship between countries is primarily affected by their  common  interests  and  has  little  significance  with  their  political  system  and  ideology  [3]. Sovereign states are motivated by their national interests rather than allegiance to the common good. In the international community, such allegiance, the so-called common moral norm, does not exist [2]. From this perspective, the signing of the Accords is based on the maintenance and contention of different political actors for their respective interests. On this basis, Neo-realism adds the perspective that relevant leaders also influence national decisions. In this context, in the research, the personal political  demands  imposed  by  the  President  of  the  US  and  relevant  leaders  of  Middle  Eastern

## Introduction


In February 2023, UNESCO launched the Global Education Monitoring (GEM) report to look at the requirements of good leadership in education, and how they may vary between countries and over time in seeking to achieve the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It argues that:

Leaders at multiple levels matter, from those within the school, to those outside of the school such as middle managers, and including those outside of education systems in government, or those working on legislature and oversight.

In this article, we use ‘school leadership’ in this broad sense to discuss its role in achieving sustainable life for humans and other species on Earth. The term ‘Anthropocene’ was coined by Crutzen and Stoermer in a newsletter for the Geological Society in 2000 to describe a new epoch, superseding the Holocene, in which the human species has had dramatic impact on the planet; we use it here for historical positioning and contemporary context.

Acknowledging that we are in the Anthropocene entails more than recognizing changes to the environment, climate, or issues of sustainability. While the term 'climate change' is well-known and widely used academically, it is insufficient as it often serves as a euphemism for a range of effects resulting from human social and economic activities, including changes in land use, soil degradation, ocean acidification, and species extinctions. These effects are essentially the consequences of humanity's ways of perceiving and interacting with the world – of capitalism, large-scale industrialization, and viewing nature as separate from us, and as a resource to exploit. While such a worldview has witnessed unparalleled advancements in technology, science, medicine, and nutrition, it has paradoxically set us on a catastrophic trajectory.

However, fixating on the 'crisis' only contributes to a sense of inevitability and, all too often, hopelessness. A recent survey conducted in 10 countries among 15-16-year-olds revealed that eco-anxiety is prevalent, with 45% of respondents stating that it affects their daily lives and 75% describing the future as frightening (Hickman et al., 2022). Therefore, we often grapple with the 'dragons of inaction' that prevent responses adaptive to this reality (Gifford, 2011).

We argue that positioning ourselves within this epoch now can stimulate new narratives for education by asking what it means to operate as teachers and leaders and policymakers within the Anthropocene. We refer to the current epoch as existing not only physically (geologically) but also psychologically and socially, necessitating a new paradigm for policy and practice:

The Anthropocene is not something we can make go away but a place where we are, a part of who we are. Therefore, we must recognize it as the starting point for any meaningful response (Schinkel, 2020, p.5).

Rather than proposing a set of solutions – too daunting a project for any one article – we present a framework for leadership in the Anthropocene that recognizes the urgency of our challenges, the fallibility of our knowledge and the uncertainty of the consequences of our actions in an unstable climate. We also explore the moral dilemmas school leaders face, and the need for both new ethical perspectives and more agential approaches to reconcile them. To do so, we must first recognize that our current crises have been created by 'educated' individuals acting within ethical parameters that are now detrimental to us and our planet. A knowledge-based, target-and-output-led approach to education that marginalizes or overlooks this crisis is evidently insufficient.

Our framework of four pillars for educational leadership in the Anthropocene draws on pragmatist philosophy and an agential approach from social ecology, expanding the concept of agency to include the preservation of a habitable planet. It also draws on two practical models – UNESCO's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Raworth's doughnut model (Raworth, 2017a and 2017b) – that help translate from theory to practice. In doing so, we aim to free school leadership (for now) from long-standing, antagonistic and essentially contested debates about the fundamental aims and purposes of education in favor of goals that build consensus around the well-understood challenges we face now, and our shared value for life on Earth. We outline principles for school leadership that emphasize diversity and sensitivity to context, especially in recognizing the disparities between the Global North and South. We demonstrate the vital role of agency, and the need to combine our energies, in spite of differing ideologies. Finally, we suggest indicators for holding each other accountable while implementing these changes.


## The significance of the Anthropocene


While the term Anthropocene is slowly gaining currency in academic literature, it has been little used in connection with educational leadership, with a few exceptions (e.g., Bottery, 2016; Carr, 2016; Kadji-Beltran et al., 2013; Kensler, 2022; Kensler & Uline, 2016; Muller et al., 2020; Pepper, 2014; Veronese & Kensler, 2013).

The term Anthropocene is contested, with debates around 1) when it started – or whether it has started; 2) whether all should be held responsible for the actions of only some humans (especially the 'global north'); 3) whether the term is too narrow or too broad; and 4) about whether we should envision a 'good' or 'bad' outcome for this epoch (see Paulsen et al., 2022). The anthropogenic effects of this epoch (i.e., sharp changes in greenhouse gases altering the atmosphere) are thought by some to have started with the industrial revolution around 200 years ago (e.g. Crutzen and Stoermer, 2000). However, it is argued that this had antecedents in earlier periods, including the agricultural revolution (which led to larger populations and the growth of cities, specialization of labor, etc.), European expansion into the Americas (leading to mass human population extinctions); and that these periods set the conditions for a more recent technological revolution, especially since the 1940s (nuclear weapons, artificial intelligence, genetics, and so on). For a thorough discussion of the Anthropocene, see Lewis & Maslin (2020) who, taking a purely geological stance, contend a much earlier starting point for the Anthropocene (around 400 years ago), while recognizing the above events as highly significant. While some writers (e.g. Ruddiman, 2013) argue that cyclical trends in  greenhouse gases began thousands of years ago, and caution about arriving at early conclusions about the Anthropocene as a new geological epoch, we argue that since the consensus is very strong that humans have already caused, and continue to cause, intense biophysical disturbances to the planet, that the term Anthropocene should thus be broadly accepted and we should consider its significance in all realms of action.

The exact starting point of the Anthropocene does not concern our central argument since common moral and philosophical stances underpin modern human behavior. Specifically, the dualist position of Rene Descartes has led us to separate not only mind from body but humans from nature. Indeed, Paulsen and colleagues (2022) argue that there is a danger in a certain anthropocentric view of this epoch that reinforces the Cartesian dualist underpinnings of human activity, leading to a failure to re-examine how humans and non-humans coexist rather than viewing nature as a mere resource for humans. This Cartesian view also morally buttresses economic models based on continuous economic growth through material exploitation (Plumwood 2002), which has led to both dramatic advances in living conditions for many millions of people (and with the potential to continue to do so for many others) while bringing us sharply to a point where we reach dangerous ecological tipping points. We therefore assert the benefits that continue to emerge from modern science and capitalist innovation, and the need for their axiological reorientation in the service of new sustainable goals.

Therefore,  educational leadership in the Anthropocene needs to address these differing societal contexts, using an economic model that ensures a good life for as many people as possible while respecting planetary boundaries. This means both shifting the dominant narratives about the economy and our relationship to nature and applying and refining contemporary technological and economic solutions. We further develop these points below.


## The need for new narratives and moral theories in educational leadership


Much of the debate surrounding education in the Anthropocene focuses on how schools can provide increased and improved environmental education to younger generations. However, as Schinkel (2021) explains, before we explore how schools can contribute to the solution, we must first acknowledge their role in bringing us to our current state:

This entails more than acknowledging that many educated people have contributed to environmental destruction, have invented greenhouse-gas-emitting machines, and so on – though this is important, too. It entails that we consider education from the perspective of deep history: what is education, from the perspective of the evolution of our species in the Pleistocene, and what has been its role in that evolution? More specifically, what was education’s role in the evolution of complex societies, and what is its role in such societies now?

Schinkel, 2021 (p.1).

The urgency of the challenges we face makes reframing the aims and approaches of schools a moral imperative. Higham (2022) has recently argued that our current educational objectives, rooted in three traditional theories of moral philosophy – utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics – are insufficient in responding swiftly and comprehensively to current threats and opportunities.  Utilitarianism, with its focus on selecting education approaches based on calculations of future human happiness and preference, relies on assumptions of socioeconomic and ecological continuity that are increasingly unreliable. For instance, prioritizing ‘giving children the skills they need for good jobs in their community’ loses significance when young people may be forced to migrate due to ecosystem degradation. Next, the deontological claim that adults have the right and duty to pass down their moral codes to children and shape their education accordingly is undermined by adults’ collective failure thus far to adequately respond to these challenges. Lastly, the virtue ethicist position, which emphasizes shaping individuals' characters and habits, fails to recognize the significance of adequate resources and a stable cohesive society in fostering moral behavior, as well as the collective nature of the responses required to address complex threats and increased interconnectivity.

Together, Higham argues, these moral theories reflect the notion that ‘what was good enough for us is good enough for you’. However, the projected life paths of today's young people and the assumptions that shaped their parents' and grandparents' generations are increasingly unsustainable (Higham, 2022). Consequently, our education leaders have a responsibility for helping shape new narratives in which current and future generations can lead secure, sustainable, and meaningful lives. As Brennan (2017) states, "What happens when the prevailing stories no longer make sense of the world?"

In their background paper for UNESCO’s Futures of Education report, the Common Worlds Research Collective (2020) set out a bold alternative story: “seven visionary declarations of what education could look like in 2050 and beyond” (p. 2), when the world as a whole has “permanently delinked education from the twin logics of infinite economic growth and human development and re-sutured it to the logics of ecological survival” (p. 7).  This stance builds on the wider critique of anthropocentrism from ecological thinkers since the 1970s in favor of biocentric or ecocentric stances seeing all living things – and even non-living things like mountains – as having ‘innate moral standing’ (Attfield 2017). We broadly share both this ambition and key critiques:  of dualism having separated humans from ‘nature’, and schools having focused on individual development rather than collective coexistence. We differ firstly, in our discomfort with its binary representations of the causes of, and solutions to, the challenges we face; secondly, in our sense of what might enable feasible trajectories from our current situation to any preferred future. Their paper imagines that “the Euro-Western human-centric stranglehold on education” (2020, p. 3) will crumble through insurgent popular rejection, spurred by mass realization of its failure, in favor of “pluriversal frameworks associated with epistemologies of the South” (p. 4) that dethrone humans as colonial masters of the Earth and resituate them as equitable cohabitants. In a political climate increasingly shaped by ‘culture wars’ built around clusters of diametrically opposed positions, often tribally defended or denounced, we do not see such a revolution in favor of highly progressive positions as likely – particularly as many different progressive groups have been divided against each other through this shift in discourse (Newman and Clarke 2022), and are politically and economically disadvantaged. Further, school leaders mostly work in relatively restrictive institutional and political contexts with a strong focus on student success based on graded individual performance; for them to explicitly reject key tenets would likely lead to the loss of their role, or inability to rise into such roles, as well as wider repercussions for their schools. Any major changes in values and operation would need to be incremental and involve a wider coalition going well beyond school leaders.

Further, as the Common Worlds Research paper (2020) acknowledges in its citations of Butler, Latour, Haraway and other radical critics, the ‘Euro-Western human-centric approach’ is not monolithic; it has always contained a diversity of voices, with many opposing totalizing narratives around individual freedom, endless growth and exploitation. Similarly, non-Western and Indigenous traditions are also diverse: for example, the value of ‘stewardship’ they denounce as Western and anthropocentric is similarly held by the Oromo people of Ethiopia, who deem it acceptable to kill animals regarded by humans as pests, but hold the destruction of a whole species to lessen the creation of God (Attfield 2017).

We argue that in the role of education leaders is not to replace one worldview with another; rather, it is to draw on theories, traditions and institutions with diverse ideological, cultural and geographical roots to explore shared crises and possibilities with open minds. Finally, we suggest that while visions of preferable futures are valuable provocations, they cannot direct or bind  school leaders – as they could only ever be realised in context, in ongoing response to both predictable and unforeseeable factors.


Pragmatism: a paradigm of intelligent response


A new approach to school leadership in the Anthropocene needs to draw on different ethical traditions to the traditional ones reviewed above. We propose starting with the pragmatism of John Dewey, who argued that a good educational aim:

"1: ... Must be based upon a consideration of what is already going on; upon the resources and difficulties of the situation...

2: ... is experimental, and hence constantly growing as it is tested in action...

3: ... Must always represent a freeing of activities." (1916/1966, p. 102)

Dewey's first radical move, echoing Schinkel above, is to start from where we are, rather than with an idea of where we want to be: the “resources and difficulties of the present situation” must inform our sense of what is necessary, desirable, and possible. This demands that we give weight to what Booth calls “imperatives ignored in the past and clamouring for attention in the present” (2011, p. 31); he cites two related imperatives: “living within the means of our biospheres” and seeking to prevent “destructive, soul-breaking conflicts in the world” (ibid). Dewey further rejects the idea that schools' aims should be represented as timeless or settled. These two criteria together redefine aims as what Dewey calls “ends-in-view”: strategic, responsive to changing circumstances, interests, and imperatives, and subject to ongoing refinement and review. If one of our educational ends-in-view were a habitable planet in 30 years' time, its value would be realized not simply by presenting curricula that address relevant issues, but through designing, pursuing, and refining activities that demonstrably help to bring that end about.

To avoid despair, increased knowledge of environmental threats must come alongside increased engagement with means of change and a growing sense of possibility resulting from repeated opportunities. Dewey's third criterion, therefore, relates to the deliberate cultivation of individual and collective agency in all school stakeholders. Drawing on Dewey's work, Biesta and Tedder (2007) argue that agency is too often understood as a personal quality divorced from context; they coin the term 'ecological agency' as something that can be "achieved, rather than possessed, through the active engagement of individuals with aspects of their contexts-for-action" (p.132). They set out its dimensions:

- Iterative – routinized action that is selectively re-activated to give it stability
- Projective – creative reconstruction of actions based on actors' values, fears, desires, and hopes
- Practical-evaluative – the capacity of actors to make informed and evaluative decisions from alternatives, to act on current challenges, demands, and dilemmas (ibid, p. 136).

Here Biesta and Tedder restate Dewey's principles in a way that allows them to be imagined and realized as objectives of a school and its curricula. The environmental connotations of their use of “ecological” are accidental, as it refers here to the Deweyan framing of humans as organisms within an environment. But it prefigures the call from Manuel-Navarrete and Buzinde (2010) for an expansion of this notion to explicitly encompass interactions with ecological structures that are under such threat as to constrain individual and collective agency:

Emerging ‘socio-ecological agents’ [also] have the task ahead of dealing with self-imposed material constraints, which surface from a clear awareness about self-inflicted threats (e.g. climate change) and with no place else to go to avoid these threats. Additionally, it is important to note that such voluntary limits are not only to be adopted by individuals and specific societies, but they must be embraced by humanity as a whole (ibid, p. 142).

In Rushton et al’s (2024) case studies of climate change and sustainability education (CCSE) in English schools, they confirmed the importance of leadership that creates the conditions for agency. Applying Biesta and Tedder ‘s dimensions of social ecological agency (2007), they concluded that the most successful leaders were advocates for CCSE across their community, working alongside other stakeholders “where shared ideas and beliefs are key enablers of agency” (Rushton et al., 2024 np).

Leadership within this model works through the dynamics and interactions of the macro, exo, meso and micro layers of the education ecosystem (e.g. Godfrey, 2019). System leaders in this context have relational roles within and outside of schools that stimulate action through the collective agency of various actors. This kind of leadership requires the ability to live with uncertainty and tensions as changes come about in complex, non-mechanistic and nonlinear-causal ways in this interconnected system. This will challenge orthodoxies about the development of school leaders and the ways in which they are held to account, which we return to later.

Pragmatism also offers new understandings of 'knowledge' and 'intelligence' that serve our reconceptualization of educational aims. Dewey’s view "was that knowing is an event that takes place between an organism and an environment rather than a static quality of either mind or reality or their correspondence" (Koopman, 2015, p. 55). Knowing is thus tied up with experience, making it "intimate, not abstract" (Dewey 1916/1966, p. 185): "... its work and aim must be distinctively reconstructive or transformatory" (Dewey, 1903, p. 100). To come to know, for Dewey, is to respond to issues we face in ways that bring about desired change, whether conceptual, material, or both. Intelligence, then, describes not the fixed processing speed of individual minds or the depth of core knowledge foundations per se, but the quality of our responses to challenges. We do not assert that this pragmatist perspective is necessarily right for all time; we do assert that it is valuable now.

An enduring critique of pragmatism is that it is scientistic, focused on problem-solving but lacking a moral core (Koopman 2015); this is in part because Dewey eschews questions about 'human nature' and 'the good life', seeking instead to expand human possibilities in an ongoing journey of improvement with no final destination. But, as Cavell (2004) points out, humans are flawed and often not minded to do the rational thing; he accuses pragmatists of not asking why our ever-growing knowledge "... fails to make us better than we are or provide us with peace" (p. 5). Pragmatists have previously offered various solutions to this problem (see Koopman 2015), but another presents itself in response to our current predicament: that life itself has value – human and non-human, individuals and ecosystems, present and future – and that it is under existential threat on this planet. In many science fiction films, it takes an alien invasion to spur divided peoples into coordinated action; in our reality, we are both the protagonists and the alien forces. We do not need global consensus on timeless human aims and capacities, nor on the superiority or inferiority on particular cultural and economic paradigms, nor on a unitary vision of the future, to agree on timely ends-in-view to guide our actions in response to existential threats.

In summary, we propose a new principle to inform good educational aims: they should enable intelligent and humane responses to the imperatives that demand our attention. This is not possible without bold, innovative, and strategic leadership. We next turn to frameworks that can support educational leaders and policymakers to enable such responses.


## Sustainable Development Goals and the role of education


The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were established following the 1992 Rio Summit on Sustainable Development, marking a significant milestone in raising global awareness of environmental and development issues. These goals encompass a broader spectrum of areas and are intended to involve all nations worldwide (for a more comprehensive description, refer to Bourn, 2022). The seventeen goals are shown below:

A cohesive approach to education for sustainability requires, at a minimum, linking our focus on education in SDG 4 with SDG 13 on climate action. However, Tosun and Leininger’s (2017) argument – that the interconnectedness of the challenges and goals detailed in the SDGs demands policy coherence and integration across multiple sectors such as food, water, energy, and climate – requires we rethink more fundamentally. Similarly, Elkington (2013) outlines how the development and use of the ‘triple bottom line’ has sought to broaden the remit and responsibility of businesses to incorporate social and ecological sustainability alongside the financial. Yet our education systems are still primarily focused on a single bottom line of academic outcomes, founded on the belief that academic disciplines alone provide "the knowledge, understanding, skills, and disposition that are to be learned by school students" (Shulman 1987, pp. 8-9). By default, they reproduce the kind of human capital currently valued for economic growth: specialization in siloed sectors within an unsustainable economic model.

Sterling (2014) argues that SDG 4 overemphasizes the (important) aims of increasing both school attendance and literacy and numeracy, neglecting UNESCO’s assertion elsewhere that Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) "...is education for social transformation with the goal of creating more sustainable societies" (UNESCO 2013, p. 33). In response, he presents a three-level model of progressive engagement in ESD in schools: from transmission of relevant information to transactional learning based on dialogue and inquiry that deepens understanding and reflects on values, to transformational learning that builds capacities for informed cross-sectoral engagement, agency, and empowerment across society (2014, p. 98) – all informed by the need to "win the future we want" (p. 94).

Our pragmatist position shares with Sterling’s model a focus on the desired end of sustainable societies, and on building people’s knowledge and capacities to realize them. However, it rejects the proposal for a tiered pedagogy, where learning about sustainability forms the foundation for subsequent critical questioning and empowered action because it reframes ESD as a curriculum area to be planned, taught, learned, and mastered before students are ready to reflect, plan, and act. A Deweyan perspective identifies sustainable development not as a subject but as a complex and evolving interdisciplinary imperative, with which even young children are already deeply engaged. This situates young people’s present realities at the center of their socio-ecological agency and expands them through addressing challenges and opportunities encountered in all spheres of life, local and global. From this perspective, the SDGs together can act as a broad cross-curricular framework to inform questioning and knowledge acquisition around how we should build a sustainable shared future, starting today.

Importantly, Facer warns that reinterpreting schools as a site to address the ecological crisis risks "abdication of the responsibility of us as adults today" (2019, p. 12). School leaders and practitioners must simultaneously undergo and model these processes to their learners since it will be too late to simply rely on the next generation having the necessary worldview.

Raworth’s Doughnut

Kate Raworth’s approach to sustainable development has gained significant recognition and use across academia, policymaking, and other fields. Raworth’s model provides a conceptual framework for  in educational leadership that responds to the challenges explored above.

Fundamental to this framework is a broader understanding of the social, economic and environmental factors that define the educational endeavor. This means leading a school system that produces more than just adults ready for production and consumption in an economy set up for ‘growth’.  Raworth (2017) likens the pursuit of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth to a cuckoo in the economic nest: just as cuckoos lay their eggs in the nests of other birds, which eventually grow and dominate the nest, GDP has become the dominant goal of our economy. The economic theories that have prevailed in recent decades fail to consider the finite resources of our planet and overlook the logical impossibility of pursuing infinite GDP growth (see Hickel, 2020; Raworth, 2017; Kallis, 2018). GDP measures are flawed also, in their inability to distinguish ‘good’ from ‘bad’ growth by including all economic activities in monetary terms, even when they harm the environment or society. Simultaneously, GDP neglects to capture valuable but non-monetized activities like parental or voluntary work (see Talberth et al., 2007).

Our school system operates within a planet of limited resources and should be led - and measured – in ways that place value on the kinds of economic activity that benefit humankind and our biosphere in the long run.  Viable alternatives to GDP exist, such as the Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare (ISEW) and the Genuine Progress Indicator, also known as "Green GDP measures." Several countries are now using  one of these measures to consider social and environmental issues alongside traditional measures of economic activity. The GDP growth model nevertheless presents a paradox: it has succeeded in improving the living standards of millions while simultaneously causing destructive consequences for the planet, particularly due to its heavy reliance on fossil fuels (Hickel, 2020). Raworth (2017) proposes a powerful solution to this contradictory situation between economic growth and environmental degradation. Her "doughnut" model outlines what humanity needs to do to thrive within planetary boundaries:

<!-- image -->

Figure 2. Raworth’s Doughnut model of sustainable economic development (Raworth 2017a, p. 47).

The light green center of the doughnut ring is described by Raworth as the "safe and just space for humanity," characterized by dignity and opportunity for everyone, supported by a regenerative and distributive economy (Raworth, 2017b, p. 44). The dark green inner ring represents the social foundation necessary for human flourishing, and the twelve social indicators outside of this ring represent the common goods that contribute to it. These indicators are derived from the Sustainable Development Goals (UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, 2015). The outer circle of the doughnut is formed by the planetary boundaries that safeguard Earth's life-supporting systems. There are nine ecological indicators that depict these planetary boundaries, which Raworth adapted from a paper by Rockstrom et al. (2009). The dark red areas on the diagram indicate where we have already exceeded planetary boundaries, while the inner circle reveals the deficiencies in meeting the essential physical and social elements required for humans to lead fulfilling lives.

Raworth's model helps distinguish and clarify the formidable challenges humanity faces. To date, there have been no examples of countries successfully lifting themselves out of poverty without concurrently increasing GDP (Raworth, 2017). Recent evidence further confirms that in the past two decades, more countries have exceeded their biophysical boundaries than ever before. While some countries, like Costa Rica, have made progress in this regard, no country currently meets the basic social needs of its citizens at a globally sustainable level (Fanning et al., 2021). Nonetheless, Raworth’s model itemizes and frames these challenges in ways that make humane and intelligent leadership responses more conceivable and directed.


## Four pillars for educational leadership in the Anthropocene


Below, we outline a conceptual framework comprising four pillars of school leadership in the Anthropocene, which takes a pragmatist perspective to guide action and uses Raworth’s Doughnut as a framework for living sustainably.

### Bridging ideologies


Regardless of our differing beliefs, we share a planet fueled by the sun, with finite natural resources and dynamic ecosystems. Thus, Raworth argues, we need to transition to a circular, regenerative economy where politicians and economists are ‘agnostic’ towards the crude indicators of GDP growth (Raworth, 2017b). Raworth's model is valuable in avoiding alienating language, such as calling for the abandonment of capitalism, which would elide benefits under-developed nations might achieve by pursuing similar aims and strategies to the wealthier nations without critical impacts on global resources.

Technological innovations will be part of the solution but not sufficient. As Curren and Metzger (2019) point out, if markets are left unchecked, prioritizing profitability and treating everything else as expendable, there is no guarantee that they will generate and scale up the necessary technical innovations to prevent catastrophic harm to billions of people and other living beings. Moreover, while drawing on scientific evidence, there is still room to recognize the potential moral power of diverse ideologies and traditions in contributing to humanity's response.

School leaders can contribute by creating inclusive environments that draw on rich and diverse historical, cultural, philosophical, and spiritual perspectives. Manuel-Navarrete and Buzinde (2010, p. 147) suggest crafting "a new creation story about where we come from, who we are as human beings, and what our future possibilities will be." We argue that these perspectives should be woven into multiple stories, embracing the diversity of perspectives and talents that will enable us to tackle various challenges with creativity and compassion. These stories should move away from a narrative of perpetual material growth and instead focus on flourishing within social and ecological boundaries, with schools playing a central role. Importantly, this approach should be embedded throughout the entire school, influencing community relationships and driving cross-curricular developments.


### Shared agency


School leadership plays a crucial role in improving teaching and learning, aligning with the objective of SDG4 as outlined in the Incheon Declaration and Framework for Action adopted by the World Education Forum in 2015.

However, there is widespread disconnection between the need to transform schools and the potential of school and system leadership to facilitate such transformation. Educational scholarship and international organizations often overlook the role of leaders in promoting not only quality and equity in school organizations but also a strongly humanistic vision and a focus on the global public good. This misconception arises from a widely held perspective that leadership is primarily concerned with managerial tasks, competition, and individual effectiveness. While this may be the case in certain contexts, leadership extends beyond technical management. It is fundamentally about vision and collaboration, within the contexts of specific school goals and the global commons.

Given the need for an agential approach in education in the Anthropocene (Bourn and Hatley, 2022), adopting inclusive and distributed models of school leadership is vital (e.g. Mincu and Granata 2021). In Gan's study of elementary school principals in Israel, the role of school leaders in creating conditions for environmental education (EE) and achieving the Green School Certificate was explored. The research highlighted the complexity of leadership in this context, and emphasized collaboration among teams of principals, teachers, students, and the community, with everyone being seen as leaders at all times, led by a principal with a strong vision. Gan highlights the importance of practical training in implementing distributed leadership models for change and learning to develop a leadership identity that incorporates environmental education.

Building upon Gan's research, four change domains for leadership have been proposed: (1) integrating EE into the school vision to promote a whole-school approach, encompassing curriculum, policies, and school culture that enhance education and promote an equitable society; (2) facilitating the learning and deep understanding of EE principles among school staff and teachers while integrating sustainable practices into the curriculum; (3) restructuring school routines and fostering shared activism to promote EE, while establishing a professional learning community; (4) adopting a comprehensive approach to teaching, learning, and leading the implementation of EE in a coherent manner (Gan, 2021, p. 1443, citing Stevenson et al., 2014).

A powerful example comes from a first-hand account from Rathfern Primary School in London, England, headteacher Naheeda Maharasingam (2020). The school enacts valued-led leadership both by embedding the SDGs across the curriculum, and by enabling teachers and students to take social action to live within planetary limits. Her approach incorporates the principles of envisioning (imagining a better future), educating (integrating the SDGs into the curriculum), and interrupting (developing metacognition and embracing new perspectives). The school provides spaces for both teachers and students to become active citizens within the school and ambassadors for the community through weekly meetings and leadership roles.

However, there are challenges for school principals when attempting to flatten hierarchies and promote shared power and decision-making in schools. In a survey of 525 environmental teacher leaders participating in the Ontario EcoSchools initiative, Acton (2022) revealed that few school principals were willing to relinquish hierarchical authority. Not all teacher colleagues supported and encouraged collaborative work, and many encountered barriers related to school scheduling, release time, or other organizational factors. Teacher leaders also found it necessary but difficult to challenge established practices, and tiring to continually explain the environmental crisis to other staff members. Most perceived the barriers to be the responsibility of the school principal. Therefore, leaders must ensure training and support that reduces such barriers (Kensler and Uline, 2016; Kensler, 2022).


### Context relevance


Another major challenge is reducing environmental excesses (the outer ring of Raworth's doughnut) primarily caused by the Global North, while poorer nations strive to meet the basic needs of their citizens (the inner ring). This does not imply that the Global North is devoid of significant social problems, nor does it suggest that the Global South should disregard environmental excesses. Rather, Raworth’s framework conceptually highlights some of the differences in priorities between regions.

Leadership at school and policy level plays a crucial role in addressing these goals in education. However, the quality of management in schools varies significantly at the country level, with higher variance than in other sectors (Bloom et al., 2015). While headteachers are expected to demonstrate leadership at the school level, the manifestation of this quality varies globally due to differences in school governance and broader cultures (Tulowitzki, 2013; Paletta, Bayste Ferrari & Alimehmeti, 2020; Hallinger, 2016). In many parts of the world, the selection process for school leaders lacks rigor and is based on checking general knowledge related to school system functioning, without specific initial or continuous training (OECD, 2019). Moreover, school leaders usually have an educational background as teachers, which means they can lack leadership and management competencies. Nevertheless, they are expected to, among other things, provide curriculum supervision, promote learning improvements, and establish community relationships (OECD, 2019). Even where more robust systems for leadership preparation exist, the theories and organizational challenges related to putting these systems into practice vary considerably across countries (Mincu, 2022).

Consequently, there are no one-size-fits-all blueprints for school leadership in the Anthropocene era as strategies and actions will depend on local issues and involve various actors both within and beyond the school. Nonetheless, school leadership development must emphasize building relationships and connections with a wider range of stakeholders.


### Intelligent and shared accountability


Given the broad and complex challenges ahead, leaders within the education system need indicators of progress towards desired goals at the macro (values) and exo-levels (national policy enactment), meso (organizational), and micro (individual, such as teacher-student) levels.

At the macro level, it is important to understand whether society, including the education system, is progressing toward sustainable forms of societal and economic well-being. This necessitates moving away from relying solely on GDP growth as the indicator used by governments in economic policymaking. Implicit in metrics such as Green GDP are notions of what constitutes a good life and a good society, including reducing inequality and poverty while fostering the development of useful technologies that enhance living conditions for humans and the environment.

Several accreditation bodies utilize sustainability metrics at the school level, such as the Green Schools Certificate for the Middle East and North Africa region (https://www.greenschools.me) and the UK's EcoSchools program (https://www.eco-schools.org.uk). Schools may also collaborate with partners or community efforts to create their own strategies. For instance, Oberlin College in the US publishes metrics to track progress toward sustainability (https://carbonneutral.oberlin.edu) and aims to become carbon neutral by 2025. Their environmental dashboard not only focuses on their own campus but also aims to inspire the wider community. Increasingly, such dashboards could be adopted across schools, businesses, towns, and cities to scale up and integrate sustainability efforts.

These efforts raise the question of who holds whom accountable, and for what? Given the exploratory, contextualized and adapting nature of school approaches required in the Anthropocene era, the dependence on external, centralized bodies using fixed summative criteria to hold actors accountable must be reduced. Instead, moral and professional accountability must be created, using standards generated from within the profession, evaluated by the profession, and employing standards co-created by stakeholders involved in the evaluation. This should include peer-based evaluations between schools and school leaders (Godfrey, 2020). Given the global and interconnected nature of the challenges, transnational approaches to peer review, as seen in the lifelong learning sector (Gutknecht-Gmeiner, 2013), could be very useful.


## Conclusions


We have argued that our four pillars model, inspired by pragmatism and socio-ecological agency, and operationalized by incorporating Raworth's Doughnut model and the SDGs, represents a way for school leadership to respond intelligently and humanely to current threats and opportunities.

In the absence of strong policy-level leadership, school leaders have a moral and professional obligation take the initiative, both individually and collectively, to create environments that foster freedom and space for teachers to question, experiment, and innovate, and for students to engage in responsive, collaborative and empowering learning experiences. Moreover, they should encourage the utilization of diverse resources and opportunities beyond school premises, while utilizing local and global issues as valuable sources of learning and growth. Simultaneously, they must advocate for a broader and more flexible set of accountability criteria that currently restrict their autonomy, enabling them to respond more effectively. This movement should bridge ideologies and traditions, necessitating contextual sensitivity while focusing on global challenges.

These challenges also question the preparation of school leaders. We argue that the skill of establishing powerful networks of connections for learning, support, or "relational agency" (Edwards, 2005), is crucial. By sharing leadership within and beyond the school, new narratives of the Anthropocene can be shared and realized.

## 1 Introduction


Statistical analyses in the health and social sciences are becoming more complex. Increases in the size and variety of data available and reductions in computational costs have led to the development of new algorithms and statistical methods as well as a general expansion of possibilities in data analysis (Lazer et al. 2009; Efron and Hastie 2021). It is increasingly common to see empirical papers including the results of tens, if not thousands, of models, be it to repeat a regression model across multiple datasets (Bann et al. 2022), to use an 'exposure-wide' (Ioannidis 2016) or 'outcome-wide' design (VanderWeele 2017; VanderWeele, Mathur, and Chen 2020), or to investigate the robustness of results across different plausible model specifications as in multiverse (Steegen et al. 2016), specification curve analysis (Simonsohn, Simmons, and Nelson 2020) and pattern mixture modelling (Leurent et al. 2018) approaches. In each of these cases, the analyst is required to write code to run many models and to present the results in a clear way. Yet, this is not a standard component of research training. Thus in this tutorial, we will see how to write efficient code to run multiple models and convey the results concisely using the programming language R .

We begin with a simple dataset: an excerpt from Hans Rosling's Gapminder project, a panel data of countrylevel indicators of development (Bryan 2023; Gapminder Project 2023). We use this to introduce some of the central ideas for running multiple models using R . Next we use data from the National Child Development Study (Power and Elliott 2006), a birth cohort of individuals born in Britain in a single week of March 1958, to apply and extend these ideas with a more realistic research example - the association between adolescent cognitive ability and allostatic load in mid-life.

## 2.4 map()

We'll use the data list-column to run a series of (sixty) regressions at the continent-year levels. Most R functions do not take lists as inputs, however, so if we want to perform an operation on a list-column , we need to iterate over its rows. This can be done using the map() family of functions. The two main inputs to map() are an object to iterate over (e.g. a list-column ) and a function to apply at each iteration. In other words, map() is a concise way of specifying a loop. 2 Below we use map() to loop over a list of two vectors, calculating the mean for each.

```
list( c(1, 4, 4), c(4, 6, 8)) %>% map(mean)
```

```
## [[1]] ## [1] 3 ## ## [[2]] ## [1] 6
```

Using the above syntax, map() passes the elements of the input object into the first argument of the specified function and returns a list the same length as the input object. Above, in the first iteration, we obtained the mean of 1, 4, and 4 ( = 3). In the second iteration, we obtained the mean of 4, 6, and 8 (= 6).

There are a number of variants of map() that return specific data types rather than lists. For instance, we can simplify the output above using map\_dbl() as this returns a numeric (double) vector.

```
list(c(1, 4, 4), c(4, 6, 8)) %>% map_dbl(mean)
```

```
## [1] 3 6
```

map() has an alternate syntax (termed lambda notation ) for cases where more complex function calls are required. This syntax can be used to specify further arguments to the mapped function or to specify the particular arguments the input object is inputted to. Below we use lambda notation to discard missing values from the vectors inputted to mean() .

```
list(c(1, 4, 4, NA), c(4, 6, 8, NA)) %>% map_dbl(~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)) # Removes missing values from calculation
```

```

```

In lambda notation, ' .x ' stands in for the current element of the input object being iterated over (e.g., the vector c(1, 4, 4, NA) in the first iteration).
