## 2.5 tidy()

Regression objects (e.g., as returned by lm() ) can be difficult to work with and typically contain extraneous information, such as the function call and the dataset used for estimation. The broom package is an extremely helpful package for extracting information from model objects. It comprises three functions -tidy() , glance() and augment() - that extract results at different level of analysis. Each returns results in tibble format.

- · tidy() returns information on individual parameters (i.e, regression coefficients and their associated standard errors and p-values).
- · glance() returns model-level information (e.g., information such as R 2 , AIC, and number of observations)).
- · augment() returns observation-level information (e.g., predicted values and residuals).

## 3 An Applied Example: Allostatic Load and Adolescent Cognitive Ability


The main ideas are now in place. We can

- 1. Use tibbles to define model specifications
- 2. Write functions which take a specification, run a model and include a tidy() step to return results in tibble format
- 3. Use map() to iterate over the model specifications, run a regression at each iteration, and place the results into a single tibble .

We will now apply these ideas using an example analysing the association between adolescent cognitive ability and allostatic load. Specifically, we will perform a specification curve analysis (Simonsohn, Simmons, and Nelson 2020), where we will examine how robust the association is using different ways of defining allostatic load and measuring cognitive ability. As part of this, we will produce a specification curve plot - a neat way of presenting the results of multiple models concisely. 3


## 3.1 Allostatic Load and Cognitive Ability


The field of cognitive epidemiology has identified broadly consistent evidence that higher cognitive ability is associated with better health outcomes and more salutary health behaviours. This includes associations with measures of physical and mental health, with clinical end-point measures such as mortality and disease incidence, and with intermediate markers of ill health, such as high blood pressure, frailty and allostatic load (Deary, Hill, and Gale 2021).

Allostatic load is a measure of the physiological damage from stress. When faced with a stressor, the body undergoes change across multiple regulatory systems - including metabolic, immune, and cardiovascular systems - in order to maintain optimal functioning. For example, heart rate increases and glucose is released into blood to increase energy availability. This process of adaption is known as allostasis (Sterling and Eyer 1988). When stressors are frequent, intense, or prolonged, the body must continuously adjust to maintain functioning. This can lead to wear and tear that damages the body over time causing disease and acute health problems. This wear and tear is referred to as allostatic load (McEwen 1998).

Importantly, as allostatic load involves multiple physiological systems in a pre-disease state, it cannot be measured with a single biomarker. Instead, to capture allostatic load, researchers combine relevant biomarkers from across multiple physiological systems - for instance, elevated blood pressure, heightened cortisol levels, high levels of inflammation, and so on. The biomarkers used by researchers depend on the data available. This differs considerably across studies and the procedure used to combine the biomarkers into a single summary measure also varies (Juster, McEwen, and Lupien 2010). Both of these make it difficult to compare results across studies and raise questions about how sensitive results may be to the definition of allostatic load. The study of allostatic load thus lends itself to a many models approach - specifically a Specification Curve Analysis (Simonsohn, Simmons, and Nelson 2020) approach - where the various ways of defining allostatic load are tested and results compared, which is what we will do here.

## 3.4 Setting Up the Model Specification Grid


Besides the specific biomarkers used, measures of allostatic load can also differ according to the procedure used to combine them. Two popular measures are sum of z-scores and sum of biomarkers in the high-risk quartile (Juster, McEwen, and Lupien 2010). In our model function, we will include code to carry out this step.

We will also iterate over the four cognitive ability measures - the association between cognitive ability and allostatic load should be observed regardless of when cognitive ability was measured in childhood (age 11 or 16) or the particular domain captured in a cognitive ability test (verbal, maths or reading skills).

Below we set up our specification grid. It has 79,264 rows.


## 3.5 Writing the Model Function


Next, we need to write the function ( allostatic\_lm() ) that takes the spec\_id , processes the data accordingly, runs a regression and extracts the results. This function will be more complex than in the gapminder example above as we need to create the allostatic load variable and generate a regression model formula based on the cognitive ability measure being used. Below, we create this function.

We first load the glue package, which contains the glue() function that can be used to create strings from the contents of R objects. We will use glue() to create a model formula using the name of the current cognitive ability variable.

The first lines of allostatic\_lm() create the allostatic load variable that will be used in the regression model. The biomarkers have already been converted to z-scores, so we add an if condition that includes extra processing steps to be carried out when the high-risk quartile aggregation method is used (i.e., to convert each biomarker to a dummy variable; high-risk vs low-risk). We also standardize the resulting allostatic load variable using scale() (mean = 0, standard deviation = 1) so that the variable is on the same scale regardless of the number of biomarkers or method of aggregation used. We run a regression and use tidy() along with filter() and select() to retain the information for cognitive ability term only.

```
library(glue) # Installed with the tidyverse but not a 'core' package allostatic_lm <-function (spec_id){ spec <-allostatic_specs %>% filter(spec_id == !!spec_id) # As spec$biomarkers is a list, spec$biomarkers[[1]] require to obtain vector curr_biomarkers <-spec$biomarkers[[1]] df_bio <-ncds %>% select( sex, # Keep sex as we determine high-risk quartile by sex all_of(!!curr_biomarkers) # Keep all variables named in curr_biomarkers ) if (spec$combine_method == "quartile"){ df_bio <-df_bio %>% group_by(sex) %>% # Determine high-risk quartile in each sex. mutate( across( # across() repeats a function over a set of columns .cols = everything(), # Specifies we want to repeat over all columns ~ ifelse(.x > quantile(.x, probs = .75), 1, 0) # =1 if high-risk ) ) %>% ungroup() # Remove grouping by sex } allostatic <-df_bio %>% select(-sex) %>% # Remove sex variable as not longer needed rowSums() %>% # Aggregate the biomarkers scale() %>% # Standardize to mean = 0, sd = 1 for comparability as.double() # Convert to simple numeric vector; scale returns metadata df_reg <-ncds %>% mutate(allostatic = !!allostatic) %>% # Add allostatic load variable select(allostatic, all_of(!!spec$cognitive_measure), bmi_11, sex, father_class) # glue() allows you to create strings using R objects # Here {spec$cognitive_measure} will be replaced by its value glue("allostatic ~ {spec$cognitive_measure} + sex + bmi_11 + father_class") %>% as.formula() %>% lm(df_reg) %>% tidy(conf.int = TRUE) %>% filter( # Keep the coefficient for cognitive ability only term == !!spec$cognitive_measure ) %>% select(estimate, p.value, std.error, conf.low, conf.high) }
```

## 3.7 Presenting the Results


Now we have the results, the problem is how to present the results concisely. Below we create a specification curve plot. A specification curve plot presents the estimates as scatter points, arranged by effect sizes and shaded according to statistical significance.

```
allostatic_res %>% mutate( rank = dense_rank(estimate), # Get rank order of estimates signif = ifelse(p.value < 0.05, "p < 0.05", "p >= 0.05") # Binary significance variable ) %>% ggplot() + aes(x = rank, # Displays rank on the x-axis y = estimate, # ...estimate on the y-axis ymin = conf.low, # ... conf.low on the y-axis (defines band of geom_pointrange()) ymax = conf.high, # ... conf.low on the y-axis (defines band of geom_pointrange()) color = signif) + # ... signif as color geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + # Adds a horizontal line through 0 (i.e., null effect) geom_pointrange(alpha = 0.01) + # Add points plus 95% CIs. (alpha adds transparency) geom_point() + # Add scatter points scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "black")) + # Define colors for signif categories labs(x = "Rank", y = "Effect Size", color = "p-value") # Axis and legend labels
```

The plot shows that cognitive ability is robustly associated with lower allostatic load. Depending on the definition of allostatic load and cognitive ability, the association varies between approximately -0.15 SD to -0.05 SD per SD increase in cognitive ability.

We can examine how estimates vary by biomarker included. This is useful for investigating which biomarkers, if any, are most strongly related to cognitive ability. Below we generate boxplots of estimates for each biomarker.

## 4 Final Remarks


We have run a Specification Curve Analysis from scratch by writing our own bespoke function. The approach we used can be generalised to other analytical approaches involving running multiple models, such as pattern mixture modelling and cross-cohort analyses. The excellent specr package offers out-of-the-box functionality to simplify running SCAs, and also includes useful plotting functions for parsing and presenting SCA results (Masur and Scharkow 2020). This package may be sufficient in many circumstances, but in complex situations involving, e.g., multiple data pre-processing steps, being able to write bespoke code may be necessary - hence this tutorial.

Where a large number of model are to be run, strategies to reduce computational time can be worthwhile. map() executes in serial on a single core. The furrr() package (which is not downloaded with the tidyverse ) can be used to run regressions in parallel, dramatically speeding up analyses (Vaughan and Dancho 2022). The future\_map() function within furrr() -and its associated variants, such as future\_map2\_dbl() -uses identical syntax to map() . In some cases, running the models on a personal computer would take too long. In this case, researchers can run RStudio cheaply on Amazon Web Services or another cloud platform (Aslett 2020).

## Introduction


On Facebook, a popular water hole for journalists considering departing the field is found in the group 'What is your Plan B?' The group offers resources, advice, and more than a few horror stories from the industry. One journalist described their editor publicly advancing the value unpaid, weekend and evening work. Other describe an expectation that journalists would clock out on time-so as to not breech corporate expectations-but then return to work afterwards. Commonly, contributors describe their bosses: at times supportive of them regardless of their career move, and at other times a key reason for their departure. As one contributor put it: 'I walked out after my boss scolded me in an open area with 'You didn't do what you were told. You were supposed to [do] what you're told.' That was the final straw' (What's Your Plan B?, 2019).

Research in general denotes the outsized role an organizational leader plays in the happiness of workers.

A great boss isn't just someone who knows their business and can delegate as easily as breathing. They're not just a decision maker. They are a teacher. A mentor. Someone who can show you your flaws and strengths and who is willing to put their own reputation on the line to recommend you to others. A person who encourages you and gives you the resources to turn confidence into legitimate, desirable product (Thibodeaux, n.d.).

The numerous challenges facing the journalism field, in regards changing economic models, the need to integrate new technology and declining audience, necessitates a robust consideration of the role of leadership in the journalistic field. Based on interviews with U.S.-based journalists (n=36), this study reflects that-while bad boss stories remain popular-journalists largely saw their bosses as exemplars within the field, inspiring their work and helping grant shape to their career goals.


## Field Theory


Through the lens of Bourdieu's (1986) field theory, journalism is considered to be a field reflecting power relationships. Field theory provides a bridge between 'structural functionalism and social phenomenology by analyzing society on both the structural and individual level through the interplay of various concepts' (Maares & Hanusch, 2022, p. 738). A field comprises several concepts reflecting the power relations between several actors: habitus, doxa , and capital .

- ● Habitus is a response structure that allows journalists to respond to the tasks before them (Bourdieu, 1977). It reflects the dispositional habits of journalists (Barnard, 2018) that provides a classificatory system for journalists to react unconsciously to reporting tasks almost unconsciously (Benson, 1999).
- ● Doxa refers to the knowledge of the game in which actors are often socialized. Actors share the essential belief that the game itself is worth playing (Benson & Neveu, 2006). In journalism this has in the past been discussed in relation to the rootedness of a journalist in news values.
- ● Capital refers to the various scarce resources that draw actors to act within the field: economic capital, cultural capital, and social capital. That said, actors with access to one form of capital at times have easier access to other forms of capital (Driessens, 2013). For example, journalists with stronger access to economic capital-money-may have a more robust ability to compete for awards within the field, a key aspect of cultural capital

(Jenkins & Volz, 2018). Similarly, journalists with strong cultural capital may also obtain easier access to developing their audience, a reflection of social capital (Nölleke et al., 2022).

Furthermore, the rules of play within the field are often determined by its dominant actors, which have often been considered in terms of genre-political journalists, investigative journalists-but could also be reflected in newsroom leaders. Newsroom leaders tend to be in a preferential location within newsrooms in that they have some say over the distribution of various resources (e.g. salaries for economic capital, nominations for national awards). Hence, through the lens of field theory, a focus on relationships with leaders would seem to be essential for understanding power relationships more broadly within the field. The location of actors within the field seems to reflect in large part their perceived 'professionalism and intimacy with the audience' (Perreault & Hanusch, 2022, p. 15). In other words, obtaining certain forms of capital can help journalists obtain a dominant position within the field and so journalists who already occupy those positions would seem to have incentive to maintain their position. Yet maintaining that dominance requires an exchange-forms of capital in exchange for the labor of journalists-and the placement of actors also assures the stability of the field (Vos et al., 2012).


## Labor in Journalism


Journalism studies scholarship has in recent years devoted more attention to the labor of news: the 'feelings of strain' (Soronen, 2018, p. 290) that accompany work practices-such as implementing innovation (Belair-Gagnon & Steinke, 2020; Ferrucci & Perreault, 2021)--and in terms of the labor of the content journalists face and the interpersonal relationships they manage (Kotisova, 2019; Wahl-Jorgensen, 2013; Pantti & Wahl-Jorgensen, 2021). This is often referred to more specifically as emotional labor , the work associated with the management of feelings (Hochschild, 1983), with emotions here reflecting: 'biologically preconditioned but to a large extent culturally determined, defined and shaped practices of feeling and thinking, … ways of practical engagement with social context, structured by our forms of understanding the context's cultural and historical specifics' (Kotisova, 2017, p. 57). Pantti and Wahl-Jorgensen (2021) similarly describe this labor as 'relating to and dealing with other people's emotions…and is shaped by the changes in the industry and specific contexts in which they carry out their work' (p.  1567). Traditionally, discussing such issues of emotion have been considered taboo in journalism studies, given that it would seem to run counter to objectivity and journalism authoritative tone (Wahl-Jorgensen, 2020). That said, it is clear that working conditions-such as relationships with supervisor-play a substantial role in news production (Wahl-Jorgensen, 2020). As Perreault & Belair-Gagnon (2021) note, journalists have suffered from institutional expectations that 'include a need to be constantly available and consistently adaptable to new and emerging digital trends' (p. 13). This would seem to point toward the centrality of management to the emotional labor at institutions.

Newsroom leaders of course want and reward passion in the newsroom (Lindén et al., 2021), which serves as a commodity to be leveraged: with passion, journalists can be asked to work at no extra cost, harder and longer (Hollifield, 2019). Journalists tend to feel more strain in their work when their work expectations require hidden, unanticipated labor: such as when journalists need explain fringe practices of journalism such as the editorial endorsement (Perreault et al., 2022) or need integrate a new form of innovation with little or no training (Ferrucci & Perreault, 2021). Yet on the other hand, there is some indication that journalists' emotional labor is responsive to their relationship with their boss (Jachimowicz et al., 2021).

Research in this area ascribes that much of an individual's passion and job satisfaction is reflected by their relationship with their leader.


## Media Exemplars / Leadership


Leadership is defined as the 'ability to build and maintain a group that performs well relative to its competition' (Hogan and Kaiser, 2005). Measuring the qualities of a leader however is a much more difficult process as various qualities, traits, competencies of leaders are used to measure elements of what makes a good leader.

Much of communication literature discusses the role of influence in leadership. One of the earliest research studies posited the role of opinion leadership through the two-step flow of communication by Lazarsfeld and Katz, as to how information in the media permeates through to opinion leaders who are able to pass on that knowledge to the public or those they have influence over (Katz,1957). Further research such as the small world study (Milgram, 1967) demonstrated the role of influence among a small group of well-connected individuals, that were able to connect different networks together. This was further reinforced by the weak-ties studies (Granovetter,1973) that showed how the use of information and influence are important attributes to diffusers of information and opinion leaders.

The role of influence is therefore a major part of what leadership is about. Three characteristics that have been identified as part of influence is connectedness, persuasiveness, and being informed (Boster et al., 2011). Connectedness provides the ability for the individual to connect groups of individuals and link multiple networks of people together, much similar to the earlier small world, and weak-ties studies mentioned above. Persuasiveness helps with the increasing influence through the use of messaging that matches one's underlying attitudes

(Hullet & Boster, 2001). And finally, Boster et al (2011), used the term 'maven' to define one who is very knowledgeable in a specific area, as the traits for being informed.

Influential leaders in the real world can be identified through different means. Quantifiably, there are several ways that capture leaders influence such as the through the use of klout scores, hype auditor, electronic word of mouth reach, and other social media assessment tools (Donohue et al, 2020). This research elaborated on the strength of leadership of such influencers through a Maxcer Quotient based on the three areas highlighted in Boster et al's (2011) research.

Leadership can also take the form of management of personnel such as individuals or people within a group.  However, measuring leadership can be difficult. In early leadership research, seven factors were identified as part of transactional and transformational leadership, meaning that a leader is able to motivate and transform the team that they lead. The seven factors identified were charisma, inspiration, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration, contingent rewards, management by exception, and laisse-faire. This led to the creation of the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ) that measured these seven factors, which later became six. Research that followed continued to look at key elements of the leader which are competence and personal characteristics (Higgs, 2003). This inspired the construction of the Leadership Dimension Questionnaire (LDQ) that highlighted three areas of measurement (Dulewicz & Higgs, 2005). The three key dimensions are the Performance of the Leader, the Follower commitment and the organization context of the leadership and leadership style. Leadership thus should not only be evaluated by the self but also by others that report to them to create a more holistic dimension of leadership.

This leads us to propose the following research questions:

RQ 1: How do journalists evaluate leadership?

RQ 2: How do journalists evaluate their leaders' employee expectations?


## Method


In order to address these research questions, this study employed in-depth, semistructured interviews with journalists (n=36) in the United States. An initial pool of 201 potential journalist participants was developed through a process of theoretical sampling (Koerber & McMichael 2008; Saldaña 2011; Ward, 2015) aimed at representing a range of mediums, specialties, and locations for journalism across the United States. The resulting sample who responded and agreed to interview (response rate was approximately 17%) included journalists at small, local news organizations-such as WECT-6 News, WLOS-13 News, the Watauga Democrat -as well as large, national news organizations-such as National Geographic, Raleigh News & Observer, and the Denver Post . The research team recruited participants by email and then conducted interviews through online video (e.g. Zoom).

The interview questionnaire probed numerous aspects of their experience with leadership, asking about both their direct reports as well as ideal-type 'exemplar' leaders. These questions were guided by similar interview-based research on labor in U.S. journalism (e.g. Ferrucci & Perreault, 2021; Perreault & Belair-Gagnon, 2022; Perreault & Hanusch, 2022). The interviews resulted in a substantial corpus of data-both qualitative and quantitative-and for this study, we are analyzing qualitative data from three areas: (1) questions about journalists' experiences with direct reports, (2) questions about how their perceptions of their leaders expectations and (3) questions regarding how they perceive exemplar, ideal-type leaders. Specific interview questions included, 'What do you think your supervisor could do better as a leader?' 'How realistic are your supervisor's expectations of you?,' and 'How is your labor valued by your supervisor??' Interviews were conducted between January 2022 and March 2022. Semi-structured interviews lasted about 45 minutes to an hour each. De-identification was granted to all participants in part because we were only interested in generating themes and general concepts regarding their experiences with leaders. Participant included 15 men, 20 women and 1 individual who identified as non-binary. Interviews were conducted by trained research students from a midsized US university and conducted until the researchers felt they achieved the appropriate information power in regard to the study participants (Malterud et al., 2016). Information power is 'determined by items such as study aim, sample specificity, use of established theory, quality of dialogue, and analysis strategy' (Malterud et al. 2016, p. 1757). The research team applied three criteria in assessing the number of interviews: (1) the high quality of dialogue in interviews, (2) the relatively narrow aim of study (leadership and labor), and (3) a specificity of sample (U.S.-based journalists). Interviews were then transcribed for textual analysis and analyzed by the authors.

The research team employed an iterative, constant-comparative approach in addressing the research questions (Glaser & Strauss, 1968). While the constant comparative method is commonly associated with grounded theory, the method is also well suited for both emic coding-driven by themes that emerge from the data analysis-as well as etic coding-driven by theory and literature (Fram, 2013). Through a series of meetings via a Zoom and in person, the researchers compared the themes that emerged in order to find associations, differences, and similarities. After identifying the themes, the researchers selected representative quotes from the transcripts that reflected the themes that emerged from the discourse (Emerson et al. 2011).

This study was done in accordance with the [REDACTED FOR BLIND REVIEW] Review Board (approval #22-0042). Participants were verbally consented for participation--and informed their participation was voluntary--and all participants were deidentified.


## How Journalists Evaluate Leadership


In regard to RQ 1, responses from two interview questions were utilized to answer this question. 'What do you think your supervisor does that makes them a good leader?', and 'What do you think they could do better as a leader?' provided themes as to how the participants felt about leadership both from a positive perspective of what they see their supervisors embody as well as the negatives of what their supervisors were lacking in the form of leadership. From the analysis of these answers, three dominant themes emerge to the forefront from the interviews. The first theme is communication, the second is expertise or being good at what the supervisors do, and finally the third theme deals with trust and autonomy.

Communication was an important theme that showed up in the majority of the participants' answers. However, it showed up more often as a lacking leadership quality than one that most of their supervisors possessed. Only one participant mentioned that their supervisor had 'Direct clear and direct and constructive communication' (Participant 14), while many others had negative comments such as 'More feedback. Yeah, more feedback' (Participant 15), 'Maybe some more checking in with people just to see how they're doing' (Participant 16), 'He could be a better active listener.' (Participant 31), 'He was hard to approach,' (Participant 21), and 'He is a lousy communicator' (Participant 33). In general, participants felt that while communication was an important leadership quality, most of their supervisors were lacking or could improve by being better communicators which would result in stronger leadership.

Expertise or being good at what they do was the second major theme of leadership that showed up from the interviews. This was demonstrated by their ability to perform a task or having expertise in the field that allows them to provide oversight to their employees. In particular, having attention to the finer aspects of the details of the job is something that respondents respect in their leaders. Several instances of this appeared as qualities that their supervisors possess. 'They are excellent at knowing the topic that is being discussed. They are also excellent at encouraging others, to be a good leader you need to know what you are talking about or doing and need to encourage and help the people lower than you (sic)'  (Participant 6) 'She's detail oriented, there's no job or just nothing that she's is too good to try and help with.' (Participant 29),  'He's very detail oriented.' (Participant 31), 'Efficient meetings so that's crucial. Being sort of on top of all the different moving parts' (Participant 10), and 'He is quite good at mentoring them and working with them to define their beat, and we still have a beat system, to help them learn how to navigate dealing with people on the local city council or the cops, you know, officials, whomever.' (Participant 33). We do see some respondents indicating a lack of leadership quality from their supervisor in this area, with comments such as 'It is clear a lot of times he has not made much effort to come up to speed on some of our ongoing stories' (Participant 23) and 'She does not have the same level of in my opinion, news judgment' (Participant 27).

The third theme is trust and autonomy. While this was seen as a minor theme based on the quantity of comments, it was mentioned as an important quality that the supervisor possessed, 'He gives us a fair amount of trust. 'I know, you're all working hard, you know, what your beats are, you know, sometimes there's something decreed from on high that we need this story or whatever it is now', but mostly, he gives us a fair amount of autonomy' (Participant 16), and 'I feel like she has my back.' (Participant 27). Negatively, respondents see the lack of trust as problematic in leadership, 'Sometimes when a topic is dropped, they can get pretty upset.' (Participant 6). As another participant put it:

I think if she took the time to put herself in somebody else's shoes, and she also created better boundaries because she contacts people at all hours of the day and night, and everything is an emergency. If she would just step back a little and take some more time to do things. With that ugly and with more intention. We might not have as many mistakes and also might not upset as many people who are getting contacted outside of work hours (Participant 29).

While this theme seems to vacillate between empathy and understanding, it seems to point mostly to the lack of support, agency, and trust from supervisors who sometimes seek to micromanage or blame-shift responsibilities on those they supervise.

These three themes are quite specific as they deal with work in journalism and some of the positives and struggles that journalists have and expect from their supervisors. Even though they are hard lined to journalism itself, we find much similarity with Boster et al's (2011) definition of influence. Influence was defined as connectedness, persuasiveness and being informed. From our research, themes of communication bear many similarities to connectedness, while trust and autonomy shares traits with persuasiveness, and expertise with being informed. How journalists evaluate their leader's expectations

Journalists overwhelming responded, in numerous ways, to reflect that their newsroom leader's expectations were reasonable. And when the expectations approached unreasonable, this was a result of field expectations and not reflective of their newsroom leader. This robust evaluation of their leaders stemmed in the questionnaire from two questions: 'how realistic are your supervisor's expectations of you?' and 'how is your labor valued by your supervisor?'

A large part the responses from journalists reflected a strong sense that their leader was informed. As participants put it, 'he gets it' (Participant 1) and 'they expect me to get my job done' (Participant 16). In the latter, Participant 16 seems to indicate that the 'job' is one that is fixed, externally assessed from the field, and the supervisor is simply the person who makes sure his employed enact their commitment to it. Similarly, Participant 26 argued that the unfair expectations of the job were not the fault of their supervisor: 'I think the news business in general right now has overblown expectations. But I think she is fairly reasonable in trying to put those on her employees' (Participant 26). Participant 13 felt that their job expectations were reasonable in that they provided means with which journalist could feel some control over their workload: 'the freedom to set your own schedule…they're very good about maintaining your hours.' Worth noting is that when journalists did not feel their supervisor's labor expectations were realistic, they often connected that to a lack of knowledge. At times this lack of knowledge was about the job of their employees-as one participant put it, 'I don't think they realize just everything that goes into my job' (Participant 24). But at times, this lack of knowledge was more expansive-about the audience or about the field in general.

Most of the time, they're fine…We seem to have a big disconnect between our long-term public mission as a print - I hate using this word - uh, product, and our website. We say that those two things are not in conflict, but I find they're in conflict all the time because stuff that we used to cover and may be part of our public mission, people don't necessarily read online, the place that we can measure it, the place that we do measure it. So, oftentimes, I'll get told to do a story about how a surrounding town needs to put out a bond issue for millions of dollars to fix their stormwater sewer system, that you know, he thinks is important, but nobody reads. So we have this real disconnect that he doesn't like to realize (Participant 32).

That said, journalists in many cases felt that they had to remind their supervisors of what they were doing-something they felt comfortable doing if granted a certain amount of connection with their supervisor. For example, participant 15 noted 'sometimes I have to kind of lay out. And just a reminder, I'm working on all these things. Yeah. I, if you want something more, something else is gonna have to wait. And he's been understanding of that.' Similarly, Participant 1 noted 'I make my limitations very clear…he understands the situation I'm in, in terms of like, you know, hours limitations and what I've got on my plate.' When there was a lack of connection with the supervisor, journalists may have felt that their labor was reasonable yet nevertheless felt a lack of value from their employer. As one participant put it 'it's valued that like they appreciate that someone is doing here but I don't think they necessarily appreciate who is doing it but like that it's getting done' (Participant 29). Participant 29 however rationalized this by arguing that their situation was normal-which it may be more generally, but was not among journalist respondents. The journalist noted 'It's not that abnormal…I think that's just how it is like literally every single job…Like this is capitalism, unfortunately.' Similarly, Participant 15 noted that while they felt connected to their supervisor, it hasn't always manifested as emotional support, but more often in terms of unplanned time away.

I mean, we don't get a lot of praise or anything, but you know, he, like, if somebody needs some time off or something, you know, he'll say, "I know you've been working hard or putting in extra hours or what have you. So, you know, don't worry about taking a sick day or whatever, you can just think about this as compensation." So that's yeah, that's a very nice thing (Participant 15).

Simply, Participant 1 noted that, for past 6 months, he had recently been carrying the sports department for their news organization as a result of departures, training for new hires; hence, participant 1 similarly appreciated encouragement from his supervisor to take time away: "There's a lot of your deal with. And so, when he says like, 'hey, you're doing a good job, you need to you need to take a day off or something,' I understand it's like 'yeah okay, I definitely do.'"

Verbal affirmation from supervisors was very important for journalists, with one journalist, for example, noting that he actually appreciated his editor so much he'd served as a reference for her as she'd sought to take a job elsewhere. They noted that their supervisor was "super supportive, and she always went above and beyond being encouraging with me, just a great team player" (Participant 3).

And while mostly, journalists reflected positively on their supervisor given their insight into the field and their connectedness to the team, there was one participant who was, in contrast, quite negative about their supervisor. Largely, they argued, that it wasn't just the lack of connectedness or field knowledge that was a problem, but also that they felt like they were not given sufficient financial support for their work.

We haven't had the cost of living increase in at least ten years...I don't get, from my supervisor...a monetary reward for my good works and my labor. 'Good job, what's next? Okay, that's what you gave me today, you gave me 2, 3 stories today, which 3 are you giving me tomorrow?' It won't be verbal, it'll mostly be in the Slack thing that we use (Participant 32).


## Discussion


There's an old saying - 'people don't quit bad jobs, they quit bad bosses' - and research in other fields suggests that, far from being just an old saw, there is actually quite a bit to the saying (Artz et al., 2015). In economics, Artz et al. (2016) demonstrated that satisfaction with a boss was the most important factor in employee's job satisfaction. They key factor for employees in judging their supervisor? Could the supervisor do their job.

We found that employees are far happier when they are led by people with deep expertise in the core activity of the business. This suggests that received wisdom about what makes a good boss may need some rethinking. It's not uncommon to hear people assert that it's a bad idea to promote an engineer to lead other engineers, or an editor to lead other editors. A good manager doesn't need technical expertise, this argument goes, but rather, a mix of qualities like charisma, organizational skills, and emotional intelligence. Those qualities do matter, but what our research suggests is that the oft-overlooked quality of having technical expertise also matters enormously (Artz et al., 2016, para. 4).

And indeed, as the present study would suggest, this would seem to be equally important for journalists. In the first research question, we sought to understand how journalists evaluate their leaders. We found that journalists primarily evaluated their supervisors based on their ability to communicate, their expertise and, less prominently, the degree to which supervisors offered trust and autonomy to their employees. In the second research question, we sought to understand how journalists perceived their supervisors' expectations. We found overwhelmingly that journalists perceived their leaders' expectations as reasonable. When journalists did see their expectations as unreasonable, it was largely seen as a result of the field-not their supervisor who was enacting the very expertise journalists lauded them for.

In conversation with field theory, journalists' perspectives of their leaders tended to reflect an evaluation of journalistic doxa . Journalists evaluated their leaders as having expertise and understanding of the nature of the game-critically informing how journalists in newsrooms ought to work-and hence, journalists were willing adjust their own habitus to accommodate this in that their supervisors were considered to be the exemplars of journalistic doxa in the newsroom (Benson & Neveu, 2006). This doxa seemed to work hand-in-hand with social capital-with great leaders, also being considered those who were well-connected and communicative in the newsroom. In the exceptional cases where journalists were critical of leaders, it seemed to be reflective of both a lack of social capital and perceived lack of doxa. When supervisors lacked economic capital (e.g. money) or cultural capital (e.g. awards), journalists tended to be more forgiving, but the lack of social capital and rooting in journalistic doxa were deemed to be essential. Prior research has reflected that forms of capital can be transferable-that is, those with great cultural capital tend to have greater access to social capital and economic capital (Driessens, 2013; Nölleke et al., 2022). Yet what journalists reflected in this study is that, while this did not always happen in the case of their supervisors, what made them perceive their leaders as being more effective within the field was a combination of doxa and internally-focused social capital.

This is an essential finding for field theory given the role individual newsroom leaders play in guiding the field-for example, with encouraging retention within the field and socializing new entrants (Gentry, 2016; Higgs, 2003)--but it also points toward less-discussed arena of wellbeing, namely the relationship between journalists and supervisors. While wellbeing has been a subject of discussion for many years in journalism studies, recent years have seen an increased focus on this topic (Wahl-Jorgensen, 2020). Journalists largely reflected a mindset that saw their supervisors as largely members of their team, and felt their supervisors set reasonable expectations and supported them to the best of their ability. This was not to say that they felt that the expectations of the field were reasonable, and while in numerous professions, leaders are often seen as the immediate face of field expectations (Hollifield, 2019) that was not the case for journalists. Journalists instead saw their supervisors as working in tandem with them to help them navigate unstable waters in the field,

Not all traits typically seen as markers of effective leadership were representative of what journalists saw as effective leadership (Boster et al., 2011; Dulewicz & Higgs, 2005): in particular, journalists reflected quite little on persuasiveness among their newsroom leaders. A much heavier emphasis was placed on their supervisor's expertise-as reflected in their doxa -and their ability to communicate effectively-which seemed to reflect a level of localized social capital.

A practical implication that is bore of this study is understanding the larger role leadership and influence in today's workplace from a bird's eye view. In an era of digital work, where remote work has become more commonplace, we also have witnessed a decline in productivity (Burns & Dunsmuir, 2022). The importance of good leadership has hence become paramount in the workplace both as a source of influence, motivation as well as positive mental well-being of employees. For journalists, the duality of maintaining personal well-being as well as motivation to work can be influenced by one's leader or boss. The two biggest criticisms were of the lack of autonomy offered and communication by leaders. Thus, in the face of digital communication (texts, video calls, etc), a leader's communication skills need to take on other facets beyond communicating the assignment alone, but understanding the affordances of different media forms, and having the ability to understand how those messages may be conveyed non-verbally. This also means understanding the technology, or in the absence of that, be able to provide greater agency to trust those that report to them to be able to manage the work. This highlights the need for journalistic leaders to adapt to the ever-evolving landscape of the newsroom to maintain a leadership that can not only motivate, but allow journalists to be both productive and have a hale mental health.

All studies have limitations and this study is no different. In particular, it is of course worth considering that while journalists were deidentified for this study, it may still be the case that journalists were reluctant to share harsher takes on their supervisor, given that interviews were conducted with research students; and they may have sought to provide socially acceptable answers and wished to avoid discouraging students. That said, it may speak to the validity of the findings that journalists nevertheless were transparent about their workload and emotional labor that are conversant with other research on journalistic wellbeing. In addition, the timing of the interviews-18 months after the beginning of the coronavirus pandemic-could have shifted responses in that the pandemic changed the nature of numerous aspects of news work (Perreault, Perreault & Maares, 2022).

Leadership comes with few perks in the field of journalism-substantial responsibilities and little financial incentive to compensate. Yet, what this study reflects is the outsized influence a leader has in journalism, as well as what journalists see as the markers of effective leadership.

## 1 Introduction


Successful insurgents in civil wars frequently capture far-reaching territory from the government. In the Sierra Leone civil war, the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) controlled

over half of the country in 1998 and could even advance into the capital of Freetown (HRW 1999). While conflict studies increasingly investigate how rebels govern during conflict (Arjona 2017, Arjona 2016 , Mampilly 2012), our understanding of their interaction with b the civilian population in newly captured territory remains limited. What does territorial takeover mean for civilians living under newly established rebel control?

We examine this research question by statistically analyzing the dynamics of violence against civilians in territory that has recently been captured by rebel groups. We argue that rebels use violence against non-combatants as a tool to establish ruling institutions when they initially lack the resources and knowledge to reign nonviolently. Consequently, transition periods between territorial capture and de facto rebel rule are particularly violent for civilians.

Our research on rebel groups' interactions with civilians after they gain new territory sheds light on the initial period of rebel governance. We contribute to the civilian victimization literature by assessing the impact of territorial takeover on civilian targeting over time. In particular, we respond to Kalyvas' (2006) logic of violence which states that civilian targeting is a strategy of armed actors to deter civilian defection and enforce compliance. We add nuance to this theory by arguing that local governance capacities matter to explain variation in civilian targeting in rebel-held territory. Violence is not simply a function of information but of whether civilians can be co-opted or are able to resist rebel rule (Arjona 2015, Kaplan 2017).

We empirically test the dynamics of violence towards civilians with a novel combination of the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) and the UCDP Geo-referenced Event Dataset (GED) in the Sierra Leone Civil War. By statistically matching battle-prone territory with territory that the RUF violently captured, we control for the fact that battles without territorial transfer also affect the probability of violence against civilians. This allows us to draw inferences on the impact of territorial takeover by rebels on violence against civilians. We do this for multiple spatiotemporal windows (Schutte & Donnay 2014), which robustly shows that violence against civilians locally increases in the short term after territorial seizure by rebels. This extension of Kalyvas' theory with a rebel governance perspective can only be identified thanks to a temporally and spatially disaggregated methodology.


## 2 Research on Civilian Targeting by Rebel Governors


Various studies have investigated when and why civilians are targeted in civil wars. The most influential theoretical contribution was made by Kalyvas in The Logic of Violence in Civil War (2006). Kalyvas (2006) argues that armed actors use indiscriminate and discriminate

violence in order to strategically enforce civilian collaboration and deter defection. Other studies have investigated why both governments (Valentino, Huth & Balch-Lindsay 2004, Schwartz & Straus 2018) and rebels (Weinstein 2006, Fjelde & Hultman 2014) use indiscriminate violence against civilians. Particularly relevant to our argument is the role of rebel resources and institutions in limiting civilian targeting (Humphreys & Weinstein 2006, Hoover Green 2016).

Recent research on rebel governance reveals more details on the question of how rebels interact with civilian populations. First, territorial control matters for peaceful interactions with civilians insofar as rebels cannot establish a system of governance without control (Arjona, Kasfir & Mampilly 2015). The more control a group has over a territory, the easier it is to establish order, to engage with civilians nonviolently, and to deter other armed groups (Arjona, Kasfir & Mampilly 2015, Kalyvas 2006). Second, the time horizon of their operations is important. In order to establish long-term control over territory, rebels need the cooperation of civilians living in that area to maintain their legitimacy (Arjona 2016 b ). Third, the objectives of the movement are important. If rebels follow an ideological agenda or strive for independence, they will be more concerned about support from the population. Conversely, if they are solely interested in looting valuable resources, they are less dependent on the active support of civilians (Mampilly 2012, Huang 2016, Stewart 2018). Lastly, others argue that the way rebels govern and interact with civilians is determined by their military means and relative strength compared to government forces (Kalyvas & Balcells 2010, Staniland 2012, Wood 2010), and whether the rebels receive external funding (Huang 2016) or military support (Wood, Kathman & Gent 2012).

Others question the deterministic nature of rebel governance and call for a more nuanced view that looks beyond the dualistic nexus of state/insurgent actors (Staniland 2012, Wood 2003, Gates 2017, Chojnacki & Branovic 2011, Risse 2011). Instead of viewing control as a zero-sum realm, in which competing actors fight for a fixed amount of power, these authors highlight the role of other states, and local and international institutions to understand rebel behavior.

Studies on rebel governance have identified different factors that explain when and why rebels dedicate efforts towards governing peacefully and those that explain civilian cooperation with non-state armed groups. However, they fall short in explaining why changes in violence against civilians occur over time in rebel-held territory if group objectives and outside factors remain constant. In response, we investigate how rebel rule evolves over time, focusing on the period immediately after territorial takeover.


## 3 Scrutinizing the Logic of Violence after Conquests


To understand the dynamics between rebel rulers and civilians in newly captured territory, we build upon Kalyvas' argument that armed actors use indiscriminate violence against civilians in contested territory due to uncertainty about civilian allegiances. Gaining control over a specific territory allows armed groups to gradually move from indiscriminate to more selective forms of violence against the population. Civilians are unlikely to comply with an overly violent ruler, so the use of indiscriminate violence against civilians is counterproductive (Kalyvas 2006, 169). This suggests that 'violence is largely a function of control' (Kalyvas & Kocher 2009, 339) and that rebel rulers that gain territorial control will increasingly spare civilian lives.

However, some empirical examples of rebel groups waging campaigns of violence after capturing territory seem to fit less well into Kalyvas' theoretical framework and need further explanation. The RUF in Sierra Leone's civil war was unchallenged in the chiefdoms of Kailahun District in 1992 but continued to engage in widespread civilian victimization (NPWJ 2004, 16). Levels of violence against civilians did not decline despite Kalyvas' prediction that increased control leads to decreased civilian targeting.

Hence, we refine Kalyvas' theory of control-driven civilian victimization with a rebel governance perspective. We argue that the initial steps towards rebel governance during civil wars are a violent process that runs counter to the incentives of rebels to use less violence in areas of established control. This initially leads to more violence against civilians after territorial takeover, and Kalyvas' control-based mechanism only sets in after rebels have violently established a minimum level of civilian compliance. After rebels gain control over a territory in a battle, they need to establish de facto control over the population. Adopting a minimalist definition, de facto control over civilians or rebel governance here refers to the establishment of behavioral guidelines for civilians that ensure compliance with rebel rulers in exchange for the provision of security. 1 We argue that the capacity to manage civilian affairs nonviolently is often lacking immediately after territorial takeover.

First, rebel groups' initial capacities are concentrated on fighting the government. During battles, resources are directed towards conquering territory from an asymmetrically stronger government. After territorial victories, rebels remain occupied with securing the borders of this territory. This reduces available capacities to plan governance structures, to police the local population peacefully, to provide dispute resolution mechanisms to regulate civilian

conflicts, and to ensure public goods provision beyond security (Mampilly 2012, 17). Until fighting units transform into rulers that can effectively generate revenue through taxation or similar institutions, they cannot provide infrastructure like local administrations or conflictresolving institutions for civilians to gain their support. When rebel groups cannot offer incentives for cooperation, they are more likely to engage in violence against civilians (Wood 2010, Wood, Kathman & Gent 2012). Violence against civilians remains prevalent until their capacities are less constrained by military objectives.

Second, rebels face an identication problem (Kalyvas 2006): who is a friend and who is an enemy? They cannot instantly identify local supporters or potential dissidents in the population (Arjona 2016 a ). Insurgents need to identify which local institutions - often embedded in customary structures - they are able to co-opt and which ones they need to dismantle and replace. While hospitals and schools may run unaffected by territorial takeovers, rebels may oust political leaders on the local level to secure their new rule. The information asymmetry regarding loyalties in the local population and in local institutions drives armed groups to use violence against civilians. Rebels may oppress the whole population by means of violence until sufficient knowledge is built up to identify opponents and establish effective local institutions for peaceful governance.

Third, rebels may be faced with active civilian resistance against their rule. If civilians push back against the establishment of new institutions in rebel territory (Guti´rrez-San´ ın e & Wood 2014, Arjona 2015), insurgents may use violence at the beginning of their rule to thwart resistance and signal firm control until the local population accepts the new rulers as expected by Kalyvas.

Overall, we expect violent interactions with civilian populations until the process of

establishing rebel institutions and governance is complete. Hence, the transition window between capturing territory and full rebel governance is likely to see an increase in violence against civilians. Figure 1 displays our theoretical expectation of violence against civilians from a rebel governance perspective. Despite the fact that contestation with other conflict actors decreases when rebels start to establish their rule, we expect civilian targeting to peak after territorial takeover in the vicinity of areas that were newly captured.

We do not argue that rebels will rely on indiscriminate violence throughout their rule and in all rebel-held territory. In the long term, rebel groups benefit from peaceful interactions with civilians due to increased willingness to provide food, shelter, and information. However, we argue that the decision to use violence against civilians is temporally and spatially dependent on the level of de facto control a group exercises over a territory. Rebels that do not have institutions to regulate civilians might require violence in newly conquered territory until they are able to establish stable governance. This leads us to our hypothesis:

Hypothesis: Violence against civilians initially increases after territorial takeover in the vicinity of the area that rebel groups violently seize.


## 4 The RUF as Extreme Case of Rebel Violence


Our empirical analysis examines the targeting of civilians by the RUF in Sierra Leone from 1997 to 2001. 2 With over 50,000 dead civilians in the 11 years of conflict (HRW 1999), we understand Sierra Leone as a crucial and extreme case of civilian victimization. In this section, we provide background information on the civil war and justify our case selection.

Sierra Leone's civil war began in 1991 when the RUF entered Sierra Leone from Liberia and recruited the country's aggrieved youth to overthrow the government. At the time, Sierra Leone was one of the poorest countries worldwide despite its richness in natural resources. Today the Sierra Leone civil war is primarily known as a grim fight over resources, particularly diamonds (Smillie, Gberie & Hazleton 2000). The dominant view is that the RUF's access to diamonds explains the group's strength, territorial successes, and their resilience in the conflict (Keen 2005). Reliance on diamonds also explains the RUF's violent behavior towards civilians (Voors, Windt, Papaioannou & Bulte 2017). While gaining territorial control, the rebel organization engaged in widespread and indiscriminate killings, abductions, and rape against all ethnic groups throughout the country (Humphreys & Weinstein 2006, Bellows & Miguel 2009, Cohen 2013). As a result, the RUF falls in the .96 quantile of the

distribution of total civilian fatalities caused by all conflict actors between 1989 and 2017 (Eck & Hultman 2007). In addition, the Kamajors, a grassroots militia force, emerged as civilians aimed to protect themselves against the violent attacks by combatants. However, the Kamajors also became deeply involved in civilian targeting. The RUF twice entered the capital during the conflict, in May 1997 and January 1999. In 1997, the RUF joined the Sierra Leone Army in a military coup against the Kabbah government, forming the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) junta that was then driven out of the capital by the Nigerian-led Economic Community of West African States Monitoring Group (ECOMOG) forces in March 1998. 3 After intense fighting, a peace agreement in 1999 and the deployment of UN peacekeeping troops, the civil war eventually ended in January 2002 (Bangura 2000).

Two reasons justify the selection of the RUF as case study to investigate initial violence against civilians after territorial takeover. First, the RUF was a highly violent rebel organization that gained large amounts of territory during the conflict which provides sufficient data to quantitatively examine how rebel governance unfolds after territorial seizure. 4 As indicated above, this large amount of civilian victimization makes the RUF an extreme case on the dependent variable. Following Seawright & Gerring (2008, 302), an extreme case selection serves as an open-ended entry into a subject.

Secondly, selecting the RUF follows a least likely crucial case design (Levy 2008). The RUF is known for extensive and cruel violence against civilians, but evidence for attempts to govern local populations is limited beyond their interest in firmly controlling civilians in diamond-rich areas in order to exploit their labor to extract resources. The group attempted to develop a system of governance that regulated social life in areas under their control following the motto 'arms to the people, power to the people, and wealth to the people' (Bangura 2000, Mkandawire 2002). Occasionally, this even included a system of alternative schooling in rebel territory (Richards 1998). In the areas around Koidu and Rutile, looted goods were distributed to civilians, hospitals were set-up for RUF fighters, and in the countryside the RUF replaced local chiefs with their own men (Keen 2005). Nonetheless, the group did not establish sophisticated administrative institutions or widely provide public goods. In contrast to extensive rebel rulers, the RUF's interaction with civilians was min-

imal and concentrated on imposing basic compliance. Therefore, we expect that it is less likely to find strong evidence for a peak of violence after territorial takeover in the case of Sierra Leone's RUF. It is more likely to find that high levels of violence prevailed in territories before and after territorial capture by the RUF. Finding evidence for an increase in violence after territorial takeover would suggest that even the RUF as limited rebel rulers used increased violence as a means to alter the political behavior of the population.


## 5 Data and Methods


Our analysis of the RUF in Sierra Leone relies on a combination of ACLED (Raleigh, Linke, Hegre & Karlsen 2010, de Bruijne 2014) and UCDP GED data (Sundberg & Melander 2013). Both datasets independently record events of deliberate targeting of civilians that we count as dependent events for our analysis. Combining these datasets is a critical step for our quantitative analysis of targeting dynamics in the Sierra Leone civil war as we aim to go beyond the qualitative evidence that has been studied previously. However, na¨ ıvely combining the two datasets would result in double-counting events from both datasets (Eck 2012, Hendrix & Salehyan 2015); we hence integrate the datasets with the meltt package (Donnay, Dunford, McGrath, Backer & Cunningham 2018) in R (R Core Team 2018). The package is based on a novel methodology that automatically integrates different event datasets while ensuring transparency and adaptability (Donnay et al. 2018, 3). Using meltt , we check whether an event of civilian targeting in one dataset is also recorded in the corresponding dataset within 10 days and 10 kilometers of one another. 5 If so, these events likely represent the same actual event reported imperfectly in the sources used by ACLED and GED, so they are combined to avoid overcounting. ACLED contains 674 instances of civilian targeting by the RUF in Sierra Leone from 1997-2001 and GED contains 143 events in the same period. The merged data contain 814 events of RUF violence in Sierra Leone. 6

The disparity in event counts between datasets can partly be explained by the different actor typologies they employ. GED only recognizes the RUF, AFRC, and Kamajors as rebel groups during this time period, so only events attributable to one of them are included. This means that subgroups such as the Superman Faction of the RUF are included, but smaller groups such as the West Side Boys Militia or Gbethis Militia are excluded from GED. In

contrast, ACLED records 16 different non-state actors during our sample period.

The two datasets have individual limitations and have slightly different foci in their data collection efforts that are important for our analysis. GED only contains events that can be linked to a known conflict according to the UCDP definition of 25 battle-related deaths per year. For an event to be included the actors have to be named, such as a government, an organized armed group, or communal groups. ACLED, on the other hand, does not have either of those restrictions. Previous research has shown that for Africa between 1997 and 2010 as much as 20% of violent events are not attributable to specific named groups in ACLED data. While GED may potentially exclude important events due to these criteria, ACLED in theory includes these events but cannot link them to specific conflicts (Eck 2012, 135).

Furthermore, GED only includes violent events. ACLED on the other hand includes both violent and nonviolent events such as protests and strategic developments. GED only includes violence against civilians that results in at least one fatality, while ACLED also includes violence against civilians that does not result in fatalities (Eck 2012, 127). This explains why ACLED has more observations than GED for our period under study and why the number of duplicate events is comparatively small.

By integrating ACLED and GED we treat violence against civilians that results in fatalities as conceptually, theoretically, and empirically equal to violence that does not result in fatalities. This decision ensures that the pattern of civilian victimization by the RUF is captured more fully. Only focusing on lethal violence against civilians may be misleading as this excludes crucial incidents of non-lethal civilian victimization (Guti´rrez-San´ ın & e Wood 2017). Given that the RUF engaged in widespread non-lethal forms of violence, such as abductions and rape, it is important to include these acts in our analyses to cover the full pattern. While fatal and nonfatal violence are different, they can both serve to cow civilians into acquiescing to rebel demands. Further, civilian-rebel interactions are prone to unexpected outcomes. Planned nonfatal shows of force can escalate to massacres after unexpected resistance or an intended slaughter is averted by miscommunication within rebel ranks, so separating them could assign intentionality where none existed.

Datasets based on news reports are inevitably prone to reporting and media bias. Reporting often differs by media outlet (Davenport 2009), may fail to accurately distinguish between military and civilian casualties (Dulic 2010), becomes less accurate as geographic remoteness increases (Weidmann 2015), and may disproportionately capture events in more connected areas (Weidmann 2016). These bias and accuracy issues are likely applicable to both ACLED and GED and should be kept in mind when interpreting our findings.

We seek to measure whether the frequency of dependent events of civilian targeting

increases in recently captured territory, but to do so we require some baseline for comparison. Our solution is to use areas where battles with no transfer of territory took place to establish a 'baseline' level of civilian targeting that occurs in conflicts. ACLED classifies battles along this distinction, which allows us to assign areas to treatment (seizure of territory from the government) and control (no transfer of territory). GED does not categorize battles accordingly so GED reported battles are not used to identify treatment and control events. Figure 2 presents the distribution of each event type in our sample. 7

To compare levels of civilian targeting in treatment and control areas, our research design requires the aggregation of point data to areal units. However, inference based on fine-grained spatiotemporal data is subject to the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP), which reflects the fact that counts of civilian victimization will depend on the choice of spatial window used to aggregate events (Cressie 1996). Accordingly, we cannot be sure that our conclusions are not an artifact of the specific spatiotemporal aggregation rule we have chosen.

To deal with this concern, we use matched wake analysis (MWA), a methodology specifically designed for robust inference in spatiotemporal event data (Schutte & Donnay 2014). MWAgenerates a balanced sample of treatment and control events by matching events along local geographic covariates. A circle around each event is then chosen to count the previous and subsequent attacks against civilians in this location during a selected time window (in days). A difference-in-differences design estimates the average treatment effect β 2 , that is the effect of territorial takeover on the post-treatment count of attacks against civilians η post .

In small temporal aggregations, such as the four-kilometer and 25-day window, treatment

and control areas are both likely to see some increase in civilian casualties due to residual violence from the initial conquest or battle. Even if the RUF only fought a battle and could not gain territory, we are likely to observe some rise in civilian targeting in the immediate days after the fight in control areas. This increase in targeting might be due to the fact that civilians die as collateral damage during the time that RUF fighting units retreat from the territory in question, which could explain the lack of significant differences in civilian targeting in shorter temporal windows.

Significantly more civilian victimization only occurs in the direct vicinity of the battle where rebels seized territory from the government. This fits our theoretical expectation: at locations where violent territorial transfer occurs, the interaction between rebels and civilians becomes even more violent. If rebels capture a village, they require more violence as a governance tool in this village but not necessarily in the surrounding area where fewer people reside or where they already had outposts before this specific territorial gain. Extending the spatial window beyond 10 kilometers does not yield any further significant results as conflict dynamics overlap and cancel out effects if space is aggregated to larger units.

The space and time combinations where we do not observe statistically significant difference between territorial conquest and regular battles are not necessarily peaceful. Due to the statistically insignificant relationship between territorial capture and the number of targeting events in these windows, we cannot be confident about whether there is a positive, negative, or null relationship.

The matching procedure substantially improves covariate balance for the two and fourkilometer and 30 and 35-day windows where we observe significant effects. Common support for these spatiotemporal windows is approximately 10 pre-matching, and around 60 postmatching, which means that treatment and control events are more similar in their values of our five matching covariates than they were pre-matching. This yields much better estimates of the treatment effect and increases our confidence in the findings.

Violations of the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA) are a threat to inference in any study involving matching (Cox 1958). In our case, we are concerned with multiple treatment events overlapping and biasing the treatment effect upward, or with treatment and control events overlapping and canceling out the treatment effect (Schutte & Donnay 2014, 4). Overlaps between treatment and control events are minimal in our sample, but the more inclusive spatiotemporal windows (e.g. 10 kilometers and 60 days) have same-type overlaps as high as 75%. To account for this potential bias, we match on the number of previous treatment and control events that overlap each event's spatiotemporal window. We also weight our difference-in-differences regression to account for the fact that

control events outnumber treatment events in our sample. 10

## 7 Discussion and Conclusion


This analysis contributes to the literature on rebel governance and civilian targeting in civil conflict. We identify temporally more violent dynamics in rebel conquered territory compared to contested areas that may be indicative of rebel efforts to violently establish governance in their territory. This result is in line with qualitative reports of the RUF committing indiscriminate violence against civilians in areas they controlled, such as reports that '[w]hile there was some targeting of particular groups, . . . the vast majority of atrocities were committed by rebels who chose their victims apparently at random. The arbitrary

nature of these attacks served to create an atmosphere of complete terror' (HRW 1999).

The results also fit Johnston's comparative case study of rebel groups' organizational structure, which shows that the RUF's rapid territorial expansion required them to delegate responsibilities to local rebel sub-units that operated relatively independently (2008). These sub-units did not necessarily have the organizational capacity to build up peaceful institutions to regulate civilian behavior. We show that civilians in territory that was recently captured, and thus may have been transferred to rebel units inexperienced in governing, experienced an increase in violence. In contrast to the finding that weak rebels are more likely to target civilians (Humphreys & Weinstein 2006, Wood 2010), we show that a group that is strong overall, such as the RUF during 1997 to 2001, can simultaneously be a temporally weak and violent ruler at the local level if the local branch of this rebel group is not accustomed to its role as ruler over civilians.

Given our extreme case selection, follow-up research should examine if other civil wars show the same violent transition period after territorial takeover. Diamond deposits reduced the importance of civilian support as a resource for rebels in Sierra Leone. 11 Other civil wars where rebel groups rely more heavily on local support for recruitment or revenue might reveal other transitional patterns. In these cases, Kalyvas' (2006) argument that violence generates civilian backlashes and is counterproductive for rebels might be more immediately applicable. This research agenda would improve our understanding of initial rebel governance and its immediate impact on civilian lives.

Furthermore, our analysis of event data does not let us systematically identify why the RUF attacked civilians. We postulate that the local population comes into conflict with the institutions rebel groups are attempting to set up in conquered territory. Rebel groups then respond with violence to enforce their new social order because they lack the knowledge or capabilities required to govern peacefully. Hence, transition periods are particularly violent for civilians. However, this causal claim needs further in-depth research on the actual motives of rebels to target civilians in newly-acquired territory.

Lastly, our findings are only possible due to recent methodological advances in integrating event data. The combination of ACLED and GED events with meltt is key to the findings of our analysis. A separate analysis using only civilian targeting events from ACLED fails to find any significant effects. 12 With only 1.38% of events overlapping between the two datasets according to our 10-day and 10-kilometer rule, our analysis highlights the need to integrate different datasets for more comprehensive analysis of micro-level conflict dynamics. ACLED

has 674 instances of RUF civilian targeting, while GED has 143, so the 817 combined RUF targeting events between the two datasets represents a 21% increase in data compared to ACLED alone. This substantial increase in data may explain why an analysis of ACLED alone yields a null result. Conflict event datasets may have different foci in their efforts to collect data, as discussed earlier, so integration is crucial when variables of interest are present in several datasets. In this case, integration also shows that looking only at certain patterns of civilian victimization rather than the full range of acts of civilian targeting may present misleading results which is why combining both fatal and nonfatal forms of civilian victimization is crucial for this analysis.

This research note examines patterns of violence against civilians following territorial conquest by rebel groups. Kalyvas assertively claims that 'gaining control over an area brings collaboration' (2006, 119). We provide a temporal extension to Kalyvas' argument by focusing on the transition from gaining control to governing territory. By combining event datasets and using matched wake analysis, we show that the RUF in Sierra Leone resorted to more violence against civilians in recently captured territory compared to areas without territorial takeover. This approach reveals that the establishment of rebel governance might be a violent process despite rebels' long term dependence on civilian support. When and under what circumstances this violent transition period turns into stable and nonviolent governance and the provision of public goods requires further research. We encourage researchers to make use of recent advancements in the collection and statistical modeling of event data to introduce more nuance into our theories of violence.
