## Discussion


Despite increasing recognition of the benefits of faculty diversity, empirical knowledge about the socioeconomic composition of university professors remains limited (e.g., Andersen 2001; Helin et al. 2019; Helin et al. 2023; Morgan et al. 2022). Using population-wide administrative microdata from Norway, this study offers a high-resolution analysis of socioeconomic diversity and inequality within the context of an egalitarian welfare state. Norway's policies, including tuition-free higher education, competitive PhD wages, and strong social welfare programs, are designed  to  mitigate  socioeconomic  inequalities.  Given  these  factors,  socioeconomic  background should arguably matter less for accessing and succeeding in academic positions; yet, our findings challenge this assumption. Despite  the fact  that  approximately 40% of faculty members come from families where neither parent holds a degree from higher education, our

findings clearly show that individuals from advantaged backgrounds are far more likely to secure faculty positions.

These disparities have remained largely stable across a period of unprecedented educational expansion. The academic landscape has undergone substantial changes over the past century (Compagnucci and Spigarelli 2020; Kerr 2001; Martin 2012; Schofer and Meyer 2005). However, these transformations have not reduced the link between social origins and the likelihood of becoming a faculty member. Similar to findings in the United States (Morgan et al. 2022), we find a stable link between having parents with higher education and the likelihood of securing a faculty position among cohorts born 30 years apart. Additionally, the relationship between parental earnings and the probability of becoming faculty members remains consistent across this period.

In this regard, a key question was whether the lack of socioeconomic diversity among academic faculty stems from processes occurring at earlier educational stages or from additional barriers between completing a PhD and gaining access to faculty positions for individuals from less  privileged backgrounds. Unlike previous studies from the United States (Morgan et al. 2022) and Finland (Helin et al. 2019), our findings reveal that differences in earlier stages of educational careers largely account for the disparities in access to faculty positions by parental education and earnings. When comparing individuals with similar educational levels, parents' education and earnings no longer predict lower likelihoods of obtaining faculty positions among those from less-advantaged families. However, individuals with faculty parents are still more likely to become professors themselves, even after adjustments of individuals' own education. Moreover, career penalties-such as lower earnings and fewer opportunities at prestigious institutions-persist for those from less privileged backgrounds, even among those who secure faculty roles. Thus, despite Norway's egalitarian welfare-state institutions, substantial barriers to socioeconomic diversity in academic careers remain.

We can only speculate why becoming a faculty member and succeeding in an academic career varies by socioeconomic background, even among individuals with similar educational levels. The early stages of academic careers are often marked by insecurity and challenging work conditions, leading many to exit the profession before securing tenure (Dorenkamp and Weiß 2018; Langenberg 2001). We hypothesized that  social  origin  could  buffer  this  stress through financial and psychological safety nets; however, our findings suggest that this is not the case, at least for parental education. Additionally, it remains unclear why hiring discrimination should differ between individuals with faculty parents and those with PhD-educated parents. One possible explanation is that faculty parents have a deeper understanding of navigating early academic careers, enabling their children to position themselves more favorably in the academic job market.

Expanding on these disparities, we find important variation across academic disciplines. Individuals  from  more  advantaged  backgrounds  are  more  likely  to  enter  certain  fields,  and within specific disciplines (e.g., medicine, law, and humanities), social origins still influence the likelihood of obtaining faculty positions even after controlling for individual education. For instance, when comparing individuals with similar educational levels, those with higher-educated parents have 50% greater likelihood of securing academic positions within the humanities and arts than those with only compulsory education, indicating that the academic career trajectories differ across fields.

Moreover, the prestige of academic positions varies, and while individuals with PhDeducated parents are no more likely to secure faculty positions than those with parents who have only compulsory education, they are still more likely to be employed in more prestigious institutions when comparing individuals with similar educational qualifications. Faculty from more advantaged backgrounds also tend to earn higher salaries, even after controlling not only for educational level and field but also sorting across institutions. This suggests that parental

education shapes academic careers beyond its effects through educational attainment. This finding aligns with observations in elite sectors of the business world, where upwardly mobile individuals often earn considerably less than their counterparts of high-status origins, indicating that  they  face  challenges  beyond  mere  entry  into  elite  professions  (Friedman  and  Laurison 2020).

Although we leverage population-wide data from Norway, our study has some limitations. Our analysis is confined to describing the likelihood of holding faculty positions by social origins  and  does  not  distinguish  between  whether  these  differences  stem  from  individual choices or barriers such as discrimination. Thus, our results should be interpreted as descriptive, as we naïvely compare individuals from different social origins with similar educational qualifications.  Individuals  from less advantaged backgrounds pursuing academic careers may be more positively selected on attributes such as academic talent and motivation, which are not fully captured in our analysis. This unmeasured heterogeneity may bias the perceived impact of social origins on career success within academia (Elwert and Winship 2014; Mare 2011).

In conclusion, although our findings indicate socioeconomic diversity among faculty members, persistent differences in the likelihood of becoming a faculty member based on social origins-particularly at more prestigious institutions-remain. Further research is needed to understand how social origins influence navigation within academic careers. However, since the differences in the likelihood of becoming faculty members are primarily explained by individual educational attainment, efforts to enhance diversity among academic faculty should prioritize equalizing educational opportunities, including ensuring fairness in the recruitment process for PhD positions.

## Introduction


In December 2022, around 1,000 business representatives attended the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15)- marking the 'first time the private sector had turned out in force for a biodiversity COP' (Hillsdon, 2022). Corporate influence at Convention for Biological Diversity (CBD) meetings is not new (Dempsey, 2016), but the private sector attendance at COP15 is indicative of current trends in biodiversity conservation: namely, the framing of biodiversity loss as a material financial risk to global capital (WEF, 2020), and the role of 'leveraging private finance' in achieving the vision of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD, 2022). Scholars have long examined the intersections of neoliberalism and conservation (McAfee, 1999; Sullivan 2013), yet there has been a rapid and recent increase in reference to 'biodiversity finance' in mainstream lexicon (OECD, 2020; UNDP, 2020).

Biodiversity (or conservation) finance broadly refers to financial flows where improving the state of biodiversity is a primary or secondary objective, or a co-benefit; encompassing public and private sources, and the use of various financial instruments (Meyers et al., 2020; OECD, 2020). While environmental markets have been in operation since at least the 1980s (Damiens et al., 2020; Lapeyre et al., 2015), more recently the private sector has been positioned as playing a major role in filling the shortfall or 'gap' in finance needed to effectively protect and restore global biodiversity has been highlighted (Bigger et al., 2021; Deutz et al., 2020; UNEP, 2021). This shift vests significant power to the private sector to play a major - if not primary - role in biodiversity governance (Auld et al., 2009)

Various discourses are mobilised to accelerate the latest neoliberal turn in conservation. To become attractive for private investors, biodiversity conservation is urged to become 'bankable' (WWF and Nature^Squared, 2020), investment-ready to 'unlock' private finance for (UNDP, 2020; World Bank Group, 2020) and 'pay for itself' (Kolinjivadi et al., 2019; Huwyler et al., 2016). Our focus on the discourses of biodiversity finance responds to a large body of scholarship on neoliberal conservation which has spanned over two decades (Apostolopoulou et al., 2021; Brockington and Duffy, 2010; Büscher et al., 2012; Holmes and Cavanagh, 2016; Igoe and Brockington, 2007; Sullivan 2013). Scholars argue that neoliberal conservation has delivered negligible finance to conservation (Dempsey and Suarez, 2016) and 'largely failed to create the profitable markets they pursue nearly anywhere in the world' (Fletcher, 2023, p. 4), yet its material effects emerge via the

entrenchment of market logics that effectively depoliticise biodiversity loss; foreclosing alternative solutions and entrenching existing power dynamics and dominant knowledge systems (Sullivan, 2013). The paradox here is that while these discourses of neoliberal natures (Bakker, 2010; Bigger and Dempsey, 2018) are significantly disconnected from conservation outcomes, they have profound, wide-reaching material consequences, and they endure.

This remarkable endurance of neoliberal conservation, in its various forms over several decades and across diverse contexts (Apostolopoulou et al., 2021), highlights the need for ongoing deconstruction of the discursive mechanics by which it is sustained, and the material consequences of these discourses. Here we contribute to this collective, scholarly labour by considering neoliberal conservation in its latest manifestation of 'biodiversity finance', drawing on data collected within 12 months of the commencement of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The GBF explicitly aims for the closure of the biodiversity finance gap of $700 billion per year, including through 'innovative schemes' including '…green bonds, biodiversity offsets and credits', and calls for governments to use 'legal, administrative or policy measures' to enable businesses to disclose biodiversity-related risks, dependencies and impacts (CBD, 2022).

Neoliberal conservation scholarship has predominantly focussed on empirical case studies in the Global South (Apostolopoulou et al., 2021). In this study we examine biodiversity finance from the sites of its discursive production in Australia, a wealthy settler-colonial state with a long track record of neoliberal conservation (Lockwood and Davidson, 2010), and largely unmatched levels of biodiversity loss (Woinarski et al., 2015). The Australian federal government is actively encouraging for-profit conservation, including through what has been called the world's first legislated national voluntary biodiversity market (NatureFinance and Pollination, 2023). This in-depth single case study generates 'local knowledge from which can be derived unique understanding' of the financialisation inherent in biodiversity finance that respects its situated complexity (Bazeley, 2013, p. 410).

Conceptually, we position our work in the context of pathways to resistance and disruption. We model the utility of an ecologies of knowledge approach, which eschews hegemonic claims of distinct knowledges and instead favours whatever configuration of heterogeneity a particular problem calls for (de Sousa Santos, 2018). We use Foucauldian Discourse Analysis (FDA) to facilitate the interrogation of knowledge and power inherent in neoliberal

conservation and overlay critical and regulatory theory to enrich the FDA. In response to the data, we consider Mbembe's (2003) Necropolitics to understand the material effects of socalled 'innovative schemes', namely biodiversity offsets and credits. Regulatory theory (Levi-Faur 2006; Braithwaite 2008) is used to further interrogate the paradoxical endurance of neoliberal conservation via ongoing government intervention (Fletcher, 2023; Kiely, 2018). In doing so, we arrive at regulation as a key site where cycles of neoliberal conservation may be disrupted. Mapping these pathways may support practiced resistance in our case study.

Our chief contribution is empirical. We identify two primary discourses of neoliberal conservation in our case study: The Innovative Spirit, and Regulation. Specifically, we highlight tradeable biodiversity units as the primary object of innovation, and the role of the 'innovators' - elite, frequently male, intermediaries with financial expertise - in promoting and enabling the endurance of neoliberal conservation in its current form of biodiversity finance. We also identify how persistent ambiguity in regulatory purpose conceals and obscures the continued reliance on government and regulation for neoliberal conservation to persist. Beneath these discourses, our findings also reveal a pervasive theme of fear, particularly around disclosure schemes, and unpacks material consequences of these discourses for threatened biodiversity in particular This offers a situated and novel empirical contribution which may offer potential pathways for disruption to neoliberal conservation.

The paper proceeds as follows. We first briefly lay out the broader context of neoliberal conservation that informs Australian discourses of biodiversity finance. Second, we unpack our ecologies of knowledge approach, whereby we first we introduce the diverse traditions of knowledge we draw from. We then briefly describe Foucauldian Discourse Analysis as vehicle for the analysis undertaken in this paper, and then detail the methodology. Following this, we explore and unpack the empirical findings from the research within our two primary discourses of innovation and regulation. We conclude by reflecting on opportunities for disruption, that is, pathways for materially better outcomes for biodiversity


## Situating discourses of biodiversity finance


Biodiversity finance in Australia is influenced by various contexts, but one that we will highlight here is that of neoliberal natures (see for example Bakker, 2005; 2010; Bigger and Dempsey, 2018; Castree 2008a,b, McAfee, 1999). The Australian move to financialise biodiversity is, as indicated above, part of a longer history that has drawn the environment

and the market - once fundamentally oppositional phenomena - together in mutually benefiting symbiosis (Bakker, 2010). Whilst the environment has fed the market since its inception, within this context of neoliberal natures, it is the market that is necessary for nature's survival. Conservation is thus 'tied to the very forces and logics that degrade and destroy nature in the first place' (Fletcher and Büscher, 2017). The environmental crisis has discursive, social and material elements (Bakker, 2010), and we acknowledge that this also is the case for solutions presented to address this crisis.

In locating its momentum in market action, conservation discourse enters into a rich scholarly debate which questions whether or not capitalism and neoliberalism can drive or even yield environmentally transformative outcomes (Holleman, 2018). Some scholars argue that the requisite innovation which is needed to reform the relationship between humans and nature is in fact born from the 'capitalist entrepreneurial spirit' (Bosch and Schmidt 2019; Herzog and Honneth, 2016). Within this framing, it is only the financial world that is conducive to the creative problem solving needed to meet the crisis of nature. In contrast, critical scholars point to the inherent contradictions contained within the logic, or faith, that capital accumulation can correct the negative ecological consequences of capitalism (Brockington and Duffy, 2010; Büscher et al., 2012; Büscher and Fletcher, 2015; McAfee, 2012), and the poor track record of neoliberal conservation approaches in delivering material finance for conservation (Dempsey and Suarez, 2016).

Financialization is a concurrent and overlapping way of understanding this relationship between capitalism and the environment, that recognizes the increased role of financial logics, actors and institutions in the economy and its governance (Epstein, 2019).While financialization is a rather nebulous concept and has a plethora of meanings (Christophers, 2015; Epstein, 2021), we use a critical definition of financialization here due to our engagement with power. Bracking (2012a: 274) defines financialization as 'a technology of power which uses the money form to quantify human and physical contexts, privilege financial parameters in decision-making, and ultimately return decisions over resources in favour of money-holders in contexts of contested uses and meanings for the non-human world'. Rendering nature into financialized forms both abstracts and conceals their power and material effects - notably, the resulting distribution of financial benefits, and loci of control in environmental governance (Sullivan, 2013; 2018).

The core success of the neoliberal conservation project has been to 'fail forward' (Fletcher, 2023) - just like cutting the head off the hydra, the failure of one 'innovative scheme' to deliver material conservation outcomes seemingly leads to the emergence of many more. While largely failing to motivate actual finance, the salience of for-profit conservation discourse is reshaping conservation and entrenching power relations; power relations which have historically primarily contributed to biodiversity decline and social inequities (Büscher et al., 2012; Büscher and Fletcher, 2015; Dempsey and Suarez. 2016; Holmes and Cavanagh, 2016; Sullivan, 2013).

A range of discursive strategies enable the continued endurance of neoliberal conservation and its material effects. Büscher et al., (2012) identified three main approaches, namely positive, 'win-win' rhetoric (Muradian et al., 2013) and promotion of easily consumable solutions to systemic, complex problems that conceal inherent contradictions, the use of 'spectacle' to promote and manage the appearance of these solutions, often via 'greenwashing' (Brockington and Duffy, 2010; Holmes and Cavanagh, 2016; Igoe et al., 2010), and silencing of dissenting voices - which may occur via active suppression, or more subtly as cathartic expressions of doubt or concern that nonetheless has no impact on the hegemonic system (Watt, 2021). More specific strategies include the use of language and metaphor which steers problems towards economic or financial solutions (Büscher et al., 2012; Coffey, 2016), disavowal of failure and simultaneous faith in the same or closely related solution, potentially with a new name (Fletcher, 2013; 2023; Redford et al., 2013; Watt, 2021), and persistent absence of what advocates of neoliberal conservation consider to be key enablers of biodiversity markets, including appropriate data, units of measurement, and government regulation (Dempsey, 2016).


## An ecologies of knowledge approach


Neoliberal conservation scholarship has drawn on a diverse range of theoretical approaches (Apostolopoulou et al., 2021), though we note that a conceptual bifurcation between poststructuralist and Marxist approaches exists in the literature. While some scholars have sought to reconcile these two conflicting approaches (Fletcher, 2013; 2023; Sullivan, 2013; Watt, 2021), in this study we employ an ecologies of knowledge approach (de Sousa Santos, 2018), which prioritises a heterogeneity of knowledges in a given intervention. Our gentle use of the poststructuralist contributions of Foucault through FDA (Foucault, 1984, 1976, 2013) is a tool of enabling this epistemic diversity.

FDA supports interrogation and recognition of power and knowledge relations, and promotes the analysis of silences alongside discourses (Escobar 1984). This is particularly relevant in the context of biodiversity governance, where the non-human object of the intervention is unable to 'speak'. That being said, Foucault's work on power and discourse is complex, arguably laden with 'cryptic philosophies', and there is an enduring lack of explicit technique to further this analysis (Khan and MacEachen, 2021). FDA may therefore draw on various aspects of Foucault's work and to abductively pull learnings from other traditions. The benefit of these engagements is to help in unpacking the material futures linked to dominant discourses on biodiversity finance.

For one, in response to the data, we bring in a brief discussion of Necropolitics, Mbembe's (2003) critique of Foucault's construction of state power. power. Necropolitics reveal a necroeconomy, which operates to subjugate life to the power of death. Whilst Necropolitics is a theory of racism, it has been extended to non-human, ecological fields (Dunlap and Laratte, 2022). Here we contend that Necropolitics has great use in deconstructing technocratic and financialised constructions masking death.

Moreover, we draw regulatory theory into the power analysis (Levi-Faur 2006; Braithwaite 2008). At is core, regulatory theory explores the steering of events to a certain outcome. Placed in the light of critical scholarship, regulatory theory can be seen as concerning the the micro and macroscopic applications of power (Drahos 2017; Foucalt 2013). Regulation changes the way society is organised, and the governance of economies and production (Drahos 2017), thus regulatory purpose can be seen as an important schema that sets out key configurations of power. Unpacking latent regulatory purposes is critical for understanding the material futures regulatory discourses are steering towards (Anantharajah, 2021).

It is important to note that critical limits exist in this analysis, the most urgent being the inclusion of Indigenous voices. This research was undertaken in a settler colonial context. Whilst Indigenous peoples are often framed as one of the potential co-beneficiaries of biodiversity finance (UNEP, 2023; WEF, 2022), including in this dataset, empirical work centring Indigenous peoples as agents of biodiversity finance remains a critical research agenda. We also note that we did not identify specific discourses related to Indigenous peoples in our data, and the absence of Indigenous voices from our research participants means that this manuscript cannot unpack how various discourses, including the role of Indigenous people in protecting biodiversity (e.g Fernández-Llamazares et al., 2024) may

lead to material consequences for Indigenous peoples in particular. In recognising this silence, we highlight that the focus of the paper stops short of recommendations of what might replace for-profit conservation, as such alternatives will be reliant on Indigenous voices and knowledges.


## Methodology


The data for this study is derived from twenty-nine (29) semi-structured interviews conducted between February and September 2022. Ethical approval was granted by the University of New South Wales Human Research Advisory Panel (HC210706). Participants were selected based on their active professional involvement in biodiversity finance and carbon farming (i.e land-based carbon offsets; Evans, 2018) within Australia, including state or federal government, agriculture, natural resource management, conservation, standards/third party certifiers, financial institutions, carbon service providers, and other relevant non-government bodies. Recruitment occurred through a combination of purposive and referral sampling, starting with existing contacts, and then actively seeking to fill gaps for maximum variation sampling (Creswell, 2012).

Participants were provided a sample interview guide and a participant information sheet prior to accepting or declining the interview request, and either written or verbal consent was obtained. Interviews took place over Zoom and were recorded using the Zoom recording (video and sound) and transcription software. Questioning was broadly structured according to the interview guide but was flexibly adapted to support conversational flow and the capture of any emergent issues. The interview transcripts produced by Zoom were checked and edited manually and then provided to all participants, who had the opportunity to check the transcript for inaccuracies or ambiguities and make any necessary revisions.

The data was analysed and coded using the software MaxQDA 2022 (VERBI Software, 2021). Triangulation primarily occurred though the use of additional investigators. MCE conducted the interviews, and KA and MCE analysed the text, following repeated rereadings. The coding process identified key discourses in the texts, including objects of the discourse, and themes (Carabine, 2001, cited in Keller, 2012). Further, alternative perspectives, or counter discourses were identified, as were particular loci of silence or marginalisation.


## The Innovative Spirit


This group of discourses captures key elements of financialised discourse (Bosch and Schmidt, 2019; Dempsey and Suarez, 2016) and contained several sub-discourses. Firstly, the endeavour of financially valuing nature was a central thread. Secondly, tradeable biodiversity units were positioned as a primary object of the discourse. Thirdly, biodiversity emerges as a subordinate object in its relationships to profit, and subsequently to carbon. Fourthly, we explore the power held by the 'innovators' of biodiversity finance. Lastly, we examine the use of temporality as a discursive strategy.


## Innovation: ascribing value to nature


The process of ascribing a financialised value to nature recurred as a preoccupation for interviewees, framed explicitly or implicitly as a missing piece or panacea:

'So, until we start to recognize that the only way we're going to crowd in the capital is to get it [nature] recognized as an asset and that we treat the capital more in the context of innovation, private sector operation, all those sorts of things, we're just going in circles' (#20).

Innovation is a central part of financialisaton, with some scholars going so far as to say that financial innovation is financialisation (Epstein, 2021, citing Vercelli, 2013). It is important here to see that what is being innovated is not only financial products, but also nature itself: it is shaped through this discourse. The translation of nature into a form that 'humanity can do business with' (Verran, 2013, p 36) means conservation occurs only when profitable (Apostolopoulou et al., 2021; Büscher et al., 2012). Yet not all aspects of biodiversity are likely to generate financial returns, such as threatened species conservation (Ward and Lassen, 2018, p 27). Research participants primarily highlighted opportunities for profit via 'sustainable agriculture and sustainable forestry, potentially sustainable fisheries' (#2) or attached to carbon revenue (#4), but articulated goals to derive income 'purely' (#2) from investment in biodiversity conservation through the future development of biodiversity credits (#2), research and innovation (#16) or involvement of government (#21).

Here, the material consequences of the discourse emerges through absence: what happens to the components of biodiversity that fail to be attached to profitable investments? As the innovation apparently required to deliver investable biodiversity projects continues to be

relegated to the future (Dempsey and Suarez, 2016), the overall trend of biodiversity loss continues.


## The discursive object of innovation: the tradable biodiversity unit


The interviews revealed the development of a tradable unit(s) for biodiversity as the primary object of innovation (Dempsey, 2016, p 180):

- '…how do you develop a unit, a proper unit… because everyone does want a tradeable unit. But it's very challenging to create' (#4)

The innovation required to develop a biodiversity 'unit' or 'metric' reduces the complexity of nature into a form that 'capital can see' (Robertson, 2006), framing it as something that is severable, and not fundamentally complex and relational. Such a characterisation furthers particular knowledge systems: nature is transformed into traditional property, something that can be owned rather than something that we, including businesses, must live in relation with (Moreton-Robinson, 2015). There are clear material risks for biodiversity in the use of generalised biodiversity units, most acutely for highly threatened, irreplaceable or slow to mature components that can, through the homogenisation required by general metrics, be substituted by less threatened biodiversity that is cheaper and easier to replace (Maron et al., 2023; Wunder et al., 2024).

Many participants acknowledged the fundamental difficulty or even impossibility of valuing nature in a quantifiable, financial sense, while simultaneously asserting its inevitability:

- '…biodiversity is not a fungible concept, except with biodiversity offset credits and so on' (#20). The interviews revealed a pervasive contradictory logic in this respect. Despite the apparent importance of developing biodiversity 'units', it was not always clear who would purchase the unit(s) or why, because the potential buyers 'haven't clarified their own drivers' (#8). Other interviewees expressed more confidence:

'So, there's two sets of buyers, I think. One set is around wanting to invest and generate a return and the other set is around wanting to have, not 'offset impact' because that's probably unlikely to be the language, I think it's more likely to be 'compensate for the impact'' (#11)

The quote above suggests an apparent disavowal of biodiversity offsets (Lapeyre, et al., 2015), but the careful use of language is also illustrative of recent discussion around so-called voluntary biodiversity credits (NatureFinance and Pollination, 2023; WEF, 2022). The term

'biodiversity credit' has often been used to refer to the units of biodiversity gains that are traded to offset biodiversity losses within regulated regimes (Wunder, et al., 2024), but has been more recently (re)defined by industry proponents as tradeable biodiversity units that aim to '… achieve a net positive outcome without directly offsetting negative impacts elsewhere' (NatureFinance and Pollination, 2023, p. 16) and differ from offsets via '…the intention of the purchase and the claims that are made around that purchase' (WEF 2022, p. 4, emphasis in original).

The distinction between offsets and so-called voluntary biodiversity credits appears blurred both in concept and in practice (Wunder et al., 2024), and indeed it is difficult to not be reminded of Redford et al.'s (2013) three steps to identifying conservation 'fads': abnegation or disavowal of the previous approach, followed by renaming of the new approach (which incorporates 'strong elements of the approach it is replacing'), and insistence of its novelty. Disavowal enables failure to be sustained, in seeking to bridge the gap between the observed and normative expectations for neoliberal conservation (Fletcher 2013, 2023; Watt, 2021).

Offsets play a foundational role in the construction of tradeable biodiversity units: indeed, throughout the data, offsets appear in many linguistic disguises. The substantive matter that is reflected by the credit is obfuscated, whereby the demand for credits is generated by '…enough destruction happening on the other side of the balance sheet to require the credits' (#1). Regardless of the varied intentions around the purchase of biodiversity credits, its core logics are predicated on death, and indeed in on-going biodiversity destruction.

The language of 'credit' disguises 'necropolitical features of the economy' hidden by normality (Dunlap and Laratte, 2022; Mbembe, 2003). Necropolitics allows us to reconceptualise the creation of biodiversity markets ('every man and their dog are trying to come up with a biodiversity credit', #9) as engaging important questions of survival, that are obfuscated by financial framings. Arguably from the discourse on biodiversity credits, it is the translation of nature through financialised logics that allows for ongoing trajectories of biodiversity decline:

- '…if … you've got a big negative side of your environment that you need to offset… is that conservation, or is that just facilitating or sanctioning of existing practices? I don't know.' (#1)

Here, despite the discourse of innovation, we can see that power rests where it historically has, and its material effects entrench biodiversity loss and 'decisions over resources in favour of money-holders' (Bracking, 2012)


## Innovating profitable biodiversity: subordinate relationships


A closely linked discursive pattern explores the relationship between profit and biodiversity. Financial profit signifies an existential benchmark ('We don't exist if we don't deliver returns to investors', #26), whereas biodiversity outcomes were consistently positioned by participants as subordinate, either implicitly or explicitly (such as through its designation as a 'co-benefit'; Mayrhofer and Gupta, 2016). This is not a surprising finding; subordination of nature has long been a recognized relational dynamic when nature is engaged through financialized processes (e.g Bracking, 2012).

How does this discursive relegation affect biodiversity in the material world? As previously discussed, it means that biodiversity will only attract private finance where the rate of financial return is deemed satisfactory by investors. This space for symbiosis is narrow (Kedward et al., 2023; Dempsey and Suarez, 2016), hence the primary beneficiaries of this discourse are those who already hold power:

'People looking at nature and climate related work, and they want to know what the internal rate of return is, they want to know how they can make money out of it. And I'm a little bit concerned with that trend because it means that the people who created the problem are turning around and making money out of solving it, and there's a problem with that' (#16)

The primacy of financial returns (at an acceptable level or benchmark) has also discursively created a relationship where biodiversity is subordinate to carbon, which is more readily commodifiable and already established as a financial product (Evans, 2018; Watt, 2021):

- '…they are used to investing in carbon, and they're going to try and think about investing in biodiversity in the same way.' (#2)

This logic further entrenches existing practices and knowledge systems, and risks overlooking components of biodiversity that are not associated with profitable carbon projects (Reside et al., 2017)


## Innovators as experts: elite relationality


Another key discursive feature was the 'innovators' themselves:

13

'They're the innovators, they know how to operate these assets, they know how to deal with customers, a whole bunch of things' (#20).

These financialised identities manifest in terms of 'big players,' 'smart guy[s]'. The innovators are celebrated:

'He was the catalyst. He was the person with the money. So, he had three billion, I think, about under management at that time' (#26).

It is important to highlight here that the expertise of these 'innovators', who are advocating marketised policy agendas or developing new biodiversity financial products, are often implicitly or explicitly men:

'I know it's only guys, [person Z], does it a bit too. He's mostly biodiversity offsets, but it's men. It is.' (#8).

Apostolopoulou et al., (2021) notes a lack of attention to the dynamics of gender (in addition to class and race) in existing neoliberal conservation literature, and our data suggests such intersections warrant further exploration.

Instances of successful financing of biodiversity were observed to be frequently the product of the relationship between elites (Holmes, 2011). One participant noted '…now it's [biodiversity finance] on the agenda because the important people say it's on the agenda, and it's affecting important things, right.' (#19) Another observed '…personal relationships matter, and that's what really drives these investments' (#8). For the actors who fail to embed themselves within these elite networks, the likelihood of attracting finance for their conservation projects thus appears slim.

The expertise of the innovators yields power (Mitchell, 2002), and is often discursively protected and maintained by a veil of complexity, which was a significant theme in the discourse:

'They're trying to sell you know green bonds and they're trying to attach a bunch of really interesting things to the equity players and all this very complex stuff, that I must admit I don't understand' (#4).

The data revealed that complexity was indeed used as a means of obfuscating the links between the discursive and the material, and moreover to uphold claims of expertise.

Power emerges as a critical consequence of this discourse: a key theme in the data was the emergence of a powerful class of intermediaries. These experts are arguably the winners of the material conditions that emerge from such discourse:

'The scheme is so complex and so convoluted that you need an intermediary with [a financial services license] and deep pockets to really engage in the space, and that's not the way it should be.'  (#16)

In the case of biodiversity finance, intermediaries are highly influential yet are not particularly visible (Tobin et al., 2023). The material benefits accumulated by this class are finance, political access, as well as the recognition of expertise. These alliances between the capitalist, financial sector and nature are uneasy ones (Irvine-Broque and Dempsey, 2023), given the former relies on 'destroying nature as an essential part of their self-reproduction.' (Spash, 2022, p. 8)


## Future temporalities


This final discursive thread comprising The Innovative Spirit , is that of future, potentially illusory temporalities. Here, the discourse emerges with the future promise of innovation: '…finally distilling something in a couple of years that may possibly be very powerful' (#4). The belief is that profitable biodiversity markets, and 'big, big money' is 'on the horizon, about to explode, just around the next corner' (Dempsey and Suarez, 2016, p.667). Or as put by another participant:

'The same is happening now with biodiversity, people saying, 'oh no one's going to buy those things'. But we'll have a massive industry around it, in the next five years, I'd say probably sooner' (#11).

Temporalities can be mobilized as a discursive strategy to legitimate the various preparatory interventions required to facilitate private investment in biodiversity (Dempsey and Suarez, 2016). A key takeaway here is that there are material impacts of discourses in biodiversity finance, including those that are ideological, fervent, and almost spiritual (Watt, 2021). The promise of future capital paves the way for various market based structural reforms that, as discussed in the following section, typically require government intervention (Fletcher, 2023).

In analyzing discourse and power surrounding biodiversity finance, it is important to acknowledge counter discourses that emerge (Keller, 2012). One particularly powerful

critique was attached to the central assumption underpinning much of the discourses highlighted in this section, the assumption that finance is the best way to solve the problem of biodiversity loss:

'So, I think that what's missing with much of this, and coming back to your topic of finance is, what is the problem we're trying to solve, and why are we assuming that it's a financial problem? That's something that I wonder, why do we think it's a financial problem? Why are we saying we need to crowd in private finance to resolve biodiversity issues? That's inconsistent with the way markets work and the way everything else works, so why are we?' (# 20).

Critiquing the inherent and foundational issue of relying on finance to fix non-financial problems is a recurrent feature of the literature (Bracking, 2015; Dempsey and Suarez, 2016; Watt, 2021). Yet the challenge remains the translation of critique into the material world: 'disciplining of dissenting voices…can perversely be stimulated as some kind of catharsis, without impacting on the broader hegemonic system' (Buscher et al., 2012) or disrupting it (Watt, 2021).


## Regulation


This discursive theme was made up of four sub-discourses. First, the interviews revealed tension between competing regulatory purposes. Second, we explore the way relationships, power and the role of government are shaped by regulatory capitalism. Third, we examine how gaps in public functions may faciltate these neoliberal discourses. Lastly, we unpack the discursive role of risk and fear in the data.


## Regulatory purpose


Despite the prominence of regulation in the interviews, there was an enduring uncertainty as to what kind of regulation was being referred to. This manifested in conflicting regulatory purposes (Parker and Braithwaite 2003). The first regulatory purpose, as described explicitly and implicitly by participants, was to create the necessary regulatory structures for biodiversity markets to be established (Dempsey, 2016, p 186). Part of creating this enabling environment involved doing so with the requisite policy certainty: 'I think no company is going to take a risk if they think they're going to become undone. So, I think there needs to be policy clarity there' (#25). Another aspect was through developing appropriate standards

and metrics for measuring and quantifying biodiversity, which one participant indicated '… is the least that government can facilitate (#20)'.

The concern, echoed by numerous participants, surrounding the need for standards was challenged by one participant who highlighted the potential disconnect between metrics and the ecological materialities they purportedly represent:

'Because you don't need better metrics to understand 80% of what's going on. And when we've been given better metrics, so say with carbon, we've had 20 years of improving carbon metrics and yet emissions continue to grow. So, I don't buy it, to be honest. Certainly, better quality information, understanding impacts better, all of those things will help us, but to have untreated sewerage going into river systems that are supporting a lot of aquatic life, it doesn't take a rocket scientist or biologist to understand that that's not going to be good for the ecology' (#21)

This links to the second, opposing regulatory purpose put forward by a minority of participants, those which centre on-ground, material conservation. One participant noted that regulation to '…protect the downside, or to encourage people to not go down that path' was critical to prevent environmental harms, but emphasised it wasn't sufficient to incentivise improved outcomes:  '…if people are sitting there thinking the regulatory framework is going to transform what happens, they are fucking deluded. It's just not going to happen' (#26).

While the participant above (#26) is referring to a compliance-based regulatory framework that seeks to minimise environmental losses, it is noteworthy that in contrast, a lack of government regulation was considered by participants as a major barrier to unleashing the transformative power of biodiversity markets (Dempsey, 2016, p 186). Ambigious reference to 'regulation' or 'regulatory environment' arguably conceals regulatory purpose (Parker and Braithwaite 2003) and the core role of government and regulation to facilitate the pathbreaking functions of the entreprenuerial 'innovators' and associated financialised biodiversity products. While the paradoxical reliance of market based approaches on government intervention is well established in both the neoliberal conservation literature (Fletcher, 2023; Kiely, 2018) and in regulatory theory (Levi-Faur 2006), here we contend that ambiguity in regulatory purpose acts as a discursive strategy that can not only assist in explaining the endurance of neoliberal conservation, but disavowal of some types of government regulation but not others.


## Regulatory capitalism, power and the role of government


Applying regulatory capitalism (Braithwaite 2008; Levi-Faur 2006) to our data sees key relational and power dynamics at play:

'So the capital allocators are the ones that can change the trajectory of the earth, not governments… the government's got to be there with the frameworks and the regulatory rules to make sure that that can happen appropriately.' (#26)

This quote directly articulates a collection of discourses that frames the private sector as the necessary leader in avoiding environmental collapse (Bakker, 2010), but also exposes the paradoxical reliance of neoliberal conservation on government intervention (Fletcher, 2023; Kiely, 2018). The government, and regulators are positioned in rhetoric as ancillary to the path breaking function of the private sector, thus affording the 'innovators' and other private actors with significant power to influence the extent to which, and the specific components of biodiversity, that will ultimately be protected, restored, or destroyed (Auld et al., 2009).

Interestingly, interviewees limit the role of government by repeated reference to the dominant interests of the market: 'To what degree, are we [government] market makers, or market facilitators, or market supporters--' (#6). There was near-silence on notion of the government as market constrainers (though see #26 above), and critically the regulatory purpose of limiting the scope and depth of commodification (Levi-Faur, 2006,  p 297).

There is also little recognition in the data on a direct role of government for conservation outside of the market rhetoric. A key element of the quote (#6) extracted above, is the fact that this view was emanating from within the public sector: these discourses were not only being produced by the private sector, they also formed a central part of how public servants saw the role of government. From both public and private zones, government is framed as useful administrators for market based responses to biodiversity, and public finance is seen as primarily the function of de-risking private finance (Gabor, 2021):

'They want government to wear the risk, they want government to put money forward and wear the risk.' (#20)

The potential for regulation to steer society towards biodiversity-centric outcomes is substantionally constrained by this subordinance to market rationales. This particular manifestation of regulatory capitalism critically links to Bracking's (2012) definition of financialisation, '…as a technology of power…' . Here, we can see the regulatory purpose of

the state being constrained by financialised logics, and this is indeed a product of power, reproduced and upheld through discourse. This raises an important question for the Australian and global community: is the primary regulatory purpose of the state to halt biodiversity decline, or to create profitable markets predicated on the death of ecosystems (Mbembe 2003)?.

## Is the private sector filling a "gap'?

Beyond the discursive power of financialised logics, other rationales for these power configurations include the critique that government has failed, and is failing to respond to biodiversity decline:

- 'And unfortunately, I see it means they're not responding to regulatory failures by raising regulatory standards, they're not spending money on things like recovery plans or they're not doing the what I would call the standard conservation things you expect from Australia…' (#1).

Australia's environmental regulations have been subject to long-term critique over their effectiveness (Woinarski et al., 2017), with an independent review concluding in 2020 that its national environmental law is 'ineffective' and 'not fit to address current or future environmental challenges' (Samuel, 2020). Similarly, public expenditure on conservation in Australia is an order of magnitude less than what is required: conservatively estimated to be around AUD 2 billion per year (Wintle et al., 2019). The Australian government has responded to this need to increase conservation funding by seeking to 'supercharge private investment in nature', because addressing biodiversity loss is 'a massive job' and government 'can't do it alone' (Plibersek, 2023a, b).

The potential for private investment in biodiversity is periliously overstated, as is the incapacity of public finance to counter the loss of biodiversity (Kedward et al., 2023). The rationale that the public sector is unable to shoulder the full cost of biodiversity conservation has gained traction as part of a broader narrative which emphasises the 'finance gap' or shortfall between the money currently available, and what is needed to cease and reverse biodiversity loss. This 'gap', naturally, can only be filled by the private sector (Bigger et al., 2021; Deutz et al., 2020). When gaps in public functions and austerity are treated 'as an immutable reality' (Dempsey et al, 2021), financial logics are able to find clear opportunities to to steer regulatory agendas towards material futures that ultimately benefit capital holders and risk further biodiversity loss.


## Fear, risk and the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD)


Fear, for the most part manifested in languages of risk, which was one of the most dominant discourses in the data. Constructions of risk tended to surround financial risk: '…what are the risks to our investments?' (#28). This included risk surrounding access to capital due to future regulation: '…we're going to get ticked off or struck off and we won't even be able to apply for finance.' (#4). Perceptions of risk also surround the potential for corporate embarrassment or shaming: 'They are shit scared …that, you know, effectively they're going to get caught out, named and shamed.' (#4). Lastly, fear was considered to be an effective motivator for the private sector to effectively address biodiversity loss: 'I mean, I love fear. This should hurt. This should be really, really painful' (#14).

The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) was repeatedly cited as a development that was generating fear, almost a future reckoning, by the majority of participants: 'I think that TNFD is a fait accompli in a way.' (#5). The TNFD is an industryled voluntary corporate disclosure initiative that seeks to enable firms to identify and report on its nature-related impacts, dependencies, risks and opportunities, with the 'ultimate aim of supporting a shift in global financial flows away from nature-negative outcomes and toward nature-positive outcomes' (TNFD, 2023). The theory of change assumed by the TNFD, that disclosure of information to the market can enable 'more positive outcomes for nature and society', has been questioned by some scholars (Christophers, 2017; Irvine-Broque and Dempsey, 2023).

The TNFD is by no means a regulatory 'stick', the lack of which was noted by participants , 1 but this does not mean it is not powerful. This is reflective of the ongoing opportunity for 'new environmental governance' where commercial and non-commercial third parties scrutinise the regulated (Gunningham et al., 1998). Yet there are also issues with state abrogation of primary regulatory responsibility - in particular, the significant opportunity for greenwashing, due to co-option or limited resources. Indeed, greenwashing emerged as a key locus for risk discourses, yet it was subordinate to the financial and public image risk discourses. Synergies are clear here with the existing work exploring archetypical discourses, such as that of 'spectacle' (Busher et al. 2012; Brockington and Duffy, 2010; Holmes and Cavanagh, 2016; Igoe et al., 2010). The palpable fear surrounding the growing expectation to disclose nature-related financial risks (which may become mandatory in future, subject to

government intervention), highlights this fear as a novel contribution and potential locus for disruption.

What does this pervasive, fear-based discourse tell us about power? Arguably, that 'no power is absolute' (Anderson, 2015). If we explore the notion that to protect biodiversity, corporate and financial actors must themselves be regulated rather than regulation operating to enable their agendas (Irvine-Broque and Dempsey, 2023), these loci of fear may prove important pressure points for regulatory intervention.


## Conclusion


The scope for biodiversity conservation that delivers financial profit is minimal: in substance comprising only 'slivers of slivers of slivers' (Dempsey and Suarez, 2016, p. 667). In Australia, as noted by participant # 8, '…it's such a narrow band of conservation that can generate a financial return'. And yet, discourse surrounding biodiversity finance inhabits grandiose dimensions, which act to maintain existing power structures and trajectories of biodiversity loss.

Here, an ecologies of knowledge approach (de Sousa Santos, 2018) and Foucauldian Discourse Analysis (FDA) has conceptually enabled the use a messy entanglement of both critical and regulatory theory to interrogate and expose power relations in our data, revealing discourses centred around innovation and regulation. In doing so, our empirical findings contribute to and build on the existing neoliberal conservation literature in several ways. First, our analysis revealed how the simultaneously impossible yet inevitable promise of tradeable biodiversity units offers capital holders a new opportunity to offset and ultimately maintain biodiversity loss while disavowing offsets. We provide new insights on the material consequences of these discourses, including the risks to highly threatened components of biodiversity that are overlooked by generalised metrics, or fail to be associated with profitable investments.  Second, we highlight the powerful role of the often-male 'innovators' in promoting and enabling marketised discourses, whose elite networks and expert knowledge are critical for navigating the complexity of biodiversity finance. Third, ambiguity in regulatory purpose could assist in explaining the endurance of neoliberal conservation. Finally, we identify fear, risk and the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures as potential loci for disruption of power relations and regulatory purpose.

In exposing existing power relations, we have found several opportunities for creative regeneration (Mahanty et al., 2023) and hopeful futures (Haraway, 2016) that may offer materially better outcomes for biodiversity. For one, we see an opportunity, or rather a necessity, to displace the market knowledges that shrink, sever and minimise nature with epistemologies that embrace the connections, relationships and indeed the centrality of nature (Brigg, 2016; de Sousa Santos, 2018). A multiplicity of knowledge must be deployed to this end, opening up space and creating momentum to displace fictitious, fantastical solutions (Fletcher, 2023, Watt, 2021). Despite the appeal of neoliberal conservation being a reduced burden on government, for-profit conservation requires significant financial and regulatory investment from government, who must continually step in to attempt market correction and 'address problems left unresolved in the process' (Fletcher, 2023). To disrupt this pattern of failure, the regulatory purpose of protecting biodiversity must be revived, both discursively and materially (Dafermos et al., 2021; Mazzucato, 2016).

## Introduction


This paper reports on the findings of a study investigating the development of Algerian University learners' intercultural competence (IC) when engaged in virtual intercultural exchanges (or  lack  thereof).  Such  partnerships  contain  activities  designed  to  help  students  become  more flexible  with  different  others  and  equip  them  with  abilities  needed  for  effective  intercultural exchanges.  Currently,  little  is  known  about  intercultural  teaching/learning  in  Algerian  Higher education  and  whether  telecollaborative  partnerships  are  likely  to  help  students  develop  their intercultural abilities. The following research question guides our study to learn more about the effectiveness of online intercultural exchanges in higher education: "To what extent can Algerian University learners' intercultural competence be promoted through online intercultural exchanges?" To develop the latter, the researchers used the framework provided by Fantini (2007) to determine the effectiveness and relevance of this technological tool and activities in developing Algerian University learners' intercultural competence.

A major contribution of this research on virtual intercultural exchanges in a monolingual Algerian context, where English is used as a Foreign Language (FL), has been to add some findings to support previous studies in the same field. Furthermore, the insights from such studies have and continue  to  draw  the  attention  of  language  instructors  to  integrate  telecollaboration  in  their language  classes  to  help  university  learners  promote  the  required  abilities  and  skills  to communicate, learn and collaborate with different partners.

This research paper begins by stating the research problem, and the main aim of this study refers then to the contribution of these research findings to the field of intercultural education in Algerian  Universities.  Next,  it  reviews  the  concept  of  culture  in  language  teaching  in  light  of computer-mediated technology and how language learners might relocate their subject positions while interacting virtually with people from different countries and cultures. Then, it unpacks the concept  of  IC  and  its  sub-dimensions.  Also,  it  reviews  previous  research  findings  on  the development of university students' IC through telecollaborative partnerships (or lack thereof). It moves  to  describe  the  research  design,  instruments,  and  procedures  for  data  collection  and analysis. Finally, it attempts to answer the research question and then discuss and interpret the findings of previous studies from the literature review section.


## Literature Review


Teaching a language as a foreign or a Second Language (hence, SL) can impact on the sociolinguistic aspect of culture (Kramsch, 2013). In the FL teaching context, where there is almost no  immediate  and/or  daily  communication  with  native  speakers  unless,  in  virtual  encounters, culture embodies a journey of discoveries on how life would look like through the eyes of target people.  FL  students,  not  least  Algerians,  learn  about  the  target  culture  with  the  only  aim  of satisfying their curiosity about otherness; they try to adapt to it or adopt it as their own only when communicating with native speakers, either while staying in the host country (Kramsch, 2013) or virtual contexts. Yet, in the SL teaching context, culture can be subjected to debates and concerns

of living and working for immigrants; they acquire a national culture that is different from their own through schooling -as a secondary socialization process (Kramsch, 1998).

In the early 21 st century, due to globalization and the rapid spread of computer-mediated technology, the ever-changing nature of the world's interconnectedness has changed the role of culture in language teaching (Risager, 2006, as cited in Kramsch, 2013).

However, the modernist perspective in which culture is researched and taught remains the same;  culture  is  still  regarded  as  linked  to  predefined  social  structures  of  particular  speech communities (Kramsch, 2013). These speech communities are focalized on individuals sharing common goals -rather than common values and memories- and belonging to many communities of practice (Pavlenko & Lantolf, 2000, as cited in Kramsch, 2013).

In their process of FL learning, language learners generally find themselves encountering other worldviews of joint activities and routines as well as different life goals, values and behaviors, thus,  some  applied  linguists  were  incited  to  espouse  a  post-modernist  (Giddens,  1991)  or ecological approach to the teaching of culture (Kramsch & Steffensen, 2008; Larsen-Freeman & Cameron, 2008).  In  this  approach,  culture  has  become  a  socially  constructed  discourse  and  is reconstructed by individuals through interactions; interlocutors from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds are likely to be displacing their cultural views in the process of understanding each other.  Here,  much  stress  is  put  on  the  relationship  between  the  self  and  others  over  multiple timescales in a decentred perspective. In a post-modernist approach, learning a foreign language does not enhance language learners to change their identity but might lead them to change their subject  positions;  consequently,  they  might  locate  themselves  in  the third  place of  discourse (Kramsch, 2009). In fact, in face-to-face or online interactions, students construct their own and their interlocutors' subject positions by asking questions about any ambiguity raised or choosing which topic to discuss or to avoid (Kramsch, 2013).


## Intercultural Competence


IC remains a concept that much like culture is difficult to define. The problem lies in the multidimensionality of the construct and in the fact that many of its proposed components are abstract concepts. The most accepted definition among scholars is the one provided by Deardorff (2004) who defined it as 'the ability to communicate effectively and appropriately in intercultural situations based on one's intercultural knowledge, skills and attitudes' (p. 196).

According to Byram and Zarate (1997), the sub-components of IC are Knowledge, skills and attitudes, complemented by the values that an individual holds as an agent participating in many social  groups.  The  foundation  of  IC  is  in  the  attitudes (savoir  être) of  the  intercultural speaker that refer to their ability to decentre. Another crucial element is Knowledge (savoirs), not essential knowledge about a particular culture, but rather a knowledge of how social groups and identities  operate  and  what  is  involved  in  intercultural  communication  (Byram,  Gribkova  & Starkey, 2002).

To see how misunderstandings can occur and they might be resolved, intercultural speakers need  the  attitudes  of  decentring  as  well  as  the  skills  of  interpreting  and  relating (savoir comprendre) , that is, comparing ideas, events or documents of two or more cultures and seeing how the  other  perspective  might  perceive  each.  Because  it  is  mainly  impossible  to  anticipate knowledge  of  all  cultures,  intercultural  speakers  need  to  acquire  the  skills  of  learning  new knowledge and integrating it with pre-existing one; this could be facilitated by asking appropriate questions about other people's unconscious beliefs, values and behaviors which cannot be easily explained,  and  hence  skills  of  discovery  and  interaction (savoir  apprendre/  faire). Finally, individuals' own beliefs, values and behaviors are deeply ingrained and can result in rejection; therefore, intercultural speakers need critical cultural awareness (savoir s'engager) of themselves and their values and those of others (Byram et al, 2002).


## The Development of Intercultural Competence through Virtual Intercultural Communication


Online intercultural communication, alternatively called virtual exchange or telecollaboration , encompasses  instructional  practices  such  as  collaborative  tasks,  collective inquiry, and opportunities for social interaction between internationally dispersed partner classes using internet communication tools (e.g., e-mail, chat, blogs, videoconferencing) without the cost of  travel  abroad  (Helm,  2015;  Lewis  &  O'Dowd,  2016).  Communication  in  telecollaborative activities  occurs  synchronously  or  asynchronously  or  combined  utilizing  various  models  and instruments.  These  online  exchanges  can  be  seen  to  promote:  (a)  learner  autonomy  through increased  techno-pedagogical  skills,  (b)  foreign  language  development  and  (c)  intercultural communicative competence (Lewis & O'Dowd, 2016). The ensuing discussion will focus on the latter competence based on reviewing some previous research findings in university class-to-class telecollaborative programs.

As mentioned above, along with promoting language skills, telecollaborative learning aims at improving learners' IC (Abrams, 2002; Belz & Thorne, 2006; Byram, 1997; Furstenberg, Levet, English, &Maillet, 2001; Kramsch & Thorne, 2002; Liaw & Bunn-Le Master, 2010; O'Dowd & Ware, 2009; Toscu & Erten,2020). O'Dowd (2007) stressed the potential of telecollaboration in assisting learners in developing their IC as opposed to traditional teaching. When encountered with linguistically  and  culturally  different  others,  learners  are  stimulated  to  reflect  upon  different worldviews (Bennett, 1993; Byram, 1997). In a research synthesis of studies reported between 2010 and 2015, Çiftçi and Savaş (2018) reported that the main claim of telecollaborative studies was that learners increased their knowledge (Lee &Markey, 2014; Schenker, 2012), interest (Liaw & Bunn-Le Master, 2010), curiosity (Chen& Yang, 2016), and awareness (Angelova & Zhao, 2016;  Chen  &  Yang,2016)  toward  both  their  own  culture  and  other  culturally-  grounded standpoints.

Furthermore,  Liaw  and  Bunn-Le  Master  (2010)  pinpointed  a  change  in  intercultural exchanges from a mere fact-based information exchange to a more advanced level of sharing personal views on the assigned topics. In their research on intercultural  learning, Liaw (2006;

2007), Jin and Erben (2007), Schenker (2012), and Chen and Yang (2016), to name but a few, showed different levels of IC among their participants. Yet, a clear developmental process among participants could not be observed. Thus, it would be fair to say that, according to Furcsa (2009), and Ware and Kramsch (2005), learners developed an awareness of the viewpoints of different individuals and their cultures. In a nutshell, virtual exchanges can be said to trigger learners to develop their IC to different extents, yet, IC was not easily measurable. Therefore, the shift in perspectives towards the target culture and reflections on own culture was used to capture instances of intercultural development (Elola & Oskoz, 2008).

Although the use of telecollaborative programs in educational settings has been reported with successful exchanges, there were still some instances of 'failed communication' (O'Dowd & Ritter, 2006) between distant learners in different locations. Bueno-Alastuey and Kleban (2016) reported that their Polish participants thought their Spanish partners lacked motivation. In addition, Ware (2013) asserts that some factors, such as a lack of stimulating context, topic development, asking questions, and risk-taking evolved into a failed exchange. In the same line of thought, Ware and Kessler (2016) identified unsuccessful communication that includes questions that were out of context and lacking in depth.

More  importantly,  opinions  differ  with  regard  to  assumed  intercultural  development through mere contact with speakers of other languages (Helm, 2013, 2016; Dooly, 2016; Flowers, Kelsen & Cvitkovic, 2019; Godwin-Jones, 2020; O'Dowd & Dooly, 2020, as cited in Dooly & Vinagre, 2022).


## Method


This  research  was  conducted  following  a  quasi-experimental  design.  The  researchers' decision can be justified by the difficulty of finding university partners for virtual intercultural exchanges and, by contrast, the availability of a pre-existing virtual classroom. More particularly, the researchers used a 'non-equivalent comparison group design without pre-test' within which an experimental and 'a comparison group is used. However, the comparison and experimental groups are not equivalent because of the non-random assignment of persons to groups.' (Hartas, 2010, p.252). Also, researchers do not often have control over the treatment; they rather scrutinize pre-existing groups that have received different treatments.


## Participants


Our  case  study  labeled Global  Virtual  Classroom (Mouhadjer,  2010)  at  the  English Department of Abou Bakr Belkaid University, Algeria , offered in  the  fall  of  2020  during  one semester, is one instance of a telecollaborative partnership. Under the guidance of their instructor, learners meet twice a week with their distant partners from Africa, Asia, Europe and America to have a first-hand experience through real-time videoconferencing, chat and emails. Participation in  this  partnership  was  a  course  requirement  for  American  students.  In  contrast,  it  was  a

supplementary class for Algerian keypals by which they can get a certificate approved from East Carolina University.

The focus group consisted of 19 Algerian students from Abou-Bakr Belkaid University engaged in virtual intercultural exchange with American partners from East-Carolina University. The control group also consisted of 19 Algerian students from the same University. The focus group consisted of 19 Algerian students from Abou-Bakr Belkaid University engaged in virtual intercultural exchange with American partners from East-Carolina University. The control group also  consisted  of  19  Algerian  students  from  the  same  University.  Participants  enrolled  in  the Department of English Language were taken from both genders (14 males and 24 females). Their age ranged between 19 to 25 years old. The sample population was selected using convenience sampling;  this  is  because,  in  educational  contexts,  true  experimental  designs  with  random assignments are rarely feasible (Mackey & Gass, 2005).


## Research Instruments


The researchers opted for a self-report questionnaire as a research instrument to conduct this quasi-experimental study. It was divided into two parts: the first part concerned participants' personal information such as gender, age, geographic area, grade level, familiarity with the concept of IC, reading about other cultures and prior intercultural experiences (traveling abroad for an extended  time  or  virtual  encounters);  While  the  second  part  encompassed  the 'Intercultural Competence Scale' developed by Fantini (2007). This scale consists of 53 items, and they are formed  as  a  5-Likert  type.  It  embraces  11  items  addressing  the  respondents'  intercultural knowledge,  such  as  culture-based  information  and  linguistic  proficiency;  10  skill  items  for assessing the participants' capability to communicate with culturally different others; 13 attitude items for evaluating the participants' respect for and openness to different cultures as well as their tolerance to ambiguities; and at last, 18 awareness items that are culture-related awareness about the self and otherness.


## Research Procedures


The participants filled in the questionnaire that included statements on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 'no competence' (0%) to 'very high competence' (100%). Statistical analyses were conducted using Excel, and then, descriptive statistics were used to examine the participants' IC level as it is disposed of in Table One.

The researchers used the visual inspection of histograms, Q-Q plots and box plots to test for normal distribution and to determine whether parametric or nonparametric tests should be used to analyze the recorded data. The findings indicated that participants' IC scores followed a nonnormal  distribution;  thus,  non-parametric  tests  were  preferred  to  analyze  data.  To  compare participants' IC scores of both control and focus groups, an initial null hypothesis needs to be formulated, which states that there is no difference between the two groups. It is expected that at the  end  of  the  study,  the  null  hypothesis  is  either  rejected  or  not  rejected.  To  this  end,  the

researchers selected the Mann-Whitney U test to compare between control and focus groups' IC scores as well as to disclose whether overseas experiences reveal any differences in participants' IC.


## Results


This  study  attempted  to  examine  the  effectiveness  and  relevance  of  engaging  Algerian University students in virtual intercultural exchanges to promote their IC.
