## Introduction


Miscarriages are spontaneous pregnancy losses before 20 to 28 weeks of gestation with the definition varying depending on the context (Quenby et al., 2021). Many studies define them as pregnancy losses before 22 gestational weeks (e.g., Feodor Nilsson et al., 2014; Lang & Nuevo-Chiquero, 2012; Larsen et al., 2013) or 24 weeks (e.g., Garcı ́ a-Enguı ́ danos et al., 2002; Maconochie  et  al.,  2007;  Norsker  et  al.,  2012).  They  are  common:  around  13  to  19%  of medically  recognized  pregnancies  (Quenby  et  al.,  2021)  and  between  20  to  30%  of  all pregnancies  result  in  a  miscarriage  (Linnakaari  et  al.,  2019).  Approximately  20  to  25%  of women 3  experience at least one miscarriage in their reproductive life.

Except for prospective clinical studies (Wilcox et al., 1988), all data types typically miss very  early  miscarriages,  for  instance,  when  pregnancies  are  not  recognized  before  the miscarriage (Strong et al., 2023). Clinical studies tend to suffer from a lack of representativity and  small  sample  sizes.  Health  records  typically  only  document  miscarriages  managed  in hospitals and, less frequently, those handled by primary healthcare providers with a selection bias  towards  those  who  sought  medical  care  due  to  a  miscarriage.  Surveys  can  collect information on all pregnancies and the circumstances surrounding them but are likely subject to  misreporting,  i.e.,  a  respondent  not  reporting  a  pregnancy  or  mistakenly  reporting  its outcome. Without a gold standard, scholars have proposed model-based approaches to correct for any possible misreporting of pregnancies, such as abortion (Tennekoon, 2017).

This  paper  focuses  on  social  inequalities  with  miscarriage  risk.  Such  questions  are problematic to assess when the extent of misreported pregnancies varies across social groups, as it may introduce bias in studies where pregnancy outcomes are of interest (Desai et al., 2021).

Thus,  another  aim  of  this  paper  is  to  analyze  miscarriage  survey  reporting  patterns  before examining its risk factors.

To  the  best  of  our  knowledge,  the  extent  of  miscarriage  misreporting  has  rarely  been studied outside the US. Therefore, building on Tennekoon (2017), we first ask whether a modelbased approach developed for abortion reporting can also be applied to miscarriages. We apply this approach to the French Fertility, Contraception and Dysfunction Survey (FECOND, 201011).  We find that most miscarriages are reported with few differences by education. Correcting for the estimated reporting rates of both induced abortions and miscarriages only slightly affects miscarriage  rates.  Thus,  we  can  investigate  further  the  factors  associated  with  miscarriages without  correcting  for  potential  misreporting.  Second,  we  employ  multinomial  multilevel regression analyses to estimate factors associated with miscarriage risk. The model estimates factors associated with the likelihood of a pregnancy to end in a miscarriage rather than in an induced  abortion  or  a live birth while  accounting  for any  time-invariant  unobserved heterogeneity  at  the  individual  level.  We  find  no  significant  socio-economic  differences  in miscarriage  risks,  but  a  positive  association  with  age  at  pregnancy  and  birth  cohort  and  a negative one with prior history of one miscarriage.


## 1. Background


Why would miscarriages be misreported in survey data?

Survey data on pregnancy outcomes are deemed incomplete with miscarriages typically expected to be underreported like induced abortions (Bardos et al., 2015; Bommaraju et al., 2016; Casterline, 1989; Lindberg & Scott, 2018; Yan & Tourangeau, 2022). This may be due to several factors.

First, because of a tendency to provide socially desirable responses, miscarriages may be omitted because of the stigma and guilt that can accompany such events (Bardos et al., 2015).

This is supported by previous research showing face-to-face interviews prompt lower reporting

rates  than  interviews  conducted  by  phone  (Jagannathan,  2001)  or  using  self-completion questionnaires with a computer (Lindberg & Scott, 2018) - which may provide a greater sense of privacy and reduce the influence of stigma. In the US, this may be particularly true for lowincome women creating social inequalities in miscarriage reporting (Lindberg & Scott, 2018).

Another common source of bias in surveys collecting retrospective information is recall bias when an event occurred years before the interview. However, recall bias may not affect reporting of miscarriages severely: in the US, the miscarriage prevalence measured for a given period is consistent across subsequent cycles of the National Survey of Family Growth (NSFG) (Lang  &  Nuevo-Chiquero,  2012).  Similarly,  a  study  comparing  medical  records  and questionnaire responses filled in by mothers found no substantial recall errors in miscarriage reporting ten years after the birth of a child (Tilley et al., 1985). However, recall biases have been documented for various reproductive health outcomes (Akuze et al., 2021; Bryant et al., 1989; Sharma et al., 2024), and miscarriages may be no exception to that.

Early miscarriages can also occur before the pregnancy is recognized by the pregnant person (Strong et al., 2023). In such cases, a miscarriage may be mistaken for the next menses. This may be particularly likely when a pregnancy is not planned. At the same time, improvements in detecting early pregnancies through pregnancy tests (Adolfsson & Larsson, 2006), including at-home ones (Lang & Nuevo-Chiquero, 2012), may have increased awareness and reporting of miscarriages over time.  Little is known on whether these factors could affect the reporting of  miscarriages  differently  across  social  groups.  Women  with  higher  socioeconomic  status might  be  more  likely  to  detect  their  pregnancy  earlier  (Watson  and  Angelotta,  2022). Pregnancies are also more likely to be recognized early when using infertility treatments, which is more common among more educated women (Goisis et al., 2023; Groes et al., 2017).

Lastly, the reporting of miscarriages can be influenced by the misclassifications of induced abortions as spontaneous, particularly in countries where inducing an abortion is not socially

accepted or permitted (Casterline, 1989). In France, which is the context studied in this paper, abortion has been legal since the Veil Law of 1975 and its acceptance has increased over time (Ohl-Hurtaud  et  al.,  2022).  Despite  this,  there  is  evidence  that  induced  abortions  are underreported in the FECOND (Scott et al., 2019), which may suggest that social stigma still affects its reporting.


## How are miscarriages reported, and how do we estimate it?


The extent of underreporting of abortions in high-income countries has been extensively studied, with reporting rates in countries like the US, the UK and France estimated to range between 25% and 86% depending on survey and context (Lindberg 2011; Lindberg et al. 2020; Lindberg and Scott 2018; Moreau, Bajos, and Bouyer 2004; Scott et al. 2019; Tennekoon 2017). Less  is  known  for  miscarriages.  They  are  deemed  to  be  less  underreported  than  abortions because they  are  allegedly  more  socially  accepted  (Bommaraju  et  al.,  2016;  Cowan,  2014; Lindberg  &  Scott,  2018).  However,  this  may  not  hold  in  all  contexts  given  the  taboo surrounding  this pregnancy  outcome  (Bardos  et  al. 2015;  Kilshaw  and  Borg  2020). Accordingly, reporting rates have been found to be close to 60% for both miscarriages and abortions  in  the  US  using  the  NSFG  (Yan  &  Tourangeau,  2022).  Casterline  (1989)  also estimated that 50 to 80% of spontaneous pregnancy losses were reported in the World Fertility surveys in the Global South.

Some researchers have developed data-driven (Yan & Tourangeau, 2022) or model-driven (Tennekoon,  2017)  approaches  to  estimate  the  misreporting  of  induced  abortion  and/or miscarriage. In this paper, we apply Tennekoon's approach (2017), which consists of estimating the true count of induced abortions by modelling and accounting for their misreporting in survey data. We apply this model to the study of miscarriage reporting and for abortions as a reference point, in the French data FECOND collected in 2010-11. Understanding the social pattern of

misreporting is crucial for the estimation of inequalities in miscarriage risks. Thus, our first aim is to assess whether the misreporting of pregnancies affects the analysis of miscarriage risks with the FECOND survey.


## Factors associated with miscarriage risk


Beyond variations in miscarriage reporting, there may also be social inequalities in the risk of  miscarriage.  Existing  evidence  often  relies  on  non-representative  data  (such  as  clinical studies)  and  is  mixed.  This  is,  for  instance,  the  case  regarding  the  relationship  between miscarriage risk and educational levels. While some studies show lower education associated with a higher miscarriage risk (Caserta et al., 2015; Norsker, Espenhain, Rogvi, et al., 2012; Parazzini  et  al.,  1997),  others  found  an  inverse  relationship  (Hegelund  et  al.,  2019)  or  no association  (Maconochie  et  al.,  2007;  Osborn  et  al.,  2000).  However,  one  could  expect miscarriage risks to be associated with a social gradient, as observed in gestational diabetes, preterm birth or neonatal death (Christian, 2012; Gissler et al., 2009; Hardie & Landale, 2013; Hein et al., 2014; Jardine et al., 2021; Joseph et al., 2007).

Socioeconomic status may be linked to a higher miscarriage risk via health-related factors. For instance, both low and high body mass index (BMI) as well as a range of specific health conditions  have  been  shown  to  increase  the  risk  of  miscarriages  (Antoniotti  et  al.,  2018; Giakoumelou  et  al.,  2016;  Kakita-Kobayashi  et  al.,  2020;  Quenby  et  al.,  2021).  Health behaviors during pregnancy, such as consumption of alcohol (Andersen et al., 2012; Garcı ́ aEnguı ́ danos et al., 2002; Larsen et al., 2013; Quenby et al., 2021), caffeine (Andersen et al., 2012; Feodor Nilsson et al., 2014; Garcı ́ a-Enguı ́ danos et al., 2002; Greenwood et al., 2010; James, 2021; Larsen et al., 2013) and tobacco (Feodor Nilsson et al., 2014; Garcı ́ a-Enguı ́ danos et al., 2002; Pineles et al., 2014; Quenby et al., 2021) may increase miscarriage risk. Because such health conditions or behaviors tend to be more prevalent among socially disadvantaged

groups (Marmot et al., 2020), they potentially contribute to social disparities in the occurrence of miscarriages.

Some studies also  hint  at  the  influence  of  the  stability  of  the  environment  in  which  the pregnancy  occurred.  For  instance,  Bruckner  et  al.  (2016)  found  that  unemployment  was associated with miscarriage rates at the country level in Denmark. In the UK, experiencing a job loss within the couple during pregnancy was associated with a higher risk of pregnancy loss (miscarriage or stillbirth) (Di Nallo & Köksal, 2023). Similarly, low incomes have been shown to be associated with higher risks of miscarriages in Denmark (Norsker, Espenhain, Rogvi, et al., 2012) and the US (Nguyen et al., 2019).

Additionally, a key factor for higher risks of miscarriages is an advanced age (around 35-40 years) at conception (Garcı ́ a-Enguı ́ danos et al., 2002; La Rochebrochard & Thonneau, 2002; Magnus et al., 2019; Nybo Andersen et al., 2000; Yland et al., 2024). Trying to conceive at these late reproductive ages is more common among more educated groups in high-income countries, hence putting them at higher risks of experiencing a miscarriage.

Finally, having prior experience with miscarriages is associated with a higher miscarriage risk (Magnus et al., 2019; Yland et al., 2024). This is possibly due to individual characteristics, such  as  endocrinological  diseases  or  uterine  abnormalities,  or  health  status  and  health behaviours. Most of the causes of recurrent miscarriages are also unknown (Garrido-Gimenez & Alijotas-Reig, 2015).

As the second aim of this paper, we explore the socio-economic factors associated with miscarriage risks in France, leveraging the contextual information on the social circumstances at the start of pregnancies available in the FECOND survey.

## 3. Results



## Miscarriage reporting


Applying Tennekoon's approach to the reporting of miscarriages in FECOND, we find that income  and  marital  status are not significantly associated with miscarriage reporting (Table A1). On average, the model estimates that 92% of miscarriages are reported (Table 1). While  the  level  of  education  was  not  significantly  linked  to  the  number  of  miscarriages  a woman had, it was negatively associated with the likelihood of reporting it (Table A1). The model estimates that all highly educated women correctly report their miscarriages, but the estimated reporting rate is 85% for lower-educated women (Table 1). Women with good selfreported health status were less likely to report a miscarriage. At young ages, the reporting of

miscarriages is particularly high in the young age group (25 or less) and lower for women aged 26 or over.

Tennekoon's model applied to abortions in FECOND yields a 55% average reporting rate (Table  A2).  This  is  within  the  range  estimated  by  Scott  et  al.  (2019),  who,  by  comparing FECOND to national French statistics on abortions, estimated a 66% (95% confidence interval: [49-89%]) reporting rate  for  induced  abortions.  We  also  find  that  there  are  no  educational differences in reporting patterns of induced abortion by education (Table A3). 7

## 4. Discussion



## 4.1 Miscarriage reporting


Previous research suggests that both abortions and miscarriages tend to be underreported in  surveys  (Lindberg  &  Scott  2018).  This  can  bias  estimates  of  the  prevalence  and  social disparities in miscarriage risk. Without a gold standard or high-quality data for comparison, a model-based approach remains the only option for estimating patterns of miscarriage reporting. In  the  first  part  of  the  paper,  we  built  on  a  model-based  approach  that  estimates  abortion reporting (Tennekoon, 2017). We estimate that 55% of induced abortions were reported, which is in line with the study by Scott et al. (2019), which compared abortion reporting in FECOND to national statistics. Applying the same model to miscarriages, we find that most of them are reported (92%). While miscarriages were less severely underreported than we expected, it is in

line  with  some previous studies suggesting a greater disclosure of miscarriage compared to abortion (Bommaraju et al., 2016; Cowan, 2014; Lindberg & Scott, 2018). Our estimate is higher than the 60% reporting rate found in the US (Yan & Tourangeau, 2022) or a maximum of  80%  in  the  World  Fertility  Survey  (Casterline,  1989)  -  although  existing  evidence  for miscarriages is scarce.

Correcting  for  abortion  and  miscarriage  reporting  rates,  we  estimate  that  13.9%  of recognized pregnancies result in a miscarriage, which is very close to what we obtain without correcting  for  misreporting  (13.8%).  Such  a  rate  is  similar  to  estimates  of  miscarriage prevalence among clinically recognized pregnancies in other high-income countries (Adolfsson & Larsson, 2006; Ellish et al., 1996; Hemminki & Forssas, 1999; Magnus et al., 2021; Nybo Andersen et al., 2000; Quenby et al., 2021; Rai & Regan, 2006). In addition, our model suggests that tertiary-educated women report all of their miscarriages, while the reporting rate is lower (85%) for lower-educated women. However, before and after correcting for this, educational differentials in miscarriage rates are small (13.7% and 14.4% for lower and higher-educated groups, respectively) and thus we did not correct for miscarriage or abortion reporting in our further analyses.


## 4.2 Miscarriage risk factors


In the second part of the analysis, we show that financial situation and partnership stability at the start of the pregnancy do not significantly influence miscarriage risk, while difficulties with work are more associated with live births than miscarriages. As highlighted in previous research (Magnus et al., 2019; Yland et al., 2024), there is a significant increase in miscarriage risk with an increase in age at the time of pregnancy. The predicted probability for a pregnancy to result in a live birth increases from 11.3 % [8.3;14.7] at age 30-34, to 18.5 % [13.6;24.2] at 35-39 and 35.5 % [22.3; 50.5] at 40+ (Figure A1). However, the positive association with prior

history of miscarriages found in the literature (Magnus et al., 2019; Yland et al., 2024) does not hold  when  controlling  for  unobserved  heterogeneity,  as  we  did  in  our  multilevel  models. Instead, we find that pregnancies preceded by one previous miscarriage have lower probabilities of resulting in another one. This may be due to random chromosomal abnormality resulting in a  single  pregnancy  loss  rather  than  systematic  reproductive  issues,  leading  these  women  to manage to achieve live birth in the next pregnancy (Miranda et al., 2011). Conversely, women with multiple miscarriages may be a selected group, potentially with more underlying risks related to health behaviours or specific genetic conditions (Garrido-Gimenez & Alijotas-Reig, 2015). Similarly, having already had at least two children at the start of the pregnancy was positively associated with miscarriage risk when accounting for individual-level unobserved factors and other factors. This could indicate that women with higher parity are more likely to experience miscarriages in later pregnancies, for instance, due to biological specific conditions, lifestyle factors or health behaviours (e.g., increased stress or physical strain). Such aspects warrant further research.

Overall, both parts of the analysis show that younger respondents report more miscarriages. These patterns may reflect cohort differences in early pregnancy recognition, with those born in the early 1980s more likely to identify and report pregnancies earlier than those born in the 1960s.  Younger  cohorts  may  also  perceive  less  stigma  than  previous  cohorts  in  disclosing miscarriages. Alternatively, these differences could stem from recall biases, presumably less severe for younger respondents.


## 4.3 Strengths, limitations and future research


In our estimation of miscarriage reporting, we assume that pregnancy outcomes other than abortions and miscarriages are correctly reported in the survey. This is likely for live births as they tend to be underreported only in contexts of high mortality at young ages (Akuze et al.,

2021; Sharma et al., 2024) and this was not the case in our study context. Ectopic pregnancies and stillbirths may also be misreported, but these events are relatively rare - for instance, less than one percent of pregnancies end in stillbirths (Taviani et al., 2024). Their underreporting is unlikely to influence the denominator much in our calculation of miscarriage rates.

Our  analyses of socioeconomic  factors associated with miscarriage risk rely on retrospective  information.  Our  findings  differ  from  previous  work  showing  a  positive association between unemployment and miscarriage risk (Bruckner et al., 2016; Di Nallo & Köksal,  2023;  Nguyen  et  al.,  2019;  Norsker,  Espenhain,  A  Rogvi,  et  al.,  2012).  These characteristics may be better indicators of socioeconomic status and conditions than the selfassessed financial situation we use.

Contrary to previous research (Antoniotti et al., 2018; Giakoumelou et al., 2016; KakitaKobayashi et al., 2020; Quenby et al., 2021), we find that BMI is not significantly associated with miscarriage risk. As BMI likely changes over the life course, particularly after early births (Lacey et al., 2017), measuring it at the time of the survey may not correctly reflect the true association between this biomarker and miscarriage risk.

Despite these limitations, survey data can capture pregnancy losses within a nationally representative sample. Our study design also highlights the importance of model choices in assessing the influence of miscarriage factors. Further research is still needed to confirm our findings, but at present, this study points to 1) a good reporting rate of miscarriages in these data,  2)  only  slight  social  disparities  in  miscarriage  reporting  and  risks,  and  that  3)  timeinvariant individual factors explain the role of recurrent miscarriages on the risk of experiencing a new one. This underscores the need for cross-country comparisons to better understand how socio-economic  and  cultural  factors,  healthcare  systems,  and  survey  designs  influence miscarriage reporting and risk.

## Introduction


Nowadays, the status of the English language has changed worldwide as it is the language of various sectors, such as tourism, business, medicine, and education (Karam, 2023). Educational institutions  have adopted the English language for a variety of reasons. Being an international language is one of the most important reasons for employing the English language in educational institutions.  However,  institutions  worldwide  are  directing  their  focus  to  internationalization. Hence, speaking English fluently is essential to becoming ahead of others in the globalized world (Aldawsari, 2022; Decorte et al., 2024). English language is not merely an academic subject but is also an instructional instrument in other academic disciplines worldwide. The status of English has changed from being a subject of study to a tool for teaching other academic subjects. Technically speaking, this phenomenon is known as English as a Medium of Instruction (EMI hereafter) to cover courses solely in English rather than using other languages (Blommaert, 2012). English as a medium of instruction is the application of the English language to teach academic topics where English is a foreign language (Bolton & Kuteeva, 2012; Celik & Yildiz, 2019). It is common knowledge  that  internationalization  procedures  have  recently  crept  into higher education establishments. Therefore, the first step in internationalizing universities can be implementing the English language as an educational tool (Borg, 2016).

The current study has multiple significances. Firstly, the primary purpose of using English is to prepare learners for the rapidly globalized world in general and educational and professional life  in  particular.  In  this  regard,  introducing  this  system  is  considered  a  means  for  expanded globalization (Celik & Kara, 2024). The trend is the same in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, which is the context of the current study, as the majority of universities are adopting the English language in teaching. Kurdish is the official language in the region and the medium of instruction from primary to high school, whereas English is a minor focus. However, some authorities implemented English as the medium of instruction in higher education in various global-orientation disciplines, such  as  accounting,  science,  engineering,  and  mathematics  (Chen  et  al.,  2020).  Secondly,  the limited exposure to English during school years may cause some students to suffer from speaking anxiety. Hence, first-year students might face issues understanding and communicating in English. Borg (2016) pointed out that despite implementing EMI courses and using coursebooks written in English, some public institutions still instruct the courses in Kurdish or Arabic. This mismatch occurs due to a variety of challenges that both teachers and students face in the English-medium environment. The primary objective of this study is to get an insight into the first-year students' perceptions and the challenges they face when implementing EMI in their major. Therefore, the current study is focusing on identifying the main challenges faced by the first-year students during the implementation of EMI through the following research questions:

- 1. What are the first-year students' attitudes towards implementing EMI?
- 2. What are the main challenges encountered by the students in EMI courses at the tertiary level?


## Literature Review


English  as  a  medium  of  instruction,  a  new  sample  of  progress  in  language  strategy, represents the target language method, which holds that teaching only in the target language and avoiding switching back to the mother tongue is the optimal course of action.   However, this viewpoint is  very  contentious.  It  raised  several  queries.  One  of  the  concerns  is  whether  these courses focus on the subject content or the language only, or both simultaneously. Another concern to take into account which is how to provide a high-quality education to learners with linguistic and comprehension difficulties (Albalawi, 2024; Chen et al., 2020). These questions indicate that introducing English presents various challenges and barriers, including language-related issues and  the  motivation  to  learn  the  language.  Therefore,  many  studies  have  investigated  various aspects of EMI, including the reasons and consequences of implementing it and teachers' and students' perceptions.


## Reasons behind the Implementation of EMI


Internationalization of universities is one of the factors behind the implementation of EMI, as  universities  are  attempting  to  attain  international  status.  Internationalizing  higher  education aims to foster intercultural and international competencies (IIC) and foreign language proficiency. Universities worldwide have used tactics like English-mediated instruction or teaching content subjects in English to accomplish this goal. EMI plays a crucial role in the development of English as a global language of communication, which has enhanced international student mobility in a process called internationalization (Corrales et al., 2016; Kara & Kucuk, 2023). These universities offer international programs and focus on applying English to their offered courses, which will eventually appeal to a more significant number of students from various parts of the world (Costa & Coleman, 2013). Blommaert (2012) has summarized the main motives behind implementing English  in  universities  as  three  goals:  appealing  to  more  international  students,  elevating  the university's  prominence,  and  equipping  the  students  for  mobility  and  the  globalized  work marketplace.

## Students' Perceptions Towards EMI


The extensive implementation of EMI in higher education has highlighted the importance of  exploring  learners'  attitudes  towards  this  system.  Hence,  a  large  number  of  scholars  have investigated  students'  perceptions.  By  examining  students'  perceptions  regarding  a  range  of factors,  such  as  English  for  education,  English  for  occupations,  English  for  globalization, conservation of tradition, both national and international identities, academic fulfillment and desire to migrate, Despitasari (2021) has shed light on EMI policy in a private higher education institution in  the  Indonesian  context.  This  policy  at  the  university  receives  excellent  feedback  from  the participants in the study.  Those participant view English as globally significant for their academic and  professional  endeavors.  They  don't  perceive  English  as  a  danger  to  the  survival  of  the Indonesian language and culture.  They are even considering moving overseas to a different nation for a more stable living and work environment. They find this policy's execution in their institution to be generally satisfactory.

Kırkgöz  (2014)  has  conducted  a  study  investigating students'  perceptions.  This  study indicated two groups. In one group, Turkish was the medium of instruction, which is the mother language of the participants, while for the other group, English was the medium of instruction. The study included a questionnaire, interviews, and an analysis of exam papers. The findings revealed that being instructed in English helped them improve their linguistic skill regarding vocabulary

In this study, there was a focus on four aspects, including investigating students' attitudes towards the variance in being instructed in English and L1, multilingual behavior adopted in the classrooms by lecturers as well as students, students' attitudes towards their own and their peers' performance and linguistic competence, and the  English  language  teaching  and  learning  events. ## Discussion


This study aimed to investigate first-year students' perceptions regarding EMI and address the  challenges  they  might  encounter  while  implementing  the  English  language  as  a  tool  for teaching and learning. The study indicated five main domains. The first domain was related to the learners' attitude towards EMI. The current study's results reflected these courses' positive impact on improving their linguistic competency. This result ties nicely with the previous study by Huang (2015), which displayed the significance of these courses in improving the learners' language proficiency.  Also,  the  results  showed  that  the  respondents  enrolled  in  these  courses  willingly. Unlike the current study, a study conducted by Yeh (2014) showed that the students enrolled in EMI courses either because they were obliged or for having no other option. The results also demonstrated  the  students'  willingness  to  learn  the  English  language.  A  study  by  Costa  and Coleman (2013) also confirmed that the respondents expressed a desire to learn English. Moreover, the findings confirmed the participants' interest in the content of the courses. Similar to previous studies,  results  by  Iwaniec  &  Wang  (2023)  showed  the  students'  motivation  to  learn  in  EMI courses  as  it  offers  the  potential  for  better  job  opportunities,  as  well  as  better  interaction  in international contexts. Moreover, these English courses offered them enhanced content learning as it improved their content-related vocabulary, eventually encouraging them to be more into these courses. The participants indicated their positive attitude to these courses as they were entertaining. This result was in line with a study by Doiz and Lasagabaster (2018) in which the respondents enjoyed the videos watched during EMI lessons. Finally, the participants confirmed their positive attitude towards these courses in general. Previous studies by (Aldawsari, 2022; Despitasari, 2021) have demonstrated similar results in line with the current study.

The study demonstrated the beneficial role of these courses on developing both contentrelated vocabulary and disciplinary knowledge of the participants. Similar findings were available in a study conducted by Chen et al. (2020) in which the participants improved regarding their vocabulary  related  to  academia  and  their  discipline.  All  in  all,  the  results  revealed  that  the participants  were  satisfied  with  taking  these  courses  because  they  significantly  improved  their knowledge and vocabulary in English.

According to the current results, the participants confirmed their development in the four skills.
