## Gentrification as a Threat to Safety Within Gentrifying Neighborhoods


To the majority of Black Cincinnatians in my sample, gentrification leverages the vehicles of physical and cultural displacement to threaten their safety within gentrifying neighborhoods. Not only do respondents see gentrification creating conditions that make these historically-Black neighborhoods unlivable, but they also observe that gentrification displaces Black people and erases Black culture from these areas in the name of 'safety.' These practices generate feelings of instability among participants, who have personally or vicariously witnessed the erasure of the city's lifelong Black and low-income residents from gentrifying neighborhoods.

Several participants expressed that the current wave of gentrification manifesting across Cincinnati makes residing in gentrifying neighborhoods unsustainable for lifelong residents. Renee, a 50-year-old lifelong Cincinnatian and Northside resident, shares that despite promises that gentrification 'will provide jobs for the neighborhood,' these economic opportunities often don't pay living wages that allow residents to support their families. 'Now sometimes I would do

security at Children's Hospital (in Corryville) and the African Americans that I saw working primarily were working those…$10/hour jobs…and that struck me because there were jobs and they did hire people, but you can't support a family on that though.' Athena, a lifelong Cincinnatian and Over-the-Rhine resident, observes that gentrification of her neighborhood and Downtown Cincinnati often leads to the forced displacement of low-income residents who cannot afford to pay more to stay. 'And again, that's just part of the gentrification…It becomes more of a class thing at that point, you know? They come out, change things, prices go up, and it's like, can you afford it or can you not, and if not, you got to go.'

But the impact of gentrification is not only felt within the inner city but also in gentrifying neighborhoods on its outskirts. Tenisha, a Louisianan that has resided in Cincinnati for three years, has seen gentrification reduce 'access to groceries and food. So, in Madisonville, they have to travel a significant distance now to get to a Kroger or to get something to eat' because 'there was a family dollar in the neighborhood that sold a lot of food and that people in the neighborhood could walk to, (but) they closed that.' Hope, a single 36-year-old Black mother who was facing eviction from her Madisonville residence at the time of our interview, describes the challenges she has faced trying to maintain stable housing amidst a rising cost of living across Cincinnati (in part due to gentrification):

So on average, a person needs to be making $45,000 just to take care of one person. Dock 12 months of items that you just have to have. 12 months of rent, and 12 months of transportation…these things added up, and you actually need $45,000 for a single person. So think about a mother who has five kids. And, of course, it's no one's fault that person chose to have that many kids, but the pay in Cincinnati is not high enough. Across the U.S., it's not high enough, and our…our living is coming up even higher now. I've been looking for a place since December and have not been able to successfully find one. And by September 30, yknow, I have to be out.

Unfortunately, Hope's sober analysis regarding the unaffordability of renting in Cincinnati for many families making a modest living aligns with findings from contemporary research

(Community Building Institute and LISC Greater Cincinnati 2017; Ellis 2022). Here, she implies that her impending eviction in the wake of COVID-19 is linked to the disparity between increasing costs of living in Cincinnati and wage stagnation in Cincinnati and across the United States. 24 These are just some examples of how gentrification exacerbates the social and economic precarities Black Cincinnatians must navigate while residing within Cincinnati's gentrifying neighborhoods.

Additionally, participants observe that neighborhoods in Cincinnati that have gentrified are no longer demographically Black and only resemble Black culture to the extent that it makes Cincinnati's gentrifying residents feel 'safe.' Kelli, 53, describes her feelings about seeing this process unfold in her childhood neighborhood of Avondale. 'I see more white people in Avondale now than I've ever seen in my entire life. It catches my eye because I want to be like, what are you doing here? You gon get in trouble, somebody's gonna get you. And then I realized, oh, you live here.' Georgia, a Black woman from New York City that has lived in Cincinnati for two years, shares how her education about Cincinnati's Over-the-Rhine neighborhood in 2018 omitted reference to its Black history and culture. 'So I did like a tour of OTR when I first moved here, and it was all white history. I think it was mostly..anything that I hear about OTR is that it used to be dangerous. It used to be a place that you could not go.' However, this did not surprise her because she 'know(s) that that's how white people tend to describe Black neighborhoods that they gentrify.' In referencing the historical 'dangerousness' of Downtown Cincinnati, participants like Aries, 27, also highlight that Cincinnati is attempting to remove poor people from this gentrifying area. 'Because it's like with Downtown, they're trying to move, I wouldn't say Blacks, but it would kind of seem like they're trying to make one population have everything. Or not even one population…They're not tryna have people in poverty or people in

low-income housing Downtown anymore.'  Here, poor people are seen as socially undesirable and needing to be removed from Downtown for the benefit of Downtown patrons (and gentrifying residents). On this matter, she elaborates that 'I see parks they've changed around Downtown, I see houses being torn down Downtown. They had a Kroger's down here that they tore down, and now they're making it into a parking lot for people's cars.' Kassidi-a Black woman in her mid-thirties that has lived in Cincinnati over ten years-confided that the cultural disruption of Cincinnati's historically-Black neighborhoods is palpable:

They just moved Cincinnati Ballet to Walnut Hills...they put the (soccer) stadium in the West End... you know, if you go on Vine Street-like it used to just be Vine Street and OTR that had all these like nice expensive shops, and now it's spread out to like Race and Sycamore, like all the way down those streets. And, you know, Walnut Hills instead of a by the slice of pizza spot, they got a whole pie pizza spot, along with like two or three new bars that are pricing out the people-some of the people in this neighborhood and, you know, they try to get rid of the Greenwich…Also, where some of my Black friends are moving honestly. If my Black friends are moving there, and there's also probably some gentrification going on of being able to buy houses in neighborhoods that are still embodying Black people and Black culture but also 'feels safe enough.' And so that, to me, is a marker that a neighborhood is changing too.

What Kassidi dispassionately describes above are more than simple 'changes' she observes across Cincinnati's gentrifying West End, Over-the-Rhine, and Walnut Hills neighborhoods, but the revaluation of valued cultural space in neighborhoods that have been historically Black. Since there are cultural amenities that are being added to (e.g., the ballet, a soccer stadium, a restaurant that serves whole pizzas, bars) and removed from (e.g., the Greenwich, a jazz club that originated in the 1960s catering to Black patrons; a neighborhood-based by-the-slice pizza spot) these neighborhoods to presumably attract well-to-do white residents and Black middle-class gentrifiers, Blackness and the working-class Black people that have historically resided in these areas are clearly being commodified (Summers 2019). 25 In this sense, she astutely observes how the cultural displacement transpiring within individual gentrifying neighborhoods shapes the

cultural erasure of others that are also undergoing gentrification. Moreover, the physical removal of Black people and longstanding communal institutions is intertwined with how Kassidi sees neighborhoods like Walnut Hills being marketed as 'safe' for (Black) gentrifiers.

However, not everyone sees gentrification as a bad thing for the city of Cincinnati. Ms. Gretta and Amiel see gentrification as a positive opportunity for financial gain. Ms. Gretta, a lifelong resident of the West End, lamented about how she often encounters people who don't realize that revitalization can lead to positive change. 'Sometimes there's revitalization, and a lot of it, it needs to happen, you know? You can't continue to live the same way, years after years, centuries after centuries.' Similarly, Amiel-a Black man from Northeastern Ohio that has lived in Cincinnati for nearly 30 years-reflected on how people often critique the wave of gentrification that has happened in Cincinnati over the past 20 years without realizing that residents who left their properties were happy to do so. 'I was convincing, going to people saying, hey look, I want to buy your building for $50,000, and they was happy to have it. They were ecstatic to have it because then no one else was coming up to sell them.' In a similar vein, other participants simply see gentrification as an economic reality. According to Ray, a 65-yearold lifelong Cincinnatian, Over-the-Rhine, the West End, North Avondale, Mount Auburn, and Walnut Hills 'are the (gentrifying neighborhoods) that come to mind more than others, and I think primarily for economic reasons. Folks are coming in, fixing up the older homes. A lot of folks want to live closer to work. That, more than anything else, is the primary reason, just sheer economics.'

Other Black Cincinnatians in this study also acknowledge that gentrification has-and does-reduce crime. Reminiscing about what Over-the-Rhine was like in his childhood, La'Darius-a Walnut Hills resident in his 30s-recalls: 'I mean, it was mostly Black, but

unfortunately it was also low income and once they started redeveloping it…(it's) been completely redone. Keep in mind, Over-the-Rhine, that was one of those spots where unless you had specific business there, there was no reason for me to go there.' According to Denise, 57, the presence of gentrification in Over-the-Rhine has brought necessary surveillance to illicit activities transpiring across the neighborhood that no one wants to be around. 'Well, you can go on the street and act a fool if you want to; you're going to be on somebody's camera...They ain't messing with these Black folks down here…But can you blame them? They pay all that moneywho wants to come outside to dead bodies?' Read another way, Denise's comment also illuminates how security logics are being used to rationalize anti-Black surveillance practices for the benefit of the Cincinnati's (presumably white and wealthy) gentrifiers.

Yet, several Black Cincinnatians in my sample expressed varying levels of alienation as a consequence of exposure to the development and cultural erasure transpiring within gentrifying neighborhoods. The hard-hitting historical reality of this situation was articulated by Mr. Jones-a 64-year-old lifelong Cincinnatian-when reminiscing about the removal of iconic institutions from his beloved neighborhood of Avondale. 'Avondale isn't the community it used to be. It's not a neighborhood anymore. We had bakeries, grocery stores, car dealerships, we had drug stores in the community, man. Family-owned drug stores. We had fresh fish and chicken and poultry stores. Of course, you're asking me, yeah, all that's gone.' Hazel, a 35-year-old lifelong Cincinnatian, finds that gentrification has destroyed the positive sense of community and intimacy among neighbors she once found in historically-Black neighborhoods like Over-theRhine.

And now being back in Over-the-Rhine from living in Price Hill, you know, I mean, I think there's that mass kind of disconnect like there's not the community here that was here when we lived in Mount Auburn for three years. Which is the neighboring neighborhood. So yeah, I mean, I think the biggest thing is the lack of responsibility that

folks that are contributing to this gentrification or this redevelopment. You know, they don't necessarily have that kind of responsibility or respect for the existing community members.

For Melloney, a 19-year-old Kennedy Heights resident, gentrification has created a sense of precarity among longtime Black Cincinnatians across her networks. 'It's just like, oh, they're just trying to…they don't really care about us or our community, they just care about pushing us out because we're not providing the money that they owe. And what Cincinnati cares about is being this really big city.' In the conversations she has participated in, people have shared 'that their grandma's house is getting foreclosed on because (developers are) trying to buy out their properties and stuff, so it's a sense of like..what's the word..a negative connotation to it.' While Mr. Jones, Hazel, and Melloney each represent different generations of Cincinnatians, gentrification has had important consequences that they are all clearly aware of.

In this section, participants embody the first tenet of the safety reimagination framework by showing how gentrification (1) exacerbates socioeconomic precarities and (2) facilitates the erasure of iconic Black cultural institutions in gentrifying neighborhoods across Cincinnati. This allows respondents to juxtapose normative assumptions that people may hold about Black Cincinnatians' core safety concerns in the wake of COVID-19 with their actual lived experiences and perspectives. Thus, across spatially-distinct neighborhoods of residence, participants in this study find that gentrification poses several threats to their individual and collective vitality within gentrifying neighborhoods.


## Gentrification as a Threat to Safety Beyond Gentrifying Neighborhoods


While the devaluation and revaluation of neighborhood infrastructure are frequently used as one sociological proxy for measuring gentrification's impact on gentrifying neighborhoods across U.S. cities (Brown-Saracino 2009; Dantzler 2021; Hyra 2017), participants in this study

observed that gentrification also has important implications for the safety of Black Cincinnatians in non-gentrifying neighborhoods. Not only do respondents illuminate that the logic of economic devaluation and revaluation has 'spilled over' into non-gentrifying areas, generally, but they also contend that the city actively divests from addressing the core safety concerns of residents in Cincinnati's non-gentrifying neighborhoods.

Black Cincinnatians in this study observe that the economic revaluation and devaluation of gentrifying neighborhoods have had important spillover effects in non-gentrifying neighborhoods. Clarence, a lifelong Cincinnatian and North Avondale resident, shares that the culture of profit accumulation associated with gentrification manifests in Cincinnati's majorityBlack, non-gentrifying neighborhoods with low property ownership rates. 'So the city will come along and put citations on the property…And people who don't have the money to get it fixed end up moving. Then developers come in, buy the property, fix it up, and charge twice what it would be for someone else giving up that property.' Micah, a Walnut Hills resident in their late 20s that moved to Cincinnati during the onset of COVID, finds that the expansion of Xavier University in Evanston has occurred in part because its neighboring communities are perceived as 'dangerous' so 'the land is cheaper just because everything around it is less desirable.' Destiny, 39, recalled the general reluctance that her neighborhood of Bond Hill showed to being approached by Cincinnati's FCC soccer club to collaborate on a neighborhood beautification project after witnessing them displace longtime, low-income residents of the West End to build the team's soccer stadium. 'If we decide to kind of give into these large organizations or companies, what's the risk factor? Do we lose our identity as the community?' Although Bond Hill remains a majority-Black neighborhood, Destiny's insights allude to the fact that members of her community see partnerships with large corporations as a threat to their communal

autonomy and cultural identity. Taken together, Clarence, Micah, and Destiny's insights highlight that the impact of neighborhood revaluation and devaluation in Cincinnati is also felt beyond the city's actively gentrifying neighborhoods.

Consequently, respondents in this study find that the devaluation of Cincinnati's nongentrifying neighborhoods leads to the provision of inadequate resources by the city to address the prevailing safety concerns of lifelong residents. Samantha, a 29-year-old Black woman from Cleveland, has lived in Cincinnati for eleven years and has noticed that 'it is normal for y'all to just literally displace whole families and communities' because the city's decision makers 'want to have all these things, but (we're often) not thinking about the people that already live here and that are from here and that will live in Cincinnati until the day they die. And I think that is our biggest kind of black eye in Cincinnati.' Danae, a forty-year-old from MI that has lived in Cincinnati for under 10 years, spoke at length about how the city of Cincinnati virtually ignores the persistence of housing scarcity and resource deprivation in her Winton Hills neighborhood without recognizing their inextricable connection to safety.

I mean, violence is important, but what about the ones that are struggling? What about the homeless  people  out  here  that  are,  you  know,  without  homes,  and  you  know  what about…Okay, they got all these stores that are closing in abandoned buildings? Why not go into trying to open these buildings up for the homeless people, you know giving to them to help them to get out of poverty, you know? Why not focus on that?

Other Black Cincinnatians in my sample associate their exposure to physical displacement to non-gentrifying neighborhoods with experiences of unsafety. Sadé is a 43-year-old Black woman who was recently displaced from her neighborhood in Cincinnati's Center City to a public housing development in Lower Price Hill, but her new residence is an environment where levels of crime and violence are palpable. As she describes:

I pay pretty much market rate, but I can't feel safe in my home. I can't leave, I can't even get out of my hallway door…and I requested several times to be removed from this area.

But because I'm not in immediate danger and because I don't have a change in my household size, I can't be moved out of this area. I don't deserve to be safe… But I guarantee you the same people who deny you wouldn't dare lay their children down in this same place every night. I think that's insane to me.

Because Sadé resides in state-funded housing, her experiences lead her to perceive that the state can move her when it wants to but not when she or her family may need to. 26 Her comments reflect an astute understanding of the politics of deservingness of safety, as she clearly expresses frustration that her family remains exposed to harms associated with social and economic precarity, crime, and violence even after being priced out of her previous neighborhood. 27 Moreover, it is clear from Samantha, Danae, and Sadé's experiences that they believe that the city of Cincinnati does not care to prioritize the needs or safety concerns of Black Cincinnatians who reside outside of gentrifying neighborhoods (Mayorga 2023).

Considering the implications of these realities, Black Cincinnatians in my sample articulated the importance of the city showing lifelong residents that their needs, agency, and existence are valued. According to Jeremiah, a formerly-homeless Black man in his late 20's, 'I understand everybody got different stuff, you know…I feel like (Cincinnati) can be in a better place for us, everybody, to see each other regardless of race, religious differences, political differences, stuff like that.' Mr. Reynolds-a formerly-incarcerated Avondale resident in his 50sstates that '(no one) want(s) to live in a neighborhood where (they) got to be scared…where (they) can't walk out in the street' because everyone wants to live somewhere where they are respected and treated with dignity, regardless of their life circumstances. Likewise, participants in this study believe that affordable housing is a crucial determinant of health (and safety) in Cincinnati that can help those struggling to get out of poverty build new lives for themselves. As Ruth-a Northside resident in her fifties-posits, 'Imagine if you're in poverty, and you had affordable housing that was safe and clean and good, like, what that would mean for you

emotionally, how you could get up every day and how much more successful you can be.' Christina, an organizer who has lived in Cincinnati for fifteen years, finds that she has taken calls to address housing instability associated with gentrification where people 'don't think about the fact that they have rights. Or even as an individual, right? They just assume that 'well, they're coming in, which means I gotta move out.' And it's like no, that's not necessarily true, you don't have to.' Rather than reinforcing this false narrative, Christina believes that lifelong and lowincome residents deserve to know 'no, you have a right to live wherever you wanna live.' Although Jeremiah, Mr. Reynolds, Ruth, and Christina are not making concrete petitions of municipal actors in Cincinnati here, the values they uplift support those who do seek to make such petitions.

Naturally, there were Black Cincinnatians in my sample who did not name gentrification as a threat to their safety in Cincinnati beyond gentrifying neighborhoods. Yet, these participants did identify proactive steps that Black residents might take to resist the undesired consequences they associated with gentrification's presence. Alexander-a 45-year-old resident of Cincinnati's North Avondale neighborhood-locates the solution to mitigating the physical displacement associated with gentrification in Black home ownership, specifically by having well-resourced Black people using their own resources to buy property that can stave off the imposition of gentrification on low-income populations. 'So, when will gentrification itself stop? It will stop when those who have the means, who look like the people who are being displaced, can invest and buy property to uphold property values in that particular area can do that, and, you know, that's where I think that there's room for improvement in Cincinnati.' For other residents, their evaluations of the relationship between gentrification and safety are a bit more complicated. Richard, a 65-year-old lifelong Cincinnatian, worries that the imposition of affordable housing

on historically-Black neighborhoods (like Bond Hill) by municipal officials and private developers accelerates the physical displacement and economic devaluation of these neighborhoods:

I'm not against that, but I'm against the overloading of Black communities with affordable housing just so they can move people around, to gentrify where they want to, you know, put in an influx of money. Meanwhile, putting some shabby buildings here and bringing in crime and blight into the neighborhood. I'm against that…And that, to me, is what affordable housing is in Cincinnati.

Richard's resistance to affordable housing in Cincinnati is tied to an implicit belief that the development of affordable housing is a vehicle of gentrification that ultimately causes more crime. Further, his perspective is complicated by his understanding as a homeowner that the installation of public housing may lead to the dilapidation of existing properties, thereby impacting future levels of municipal (dis)investment in his neighborhood and others across Cincinnati where these problems exist (Pattillo 2007). However, while Richard believes that these practices will inevitably continue, he argues that Black Cincinnatians must decide 'who's coming and who's going. If we don't say it, then they're gonna bring them in here. And it..won't be long before it becomes a blighted area and housing prices go down, they start to move in, and they move them out somewhere else. You know. And the neighborhood is gentrified again. So it's up to the residents to secure their neighborhoods.' 28,29 For Richard, keeping Black Cincinnatians safe requires a concerted effort to not only protect their property (security) but also resist the imposition of economic precarity and communal erasure he associates with gentrification (safety). Thus, even within the unsafe environment that gentrification has created (and exacerbated), Black Cincinnatians in this study identify that they have the power to fight for a Cincinnati that is 'safe' and 'livable' by resisting the coordinated efforts of municipal actors and private interests to devalue their neighborhoods.

Here, participants embody the second and third tenets of safety reimagination . They invoke the second tenet of safety reimagination by demonstrating how the spillover effects of gentrification in Cincinnati lead to (1) the devaluation of the city's non-gentrifying neighborhoods and (2) the provision of inadequate resources to address residents' prevailing safety concerns. To achieve this, respondents simultaneously identify underrecognized forms of power and acknowledge myriad forms of violence they must negotiate as a consequence of relative deprivation. Consequently, they activate the third tenet of safety reimagination by illuminating gentrification as a critical site of resistance and possibility for the longevity of Black communities in Cincinnati. This evidence collectively suggests that Black Cincinnatians in this study also see gentrification as a threat to their safety beyond gentrifying neighborhoods.

Gentrification as a Vehicle of Anti-Blackness and City-wide Communal Erasure As previous sections illustrate, Black Cincinnatians in this study have an extremely nuanced understanding of the consequences of gentrification for Cincinnati's gentrifying and nongentrifying neighborhoods. While respondents are attuned to the fact that the local government, private developers, and locally-based corporations play a role in catalyzing gentrification, they also recognize that Cincinnati's 'routine' practices of displacement and disruption have created a culture of intolerance that Black residents experience in how they are treated by white Cincinnatians (and others) within and beyond gentrifying neighborhoods. Ultimately, participants find that this culture of anti-Blackness translates to a city-wide erasure of Black people, Black culture, and Black history that is felt by short- and long-term residents alike.

Black Cincinnatians in this study observed that gentrification has allowed for the increased visibility of anti-Blackness in everyday life across Cincinnati. Freddie, a Pleasant Ridge resident that has lived across different Cincinnati neighborhoods for over 10 years,

confides that 'When I was in West Price Hill, I never told people I was from…I stayed at West Price Hill because I already knew the connotation that came along with that…I mean, if you say you in certain communities…it's like, oh, you kind of belong to a certain extent.' Recalling an experience he had with a cab driver coming home from the airport, 'I was like, hey, I stay downtown because I mean, at the end of the day, the West End is downtown. And I gave him my address, and he was like, oh no, this is ten dollars more. But if I was a couple of blocks away, the price was cheaper.' Lifelong residents like Belinda, 36, suggest that she does not feel safe in Cincinnati neighborhoods that are actively being gentrified because the culture of 'pushing' Black people out extends to how she is treated as a restaurant patron.

Belinda: I actually do sometimes feel uncomfortable in Over-the-Rhine.

Interviewer: What is it about Over-the-Rhine that makes you feel uncomfortable?

Belinda: It's kind of some weird combination of how Black it used to be there, and now how it's been gentrified, it's just kinda like ugh…and I've never really felt like they're super receptive to Black people...Sometimes it just feels like they would prefer that we didn't come out down there or something. 30

Other respondents in this study also see the culture of 'pushing' Black people out reflected in how housing-insecure and lifelong residents are treated across Cincinnati. For instance, Bailey-a forty-year-old Westwood resident originally from Cleveland-sees '(anti-Black) racism operating in the declaration that it was too unsightly for homeless tent camps to remain on Third Street because people who were going to work didn't want to see that.' Hazel, a lifelong resident in her mid-thirties, is saddened that 'now being back in Over-the-Rhine from living in Price Hill I think there's that mass kind of disconnect like there's not the community here that was here when we lived in Mount Auburn for three years, which is the neighboring neighborhood.' Moreover, she is frustrated by 'the lack of responsibility that folks that are contributing to this gentrification or this redevelopment have you know they don't necessarily have that kind of responsibility or

respect for the existing community members.' Thus, the lack of respect shown toward residents of gentrifying neighborhoods is seen by participants as 'linked' to the treatment of Black Cincinnatians across the city as a whole.

Respondents also contend that Cincinnati's disdain for its Black population is evident in city-wide efforts to dissociate from majority-Black neighborhoods while quietly pushing residents and Black-owned businesses to neighborhoods on the city's outskirts. Dameon, a lifelong Cincinnatian and Mount Airy resident in his fifties, has watched the city of Cincinnati rebrand itself over the last 10 years using these tactics. 'What they've done is, instead of saying that a business is in Avondale, you know, they would rather call it Uptown, you know? They didn't want to use the term Avondale or uh, it's easier to say that it's in Clifton because it sounds whiter.' From his perspective, the motive driving this decision-making is clear: 'They don't want to associate anything like Children's Hospital or University Hospital or anything like that as being an Avondale, but that's where it is, you know? They'd rather call it Uptown because somehow it has some kind of negative connotation to it.'

Other participants in this study are attuned to these rebranding practices, too. Vic, a thirty-year-old Black man from Chicago that has lived in Cincinnati for eight years, discerns that 'When they do things like that, that's when they plan on moving theyselves back in, that's what they call taking back what's theirs.' Nikki, 41, is torn because although she is happy that 'Black Cincinnati is improving in more Black-owned businesses being started,' she recognizes that 'at the end of the day, this city is not built for us…And so that's what's so discouraging is that you have all this gentrification going on, people coming in and being able to benefit where it's just so hard for Black people to get that same opportunity.' Ms. Williams, a 65-year-old North Avondale resident and lifelong Cincinnatian, regards the denial of opportunities for Black Cincinnatians to

live in the city as an ongoing practice. 'I remember there was this major trend where we were being moved out to, or, people of color being moved out to like Mount Washington and all these other places that they would have never been, you know. Back in the day, they were certainly pretty much white neighborhoods.' Milton, an East Price Hill resident in his mid-30s, concludes that Cincinnati's rebranding efforts and denial of history plays a part in the communal erasure of Black Cincinnati and Black Cincinnatians 'especially in some areas Black people were almost forced into because they didn't want Black people in certain areas. So it's like, alright, you pushed us here, and now we're here, and you want us to move again?'

Collectively, these intergenerational insights lead participants to observe that the erasure of Cincinnati's Black population within and beyond gentrifying neighborhoods leads to the erasure of Black culture and Black history across Cincinnati. Reflecting on the erasure of important Black communal landmarks across Cincinnati, Titus-a 54-year-old lifelong Cincinnatian and Downtown Cincinnati resident-shares:

Interviewer: So, when you say that, can you say more about that, the Black landmarks that have been erased? Like, are you talking about…

Titus: Erased, that something has been done with the building differently. You know, like the Warner Studios off of Central Parkway where James Brown used to perform and everything at, they're eventually gonna do something different with that. We should have made it a historical site, you know, stuff that needs to be historical, they're not making it historical. Regal Theaters has been down there on Linn forever. They're saying they're making some condos or something...that's just hearsay, but I mean, that's what I'm hearing. I live down that way, so maybe part of that could be true, part of it fantasy, it's 50/50. So a lot of things like that's going on, and, if the city, the company for 3CDC is the company that's doing all of the work…but that company came out of nowhere and bought up everything and redeveloped it. But when they redeveloped it, they didn't think about the small people, the little people. So it's like, downtown is nice, but you don't have any culture in it, within the city limits either…

A growing body of empirical research corroborates Titus' assessment that 3CDC has played an important role in catalyzing gentrification and 'urban renewal' in Cincinnati over the past twenty

years (Addie 2008; Ehrenfeucht and Nelson 2020). Additionally, his testimony sheds light on how the removal of Black cultural landmarks from historically-Black Cincinnati neighborhoods associated with gentrification leads to a sense of unsafety that is felt by Black Cincinnatians residing across the entire city (Freeman 2006; Hyra 2017; Pattillo 2007). The consequences of this erasure are not just felt by longtime Black residents but by short-term Black residents, too. Amber-an East Price Hill resident in her late 30s-recalled this 'feeling' of gentrification when she first moved from California into her predominantly Black, working-class neighborhood. 'Gentrification is a very scary feeling, and I'm not even from here, so I don't know how much that would be compounded if, like, I was born and raised in this neighborhood for 20 years.' Thus, considering Titus' observations that developers like 3CDC are not taking active efforts to preserve the history of Cincinnati's historically-Black neighborhoods prior to redeveloping (and gentrifying) them, it is unsurprising that the effects of city-wide Black communal erasure are also felt by respondents beyond Cincinnati's gentrifying neighborhoods.

Likewise, other study participants expressed concern about the safety implications of these processes of Black communal erasure for longtime Cincinnati residents. Here, respondents are particularly concerned about how decisions are made about what neighborhoods are allowed to gentrify, what populations are worthy of protection, and what that protection looks like in practice. Latrell, a lifelong Cincinnatian in his late 30s who resides in Westwood, isn't against gentrification in principle but is against how he knows it actually operates in practice. 'I don't have any problem with seeing a Starbucks or Jimmy Johns in Black neighborhoods…just as long as the people that were once in that area are given a chance to benefit also, and not just lose memories, heritage, and be forced to move to College Hill.' However, he mentions that 'I've been hearing that eminent domain clause passed around a lot when I hear terms of

gentrification,' suggesting that he associates the targeting and cultural devaluation of Cincinnati's historically-Black neighborhoods with distinct practices of racial and economic exploitation that clash with his previously-stated values (Rucks-Ahidiana 2021). In weighing out how decision makers in Cincinnati might overcome prevailing anti-Black logics that govern how the city participates in gentrification, A.J.-a Cincinnati police officer and Northside residentponders: 'When we're talking about infrastructure, could we (have made those changes) with the population that existed prior to the white population? Could we have done that?…And do we value that population enough to put those steps in place?'

Other Black Cincinnatians in this study echo Latrell and A.J.'s calls to 'valuing populations' that are being disproportionately impacted by gentrification in Cincinnati, leading them to make concrete petitions of the state. For Ruth, 53, the mandate is simple: 'Quit making people move out of their neighborhoods when you renovate things. Include them in that process and show them ways to live in a renovated society. If you're worried about how they'll treat the property, then show them how to (do it). Like, build a relationship and a connection.' This is a petition to the City of Cincinnati to halt contemporary practices of (re)imposing precarity on longtime Black, low-income residents in favor of building authentic connections to these residents that currently don't exist. Hope echoes the sentiment that everyone deserves respect and a right to a safe life in Cincinnati, sharing that 'Everyone wants to be happy, might be in a different way [laughs], but everyone wants to be happy. Everyone wants to feel safe, and everyone should be respected. You treat others as you would have others treat you.' This is another petition imploring the City of Cincinnati to quell its routine practices of communal erasure and anti-Blackness in Cincinnati happening concurrently with gentrification. Moreover, in explicitly stating that 'everyone wants to feel safe,' Hope is compelling municipal actors in

Cincinnati to protect Black Cincinnatians from the broad categories of harm that shape their holistic understandings of safety (inclusive of, but not limited to, crime and violence; Okechukwu 2021). Beyond describing respect as an amenity, Latrell, A.J., Ruth, and Hope's comments above describe respect as an essential determinant of safety in Chocolate Cities like Cincinnati, where the implications of gentrification are felt by Black residents beyond the context of gentrifying neighborhoods.

In this section, participants embody the final tenet of the safety reimagination framework by showcasing how the erasure of Cincinnati's Black population within and beyond gentrifying neighborhoods leads to the erasure of Black culture and Black history across Cincinnati. This allows them to offer tangible solutions for how Cincinnati's city officials and residents might collectively manifest a world where Black communities across Cincinnati have everything they need to survive and thrive. Although addressing the lingering effects of anti-Blackness and communal erasure in Cincinnati will not happen overnight, Black Cincinnatians in this study articulate a willingness to begin the process of building these new relations.

## Background


Socio-economic inequalities in common mental disorders (CMDs) such as lifetime prevalence, treatment utilisation, and perceived treatment helpfulness have been documented in various settings. However, whether these inequalities are present globally (in both HICs and LMICs) and what factors explain between-country variation is unclear because of inadequate cross-national data. We therefore examine this question using a recently published global, individual-level survey data.


## Methods


This study uses a nationally representative individual-level survey dataset (Wellcome Global Monitor 2020), in 111 countries (N= 117,088) to test if socio-economic factors (household income quintile, education), psycho-social factors (local stigma perception, trust in health professionals) and country-level factors (GDP, Gini, health expenditure) predict (1) CMD lifetime prevalence, (2) utilisation and (3) perceived helpfulness of talking to a mental health professional and taking prescribed medication. Multi-level logistic regression models were used.


## Findings


Across both HICs and LMICs, individuals in higher household quintiles are less likely to experience anxiety or depression (OR=0.90 for each increase in income quintile, 95% CI[0.89-0.91]), more likely to talk to a mental health professional (OR=1.05[1.03-1.07]) and more likely to perceive this treatment as 'very helpful' (OR=1.06[1.03-1.09]). Income is not, however, linked to utilisation (OR=0.98[0.97-1.01]) and helpfulness of taking prescribed medication (OR=1.02[0.99-1.05]). Perceived stigma reduces mental health professional utilisation (OR=0.93[0.90-0.97]) and helpfulness (OR=0.76[0.72-0.81]), while trust in health practitioners increases both utilisation (OR=1.10[1.06-1.14]) and helpfulness (OR=1.32[1.24-1.40]). Country-level health expenditure is related to higher mental health professional utilisation (OR=1.11[1.04-1.19].


## Interpretation


This analysis reveals a global 'triple inequality effect', whereby the disadvantages of lower SES individuals persist in each outcome (lifetime prevalence, treatment utilisation and helpfulness). But these inequalities are moderated by background factors such as stigma and trust in health

professionals, and depend on the type of treatment. These findings suggest that addressing inequalities in CMDs cannot focus on only one of these inequalities alone nor can efforts ignore the social context in which they are embedded.


## 1. Research in Context



## Evidence before this study


We conducted searches in Google Scholar and PubMed for publications up to February 2023 on papers coving cross-national work on social inequalities in mental health. We used the terms such as 'global inequalities in mental health', 'socio-economic status and mental health',  'global mental health survey', 'mental health treatment gap', 'inequalities in mental health treatment utilisation', 'perceived treatment helpfulness for depression'. Our search finds a strong, crossnational evidence base on CMD prevalence based on the Global Burden of Disease studies. Further, we found a variety of studies based on the WHO World Mental Health surveys and the Eurobarometer surveys 2006 and 2010 that find evidence for within-country socio-economic inequalities in treatment utilisation. One study found evidence that education is linked to perceived treatment helpfulness. Research frequently identified stigma as a barrier for CMD treatment utilisation. However, the studies on treatment utilisation and treatment helpfulness are limited to datasets that cover less than 30 countries. So far, the biggest cross-national survey datasets on treatment utilisation are based on the EU's Eurobarometer surveys. Therefore, between-country variation and predictors as well as differences between LMICs and HICs could not be thoroughly examined. Further, we did not find any cross-national study that investigates social inequalities of different mental health outcomes (e.g., prevalence, treatment utilisation, and helpfulness) together in one study to identify how social inequalities deepen across different health outcomes.


## Added Value of this study


To our knowledge, this is the first study that uses a new, global survey dataset that covers 111 countries (both LMICs and HICs) to investigate socio-economic and psycho-social inequalities in three different CMD health outcomes. It is also the first study covering a sufficient number of countries to investigate country-level predictors of treatment utilisation and helpfulness. Our analysis uncovers a global 'triple inequality effect' in CMD prevalence, treatment utilisation and perceived treatment helpfulness in both LMICs and HICs, whereby disadvantages for lower SES individuals persist and deepen at each health outcome. This effect is moderated by psychological and country-level factors: Our study is the first one to show that trust in health practitioners is highly associated with both treatment utilization and treatment helpfulness. Finally, we discovered a notable exception to the 'triple inequality effect' as it does not persist for pharmacological treatment: In LMICs, more affluent individuals were less likely to take prescribed medication when affected by anxiety or depression.


## Implications of all the available evidence


Our findings suggest that efforts to reduce mental health inequalities need to account for how socio-economic factors simultaneously influence a variety of related health outcomes and consider the social context in which such efforts are embedded. For the design of policies and scaling up mental healthcare, policy makers and health practitioners need to focus on social inequalities in several different health outcomes throughout the cascade of care. This study also points to the need to consider the root causes of social inequality to improve multiple health outcomes at the same time. Finally, this study shows that psycho-social factors such as stigma and

trust in health professionals not only determine treatment uptake, but also to the perceived benefit of treatment.


## 2. Introduction


Common mental disorders (CMDs), which include depression, anxiety, and somatoform disorders, are a primary cause of global disease burden  . 1

Notably, CMDs are socially stratified. This becomes clear in the association between socioeconomic status (SES) and three related health outcomes: Individuals with lower SES (1) have a higher lifetime prevalence of CMDs, (2) are less likely to utilise professional treatment (3) are less likely to perceive treatment as helpful when they do receive it 2-4 . This sequence of socioeconomic inequalities suggests that inequalities deepen as individuals move from being affected to experiencing treatment outcomes. Besides socio-economic inequalities, psychosocial factors (e.g., stigma and attitudes) and country-level factors (e.g., economic conditions and healthcare spending) may play a role to determine who receives and who benefits from treatment 2,5 . While we have some evidence documenting these associations across countries, most of this work has been carried out almost entirely in high income countries 6,7 . Therefore, we do not know if socio-economic and psycho-social patterns in lifetime prevalence, treatment utilisation and perceived helpfulness exist universally, and what factors explain betweencountry variations. This study addresses this gap by investigating what socio-economic, psycho-social and country-level factors are correlated with these three health outcomes in a global survey across 111 countries.


## Socio-economic factors


Out of the different health outcomes in this study, the link between SES (income and education) and CMD lifetime prevalence the most thoroughly documented across country contexts as lower SES individuals are more frequently affected by depression and anxiety  . 8 Theories on the pathway between income and mental health identify material circumstances, psycho-social stress, and behavioural differences  . SES also affects treatment utilisation for 4

CMDs  3 . Generally, only a minority of affected individuals receives minimally adequate treatment  . Evidence from the European Union and Switzerland suggests that those 9 individuals who do utilise treatment have higher educational attainment and income 5,10 . Lastly, SES is associated with treatment effectiveness. Two systematic reviews using studies from the US and Europe showed that the effectiveness of psychological therapies 11 and antidepressant treatments 12 is lower for low SES individuals. As an explanation, lower SES individuals might face more socio-economic stressors which cannot be relieved by treatment 13 . Besides treatment effectiveness, perceived helpfulness is as a patient-centred way to measure treatment outcomes 14 , that yields high levels of external validity (Edlund et al., 2015). Using data from WHO's World Mental Health (WMH) Survey Initiative across 16 countries, researchers found that individuals with higher education perceive depression treatment as more helpful  . In summary, we do not know if the association between SES and mental health 2 outcomes is stable across all country contexts. We hypothesise that SES is associated with lifetime prevalence, treatment utilisation and helpfulness in both HICs and LMICs (H1).


## Psycho-social factors


Mental health stigma and negative help-seeking attitudes are well-documented barriers for utilising CMD treatment and explain part of the relationship between SES and treatment utilisation 16 . Stigma is a particularly widely studied barrier to treatment-seeking, with crossnational evidence stemming from the 2006 and 2010 Eurobarometer surveys  . Other psycho7 social factors gained less attention. Qualitative evidence suggests that trust in mental health practitioners and services is an important determinant of help-seeking 17,18 . However, trust has not been examined in quantitative, cross-national studies. Psycho-social factors might also be associated with the abovementioned measure of perceived helpfulness. The implications of outcome expectations and associated placebo effects for pharmacological treatments and talking therapy are well documented 19 . However, whether stigma or trust in health

practitioners are correlated with perceived treatment helpfulness has not been investigated across countries. Again, cross-national evidence on treatment utilisation and helpfulness is limited to European countries, and the role of trust is under-researched. We hypothesise that stigma and trust in healthcare professionals are associated with treatment utilisation and helpfulness across a sample of 111 countries (H2).


## Country-level factors


Lifetime prevalence of CMDs varies across country contexts. The Global Burden of Diseases study shows that HICs tend to have a lower prevalence than LMICs  . Regarding treatment 1 utilisation, the size of mental health treatment gaps varies depending on country-level economic and healthcare capabilities. The WMH Survey Initiative shows that 36% of people affected by anxiety disorders utilise treatment in HICs, and only 13% in lower-middle-income countries 20 . Evidence on country-level variations in healthcare utilisation is based on the Eurobarometer surveys 2006 and 2010. In Europe, healthcare spending and the available mental healthcare workforce explain cross-national variation in antidepressant use  . 5

Country-level variation in treatment helpfulness is not well-documented. The only two studies on this topic using the WMH Survey Initiative involved too few countries to include specific country-level predictors 2,21 . Surprisingly, patients in LMICs reported a higher treatment helpfulness for antidepressants than in HICs 21 . However, it is unclear if national-level differences in healthcare spending or quality-of-care influence treatment helpfulness. We hypothesise that GDP, health expenditure and lower out-of-pocket health expenditure are associated with higher treatment utilisation and helpfulness (H3).


## Study rationale and hypotheses


Overall, there is a lack of global cross-national evidence to understand the within and between country variations of three central CMD health outcomes (lifetime prevalence, treatment utilisation and treatment helpfulness). Using an individual-level survey dataset in 111

countries, we investigate if socio-economic and psycho-social inequalities in the three health outcomes exist universally, and what factors explain between-country variation.

There are two main reasons for studying the three health outcomes together. First, we cannot fully understand the mechanisms behind inequalities in the burden of disease by studying single health outcomes if inequalities exacerbate over different health outcomes. Research on infectious diseases and depression 22,23 used cascades of care approaches to examine at what points of the treatment journey patients drop out. Here, we apply this thinking to CMDs and examine three major health outcomes (who is affected, who receives treatment and who perceives treatment as helpful), while our interest is in understanding inequalities at each step. Notably, we focus three key health outcomes in many countries, instead of a larger healthcare cascade in one specific context. Second, differences in the determinants of the three health outcomes might have differential implications on what policies are needed to reduce health inequalities. Studying the outcomes together in one study can make such differences explicit.


## Hypotheses


In summary, existing work in this area suggests 3 hypotheses relevant to our main research objective.

H1(SES). Lower SES individuals have a higher CMD lifetime prevalence, are less likely to utilise professional treatment and to perceive this treatment as helpful, irrespective of HIC/LMIC country context.

H2(Psycho-social) . Lower levels of stigma perceptions and higher levels of trust in health practitioners is associated with higher treatment utilisation and perceived helpfulness. H3(Country-level/Macroeconomic). Higher GDP and health expenditure, and lower out-of- pocket health expenditure are associated with higher treatment utilisation and helpfulness.


## 3. Methods



## Sample


The data was collected via telephone between August 2020 and January 2021 by Gallup commissioned by the Wellcome Trust. The dataset is publicly available online, alongside research and methodology reports 24 . The dataset included representative population-based surveys in 113 countries. Two countries were exluced because in Tajikistan, the mental health items were not included and in Venezuala, the variable on participants' household income is missing which is central to estimate socio-economic inequalties. Therefore, the final sample included 111 counties and 117,088 participants (see supplamentary Table S9). Data collection was situated in the context of the Covid-19 pandemic. Survey development was concluded before the pandemic and data collection had started before being interrupted in March 2020. Yet, the conclusions of this study aim to be relevant beyond the pandemic's context: All outcome variables used in this study refer to lifetime experiences rather than pandemic-related events.

Variables


## Dependent variables


Lifetime prevalence of anxiety or depression was measured using a single item 'Have you ever been so anxious or depressed that you could not continue your regular daily activities as you normally would for two weeks or longer' with 'Yes' or 'No'  The item was designed by . Wellcome Trust researchers considering the general diagnostic criteria for anxiety and depression with the goal to elicit analytical comparisons across country-contexts and cultures (rather than epidemiological precision of prevalence) 24 . The item underwent cognitive testing to fulfil this purpose of cross-country comparability. Respondents who reported lifetime experience with anxiety or depression were asked about two types of treatment utilisation: 'When you were feeling so anxious or depressed, did you ever do any of the following to

make yourself feel better? Talk to a mental health professional' and 'Take medication prescribed by a healthcare professional' ('Yes' / 'No'). Both items underwent cognitive testing in 10 countries to confirm interpretability across countries. This showed that 'talking to a mental health professional' was interpreted by the participants in a variety of ways such as 'talking to a therapist, doing talk therapy, or talking to a mental health professional' . Similarly, for 'taking prescribed medication', the type of medication was intentionally left open.

Those who answered treatment utilisation questions with 'Yes' were questioned on their perceived treatment helpfulness "Did you find the following very helpful, somewhat helpful, or not helpful in making you feel better?' regarding both treatment types (3= Very helpful , 2= Somewhat helpful , 1= not helpful ). To ensure consistency of interpretation and effect sizes across all statistical models (see Figure 1 and Table 2), categorised ' not helpful ' and ' somewhat helpful ' together as ' not entirely helpful ' (contrasted with the category ' very helpful '). Sensitivity tests showed that results remained stable compared to the original coding (see supplementary Table S8).


## Socio-economic factors


Out of the different health outcomes in this study, the link between SES (income and education) and CMD lifetime prevalence the most thoroughly documented across country contexts as lower SES individuals are more frequently affected by depression and anxiety  . 8 Theories on the pathway between income and mental health identify material circumstances, psycho-social stress, and behavioural differences  . SES also affects treatment utilisation for 4

CMDs  3 . Generally, only a minority of affected individuals receives minimally adequate treatment  . Evidence from the European Union and Switzerland suggests that those 9 individuals who do utilise treatment have higher educational attainment and income 5,10 . Lastly, SES is associated with treatment effectiveness. Two systematic reviews using studies from the US and Europe showed that the effectiveness of psychological therapies 11 and antidepressant treatments 12 is lower for low SES individuals. As an explanation, lower SES individuals might face more socio-economic stressors which cannot be relieved by treatment 13 . Besides treatment effectiveness, perceived helpfulness is as a patient-centred way to measure treatment outcomes 14 , that yields high levels of external validity (Edlund et al., 2015). Using data from WHO's World Mental Health (WMH) Survey Initiative across 16 countries, researchers found that individuals with higher education perceive depression treatment as more helpful  . In summary, we do not know if the association between SES and mental health 2 outcomes is stable across all country contexts. We hypothesise that SES is associated with lifetime prevalence, treatment utilisation and helpfulness in both HICs and LMICs (H1).


## Psycho-social factors


Mental health stigma and negative help-seeking attitudes are well-documented barriers for utilising CMD treatment and explain part of the relationship between SES and treatment utilisation 16 . Stigma is a particularly widely studied barrier to treatment-seeking, with crossnational evidence stemming from the 2006 and 2010 Eurobarometer surveys  . Other psycho7 social factors gained less attention. Qualitative evidence suggests that trust in mental health practitioners and services is an important determinant of help-seeking 17,18 . However, trust has not been examined in quantitative, cross-national studies. Psycho-social factors might also be associated with the abovementioned measure of perceived helpfulness. The implications of outcome expectations and associated placebo effects for pharmacological treatments and talking therapy are well documented 19 . However, whether stigma or trust in health

practitioners are correlated with perceived treatment helpfulness has not been investigated across countries. Again, cross-national evidence on treatment utilisation and helpfulness is limited to European countries, and the role of trust is under-researched. We hypothesise that stigma and trust in healthcare professionals are associated with treatment utilisation and helpfulness across a sample of 111 countries (H2).


## Country-level factors


Lifetime prevalence of CMDs varies across country contexts. The Global Burden of Diseases study shows that HICs tend to have a lower prevalence than LMICs  . Regarding treatment 1 utilisation, the size of mental health treatment gaps varies depending on country-level economic and healthcare capabilities. The WMH Survey Initiative shows that 36% of people affected by anxiety disorders utilise treatment in HICs, and only 13% in lower-middle-income countries 20 . Evidence on country-level variations in healthcare utilisation is based on the Eurobarometer surveys 2006 and 2010. In Europe, healthcare spending and the available mental healthcare workforce explain cross-national variation in antidepressant use  . 5

Country-level variation in treatment helpfulness is not well-documented. The only two studies on this topic using the WMH Survey Initiative involved too few countries to include specific country-level predictors 2,21 . Surprisingly, patients in LMICs reported a higher treatment helpfulness for antidepressants than in HICs 21 . However, it is unclear if national-level differences in healthcare spending or quality-of-care influence treatment helpfulness. We hypothesise that GDP, health expenditure and lower out-of-pocket health expenditure are associated with higher treatment utilisation and helpfulness (H3).

## Psycho-social factors (H2)


H2, which states that psycho-social factors are associated with treatment utilisation and helpfulness, is confirmed by the results shown in Table 2. Perceived stigma (OR=0.93[0.900.97]), belief in science to treat mental health conditions (OR=1.08[1.05-1.12]) and trust in health professionals (1.10[1.06-1.14]) all predict mental health professional utilisation and also significantly predict the utilisation of prescribed medication in the same direction (see Table 2). Similarly, perceived stigma (OR=0.76[0.72-0.81]) and trust in health professionals (OR=1.32[1.24-1.40]) also predict the perceived helpfulness of both types of treatment in the hypothesised direction. ## Country-level factors (H3)


H3 states that country-level economic and healthcare factors explain between-country variation in the health outcomes. Table 2 highlights several significant country-level effects. Higher income inequality (Gini) is associated with a higher prevalence of anxiety or depression (OR=1.02[1.004-1.03]). GDP (OR=1.26[1.08-1.47]) and health expenditure (OR=1.11[1.04-1.19]) are related to higher mental health professional utilisation. In contrast, for utilisation of prescribed medication, such country level effects were small and not significant.
