## 5. Discussion


This study used a survey dataset in 111 countries to investigate within and between country inequalities in the three mental health outcomes of CMD lifetime prevalence, treatment utilisation and perceived treatment helpfulness.

This study demonstrates that socio-economic inequalities cut across the three health outcomes of prevalence, mental health professional utilization, and perceived helpfulness in both HICs and LMICs. Firstly, in line with previous research individuals with lower SES (income and education) have a higher lifetime prevalence of anxiety and depression 4,8 . Secondly, individuals with higher SES are more likely to talk to a mental health professional when they are affected by anxiety or depression. These results indicate that higher SES individuals are more likely to engage in talking therapy and specialist mental health care. This is in line with Europe-based research on treatment utilisation for mental health services 3,10 and specialist medical healthcare 26 . Thirdly, talking to a mental health professional was perceived as more helpful by higher SES individuals. As potential explanations, talking therapy might be better tailored to the needs of those higher education 27 and might more readily provide perceivable progress for individuals without poverty related pressures 13 . In conclusion, these findings point to a global 'triple inequality effect', whereby disadvantages of lower SES individuals deepen along each of the three health outcomes.

However, this 'triple inequality effect' was only shown for the utilisation of mental health professionals, and not regarding utilisation and perceived helpfulness for pharmacological treatments. SES had no significant association with utilisation with taking prescribed medication in HICs, while in LMICs, the reversed social gradient was shown for utilisation. In LMICs, richer and more educated individuals were less likely to take prescribed medication when affected by anxiety or depression. Different explanations for these effects can be considered. First, antidepressant medication tends to be cheaper and easier to access for both healthcare

providers than specialist care and talking therapy 5,28 . Therefore, income might not be an important determinant for medication. Relatedly, medication is often prescribed by primary health care professionals 29 which is - opposed to specialist care - is more frequently used by lower SES individuals 26 . As a second potential explanation, the item to measure treatment utilisation might have been interpreted differently across countries. As the survey item did not specify what type of prescribed medication was taken, the types of pharmacological treatment might differ between HICs and LMICs. As in LMICs, depression and anxiety are particularly strongly underdiagnosed, people reporting with CMD symptoms might be treated for their somatic symptoms  30 . In such cases, higher SES individuals might be less likely to take such potentially unsuitable medication. Future research needs to differentiate between the specific types of treatment and find explanations for the different socio-economic effects.

Besides stigma perceptions, trust in healthcare professionals was identified as predictors for treatment utilisation. Especially with the sensitive topic of mental health, trust is an important condition to disclose personal problems and seek help 18 . This finding highlights the importance to increase trust between patients and healthcare providers. Interestingly, stigma and trust were also associated with perceived helpfulness of both treatment types. Thus, treatment helpfulness might be influenced by psychological factors that shape expectations and interactions during the treatment. Conversely, a successful therapy might influence perceptions of stigma and trust. Future research should attempt to disentangle these two alternative causal pathways.

This paper extents previous findings on national-level treatment variation in Europe 5,7 and shows that GDP and health expenditure are important predictors of treatment utilisation globally. The richer a country, the more likely are its citizens to access mental health specialists. However, health expenditure and GDP do not explain cross-national variations in the use of medication in this study. As highlighted earlier, this might be because providing

and using medication requires fewer country-level financial resources than providing specialist mental healthcare. Surprisingly, higher GDP is negatively associated with perceived treatment helpfulness of both types of treatment. Based on H3, we expected that higher country-level economic resources would entail with higher service availability and quality of care, and therefore relate to higher treatment satisfaction. Previous findings also indicate that antidepressant treatments were perceived as more helpful in LMICs than HICs 21 . Possibly, richer countries might have higher expectations in treatment helpfulness which are harder to fulfil. This effect should be thoroughly investigated in future international research.

Several limitations should be highlighted. First, the study uses cross-sectional data and memory recall for lifetime events, which make the results prone to response biases. Second, the data collection during Covid-19 might have changed the salience of mental health related topics. Third, the item to measure lifetime experience of anxiety or depression was designed to allow international comparisons of lifetime experiences, but not clinically precise measurement. No distinction between anxiety and depression can be drawn as they are measured in one item. Forth, differences in the meaning for "talking to mental health professional" and 'taking medication prescribed by a healthcare professional' leave some uncertainty around the results as highlighted in the discussion. Future research should use longitudinal designs and distinctive measures for anxiety, depression, and treatment types to validate our findings.

## 1 Introduction 1


The role of social media, and digital networks more generally, in civic society is a growing scholarly and public concern (Bennett and Segerberg, 2012; Earl and Kimport, 2011; Liu, 2020). The use of social media in both spectacular events, such as the attack on Capitol Hill, and for ordinary everyday coordination within local sports clubs points to the large uptake of social media for a broad spectrum of civil society. The capacity of social media groups to recruit members and facilitate civic participation is, therefore, of great importance. This was especially true during the COVID-19 pandemic. The pandemic and government lock downs of large parts of society, including the provision of both public and private welfare services, resulted in an urgent and diverse set of needs. The elderly and sick needed help with shopping and errands while isolating to avoid infection, the shut down of schools and child-centers left parents alone with their children while still having to work, citizens needed information about the illness and the regulations put in place to contain it, and economic recession and sharply rising unemployment rates, left many economically vulnerable. Due to the pandemic's requirement for social distancing and the lockdown of large parts of society, digitally mediated organizing became necessary for civil society actors' coordination of social support. In response to these needs and the

altered circumstances, we witnessed massive mobilization of voluntary help and support, especially within digital networks, in civil societies across the world (Bertogg and Koos, 2021; Borb´th et al., 2021; Carlsen, Toubøl, and Brincker, a 2021; Miao et al., 2021; Woodman, 2020). This development poses central questions concerning the ability of social media networks to facilitate help, particularly with regard to the volume and type of the help facilitated, and the persistence and demography of the volunteers. In this paper, we seek to answer these questions, central to the ongoing debates in studies of online facilitated civic participation.

Current research finds divergent results regarding most of the above questions. While social movement scholars found that social media was a powerful vehicle for mobilization (important in terms of volume ) in cases such as the Arab spring and Gezi park (Steinert-Threlkeld, 2017; Tufekci, 2017; Wolfsfeld et al., 2013), other studies comparing the likelihood of actual participation given digital participation typically find that very little participation coming from digital mobilization (Lacetera et al., 2016, Lewis et al., 2014). With regard to type of civic participation, scholars have, on the one hand argued that digital modes of organization only facilitate cheap activism, which has been referred to as clicktivism (Diani, 2000; Eimhjellen, 2019; Laer and Aelst, 2010; Morozov, 2011), while others have pointed to a broad set of civic activities coordinated through digital platforms (Carlsen, Toubøl, and Ralund, 2021; Gundelach and Toubøl, 2019). Relating to persistence , some research has found that digital activists are periodically active and by far the majority activists are one-time activists (Lewis et al., 2014), rendering digital activism an ephemeral and loose form of organizing that is unable to organize enduring efforts. Others find that online organized civic organizations may be able to persist and organize continual activities for a substantial time span (Carlsen et al., 2020; Toubøl, 2017). Finally,

it has been argued that digital modes of organizing are demographically biased in the sense that they affect a participation gap across socio-economic strata and generations driven by unequal access to digital platforms and possession of digital skills (Schradie, 2018). Others, argue that the cheapness of digital activism enables participation from a broader spectrum of the population (Earl and Kimport, 2011). In support of the latter hypothesis Eimhjellen and Ljunggren, 2017, find that in Norway those with a short education are more likely to participate in digital volunteering (administrate forums or fund raise). In sum, critics argue that digital networks support little, cheap, periodic and biased civic participation, while others argue the exact opposite. However, there is a lack of rigorous empirical investigation and testing of these claims, which, in combination with the phenomena still being young and in rapid development, leaves the questions relatively open.

To investigate these issues in an empirically rigorous fashion, this paper exploits original data encompassing a three-wave panel survey data set covering the adult Danish population and a comprehensive data set on volunteering organized in 247 Facebook groups in the spring 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic in Denmark. The results paint an overall more favorable image of the potential of digital participation, but they also confirm some of the critical assessments of this kind of civic organization. We show that in the COVID-19 crisis, the volume of help provided by digital networks was quite significant and also displayed the trademark of digital activism observed elsewhere, namely the ability to mobilize extremely fast, thereby, being able to respond almost instantaneously to the urgent needs for help in the population. Second, by direct comparison with the types of activities carried out in traditional formal civil society organizations (CSOs) we show that digital networks did not facilitate cheaper types of help than traditional formal CSOs, thus rejecting the click-

tivism hypotheses. With regard to persistence, survival analyses confirm that social media networks are less successful in terms of sustaining engagement at the individual level compared to formal CSOs. Finally, turning to demography, the digital gap with regard to age is confirmed, but with regard to social strata, the evidence suggests that digital networks are more successful in terms of engaging individuals with a relatively short education. These insights suggests that traditional formal CSOs and digital networks may complement each other and thereby strengthen the overall civic effort in a given cause.

In this paper, we focus on specific aspects of digital participation, namely what Earl and Kimport (2011) has call e-mobilization, which is the use of online infrastructures to coordinate and mobilize actors civic participation both on- and offline. Furthermore, we are interested in participation organized in informal digital communities and networks. When we refer to digital networks or organizing, we mean informal groups that have mobilized via digital platforms and use digital platforms, such as Facebook groups, as their main organizational vehicle. We thereby exclude formal civic society organizations that use social media groups to communicate with volunteers.

We proceed by discussing the current state of the art in the literature on digital civic participation in the following section. We then outline our research design and motivate why our comparative strategy is well suited to address central questions regarding the volume, type, persistence and demography of online civic participation. We begin the analyses by describing the context around the COVID-19 pandemic in Denmark in the spring of 2020 and then we turn to addressing the questions of the volume, type, persistence and demography of participation facilitated through digital networks as opposed to those facilitated through formal CSO.


## 2 A comparative approach to digital organizing


The various different approaches to studying digital participation have had important contributions in trying to specify digital participation vis-`-vis a other modes of organizing participation. Schematically viewed, one can say that case studies of prominent digital mobilizations contributed to recognition of a new medium of organizing that should be taken seriously (Bennett and Segerberg, 2012; Tufekci, 2017). Population studies of 'members' of digital networks have empirically demonstrated that we should not equate digital engagement with activism or volunteering: very few of those who are digitally active contribute with actual participation (Lacetera et al., 2016; Lewis et al., 2014). Most recently, field level approaches have tried to specify consequences of digital participation for the competition between organizations from different socio-economic strata within a specific issue domain (Schradie, 2018). The latter approach holds the issue and political context constant and compares digital participation across different groups.

Combining multiple insights from the prior literature, the main conceptual point in this paper is that we should compare digital organizing forms of civic participation to other modes of organizing (e.g., CSOs churches, public and semi-public institutions and so on) within the same mobilization or related to the same cause in order to assess how digital civic participation differs in a comparative perspective. This should be done by comparing the participation facilitated in terms of volume and type, and the population activated in terms of persistence and demography, in order to understand and evaluate digital organizing's contribution to the overall mobilization of volunteers.


## 2.1 The problem of comparison in the current literature


One of the main arguments against the importance of participation on social media is that the average digital activist is not very active and the type of engagement happening online is not really activism (Eimhjellen, 2019). In other words, the contribution is small and cheap. Lewis and colleagues (Lewis et al., 2014) find that a very small fraction of those who are active in the Facebook groups around the Save Darfur humanitarian cause donated any money or recruited new members. The vast majority was passive. Lewis et al. conclude 'that Facebook conjured an illusion of activism rather than facilitating the real thing' (2014:1). Similarly, Lacetera et al., 2016 find that although a charity campaign generated a lot of digital activity, it only resulted in 30 donations out of 6.4 million users exposed. These findings provide strong support for not equating likes and online membership with activism. While some authors have conceptually rethought activism in the light of these new and very cheap forms of participation (Earl and Kimport, 2011), it is important to handle this heterogeneity and not uncritically assume that online traces such as likes and comments, imply more weighty forms of participation such as donations, protest behavior or social support.

The strength of Lewis et al.'s (2014) study is that they have an actual measure of participation. Yet, from the fact that most group members do not engage in anything but clicktivism, it does not necessarily follow that digital networks are not important for the overall mobilization. Even though the active members only make up a small fraction of the total pool of members, it still might be a quite substantial fraction of the total share of participation related to the given issue across all kinds of organizational settings, offand online. The ease of joining online groups should make us expect that many do so out of curiosity and/or sympathy for the cause. Hence, digital groups and networks often con-

tain a heterogeneous set of actors, ranging from curious bystanders and those who sympathize with the cause but do not participate - what social movement scholars call the sentiment pool - to what we might call actively engaged, a category that is itself heterogeneous, ranging froom plugin participants, rank and file members to highly active core members. The fact that the pool of sympathizers and curious bystanders are many times larger than the comparatively minuscule fraction that actually participate in a given mobilization is well known in the social movement literature (e.g., McAdam, 1986) and when this point of comparison is chosen, almost any form of civic participation appears to be relatively small. What has changed with digital organizing is that the larger sentiment pool leaves traces of support on digital platforms, but this does not mean we should treat them as digital activists.

That said, the few population-level surveys that compare digital volunteering with traditional volunteering find that digital volunteering is a rather limited phenomenon (Eimhjellen, 2019). However, many case studies of online mobilization suggests that this might be because online organizing is primarily used in times of crisis (e.g., political struggles (Steinert-Threlkeld, 2017; Wolfsfeld et al., 2013), natural disasters (Albris, 2018)) and therefore displays low participation rates in more peaceful times.

A number of studies have reached the opposite conclusion to the clicktivism hypothesis. They find that online networks facilitate large mobilization of highcost and high-risk activism (Carlsen, Toubøl, and Ralund, 2021; Gundelach and Toubøl, 2019; Tufekci, 2017). The problem with these affirmative studies of social media's importance is that they sample on the dependent variable and they typically do not compare online activism to other organizational settings. Theocharis et al., 2017, for example, investigate the digitally mediated solidarity activism in the wake of the financial crisis, but the study draws on a single

digital initiative and hence can't answer comparative questions regarding the importance of digital organizing relative to formal CSOs. Several reinforcing misunderstandings can result from these methodological issues. First, inferring from cases that have already proven to be successful on social media without taking into account all the unsuccessful mobilization attempts is an obvious problem if used to conclude something more general about digital organizing (or any other form of civic mobilization for that matter (McAdam and Boudet, 2012)). Second, if one does not compare with other vehicles of mobilizing, there is no way of knowing wheather the observed online mobilization is relatively large or small given other organizational modes of mobilization.

Students of online civic participation also disagree about whether digital organizing might facilitate participation for those who are underrepresented in traditional formal CSOs or whether it excludes groups that lack digital literacy creating a digital gap in civil society. Earl and Kimport (2011) present a resource centered argument saying that online infrastructures might mobilize low resource individuals due to the reduced cost of coordination and participation, thereby countering the normal inequalities in participation in civil society that have been documented again and again. Various empirical studies supports this thesis. Eimhjellen and Ljunggren, 2017, find that individuals with short-term education are likely to engage in digital volunteering. Tai et al., 2020, find that the association between e-participation and offline participation is strongest for the less affluent. Ackermann and Manatschal, 2018, drawing on a population-based sample, find that digital volunteering is not dependent on resources, where offline volunteering is. Ackermann and Manatschal, 2018, also find support for the hypothesis that digital volunteering helps mobilize younger cohorts normally underrepresented in offline volunteering. However, Schradie, 2018 argues against the equalizing potential of digital activism and

shows how digital activism reestablishes divides between high and low resource groups. Typically, communicating online demands certain literacy and digital competencies associated with and gained through long-term education.

Schradie(2018) study compares civic groups from different social strata and their relative engagement online, but does not compare this with non-digital engagement. Furthermore, she operates at an organizational level and does not address individual level variation. This makes it difficult to understand and evaluate the ability of digital networks to activate new parts of the population. It seems unlikely that any given organizational mode will be representative of society at large, hence, from this perspective, any given organizational mode will always be biased. While these biases in organizational modes are important to locate, we need to supplement them with an analysis of their role within the overall ecology. This means we need to specify the role of digital networks in facilitating different parts of the population in comparison with other forms of organizing.

Thus, the studies that provide the foundations for assessing whether digital civic participation is large or small, cheap or costly, sustained or periodic, equalizes civic participation or reinforces digital gaps, only provide tentative evidence to support their diverging answers to these questions. This points to the need for research designs that better allow us to address these questions using appropriate comparisons between this new, and still developing form of civic participation and traditional forms.


## 3 Digital and survey data


This paper uses data from two separate data sets. The first data set is a comprehensive sample of COVID-19 help groups on Facebook with information the timing of their formation and locality. The data also contains information on

activity within the groups, posts and comments, but these are not used in the present analysis. The Facebook groups were located using an extensive search strategy which varied both keywords and location referent, resulting in more than 5000 groups of which 247 where deemed to be about facilitating help during the COVID-19 crisis (Carlsen, Toubøl, and Brincker, 2021).

The second, and main data source, is a national three-wave panel survey on solidarity, volunteering and support during the COVID-19 crisis conducted between 3 April and 11 May 2020 in Denmark. The survey section of Statistics Denmark (DST Survey) collected the responses from a random sample of the Danish population in the age range of 16-99 years old. The online questionnaire was distributed electronically to the inbox of e-Boks that the vast majority of the population have and use to communicate with public authorities and institutions as well as private companies such as banks and insurance companies. The small group who opted out of e-Boks received an invitation by post. The invitations were followed by telephone reminders offering the opportunity of being interviewed by phone.

For the first wave, 42.6 percent (3,389 respondents) out of a total sample of 7,964 individuals completed the survey. This response rate is similar to the general level of response rates in these types of studies (Toubøl and Frederiksen, 2019). When testing for representativity, the response sample displays the expected patterns of under-representation of ethnic minorities and overrepresentation of the elderly, people with higher education, and people with high incomes. To counter these biases, we apply analytical weights constructed from the distributions of age, gender and occupational status when we report descriptive statistics on the helping behavior of the population.

To assess the persistence of activists, we also use data from the second and third waves of the panel. The invitations to participate in the second and third

waves were distributed in a dynamic way relative the timestamp of the prior response aiming for a ideally 3-4 week time gap between the three points of observation for each individual. This means that the second round of responses were roughly collected during the month of May and the first half of June 2020 and the third round was collected in June and the first half of July 2020. 25 percent of the original sample (2,000 respondents) provided complete responses to all three waves.

In addition to measuring standard factors related to personal biography and household, socio-economic status and social capital the questionnaire inquired about each respondent's participation in voluntary support related to COVID-19 in the role of provider as well as recipient of such help. For the present analysis, our key survey items are questions concerning the type of help respondents undertook and which organizational context this was done in. It also asked about the respondent's embeddedness and activities in the wider civil society before the COVID-19 crisis commenced. Questions on the respondent's general as well as specific attitudes toward COVID-19, such as trust in the ability of different actors to handle COVID-19 and perceived personal risks of contracting the disease were also included, as were questions regarding perceived personal health and specific medical history of COVID-19 of themselves and their close relations.

## 4.1 The Mobilization of COVID-19 support on Facebook in Denmark


Denmark was among the first countries to impose a comprehensive lock-down on large parts of society, including the majority of health and welfare services. This also encompassed traditional CSOs which had to temporarily shut down street level services and reorganize activities to conform to requirements regarding distancing and isolation that were imposed by the government in order to contain the disease. Hence, a move to digital platforms became necessary. Whilst formal CSOs also use digital platforms to organize their activity, in this analysis,

when we refer to digital organizing, we refer to largely informal organizing that has digital platforms as its core arena of both recruitment and organization. In a Danish context, the digital platform used by informal groups is typically Facebook. One very central aspect of Facebook in a Danish context is that up to 70 percent of the Danish population use Facebook (Tassy 2018), and 53 percent use it on a daily basis. Hence many Danish citizens are familiar with the mode of communication, which makes it easy to join and more predictable in social and cultural terms. Large parts of the Danish population know what it implies to be a member of a Facebook group and it is routinely used to mobilize large scale voluntary efforts (e.g., Carlsen et al., 2022; Carlsen, Toubøl, and Ralund, 2021.

As Figure 1 clearly illustrates, Facebook COVID-19 help groups were formed in direct response to the lockdown announcement by the Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, on the 11th of April. On The 11th of April alone, 59 groups were formed and by the end of March almost 250 groups had been created. These groups were not just empty containers with no members. Not long after they had opened, they counted over 100 000 members wanting to help with everything from information sharing to shopping, from the production of health equipment to dog walking. As Figure 2 shows, the groups opened up all around Denmark. The groups depicted in Figure 2 are only the local and regional groups, and in addition to these, several national groups also emerged.

This data clearly indicates that there was a massive attempt at mobilizing help using digital infrastructures, and it demonstrates success in terms of attention, i.e., the groups were discovered by large numbers of Danish citizens many of whom joined. Based on the numbers of groups and members alone, the COVID-19 mobilization of voluntary help was massive compared to other recent online mobilizations of voluntary help and support (Carlsen et al., 2022;

## 5 Conclusion and discussion


Using an original population representative, three-wave survey panel data set we have mapped voluntary participation during the COVID-19 crisis in the

spring 2020 in Denmark. The paper provides insight into the following four central topics of debate in civil society studies concerning the role of socialmedia-organized civic participation in the overall voluntary efforts of civil society in response to the COVID-19 crisis: 1) volume of participation and 2) type of participation and 3) the persistence and 4) the demography of the online volunteers compared to the type of volunteering organized in formal CSOs.

The results indicate that the volume of voluntary help organized online during the early phase of the COVID-19 crisis was quite substantial, amounting to around 2/3 of that organized in formal CSOs. With regard to the types of activity and the frequency of helping of the individual volunteer, overall, we do not observe substantial differences between the two forms of organizing. These findings suggest that we should not discount digital networks and social media as a source for mobilizing substantial and much needed voluntary efforts in times of crisis. Notions of 'clicktivism' do not apply in our case since the effort of the online volunteers cannot be said to be cheap relative to that of the formal CSOs. Our results also show that digital networks were not the only relevant mode of organizing despite lockdown measures having given digital forms of participation an obvious advantage. Informal personal networks and formal CSOs where still the dominate modes of participation. In terms of persistence, we find digital volunteers to be less persistent compared to volunteers organized in formal CSOs, which is in line with other results in the literature (e.g., Lewis et al., 2014). Lastly, in terms of demography, we find that, compared to formal CSOs, digital organizing, relatively speaking, facilitates more participation from those with a short education.

Our results clearly demonstrate that digital organizing should be taken seriously as a mode of organizing participation. Yet, even during the COVID-19 pandemic, which disadvantaged forms of organizing that rely on physical co-

presence, it should not be considered as the only relevant form of volunteering. Our comparative research design has some clear advantages in characterizing digital organizing through an adequate comparison to other forms of organizing. The comparative outlook also points to the need to move beyond analyzing digital organizing in isolation and towards focusing on its role in the wider voluntary efforts.

We end by discussing how our results suggest that we should specify the role of digital organizing in comparison to formal forms of volunteering, and point to future productive areas of research. Digital organizing played the role as civil society's first responder during the COVID-19 pandemic. Within days of the lockdown, hundreds of help groups had been formed covering most of Denmark and supporting a substantial amount of participation. Almost all of the volunteers in digital networks were only active in the first period of observation, while volunteers in CSOs had a higher rate of persistence. From this perspective, the role of digital networks was to support mobilization immediately in the wake of a crisis, providing help until larger formal organizations adapted and started their volunteering initiatives. This first responder characteristic of digital organizing points to its importance in emergency and crisis situations. Social media has played a similar role in responding to local floods (Albris, 2018) and service provision for refugees (Toubøl, 2017) and more. In contrast, studies conducted in times not characterized by an immediate crisis (Eimhjellen and Ljunggren, 2017) found little evidence that online-mediated volunteering played a significant role.

We also find that digital networks and CSOs complement one another in regards to the parts of the population they mobilize. Digital networks mobilize actors who have shorter educations compared to those in CSOs. While there might be technical and literary skills associated with social media usage

(Schradie, 2018), these result in less educational bias than the processes related to participation in CSOs. This mirrors the findings from resource mobilization theory (Wilson, 2000; Wilson and Musick, 1998) suggesting that participation in formal CSOs requires the ability to navigate complex organizations and a bureaucratic talent which presupposes a certain level of cultural capital acquired through education. Thus, our interpretation suggests that, to potential volunteers, digital networks constitute an alternative that allows for direct help without having to navigate a complex organization. In short, the idea of complementarity suggests that CSOs and digital networks supplement one another in order to maximize the total amount of help and temporal coverage of help during a crisis.

Future research should seek to investigate digital networks as stepping stones to more enduring voluntary engagement in CSOs and/or personal networks. Do digital networks cultivate a preference for voluntary work in its participants that later results in the participants moving on and joining an established CSO? Do digital networks translate into enduring support relations between the provider of help and the recipient of help? More generally, researchers should start to view digital networks as an organizational form amongst other forms active in the voluntary efforts. Research can then start to address the central question of complementarity and/or competition between digital networks and other ways of organizing social support.

Finally, we would like to make a reservation with regard to the external validity of our study's findings relating to the specificities of the COVID-19 crisis. One might ask whether our results generalize beyond the COVID-19 crisis situation during which digitalization was unprecedented and which might relate to the requirements of physical distancing. While the precise consequence of physical distancing on civil-society participation remains unknown, the pat-

tern of digital mobilization of civic participation occurring in relation to major events and crisis has been found in multiple empirical studies (e.g., Albris, 2018; Carlsen et al., 2022; Carlsen, Toubøl, and Ralund, 2021; Tufekci, 2017). Thus, as also discussed in the preceding, our findings might not generalize to more stable periods in which studies find that digital networks play a more restraint role. On the other hand, our results might very well be transferable to other crisis situations, be they due to political turmoil, natural disasters, or something else stirring up social life.

## Data Collection Procedure


The  use  of  innovative  computer  technologies  provides  an  opportunity  to  create  a qualitatively new information educational environment without borders and with the possibility of organizing a global system of distance learning. Distance learning is a component of creating an open education system that provides nationwide access to educational resources.

Uzhhorod National University offers online learning via Google Meet, Classroom, and Moodle e-learning platforms (E-Learning. Uzhhorod National University).

Tests with automatic checking allow you to organize a quick assessment of the level of mastering  the  educational  material  students.  Typically,  test  systems  can  create  questions  of different types (multiple choice, text or numerical answer, ordering, matching, etc.). Libraries of ready-made questions are often available that you can add to your testing sessions, modifying them as needed. Most services provide the ability to create questions, sometimes with multiple-choice answers, using images, audio, and video clips. This way, you can form a whole trajectory of a single topic. Typical settings for online tests include the ability to shuffle questions and answer choices within them, set time limits (time to attempt, time to open the quiz for completion), limit the number of attempts, and the method or time of reporting test results. If testing is used for educational purposes, you can loosen the strictness of these parameters. If the testing is for control purposes,  then  more  severe  restrictions  can  be  applied,  and  students  can  be  reminded  of  the importance  of  academic  integrity.  It  should  be  noted  that  automated  testing,  although  it dramatically  simplifies  the  routine  work  of  the  teacher,  is  sometimes  insufficient  to  reliably diagnose the success of mastering the topic. Therefore, supplement test tasks with practical tasks, exercises, essays, etc. The teacher can provide feedback on the test results individually or take into account the dynamics of student responses in planning different classes (Organization of Distance Learning at School Methodological Recommendations, 2020, pp. 33-34).

At the Faculty of Philology, training is organized in a mixed form. Some students work in the classroom, and some stay at home. The part of students who work remotely usually receives educational material via the Google Meet platform, and the systematic consolidation of what has been learned, self-study, etc., takes place on the Moodle e-learning site.

The use of distance learning technologies increases and improves the effectiveness of the educational  process,  which  largely  depends  on  the  level  of  preparation  of  teachers  for  the implementation of distance learning, as well as on the readiness of students to study in distance education  (Tkachenko,  Khmelnytska,  2021,  p.  91). ## Discussion


Platforms  Moodle,  LearningApps,  and  Kahoot!  can  be  ways  of  synchronous  and asynchronous  learning.  Among  the  advantages  of  synchronous  learning  is  the  involvement  of participants in the learning process directly during the lesson. This mode provides quick feedback from the teacher, correction, and explanation of unclear points; organization of group activities; development of communication and collaboration skills; motivation to  learn  in  the  process  of communication  (Tkachenko,  Khmelnytska,  2021,  p.  93).  The  disadvantages  of  synchronous learning include the current realities associated with problems with electricity and communication in Ukraine. The modern student of higher education does not always want to be squeezed into the

limited time frame of the educational process, so the synchronization of the schedule can also interfere  with  the  mastering  of  the  specialty.  The  asynchronous  format  is  characterized  by  the flexibility of the program; lack of dependence on communication interference; the ability to learn the educational material at one's own pace; availability of educational materials at a convenient time for the student; development of self-organization skills and knowledge to learn (Tkachenko, Khmelnytska,  2021,  p. 93).  It  is  clear  that  the  lack  of  understandable  organization  of  the educational process can be a disadvantage. In today's conditions, higher education students should strive to master soft skills, increase information and digital competence and build their trajectory of educational development. Therefore, web resources Moodle, LearningApps, and Kahoot! are effective ways to check the level of mastery of academic material by students, provided they are aware  of  the  applicant's  role  as  an  active  participant  in  the  educational  process.  A  promising direction for the development of distance learning in higher education institutions of Ukraine is the close cooperation of developers of software products for distance learning, distance education methodologists, and teachers of higher education institutions to develop strategies for the use of new information technologies in distance learning (Osadcha, Sysoeva, 2019, p. 277).


## Conclusion


Thus,  the  modern  educational  process  in  higher  education  institutions  to  improve  and modernize, is in search of new information forms of education. The classical form of education cannot  fully  ensure  the  development  of  personal  and  professional  competencies  of  higher education students. Modern tools for the implementation of distance learning make the educational process  dynamic  and  exciting.  The  most  effective  in  establishing  optimal  interaction  between teacher and student during the war were web resources Moodle, LearningApps, and Kahoot! In addition, they teach students to organize their time, spending it on development. Higher education institutions in Ukraine face challenges in the conditions of war due to both current events and the requirements of digitalization. Today, specialists competent in information and communication technologies motivated to develop and improve are in demand. Therefore, the main task of higher education  institutions  is  to  create  appropriate  conditions  for  teachers  and  students  to  distance learning. The use of distance learning tools increases the motivation, and initiative of students, improves  the  quality  of  education  and  educational  services,  and  increases  the  flexibility  of educational goals of higher education institutions.

## INTRODUCTION


Museums are the representative of our cultural heritage. It plays a crucial role in preserving the art and craft of culture by careful documenting and preserving the artifacts. Due to such effort of documentation, culture can be recorded and remembered for a regardless time in future. In this way museums converted in such places where an ample number of cultural objects are accessible for  the  exploration,  learning  and  enjoyment  to  various  kinds  of  visitors  like  children,  adult, student and travelers.

However, the policy of exclusion for various kind visitors is also prevalent in the museum due to vision-centric nature of museum and architecturally designed for people without any difficulties. One such example is the exclusion of visually impaired people from the museum.

Modern  museums  are  vested  with  the  task  of  unfolding  the  importance  of  their  exhibits  and communicating  their  significance  and  value  to  the  people  at  large  who  reserve  the  right  to understand and enjoy the cultural heritage of the country. Every museum has a wide and diverse audience base, which includes people from all occupations and different backgrounds; the able and the disabled. The real question is that how many museums have taken initiatives to plan their activities; keeping in mind the needs of the disabled. They constitute a very important fraction of the visitor profile and have all the rights to get access to the museums and other resources that the able-bodied have. The museums have to chalk out permanent measures and set of activities keeping in consideration the disabled community. The museum needs to consciously understand its audience who visit and who do not visit. It needs to make accessible its educational potential to visitors of all kinds.

The exclusion policy of the museum was started with the development of traditional practices of the  museum  in  India  as  well  as  in  the  world  until  the  development  of  modern  technologies. However,  in  case  of  development  of  the  museum,  the  science  and  technologies  played  an enigmatic and energetic role in creating the policy of inclusion as well as assimilation. However, the denunciation of technological advancement is justifiable on the scale of moral development in  societiesbutthe  new  advancement  of  technology  has  accelerated  the  development  of  an inclusive museum for all visitors.


## Vision centric nature of museum


All  focus  group  participants  or  visitors  expressed  interest  and  desire  to  participate  in  museum experiences whether they are disable or nondisabled. It is human behaviour, that one likes to visit that place which is unique and informative, and museum is one such places. Same thing happens to visually impaired people but whenever they visit a museum they go through the trouble of not understanding the essence of culture because of the vision centric orientation of museums and lacunae  in  the  facilities  provided  by  the  museum  architecture  and  staffs.Museum  curators generally display objects of our tangible and cultural intangible heritage but in some cases the structure  of  museum  creates  a  situation  of  physical  harm  or  emotional  harm.  For  example,  a inadequately plan pathway and use of slippery material like tiles for the construction, sometimes leads old people, child of joyful nature, people who are not used to on walking over this kind of material as well as the pregnant lady, to suffer or face the physical harm due to falling down over slippery material. In the same way people having low sight, partially or visually impaired as well as  differently  abled,  face  difficulties  due  to  lacuna  or  drawback  in  planning  of  museum  or gallery,  which  leads  the  visitors  to  an  inferiority  complex  and  became  a  creator  of  emotional harm. ## 1. Introduction


Ranked Choice Voting (RCV) is the most publicly debated and rapidly expanding electoral reform in the United States. Rather than voting for a single candidate, voters under RCV can rank multiple candidates. 1 If any candidate wins a majority of first preferences, she is elected. If no candidate wins a majority of first preferences, the candidate with the fewest first preferences is eliminated, and each of her ballots transfers to the next-ranked candidate. The process repeats until a single candidate wins a majority of the remaining ballots.

RCV is widely employed in local and state elections, both in general elections and in the primaries of both major US political parties. 2 A notable recent example is New York City, which adopted RCV in its primary elections for both Mayor and City Council in 2019. The change was endorsed by a broad coalition of political actors and hailed as 'a smart, tested reform that would make certain that New Yorkers elect candidates who have the support of a majority of voters' (New York Times 2019). More recently, Alaska adopted RCV for its state and federal elections through a voter initiative in 2020.

In this paper, we develop a new theoretical framework to analyze electoral competition under RCV, and we use it to examine widely held contentions about RCV's benefits relative to a plurality rule. 3

The first contention we assess is that RCV encourages candidates to pursue a broad electoral appeal instead of focusing on their core supporters. The contention rests on the following logic: under plurality, a candidate only benefits from the support of voters that prefer her to every other candidate. This encourages a candidate to focus on mobilizing the narrow segment of voters that are most likely to prefer her over all other candidates-usually, an ideological, social, or ethnic base. Under RCV, by contrast, a candidate can benefit from

the support of voters that do not like her the most. The prospect of winning voters' second preferences is expected to raise a candidate's relative benefit from broadening her platform in order to attract support from these voters, rather than focusing exclusively on her base. This contention is advanced by scholars (Horowitz 2004; Drutman 2020), pundits, and electoral reform advocates including Common Cause and FairVote in the United States and the United Kingdom's Electoral Reform Society .

The second contention we assess is that RCV better aligns electoral outcomes with voters' preferences-in particular, by weakening the prospect that a 'Condorcet loser' wins a multi-candidate contest. A Condorcet loser is defined as a candidate that would lose in headto-head competition with any other candidate. By definition, a Condorcet loser cannot win a two-candidate contest; she may nonetheless win a multi-candidate contest if voters divide their ballots across multiple candidates. RCV is expected to reduce that risk by allowing voters to transfer their ballots to other candidates in the event that their most preferred candidate is eliminated.

This paper examines-and writ large rejects-these contentions using a formal-theoretical model featuring three office-seeking candidates: a , b , and c , who compete for the support of an electorate divided into three groups: A B , , and C . Voters in groups A and B are collectively a majority, but voters in group C are a plurality. An example could be a district in which moderate (group A ) and conservative (group B ) Republicans are a majority of voters, but Democrats (group C ) outnumber either of the two Republican groups.

Each candidate j ∈ { a, b, c } chooses whether to pursue a broad campaign that appeals to all voters, or instead pursue a 'base' campaign that targets (via material benefits and/or symbolic appeals) voters in corresponding group J (so that group A is a 's base, group B is b 's base, and minority group C is candidate c 's base). In a distributive politics setting, the broad strategy represents an efficient spending allocation, versus a targeted policy that skews spending towards a candidate's core supporters or co-ethnics (e.g., Burgess et al. 2015). Alternatively, the policies could distinguish issues that all voters care about (e.g., the economy) from narrow issues that tend to excite only that candidate's base (e.g., culture wars). A candidate's base is defined as the voters that she can exclusively target, possibly reflecting differences in the candidates' clientelistic networks (Dixit and Londregan 1996), or their credibility on ethnic or

ideological issue cleavages (Robinson and Torvik 2005).

After the candidates choose policies, an aggregate preference shock is realized, and voters choose whether to turn out or abstain. Under plurality, a voter that turns out casts a ballot for a single candidate; under RCV, a voter that turns out chooses whether to rank one or more candidates. Voting decisions are guided by a simple heuristic based on abstention due to alienation , developed theoretically in Hinich, Ledyard and Ordeshook (1972), Callander and Wilson (2007), and Zakharov (2008). In this heuristic, a voter always ranks candidates according to her sincere preference, but she only awards a preference to candidates she likes enough. Implied turnout patterns find empirical support in plurality rule elections (Adams, Dow and Merrill 2006, Stewart 2020); we document evidence-including from our own voter survey conducted during the 2020 New York Democratic mayoral primary-that our model matches real-world RCV voting patterns. 4

Candidates' platforms can therefore persuade voters to support them, but they can also mobilize turnout. Broad policies are more effective at changing voters' preferences over the candidates, but narrowly targeted policies are more effective at turning out a candidate's core supporters.

Under plurality, a candidate wins if and only if she receives more votes (first preferences) than every other candidate. In our three-candidate RCV setting, a candidate wins if and only if (a) no other candidate wins a strict majority of first preferences, (b) she herself does not win the fewest first preferences, and finally (c) her combined first and second preferences exceed those of whichever candidate does not receive the fewest first preferences. Two facts about RCV follow: winning second preferences from voters that do not like a candidate the most is valuable, and winning voters' first preferences may not be necessary to benefit from their support.

Our paper's main insight is to show that these two facts need not encourage a candidate to pursue a broad strategy; they may have the opposite effect and intensify a candidate's incentive to target her base.

The key intuition underlying our result is that the possibility of winning second preferences under RCV changes how the candidates pursue first preferences. Under plurality, a candidate needs to win more first preferences than every other candidate. Under RCV, a candidate may instead focus on winning more first preferences than candidates whose voters are likely to rank her second . By defeating these candidates, she accrues a valuable dividend of second preferences that can strengthen her hand against the other candidates. Even if a candidate only wins first preferences from her core supporters, her ability to benefit from the second preferences of voters that do not rank her first may reduce her urgency from trying to capture these voters' first preferences with a broad campaign.

As a consequence, we unearth broad circumstances in which RCV intensifies the candidates' incentives to target their core supporters and eschew broad campaigning strategies. In particular, this arises in political contexts characterized either by high partisanship, or low baseline participation in elections. Ironically, these are the contexts in which reform advocates argue that RCV is most urgently needed.

We then turn to RCV's impact on the alignment of electoral outcomes with voter preferences. In our model, minority candidate c is a 'Condorcet loser' whenever partisanship, i.e., the division between majority (A and B groups) and minority (group C) is sufficiently large (so that c is always the least preferred option of all majority voters). As Grofman and Feld (2004) observed, RCV necessarily weakens the Condorcet loser's victory prospects when the candidates' strategies (i.e., the set of alternatives) are fixed. We nonetheless show that the candidates' strategies under RCV can shift to an extent that the Condorcet loser enjoys a strictly higher probability of winning, relative to plurality rule.

To understand why, recognize that under either plurality or RCV, a Condorcet loser wins only when the majority of voters that oppose her divides between the remaining candidates. When the majority divides under plurality, candidates draw votes (i.e., first preferences) from one another. RCV alleviates the majority's vote-splitting problem by allowing voters to transfer their ballots via second preferences to other candidates. In fact, second preferences are

irrelevant when the majority unites behind a single candidate. RCV therefore benefits a majority of voters only if they disagree over their preferred candidate. This is the channel through which RCV is expected to reduce the risk that a Condorcet loser wins.

For the same reason, however, RCV benefits a candidate's election prospects only if the majority divides. These divisions are more likely when the candidates adopt differentiated policies. Relative to plurality, RCV therefore tends to insure candidates' electoral prospects against the vote-splitting problem to a greater extent when they pursue policies that are less likely to unite the majority. This can benefit a candidate's individual election prospects, but it may incentivize electoral strategies that divide the majority to such a degree that the Condorcet loser's victory prospects increase, relative to plurality.

Contribution. Electoral systems can be assessed according to their effect on voters, and their effects on candidates. Existing work almost exclusively studies effects on voters, presuming that the set of alternatives (i.e., candidates and their policies) is fixed. In that vein, existing work highlights both experimentally (Van der Straeten et al. 2010) and computationally (Eggers and Nowacki 2021) that RCV can attenuate voters' incentives to cast strategic ballots, relative to plurality rule.

Two papers study policy outcomes and the number of candidates under RCV in a spatial model of elections: Callander (2005) and Dellis, Gauthier-Belzile and Oak (2017). Both characterize equilibria with two candidates who locate at polarized platforms: polarization is bounded by the threat of another candidate contesting the election at a centrist position between the two platforms.

In a citizen-candidate framework, Dellis, Gauthier-Belzile and Oak (2017) show that this bound is tightest under RCV. The reason is that a centrist entrant wins so long as she doesn't receive the least first preferences, since her centrist platform wins every voter's second preference. Under plurality, by contrast, a centrist entrant wins only if she receives the most first preferences. The authors conclude that RCV sustains less policy polarization than the plurality rule. Callander (2005) characterizes a continuum of equilibria in his office-motivated Downsian framework, highlighting the co-existence of equilibria with full median convergence under RCV, alongside equilibria with polarized platforms. Under plurality, by contrast, median convergence with three or more candidates cannot be supported (Cox 1987).

Because all voters turn out and fully utilize their ballots in both papers, and because candidates are differentiated solely by platforms, these frameworks do not address how candidates use their policy commitments to mobilize core supporters versus moderates. While our threecandidate framework abstracts from the question of how many candidates can be supported under RCV, both Callander (2005)'s and Dellis, Gauthier-Belzile and Oak (2017)'s analysis with endogenous candidacy highlights the stability of three-or-fewer candidate competition under RCV. This is also consistent with evidence from real-world elections documented in Jesse (2000) and Farrell and McAllister (2006).

These observations underlie the comparison of plurality versus RCV that is the main message of our paper. Under plurality, candidates who tend to appeal to similar groups in the electorate draw votes from one another when their voters disagree about who to rank first. RCVmakesvote-splitting less costly by allowing voters to express more preferences. The ability to express more preferences implicitly solves the voters' coordination problem that exists if the majority divides. Nonetheless, the vote-splitting problem only arises when the majority divides, and the majority is prone to divide when the candidates offer distinct policies. Since RCV's benefit to candidates accrues when their voters divide, it provides comparatively less discipline against electoral strategies that generate division.

Simply because second preferences are valuable does not imply that candidates choose policies to maximize them. Second preferences are only valuable from voters who ranked some other candidate first, and whose most-preferred candidate has already been eliminated from the contest.

Figure 6 and the accompanying discussion starkly illustrate this point. They show how RCV changes a candidate's value from winning first preferences. Under plurality, she needs more first preferences than every other candidate . Under RCV, her an alternative path to victory may be to securing more first preferences than other candidates whose voters are likely to rank her second . When this path calls on a candidate to differentiate from those candidates, we may observe policy divergence under RCV in contexts where plurality guarantees convergence.

## 5. Preference Alignment


We now ask whether RCV better necessarily aligns electoral outcomes with voters' preferences to a greater extent than plurality.

Recall that a Condorcet Winner is a candidate that defeats every other candidate in pairwise majority voting. We cannot define an ex-ante Condorcet Winner in our framework because that candidate's identity depends on her (endogenous) campaigning strategy. However, we can define a related concept of a Condorcet Loser . A Condorcet loser is a candidate that is defeated by any other candidate in pairwise majority voting. By definition, a Condorcet loser cannot win a two-candidate contest, but may prevail in a multi-candidate election due to vote-splitting.

In our framework, candidate c is an ex-ante Condorcet loser so long as θ is sufficiently large: in particular, when θ > 1 every voter in the majority likes candidate c the least regardless of the preference shock τ 's realization, and regardless of the candidates' campaigning strategies. Recall that for some parameters we may have multiple equilibria under both systems. Focusing on primitives for which there is a unique equilibrium under both systems, the next result identifies conditions under which RCV increases a Condorcet loser's probability of winning the election, relative to plurality.

Proposition 7. Suppose θ > 1 , so that candidate c is a Condorcet Loser. Then, c 's probability of winning is lower under RCV than plurality if ρ > ρ , but higher under RCV than plurality if ρ < ρ and α > α plu .

Depending on parameters, the orderings may be weak or strict. Recognize that for fixed strategies, RCV always (weakly) improves the probability that a majority candidate wins. Remarkably, Proposition 7 shows that the strategies pursued by the majority candidates may distort outcomes to such a degree that c 's victory prospects increase . This occurs when the unique equilibrium under plurality leads the majority candidates to pursue a broad strategy, whereas the candidates instead target their bases under RCV's unique equilibrium.

Regardless of whether c 's prospects improve or weaken under RCV, the next result shows that candidate a with the relatively larger base of cores supporters is always better off under

## Interpreting the Modeling Framework


We briefly discuss some of our modeling assumptions.

Divided Majority. Our restrictions on preferences result in a form of 'Divided Majority' setting, with the novelty that the candidates in our setting strategically choose platforms, rather than representing a fixed position as in existing models. While our preference restrictions serve primarily to facilitate analysis, they serve substantively important purposes.

First, the Divided Majority setting is central to positive and normative analyses of election systems-famously, Borda (1781) and Condorcet (1785), but also in contemporary work by Myerson and Weber (1993), Piketty (2000), Martinelli (2002), Dewan and Myatt (2007), and Myatt (2007). Bouton and Gratton (2015) nest the divided majority in a general set of voter preferences. In addition to the novelty of endogenizing the set of alternatives, our preference restrictions are weaker than almost all existing models in that we do not assume that voters in the majority like candidate c the least. On the contrary, our assumptions allow minority candidate c to choose policies that secure some majority voters' second preferences.

Second, our setting matches many real-world elections. The papers cited offer an abundance of historical examples, but Alaska's August 2022 special congressional election also fits. Presuming-as we do-that voters' ballots reflect their sincere preference orders, a majority of voters favored a Republican: 31% of ballots ranked Palin (R) first, 29% ranked Begich (R) first, and 40% ranked Peltola (D) first; further analysis of second preferences concludes that Begich was the Condorcet winner. Nonetheless, vote-splitting and ballot exhaustion amongst Republicans likely facilitated Peltola's victory despite RCV's potential benefits.

Third, arguments about RCV's benefits over plurality seem especially compelling in a divided majority context. In the absence of preference cycles, second preferences matterand only matter-when a group of voters that are collectively a majority divide over which candidate they like the most, therefore creating the risk of electing the minority-preferred candidate. Because broad platforms help any candidate (including minority c ) win second preferences even from voters that do not like her the most, they should be particularly attractive under RCV.

Voting Behavior. We assume voters cast their ballots sincerely. Eggers and Nowacki (2021) highlight the complexity of strategic voting incentives under RCV; indeed, there is presently no game-theoretic formulation. Sincere voting yields necessary tractability to maintain our on strategic candidates.

We also assume that voters can abstain both from turning out, and from fully utilizing their ballots. Turnout is a critical margin in real-world elections (Hall 2015). Under plurality rule, the 'reservation utility' could be interpreted as cost of voting, as in models that share our perspective that voters abstain due to alienation, such as Hinich, Ledyard and Ordeshook

(1972), Callander and Wilson (2007), and Zakharov (2008). Under RCV, of course, there is no marginal cost of ranking additional candidates. Nonetheless, many voters do not fully utilize their ballots. For example, in our own exit poll of New York voters during the 2021 Democratic primary, 52% of voters reported that they did not rank every candidate. Of those voters that ranked only one candidate, 67% reported the reason was ' that was the only candidate I liked '. This is precisely the behavior our voting heuristic captures.
