## 1 - Measuring the social opportunity structure


The concept of 'social opportunity structure' (SOS) refers to the set of all individuals that are available to form social ties under conditions of repeated interaction (Stauder, 2014). The SOS can thus be thought of in terms of 'exposure' to others (Bojanowski and  Corten,  2014:  15)  or  as  concerning  the  'availability  of  potential  relationships' (Lenkewitz, 2023: 247). These notions are difficult to measure empirically for at least three reasons. First, the concept of SOS requires capturing opportunities for contact, rather than actual social interaction. Individuals may  not  be  aware  of  such opportunities or may be unable to report on them accurately. For instance, individuals may not be aware of how many neighbors live in their building or may not be able to identify  what  social  groups  they belong  to. Second,  there  is  a  possibility  that  such potential contacts that are hard to identify are the most relevant for the outcome of interest.  For  instance,  they  may  be  weak  ties  that  occupy  a  brokerage  position between  one's  social  group  and  other  groups,  especially  under  conditions  of

segregation (Love and Levy, 2019). Third, the fact that interaction opportunities are distributed across multiple contexts (e.g. workplaces, neighborhoods, sport associations)  requires  adopting  a  multi-context  perspective  to  fully  understand  an individual's  social  position  (DiPrete  et  al.,  2011;  Mollenhorst  et  al.,  2012;  Stauder, 2014). The first two reasons make it difficult to measure SOS through self-reported data from surveys, while the third reason makes it difficult to measure SOS through aggregate sociodemographic data (e.g. about neighborhood composition; Huijts et al., 2014; Kruse, 2017), as such data is rarely available for multiple contexts at once.

An alternative approach for  mapping SOS is the collection of  social  network  data. Personal network items are regularly used in surveys to measure the notion of SOS (e.g. Stauder, 2014). In general, the use of position and name generators facilitates data collection by improving recall. For instance, DiPrete et al. (2011) used position generators  in  the  General  Social  Survey  to  measure  the  number  of  individuals  of different groups in the acquaintanceship and trust networks of respondents across four different contexts (family, neighborhood, workplace, and schools plus other venues). However, the issues identified above create obstacles in measurement. If the intention is to identify potential contacts, asking respondents to recall the individuals in a social context may not yield an accurate image of the pool of potential contacts, but rather portray perceived segregation or those contacts with whom interaction takes place at least  somewhat  regularly  (DiPrete  et  al.,  2011).  If  interaction  is  segregated,  the measures may be biased. An option to address such potential bias and to capture weak ties explicitly is to measure the full network of a given context via a survey, as is common in research on schools (Lenkewitz, 2023; Moody, 2001), but this approach is

too  costly  to  be  applied  to  nationally  representative  samples  and  multiple  social contexts at once.

The proliferation and increasing collection of online social network data has helped push beyond some of these limitations. The large-scale nature of datasets on social media friendships and followers allow to measure the notion of SOS across much larger samples. These data sources can also capture the types of weak ties that may provide important opportunities for intergroup contact but not be identified via surveys or other data sources (Hofstra et al., 2017). Chetty and colleagues' (2022) work on class  mobility  using  Facebook  friendship  data  is  a  seminal  example  of  this  line  of research. At the same time, the lack of representativity of these samples, the influence of platform algorithms on tie formation, and the specificity of online interaction have sparked concern about the validity of these data sources (e.g. Lazer et al., 2021). Online social media data thus helps measure the notion of SOS in a manner that is more aligned with the idea of potential contacts but may not translate accurately to the study of offline behavior.

We  focus  on  a  promising  newcomer  to  the  field:  population-scale  network  data sourced from administrative registers (Bokányi et al., 2023; Cremers et al., 2024; Van der Laan et al., 2023). These datasets measure formal relationships identified through shared membership in institutional contexts (e.g. households, workplaces, schools). The main advantage of this type of data is that it identifies all individuals who are affiliated with each context (e.g. all workers in a workplace, all students in a school) through unique personal identifiers, which also allow to link to sociodemographic data (e.g.  registered  gender,  country  of  origin,  declared  income).  In  this  way,  network

register data allows to efficiently capture all potential regular contacts in a context, as required by the notion of SOS, including weak ties. Crucially, this can be done across multiple  contexts.  This  type  of  data,  therefore,  offers  a  promising  avenue  to counterbalance some of the main limitations of survey and online social network data for the study of segregation and intergroup relations (Kazmina et al., 2024a; 2024b; Van der Laan et al., 2023).

To further previous work in this approach, we link population-scale network register data to survey data that contains social network generator items. In this way, we exploit the advantages of the register data when measuring the notion of SOS, but also exploit the capacity of survey data to provide valuable information on individuals' sets of active ties, allowing us to situate self-reported intergroup social ties in their social context. Throughout the process, we document the main methodological choices, strengths, and  limitations  that  characterize  this  population-scale  network  approach  to  data linkage.


## 2 - Data and methods



## 2.1 - Data


The population-scale network data was created by Statistics Netherlands and contains as nodes the 17.2M individuals in the Dutch census of October 2018. Edges capture membership in households, workplaces, and school cohorts, as well as relationships with  family  and  next-door  neighbors,  forming  a  multi-layer  network  (827M  edges). These  are  institutionally  defined  'formal'  ties,  some  more  active  than  others.  The family layer contains ties to parents, children, siblings, grandparents, grandchildren, uncles, aunts, cousins, and nephews. The household layer identifies individuals living

together in the same address and acting as a joint economic unit. Formal partners are included in this layer and not in the family one. The work layer identifies co-workers based on their major employer. For workplaces with more than 100 employees, the work layer samples the 100 colleagues that reside closest to the individual. The school layer  is  composed  of  institution-cohort  ties.  The  last  layer,  next-door  neighbors, contains ties to all members of the ten closest households within fifty meters of an individual's address,  sampling  randomly  when  there  are  more  than  ten  such households. For further details see Van der Laan et al. (2023). We refer to this data as the register data.

The  survey  data  is  sourced  from  the  Longitudinal  Internet  studies  for  the  Social Sciences  (LISS).  LISS  is  an  online  panel  survey  of  individuals  nested  within households. It surveys household members who speak Dutch and are over 16 years old. The sample has been updated via stratified sampling to correct for under- and over-representation of subpopulations. Here we use the 2018 'Social Integration and Leisure'  and  'Background'  modules,  both  collected  in  October,  comprising  6586 individuals with a non-response rate of 15.3%, resulting in 5577 responses. We refer to this data  as  the survey  data. We  link the register and  survey  data  via pseudonymised personal identifiers provided by Statistics Netherlands. Due to missing link data, 736 cases cannot be matched. Privacy and data security are ensured via several checks and balances (see Appendix 1).


## 2.2 - Variables


The analysis concerns how the likelihood that natives report intergroup social ties with immigrants depends on the composition and type of social contexts of natives. We explore this relationship through multivariate regression analyses.

By natives we refer to individuals born in the Netherlands. By immigrants we refer exclusively to individuals who have been born outside of the Netherlands. We count the individuals who have at least one immigrant parent as natives because they have been born and brought up in the Netherlands, but acknowledge their origins through a dummy variable for immigrant descent. We restrict our analysis to all individuals born in the Netherlands, regardless of the country of origin of their parents (N=4438).

To measure intergroup ties we rely on a survey battery of ego-network items where respondents  provide  information  about  up  to  five  'close  contacts  with  whom  they discuss important matters'. 93.86% of the 12227 alters are reported to be of Dutch 'origin'  (659  are  not  Dutch,  92  are  of  unknown  origin).  We  operationalise  our dependent variable as a dummy that captures whether at least one of the alters in the survey ego-network is of non-Dutch origin, i.e. an intergroup social tie. We do not use a count variable due to the large class imbalance and the variation in the number of alters reported (see Appendix 2, Table 2). We exclude the 894 respondents (20.14% of  the  total)  that  report  no  ties  or  do  not  know  or  report  the  origin  of  any  alters, decreasing the sample size to 3544 individuals.

We measure the SOS by extracting the ego-network of respondents from the register data.  The  register ego-networks of the survey respondents in our analysis sample contain a total of 305230 alters, with a mean number of alters per network of 86.27

(see Appendix 2, Table 2). We interpret each network layer as a distinct social context. For some parts of the analysis, we combine all layers and view them as an aggregate SOS. In that case, we measure context composition as the percentage of immigrants and immigrant descendants present in the register ego-network. We identify migration background via a variable with the same categories as the one used to define the analysis sample.

For other parts of the analysis, we disaggregate these measures into social contexts of public and private nature. We classify the social ties in households and families as private contexts, and the social ties in the next-door neighborhood, workplaces, and schools  as  public  contexts.  We  make  this  distinction,  even  if  public  and  private contexts overlap (Mollenhorst et al., 2012), because individuals in private contexts will most often be active social ties rather than potential ones, with some exceptions (e.g. nephews may not be active ties). By accounting for the presence of outgroup members in private contexts we partly control for selection, account for potential indirect contact through close social ties (Dovidio et al., 2017), and provide a useful point of reference to  gauge  the  importance  of  public  contexts,  which  are  the  focus  of  most  previous literature  (e.g.  DiPrete  et  al.,  2011;  Krause, 2017;  Lenkewitz, 2023). To do so, we calculate the percentage of immigrants and the percentage of immigrant descendants separately for private and public contexts. If a respondent has no social ties in public contexts, we impute the mean percentage of immigrants and immigrant descendants in public contexts from the rest of the sample. We do the same for private contexts. We do so to keep the analytical sample constant across regression models. Imputation is performed for 50 cases for public contexts and 33 for private ones.

We control  for  factors  that  may  affect  the  relationship  between  social  context  and having intergroup social ties with immigrants. First, we control for the size of the social context, measured as the number of alters in each network layer. When we aggregate all layers, we count each alter only once even if they are present in several network layers.  At  the  individual  level,  we  control  for  immigrant  descent  (binary),  highest educational  attainment  (6  categories),  age  (continuous),  and  gender  (binary).  We measure  immigrant  descent  and  age  through  the  register  data  to  avoid  typical problems of survey self-reports. We use the survey data to measure gender, because self-reports are more representative of gender identity, and education, because the register data lacks information for a third of the sample. Excluding six observations with missing information in at least one of these variables yields a final analysis sample of 3538 individuals nested in 2753 households. Tables 2 and 3 in Appendix 2 present descriptive statistics of all variables.


## 2.3 - Modelling approach


We use binary logistic regression models. To circumvent well-known issues with the interpretation of log-odds coefficients, we focus on calculating and visualizing average marginal effects (AMEs) and predicted probabilities. We check all models for model fit,  nonlinearity  in the effects of the continuous predictors, multicollinearity, outliers, and influential values. All models show slight nonlinearity in the effect of the context size  variables. We account for  nesting of respondents in households via clustered standard errors at the household level.


## 3 - Results


Model  1  regresses  the  binary  variable  of  reporting  an  intergroup  social  tie  on  the percentage  of  immigrants  and  immigrant  descendants  in  the  SOS,  its  size,  and individual-level  factors.  Table  1  in  Appendix  2  presents  the  full  regression  output, which we discuss in the text in terms of average marginal effects (AMEs).

Natives who have a higher percentage of immigrants in their SOS are more likely to report an intergroup social tie (AME = 0.002076, SE = 0.000582). A higher percentage of immigrant descendants in the SOS is also associated with a higher probability of reporting an intergroup social tie (AME = 0.005495, SE = 0.000670). However, we cannot discard the possibility that this positive effect may be  inflated  if  survey  respondents  classified  close  contacts  who  are  immigrant descendants as of non-Dutch origin. ## 4 - Conclusion


We have  proposed  a  new  measurement  approach  to  study  how  the  formation  of intergroup  social  ties  is  related  to  the  'social  opportunity  structure'  (SOS)  of individuals.  Our  contribution  lies  not  in  causal  inference  but  rather  on  improved

measurement of the notion of SOS through a population-scale network approach that exploits the linkage of social network register and survey data. We have provided stepby-step documentation of the choices and trade-offs that the linkage process implies. We have also showcased our approach by analyzing how the existence of intergroup social  ties  between  natives  and  immigrants  in  the  Netherlands  is  related  to  the composition and type of social contexts in which natives are embedded. We find that natives whose SOS is composed by a higher percentage of immigrants, but especially by  a  higher  percentage  of  immigrant  descendants,  are  more  likely  to  report  an intergroup social tie. These relationships hold in public contexts (next-door neighborhoods,  workplaces,  and  schools)  even  when  controlling  for  exposure  in private contexts (households and families).

The population-scale network approach is promising for the study of intergroup contact and  segregation.  It  does  not  suffer  from  response  biases  when  assessing  the composition  of  the  SOS,  can  capture  (very)  weak  ties  that  may  be  of  special importance in contexts of social segregation, and can gauge SOS composition across multiple contexts at once. There are important extensions to our analyses that would expand  this  list  of  contributions.  First,  both  the  register  and  survey  data  are  now available in longitudinal format. The  addition  of a temporal  dimension  offers unprecedented opportunities to study processes of intergroup contact and segregation as  they  unfold  (e.g.  how  the  formation  of  intergroup  marriages  is  shaped  by  and reshapes the SOS of individuals; Blau and Schwartz, 1997). Longitudinal data can also be used to further the other main line of methodological research in the field: causal theorizing and inference (Wimmer and Lewis, 2010: 636). Second, data linkage allows to incorporate into the analysis a host of both predictors (e.g. personality traits,

party  identity)  and  outcomes  (e.g.  attitudes  towards  immigrants;  Kazmina  et  al., 2024a) that are of substantive interest but may not be regularly included in targeted data  collection  efforts  nor  collected  at  a  large-scale.  Third,  the  fact  that  our  SOS measures  are  based  on  network  data  at  the  population-scale  allows  to  include measures  of  presence  of  outgroup  members  in  multiple  contexts  at  once  or opportunities  for  contact  at  multiple  degrees  of  separation  (Bokányi  et  al.,  2023; Kazmina et al., 2024a). These new measures would allow to test arguments about the role of indirect contact and weak ties in segregation processes at a large-scale and longitudinally (Dovidio et al., 2017; McPherson et al., 2001).

However,  our  approach  is  not  without  limitations.  We  did  not  separate  SOS  from selection  effects,  so  our  results  remain  a  descriptive  confirmation  of  a  correlation between  SOS  and  personal  network  composition  (Blau  and  Schwartz,  1997; McPherson  et  al.,  2001).  Future  research  should  ascertain  whether  the  SOS influences  tie  formation  net  of  (and  in  interaction  with)  homophily  and  other  tie formation  mechanisms  (Bojanowski  and  Corten,  2014;  Wimmer  and  Lewis,  2010), attending to whether private contexts can be considered part of the SOS or function as a measure of selection into intergroup ties. Another limitation is our assumption that the self-reported identification of alters' migration background distinguishes immigrants  and  their  descendants:  it  may  be  the  case  that  (some)  Dutch  natives identify immigrant descendants as immigrants. This would bias our outcome variable but not affect the population-scale network approach, which could still be used with other  outcome  variables.  Disaggregation  of  the  label  'immigrant'  into  groups  of different national origin, which the data allows, would provide a more realistic account of intergroup interaction dynamics. More generally, our approach suffers from a lack

of  data  on  informal  interaction  contexts  (e.g.  sport  clubs,  associations,  religious spaces) which are key in the formation of intergroup social ties (e.g. DiPrete et al., 2011). The large size of some contexts (e.g. very large workplaces) may not fit with the conditions of regular interaction implicit in the notion of SOS (Stauder, 2014), but this can be interrogated by incorporating context size in statistical modeling. We hope to see future research taking these limitations into account to leverage the advantages of the population-scale network approach to the fullest.

## Materials and methods


This research project was approved by the Curtin University Human Research Ethics Committee (HRE2021-0483).


### Participants


An online survey was completed by Australian parents and carers of school-aged children (hereafter “parents”) in 2021. The initial cleaned sample size was 2,427. Several respondents with conflicting answers on the gender demographic question were also excluded from this analysis, giving a final sample size of 2,418. The methodology and general characteristics of respondents are described elsewhere (Hendriks et al. 2023).

School-sector enrolments amongst respondent families are compared with the 2021 school enrolment (“Enrol”) census figures in Table 1. While exact comparisons cannot be made since the survey base (families/any child enrolled in school sector, total number of children unknown) is different from the enrolment census base (all students), respondent characteristics suggest representative overall sampling. A slight oversampling of families with students at non-faith independent schools might suggest greater involvement of those parents in their children’s education, possibly making them more likely to opt into a survey on the subject.

Few respondent families (8.9%) had children enrolled across more than one school sector.

### Measures



#### School sectors


Australian schools are commonly divided into sectors of government, Catholic, and independent. Most independent schools are faith-based — aligned with a particular religion or religious denomination — while a small minority are non-faith-based. This analysis adopts the following classification:

“Secular only” or “None” means none of the respondent’s children attend a religious school: that is, all the respondent’s children attend either a government school or a non-faith-based independent school.

“Any Catholic school” means at least one of the respondent’s children attends a Catholic school.

“Any independent faith school” means at least one of the respondent’s children attends a faith-based independent school.


#### Religion and religiosity


Religion was measured by respondent religious affiliation. Of the minority of respondents who chose “Other” (n=98), all provided sufficient further information to reliably classify them into None, Catholic, Anglican, Other Christian, or Other non-Christian. “Religiosity” was measured by respondent rating of the importance of religion in their everyday life: not at all, not very, somewhat, or very.


#### Attitudes


Parental attitudes regarding potential discrimination against LGBT persons were measured by their attitudes towards four statements: “Relationships and sexuality education should…”

Be inclusive to all students, regardless of gender identity.

Be inclusive to all students, regardless of sexual orientation.

Reduce homophobia (i.e., prejudice and discrimination against lesbian, gay, and bisexual people).

Seek to include gender diversity and reduce transphobia (i.e., prejudice and discrimination against transgender or gender diverse people).

The response frame for each question was pre-coded strongly agree, agree (hereafter “Total agree”), neither agree nor disagree (“Neither/nor”), disagree, strongly disagree (“Total disagree”). The small minority of respondents who chose don’t know/prefer not to say were excluded from each attitudinal analysis: question 1=1.5%, 2=1.2%, 3=2.1%, 4=2.3% of respondents.


### Data Analysis


A crosstabulation was used to examine parental religious affiliation and religiosity by school sector.  Additional crosstabulations examined parental attitudes by religiosity and by school sector. Net approval values for each of the attitudinal statements were obtained by subtracting the Total disagree from Total agree. These values summarise the extent to which parents support or opposes the tested domain.

Pairwise comparisons were used to examine parental attitudes by the same religiosity and whether their child/ren were enrolled in a secular or religious school. As Catholicism has its own school sector within Australia, parental attitudes were also examined in respect of their child/ren’s enrolment in a secular school versus the Catholic school sector. Net approval values and percentage differences were also calculated. Chi-square analysis was used to determine statistical significance for all tests.

## Discussion


In considering the main findings, it is important to note that the sample achieved in this study closely matched population estimates. Most Australian parents who sent their child to a religious school were not very religious, and across the religiosity spectrum – including even very religious parents - the clear majority supported schools to be inclusive spaces for sexual and gender diversity and to reduce homophobia and transphobia. These results are timely in the context of proposed legislative reform regarding discriminative practices within religious educational institutions. They also add to the current body of evidence that the Australian public (Karp 2018,  2022; Ezzy et al. 2022) and school teachers (Burns et al. 2023) oppose discrimination based on sexuality or gender identity. Previous studies of Australian parents, with more limited sampling frames, also report similar findings (Ullman, Ferfolja, and Hobby 2022; Francis 2022).

Parental religion and religiosity, by school sector

Parents with children enrolled in Australian religious schools were more likely to have a religious affiliation and to consider religion important to their everyday life than parents with children only at a secular school. However, the differences were modest. At Catholic schools, nearly a quarter of parents (22.5%) had no religious affiliation, and just over half (54.0%) were Catholic. More than half (53.3%) said that religion was personally not at all or not very important. At faith-based independent schools, a quarter of parents (25.6%) reported no religious affiliation, and half (49.5%) said that religion was not at all or not very important. To our knowledge, this is the first Australian study to document parental religious affiliations or personal importance of religion across different school sectors.

While some parents may indeed enrol their children in religious schools specifically for religious reasons, these findings are more consistent with most parents choosing non-government schools for perceived high teaching quality, student care, and discipline (Beamish and Morey 2013). Individual school sectors and schools should be cautious about assuming the values of their families or their motivations for enrolment without specifically collecting this data via professional, unbiased methodologies.


### Parental attitudes, by religiosity and school sector


The contention that religiosity correlates strongly and positively with negative attitudes towards LGBT persons can be rejected in light of these research findings. While there was a positive statistical association between religiosity and negative attitudes, the differences were small.

Even amongst the most religious parents (religion very important in daily life), clear majorities were in favour of schools being inclusive spaces for students with diverse sexual orientations (77.2% support) and gender identities (77.9%), and for schools to work to reduce homophobia (63.6%) and transphobia (63.9%). Such opinions are antithetical to a desire to discriminate. Further, amongst these most religious parents only small minorities expressly disagreed with the four concepts (9.5%, 10.5%, 14.9% and 19.9% respectively) and a small proportion (4.7%) disagreed with all four.

Across all school sectors most parents supported all four attitudinal statements and only small minorities of parents expressly opposed them. Even for the most negatively polarised principle (reducing transphobia) in the most negatively polarised school sector (independent faith-based), fewer than one in six parents (15.3%) expressed an opinion directly consistent with a potential desire to discriminate against LGBT persons. These low rates of opposition are not surprising given majority support for the four attitudinal statements amongst even very religious parents, and that many parents at religious schools are not at all or not very religious.

Pairwise comparisons, that considered 16 permutations, determined few instances where parents with the same level of religiosity held statistically different attitudes to parents enrolled in a different school sector. These related to parents at the extreme ends of the religiosity spectrum.

Catholic parents with any child at a Catholic school showed higher (not lower) net approval than those with children only at secular schools, though the differences were not statistically significant. These findings do not support the contention that Catholic parents are more likely to choose Catholic schools because they support Catholic church doctrine on LGBT matters. To the contrary, many Catholic parents appear to choose a Catholic school despite disagreement with church doctrine. At the present time, although it promulgates compassion, the Catholic Church currently condemns same sex relationships and diverse gender identities (Catholic Church 2000; Congregation for Catholic Education for Educational Institutions 2019).

Regardless of a parent’s religious affiliation, the strength of their religious practice, or the school sector in which they enrol their child/ren, significant majorities expressed support for schools to be inclusive spaces for individuals with diverse sexual orientations or gender identities, and to actively challenge homophobia and transphobia. These findings align closely with previously cited Australian studies and polls (Karp 2018,  2022; Ullman, Ferfolja, and Hobby 2022) The small degree of opposition suggests intrinsic support for LGBT persons and contests the assertion that there is widespread support for discriminative practices amongst religious families.


### Strengths, limitations, and future directions


The dataset did not include direct questions regarding religious schools’ right to discriminate. However, such questions can be problematic due to the potential for various forms of bias. Firstly, they can be subject to perception bias, where parents may assume the untested belief that religious parents would send their children to religious schools in support of LGBT discrimination. They can also be subject to normative bias, that it is historically “natural” for religious school administrators to argue for the right to discriminate. Finally, they can be subject to acquiescence bias, acceding to the apparent authority of religious school administrators. For these reasons, intrinsic measures of parental attitudes toward what their children ought to be taught regarding sexual orientation and gender diversity, such as those employed in this study, are more likely to provide more meaningful measures of parental attitudes.

Future research should investigate the attitudes of the general adult population, with parents of school-age children. This would help to determine if there are any real difference in societal attitudes, or, as previously noted, if direct questions regarding support for religious school rights to discriminate introduce potential biases.

This survey obtained a slight oversample of females. It is unclear whether female respondents of this survey were more likely to be involved in their child/ren’s school selection and education, had more time to participate in the survey, or whether some other reason explained the discrepancy. However, previous Australian research amongst primary school families, has indicated that females do most of the background research when it comes to school selection (Australian Institute of Family Studies 2016). We tested the effect of weighting for gender equality against several variables and found only trivial differences in statistical results. For these reasons we did not employ gender weighting.

The survey did not capture data on socio-economic status (SES). Therefore, potential confounding effects on attitudes could not be assessed. However, since independent faith-based school fees tend to be high for all their enrolees (religious or not and scholarships aside), we anticipate that SES would not make a significant contribution regarding attitudes toward these moral matters — but are more likely to in respect of economic matters which were not the subject of this study. Unsurprisingly, Australian parents with higher occupational status (key metric household income) are more likely to enrol their children in private, fee-based schools (Beamish and Morey 2013).

Moving forward, any effort to amend Australian anti-discrimination laws as they relate to religious educational institutions, should not assume parents are supportive of these organisations discriminating against staff or students based upon sexual orientation or gender identity. These research findings clearly outline that there is overwhelming support for all school sectors to be inclusive of sexual orientation and gender diversity, and to actively challenge homophobia and transphobia.

The engagement of parents and families is a known factor for the successful implementation of comprehensive sexuality education within schools and various success stories have been documented (Marson 2019). Educational bodies should therefore meaningfully consult with families when developing curricula or school policy (e.g., Department for Education 2019) Schools should also keep families informed about classroom content to help foster at-home conversations (e.g., BZgA and IPPF European Network 2016a). Additionally, they may also choose to offer information sessions or educational materials for parents to supplement their own education (e.g., BZgA and IPPF European Network 2016b).

Finally, sexuality education programs should also be respectful of faith perspectives. Although, as noted by Wareham (2022), policies that restrict access to comprehensive lessons can be highly problematic if ideological pluralism is not provided. As one example, Philips et al. (2023) have recently outlined their evidence-based teaching resources where faith is both recognised and respected.

### Conclusion

The contention that most or many parents who send a child to a religious school importantly do so on the grounds of “traditional” sexuality concerns — negative or discriminatory attitudes toward LGBT persons — is contradicted by the findings of this study. While there was a very small minority of parents (many but not all of them religious) who held negative attitudes; most parents, including most religious parents with children at religious schools and even the very religious, wanted schools to be inclusive of sexual orientation and gender diversity, and to actively challenge homophobia and transphobia. It is therefore inaccurate to assume that these parents hold an intrinsic desire to discriminate against LGBT students or staff. Arguments that Australian religious educational institutions should be exempt from anti-discrimination laws, based on the expressed wishes or expectations of parents, are misinformed and counterfactual. In contrast, the empirical evidence that has been presented, should provide all school sectors with greater confidence that they have widespread parental support to affirm diversity of sexual orientation and gender diversity.

## 1 Introduction


Text is not produced in a vacuum. Rather, text is produced by people from different social contexts and backgrounds who engage various linguistic practices for particular audiences and for particular purposes. Despite the growth of computational text analysis in the social sciences, our knowledge of the social influences on textual production in large scale processes is limited. Computational analyses of text often seek to correlate or predict content with representations of ideas, people, and entities or broader social processes (like healthcare, for example [1, 2]), typically without regard to how and by whom the texts were produced. Recent studies have found that authorship characteristics such as gender and socioeconomic background are strongly related to both the ways people write and what they write about [3 ? -6]. Further establishing the relationship between authorship information and text could point to large new sources of data for digital demography beyond traditional digital trace data like social media likes [7]. Following theoretical movements in social geography [8], sociological study of text production could meaningfully benefit from simultaneous exploration of multiplex author identities and space-based influences such as social context, social relations, and inequality. Such study is particularly important given the spatial dependence of so much of human experience [9, 10]. Developing a stronger understanding of the relationship between demography and text is produced is important for many academic disciplines given the implications the ways that text is so prominent in modern life and, with the advent of large language models (LLMs), will become increasingly prevalent. It also has practical implications for the way we use text in key moments of evaluation, like college admissions, and assumptions about the social origins of machine bias.

Related work has alluded to the social and spatial nature of text production by analyzing texts of authors with known background information such as novels written from specific literary families [11], fiction by writers from specific birth cohorts [12], and campaign messages of politicians of known gender and race [13]. While informative, author characteristics outside of these kinds of public figures are scant and typically ignore external social dimensions. Recent work by psychologists and linguists have studied similar relationships between author characteristics and texts, but it has mostly focused on text as indicators of authors' cognitive and affective states [14, 15]. It remains unclear how text, like spoken language, is shaped by and reflective of social conditions or with respect to specific social conditions. Attention to authorship remains significant for producing insights about unique forms of social inequality [16-18] and how they form and change over time [19]. Given that authored texts are central to consequential processes like school admissions and job hiring, these types of analyses should begin to consider how writing choices and styles reflect authorial information in more complex ways, including the consideration of intersectionality and various spatial dependencies. Considering how authors' multifaceted identities as well as their positioning within and across social contexts is integral to how they produce text and what informs the language they utilize. .

In this study, we examine textual production in selective college admissions. While other studies have focused on the mechanics and process of admitting students [2022], we focus on the forces that influence the creation of a key element of the modern

application: the admissions essay, required by a majority of U.S. selective institutions. We analyze a corpus of 254,814 admissions essays and associated metadata submitted by 83,536 applicants to the University of California system over two admissions cycles (2015-2016 and 2016-2017). These essays represent the entire universe of in-state applicants who identified as Latinx/Hispanic, enabling important insights into intragroup variation that is not always possible 1 . Specific metadata include gender identification, reported household income, whether they were the first in their family to attend college or not, and the ZIP code of the applicant's high school; additional details are described in the Materials and Methods section. The majority of the applicants in our dataset either identified as first generation college students (approximately 77% for each year) and/or as women (approximately 60% for each year). The median household income for our data (approximately $ 65,000 for each year) is also below the state median ( $ 84,000 ). The University of California system is an ideal site to study the 2 textual influences of author identity and spatiality as it garners applications from a diverse set of students residing in vastly different local contexts. Particularly amongst the Latinx students that apply, there is notable diversity in gender, country of origin, socioeconomic class, parental education, locale (rural, urban, suburban), and language used at home, all of which would theoretically contributes to intra-group variation in text production. By sampling within a single ethnic/racial group, we can study more complex identity markers (beyond typically-studied racial differences) and contexts than has been studied to date and contribute to research illustrating the false nature of monolithic demographic categories. We use these data to examine their relationship to essay content and style. Assuming spatial dependence, we also consider the extent to which students of particular identities write similarly or different from others in their local contexts.

Our study focuses on how spatiality and author identity shape text. The strength of our results forward an understanding of text as a source of data with strong demographic imprints made discernable using computational tools, especially in critical social processes like college admissions. In this vein, we employ and find support for a sociolinguistic perspective that assumes a correspondence between individual identities, local context, and communicative practices, but with written language as opposed to spoken language [6, 23]. Analyzing the relationship between people, places, and the text that people produce yields important insights into communities and groups of people in ways that might be hard to measure directly outside of spoken language [24]. Further, this approach can extend past theories and studies on the relationship between language, society, economy, and policy in fresh ways [25]. In our case, we find that text reflects specific forms of social variation, stratification, and localized patterns of social exchange and networking as well as complex, multidimensional identities.

Studying textual production from a sociolinguistic perspective is useful because linguistic variation often entails many forms of social variation and complex forms of social inequality [26]. Social scientists have begun to explore the possibilities of computational analyses for other sorts of unstructured data like pictures [27] and audio

[28-30], but computational text analysis is potentially unique in how it can be connected to broader social processes, like the sorting of students in selective admissions processes in the US. While we do not make any specific claims about inequality in college admissions in this paper, we do argue that the high dimensionality and scale of textual data, and the social conditions in which they are produced, are uniquely suited to deepen collective understandings of how text is encoded spatially and with key markers of personal identity.

Thinking of text as a social product as much as it is the outcome of an individualized process could also prove useful in developing a more nuanced understanding of potential promises and pitfalls when used in contexts like college admissions. For example, if admissions essays are intended to provide some kind of information that is unique about a student but other students from analogous spatial contexts or with similar intersecting identities are providing very similar information, it may be that the assumptions of the unique information text provides have butted up against the modern digital world. Scholars interested in social capital and the many different life experiences and outcomes it often predicts might also consider adopting computational text analysis methods into their analysis. Sociologists, economists, psychologists, and other social scientists outside of linguistics have long used text as data [31-33], but modeling text itself as a social artifact (similar to the conceptual starting point of sociolinguists) could yield generative perspectives into how the ways that we write are shaped by our social experiences. The spatial features we select are also closely tied to understandings of socioeconomic inequality, pointing to the potential for scholars of this topic, regardless of discipline, to develop new tools and perspectives through text analysis. Especially as we consider the various high-stakes situations that require text production, such as college and job applications, it is essential that social scientists leverage new tools and methods to consider how identities, spatiality, and text converge and may produce distinct outcomes. Finally, modeling these patterns with computational tools can also generate a broader understanding of the relationships between textual production, spatiality, and multidimensional identity and how these patterns are socially complex but predictable.


## Identity and Text


By capitalizing on the large volumes of textual data generated through digital platforms and social processes, researchers can reveal overlooked patterns of representation, inequality, and social stratification. Recent advances in machine learning provide a new set of tools for studying such identity and demographic phenomena in text. But these include and also go beyond traditional single categories of demography and identity. As one example, sociologist Laura Nelson [34] argues that machine learning 'is foundationally compatible with the epistemology of intersectionality' (p. 3) and calls for expanding computational analyses beyond predominantly deductive, inferential approaches. In this paper, we respond to that broader call by examining how author identities are embedded in social data production processes, specifically through textual data, with intersectionality serving as a key illustration of how multiple axes of identity can be explored and understood alongisde single dimensions of identity (e.g., gender).

Sociolinguists have taken similar approaches to the study of spoken language by demonstrating how the same social factors which shape society by identity and socioeconomic processes eventually play an active role in shaping language [5, 35]. Although there is nothing inherently better or worse about any particular linguistic style, but through social and demographic associations certain patterns become reinforced and, in moments of social interaction, imbued with meaning from others. While this study does not focus specifically on meaning or meaning making, we do consider how the components of meaning in this moment of evaluation (as communicated through college admissions essays) are strongly influenced (or not) through social factors to better understand whether authorship characteristics and contexts inform the production of big text data. Given our considerations of spatial dependence and influence, identity, and authorship, our dataset of college admissions essays are ideal to consider the ways we might extend these how collective identities inform social patterning of language as presented through self-narration in a key moment of evaluation (college admissions). These could have implications for future studies with text data as well by potentially pointing out the ways that patterns in aggregated text might be more accurately reflecting dominant group tendencies. While not every dataset will have information about specific authors, we hope this analysis can nevertheless be generative towards unpacking the social influences that shape the production of text.

We utilize computational methods to study identity in the context of a consequential narrative moment: the construction of the college admission essay. These data are more standardized compared to other sources of textual data because students have to write to similar prompts (most of which ask applicants to write about different aspects of their personal lives) under similar time constraints, making them ideal for investigating the relationship between author identities, contexts, and textual production. Furthermore, previous social science inquiries that leverage large-text data to analyze identity do so through the examination of high-profile people, like politicians [13]. Although these types of analysis can tell us a lot of power dynamics and elite settings, they do not represent everyday people. What our dataset of college admissions essays to one of the largest public university systems in the nation can tell us is how everyday people produce text, especially within high-stakes circumstances like college admissions. Additionally, our dataset includes a diversity of intersectional identities, such as gender, socioeconomic class, language spoken at home, and others.


## Sociospatiality and Text


Advances in big data and digital technology have created new opportunities to study local and more distal contexts spatially. For example, sociolinguists have traced a wide array of linguistic trends and patterns across space [6] and likewise have examined the relationships between neighborhood composition and life trajectories [36]. Though these are usually not causal claims, they illustrate that human interaction and behavior at scale are highly correlated with, and predictable by, spatial context.

In the same way, one's identities variably matter within contexts and therefore should be studied alongside other axes of analysis [37]. For example, studies of transnational families demonstrate that families must negotiate differing gendering roles from two distinct nations and the interaction of their identities depends on the place they

are in [37]. Studies of health and big text data have also found strong connections between what people write, authorship characteristics, and various health outcomes and measures. Often, these studies examine language from a psychological perspective, such as a study showing that geotagged social media text data are stronger predictors of heart disease mortality than traditional co-morbidities [1] and strong predictors of medical depression [38]. Social science focused on studies of social inequality, stratification, mobility, culture, demography, and other typically non-cognitive lines of inquiry, however, have also been able to leverage big (spatial) data.

Opportunity Insights, a policy institute at Harvard, has been at the forefront of examining the socioeconomic characteristics of the US through a spatial lens. One of their core arguments is that social capital and social mobility are distributed geographically, meaning that one's life trajectory with respect to social and economic opportunity is geographically determined [36]. Social capital is 'the ability of actors to secure benefits by virtue of memberships in social networks or other social structures' [39]. However, access and possession of social capital is stratified by social class and race/ethnicity [40], which themselves are stratified spatially [41]. They used data from the American Community Survey (ACS) and Facebook friendship networks to generate various measures of social capital across U.S. ZIP codes [36, 42]. They found that social capital metrics such as local inter-connectivity on social media and neighborhood level economic exchanges were strongly associated with economic mobility, or increases in one's socioeconomic status. The network was constructed using 44 billion connections and includes socioeconomic status information about each person in the network. According to the authors of the study, metrics generated from this network represent the most powerful predictors of social mobility and capital in a given zip code. These include cross class friendships (i.e., economic connectedness, the extent that high SES individuals have friends from lower SES backgrounds). Beyond the size and scope of this data, they also surface unique implications about the dynamic relationships between socioeconomics and space: rather than static and immobile measures of wealth, these represent information about relationships and social activity in a given ZIP code.

Computational tools enable social scientists to analyze the complex dynamics of social interaction with spatial contexts and their relationship to the production of cultural artifacts. In the current study, we examine whether Latinx college applicants across California write in similar and distinct ways from each other, with particular attention to the relationships with author identity markers and measures of their spatial context. This is a departure from previous work in sociolinguistics that focuses on spoken language almost exclusively. Demonstrating the dependence of textual production on authorship characteristics and spatial contexts poses a challenge to more individualistic, idealized notions of authorship and the production of text. It may also, however, open up an avenue of research that complements Chetty's work on social mobility to get more precise measurements and understandings of how tendencies in writing reflect spatial and demographic patterning, much like other social interactions and processes.


## Materials and Methods



## Data


Our data are extracted from a corpus of first year applications written by every Latinx identifying applicant to the UC system for the 2015-2016 and 2016-2017 admissions cycles. Focusing on Latinx students allowed us to focus our study intersectionally and intra-racially [43] and implicate future research directions focused on this population. Applicants to the UC system fill out one application and then choose which campuses receive their materials for admissions consideration. Our data also included Latinx out-of-state, international, and transfer applicants. We filter out these applicants and focus our analysis only on in-state applicants from California. This allowed us to circumscribe local contexts to the same state of residence to retain a level of fixed local conditions (students living within a larger common economy and statewide legal and educational system). Out-of-state and international applicants come from cultural contexts that may introduce further complexity into our analyses, and their disproportionately higher family incomes also affect textual production. The essay format changed from 2015-2016 to 2016-2017. Applicants used to write two essays responding to the same two prompts, but starting in 2016-2017 applicants had to write four essays in response to eight prompts. We focus instead on the merged text of all essays provided by the applicants, following [4]. This approach enabled us to maximize power and produce stable computational results in our text analysis. Along with the essay text, our data include the high school code of the applicants, and the variables used to create our multidimensional identity variables. See Table 1 for the descriptive statistics of our data.

Although outwardly studying only Latinx students in the applicant pool may seem limiting, there are many ways in which this data allows us to do important authorship and spatial analyses. Firstly, the Latinx/Hispanic panethnic community is not a monolith. Rather, as the largest racial minority group within the United States, variations in country of origin, socioeconomic class, parental education, gender, and other identities allows for an ample examination of authorship identities (and different intersections) by holding the race/ethnicity category constant. Furthermore, Latinx students are the largest group of students and UC applicants, making them a particularly critical group to study as they are not necessarily the majority at UC campuses. Past research has demonstrated variation at the ethnic level (e.g., Mexicans vs. Cubans) [44-46], something we do not explicitly consider here. Therefore, our research utilizes intra-group variation as an opportunity to understand how the intersection of other identities and context shape text production in nuanced ways.

Applicants were matched to the ZIP codes of their respective schools; we do not share information about individual schools for privacy. The spatial data takes our analysis a step beyond given its relationship between identities, spatiality, and its connection to many different measurable contextual factors. The spatial data describe structural features of ZIP codes, including a variety of socioeconomic and demographic features (e.g., racial composition, percent college-educated, percent living in poverty, median income), as well as processual aspects of contexts, including social capital.

## Text Processing and Statistical Methods


A well known obstacle in using any topic modeling approach is the need to predetermine an appropriate number of topics to generate. In our case though, we are just using the topics as predictors and are less concerned with the actual content of the topics. Therefore, we take a more agnostic approach to selecting a number of topics and use a more purely data-driven approach. Using the ldatuning package, we tested models ranging from 10 to 150 topics for each year of data. For the 2015-2016 essays we selected 60 topics and for the 2016-2017 essays we selected 70. See Figures SM1 and SM2 for visualizations and details of this process. Since topics sum to unity, we remove the topic least correlated with a given outcome in our analyses. After generating the essay features using correlated topic modeling (CTM) and LIWC, we use them as inputs for two tasks: document classification and ZIP code feature explanation. We use logistic regression models as our classifiers. We explain these methods in more detail below. The classifier was used to classify student demographic features or combinations of features (e.g., gender vs. gender and low income). Our ZIP code feature analysis takes average essay features within each ZIP code and uses them to predict ZIP code characteristics.


## Document Classification Based on Authorship


We use essay content and style features to see how well essays predict different characteristics of the applicants. Two metrics were used to report classification accuracy: accuracy (correct labels over total number of guesses) from repeated undersampling with cross-validated classification; and a new metric called the intermodel vigorish designed for measuring classification accuracy with imbalanced data [47]. The undersampling with cross-validation creates samples of equal size, and the results can be interpreted as 'accuracy above 50%.'

The IMV works by comparing a predictive model with another model that only predicts the mode outcome using the same data. The results from this method are comparable to the common vigorish (percentage of winnings deducted from players) of 1% in blackjack which, on average, becomes 0.0099 cents per dollar for the casino. ## Linear Models of Essay and Spatial Features


We estimate the relationship between essay content and style and several measures of sociospatial context taken from the ACS and the Opportunity Insights Lab. Specifically, we take the average essay features per ZIP code and use them to explain characteristics of the ZIP code using linear regression. This reduces the number of observations from tens of thousands to hundreds. To account for this drop, we do not include any out-of-sample classifications and just report regression outcomes based on all of the data available. We use the amount of explained variance ( R 2 and adjusted R 2 ) as the reported outcome to put these results in conversation with a previous analysis of essays, SAT scores, and income [4]. The strength of these previous results, which also used linear regressions, informed our decision to use a linear model as opposed to a more flexible model.


## Misclassification Analysis


Finally, we combine insights from studies one and two to analyze patterns in essays that were misclassified. First, we repeat the undersampling procedure from study one but without cross-validation. Instead, we repeat the procedure with three different random samples of equal size and label each essay as being classified as either correct or incorrect along with how exactly the essay was misclassified (Type I or Type II errors). This was done ten times to ensure less biased, stronger statistical outputs. After performing ten sets of classifications, we then counted the number of essays that were correctly and incorrectly classified for each ZIP code and calculated the average proportion of essays that were misclassified. Our spatial features were then used as predictors for the proportion of misclassified essays by ZIP code.

To determine which predictors to include in this model, we use forward, backward, and both direction stepwise regressions and compare outputs. These procedures compare models that add or remove variables and then compare models based on their respective different outcome metrics, including the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) value, to see which model fits the data most parsimoniously [48].

After running these procedures, we selected the model that contained ZIP code level information about median income, proportion of White residents, the Facebook friend clustering metric, and the mutual friends ratio. The R 2 for this model and the model containing all of the variables differed by approximately 1%, further assuring the results from the stepwise regression approach. ## Results



## Topic models and dictionary features to quantify essay content and style


We use correlated topic modeling (CTM; [49, 50]) and the linguistic inquiry and word count (LIWC; [51]) software package to generate variables that capture the content and writing style of the essays. The same rationale applies to our decision to merge the essays rather than analyze them by prompt. We use the 'ldatuning' package in R [52] to select the number of topics to generate. Additional details are presented in the materials and methods section. This process suggested that the final model generate 60 topics for the 2015-2016 essays and 70 for the 2016-2017 essays. The essay format changed over the two years of data, and for this reason we analyze the documents by

year; in the first year, all students wrote essays for the same two prompts, but in the second year applicants had to select four prompts from eight possible choices. To generate features of multidimensional identity, we use the combinations of gender, family income (above or below median), and parents' education (first-generation student or not) as provided by the applicants in our dataset. These were chosen because past studies have found these characteristics to be important in college admissions individually, but using text can allow us to generate new perspectives about how their intersections are also important. We labeled the topics by hand; see Table S1 and S2 for the full list of topics and labels. To model spatiality, we averaged the essay content and style metrics by ZIP code and predicted similarly averaged 2014-2018 ACS 3 data and social capital data from the Opportunity Insights Lab 4 .

With topics and dictionary features generated for each year of data, we compared different groups of applicants with regard to the prominence of specific content and style features in their essays. We use Welch's t-tests to compare average values by group while also accounting for the differing group sizes. Of the 60 topics generated from the 2015-2016 essays, 58 were significantly more prevalent for either first-generation, low income women (31 topics) or students who did not identify that way (27 topics). And of the 93 dictionary features, 79 were significantly larger for first-generation, low income women (46 features) or students who did not identify that way (33 features). These results were similar for the 2016-2017 essays. First-generation, low income women tended to write more about other people ('People, kindness', 'Kid friend', 'Extended family') and common issues associated with Latinx populations in California ('LA neighborhoods', 'Spanish bilingualism'). Students outside of this group wrote more about sports and activities ('Team sports', 'Dance and theater') and specific academic interests ('Reading and writing', 'Engineering sciences'). Stylistically, first-generation, low income women used more pronouns, function words, and Authentic (a composite metric of several LIWC features) language. Conversely, students who did not identify this way used more analytic language, words of six letters or more, and more words per sentence. See Table S3 for a full list of topic and dictionary features more strongly associated with first-generation, low income women. This is noteworthy as low-income, first-generation women are marginalized on the account of socioeconomic class and gender, and as such the fact that they write more about people/community issues as well as through distinct language properties shows that authorship identities effectively shape the topics and ways in which they write.

There are also strong correlations between individual essay features and spatial characteristics (see Figures 2 and 3). For example, the ACS variables had correlations with the essay features in the range of ∼ -0.60 and 0.60; for spatial variables the range was between ∼ -0.55 to 0.50. For comparison, the strongest correlations here are larger than the relationship between essay content and style and an applicant's reported household income and test scores (adjusted R 2 = 0.17 and adjusted R 2 = 0.53, respectively [4]). In other words, for some measures of essay features, an applicant's neighborhood appears to be more strongly encoded in admissions essays

## Essay Features and Spatial Characteristics


The primary results for Study Two are presented by ZIP code variable groups: those from the ACS survey and those from the Opportunity Insights Lab. We present R 2 and adjusted R 2 as measures of the extent to which student narratives are associated with local social and economic conditions. Overall, spatial features had very strong relationships with essay content and style. Figure 4 presents the results for the 20152016 essays; Figure S3 presents similar results for the 2016-2017 essays.

All of the ACS variables and most of the spatial variables had stronger relationships with the essays than did applicant income as described in past studies (adjusted R 2 = 0.17; [4]). Comparatively fewer of these same variables had stronger relationships than SAT scores and essays when comparing adjusted R 2 , however (adjusted R 2 = 0.53). Among the ACS variables, the proportion of residents with Bachelor's degrees was higher (adjusted R 2 = 0.59) and the proportion of Hispanic residents (adjusted R 2 = 0.52) was similar to the results comparing essays and SAT but much stronger than essays and income. These comparisons do not imply that the other variables had weaker relationships, however. On the contrary, nearly all of the ZIP code variables had very strong relationships with the averaged essay features. This suggests that not only is author socioeconomic class important but that this relationship is also salient spatially (by ZIP code). Looking at both axes of analysis helps us understand the interaction between identity and context, which further shapes text production and authorship.

With regard to the spatial measures, averaged essay features explain nearly 60% of the variance in ZIP code level economic connectedness (adjusted R 2 = 0.56) and more than 50% of levels of outside class exposure (adjusted R 2 = 0.52). As a comparison, we also measured the relationship between the average applicant income by ZIP code and the spatial features for the 2015-2016 data. Explained variance was also high but not as large as for essay features (adjusted R 2 = 0.44 for the ACS variables, 0.34 for the spatial variables). The relationship between average income and essay features within ZIP codes was quite robust, however (adjusted R 2 = 0.65). Combined, these results show that spatial features, including those indicating static descriptors of a ZIP code (eg. median income for a ZIP code like with the ACS data) and attempts at modeling more dynamic social aspects (eg. economic connectedness and exchange in a given ZIP code like with the spatial data) have a very strong relationship to the types of text students generate and eventually submit as part of their college admissions essays. These results demonstrate the complex, highly social nature of textual production.
