## Discussion


The massive increase in the availability of textual data, along with concurrent increases in processing power and algorithmic sophistication, has spurred interest in computational text analysis across the social sciences. Textual data represent communications between people and organizations; describe ideas and people; and present arguments and rules. Our results show how this particular form of text is strongly influenced by authorship identity and spatiality. Given that massive amounts of text are being produced and stored everyday, this is a trend that is unlikely to change anytime soon, raising questions about how existing lines of social variation are encoded in texts written beyond the context of college admissions. Future studies might more directly consider how social conditions such as inequality are also encoded into text, along with the comparative strength of those relationships.

In this paper, we used various computational methods to examine whether variation in textual production explains variation in who applicants are and the context in which they live. We find that spatial features, namely variation in social and economic characteristics in a given ZIP code, are embedded in admissions essays; this is also the case for multidimensional identities. A number of our models relating spatial

conditions to essays produced adjusted R 2 values above 50%, meaning that topics and writing styles are more than 70% correlated with the sociodemographic features of their local environment. These results are comparable to other studies using text data as well as others using social media data [56]. We also found it is hardest to predict students' content and writing styles in places with sociodemographic profiles that differ markedly from the personal identities of students hailing from those places, such as Latinx applicants from communities with higher proportions of White residents. Generally, areas of sparse population (a repeated sampling approach helped address our concerns about a lack of data) and lower values for the spatial metrics also had higher levels of document misclassification, pointing to another social dimension to textual production. Given the importance of identity in one's life course and as a key dimension in the social sciences, this result is important because it shows that how we write might be better reflected by who is around us rather than the identity boxes we check. These results also challenge standard notions of authorship centered on the individual rather than their identity and context, an important consideration in moments of evaluation like college admissions. Future research will need to further examine the mechanisms behind why geography matters in writing style, why these patterns vary from place to place, and the reasons why otherwise strong geographic patterns occasionally break.

Additionally, although we only focus on the Latinx applicant pool as they constitute the highest proportion of applications to the University of California as well as the state's majority population, our findings surrounding the importance of authorship identity and context extends beyond this group. The relationship between intersectional identities and their context is evidently strong, meaning that future studies should look at different identity groups and spatial contexts to see how they shape text production, as we anticipate they would look different from the essays we had access to. California is a particularly unique context as Latinx students are the majority population but in states with more sparse representation or amongst other raciallymarginalized groups, we could expect their compounding identities and social contexts to shape similar essays in different ways than the students in our corpus.

Our results also point to additional avenues of digital demography research for intersectionality, spatiality, and any number of sociological studies that use text and machine learning methods. For example, if we assume there are strong patterns with respect to authorship identity and spatiality in other moments of self-narration aside from college admissions (a not uncommon scenario), there could be the potential to misattribute trends as being evenly distributed throughout society. Modern AI, specifically LLMs, are widely lauded for their ability to generate 'human-like text', but their low levels of variance and tendencies to write like people from high socioeconomic backgrounds [57, 58] could not only mask the trends we document here but also create new forms of marginalization and stigmatization: if the ways that one self-present are strongly connected to their identity and context, AI might inadvertently highlight who writes more or less like AI. In the domain of college admissions, new attention has been placed on the essays as a vehicle to communicate racial hardships, but as we show those narratives are just as likely to be grounded in intersectionality and social contexts.

In addition to shedding light on the ways that textual production is shaped geographically and socially, this study highlights the importance of studying textual production in relation to high stakes social processes like college admissions. Accordingly, our work is connected to trends in reassessing high stakes contexts and data with computational tools [59, 60]. These systems are often designed to give people an opportunity to highlight why they are unique and meritorious, but using computational tools gives us the opportunity to see how identity and social context are deeply embedded in these materials . By analyzing these patterns with data widely used in the social sciences, we show how computational tools can be integrated into social scientific inquiry in a purely methodological sense (ie. using computational tools for analysis) but also substantively. Scholars of identity, social capital, socioeconomics, and other related domains might consider how the social processes which inform their work could also capture patterns of textual production as we highlight here. For example, text, language, and writing might be strong predictors not just of current social context but also long term life trajectories, a type of data not considered in the Fragile Families Challenge [61]. This is especially true for college admissions after the SFFA v. Harvard Supreme Court case ended traditional affirmative action policies but still allowed room for applicants to describe instances where they experienced racism, presumably through the admissions essay. While some have speculated the ruling might end the use of essays 5 , the unprecedented scrutiny on them could also push for further investigation into other sources of text across social sectors.

While the future of college admissions protocols is currently unclear, this study provides important context by extending prior research on the relationship between identities and text production by showing how students' multifaceted context shapes what they can write about and how they do it. Previous research has focused on descriptions and language of intersectionality within a given text [34], but this study goes further by exploring how complex representations of author identity and context can shape the production of text. Moreover, scholars of intersectionality can use this framework and methodology to demonstrate how intersectional experiences relate to other processes of data generation beyond the admissions essay. By expanding the application of this framework, researchers can better understand how intersectionality shapes materials and experiences in various contexts, and how these factors contribute to broader social processes.

The strength of the spatial results points to the importance of geographically distributed socioeconomic activity (a key feature of social capital producing processes [36, 42]) as a predictor of sociolinguistic practices (in this case, writing an admissions essay). Future studies of social capital, socioeconomic inequality, and other similar topics might also consider adopting textual data and computational tools to add depth and richness. Conversely, studies of language and social interaction might also consider the types of social processes and outcomes measured in the spatial data. Computational researchers of bias and fairness might likewise extend their analyses to consider the role of authorship in producing a given dataset.

Creating textual datasets has become much easier for social scientists over the past few decades. This, of course, comes at the cost of working with a dataset where authorship information is either unknown or less reliable. Given this tension but also recognizing the value in different approaches of scholarship, we envision parallel streams of research using textual data: studies where data are massive but authorship is unknown and studies where authorship is known but data are not massive. Similar suggestions have been put forth by other researchers (e.g. [62]). Having a stronger understanding of the dynamics between text and society could also be useful as generative AI grows in popularity, specifically with regard to understanding how these dynamics might contribute to the responsible development and deployment of generative AI technologies in a diverse society. The current study highlights the intersection of both streams of research by examining the dense connections between textual production and author attributes pertaining to social identity and geography. We hope this work can help social scientists become more precise in their conceptualization of textual data and how spatiality and personal identity markers shape the production of textual data, especially those used in high stakes evaluations like college admissions.

## Introduction


Pragmatic  competence,  the  ability  to  use  language  appropriately  in  social  contexts, encompasses understanding not just literal meanings but also implied intentions and social nuances conveyed through language. Teaching this competence poses challenges for language instructors (Metruk, 2021), requiring authentic materials and opportunities for honest communication. They train  their  students  to  be  skillful  in  using  cooperative  principles  and  politeness  strategies, appropriate exchange of speaking turns in face-to-face interaction (Duncan, 1972; Kendrick et al., 2023), and correct use of speech acts like requests, apologies, promises, invitations, refusals, and complaints. Moreover, they guide discussions on sensitive topics, bridging differences to facilitate agreement. Imparting cultural norms and fostering intercultural empathy is an inseparable part of this process, too (Handzilevska et al., 2021).

Hedging language represents a  part of the target culture that foreign language learners should know. The challenge is that even with all the goodwill in the world, miscommunication is likely to happen, especially when there are significant cultural differences between communicators (Fabian, 2018). If the speakers misinterpret hedges in an utterance, they may misunderstand the interlocutor´s intent.  At the same time, if the speakers fail to hedge correctly, they may be seen as rude, impolite, or arrogant. One of the ways how to develop this competence and awareness of the use of hedging language in spoken and written performance is to incorporate working with corpus texts into language teaching. Using cautious language, teachers demonstrate humility and openness to alternative viewpoints, fostering trust and cooperation among learners. This is reinforced by the importance of educating tolerance as one of the qualities of a humane personality (Fabian et al., 2022). This approach encourages active engagement and effective collaboration towards common goals.  As  specialists in  pragmalinguistics and  corpus  linguistics, we  chose  to  delve  into  this linguistic phenomenon through corpus analysis of the British National Corpus, focusing on spoken discourse, where pragmatic competence is most evident.


## Literature review


Hedges as the basic concept were introduced for the first time by the cognitive linguist George Lakoff. He defined them as cautious words and phrases that make utterances and speech acts  fuzzy  (Lakoff,  1973).  Hassan  &  Said  (2020)  pointed  out  that  they  'convey  intentional vagueness, mitigation, tentativeness, politeness, indirectness, possibility, evasiveness, lack of full commitment  and  show  deference  to  the  readers  as  opinions  are  kept  opened  of  other interpretations' (p. 60). Udin & Zulkhaeriyah (2022) added that they serve to demonstrate the roles we adopt for ourselves and impose on others. Hedges function as a shield for the speaker or text writer and protect them from potential regrets by modifying their utterances.

Kraus (2008) presented a parallel concept to hedges, termed modalizer. He defined it as a means  of  expressing  modification and  evaluation of  the  spoken  content,  often  involuntarily revealing the speaker's bias. Modalizer weakens the certainty and assertiveness of statements and shifts responsibility for their validity away from the speaker. Not only does it have the ability to modify the statement, but  it can also  fundamentally alter its overall meaning. Graefen (2000) elucidated  that  when  the  notion  of  hedge  in  public  life  is  mentioned,  almost  everybody immediately associates  it  with  specific  investment  strategies.  However,  only  a  minority  of individuals know that the English term hedge carries additional meanings such as protect or shield.

Drawing a metaphorical parallel to a green hedge in a garden, hedges offer protection and distance. They are essential for maintaining polite communication, as politeness is a universal and

Hedging strategies allow interlocutors to reduce the impact of imposing, authoritative, or direct comments (Jovic et al., 2023; Chaqmaqchee & Jasim, 2022). They play a vital role in communication by contributing subjectivity to utterances, facilitating differentiation and relativization of truths, and signaling caution and  willingness to  make  concessions. Hedges  acknowledge  the  presence of uncertainties, doubts, and vagueness in the world, enhancing the acceptability and credibility of statements while mitigating negative impositions (Fischer, 2005).

Contemporary  perspectives  on  hedges  have  broadened  the  notion  beyond  semantic modification to encompass elements such as uncertainty, lack of commitment, and perception. Although  there  is  no  consensus  among  linguists regarding  their precise  purpose,  hedges  are generally  acknowledged  as  discourse  features  aimed  to  enhance  precision,  politeness,  and mitigating negative  impositions (Johansen,  2020).  Researchers  approach  hedges  from  varied perspectives, considering different variables when categorizing them. For instance, Laghari et al. (2022) have concentrated on softening propositional statements and claims in academic writing, Liu (2020) expounded on hedging in terms of politeness strategies, Demir (2018) analyzed lexical hedges,  and  Hyland  (1996)  introduced  content-oriented and  reader-oriented hedges.  Contentoriented hedges  delineate the relationship between the  proposition and  a  representation of the world, whereas reader-oriented hedges are deployed to garner the reader's acceptance. The former encompasses accuracy-oriented and writer-oriented hedges. Accuracy-oriented hedges facilitate the expression of uncertain statements with appropriate caution, reducing the risk of accusations, whereas  writer-oriented hedges  allow  authors  to  shield themselves from  criticism. However, Hyland's classification has drawn criticism for its overlap and challenging differentiation despite its widespread use in scientific discourse (Johansen, 2020).

Conversely, Prince et al. (1982) presented a classification framework for hedges in spoken interaction, dividing them into two primary classes: approximators and shields. Approximators are responsible for  introducing fuzziness  within  the  propositional content. Shields  correlate with fuzziness in the relationship between the propositional content and the speaker's commitment to the truth of the conveyed proposition. Approximators are further categorized into adaptors and rounders,  indicating deviation from  the  prototypical situation. Shields  encompass  plausibility shields, indicating speaker uncertainty about the content, and attribution shields, enabling speakers to attribute beliefs expressed in the proposition to others.

Chan & Tan (2009) developed Salager-Meyer's theory (1995) on categorization of hedges in the written discourse. According to them all hedges can be grouped into modal auxiliary verbs, modal lexical verbs, adjectival, adverbial, and nominal modal phrases, approximators of degree, quantity, frequency, and  time, introductory phrases, "If"  clauses, and  compound hedges. Their taxonomy stems from an  analysis of  hedge  frequency across  different written  genres,  noting variations in their prevalence. Similarly, Caffi (1999) proposes a classification of hedges under the concept of  mitigation, emphasizing their role in  mitigating adverse effects on  communication participants. He identifies three main types of mitigating mechanisms: bushes, hedges, and shields.

Each framework for classifying hedges offers unique insights into their functional aspect. The  choice of  classification depends on the researcher's aims and  focus. For our research, the classification by  Prince et  al.  (1982)  has  been  adopted  due  to  its clarity and  applicability to observed  interactions among  physicians in  intensive care  settings. This  framework delineates hedges into approximators and shields, facilitating precise research focus.

Most of the present studies have been devoted to hedges used in the written discourse, in consequence of much greater difficulty, higher cost and slower speed of collecting spoken forms of language. However, access to the corpus of informal spoken conversations in English, to the spoken British National Corpus 2014, enables researching hedging in discourse and provides a unique resource for examining hedging in authentic everyday conversations (Johansen, 2020). The Spoken BNC 2014 was compiled by the ESRC Centre for Corpus Approaches to Social Science at Lancaster University and Cambridge University Press. It is the first publicly available corpus of English spoken today, as the spoken component of the original BNC 1994 is still used as a proxy for the present-day English in research. It contains transcripts of 1,251 conversations recorded by 668 speakers from the UK public between 2012 and 2016. The compilation of the Spoken BNC 2014 is primarily based on the original BNC´s spoken component (Love et al., 2017). The corpus contains  informal  everyday  spontaneous  interactions  recorded  by  volunteers  who  selected contributors by age, gender, social class, and geographic region (Kennedy, 2003).

Out of many corpus analysis tools available for BNC, the Sketch Engine has been chosen. 'Sketch Engine refers to two different things: the software, and the web service. The web service includes, as well as the core software, many corpora pre-loaded and ´ready for use´, and tools for creating, installing, and managing corpora' (Kilgarriff et al., 2014, p. 8). Moreover, the Sketch Engine tools make it possible to investigate the natural language and apply such research results for the needs of teaching languages (Lacková, 2021, p. 135).

After  choosing  BNC  2014  as  a  linguistic source  and  Sketch  engine  as  a  toolbox  for linguistic discovery, we could start to solve the research problem - quantitative and qualitative analyses of hedging language existing in English spoken discourse.


## Methodology


The  overarching aim of  the  present research is  to  study  the  occurrence and  linguistic context of hedges in the English spoken discourse with a specific emphasis on comparing their frequency across varying demographic groups based on gender, age, and educational attainment. Age is categorized into distinct groups, ranging from 0-10 to 80-89, along with a category for unspecified age.  Gender is  delineated as male, female, or  unspecified. Educational attainment includes  seven  levels: primary, secondary,  sixth  form,  graduate, postgraduate,  unknown,  and unspecified.

The research process is guided by two central questions:

- Q1: Do differences in the usage of approximators and shields exist among men and women across different age groups?
- Q2: Are there variations in the usage of approximators and shields among men and women with different levels of educational attainment?

To  address these questions, the chosen variables encompass two primary categories of hedges:  approximators  and  shields.  From  an  exhaustive  examination  of  potential  variable combinations, three hypotheses crucial for the research implementation are formulated:

The analysis of corpus data in Women 30-49 and Men 30-49 has ascertained that the most commonly used adaptors in both sub-corpora are quite, really, kind of, and sort of , whereas the most distinct difference between men and women of the same age relate to frequency of use of adaptor really. The research points out to a tendency for women to intentionally repeat this adverb in a sentence to convince the hearer of the truth of the utterance. The research has proven the fact that men do not tend to be personal and do not repeat expressions in their spoken performance because their conversational style is different. Even though there are some adaptors and rounders that are used more frequently by men, in general, the results confirm that women use slightly more approximators in speech.

Overall, the results show that shields are more frequent in spontaneous speech. The findings of this research study indicate that English language has emerged as an important medium of education in Saudi Arabia, and learning of the language is widely promoting its culture. ## 1. Introduction:


Learning English as a foreign language (EFL) has become a vital skill for millions of people worldwide due to its status as a global lingua franca. Among the various linguistic competencies required for effective English communication, pronunciation is an essential aspect that significantly affects a speaker's intelligibility. However, acquiring accurate English pronunciation can be challenging for EFL learners, particularly those from different language backgrounds. This research paper focuses on English pronunciation errors made by Libyan students, exploring the factors contributing to these errors and their implications for language education.


## 1.1. Background of the Study:


Libya is an Arabic-speaking country in North Africa, where English is taught as a foreign language in schools and universities. Despite the increasing demand for proficient English speakers in the country, Libyan EFL learners often face difficulties with English pronunciation. These pronunciation errors can be attributed to various factors, including the influence of the learners' first language, insufficient exposure to native English speakers, and inadequate pronunciation instruction. Understanding and addressing these pronunciation errors is crucial for improving the overall English language proficiency of Libyan students and enhancing their communication abilities in global contexts.


## 1.2. Research Objectives:


The primary objectives of this research paper are to:

- 1. Identify the common English pronunciation errors made by Libyan students learning English as a foreign language.
- 2. Analyze the possible factors contributing to these pronunciation errors, with a focus on the interference of the students' first language (Arabic).
- 3. Investigate the implications of these pronunciation errors for language education and teaching practices in Libya.
- 4. Provide recommendations for language educators to address these errors in pronunciation, facilitate improved English language acquisition among Libyan students, and promote effective communication in English.


## 1.3. Scope and Limitations:


This study focuses on Libyan students learning English as a foreign language, with a specific emphasis on their pronunciation errors. The research encompasses various educational levels, including high school and university students. However, the study does not cover all aspects of English language acquisition, such as grammar, vocabulary, or listening comprehension. Additionally, while the investigation includes the influence of the Arabic language on English pronunciation, it does not delve into other factors such as motivation, language learning strategies, or individual learner differences.

## 2. Literature Review


This section presents a comprehensive review of the literature on English pronunciation challenges for Arabic speakers, factors contributing to pronunciation errors, and previous studies on Libyan EFL learners' pronunciation errors. The review aims to provide a solid foundation for understanding the context of the research and to identify gaps in the existing literature that this study seeks to address.


## 2.1. English pronunciation challenges for Arabic speakers:


Arabic and English are linguistically distinct languages, and the differences between them can lead to significant pronunciation challenges for Arabic speakers learning English. Some of the primary pronunciation issues arise from the phonetic and phonological dissimilarities between the two languages, such as the presence of sounds in English that do not exist in Arabic, different stress patterns, and variations in consonant clusters (Rabab'ah, 2005; Ghaleb, 2010). For instance, the English /p/ sound is often problematic for Arabic speakers since it does not exist in Arabic, leading to the common substitution of /b/ for /p/ (Al-Khresheh, 2010). Similarly, the English /v/ and /θ/ sounds are frequently replaced by /f/ and /s/ or /z/, respectively (Barjesteh,

2012). Additionally, difficulties in distinguishing between short and long vowels, as well as inconsistencies in applying English stress patterns, can contribute to reduced intelligibility and misunderstandings in communication (Munro & Derwing, 1995).


## 2.2. Factors contributing to pronunciation errors:


Several factors have been identified in the literature as contributing to pronunciation errors among EFL learners. First, and perhaps most notably, is the influence of the learners' first language, or the phenomenon of native language (L1) interference (Odlin, 1989). As previously discussed, the differences between Arabic and English phonetics and phonology can lead to pronunciation errors among Arabic-speaking EFL learners.

Second, insufficient exposure to native English speakers can also contribute to pronunciation errors (Gilakjani, 2011). When students have limited opportunities to interact with native English speakers or listen to authentic English materials, they may not develop an accurate model of English pronunciation, which can hinder their ability to produce accurate English sounds and stress patterns (Neri et al., 2002).

Third, inadequate pronunciation instruction is another factor that can lead to errors in pronunciation. Many EFL teachers may not have received sufficient training in teaching pronunciation or may not allocate enough time to pronunciation instruction in their curricula (Derwing & Munro, 2005). Consequently, students may not receive the necessary guidance and practice to improve their pronunciation skills.


## 2.2. Previous studies on Libyan EFL learners' pronunciation errors:


Several studies have investigated pronunciation errors among Libyan EFL learners. For example, Al-Khresheh (2010) found that Libyan students had difficulties with English consonant sounds such as /p/, /v/, and /θ/, as well as vowel length distinctions. A study by Ham ouda (2011)

also reported challenges with English stress patterns, consonant clusters, and vowel quality.

These studies have provided valuable insights into the pronunciation issues faced by Libyan EFL learners, highlighting the need for targeted pronunciation instruction and practice.

However, there remains a need for a more in-depth investigation of the specific factors contributing to these pronunciation errors and their implications for language education in Libya. Furthermore, research on the effectiveness of various teaching strategies and approaches for addressing these pronunciation errors among Libyan EFL learners is limited, necessitating further exploration in this area.

This study aims to build upon the existing literature by providing a detailed analysis of the common English pronunciation errors made by Libyan students, examining the factors contributing to these errors, and offering recommendations for language educators to address these pronunciation challenges effectively.

In conclusion, the literature review has revealed that Arabic-speaking EFL learners, including Libyan students, face numerous pronunciation challenges due to the phonetic and phonological differences between Arabic and English, L1 interference, insufficient exposure to native English speech, and inadequate pronunciation instruction. Previous research on Libyan EFL learners' pronunciation errors has provided valuable insights into their pronunciation difficulties, but further investigation is needed to better understand the specific factors contributing to these errors and their implications for language education. This study seeks to fill this gap by examining the pronunciation errors of Libyan EFL learners, analyzing their underlying factors, and offering recommendations for addressing these errors in language education.


## 3. Methodology:


This section describes the research methodology employed in the study, including participant selection, data collection, and data analysis. The research design is qualitative in nature, aiming to provide an in-depth understanding of the English pronunciation errors made by Libyan students and the factors contributing to these errors.


## 3.1. Participants:


The participants of this study were 30 Libyan EFL students, comprising 15 high school students and 15 university students from various institutions in Libya. The age of the participants ranged from 16 to 25 years old. All participants had studied English as a foreign language for at least six years, and their proficiency levels ranged from intermediate to advanced, as determined by their performance on the Oxford Placement Test.

A purposive sampling technique was employed to select participants who were willing to participate in the study and who had experienced pronunciation difficulties, as reported by their English teachers. The gender distribution was balanced, with equal numbers of male and female participants.


## 3.2. Data Collection


Data was collected through audio recordings of the participants, who were asked to read aloud a series of English texts designed to elicit a wide range of English sounds, stress patterns, and intonation contours. The texts included short paragraphs, sentences, and word lists containing minimal pairs to capture potential pronunciation errors.

In addition to the reading tasks, semi-structured interviews were conducted with each participant to gather information about their learning experiences, pronunciation difficulties, and strategies they had used to overcome these challenges. Interviews were conducted in Arabic to ensure participants felt comfortable expressing their thoughts and experiences.


## 3.3. Data Analysis


The audio recordings were transcribed using phonetic symbols to represent the pronunciation errors observed in the participants' speech. A qualitative content analysis approach was employed to identify and categorize the common pronunciation errors made by Libyan EFL learners. The analysis focused on segmental errors (i.e., errors related to individual consonant and vowel sounds) and suprasegmental errors (i.e., errors related to stress, rhythm, and intonation). Errors were further classified based on the type of error, such as substitution, deletion, or addition of sounds.

The interview data was transcribed and translated into English. Thematic analysis was used to identify recurring themes and patterns in the participants' learning experiences, pronunciation difficulties, and strategies for overcoming these challenges. The interview data was then triangulated with the findings from the audio recordings to gain a deeper understanding of the factors contributing to the pronunciation errors observed in the participants' speech. To ensure the reliability and validity of the findings, two independent raters were involved in the analysis of the audio recordings and interview data. Any discrepancies between the raters were resolved through discussion and consensus. Moreover, member checking was conducted by sharing the findings with the participants to confirm the accuracy of the identified errors and the interpretations of their learning experiences.

In conclusion, the methodology employed in this study involved collecting data through audio recordings of Libyan EFL students' speech and semi-structured interviews to gain insights into their pronunciation errors and the factors contributing to these errors. A qualitative content analysis approach was used to analyze the data, with a focus on segmental and suprasegmental errors. The findings from the audio recordings and interviews were triangulated to provide a comprehensive understanding of the pronunciation challenges faced by Libyan EFL learners and their implications for language education.

## 5. Discussion:


This study aimed to investigate the English pronunciation errors made by Libyan EFL students and the factors contributing to these errors. The results revealed several segmental and suprasegmental pronunciation errors and highlighted the influence of Arabic on the students' English pronunciation. ## 5.1. Implications for English language education:


The identification of common pronunciation errors among Libyan EFL students can help language educators tailor their instruction to address these challenges more effectively. For instance, teachers can provide targeted practice on problematic sounds, such as /p/, /v/, and /θ/, and help students differentiate between short and long vowels. Additionally, educators can focus on improving students' stress placement, rhythm, and intonation to enhance their overall English pronunciation.

Given the influence of Arabic on the students' English pronunciation, educators must raise learners' awareness of the differences between Arabic and English phonetics and phonology. This can help students recognize the potential for L1 interference and develop strategies for mitigating its impact on their English pronunciation.

Furthermore, the findings highlight the importance of providing students with ample exposure to native English speech. Language programs can incorporate authentic English materials, such as audio recordings, videos, and podcasts, into their curricula to familiarize students with nativelike pronunciation. Additionally, creating opportunities for students to interact with native English speakers, either in person or through online platforms, can help them develop a more accurate pronunciation model and improve their listening and speaking skills.

The role of pronunciation instruction in English language courses should also be re-emphasized, as many participants reported dissatisfaction with the pronunciation instruction they had received. Teachers should receive adequate training in teaching pronunciation, and pronunciation should be integrated into the curriculum, rather than being treated as an isolated skill. Providing targeted feedback on students' pronunciation errors and encouraging the use of effective learning strategies can further support students in overcoming their pronunciation challenges.


## 5.2. Implications for future research:


This study has provided valuable insights into the pronunciation errors made by Libyan EFL students and the factors contributing to these errors. However, further research is needed to explore the effectiveness of various teaching strategies and approaches for addressing these pronunciation challenges.

For instance, experimental studies comparing different pronunciation teaching methods, such as explicit instruction, implicit learning, or the use of technology, can provide evidence-based guidance for educators seeking to improve their students' pronunciation skills. Additionally, longitudinal studies tracking students' progress over time can shed light on the long-term impact of targeted pronunciation instruction on learners' overall English proficiency.

Moreover, future research could investigate the relationship between students' pronunciation skills and their performance in other language skills, such as listening, speaking, reading, and writing. This could help to better understand the role of pronunciation in overall language development and inform the design of integrated language courses that effectively address all aspects of English proficiency.

In conclusion, the results of this study have important implications for English language education in Libya, emphasizing the need for targeted pronunciation instruction and practice to

address the common pronunciation errors faced by Libyan EFL students. The findings highlight the influence of Arabic on students' English pronunciation and underscore the importance of providing students with ample exposure to native English speech and effective pronunciation instruction. By focusing on these areas, English language educators can better support Libyan students in overcoming their pronunciation challenges and achieving success in their English language learning journey.

Future research should continue to explore the effectiveness of various teaching strategies and approaches for addressing pronunciation errors and investigate the relationship between students' pronunciation skills and their performance in other language skills. Such research can further contribute to our understanding of English pronunciation development among Libyan EFL learners and provide valuable guidance for educators seeking to enhance their students' overall English proficiency.


## 6. Recommendations:


Based on the findings of this study, the following recommendations are proposed for English language educators, curriculum developers, and researchers to address the pronunciation challenges faced by Libyan EFL students and to enhance their English language proficiency.


## 6.1. For English language educators:


- 1. Emphasize pronunciation instruction: Integrate pronunciation practice into regular English lessons and provide targeted instruction on problematic sounds, stress placement, rhythm, and intonation. Ensure that pronunciation is treated as an essential component of language learning, alongside grammar, vocabulary, and other language skills.

- 2. Raise awareness of Arabic interference: Help students understand the potential influence of their native language on their English pronunciation and provide guidance on strategies for mitigating L1 interference.
- 3. Provide ample exposure to native English speech: Incorporate authentic English materials, such as audio recordings, videos, and podcasts, into the curriculum to familiarize students with native-like pronunciation. Encourage students to interact with native English speakers, either in person or through online platforms.
- 4. Offer individualized instruction and feedback: Recognize that students may have different pronunciation challenges and provide personalized instruction and feedback to address their specific needs. Encourage self-assessment and peer feedback to help students become more aware of their pronunciation errors and monitor their progress.


## 6.2. For curriculum developers:


- 1. Develop a pronunciation-focused curriculum: Design a curriculum that emphasizes pronunciation skills and incorporates regular pronunciation practice into English language courses. Include pronunciation-focused activities and assessments to monitor students' progress.
- 2. Offer teacher training in pronunciation instruction: Provide English language teachers with adequate training in teaching pronunciation, including guidance on effective teaching strategies and techniques for addressing common pronunciation challenges faced by Libyan EFL students.
- 3. Utilize technology to enhance pronunciation learning: Incorporate technology, such as computer-assisted language learning tools, pronunciation apps, and online resources, into the curriculum to support students in practicing pronunciation skills both in and outside the classroom.

- 4. Foster a learner-centered approach: Encourage the development of learner autonomy by providing students with opportunities to take control of their own pronunciation learning, set personal goals, and employ effective learning strategies.


## 6.3. For researchers:


- 1. Investigate the effectiveness of various pronunciation teaching methods: Conduct experimental studies comparing different pronunciation teaching approaches, such as explicit instruction, implicit learning, or the use of technology, to provide evidence-based guidance for educators.
- 2. Explore the relationship between pronunciation skills and other language skills: Examine the impact of improved pronunciation on students' performance in listening, speaking, reading, and writing to better understand the role of pronunciation in overall language development.
- 3. Conduct longitudinal studies tracking students' progress: Monitor the long-term impact of targeted pronunciation instruction on learners' overall English proficiency to inform curriculum development and teaching practices.
- 4. Investigate the role of learner factors: Examine the influence of learner factors, such as motivation, attitude, and learning strategies, on pronunciation development to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the challenges faced by Libyan EFL students and inform the design of effective learning interventions.

By implementing these recommendations, English language educators, curriculum developers, and researchers can contribute to addressing the pronunciation challenges faced by Libyan EFL students and support their journey towards achieving English language proficiency.

## 1. Introduction


Global supply chains have evolved into highly complex networks involving numerous stakeholders, cross-border transactions, and regulatory frameworks, making them increasingly vulnerable to illicit trade activities such as fraud, counterfeiting, and smuggling (Paraje, Pruzzo, & Muñoz, 2023; Owoade et al., 2024). Traditional supply chain management has long relied on paper-based documentation and fragmented communication systems, leading to inefficiencies, lack of transparency, and security gaps. To address these challenges, digital technologies such as blockchain, artificial intelligence (AI), and the Internet of Things (IoT) have been explored to enhance security, efficiency, and resilience in supply chain operations (Rejeb et al., 2019; Saberi, Kouhizadeh, Sarkis, & Shen, 2018).

One of the most ambitious attempts at applying blockchain technology in supply chain management was TradeLens, a platform co-developed by Maersk and IBM. TradeLens aimed to provide real-time, immutable, and decentralized data sharing among supply chain stakeholders, offering a unified view of shipment movements, customs documentation, and transaction histories. By reducing reliance on manual record-keeping and enabling seamless collaboration, the platform sought to improve efficiency, minimize risks, and combat illicit trade (Zheng et al., 2018; Khan, Piprani, & Yu, 2023; Ventura et al., 2019). Its adoption by ports, regulatory authorities, and logistics providers demonstrated the potential of blockchain to revolutionize maritime shipping.

Despite its early success and widespread industry participation, TradeLens was discontinued in early 2023, signaling the significant challenges associated with implementing blockchain in global trade. ## 2. Literature Review


Supply chain management (SCM) literature consistently highlights transparency and efficiency as essential drivers of competitive advantage within increasingly complex value networks. Digital technologies, particularly the Internet of Things (IoT), blockchain, and artificial intelligence (AI), are recognized as transformative tools that enhance operational visibility, prevent fraud, and promote sustainability in global supply chains. The adoption of IoT has significantly improved product monitoring across supply chain nodes, resulting in enhanced operational efficiency and improved risk management (Rejeb et al., 2019). When integrated with blockchain, IoT facilitates scalable and traceable solutions that foster trust among business-to-business (B2B) partners while streamlining warehousing, manufacturing, and transportation processes. Additionally, IoT-supported Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM) strengthens resilience against disruptions by refining risk mitigation strategies (Birkel & Hartmann, 2020).

Blockchain has garnered particular attention for its ability to secure global supply chains by improving traceability, reducing fraudulent transactions, and increasing stakeholder trust (Chelh et al., 2023). By providing a decentralized and immutable ledger, blockchain ensures transparent and tamper-proof record-keeping in logistics. The integration of AI further enhances these capabilities by leveraging predictive analytics to detect anomalies, thereby mitigating risks associated with human error and fraud (Omoyemi & Joy, 2024). Collectively, these technologies foster a more adaptive and compliant supply chain ecosystem.

Despite its transformative potential, blockchain adoption in global logistics faces significant barriers. One of the most ambitious blockchain-driven SCM initiatives, the TradeLens platform, was developed by Maersk and IBM to enhance supply chain transparency through real-time data exchange. Initially, TradeLens demonstrated blockchain's potential by reducing shipping delays, improving documentation efficiency, and mitigating illicit trade vulnerabilities (Zheng et al., 2018; Khan, Piprani, & Yu, 2023; Ventura et al., 2019). However, despite early adoption by key industry players, TradeLens was discontinued in early 2023 due to challenges in achieving industry-wide collaboration and financial sustainability. Its failure underscores persistent challenges in large-scale blockchain implementation, including reluctance among competitors to share proprietary data, regulatory fragmentation, and high system integration costs (Saberi et al., 2018).

The challenges faced by TradeLens reflect broader concerns in the literature regarding blockchain's feasibility in global supply chains. Kshetri (2018) acknowledges blockchain's potential to enhance efficiency, trust, and operational reliability but notes that adoption remains hindered by governance complexities and the necessity of extensive interorganizational cooperation. Wieland (2021) critiques traditional supply chain theories, advocating for adaptive strategies that better align with dynamic market conditions. TradeLens' failure exemplifies this need for more flexible, collaborative digital transformation models rather than rigid, centralized platforms.

For blockchain-based SCM solutions to succeed in the long term, factors beyond technological capability must be considered. Al-Nawafah et al. (2022) argue that digital transparency can significantly enhance green supply chain management (GSCM) by optimizing routes, reducing waste, and minimizing carbon footprints. However, broad adoption of blockchain in SCM necessitates not only industry commitment but also supportive policy frameworks that incentivize data sharing and interoperability among stakeholders.

The COVID-19 pandemic reinforced the necessity of resilient supply chains, emphasizing the relevance of digital platforms like TradeLens (Rai et al., 2018). Blockchain's ability to enhance logistics visibility and enable real-time collaboration among trading partners is crucial in mitigating disruptions. Huang et al. (2022) link technology adoption to measurable improvements in logistics performance, resource allocation, and inter-firm coordination. However, the discontinuation of TradeLens suggests that achieving widespread blockchain adoption requires more than technological innovation; economic incentives, governance structures, and regulatory harmonization are equally critical.

The IBM-Maersk partnership that underpinned TradeLens highlighted blockchain's potential in supply chain finance (Lerman et al., 2022). By reducing transaction costs and improving financial transparency, blockchain offers significant economic advantages in global logistics. However, TradeLens' failure demonstrates that without a sustainable financial model to support multi-stakeholder collaboration, such platforms may struggle to remain viable.

In contrast, IBM Food Trust, another blockchain initiative, achieved widespread adoption among major retailers like Walmart and Carrefour. Its success stemmed from addressing a critical industry challenge-food safety and recalls-where blockchain provided immediate, tangible benefits. Additionally, the initiative faced less competitive resistance, as retailers were more willing to collaborate than players in the highly competitive ocean shipping industry. This comparison underscores the importance of industry-specific dynamics in blockchain adoption.

Similarly, VeChain's blockchain platform has gained traction in the luxury goods sector, particularly in product authentication for brands like Louis Vuitton. Unlike TradeLens, which targeted global logistics, VeChain found success in a niche market where data transparency directly benefits all participants. This illustrates that blockchain adoption is more viable in sectors where consumer trust and product verification are paramount.

Everledger also achieved initial success by using blockchain to track diamonds, ensuring authenticity and reducing fraud. However, like TradeLens, it encountered challenges in widespread stakeholder adoption. This suggests that blockchain is more effective in highvalue, low-volume industries like diamonds than in high-volume, low-margin industries like global shipping, where adoption hurdles are more pronounced.

In conclusion, while blockchain, IoT, and AI offer promising advancements for SCM, their successful implementation depends on various factors, including industry collaboration, economic incentives, regulatory alignment, and sector-specific applicability. The cases of TradeLens, IBM Food Trust, VeChain, and Everledger illustrate that technological innovation alone is insufficient-successful adoption requires strategic alignment with industry needs and a supportive ecosystem for collaboration.


## 3. Towards a Conceptual Framework


The growing complexity of global supply chains necessitates innovative approaches that integrate digital technologies to enhance transparency, security, and operational efficiency. Existing literature underscores the transformative potential of IoT, AI, and blockchain in addressing challenges such as supply chain fraud, regulatory compliance, and logistical inefficiencies (Rejeb et al., 2019; Saberi et al., 2018). These technologies, when effectively integrated, provide real-time insights, predictive analytics, and immutable data records that can fortify supply chain resilience and mitigate risks.

However, as demonstrated by the discontinuation of TradeLens in early 2023, technological innovation alone is insufficient to guarantee widespread adoption and long-term viability. Despite its promising features-such as secure digital documentation, real-time shipment tracking, and automated workflows-TradeLens faced barriers related to industry collaboration, competitive interests, and financial sustainability. This raises critical questions about how digital transformation efforts can overcome structural and strategic challenges in supply chain management.

To address these issues, we propose a conceptual framework that integrates key digital components necessary for a secure and efficient supply chain. This framework consists of three interrelated components:


## 3.1 Data Acquisition and Integration


A fundamental challenge in supply chain management is the fragmentation of data across various stakeholders, leading to inefficiencies and vulnerabilities to illicit trade (Saberi et al., 2018). Effective supply chain security requires the aggregation of real-time, multisource data-including logistics, customs, and sensor data-into centralized or interoperable platforms. TradeLens attempted to achieve this through blockchain-based data sharing, but its inability to secure universal participation among industry players limited its effectiveness (Zheng et al., 2018). Future digital platforms must focus on open data standards and interoperability to encourage broader adoption and collaboration.


## 3.2 Advanced Analytics and Decision Support


Predictive analytics and AI-driven insights play a crucial role in modern supply chain risk management. By leveraging machine learning algorithms, companies can detect anomalies in shipment movements, anticipate supply chain disruptions, and optimize decision-making (Omoyemi & Joy, 2024). TradeLens sought to provide these capabilities, but its discontinuation suggests that digital platforms must offer clear economic incentives for participants to contribute and utilize data insights meaningfully (Birkel & Hartmann, 2020). Future frameworks should emphasize incentive structures that align the interests of various stakeholders, ensuring sustained engagement and data sharing.


## 3.3 Digital Trust and Transparency


Blockchain technology is often promoted as a solution for enhancing digital trust by creating immutable records of transactions (Chelh et al., 2023). While TradeLens successfully demonstrated blockchain's ability to streamline documentation and reduce shipping uncertainties, its closure highlights the challenges of implementing governance models that balance transparency with competitive concerns (Kshetri, 2018). Moving forward, digital trust mechanisms must incorporate flexible governance structures that allow stakeholders to retain control over proprietary data while still benefiting from shared insights.


## 3.4 Adapting Lessons from TradeLens


The discontinuation of TradeLens underscores several key takeaways for future digital transformation initiatives in supply chain management:

- · Scalability and Adoption: Digital platforms must prioritize industry-wide interoperability rather than relying on proprietary frameworks that exclude potential adopters (Wieland, 2021).
- · Economic Incentives: A viable business model must ensure that all stakeholdersshippers, carriers, customs agencies-benefit from data participation (Al-Nawafah et al., 2022).
- · Regulatory Integration: Governments and international trade organizations must collaborate to develop standardized digital compliance frameworks, ensuring alignment with evolving regulatory requirements (Rai et al., 2018).
- · Sustainability and Resilience: Digital solutions should not only enhance efficiency but also contribute to environmental sustainability and supply chain resilience, particularly in response to disruptions like the COVID-19 pandemic (Huang et al., 2022).


## 4. Lessons from TradeLens and the Future of Digital Supply Chains


The case of Maersk's TradeLens provides a compelling exploration of both the potential and limitations of blockchain-enabled digital transformation in global supply chains. While the initiative demonstrated how distributed ledger technology (DLT) could enhance supply chain transparency, efficiency, and security, its discontinuation in early 2023 reveals critical structural, strategic, and economic challenges. This discussion examines the key takeaways from the rise and fall of TradeLens and provides insights into how future digital supply chain innovations can overcome similar hurdles.


## 4.1 Why TradeLens Failed: Key Challenges


Despite its technological sophistication, TradeLens faced several significant challenges that ultimately led to its discontinuation.

## 4.1.1 Industry-Wide Adoption and Competitive Concerns

One of the fundamental challenges was the reluctance of major industry players, especially competing shipping companies, to fully adopt TradeLens. Many stakeholders feared that Maersk's dominant role in the platform would give it an unfair competitive advantage, creating an uneven power dynamic (Birkel & Hartmann, 2020). Trust and neutrality are critical for digital transformation initiatives that rely on data-sharing ecosystems, and any perception of centralized control can deter adoption (Saberi et al., 2018).

## 4.1.2 Lack of Interoperability and Standardization

For any digital supply chain solution to be successful, it must seamlessly integrate with existing logistics platforms and comply with diverse regulatory environments. While TradeLens aimed to be a single source of truth for supply chain transactions, its limited interoperability with other platforms created significant barriers (Omoyemi & Joy, 2024). A successful blockchain-based supply chain network requires open data standards to ensure compatibility across multiple industry stakeholders (Rejeb et al., 2019).

## 4.1.3 Economic and Commercial Sustainability Issues

Blockchain-based platforms require significant investment in infrastructure, integration, and maintenance. While TradeLens offered efficiency gains, its financial model did not provide sufficient incentives for all stakeholders (Lerman et al., 2022). Many supply chain participants were unwilling to bear the costs associated with joining the platform, especially when the benefits were perceived to be unevenly distributed (Paraje, Pruzzo, & Muñoz, 2023).

## 4.1.4 Regulatory and Compliance Barriers

Although blockchain has the potential to simplify compliance with customs regulations and trade policies, the absence of unified global digital trade regulations hindered TradeLens's adoption. TradeLens struggled to harmonize blockchain-based documentation with the varying requirements of different governments and customs authorities (Rai et al.,

2018). This issue highlights the broader challenge of regulatory fragmentation, which continues to be a major barrier to digital innovation in supply chains (Huang et al., 2022).


## 4.2 Key Lessons for Future Digital Supply Chain Initiatives


The discontinuation of TradeLens does not indicate that blockchain and digital technologies have no future in supply chain management. Instead, it provides valuable insights into how future digital transformation efforts can be designed for long-term success.


## 4.2.1 The Need for Decentralized Governance Models


A major takeaway from TradeLens is that digital supply chain platforms must be built on neutral, decentralized governance structures. Instead of a single corporation leading the initiative, consortium-based models, where multiple industry players share decisionmaking power, can increase trust and encourage widespread adoption (Al-Nawafah et al., 2022).


## 4.2.2 Prioritizing Interoperability and Open Standards


Future blockchain-enabled supply chain solutions must emphasize interoperability with existing logistics systems. Unlike TradeLens, which functioned as a closed ecosystem, next-generation platforms should adopt open APIs and industry-wide data standards to facilitate seamless integration and cross-platform compatibility (Wieland, 2021).


## 4.2.3 Aligning Economic Incentives Across Stakeholders


One of the primary reasons TradeLens struggled was that stakeholders did not see a clear return on investment. Future platforms must ensure that economic benefits are equitably distributed-this could include cost-sharing models, incentive-based participation, or blockchain-powered supply chain finance solutions (Chelh et al., 2023). Tokenization models-where participants are rewarded for contributing data-could also provide new financial incentives for engagement (Phiayura & Teerakanok, 2023).


## 4.2.4 Enhancing Regulatory Collaboration and Compliance Integration


TradeLens demonstrated that regulatory alignment is critical for digital transformation in supply chains. Future initiatives must actively collaborate with government agencies and international trade organizations to develop standardized, legally recognized blockchain documentation systems (Rodrigo et al., 2023). Ensuring that smart contracts and digital bills of lading comply with global trade laws will be essential for wider adoption.


## 4.2.5 Balancing Transparency with Data Privacy


While blockchain provides enhanced traceability and trust, many companies remain hesitant to share supply chain data due to competitive concerns. Future platforms must offer flexible privacy controls, allowing stakeholders to decide how much data they share while still benefiting from blockchain verification (Zheng et al., 2018).


## 4.3 The Future of Digital Supply Chain Management: Beyond TradeLens


Although TradeLens was discontinued, it laid the groundwork for future innovations in digital supply chains. The lessons learned from its failure highlight the importance of balancing technological innovation with industry collaboration, economic viability, and regulatory adaptability.

Moving forward, blockchain, AI, and IoT will continue to play a significant role in modernizing supply chain operations. However, success will depend on rethinking digital transformation strategies:

- · Industry-wide standardization and collaboration must take precedence over proprietary systems.
- · Regulators and trade organizations must play a proactive role in shaping digital supply chain policies.
- · Financial models must ensure that all stakeholders see clear value from participation.
- · Privacy, security, and competitive concerns must be addressed through customizable governance models.


## 5. Conclusion


This paper has examined the role of digital transformation in supply chain management, using Maersk's TradeLens initiative as a central case study. While TradeLens was initially seen as a breakthrough in supply chain transparency and security, its discontinuation in early 2023 underscores the complex challenges of adopting blockchain technology at scale. The analysis highlights that while real-time data integration, advanced analytics, and blockchain technology can enhance supply chain security and efficiency, their success depends on overcoming critical barriers related to industry-wide adoption, governance structures, regulatory integration, and economic sustainability.

The case of TradeLens provides key insights into why technological solutions alone are insufficient for digital supply chain transformation. The lack of interoperability, competitive concerns among stakeholders, and unclear financial incentives ultimately prevented the platform from reaching its full potential. These findings emphasize that future digital supply chain initiatives must focus on collaborative governance, open data standards, and equitable economic incentives to ensure long-term viability.


## Future Directions in Digital Supply Chains


Despite its discontinuation, TradeLens serves as a valuable learning experience that can inform the next generation of supply chain innovations. The following key areas will shape the future of digital trade networks:

- 1. Decentralized and Industry-Wide Governance Models: Future digital supply chain platforms should adopt decentralized or consortium-based governance structures to ensure neutrality and build industry trust. Unlike TradeLens, which was largely controlled by Maersk, successful blockchain initiatives must encourage participation from multiple industry players with equitable decision-making power.
- 2. Interoperability and Open Standards: The next generation of digital trade platforms must prioritize interoperability. Open APIs, standardized digital documentation, and cross-platform compatibility will be crucial in ensuring seamless integration with existing supply chain ecosystems and regulatory frameworks.
- 3. Blockchain in Trade Finance: While TradeLens struggled in logistics, blockchain has immense potential in trade finance. Smart contracts, tokenized transactions, and decentralized financial solutions can enhance efficiency in areas such as letters of credit, payment processing, and fraud prevention.
- 4. Regulatory Collaboration and Compliance Integration: Governments and international trade organizations must actively collaborate to create standardized digital trade documentation laws. Future blockchain-based platforms should integrate compliance-friendly smart contracts that automatically enforce trade regulations, customs protocols, and tax requirements.
- 5. The Role of AI and IoT in Enhancing Digital Supply Chains: Artificial intelligence and IoT-driven predictive analytics will play a critical role in supply chain optimization, risk mitigation, and fraud detection. Blockchain-enabled digital networks should incorporate AI to analyze vast amounts of supply chain data in real-time and proactively address potential disruptions.

## BACKGROUND AND EXPECTATIONS


In the American popular consciousness, Russia (formerly the Soviet Union from 1922 to the Cold War's end) has often served as the 'anti-nation.' America was Anglo Protestant, capitalist, moral, and free, while the Soviet Union/Russia was foreign, atheist, communist, evil, and oppressive (Du Mez 2020). Historically, leaders of Christian Right were among the most suspicious toward the Soviet Union/Russia because they were the most adamantly ethnonationalist and anti-Communist, associating communism with ethno-racial outsiders and Civil Rights agitators, leftism, and atheism (e.g., Falwell 1980). Reflecting the USSR's status among conservative Anglo Protestants, it was also identified with anti-Christian forces in End Times books and movies made by premillennial-dispensationalist white evangelicals (Lindsey 1970). Unsurprisingly, data from 1974 to 1994 shows both political and religious conservatives held the most antipathy toward Russia. 2

After the Soviet Union's collapse, Gallup (2022) data show American's views toward post-Soviet Russia were generally more positive throughout the 1990s and then ebbed and flowed throughout the 2000s into the early 2010s. However, following Vladimir Putin's election as Russian President in 2012 and Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2014, Americans' attitudes quickly became unfavorable. Throughout much of this time, pollsters like Gallup and Pew Research Center showed Democrats and Republicans typically moved together in their views of Russia largely in response to Russia's geopolitical behavior, though Democrats tended to be slightly more favorable than Republicans (Reinhart 2018). These patterns changed almost

immediately following the 2016 election of Donald Trump. Data from multiple surveys before and during Trump's presidency show favorability toward Russia and Vladimir Putin increased considerably among Republicans while plummeting among Democrats (Huang and Cha 2020; Pew Research Center 2019; Reinhart 2018; Swift 2017). 3

These more recent shifts could suggest that Americans' changing views about Russia and Putin are driven largely by partisan allegiance which has becoming tightly correlated with ideological identity in the past few decades (Perry 2023). Early on in his candidacy and throughout his Presidency, Trump expressed admiration for Putin's leadership and encouraged Americans to see Russia as America's ally (Riccardi-Swartz 2022b). Part of this was almost certainly because of well-documented financial ties between Trump and Russian oligarchs (Snyder 2018). But the other part is that while the former USSR was demonized because of 'godless communism,' Putin's Russia now represents much of what Trump advertised and valued in his own leadership: law and order, challenging mainstream media, white ethnonationalism, and traditional (in Putin's version Orthodox) 'Christian' values that did not depend on personal piety, but on nativism and traditionalist moral stances (Stoeckl and Uzlaner 2020; Riccardi-Swartz 2022a, 2022b).  In this sense, the 'Christianity' of both Russian and American 4 Christian nationalism cannot be understood apart from their connection to ethnicity, in the latter

case, whiteness (Butler 2021; Perry 2023). Whiteness is thus the subtext of Christian Right discourse on Russia's protection of borders or preservation of culture. For example, in 2017, farright activist Christopher Caldwell spoke at Hillsdale College: '[I]f we were to use traditional measures for understanding leaders, which involve the defense of borders and national flourishing, Putin would count as the pre-eminent statesman of our time (Caldwell 2017).

Other prominent leaders on the Christian Right have praised Putin as a warrior for traditional Christian culture. Pat Buchanan (2014) explained, 'In the culture war for the future of mankind, Putin is planting Russia's flag firmly on the side of traditional Christianity.' Similarly, former GOP Senate candidate for Delaware, Lauren Witzke (a catechumen to Russian Orthodoxy) explained, 'Russia is a Christian nationalist nation so…I actually support Putin's right to protect his people and always put his people first, but also protect their Christian values. I identify more…with Putin's Christian values than I do with Joe Biden' (Henderson 2022). And still others on the Christian right have sought to blame Ukraine, not Putin. Just before Russia's invasion, founder of Turning Point USA Charlie Kirk told listeners, 'It feels as if Putin is going into places that want him. They have voted overwhelmingly to be part of it' (Media Matters 2022). Similarly, Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (GA-R), who has called herself a 'Christian nationalist' on social media and speeches, blamed Ukraine for the invasion saying it 'just kept poking the bear, and poking the bear, which is Russia, and Russia invaded' (Fedor 2022).

We propose that, beyond partisanship or conservative political identity, Christian nationalist ideology undergirds support for both Russia and Putin since the rise of Trump. Much recent research affirms cultural factors drove support for Trump's brand of populist, autocratic, and nationalist leadership that frequently leveraged nostalgia for America's mythical Anglo Protestant past (Butler 2021). Though various names have been used, scholars have identified

Christian nationalism as a key driver of Americans' support for Trump's candidacy and policies in 2016 (Gorski 2017; Whitehead et al. 2018) and again in 2020 (Braunstein 2021). Subsequent research has also documented that Christian nationalist ideology is rooted in assumptions of white male Christian hegemony (Butler 2021; Du Mez 2020), and consequently, is powerfully associated with authoritarian, anti-democratic, and exclusionary political views (Gorski and Perry 2022). Flowing from this, we theorize that Americans' are drawn to Russia and Putin, not only because of partisan loyalty or conservative identity, but because of Christian nationalist ideology that favors authoritarian, autocratic means to restore a mythical ethno-cultural order. 5

First, we expect Christian nationalism inclines Americans to view Russia as a political ally working toward similar goals of moral securitization of the public sphere. However, as support for Russia has ebbed and flowed, we expect Christian nationalism's relationship with support for Russia will be contingent on its geo-political activity vis-à-vis the US (see work on threat perception, e.g., Gries 2022). At times when Russian-US hostilities are more relaxed (before Ukraine), we would suspect Christian nationalism would be associated with more friendly views toward Russia. But following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, we would expect Christian nationalism would perceive Russian power as a threat. In contrast, we theorize Christian nationalism, being primarily about restoring a mythical white ethno-cultural order, will be positively associated with Putin support due to his authoritarian ethno-nationalist leadership style (Riccardi-Swartz 2022a, 2022b). And we anticipate Christian nationalism will be positively associated with Putin support regardless of how Russia is perceived.


## METHODS



## Data


Data for this study are taken from three sources, the Public Religion Research Institute's (PRRI) 2018 American Values Survey (Vandermaas-Peeler et al. 2020), Pew Research Center's American Trends Panel, Wave 84 (ATP 84); and the 2022 National Addiction and Social Attitudes Survey (NASAS) (see Authors). The American Values Survey (AVS) is PRRI's annual survey of religion, culture, and politics. The AVS is conducted by AmeriSpeak, a probabilitybased panel administered by NORC at the University of Chicago, designed to be representative of the US adult population. Sampling weights are provided and applied to account for probability of selection into the sample and to ensure representativeness with the US population parameters for gender, race, education, age, housing type, and telephone usage. The AVS includes 2,509 cases. After adjusting for missing cases, our analytic samples include from 2,168 to 2,377.

Pew's ATP Wave 84 was fielded in March of 2021 by Ipsos, a global market research and polling firm. The ATP surveys are taken from nationally representative panels of randomly selected U.S. adults. Panelists participate via self-administered online surveys. Ipsos develops and provides sampling weights to account for the multi-stage sampling process and bring the survey into alignment with nationally representative norms (for more information, see Keeter 2019). The resulting original survey included 12,055 cases that were weighted. After accounting for missing information, our final analytic sample is 9,550 cases.

The 2022 NASAS was designed by the authors and fielded in March 2022 by YouGov, an international research data and analytics company. YouGov recruits a panel of respondents through websites and banner ads. In order to draw a nationally representative sample, YouGov employs a method called 'matching.' Drawing a random sample from the American Community

Survey, YouGov then matches a respondent in the opt-in panel who is the closest to the Census respondent based on key sociodemographic factors. YouGov also develops sampling weights to ensure the survey sample aligns with nationally representative norms for age, gender, race, education, and census region. The resulting original survey sample included 2,809 Americans that were matched and weighted. Our final analytic sample in full models is 2,804 cases.


## Attitudes toward Russia and Putin in 2018, 2021, and 2022


The 2018 AVS asked three questions regarding Russia and Putin. Respondents were given a list of names and entities including 'Russia' and 'Russian President Vladimir Putin.' They were asked to indicate whether their overall opinion of each was 1 = very unfavorable, 2 = mostly unfavorable, 3 = mostly favorable, or 4 = very favorable.  Respondents were also asked 6 'Do you consider Russia an ally of the United States, friendly but not an ally, unfriendly, or an enemy of the United States? Response options ranged from 1 = enemy, 2 = unfriendly, 3 = friendly, or 4 = ally. The 2021 ATP 84 only asked a question about Putin, which was identical to the question asked in PRRI's 2018 AVS survey. Response options also ranged from 1 to 4. The 2022 NASAS asked two questions regarding Russia and Putin. Respondents were asked to indicate their level of agreement with the statements: 'Russia's power and influence are a major threat to the well-being of the United States,' and 'Vladimir Putin exhibits leadership qualities that I respect.' Responses ranged from 1=strongly disagree to 5=strongly agree.


## Christian Nationalism


Christian nationalism has been measured in a variety of ways (Al-Kire 2022; Davis 2018; Gorski and Perry 2022; McDaniel et al. 2022). Among the measures commonly used (see AlKire et al. 2022; Whitehead and Perry 2020), the 2018 AVS asked respondents 'Which of these

statements comes closest to your view? America has always been and is currently a Christian nation, America was a Christian nation in the past but is not now, or America has never been a Christian nation.' We recoded this measure into binary variables with those who believe America was never a Christian nation as the reference category.

The 2021 ATP 84 asked a series of seven questions assessing how Americans view church-state relations, with many modeled off of questions included in Whitehead and Perry (2020; see also Gorski and Perry 2022). Respondents were given two statements and asked which came closer to their view such as 'The federal government should declare the United States a Christian nation' or 'The federal government should never declare any particular religion as the official religion of the United States.' For a full list of the questions used, see Appendix Table A1. We coded all responses so that 1=affirming the Christian nationalist answer, 0=rejecting the Christian nationalist answer. We then added up responses to create a scale ranging from 0-7 (alpha = .73) with higher scores indicating greater Christian nationalism.

The 2022 NASAS introduces a new measure of Christian nationalism that incorporates questions from multiple studies (Davis and Perry 2021; Gorski and Perry 2022; McDaniel et al. 2022). Respondents were asked to indicate their level of agreement with the following statements: 'America holds a special place in God's plan,' 'It is critical that our government maintains a separation of church and state' (reverse coded), 'The federal government should declare the United States a Christian nation,' 'I consider the founding documents like the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution to be divinely inspired,' and 'I consider being a Christian an important aspect of being truly American.' Response options ranged from 0=strongly disagree to 4=strongly agree. We combined items into a scale (Cronbach's alpha = .84) from 0-20 with higher scores indicating greater agreement with Christian nationalism.
