## RESULTS


OLS models in the first analysis (Appendix Table A5) predict Americans' attitudes toward Russia and Putin in the 2018 AVS. The first model predicted more favorable views toward Putin. The key finding is illustrated on the far left side of Figure 1. Even with controls in place, Americans who affirm the nation's Christian heritage in the past and/or the present tend to score higher on favorability toward Putin. Turning the focus to Russia, only those Americans who believe the United States was and is currently a Christian nation (the most extreme category on the Christian nationalist measure) tend to be more favorable toward Russia than those who say America was never a Christian nation. Lastly, the far right side of Figure 1 presents results from our third model predicting whether Americans consider Russia more of an ally than an enemy. Compared to those who believe America was never a Christian nation, those who affirm America was a Christian nation (even if they disagree on whether America is currently) score higher on viewing Russia as a friend or ally. Together these findings support our expectation that Christian nationalist ideology leads Americans to be more favorable toward Russia and Putin.

Figure 2 illustrates the clear linear association we observe from our OLS analysis with data from the March 2021 ATP 84 (Appendix Table A6) predicting that Americans hold more favorable views toward Putin. Even after accounting for party identification, ideological identity, and conventional religious measures, as Christian nationalism increases from 0 to 7, Americans consistently score higher on favorability toward Putin.

For the third analysis, we predicted outcomes related to Russia and Putin in the 2022 NASAS (Appendix Table A7). Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, we anticipated that Christian nationalism (as a form of nationalism ) might incline Americans to view Russian power

as more of a threat. In our first Model, Christian nationalism was indeed positively, but weakly, associated with viewing Russia as a threat to the United States ( p < .05). However, after plotting out the bivariate pattern between Christian nationalism and the threat perception outcome, it was clear that the association was more curvilinear. Consequently, when we included quadratic term (see Model 2 in Appendix Table A7), both the initial term and the quadratic term become strongly significant predictors in the opposite directions. Panel A in Figure 3 illustrates this Ushaped curvilinear trend. Americans who either strongly reject Christian nationalism or strongly affirm Christian nationalism are more likely to view Russian power as a threat to the United States than those Americans who score in the middle on the Christian nationalism measure.

Our last Model focusing on Putin showed a different pattern, illustrated in Panel B, Figure 2. Even after accounting for political, religious, and demographic characteristics, the more Americans affirm Christian nationalist ideology, the more likely they agree that Putin exhibits leadership qualities they respect. Once again, this affirms that the more Americans embrace Christian nationalist ideology, the more favorable views they hold toward Vladimir Putin.


## DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS


Following Trump's election in 2016, voices on the political and religious right warmed toward both Russia and Putin, likely reflecting a variety of historical, political, and ethno-cultural conditions (Moreton 2022; Riccardi-Swartz 2021; Stoeckl and Uzlaner, eds. 2020). Even after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, prominent far-right and Christian Right voices have expressed admiration toward Putin and warmer feelings toward Russia than Ukraine. In this study, we tested whether Christian nationalist ideology, in addition with conservative ideological identity and Republican partisanship, inclines Americans to hold more positive views toward Russia and Putin before and after the 2022 Ukrainian invasion. Data from 2018 showed that affirming

America's Christian heritage and character inclined Americans to view Putin and Russia more favorably and Russia as more of an ally. Similarly, data from 2021 showed Christian nationalist ideology was linearly associated with greater favorability toward Putin. And data from just after the Ukrainian invasion in 2022 (an invasion in which Russia showed military strength and aggression) revealed that extreme orientations toward Christian nationalist ideology inclined Americans toward viewing Russian power as a national threat. In contrast, Christian nationalism was a positive, linear predictor of respect for Putin's leadership.

Our findings nuance current understandings of the Religious Right and Russia in several important ways. First, we demonstrate that Christian nationalist ideology seems to influence Americans' views toward Russia and Putin beyond traditional indicators of partisanship, ideological identity, or religion. Though for Russia, this may be connected to whether it is perceived as a geopolitical ally or threat (thus the difference between 2018 and 2022), for Putin, Christian nationalism finds consistent ideological approval. Americans who subscribe to Christian nationalism in 2018, 2021, and 2022 were warmer toward Putin, in part, because they subscribe to certain views about America's mythic Christian past and a vision for its future (Riccardi-Swartz 2022b). This 'future' orientation is potentially what distinguishes a Christian nationalist right from traditional 'values conservatives.' Putin is returning Russia to its 'traditional' Christian values and ethno-cultural purity by radical action. The fact that Christian nationalism would attract Americans to his leadership makes sense given recent research showing Christian nationalism is associated with support for ethno-racial purity, anti-democratic policies, and various forms of authoritarian violence that serves to control problem populations (Armaly et al. 2022; Davis 2018; Gorski and Perry 2022; Riccardi-Swartz 2021, 2022a).

Why was Christian nationalism's relationship to perceived Russian threat in 2022 curvilinear? It is almost certainly for different reasons on the left and the right. For those who strongly reject Christian nationalism, Russian power is indistinguishable from Putin's and thus both are associated with authoritarian ethno-traditionalism. But for those who score higher on Christian nationalism, support for Russia and Putin may be less tightly coupled. Though Putin's leadership style and perception as a strongman leader and friend to other such strongmen is consistent, how Americans evaluate the Russian nation appears more contingent on its geopolitical activity vis-à-vis the United States. As numerous surveys have shown (Huang and Cha 2020; Pew Research Center 2019; Reinhart 2018; Swift 2017), Americans' views toward Russia have historically ebbed and flowed in response to Russia's geopolitical activity. And it was only in recent years that Republicans and Democrats became sharply divided due to Russia's interference on Trump's behalf in the 2016 election. Since the 2022 military invasion of Ukraine, however, Russia's identity as a geo-political threat has likely become more salient. For those who strongly affirm Christian nationalism, it may be that the 'nationalist' elements of Christian nationalism incline Americans to view any aggressive military force as a threat. Gries (2022) shows that ideologically motivated perceptions of threat (e.g., nationalism) incline conservatives to be more suspicious of foreign power and this would be consistent with our findings. Other military forces could be viewed as threats, even while the same ideology inclines Americans to respect authoritarian leaders like Putin or Victor Orban (Moreton 2022; Riccardi-Swartz 2022a).

This last point speaks to the important implications of our findings. To the extent that Christian nationalist ideology 'threatens democracy' (Gorski and Perry 2022), it is not necessarily because it aligns us with military enemies who might harm us, but that it attracts Americans to demonstrably authoritarian strongmen who promise to return their nations to a

mythical ethno-culturally 'pure' past. This is consistent with findings showing Christian nationalism is associated with support for Trump (Whitehead and Perry 2022), restricting voter access (Perry et al. 2022), and political violence (Armaly et al. 2022). But here we see Christian nationalism can even warm Americans toward authoritarian leaders of former geopolitical enemies, or even those viewed as current military threats.

Several data limitations should be acknowledged. While these three data sets provide large, representative samples of Americans over time with valid measures of Christian nationalism, the ideal would be to leverage panel data with identical measures of Christian nationalism and attitudes toward Russia and Putin to observe change. This limitation manifests itself in our study in that we cannot be certain that it was the Russian invasion of Ukraine that caused the curvilinear relationship between Christian nationalism and Russia support. This conceivably could have been the case before. Future research should also be conducted to tease out precisely what characteristics groups of Americans appreciate about Putin or what Russia means to the United States. Select quotes from far-right Christian pundits strongly suggest these are traditionalist moral values and authoritarian social control. And the associations we document with Christian nationalism would affirm this. Nevertheless, more precise measures would allow researchers to determine how prevalent these views are across the general populations and which reasons resonate the most with ideological commitments we document. Lastly, our data only focus on Putin and Russia. But future research should expand the focus to examine how Christian nationalist ideology influences Americans to evaluate a variety of global leaders and regimes. Given our findings here, it is likely that Christian nationalist ideology may incline Americans to distrust economic competitors and potential military threats (e.g., China) while still applauding the strength, traditionalism, and control exercised by their leadership.

## 1 Introduction


The objective of this work is to employ the key idea behind social physics that, under appropriate conditions, the tools developed to describe physical systems can be used to describe certain social systems [1, 2]. We focus on fundamental mechanical concepts to contribute towards understanding social change, its nature and its causes. Even more, establishing appropriate analogues of mechanics in social phenomena contributes to further explore connections of other physical concepts in a systematic way. This may be so since mechanical concepts are foundational to other areas of physics like thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, and general relativity, given the appropriate mechanisms like statistical mechanics, quantization and covariant formulations, respectively.

We are looking for a description of social phenomena in terms of stances about a social question (position) [3-5], social change (motion) [6, 7, 17], predisposition to

change (inertia) [8-11], advocacy and compellingness (forces and interactions) [12, 13], and others in a similarly fashion. However, we expect the analogy not to be perfect, but a useful approximation [14, 16]. We also expect there to be differences in the relations among them compared to what happens in physics. In other words, one would expect that a possible mechanical theory of social change be a genuine social mechanics in its own right.

In a substantial part, this proposal aims to provide a mathematical framework to observations about social change like the following, taken from [17]: 'It is important to emphasize that with small variations in starting points and inertia, resistance, or participation at the crucial points, social change may or may not happen. Suppose that a community has long had a norm in favor of discrimination based on sexual orientation; that many people in the community abhor that norm; that many others dislike it and that many others do not care about it; that many others are mildly inclined to favor it; and that many others firmly believe in it. If norm entrepreneurs make a public demonstration of opposition to the norm, and if the demonstration reaches those with relatively low thresholds for opposing it, opposition will immediately grow. If the growing opposition reaches those with relatively higher thresholds, the norm might rapidly collapse. But if the early public opposition is barely visible or if it reaches only those with relatively high thresholds, it will fizzle out and the norm might not even budge'. This considerations show similarities between evolution of social systems and that of physical systems. Indeed, the coincidences mostly distil from the more fundamental concept of change with respect of time.

Indeed, the work presented here belongs to the realm of quantitative methods and mathematical models for human and social research [15]. As such, it does not give a fundamental explanation of why such systems behave the way they do. What it does is to provide tools to model this behaviour to help investigate its nature through measurable traits. We do not pretend to substitute already existing theories about social behaviour, but to aid them by introducing quantitative tools based on well known results about analogous models in physics.

We are confident that the results will prove interesting to both social researchers, as well as physicists. On the one hand, investigators of social phenomena can put these results to test while also using them to characterize individuals and populations, their traits and conditions, as well as the possible relations among all of them. On the other hand, we believe that physicists will find that the resulting generalizations of physical concepts yield novel and fascinating possibilities to further develop them.

The rest of the article is organized as follows: In Section 2 we introduce and develop fundamental concepts for a mechanical theory of social change analogously to classical mechanics in its Newtonian formulation. In Section 3 we use those fundaments to describe some initial models. Specifically, we study the motion of a particle subject to free motion, a force described by Hooke's law, and a stochastic interaction, governed by the Smoluchowski equation. As an example of the use of this last one for modelling real data, we describe partisan preferences in the United States as outlined by presidential elections. In Section 4 we briefly discuss how other formulations of mechanics, known to be equivalent to the famous Newton's laws can be understood in the light of our

proposal. Finally, in Section 5 we present the concluding remarks of this investigation, as well as a some prospective lines to continue this research.


## 2 Fundamental concepts


In this section we will present the concepts that will allow us to build a mechanical theory of social change. A particle in our social models represents an single conviction held by a unit of the social universe. Just like in physics, here a particle is an idealization [18]. It helps to describe the simplest component of matter, here understood as a society, and upon aggregation with other particles yields more complicated forms of social matter. Actually, this illustrates a powerful trait of physics: it departs from simple cases to be aggregated non-trivially to explain more complex phenomena.

Since societies are composed of individuals, a particle can be readily identified with the convictions of an individual person. However, other realizations of a particle could be made [19]. For example, a social group fairly homogeneous with respect to a trait of interest could be identified with a particle, just like the centre of mass of an extended object, e.g. a ball, can be identified with a particle, although it is composed of more fundamental particles.


## 2.1 Position


The first concept that we wish to discuss is that of position or, more generally, configuration . The position of a social system should describe its status with respect to an attribute of which change (or lack thereof) occurs. More concretely, a positions can be identified with beliefs, convictions or stances about a social question. Then, a position in social mechanics is treated here in the sense of the common phrasing 'what is your position on this topic?-My position on it is...' and others similar to these.

We also require the position to be describable by coordinates in a space. Thus, this space is generally the set of all possible positions an individual can take on a topic. More specifically, the system at hand shall give us hints on the mathematical properties of such a space. For brevity, we can think of this space as a subset of R n , that is, we can specify a position by n real coordinates in the usual notation ( x , x 1 2 , . . . , x n ).

This picture has some underlying assumptions about the type of characteristics that can be modelled by it. We suppose that in the space of social positions we can assign univocally a set of coordinates ( x , x 1 2 , . . . , x n ) to a given stance. That is, we can somehow measure stances or, at least, there is a proxy way of measuring them. We also suppose that there is a 'well-behaved' way of comparing different stances. This is a matter that is readily found in the fundaments of some already existing conceptual frameworks around social phenomena, like in the utility theory of economics.

an observation about how this trait evolves in time. Even more, it claims a change in time very much familiar to physics: an oscillatory motion. Such a model of a trait varying in time is not new in social sciences and should be understood closely related to the method of analysing time series.

## 2.3 Inertia


So far the concepts we presented have not been particularly heavy on physics. Position as a stance on social issues and motion as a a change in position over time have been used in social sciences by other names in a transparent way. Now, we proceed to a concept that is in the kernel of mechanical treatments in physics: inertia.

Inertia is the tendency to maintain a specific state of motion, usually called free motion . Conversely, this tendency can be understood as an opposition to change the state of motion in response to efforts to modify it. Upon observations of different systems we can assign a parameter quantifying said opposition. We call it inertial mass or just mass, for now. This mass, usually denoted by m , provides us with a powerful quantifiable property to characterize how individuals, or groups of them, respond to change. In physical heuristics, there are individuals that are heavier or lighter than others depending on how difficult or easy it is to provoke a change in their motion, respectively.

From Newton's first law of mechanics, the state of free motion in physics is the uniform linear motion. In turn, this is closely related to the idea of particles having a constant inertial parameter, that is, mass. However, there is no reason for this to be the case for social phenomena. In fact, we shall see that it makes sense to have social masses that depend on the position of the particle. This is one of the interesting generalizations resulting from applying physical ideas to social studies.

There is another quantity closely related to mass. It is the momentum , usually denoted by p = m d x i d t , that is, the product of the mass m and the velocity d x i d t , which is the rate of change of the position x i in time, obtained by deriving c i with respect to time t . It is closely related because, as we shall see, it is the quantity upon which externalities act more directly and transparently. The reason being that p encompasses, by definition, both the state of motion and the opposition to change it. Thus, when we refer to the state of motion we mean a given momentum p .


## 2.4 Interaction


Mass is a property of the particle susceptible of motion, even if it depends on its position. On the other hand, we still need to describe externalities, that is, the action of others on the particle. We do this through the concept of force . Forces are in general functions of position and time: F = F x , t ( i ), where i = 1 , . . . , n and the specific mathematical expression is proposed and confirmed for each social phenomena.

In line with previously introduced concepts, a force is an influence causing a change in the state of motion of a particle. Similarly, here an interaction is the exercise of forces among several particles. We say 'here' because in physics there are other formulations of mechanics. For now, we shall stick to the use of forces since they are valuable in explaining intuitively the comparison between physical and social phenomena.

A concept closely related to motion and force is that of equilibrium in that it is observed as a lack of change in the motion due to the exact balance of opposing forces. Indeed, the lack of a net resulting force on a particle is not rest but the continuance of its current motion.

Before we move on, a caveat is at hand. we have described position as points in a space of possible stances and, with it, we have disregarded physical space, that is geographical separation between individuals and societies. So, how are they interacting? Certainly, there must be a physical channel carrying interactions. Whether it be in-person conversations, interactions through social media, action through an intermediate individual, or other ways, it does not matter for our current formulation.

In this work we are concerned about the effect of the interaction on the stances of each participant in a social group and with a given social environment. We do not mean to say that physical distance is unimportant. Rather that we assume that a channel for communicating interactions is already established of which the physical separation, as well as other properties, form the set of parameters shaping the interaction in the space of social positions.

Modernity is key to the relevance of this framework. In the past, when social systems contained a smaller population, the exchange of ideas only occurred when people physically encountered each other and in a slower rate. Nowadays, there is a bigger, faster and more interacting community. There is also more data available to be understood on itself, but also to better understand social change, in general.

## 5 Conclusions


In this work we have explored the idea behind social physics that analogies between some social and physical systems may occur under certain circumstances. While an analogy can take place as mathematical formulations coincide, this work studies further comparisons. Thus, physical concepts are employed to describe social change, taking advantage of the well established heuristics behind physics. That is to say a more genuine social physics framework than just a coincidence in mathematical tools.

For the sake of systematicity, the investigation commenced with the a proposal to connect fundamental concepts in physics with notions regarding social change. Specifically, we explored the concepts of particle, position, space, motion, inertia, mass,

momentum, force, interaction and equilibrium. They key idea is to represent stances on a social question as positions in a configuration space.

Once the initial concepts were established in a social change context, we used the resulting connections to describe a particle moving freely and one moving under the influence of a net force. An important caveat is the generalization of the concept of mass. On the one hand, mass can be either positive or negative. The first case represents a resistance to motion under an external influence that increases with the magnitude of the mass. The second case can be understood as a back reaction to the external influence that produces a motion in the opposite direction of it and it also increases with its magnitude.

On the other hand, the mass is also generalized to be a function of position. With it, we can distinguish the responses to social influences and characterize the social unit depending on its current stance on the topic. This encompasses the assumption of a consistent individual, where, upon having the same stance, it shows the same inertial response to a certain interaction. Although one can imagine more general mass functions, like one that is also explicitly time dependent or with hysteretical behaviour, these cases are not explored here.

Notably, here we used the Newtonian formulation of classical mechanics. Thus, a remark on well-known Newton's laws is at hand. As in the first law, there is a tendency to maintain a particular motion when no forces act on an object: free motion; as well as a measure of this tendency: inertial mass. However, these differ from the physical case since, although the mass is a characteristic of the object, it varies with its position. Still, one can use the mathematical expression for the second law, stating that the net force on a particle produces a change in the state of motion through the derivative of momentum with respect to time. Finally, generalizing the third law, while human interactions can be two-way, one can imagine the reciprocity not being identical. In this regard, some asymmetries could be incorporated in the model by means of distinct mass functions among interacting particles. Nonetheless, it seems that this would need to be validated for a given specific phenomenon.

We also briefly described the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian functions corresponding to the proposed framework. However, as is well known, the resulting system is non holonomicaly constraint due to the position dependent mass. They could be connected to formulations of social behaviour based on extremization of functions like utility theory.

Finally, we showed how stochastic considerations can be incorporated by passing to a mechanical description based on distributions instead of trajectories. As an example we used the Smoluchowski equation to describe partisan stances corresponding to the outcomes of USA's presidential elections since 1856.


## 5.1 Future work


From the various considerations presented in this work, there are some immediate prospective directions to continue the investigations presented here. One can study other possible generalizations of mass functions or different specific cases of forces and interactions. Notably, we have used one-dimensional systems for simplicity, however multiple social issues in the form af additional dimensions can be considered. One

can also investigate the many-body problem in social mechanics and even develop an statistical mechanics explanation of how individuals aggregate to produce social configurations, analogously to how small particles aggregate to produce solids, liquids or gases, or even more complex states.

There are two more possible directions for the kind of research conducted here: social systems analogous to quantum physics and general relativity. Although seemingly strange, the first is a reasonable direction since quantum mechanics incorporates fundamentally the notion of stochasticity of a single particle. The uncertainty is fundamental and we do not know why it must be accounted for in the quantum theory, so it is postulated. An attempt could be made to see if the results from quantum mechanics yield mathematical tools to deal with uncertainties in an individual's motion, even if they are not fundamental, but only effective due to the unpredictability of human behaviour [25, 26].

General relativity offers possibilities in applying analogous reasoning to social systems. The novelty of general relativity is an intertwine between the nature of the space of positions and the objects moving on it. This can help generalize the notion that the positions accessible, i.e. the space, are previously fixed to be occupied by individuals, moving towards a picture in which the space of stances is dynamical and changes as a society evolves. While the mathematical framework for general relativity is differential geometry, where space-time is a manifold, there are already social stances describable in these terms, for example, the concept of equilibrium manifold in economics [27]. Of course, no connection between them is claimed now, but they are susceptible of investigation for possible analogies. It is worth mentioning here that there is already an empirical result in economics known as the gravity model of international trade stating that 'the volume of trade between two countries is proportional to their economic mass and a measure of their relative trade frictions' [28]. Although, it is analogous to non-relativistic gravity.

In any of these prospectives there is always the opportunity to find data susceptible to be described by each resulting model that, in turn, can help to test and tune it.

Before we finish this exposition, a warning is necessary: as with other frameworks exploiting analogies, the connections made through social mechanics should be treated as effectively describing social phenomena, as opposed to fundamental explanations. Any statement on the fundamental nature and mechanisms of an attempted 'true' description of human behaviour must be rigorously tested against robust data, with great scepticism. People are not machines.

Since then, artificial intelligence has become deeply integrated into daily life (Devlin et al., 2023; Maslej et al., 2024), with nearly every sector of the economy adopting the technology to enhance efficiency and improve outcomes (Rashid & Kausik, 2024). ## The Physical Infrastructure of Artificial Intelligence: Data Centers and Minerals


The frequent mention of Artificial Intelligence in news reports, often accompanied by abstract terms such as Cloud, Big Data, Algorithms, Machine Learning, and Virtualization, can create the misleading impression that these technologies operate immaterially, detached from any physical infrastructure.

However, behind  these  terms  lies  a  vast  and  complex  network  of  physical  systems, primarily housed in data centers. These facilities are designed to accommodate and operate thousands of servers organized in racks, alongside storage systems (such as SSDs and HDDs),

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

networking  devices  (switches,  routers,  and  firewalls),  processing  units  (CPUs,  GPUs,  and TPUs), power supply and backup systems (generators and UPS), cooling mechanisms (fans, chillers, and liquid cooling), environmental monitoring sensors, connection cables, and various other essential components (Avelar et al., 2023; Chatterjee & Venugopal, 2023).

Data  centers  serve  as  the  backbone  of  an  AI-driven  world,  providing  the  critical infrastructure  necessary  to  meet  the  increasing  demands  for  computational  power  and  data storage. The construction of these facilities depends on a broad range of minerals and metals including gallium, germanium, metallic silicon, tantalum, platinum-group metals, copper, rare earth  elements,  silver,  and  gold  -  ranging  from  abundant  materials  to  highly  critical  raw resources (Pehlken et al., 2019; Crawford, 2021; Robbins & Van-Wynsberghe, 2022).

These resources undergo extensive extraction and refining processes to achieve the high levels  of  purity  required  for  the  electronic,  magnetic,  mechanical,  and  optical  properties essential to AI systems (United Nations, 2024). It is estimated that the production of complex electronic devices consumes between 50 and 350 times the final weight of the product in raw materials (Ademe, 2021). For instance, manufacturing a laptop requires mobilizing approximately 600 kg of materials, while an internet router demands around 500 kg (Ademe, 2021).

Currently, there are approximately 12,000 data centers worldwide (Statista, 2024b), of which  992  are  classified  as  hyperscale  (Statista,  2024c).  Although  no  universally  precise definition exists, IBM - a multinational technology company - suggests that a data center must house at least 5,000 servers and span more than 10,000 square feet (approximately 929 m²) to be  considered  hyperscale  (Powell  &  Smalley,  2024).  However,  the  largest  data  centers  far exceed this scale. A striking example is The Citadel Campus in Reno, Nevada, USA. Operated by  the American  company  Switch,  which  specializes  in  designing,  building,  and  managing large-scale data centers, this facility spans 7.2 million square feet (approximately 669,000 m² or 66.9 hectares) (Switch, 2024). These figures highlight the enormous volume of minerals required to sustain this critical infrastructure.

## Minerals, Artificial Intelligence, and Geopolitics


In recent years, it has become increasingly evident that the supply of critical minerals essential for artificial intelligence infrastructure is not dictated solely by market dynamics but is also deeply shaped by geopolitical factors. The availability of these minerals, along with the technologies associated  with them, has become a central element in the global struggle for supremacy between the United States and China (Lee, 2018; Kalantzakos, 2020; Nakano, 2021; Xinyue, 2024; Zhou, 2024), triggering intense confrontations.

Currently, China dominates the market for critical minerals essential to AI infrastructure, including antimony, gallium, germanium, and rare earth elements (Areddy & Follow, 2023; Xinyue, 2024). In contrast, the United States leads in the manufacturing stage of AI-related products  -  a  process  that  relies  heavily  on  advanced  expertise  in  areas  such  as  intellectual property, design, automation, and fabrication technology (Xinyue, 2024).

Amid an escalating technological, economic, and political rivalry - which began at least as early as 2018 during the Trump administration and intensified under Joe Biden - the U.S. government announced measures in October 2022 aimed at restricting the export of advanced technologies to China (Reuters, 2023). These actions included prohibiting the sale of advanced chips  and  imposing  export  restrictions  on  semiconductor  manufacturing  equipment  (United States, 2022).

In July 2023, in response to these restrictions, China imposed limits on the export of two  essential  minerals  for  AI-related  technologies:  gallium  and  germanium,  of  which  it

Together, Nvidia and TSMC dominate the global market for high-efficiency chips designed for artificial intelligence (Statista, 2024g).

Amid these disputes, both the European Union and the United States are seeking new strategies to secure access to critical minerals essential for technological development (Zhou, 2024). In the case of the United States, the White House has launched a series of initiatives estimated  at  over  $120  billion  -  aimed  at  strengthening  national  supply  chains  for  critical minerals to reduce dependence on China (The White House, 2024).

This launch occurred despite the restrictions and prohibitions  imposed  by  the  Biden  administration  on  access  to  advanced AI  chips  (United States, 2022; Hoskins, 2023; Freifeld & Potkin, 2024). Within days, the application became the most downloaded app on Apple's App Store in the United States, significantly impacting the global AI market (Field, 2025).

As a result, American technology companies lost approximately $1 trillion in market value in a single day. Nvidia, the leading manufacturer of high-efficiency AI chips and, until then, the most valuable company in the world, experienced a historic decline of around $600 billion in its market valuation - the largest single-day depreciation ever recorded in the U.S. stock market (Milmo et al., 2025).

These events underscore the strategic role of artificial intelligence and critical minerals in contemporary global geopolitics, suggesting that further significant developments are likely to unfold in the coming years.


## Energy Consumption of Artificial Intelligence and Data Centers


Artificial intelligence  models  generally  consume  significantly  more  energy  than traditional  applications  such  as  email  access,  data  retrieval,  communication,  or  content streaming  (EPRI,  2024;  Luccioni  et  al.,  2024a).  This  high  energy  demand  arises  from  the reliance of modern large language models (LLMs) on complex neural networks with billions of parameters,  which  are  fine-tuned  during  training  to  recognize  patterns  and  contextual relationships  within  vast  datasets  (Naveed  et  al.,  2023). Additionally,  the  management  and transfer of these massive datasets across thousands of physical infrastructure components - such as  memory  units  and  processors,  typically  housed  in  data  centers  -  further  amplify  the substantial energy requirements of artificial intelligence processes (Bourzac, 2024).

For instance, a single query in OpenAI's ChatGPT consumes approximately ten times more  electricity  than  a  traditional  search  on  Google  (EPRI,  2024).  Emerging  AI-driven technologies,  such  as AI-generated  audio,  images,  and  videos,  exhibit  even  higher  energy consumption.  In  a  series  of  experiments  measuring  the  energy  usage  of AI  models  across different tasks, Luccioni et al. (2024b) found that the most energy-intensive image generation model consumed approximately 1,600 Wh (watt-hours) to create 1,000 high-definition images - equivalent to 70 smartphone charging cycles.

Since the successful launch of ChatGPT in late 2022 - reaching 100 million users within just two months (Milmo, 2023) - Big Tech companies have increasingly integrated AI into a growing number of online interactions and digital tools (Vries, 2023). With 5.52 billion active internet users worldwide  (Statista,  2024h)  engaging  more  frequently  with  AI-powered technologies, the energy consumption associated with these interactions continues to escalate.

While some researchers argue that advancements in hardware have historically been accompanied by improvements in energy efficiency - playing a key role in mitigating the rapid rise  in  energy  demand  (Desislavov  et  al.,  2023;  Bourzac,  2024)  -  progress  in AI-specific processors appears to challenge this trend. Moreover, significant architectural changes in AI GPUs are not expected in the short term due to high costs, complexity, and lengthy development cycles (Bourzac, 2024). As a result, although new processors achieve higher performance per watt compared to their predecessors, their increased capacity and large-scale deployment have contributed to a continuous rise in overall energy consumption (Kindig, 2024; United Nations, 2024). Additionally, Jevons' Paradox (Alcott, 2005) suggests that efficiency improvements can paradoxically lead to an increase in total energy usage over time (Coskun, 2024).

As a consequence, the International Energy Agency (IEA, 2024) - a leading authority on global energy trends - estimates that data centers, cryptocurrencies, and artificial intelligence collectively consumed approximately 460 TWh of electricity in 2022, accounting for about 2% of global electricity demand. The same report projects that this figure could double by 2026, reaching between 620 and 1,050 TWh. At the lower estimate, this increase would be equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of Sweden, while at the higher estimate, it would match that of Germany (IEA, 2024).

In countries with a high concentration of these infrastructures, energy consumption is already substantial. The United States, which has the largest number of data centers in the world (Statista,  2024b),  sees  these  facilities  account  for  approximately  4%  of  national  electricity demand (IEA, 2024; EPRI, 2024). Driven in part by AI advancements, this share is projected to rise to 6% by 2026 (IEA, 2024) and up to 9.1% by 2030 (EPRI, 2024). In China, electricity demand from data centers is expected to reach approximately 300 TWh in 2026 and 400 TWh by 2030 (IEA, 2024). Meanwhile, in Ireland - a country that offers tax incentives for data center installations  -  these  facilities  already  account  for  approximately  21%  of  the  nation's  total electricity consumption, with projections indicating an increase to 31% within the next three

An  investigative  report  published  by  Bloomberg,  conducted  by  Saul  et  al.  (2024), revealed that the rising electricity demand from data centers has surpassed available supply in multiple regions worldwide. This imbalance has placed strain on local power grids, raising concerns among residents about potential supply disruptions and rising electricity costs.


## Energy Transition and Minerals in the Context of Artificial Intelligence


Major technology  companies  have  been  intensifying  their  investments  in  renewable energy  sources  as  part  of  sustainability-driven  strategies.  These  initiatives  aim  not  only  to reduce their carbon footprint but also to enhance their corporate image among the public and investors, particularly amid the growing global debate on energy transition (Thompson, 2024). Although renewable energy is not always directly used in operations, these companies often sign contracts to purchase clean energy in volumes equivalent to their consumption, thereby contributing to the global energy transition (BNEF, 2023). For example, Google and Amazon both claim to offset 100% of their energy use - including that of their data centers - through corporate power purchase agreements (Amazon, 2024a; Google, 2024b), while Microsoft has committed to reaching this goal by 2030 (Welsch, 2022).

To achieve these targets, Amazon reports owning or partnering in approximately 500 solar and wind projects worldwide (Amazon, 2024a). Meanwhile, Google stated that between 2010  and  2023  it  signed  over  115  clean  energy  purchase  agreements,  corresponding  to  a generation capacity equivalent to approximately 36 million solar panels (Google, 2024b). In 2024, Google also announced that its future data centers would be strategically located near solar and wind farms to ensure direct energy supply from these renewable sources (Calma, 2024a). That same year, Microsoft revealed the signing of one of the largest corporate future renewable energy procurement contracts, valued at approximately $17 billion (Calma, 2024b).

As demonstrated in Global Geography of the Energy Transition and Mineral Extraction (Stacciarini  &  Gonçalves,  2025b),  this  trend  has  intensified  largely  due  to  the  increasing economic viability of solar and wind energy, whose costs have dropped drastically over the past decade, making them highly competitive in various regions (Statista, 2024i; Statista, 2024j). Between 2013 and 2022, solar (47.8%) and wind (38.7%) energy accounted for approximately

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

86.5% of the $3.4 trillion invested in global renewable energy infrastructure (IRENA & CPI, 2023).

However, similar to chips and other data center components, solar and wind energy technologies  depend  heavily  on  critical  minerals  (WB,  2020;  IEA,  2021;  IRENA,  2021; Stacciarini &  Gonçalves,  2025b).  This  dependency  stems  from  intrinsic  technological characteristics, such as lower energy density. For example, wind turbines generate energy more gradually  compared  to  fossil  fuel-powered  turbines,  requiring  larger  infrastructure  and, consequently, greater use of mineral resources to achieve equivalent energy production levels (Stacciarini & Gonçalves, 2025b).

Data from the International Energy Agency (IEA, 2021) indicate that an onshore wind power plant can consume up to nine times more mineral resources than a natural gas plant of similar capacity. In offshore wind projects - where Amazon claims to be the world's largest corporate buyer of energy (Amazon, 2024b) - critical mineral consumption can be up to fifteen times higher, due to the need for large foundation piles, underwater structures, and extensive networks of submarine cables and pipelines.

The issue of energy density also applies to solar panels. Modern solar farms often consist of millions of panels, and because this technology relies on a significant set of critical minerals (WB, 2020; IEA, 2021; IRENA, 2021; Stacciarini & Gonçalves, 2025b), pressure on mineral extraction continues to grow (Stacciarini & Gonçalves, 2025a). A notable example is the Orion Solar Belt complex in Texas, designed to supply power to Google's data centers. With over 1.3 million solar panels and a generation capacity of 900 MW (SP Energy, 2024), a proportional analysis suggests that to meet the projected 35 GW energy demand of U.S. data centers by 2030 (Newmark, 2024), approximately 50 million solar panels would be needed if the entire energy supply were sourced from solar power.

Another challenge is the significantly shorter lifespan of solar and wind installations compared to traditional power plants. While coal-fired or nuclear power plants can operate for 40 to 50 years, solar installations are estimated to last 25 to 30 years, and wind farms 20 to 25 years (Statista, 2024k). This more frequent replacement cycle, combined with the limitations of recycling processes for these structures (Chowdhury et al., 2020; Jensen et al., 2020; Massoud et al., 2023), further intensifies the demand for minerals.

## Conclusions


This study analyzed the complex and often overlooked interconnection between Data Centers, Critical Minerals, Energy, and Geopolitics as the foundational elements of Artificial Intelligence .  Initially,  it  highlighted  how AI  -  currently  driving  approximately  $250  billion annually, with projections reaching $830 billion by 2030 - has become a central element in global debates, integrating deeply into various aspects of daily life.

Although  often  perceived  as  immaterial,  this  study  demonstrated  that  artificial intelligence depends on a vast and intricate physical infrastructure, primarily concentrated in data  centers.  These  facilities  house  essential  components  such  as  servers,  storage  systems, processing  units,  and  cooling  mechanisms,  all  designed  to  meet  the  growing  demands  for computational power and data storage. The production of these systems requires a broad range of minerals and metals, many of which are classified as critical. For instance, manufacturing a single internet router can necessitate the mobilization of up to 500 kg of raw materials.

Another critical issue identified is the short lifecycle of data center equipment, typically ranging from two to five years. The improper disposal of these devices  - without adequate recycling processes - not only removes valuable metals from the supply chain, increasing the need for primary extraction through mining, but also poses significant risks to human health and the environment due to the presence of toxic substances. Furthermore, the extraction of these  resources  is  frequently  associated  with  environmental,  social,  economic,  and  political imbalances, particularly in regions of the Global South.

Data collected indicate that approximately 12,000 data centers are currently in operation worldwide, with the number of large-scale hyperscale data centers having quadrupled in the past  eight  years,  now  totaling  992  facilities.  Projections  suggest  that  this  expansion  will continue in the coming years.

Although  precise  studies  on  the  volume  of  minerals  used  in  the  construction  and maintenance of this infrastructure are still lacking, supply shortages of certain resources have already  been  observed,  exacerbated  by  geopolitical  and  strategic  tensions.  The  ongoing competition  between  the  United  States  and  China  over  the  control  of  critical  minerals  and leadership  in  AI-related  technologies  exemplifies  these  disputes.  Since  2022,  the  U.S. government has implemented a series of restrictions on the export of advanced technologies, such as chips and semiconductors, to China, which, in response, has imposed limitations on the export of essential minerals required for manufacturing AI-related technologies.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

The  study  also  underscored  the  high  energy  consumption  associated  with  artificial intelligence applications. As the number of users engaging with AI technologies continues to rise, energy demand is expected to increase further. Currently, data centers, cryptocurrencies, and AI collectively account for an estimated 2% of global electricity consumption - a proportion that  could  double  in  the  coming  years.  In  the  United  States,  data  centers  already  represent approximately 4% of national electricity use, with projections reaching 9.1% by 2030. In some regions, local power grids are already experiencing strain due to the increasing energy demand.

Although major technology companies are investing in renewable energy sources such as solar and wind to meet the electricity needs of their data centers and AI applications, these sources also require substantial amounts of critical minerals due to intrinsic factors such as lower energy density, shorter lifespan, and recycling limitations. For example, an onshore wind power plant can consume up to nine times more minerals than a natural gas plant of similar capacity,  while  offshore  wind  projects  can  demand  up  to  fifteen  times  more.  Large-scale projects such as the Orion Solar Belt - which is installing over 1.3 million solar panels in Texas (USA) to power Google's data centers - illustrate this increasing reliance on critical minerals.

This body of data and analysis demonstrates that the expansion of AI and its associated infrastructure presents challenges that extend beyond technology, encompassing environmental, social, economic, and geopolitical dimensions. Understanding these interconnections is essential for the scientific community, society, policymakers, corporations, and  nations  to  critically  assess  the  trade-offs  involved  and  explore  viable  alternatives  and solutions  to  these  challenges  -  especially  if  the  trajectory  toward  widespread AI  expansion continues.

- 1. What discourse is occurring in #DisruptJMM about social justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion (hereafter referred to as SJEDI)?
- 2. What other discourse is happening in #DisruptJMM that creates a social organizing movement?
- 3. What is the evidence that #DisruptJMM has made an impact?

To answer these questions, below we develop a qualitative analysis framework by which to analyze Twitter #hashtag movements calling for SJEDI in STEM.


## 2 Twitter use for mathematics community building and advancing equity and inclusion


Twitter is a social media platform centered on the use of short 'tweets' of less than 240 characters and a network of accounts users follow to which creates a

tweet feed. While original content tweets can be authored, it is also common for other tweets to be reshared or 'retweeted' either as-is or as a 'modified tweet,' which adds some additional context or commentary. In order to develop community conversation on Twitter, #hashtags are often used, which allow users to see only the tweets which incorporate the #hashtag into an original tweet or into the modified tweet.

Among academics, an early widespread use of #hashtags was to create 'conference backchannels' [21, 29]. For example, the official conference hashtag of the 2020 Joint Mathematics Meetings was #JMM2020. A conference hashtag allows the conference organizers as well as attendees to make announcements, drum up excitement for talks, share resources, and interact with conference participants. More importantly, because of the tendency for Twitter accounts to be public, #hashtags can facilitate the engagement of individuals and organizations with the conference even if they are not attending in person.

Utilization of Twitter conversation, however, goes beyond conference hashtags. Many academics utilize social media platforms, and Twitter in particular, to network and advance research, as a professional learning network to develop new skills, and/or to build community through continued discourse with one's intellectual and disciplinary community, particularly between professional society meetings [12, 14, 16, 20].

Twitter has been well known as a platform for social change movements, gaining particular attention during the Arab Rising [28]. To organize for change, marginalized communities form counterspaces to engage in discourse to challenge norms [25]. Twitter acts as a public counterspace where a network can engage in discourse, a ' networked counterpublic' [9]. Hashtags allow for connection of both diverse people and ideas across the digital world. Notable hashtag-driven social change movements for equity and inclusion in the United States include #Ferguson, #GirlsLikeUs, #GeorgeFloyd, and #BlackLivesMatter [8, 9, 10, 17, 31].

There is no one way that equity and inclusion advocacy happens on Twitter and no one way that advocacy turns into a movement; however, the book #HashtagActivism offers a glimpse into the tools and conversations that may occur in networks for racial and gender social justice hashtag advocacy in the United States [9]. Key ideas include (1) bringing awareness to issues with an emphasis on amplifying the voices of those affected, challenging stereotypes or current mindsets and practices, and increasing visibility, (2) organizing, building and activating community, and (3) leveraging hashtags and allies to broaden the conversation and the counterpublic.

Twitter #hashtag analysis can be quantitative, qualitative, or both. Typically quantitative analysis involves computational analysis of the structure of the network, identifying key users or tweets and patterns in the connections between them. Qualitative analysis can include analyzing sentiments, themes of the discourse, the users, and the context. Because of the sheer number of tweets often involved in a widespread hashtag, often a subset of tweets are considered and computational text analysis is employed in order to understand the sentiments or themes [1].

In this paper, we use the thematic features noted by Jackson et al. [8] in their analysis of community building in #GirlsLikeUs, a trans advocacy movement, to build a qualitative codebook and framework to help understand community building in the hashtag #DisruptJMM. While the two movements have different content foci, both focus primarily on social justice movements in the United States and have a strong community building and support emphasis. Building this framework will allow us to understand how Twitter is used by the math community as a public counterspace to advance social justice in the mathematics community.

## 3.2 Qualitative Analysis and Frameworks - Girls Like Us application and modification


We used tweet data collected and cleaned by Dr. Bork Rodriguez as part of an earlier stage of this study [5], publicly available on GitHub [4]. This dataset includes every tweet which used #DisruptJMM, up to the date September 21, 2021 when the first study was completed. Of the complete set of 1129 tweets, 299 were original tweets (including replies and quote tweets); the remainder were retweets. We also used Twitter search functionality when close-reading tweets to better understand a tweet's context as necessary.

Weused an inductive coding approach to create a codebook. Two researchers (Diaz Eaton and Roca) independently reviewed the original tweets in the data set, and each constructed a set of codes. With a preliminary code list in hand, they observed the emergence of three themes: self-organizing, community building, and social justice, equity, diversity and inclusion (SJEDI). After a review of qualitative analysis of social justice movements on Twitter based in communitybuilding, we added three additional themes based on the work of Jackson et al.

in #GirlsLikeUs: creating change, celebrating lives, and broadening the counterpublic [8].

The entire research team discussed final reconciliation and code consolidation of both the broad themes and the codes. This resulted in a codebook with 36 codes under 5 themes: 'Self-organization,' 'Building Community', 'Broadening the Counterpublic', 'Creating Change in Math', and 'SJEDI' (Table 1). It was decided to incorporate the theme of celebrating lives from [8] into the emergent theme 'Building Community'.

Some code choices were specific to the context. For example 'talk support' describes individuals advertising their talk at the 2020 JMM, individuals responding that they would be there to show support, individuals sharing pictures of the talk on Twitter, and retweeting others' tweets related to these actions.

We also made the intentional decision to disaggregate the code for tweets referring to Indigenous social justice issues. While we could have grouped this under the 'BIPOC' code more broadly, one of the first talks of the 2020 JMM was by Dr. Belin Tsinnajinnie, [27] an Indigenous mathematician who studies settler colonialism in mathematics education. Among the co-authors, there was agreement that this significantly elevated the discourse on Indigenous issues within the mathematics community. In addition, Dr. Tsinnijinnie reminded us in his talk that often Indigenous data is aggregated or excluded in analysis due to low sample size - using a scientific method which leads to systemic erasure. We choose instead to intentionally center this data in our work.

Three researchers (Hibdon, Lewis, and Roca) then used the codebook to code the entire dataset. To establish inter-coder reliability, all three independently coded a first sample of 29 tweets. After discussion and establishing consensus codes for this sample, a second sample of 30 tweets was independently coded by each of the three coders; this led to an average pairwise agreement at the theme level of 80%. The remaining 240 tweets were then randomly assigned and coded by a single coder.

When coding tweets, the context of the tweet was considered. In particular, if a tweet quoted another tweet or included an image, the content of the included tweet or image was also used to determine applicable codes. One prominent example of this was the many tweets that included an image of a slide from a JMM presentation; in addition to being coded as 'talk support' for live tweeting a JMM talk, the content of the slide in the image was also coded as applicable. Tweets were often placed in more than one theme and had multiple codes attached to them (see Figure 3).

Since retweets have the same content as original tweets, we simply duplicated the codes for these. This decision has the effect of giving a weight to the original tweets in our analysis, based on the number of times it was retweeted. Unless otherwise specified, all frequencies and percentages below will be in reference to the entire data set, including retweets.

## 4 Results and Discussion



## 4.1 Theme and code prevalence


The most prevalent theme in our tweet dataset was Building Community (Table 1). We also examined codes within themes (Figure 4) to understand what activities were occurring within themes.


## 4.2 Discourse on SJEDI in #DisruptJMM


Two of our five themes directly address SJEDI issues: SJEDI and Creating Change in Mathematics, which was the application of SJEDI issues to mathematics more specifically. Within the #DisruptJMM tweets, approximately 61% had SJEDI themes and 42% had Creating Change in Mathematics themes (Table 2).

Within SJEDI, the top code noted was 'representation' ( n = 276) which was broadly about diverse representation or the lack thereof in mathematics and or mathematics meetings. This is not particularly surprising; Dr. Piper H. originally called for increased diversity and inclusion on the mainstage of JMM, not being relegated to special sessions. ## 4.3 What other discourse is happening in #DisruptJMM that creates a social organizing movement?


Preliminary investigation [5] had already led researchers to believe that Building Community would be a key theme. It was indeed the most common theme, with over 75% of all tweets involving this aspect. The foundation of the Building Community theme is the support of those that gave talks at JMM ( n = 545). This included asking for support, showing up to the talk, tweeting slides of the talk, and virtual cheering and encouragement. The vast majority of solicitations for talk support were related to talking about equity and inclusion issues at JMM during their talk. It was clear that talking about equity and inclusion within the context of a mathematics meeting was against the norm, and participants sought solidarity in the effort. This also created an in-person counterpublic in companionship with the virtual effort.

The support between #DisruptJMM users went beyond the conference talks. 'Emotional support' was the second most common code ( n = 117) indicating

that the support went beyond math and was about emotionally supporting people. This is similar to what is presented in the humanizing aspect of Creating Change in Math - #DisruptJMM effectively blended conversation about the human experience with the mathematical experience and indicates a possible shift beyond slides at talks. People described that #DisruptJMM was making an impact. Speaking to this is the third most common code, 'BC impact' ( n = 112) , which included testimonials about the impact of the community formed and tweets, which treated the hashtag like a listserv - advertising opportunities, seeking feedback from like-minded individuals.

The final two themes speak to strategic community organizing. Self-organization, which was 66% of the tweets in our dataset, defined the hashtag in the present and possibilities for the future. The foundation of these tweets was 'amplification' ( n = 625) which shared JMM talks using the hashtag, and also brought issues or related conversations to the attention of the #DisruptJMM community. Of the tweets coded 'amplification', 67% were also coded 'talk support'; the vast majority of these were tweets seeking to amplify ideas shared in a JMM talk. Broadening the Counterpublic was present in 47% of our tweets. Retweets were not part of the amplification only by virtue of retweeting; recall instead they were coded according to the content retweeted alone. However, quote tweets which added #DisruptJMM to an existing tweet were included. Many tweets intentionally broadened the conversation to other hashtags, using the official conference hashtag, or hashtags of related conversations. Tweets in this category also commonly tagged other handles ('influencers', n = 341), either users with large following, particular expertise, or the official JMM related account handle. One tweet reported on the emergence of the #DisruptJMM hashtag in the French language.

In the foundational codes for each of these themes, we see the synergistic effect between the in-person meeting and #DisruptJMM. Tweets where talk content was shared by audience members were coded as both 'talk support' as well as 'amplification.' In addition, these tweets were also often co-tagged with other hashtags or influencer accounts (like the official JMM Twitter handle and hashtag), part of Broadening the Counterpublic.


## 4.4 The impact of #DisruptJMM


Within each theme, we created codes for tweets that displayed evidence of impact. In most cases, the 'impact' codes were a small proportion or just emerging. The exception was impact related to Building Community; we were able to see that #DisruptJMM users were treating the hashtag like a listserv or more accurately, a networked counterpublic. Also in this theme was 'thankful' ( n = 84), in which community members expressed gratitude to people for showing up, creating the counterpublic space, and replying to questions. This category overlapped with 'Self-Organization impact' ( n = 38) which was specifically about the impact of organizing #DisruptJMM. Within SJEDI there were a number of tweets that spoke to a general feeling of needed challenge and 'learning' in SJEDI conversions ( n = 32), or recounted what someone did

differently in class or in a department meeting as a result ( n = 10).

In particular, we want to highlight that this present work is a result of the Broadening of the Counterpublic seen in our data set. While our analysis was restricted to the #DisruptJMM hashtag, a co-occuring hashtag #DisruptMath was used by author Diaz Eaton to start a conversation about organizing a semester-long program at the Institute for Computational and Experimental Research in Mathematics on the theme of applying mathematical tools for social justice. This program eventually took place in the summer of 2022, and is where this present collaboration was initiated.

At JMM 2020 Dr. Belin Tsinnajinnie's talk was the first time Dr. Joseph Hibdon, Jr. saw another Native American mathematician talk about Native Identity in the mathematical community.

'Being at JMM is important to me but not once I have felt like the community at JMM was welcoming and open to Native and Indigenous people. Personally I have tried to connect with other Native And Indigenous mathematicians at JMM but there was never a place. The only time I get to meet other Native and Indigenous people in math and science is at the Society for the Advancement of Chicanos/Hispanic and Native Americans in Science (SACNAS) national conference and the American Indian Science and Engineering Society (AISES) conference. Seeing Dr. Tsinnajinnie and finally getting to meet him in person made JMM feel a little more comforting. Getting to talk about our Native history and pathways into math made me realize that there can be a place for Native Americans and Indigenous people in the mathematical community; we just have to be given opportunities to showcase that we exist.'

-Dr. Joseph Hibdon, Jr.

Dr. Hibdon's contributed reflection illustrates how important the highlighting and discussion of Indigenous scholars and authors was. In addition to Dr. Tsinnajinnie's talk raising visibility of colonialism in mathematics, the visibility of representation also made a huge impact.


## 5 Conclusion


To our knowledge, the framework proposed here is the first to apply #Hashtag Activism theory to qualitative research on equity and inclusion in STEM. In drawing on work in multiple disciplines, we noticed some key similarities and differences between this type of movement and others. #DisruptJMM other #HashtagActivism movements both had strategic organizing components and discussion of issues of equity and inclusion [8, 9]. However, we noticed that in addition to general SJEDI discussion, our communities also had specific discussions on what SJEDI meant within the context of the discipline and what change might look like (Creating Change in Math). Also, this particular movement was about grassroots organizing within the discipline, not meant as a public movement. Therefore we did not have highlighting of diverse people and their

successes generally, but rather more focused on amplifying the #DisruptJMM conversation at the meeting. Because this movement focused on a counterpublic hashtag associated with an annual meeting, it exhibited temporal spiking during the conference, with relatively little activity between the annual conferences. While there was some effort to introduce #DisruptMath as a year-round effort and the suggestion to 'disrupt everything' ( n = 10), this effort did not take off.

Despite the limitations of the engagement with #DisruptJMM in comparison to most national equity and inclusion movements, the hashtag still made an impact within the mathematics community. Because of the nature of academic use of Twitter, we expect that other disciplines may have experienced similar efforts on Twitter. We would encourage collaborations exploring niche #HashtagActivism movements within other disciplines.

We also note that the present work is limited to tweets that themselves contain the #DisruptJMM hashtag. It is our sense as observers, and sometimes participants, that there are important conversations happening, for example, in replies to a #DisruptJMM tweet. However, if the replies themselves do not contain the hashtag, they are not represented in the data set we examined. We would welcome further study into such an expanded data set.

While [5] focused on an initial look at the network structure of this data set and exploration of themes from those involved in the #DisruptJMM conversation, we have focused on the content of the tweets themselves. This leaves us with a natural next step of considering the two together. How do ideas move across the network? How do they propagate beyond the network? This combination of structural and qualitative work would give us the most insight.

## Introduction


The Kingdom of Thailand is a Southeast Asian country at the center of the Indochinese Peninsula. It is the only country in this region to have avoided European colonial rule, acting as an independent buffer between Britain and France's respective colonies in the region instead. Before the events of the 1932 Siamese Revolution, Thailand was an absolute monarchy. Since then, Thailand has been a constitutional monarchy and has had 17 constitutions, the most recent drafted in 2007. 1 The monarch acts as the Head of State, while the Prime Minister serves as the Head of Government.

In 2011, Thailand graduated to an upper-middle income country. Its GDP before the pandemic had been growing at a rate of 2% (2019). 2 As of 2020, the GDP is estimated to be USD501 billion. 3 Contributing to these numbers is a labor force of 38 million people, 59% of whom are female. Informal employment in Thailand makes up only 37% of the total employment, one of the lowest rates in ASEAN. 4 Informal employment is more prevalent

<!-- image -->

among the oldest age groups and consists of slightly more males than females. 5

Ranking 75th in the World Economic Forum's 2020 Global Gender Gap Index , Thailand still has some way to go in its protections for women, especially at the workplace where women are relatively well-represented. 6 As this report will highlight, improvements to employment protections for women returning from maternity leave and nursing support at the workplace are much needed. Protections for other caregivers are also missing from the legislation.

As for paid careworkers, such as domestic workers, amendments to national labor laws in 2012 have afforded them some level of protection. However, protections such as minimum wage and social security benefits have yet to be extended to them. In Thailand, only citizens from Cambodia, Myanmar, Lao PDR, and most recently Vietnam, are legally permitted to enter in search of domestic work, owing to Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) on employment cooperation that their governments had signed with Thailand. 7 It is estimated that this group of workers make up 50% of Thailand's domestic workers. 8 Hence, it is crucial that these protections are afforded to them as well.

Overall, Thailand scored 4.32 (out of 10) in the GCPI, placing it on the high end of the 'Emerging' band of the index. Its score in Sub-Index A was 2.65 (out of 10), significantly lower than its score of 6.00 (out of 10) in the Sub-Index B.

Thailand's key legislation governing employment is the Labor Protection Act (1998), which regulates the rights and duties of employers and workers by laying down minimum labor and employment requirements. All 'employees' in Thailand, including migrant workers, are covered under this Act. Domestic workers, however, are excluded from certain provisions. It was only in 2012 that some of their rights were expanded. Currently, this Act

## Recent Care Policy Developments



## Increased maternity leave period


According to an amendment to the Labor Protection Act that was published in the Government Gazette on April 5, 2019 and came into effect on May 6 that same year, 9 maternity leave entitlements for pregnant workers are now set at 98 days per pregnancy, extended to leave taken for prenatal care. Previously, this leave period was only set at 90 days.


## Better protection of domestic workers' rights


On 9 November 2012, Ministerial Regulation No. 14 entered into force. The Regulation was issued under the Labor Protection Act, and extends new rights and protection provided under the Act to workers who perform domestic work which does not involve business operations. Though lacking, this Regulation was a step in the right direction as domestic workers were now entitled to some of the basic rights other workers had been afforded for decades, including rights to proper leave periods and regular payments of salaries, and entitlements to lodge complaints.

https://learn.asialawnetwork.com/2019/04/12/thailand-legal-update-new- amendment-thailands-labour-protection-act/


## 'Regularizing' migrant workers


In recent years, Thailand has stepped up efforts to provide more social protections to migrant workers, on whom the country heavily relies for domestic work. In 2015 and 2016, for example, they revised their MOUs to broaden cooperation on skills development and social protection. The government has also set up programmes for undocumented migrants already working in Thailand to come forward and formally register themselves through nationality verification (NV) processes meant to regularize their status. NV for migrants from Laos PDR and Cambodia began in 2006, whereas that for migrants from Myanmar only began in 2009. 10 The most recent round of registration, which began in July 2017 and closed in June 2018, saw the opening of 80 'One-Stop Service Centres', which were designated points located across Thailand where workers could obtain ID documents, work permits, health insurance and temporary permission to remain, all for a fee and subject to medical exam results, proof of employment and the official approval. 11

One added benefit of these registrations is that migrant workers under the MOU or who have passed NV can, in theory, be registered under the Social Security Fund. 12 However, the main problem for domestic workers is that, regardless of their nationality, they are excluded from the Social Security Act (1990) which defines 'employee' as 'a person agreeing to work for an employer in return for wages irrespective of designation but excluding an employee who is employed for domestic work which does not involve in business.' As a result, migrant domestic workers still struggle twice as much as other migrant workers in seeking protection.
