## Introduction


It has become increasingly clear that preparing students with skills germane to science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) careers is a central thrust of postsecondary education and critical the future development of the workforce (National Science Foundation, 2020a). It is also clear that strategies to support engagement and persistence for low-income, racially minoritized, and first-generation (at-promise students ) are needed to ensure advancement and 1 broader participation in this future workforce (National Science Foundation, 2022). Within this context, it is incumbent on university graduate programs to look for new ways to facilitate highquality educational practices that advance students' research capacity whilst ensuring an inclusionary approach.

A growing body of research has recognized the learning community format as a means to improve student engagement and persistence in graduate work (Jiang & Koo, 2020; Parker, 2009; Romsdahl & Hill, 2012), as well as improve the experiences of at-promise students (Culver et al., 2021; Dagley et al., 2016; Russell, 2017). Among several iterations, learning communities (LC) have been defined as cohort-based, curricular-centric groups that use a horizontal co-learning model rather than a hierarchical teacher-student structure (Brower et al., 2007; C. Smith & Bath, 2006). Given that research at the intersection of graduate school pedagogy, STEM career skill attainment, and at-promise student experiences is still developing (National Science Foundation, 2020a), the learning community format may offer promise.

This article describes a graduate, research-focused learning community developed over a period of four years at Auburn University, called the Quantitative Methods Education for Research (QMER) learning community. QMER was based on an understanding of the literature on learning communities, the desire to advance graduate skills associated with STEM, faculty observations of at-promise student needs, and a vision to create a more inclusive environment for student growth. Through a combination of collaborative workshops, research teams, and extracurricular support groups, the QMER learning community has focused on improving access to, and attainment of: (1) academic professional skills and competencies; and (2) foundational STEM skills and advanced research methods.

Below, we describe QMERs design and use a mixed methods approach to assess the program thus far in terms of its impact on student perceptions of (1) self-efficacy in graduate work, (2) self-efficacy in research, (3) inclusivity, and (4) belongingness. Results suggest that graduate all participants in QMER felt an increased sense of self-efficacy, inclusivity, and belongingness. However, the magnitude of these feelings were stronger for Black, at-promise, and international graduate students.


## The QMER Learning Community Model


The Quantitative Methods Education for Research (QMER) learning community was started by a pair of assistant professors at Auburn University under the observation that graduate students in Education pursuing in advanced-level quantitative, empirical research tended not to be from diverse backgrounds. At the same time, there was a desire to enhance methodological

options for students beyond the standard three course graduate sequence to better support and improve foundational STEM skills, including data literacy, analysis, coding, statistical reasoning, and reproducible research techniques (Gibson & Mourad, 2018; Kasza & Slater, 2016; National Science Foundation, 2020b). QMER was developed under the guiding mission: ' To improve the rigor, quality, and inclusivity of quantitative research in Alabama and beyond ,' and its core values were: (1) collegiality and collaboration ; (2) distinction in scholarship and preparation ; (3) open access and open science ; (4) continuous improvement . Over the course of four years, QMER has grown rapidly, hosting 50+ learning community workshops, two research teams, and multiple other gatherings. It has retained a highly diverse group of students, and hosted students from virtually every academic discipline on campus. Below we detail the pedagogical model and curricular design, followed by


## Pedagogical Structure


QMER was designed on the Learning Community model, with specific consideration of the barriers that students often face when engaging in advanced quantitative research. Given that at-promise students have often shown great benefit from approaches that emphasize personal value, contribution, group belonging, and academic-self efficacy (Buckley & Park, 2019; Litson et al., 2021; Murphy & Destin, 2016), the learning community model's structural focus on community, diversity, relatedness, and engagement (Lenning et al., 2013; B. L. Smith et al., 2009) offered an ideal format.

Specifically, QMER seeks to directly address resource inequalities common to at-promise students engaging in foundational STEM learning. While the research is growing in this area, atpromise students are often overrepresented in schools less able to prepare students for graduatelevel work (Ghose et al., 2018). This preparation may also not provide exposure with the technology and tools common to STEM and quantitative research (Estrada et al., 2016a), provide familiarization with the specific disciplines, specializations, and institutional supports (Johnson, 2016), or model social and professional norms common to the institutional culture and expectations of graduate programs (Okahana et al., 2018). Moreover, lower levels of representation of at-promise students often results in fewer role models with similar backgrounds, including smaller peer groups (Estrada et al., 2016a), and fewer representative mentors (Griffin et al., 2020).

To facilitate QMER's mission of inclusivity as well as it's values of collegiality and collaboration, the learning community is designed as a voluntary, supplementary organization that operates independent of student's coursework. It provides topical discussions where all graduate students at the university are invited attend for as many or as few events as needed. At the beginning of each QMER workshop, research team meeting, or event, a statement is given that this is a learning community where there is no hierarchy of knower-learner, there are no grades and therefore no risk of failure, everyone is at a different place in their academic development, no prior knowledge is expected, and all questions are welcome (Culver et al., 2021; Lenning et al., 2013; Parker, 2009). After the announcement, the facilitator begins with questions and conversation around a particular topic (e.g., graphics in R), and aims to use personal stories, anecdotes, and concrete examples in the lesson. Faculty and students offer individualized instruction to others, and instances of collaborative experience-sharing (e.g., student's sharing how they approached a task) are featured. At the end students are offered a survey for reflection.

Given the aforementioned issues surrounding academic and technological exposure, QMER followed the Open Science and Open Educational Resources (OER) models whereby all resources, including manuals, articles, software, and computer access would be free and available beforehand and afterwards (National Academies of Sciences Engineering Medicine, 2018; Nipa & Kermanshachi, 2020). To ensure transportation or scheduling were not problems, events would be held in a common campus room and/or over video and would be recorded and posted for free at a non-public hosting site meeting all university accessibility criteria (Panopto) afterwards, with a posted space online to ask questions and maintain discussion asynchronously (Jiang & Koo, 2020; Nipa & Kermanshachi, 2020). In sum, these techniques have been used to address the needs for at-promise students, while removing barriers to research participation and persistence in graduate and STEM programs (Dagley et al., 2016; Estrada et al., 2016a; Griffin et al., 2020; C. Smith & Bath, 2006).


## Curricular Design


QMER has designed two tracks of topics that are discussed in the learning community: (1) professional skills and (2) research skills. Topics are co-designed between graduate students and faculty as part of a group visioning session that occurs each semester, with continuous feedback from participant students. First, given the research on inequities in socialization and expectations (Johnson, 2016; Okahana et al., 2018), the professional skills workshops emphasize the academic norms, expectations, and social elements of higher education. Topics have included: professional identity development, conference and publication process, job market and interview skills, organizing and planning projects, working with your advisor, and more. Second, the research skills track emphasizes skills foundational for-but not isolated to-STEM research competencies including complex modeling and data science (Gibson & Mourad, 2018; Kasza & Slater, 2016; National Science Foundation, 2020b). Topics include specific skills such as data cleaning, visualization, coding, or techniques for reproducible research. Other workshops focus on advanced techniques outside of the normal statistical course sequence such as multilevel/mixed effect modeling or time-series analysis.

The curriculum and design of each workshop emphasizes an integrated set of techniques aimed of promoting the type of thinking and problem-solving aligned with foundational STEM skills (Gibson & Mourad, 2018; National Science Foundation, 2020b; Nolan & Temple Lang, 2010; Steen, 1992). Workshops center around a problem to be addressed, and are discussed using the design thinking process (empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test) (Li et al., 2019; Simeon et al., 2020). Workshops focusing on research skills model problem-solving through combination of computational thinking or statistical reasoning processes. For computational thinking, the process of decomposition, abstraction, algorithmic representation, and pattern recognition are used (Li et al., 2020; Lyon & J. Magana, 2020; Swaid, 2015). Statistical reasoning emphasizes concepts of aggregation, distribution, randomness, variation, and trend-seeking are based on practicing connections from a problem based standpoint (Son et al., 2021). These models (design, computational, and statistical reasoning) are aimed at offering the metacognitive structures to pursue success in advanced research that are often not overtly integrated in postsecondary education (Lyon & J. Magana, 2020).


## Method



## Data


To assess the impact of the QMER learning community approach, we collected data from a participant survey sent to every student who engaged with QMER over a three-year period, and in-depth follow-up interviews with students who were involved in the learning community. The survey and interviews were designed to assess perceptions of two main aspects of the learning community: academic self-efficacy and belongingness.


## Academic Self-Efficacy


First, we included questions regarding academic self-efficacy , which can be defined a students' beliefs about their ability to manage research demands, preserve during difficult times in their studies, or handle challenges (Cheng et al., 2019). As noted from by Bartimore-Aufflick et al. (2016, p. 1918) 'Perhaps the single most important (and reliable) predictor of university student achievement in recent decades is self-ef fi cacy.' Academic self-efficacy has been linked with improved academic performance, resilience, and persistence (Chemers et al., 2001; Cheng et al., 2019; Schunk & Pajares, 2002). Adapting questions from Cheng et al., (2019), we included two scales of academic self-efficacy, self-efficacy of graduate studies ( SEG ) and self-efficacy of research ( SER ). SEG included questions surrounding a student's confidence in comprehending graduate school concepts and performance (e.g., 'I am confident I can take more advanced courses'). SER included questions aimed at evaluating a student's confidence in being an independent scholar (e.g., 'I'm confident I can develop my own research').


## Belongingness


Second, we included questions regarding belongingness , which refers to students' general sense of value, acceptance, inclusion, connectedness, care, respect, and importance in a group or among others on campus (Stachl & Baranger, 2020; Strayhorn, 2018). Research has found that belongingness is associated with important educational outcomes such as academic self-concept, academic success, motivation, persistence, and self-efficacy (Hausmann et al., 2007; Ostrove et al., 2011; Strayhorn, 2018). Specifically, graduate student belongingness has been found to be positively influenced by factors such as professional relationships, mentoring, and microaffirmations (O'Meara et al., 2017). Moreover, socialization with diverse groups and displays of inclusive goals have shown to improve feelings of belongingness (Maestas et al., 2007).

Considering the literature surrounding the importance of a sense of belonging, specifically for at-promise students, we included a scale of perceptions of inclusivity and belongingness , developed and validated by Maestras et al., (2007). Inclusivity deals with perceptions of the social inclusiveness of the learning community itself (e.g., 'I feel that the learning community values and respects all students' voices and opinions'). Belongingness addresses a student's sense of personal acceptance into the community (e.g., 'I feel like I can share my thoughts freely with others').

## Sample


As noted above, the survey was sent to each student that had participated in a QMER event over the past three years. All graduate students at the university were invited to QMER workshops through a graduate student listserv and interested students could register for any workshop using a Qualtrics registration link. Since workshops were held virtually over Zoom, emails of students attending workshops were compiled from Zoom reports. From this list, emails were sent to each student who had attended a workshop. Five $15 dollar gift certificates were raffled off to incentivize participation in the email survey invitation. Of the 160 registered participants, 59 completed the survey, resulting in a 37% response rate. Table 2 provides the compositional characteristics of the sample.

Notably, our sample includes a relatively high proportion of Asian and Black students, considering the graduate student population at the host university is roughly 3% Asian, 8% Black 4% Latinx, and 65% White. Much of the sample is comprised of first-generation, low income, and international students, the last of whom make up roughly 17% of the graduate student population but represent 47% of the sample. Also, it shows a high proportion of first generation and low-income students. Given that those three indicators were not mutually exclusive, 72% of the sample identified themselves as being at-promise in one or more dimensions. Respondents also came from virtually every college across the university, including agriculture, architecture, biosystems engineering, forestry, mechanical engineering, political science, educational psychology, and more. Overall, respondents attended just over 4 events, and were in their 3 rd year of graduate school. However, it is notable that White students attended relatively fewer events (2) compared to Latinx (6) and Black (4.8) students. In addition, first-generation and lowincome students attended nearly 5 events each.


## Analysis & Limitations


## Table 2. Survey Sample Characteristics

The goal of this analysis is to gain an understanding of the value the learning community approach for students in terms of professional efficacy and belongingness, as well as to see what differences may exist between student groups, particularly at-promise students. We therefore present descriptive statistics to demonstrate broad trends and group differences, supported by qualitative responses to help explain these trends.

To present our survey data, we constructed scores for each scale using STATA's alpha function. In this manner, each scale score is reported on a continuum of 1-5, with 1 representing a low agreement score ('strongly disagree') on SEG, SER, Inclusivity, or Belongingness, and 5 representing a 'strongly agree' score on the respective scale. This is followed with a series of themes presented from our open-ended questionnaire. Responses to questions on how students felt about their self-efficacy and belongingness were independently coded, cross-checked, and reconciled by the researchers until certain themes developed. These themes are presented following the descriptive section.

It should be noted that our sample is not random nor necessarily representative. While the authors can anecdotally note that the demographic makeup of the sample does seem to align with observations, we do not collect information on students participating in QMER events, as we do not want self-identification to be a barrier to participating. Given the low number of observations (59) and non-random sample design, representation of sub-groups is limited. For this reason while we report t-test results to demonstrate sample group differences, these are not to be considered representative of all participants.  In addition, selection bias is a concern, and it is possible that, for example, certain types of students are more likely to take surveys or be motivated by financial incentives. Our goal is not to actively posit that the QMER learning community causes certain differences, but rather make an introductory case that it may be perceived by some students differently, and that this may serve as grounds for future research.

## RQ2: How has QMER impacted academic self-efficacy and belongingness?


Given the above results reporting that QMER participation has improved students' sense of academic self-efficacy and belongingness-particularly for at-promise and Black studentswe now turn to provide a deeper sense of ways in which the program has been viewed. Using open-form responses from participants, we provide further information on the ways in which the program has been viewed by students, organized into themes aligning with academic selfefficacy and responses aligning with belongingness.


## Practical and Supplementary Approach


Several participants noted that they experienced improved mastery with statistical software, as well as translating it into coursework and research. This was often attributed to the emphasis on supplementary practical skills that did not repeat what was in the normal coursework sequence. In response to a question on what was helpful about participating in QMER, one student noted:

Overall, QMER equipped me with the motivation and confidence to be an independent graduate student and a future researcher. I have been exposed with the requisite research skills and tools to initiate and complete a research project on my own. First-generation, low income, international Black, male, Educational Leadership student .

Some students noted the opportunities to 'slow down' and 'process' much of the material, noting that '…the information is valuable and more personable than regular classes.' As noted by one student:

Essentially [QMER is] a place to apply practically the knowledge we are learning in Grad School. To be frank, this is the most needed practical experience that is not taught in Grad School. First-generation, low-income, Black, male, Adult Education student .

Several students noted the importance of simply introducing the software that is used in coursework (such as R), while others emphasized the practical and developmental nature of the curriculum:

QMER helped me in different stages in my program. To be specific, it helped me with getting familiar with statistical methods, software usage [R, SPSS], and research workflow in the first year of my PhD program. It helped me to navigate the process of journals and conferences. It helped me as I started manuscript writing when I was in the second year of my program. First-generation, low-income, international, Asian, female, Educational Psychology student .


## Focus on Academic Soft Skills


A second theme that developed under the area of improving academic self-efficacy was an emphasis on the soft skills surrounding academic research, which has shown to be particularly difficult for underrepresented and at-promise students (Estrada et al., 2016b; Okahana et al., 2018). Several at-promise and underrepresented students emphasized the importance of 'hearing the personal experiences of professors,' as well as emphasis on 'professional development […] and assistance with preparing [my] work to align with my goals.' Others emphasized the treatment of soft skills such as job market preparation, resume building, networking, 'communication with my advisor,' and 'learning how grad school works in general.' One student noted:

I truly enjoyed the workshops on succeeding in our graduate programs. I found learning about the doctoral journey […] leading towards dissertation necessary and helpful. Firstgeneration, low-income, Black, female, Higher Education Administration student

Another student, a Black, first-generation, low-income woman in Agriscience brought up that 'QMER opened my eyes to ways to prepare myself for the job market.'


## Connecting Students Outside of Programs


Several students noted the importance of meeting with others outside of their programs and even colleges, supporting the notion that graduate student's sense of belongingness is found to be positively influenced by factors such as socialization with diverse groups (Maestas et al., 2007) and professional relationships (O'Meara et al., 2017). For example, a fourth-year doctoral student stated that participating in QMER gave her:

- …the opportunity to feel connected. I have been done with my coursework for some time now and there is very little within the program that created a similar sense of graduate student community once coursework is completed…it is a relief that there are student peers and faculty who are willing and available to answer your questions or help you problem solve…-White, female, Adult Education student

A student from Human Development and Family Studies noted 'Often it's too easy in the later years of graduate school to become siloed, and QMER offers some connections.' As noted earlier, while QMER started with students in the College of Education, it had drawn participants from across the university, including chemical, civil, and mechanical engineering, biomedical science, computer science, rural sociology, agriscience, pharmacology, fisheries, aerospace, and industrial systems. This diverse connection was important for both social support and learning, with one student noting that '…joining [QMER] taught me different perspectives and approaches to research that I now use myself in my daily work.'


## Removing Risk


Finally, several students noted that since the learning community existed outside of the traditional class setting it did not have the normal teacher-student hierarchy and had no grades or assessments attached. This allowed for learning to take place in a low risk environment. As one at-promise student in Counseling Psychology stated, 'It feels very open. I don't feel judged.' Students noted that QMER was 'more personable than regular classes' and that it has a 'welcoming environment.' This low-stakes environment allowed for better overall connections as well:

I was able to connect with students and faculty members more easily in this setting, and able to learn things that were not dealt with during the class, or things that I wanted to learn in-depthInternational Asian female Adult Education student .

Following the abovementioned barriers to at-promise students in higher education, such as unfamiliarity with academic norms, feelings of inadequacy, or fear of failure (Estrada et al., 2016b; Maestas et al., 2007; O'Meara et al., 2017), operating in a low risk environment appears to support further learning in spaces that might otherwise be prohibitive.


## Discussion


The goal of this paper has been to describe and evaluate the QMER learning community model in terms of its effect on academic self-efficacy and belongingness for graduate students. The model of supporting foundational STEM research techniques through a supplementary, interdisciplinary, and professional-skills oriented learning community format has shown that (1) generally students felt QMER supported greater self-efficacy in research, self-efficacy in graduate studies, inclusivity, and belongingness; (2) Black, first-generation, low income, and international students reported statistically higher perceptions of self-efficacy in graduate studies, inclusivity, and belongingness than their peers; and (3) the supplementary approach, soft-skill focus, connections, and low-risk environment were aspects of the QMER learning community model that stood out to students. Following these results, we believe the QMER model holds promise for supporting foundational STEM skills through programs that supplement regular coursework and address the specific barriers of efficacy and belongingness that at-promise, international, and students of color often encounter.

This work reveals three key implications for institutions looking to simultaneously improve students' experience and capacity. First, instructional structures that operate outside of the traditional methods sequence may be increasingly important as more specialized and differentiated research expertise is needed in many areas of the workforce (Sengupta et al., 2018; Tytler, 2020), and  high student-to-faculty ratios in many programs make socioemotional supports and communication more difficult to foster (Crocker et al., 2014; O'Meara et al., 2013). Second and related, explicit attention to professional norms (e.g., what to put on a CV), soft skills (e.g., networking at conferences), and baseline competencies (e.g., version control) surrounding foundational STEM skills may offer a means to further support underrepresented and at-promise students who have less exposure and mentorship within their respective field (Estrada et al., 2016b). Whether addressed within the traditional class structure or not, students were clear that these supplementary skills were needed. Third, offering a format for students to meaningly interact across disciplines towards common academic goals may help foster notions of shared identity and community that may serve to improve both goals of research equity and excellence (Culver et al., 2021). As some students felt 'siloed' in their programs, learning to find commonalities that allow for interdisciplinary communication may help student feel a greater sense of shared belonging as well as prepare them to engage in convergence research (National Science Foundation, 2022; O'Meara et al., 2017; Stachl & Baranger, 2020).

Given that this learning community has multiple facets, it is difficult to pinpoint specific aspects that had the greatest contribution to the success of the program. However, it was clear that QMER's structure operated best alongside regular coursework, rather than in lieu of it. Students reported that much of its importance was in offering a 'different perspective' on the same skills, furthering understanding and context needed for learning (Hilliard, 2012). To gain a better understanding of just which aspects are most important, it will be important to continue with research on which specific learning outcomes have resulted from the program-which is a limitation of the current study. While the present study has focused on self-efficacy and belongingness, it is our aim to assess learning objectives, as well as other aspects of student success including persistence, time to completion, and placement. Moreover, it will be important to assess the capability of scaling the program. As participation has more than tripled in the past two years, maintaining personal and individual connections will become more difficult, and administration the program may become more complex. However, these preliminary results do offer a promising start to-and proof-of-concept for-the QMER learning community as a model that may create a more asset-based, inclusive environment for students while simultaneously push their research capabilities to advance the future workforce.

This research focuses on several main aspects to provide a comprehensive understanding of the impact of social media on teenagers' social values. Identify Changes in Social Values Examining the types of social values that change among teenagers due to interactions on social media. Long-Term Impact Evaluate the long-term impact of these changes in social values on future social dynamics, including relationships between youth, family interactions, and participation in the community.

This research uses the Symbolic Interaction Theory proposed by George Herbert Mead and Herbert Blumer. This theory, although relatively new in communication studies since the early 19th century, has developed to this day and has indirectly become a branch of sociology from an interactional perspective. According to the interactional perspective, Symbolic Interaction is one of the perspectives in communication studies that is perhaps the most "humanist". This perspective emphasizes the greatness and value of the individual above the influence of existing values. This perspective argues that every individual has the essence of culture within himself, interacts in society, and produces meaning that is collectively agreed upon. In the end, it can be said that every form of social interaction carried out by an individual will take into account the individual's personal side. This is one of the characteristics of an interactional perspective based on symbolic interactionism. (Siregar 2016).

Symbolic interaction theory emphasizes the relationship between symbols and interaction, with a primary focus on the individual. Many experts in this perspective argue that the individual is the most important element in the sociological concept. This theory emphasizes that social meaning and values are formed through social interaction. Social media, as a digital interaction platform, functions as a space where teenagers communicate and share symbols (such as images, texts, videos) that influence their perceptions and values. In this context, dominant symbols on social media can encourage teenagers to adopt new values that are different from traditional values.


RESEARCH METHODS


This research uses a qualitative design with a case study approach. This design was chosen to gain an in-depth understanding of a complex and dynamic phenomenon, namely the influence of social media on changes in social values among teenagers. Case studies allow researchers to explore in detail adolescents' experiences, perceptions, and interpretations of their interactions on social media. The main data collected in this research includes in-depth interviews. Data in the form of interview transcripts with teenagers who actively use social media. This interview will reveal their views and experiences regarding the use of social media and the changes in social values they perceive.

Participant Observation Observational data about teens' activities on social media, including the types of content they consume and share, and their interactions with other users. Content Analysis Data in the form of content from teenagers' social media accounts, including posts, comments and messages, to understand how they express and accept social values. The data source in this research is teenagers aged 15-19 years. As the main research subjects, teenagers were chosen because they are active social media users and are in a critical phase of identity development. Social Media platforms such as Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and Twitter as secondary data sources for content analysis and participant observation.

Purposive Sampling Research Technique: This technique is used to select respondents who meet certain criteria, namely teenagers aged 15-19 years who actively use social media. The aim is to obtain a relevant and representative sample. In-depth Interview, This technique is used to collect qualitative data directly from respondents. Interviews were conducted in a semi-structured manner to allow flexibility in topic exploration. Participatory Observation: This technique involves direct observation of teenagers' social media activities. The researcher acts as a participant observer to understand the natural context of the interaction. Content Analysis, This technique is used to analyze text, images and videos posted by teenagers on social media. This analysis aims to identify key themes and patterns that indicate changes in social values.

This research was designed to provide an overview of how social media influences social values among teenagers, with a comprehensive and in-depth approach to the data collected.


RESULTS AND DISCUSSION



Changes in Social Values



- Values of Togetherness and Solidarity


The use of social media has changed the way teenagers interact with their friends. Interview results show that although teenagers feel more connected through platforms such as Instagram and WhatsApp, the frequency of their face-to-face interactions has decreased. One respondent stated, "I feel closer to my friends through chat groups on Instagram, but we rarely meet in person now." This indicates a shift in the value of togetherness from direct interaction to virtual interaction.

In addition, increasingly focused social interactions in cyberspace can trigger feelings of isolation and loneliness, which in turn can increase the risk of depression. The inability to separate oneself from the virtual world and find a balance between online interactions and real life can lead to mental overload. Therefore, it is important to reduce this risk by educating teens about wise use of social media, providing emotional support, and teaching stress management skills. Communities, schools and families also have an important role to play in creating an environment that supports youth mental health, by promoting open dialogue and providing adequate resources to overcome mental challenges that may arise from excessive use of social media. (Setiawan and Aryani 2023).


- Value of Individualism


Social media emphasizes personal achievement and popularity, encouraging teens to become more individualistic. Many respondents felt pressured to present themselves in a certain way to gain attention and recognition from their followers. One teenager expressed, "I often feel like I have to post something cool to get attention. It feels like a competition for who is the most popular."

The most dominant social media users are teenagers. The social media most frequently used by teenagers include Facebook, Twitter, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, LINE, and WhatsApp. Each platform has special advantages that attract many users. However, the most popular currently is Instagram. Teenagers, who are trying to find their identity, are easily influenced by an unstable and contradictory environment. This can cause them to experience mental anguish, anxiety, uncertainty, and doubt. As a result, many Indonesian teenagers experience behavioral disorders, which can endanger themselves, both now and in the future.

Adolescence is a phase where individuals experience many emotional and psychological changes due to the influence of the surrounding environment. Teenagers tend to be vulnerable to outside influences and often imitate behavior that is considered cool or popular, without considering risks or religious norms.

Today's adolescent behavior tends to move in a negative direction, along with the development of adolescent lifestyles and behavior in the era of globalization. Adolescents' social interactions are often influenced by lifestyles from abroad, which causes them to lose local cultural values. This happens because foreign cultures are often not filtered before being adopted by teenagers. As a result, many Indonesian traditions and cultural values are starting to fade and be forgotten by the younger generation. Teenagers tend to prefer foreign lifestyles without considering good or bad values. For example, promiscuous behavior in romantic relationships that makes parents anxious, or dating openly in public, is considered normal by today's teenagers. However, this behavior is often the result of a mixture of foreign cultures that adhere to the principles of promiscuity.

Teenage behavior via Instagram usually posts about their personal activities, stories, and photos with their friends. They think that the more active a teenager is on social media, in this case Instagram, the more they will be

increasingly considered cool and slang. Well, this is what makes them individualistic, they post something just to attract followers, even if they take photos with friends, but teenagers only think about how to increase their followers. They gather just to play on their cellphones alone and take photos together just to show that they enjoy having friends even though they only gather and take photos just to upload stories so they can add followers. However, teenagers who do not have social media are usually considered old-fashioned, out of date, and less social. This kind of mindset makes teenagers behave far from the values of togetherness and solidarity, encouraging teenagers to behave individually (Ferlitasari, Suhandi, and Rosana 2020).


- Consumptive Value


Consumptive behavior among teenagers is a serious concern due to their increasing exposure to advertising and commercial content through social media. This phenomenon shows the significant impact of the digital environment on purchasing decisions and value priorities among the younger generation. The rapid growth of platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok has provided space for product promotions and consumer lifestyles that can influence the mindset and behavior of teenagers.

Teenagers, as a vulnerable group, are often exposed to various advertisements aimed at attracting attention and triggering the desire to consume. For example, content that showcases glamorous lifestyles, the latest fashion products, or advanced technology can create unrealistic expectations and the urge to follow the latest trends in consumption. Constant exposure to these messages may shape adolescents' perceptions of their self-worth based on their possession of material goods. (Paulina 2023).

Ease of access to products and trends through social media increases consumer behavior among teenagers. They more often buy items that are popular on social media to stay up-to-date. For example, one respondent said, "I often buy things I see on TikTok, even though I don't really need them."

Additionally, the use of clever marketing tactics, such as exclusive discount offers or attractive advertising models, can increase the appeal of a product. This can lead to impulsive behavior among teenagers, who may be tempted to buy things they don't really need. Apart from that, conforming to consumer norms displayed on social media can also create social pressure that encourages teenagers to follow trends without careful consideration (Paulina 2023).

The role of parents and education has a crucial role in responding to the challenges of consumer behavior. Providing a solid understanding of media literacy, guiding teens to develop critical skills in evaluating advertising, and holding discussions about the values underlying consumer decisions can help teens become smarter and more responsible consumers.

Additionally, an emphasis on financial education and understanding the psychological impact of consumer behavior can help build financial intelligence and mental health among teenagers. This education can increase teenagers' resilience to consumer pressure from social media, enabling them to make wiser and balanced consumption decisions. Thus, a holistic approach involving various parties can help shape healthier consumer behavior among the younger generation. (Bomantara et al. 2023).


Mechanisms for Change in Social Values



- Influencer Influence and Viral Content


Influencers are considered convincing and trustworthy figures by their audiences, both in expressing opinions and providing reviews about products. They are also skilled at creating interesting content and editing it well so that it is liked by the audience. Apart from that, influencers have the same appeal and interests as their audience in various fields such as travel, fashion, gaming, film, music, and so on. The presence of influencers also creates admiration among teenagers who watch, because they are considered to have great referential power, which means they are considered to have authority when they serve as role models or inspire other people, this is often done by influencers with their audience.

Influencer content uses language that is easy to understand and informative, and has elements of entertainment, making it a favorite for most teenagers. The majority of teenagers admit that influencer content is popular and is a means for them to express themselves. They also consider watching influencer content as a hobby and even a necessity because the content provides entertainment, inspiration and information according to their needs. (Mahdia 2018).

Influencers and viral content on social media have a big influence in shaping teenagers' values. Many respondents stated that they idolize influencers and emulate the lifestyle and values they promote. "I follow many fashion influencers on Instagram and often buy the products they recommend," said one respondent.


- Peer Interaction and Pressure


Soekanto (2003) explains that interaction is a series of activities that occur in a social relationship, where individuals have expectations about appropriate behavior in social relationships. This interaction creates a social situation in which there is interconnectedness between individuals due to the instinctive urge to live together and the desire to adapt socially and interact with other people. Meanwhile, Thibaut and Kelley define interaction as a process of mutual influence between two or more people when they are present together. They mutually create impacts or communicate with each other. In the context of interaction, the actions of each individual aim to influence other individuals.

The role of peers in adolescent interactions is increasingly seen as significant, in line with the increasing interest of individuals in building friendships and joining groups. Peer groups also act as learning communities where roles and social norms are formed regarding achievements and activities. Environmental influences on adolescents often start from interactions with peers. In the age range of 9-15 years, teenagers are undergoing a process of searching for identity, which often occurs through close relationships with peers who share interests, interests, feelings, and support each other in solving problems together.

In this process of searching for identity, teenagers often identify role models from their social environment, where peer groups have an important role in the process of selecting figures who are considered role models. Adolescents have a strong desire to be accepted and recognized as equal members of their peer group, both in the school environment and outside of school. As a result, they tend to adopt views and behavior similar to those of their peer group members. (Ni’mah, Hardjajani, and Karyanta 2010)

As explained above, peers influence how a teenager does something. Well, interactions on social media are also often influenced by peer pressure. Teenagers feel the need to follow the trends adopted by their friends to remain accepted in their social group. One respondent said, "If my friends use certain apps or follow certain trends, I feel like I have to join in so I don't get left behind."


The Impact of Online Gambling on Weakening Social Values in Adolescents


Every action carried out by a human must produce an impact, both positive and negative, which can be directly felt by the perpetrator and observed by other people around him. This also applies to teenagers involved in online gambling games; they will feel the impact of their decisions. These impacts include the risks of the actions taken, and although the impacts can vary, they generally tend to be negative or detrimental, both to oneself and others.

Online gambling games are often considered deviant behavior in society, because the majority of people think that gambling is not in accordance with norms and is considered not good. For teenagers who are involved in online gambling activities, they will experience various impacts which can result in a weakening of the teenagers' social values. This research aims to collect data about the impact of the online gambling phenomenon on the decline in social values in teenagers. The focus of this research will be on social values as explained by Notonegoro, namely material values, vital values and spiritual values.


- Material Value


Material values, namely everything that is useful for human life, related to material values that are useful for human physical life or human physical needs. So anything that can be useful as a spiritual or physical filler has material value.

Online gambling has a negative impact on teenagers, especially in terms of weakening material values, such as running out of money they have. Losing money is the most striking negative impact of playing online gambling. Money has a central role in this gambling activity; teenagers bet money, and if they lose, the money wagered is lost. If they often lose when gambling, their money will gradually run out. As a result, teenagers may have to borrow money from friends to meet their living needs if they do not have their own money.


- Vital Values


vital, namely everything that is useful for humans to be able to carry out life activities or is useful for humans to be able to carry out activities or activities.

Online gambling has a negative impact on the vital values of the teenagers involved, where when they lose in gambling, they tend to take extreme actions such as pawning their personal assets. For example, some teenagers even pawn valuable items such as their cellphones or motorbikes to fulfill their needs or desires in playing online gambling.


- Spiritual Values


Spiritual values, namely everything that is useful for human spirituality, spiritual value is the same as the human soul or heart. These spiritual values can be divided into four types: (1) truth values, which originate from human reason (ratio, mind, creativity), (2) beauty values or aesthetic values which originate from human feelings (aesthetic, gevoel, rasa), (3) goodness, or moral values, which originate from human will (will, will, intention), (4) religious values, which are the highest and absolute spiritual values. This religious value originates from human belief or belief.

Online gambling has a negative impact on teenagers who do it, namely weakening spiritual values, including teenagers abandoning religious obligations such as prayer or prayer and fasting in the month of Ramadan, carrying out actions that violate community norms such as drinking alcohol and the like (Zurohman, Astuti, Sanjoto 2016).

So the point is that online gambling is a social media tool that can eliminate the social value of a teenager. In fact, online gambling is a social media site that has no positive value, online gambling will only bring teenagers into misery.


Long Term Impact



- Loss of Traditional Values


A strong tradition is a tradition that has been implemented for a long time and is deeply rooted in society. However, as time goes by, many traditions are starting to be abandoned by society due to the influence of new values that emerge through social media. For example, traditions such as mutual cooperation and good manners, which have been part of the cultural heritage passed down from generation to generation, are now threatened by changes in new values that are developing in this digital era.

WS Renda highlighted the significance of tradition by stating that its existence is very important to maintain neat social interactions and prevent people from immoral behavior. The essence of tradition is the transmission of information from one generation to the next, either verbally or in writing, because this is vital for the survival of a tradition. Without this process, a tradition could experience extinction.

Paying attention to the very important role of tradition in a society, which not only reflects the behavior of community members in everyday life but also in the spiritual and religious realm, shows that tradition is an integral part of a nation's culture. Culture itself is reflected in various traditions passed down from generation to generation. Unfortunately, in Indonesia, many traditions are starting to be abandoned and the values contained in them are becoming increasingly faded. This could result in a decline in Indonesian national culture because various important traditional values such as the tradition of respect for parents, good manners, the spirit of sharing and mutual cooperation have been forgotten. Many teenagers today prefer to imitate foreign culture because of the influence of social media, which ultimately causes the disappearance of some local cultures. The inability of the younger generation, especially teenagers, to maintain and preserve traditional Indonesian values is one of the main factors causing the loss of various aspects of this culture.

However, when society is not fully ready to accept these changes, this can have a negative impact on the social conditions of society. (Rohimah, Hufad, and Wilodati 2019).

The research results show that several traditional values, such as mutual cooperation and courtesy, are starting to be eroded by new values formed through social media. ## Introduction


The variability in the ages at which individuals die (also known as 'lifespan inequality') is unarguably 'the most important of all inequalities' because all other inequalities one might care about are conditional on being alive (van Raalte et al 2018, page 1002). During the last decades, investigations around this topic have expanded in several directions, documenting the levels and trends in lifespan inequality both across and within countries (e.g., Wilmoth and Horiuchi 1999, Edwards and Tuljapurkar 2005, Smits and Monden 2009, Edwards 2011, van Raalte et al 2012, 2014, Sasson 2016b, Colchero et al 2016, Permanyer and Scholl 2019).

A fundamental issue that remains poorly understood in this literature has to do with the sources of lifespan inequality. Which factors are the most important drivers of such inequality and its changes over time? Individuals are heterogeneous in multiple characteristics (e.g., sex, place of residence, country of birth, education, income, race, ethnicity, religion, and so on and so forth), but some of those characteristics are more important than others when explaining the variability in the ages at which they die. For instance: Are differences in individuals' length of life more strongly determined by their place of residence or their educational attainment? What role do gender or ethnicity play in explaining those differences? Unfortunately, current approaches fail to appropriately address this important research question.

An overly simple method to tackle this important question would be to apply standard decomposition techniques for each of those characteristics separately . That is, one could tentatively estimate the source of variation explained by each factor, one at a time, and then identify the ones with higher or lower explanatory power. However, this approach has one key limitation. It treats the different factors as if they were operating independently, an unrealistic assumption that is often not satisfied in practice, thus missing the mediating pathways and interactions that might exist between them. Consider the hypothetical age-at-death distributions shown in Figure 1, and assume that we are interested in determining the influence of two factors (say, 'sex' and 'race') on lifespan inequality. In scenario A, most of the differences in length of life are attributable to race, with sex playing a minor role (i.e., in that scenario, the race of individuals is a better predictor of their longevity than sex). In scenario B, sex and race play a similar role separately, but the interaction between the two that plays a prominent role that was not observed before. What determines the worse longevity outcome (i.e., a shorter lifespan) is not sex or race, but some combination of the two (in this example: being a 'black men').

In this paper we propose a novel decomposition approach to address this question. The suggested method: (i) Allows measuring the contribution to lifespan inequality of several factors simultaneously , hence capturing the interactions that might exist among the different factors one is interested in, and (ii) It can be applied to the absolute and relative Gini indices, the Variance and the coefficient of variation squared (which can be thought as a dimension-less version of the variance), a group of popular indicators that have been widely used to document levels and trends in lifespan inequality (e.g., Andreev et al 2003, Smits and Monden 2009, Gillespie et al 2014, Seligman et al 2016, Permanyer and Scholl 2019, Permanyer et al 2023). In the empirical illustration, the proposed method is applied to US data to explore how sex, race, and educational attainment have contributed to lifespan inequality in 2010.

## Interpreting the interaction coefficients


The interpretation of the multiple-way interaction terms is not straightforward. At one extreme, whenever they take very small values, one can safely assume that the different factors operate independently, so to speak - meaning that the contribution of one factor to overall lifespan inequality is not influenced by the values that the other factors can take. An example of a pair of factors with low interactions could be 'Day of the week where the death occurred' and 'Sex', because one does not expect the deaths of women and men to occur in different days of the week. At the other extreme, high interaction coefficients  would  be  indicative  of  the  existence  of  non-trivial  associations  between factors and suggest that the contribution of one factor is indeed contingent on the values of the other factors (as is the case in Scenario B from Figure 1).

Even  if  the  interaction  coefficients  might  be  challenging  to  interpret,  they  signal  the existence of potentially complex patterns of association between the different variables and the outcome of interest (in our setting: length of life), thus inviting further exploration to  gain  better  understanding  of  the  underlying  explanatory  factors.  For  example,  an interaction between 'Sex' and 'Education' may reflect the differential health returns to schooling  that  have  been  observed  between  men  and  women  (Hayward  et  al.,  2015; Zajacova & Hummer, 2009).


## Illustration: The contribution of sex, race, and educational attainment to US lifespan inequality


We illustrate this decomposition method using three known social determinants of US adult mortality: sex, race, and educational attainment. Sex differences in mortality are thought to reflect differences between men's and women's health behaviors and lifestyles, socioeconomic status, social ties, and biological factors, as well as the complex pathways linking social and biological factors within specific institutional contexts (Bird & Rieker, 2008; Richard G. Rogers et al., 2010). Black-white disparities in mortality in the US similarly reflect a complex web of mechanisms relating to the systematic and unequal treatment of black individuals and communities, resulting in differential access to health-preserving and healthcare resources (Hummer & Chinn, 2011; Williams & Sternthal, 2010). Educational attainment in understood both as a proxy for socioeconomic status and a health resource in itself (Baker et al., 2017). It is a primary resource in accessing healthy environments, medical information and technologies, and beneficial social ties (Link & Phelan, 1995). It is also a potential pathway through which sex and racial disparities in mortality manifest (Geruso, 2012).

Importantly, whereas the sex gap and black-white gap in life expectancy at birth peaked in the US, respectively, in the 1970s and late 1980s (Arias & Xu, 2019; Firebaugh et al., 2014), education gaps in life expectancy have increased steadily for several decades (Bound et al., 2015; Meara et al., 2008; Sasson, 2016b). These descriptive trends are widely recognized (Crimmins & Zhang, 2019), though their dynamics have not been previously formalized and evaluated in a single framework.

While sex, race, and educational attainment have long been established as important predictors of length of life, their relative contributions to overall lifespan inequality has rarely been assessed in combination . Prior research has tended to focus on one determinant at a time while treating the others as statistical nuisance-either controlling for the other factors within a survival analysis framework or stratifying life tables within a formal demography framework (e.g. educational attainment by sex). For example, a study across several European countries found that sex accounts for up to 9.9 percent of the total inequality in lifespans, measured using the Theil index, and that education accounts for as much as 10.9 percent of the inequality (van Raalte et al., 2012). However, each of these contributions was estimated independently of the other, so their combined contribution is likely much smaller than the sum of the gross effects. A comprehensive analytical framework is thus needed to address both within and between-group inequality across multiple social factors.


## Data


We use previously published US life tables from 2010 for adults aged 25 and over by sex, race, and educational attainment (Sasson, 2016a, 2016b). For simplicity, our illustration includes only two levels in each factors: female/male, black/white, and low/high education. However, by altering the set of dissimilarity vectors to account for all possible pairwise comparisons, the method can be generalized to include additional factors or more than two levels per factor. Prior research has shown that by 2010 having a BA degree was the most salient educational distinction for predicting life expectancy in the US (Case & Deaton, 2021; Sasson & Hayward, 2019). Thus, we define 'low education' as those without a BA degree and 'high education' as those having a BA degree or higher. Applying our methodology, we estimated the absolute Gini coefficient of US lifespans in 2010, conditional on survival to age of 25, and decomposed it to the three factors and their interactions.


## Results


The results of the decomposition are shown in Figure 2. In 2010, the total Gini coefficient of US lifespans over the age of 25 was 7.76 years. Our additive decomposition further reveals that within-group inequality accounted for 1.63 (21.0%) of the total whereas between-group inequality accounted for 6.12 (79.0%). We further decomposed the between-group component to contributions by Sex, Race, Education, and their two-way and three-way interactions. With respect to the main effects, the Sex component contributed 1.70 (27.7% of the between-group component), Race contributed 0.62 (10.1%), and Education contributed 1.19 (19.4%). The two-way interaction effects had non-negligible contributions: Sex × Race contributed 0.64 (10.5%), Sex × Education contributed 1.22 (19.9%), and Race × Education contributed 0.37 (6.1%). Lastly, the three-way interaction between Sex × Race × Education contributed 0.38 (6.2%) to the between-group component.

With respect to main effects, sex appears to have the largest contribution, followed by education, followed by race (black/white). Furthermore, the interaction effects cannot be ignored in this instance, and together make up 42.7% of the between-group inequality. The interaction between sex and education is especially large, which is supported by prior research showing that, irrespective of race, the sex gap in life expectancy tends to be smaller at higher levels of education and larger at lower levels of education (Sasson, 2016b). By contrast, black and white Americans in 2010 had similar levels of life expectancy at lower levels of education (men in particular), but blacks suffered a substantial penalty at higher levels of education.

## Discussion and Conclusion


This paper presents a novel method to decompose lifespan inequality in those settings where the population under study is partitioned across several factors/characteristics simultaneously (e.g., race, sex, ethnicity, education, and so on) and we wish to know which one of them is its most important determinant. More specifically, the proposed method allows determining the contribution of those several factors and their multipleway interactions to overall lifespan inequality. This method can also accommodate factors with more than two levels (e.g., Low/Medium/High education or multiple regions). Unlike traditional approaches that inspect the influence of each factor on the outcome of interest separately, the suggested method does not require subpopulations to be mutually exclusive, and takes into consideration the fact that the different factors might interact with each other.

The methodological approach proposed here applies to those measures of inequality that are based on the outcome comparison among all pairs of observations. Prominent examples of such measures include the absolute and relative Gini indices, the variance and the coefficient of variation squared - which are commonly used as measures of lifespan inequality (e.g., Shkolnikov et al. 2003, Monden and Smits 2009, Gillespie et al. 2014, Permanyer and Sholl 2019). Importantly, those measures allow certain decompositions 'within-' and 'between-groups' that differ in fundamental ways with respect to standard ANOVA-like decompositions (see Permanyer et al. 2023 for further details). For the latter, the between-group component has a single term that measures the inequality that would be observed in a hypothetical distribution suppressing variability within each of the groups in which the population is partitioned. For the former, the between-group component contains many terms indicating how 'close' or 'far away' any two group-specific age-at-death distributions are. Future research should determine whether the ideas presented in this paper could be extended to broader families of inequality indices, like the Generalized Entropy Measures.

Some limitations should be highlighted. On the one hand, the results of the decomposition might be contingent on the number of values (or categories) that the different factors can take. Ceteris paribus , a factor with a high number of categories (say, 'State' in the US context) might contribute to a larger extent to overall lifespan inequality than other factors with lower number of categories (like 'Sex'). For this reason, it is important to keep the number of categories fixed whenever performing comparisons across time or space. On the other hand, the interpretation of multiple-way interaction coefficients remains a challenging issue. Indeed, non-negligible interaction coefficients suggest the existence of non-trivial patterns of association between factors that warrant further efforts to understand the underlying dynamics.

The ideas proposed in this paper hold promise to be useful for the analysis of 'intersectional inequalities' - a field of research that is rich in qualitative hypothesis but often lacks quantitative tools to test competing hypotheses (Kapilashrami et al., 2015). Indeed, most qualitative research suggests that different axes of inequality do not operate independently but rather compounding each other to the detriment of

individuals' well-being - a fundamental research program that might be approached from a quantitative perspective taking advantage of the tools presented here.
