## Introduction


Several studies across very different fields have identified various traits said to be necessary for supporting cooperation and social cohesion within increasingly large, complex, and diverse societies. Though scholars disagree about which particular trait or set of traits are most essential in this process and when exactly these  features  become  widespread  in  different  parts  of  the  world,  there  is  wide  agreement  that  as societies became larger and more populous, some set of core features were adopted to maintain cohesion and so survive (and perhaps thrive) in inter-state competition (Acemoglu and Robinson 2012; Eisenstadt 2010; Fukuyama 2011; 2012; Levine 2005; Mouzakitis 2017; Sanderson 1999; Turchin, Whitehouse, et al. 2021; Wagner 2012). These include accessible political institutions, constitutional law, limitations on the exercise of power, and a suite of ideological and philosophical traits promoting moralizing, universalizing, egalitarian, and prosocial ideals.

Previous analyses of historical data compiled in Seshat: Global History Databank have suggested that as societies grow in scale and complexity, extreme forms of inequality -autocratic forms of governance, rulers appearing as living gods and legitimated by access to divine authority,  oppressive treatment of religious or socio-economic groups -no  longer provide a viable method of maintaining cohesion and cooperation. This process is seen most dramatically in large, multi-ethnic empires where cross-cutting group alignments can foment internal conflict and weaken military capacity. The rise and adoption of certain  features  typical  of  moralizing  religious  systems  along  with  different  forms  of  governmental administration stand out as being critical mechanisms for maintaining cooperation at increasing scales and levels of complexity. These developments were also found to be driven by competition between societies, as those able to develop such features generally outcompeted others in inter-state conflict, leading to their spread in different areas and cultural contexts (Turchin, Whitehouse, et al. 2021).

The relationship between these different supposedly critical traits that support social cooperation and cohesion, and the abandonment of alternate social forms, however, has not been subjected to large-scale systematic analysis. It has thus been difficult to pin down an understanding of how these traits not only evolved and spread in different times and places, but how they interact with each other. A number of pressing  questions,  then,  remain:  Which  of  the  many  features  identified  as  being  foundational  for cooperation is actually the most consistent across a large number of historical cases? Is there merit to the arguments that a suite of traits adopted at roughly the same time are all necessary for this process? And does the proposal  of a  'megasociety  threshold' at  roughly  1  million  inhabitants  that  creates  a  strong distinction between modes of social life withstand empirical scrutiny?

Here, we investigate the rise, spread, and force of cooperation-promoting institutions and ideologies in societies by leveraging Seshat: Global History Databank (seshatdatabank.info), an important resource for exploring such long-term social dynamics on a stratified global sample of past societies (François et al. 2016;  Turchin  et  al.  2015;  Turchin,  Whitehouse,  et  al.  2018).  Using  the  extensive  body  of  empirical historical information gathered by the Seshat project, we explore a range of new variables relating to levels of inequality, political domination, ideology, and  religion  to uncover how the different features proposed as critical factors in social cooperation have evolved and to assess their relationships to each other. We find that while certain forms of religious and ideological thought do tend to arise as societies become larger and more populous and then become widespread and resilient, other putative elements of increasingly complex societies -such as institutionalized constraints on authority or the institutionalization of prosocial and egalitarian ideals -do not follow the same pattern. Our findings build on previous work, suggesting that the role of moralizing religion, formalized governmental administration, and the provision of public goods helped to facilitate cooperation across divisions of ethnicity, class, and caste while preserving sufficient levels of well-being and administrative capacity needed to maintain social cohesion  within  large  and  diverse  societies.  Yet,  adopting  these  features -even  when  embracing moralizing religions and appealing to universalizing and egalitarian ideals -did not prevent certain forms of  structural  inequality  from  arising  or  persisting.  Indeed,  arguably  such  ideological  structures  arose precisely to mitigate such material and social inequality (Graeber and Wengrow 2021).

This paper provides a quantitative analysis of the relationship between the key factors highlighted in these works, focusing on ideological features such as aspects of moralizing religion and egalitarian, prosocialpromoting thoughts, as well as institutional features such as  limitations  on  authority  and  restrictions about ruler's claims to supernatural authority. We then explore several regional case studies (central Italy, the Nile Valley of Egypt, and northern China) to explore in more fine-grained detail the dynamics that these factors displayed in specific historical contexts. This article, thus, combines statistical analysis of a relatively large sample of empirical data with more traditional historiographical discussion. Combining quantitative  and  qualitative  research  in  this  way  provides  unique  insights  that  would  be  impossible adopting one approach alone. We close this piece with a discussion of our main findings and highlight their implications for how we conceive of long-run trends in global cultural evolution.


## Theoretical Background and Core Hypotheses to be Tested


From  the  late  Neolithic,  human  societies  have  grown  generally  larger  and  more  complex  over  time (Richerson and Boyd 2005; Turchin 2015; Watkins 2019). At its core, this long-run social evolution has hinged on the ways that humans have solved coordination and collective action problems at growing scales and within increasingly complex systems (Blanton and Fargher 2016; Carballo, Roscoe, and Feinman 2014; G. A. Johnson 1982; Gavrilets and Richerson 2017; Olson 1965; Ostrom 1990; Whitehouse and Lanman 2014). In particular, as social groups have expanded, they have had to figure out new ways to manage increasingly large and diverse populations and to facilitate cooperation at ever higher scales and levels of complexity. A key ingredient in this process seems to be humans' inclination towards prosocial behaviour, namely the willingness of individuals to accept some personal costs -expending time, energy, resources, even risking their own life -for the benefit of their social group (Tomasello 2009; Francois, Fujiwara,  and  Ypersele  2018).  When  societies  failed  to  solve  these  challenges  or  to  elicit  prosocial behaviour among inhabitants, they generally encounter turmoil, crisis,  and sometimes collapse,  their territory and surviving populations subsumed by societies that had better managed these collective action problems. In this way, the more successful advances and adaptations in social systems became adopted -or  imposed -in  more  and  more places leading to the  spread of traits we encounter in most large, modern societies today.

Various schools of thought have tried to understand exactly how these processes played out in the past, and pinpoint which innovations or 'revolutions' were particularly central in these evolutionary successes. These works generally seek to identify the critical practices and institutions that allowed certain groups to maintain stability and even expand, features which were then adopted and adapted by other societies until  they became widespread across multiple regions and cultures.  These conjectures can be broken down into three essential schools, though it should be noted that there is some overlap between these areas in many scholars' arguments : institutional studies focus on the development of political institutions and systems of governance and administration needed to manage increasingly populous and territorial extensive societies; ideological studies, on the other hand, highlight the normative and cultural features that promote social coherence and adherence to shared values that can support cohesion among large, diverse populations; finally, package of traits theories argue that various sets of cultural traits, including both institutional and ideological features, tend to coevolve together along with social scale, often in an iteratively reinforcing feedback loop where an increase in societal scale demands the adoption of some of the above-mentioned traits, which supports a further increase in scale, additional adoptions, and so on.

Below, we survey briefly these three prominent schools of thought, highlighting the key features advanced by each perspective. At the end of this section, we present a table of the core hypotheses derived from these previous studies that we then test against empirical historical data.


## Institutional Developments


Many influential theories  from  anthropologists  and  political  theorists  highlight  political  institutions as central in the evolution of increasingly large and complex societies. These works typically argue that the development  and  spread  of  more specialized  and  formalized  forms  of  governance allowed  for  the management and coordination of increasingly large and diverse populations scattered over wider and wider  territories  (DeMarrais,  Castillo,  and  Earle  1996;  Mann  1986;  Eisenstadt  2010;  Fukuyama  2012; 2014). A complimentary line of scholarship emphasizes the heterogeneity of large-scale government, with the tailoring of policies to local contexts and the reliance on differing degrees of administrative intensity (Doyle 1986; Berdan 1996; Covey 2014).

In  a  similar  vein,  many  scholars argue  that  a critical  institutional innovation was establishing  effective constraints on predation and the use of arbitrary force by rulers and other elites. (Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson 2005; Acemoglu and Robinson 2012; Crone 1989; Harrington, Boski, and Gelfand 2015; Levi 1988;  Skocpol  1985).  This  involved  developing  new  rules  around  authority,  or  extending  existing institutions that regulated the behavior of the majority population to apply, for the first time, to rulers as well.  Such  constraints  are  said  to  have  limited  the  autocratic  and  exploitative  forms  of  rule  that characterized  archaic  states,  which  may  have  facilitated  cohesion  and  prosocial  behaviour  among increasingly large populations by reducing the sense of unfairness and preventing at least some abuses of power and impoverishment that were present in societies without such constraints.

Rules and norms that abolished rule by 'god kings' -such as the Pharaohs of ancient Egypt who were positioned  as  living  supernatural  beings -or  having  rulers  base  their  legitimacy  and  authority  on maintaining special access to supernatural powers are thought to be particularly important constraints in this line. This is especially prominent in the work of proponents of the Axial Age theory (see below).

Others  emphasize  institutions  that  ensure  the  generation  and  maintenance  of public  goods such  as irrigation works, food storage and drinking water provision, support for the movement of goods, people, and information (such as maintaining roads, ports, postal services, etc.). These institutions are thought to help incentivize cooperation and prosocial behaviour among the beneficiaries of these goods, who have a  'stake'  in  the  continued  successful  operation  of  the  state  systems  that  support  them (Blanton  and Fargher  2009;  Brewer  1990;  Witoszek  and  Midttun  2018;  Wittfogel  1957;  Wong  2019).  Though  it  is important to note that not all public goods are equally 'public', in that sometimes notionally accessible resources like a water supply facility are actually available only to certain communities within a society. Nevertheless,  such  theories suggest  that the greater number  and  wider  availability of critical infrastructure and social programs in a given society, the greater the likelihood that the society will see high levels of cooperation and prosocial engagement from inhabitants.


## Normative Ideologies


A different approach to this critical question looks not to state structures or institutions, but focuses on normative ideologies. A number of scholars in the emerging field of cognitive science of religion notably contend that belief in moralizing supernatural powers incentivizes prosocial behaviour among adherents (Baumard and Boyer 2013; Bulbulia et al. 2013; Casanova 2012; D. D. P. Johnson 2005; Henrich 2020; Norenzayan  2013;  2015;  Peoples  and  Marlowe  2015;  Purzycki  et  al.  2018;  Stausberg  2014).  Scholars pursing this direction argue that such belief systems helped individuals internalize norms of cooperation and  group  cohesion,  promoting  prosocial  behaviour  among  adherents  and  cooperation  among increasingly large communities. The nature of the relationship between religious ideology and complexity, though, is  itself  the  subject  of  fierce  debate,  with  one  side  arguing  that  beliefs  in  morally-concerned supernatural  powers  preceded  and  indeed  played  a  causal  role  in  the  rise  of  increasingly  large  and complex societies (Norenzayan 2013; Watts et al. 2015), while the other argues that these ideological developments arose as part of a package of traits including many institutional features as well (explained below; (Turchin, Whitehouse, Larson, et al. 2022)).

Another, similar line of argument holds that many norms develop outside of religious or other moralizing belief systems that promote egalitarianism and/or expressly advocate for prosocial behaviour among constituents (Curry  2016;  Whitehouse  et  al.  2019).  While  the  specific  content  of  these  norms  differs widely between cultures, they share as a common feature the intent to engender prosocial behaviour among adherents. Critically, this would be true whether or not these norms of morality are accompanied by beliefs in moralizing supernatural powers.


## Packages of Key Traits


A popular composite perspective comes from Axial Age arguments i . In essence, this line of thought holds that certain Eurasian societies  during the mid-1st millennium BCE developed a suite of novel ideological, ii cultural, and political ideas that transformed their social order. Many axial age works argue that these ideas  not  only  spread  throughout  the  world  in  subsequent  centuries,  but  are  integral  pieces  of contemporary social formations. The notion holds clear appeal; it offers a simple, compelling account of when and how past civilizations made the grand transition -the axis on which world history turned -from 'archaic', despotic forms  of rule to more inclusive, constrained, and 'modern' societies (Abrutyn 2014; J. P. Arnason, Eisenstadt, and Wittrock 2005; Baumard, Hyafil, and Boyer 2015; Bellah 2005; 2011; Bellah and Joas 2012; Black 2008; Boy and Torpey 2013; Eisenstadt 1986; Halton 2014). Axial Age theories suggest that the major innovations outlined above should arise together and roughly simultaneously , whether  as  part  of  the  initial  axial  cases  or  being  spread  together  as  part  of  a  single  package  of transformations. We have elsewhere challenged these ideas (Mullins et al. 2018; Whitehouse et al. 2019), suggesting that the rise and spread of axial transformations were much more varied than traditionally thought. Nevertheless, the theory continues to hold prominence and further empirical testing is needed to flesh out the different aspects of axial arguments.

Several members of the Seshat project, including many of the authors on this paper, have also contributed to the package of traits line of thought.  Our prior work illustrated that social complexity tends to involve the  co-evolution  of  a  suite  of  factors -including  territorial  extent,  governance  and  administrative functions, informational technologies, and other elements  (Turchin, Currie, et al. 2018) -as well as the adoption of moralizing normative ideologies as these aspects of complexity grow (Turchin, Whitehouse, Larson,  et  al.  2022).  A  recent  paper  further  scrutinized  these  patterns,  finding  that  these  various developments  all  respond  to  innovations  in  military  technologies  along  with  advances  in  agricultural productivity needed to maintain subsistence among growing populations  (Turchin, Whitehouse, et al. 2021).  Other  research  exploring  these  patterns  highlighted  that,  while  all  of  the  factors  identified  by Turchin et  al.  (2018)  are  indeed  highly  correlated  overall,  jumps  in  social  scale  (territorial  extent  and population numbers) tend to rise first, with information technologies and other elements following (Shin et al. 2019; 2020; Kohler, Bird, and Wolpert 2022).

Another recent proposal (Whitehouse et al. 2019) suggests that when any society exceeds a population of roughly one million people -the 'mega society threshold' (MST) --it simply cannot function well or survive inter-state competition without adopting several interrelated features. In other words, one million inhabitants may be the point at which social groups become too large to manage or maintain cohesion without developing a particular package of traits, including all of the institutional and ideological features noted above. This is similar to the suite of traits associated with the Axial Age, though it offers a different causal mechanism for how and why these traits were adopted (or not) in different places at different times.

## Materials and Methods Defining Primary Measures


In this section, we describe the measures used to test the core hypotheses identified in Table 1. Details on how each measure was constructed and data was collected are provided in the SM. Measures are collected as a timeseries for large-scale polities world-wide from the fifth millennium BCE to 1900 CE, sampled every 100 years.

1) Governance. To measure the sophistication and inclusiveness of governance structures ( Gov ), we utilize data previously collected and analyzed by members of the Seshat project (Turchin, Currie, et al. 2018; Turchin, Whitehouse,  Gavrilets, et al. 2022). This measure  combines  variables  concerning  the professionalization of administrative and legal functions (bureaucrats, soldiers, priests), the presence of examination systems and merit-based promotion of officials, and the existence legal codes, lawyers and judges, as well as courthouses and other dedicated government spaces.

2) Constraints. We explore institutions constraining the exercise of power and basis of legitimate authority by rulers through two measures. First, we measure the presence of formal, institutionalized constraints on rulers ( Constrain ), such as constitutional limits on ruler authority or the right of veto power held by other officials. Second, we measure the extent that rulers base their authority  on aspects other than religious  grounds  ( NoGodRule ).  This  measure  assesses  whether  rulers  are  conceived  of  as  gods  or supernatural powers or base their rule primarily on access to supernatural power, such as through certain rituals only they are permitted to perform -if so, this will result in a lower score; if rulers do not base their authority on these grounds, that results in a higher score.

3) Public Goods. We measure the provision of public goods ( Infra ) by utilizing the same data and analysis as with the Gov measure. Infra focuses on infrastructure typically provided by state resources or elites associated  with  governing  functions  and  which  are  relatively  readily  identifiable  in  the  historical  and archaeological sources.

- 4) Moralizing Religion. Following the procedure described in (Turchin, Whitehouse, Larson, et al. 2022), we measure the presence and degree of moralizing supernatural punishment and reward ( MSP ) in the prevailing  ideology  of  each  of  the  polities  in  our  sample.  MSP  here  refers  to  a  cluster  of  beliefs  and practices postulating a system of supernatural punishment and reward for morally salient behavior, where such systems are primarily concerned with the way humans interact with other humans, rather than how they interact with supernatural forces. We code 9 separate measures (detailed in SM) of such moralizing beliefs  and  practices,  whether  enforced  by  supernatural  agents  or  non-agentic  forces,  e.g.  karmic principles.

5) Prosocial Norms. We measure ideals that espouse moralizing and egalitarian beliefs ( EgalID ), whether they are expressed in religious works and contexts or other normative ideologies, such as works of political or  social  philosophy  (the  writings  of  Plato,  for  instance).  Similarly,  we  measure  ideals  that  promote prosocial behaviour among adherents ( Prosoc ), again whether these are expressed in religious or other ideological contexts.

- 6) Axial Age. This theory touches on all of the aspects discussed above, which together constitute the 'axial' package.
- 7)  MST .  We  explore  the  potential  impact  of  societies  crossing  the  'mega society  threshold'  ( -MST )  by determining the date at which any polity in each of the Natural Geographic Areas (NGA; see SM for details) exhibited a population greater than one million. We then used that date to establish the relative time from the MST for each datapoint in our sample. For example, in the Latium NGA the first polity to cross the MST was the middle Roman Republic in the late 3 rd  century BCE, so we set the threshold year for that NGA to  200  BCE,  since  we  sample  at  century  timesteps.  A  datapoint  from  100  CE  under  the  Roman Principate, which occupied Latium during most of the first three centuries CE, is thus coded as being +300 relative to the MST year.


## Defining Additional Measures


In addition to the key response measures detailed above, we employ a number of other measures needed to test the core hypotheses from Table 1.

In  particular,  every  theory  identified  here  involves  the impact  of  increasing  social  scale  in  driving  the advent and adoption of other traits. We measure this ( Scale ) as the first principle component of a polity's territorial  extent,  overall  population,  and    population  of  the  largest  settlement,  as  in  previous  work (Turchin, Whitehouse, Gavrilets, et al. 2022; Turchin, Whitehouse, Larson, et al. 2022).

Some of the identified theories involve the impact of military competition between rival polities. We proxy that competition by a measure of the sophistication of military technology deployed by different polities ( MilTech ), as well as a simplified measure capturing the use of iron metallurgy along with cavalry warfare ( IronCav )  adapted from previous work (Turchin, Hoyer, et al. 2021). The latter measure highlights the importance of these technologies in macro-social evolution (cf Turchin et al. 2022).

For some of the analyses below, we also include other factors that may have played important roles in the development of our primary response measures, although these are not featured prominently in the body of theories we review above. These are taken from our prior work assessing the primary causal drivers of different aspects of social complexity, including Scale and Gov, as well as of moralizing religions. These include a measure of each polity's agricultural productivity ( Agri ) as well as a term capturing the time  from  the  adoption  of  agriculture  in  each  reach  ( AgriLag ),  adapted  from  previous  work  (Turchin, Currie, et al. 2021). We also include a number of possible autocorrelative factors, including a measure of the spatial distance between polities ( Space ) and linguistic affinity ( Phylogeny ). Further details on how these measures were conceptualized and coded are included in the SM.

While the various theoretical  perspectives discussed  above  highlight  different  principal  drivers  in  the evolution of large, complex societies, they generally agree that whatever measure is highlighted should closely track increases in social complexity and especially in social scale. Overall, however, we find only partial support for this.

Three main conclusions follow from the analyses presented below. First, these various factors are poorly correlated with each other. Second, there is a clear divergence in how well they align with social scale and other  aspects  of  social  complexity:  on  one  hand,  certain  ideological  features,  notably  adherence  to moralizing religions, as well as some institutional ones, namely public goods provision, do rise sharply as social scale increases -particularly as societies cross the MST -in line with the predictions of cultural evolutionary theory, cognition science of religion scholarship, and certain Axial Age arguments; on the other hand, we find that other ideological aspects of equality and prosociality, as well as institutional features constraining ruler' s power,  do  not  follow  these  same patterns, in contrast to many anthropological and political theory perspectives as outlined above, as well as to the expectations of the MST idea. Lastly, dynamic regression analysis confirms these mixed results, as some features are well predicted  by  prior  developments  in  military  technology  and  agricultural  productivity,  consistent  with previous findings (Turchin, Whitehouse, Gavrilets, et al. 2022), while others are not well described by any of the factors explored here. We describe in detail the significance of these findings in the Discussion section below, after we explain each of these results in turn.

We performed a number of different analyses exploring the hypothesized relationships between our key measures, defined above. First, we performed crosscorrelation analysis using Pearson's method (see SM) to investigate the relationship between our primary measures as well as Scale; see Figure 1. Some features are indeed strongly correlated with each other, namely Infra and Gov, Infra and MSP, and MSP and Gov. Similarly,  Scale  is  strongly  correlated  with  MSP,  Infra,  and  Gov,  consistent  with  previous  findings. However, Constrain, NoGodRule, EgalID, and Prosoc show no significant correlations with each other, with the other primary measures, or with Scale, contrary to the expectations of many hypotheses. This suggests that these measures evolved somewhat independent of each other and thus were not all part of a single 'package' of adaptations coevolving in different times and places around the globe.

Lastly,  we  sought  to  move  beyond  such  synchronous  correlations  to  explore  the  potential  influences driving changes in our key measures. We followed our established Dynamic Regression procedure for detecting causal patterns in time-series data (Turchin 2018; Turchin, Whitehouse, Gavrilets, et al. 2022). Indeed, this is one of the crucial advantages of the long time-series data afforded by historical evidence, as collected by the Seshat project. As causes tend to precede their effects in time, we can measure the significance  of  the  relationship  between  different  predictor  variables  measured  at  one  time  step  ( ) t against the response variable measured at the next time step ( t+1 ).  We explored each of our primary response measures in turn against a host of other measures, including the other primary measures and additional measures for military technology (MilTech and IronCav) and agricultural productivity (Agri and AgriLag) as explained in Materials and Methods above. We also included measures to assess possible autocorrelations, including those due to spatial (Space), temporal (Time), and cultural affinity (Phylogeny). See the SM for details and full results.

Overall, the dynamic regressions provide further support to the results indicated by our previous analyses. We find that military competition (particularly the IronCav measure) and agricultural productivity (Agri) display significant relationships with later values of MSP, Gov, and Infra, consistent with earlier findings (Turchin, Whitehouse, Larson, et al. 2022; Turchin, Whitehouse, Gavrilets, et al. 2022). This is an important confirmation, as the current study includes several ideological and institutional factors (notably EgalID, Prosoc, Constrain, and NoGodRule) not included in the earlier analyses, lending additional strength to the prior results. All three of these measures -MSP, Gov, and Infra -also show significant effects for some of the autocorrelative measures. MSP is driven by values of MSP at the previous timestep, and shows a significant and negative effect with the square term (MSP.square). This highlights the change we see in our data where many regions acquire high levels of MSP after a certain point, and then retain those high levels even as individual polities rise and fall in that region. Likewise, the previous time step measures (both 1 and 2 time-steps earlier) appear as significant effects on later values of Gov and Infra, as do the square terms, though all with positive coefficients. This may indicate that these features tend to grow steadily over time, but also ten d to retain high values featuring few major 'turns' or losses. It is notable too that the dynamic regression models for these three measures produce fairly strong fits, with r  values 2 above 0.8 in each case.

A more surprising result is that these same measures do not appear to be significant drivers for the other measures -EgalID, Prosoc, Constrain, and NoGodRule. None of the military competition or agricultural productivity measures show significant effects on any of these measures, nor do the autocorrelative terms apart from the 1 time-step previous measures. This 1-time-step autocorrelation result suggests there is some  'stickiness'  with  these  measures,  but  the  lack  of  significant  autocorrelations  with  2  ti me-step previous terms indicates that this stickiness does not last. Further, the lack of significant autocorrelated square terms may suggest a fluctuating pattern. Note also that these regression models have moderate r   values,  ranging  between  0.6  and  0.8.  The  lack  of  a  strong  pattern  between  these  factors,  which  is 2 expected by several theories, is thus surprising. We return to this significant result in the Discussion.

The above analyses explore general trends and the relationship between these various factors at the macro-level, combining data from our full global sample of historic polities. The Mediterranean Basin has seen the rise and fall of numerous complex polities over many thousands of years. After the Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BCE (Dickinson 2012; Drews 1993; Milisauskas 2002) and the demise of large states like the Hittite and Assyrian Empire and the relatively large Mycenaean kingdoms  in  the  Aegean,  the  region  was  fragmented  into  many  small-scale  political  units.  However, archaeological evidence shows that this was not a static period in which social life shrank to the level of the farming village. Instead, it was a time of population movements and long-distance trading networks (with different nodes and hubs, now that the major Bronze Age powers had left the stage), as well as nearconstant warfare -an interregional warring states period. This military intensification shows up in the increased variety and sophistication of weapons, armor and fortifications during these centuries.

After 500 BCE, we see the emergence of larger-scale, centralized polities: the expanding Roman Republic, the regionally dominant Athenian city-state, and the Punic Empire, founded by colonists from Phoenicia and centered on Carthage on the North African coast. This is reflected in the growing Scale seen in the region around this time (Figure 4). All these powers were in fierce conflict with their neighbors, clashing on land and - thanks to developments in naval technology (McGrail 2008) -at sea. Aegean societies faced the additional threat of an expansionist Persia to the east.

The political arrangements at the heart of the mid-millennium states and burgeoning empires aimed to break the stranglehold of control by a few royal or elite families. They set in place organs of representative government, checks and balances on central authority, and mechanisms to prevent dynastic succession, such as term limits on public offices in the Roman Republic, though notably these rise at relatively low social scales, well before the MST is reached in the region (Fig 4b). This process has long been recognized in Western historical scholarship in the case of Greece and Rome, which often serve as the quasi-mythical ancestors of democratic nation-states (Fukuyama 1992; Ober 2008; 2015). However, there are signs that these political innovations were not limited to what is now Europe. Due to the scarcity of Punic written sources, much less is known about the government of ancient Carthage than about its neighbours to the north,  but  it  appears  that  it  was  a  monarchy  (albeit  probably  an  elective  one,  and  with  a  powerful consultative body) until the fourth century BCE, and an oligarchic republic thereafter (Picard 1994, 371 -75). Nevertheless, it should be noted that all these republican and democratic political arrangements were short-lived experiments compared to the longer sweep of this history. Rome became an empire with a thriving cult to a divinized Emperor, various Greek city-states fell under the rule of divinized Hellenistic kings, and the Punic Empire collapsed completely, absorbed into Rome.

The last millennium BCE also saw an explosion of new ideological thought around ethics and the best way to organize societies, the nature of virtue, and the role of the gods in relation to humans. In the Greek Aegean, the pre-Socratic thinkers tackled the nature of the cosmos from the sixth century onwards, but here we are less interested in this relatively abstract philosophy than in the political and moral thought that  came  later,  starting  in  the  fifth  century  with  Socrates  and  Plato  in  Athens  and  quickly  spreading throughout the Mediterranean littoral. These burgeoning philosophies for which 'Socrates,' 'Plato' and 'Aristotle' serve as shorthand could not be considered 'egalitarian' in the modern sense - and in fact '[i]t is easier to find critics of democracy than supporters' in this period (Johann P. Arnason, Raaflaub, and Wagner 2013, 2). However, they had in common a universalizing frame of reference, attempting to develop a generally applicable morality, discover the best form of government, and ask how humans could be made more virtuous. It was clear that pre-existing social hierarchies, rights and privileges could no longer be taken for granted. Interestingly, while these philosophical perspectives were largely adopted in Roman Italy -at least by many elite Romans -this emphasis on universal moral and ethical principles did not  translate  into  explicit  exhortations  towards  prosocial  behaviour  (Fig  4a).  It  is  important  to  note, however, that there was a strong cultural and political tradition of benefaction across the Mediterranean, including in Italy through the Republic and Principate periods (Hoyer 2018; Lomas and Cornell, Timothy J. 2003; Verboven 2012; Zuiderhoek 2009). Prosocial behaviour, thus, was certainly not lacking in Italy at this  time,  perhaps  reflected  in  the  'rebound'  in  Prosoc  demonstrated  in  the  later  Principate  to  early Dominate period. Still, it is notable that this did  not feature in the dominant religious and  normative ideologies of the period the way it did in contemporary systems of thought in other parts of the world including the Greek world as well as Egypt, China, and Persia.

The new philosophical and political thought continued to flourish and develop long after the Greek citystates  had  been  brought  under  dynastic  rule.  Indeed,  some  of  the  most  explicit  expressions  of universalizing ethics in the Greek-speaking sphere, such as the thinking of Epicurus or the Stoic Zeno of Citium, date to the Hellenistic period (Long 2006). Variants of Stoicism, Cynicism, Epicureanism and other schools also found fertile ground as the Roman period wore on, particularly through the Principate and into the Dominate period well after the region had crossed the MST (Fig 4a). This is reflected in the rise of MSP leading into and through the adoption of Christianity as state religion during the early 4 th century CE. Egalitarian ideals follow a similar path, though notably  decline (unlike with MSP) near the end of the Roman period. Critically, these moralizing and universalizing egalitarian ethics were thriving at the same time as the checks and balances of Republican rule were being steadily eroded. This is similar to what we see in China, discussed below.

Everywhere in the Mediterranean, increasingly autocratic political forms coexisted with (semi-)egalitarian and universalizing, prosocial ideologies, at least among elite circles. While an emphasis on moralizing concerns remained active into Late Antiquity and through the Early Modern Period, we find that these other aspects decline in the mid-first millennium CE, only to rise, fall, and rise again over the next thousand years. In the history of the Mediterranean there is, thus, no identifiable package combining representative government and constraints on power with 'modern' or 'axial' ideologies, nor a consistent and stable development of these ostensibly crucial traits save for an adherence to moralizing religious beliefs.

Mid1st millennium BCE China was one of Karl Jaspers' original axial cases, and has featured in virtually every subsequent formulation of the Axial Age theory. Arguments for its inclusion among 'axial' societies, and thus as one of the roots of later modernity, rest largely on the philosophical, religious, and political thinkers of the Spring and Autumn (771-476 BCE) and Warring States (475-221 BCE) periods, whose ideas were written down and systematized somewhat later. We focus here on what is now northern China, the Middle Yellow River Valley.

In a parallel trajectory to the Mediterranean, the region in the late Bronze Age was dominated by a large, complex  and  hierarchically  organized  state,  the  Shang.  The  social  scale  of  early  societies  in  China surpassed those in Europe, witnessed by the region crossing of the MST around 1600 BCE (Fig. 5). The Shang were overthrown by the Western Zhou around 1000 BCE, who claimed that the Shang had lost the 'Mandate  of  Heaven',  meaning  divine  support  for  their  ru le,  through  their  wickedness  and  immoral behaviour (Shaughnessy 1999; Zhao 2015). However, after about 75 relatively peaceful years of Zhou rule over a large portion of the central plains of China, vassal rebellions and popular unrest began to increase. The  centuries  after  the  fall  of  the  Western  Zhou  in  771  BCE  were  characterized  by  political  flux  and endemic  conflict  between  many  small  polities,  and  the  scale  and  intensity  of  warfare  increased dramatically. In the last millennium BCE the agrarian societies of the Middle Yellow River Valley also faced a threat from nomadic groups based on the steppe (Di Cosmo 2015; Kradin 2011; 2014).

Amid the political fragmentation of the later Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, a 'hundred schools' arose: many philosophies and ethical systems, later categorized as Confucian, Mohist, Daoist, Legalist, and so on. They differed  widely  in their approaches to hierarchy and inequality, but they all sought  a  universally  applicable  ethics.  Even  Confucianism,  which  valued  hierarchical  relationships  as contributing to stability and social harmony, found itself having to mount a defense of a state of affairs that in former times was taken for granted. For example, 'nobility' was reframed as a matter of wise conduct  and  personal  virtue  rather  than  inherited  status,  but  stark  inequities  between  members  of different classes were not only tolerated, but lauded, meaning this universalizing ideology was far from egalitarian  (Fig  5a).  Like  much  of  Greco-Roman  philosophy,  Warring  States  period  thinkers  tackled practical questions about the best way to organize and rule a polity. Wandering advisor-sages offered their philosophies up to rulers, and attempted to sway them towards more virtuous and wise styles of government.

It is important to emphasize that although these ideas largely developed within this context of prolonged inter-state conflict, they did not become widely adopted throughout the region until the consolidation of the Qin and early Han Dynasties around the turn of the first millennium CE, which witnessed a fairly strong increase in social scale. This is reflected in the 'jump' in moralizing beliefs and promotion of prosociality during the Han and the other imperial dynasties which followed, although egalitarian ideals remained largely absent (Fig 5a).

This did not,  however, translate into increasing  formal  constraints on executive authority; in  fact, we observe the opposite. We find that constraints on the power of rulers dipped sharply during the last millennium BCE, especially in its final centuries in the midst of Warring State conflict and through the early imperial period (Fig 5b). Following a remarkably similar pattern to that seen in the transition from Republic to Principate in Rome, when China was unified under its first imperial foundation, the Qin Dynasty, in 221 BCE, the first emperor attempted to quash further conflict by imposing strong, centralized, autarchic rule over this polity, which was much larger and more populous than any previous state in the region. The Qin ruler embraced this eve n more explicitly than in Rome, assuming the role of 'supreme divine being' (Lewis 1999, 167) (Fig 5b). Subsequent emperors were also deified after death, lavish rituals involving massive state expenditure (Puett 2014). However, it is worth noting that from the Zhou period onwards rulership had been viewed in a moralizing light: the incumbent dynasty ruled with the approval of Heaven, but this would be withdrawn if they oppressed the people. In the late first millennium BCE we also see the creation of  a  professional  bureaucracy,  long  before  equivalent  developments  in  Europe.  Civil  servants  were educated in the 'axial' -style schools of thought that had developed in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States period. By codifying and regularizing the process of government, this system likely served as a check on  arbitrary  executive  power  and  weakened  the  traditional  aristocracy  even  without  a  formal, institutionalized system of political constraints. Incorporating these philosophies into official practices, however, likewise institutionalized the hierarchical, in many ways egalitarian precepts they espoused, as noted above.

These  broad  trends,  coupled  with  the  results  of  our  quantitative  analyses,  suggest  that  periods  of centralization  followed  by  fragmentation  and  intense  inter-polity  warfare  pushed  societies  in  China towards the adoption of cooperation-promoting ideologies, cemented within the subsequent phase of consolidation and centralization. The role of institutional reforms aiming to curtail arbitrary or oppressive power is much less evident than in the ancient Mediterranean, and again there appears to be no necessary link  between  'axial' -type  schools  of  thought  and  institutionalized  constraints  on  rulers.  It  is  also noteworthy  that  Buddhism,  an  explicitly  moralizing,  prosocial  religion  that  stressed  compassionate treatment of all beings, was widely adopted in China only much later, after the Han Dynasty fell and the region again descended into intense warfare between rival small polities in the Three Kingdoms period. Even this, though, did little to curtail the supernaturally based, largely unconstrained power of rulers (Fig 5b).

Towards the end of the fourth millennium BCE, the Nile Valley became home to some of the earliest largescale,  complex  societies  in  the  world.  Figure  6  shows  clearly  the  sharp  rise  in  Scale  during  the  4 th millennium and very early crossing of the MST. By around 2650 BCE, the start of the Old Kingdom, a centralized, hierarchically organized state, ruled by a divine king, stretched from the Nile Delta in the north to the island of Elephantine in the south. Over the course of Egyptian history, the central administration periodically lost control of some of this territory and rival powers (such as the priests of Amun at Thebes, provincial elites, or newcomers from Nubia, Libya and the Levant) vied for control. These more politically fragmented phases are known as 'intermediate periods'. Written documents belonging to the genre of Chaosbeschreibungen (accounts  of  chaos)  likely  overemphasize  the  immiseration  of  the  intermediate periods to serve political purposes. However, the alternation between long periods of centralized rule and shorter phases of disintegration is a recurrent feature of Egyptian history.

Several  contributors  to  the  Axial  Age  debate  (notably  (Assmann  2005;  2012))  have  noted  that  Egypt appears precocious in its development of 'axial' ideologies, with evidence  for universalizing thought, limited forms of egalitarianism, and a profoundly ethicized view of the cosmos well before the traditional dates of the Axial Age (c. 800-200 BCE) as described by Karl Jaspers. Some early glimmerings of these traits can be discerned as early as the Old Kingdom, c. 2650-2150 BCE, growing after the MST is crossed as predicted by that body of theory (Fig 6a).

Despite the persistence of many ideological and institutional systems throughout the Pharaonic period, Egyptian thought was not static over the thousands of years of its development. This is best illustrated by the evolution of the ethical concept of maat . Variously translatable as truth, justice or harmonious order, maat was a central pillar of ancient Egyptian culture throughout the Dynastic period. The gods, rather than being capricious or merely self-interested, desired the maintenance of maat on earth. During the Old Kingdom this was the duty of the king, who was the point of contact between the gods and the world of humans. From the First Intermediate Period and Middle Kingdom onwards, writings from tombs and funerary monuments suggest that l iving a virtuous, just, and ordered life - a 'maatian life' - had become the responsibility of non-royal elites as well as the upwardly mobile middle classes. Texts focused on the afterlife, such as the Coffin Texts (First Intermediate Period onwards) and the Book of Going Forth by Day (the Book of the Dead, dating from the New Kingdom) show an increasingly strong emphasis on inevitable divine judgment after death for one's moral conduct.

There was no doctrine that elites were ontologically different from commoners. For instance, one spell from the Coffin Texts has a creator god declare:

I made the four winds, that every man might breathe, wherever he may be … I made the great inundation, that the bereft might share in it like the great … I made every man like his fellow; I did not command them to do evil, but it was their own hearts which overthrew what I devised … I created the gods from my sweat, and men are the tears of my eye (Ray and Ray 2002, 30).

This  notional  egalitarianism  appears  to  have  become  more  inclusive  in  practice  over  time.  This  is  an important point, as it is not directly reflected in our quantitative assessment of EgalID, which measures only the notional level. Whereas in the Old and Middle Kingdoms foreigners represent embodiments of chaos and threats to the ordered state, several New Kingdom and Late Period texts portray lands beyond the Nile Valley as important parts of creation. Their inhabitants now appear as fellow humans presided over by the benevolent gods. These ideals become superseded, or at least partly suppressed, in later periods when new ideologies were introduced by conquest (from Persia, Alexander the Great and his successors, and Rome), at least among the ruling elites; their adoption among the general population remains  unclear  (Bard  2015).  This  suggestion  of  increasing  implementation  or  perhaps  behavioural manifestation of this principle adds nuance to the picture given in Figure 6a.

Despite  such  universalizing  strands  in  religious  thought,  stark  inequities  within  Egyptian  society  were accepted  throughout  this  time  -  and  even  positively  valued.  Indeed,  respect  for  hierarchy  was  one component  of maat .  Maatian  justice  did  not  require  redistribution  of  wealth  or  any  other  form  of economic levelling. Instead, elites portrayed themselves as taking an attitude of paternalistic benevolence towards their social inferiors: clothing the poor, feeding the hungry and providing for widows and other vulnerable people, similar to the culture of beneficence seen throughout the Mediterranean world. It is not clear to what extent this was put into practice, but such texts are a clear example of support for prosocial behavior, which is sometimes (implicitly or explicitly) considered a hallmark of axial or 'world' religions.

What  about  the  role  of  the  Egyptian  Pharaoh,  long  considered  the  quintessential  archaic  god-king? Festivals, monuments and funerary practices all served to legitimize the king's authority and cement his role as the mediator of the divine and human worlds (Fig 6b). That said, some Egyptologists have identified a  gradual  desacralization  of  the  king's  role  over  time,  so  that  in  later  periods  he  was  sometimes represented as merely chosen by the gods, or as god's servant (Bellah 2011). In the Late Period, the king was  increasingly  described  as  an  'instrument'  of  the  gods,  a  shift  in  terminology  that  reflected  the pharaohs' decreasing political and religious influence in the last millennium BCE (O'Connor 1983) . Further, the development of bureaucratic administration and a trend towards more impersonal and routinized modes of governance over the course of the Pharaonic period, including by powerful religious officials, also provided some constraints on the arbitrary exercise of power by rulers. On the other hand, there were virtually no explicit institutional constraints on the king's power from governmental sources. There was no formal separation between executive, judicial, legislative and military power in the Old, Middle or New  Kingdoms,  providing  the  Pharaoh  and  his  advisors  virtually  limitless  scope  for  action.  Perhaps because these constraints were more informal and based on the relative power of the priestly class, they fluctuated fairly significantly over the course of the Pharaonic period (3000 -300 BCE), conflicting with the expectation of a more constant, monotonic growth given by the theories discussed above.


## Discussion and Concluding Remarks


The most significant and perhaps surprising finding is that the various traits we explore here do not all follow  a  similar  trajectory  over  long  periods  across  different  regions,  as  several  of  the  theoretical perspectives surveyed at the beginning of this paper would suggest. We find a clear distinction between MSP, Gov, and Infra -which follow more closely the patterns expected from previous work -and the other  measures,  EgalID,  Prosoc,  Constrain,  and  NoGodRule,  which  diverge  significantly  from  these patterns. The findings regarding NoGodRule are particularly striking, as we not only fail to find a support for hypotheses suggesting that rulers would become less reliant on claims of divine or religious authority as societies become larger and more populous, but we actually find the reverse; in our sample, rulers become  more  likely  to  base  their  authority  on  grounds  of  access  to  supernatural  powers  as  Scale increases.

Our results generally support a cultural evolutionary interpretation, though with significant qualifications. We  find  that  increasingly  intense  interstate  competition  and  conflict,  proxied  here  by  IronCav  and MilTech, acted as a major driving force behind the rise and spread of MSP as well as the production of public  goods  and  advances  in  governmental  sophistication.  Notably,  however,  we  find  that  other ideological expressions of prosocial, egalitarian ideals are not driven by these same factors, nor do they follow the same trajectory as MSP. This suggests that the benefit of moralizing religions is not necessarily that they fostered cohesion based on any egalitarian values, but that they did so mainly by spreading universalizing ideologies that facilitated cooperation across divisions of ethnicity, class, and caste, though in some cases endorsing hierarchical and exploitative social formations as seen clearly in the case studies described above. Prosocial  and  egalitarian  beliefs  offered  perhaps  alternative  'options'  for  generating social  cohesion,  though  perhaps  less  powerful  ones  as  they  fluctuate  more  widely  than  MSP.  This  is consistent with Ideological theories stressing the important role of moralizing religions in fostering social cohesion, but adds nuance by demonstrating the divergence between the force of adopting a moralizing religion and other cooperation-enhancing traits.

Likewise, we find that many rulers were able to persist in legitimating their authority on religious grounds and avoid formalized constraints on their authority, despite their societies adopting ideological precepts that explicitly promoted egalitarian and universalizing ideals iv . The case of north China illustrates this well, as by any definition the  region  was home to large, complex, advanced societies with well-developed, 'axial' -type ideologies from the early imperial period, yet rulership remained tied with divine power and largely unconstrained throughout the first millennium CE. This suggests that restricting claims to divinity or  divine  favour  by  rulers did  not  convey  the  same  adaptive  advantage  to  large,  complex  societies, otherwise we should expect to see them covary with the ideological measures much more closely than we do.

We also find only limited support for the MST hypothesis. While several traits are notably different in regions before and after crossing this threshold, this is not consistent across the measures we explore here. Even in the measures where this difference is significant, values remain fairly variable even after the MST is crossed (see Figure 3 above), suggesting it is not a particularly strong effect or sufficient driver to explain the dynamics observed here. Societies organized above the MST do seem to have enjoyed an external military advantage as long as they could maintain internal cohesion to keep the costs of policing and enforcement low and the ability to marshal significant resources to military and other collective actions high. Our results indicate, however, that this cohesion could be effected in a variety of different forms.  These  are  quite  striking  results,  particularly  regarding  institutionalized  constraints  on  political authority, as they run counter to assumptions about the predominance and importance of such features not only in the past, but as key traits to be promoted generally as a means to facilitate development globally (Acemoglu and Robinson 2012; Fukuyama 2012; 2014; Rodrik 2008). While our study does not explore democratic political features directly as some of these scholars highlight, our focus on egalitarian norms and formalized constraints on rulership allow us to trace the rise and fall of these more inclusive, representative types of rule in different contexts.

The variability seen in many of the traits explored here even in societies far past the MST may reflect the ebb-and-flow of stability and unrest within these societies themselves. Based on prior work by ourselves and others (Goldstone 2017; Hoyer et al. 2024; Korotayev, Malkov, and Khaltourina 2006; Turchin 2003; Turchin and Nefedov 2009), we reason that internal social dynamics operating on finer time-scales than we explore here (decades to perhaps a generation or two) generated this volatility alternating between essentially two distinct periods: one of societal growth and cohesion, which promoted the imposition of constraints on authority and (to some degree, when emerging from a prior period of intense inter-state competition) the reduction of divine claims to authority; and another of disintegration and fragmentation in which these constraints are eroded or co-opted by power holders, or as inter- and intra-state conflict grows creating 'emergency situations' promoting a concentration of power in defense (Tainter  1988; Kemp 2023; Hoyer et al. 2024). These results require further research to unpack fully, though we argue that the method presented in this paper provides a fruitful means of exploring and comparing different and divergent - societal dynamics on a macro scale.

The case studies discussed here raise the appealing, though somewhat preliminary notion that a relatively fragmented geo-political context - namely, 'warring states' type periods -played a key role in driving the adoption of new moralizing religious traditions and deepening governmental functions to facilitate societal  cooperation  and  cohesion  at  increasing  scales and  under  increasingly  centralized,  demanding states. This interpretation would explain both the precociousness of the idea of maat developing in Egypt in the midst of the chaos of the First Intermediate Period as well as the relatively late, 'axial' developments of platonic philosophy among the poleis of the eastern Mediterranean and legalist and Confucian schools in Spring/Autumn and Warring States northern China during the mid-1st millennium BCE, despite the fact that both Anatolia and north China had experienced intense military competition and the rise of large, complex societies centuries earlier.  Even  much  more  recent  examples  fit  this  pattern,  as  the  political fragmentation and long-lived competition between states in early modern northern and western Europe has  been  singled  out  by  numerous  scholars  as  a  key  factor  explaining  Europe's  dramatic  ris e  as  the dominant global region during Industrial Revolution and the age of imperialism that followed (FernándezVillaverde et al. 2020; Goldstone 2021; Scheidel 2019; Stasavage 2019).

These patterns withstand scrutiny in a variety of contexts. In addition to the case studies documented here, we find that Anatolia, Mesopotamia, and northern India exhibit similar patterns as Egypt, seeing a rise in social scale and other aspects of complexity in the early-mid 2nd millennium BCE within a context featuring close-packed groups of relatively small, culturally similar populations in intense competition both from each other as well as nearby nomadic populations. Later in time, we find that areas such as Cambodia and Japan remain as relatively small, disaggregated polities until the late first millennium BCE, when increasing development in a highly localized area seems to produce knock-on effects leading to increasing inter-state competition and, of course, the other developments that follow it. This process is later amplified as these increasingly large and complex societies come into contact with their even larger, more  complex  neighbors,  notably  China  in  the  case  of  Cambodia  and  Japan,  or  the  arrival  of  large European imperial states into the western Hemisphere and Polynesia. This contact initiates a new round of even sharper competition and, unsurprisingly, the imposition of a major (Eurasian-based) moralizing religious tradition and European forms of governance, or at least imperial magistrates overseeing -and superseding -local governance systems.

It is important to stress that our sample of past societies is skewed towards larger, historically-attested states in Afro-Eurasia. While we do sample societies from all major world regions, including many smallerscale, less centralized, archaeologically-attested ones, they do not form the bulk of our dataset. Our focus on Scale and MST in this article, thus, may obscure some of the important developments that occurred within societies and regions which never surpassed the MST, at least before the early modern period. For instance, IronCav appears to play a significant role in driving major Scale increases once it appears in North and South America after contact (and conflict) with European imperial powers. It is likely, though, that before  the  introduction  especially  of  horses  into  these  regions,  there  were  other  similar  militarilyimpactful technologies that drove the scale increases seen in places like Mexico and Peru, home of largescale and complex pre-contact empires like the Inca and Maya. Indeed, our results are generally consistent with the idea that smaller-scale, yet still expanding, societies adopted certain ideological and institutional features beneficial to maintaining cohesion at these increasing scales, even if the levels of MSP, Gov, and Infra demanded by expansive megasoceities seen in earlier periods across Afro-Eurasia were not needed until much later.

The analyses presented here offer novel insights into ideas that have preoccupied scholars across a host of  disciplines,  from  political  theory  and  philosophy  to  cultural  evolution  to  cognitive  psychology.  Our results are significant both for providing additional support and extending on prior findings, as well as identifying  limitations  of  several  prominent  theories.  The  case  studies  discussed  provide  additional nuance and contextualization to the general patterns explored here, revealing an intriguing potential explanation for these broad findings. Future work is needed to more fully unpack these results, but we suggest the framework and historical data compiled by the Seshat project offer a fruitful avenue for these investigations.

## Introduction


When do forcefully displaced people feel like they can return home - and to what extent are their motivations similar or different to other migrants? Latest estimates suggest that there are 108 million forcibly displaced people globally, a number that has more than doubled in the last decade (UNHCR 2022). While the majority remains internally displaced, 35.5 million had to leave their home country (UNHCR 2022), embarking into an often perilous and difficult future. And although many of these forcefully displaced people hope to establish themselves in their new host countries, many others ultimately wish to return home (Ghosn et al. 2021; Zakirova and Buzurukov 2021), since forced displacement is associated with lower mental and physical health (Zilic 2018) and significant economic hardship (Torlinska, Albani, and Brown 2020). The desirability (and feasibility) of such a return is complicated further by declining acceptance of forcefully displaced peoples and refugees in receiving countries.  Real (and often imagined) 1 costs  of  sheltering  and  integrating  refugees  into  host  societies  have  led  to  increasing polarization around the acceptance of refugees, mirroring polarization over migration more

generally  (Lönnqvist,  Ilmarinen,  and  Sortheix  2020;  Schmidt-Catran  and  Czymara  2022; Simonsen and Bonikowski 2022). The development of incentives to encourage voluntary return to the countries of origin has therefore been a focus for some time (Hatton 2020).

However, while we know a considerable amount about the factors shaping return intentions among migrants in general, we still know surprisingly little about the extent to which these factors are similar (or different) for internationally displaced peoples. On the one hand, the roots of forced displacement is often war or other forms of large-scale violent conflict, so that other factors may simply not matter. On the other hand, existing research suggests that the decision to flee in the first place appears contingent, even in highly dangerous circumstances (Adhikari 2013). Moreover, given the qualitative and observational nature of most existing research, it is difficult to determine the causal impact that home country conditions have on return intention of forcefully displaced people. In short, it remains an open question to what extent the factors identified in the general return migration literature could also apply to the return intentions of internationally displaced people.

The goal of this paper is to address this question explicitly: Focusing on individuals forcefully displaced by the war in Ukraine, we use a factorial experimental framework to compare and contrast the relative causal effects that different aspects of home country conditions have on the return intentions.


## Theory


There is a sizable literature discussing the factors that drive migration (Arango 2000; HagenZanker 2008), and return intentions of migrants in general (for an overview see (King and Kuschminder  2022)).  However,  research  on  return  intentions  of internationally  displaced people is comparatively sparse. Two competing perspectives have emerged: One focuses on peace and security and thus the unique position that displaced people face, and one that focuses on  social  and  economic  prospects  more  generally,  thus  embedding  the  return  intentions  of displaced people in the literature on return migration more generally (Alrababah et al. 2023; Camarena and Hägerdal 2020; Ghosn et al. 2021). To complicate adjudicating these different approaches  further,  most  existing  research  on  return  intentions  of  refugees  and  displaced peoples uses either qualitative research or non-experimental survey data (see (Alrababah et al. 2023) for a notable exception). As such, it is difficult to assess the causal impact that these factors have.

The first strand of the literature contends that in most cases the unique situation of displaced persons  is  not  considered  in  theoretical  development  -  even  in  theories  addressing  the circumstances  of  return.  In  particular,  most  general  theories  of  migrant  return  intentions disregard the fact that the displacement was forced in the first place, and that individuals would have to return into a country that either once persecuted them or was in a state of (civil) war (Alrababah et al. 2023). Indeed, there is some evidence that economic factors matter little for refugee return intentions, while  political factors in general, and reduction in human rights violations, violence and conflict in particular, are the primary drivers of return (Zakirova and Buzurukov 2021). Similarly, increased stability and protection from violence have been found as  key  drivers  of  return  intentions  among  Syrian  refugees  in  Germany  (Kaya  and  Orchard 2020). Focusing on displaced people's unique situation, our first hypothesis is therefore:

Hypothesis 1 - Peace Hypothesis: Return intentions of internationally displaced people is driven primarily by the end of conflict in the country of origin.

One important caveat to this hypothesis is that refugees fleeing conflicts may be hesitant to return home despite the end of conflicts, especially if "peace" was achieved through a major (military)  defeat  of  their  political,  ethnic,  or  religious  group.  While  such  a  peace  may technically  indicate  a  return  to  peaceful  conditions,  such  conditions  do  not  necessarily correspond to a return to safe conditions for the displaced person that has fled the country. Similarly, an end to the conflict itself may not provide a guarantee of future peace and security, as the likelihood of future conflict is shaped not just by conditions in their home country, but also by international context factors such as stability in the region or the support of international and supranational organizations. Our second hypothesis is therefore as follows:

Hypothesis  2  -  Political  Integration  Hypothesis: Return  intentions  of  internationally displaced people is driven by future security in the country of origin - guaranteed here through integration into supranational organizations

Although peace and future stability should be a self-evident driver of return intentionality, existing  research  suggests  that  return  intentionality  among  forcibly  displaced  people  is considerably more complex. Indeed, there is evidence that internationally displaced individuals return to their country of origin even during ongoing conflicts. Moreover, the research on return intentions  of  refugees  highlights  not  only  considerably  heterogeneity  among  the  displaced (Ghosn  et  al.  2021;  Müller-Funk  and  Fransen  2022),  but  also  the  importance  that  social attachments  and  economic  conditions  play  in  decisions  to  return  (Alrababah  et  al.  2023; Camarena  and  Hägerdal  2020;  Klinthäll  2007).  As  such,  return  intentions  may  mirror  the factors identified by the return migration literature more generally: Economic factors and social conditions in the home country. Specifically, migrants may return home for economic reasons, either  because  conditions  in  the  country  of  origin  have  improved  compared  to  the  hosting country or because the migration cycle ends because immigrants have fulfilled their goal in raising  their  economic  outlooks,  supporting  their  family  back  home,  or  have  successfully achieved  a  higher  qualification.  Forcefully  displaced  people  may  therefore  return  home  if economic conditions have improved in the home country (for an overview see Stark & Bloom,

1985).  Similarly,  social  network  theory  has  underscored  the  role  of  familial  and  social connections in return decisions, emphasizing the role of family and different family linked role relations migrants consider when deciding to move back home, especially when (close) family is considered a strong pull factor for returning home (Czeranowska et al., 2023).  Following these arguments, an alternative set of hypotheses is as follows: Hypothesis 3 - Economic Conditions: Return intentions of internationally displaced people mirror that of migrants more generally and are driven by economic conditions in their home country.

Hypothesis  4  -  Social  Conditions :    Return  intentions  of  internationally  displaced  people mirror  that  of  migrants  more  generally  and  are  driven  by social conditions  in  their  home country.

## Experimental Design


To  analyze  which  conditions,  increase  refugees'  return  intention,  we  used  a  vignette experiment  that  describes  potential  return  scenarios,  with  conditions  varying  along  five different dimensions regarding peace, social, and economic conditions (4*3*2*2*2=96 unique vignettes).  Each  respondent  received  three  vignettes  resulting  in  1,102  total  evaluated scenarios. 4

Most  importantly,  we  vary  two  aspects  shaping  peace  and  security  (Hypothesis  1  and  2): Territorial  integrity  and  integration  into  international  organizations.  To  vary  conditions  for territorial integrity, we compare the baseline scenario of ongoing hostilities with Russia to three 'peaceful' conditions: (1) Ukraine has regained its full pre-2014 territory, including Crimea, (2) Ukraine has regained its Eastern parts but not Crimea, or (3) peace but with the Donbass and Crimea now under Russian control. To vary international political integration and thus future security, we also propose different scenarios for Ukraine's status regarding the European Union. The baseline scenario is Ukraine as a neutral state, which has no formal association with the European Union, while alternative scenarios propose either (1) a special association

status  with  the  European  Union  akin  to  Norway  or  Switzerland,  or  (2)  a  guaranteed  EU membership. 5

To assess  the  impact  of  the  traditional  return  migration  literature,  economic  prospects  and social bonds  (hypothesis  3  and  4)  we  vary  economic  prospects  through  employment opportunities (low vs. high levels of unemployment in Ukraine) and the conditions of industry (destroyed and unable to be rebuilt vs. quick restoration of key industrial sectors) and social conditions  by  varying  how  many  other  Ukrainians  have  returned  (most  vs.  few).  A  full breakdown of the conditions and the vignette wordings can be found in the Supplementary Information, Table A1.

The main outcome is return intention, which asks respondents after each vignette how likely, on a scale from 0 'not at all likely' to 10 'very likely', they would be to return to Ukraine under these conditions.


## Identification Strategy


To identify the causal effect of different scenario characteristics on return intentions, we use a simple  OLS  model,  which  includes  all  dimensions  of  the  Vignette  as  explanatory  factors (Bansak et al. 2021), and with return probability as the dependent variable.  The randomization of choice characteristics allows us to determine the causal effect that each characteristic has on respondents' final choice.  To account for the use of several vignettes per respondent, we cluster standard errors at the individual level and include a control for the vignette order, i.e. whether

the vignette was asked as first, second or third option. 6 In the results section, we show Average Marginal Component Effects (AMCE) (Bansak et al. 2023), that is the average causal effect of each  choice  characteristic  on  the  final  choice,  holding  all  other  dimensions  constant. 7 All replication files were uploaded to OSF. 8

7 While  it  would  be  interesting  to  see  how  individual  level  characteristics  such  as  age, parenthood, or the level of social integration in the host country would affect the relationship between vignette characteristics and return intentions, the limited number of observations does not provide sufficient power to detect moderation effects. We also tested interactions between the peace condition and all other characteristics but did not detect any significant interaction terms.

However, our results also show that the type of peace achieved does not uniformly affect return intentions.

Similarly,  international  political  integration  also  emerges  as  an  important  driver  of  return intentions.
