## Discussion and Conclusion


When do internationally displaced peoples and refugees consider returning to their country of origin? And to what extent do these factors mirror those of migrants more generally? In general, our findings support the literature that focuses on the unique conditions that drive forceful displacement,  e.g.  security  and  political  concerns.  In  short,  peace  and  security  are  more important for return intentionality than economic factors.

However, our results also show that not all forms of peace are created equal, and that security can be created in different ways. Although our results show that compared to a scenario of ongoing conflict, most peace scenarios lead to significantly higher return intentions, peace with significant  losses  of  territory  and  the  associated  infringements  on  national  security  and sovereignty are indistinguishable to ongoing conflict regarding return intentions. Conversely, security  does  not  have  to  be  driven  by  domestic  factors.  Integration  into  international associations such as the European Union also causes increased return intentions, partially at least because such integration also provides greater security. Of course, EU integration would reduce not only the probability of future attacks, but it would also likely increase economic opportunities. Nevertheless, given the low or insignificant effects that other economic factors play, the importance of international security provisions for increased return possibilities is an important additional finding of our research.

Of course, there are several limitations to our research. First, while our experimental approach allows  us  to  identify  causal  relationships  between  scenarios  and  return  intentions,  the generalizability of our results may be limited in several important ways. Although our sample captures  a  wide  variety  of  Ukrainian  displaced  peoples  and  refugees,  our  sample  cannot guarantee  representativeness  of  all  Ukrainians,  let  alone  experiences  beyond  Ukraine. Expanding this design to other populations may provide important evidence for the overall generalizability of our findings.

Second, the vignette design and the hypothetical nature of the scenarios may create a greater disconnect  between  return  intentions  and  actual  behavior  and  may  not  capture  the  full complexity of refugees  decision-making process in real-life situations, especially  given the geopolitical  and  personal  complexities  of  their  experience.  However,  an  exploratory  data analysis of data from the subsequent fourth wave of the panel, fielded from February to April 2024 suggests that out of the 216 people that took part in both waves that live outside of Ukraine in wave 3, 18 had returned by wave 4, and that more importantly, that this correlates strongly with pre-treatment return intention measured in wave 3 (r=0.27, p < 0.001, N = 216). In other words,  stated  return  intentions  and  actual  behavior  do  appear  to  have  meaningful  relation. Nevertheless, more follow up analyses of actual behavior is clearly necessary. Additionally, this research should be combined with qualitative research on the logics underpinning refugees' return intentions, such as in-depth interviews or personal narratives. Such research would not only allow for greater insights into the decision-making process, it would also enable more realistic vignette designs for future quantitative and experimental research.

These  issues  notwithstanding,  our  results  provide  important  insights  for  researchers  and policymakers alike. Policymakers, especially in host countries and international organizations, should recognize that the decision of displaced peoples to return to their home countries is multifaceted, but that peace and security are paramount and more important than economic or social conditions. Moreover, it is important to recognize that not all forms of peace and security are created equal. The design of refugee and repatriation policies should embrace this nuance and  consider the importance  of  territorial integrity and  international integration. For researchers,  this  study  highlights  the  need  for  more  comprehensive  and  context-specific investigations into refugee return dynamics. Our paper demonstrates that simple binaries such as war vs. peace do not adequately capture the complexities of refugees' decision making, and the ways in which experimental studies can be used to tackle these complexities.

## 1 Introduction


On March 31, 2017, Netflix released the first season of its series 13 Reasons Why , a fictional drama about the aftermath of a teenage girl's suicide. The show's graphic depiction of this suicide incited controversy, with some mental health professionals warning about the potential for 'copycat' suicides (Libbey, 2018). Netflix ultimately removed this scene, but not until years later (Brito, 2019).

I present evidence that 13 Reasons Why 's release caused an increase in ER visits for intentional self-harm among teenage girls in the United States. The findings speak to

long-standing sociological debates over contagion -the idea that observing a behavior in others makes it more likely that a person will exhibit similar behavior Abrutyn and Mueller (2014b). In particular, the results support the idea that contagion is partly facilitated by perceived similarity. That is, when I view somebody else as similar to me, I am more inclined to adopt their behaviors as my own.

Suicide contagion-also called suicide suggestion or imitation -has a complicated history in sociology. In his foundational study of suicide, Durkheim (1897) dismissed Tarde's (1903) work on imitation as 'purely psychological,' and Tarde has been largely forgotten by American sociology. 1 Phillips (1974) revived sociological interest in imitative explanations of suicide, and a growing body of empirical work supports the contagion thesis Domaradzki (2021). These findings have inspired new theoretical work as well. Abrutyn and Mueller (2014b), for instance, revisit Tarde's work and show that it was more social -psychological than Durkheim suggested. They argue-compellinglythat we ought to incorporate Tarde's insights into a revised Durkheimian theory of suicide.

The empirical literature on suicide contagion, while impressive, leaves some questions unanswered. Studies largely focus on the effects of celebrity suicides-such as Robin Williams's or Marilyn Monroe's-which limits our understanding of contagion in two ways. 2 First, the behavioral models -that is, the celebrities who die by suicideare real people. This raises the question of whether fictional suicides might produce similar imitative effects. Second, celebrities are high-status, well-known, and often widely beloved. This raises the question of whether a lower-status person's suicide might produce similar imitative effects.

While some studies have examined the effect of fictional suicides, the findings are mixed (Domaradzki, 2021), and analyses suffer from different methodological shortcomings. Gould and Shaffer (1986), for instance, rely on a before-and-after design to estimate effects of television movies on suicidal behavior, which fails to account for seasonal trends in suicide. Stack et al. (2014) rely on survey data to assess the effect of cumulative exposure to movies featuring suicide on suicide attempts, but unmeasured confounding likely biases treatment effect estimates. Some studies present evidence of contagion with non-celebrity behavioral models, but these too face methodological issues. Using social network data, Abrutyn and Mueller (2014a) argue that suicidal behavior spreads across friends, but the analysis is likely affected by unmeasured confounding-as well as network-specific problems like homophily bias and partial censoring of the peer group (Shalizi and Thomas, 2011; Griffith, 2022). The present study seeks to provide more robust evidence that imitation persists when behavioral

models are fictional or low-status.


## 1.1 Prior Work on 13 Reasons Why


Bridge et al. (2020) present evidence that 13 Reasons Why 's release caused a spike in suicide mortality among teenage boys-but not girls-in April 2017. Niederkrotenthaler et al. (2019) find evidence of contagion for both boys and girls, but effect estimates for both groups are noisy, making it difficult to reliably compare the magnitudes. The results are puzzling: the contagion literature suggests the effect should be larger for girls since the show revolves around a girl's suicide. Celebrity suicides, for instance, tend to produce larger spikes in suicide mortality for people of the same gender as the celebrity (Fink et al., 2018; Domaradzki, 2021). The absence of effects for girls led some to cast doubt on Bridge et al.'s (2020) findings (e.g., Romer, 2020a; Grady, 2019).

The two studies on 13 Reasons Why raise methodological concerns as well. Both studies employ the interrupted time series (ITS) method. This procedure consists of two steps. First, we build a forecasting model for suicide mortality using data from before the show's release but not after-i.e., the pre-treatment period. Second, we use this model to predict what suicide mortality would have been in the post-treatment period absent the show's release. Consequently, the accuracy of our treatment effect estimates hinges on the accuracy of our forecaster. Romer (2020a) argues that Bridge et al.'s (2020) forecasting model failed to account for strong temporal trends in suicide. Suicide mortality for teenage boys was rising prior to the show's release, he contends, so it is plausible that mortality would have continued to rise in April 2017 absent the show's release. Media coverage of Bridge et al.'s (2020) study urged caution in drawing causal conclusions from the results (Grady, 2019; D'Zurilla, 2019).

More broadly, methodologists have put forward several critiques of ITS methods and practice. Zoorob (2020) highlights the model-dependent nature of ITS, and Berk (2021) argues that standard ITS model-selection strategies invalidate confidence intervals. Baicker and Svoronos (2019) find that ITS produces estimates that are large in magnitude, statistically significant, and of the wrong sign when applied to data from the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment. Romer (2020b) also raises concerns about the accuracy of forecasting models used in ITS studies.


## 1.2 Contributions


Three issues motivate this paper. First, we lack strong evidence about suicide contagion caused by fictional and low-status suicides. 13 Reasons Why 's release offers an opportunity to study these issues because the character who dies by suicide is not popular or high-status in her school-she is bullied and assaulted by her peers. Furthermore, the actress who plays this character-Katherine Langford-was fairly unknown prior to the show's release. This study provides evidence that the suicides of such fictional characters can affect self-harm behavior. It also indicates that previous studies on suicide

contagion-which typically restrict attention to suicide mortality-may understate the full extent of imitation effects.

Second, prior research on 13 Reasons Why introduces a puzzle: why would the show increase suicide mortality for boys but not girls? This study resolves the puzzle by changing the outcome of interest from suicide mortality to self-harm behavior, which is typically non-fatal among teen girls. More specifically, I find that the show's release caused a temporary spike in emergency room (ER) visits for self-harm among teen girls but not teen boys. The result-coupled with null effects for suicide mortality among girls-fits with a well-known gender 'paradox' in suicide: while men die by suicide more often than women, women attempt suicide more often than men (Canetto and Sakinofsky, 1998). 3

Finally, the methodological critiques of ITS in general-and of 13 Reasons Why studies in particular-motivate this project. I show how to use ITS to make credible causal claims in the absence of perfect identification. ITS, like all observational causal inference methods, requires strong identification assumptions. These assumptions almost certainly fail in any practical setting. Accordingly, I make no claim that my ITS analysis produces exactly unbiased treatment effect estimates or perfectly valid confidence intervals. Instead, I use various supplementary analyses to show that the bias is likely small and that the large, post-release spike in self-harm visits primarily reflects a causal relationship. I also import several tools from the statistics and forecasting literatures that improve upon standard ITS practice.

The paper proceeds as follows. In Section 2, I motivate the core causal question, and Section 3 clarifies the nature of the treatment. Section 4 describes the data, and Section 5 details the methodological approach. I present the main results in Section 6 along with supplementary findings that both further our understanding of the 13 Reasons Why effect and provide additional evidence that the post-release spike in self-harm visits reflects a causal relationship. Section 7 reports numerous additional analyses to address potential methodological problems underlying the results. Section 8 concludes.

A note on terminology: Throughout the paper, I use 'self-harm visits' as shorthand for 'ER visits for intentional self-harm.' When no demographic group is mentioned explicitly, I am referring to self-harm visits for teen girls.


## 2 Studying 13 Reasons Why Can Enhance Our Understanding of Suicide Contagion


I aim to answer a straightforward question: did the release of Netflix's 13 Reasons Why cause a temporary spike in ER visits for self-harm among teenage girls? The answer is important for at least three reasons. First, the answer can inform how studios portray suicide in TV and film. Second, the answer can shed light on how fictional stories

influence real-life behavior more broadly. Third, the answer can clarify the role that social status and admiration play in suicide contagion. I expand on each reason in turn.

Understanding whether 13 Reasons Why led to a spike in self-harm behavior can inform how writers and studios approach fictional portrayals of suicide, particularly for young viewers. The initial release of 13 Reasons Why was controversial precisely because of concerns about copycat suicides. The show featured a graphic depiction of suicide that was ultimately removed years later, and Netflix later added warning cards to the start of each season warning viewers about the show's themes (Brito, 2019). Concerns about suicide contagion, then, have already influenced the way Netflix presents 13 Reasons Why and have likely affected how writers and studios approach suicide. But providing more rigorous evidence of the effect in question can draw more attention to the need for such changes. Furthermore, demonstrating that the show's release affected non-fatal self-harm behavior would suggest that the show caused more harm than previously thought.

The effect of 13 Reasons Why on suicide attempts can inform the broader study of the effects of fictional stories on real-life behavior and attitudes. The effect of fictional stories on drug use and gun violence are hotly debated in the press, and finding effects for suicide contagion might shift our expectations about effects in other domains. Researchers have also examined the effect of fictional stories on political and social attitudes (Paluck, 2009). This study therefore contributes to a broader evidence base on the effects of fiction on real-life behavior and attitudes.

Popular fictional portrayals of suicide offer a way to study how social status and widespread admiration affect suicide contagion. A large literature demonstrates that widely-reported celebrity suicides cause short-term increases in suicide mortality (Fink et al., 2018; Phillips, 1974; Domaradzki, 2021). One explanation for the effect is that the deaths make the idea of suicide more acceptable and cognitively accessible to atrisk populations, such as people suffering from depression (Abrutyn and Mueller, 2014b; Patterson, 2014). Relatedly, Tankard and Paluck (2016) argues that stories influence norm perception-that is, what people think the current social norms actually are.

How celebrity suicides affect perceived acceptability remains an open question. A death might influence perceptions through the celebrity's social status or popularity. Virtually all celebrities are high-status, and many are widely adored. Alternatively, the effect could stem from personal identification with a celebrity. 4 If J views K as similar to her, and K dies by suicide, this might make the idea of suicide more acceptable or cognitively accessible to J .

Netflix's 13 Reasons Why provides an opportunity to study suicide contagion while separating the effects of social status from the effects of personal identification with the deceased. The character who dies by suicide is bullied and assaulted by her peers, and the actress playing her was not well-known prior to the show's release. Studying 13 Reasons Why , then, can shed light on how it is that widely-reported events or widely-

consumed stories can influence behavior.


## 3 What Exactly is the Treatment? Why Focus on This Subgroup?


Two issues require clarification: the nature of the treatment and the decision to focus on effects among teen girls. In short, the treatment is the show's release -not the actual watching of the show-and I focus on teen girls both to resolve the substantive puzzle raised by earlier studies and because I expect effects to be largest among this subgroup. I expand on each point below.

This study examines the effect of the show's release but not the actual watching of the show. The distinction is important: the show's release plausibly affected self-harm behavior among those who had not even seen it. Figure 1 illustrates how. Suppose that J watches the show, causing her to self-harm. J 's self-harm behavior might cause her friend, K , to self-harm as well. Thus, even if K had not watched the series, the show's release could have indirectly caused her to self-harm. Furthermore, the graph does not exhaust all possible causal pathways through which the show's release might cause J or K to self-harm. For instance, seeing social media posts about the show might cause J to talk to K about self-harm, which could in turn cause K to self-harm. 5

Clarifying the treatment raises another question: why focus specifically on effects for teen girls? As I have defined the treatment, everybody was exposed to it. Anyone could have watched 13 Reasons Why , and contagion effects could be present for any age group or gender. I focus on teen girls for two reasons, one substantive and one practical. Substantively, I hope to resolve the puzzle raised by Bridge et al. (2020):

why did we observe no mortality effects for teen girls, who should theoretically be the most susceptible to contagion effects? Practically, we are most likely to detect treatment effects among this group. Teen girls were among the most likely demographic groups to watch the show, and the literature on suicide contagion suggests that teen girls should be the most affected by the depicted death. Since ITS makes it difficult to detect small effects, I focus the analysis on teen girls.


## 4 Data


I use data from the National Emergency Department Sample (NEDS) collected by the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (HCUP) to estimate national monthly counts of emergency-room (ER) visits for intentional self-harm by girls aged 10-19. 6 These counts include fatal and non-fatal visits, but the proportion of fatal visits typically falls below 1%. 7 The NEDS is the largest survey of ER visits in the US. It contains data on approximately 30 million ED discharges per year. The data is collected through a stratified, single-stage cluster sample: HCUP constructs strata based on hospital characteristics, and, every year, takes a stratified random sample of hospitals, obtaining 100% of discharge records for each hospital. The yearly change in the sample of hospitals raises methodological concerns that I address in Sections 6 and 7.

Intentional self-harm was categorized using ICD-9 and ICD-10 diagnosis and injury codes listed under 'self-inflicted harm' by the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (2021). I included ER visits that had intentional self-harm listed for any injury or diagnosis (i.e., whether primary or secondary). Appendix A details the coding schemes for both the main analysis and supplementary analyses, and Appendix B shows that the results are robust to alternative coding schemes. National estimates were obtained using discharge-level weights in the NEDS. HCUP calculates discharge weights by dividing the total number of ER visits within a stratum by the total number of sampled ER visits within that stratum, obtaining the total number of ER visits from the American Hospital Association. Results using unweighted counts are similar (Appendix B).

I drop observations that are missing gender, age, or month of visit to obtain these counts. This typically results in a loss of approximately 15% of observations per year, with exact figures presented in Appendix C. ## 5 Methods


This section outlines the methodological approach I take. Section 5.1 motivates the interrupted time series (ITS) design in this particular study and reviews how ITS works. Section 5.2 highlights three problems with conventional ITS practice and describes the steps I take to avoid these issues.


## 5.1 When to Use ITS and How It Works


The ideal setting for ITS has three distinguishing features. First, we have a time series of an aggregate outcome for some group-such as total self-harm visits for teen girls. Second, this group becomes treated all at once at some point in time. In this case, the group becomes treated on March 31, 2017, when 13 Reasons Why is released. Recall that 'treatment' refers to the release of the show rather than the actual watching of the show (see Section 3). Finally, ITS is most appealing when we lack data on a plausible control group-or when plausible control groups exhibit different trends and seasonality than the treated group. 8

ITS is especially useful in such settings because it requires no data on a control group. The core insight of the method is that we can use the treated group's pretreatment outcomes to predict its counterfactual outcomes in the post-treatment period, as shown in Figure 2. To begin an ITS analysis, we select a forecasting model and fit it to the pre -treatment series-in this case, the series of self-harm visits prior to 13 Reason Why 's release. We then use this model to forecast outcomes for the post -treatment period-the period immediately following the show's release. Finally, we compare these forecasted post-treatment outcomes with the observed post-treatment outcomes. The intuition is that the model can predict what would have happened in the absence of treatment since it was built using observations that had not yet been exposed to the treatment.

We can describe this procedure more formally with potential outcomes notation. Our goal is to estimate the causal effect of releasing 13 Reasons Why on the number

of self-harm visits among teenage girls. Y t (1) represents the number of self-harm visits we would observe in period t had 13 Reasons Why been released that period, and Y t (0) represents the number of ER visits we would observe in period t absent 13 Reasons Why 's release. We define the causal effect in period t as τ t = Y t (1) -Y t (0)-the difference between the potential outcome under treatment in period t and the potential outcome under control in period t .

Used to train forecasting model

The fundamental problem of causal inference is that we observe only one of these two potential outcomes in any given period. From January 2006 to March 2017-the pre-treatment period-we observe only Y t (0). In April 2017, we observe only Y t (1). The ITS solution is to use the pre-treatment series to build a forecasting model for the potential outcomes under control, Y t (0). We can then use this model to impute Y t (0) for the post-treatment period. We then estimate our treatment effect as ˆ τ t = Y t (1) -p Y t (0), where Y t (1) is observed and p Y t (0) is estimated from our forecasting model.

ITS relies on two central assumptions (Morgan and Winship, 2015). First, we assume that we can recover the correct model specification for the potential outcomes under control. This is a strong assumption that will virtually always be violated in practice. Second, we assume that this model specification remains unaltered in the post-treatment period. This latter assumption might be violated in the presence of

concurrent changes that affect the outcome-that is, concurrent treatments. 9 For instance, if a beloved celebrity died by suicide the same month as 13 Reasons Why was released, we would be unable to separate the effects of show from the effects of the celebrity death.


## 5.2 Improving the ITS Design


This subsection describes three problems with conventional ITS practice and offers three potential solutions. In this particular application, the methodological improvements change the results very little, so uninterested readers may skip to Section 6 without much loss of understanding. Appendix E more thoroughly outlines the approach.

Critics have identified (at least) three problems with standard ITS practice. First, Romer (2020a) points out that practitioners may fail to account for trends and seasonality in the data. Failing to account for an upward secular trend in self-harm visits may lead us to underestimate the counterfactual outcome in the post-treatment period and overestimate the treatment effect of 13 Reasons Why .

Second, Berk (2021) recognizes a more subtle problem with current practice. Researchers typically use the pre-treatment time series to both select and estimate a forecasting model. For instance, we might fit many models to the pre-treatment series of self-harm visits and select one according to AIC or time-series cross-validation. We then use this same data to estimate the model parameters and forecast the counterfactual outcomes. The problem is that the selected model may overfit the data, generating artificially small residuals and producing prediction intervals that are too narrow. Re-using data in this manner can thus invalidate prediction intervals. 10

The third and most fundamental problem with ITS is that the selected model will almost always be misspecified, generating bias and invalidating conventional confidence intervals. With potentially infinite reasonable models to choose from, it is exceedingly improbable that we select the true specification-which may be too complex to reliably estimate, anyway. 11 The first two problems can be seen as a special case of this one, but they are worth discussing separately: even when we account for trends and avoid re-using data, our model will likely be misspecified.

I use several tools to circumvent these problems, summarized in Table 1. To account for trends and seasonality, I perform all analyses on data that has been firstand seasonally-differenced. 12 Visual inspection and statistical tests suggest the data are stationary after this double-differencing.

Table 1: Methodological improvements to standard ITS practice. Methodological practices I follow for the main ITS analysis. I describe my approach in more detail in Appendix E. A supplementary analysis uses sample-splitting to further guard against overfitting, and the findings are similar (Appendix B).

I employ two strategies to avoid overfitting. First, I use national monthly suicide mortality data from the CDC as an exploratory dataset to test a wide variety of forecasting models. The logic is that suicide mortality data exhibits similar seasonality and trends to the self-harm data without sharing any idiosyncratic randomness. I assess model fit using time-series cross-validation and find that AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) models with no additional covariates (e.g., monthly economic indicators) outperform others. I use the auto.arima() function in R , which selects the order of the ARIMA model using AIC-guided stepwise selection (Hyndman and Khandakar, 2008). I only run ARIMA models on the self-harm data, and I only use specifications chosen by this stepwise selection algorithm.

Second, I employ the main ITS analysis with and without sample-splitting. For the split-sample analysis, I use the first half of the differenced pre-treatment series to select a model specification using stepwise selection and then use the second half to estimate the model parameters with the chosen specification. Results of the analysis are extremely similar regardless of whether sample-splitting is used, and simulations suggest that, when conducting stepwise selection with no added covariates, using the entire pretreatment series improves predictive accuracy without undercovering (Appendix F). All analyses use the entire pre-treatment series to both select and fit the model unless otherwise specified.

Finally, to address model misspecification, I use conformal predictive inference, which can provide exact prediction (and confidence) intervals even when the model is misspecified (Shafer and Vovk, 2008; Lei et al., 2018; Chernozhukov et al., 2021). In particular, I employ Chernozhukov et al.'s (2021) procedure, which extends the standard conformal approach to the time-series setting. 13 As a result, even if ITS treatment effects are biased, we can still construct valid confidence intervals for the treatment ef-

fect. 14 Conformal inference ensures that, even when our model is wrong, it can still be useful. This shifts the goal of the analysis from unbiased treatment effect estimation to valid inference (i.e., confidence intervals) for the treatment effect. In this setting, the conformal inference prediction intervals and the standard ARIMA intervals are virtually identical. I briefly walk through the mechanics and assumptions behind conformal inference in Appendix E.

## 6.2 Understanding the 13 Reasons Why Effect


In this section, I present results from two additional analyses. The first explores the duration of the treatment effect, and the second examines forms of self-harm used during the post-treatment period. I find that the effect persists for two months, which is consistent with Niederkrotenthaler et al.'s (2019) finding that social media posts about the show had largely dissipated by June 2017. I also find that ER visits for cutting-the method of suicide portrayed in 13 Reasons Why -are particularly high in the post-treatment period.

These analyses serve two purposes. First, they help us better understand the 13 Reasons Why effect. The imitation of method, for instance, suggests that the effect may operate through similar mechanisms as celebrity effects. Second, the results make us more confident that the post-release spike in self-harm visits largely reflects a causal effect. While the estimated treatment effects are imprecise and likely biased, the additional evidence makes it more difficult to believe that model misspecification or concurrent changes can explain the entire post-release rise in self-harm visits.


## 6.2.1 The Treatment Effect Persists for Two Months


To assess the duration of the treatment effect, I use the fitted ARIMA model from Section 6.1 to forecast 4 months ahead with 95% prediction intervals. The prediction intervals are constructed using bootstrapped residuals because the conformal inference approach of Chernozhukov et al. (2021) does not easily extend to the multi-step-ahead setting. The post-treatment observations are not used for these forecasts since the goal is to forecast the potential outcomes under control.

Figure 5 plots the results. The observed counts of self-harm visits are much higher than the forecasted values in April and May. In June and July, however, the observed counts are close to the forecasted values and well within the prediction intervals. A duration of two months is consistent with findings from Niederkrotenthaler et al. (2019). They find that social media posts related to 13 Reasons Why were highest in April 2017 and had largely dissipated by June 2017.

Two factors could explain why these durations align. First, social media activity serves as a proxy for public interest in the show. Second, social media coverage of the show might mediate the effect of the show's release on self-harm visits (see Figure 1). That is, viewing social media posts related to the show may trigger self-harm behavior even among people who have not watched it. The analysis provides no direct evidence of mediation, but the results suggest we should not rule it out.

The findings also shed doubt on competing, non-causal stories about the post-release spike in self-harm visits. Consider the idea that model misspecification explains the gap between observed and forecasted counts in April and May. Why, then, are the forecasts for June and July so accurate? And why does the duration of the apparent treatment effect happen to align with 13 Reasons Why -related social-media activity? The results

## 7 Addressing Methodological Concerns


In section, I address potential methodological problems that might undermine the results, such as model dependence, invalid prediction intervals, anticipation effects, and differential measurement error. The discussion reinforces the study's main thesis: while treatment effect estimates likely suffer from some degree of bias, the causal effect of 13 Reasons Why 's release probably explains the vast majority of the post-release spike in self-harm visits. Indeed, results in Section 7.2 suggest that some ER visits for intentional cutting may have been misclassified as accidental, leading us to underestimate the effect of the show on self-harm visits.


## 7.1 April and May 2017 Forecasts are Virtually Unaffected by Alternative Post-Treatment-Period Cutoffs


The canonical ITS setup requires a clean separation between pre- and post-treatment periods. The unit is untreated in one period and becomes treated in the next. The 13 Reasons Why promotional period complicates this separation. On March 1, 2017, a month before the show came out, Netflix began promoting the show's first season,

and a trailer for the show began airing (Bridge et al., 2020). Because the widespread promotion plausibly affected self-harm behavior, we might think of March 2017 as a 'partially treated' period.

If March 2017 represents a partially treated period-rather than a true control period-it poses two problems for the analysis. Second, even if the observation is not used to select a model, an autoregressive model will use March's count of self-harm visits to forecast April's count of self-harm visits. The model is built to forecast a future control outcome using a past control outcome, but using March means we are using a partially treated outcome to forecast a control outcome. Appendix G provides a more formal discussion of these problems.

Fortunately, using March 2017 to select a model-or forecast April 2017's count of self-harm visits-matters very little. ## 7.2 ER Visits for Accidental Cutting and Poisoning are Not Especially Low in April or May 2017


The central causal claim I have advanced is that the release of the show 13 Reasons Why temporarily increased self-harm behavior among teen girls. But there is a competing story we can tell about the data: the show's release could have caused physicians to misclassify accidental cuttings and poisonings as intentional. 20 If a doctor's awareness of 13 Reasons Why increased her propensity to classify a particular drug overdose as intentional, we might see a rise in ER visits for 'intentional' self-harm in the absence of any change in actual self-harm behavior. In short, 13 Reasons Why may have changed doctors' behavior rather than girls'.

To explore this possibility, I compare ER visits for intentional and accidental injuries. Specifically, I focus on ER visits for poisoning and contact with sharp objects among teen girls, which make up roughly 97% of intentional self-harm visits for teen girls in April 2017. The ICD-10-CM classifies poisonings and contact with sharp objects as either accidental, intentional, or of undetermined intent. If the data reflect a change in doctors' behavior, we would expect the rise in 'intentional' poisonings to be coupled with a decline in poisonings coded as accidental or of undetermined intent. 21 Figure 8

## 7.3 Prediction Intervals Show Good but Imperfect Coverage in Repeated Placebo Tests


Conformal prediction intervals rely on weaker assumptions than conventional prediction intervals, but these assumptions might still be violated. 22 One way to assess the validity of the intervals is with a repeated placebo test procedure. More precisely, this procedure will assess the validity of conformal intervals when we have used the data to select the model. We can thus see it as assessing the validity of the ITS method (as implemented in this study) as a whole.

To understand the logic of this procedure, consider one placebo test in isolation. First, we select an ARIMA model using the first half of the pre-treatment data-that is, the first 61 first- and seasonally-differenced periods. Call this the training period. Next, we fit the chosen model to these 61 periods. Finally, we use the fitted model to forecast the 62nd period's count of self-harm visits with a 95% conformal prediction interval. Call the 62nd period the test period.

This test period is pre-treatment, and thus represents a potential outcome under control. Consequently, the observed count should lie within the prediction interval with probability 0.95. If the prediction interval fails to cover the observed count of self-harm

visits, we might doubt the validity of the intervals. If the prediction interval covers the observed count, we will say that the ITS method passes the placebo test.

Conducting just one placebo test, however, fails to provide an accurate picture of how well our prediction intervals cover. For instance, if nominal 95% prediction intervals cover the truth only 80% of the time, they are invalid but still provide a high probability of passing the placebo test. To better gauge the performance of these intervals, we can repeat this placebo test many times.

To repeat the test, I iteratively expand the training period, refitting the ARIMA model each time (but without changing the specification chosen for the initial test). For instance, the second placebo test fits the ARIMA model to the first 62 periods and forecasts the 63rd period with 95% prediction intervals. The third placebo test fits the ARIMA model to the first 63 periods and forecasts the 64th period, and so on. I repeat this procedure until I reach the post-treatment period. Figures 9 and 10 plot the placebo test results alongside the estimated treatment effect in the post-treatment period for comparison. Note that the black lines in Figure 9 represent out-of-sample predictionsthey are forecasted using models that were selected and fit using only previous time periods. The confidence intervals in Figure 10 are computed by subtracting the upper and lower limits of the prediction intervals from the observed count of self-harm visits as in Chernozhukov et al. (2021).

The plots depict seven missed observations, but one of these occurs in August 2014, when Robin Williams died by suicide. Excluding this period, the conformal prediction intervals miss six out of 60 (10%) of observed values. This performance is neither stellar nor terrible. The intervals are likely invalid, but they do not severely undercover. Appendix B includes results with different block sizes. 90% conformal intervals with a block size of 3 appear to overcover, failing only 3 of 61 placebo tests. The estimated treatment effect in the post-treatment still maintains statistical significance with this block size.

Three additional facts about the placebo test results are worth noting. First, the effect estimate for April 2017 is larger in magnitude than any placebo test estimateincluding the estimate following Robin Williams's suicide. Thus, while the prediction intervals may undercover, the placebo test procedure suggests that the count of ER visits in April 2017 is the most unusual of the bunch. 23 Second, the absolute mean of the 60 placebo effect estimates is approximately 6.5-quite close to zero considering the estimated standard deviation of the placebo estimates is roughly 418. This provides some assurance that our method for estimating treatment effects is nearly unbiased. Finally, the performance of the placebo tests seems to improve as the size of the training period grows, making us more confident in the main treatment effect estimate.

Figure 15 shows that the effect estimate in April 2017, the post-treatment month, is unusually large relative to the distribution of pre-treatment effect estimates. Across all three control groups, the April 2017 estimate is near the 95th percentile of the pre-treatment point estimates.

## 7.7 A Causal Effect of 13 Reasons Why Remains the Most Plausible Explanation for the Post-Release Spike in SelfHarm Visits

Before concluding, it is worth briefly reviewing the evidence presented in this study. While the ITS estimator is likely biased, placebo tests on plausible control groups-and on pre-treatment data for teen girls-indicate the bias is probably small (Sections 6.1 and 7.3). ER visits for intentional cutting are particularly high in April and May 2017, matching the method of suicide depicted in 13 Reasons Why , and the treatment effect persists for two months, consistent with show-related social media activity (Section 6.2). Self-harm visits for teen girls show slight elevation prior to the show's release, but this was plausibly caused by Netflix's promotion of the series. Skeptics of such a promotional effect, however, need not worry: an unusually high count of self-harm visits in March 2017 should prompt our model to forecast an even higher value for April 2017, not lower. Furthermore, both model residuals and careful inspection of the raw data suggest that April and May's counts are far more unusual than March's (Sections 7.4 and 7.5). Finally, self-harm visits return to expected levels by June 2017 (Section 6.2). If the elevated counts in April and May merely reflect secular trends in the outcome, such a return would represent an extraordinary coincidence.


## 8 Conclusion


In this study, I presented evidence that the release of 13 Reasons Why led to a temporary spike in the number of ER visits for intentional self-harm among teenage girls. The study provides new evidence that fictional stories can affect suicide attempts, contributing to literatures on both suicide contagion and the effects of fiction on behavior. It provides additional support for theories of suicide that emphasize the importance of imitation, a view Durkheim famously rejected (Abrutyn and Mueller, 2014b). In contrast to work on celebrity suicides, this study shows that the deceased need not be high-status or widely admired to prompt imitation effects. Furthermore, the imitation of method suggests that cognitive accessibility may partly explain suicide contagion.

The study also showcases how to make credible causal claims when data is imperfect and identification assumptions are violated. ITS requires implausibly strong assumptions, and measurement error likely affects the time series of self-harm visits. Accordingly, I make no claim that treatment effect estimates are exactly unbiased or confidence intervals perfectly valid. Instead, I show through a series of supplementary

analyses that a causal effect of 13 Reasons Why 's release remains the most plausible explanation of the large post-release spike in self-harm visits.

Researchers sometimes avoid making explicit causal claims even when methodological choices-such as conditional on many confounders-presuppose causal goals (Hill, 2015; Hern´n, 2018; Spirling and Stewart, 2022). a The practice stems from the valid concern that causal identification assumptions are probably violated in most observational studies. But explicitly acknowledging our causal goals-and that our causal effect estimates are likely biased-opens the door to a more fruitful exercise: conducting additional analyses that diagnose how severe this bias might be (Rosenbaum, 2015; Hill and Hoggatt, 2018). Suicide contagion provides an ideal case for such an exercise since controlled randomization is prohibited in this setting. In this study, results suggest the bias is likely small, allowing us to say that 13 Reasons Why probably did cause an increase in ER visits for self-harm among teen girls.

## 1. Introduction


Having a great interest in experimental research that develops new interventions to make tourists behave in more sustainable ways (Dolnicar, 2020), we were very excited to see a paper published in Tourism Management that asked the provocative question: “Can colored sidewalk nudge city tourists to walk?” (Chen, Lehto, Lehto, & Day, 2023). The title of the article suggested that the study would deploy nudging interventions and measure whether they have an impact on how much tourists walk. With great interest we read the article and were delighted to find that the authors set out to “investigate how to nudge tourists to walk under an urban context” (p. 2). Jumping straight to the conclusions section, we found that the study “lends empirical evidence for how environmental cues can encourage city tourists to stay active” (p. 8) and that the study “suggests several effective ways to nudge city tourists to walk” (p. 10). A closer look at the methods section, however, revealed that neither of those statements were accurately reflecting the research findings because walking behaviour was never observed. Rather, self-reported interest in walking served as the dependent variable in this survey experiment. The authors were not trying to conceal this; they explained their research design clearly, yet, throughout the paper they made statements that overreached the scope of the study.

We sincerely apologize to the authors for using their paper as an example. It is a great paper, which we have thoroughly enjoyed reading because it offers such a creative new solution that may indeed have the potential to influence environmentally significant behaviour as well as to increase physical activity. We could have chosen any of 28 experimental papers published in Tourism Management, the Journal of Travel Research or Annals of Tourism Research in 2022 that included statements, which were not accurately reflecting the permissible conclusions given the research design. And there is no doubt that we ourselves have also used misleading language. For example, the first author overstated the clinical implications of a cross-sectional self-report study on the association between emotional difficulties and self-injury by stating “The results highlight the clinical utility of building emotional acceptance (i.e., decreasing experiential avoidance) specifically for men in the treatment of self-injury” (Greene, Hasking, & Boyes, 2019, pp. 464). Unintentionally, this statement implies a clinical trial was conducted that measured self-injury pre-treatment and post-treatment - which it was not. This commentary is not specifically about the article written by Chen and colleagues. It was the study by Chen and colleagues, however, which raised the following question for us: how often do we as tourism scholars give readers the impression – in the title of an article, in its abstract, in the conclusions section or in the managerial implications section – that our findings are more powerful than they are? This is the question we investigate empirically in this commentary.


## 3. Methodology


As the starting point for our investigation, we used articles published in 2022 or in-press to be published in upcoming issues of Tourism Management, the Journal of Travel Research or Annals of Tourism Research as of the 1st of December 2022. To be included in our study, an article had to comply with the following criteria: (1) it had to be an experimental study that aimed to change at least one behaviour or behavioural intention, and (2) it had to measure at least one behaviour or behavioural intention. Experimental studies that included only proxy measures (e.g., eye tracking or skin conductance) or emotion-based measurement (e.g., self-report anxiety or facial muscle analysis) or evaluation (e.g., satisfaction with service) were excluded. Also excluded were cross-sectional survey studies with no experimental manipulation, reviews, and qualitative enquires. We first screened papers at abstract level and removed irrelevant studies. The remaining articles were analysed at full-text level for compliance with our selection criteria.

Sixty articles complied with these criteria. We inspected in detail the research design of each of those studies and classified each study in one of the following categories: (1) survey experiment, (2) laboratory experiment, (3) retrospective natural field study and (4) field study. If a paper contained multiple experiments, it was coded based on the study with the strongest research design with respect to the ability to derive valid, causal, and generalisable conclusions (Viglia & Dolnicar, 2020); field studies ranked first in strength, followed by retrospective natural studies, laboratory experiments and survey experiment. We did not identify any natural field studies that were not retrospective.

Next, we coded whether the paper measured (1) behavioural intentions or (2) actual behaviours. Imaginary-scenario based experiments where the participant had to make a choice from a series of options, such as choosing a meal from a menu or a hotel for an imaginary holiday, were coded as intentions. Finally, the title, abstract, aims, methods, results, discussion, and implications sections were coded for misleading language. Specifically, we coded if the language used indicated actual behaviour, and, if so, whether such statements were permissible given the data collected by the authors. For example, the title “Effect of Time Pressure on Tourism: How to Make Non-impulsive Tourists Spend More” (Li et al., 2022) implies that the study had measures real tourist spending and attempted to develop an intervention to increase real spending. Yet, the research design clarifies that the self-reported impulse purchase intentions served as the dependent variable. Many articles switched between referring to behavioural intentions and actual behaviour when describing their own study. A section of a paper was coded as having misleading language even if it occurred only in one or two sentences. Considering that people tend to skim academic articles, one sentence is enough to cause misinterpretations of the findings.


## 4. Results and discussion


The first key insight is that survey studies continue to dominate tourism research, as shown in Figure 1. This is unsurprising in view of the ever-increasing publication pressure academic researcher face, especially early career researcher. It is surprising, however, in view of the substantial technological progress made over the past decade, which enables researcher to obtain data from a much wider range of sources, including behavioural data from secondary sources and behavioural data collected specifically for the purpose of the study, such as GPS tracking (e.g., Shoval & Isaacson, 2007; Hardy, Vorobjovas-Pinta, Wells, Grimmer, & Grimmer, 2022) and psychophysiological measures (e.g., Li, Walters, Packer, & Scott, 2018). Despite these opportunities, only 10% of the articles included in this review collected data in a laboratory (e.g., Ying, Tang, Ye, Tan, & Wei, 2022; Zhao, Wong, Tong, Li, & Xiong, 2022) and less than 2% collected data in real-life contexts (e.g., Lv, Lu, Xu, Sun, & Yang, 2022). Fewer than 4% of studies used secondary data to conduct retrospective natural experiments (e.g., Leung, Wu, & Sun, 2022; Kapoor, Balaji, Jiang, & Jebarajakirthy, 2022).

The second key finding – illustrated in Figure 2 – is that most empirical articles (95%) measure stated behavioural intentions; only 5% measure actual behaviour. It is much easier, of course, much more convenient, and much cheaper to measure stated behavioural intentions than to measure actual behaviour, but it is also less informative, undermining substantially the ability to generalise conclusions to actual behaviour. Just because people express a greater interest in walking, for example, does not mean that they will in fact walk more. The only way to determine if a specific intervention will increase actual walking behaviour is to observe people walking, either by watching them or by monitoring them with a GPS tracker, for example.

It is becoming easier to measure actual behaviour. Much travel-related behaviour manifests online and, as such, is accessible. Additionally, technology, such as GPS tracking makes it more feasible today to measure actual movement. Traditional observation, of course, always remains a viable option. Yet, the publication patterns we observed in our review suggests that, collectively, we have settled on accepting behavioural intentions as a good enough substitute for behaviour. This is concerning because there is an entire body of work that shows how large the gap between stated intentions and actual behaviour can be in general (e.g., Nguyen, Faulkner, Yang, Williams, & Tong, 2022; Webb & Sheeran, 2006), and in tourism specifically (Karlsson & Dolnicar, 2016). But, if indeed, collectively, we accept stated behavioural intentions as a dependent variable in some instances, then we must ensure to accurately report findings. Our findings then only predict stated behavioural intentions, with the translation rate to actual behaviour unknown.

Finally, and this relates directly to the initial question we asked ourselves: do authors accurately represent the findings of their studies throughout the manuscript. To answer this question, we analysed in detail the full article and identified any sections that make statements about a measured behaviour (intention) that were not backed by the research design. For example, if a paper studied the effect of colouring the sidewalk on the self-reported stated interest in walking, and the authors concluded that colouring sidewalks is a good practical measure cities can take to increase physical activity, this latter statement is not permissible, and we coded it as such. As can be seen in Figure 3, nearly half (47%) of the articles under study made misleading statements about behaviour at least once in the article.  Looking specifically at the sections in which such misleading statements occur, we conclude that, most frequently, inaccurate statements are made in the title, followed by the discussion section and the abstract. This is unfortunate because the title and the abstract, arguably, are the most read parts of any academic article. It is particularly important, therefore, that those sections contain no misleading statements and allow the reader to understand clearly what has been done and, as a result, which conclusions can legitimately be drawn from the research.

Titles were classified as misleading if they mislabelled behavioural intentions as actual behaviour in their title or used causal language that implied the study contained an experiment that impacted actual behaviour (e.g., “Gamified environmental interpretation as a strategy for improving tourist behaviour in support of sustainable tourism: The moderating role of psychological distance”; Frías-Jamilena, Fernández-Ruano, & Polo-Peña, 2022). We also note, many authors did provide clear titles that could not be misinterpreted (e.g., “Mitigating Tourism Social Costs during a Pandemic: Evaluating Residents’ Perceptions and Behavioral Intentions”; Li, Li, Song, & Chen, 2022).

In the abstract, 22% of the reviewed articles used misleading language when referring to behaviour or behaviour intentions. Chan and Gohery (2022), for example, state that “higher perceived control manifests in travel behavior in the form of fewer perceived risks while traveling” (p. 1), although only behavioural intentions were measured. The authors use correct language throughout the remainder of the abstract “We observe that powerless (vs. powerful) participants perceive greater control (Experiment 2) and fewer risks while traveling (Experiment 3) when the destination is anthropomorphized, explaining their higher travel intentions (Experiments 1–3)” (p. 1).

The rate of misleading information in the aims and/or hypotheses section was relatively low (18%). Typically, intention-based studies coded as misleading did not specify behavioural intentions in their hypotheses “Conservative consumers are less likely than liberal consumers to stay at hotels that have donated rooms to homeless people” (Bae, 2023, p. 3). This study measures an individual’s intention/preference to stay in one room over other hotels or willingness to stay at a specific hotel but not their actual hotel stays.

Misleading language in the methods was less common; most authors stated accurately whether they measured intentions or behaviours. Nevertheless, in some instances, language is misleading even in the methods section (17%). For example, a survey scenario study that investigated the impact of pro-customer deviance on customer citizenship behavioural (intentions) failed to state throughout the methods section that their measure was not actual behaviour but rather intentions: “Five items measuring customer citizenship behaviour were adapted from Yi and Gong (2013) (e.g., If I have a useful idea on how to improve service, I let the employee know; I will recommend this hotel to others)” (Hu, Ma, Xu, & Liu, 2022, p. 6). Further, the terms field study or field experiment were used by some authors when describing their methods to refer to field surveys where participants were recruited at a tourist location, but the actual experiment took the form of survey study. A clearer term in this case would be “field survey experiment” if the authors wish to distinguish it from an online survey experiment.

Mirroring findings relating to the methods section, authors rarely use misleading language when reporting on the results (15%). Exceptions exist. For example, Li, Wang, and Li (2022) conducted a laboratory study that manipulated the effect of time pressure on impulse buying (intentions). It was clear from the methods that actual impulse buying was not measured “You find a nice local product which you would expect to cost around 90 RMB. But the actual price of this product is 139 RMB. Please indicate the tendency that you would buy this product.” (Li et al., p.6) but in the results the authors consistency used the term impulse buying without specifying intentions (e.g., The results confirmed the main effect of time pressure on impulse buying was significant”; p.7).

About a quarter of the reviewed studies used misleading language in the discussion section of their manuscripts. Most of these referred to behaviour rather than intentions (e.g., “The current study lends empirical evidence for how environmental cues can encourage city tourists to stay active”; Chen et al., p. 8). Authors who conducted intention studies typically did not overstate their implications (18%), often using tentative language around what their intervention could mean for real world behaviour. However, some authors did make claim implications beyond intentions. For example, a study by Karl et al. (2022) that manipulated episodic memory to increase travellers’ intentions towards holiday accommodations stated in their managerial implications that “A big picture implication for tourism and hotel managers is that engaging potential travelers in affective forecasting has direct effects on their attitudes and behaviour, especially in times of a pandemic” (p. 16). This claim is not permissible given the research design implemented.


## 6. Conclusions, recommendations and limitations of the study


Empirical studies cannot draw conclusions that are not supported by the implemented research design. Studies that measure behavioural intentions, for example, cannot validly draw conclusions about actual behaviour. We conducted this review with the aim of identifying how commonly we, collectively as tourism researchers, use imprecise language about behaviour or behavioural intentions. Almost half the empirical articles published in 2022 in three of the leading tourism journals (47%) contained misleading statements in at least one section. Because readers may not read the entire article, instead skimming the article, or focusing on the abstract and conclusions, it is critically important that statements made throughout the entire article are supported by the empirical data collected. It is particularly important for titles, abstracts and conclusions because they are the most read parts of manuscripts.

We also recommend caution to authors when using the term “field experiment”. Some authors , refer to survey experiments as field studies or field experiments because they recruited participants for their study at a specific tourist location. The authors did not intend to mislead readers into thinking they conducted a field experiment; they clearly describe the use of survey materials and manipulations in the methods. Nevertheless, a reader skimming the methods section might see the term field study and assume actual behaviour was measured. We suggest the terms “field survey experiment” or “location-based survey study” if authors wish to distinguish this approach from other types of online survey experiments.

## This review study has several limitations. The articles were coded by one person with a psychology degree and English as her native language, which may have influenced coding. Her interpretation of the language used in an article may not be equivalent to others from different cultural backgrounds and/or disciplines and/or have English as their second language. We do not expect any potential bias resulting from this leading to substantially different insights. Also, for feasibility, we restricted our search to studies published in three of the leading tourism journals internationally and to the year 2022 only. Our results, therefore, reflect this section of the literature. Furthermore, in this study, our focus was on language surrounding behaviour and behaviour intentions. However, as highlighted by Olaussen, Abetz, Qin, Mitra and O’Reilly (2022) in their review of misleading language used in conclusions not supported by evidence in the medical literature, misleading language around null findings are also of concern. In fact, they found that 10% of authors used inaccurate language to describe null findings (Olaussen et al., 2022). Future reviews could investigate whether this is also an issue for the tourism literature.

## Introduction



## Background


The integration of technology in education has revolutionized the way students learn and acquire new knowledge. An emerging area of interest is the use of video games for educational purposes. Therefore, it is important to consider the impact of such games, the types of games that are most effective, and  students' perceptions of  games in the  language learning environment. Video games, traditionally perceived as mere sources of entertainment, have shown potential in enhancing cognitive and language skills. Therefore, this study explores the efficacy of video games in aiding vocabulary acquisition among Saudi university students, aiming to provide empirical evidence  for  the  educational  value  of  video  games.  Furthermore,  video  games  provide  an interactive and engaging platform catering to various learning styles, making them an attractive alternative to  traditional learning  methods.  The  immersive  environments and  contextualized language used in video games can offer learners practical applications of new vocabulary in realtime scenarios. As digital natives, today's students are increasingly comfortable with technology, and leveraging video games for education can bridge the gap between entertainment and learning, as shown in a systematic review on the use of video games for academic learning by Martinez et al (2022).

Given the increasing globalization and the importance of English as a global lingua franca, innovative methods to improve language proficiency are essential. Furthermore, this study seeks to understand not only the quantitative impact of video games on vocabulary learning but also the qualitative experiences of students engaging with this medium.

## Main Aim and Significance

The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the impact of video games on vocabulary acquisition among Saudi university students. Additionally, the study aims to identify students' perceptions  and  preferences  regarding  using  video  games  for  educational  purposes,  thereby providing insights into the potential of integrating video games into language learning curricula. This research is particularly significant in Saudi Arabia, where traditional educational methods predominate and  there  is  a  growing  need  for  innovative approaches  to  engaging  students in learning. Traditional methods often rely heavily on rote memorization and passive learning, which can lead to disengagement and a lack of practical language skills (Al-Seghayer 2021).

By  investigating the  role  of  video  games  in  vocabulary  learning,  this  study  aims  to contribute to the existing body of knowledge and offer practical implications for educators and policymakers  in  the  region.  It  highlights  the  potential  for  a  shift  towards  more  active  and experiential learning methodologies that can better prepare students for real-world communication challenges. Additionally, this  study addresses the  gap  in  research specifically focused  on  the Middle Eastern context, providing insights that are culturally and regionally relevant.

## Research Questions

The following research questions form the focus of this study:

- 1.      Do video games facilitate vocabulary acquisition among Saudi university students?
- 2.      What types of video games are most effective for vocabulary learning?

3.      How do students perceive the use of video games in their language learning process? The findings of this study could pave the way for curriculum designers to incorporate more engaging and effective learning tools, ultimately enhancing the educational outcomes in the

## Literature Review



## Theoretical Framework


The study is grounded in two key theoretical frameworks: Mayer's Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning and Krashen's Input  Hypothesis. Mayer's theory posits that people learn more effectively when  words and images are presented together rather than separately (Mayer 2024). This multimedia learning approach suggests that video games which combine visual and auditory stimuli, can enhance vocabulary acquisition by providing a rich contextual environment. Krashen's Input Hypothesis emphasizes the importance of exposure to comprehensible input in second language acquisition, arguing that language learners acquire new vocabulary when exposed to language slightly above their current proficiency level.

Video games can provide such comprehensible input engagingly and interactively, which can be particularly beneficial for learners who might struggle with traditional learning methods. Mayer (2024) recommends conducting research in  natural learning environments, such  as the current study, to examine the effectiveness of multimedia learning in relation to its 'practical role in improving instruction and training' (Mayer 2024 p.8). In  addition, Hartt et al (2020 p.590) explain that students can be motivated as 'In the classroom, one important advantage is the ability of games and game-based activities to entice internal learning motivation by introducing various 'joyful' elements.' Furthermore, in their research with undergraduate students, they found that 'students favored and were more engaged in the game-based lecture' (Hartt et al., 2020 p.589).


## Video Games and Language Learning


Video games offer an immersive environment that requires players to follow instructions, solve problems, and interact with characters, all of which can facilitate language practice. Several studies have highlighted the potential of video games in language learning. For instance, Peterson (2016) found that massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs)  can enhance second language learners' communicative competence by providing opportunities for meaningful interaction in a target language context. Additionally, Reinders and Wattana (2015) demonstrated that digital games could increase learners' motivation and reduce language anxiety, contributing to  more  effective language  learning. These  interactive elements make  video  games  an  ideal medium for practicing language skills in a low-stress environment.


## Vocabulary Acquisition


Vocabulary acquisition is a critical component of language learning, as a rich vocabulary base allows learners to communicate more effectively and comprehend written and spoken texts. Research  has  shown  that  repeated  exposure  to  vocabulary  in  various  contexts  can  improve retention and understanding. Nation (2001) emphasizes that vocabulary knowledge involves not only the ability to recognize and recall words, but also the ability to use them appropriately in different contexts.  Video  games,  with  their  interactive and  contextualized language  use,  can provide  such  repeated  and  varied  exposure,  making  them  a  valuable  tool  for  vocabulary acquisition.

In  addition, deHaan, Reed, and Kuwada (2010) found that playing a music video game significantly improved learners' recall of new vocabulary compared to traditional study methods. Similarly, Miller and Hegelheimer (2006) reported that students who played an adventure game showed better retention of target vocabulary than those who engaged in traditional learning activities. Moreover, Karakoç et al (2022) conducted a metaanalysis that combined the results from experimental studies carried out between 2000 and 2018 on game-based learning  and the academic achievement of students, and they concluded that 'it can  be  asserted  that  game-based  learning  positively  affects  student  achievement  in  all  the disciplines and it is appropriate to be used in all kinds of courses' (Karakoç, 2022 p.12). These studies suggest that video games can be an effective medium for vocabulary learning, providing both  immediate and  long-term benefits. Recent  research continues  to  support  these  findings, indicating that 'video games can serve as a complementary tool to traditional learning methods, providing a dynamic and interactive platform for language acquisition' (Smith & Jones, 2022).


## Impact of Game Genres and Cultural Relevance on Learning


Different genres of video games may have  varying impacts on vocabulary acquisition. Adventure and role-playing games (RPGs) often require players to engage in dialogues and follow complex narratives, which can introduce and reinforce new vocabulary (Torres-Rodríguez et al., 2022). Puzzle and strategy games, on the other hand, might focus more on problem-solving skills but can still enhance language skills through in-game instructions and feedback. Understanding the specific impacts of different game genres can help educators choose the most effective games for vocabulary learning. For instance, games that involve storytelling and character interactions (Corbitt 2023) might be more beneficial for practicing conversational language skills, while games that  require  reading  and  following  instructions  can  improve  comprehension  and  contextual vocabulary use.

It is also important to consider the cultural relevance of video games used in educational settings. Games that incorporate culturally relevant content can be more engaging for students and provide  contextually appropriate examples of  language  use.  This  is  particularly important in regions like Saudi Arabia, where cultural norms and values play a significant role in education (Elyas,  2021).
