## INTRODUCTION


Prosecutors are locally elected officials with significant discretion at the front-end of the criminal legal system. In recent decades, prosecutors in the United States have wielded their power in a way that contributes to mass incarceration and its racial disparities (Frohman 1997;

Pfaff 2017). More recently, a growing number of 'progressive' prosecutors have campaigned on promises to mitigate these harms by using their discretion to reduce charges, the use of cash bail and pretrial detention, and racial disparities (Davis 2019). Progressive prosecutors have also generally pledged to meet growing calls for accountability of police violence, a key demand of the Movement for Black Lives (BLM; ibid). As progressive prosecutors have been elected in growing numbers, particularly since 2016, so too has resistance against them. Challenges to progressive prosecutors include the recall of former District Attorney Chesa Boudin in San Francisco, the forced resignation of former Circuit Attorney Kim Gardner in St. Louis, and the suspension of two locally elected prosecutors in Florida by Governor Ron DeSantis.

Although these cases have been well-publicized, less is known about the broader extent of or dynamics underlying concerted challenges to prosecutors. To date, little is known about how widespread such challenges are, and whether challenges to prosecutors are primarily targeted at progressives or other groups. Moreover, there has yet to be a systematic examination of the leadership, forms, and function of concerted challenges to prosecutors outside of regularly-scheduled elections. Understanding these dynamics may have implications not only for criminal justice reform, but also for local politics in the United States more generally. In an era of national reckonings over racial injustice (Oliver 2021), the movements for and against local prosecutors offer microcosms into the broader state of our polarized politics (Grumbach 2018).

This study explores the origins, extent, and impact of concerted challenges to prosecutors. Toward this end, I constructed an original database of all local prosecutors in office or elected in 2012 and/or 2022 in the country's 300 most-populous jurisdictions in which local prosecutors are elected. Collecting data at these two timepoints enables comparisons of the field of prosecution prior to and after progressive prosecutors' rise, a timeframe scholars tie to BLM

(Davis 2019; Butler 2023). To construct this database, I conducted archival research and documented prosecutor political orientations, demographics, and professional backgrounds; partisan variation in control over state executive and legislative branches (henceforth, state politics); and extra-electoral challenges , which I define as organized efforts to remove a prosecutor from office or constrain a prosecutor's power outside of a regularly-scheduled election. I also operationalize a novel, systematic definition of the term 'progressive,' which has been often-used but inconsistently defined in scholarly literature (Godsoe 2022; Woodly 2022; Foglesong et al. 2022). I define prosecutors as progressive if they sign-on to professional letters pledging their commitments to reform goals. These letters are publicly issued by Fair and Just Prosecution (FJP), a national organization that convenes and trains prosecutors to 'reimagin[e] public safety and … end mass incarceration' (FJP 2024). Thus, my definition is based in the on-the-ground movement for prosecutor reform and systematically constructed for consistent use in future research.

Analysis of this original dataset enables me to make several contributions to ongoing scholarly debates. First, this research is the first national and empirical study evaluating the reach and impact of challenges to prosecutors. It reveals three core findings: extra-electoral challenges appear to be correlated with (1) prosecutor demographics, disproportionately affecting Black women prosecutors; (2) politics, disproportionately affecting progressive prosecutors, especially those in Republican-controlled states; and (3) contemporary political polarization, as extra-electoral challenges to prosecutors nearly tripled over the last ten years and disproportionately coalesces around ongoing debates over perceptions of crime, BLM, and abortion. In addition to descriptive statistics and linear probability models, I use qualitative archival analysis and consider counter-hypotheticals to strengthen my findings. For instance, I

show that prosecutors who are white, male, and not progressive do not face extra-electoral challenges even when there is evidence of their gross misconduct.

Second, this study theorizes extra-electoral challenges against prosecutors as an emerging movement repertoire used by the political right to legally mobilize against racial justice. In this way, it resembles earlier countermovements in the United States to contest progress towards equity. Throughout the country's history - including following Reconstruction and the 1960s Civil Rights Movement - progress advancing legal rights and protections of African Americans has been met with vitriolic backlash to undermine and undo these rights (Du Bois 1935; Francis and Wright-Rigueur 2021; Weaver 2007). The movement against progressive prosecutors appears to follow this historical arc. Efforts to elect progressive prosecutors were framed as part of a broader racial justice movement to combat the racialized harms of mass incarceration and to strengthen accountability for racialized police violence (Davis 2019; Butler 2023). Progressive prosecutors, disproportionately people of color, who ran on platforms to advance these goals, have been met with unprecedented constraints on their discretion and efforts to remove them from office outside of regularly-scheduled elections. Those seeking to thwart progressive prosecutors' agenda for racial justice frame their efforts in language of law, order, and public safety, mirroring historical rhetoric and tactics (Alexander 2010; Anderson 2017).

Moreover, I detail the strategies comprising extra-electoral challenges - such as removal proceedings, state legislation, and oversight committees - thus shedding light on a contemporary countermovement tactical innovation. These extra-electoral strategies have been used to remove elected prosecutors from office and replace them with non-elected individuals, thus appearing to deviate from democratic norms. Additionally, these strategies appear to be growing not only against prosecutors but also against members of local school boards and state officials (Spivak

2020). Although these extra-electoral procedures are designed to ensure accountability for official misconduct, I show that they are in fact being used increasingly against prosecutors for ideological purposes. I contend that challenges to progressive prosecutors are designed to maintain racialized social strata, both within the carceral system and within the offices of those who enforce it. It is also worth noting, however, that these strategies appear to be expanding beyond challenges to progressive prosecutors, as there is evidence of their nascent use against moderate and conservative prosecutors. For instance, the newly elected Democratic Governor of Arizona recently forbade conservative prosecutors from charging abortion-related offenses, a strategy to curb prosecutorial discretion that fits within my definition of extra-electoral challenges and may indicate broader political polarization.

Finally, this article provides a novel dataset, operationalized variables, and statistical patterns that generate theories for future studies to test. My analysis shows that prosecutor demographics, state politics, and contemporary polarization are all important when considering extra-electoral challenges . Future research can further disentangle these variables and consider additional potential factors that may influence extra-electoral challenges , such as local wealth inequality, specific policies, or other factors beyond the scope of this study. Other studies may also put this database into conversation with content analysis of media articles or ethnographic studies of prosecutors' offices. Researchers studying legal mobilizations beyond prosecution might consider this article's definition of extra-electoral challenges to understand the extent or impact of similar movement repertoires in other public realms. Thus, this research adds to and poses nascent tools for the literature on movements for and against racial justice.

In what follows, I review the literatures on prosecutors and legal mobilizations around racial justice. I then describe my data and methods, followed by my findings. I conclude with a

summary and discussion of what the movement against progressive prosecutors today reveals about legal mobilizations to counter and constrain racial justice in the United States.


## PROSECUTORS



## Prosecutors and Mass Incarceration


Extensive research reveals the growth of the criminal legal system in the United States since the 1970s. This scholarship suggests that this historically and internationally unprecedented growth was not a response to rising crime rates, but rather stems from policy changes that are part of a longer history of racialized social control in this country (Weaver 2007; Beckett and Francis 2020). Myriad studies document how the criminal legal system operates as a 'racial caste' system (Alexander 2010: 12) that disproportionately targets and harms Black and Indigenous people of color and low-income communities, including their health, wealth, and civic participation (Turney and Wakefield 2019).

Prosecutors have had an important role in fueling mass incarceration. Research reveals how prosecutors categorize places and people across race, class, and gender stereotypes, and use these stereotypes as they decide whether to accept a case and when conveying it to juries (Frohmann 1997; Gottschalk 2016). Other studies show that prosecutors' discretion grew with federal sentencing reforms that limited judicial discretion, ultimately leading to more felony filings and pressure on defendants to enter plea deals (Lynch 2016; Pfaff 2017). With this expanded power, prosecutors contributed to a growing number of people, disproportionately people of color, going to prison for longer.

Studies show how prosecutors contribute to racial disparities within the criminal legal system. For instance, Nicole Gonzalez van Cleve (2016) uses ethnographic data to convey the role of prosecutors in the 'racial abuse' constituting the court system, describing the courts as a

'theater of racial degradation' (2022). Other studies on prosecutorial discretion show that 'defendants' or victims' race directly or indirectly influences case outcomes, even when a host of other legal and extra-legal factors are taken into account' (Kutateladze et al. 2012: 17). Angela J. Davis analyzes the history of race and prosecution in the United States, and proposes ways prosecutors can use racial impact studies to guide their discretion and 'eradicate the discriminatory treatment of African Americans in the criminal justice system' (1998: 18).

Scholars have also examined prosecutors as elected officials, illuminating the political dynamics that contribute to prosecutors' traditional role in contributing to mass incarceration and racial disparities (Davis 2019; Degenshein 2023). This literature emphasizes that prosecutors historically have faced little scrutiny at the ballot box. For instance, prosecutors are the most frequently elected local law enforcement official (Ellis 2012), yet incumbent prosecutors are more likely to run unopposed than other incumbent officials (Wright 2008). When prosecutors do face opposition in elections, they have often relied on punitive rhetoric, measuring and touting their success in terms of conviction rates (Pfaff 2017; Beckett 1997). In recent years, social movements focused on the harms of the criminal legal system and its role in structural racism have gained traction in public discourse (Dunivin et al. 2022). In this context, some reform advocates suggested that prosecutors could, and should, curtail mass incarceration (Travis et al. 2019; Sklansky 2021). More specifically, if the public demands a smaller and more equitable criminal legal system, they can hold prosecutors to account on these goals through the ballot box. The Movements for and against 'Progressive' Prosecutors

'Progressive' prosecutors are those who pledge to work towards these aims to reduce the scale of and disparities within the criminal legal system. Davis (2019) traces the movement for prosecutor reform to the Movement for Black Lives (BLM), arguing that impunity of police

officers following lethal use-of-force led to public outrage and a new focus on prosecutors (see also Tillery 2019; Weaver et al. 2020; Soss and Weaver 2017). More specifically, BLM emphasizes the perceived and genuine closeness between police and prosecutors, and the conflicts of interest that ensue from their collaboration on cases as well as campaign donations and endorsements from police unions (Austin et al. 2019).

Outrage over impunity for police violence led organizations like Color of Change and the American Civil Liberties Union to coordinate education campaigns about the power of prosecutors. These organizations supported the election of a growing cohort of elected progressive prosecutors, particularly since 2016 (Davis 2019). In addition to national advocacy organizations, foundations such as the Open Society Foundation, MacArthur Foundation, and Arnold Ventures invested in convening prosecutors and launching research projects to examine prosecutorial discretion. These organizations fostered broad coalitions to 'reimagine the role of the prosecutor' from a mechanism of mass incarceration to partner in reform (Travis et al. 2019).

As progressive prosecutors were elected in growing numbers and saw a rise in institutional support, they also encountered a burgeoning countermovement opposing their elections and tenures in office (Davis 2019). Scholars suggest resistance to progressive prosecutors often stem from assistant district attorneys  (ADAs) within their offices, other 2 criminal legal actors or public officials in their jurisdictions, and powerful local institutions,

including police unions and the bail bonds industry (Barkow 2021; Richardson and Kutateladze 2021). Some argue that rising crime contributed to this resistance, although there is limited empirical support for this claim (Foglesong et al. 2022; Stone 2022). Davis (2019) emphasizes the important role that race and gender play in pushback to progressives. While past research offers compelling theoretical claims and insight from individual offices, this study offers the first empirical investigation nationally into the origins, reach, and impact of resistance to prosecutors.


## LEGAL MOBILIZATIONS FOR AND AGAINST RACIAL JUSTICE



## Legal Mobilization


The literature on legal mobilization offers a useful analytic frame for making sense of the movements against locally elected prosecutors. Legal mobilizations are specific social movement repertoires, or the 'whole set of means [a group] has for making claims,' that centers the law as a movement tool (Tilly 1986: 2; Lehoucq and Taylor 2020). I draw on Lynette J. Chua's definition of legal mobilizations as 'socially constructed political processes … [in which] people mobilize the law in series of ongoing social interactions, by forming their own understandings about law and putting law into action in their struggles and dealings with one another' (2019: 359). Although this study focuses on legal actors - prosecutors - Chua's definition of legal mobilization provides a capacious understanding of how movements for and against them impact society beyond the courtroom or interactions with agents of the state.

This understanding of legal mobilization reveals how the law is both 'constitutive and instrumental' (ibid), shaping myriad aspects of identities and everyday life (Merry 1998). The law has the potential to shape not only our understanding of our own and each other's rights and restrictions, but also our 'common sense' of social norms, order, and alternative possibilities (Gramsci 1973). In this way, the law shapes dominant views of individuals' and groups' various

social positions, which in turn shapes actors' capacity to utilize or contest the law for their claims. This relational view of legal mobilization reveals how various groups compete for hegemony of political fields (Lehoucq and Taylor 2020). As Michael McCann argues, 'the primary project of legal mobilization analysis is aimed at the constitutive role of legal rights both as a strategic resource and as a constraint … for struggles to transform, or to reconstitute, the terms of social relations and power' (2006: 22).

This study broadens the lens of legal mobilizations to consider contests over the field of prosecution as competing movements for and against racial justice. My analysis suggests that legal mobilizations against progressive prosecutors are aimed at specific 'terms of social relations and power' (ibid), particularly across race and gender. The dominant, traditional understanding of prosecutors' role within the criminal legal system is to pursue charges and convictions against those who violate the law. Although prosecutors have always utilized their discretion in myriad ways (Sklansky 2018), explicitly expressing a professional commitment to challenge the racialized harms of mass incarceration counters the dominant understanding of the prosecutor's role.

In this context, I argue that claims against progressive prosecutors reflect the fear that they will transform the racialized social order. Progressive prosecutors do this through their efforts to reduce racial disparities, as well as via their demographic positionality as an increasingly diverse group of elected officials (Davis 2019; Butler 2023). Extra-electoral challenges against progressive prosecutors, then, can be understood within the country's longer history of legal mobilizations against racial justice.

Racial Justice

Within the United States, the law has generally been used to protect white people and their property, often at the expense of and based on the direct exploitation of people of color (Robinson 1983; Merry 1998; Francis and Wright-Rigueur 2021). Indeed, laws were specifically created to justify the country's founding on chattel slavery and Indigenous dispossession (Jenkins and Leroy 2021). Efforts to expand protections and rights for people of color have been met with quick and vitriolic backlash, including 'through the courts, the legislatures, and a range of government bureaucracies' (Anderson 2017: ix; Du Bois 1935; Bracey 2021). For instance, as Carole Anderson (2017) shows, white mobs terrorized Black people following Reconstruction as well as the 1960s Civil Rights Movement (see also Wells 1969). These mobs, like earlier iterations of racist violence, had both de jure and de facto support of states and the federal government. Perpetrators of mob violence were rarely arrested. Instead, their actions were often justified through the criminalization of their victims, a facet of racialized violence that persists today (Burch 2022; Austin et al. 2019). The movement to elect progressive prosecutors was motivated in part to resist this obstinate historical trend (Davis 2019).

BLM has brought renewed attention to the law's potential and limits for protecting the rights and life of Black people and other marginalized groups (Taylor 2016; Oliver 2021). A burgeoning literature is documenting and debating the impacts of BLM (Dunivin et al. 2022; Caren et al. 2023), and situates BLM within the longer history of legal mobilizations for racial justice. For instance, Megan Ming Francis and Leah Wright-Rigueur (2021) draw parallels between Ida B. Wells's work (1969) documenting instances of lynchings in the early 20th century and BLM activists' efforts to quantify instances of police violence in the absence of a government database. Thus, BLM legally mobilizes to strengthen protections for Black lives, including by producing knowledge about state-sanctioned violence. Magda Boutros's (2022)

ethnography of activists contesting racialized police brutality in France further elevates the epistemic potential of legal mobilizations. Boutros shows how activists overcome the country's legally mandated colorblindness to document patterns and practices of discriminatory policing against Black and Arab young men. This research sheds light on how the law can obscure past and present legalized harms: France's official policy of colorblindness serves to erase its history of colonization, a period in which the law's use to create and maintain racialized social hierarchies is particularly evident (Fanon 1961).

Several U.S. policies more explicitly reveal parallels between past and present racialized legal systems (Hinton and Cook 2021; Weaver 2007). For instance, Michelle Alexander (2010) frames mass incarceration as an extension of earlier racialized systems and statutes, such as vagrancy laws, Black Codes, and Jim Crow, that subjugate Black people and deprive them of the right to vote. From this perspective, the criminal legal system serves a dual, interconnected purpose to criminalize people of color and, in turn, to limit their citizenship and participation in democracy. Indeed, felon disenfranchisement did not become widely adopted until Reconstruction, after Black people secured a right to vote via the 15th Amendment: '[b]etween 1865 and 1900, 19 states adopted or amended laws restricting the voting rights of criminal offenders' (Uggen et al. 2005: 308).

Felon disenfranchisement today remains emblematic of racialized voter suppression (ibid). Prosecutors have direct influence over felony filings and carceral sanctions, thus impacting criminal legal consequences for democratic participation. However, progressive prosecutors are explicitly challenging the law as a tool to constrain civic engagement. For instance, in Florida, several prosecutors waived fines and fees for formerly incarcerated people so that they can vote (Gardner and Rozsa 2020). In Florida, two of the prosecutors engaged in

these efforts - Monique Worrell and Andrew Warren - were removed from their elected positions overseeing racially diverse jurisdictions and replaced with non-elected officials.

I view this and other examples of extra-electoral challenges against progressive prosecutors, detailed below, as legal mobilizations to maintain the existing racialized status quo and to resist the 'transform[ation of] … the terms of social relations and power' (McCann 2006: 22). Thus, extra-electoral challenges can be understood as part of the United States's ongoing processes of struggles for and against racial justice. While earlier countermovements sought to utilize the law to constrain progress towards equity following Reconstruction and the 1960s Civil Rights Movements, extra-electoral challenges against progressive prosecutors today can be viewed as a tactical innovation and legal mobilization against BLM.


## DATA AND METHODS



## Prosecutor Sample


This study examines the form, function, and outcomes of challenges to the tenure and discretion of locally elected prosecutors. To do so, I constructed an original database of all local prosecutors who were in office or elected in 2022 in the 300 most-populous jurisdictions in the United States where local prosecutors are elected. I created this database first using population data from the U.S. Census Bureau to identify the country's most-populous counties. I then refined this list, excluding locales where prosecutors are not elected (n=26) and combining counties that share a common prosecutor (n=9), resulting in 265 distinct prosecutor jurisdictions.  I identified the 2022 local prosecutors for each of these jurisdictions. For 3

jurisdictions where an incumbent left office in 2022 (n=40), I include both the outgoing prosecutor as well as his or her successor. Thus, there are 305 prosecutors in the 2022 prosecutor database who, collectively, represent about 61 percent of the 2022 U.S. population. 4

I collected similar data for prosecutors in these jurisdictions in 2012 to compare extra-electoral challenges before and after a first wave of progressive prosecutors were elected. 5 The selection of that date reflects the fact that the 2016 elections marked a notable shift away from incumbent prosecutors running largely uncontested races on punitive platforms. Scholars credit this shift, in large part, to BLM (Butler 2023; Davis 2019; Soss and Weaver 2017). For instance, following the 2014 murders of Michael Brown in Ferguson and Laquan McDonald in Chicago, and the impunity of the officers who killed them, prosecutor candidates Kim Gardner and Kim Foxx were elected in these jurisdictions,  respectively, on campaign promises of police 6 accountability and broader criminal justice reform. My research also suggests 2016 marked the first-time donors significantly invested in prosecutor races. Thus, 2012 data offers a window into the field of prosecution before the shift towards prosecutor reform.

There are 94 prosecutors who were elected in 2012 or earlier and remained in office in 2022. These individuals are included in both the 2012 and 2022 databases. To ensure counts of extra-electoral challenges are not distorted by prosecutors in office in both 2012 and 2022, I confine extra-electoral challenges to include challenges only within the preceding decade. I used archival methods (Benzecry et al. 2020; Lara-Millan et al. 2020) to collect data on each prosecutor's race, gender, professional background, political affiliation, and potential instances of extra-electoral challenges , described further below. I collected this data from prosecutors' web pages, campaign materials, and the top ten most-relevant media articles about them according to Google News searches. Systematically reviewing and collecting data from multiple public sources enables triangulation and replicability in future empirical research.

Prosecutors' professional background were coded for whether they previously served as assistant district attorney, other state or local law enforcement official, other state or local elected official (not law enforcement), public defender (for indigent clients), or other. Prosecutors who ever served as an ADA were coded as such, even if they also pursued other careers. This is based on the hypothesis that those who previously served within a prosecutor's office are less likely to

encounter concerted resistance and better able to navigate internal dynamics. For those who did not serve as ADA, their most recent profession prior to serving as chief prosecutor was coded.

For political affiliation, I used two measures: political party and ideology. Political party is an imperfect measure, as prosecutors in several states are nonpartisan,  and there is significant 9 variation of practices within the broad parties of Democrat and Republican. Additionally, I consider counterarguments to my analysis. Opponents of progressive prosecutors often argue that they go beyond the limits of their offices' mandates or are acting inappropriately in ways that justify action against them. Therefore, I coded for all instances of prosecutors' potential misconduct apparent in the archives, ultimately identifying seven prosecutors in 2022 who are not facing extra-electoral challenges despite actions that could be considered violations of the ethics or norms of the office. These prosecutors, all of whom are white, most of whom are men, and none of whom are progressive, have been accused gross misconduct, yet none have encountered concerted efforts to limit their power or oust them from office. I detail these instances and their implications below.


## FINDINGS


This study scrutinizes the field of prosecution to assess whether there are discernible patterns in extra-electoral challenges , which seek to curb the discretion and tenure of elected officials. Through original data analysis of all locally elected prosecutors in 2012 and/or 2022 in the country's most-populous jurisdictions, I find that 45, or nearly fifteen percent of prosecutors in 2022, encountered extra-electoral challenges , nearly triple the proportion a decade prior. Closer examination reveals the importance of prosecutor demographics, politics, and contemporary political polarization in extra-electoral challenges .

## Prosecutor Demographics


My analysis shows that contemporary extra-electoral challenges vary by prosecutor demographics. For instance, people of color comprise only one in five locally elected prosecutors, yet comprise nearly half of those facing extra-electoral challenges (see Table 1 and Figure 1). Results from LPM are consistent, showing that prosecutors of color are over 12 percent more likely than white prosecutors to face extra-electoral challenges , and this difference is statistically significant (see Table 2). An additional model where race is considered as a categorical as opposed to binary variable reveals that this difference is driven by extra-electoral challenges against Black and Latino prosecutors, likely due to the small number of Asian and Native American prosecutors (six and one, respectively).

Similarly, fewer than one in three locally elected prosecutors are women, yet 42 percent of those facing extra-electoral challenges are women. Although LPM results do not suggest the difference in extra-electoral challenges confronting men and women is statistically significant, they do suggest a strong effect when considering the interaction of race and gender: Women of color are 26 percent more likely to encounter extra-electoral challenges compared with white men (see Table 2). This is particularly apparent when looking at Black women, who comprise less than seven percent of locally elected prosecutors, yet comprise twenty percent of those facing extra-electoral challenges . These findings support earlier work suggesting race and gender play a meaningful role in challenges to prosecutors specifically and elected officials generally (Davis 2019; Nelson 2021; Anderson 2017).

In considering the white male prosecutors who do encounter extra-electoral challenges , resistance seems to focus on their commitments to racial justice. For instance, DAs who were formerly public defenders - and thus, tasked with defending poor people, often people of color

(Harris 2016) - face a disproportionate amount of extra-electoral challenges : public defenders comprise nearly sixteen percent of those facing extra-electoral challenges , yet comprise only four percent of prosecutors generally. Larry Krasner and Chesa Boudin, who each faced extra-electoral challenges , were public defenders before being elected DA. However, the number of former public defenders serving as chief prosecutor is so small (thirteen, with seven facing extra-electoral challenges ), that further research is warranted before any conclusions are drawn. Unsurprisingly, those who previously served as ADAs appear to be under-represented as those facing extra-electoral challenges (75 percent of prosecutors generally, compared with 56 percent facing extra-electoral challenges ). No other professional backgrounds had notable discrepancies between their composition as prosecutors generally with those facing extra-electoral challenges . Politics

In addition to analyzing prosecutor demographics and professional backgrounds, I consider the role of prosecutor and state politics in extra-electoral challenges . To do so, I first compare extra-electoral challenges against progressive prosecutors with those against non-progressives using the definitions described above. This analysis shows that over 55 percent of prosecutors facing extra-electoral challenges are progressive, although they only comprise sixteen percent of prosecutors generally (see Table 1). LPM results support this finding, showing that progressive prosecutors are 36 percent more likely to face extra-electoral challenges than non-progressives, and this finding is statistically significant (see Table 2). Given that progressive prosecutors are those with explicit commitments to ending the racialized harms of mass incarceration, this finding corroborates extra-electoral challenges as a legal mobilization against racial justice.

To further consider the role of politics in extra-electoral challenges, I also consider political party. Although this is an imperfect measure given that there is significant variation within political parties and prosecutors are nonpartisan in several states, progressives are most often registered as Democrats, thus enabling this comparison to further test my results. Indeed, Democrats are overrepresented among those experiencing extra-electoral challenges (71 percent), compared with their representation among prosecutors generally (41 percent). In contrast, only eleven percent of Republicans face extra-electoral challenges , although they constitute 39 percent of prosecutors generally (see Table 1).

In addition to individual prosecutors' political affiliations, state politics appear important for extra-electoral challenges . Over half (56 percent) of prosecutors facing extra-electoral challenges are in states where both state legislative bodies and the governor's office are controlled by Republicans (i.e., 'Republican Trifectas'), compared with 41 percent of prosecutors generally. 15 Indeed, LPM results show that prosecutors in states with Republican Trifectas are about 14 percent more likely to face extra-electoral challenges than those in states with Democrat Trifectas (see Figure 2).

Considering the interaction between prosecutor and state politics is also revealing. Progressives are statistically significantly more likely to encounter extra-electoral challenges than non-progressives in every type of state, but particularly so in states with Republican trifectas and divided governments (64 percent and 41 percent, respectively; see Table 2). The archives also reveal that in states with divided governments or that are controlled by Republicans, prosecutors in jurisdictions governed by local Democrats seem to be particularly

affected by extra-electoral challenges , discussed further below. Furthermore, it appears that even non-progressives in Republican controlled states are statistically significantly more likely (eight percent) to face extra-electoral challenges than are non-progressives in Democrat-controlled states. For instance, Rachel Mitchell, an Arizona prosecutor, was recently censured by the state's Republican Party, her own party, for sanctioning Kari Lake, a Republican gubernatorial candidate who made false statements to the court about election fraud.

The primary leadership of extra-electoral challenges against prosecutors also appears to vary based on state politics (see Table 4). Most prosecutors facing extra-electoral challenges in states with Democrat Trifectas encounter resistance led by state and local law enforcement, frequently police unions. 16 For instance, Pamela Price, DA of Alameda County, California (which includes Oakland), is a Black woman and former civil rights attorney who was elected in 2022. She encountered a recall campaign less than six months into her tenure surrounding allegations that her office's policies to decline prosecuting certain offenses was contributing to rising crime, a claim empirically unjustifiable given her limited tenure in office. Nevertheless, local law enforcement vocally ridiculed Price and supported the recall effort, as they also did for the successful recall against neighboring San Francisco DA Chesa Boudin less than one year prior. The archives also show law enforcement contributed to the campaign of Price's opponent in the general election. Price was recalled half-way through her four-year term in fall 2024.

Allegations of rising crime were also used in efforts to remove Los Angeles County DA George Gascón from his post within his first year of taking office. Again, it is empirically

unjustifiable for a change in prosecutor to lead to a rise in crime in such a short period of time, especially in a city like Los Angeles where longstanding impunity for violence is well-documented (Leovy 2015). Gascón faced two recall attempts, both of which failed to garner sufficient signatures to get on the ballot. The latter recall effort was organized by the Assistant District Attorneys Association, a union that includes hundreds of assistant prosecutors, including many within his own office, who also filed a lawsuit against him. The Sheriff of LA County also supported the recall effort. Gascón is a former officer with the Los Angeles Police Department and the former chief of Mesa, Arizona's police department. He was also the DA of San Francisco prior to his move to Los Angeles. While in San Francisco, he did not face the sort of extra-electoral challenges that his successor encountered nor that he faced in Los Angeles, indicating a shift in political dynamics, discussed further below. He lost his bid for reelection in 2024.

In addition to claims over rising crime, abortion has emerged as a central point of contention in states with Republican Trifectas or divided governments. For instance, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis suspended two locally elected prosecutors, Hillsborough State Attorney Andrew Warren and Orange-Osceola State Attorney Monique Worrell, after they said they would not charge people seeking or aiding abortion. 17 DeSantis replaced Warren and Worrell by

appointing two non-elected attorneys, Susan Lopez and Andrew Bain, respectively. Both Warren and Worrell were proactively progressive in their campaign messaging and policies, whereas Lopez and Bain are aligned with DeSantis's right-wing agenda, which extends beyond challenges to local prosecutors to also include bans on books and LGBTQ equality. Indeed, Lopez and Bain are both members of the Federalist Society, a right-wing association of attorneys who legally mobilize for judicial appointments in order to advance conservative policies. 18

In addition to governors, state legislators also seem to lead extra-electoral challenges against prosecutors in Republican-controlled or divided states. For instance, Florida legislators introduced a bill to strip cases from or implement oversight committees over progressive prosecutors. Similar statutes have been introduced in Georgia, Texas, Tennessee, Indiana, and Wisconsin. While some of these statutes name the prosecutors they target, others focus on specific policies, such as taking over abortion-related cases from prosecutors who decline to charge them. The majority of prosecutors targeted by these statutes are people of color or are in majority-minority districts, thus overruling the will of voters who have been historically disenfranchised.

These tactics' efficacy has not gone unnoticed by officials on the other side of the political aisle, who are beginning to adopt similar strategies to thwart the discretion of prosecutors with whom they disagree. For instance, newly elected Arizona Governor, Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, prohibited prosecutors from charging people seeking or aiding abortions through an Executive Order. Several Republican prosecutors in the state, including Rachel

Mitchell of Maricopa County and Kent Volkemer of Pinal County, are now challenging this order. Similar dynamics are apparent in Michigan.


## Contemporary Political Polarization


These points of contention - perceptions of crime, BLM, and abortion - further suggest that extra-electoral challenges against prosecutors relate to the broader contemporary political moment defined by polarization (Grumbach 2023). For instance, the proportion of prosecutors facing extra-electoral challenges nearly tripled from about five percent in 2012 to nearly 15 percent in 2022. Prosecutors in office in 2012 who used their discretion in unpopular ways were more often voted out of office during regularly-scheduled elections rather than removed via extra-electoral strategies.

For instance, Bob McCulloch served as prosecutor from 1991 through 2019 in the jurisdiction that included Ferguson, Missouri. McCulloch rarely faced electoral opponents and never faced extra-electoral challenges . Throughout his tenure, he never indicted an officer for use-of-force, including in 2014, when he failed to indict police officer Darren Wilson for shooting Michael Brown. He lost his subsequent election in 2018. Former Duval County, Florida State Attorney Angela Corey also lost her reelection campaign in 2016 after she was accused of mishandling the prosecution of George Zimmerman, who murdered Trayvon Martin in 2014. The murders of Brown and Martin, and impunity for those who killed them, helped to launch BLM and focus on prosecutors' discretion in police accountability (Davis 2019; Oliver 2021). These events contributed to the movement to elect progressive prosecutors, but did not seem to result in extra-electoral challenges .

In contrast to these defeats at the ballot box, the extra-electoral challenges that occurred in the early aughts and 2010s were used primarily to remove or constrain the discretion of

prosecutors accused of gross misconduct, as opposed to policy or ideological disagreements. For instance, William Mason, a white male prosecutor in Cuyahoga County, Ohio from 2009 to 2012, was forced to resign over federal inquiries into pay-to-play corruption related to donations to his office and other local officials. Former Cameron County, Texas District Attorney Armando Villalobos, a Latino man, was also forced to resign after being indicted on federal charges of bribery and extortion.

These local prosecutors' forced resignations for official misconduct and federal offenses stand in stark contrast to that of Kim Gardner, a Black woman and prosecutor of St. Louis from 2016 to 2023. Gardner was elected in a jurisdiction that neighbored McCulloch's, where Michael Brown was killed, on a promise of police accountability. One of Gardner's early actions as prosecutor was to update her office's Brady policy, which limits prosecutors' collaboration with police officers who have allegations of misconduct - such as not taking these officers' evidence or testimony. The police department issued threats towards and obstructed Gardner's discretion immediately after she took office and throughout her tenure. She ultimately resigned halfway through her second term while facing opposition from the police, mounting pressure from a lawsuit by the Missouri Attorney General, and state legislation that sought to seize her cases. These challenges were not levied against her predecessor or neighboring prosecutors.

Contemporary extra-electoral challenges , such as those facing Gardner, are based on ideological disputes and political retribution, as opposed to the official misconduct that led to extra-electoral challenges to prosecutors in 2012. In contrast, my archival research shows seven prosecutors in office in 2022 accused of official impropriety who have not faced extra-electoral challenges . This impropriety includes evidence of corruption, improper investigations, overt racism, domestic violence, and drunk driving. All of these prosecutors accused of misconduct are

white, most are male, none are progressive. None have encountered extra-electoral challenges . I consider this impunity for officials accused of misconduct as an important complement to, and contrast with, legal mobilizations against officials advancing racial justice. The absence of extra-electoral challenges to prosecutors facing allegations of impropriety today offers further evidence that efforts to constrain the power of progressive prosecutors are intended to limit steps towards racial justice, rather than to uphold high ethical standards of DAs.

The ideological basis, as opposed to official misconduct, driving extra-electoral challenges today is also apparent in the tenures of prosecutors facing resistance. For instance, prosecutors elected since 2015, when the first cohort of progressives entered office, are overrepresented as those facing extra-electoral challenges , comprising less than 60 percent of prosecutors generally compared with 80 percent facing concerted resistance. Nearly half (47 percent) of those facing extra-electoral challenges encountered these challenges less than two years into their first term, prior to any potential policy impacts or evidence of misconduct from materializing.

Of the seven prosecutors who have been in office for over a decade and are now encountering extra-electoral challenges , this opposition began in 2020 or later. Challenges against six of these DAs are centered around the prosecutor's policies on police violence or abortion, debates that have come to the fore and been increasingly polarized in recent years. For example, John Chisholm, who took office in Milwaukee, Wisconsin in 2006, began encountering extra-electoral challenges in 2020. Milwaukee is home to about 60 percent of Wisconsin's Black population. It is a blue city in a purple state where the Democratic governor frequently battles with the Republican state legislature over his discretion. These debates now seem to be spilling over into the prosecutor's office.

Chisholm is a white man and career prosecutor who was one of the first DAs to partner with researchers to analyze, with aims of rectifying, racial disparities in his office's case filings (Kutetaladze and Andiloro 2011). He co-authored with Angela J. Davis a paper on the history of institutional racism in prosecution (Davis, Chisholm, and Noble 2019). Chisholm was elected a decade before progressive prosecution was a widely recognized term, yet he is credited, along with former King County, Washington prosecutor Dan Satterberg, for creating a roadmap for prosecutors who seek to reduce the racialized harms of mass incarceration (Davis 2019).

Despite years of public efforts to advance reform, Chisholm only began to encounter extra-electoral challenges in 2020. For instance, the 2022 Republican candidate for Wisconsin Attorney General pledged that he would restore law and order in Milwaukee, which he described as a 'shooting gallery,' by taking cases from Chisholm (Whalen 2022). Both Chisholm and his neighboring prosecutor Izmael Ozanne of Dane County, a moderate DA who has been in office since 2010 and is the first Black person elected prosecutor in Wisconsin, face extra-electoral challenges surrounding their handling of cases related to police violence and abortions.

Protesters in support of BLM want their offices to pursue more charges against officer use-of-force, while groups on the other side of the political spectrum have protested what they perceive as their lax charging and bail policies. After both DAs said they would decline to charge abortions, anti-abortion groups lobbied the state to take over their cases. Chisholm announced in January 2024 that he would not seek another term.


## CONCLUSION


This study uses challenges to prosecutors to elucidate a novel legal mobilization used by the political right to thwart racial justice efforts following BLM. Extra-electoral challenges are organized efforts to constrain elected officials' discretion or tenure outside of

regularly-scheduled elections. As progressive prosecutors have been elected in growing numbers since 2016 on pledges to combat the racialized harms of mass incarceration, they have faced unprecedented constraints on their power. The burden to advance racial justice and combat mass incarceration falls disproportionately on prosecutors of color, especially Black women prosecutors, who then endure extra-electoral challenges throughout their tenures. This opposition occurs most often in states with Republican-controlled or divided governments. It is frequently led by governors, state legislators, and local police unions, and justified under the language of law, order, and public safety. In this way, extra-electoral challenges are reminiscent of historical legal mobilizations against racial justice, including strategies designed to counter progress towards equity following Reconstruction and the 1960s Civil Rights Movements.

This study offers the first empirical investigation into the origins, extent, and impact of challenges to prosecutors nationally. Future research might consider extra-electoral challenges in other public realms or might further probe the relationship between prosecutors and legal mobilizations for and against racial justice. For instance, an expanded database with additional prosecutors and datapoints might enable more sophisticated statistical analyses that can further disentangle the relationships between prosecutor demographics, policies, politics, contemporary polarization, and other variables. Qualitative research, including ethnographic or archival case studies of specific jurisdictions, might further clarify the mechanisms driving extra-electoral challenges. Future scholarship might pay particular attention to apparent anomalies, such as Satana Deberry, a Black woman in North Carolina, a state with evidence of democratic contraction (Grumbach 2023), who does not seem to encounter extra-electoral challenges . While this study is unable to address these important questions, it lays the groundwork for future

studies to probe them more deeply. Finally, this study utilizes a novel database and operationalized terms that may be used in future empirical research.

In our contemporary era, defined by the country's first Black President followed by the subsequent election of Donald J. Trump, movements for racial justice focused on the local level, where democratically elected prosecutors pledged to use their discretion to combat the racialized harms of the carceral system (Davis 2019). As they have attempted to do so, the backlash has been vitriolic, with ramifications for efforts to create a more equitable legal system. Moreover, as questions over political polarization at the national level return, this research emphasizes the importance of careful attention to local actors entangled in dueling legal mobilizations for and against racial justice. Prosecutors have effectively served as mechanisms of mass incarceration and racial disparities in the criminal legal system over the last four decades. Whether they are able to effectively utilize their discretion and meet recent calls to combat the racialized harms of the criminal legal system remains to be seen.

## Introduction


The academic needs of young immigrants have long constituted an important topic for research. Yet we know little about the academic outcomes of a unique and growing group: foreign-born children of return migrants. Azose and Raftery (2019) estimate that about one in four migration events are a return to a person's country of birth, amounting to millions of return migrants worldwide. Thousands of foreign-born children have accompanied these returnees; for example, 500,000 American-born minors are living in Mexico, amounting to about 2 percent of school enrollment (Masferrer 2021:39).

Do these young migrants benefit from an 'immigrant advantage,' or do they struggle to succeed in a country at once foreign and familiar? What does it mean to incorporate into a

society where ethnic, cultural, and legal barriers are at a minimum? How can schools best support this unique - and often invisible - population? Although small, single-country analyses exist, we know little about how parents' return migrations influence children's educational trajectories on a larger scale, or how these experiences vary by country and country-level institutions.

This paper attempts to answer these questions by relying on the Program for International Student Assessment (PISA), which assesses 15-year-olds' reading, math, and science skills every three years in dozens of countries worldwide (Schleicher 2019). Pooling PISA data from 2012, 2015, and 2018 results in 3,480 children of return migrants from 72 birth countries and 43 countries of residence. It compares them to 431,212 non-immigrants in their parents' origin country as well as 7,781 comparable children of migrants in children's birth countries. This twofold comparison allows the estimation of both descriptive and causal estimands: the descriptive gap between children of return migrants and locals, and the causal effect of following one's parents on a return migration journey. I also use meta-analytic and fixed effects models to examine policies as well as features of origin and destination countries that shape integration of return migrant children.

I find that, on average, these children obtains slightly lower PISA scores compared to local children in their parents' country of birth. But compared to children of similar migrants in their country of birth, they perform significantly worse, at one-fifth of a standard deviation lower. However, these averages hide great variation between particular groups.

This paper makes empirical, methodological, and theoretical interventions in the sociology of immigrant education. Empirically, it is one of the first large-scale assessments of the academic achievement of children of return migrants. This growing population is often

invisible to educators, and we know little about how these children are doing in school. It also advances theory of immigrant education. It contributes to immigrant incorporation theory by showing how assimilation processes function in a context where ethnic, cultural, and legal barriers are at a minimum and explores the importance that institutional factors can assume in educational integration.


## Background


Although the education of young migrants and children of immigrants in destination countries has been an active area of research for decades, the migration process of children is only recently receiving concerted scholarly attention (Dobson 2009; Orellana et al. 2001). This is especially true for children involved in return and circular migration, despite the large size of these populations. About one in four migration events are a return to a person's country of birth. The four largest return flows from 2010 to 2015 were United States to Mexico (1.3 million), United Arab Emirates to India (380 thousand), Ukraine to Russia (358 thousand), and India to Bangladesh (350 thousand) (Azose and Raftery 2019:118). Thousands of children born to migrants abroad have accompanied their parents on their return to their home countries.

Scholars are beginning to study children of return migrants. They have focused predominantly on the Mexican case, the largest in the world. In 2000, the Mexican census counted 258,000 U.S.-born minors (Gonzalez-Barrera 2021); by 2020, this had nearly doubled to 500,600 minors, or about 2 percent of the school-age population (Masferrer 2021:39).

Although quantitative work remains scarce (for an exception, see Hoffmann 2022b), qualitative researchers have begun to study these youths, both in Mexico and elsewhere. The findings from researchers working in this domain have been mixed. Most of this work emphasizes the difficulties that children of return migrants face in their parents' country of

origin. Despite usually possessing oral proficiency in two languages, their written competency tends to lag behind (Santibañez 2021). Especially when they first arrive, their peers often treat them as outsiders (Meyers 2014), and the stigma they face can be exacerbated by the political climate (Bybee et al. 2020). Conflicts also occur psychologically, as these children struggle with their identity and feelings of belonging (Bybee et al. 2020). Yet their appearance and oral fluency often renders them invisible to teachers (Sánchez García and Hamann 2016), and resources for immigrant students are lacking in countries such as Mexico (Santibañez 2021). Even navigating the complicated bureaucracy to enroll in school or finding the money for transportation, uniforms, and school supplies may be out of reach for return migrant families (Mateos 2019). Furthermore, family separation is a frequent, stressful feature of migration that is common for children of return migrants as well (Zúñiga and Giorguli Saucedo 2018).

In some of the rare work that considers contexts outside of North America, Vathi, Duci, and Dhembo (2016) produces strikingly similar findings in the case of children of migrants who return from Greece to Albania. These children face barriers in school stemming from both individual and institutional factors. They lack knowledge of the Albanian language and struggle with changes in curriculum, especially at older ages. Although education policies are in place to provide extra support to ease their transition to Albania, these are rarely implemented, and teachers' 'assimilationist teaching practices' (Vathi et al. 2016:167) neglect diversity of experiences in their classrooms. All of this results them falling behind in school, often performing poorly academically and even being held back a grade or two.

In another non-American context, Koo, Ming, and Tsang (2014) bring a Bourdieusian perspective to their interview-based study of children in China who return from Beijing to rural areas in the neighboring Hebei province where they were born. At the time of their study, China

required students intending to apply to college to attend high school and in their place of birth. At a young age, their parents brought them to Beijing, where they were seeking work. Koo et al. (2014) argue that children learn the habitus of the big city, most notably in speaking the urban dialect and adapting to different teaching practices and academic performance standards. But the change of social field upon return makes these strategies sources of weakness rather than strength. Furthermore, since their parents usually stay in Beijing to work, these children benefit less readily from their social capital. The authors argue that these children are doubly disadvantaged: once when they move to Beijing, and again when they return to the countryside.

Yet not all work on return migrant children conceives of them as consigned to disadvantage. Zúñiga and Giorguli Saucedo (2018) and Hernández-León, Zúñiga, and Lakhani (2020) see some of the children of return Mexican migrants in their studies benefiting from dual nationality. Similarly, in an intensive ethnography in two schools in central Mexico, Bybee et al. (2020:135) observe a 'star student' discourse: 'The notion of American-Mexican pupils as 'good students' was common enough in both schools that it extended beyond English classes where they had an obvious advantage.' Although these students experienced bullying and exclusion due to their perceived foreignness, the privilege of binational education and other resources gave some of them a leg up in school.

Despite the advances this recent research has made in our understanding of children of return migrants, results have been particular to small-scale research contexts and limited mostly to Mexico. Furthermore, with some studies emphasizing challenges while others highlight strengths, we do not know whether children of return migrants tend to be advantaged or disadvantaged in school. Large-scale, cross-national work - as this study accomplishes - is necessary to characterize the overall situation of foreign-born children of return migrants around

the world, as well as to elucidate which education policies are likely to enable the academic success of these children.


## Theory



## Individual Explanations


How can we understand the mixed results from previous studies of children of return migrants? Theories of return migrant integration point to possible explanations for both positive and negative outcomes of their foreign-born children. First, they help us understand possible disadvantage . The perspective of neoclassical economics suggests that return migrant families may not found lucrative employment in the host country (Todaro 1980). Even in cases where they have, a transnationalist perspective (Basch, Glick Schiller, and Szanton Blanc 1994) emphasizes that alienation and exclusion in the 'home' society can still afflict return migrants and their children as they struggle with their identities. Institutions for investment and activation of resources gained abroad may also be lacking (Hagan and Wassink 2020:539). In addition, migrants who are not ready and willing to migrate (Cassarino 2004) - as in the case of deportation - are less likely to possess the resources to ease re-entry into society. The result can be traumatic for children, and may give rise to the difficulties documented in the ethnographic research cited above.

Yet these students may also be among the privileged in their new country of residence. The New Economics of Labor Migration (Stark and Bloom 1985) highlights how voluntary return migration can be evidence of economic success, with parents accumulating sufficient resources to lead a comfortable life in Mexico. Following Cassarino's (2004) resource mobilization-preparedness framework, if children benefit from resource-rich social networks and

parents who have achieved their goals in acquiring skills and capital while abroad, and if the family is ready and willing to move, they are more likely to be well supported upon return to the parents' country of origin. Scholars suggest that at least some of these children benefit from resources such as dual nationality, bicultural facility, and experience in better resourced schools (Bybee et al. 2020). Furthermore, in the absence of most social markers of difference, assimilation theory predicts that integration should be straightforward and rapid (Alba and Nee 2003). As Bybee et al. (2020) document, these foreign-born children of return migrants may be 'star students.'


## Institutional Explanations


Individual resources or encumbrances may not be as important as the institutional context in which these children find themselves. In recent years, scholars of immigrant incorporation have found that institutional features of national systems may be at least as important as individual factors in accounting for incorporation outcomes (Schneider, Crul, and Pott 2022; Thomson and Crul 2007). Previous work on immigrant academic achievement in general has highlighted certain factors that will likely matter for children of return migrants. Perhaps the most studied policy in this area is academic tracking. Within-school tracking refers to grouping children in classes by 'ability' or 'aptitude' (in the U.S., these might be Honors or AP classes). Betweenschool tracking describes systems where students are sorted into different types of schools, such as vocational, technical, or college preparatory. Although within-school tracking has shown mixed effects for immigrant-origin students, (Cobb-Clark, Sinning, and Stillman 2012; Teltemann and Schunck 2016), between-school tracking shows more clearly negative effects (Borgna and Contini 2014; Dronkers and de Heus 2016; Ruhose and Schwerdt 2016; Teltemann and Schunck 2016).

Another policy that can negatively affect immigrant achievement is school segregation: when schools are stratified by socioeconomic status, immigrant students tend to suffer (Dronkers and Levels 2007). Lack of familiarity with the language of instruction can be a major barrier to learning for immigrant students (Cobb-Clark et al. 2012; Dustmann, Frattini, and Lanzara 2012). Hence, designated classes for learning the host country language can help immigrant achievement. Finally, the presence of a large coethnic community can help ease the integration process (Portes and Zhou 1993); it is likely that children of return migrants will do better in areas with more return migrants. Such a community is likely to be especially beneficial when it is well resourced (Lee and Zhou 2015).


## Analytic Strategy


For children of return migrants, how do we define 'positive' or 'negative' outcomes in school? Much depends on the comparison group and estimand. One important consideration is accounting for immigrant selection. Selection can be incorporated into statistical models of children's education in two ways. It can be directly included as a covariate measuring relative educational attainment, at either the group (Feliciano 2005) or individual (Feliciano and Lanuza 2017) level. Alternatively, the researcher can find a suitable comparison group that implicitly accounts for immigrant selection. For example, in previous work I use propensity-score matching to compare young Eastern European migrants in Western Europe to similar co-nationals who stayed behind in the East (Hoffmann 2022a). This second approach has the benefit of accounting for more than measured educational selectivity: many skills are not captured by measures of formal education (Hagan, Hernández-León, and Demonsant 2015), and immigrants are selected in ways not related to skills at all. Further adjustment for observed individual differences can render the groups even more comparable.

This chapter makes both types of comparisons. First, it places foreign-born children of return migrants in the local educational context by comparing them to local children without migration backgrounds, providing an estimate of the descriptive gap in achievement between locals and foreign-born children of return migrants. This set of analyses follows the tradition of assimilation literature, showing how similar to locals these migrant children have become. Second, this study compares these children to a suitable 'control' group: children of samenationality migrants in their country of birth. For example, for the Mexican case, this the comparison group will be U.S.-born children of Mexican migrants in the U.S. The target here is a causal estimand: the scores these children would have obtained had they not followed their parents' return migration. Finally, this paper examines institutional features of both country of birth and country of residence, elucidating which help or harm academic achievement. By considering both country of origin and destination, this paper employs a cross-border perspective (Waldinger 2017) that sheds greater light on the process and outcomes of migration than a single-country analysis would.

Education researchers typically use methods such as OLS regression that assume linear effects of covariates, but the data-generating process is often nonlinear and complicated. Failure to account for nonlinearity and interactions can severely bias effect estimation (Dorie et al. 2019). Recent advances in flexible machine learning methods have provided new tools for estimation that bypass these pitfalls, but these methods have been rarely implemented in education research. For both the descriptive and causal estimands, I will employ Double or Debiased Machine Learning, (DML, Chernozhukov et al. 2018) a method designed to be flexible enough to handle many potentially confounding variables but to not overfit the model to the data. [Note to reader: In this draft, I have not yet implemented DML. I use OLS to estimate the results

below.] Through subsequent regularization (prevention of overfitting) and de-biasing, DML allows consistent estimation of treatment effects while making only minor functional form assumptions. I will use the DoubleML package and random forests from the mlr3 library to implement this method in R.

I will employ DML to estimate both the descriptive gap between children of return migrants and locals in their country of residence, as well as the causal gap between these children and similar children of migrants in their country of birth. These estimation strategies will control for pre-migration characteristics outlined below. Finally, I will use methods of metaanalysis (Chmielewski 2019) to aggregate estimates into weighted measures of the relative performance of children of return migrants to locals and to children in their countries of birth. The multilevel models employed in meta-analytic techniques are ideally suited to handling country groups with small numbers, and they make the analysis of the country-level variables described below straightforward (Singer and Willett 2003).

I also use techniques from meta-analysis to aggregate dyad-level results. I compare results from pooled estimates that do not take the dyadic structure of the data into account, fixed effects meta-analysis, and random effects meta-analysis (Borenstein et al. 2010). For analysis of policies, I use random effects meta-analysis and OLS models with country fixed effects and clustered standard errors. I use the metafor (Viechtbauer 2010) and fixest (Bergé 2018) packages in R.


## Data


Data for this paper come from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). Every three years, the OECD administers this achievement test for reading, math, and science to

15-year-old students in dozens of countries around the world (Schleicher 2019). The exam was created in the late 1990s to provide reliable, internationally agreed upon indicators of student performance, ensuring maximum comparability across school systems. These data constitute one of the few large-scale, internationally comparable measures of academic outcomes for adolescents, making it ideal for the present project.

Outcome variables consist of reading, math, and science scores, which the OECD constructs to have a global mean of 500 and standard deviation of 100 within each test year. I use the first five plausible values for scores. No student answers every question in PISA exams, and hence these values represent the uncertainty from imputation of scores by the OECD. I perform all analyses five times - once for each plausible value - and aggregate estimates and standard errors using using 'Rubin's Rules' (Rubin 1987), as suggested by the PISA Technical Report (OECD 2017:148).

Pooling PISA data from 2012, 2015, and 2018 results in 3,480 children of return migrants. These are defined as children born in a different country from their country of residence at the time of PISA (at age 15), and who have at least one parent who was born in the country of residence. This sample contains 72 birth countries and 43 countries of residence, or 146 unique dyads for birth country-country of residence pairs.

For the descriptive comparisons within the country of residence, the control sample is defined as non-immigrant children of two non-immigrant parents ( 𝑛 = 431,212). For the causal comparisons with country of birth, the control group is defined as children born in the country of birth to at least one immigrant parent from the country of residence ( 𝑛 = 7,781). For example, one member of the 'treatment' group may be a girl born in Serbia to one parent who was born in Montenegro, but who is residing in Montenegro at the time of the PISA test. For the descriptive

comparison she is compared to children born in Montenegro to two Montenegrin parents. For the causal comparison she is compared to children of at least one Montenegrin parent who were born in Serbia and residing in Serbia at the time of the test.


## Country-Level Variables


PISA data also provide country-level variables that can be used in analysis of institutional features that may help or harm the academic achievement of children of return migrants. Most of these come from surveys of school principals or administrators. Perhaps the most studied policy in this area is academic tracking, or the sorting of students by academic rigor, focus, or 'ability.' Within-school tracking has shown mixed effects for immigrant-origin students, (Cobb-Clark et

al. 2012; Dronkers, Van Der Velden, and Dunne 2012; Marks 2005; Teltemann and Schunck 2016), between-school tracking into different types of schools - such as vocational, technical, or college preparatory - shows more clearly negative effects (Borgna and Contini 2014; Dronkers and de Heus 2016; Entorf and Lauk 2008; Heath and Brinbaum 2014; Ruhose and Schwerdt 2016; Teltemann and Schunck 2016; van de Werfhorst and Heath 2019).

I consider three types of tracking. First is ability grouping : the sorting of students within classes in a school. In 2012, school administrators were asked to respond to the statement 'Students are grouped by ability within their mathematics classes' by choosing 'for all classes,' 'for some classes,' or 'not for any classes.' Schools whose administrators answered 'some' or 'all' receive a value of 1, and those that answered 'none' are coded as 0. In 2015 and 2015, administrators were asked about ability grouping within classes by subject; those who answered 'some' or 'all' subjects receive a value of 1, while those who respond 'not for any subject' receive a value of 0. Although the 2012 question is not the same as the 2015 and 2018 question, ability grouping for math is the most common type; if a school does not have ability grouping for math, it is unlikely it has ability grouping for other subjects. To obtain a country-level measures, I calculate the proportion of schools in the country with a value of 1 for ability grouping.

Next I consider within-school tracking : the sorting of students between classes in a school. Similarly to ability grouping, school administrators were asked about tracking practices for math in 2012 and for all subjects in 2015 and 2018, and I code responses in the same manner. As above, I calculate the proportion of schools within-school tracking occur to obtain a countrylevel variable.

The third measure of tracking is between-school streaming of students. In many countries, students are sorted at the secondary level into different types of schools depending on

their career plans or academic history. In 2012, 2015, and 2018, students were asked whether their current school (at age 15) was general, pre-vocational, vocational, or modular. To obtain a measure of country-level streaming, I find code these school types as equal to 1, 2, 3, or 4, then find the standard deviation across schools surveyed in the country.

I consider two other country-level features. The first is segregation by socioeconomic status, which has been shown to negatively affect immigrant student achievement (Dronkers and Levels 2007). I rely on the index of economic, social and cultural status (ESCS), which PISA derives in each year as 'a composite score built by the indicators parental education (PARED), highest parental occupation (HISEI), and home possessions (HOMEPOS) including books in the home via principal component analysis (PCA)' (OECD 2017:339). I standardize this variable to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1 within each survey year. To measure segregation, I find the mean ESCS by school, then calculate the standard deviation across schools in a country in each year.

Finally, some scholars point to the importance of a strong coethnic community. Portes and Zhou (1993) argue that a large coethnic community can promote immigrant success by providing resources, opportunities, and protection. Levels, Dronkers, and Kraaykamp (2008) find immigrant students tend to do better in school when their coethnic community has higher socioeconomic capital than the country majority. I measure the community size of return migrants by calculating a weighted proportion of students in the country who are foreign-born children of return migrants, by dyad. I measure community SES by calculating the difference in average ESCS between children of return migrants and local students.

Where are foreign-born children of return migrants most prevalent? Although PISA does not survey every country or provide data about all migrant groups, large groups in this sample are worthy of attention. Table 1 shows the largest fifteen birth country-country of residence dyads in this sample and their average reading, math, and science scores. The largest dyads in

Scores vary substantially around the global mean of 500; dyads such as Russia-Georgia and Croatia-Bosnia and Herzegovina have fairly low average scores, but others such as United Kingdom-New Zealand and United States-Canada have high scores.

Without placing these scores in context, it is difficult to evaluate whether these foreignborn children of return migrants are excelling in school or falling behind. How do they compare to the native-born in their country of residence? And how do they compare to children in the migrant community they left?

The left panel of Figure 1 presents simple difference-in-means (DIM) estimates comparing foreign-born children of return migrants to locally born children in their country of residence (i.e., their parents' birth country) for the fifteen largest dyads presented in Table 1. Many foreign-born children of return migrants outperform locals. For example, children born in the United States to Israeli parents who move to Israel obtain scores about 50 or more points higher - or half a standard deviation - than Israeli-born children. Scores are also relatively high for the birth country-country of residence dyads of United Kingdom-New Zealand, MalaysiaBrunei, United States-Canada, and New Zealand-Australia. The relatively high performance of children of return migrants with experience in anglophone countries is notable.

Dyads at the bottom of the graph show children of return migrants who tend to score lower than locals. These include France-Belgium, Argentina-Uruguay, Germany-Belgium, Sweden-Finland, and Russia-Georgia. These differences are minor, however, amounting to less than a quarter standard deviation.

Due to the limitations of PISA data, not all dyads are present in the data. Results are fairly similar to those in Figure 1: Children of return migrants who are advantaged relative to the local population tend to be advantaged compared to the migrant community they departed. One exception is for Serbian-born children of Montenegrin return migrants: While these children slightly outperform Montenegrin children, they perform about one-quarter of a standard deviation worse than children of Montenegrin children in Serbia.

To help visualize the distribution of dyad-level differences in scores, Figure 3 displays histograms of both country-of-birth and country-of-residence comparisons. For both, there is great heterogeneity: Although the distributions are centered close to 0, some groups of children of return migrants score substantially lower than locals or the communities they left, while others outperform. On balance, negative disparities tend to be more extreme than positive ones.

These differences do not account for migrant selection. How do these differences change in models that adjust for pre-migration characteristics? The right panel of Figure 1 shows adjusted estimates for country-of-residence comparisons.
