Across countries, there is great variation in the PISA scores of children of foreign-born return migrants. Whether we take the country of residence (parents' birth country) or country of birth as the comparison group, many groups of children of return migrants excel on these tests, although some fall behind. The next section considers trends for this population as a whole.


## Overall Findings


How can we characterize the overall situation of children of return migrants? Figure 4 presents results in a few ways. The left panel uses the country of residence (parents' birth country) comparison group. At the top are estimates from pooled OLS regressions with a single coefficient indicating being a child of a return migrant. On average, the global sample of children of return migrants performs slightly better on PISA tests than children without migrant background, although this advantage is statistically significant only for math. The second set of estimates adds individual controls to this model; once the pre-migration characteristics are

accounted for, the average child of return migrants scores slightly lower on PISA, although the confidence intervals overlap 0.

The next set of estimates ('FE') comes from a fixed effects model usually used for metaanalysis that combines estimates for all dyads in the sample (Borenstein et al. 2021). This model assumes there is a common effect for children of return migrants, and that variations by dyad reflect random noise. In these models, children of return migrants perform significantly worse than their local counterparts without migrant background. The negative disparity is somewhat greater when individual controls are included. Although the differences are significant, they are substantively small, at under one-tenth of a standard deviation.

The final sets of estimates come from a random effects meta-analysis model, which assumes that the effect varies by dyad. Here, effects are more negative: In models with and without individual controls, the disparity is greater than one-tenth of a standard deviation.

The right panel of Figure 4 uses the country of birth's migrant community as the comparison group, presenting corresponding sets of estimates. Here results do not vary greatly by model: Compared to children of the same migrant group in the target group's country of birth, children of return migrants perform worse on PISA tests. Science scores are generally somewhat higher. In the random effects models, coefficients are imprecisely estimated; for math and science, the 95-percent confidence intervals overlap with 0.

On average, across dyads in the sample, foreign-born children of return migrants appear somewhat disadvantaged in PISA tests. Whether the comparison group is local children without migrant background or children of similar migrants in the birth country, foreign-born children of return migrants obtain somewhat lower PISA scores.

What explains great variation in PISA score disparities shown in Figures 1 and 2? Part of the explanation may lie in country-level institutions and policies. Due to the nationally bounded nature of these institutions, this part of the analysis compares children of return migrants to only children in the country of residence.

The first institution considered is within-class ability grouping. In both panels, this coefficient is close to 0; the proportion of schools that group students by ability does not seem related to PISA scores for children of return migrants.

Next I consider within-school tracking, or the sorting of students into different classes based on ability. In the left panel, the coefficients are positive and significant, suggesting that, in countries where within-school tracking is more common, children of return migrants tend to perform better than local children. But the right panel shows the opposite: In countries that move toward greater within-school tracking, children of return migrants tend to perform worse on PISA. These differing results suggest that children of return migrants who do well on PISA tend to live in countries with more within-school tracking, but that a change to greater tracking may actually detract from their PISA scores.

The final measure of tracking is between-school streaming, or the extent to which countries formally differentiate schools. Coefficients in both models are nonsignificant for this variable.

The next measure considers inequality: SES segregation, calculated as the standard deviation of the average economic, social, and cultural status for schools. The coefficients here are also nonsignificant.

The final two factors relate to the community of children of return migrants: its size and its SES, relative to the majority. The community size does not have significant coefficients, but the community SES does. In countries where the return migrant community has higher SES than the majority, children of return migrants tend to perform better than locals, even when individual SES is controlled for. A one standard deviation increase in community SES is associated with a

quarter standard deviation increase in PISA score advantage. This coefficient is similar in size in the fixed effects regression, suggesting a causal interpretation.


## Discussion and Conclusion


Despite numbering in the hundreds of thousands worldwide, foreign-born children of return migrants have received little scholarly attention outside of a handful of case studies. This group is important to study both due to its size but also because it can tell us about the dynamics of immigrant incorporation and policies related to immigrant achievement more broadly.

This paper aimed to characterize the academic achievement of these foreign-born children of return migrants by analyzing 146 birth country-country of residence dyads from PISA data for 2012, 2015, and 2018. How do these children compare to locals in their parents' country of birth and to children of migrants who do not return? Across dyads, there is great variation in PISA score disparities for children of return migrants. Some of the most advantaged birth country-country of residence dyads are United States-Israel, United Kingdom-New Zealand, and Malaysia-Brunei. The most disadvantaged include Sweden-Finland, ArgentinaUruguay, and France-Belgium, however these disadvantages are relatively minor. Results vary little whether the comparison group is locals or the migrant community these children left; children who are (dis)advantaged compared to locals tend to be (dis)advantaged compared to the migrant community they left.

When estimates are aggregated into a meta-analytic framework, models show that the general situation of children of return migrants is of slight disadvantage, relative to both locals and to children of migrants in the communities they left. Two country-level features help explain the variation across countries. First, within-school tracking into classes of different 'abilities' is associated with an advantage for children of return migrants relative to locals. But countries that

move toward greater within-school tracking may see the opposite effect. The socioeconomic status of the return migrant community, relative to local non-migrants, shows a more clearly positive effect: Children of return migrant communities that are relatively advantaged tend to excel on PISA tests, even when their individual SES is accounted for.

These results support three main conclusions that put into perspective the mixed results from previous, small-scale studies. First, there is great variation across the experiences of children of return migrants around the world, as shown in Figures 1 and 2. In many countries, children of return migrants enjoy a distinct advantage compared to both locals and to children in the migrant communities they left. However, secondly, the average child of return migrants experiences a disadvantage in school, scoring slightly lower on PISA than comparison groups. Figures 1 and 2 present only large return flows, at least as represented in PISA data; this suggests that children in smaller return flows are the ones falling behind. Finally, the analysis of countrylevel institutions showcases the importance of group-level resources that return migrants bring with them: Even when a child's return migrant parents have few resources, an advantaged returnmigrant community may fill in with the resources and knowledge necessary for these children to do well in school. Groups with more resources appear better able to weather the travails of migration. Reverse causality is also possible; groups with smoother return migration experiences may be able to accumulate more resources.

This research suggests a number of avenues for future research. This study is limited by the data availability of PISA; not all countries administer PISA, and some countries do not ask students for their or their parents' birthplaces. Future research should study populations not covered by PISA data. Furthermore, not all students in a country take the PISA test; in Mexico, scholars have found that bureaucratic hurdles prevent the most disadvantaged students from

enrolling in school (Mateos 2019; Zúñiga and Carrillo Cantú 2020), and hence are excluded from the PISA sample. Finally, since only 15-year-olds take PISA, we do not know if achievement varies by age at test time. Disparities for children of immigrants may be wider at younger ages (Hoffmann 2018; Strand, Malmberg, and Hall 2015), and educational success may not lead to success in the labor market (Lee 2021:192-93). Future research should study academic achievement at younger ages, enrollment in higher education, and the school-to-work transition for children of return migrants.

These results have broader implications for studies of immigrant incorporation. Assimilation theory predicts that when an immigrant group lacks social markers of difference, assimilation should be rapid and straightforward. But even in this case - a group that has locally born parents, speaks the language, and is visibly indistinguishable from children without a migrant background - a slight disadvantage in school remains, on average. This phenomenon highlights that migration is a difficult process. Some return migration flows - such as from the U.S. to Mexico - involve high levels of deportation. Although U.S.-born children are not at risk of deportation, many undergo the trauma of accompanying their deported parents (Waldinger 2021). Return migration may also involve separation from loved ones, financial hardship, and difficult cultural adjustments that can negatively impact academic achievement.

## 1. Introduction.


In  St  Thomas  Aquinas' Summa Theologica (Aquinas,  1265-73),  the 'Angelic Doctor' asks if God's existence can be proved, and answers in the affirmative, the second of his 'Five Ways' ( Quinqae Viae ) being:

'The second way is from the nature of the efficient cause. In the world of sense we find there is an order of efficient causes. There  is  no  case  known  (neither  is  it,  indeed,  possible)  in which a thing is found to be the efficient cause of itself; for so it would be prior to itself, which is impossible. Now in efficient causes  it  is  not  possible  to  go  on  to  infinity,  because  in  all efficient causes following in order, the first is the cause of the intermediate cause, and the intermediate is the cause of the ultimate cause, whether the intermediate cause be several, or only  one.  Now  to  take  away  the  cause  is  to  take  away  the effect.  Therefore,  if  there  be  no  first  cause  among  efficient causes, there will be no ultimate, nor any intermediate cause. But if in efficient causes it is possible to go on to infinity, there will be no first efficient cause, neither will there be an ultimate effect, nor any intermediate efficient causes; all of which is plainly false. Therefore it is necessary to admit a first efficient cause, to which everyone gives the name of God.'

The  Kalam  cosmological  argument  may  be  somewhat  more  briefly stated, as a syllogism (Craig, 1997, p.236):

## '1.  Whatever  begins  to  exist  has  a  cause.  2.  The  universe began to exist. 3. Therefore, the universe has a cause.'

There is, here, no need to go into any discussion about what is meant by Aquinas' (and Aristotle's) term 'efficient cause' (see Carr, 2022). It should be noted that Craig's version of the argument differs from alGhazâlî's original to the extent that, for al-Ghazâlî, given his understanding of causation, Allah had to keep intervening in the order of creation to keep the chain of cause and effect going, as - for him this was not automatic, as Griffel (2020) explains.

It is generally accepted that the syllogism, as such, is valid, and that  the  major  premiss  is  true;  it  is  the  minor  premiss  that  has  been subjected to the greatest challenge. Scientists like Penrose (2010) argue for an eternal, cyclic Universe. The present author has made his own contribution  to  that  particular  debate  (Blaber,  2023c).  Philosophers such as Oppy (1991a, 1991b, 1995) invoke Cantor (1874, 1879) and set

theory (Gray, 1994; Alfeld, 1996; Bagaria, 2023) to argue in favour of infinite  causal  regresses.  However,  there  are  defenders  of  causal finitism, among them Pruss (2018a, 2018b) and Schmid (2021, 2023), as well as opponents, such as Puryear (2014).

The entire discussion must be set in the context of whether or not the concept of God is coherent, which it is our contention here that it is (see  Blaber,  2023b).  It  should  be  noted,  though,  that  the  Kalam cosmological argument does not, of itself, justify belief in a personal Creator, merely, if true, in a cause, whether personal or impersonal, of the Universe.

## 3. A Finite Chain of Causation.


Pruss (2018a, op.cit., p.3, pdf.) defines 'causal finitism' as

## 'a family of views on which, roughly, an infinite number of things cannot be causally prior to one thing.'

It follows, he says, that, if causal finitism is the case, there can be no infinite regress of causes (see p.1),

'since  each  of  the  infinitely  many  items  in  a  causal  regress would be causally prior to the item from which the regress started' (p.3, ibid.).

Schmid (2021, op.cit.,  p.1,  pdf.)  states  causal  finitism  ('CF')  as  the proposition that 'Necessarily, every  causal history is finite'. Schmid (2023, op.cit.) cites Gel's (2022) defence of 'pure act theism' against Oppy's  (in  Goldschmidt,  ed.,  2013,  Ch.3,  pp.46-63)  naturalistic explanation of the first cause, or 'First Cause', as Gel capitalises it.

Schmid  gets  somewhat  bogged  down  in  whether  or  not  Gel's argument satisfies, or does not satisfy, the criterion of Ockham's Razor - whether stated in William's own formulation, Numquam ponenda est pluralitas  sine  necessitate ('Plurality  must  never  be  posited  without necessity'),  or  in  John  Punch's  more  famous  one, Entia  non  sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem ('Entities  must  not  be  multiplied beyond  necessity')   hardly  matters.  All  that  need  be  noted  is  that 5 Oppy's  argument  fails  because  everything  in  nature  is contingent , whereas what is needed of a First Cause is that it be necessary . Only a self-caused, self-existent being, whose essence entails existence, will do.

Hume (1779, 1990, 2017, Part 9, pp.38-40) argues that there is nothing contradictory about any infinite causal sequence, and there is no need to posit a cause for the whole sequence. Uniting the sequence into a whole is a mere mental construct, he says - 'an arbitrary act of the mind'. Furthermore (and this is also an attempt at a refutation of the ontological argument), Hume tells us that (a) nothing is demonstrable unless its contrary implies a contradiction; (b) nothing that is distinctly conceivable  implies  a  contradiction;  (c)  whatever  we  conceive  as existent, we can also conceive as non-existent; (d) [therefore] there is

no being whose existence is demonstrable. By 'demonstrable', Hume means provable a priori . It is clear that premiss (a) is true, so those of us who disagree with him must disprove premisses (b) and, especially, (c) to defeat his argument.

Hume tells us that that the phrase 'necessary existence' has no meaning, on the basis of his line of reasoning just stated, but then asks 'why  shouldn't  the material  universe be  the  necessarily  existent being?' He is merely playing games at this point. His substantial point is  that  there is no  'necessarily  existent  being',  no  'first  author  of existence',  no  priority  in  time,  no  beginning  of  existence  -  in  other words, no God. It is clearly incumbent on all defenders of monotheism to dispute his case.

Zarepour (2021) notes that there are varieties of causal finitism that it is not, in other words, an intellectual monolith. The bulk of his argument,  however,  is  concerned  with  whether  or  not actual (as opposed to potential, or theoretical) infinities exist. (There is no doubt that mathematical infinites exist: there are infinite sets; if we divide 1, or any other finite number, by 0, the quotient is infinity .) He outlines 6 his own version of the Kalam cosmological argument, to incorporate this issue (we will elide his arguments 'A' and 'B' here, for reasons of brevity):

'(A1/B1) The universe exists; (A2/B2) If the universe has no beginning, an infinite temporal regress of events exists; If the universe has no end, an infinite temporal progress of events exists;  (A3/B3)  An  infinite  temporal  regress  of  events  is  an actual infinite; An infinite temporal progress of events is an actual  infinite; (A4/B4)  An  actual  infinite  cannot  exist; (A5/B5) Therefore: The universe [had] a beginning [and will have] an end' (pp.302-303, emphases added).

Zarepour seems to think B5 - the idea that the Universe will have an end - contradicts religious belief in an eternal afterlife (p.304), but is

in  this,  rather  obviously,  confusing  the  physical  Universe  with  the spiritual realm. There is no such contradiction. It is doubtful that Craig (2008, p.116) shares his confusion, although Zarepour (ibid.) appears to believe that he does.

What might well be fatal to his argument that there are 'absurd consequences' to the existence of actual infinites is his insistence on referring  to  them  being  'instantiated  in  the  mind-independent  real world' (p.305).

But what if there is no 'mind-independent real world'? What if Berkeley's  (1734,  2002),  or  some  other  form,  of  idealism  is  true? Actual infinites must be a metaphysical and ontological impossibility (Zarepour, ibid.) in a Berkelian Universe - especially given the fact that Berkeley was a Church of Ireland Bishop, and a staunch defender of theism,  see  Downing  (2021,  1;  3.1.3).  There  must  be  a  way  of differentiating between the physical and the mathematical in idealistic metaphysics, even though 'mathematics is the language of nature', as Galileo pointed out (Galilei, 1623, p.4) . Speculation on how this might 7 be achieved, though, is beyond the scope of this paper.


## 4. Objections Grounded In 'Anti-Theodicy'.


The  present  author  has  dealt  with  many  of  the  issues  raised  here elsewhere (Blaber, 2023a, 2023b), so will not rehearse them extensively again.

As is well-known, Leibniz (1710, 1951) argued we were living in 'the best of all possible worlds', created by an omnibenevolent deity. Leibniz was quite sanguine about all the evil and suffering in the world, and was happy to accept the idea that the vast majority of the human race would end up suffering eternal torment in Hell. This was merely a manifestation of the 'justice' of God! Needless to say, later philosophers, like Voltaire (1759, 2005) did not think much of these ideas.

The experience of the twentieth century, and particularly of the Jews  at  the  hands  of  the  Nazis  in  the  Holocaust,  caused  many  to

abandon belief in God altogether - but not Elie Wiesel (Wiesel, 1958, 1972, 1985, 2006), whose powerful, vivid and distressing account of his  time  as  a  teenager  in  the  Auschwitz,  Buna  and  Buchenwald Concentration  Camps  between  1944-45,  ought  to  be  compulsory reading in schools.

If  it  not the  case,  to  quote  Stendhal (Marie-Henri Beyle, 17831842),  that  'God's  only  excuse  is  that  he  does  not  exist'  ( 'La  seule excuse de Dieu ce n'existe-pas' ), perhaps it is rather the case that ' Dieu existe,  donc  il  n'a  aucune  excuse '  ('God  exists,  therefore  he  has  no excuse'). In other words, while we can posit the existence of a 'God', or god, that God will not be the traditional one, with all the attributes traditionally ascribed to him, including moral perfection, but a God that lacks  omnibenevolence  and  foreknowledge,  for  reasons  outlined  in Blaber (2023b). This 'God' is rather more like the Gnostic 'Demiurge' than the God of Judaism, Christianity or Islam - see McPeters (2022).

It should, in fact, be acknowledged that the 'First Cause' posited by the Kalam cosmological argument is not necessarily personal at all, and  thus  might  well  not  be  endowed  with  'free  will'  and  the  moral responsibility entailed by free will. Article I of the Church of England's XXXIX  Articles  describes  God  as  being  'without  body,  parts  or passions', and it is difficult to see how an impassible being (which the God of traditional theism is ) can be truly personal, in any sense that 8 does  not  stretch  the analogia  entis ('analogy  of  being') to  breaking point.


## 5. The Kalam Cosmological Argument.


The chief recent exponent of the Kalam cosmological argument, as we have previously stated, has been Craig (1991, 1997, 1998, 1999, 2006, 2011)  and  Craig  and  Sinclair  (in  Craig  and  Moreland,  eds.,  2009, pp.101-201),  but  he  has  been  joined  by  Loke  (2022)  in  linking  the Kalam  argument  to  the  teleological argument  (the 'fine-tuning' version,  in  their  case),  whilst  Craig  himself  dovetails  the  Kalam argument with the teleological (design) argument for the existence of God (1998).

In Defence of the Kalam Cosmological Argument.

Mushtaq (2018) examines the Kalam and teleological arguments from  an  Islamic  perspective,  whilst  Morriston  (2000)  joins  those criticising the Kalam argument, asking if it is necessarily the case that the  Universe had a personal cause  (which,  in  fact,  the  argument, as stated , does not imply - additional premisses are required, as we have already noted).

It is as well to re-state the Kalam argument once more, making use of Zarepour's formulation (op.cit.):

- (1). The Universe exists.
- (2). The Universe has a beginning, and it has an end.
- (3). Whatever exists, has a beginning and an end has a cause.
- (4). Therefore, the Universe has a cause.

We will defend this particular version of the argument, before turning to examine Craig's, et al 's discussions.

'[T]ime, that takes survey of all the  world,/Must have  a stop,' (Shakespeare, Henry  IV , Part  1,  Act  V,  Scene  4,  ll.81-82).  It  is fundamental to Jewish, Christian and Islamic belief that the physical Universe had a  beginning  and will  have an  end,  with  a  Day  of Judgement:  see  Daniel  11-12; Zephaniah  1:2-18;  Zechariah  14; Revelation  6-21;  Qur'an  7:8,  40-51;  43:63-76.  We  have  already adduced  our  own  reasons  why  these  beliefs  may  be  reproduced  in physical fact.

Huby (op.cit.) asks whether an actual ,  as  opposed to potential, infinity  is possible  (p.123).  She,  like  Zarepour,  writes  from  the perspective of what  Kant termed 'transcendental realism'  - in other words,  the  idea  that  the  Universe  is  objectively  real  and  exists independently of minds (p.124), and this is a weakness of her argument. The issue ought not to depend on realist versus idealist metaphysics. As stated above, an actual infinity could well be ruled out, even if Esse est percipi aut percipere ('To be is to perceive or to be perceived', see Berkeley, op.cit.). Indeed, it is arguable that it is more likely to be ruled out if  that  is  the  case  -  since  we  cannot  perceive  infinities.  We  can conceptualise them, but not perceive them.

One thing Huby says that is particularly worth commenting on is this:

'the  transcendental  realist...  must  hold  that  there  is  an unbroken continuity between any past state of the universe and the present, however distant in time that past state may be, and that the same Laws of Nature, or at least related ones, hold everywhere in the universe, however far away' (ibid.).

Whilst  it  is  perfectly  reasonable  to  adhere  to  the  first  part  of  this statement, both it and the second part are unproved, and unprovable, assumptions,  which may be  true,  but  may not be,  and  the  second assumption  is  less  reasonable  than  the  first.  The  problem  is  the transcendental realism, and indeed, the realism. We cannot know what is independent of our minds - we only know the phenomenal world, and  to  argue,  as  Kant  (op.cit.)  did,  for  a  'noumenal'  one,  is  an unprovable assumption. It is sufficient to note that Huby tells us

'now that, thanks to Riemann and Einstein, it is no longer necessary to assume that space must be infinite, arguments for the infinity of matter collapse too' (p.125).

One final point she makes is also worth recording, and that is this, on p.129 (emphasis original):

'Cantor did not make an actual infinite respectable in the sense that he enabled us to understand how there could be an infinity of actual numbers: rather he introduced techniques by which we can deal satisfactorily and unambiguously with a certain kind of potential infinite.'

The  German  mathematician  David  Hilbert  (1862-1943;  Hilbert  in Benacerraf and Putnam, eds., 1964, 1984, pp.183-201) stated that an actually realised infinite quantity 'is nowhere to be found in reality'.

Erasmus and Luna (op.cit.), as stated earlier, present a philosophical argument for a beginning of time, but undermine their case from the beginning because of their understanding of set theory, criticising what they call the 'Infinity Argument' (pp.161, et seq. ). By this, they mean the argument that:

'it  is  metaphysically  impossible  for  an  infinite  number  of things (such as events) either to exist (i.e., be instantiated in the real  world) simultaneously or to come into existence in such a way that there is a time at which all the infinitely many things have already occurred. Thus, since an infinite sequence of  events  cannot  be  completed,  the  sequence  of  past  events must be finite' (p.162).

They  claim  (ibid.)  this  argument  is  'problematic'  (as  opposed  to 'unsound') because (1) set theory is consistent with an actual infinite (but see Huby, op.cit., above on this); and (2) because

## 'the Infinity Argument brings into question the view that God predetermined an endless future.'

Whence the idea that he did? Once again, as with Zarepour, we see this almost incomprehensible confusion between  the eternity of the physical Universe and that of the spiritual one, bordering on the absurd.

Craig and Sinclair (in Craig and Moreland, eds., 2009, op.cit., p.102) cite al-Ghazâlî's Al-Iqtisād fī al-I'tiqad ('Moderation in Belief'; al-Ghazâlî,  1962  [2013],  pp.15-16),  giving  the  original  form  of  the Kalam cosmological argument:

'Every being which begins has a cause for its beginning; now the world is a being which begins; therefore, it possesses a cause for its beginning.'

In  defence of the second premiss, Craig and Sinclair say (ibid.), alGhazâlî  argued  that  an  infinite  regress  of  temporal  phenomena  was impossible, and so there could not have been an infinite past. The finite past must, for al-Ghazâlî (1963, p.33):

## 'stop at an eternal being from which the first temporal being should have originated.'

Craig (1998) tells us that:

'The cosmological argument aims to prove that there exists a First  Cause  or  Sufficient  Reason  for  the  existence  of  the cosmos; the teleological argument aspires to show that there is  an  Intelligent  Designer  of  the  order  in  the  cosmos.  The teleological argument shows that the First Cause demonstrated  by  the  cosmological  argument  is  not  some mindless 'ground of being,' but a personal, intelligent Mind.'

Here,  of  course,  Craig  is  taking  an  obvious  swipe  at  Tillich  (1973, pp.235-236), but his stricture is, in effect, equally directed at Spinoza (1671?,  1910;  1665,  1677,  1996,  2017).  It  also  encompasses  the impersonal  idealistic  pantheist  deity  (if  'deity'  is  the  right  word), Brahman 9 ,  of  Hinduism  (Tunga,  2015),  and  it  is  grossly  unfair  to characterise it (the noun is neuter in Sanskrit) as 'mindless'. See also Dalal  (2021).  The  design  argument  is  exposed  to  the  sort  of  attack aimed at it by the likes of Dawkins (1986, 1991, 2006), although his direct  target  is  William  Paley  (1743-1805)  and  his  'watchmaker' version of the argument, to be found in Paley (1802).

Loke  (op.cit.,  Ch.4,  4.3.3)  argues  that  the  'fine-tuning'  of  the Universe (by which he means, and which is meant, such things as the facts, which Davies, 1982, pp.69-70, 71-73, points out, that changes to the relative strengths of the strong nuclear, gravitational and electromagnetic  forces  would  have  profound  consequences,  which would render life in the Universe highly improbable, if not impossible - Davies, op.cit., pp.110-115) is 'fundamentally due' ( sic ) to 'Design'.

His problem is that cosmologists such as Carter (1974, pp.293294)  have  explained  'fine-tuning'  in  terms  of  either  the  'weak'  or 'strong' anthropic principles, and  Tegmark's  (2007)  'Level  IV' Multiverse (p.15) is comprised of a putative set of universes parallel to, and including, this one, with different physical laws and constants, and different  initial  physical  conditions,  so  there  will  be  life  in  some  of them, but not in others, with no need to invoke a cosmic designer.

Ross (in Goldschmidt and Pearce, eds., 2017, Ch.15, pp.246-258) defines what he terms 'strong fine-tuning for consciousness' as:

'[The  fact  that]  a  large  number  of  fundamental  physical parameters  (e.g.,  the  constants  that  figure  in  the  laws  of physics) are strongly fine-tuned for the existence of consciousness' (p.250).

Ross thinks that the essence of scientific explanation is reduction of the total  number  of  independent  phenomena  that  we  have  to  accept  as 'ultimate', or 'given' (what medieval philosophers would have called 'saving  the appearances',  a  translation of Simplicius' sōzein  ta phainomena ,  see  Lewis,  1964,  pp.14-15),  and  -  in  consequence  believes  that  parsimony  (Ockham's  Razor)  is  essential,  as  are  the criteria of stringency, which he defines as 'the degree to which... tight constraints'  are  imposed  on  the  elements  of  a  scientific  theory's inferences, and strength, which is:

'the scope of known propositions that can be inferred from other known propositions... on the basis of these inference[s]' (p.251).

He then proceeds to defend what he calls 'nootropic reasoning' (ibid.), which he defines as:

'reasoning from the premise that consciousness exists, together with the premise that consciousness can only exist if the universe is thus-and-so, to the conclusion that the universe is thus-and-so' (pp.251-252).

He gives as an example the following:

- '1. Consciousness exists. 2. Background conditions [b.c.s] A, B, [&] C obtain. 3. If [b.c.s] A, B [&] C obtain, consciousness can exist  only  if  the  gravitational  constant  lies  between  6.5 and  6.8  ×  10-11  m   kg 3 -1 s -2 .  4.  Therefore,  the  gravitational constant lies between 6.5 and 6.8 × 10 -11  m  kg 3 -1 s -2 ' (ibid.).

Ross concludes:

'if nootropic inferences are explanatory, then numerous facts about the fundamental physical parameters can be explained in  part  in  terms  of  the  existence  of  consciousness...  [W]e defined explanatory idealism as the view that mentalistic facts play an  important  role  in  explaining  a wide  range  of phenomena that appear, prima facie , to be mind-independent. Now, clearly, the fact that consciousness exists is a mentalistic fact. And, equally clearly, this fact plays an important role in nootropic explanation. Moreover, facts about the fundamental physical constants are  paradigmatic examples of prima  facie mind-independent  facts...  if  Strong  FineTuning  for  Consciousness  is  true,  then  so  is  explanatory idealism' (pp.252-253, emphases added).

However, Ross' argument is as vulnerable to the objections of those advocating one version or the other of the anthropic principle, and/or the  'Level  IV'  Multiverse,  as  Loke's  (op.cit.)  is,  and  'explanatory idealism'  is  a  weak,  and  rather  insipid,  cousin  to  that  advocated  by Berkeley (op.cit.).

Mushtaq (2018) points out that the Kalam cosmological argument is  deistic,  as  well  as  theistic  (p.38),  before  rehearsing  the  argument against actual infinities.

'Why is there a necessity of a First Cause? The primal reason is  the  impossibility  of  actual  infinity.  Aristotle  argued  that there  are  two  kinds  of  infinities  -  Potential  and  Actual. Consider prime numbers which have a starting point from the numeral 1. Now go on adding numbers and you will never stop and there will be always another number which could be added to the previous number. Now consider a set of numbers within  a  space  that  has  a  beginning  and  an  end  but  the numbers within this space are infinite. This is paradoxically not  possible  because  you  cannot  add  any  number  to  a complete set, hence it can't be infinite. Similarly, infinite time, where there is no temporal beginning and ending, is logically not possible. If you travel backward in time and tried to find

where it all began, you won't stop anywhere and no matter how many billions and trillions of years you go back there still will be billions and trillions of years to travel. Since an infinite temporal regress is akin to an actual infinite, it can't exist in reality and if there is no beginning to the universe and there is  an  infinite  past,  we  can't  reach  to  the  present  moment' (ibid.).

This  is  fair  enough,  but  when  Mushtaq  turns  to  the  teleological argument, and says (p.40):

'Most of the phenomena in nature are so delicate and complex that  many  people  regard  it  highly  improbable  that  these things  came  into  existence  by  mere  chance  and  random unconscious  factors. Teleos or  purpose  is  deemed  behind every biological aspect of life. An eye is not a random socket but it has a purpose which is to see and perceive the external reality.  Most  people  since  time  immemorial  have  found  it difficult to believe that such an exquisite design could be an accident  as  atheists  want  us  to  believe.  Theists  deduce  a Volitional  Mind  behind  all  these  intricate  phenomena.  Not only in the living beings but in the formation and the stability of  the  universe,  there  is  a  fine  tuning  in  the  cosmological constants without which a universe couldn't form. Physical laws of nature are so refined that it necessarily demands a Law-Giver' (emphasis original), he is on much weaker ground, for reasons already adduced. It would seem that, if one wishes to defend the idea of the First Cause being a Personal Creator or Designer, one must employ another line, or lines, of reasoning to that of the teleological argument.


## 6. Conclusion.


The principle ouden ex oudenos was first articulated by the pre-Socratic Greek philosopher Parmenides ( fl. late 6 th -early 5 th Century BCE; in his Fragments 1-19, Fragment 6), and is to be found in Aristotle's (350

In Defence of the Kalam Cosmological Argument.

BCE) Physics Book 1, Parts 4 and 8. In Lucretius' poem, De Rerum Natura (The Nature of Things, c. 50s-40s BCE), he translates the phrase into Latin: ex nihilo nihil fit:

'For  certainly  all  men  are  in  the  clutches  of  a  dread  /Beholding  many  things  take  place  in  heaven  overhead/Or here on earth whose causes they can't fathom, they assign/The explanation for these happenings to powers divine./ Nothing can be made from nothing - once we see that's so,/Already we are on the way to what we want to know:/What can things be fashioned from? And how is it, without/The machinations of the  gods,  all  things  can  come  about?/'  (Book  1,  ll.151-158, emphasis original.)

Against 'nothing will come of nothing' (the same phrase quoted by King  Lear  in King  Lear ,  Act  1,  Scene  1,  l.89),  orthodox  Christian theology opposes creatio ex nihilo , creation from nothing. John Milton (1825, Book I, Ch.VII, p.178 [p.230, pdf.]), dissents from this view:

'Thus far it has appeared that God the Father is the primary and efficient cause of all things. With regard to the original matter  of  the  universe,  however,  there  has  been  much difference of opinion. Most of the moderns contend that it was formed from nothing, a basis as unsubstantial as that of their own theory. In the first place,  it  is certain  that  neither  the Hebrew verb [ bara ] 10 , nor the Greek [ ktizein , ]  nor the Latin creare , can signify to create out of nothing. On the contrary, these  words  uniformly  signify  to  create  out  of  matter...  To allege... that creation signifies production out of nothing, is, as logicians say, to lay down premises without a proof; for the

passages of Scripture commonly quoted for this purpose, are so far from confirming the received opinion, that they rather imply the contrary, namely, that all things were not made out of nothing.' (Emphases original.)

The problem arises from this, of course, that we are left with a belief in the  pre-existence  of  matter  (and  energy,  given  their  equivalence,  of which Milton could have known nothing). Whence did it come? Only from God, if he is the Creator, and only either (a) out of nothing; or (b) out of his own substance, of which, Spinoza tells us, he is the cause (Spinoza, 1665, 1677, 1996, 2017, op.cit., Part I, Definitions D1, D3, D6 & D8, p.1, pdf.). If it is true, as Parmenides, Aristotle and Lucretius (see above) contended, and as Milton did, that 'nothing can come of nothing',  God  created  finite  matter  and  energy  from  his  own,  and obviously  eternally  pre-existing,  infinite  substance.  Furthermore,  if Spinoza is correct, this was not a volitional act, but a necessary one (op.cit., Part I, Definition D7, p.1, pdf.).

If the present author is correct (Blaber 2023c, see p.5, above), the Universe did not originate ex nihilo , but from an extremely dense point, some ~13.8 billion years ago, when all the matter in the cosmos at that time  -  possibly  only  the  Planck  mass  -  was  concentrated  in  an extremely  dense  point  at  the  centre  of  a  black  hole,  itself  inside  an infinite, almost empty, Euclidean space.

There  is  no  known  physical  law  that  would  have  permitted  a spontaneous, natural transition from that state to the subsequent cosmic history - it would have required a supernatural intervention: in other words, the hand of God.

It may be that this theory is incorrect: but it seems, to the present author, at any rate, to be rather more coherent than any which proffer, as an alternative, 'fluctuations' in a 'quantum vacuum' which turns out not to be a 'vacuum' in any meaningful sense at all, and which violate the law of mass-energy conservation (Jaki, op.cit., pp.133-136).

## Introduction:


On 14 th October 2023, Australian voters participated in the Indigenous Voice to Parliament Referendum (hereafter the Voice referendum or the Voice). Australians were required to vote in a referendum that proposed a constitutional amendment aimed at establishing the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice. This body, as envisioned, would serve the purpose of advising both the Parliament and the Executive Government of the Commonwealth on matters pertaining to laws and policies that affect Indigenous Australians. The creation of this advisory body would be a form of Constitutional recognition of Indigenous people as the First People of Australia (Reconciliation Australia 2023).

The Constitutional amendment required a 'double majority' from the voting electorate, requiring a national majority from all electors, and a majority of electors in the majority of states (Australian Electoral Commission 2023). The Voice referendum results did not meet that threshold, with 60.1% of Australians voting No, while 39.9% supported the referendum, leading to the rejection of the Voice.

The vote was preceded by substantial campaigning by  Yes  and  No  groups with ties to civil ' ' ' ' society, party politics, and business interests (the latter seeing an opportunity to pledge a progressive politics to historical injustices in Australia). The campaigns accompanied heated debate online and showed the limits of Australian digital media regulations in platforms such as WeChat, where Chinese Australians go for news and information.

No study to date has systematically captured or analysed the discourse on WeChat about the Voice, which we report on here via our novel methods. The paper also shows how the regulatory limits manifest, based on systematic quantitative and qualitative assessment of the WeChat posts dealing with the Voice positioned towards Australian audiences.

Timothy Graham's (2023) research of English digital media discourse analysed online discussions related to the Voice referendum on Twitter (now 'X'). Graham found that, leading up to the referendum, the English-speaking Australian Twittersphere was characterised by confusion and intense polarisation. Notably, conservative politicians and media outlets played a significant role in shaping discussions on Twitter. Both Yes and No camps engaged in coordinated activism. The Yes campaign, with a higher prevalence on Twitter, demonstrated organised efforts countering No campaigners and addressing biased media coverage. Within and adjacent to the No camp, Graham shows notable spikes in the activation of suspicious accounts that propagated misinformation and conspiracy theories.

This paper seeks to build upon Graham's discussion by examining the discussion and sharing of information about the Voice referendum on WeChat -a social media application owned by China-based tech giant Tencent -and targeted to Mandarin-speaking Australians. The research is guided by the following questions:

- 1) Who were the domestic and international actors engaging on WeChat to shape the discussion of the Voice referendum? What features of the app did they use and what content did they disseminate?
- 2) What proportion of content involved misinformation and disinformation?
- 3) How much support did the Yes and No position receive among WeChat users, as evident from engagement metrics and comments?
- 4) What lessons can be learned for effective political communication on WeChat or other social media platforms with Mandarin speaking Australians, particularly in anticipation of the 2025 Australian federal election?


## WeChat and Chinese Australians:


WeChat is a multifaceted platform encompassing interpersonal and group messaging, news publication, payment services, short videos, and live streaming that is the most popular digital Chinese language platform in Australia. Since the launch of the 'WeChat Official Accounts' function (WOAs) in August 2012, Chinese diasporic media organisations, ethnic Chinese businesses, and individual content creators have taken up WOAs to keep Chinese Australians informed about local and global affairs. WOAs are recognised as the predominant news source among Chinese-speaking communities and play a critical role in both informing and shaping public opinions (Sun 2018; Hsu 2023). The economic model of the majority of Chinese diasporic media WOAs is that they collate news stories from English media, translate, and then edit posts for public consumption on their own WOAs. WOAs on WeChat operate as a fully-fledged business with the autonomy to monetise its content and readership through advertising. Despite operating overseas, each WOA in Australia is registered with a China-based brand and remains subject to Chinese internet governance. This entails platform censorship and self-censorship of politically sensitive topics disapproved by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) (Yang 2023). Each media account is allowed a maximum of eight daily posts, except for state-approved accounts such as China Daily or People's Daily , which are exempt from this restriction but work under a different (state-sponsored business model).

Despite facing competition from the short-video and live-streaming features of the emerging app Red (also known as Xiaohongshu) and WeChat's own similar new functionality ' WeChat Channel , WOAs continue to serve as a recognised and effective communication ' medium for Australian institutions targeting with Chinese communities. Analysis on the dynamics and information flow on WeChat in the context of the Voice referendum is essential for Australia's public sector and non -governmental organisations to understand actors, content, and perspectives that shape the opinions of Chinese Australians on the platform. This significant insight will also contribute to enabling the design of strategies to address any potential influences from WeChat and media accounts, ensuring that ChineseAustralian voters can make well-informed political decisions in the 2025 Australian federal election.

With 1.4 million Australians of Chinese ancestry, comprising 5.5% of the population, this community constituted a significant voting bloc in shaping the outcomes of the Voice referendum. It is important to note that our analysis can only capture online public opinions generated predominantly by Chinese-speaking migrants in Australia, and this may not match the actual referendum result. Nevertheless, the significance of online opinions persists, given their potential to influence eligible Chinese-Australian voters and future participants in the electoral process.


## Research methods:


The research initiative originates from an ongoing project begun in 2019 that is dedicated to the systematic monitoring and analysis of public opinions and sentiments concerning Australian politics on Chinese social media. Our current research focus includes WeChat and Red (or known as Xiaohongshu in Mandarin). With the novel computational tool  Share-' Capture ' (Fordyce et al., forthcoming), the project has captured over 17 thousand public posts from WeChat, standing as the largest collection of research data on WeChat outside of China.

In the context of the Voice referendum, our research team has subscribed to 135 public accounts on WeChat. An English-Mandarin bilingual researcher monitors the public posts from the subscribed accounts daily, copies the URLs of public posts discussing Australian politics on WeChat and then pastes them into a private channel on Telegram. This facilitates the exportation of public posts from WeChat, enabling future data scraping, storage, and analysis. The private Telegram channel consists of two researchers and a bot designed for scraping inputs.


## Referendum-related sample


Within the sample collected using the above method, the first post addressing Australia's forthcoming referendum surfaced 9 months prior, in January 2023. Over the period spanning from the 8 January to 8 December 2023, our tool 'Share Capture' -collected a total of 3,002 items related to the Voice referendum, which included:

- · 262 public posts from WeChat that discussed the Voice referendum. 18 public posts were removed after data collection, with 12 of them originally provided by the Australian Electoral Commission 1 .
- · 20 short videos published through WeChat's 'Channel' feature a public feed of video and photo content. Content published on the Channel is pushed to WeChat users -including subscribers and non-subscribers -based on their registered interests and demographic features.
- · 2,715 anonymous comments by users (including 133 comments reacting to public posts and 2,582 comments responding to the short videos).

The collected data was subject to both quantitative and qualitative content analyses. Quantitative content analysis (Neuendorf 2002) was used to analyse the coverage of the Voice referendum and the key international and domestic actors involved in shaping the discussion. This process entailed counting, ranking, and categorising the hashtags, and identifying correlations between variables. Based on the quantitative analysis, the authors conducted qualitative coding of public posts, user comments, and short videos. We categorised the stance of public posts, indications of misinformation and disinformation, and users' expression of support (vote ' Yes ) or objection (vote  No ). Posts as we code them ' ' ' includes content created and posted by the account itself, as well as any sponsored ads/banners paid by other actors that appear in the account's 'post'. In cases where the stance is not explicitly stated or the comment is unrelated to the Voice referendum, we classified it as 'Uncertain/Irrelevant.'

The Voice referendum is a part of our ongoing project that monitors and analyses Chinese Australians' public opinions on Chinese social media services. As we enter 2024, we continue identifying discussions of the Voice referendum with a particular focus on the potential implications of this event on the upcoming 2025 Australian federal election.

## Analysis of content and stance of videos and Chinese-language media posts


In stark contrast to the multiple topics within WOA posts that touched on the Voice, shortvideo accounts exhibited more pronounced stances in their commentary. We noted that content creators expressed their positions -vote Yes or No -explicitly through short videos. Among the 20 short videos collected, 8 supported the No campaign, 10 supported the Voice referendum and Yes campaign, and 2, from official channels (SBS Chinese and the Victorian Labor), discussed Chinese polling of the Voice referendum and educated the Chinesespeaking public about the political event.


## The presence of misinformation and disinformation


In the collection of short videos, we identified narratives containing misinformation and disinformation. Our categorisation of disinformation and misinformation drew guidance from fact-checking sheets provided by the Guardian (Remeikis and Butler 2023) and the Australian Electoral Commission (2023) 3 . However, we observed that the provided factchecking sheets were shaped by misinformation and disinformation that originated from English-speaking social media, with limited attention to misleading content presented in non-English languages. The following part will identify the narratives of dis- and misinformation articulated in Mandarin that fell outside the purview of English journalism or Australia's public institutions.

The shared narratives of misinformation and disinformation:

- · The Voice will increase taxes or cost your money.
- · There are no details about the Voice (as proposed in the referendum question, or proposal).
- · The Voice will destabilise democracy and the integrity of Australia's constitution.
- · The Voice will divide the nation.

Variations of misinformation and disinformation circulated in the short videos on WeChat include:

- · Anti-Labor sentiment:
- -Portraying the Voice as the government's attempt to shift responsibilities to the parliament and Australian citizens.
- -Framing the 'Vote No' stance as opposition to the Labor government rather than discrimination against Indigenous communities.
- · Denial of colonialism:
- -Alleging that migrants are appealed by a civilised, white Australia.
- -Claiming that colonialism has no relevance to contemporary Australian citizens.
- · Reinforcement of Indigenous privileges:
- -The Voice will lead to racism against Chinese communities.
- -The Voice is comparable to the Eight Banners under the Qing Dynasty in China, which led to the collapse of the Qing dynasty.
- · Reinforcement of existing stereotypes against Indigenous communities:
- -Depicting Indigenous people as uncivilised.
- -Alleging Indigenous people abuse government systems and resources.
- · Misinterpretation of the result:
- -Falsely claiming that only social elites voted Yes.
- -Incorrectly stating that Indigenous states voted No.

Discussion and Analysis:

In the covering the Voice referendum, the study underscores the enduring influence of Chinese diasporic media accounts on WeChat in keeping Chinese Australians informed about both domestic and international matters. WeChat Official Accounts managed by diasporic media entities remain a pivotal tool for political communication, acknowledged by Australian public institutions, politicians, and NGOs. However, the emergence of short-video accounts on WeChat's Channel, particularly those operated by individual con tent creators, has challenged the prevailing influence of Chinese diasporic media accounts. The content creator individuals -vs. registered WOA accounts, offer a new set of actors in WeChat public exchanges with Chinese Australians. More research on their origin is warranted.

The short-video accounts, in the meantime, has given rise to a space where misinformation and disinformation thrive. Analysis of user comments on WeChat indicates a notable preference for pro-No short videos which garnered higher public engagement compared to pro-Yes videos and articles reporting the referendum. From the metrics of the comments, a significant portion of the Chinese Australian online community expressed a preference for voting No. Further discussion and reflection are warranted considering the research findings above.

- · Difference in stance between content creators versus users comments

While the research team has captured more pro-Yes campaigns compared to pro-No campaigns (Figure 5 above), our analysis reveals that 90.1% of user comments collected from both WeChat's public posts and short videos leaned towards a No vote, with only 6.08% expressing support for a Yes vote.

- · Difference in medium/type of content in terms of user engagement

Compared to the text-based WeChat Official Account feature which contributed greatly to covering the Voice referendum, the short-video feature, WeChat Channel, attracts public engagement more effectively and such engagement is manifested in the form of user comments, likes, and shares. Yes23, the Australian Government, and the Australian Electoral Commission devoted resources in influential WeChat Official Accounts but received very limited public response. Pro-No advocates employed short videos and garnered more active user interactions compared to the Yes camp.

- · Presence/absence of influence -direct or indirect -from Beijing?

In our analysis of WeChat's coverage and public opinions of the Voice referendum, we did not find evidence indicating that Beijing's official propaganda or foreign influence apparatus placed significant emphasis on the outcome of the referendum or attempted to influence Chinese Australia voters. The WOA operated by the Chinese embassy in Australia did not cover the Voice referendum but instead focused on the activities of the Chinese ambassador Qian Xiao in Australia and China's international activities. It is important to note that we did not delve into the political economy of Chinese diasporic media accounts or individual content creators, and as such, we refrain from speculating on the accounts' ties with Beijing, if any.

Furthermore, WeChat's rules and regulations, particularly those governing eligibility for public-facing accounts, inadvertently shaped the landscape for individuals, entities, or media within the Chinese diaspora or the broader Australian political spectrum to use the platform for expressing opinions or disseminating information related to the referendum. WeChat exercises lenient content control for matters unrelated to or not of concern to Beijing. For example, WeChat's guidelines prohibit content that 'incite ethnic discrimination' (Weixin, n.d.). However, this restriction is limited to activities within China and does not extend to racially discriminatory content outside the country. As demonstrated in our findings, racially discriminatory discourses against Indigenous communities were prevalent sources of misinformation and disinformation on WeChat.


## · Importance of language and identity in content for engaging Chinese Australians


It would appear that content generated in the Chinese language, whether from those who are of Chinese or non-Chinese ethnicity were more effective and impactful than content in English -even with Chinese subtitles.  For example, a short video released by the Victorian Labor featuring Carina Garland interviewing Mark Dreyfus about the Voice referendum on 18 September 2023 received no comment from viewers. This lack of engagement can be attributed to the interview being conducted in English, despite the presence of translated captions in Chinese, and involving two public figures who are white and of non-Chinese ethnicity. In contrast, 5 Yes campaigning videos featuring Linda Jaivin, a sinologist (white), in Chinese received a total of 485 comments despite the majority of WeChat users in our sample supporting the No campaign. 8 No campaigning videos presented by 3 Chinese migrants garnered 1,625 comments, while 2 anti-disinformation Yes campaigning videos conducted by a Chinese-Australian academic received 123 comments.


## · Substantive gaps in content across full sample


Alongside the above analysis of what was contained in WeChat posts and videos about the referendum, it is worth noting what types of information or argumentation were absent. ' No  advocates expressed concern for or sympathized with  anxieties within Chinese migrant ' communities regarding potential disempowerment post-Voice referendum, reinforcement of racial inequality between Chinese and non-Chinese Australians as Indigenous communities gaining sociopolitical 'privileges', scepticism towards the Albanese government, apprehension about to-be-increased taxation with the creation of the Voice, and the propagation of racially discriminatory discourses against Indigenous communities.

These concerns, deeply rooted in Chinese migrant communities, in fact reflected broader issues related to anti-Chinese racism in Australia, distrust in the Labor government especially regarding their economic management, and tensions between migrants and Indigenous communities and between ethnic communities.

Effective political communication should be tailored to the literacy levels of migrant communities. The advocacy for the Yes campaign lacked nuanced perspectives on Chinese communities. The development of the campaign overlooked the fact that Chinese Australians have become a part of Australia's colonial history and establishment through immigration and naturalisation processes. Migrants in Australia exhibit varying levels of literacy and emotional responses regarding colonialism and postcolonialism. Standard campaigns differentiated only by languages would hardly influence public opinions within non-English migrant communities. Further, they faced resistance from the community due to their top-down approaches.

- · Actual impact on vote - difference between user comments' stance and actual voting results among Chinese majority areas

It is important to note that our data diverged from the final voting result, as evidenced by the Yes vote of 49.59% in the Victorian seat of Chisholm, which has the country's largest Chinese population (McCubbing 2023). With the discrepancy, we suggest the following factors:

- · Yes voters online may be marginalised while No voices are amplified.
- · The eligibility of online Chinese Australians to vote.
- · The referendum results were calculated according to electorate sectors without specifying ethnicities or cultural backgrounds.
- · Generational patterns of social media use and information consumption habits are not addressed in national surveys or academic research.


## Conclusion and recommendations


Chinese-language media accounts on WeChat continue to serve as a key forum for members of broader Chinese migrant/diaspora communities in Australia to receive information and discus the referendum. Australian public institutions, politician, and grassroots organisations recognsied the role of Chinese diasporic media accounts on WeChat and exerted their influence through popular WeChat Official Accounts leading up to the Voice referendum. WeChat's short video feature 'Channel' -was presented as a crucial site for effective user engagement in the context of the Voice referendum. Although pro-Yes campaigns had a more extensive presence on WeChat than pro-No campaigns, the latter garnered more significant and resonant responses. Among the collected comments, over 90% of online users expressed to vote No.

In conclusion, this paper emphasised the importance of where to communicate, who to communicate, and what and how to communicate -for effective political communication. We suggest that effective communication from Australian public institutions on Chinese social media is crucial for enabling Chinese migrants to make well-informed political decisions amidst disinformation and misinformation. Specific actions that could be taken include:

- · Political communication in not-English languages ought to steer clear of tokenism. Effectiveness in communication should be built on genuine engagement with migrant communities, including tailoring communication strategies based on the literacy levels and information consumption habits of migrants and maintaining consistency in communication. The Australian Government made good efforts here for COVID vaccination campaigns, but the lessons seem to not have been applied by politicians themselves.
- · Closing regulatory gaps regarding mis and disinformation in non-English languages. Disinformation and misinformation in English-language are scrutinised by Australian public institutions and audience. However, content in non-English languages and disseminated outside dominant platforms (i.e., Google and Facebook) will remain beyond the scope of the Combatting Misinformation and Disinformation Bill, a new legislation set to be enacted by the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) in 2024.
- · Establish and regularly update a set of parameters to differentiate and identify disinformation and misinformation, particularly during significant political events and crises, across platforms.
- · Australian public institutions and media should bear the responsibility of enhancing public awareness regarding misinformation, disinformation, and facts.
- · Government support should be directed towards organisations and communities actively involved in fact-checking, monitoring and reporting misinformation and disinformation originating from social media.
- · Funding initiatives should be extended to provide training to ethnic media organisations and their journalists.
- · WeChat 's regulations should demonstrate consistency in both practice and agreement. The platform should assume the responsibility of regulating content and behaviours that threaten humanity, human rights, and equity, rather than narrowly prioritising the protection of Beijing's political interests.
- · For Australian public institutions, it would be necessary to develop a code of conduct for self-media to tackle issues discussed in this study.

## Overview of Foreign Studies


The PAD class is a localized teaching model proposed based on the practical teaching context in China. Therefore, there is relatively little research on this topic in foreign countries. Most of the existing foreign literature is published by Chinese scholars in foreign conferences and journals (Geng et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023). By searching Springer with keywords such as PAD Class or PAD teaching  model ,  it  was  discovered  that  foreign  research  on  PAD  class  started relatively late, and the overall quantity of literature is limited.

Foreign studies have primarily focused on the practical implementation of PAD classes in specific educational settings. For example, Liu et al. (2019) applied the PAD class to the teaching of C Language and found that it improved students' academic performance, offering new insights for  higher education reforms. Yang et al. (2020) adopted the PAD teaching model in Medical Genetics and concluded that PAD class is conducive to students' self-directed learning. Liu (2021) analyzed the concept and functions of PAD class and effectively resolved issues such as high absenteeism and student apathy through PAD class. Pan et al. (2022) applied the PAD model in vocational colleges and found that the implementation of this teaching model improved students' communication skills and optimized teaching effectiveness. Sun and Asmawi (2023) applied the PAD model to the teaching of Business English and  concluded that PAD classes can enhance students' interest in their business English writing.

Although  research  on  the  PAD  class  model  is  quite  limited  internationally,  it  must  be admitted  that  foreign  studies  have  provided  strong  theoretical  support  for  developing  critical concepts in the PAD teaching model. The term 'internalization' was first proposed by French scholar  Emile  Durkheim,  who  defined  it  as  the  transformation  of  social  consciousness  into individual consciousness, involving the transfer of ideological elements into individual consciousness (Cheng, 2010). Later, Vygotsky (2003), a representative of Constructivist Theory, introduced the concept of 'internalization' to analyze the formation process of intelligence. The foreign research on 'internalization' provides a theoretical foundation for the 'Assimilation' stage in  PAD  class.  Professor  Mazur  at  Harvard  University  (2009)  innovatively  proposed  the  peer instruction method, which laid the theoretical foundation for the 'Discussion' stage in PAD class. This  teaching  method  embodies  the  student-centered  teaching  philosophy  and  emphasizes interaction and cooperative learning among students.


## Overview of Domestic Studies


Research on PAD classes in China began in 2014. To provide a more detailed overview of domestic research on the PAD class, a search was conducted in CNKI (China National Knowledge Infrastructure, a comprehensive Chinese academic database platform that provides access to vast amounts of scholarly journals, theses, dissertations, and other academic resources in various fields, facilitating research and knowledge sharing) using PAD class as the main keyword. Through the analysis of related literature, it can be observed that research on PAD class in domestic studies mainly falls into two categories: 'theoretical research' and 'practical research'.

Theoretical research on PAD class encompasses three main aspects. Firstly, researchers have focused on the fundamental concepts of PAD class, as evident in studies conducted by Zhang (2014), Qiu (2016), Tian et al. (2017), and Liu et al. (2019), among others. Secondly, research has examined the role positioning of teachers and students in PAD classes, which has been explored in studies by Yang et al. (2015), Zhao (2017), Fu and Xu (2020), and others. Lastly, studies have explored the reform of the PAD class, as investigated by Du and Zhang (2016), Hu et al. (2019), Li (2020), and others.

Practical research on PAD class can be categorized into three clusters. The first cluster focuses on the application of PAD class in specific subjects or courses, with studies conducted by Chen  (2020),  Yang  (2020),  Wei  (2018),  and  others.  The  second  cluster  investigates  the combination of the PAD class with other models or platforms, as explored in studies by Li et al. (2020), Dai et al. (2021), Huang (2021), Zhang and Wang (2024) and others. The third cluster examines the application of the PAD teaching models in various educational stages, as studied by Zhao (2015), Han and Guo (2016), Yang (2021), Xu (2024) and others.


## Review of Current Research


In general, research by foreign scholars on the theory of internalization and peer instruction has laid a theoretical foundation for the design and application of PAD class teaching models. This is beneficial for the further development and optimization of the PAD class in China. Although the quantity of foreign literature on the PAD class is relatively small, it is continuously increasing, and the scope of research is expanding. However, foreign research doesn't go deep enough into theory, teaching methods, or critical studies (Romero et al., 2024; Gö ç en & Bulut, 2024). The focus of teaching practice is mainly on higher education, with a lack of research on the application of PAD classes in other educational stages.

On the other hand, domestic research on the PAD class is relatively abundant, with a wellestablished research system and increasing research interest. The scope of practical research is also expanding. Local scholars have shown that PAD classes work well in authentic teaching, providing many helpful examples and ideas for future research and teaching (Zhang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019; Sun & Asmawi, 2023). However, domestic research also has some shortcomings. For example, there is a lack of theoretical innovation, with superficial descriptions mainly focusing on basic concepts and a lack of in-depth research and exploration. Research methods tend to be overly singular, lacking sufficient in-depth quantitative studies. Additionally, the integration of multidimensional teaching content with PAD classes is still in its infancy.

In summary, both domestic and foreign research have strongly confirmed the feasibility and effectiveness of PAD classes in practical teaching. This provides a solid theoretical foundation and valuable insights for this study. Building on the work of scholars worldwide and inspired by the OBE concept, this study develops a new blended teaching model by restructuring teaching content, organizing tiered teaching activities, and creating intelligent learning environments. Both

qualitative and quantitative methods are employed to assess how well PAD classes work in the Introduction to Linguistics course. The findings of this study will provide a theoretical basis for further PAD class research and offer valuable examples for applying PAD classes to core courses in universities.

Both classes are taught by the same teacher, following an identical curriculum and utilizing the same textbook. ## Research Procedures


This  study  involved  two  classes  from  the  major  of  translation  and  interpreting  at  our university, aimed at evaluating the efficacy of the new PAD teaching model in professional course instruction.

In  the  first  phase,  researchers  selected  two  sophomore  translation  major  classes  and compared their average grades from the previous semester's core courses. Finding no significant differences in academic performance between the two classes, one (Translation Class 2204) was randomly assigned as EG and the other (Translation Class 2203) as EG. After that, students in EG were  asked  to  complete  an  initial  questionnaire  to  gather  baseline  data  on  their  self-directed learning abilities, practical application skills, and values.

In the second phase, the teaching experiment formally started. CG received traditional faceto-face instruction, while EG underwent the new PAD teaching guided by the OBE principle. At the end of the semester, EG participated in the same questionnaire survey once more to assess any changes in these three dimensions. Additionally, both groups took the identical comprehensive final test to evaluate their mastery of the subject.

In the third phase, the test scores were compared using an independent sample t-test to detect if there existed a significant difference between the two groups. Besides, paired t-tests were used to examine the changes within EG across the survey dimensions before and after the teaching period. Detailed discussions were then conducted based on the experimental results.

Additionally,  students  have  exhibited  an  increased recognition  of  their  chosen  major  and  a  stronger  sense  of  value  qualities.  Students  have  also developed a robust sense of confidence and determination, ready to apply their skills in service to their country and to promote Chinese culture internationally. This holistic educational approach has thus proven to be highly effective in preparing students for professional success and ethical leadership in their future careers.


## Discussion


The implementation of the PAD teaching model has yielded significant enhancements in students' academic performance, self-directed learning abilities, and practical application skills. This confirms the hypothesis that interactive and personalized learning environments substantially benefit  student  engagement  and  academic  achievement.  Such  improvements  are  supported  by findings from Kennedy & Birch (2020) and Mohieldein (2017), who noted that active learning frameworks significantly contribute to personal growth and better learning outcomes.

Moreover,  the  model's  influence  on  students'  intrinsic  motivation  and  self-directed learning abilities corroborates Narayanan's (2020) assertions that learner-centered approaches are pivotal  in  fostering  student  autonomy  and  engagement.  The  noted  enhancement  in  students' practical application skills also aligns with the research by Tran & Ma (2021) and Ge et al. (2021), highlighting the critical role of integrating practical activities into theoretical learning to solidify knowledge and prepare students for real-world challenges.

These  results  provide  substantial  evidence  supporting  the  effectiveness  of  the  PAD teaching model in addressing the pain points of traditional teaching methods. By comparing these outcomes with previous studies, it is evident that the PAD model not only meets but potentially exceeds traditional educational frameworks in fostering comprehensive student development.


## Implications for Practice


The  findings  from  this  study  have  significant  implications  for  educational  practice, particularly in higher education. The successful implementation of the PAD model suggests that similar approaches could be adopted across various disciplines to enhance educational outcomes. Educators and  curriculum  developers  are  encouraged  to  consider  integrating  multidimensional smart teaching tools to create more dynamic and responsive learning environments. Such tools can help bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application, crucial for student success in professional fields.

Furthermore, the enhancement of professional identity and national consciousness among students underscores the importance of incorporating national values and professional ethics into the curriculum. This approach not only aids in academic and professional development but also fosters a well-rounded educational experience that prepares students to contribute positively to society.


## Limitations and Further Recommendations


While the results of this study are promising, certain limitations must be acknowledged.

By incorporating multidimensional smart teaching tools, the model not only strengthened students' professional identity and national consciousness but also facilitated their holistic development.
