## Introduction


In social science research, integrity and reliability are critical to the quality of research instruments. Given  the increasingly complex  research  methodologies  nowadays,  rigorous instrument  validation  is  called  for  more  than  ever  (Boateng  et  al.,  2018).  In  this  regard,  the Research  Instrument  Validation Framework  (RIVF)  by  Villarino  (2024)  has  provided  a comprehensive  approach  toward  such  a  challenge  by  integrating  face,  content,  and  construct validity  assessments,  but  applying  such  a  framework  presents  significant  challenges  explicitly novice researchers (Kyriazos et al., 2018).

Recent  developments  in  artificial  intelligence  and  web-based  technologies  hold  the potential to address these challenges. Moreover, the development of this ecosystem is based on valid theoretical frameworks-that of the unified validity theory by Messick in 1995, as well as the argument-based approach by Kane in 2013. These theories offer the foundations from which AI algorithms will step users through validation processes at a detailed level, which is currently identified  as  best  practice  within  educational  and  psychological  research.  Implementing  these theories in an AI-driven platform would include a new approach for instrument validation, likely bridging the gaps between theoretical understanding and its applications in practice.

This work applies the theory of perceived usefulness, ease of use, and effectiveness to extend its practical applications in the RIVF system. It asserts that perceptions about a system's usefulness and ease of use significantly affect user acceptance and efficacy. Integrating this theory, the  AI  chatbot  and  website  are  theoretically  sound,  user-friendly,  and  effective  in  real-world applications. This study is set to develop and evaluate a novel AI-powered instrument validation ecosystem in social sciences, specifically focusing on educational research. The first objective of this study is to create an AI chatbot utilizing the Poe platform, which facilitates conversational AI agent development. This chatbot, RIVF Validator, was designed to help walk a researcher through the instrument validation process using the Research Instrument Validation Framework.

Meanwhile, the authors developed a detailed website using WordPress for this framework that would be a central home base with resources, interactive tools, and community engagement concerning RIVF. A website was also designed for this chatbot; detailed descriptions and tutorials were  mentioned  on  this  website,  and  the  website  was  also  provided  to  the  researchers  for experience sharing and best practices. In addition, this research also evaluated the effectiveness of the RIVF system in enhancing instrument validity by administering two graded instruments for measuring pre-RIVF and post-RIVF scores regarding face, content, and construct validity and by examining  user  perceptions  about  the  chatbot  and  website.  Also,  this  study  explored  the relationship between user perceptions and the overall improvement in the validity of instruments.

Additionally, this research can potentially improve the quality and replicability of social science studies in general. At a time when concerns related to the credibility of research are at the forefront, tools that support rigorous instrument validation could not be more  urgently needed. Applying  current  and  cutting-edge  validation  techniques,  such  a  milieu  may  also  democratize access  to  research  methods  more  broadly  for  early-career  researchers  and  those  working  in resource-constrained settings. The succeeding sections provide an overview of the RIVF Validator chatbot and the related website, including their development, features, and possible impacts on research practices. They also critically assess the challenges encountered.


## Theoretical Framework of the RIVF AI-Chatbot and Website


The whole theoretical framework behind the multilevel base of the RIVF AI chatbot and website integrates critical concepts from instrument validation theory, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and web-based learning systems, as shown in Figure 1. It is an approach to make a comprehensive and user-friendly tool for researchers in education, psychology, and social sciences.

At the foundation of RIVF is Messick's (1995) integrated construct-based validity model, terminally orienting toward the holistic judgment of the validity of score interpretation and use. This is complemented by Kane's (2013) argument-based approach, which urges clear statements of  interpretative  arguments  and  solid  evidence  gathering.  These  foundational  underpinnings inform  the  structure  and  content  of  the  AI  chatbot  and  the  website,  providing  users  with  a theoretically sound validation method.

Artificial  intelligence  theories  and  natural  language  processing  are  at  the  root  of  the development  of  this  AI  chatbot.  The  chatbot  uses  transformer-based  language  models  to comprehend  and  respond  to  user  inquiries.  It  is  combined  with  different  domain-specific knowledge  representation  techniques  to  capture  the  theory  justifiably  and  apply  instrument validation. Theories of Web-based learning and user experience guide the design and functionality of the website. Based on the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, information presentation should be guided by Mayer, 2002, wherein text and visual elements are integrated cohesively for comprehension.  The  theory  of  distributed  cognition  will  also  be  discussed  in  the  design  of interactive elements since it is realized that the website acts just like an extension of the user's cognitive processes during a validation task.

Incorporating Classical Test Theory and Item Response Theory in the RIVF provides a robust  statistical  base  for  the  validation  process.  These  theories  underlie  the  weighted  scoring system type, which provides more nuanced scores for instrument quality entered into the chatbot and  website.  Finally,  cross-cultural  validity  considerations  are  included  in  this  framework,  as stated by Villarino et al. (2022) and van de Vijver and Tanzer (2004). Parameters include the fact that the RIVF is applicable across different cultures. This is crucial since most of the research work today is global and needs to have validated instruments for cross-cultural studies.


## Methodology


This study utilized a quantitative approach to develop and evaluate the RIVF AI chatbot and website. The research design comprises three main phases: development, implementation, and evaluation.


## Phase 1: Development


As presented in Figure 2,  the development phase began with a comprehensive literature review to refine the theoretical foundations of the RIVF  based on the study conducted by Villarino (2024).  The  RIVF  was  created  following  a  modified  Delphi  study  involving  22  experts  in educational  measurement  (n=7),  psychological  assessment  (n=6),  social  science  methodology (n=5), and cross-cultural validation (n=4). The Delphi process was conducted over three rounds, and consensus was reached on the key components and criteria of the RIVF (Villarino, 2024).

## Phase 2 and 3: Implementation and Evaluation


A survey was administered to 100 researchers who volunteered and requested to use the RIVF system to validate their adapted instruments. The survey assessed the perceived usefulness, ease of use, and effectiveness of both the AI chatbot and the website using a 5-point Likert scale.

To ensure adequate statistical power, G*Power analyses were conducted. For the paired ttests (n=100), assuming a medium effect size (dz=0.5) and α=0.05, the power was calculated to be 99.73%. For the one-way ANOVA assessing correlations between user perceptions and overall validity improvement (n=100), assuming a medium effect size (f=0.25), α=0.05, and four groups, the power was 80.95%. These calculations confirmed that the sample size was sufficient to detect medium effect sizes with high statistical power for the analyses.

## Ethical Considerations


The  study  was  guided  by  ethical  research  principles  with  particular  attention  to  the international  characteristics  of  the  participants.  The  participants  contributed  information  under informed  consent  about  the  study's  purpose  and  procedures,  and  participation  was  strictly voluntary,  confidentiality  was  maintained,  and  all  data  gathered  were  anonymized  (Philippine Council  for  Health  Research  and  Development,  2017;  Hernandez  et  al.,  2020;  American Educational  Research  Association  et  al.,  2014).  Moreover,  the  participants  had  the  right  to withdraw from the study at any time (Li et al., 2021). The risk was minimal as only professional opinions were sought, anchoring on Cook and Hatala's  survey in 2016. The expert's time and efforts were rightly justified by having a comprehensive validation framework output with the benefits for the participants to use, replicate, and enhance the existing version of the RIVF for further studies (Zorek et al., 2022). This process is explicitly carried out to maintain high ethical standards  while  accommodating  the  explicit  aspects  of  international  expert  consultation  in instrument validation research.

## Summary of Validity Improvement and User Perception Factors using the RIVF System


This section presents a comprehensive analysis of the instrument validity improvement and user perceptions of the Research Instrument Validation Framework (RIVF) system, as indicated in Table 3.

The analysis detailed in Table 3 reveals significant improvements in instrument validity after implementing the Research Instrument Validation Framework (RIVF) system. aligns with findings by authors such as Streiner and Norman (2015), who highlight the importance of  face  validity  in  ensuring  that  items  are  clearly  understood  and  perceived  as  relevant  by respondents.

This change, marked by a t-value of 14.14 and a p-value < 0.001, reflects the RIVF system's effectiveness in reinforcing the theoretical underpinnings of the instruments. This finding is consistent with the work of Campbell and Fiske (1959), who emphasize the critical role of construct validity in measuring theoretical concepts accurately.

Overall  validity  scores  also  indicate  a  significant  increase  from  2.80  (±0.60)  to  3.90 (±0.50), with a mean difference of 1.10 (±0.40), a t-value of 19.40, and a p-value < 0.001. This comprehensive  enhancement  suggests  that  the  RIVF  system  effectively  improves  the  overall robustness of research instruments, echoing findings from researchers like Nunnally and Bernstein (1994), who discuss the importance of overall validity in ensuring research quality.

The consistent improvement across all domains (p < 0.001) highlights the RIVF system's comprehensive approach to validation. The major improvement is observed in construct validity (M=1.20, SD=± 0.60), followed by content validity (M=1.10, SD==± 0.50), and overall validity (M=1.10,  SD==± 0.40),  which  highlights  the  system's  strength  in  addressing  complex  validity aspects.  While  face  validity  (M=0.90,  SD=±  0.40)  showed  the  smallest  improvement,  it  still demonstrated  significant  gains,  indicating  that  the  RIVF  system  also  refines  the  surface-level aspects of research instruments.

Statistical significance, evidenced by high t-values and low p-values, confirms that these improvements  are  robust  and  unlikely  due  to  chance.  The  findings  suggest  that  researchers employing the RIVF system can expect enhanced instrument validity, leading to more reliable data collection and research outcomes. This balanced improvement across various validity domains supports the RIVF system's value as a tool for developing high-quality research instruments, as reinforced by prior studies on validation methodologies.

## One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) that assessed the relationship between user perceptions and overall validity improvement.

Table 4 presents the results of a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) that assessed the relationship between user perceptions and overall validity improvement. The F-value represents the  ratio  of  the  variance  between  groups  to  the  variance  within  groups,  and  a  higher  F-value indicates a stronger relationship between the variables. The p-value indicates the probability of obtaining  a  result  as  extreme  as  the  one  observed,  with  a  lower  p-value  indicating  a  stronger relationship. Partial η² represents the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable, with a higher value indicating a stronger relationship.

The one-way  ANOVA results in Table 4 reveal  significant  relationships  between  user perceptions and overall validity improvement in the RIVF system. All four factors  - perceived usefulness,  ease  of  use,  effectiveness,  and  overall  satisfaction  -  show  statistically  significant correlations with validity improvement (p < 0.01).

Effectiveness is the strongest predictor of validity improvement (F = 22.36, p < 0.001, partial  η²  =  0.32),  explaining  32% of the variance. This suggests that users who perceived the system as more effective were likely to significantly improve their instrument's validity. Overall satisfaction follows closely (F = 18.64, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.28), indicating that users' general contentment with the system is strongly associated with better outcomes.

Perceived usefulness also strongly correlates with validity improvement (F = 15.27, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.24). This implies that users who found the RIVF system more useful were more likely to see substantial improvements in their instrument's validity. While still significant, ease of use shows the weakest association among the factors analyzed (F = 8.92, p = 0.004, partial η² = 0.15). This suggests that while user-friendliness is essential, it may not be as critical as other factors in determining the system's effectiveness.

These findings highlight a clear hierarchy of the importance of user perception factors, with effectiveness and overall satisfaction at the top, followed by perceived usefulness and ease of use. This hierarchy suggests that users value tangible results and a positive overall experience more than specific aspects like ease of use. It also implies that users may be willing to navigate a more complex system if it delivers superior results in improving instrument validity.

The strong correlations between user perceptions and validity improvement emphasize the value of user experience in achieving desired outcomes. Furthermore, the findings suggest that a positive user experience, particularly in terms of perceived effectiveness and overall satisfaction,

may motivate users to engage more deeply with the system, potentially leading to better results in instrument  validation.  These  results  provide  valuable  insights  into  the  complex  relationships between user perceptions and the effectiveness of the RIVF system and highlight the importance of focusing on system effectiveness and overall user satisfaction to achieve optimal outcomes in instrument validation processes.


## Discussion


This  study  aimed  to  evaluate  the  effectiveness  of  the  Research  Instrument  Validation Framework (RIVF) system, focusing on its ability to improve instrument validity and assess user perceptions of its AI chatbot and website components. The research addressed the growing need for robust,  technologically-enhanced  validation  tools  in  an  increasingly  complex  research landscape.

The findings reveal significant improvements in instrument validity across all domains after using the RIVF system, with construct validity showing the most substantial enhancement. This comprehensive improvement aligns with the multifaceted approach to validity advocated by modern validity theorists such as Kane (2013) and Messick (1995). The marked improvement in construct validity addresses a critical aspect of instrument development that is often challenging to refine (DeVellis & Thorpe, 2022). This finding not only supports recent studies emphasizing the  importance  of  construct  validity  in  developing  robust  research  instruments  (Kramer  et  al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018) but also suggests that AI-driven systems may be particularly adept at enhancing this complex aspect of instrument validity.

The comparative analysis between the AI chatbot and website components of the RIVF system  yielded  results  that  align  with  and  challenge  existing  literature.  The  AI  chatbot  was perceived as significantly more  valuable and practical than the website, echoing findings from studies on AI-assisted research tools (Guinart et al., 2021; Lameier et al., 2018). This preference for AI-driven systems in complex tasks like instrument validation suggests a shift in researcher attitudes toward embracing advanced technological solutions. However, this finding also raises important questions about the role of human expertise in research validation processes and the potential for over-reliance on AI systems.

While the AI chatbot was preferred for effectiveness, the website was rated higher in ease of  use,  consistent  with  findings  from  Or  and  Chapman  (2022)  on  the  importance  of  familiar interfaces  in  assessment  tools.  This  dichotomy  highlights  a  crucial  challenge  in  developing research  support  systems:  balancing  advanced  AI  capabilities  with  user-friendly  interfaces.  It suggests that future developments in this field may need to focus on making AI-driven tools more intuitive and accessible, perhaps by incorporating design elements from traditional web interfaces. The  strong  correlations  between  user  perceptions  and  validity  improvement  underscore  the importance of user experience in the effectiveness of validation tools. Effectiveness emerged as the strongest predictor of validity improvement, followed by overall satisfaction.

This  finding  further  aligns  with  recent  studies  emphasizing  the  role  of  perceived effectiveness in adopting and successfully using assessment tools (Kyriazos et al., 2018; Shim et al., 2023).  However,  the  relatively  weaker  relationship  between  ease  of  use  and  validity improvement contrasts with some earlier research that emphasized user-friendliness as a critical

factor (Bolarinwa, 2015). This suggests a potential paradigm shift in how researchers approach sophisticated  research  tools,  prioritizing  effectiveness  over  simplicity.  It  also  raises  questions about the applicability of general technology acceptance models to specialized research tools.

From  an  interdisciplinary  perspective,  the  RIVF  system's  effectiveness  across  various validity  domains  suggests  its  potential  applicability  in  diverse  research  fields.  This  broad applicability  could  have  significant  implications  for  standardizing  validation  processes  across disciplines, potentially enhancing the comparability and rigor of research instruments in fields ranging  from  psychology  to  education  to  health  sciences.  However,  adopting  such  AI-driven systems in research methodology raises critical ethical considerations. While the RIVF system demonstrates clear benefits, there is a need to consider potential biases in AI algorithms, data privacy concerns, and the risk of diminishing human critical thinking in the validation process. Future research and development in this area should actively address these ethical dimensions.

Moreover, the findings suggest that research institutions and individual researchers may consider incorporating AI-assisted validation tools like the RIVF system into their methodological processes. However, this integration should be done thoughtfully, focusing on training researchers to use these tools effectively and critically. Institutions might consider developing guidelines for the appropriate use of AI in research methodology to ensure that these tools enhance rather than replace human expertise.

## Limitations

Despite its strengths, this study has several significant limitations when interpreting the results. Firstly, while adequate for statistical analysis, the sample size may  limit the generalizability  of  findings  across  diverse  research  disciplines.  Future  studies  should  consider larger,  more  diverse  samples  to  enhance  external  validity  and  explore  potential  variations  in effectiveness across different fields. Secondly, the study's focus on immediate improvements in instrument  validity  does  not  account  for  long-term  effects  or  the  possible  need  for  iterative refinement of instruments. Longitudinal studies could provide valuable insights into the sustained impact of the RIVF system on research quality over time. Thirdly, while the survey compared AI chatbot and website components, it did not explore their potential synergies.

Moreover, further research could investigate how integrated use of both components might yield optimal results in instrument validation. Additionally, the study's reliance on self-reported perceptions of effectiveness may introduce some bias; future research could benefit from more objective measures of improvement in instrument quality. Lastly, the study did not control for participants' prior experience with AI tools or their general technological proficiency, which could have influenced their perceptions and the effectiveness of the RIVF  system. These limitations provide  important  directions  for  future  research  and  should  be  considered  when  applying  the findings of this study in practical contexts.


## Conclusion and Recommendations


The  Research  Instrument  Validation  Framework  (RIVF)  system,  integrating  an  AIpowered  chatbot  and  interactive  website,  demonstrates  significant  potential  in  enhancing  the validity of research instruments in social sciences. The study reveals substantial improvements across all validity domains, with construct validity showing the most marked increase. Despite the

latter's superior ease of use, the AI chatbot's higher perceived usefulness and effectiveness than the  website  indicates  a  growing  acceptance  of  advanced  technological  solutions  in  research methodology. Strong correlations between user perceptions, particularly effectiveness and overall satisfaction, and validity improvement further underscore the system's value.

These findings suggest that AI-assisted validation tools can potentially enhance the quality and  rigor  of  research  instruments.  The  RIVF  system's  effectiveness  across  various  validity domains points to its potential for  standardizing  validation  processes  across  different  research fields, potentially improving the comparability and reliability of research instruments in diverse disciplines.  However,  implementing  such  systems  requires  careful  consideration  of  ethical implications,  the  role  of  human  expertise,  and  the  need  for  critical  thinking  in  the  validation process.

To maximize the benefits of the RIVF system and similar AI-assisted validation tools, the authors recommend the following: 1. research institutions may consider integrating AI-assisted validation tools like RIVF into their methodological processes, developing appropriate guidelines for  their  use;  2.  future  developments  should  focus  on  optimizing  the  balance  between  AI capabilities and user-friendly interfaces to enhance effectiveness and ease of use; 3. comprehensive training  programs  should  be  developed  to  educate  researchers  on  effectively  using  these  tools while maintaining critical thinking skills; 4. to further validate the long-term impact of AI-assisted validation,  longitudinal  studies  should  be  conducted  to  assess  its  sustained  effect  on  research quality; 5. the application of the RIVF system should be explored across diverse research fields to enhance  its  versatility  and  broaden  its  impact;  6.  comprehensive  ethical  guidelines  should  be developed for  using  AI  in  research methodology,  addressing  potential  biases and  data  privacy concerns; and 7. the RIVF system should be continuously improved and refined based on user feedback and technological advancements to ensure its ongoing relevance and effectiveness. This iterative process will help maintain the system's value in the ever-evolving landscape of research methodology.

## Introduction


Mental health is an absent state of mental disorders (Lukat et al., 2016). However, a new definition has  been  proposed,  which  not  only  involves  the  absence  of  a  disease  but  also  involves  aspects present in the individual, such as optimism, life satisfaction, and resilience (Bieda et al., 2017). The previous concept is Positive Mental Health (PMH), defined as the general presence of emotional, psychological, and social well-being (Lukat et al., 2016). In this alternate definition, the individual can identify strengths they have to face their daily activities (Gómez-Acosta et al., 2020). Therefore, PMH is now considered a protective factor for mental health disorders and even a predictor in their recovery (Huang et al., 2021). According to this, it is possible to understand how PMH elements can be present simultaneously as a mental health disorder and be important to recovering from it (Lukat et al., 2016).

The  perceived  stress  in  young  phsyisician  constitutes  a  physical  and  psychological  problem  for these  individuals.  Various  sources  of  stress  have  been  identified  and  studied.  These  sources  are multifactorial  and  are  referred  to  come  from  study  programs  and  sociodemographic  variables, among others (Huang et al., 2021). Currently, young phsyisican are exposed to a high academic load, which requires high levels of self-efficacy and tolerance for frustration. PMH is a mechanism to deal with mental disorders and achieve better academic performance and quality of life (Machado & Bandeira, 2015) .  It  was  identified  that  high  levels  of  self-efficacy  are  related  to  deeper  study strategies,  while  young  physicians  with  lower  PMH  scores  used  a  more  straightforward  study approach  (DaLomba  et  al.,  2021).  It  has  even  been  researched  how  young  physician  with  more PMH, resilience, and Grit approach face challenges better and have better academic performance regardless of IQ (Kryza-Lacombe et al., 2019).

Different instruments have been used to measure Positive Mental Health over the years (GonzálezArratia-López-Fuentes  &  Valdez  Medina,  2016;  Hankir  et  al.,  2014) , with  domains  such  as emotional-cognitive well-being, environmental domain, social skills, empathy, physical well-being, self-reflection, and psychological distress (Teke & Baysan Arabaci, 2018) . Some examples include Maria Teresa Lluch's Scale from 1999; Barrera and Flores' Scale, which was applied to Mexican youth  in  2015;  Warwick-Edinburgh  Mental  Well-Being  Scale,  written  in  2007,  containing  six domains assessed on 14 items; and Justina Lukat's Positive Mental Health Scale (PMH-S), created in  2016  which  consists  of  9  items  that  were  taken  from  similar  instruments  and  no  domains (Ramirez-Schneider,  Edgar  and  Rodriguez-Valenzuela,  Alejandro  and  Restrepo-Jaramillo,  Martín and Oliveros-Castro1, Jose Luis and Palencia-Sánchez, Francisco and Riaño-Casallas, 2022).

Lukat's  PMH-S  has  been  validated  across  different  groups  of  interest  and  has  shown  excellent internal  consistency  and  one-dimensionality  across  samples.  The  measurement  invariance  of  the PMH-S has been tested for its items across eight countries, age groups, and genders (Velten et al., 2021).  Results  for  PMH-S  gender  comparisons  were  inconclusive,  with  studies  showing  no significant  differences  (Çeçen  et  al.,  2021),  higher  levels  of  PMH-Scale  for  men  than  women (Velten et al., 2021), and higher levels of PMH-S for women than men (Huang et al., 2021). The psychometric properties of the PMH-S are valid and reliable among university students (Çeçen et al., 2021) and healthcare students (Yavas et al., 2022).

Conversely, Grit is defined as a personality trait that measures levels of passion and perseverance for  long-term  goals (Stoffel  &  Cain,  2018) .  It  has  been  related  to  good  academic  performance, determination, lower burnout (Kannangara et al., 2020)(Brateanu et al., 2020), performance, and job satisfaction  (Ursua  et  al.,  2020).  The  ability  to  quantify  these  traits  was  achieved  by  Professor Angela Duckworth, who developed an original 12-item scale (Grit-O) that also has a short version with eight items (Grit-S) (Duckworth, 2023). This instrument was applied to medical students and physicians of different specializations (Abd Elwahab & Lowery, 2017) ,  associating the perception of  exhaustion  with  lower  levels  of  Grit  (Cortez  et  al.,  2019).  In  similar  studies,  it  was  linked  to empathy with the patient (Isenberg et al., 2020), passing the semester  (Alejandra Catalina Borda Piñeres,  Tomás  Galvis  Pulecio,  Paola  Lozada  Estrella,  Camila  Mejía  Barrantes,  Valeria  Mojica Sierra, 2022), and even the choice of surgical subspecialties with greater demand (Huo et al., 2022). Two studies reported a slightly higher but less significant score difference in women than men in Grit values (Huo et al., 2022), (Ursua et al., 2020). Others did not make comparisons of the scores according to gender (Domínguez-Torres et al., 2022), (Shi et al., 2022).

Several  studies  have  linked  Grit  to  the  academic  performance  of  young  physician,  as  well  as Positive Mental Health scores as a coping mechanism for mental disorders (Schönfeld et al., 2019). However,  to  our  knowledge,  an  association  between  PMH  and  Grit  has  yet  to  be  established, especially  in  healthcare  workers  (Lee  et  al.,  2022).  This  paper  analyzes  the  relationship  between mental health and Grit through Dr. Ducksworth's Grit Scale results and the PMH-S results of young doctors;  finds  a  relationship  that  encourages  the  search  for  strategies  that  improve  physician' wellbeing.

In a country like Colombia, where the training of doctors is essential but where, due to costs and access to education, it is difficult to guarantee the training of new professionals, they must complete their  training  satisfactorily.  For  this  reason,  identifying  actions  to  promote  mental  health  or  how present it is in them can help design learning strategies for medical students (Yee Chow & Yiu Choi,

2019) .


## Methods


an  observational  cross-sectional  study  was  carried  out  using  a  non-probabilistic  sampling  of  the purposeful type with the inclusion criteria of being a young phsyisican of the Pontificia Universidad Javeriana for the first period 2023. There were no exclusion criteria for this study. An anonymous survey that includes quantitative variables was used as a measurement tool to establish measures of central tendency and perform data analysis. Each research participant agreed to informed consent to answer this survey. Sociodemographic variables were included to characterize the sample, and the Positive Mental Health Scale and the Grit-O Scale were used following the objectives of this study.

The  Positive  Mental  Health  Scale  developed  by  Lukat  consists  of  9  statements  with  Likert-type response options. This survey evaluated the individual's general, emotional, and global psychological  well-being  (Psychometric  properties  of  the  Positive  Mental  Health  Scale  (PMHscale).  This scale is not validated in Spanish, for which a translation was done to apply it in the target population as an initial approach to validate this scale in the native language. Two experts in occupational  health  validated  this  translation:  one  of  administrative  science  and  another  of biomedical sciences.

The Grit-O Scale contains 12 statements with Likert scale-type response options. The scale assesses an individual's ability to maintain focus or interest and persevere in achieving long-term goals. A short-scale  version  contains  nine  items  and  is  known  as  Grit-S.  We  decided  to  use  the  original version since we have used the scale previously (Alejandra Catalina Borda Piñeres, Tomás Galvis Pulecio,  Paola  Lozada  Estrella,  Camila  Mejía  Barrantes,  Valeria  Mojica  Sierra,  2022);  it  is recommended  by  the  author  (Duckworth,  2023),  and  it  is  the  only  one  validated  in  Colombia (Collantes Tique et al., 2021).

Finally, an analysis of the results was carried out utilizing Excel and SPSS. A descriptive analysis of the population was performed along with descriptive characteristics for each scale. A correlation analysis was made between the two scales, and an internal structure analysis for the items to assess the consistency of each one.

Given that the Positive Mental Health Scale instrument did not have a Spanish version, a translation and  back-translation  were  carried  out  by  experts  to  guarantee  the  cultural  adaptation  of  the instrument. Likewise, the statistical reliability of the instrument was corroborated by performing a reliability analysis using Cronbach's alpha. For this purpose, atypical observations were removed. Secondly, descriptive statistics were obtained, and finally, Cronbach's alpha was calculated.

## Discussion


The  results  of  the  descriptive  analysis  allowed  us  to  identify  that  in  our  population,  there  is  an average  on  the  Grit  scale  of  3.16.  In  a  2020  applied  study,  a  Grit  level  of  3.83  was  established (Isenberg  et  al.,  2020),  which,  without  being  negligible,  is  higher  than  the  average  in  our population.  Similarly,  a  previous  study  from  the  Pontificia  Universidad  Javeriana  found  that  the scores  of  fifth-year  students  were  mostly  between  3  and  5  (Alejandra  Catalina  Borda  Piñeres, Tomás  Galvis  Pulecio,  Paola  Lozada  Estrella,  Camila  Mejía  Barrantes,  Valeria  Mojica  Sierra, 2022). In contrast, our population had a very marked tendency to score 3, and the highest score was established at 4.33.

The  results  also  revealed  a  similar  pattern  of  results  between  men  and  women.  Previous  studies have reported a slight  tendency  for women to  have  greater Grit  (Huo  et  al.,  2022)  (Ursua  et  al., 2020); nonetheless, our results include a heterogeneous pattern in which men have more remarkable Grit than women.

The  results  were  not  analyzed  by  separating  the  two  dimensions  of  the  Grit  scale:  passion  and perseverance.  However,  it  would  be  interesting  for  further  studies  to  analyze  the  relationship between the two dimensions of Positive Mental Health.

When analyzing PMH-Scale results, a study that applied the scale in 8 countries (France, Germany, Poland, Russia, Spain, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and the United States) identified a PMH score of 17.05 for women. In contrast, for men, at 17.43 (Velten et al., 2021). Our PMH-Scale analysis identified an average for both sexes higher than the estimated in this study, with the score for men at 19.12 and the score for women at 17.88. This same study estimates the average PMH for 18 to 24 years at 16.40. This places our population 2 points above (18.27) (Velten et al., 2021)

As mentioned previously, our results showed a PMH-Scale score for men higher by 2 points than for  women.  This  outcome  was  different  from  those  found  in  earlier  studies,  which  have  had inconclusive results  (Çeçen et al., 2021). Age comparisons were not made since it is a population with very homogeneous ages.

The study results indicate that with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.28, there is a weak linear association between Grit and PMH in medical students. However, it is essential to note this study's limitations  that  may  affect  the  result  of  this  association,  such  as  its  small  sample  size  and homogeneity.


## Conclusion


In  conclusion,  this  study  provides  insight  into  Grit  and  Positive  Mental  Health  levels  in  young physicians and the significant differences from previous studies where the Grit scale was applied to medical  students.  Additionally,  when  making  gender  comparisons  between  the  Grit  and  Positive Mental  Health  levels  obtained,  we  identified  higher  scores  in  men  rather  than  women.  The correlation of these two variables suggests a weak but not negligible linear relationship. This raises the question of how to develop higher levels of Grit in women and whether pedagogical strategies used  in  the  training  of  medical  students  can  influence  positive  mental  health.  However,  further research is needed to expand our knowledge and understanding of the relationship between these variables, not only for the benefit of medical students but all students, by promoting interventions that aim to improve Grit and Positive Mental Health in this population.

Considering  this study's limitations, further research, including a larger and  more  diverse population, is needed to understand the relationship between Grit and Positive Mental Health. It is also important to remark that Positive Mental Health and Grit are familiar to everyone. Therefore, it would be interesting to apply this study's methodology to new populations different from medical students to explore the impact of this demographic variable in this association. Also, considering our results revealed higher levels of Grit and Positive Mental Health for men compared to women, this study provides a groundwork for further studies that aim to analyze the causes and relationships between  women's  Grit  and  Positive  Mental  Health  compared  to  men.  Finally,  the  creation  of  a Spanish version of the PMH-Scale made for this study opens an opportunity for future validating studies in our country.

## Findings


Based on the empirical data on municipal waste management costs, on average, the size and the average cost of the service  are  inversely  related.  This  trend  is  supported  using  subsets  defined  by  the  quantity  of  waste  managed. Multiple factors aid in explaining this result, and among others, due to scale and scope, factors such as transition costs increase with the number of players running different services.


## Practical implications


The provision of public services of economic interest should favour the participation of more companies wherever possible to the extent that social surplus is produced. However, pursuing this principle to the detriment of efficient service  delivery  is  not  ideal.  This  paper  demonstrated  that  a  single-provider  waste  management  business  model  is efficient under specific conditions, as in this article.


## Originality


This  paper  presents  an  original  research  methodology  for  comparatively  analysing  waste  management  service efficiency in urban areas and provides adequate evidence using alternative measures of costs according to the phase of the waste management chain, the scale, and ultimately the scope of municipal solid waste management services.


## 1. Introduction


Public services of general economic  interest are fundamental  to the nation's economic development and significantly impact social welfare (Boggio, 2016). The operational efficiency of the  municipal  solid  waste  (MSW)  management  industry  has  become  increasingly  significant  for achieving sustainable development objectives (Zorpas, 2020). Business and governance models of MSW management need to evolve towards efficiency levels compatible with the achievement of economic and environmental objectives (Kaza et al. , 2018). Research has exposed the critical need for  assessing  different  models  of  governance  and  organisation,  and  entrusting  services  for  the governance  and  delivery  of  public  services  (Soukopová et  al. , 2017).  Trade-offs  between  the competitive dimensions in industrial structures characterised by imperfect competition must also be considered.

Typically,  local  authorities  can  choose  between  three  models  and  procedures:  entrusting  the service  to  third  parties  through  public  procedures,  the  provision  of  the  services  through  hybrid public-private  firms  and  in-house  provision.  Free  market  and  competition  rules  apply  to  actors entrusted  with  providing  public  services  for  economic  interests  as  long  as  these  rules  do  not prevent them from fulfilling their general mission (European Commission, 2022).

Additionally, the principle that underpins European competition and public procurement legislation  since  the  introduction  of  Directive  2014/24/EU  is  important,  which  is  to  encourage small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to participate in public procurement and, thereby, in the  provision  of  public  services.  However,  this  principle  can  be  abandoned  by  considering integrated utilities, which can provide more services at various stages of the chain, owing to the economies  of  scale  and  scope  resulting  from  their  production  efficiency.  Subdividing  large municipalities  can  be  assumed  to  lead  to  greater  competition,  fostering  growth  among  service providers  (Sarra et  al. ,  2020).  However,  on  the  contrary,  a  recent  empirical  study  focused  on Barcelona revealed that multiple firms can strategically interact to maximise producer surplus at the expense of social welfare (Be l and Sebő, 2021).

MSW management can be regarded as  an  industry  with  two  or  more  intertwined  phases.  The market structure in the first phase is mainly labour-intensive, while the second phase is capitalintensive and supported by enabling infrastructure, such as waste treatment plants. Both phases are subject to the risk of market failure, and in certain circumstances, the market can effectively manage one or more services (Di Foggia and Beccarello, 2018).

The industrial  organisation  of the  collection phase  often  involves  local monopoly  configurations justified  by  the  economies  of  scale  resulting  from  the  size  of  the  service  and  its  economies  of scope  (AGCM,  2016).  Much  has  been  written  regarding  the  existence  of  scale  economies,  an important  issue  with  some  consensus  (Callan  and  Thomas,  2001),  as  confirmed  in  previous analyses  that  also  found  scale  economies  and  some  efficiency  differences  between  public  and private providers (Tickner and Mcdavid, 1986). Early research in the field of economies of scale focused on the interrelationships of scale, market structure, and costs, with scattered evidence in

the beginning, based on the little evidence of the existence of certain scale economies (Stevens, 1978).

In this regard, the more recent findings on economies of scale have provided mixed results. For example,  a  recent  study  found  that  less  than  half  (40.4%  of  the  municipalities  evaluated), presented  negative  economies  of  scale  (Llanquileo-Melgarejo  and  Molinos-Senante,  2021). Another study underscores the drivers of costs under alternative cost definitions (Di Foggia and Beccarello,  2020).  Similarly,  a  third  article  concluded  that  population  and  size  are  important factors for scale economies, and the implication is uncertain (Wowrzeczka, 2021). This uncertainty is  partly  due  to  information  asymmetries  that  complicate  comparative  analyses.  Another  factor that concurs with mixed results is the unit of analysis.

Indeed, many studies aimed at understanding the economies of scope in MSW management by focusing on the input factors of firms and very different output variables, failing to differentiate among collection costs, total costs, and treatment costs or using per capita cost against costs per unit of waste.

Scale  economies  in  a  public  service  of  general  interest  such  as  waste  management  should  be evaluated from the perspective of the contracting authority, paying more attention to exogenous factors affecting the organisation of the service that must be used at the same level as the input factors of firms. Indeed, failing to consider the above may result in formally correct results but be biased  in  practice  if  the  subadditivity  of  costs  is  not  considered.  Consequently,  the  contracting authorities  may  decide  it  inappropriate  to  divide  the  contract  into  lots  to  avoid  the  risk  of rendering the execution of the contract excessively technically difficult or expensive and because coordinating the different contractors for the lots could risk undermining the proper execution of the contract.

Some scholars have empirically evaluated the impact of different regulated business models on MSW management and suggested that their efficiency can  be  increased  by  limiting  the  size  of these service areas so that the system encourages large service providers to compete for service allocation  in  a  large  number  of  small  areas,  thus  intensifying  the  positive  effects  of  market competition (Sarra et al. ,  2020). However, it could be argued that reducing the size of the areas that can be allocated to a single firm may promote anti-competitive strategies aimed at creating divisions between several theoretically competing operators.

Strengthening market competition and realising economies of scale by integrating organisations (and  thus  reducing  the  number  of  individual  economic  actors)  can  be  considered  appropriate choices for achieving economic and environmental efficiency. First, this idea is supported based on an econometric model that identifies the main determinants of service costs. Then, the focus was on the analysis of multiple case studies, using a sample consisting of the ten most populous Italian

cities. Third, a single case comparing a 'business -asusual' model involving a single economic actor with an alternative scenario consisting of four firms was analysed.

Evidence suggests that as the size of the service increases, the average cost tends to decrease. The case  study  confirms  the  presence  of  economies  of  scale,  resulting  from  the  specific  factors employed in the production of the service.

## 2. Background and literature


The complexity of the WM industry raises concerns about the technologies it relies upon and the sustainability of its business models (Björklund et al. , 1999), which also depend on how contracts between MSW management providers and institutions are structured (Walls, 2005). In light of the challenging  environmental  goals,  the  efficiency  of  MSW  management  business  models  has become an increasingly important concern (Kinnaman, 2009); thus, their sustainability as well as their  emergent  role  in  local  communities  is  critical  (Avilés-Palacios  and  Rodríguez-Olalla,  2021; Esmaeilian et  al. ,  2018).  As  such,  the  relationship  between  efficiency  and  economies of  scale  is attracting  more  attention  at  both  the  political  and  the  organisational  levels.  Accordingly,  the number of studies on the cost of MSW management has grown, such as the analysis of the cost functions (Bohm et al. , 2010) or the cost of recycling environmental policies (Da Cruz et al. , 2014).

Previous literature has focused on the determinants of demand for MSW management services (Diaz-Farina et  al. ,  2020),  organisational  forms  and  modes  of  supply  (Zhang et  al. ,  2015),  policy implications (Goddard, 1995), cost structures (Callan and Thomas, 2001; Pérez-López et al. , 2016), and the need to develop strategies to achieve sustainability goals. Regarding sustainability goals, geopolitical contingencies  make  it  difficult  to reach  the  binding  agreements  and  credible commitments made by policymakers (Darus et al. , 2020).

Different approaches have been proposed to analyse the economic efficiency of MSW collection firms.  For  example,  a  recent  study  identified  a  relation  between  costs  and  environmental efficiency, although this relationship is nonlinear, as a rise in the separated waste collection rate increases total costs by a less-than-proportional amount, which provides evidence of the existence of economies of scale (Bartolacci et al. , 2019).

Economic  and  technical  efficiency  have  emerged  as  prominent  factors  in  explaining  costs  (lo Storto,  2021).  Given  the  increasing  pressure  governments  face  to  increase  cost  efficiency,  they

may transfer waste disposal services to private firms  (Jacobsen et  al. ,  2013). This  possibility has raised the dilemma of whether for-profit enterprises are compatible with outcomes that maximise social welfare (Kinnaman, 2009); the available findings are mixed (Bel and Fageda, 2010; Simões et al. , 2012).

Empirical evidence based on the existing MSW management business models is important, as it shows how economic and political factors exert different impacts on MSW management via both private  and  public  firms  (Plata-Díaz et  al. , 2014).  Other  studies  indicate  that  private  MSW management operators are not necessarily better performers than public firms (Bel and Fageda, 2010).

Additionally,  firm  size,  inter-firm  relations,  and  alternative  technologies,  as  found  in  studies  on green  reverse  logistics  technology  (Mugoni  et  al.,  2023),  can  be  argued  to  significantly  impact MSW management strategies (Lombrano, 2009). Considering that the size of firms that perform public services may correspond to a greater propensity to innovate, it is intuitive that advancing MSW business models can improve the net economic benefit they provide  (Marashlian and ElFadel,  2005).  Broadly  speaking,  business  models  and  MSW  management  methods,  such  as  the organisation of collection services, have received limited attention (Guerrini et al. , 2017).

These methods are crucial because they significantly impact the organisation of work (Allesch and Brunner,  2014),  and  both  controllable  and  noncontrollable  factors  can  significantly  impact  the costs of MSW management (De Jaeger and Rogge, 2013).

Furthermore,  the  way  the  service  is  provided,  and  the  size  and  density  of  the  population  also affect  the  costs  of  MSW  management  due  to  economies  of  scale  (De  Jaeger et  al. ,  2011).  The characteristics of the waste produced also play an important role (Chifari et al. , 2017; Greco et al. , 2015). Worth remembering is that morphological and geographical factors (Passarini et al. , 2011), socioeconomic conditions (Mazzanti et al. , 2008), and policies and legal frameworks (Benito-López et al. , 2011) are also central to forming cost structures. Environmental objectives (Beccarello and Di Foggia, 2016), production technologies (Swart and Groot, 2015; Tisserant et al. , 2017), and the use of waste management facilities (Chu et al. , 2019) also play a role in this process.

With  respect  to  how  the  competitive  environment  and  business  strategies  influence  agility, adaptability, and alignment -which are linked, as reported by a recent study (Garrido-Vega et al. , 2021) -there  is  a  paucity  of  articles  focusing  on  the  strategic  behaviour  of  MSW  management firms. Some  studies  have  drawn  conclusions  concerning  the  degree  and  type  of  market competition (Bel and Sebő, 2020, 2021) .


## 3. Methodology



## 3.1 Context


The  waste  management  industry  is  a  hybrid,  regulated,  and  market-driven  sector  as  the  main activities  in  the  collection  phase  are  often  allocated  to  legal  monopolies,  whereas  those  in  the treatment phase, for example of waste electrical and electronic equipment (Roy et al., 2022), can mostly be fulfilled by the market.

Therefore, analysing  economic  and  environmental  efficiency  based  on  identifying  economies  of scale  and  scope  is  particularly  complicated.  As  evidence  of  this,  the  results  in  the  previous literature do not necessarily reach the same conclusions. There are many reasons for this. Studies have  been  conducted  in  different  disciplines;  also,  the  type  of  cost  analysed  as  a  dependent variable  (e.g.  total  costs,  costs  of  separated  collection,  costs  of  nonsegregated  collection,  sales prices) differs depending on the context. The unit of analysis may contribute to the variance in the results, and the analysed phase plays a large role in this phenomenon.

We  refer  to  the  combination  of  the  transaction  cost  approach,  economies  of  scale,  and  the competitive  aspects  that are becoming  increasingly  important  in  defining  how  the  MSW management industry should function.

The idea of transaction costs is applied in many contexts, from simple situations to more general ideas that consider various methods for allocating resources and coordinating economic activity (Klaes, 2016). Transaction costs are a necessary first step in separating the factor market from the product  market.  It  may  be  impossible  to  distinguish  between  markets  in  service  industries characterised by a supply chain with a significant number of suppliers. Therefore, distinguishing one  organisation  from  another  is  often  difficult  when  decisions  are  contractually  binding. Furthermore,  transaction  costs  are  often  difficult  to  measure  and  separate  by  type  (Cheung, 2016).

Transaction  costs,  like  production  costs,  are  a  wide-ranging  designation  for  a  heterogeneous assortment of inputs and transaction functions that may show diminishing, constant, or increasing returns;  in  general,  economies  of  scale  are  often  pronounced.  Compared  to  a  theoretical  state without  transaction  costs,  transaction  costs  inevitably  reduce  social  welfare  due  to  the  loss  of allocative  efficiency  they  incur.  Efficiency  problems  also  arise  in  a  more  general  context.  As complicated transactions may include multilateral contracts with many parties, transaction costs tend to increase (Niehans, 2016).

## 3.2 Research design


The analyses were developed at two levels to increase the robustness of the results; two research questions were developed to investigate this topic.

RQ1: What is the relation between the size of the service and the cost? An econometric analysis based on 54% of Italian municipalities was developed to identify the impact of the determinants of MSW  management  costs.  Then,  a  sensitivity  analysis  of  different  samples  was  performed  by dividing the sample into 3, 5, 10, 15, and 20 subsamples. The hypothesis is an inverse relationship between scale and cost.

RQ2: Which factors impact the optimisation of MSW management services? A case study was used to test the best option between assigning MSW management to a single firm or dividing the city into four lots and assigning the service to four firms. The observed cost was reclassified, based on the 56 subservices (see Annex 1 for additional details) that constitute the service. An alternative scenario in which four firms provide MSW management services was simulated for comparative purposes.

This scenario first considered the organisational structure of the incumbent, which is divided into four branches referring to four subareas of the city of Milan. Then, a hypothetical total cost was calculated, based on the four existing operating divisions. The case study analysis aimed to shed light  on  the  operating  and  organisational  factors  that  have  received  little  attention  thus  far  in MSW  research  on  scale  and  scope.  The  hypothesis  is  that  a  single  contractor  is  expected  to provide MSW management services more efficiently due to organisational issues and transaction costs.


## 3.3 Data collection and variables


The official data from the municipal waste cadastre published by the Italian national environmental protection institute (ISPRA) and openly accessible from the ISPRA web portal were used  to  run  the  analyses.  The  cadastre  database  contains  data  referring  to  the  cost  of  MSW management,  treatment  options,  and  waste  production  at  the  municipality  level.  Similarly,  the data available in the public balance sheets of the city of Milan were used. Only municipalities with available  data  were  included  in  the  sample.  The  morphological  and  geographical  data  were retrieved  from  the  Italian  Statistics  Institute  portal,  which  contains  the  data  on  all  Italian municipalities, which are publicly available for download. We aimed to increase the robustness of the  analysis  at  the  subsample  level  by  rerunning  the  econometric  analysis  using  comparable municipalities by size, as reported in the sensitivity analysis.

## 5. Discussion


Economies of scale can play a significant role in defining business models even though they may seemingly  conflict  with  the  common  knowledge  that  policymakers  should  favour  SMEs  in  the provision of public services to create new opportunities and support the growth of SMEs, which in turn can make a significant economic contribution. It is worth emphasising that the involvement of SMEs  in  public  procurement  allows  contracting  authorities  to  broaden  their  base  of  potential suppliers  and  to  benefit  from  the  increased  competition  for  public  contracts.  However,  such positive  externalities  in  terms  of  efficiency  and  market  development  gains  vanish  in  certain circumstances. Indeed, the arguments regarding the presence of economies shall be contextualised to fit with the cases. Considering that a few studies have stated that the existence of scale economies, to a certain level, does not indicate that it can be generalised to all cities. In fact,  most  studies  have  analysed  samples  only  with  no  or  just  a  few  large  municipalities.  In contrast,  this  article  deeply  analyses  the  MSW  cost  structure  in  a  1.38-million  inhabited  city, suggesting that the MSW service is large and complex enough to require specific analyses.

In cities where public or private incumbent monopolies have long-run MSW management services, policymakers should not allow for excessive exemptions, such as splitting a city's area into several subareas to allow more firms to participate in MSW management. Nevertheless, it is possible to argue that splitting the municipal area into several subareas or the MSW management service into subservices  each,  or  some  of  them  corresponding  to  many,  may  encourage  anti-competitive strategies. This action limits the number of lots in which a single economic operator can run the service  and  may  even  lead  to  covert  agreements  between  competitors,  which  would  in  turn worsen social welfare, for example, due to transaction costs (Cheung, 2016; DaSilva and Trkman, 2014) that have received little attention in MSW management studies.

Analysing the city of Milan enabled the determination of the efficiency of the business model by including  costs  sourced  from  public  information  regarding  the  incumbent,  and  the  results conveyed  that  a  single  firm  was  more  efficient  than  four  firms.  The  main  reasons  highlighted include  the  differences,  especially  regarding  the  separated  collection  of  materials  (e.g.  streetsweeping  activities  and  bin-emptying  activities),  given  that  the  production  factors,  employees, means of production, and containers required are proportional in the two scenarios analysed in this article. However, this study found several issues related to transaction costs. Furthermore, the results indicate that the incumbent is more efficient from an economic standpoint.

The services causing the greatest cost burden are those related to collection, which include the sorting  of  bulky  waste,  durables,  batteries,  pharmaceuticals,  and  spent  toner  cartridges,  the collection of residual and differentiated waste with dedicated containers, the collection of residual and  differentiated  waste  in  cemeteries,  the  cleaning  of  markets,  the  collection  and  disposal  of small  items  containing  asbestos,  the  separated  collection  of  used  clothing,  the  separated collection of used oil, and some sweeping activities such as cleaning the banks of watercourses, collecting  leaves,  cleaning  tree  rows  and  their  areas,  mowing  and  weeding  pavements,  and washing tunnels, arcades, and subways. Similarly, other activities, including on-demand services, have been shown to experience a significant increase in costs. Some production factors are not divisible or shareable between firms, which would entail the duplication of that production factor and therefore its cost.

Evidence suggests that entrusting MSW management services to a single firm may positively affect the community given the potential cost savings (-6%) and, thereby, the waste tax that citizens pay to  finance  them.  The  main  drivers  increasing  production  costs  are  the  need  for  personnel  and means of production -namely, vehicles -to provide the same level of service if they were to be provided  by  several  firms.  The  above  results  are  correlated  with  strategic  management  and uncertainty-coping strategies, given that uncertainty plays a substantial role in strategic decisionmaking processes and increases the risk and ambiguity of innovation (Beraha et al. , 2018), which is needed to improve the performance of the MSW management industry.

Interestingly, a recent study focusing on the city of Barcelona showed that dividing the region into four  lots  discriminated  in  terms  of  quality  and,  furthermore,  differentiated  service  quality.  The study  analysed  the  effects  of  competition  by  focusing  on  the  strategic  behaviour  of  firms  and illustrated  the  incentive  to  strategically  determine  the  quality,  based  on  the  operating  distance from competitors, which is an approximation of competitive pressure. This is, therefore, a risk if the principle of universality of service quality is to be respected. It is important to avoid triggering strategic behaviours  that  increase service quality only in the most  relevant  and  directly comparable areas (Bel and Sebő, 2021).

However, both positive and negative aspects  should  be noted  to exist even when  a  single  firm provides the service, as shown in Table III.
