The results also provide information on the compatibility of such strategic behaviour of firms with the principle of universality of service. This is an essential element and a principle that cannot be derogated from and a risk that may emerge. A further risk lies in the information asymmetries between  local  authorities  and  contractors,  which  could  reduce  the  efforts  of  the  latter  in neighbourhoods farthest from those where there is more competition.

The main contribution of this paper is threefold. From a theoretical perspective, it summarises the previous literature on economies of scale and scope in MSW management and provides thoughtprovoking results that further the discussion on competitive policy and the regulation of public services. From a managerial perspective, the results offer new insights into critical organisational and operating factors that may emerge in running such services, which, due to transaction and other costs, may lead to suboptimal levels of output and economic inefficiency. This paper also has policy  implications  given  that  the  abovementioned  considerations  can  serve  as  a  reference  for public decision-makers in designing municipal strategies that consider economic and social welfare outcomes. Managerial and practical perspectives are also straightforward for both bit utilities and SMEs, which shall analyse in detail the organisational and transaction costs they may experience in running this service in complex circumstances.

Our results also suggest that additional research is needed to evaluate the relation between scale and MSW management costs, which is a public service of general interest. Its effectiveness should be evaluated from a contracting authority -often municipality -perspective, not only from the firm perspective, paying more attention to the exogenous factors affecting the organisation of the

service.  Indeed,  failing  to  consider  the  above  may  result  in  formally  correct  results  but  bias  in practice  if  the  subadditivity  of  costs  is  not  considered.  In  fact,  a  paradox  may  emerge.  When analysing samples of firms the results of relatively small-scale economies may suggest the optimal size  that,  if  put  into  practice  in  relatively  large  cities,  resulted  in  multiple  firms  operating conjunctively, paving the way to transition costs and organisational failures that lead to negative externalities: one pitfall relates to costs, and the other downside refers to different quality levels that may occur in different parts of the cities because the service is run by different companies, and  other  hypothetical  problems  emerge  in  the  potential  strategic  behaviour  of  firms  and difficulties in regulating more firm issues.


## Conclusion


This  paper  investigates  the  scale  and  scope  of  MSW  management  business  models  in  terms  of their economic efficiency to provide empirical evidence to support both the debate and the design of competitive waste management policy strategies. On one hand, it is generally recognised that the broad participation of SMEs in the provision of public services is a public policy goal. On the other hand, monopolistic competition outperforms other models in certain circumstances -for example,  in  that  of  integrated  utilities,  which  can  provide  more  services  at  more  stages  of  the supply  chain,  owing  to  economies  of  scale  and  scope  resulting  from  their  optimised  and streamlined production models.

A novel contribution of this paper is in its effort to analyse and test the same hypothesis across different conditions. From a national perspective, based on an econometric analysis of a significant sample of Italian municipalities, the results confirm the presence of an inverse relation between the scale and the average cost of the service. This finding is important considering that as the size of the service increases by 1%, the average cost of MSW management services decreases by 0.46% nationwide.  From  the  results,  the  inverse  relation  between  service  scale  and  costs  can  also  be inferred to persist even under different hypotheses, as confirmed by our scenario analysis.

To fine-tune the analysis and provide useful insights that benefit managers and local administrators,  a  simulation  has  been  carried  out  for  the  city  of  Milan  by  testing  whether  the service costs were lower when run by a single firm compared to when run by four different firms. The evidence suggests that MSW management is more efficient when carried out by a single firm given the industry structure, resource and labour force optimisation, and lower transaction costs, which,  in  certain  circumstances,  overcome  the  efficiency  gains  of  the  market,  envisaged  by economic theory.

The  simulation  revealed  that  dividing  the  city  into  subareas  may  lead  to  diseconomies,  thus undermining economic efficiency and general service quality and creating undesirable consequences for social welfare and the equal treatment of citizens. Therefore, there are  cases where contracting authorities shall decide that it is not appropriate to divide the contract into lots

due  to  the  risk  of  rendering  the  execution  of  the  contract  excessively  technically  difficult  or expensive and because coordinating the different contractors could risk undermining the proper execution of the contract to the detriment of equity and quality.

This  study  has  certain  limitations.  The  results  are  extendable  and  relevant  to  other  cities  only when the spatial and socioeconomic characteristics are comparable given that the factors used to identify whether a single firm is more efficient can lead to varied results in cities characterised by nonhomogeneous conditions or in larger multicentric cities. In fact, the land of the city of Milan is flat,  with  an  altitude  of  approximately  130  metres,  on  an  administrative  area  of  approximately 181.7  square  kilometres,  with  a  population  of  slightly  less  than  1.4  million  inhabitants:  7,315 inhabitants  per  square  kilometre.  Consequently,  a  very  different  situation  with  respect,  for example, to Rome: approximately 2,860,889 residents in 1,285 km 2 , 2.226 inhabitants per square kilometre, and varied land characteristics. In such urban conditions, the results in terms of optimal business  organisation  may  significantly  change,  preventing  our  results  from  being  extended  to geographically significantly different cities.

In  the  context  of  large  cities,  both  the  advantages  of  dividing  the  municipal  area  into  smaller subareas -or the service into more lots -to facilitate the potential entry of smaller operators and the a priori advantages related to the existence of economies of scale need to be further studied and contextualised to avoid a strategic drift in municipal waste service planning.

The  future  research  should  focus  on  two  topics.  First,  the  activities  that  comprise  waste management services should be broken down to investigate the opportunities presented by and costs  of  alternative  forms  of  management  for  each  subservice  according  to  scale  and  other exogenous factors. Second, provided that cross-sectional studies struggle due to sampling reasons, an analysis of the impact of economies of scale and scope in large cities is needed using case study approaches.

## Introduction


The past two decades have brought an onslaught of policies that criminalize immigrants in the United States, making their lives more precarious and threatened by surveillance, detention, deportation, and exploitation. Yet, immigrants are also often held up as contributors to U.S. society and key institutions. This duality reflects the fraught and often contradictory position immigrants hold in the American psyche. As Bosniak (2006) and other political theorists have highlighted, these narratives serve each other. Demarcating the alien helps clarify the boundaries of who is a citizen. The inclusion of some immigrants in the U.S. economy and political membership is also often justified through exclusion of other immigrants and non-immigrants (De Genova 2005; Paret 2014). This ambivalence is reflected not only in immigration legislation and other laws but can be seen in the organizational narratives of key U.S. institutions across the political spectrum.

We might assume that political differences would generate distinct discursive strategies around immigration policy, and that differing institutional fields would produce different narratives about immigrants (Benford and Snow 2000; Bloemraad, Silva, and Voss 2016; T. K. Wong 2017). This paper examines these dynamics through a comparative study of organizational discourses on immigrants in two cornerstone U.S. institutions over the last two decades. We focus on labor unions and the U.S. military as powerful players in setting the terms of immigration debates and immigration policies in the United States. While not parallel institutions in terms of organizational form nor relationship to the state, they are both key sites of partisan influence, and both labor unions and the military have an outsized impact on the socio-economic outcomes of their members.  A focus on the U.S. labor movement and military also provides analytical leverage because each arena is associated with distinct political factions and policy positions.  As such, we interrogate how each institution frames the significance of immigrants as members and workers, and how they relate to the larger punitive and criminalizing context for immigrants in the United States. We do so as a way to better understand the nature of immigration discourse in the United States.

Further, we focus on these two institutions because they each reflect a slice of U.S. politics with wide mainstream appeal and comparable proportions of U.S. adult population: 6 percent union membership (Bureau of Labor Statistics 2023) and 7 percent of adults who have been members of the U.S. armed forces (U.S. Census Bureau 2022). We argue that in unpacking how unions and the military talk about immigrants’ contributions and utility, we can learn a great deal about the immigrant qualities each institution frames as exemplary, thus making select immigrants palatable. This paired institutional comparison also allows us to extend theoretical and comparative work on diversity ideologies and policies (Nkomo 2012; Berrey 2015; Ray 2019) into new empirical sites that engage with racialized immigrant populations.  The common frames we uncover are rooted in U.S. economic nationalism and a fictive ideal of prosperity.  They stem, we argue, from fundamental ideologies shared between institutions that maintain a global capitalist society, which glorify imperial pasts, and which offers a justification of rights based on economic value.  For both U.S. unions and the U.S. military, immigrants represent a population and member base that reinforce the goals of these ideologies.

Both the U.S. labor movement and the U.S. military have long and complex histories with immigrants and immigration.  For many years, U.S. labor unions supported restrictive immigration policies and even excluded immigrants, whom they viewed as a threat undermining U.S.-born workers. This is part of a broader capitalist political economy whereby immigrants were conceptualized primarily as labor inputs. Restricting, or increasing the barriers to entry, for new immigrant workers was seen as a necessity for protecting the labor market position of U.S. workers. Then and now, this form of social closure is highly racialized (López-Sanders 2024)

Over time, however, immigrants have grown their share in key industries such as agriculture, with debate and divisions within the labor movement about the growing undocumented labor force (Garcia 2012). In response, beginning in the late 1980s, some major unions started to organize these new populations, culminating in such iconic moments in the labor movement as the Justice for Janitors campaign (Zlolniski 2006). By the early 2000s, and thanks to the work of grassroots immigrant leaders, most major traditional labor unions at least nominally supported broad immigrant rights proposals (Milkman 2011; Ness 2005). Today, immigrants account for 17 percent of the U.S. labor force (Bureau of Labor Statistics 2021), though only an estimated nine percent of union members in the United States are foreign-born (Milkman and Luce 2021). Given the declining union membership numbers, immigrant workers are a site of growth and strength for the labor movement (Hamlin 2008). This is despite the fact that U.S. union membership has been actively decimated by an erosion of protections for collective worker actions (Rosenfeld 2014). Unions remain, however, one of the most influential institutions in the creation of labor, trade, and social protection policies in the United States – at national and subnational levels (Turner and Cornfield 2007; Tattersall 2010; McAlevey 2020).

Labor unions organize and represent immigrant workers, and have become an important institution for social mobility, immigrants included. Meanwhile,  the U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) is the largest employer in the United States, with enormous influence on public policy (Donnelly 2020; Office of Senator Elizabeth Warren 2022). Immigrants have fought in the U.S. military in all of its many wars, starting with the Revolutionary War (C. Wong 2007). In the 21st century, the military tends to laud immigrants as workers with language, cultural, and other skills that are critical to military operations. This parallels ever-present currents of anxiety about their loyalty and potential for breaching security (Aptekar 2018; 2023). Without a draft since 1973, the five branches of the U.S. military rely on an all-volunteer force in a context when fewer and fewer U.S. youth are either willing or qualify to enlist. Given shortfalls in recruitment, immigrants are an important source of labor for the military, and there are targeted military marketing campaigns to recruit them (Aptekar 2023). Since early 2000s, the DOD has been a supporter of immigration reforms such as the DREAM Act, which would provide a path to citizenship for immigrant youth by, in part, channeling more immigrant youth into the military labor force. While military service does not provide an automatic pathway to U.S. citizenship, it reduces time to eligibility for naturalization for permanent lawful residents. This is used by military recruiters as a selling point to attract immigrants. However, in practice, the securitization around immigrant servicemembers has significantly delayed the realization of this benefit (Aptekar 2023). In less tangible, but still significant, ways, military service can provide some immigrants with economic mobility, as well as symbolic benefits that can bolsters a sense of belonging.

Our research confirms a keen interest by both institutions – U.S. labor unions and the U.S. military – to recruit and count immigrants among their ranks.  Though both institutions clearly need immigrants as workers and members, they are ultimately oriented towards immigrants in different ways given their structural differences and partisan influence.  We would therefore expect each to engage in differing discourses around immigrant inclusion.  Yet, our analysis of union and military communications reveals that despite significant differences, they share several core themes in their framing of immigrants. While popular discourse positions the United States as having a more pluralistic political and cultural sphere than societies deemed authoritarian by U.S. commentators, our research cautions against such conclusions about U.S. exceptionalism. U.S. national ideologies shape how immigration is framed in public discourse.  These dominant narratives emerge across different institutions and organizational forms in society.

In what follows, we synthesize existing research on labor unions and the military to contextualize these commonalities, engaging sociological theory on diversity ideology and organizational discourse.  Specifically, we explore the following discursive themes: immigrants as (1) potential threats, (2) as essential workers, and finally, (3) as a source of organizational diversity. We conclude by discussing the implications of these discursive strategies on immigrants and immigration policies writ large in the United States.


## Literature Review



### Diversity, Immigrants, and Organizational Discourse


Given the multiplicity of cultural schema around immigrants in the United States that they could draw on, we might expect that unions and the military would have different organizational discourses on immigrants. For unions struggling under a capitalist system with an increasingly challenging labor organizing environment, immigrants may come to be seen as part of a reserve army of labor and a threat to worker power, or as a source of worker power themselves. The military, by contrast, is both a protector of national borders and responsible for recruiting and maintaining a war-ready military labor force, which includes immigrants.  This convergence of nationalism and capitalist efficiency would lead us to expect its orientation to be more utilitarian, albeit colored by concerns about foreigners’ loyalty.

This is not to say that institutions or institutional cultures are static. They respond to changing resource and cultural imperatives and may respond to pressure from grassroots movements as well.  Legitimacy with members is an important currency for organizations, which can in turn shape prevalent discourses (Pfeffer and Salancik 1978). For instance, the shift in unions over their approach to immigrant workers is in part the result of the demands of immigrant worker organizers from below (Tait 2005).

Institutions are also responsive to multiple external constraints and pressures, which both the U.S. military and unions are facing in the 21st century. The U.S. military struggles to get enough enlisted workers (Linn 2023), while unions struggle for membership in an era of at-will employment, the fissured workplace, and weakening National Labor Relations Act (Rosenfeld 2014). While there is a recent uptick in the legitimacy of unions among the U.S. public, the military has both struggled with recruitment and legitimacy around its major wars (Doherty and Kiley 2023). However, even in times of austerity, the U.S. military enjoys unrivaled flows of material and symbolic resources and bipartisan support.

For both unions and the military, immigrants are necessary to reproduction and success. At minimum this reflects U.S. demographic realities affecting both institutions. Further, these similarities might occur despite distinct justifications and resource needs of each institution. Organizations are embedded in larger societal structures and hegemonic ideologies that transcend organizational forms. Unions and the military must engage with the larger structures and cultural material (Lune 2010) that is shaped by white supremacy and settler colonialism, and they must conform to dominant understandings of race to get resources, including in the form of people (Nkomo 2012; Wooten 2019). In the United States, cultural schemas around immigrants and immigration are inextricable from processes of racialization that typically position immigrants as outsiders to the nation (Kretsedemas 2013). Diversity ideologies have become increasingly popular, in response to calls to address racial inequalities in society and these respective organizations. They are, however, contradictory, and exist simultaneously alongside policies and practices of exclusion.

Labor unions and the military are both racialized and are racializing agents themselves in the United States (Ray and Purifoy 2019). This is clear in the way the dominant labor movement long reflected nativist and white supremacist ideologies (Honey 2000; Nelson 2002), capitalizing on the wages of whiteness at the expense of undermining working-class power (Roediger 1991). This history of exclusion is part of the genealogy of the U.S. labor movement and continues to structure it today. This is true even as labor unions also played an important movement in civil rights organizing (Honey 1993; Jones 2013), and more recently centering immigrant rights and racial justice. Similarly, racial hierarchies, white supremacy, and settler colonialism were instrumental to the very formation of the U.S. military as a force for maintaining chattel slavery and settler dominance (Dunbar-Ortiz 2021).  This reality does not negate the role of the military in the upward mobility of some communities of color. But the foundational racial oppression remains true despite a shift towards greater inclusion (Burk and Espinosa 2012). Indeed, the ideological exigencies of the Cold War in large part forced the U.S. military to be more racially inclusive after resisting desegregation efforts as compromising efficiency.  But it did so by assimilating military workers into a racialized labor hierarchy in the service of empire (Kiang 1991; Bailey 2023). Given these similarly fraught organizational histories, we might expect overlap in the union and military discourses around immigrants.

Another reason to expect similarities between unions and the military in how they frame immigrants is the dominance of the diversity ideology among 21st century organizations (Embrick 2011; Nkomo 201; Mayorga-Gallo 2019). Isomorphism in organizations means that they replicate each other’s policies, structures, and discourses, and these become taken for granted and commonsensical (Meyer and Rowan 1977; DiMaggio and Powell 1983; Mizruchi and Fein 1999).  The isomorphism could be arrived at through different mechanisms – bowing to dominant narratives, imitations, or shared professionalization (DiMaggio and Powell 1983) – but the result is similarities in how organizations signal their orientations towards racial and other forms of diversity. Beyond isomorphism, diversity is also an ideology, that is, a system of beliefs that organizes the social world.  Scholars have demonstrated that diversity ideology is used to signal inclusiveness rather than remedy material inequities (Collins 2011; Embrick 2011; Berrey 2015).

One might also expect unions and the military to produce similar discourse on immigrants as part of efforts to promote diversity as good for productivity and competitiveness (Berrey 2015; Thornton and Ocasio 1999).  Indeed, the business case for diversity is a leading justification for DEI trainings and new managerial positions dedicated to the implementation of DEI goals (Dobbin and Kalev 2022).  For example, the U.S. military effectively promotes itself as a racially egalitarian institution in recruiting people of color as workers (Ray 2018a; 2018b). It also defends affirmative action (Loewenson 2022). The labor movement, too, has argued in favor of embracing immigration for the “diversity and values they bring” (AFL-CIO 2005).

Both the U.S. labor movement and U.S. military institutions have strong currents of “colorblind” ideologies (Bonilla-Silva 2007; Ray and Purifoy 2019): unified working-class solidarity for unions and the emphasis on conformity for the military (Ray 2018b). The prevailing imaginary of the worker and the soldier has been and to a large extent continues to be a white U.S.-born man. This is reflected in much of the higher ranks of union and military leadership in the public arena.  Further, while an increasingly popular part of organizational branding, research confirms that efforts to increase diversity and promote DEI goals are readily cast off if these threaten other institutional priorities.  These realities reflect the contradictions of diversity ideology, as a prominent, but easily discarded and materially shallow, organizational goal (Smith and Mayorga-Gallo 2017).

While there are theoretical reasons to expect differences and similarities in the discourses of unions and the military around immigrants, we must also attend to the nuances in these discourses within each institution. This is essential because of the nature of cultural schemas around immigrants in the United States: there are tropes framing some racialized immigrants as criminals, demographic threats, fiscal burdens, and economic competitors (Chavez 2008; Rodriguez 2008), while others are lauded as humanitarian victims seeking relief and critical economic inputs (Nawyn 2011; Gleeson 2015; Huber 2016). The distinctions made among immigrants follow a larger cultural (and often legal) prerogative of deservingness politics, positioning some groups of immigrants as more worthy of rights and belonging than others, even among those fighting on behalf of immigrants and immigrant organizers themselves (Yukich 2013; Huber 2016). Given these tropes of relative worth, imbricated with racial hierarchies, it would not be surprising to find contradictory framings of immigrants within institutions. Support for immigrants is often conditional, limited by broader institutional goals, and reflective of broader social anxieties around immigration.


### Unions and Immigrants


Unions are many things, but could be defined as working class political institutions, organized through (ideally) democratic structures, whose purpose is to concentrate the power of labor to improve workers lives.  Yet, whose labor and which workers has always been a point of debate for unions in a resource scarce environment.  Organized labor’s stance towards immigrants has fluctuated between restrictionist and expansionist (Fine and Tichenor 2009),  including various incarnations of red scare politics branding immigrants as untrustworthy national security threats, part of the industrial reserve army, a notably militarized term Marx used to denote “a mass of human material always ready for exploitation” (Marx 1867). More radical wings of the US labor movement did sometimes view the industrial reserve army of immigrants as an organizing opportunity, even as they may supported more immigration control (Rosenberg 1995). Mid-century civil rights struggles began to highlight the plight of immigrant workers and their need for protection, but labor leaders (most famously Cesar Chavez) often had a complicated relationship with undocumented migrant workers who were seen as scabs threatening organizing efforts (Garcia 2012). By 1986, when the Immigration Reform and Control Act was passed, the compromise issued by the AFL-CIO was a mass legalization of 3 million immigrants paired with employer sanctions that would set the course for punitive workplace immigration enforcement practices.

These protectionist positions adopted by the AFL-CIO – which framed immigrants as competitors who played no role in the organizing agenda – were reflective of their opposition to free trade policies that might rob American workers of jobs in industries that were rapidly outsourcing production (Kay 2011).  Over time, however, the AFL-CIO (and its sister organizations like the Solidarity Center) would begin campaigns of transnational solidarity to shore up worker power, with the hope of improving conditions to keep would-be migrants home and reduce firms’ search for cheaper labor. While some critics have called into question the nature of this transnational solidarity (Scipes 2010), these connections would prove significant to later efforts to organize immigrants. A growing cadre of labor leaders (many of them women of color) were pushing from below from affiliate unions in key immigrant industries to demand that the AFL-CIO change its approach to immigration policy and its immigrant membership (Sherman and Voss 2000). By 2000, the AFL-CIO had changed its position to one that called for the repeal of employer sanctions, and which demanded a pathway to citizenship for the growing undocumented population (AFL-CIO 2001b).

Opinion polls have tracked a steady opposition to increased immigration in the United States since the passage of the 1965 Immigration Act, with a decline in anti-immigrant sentiment in the late 1990s.  However, restrictionist views intensified in the years following the attacks of September 11, 2001, with opinion polls showing a spike in the proportion of Americans who wanted to see immigration decreased (Gallup Inc. 2024). Some labor organizations resisted, such as when participants in the 2003 Immigrant Workers Freedom Ride chanted “we are workers not terrorists” (Stuteville 2003). What followed was a heyday of immigrant union victories across the country that made clear the critical role of immigrants in the U.S. labor movements’ organizing priorities and political platform (Ness 2005; Milkman 2006; Milkman, Bloom, and Narro 2010). The second Bush administration was marked by workplace raids and other spectacles of interior enforcement, paired with repeated failed attempts to pass a comprehensive immigration reform bill (T. K. Wong 2017). In many cities, the mass immigrant rights marches of 2006 had labor unions at the helm, as well as the breakaway Change to Win coalition (led by Service Employees International Union – SEIU) that centered new worker organizing as part of its new agenda (Voss and Bloemraad 2011; Zepeda-Millán 2017; Nicholls 2019).

This shift away from viewing immigrants solely as competitors was reflected in both labor organizing campaigns and union policy positions.  These remained, however, nuanced on the question of immigration  By 2012, the AFL-CIO executive council platform cosigned a moderate stance of “rational operational control of the border,” endorsed a pathway to legalization for the undocumented, but still opposed the expansion of guestworker programs (Fine and Tichenor 2012). These exemplified the attempts of the federation to circumscribe solidarity inside national borders while still critically examining the position of the U.S. working class within the capitalist political economy.

In the 2010s, student organizers cornered union leadership into endorsing the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) and (the later failed) Deferred Action for Parents (DAPA), which were instituted by executive decree, circumventing a perennially unsuccessful congressional strategy (Nicholls 2013; de Graauw, Els and Gleeson 2021). While the number of deportations of immigrants from the interior of the United States were at record high in the first Obama administration, declining through his second administration and that of Trump (Bush-Joseph and Chishti 2024), the number of detentions continued to rise (Shah 2024) and continued unabated right into the Trump era.  This once again pushed the AFL-CIO and other unions into a defensive stance to counter the hardening of all openings for immigration reform and attacks on Muslim and communities racialized as foreign (Gleeson 2018). The labor movement as a whole remained split, with some factions in favor of a unionized border patrol and union-made border wall (Loomis 2017).  This marked one of many dividing points between the reigning status quo in the labor movement, and the emergent progressive (some argue, new radical) flank of U.S. unions (Chacón and Davis 2018).

The labor movement cannot ignore the 17 percent of the private workforce currently made up of immigrants (Bureau of Labor Statistics 2021).  This paper seeks to understand how a hegemonic diversity ideology works alongside this demographic reality to shape the labor movements’ discourse on immigrant inclusion.  We demonstrate that rather than a unique feature of union strategy, this discourse is also apparent in statements issued by the leadership of another very distinctly positioned U.S. institution: the military.  The similarities in these two institutional approaches to immigrant incorporation simultaneously rely on narrow definitions of immigrant utility and deservingness.


### Military and Immigrants


As institutions that use armed violence to defend the nation state and carry out its foreign (and often domestic) policy, militaries assume a different institutional form than do labor unions. The U.S. military is inherently undemocratic and hierarchical in structure. It is spread over 900-plus bases across the globe and engaged in multiple conflicts at the same time (Vine 2015). In 2022, there were 1.3 million active-duty armed forces personnel with about 172,000 troops overseas (Gibbons-Neff and Schmitt 2019; Defense Manpower Data Center 2023). Immigrants continue to be seen as an important source of labor for the U.S. military struggling with recruitment. Approximately five percent of U.S. service members are foreign born, which includes naturalized U.S. citizens, legal permanent residents, and non-citizens on temporary student and employment visas (Batalova 2008). About 80,000 non-citizens enlisted in the Army, Navy, Marines, and Air Force between 1999 and 2010. Immigrants who enlist without U.S. citizenship are more likely to be women, people of color, older, and have dependents than enlisted citizens (Center for Naval Analyses 2011).

The military is a powerful institution with its own immigration policy agenda and ability to shape immigration debates and immigration narratives. Historically, the United States has used naturalization and the promise of citizenship to fulfill its needs for military labor, including to avoid having to institute military draft, via proposals that would require immigrants to perform military service, and through the use of  colonized populations as soldiers (Lutz 1990; Salyer 2004; Bailey 2007). In the 21st century, the DOD has supported the DREAM Act, which would channel a new pool of recruits into the military in exchange for a path to citizenship (Mariscal 2007).

The military tries to distinguish military labor from civilian labor, notably squashing attempts to unionize military workers in the 1970s (Mittelstadt 2011). The military also competes against other entry-level employment opportunities, actively marketing itself as a desirable employer.  In fact, the U.S. military has won major advantages in competition for workers, including gaining unprecedented access to youth in schools and colleges. It also brands itself as a colorblind engine of social mobility, particularly in respect to African Americans (Moskos and Butler 1997). In a clear example of the commodification aspects of diversity ideology identified by Mayorga-Gallo (2019), the image of the military as a racially progressive employer helps it recruit workers and maintain legitimacy (Ray 2018b). Scholars note racial inequities in the military, such as suppressed discrimination claims and disparate treatment of service members of color in military justice and military health care (Burk and Espinoza 2012). Ray (2018a) demonstrates the persistence of a racial hierarchy in the U.S. military, and “the assumption… that minorities must integrate into the military, revealing the unmarked white background on which this assumption rests.” (289) Through interview-based research, Ray (2018a) shows the gap between military’s framing of diversity as a force multiplier – which we also see in our analysis – and the resistance by white members of the military to systemic change that would address racial inequity.

At a time of heightened anti-immigrant discourse and cruel immigration enforcement policies, immigrants are pressured to prove themselves worthy, deserving of rights and protection, and different from other, undeserving immigrants. Rhetorically positioned as eternally in debt on U.S. soil, immigrants attempt to prove their deservingness to belong through their service in the military (Cacho 2012; Pacleb 2009). This can be a difficult position, as it "forces them to prove their loyalty and Americanness in the face of rejection of their own ethnic communities by the very same state that employs them” (Pacleb 2009, 147). In the immigrant rights movement and mainstream politics, narratives of immigrant service members are used as the ultimate example of a deserving immigrant. Pacleb (2009) argues that immigrant service members are increasingly framed as the new model minority because they are ostensibly willing to die for the United States even before becoming a citizen. Open discussions of immigrant service members dying in combat are at odds with the recruitment prerogatives of the U.S. military, and it remains to be seen how model minority frames might manifest in the official discourse of the military itself. Critical analysis sets up our understanding of the way immigrants fit into the U.S. military, yet more research is needed that looks directly at how the military itself frames immigrants and immigration. How do the military’s discourses on immigrants reflect and grapple with these tensions, as well as recruitment needs and legitimacy prerogatives within multiple audiences?


## Methods


This research project investigates how traditional labor unions and the U.S. military have incorporated immigrant members into their respective institutions.  Both institutions are public facing and politically relevant and engaged.  To be sure, this political activity is cast in different ways.  Generally, unions are seen as an important arm of the Democratic Party in the United States.  But they also represent large swaths of the poor white working class that vote Republican (Frymer and Grumbach 2020).  While the military is commonly thought of as apolitical, in fact it has been actively involved in the immigration policy-making (Scroggs 2000; Hobson 2008; Kambrod 2013).  Indeed both are influential actors in U.S. politics.

In studying how labor unions frame immigrants, we focus on AFL-CIO, the largest federation of unions in the United States, the breakaway (though still very enmeshed) Change to Win coalition led by the SEIU and United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW), and the more muted North America’s Building Trades Unions (NABTU). We also analyzed how the U.S. military has articulated its stance on immigrants, as well how immigration and elected officials discuss immigrant labor in the U.S. armed forces.  For both sets of archives, we searched for the terms “immigrant,” “immigration,” and “foreign-born.” Each set of textual material was analyzed for salient frames, which we then compared for analytical coherence and overlap.

While not a monolith, we focus on the apex of each institutional landscape to understand the public messaging emanating from each.  The differences in these two institutions produced distinct source material that became the basis of ascertaining each set of discourses on immigrants.  For U.S. unions, we examine archival materials and media statements of the aforementioned national labor organizations, including using keyword searches on the archives of the AFL-CIO.  For the U.S. military, we conduct a systematic search of DOD websites, Congressional records, and federal court records since 2001, as well as military-related media. We focus on reports contracted by the military, congressional testimony, and immigration-themed op-eds written by military leaders. The data set includes reports and texts analyzing the military’s recruitment strategies, performance of immigrant service members, military diversity policies, and the impact of immigration policies on military staffing.

We acknowledge that the source material described here does not necessarily fully encompass the entirety of each institution’s positions, and that public proclamation may very well differ from practice and internal interpretations and debates. ## Findings


In analyzing the ways in which the AFL-CIO and some of its member unions and affiliates and the U.S. military talk about immigrants, we first outline the ambivalence both institutions have had towards immigrants, then home in on two key frames they have each developed in their support: immigrants as essential labor, and immigrants a source of diversity. Despite the different nature of the two institutions, we found a convergence in institutional discourses, even as they are complex and multivalent.


### Immigrants as potential threat


Both unions and the military navigate the tension between inclusion and the threat that immigrants pose to their goals. Our analysis uncovers a persistent anxiety that both unions and the military express around the potential threat posed by immigrants. For unions, immigrants can be seen as competition and wage depressor for non-immigrant workers. For the military, immigrants are suspect foreigners whose loyalty is under question.


#### UNIONS


Unions are constantly striving to build external legitimacy with the public and there have been recent upsurges in support for unions (Saad 2023). Yet, they have also struggled to reconcile the pro-immigrant support of national union leadership with the lingering anxieties of the predominantly native-born rank and file.  Indeed, immigration has been a constant field of contestation for the U.S. labor movement internally and externally.  Despite an undeniable demographic shift in the labor force, immigrants have long been framed as a threat to union jobs and organizing, as described above.

Careful analysis of official AFL-CIO statements reveals continued ambivalence and a house of labor that is not united on the specifics of immigration policy. While calls for a “comprehensive immigration reform” abound, the specific standalone bills languishing in Congress have uneven union support.  The United Farmworkers (no longer affiliated with the AFL-CIO), have long disagreed with the AFL-CIO regarding efforts to expand a guestworker program, which the latter insists would only repeat the exploitation of years past. Additionally, the AFL-CIO has wavered on attempts to increase temporary highly skilled visas. In a 2003 statement, the AFL-CIO Executive Council urged restricting this program to “minimize the impact on all professional workers,” presumably those already in the United States. (AFL-CIO 2003b).  A decade later, it focused on tech employers’ abuse of the program and the injustices of denying tech workers a path to citizenship (AFL-CIO 2015).

When the leadership of AFL-CIO argued for a path to citizenship for the undocumented population in 2006, it also expressed concern about what the presence undocumented workers does to the working conditions of “U.S. workers who labor in the same industries” (AFL-CIO 2006).  The federation has since largely shifted its position to frame undocumented immigrants as an asset to the labor movement, even as they are particularly vulnerable to workplace abuse.  These dualities betray some lingering anxieties about which immigrants will be privileged, and their potential impact and contribution.  These positions reflect not necessarily a blanket split between pro- and anti- immigrant contingents of the labor movement.  Rather, they start to paint a picture of the type of immigrant and immigration policy that unions find favorable.  For example, when the AFL-CIO argued in 2017 for extending Temporary Protected Status (a humanitarian program for migrants from designated countries who cannot safely return), its press release painted a dire picture of immigrants in the “shadow economy” who undermine the unions’ struggle for good working conditions and equity (AFL-CIO 2017a).

Parallel to these economic anxieties are ongoing concerns about the quality of migrant flows and their impact on broader social life. As the AFL-CIO has argued, immigration reform is for “workers who have paid taxes and made positive contributions” (AFL-CIO 2006). These characterizations reflect a particular ideal type of immigrant, but no doubt also an idealized ethos of the working class. More poignantly, and in the post 9/11 context especially, unions embraced the trope of “the nation of immigrants” while also making calls for border security to “deter terrorists or other ill-intentioned person who enter the United States to do harm.” These ill-intentioned persons are contrasted to “honest, hardworking immigrants” (AFL-CIO 2001b).

In sum, the labor movement remains ambivalent over the growing immigrant workforce, even as it has embraced calls to ease off of immigration enforcement measures that threaten immigrant union members and their families.  Though as it shifts to a stance of solidarity, it has drawn a bright line around the qualities that make immigrants an important target for unions, focusing especially on their role as essential workers, and as a source of diversity.


#### MILITARY


Similarly, the military views immigrants with some suspicion. That suspicion of the foreign-born – or native-born racialized as foreigners – is not a new phenomenon but since 2017, it has revealed itself in policies that have burdened immigrant service members with new document and security checks, hampered their naturalization, and suspended immigrant-specific programs. In military texts, we see a tension between the recruitment of immigrant workers – particularly the use of U.S. citizenship as a recruitment enticement – and security concerns that their presence in the military evokes for some military leaders. Are immigrant recruits presenting fraudulent documents? Was access to citizenship made too easy for potential spies, mercenaries, and terrorist infiltrators?

For example, in Congressional testimony in 2003, Representative Doug Bereuter argued against expedited naturalization for immigrant service members by invoking the fall of the Roman Empire:

Enacting such excessive inducements for joining the US military is a step in the wrong direction, particularly if it results in this country increasingly depending upon what could come to be thought of and called foreign mercenaries to serve in the Armed Forces. This practice has too many similarities to the mercenary forces of the Roman Empire in its decline as Roman citizens themselves became unwilling to serve in the Roman legions. Imagine, too, the reactions of foreign nations that begin to see our forces as forces that serve to gain citizenship for themselves and their families.

In a 2005 report, Center for Naval Analyses (CNA), a non-profit research center consulting the DOD, expressed concerns about the recruitment of native speakers of Middle Eastern languages. Although these immigrants were seen as much needed for warfare against Middle Eastern countries, their recruitment raised worries: “There also are security concerns about accessing native speakers – particularly those from countries that are considered hostile. Because of these concerns, all initiatives are proceeding carefully.” As much as the military has invested in targeting Hispanics for recruitment, a 2004 CNA report expressed concerns that Hispanic immigrants would have a hard time adjusting to military life compared to citizens and recommended that even for U.S.-born Hispanic service members, the military track their identification with other countries.

Fears about immigrant military workers presenting a security threat ended the 10-year-old Military Accessions of Vital National Interest (MAVNI) program in 2017, stranding hundreds of mostly Asian immigrants in a precarious legal situation. Defense of the MAVNI program drew on model minority language to describe immigrant recruits and emphasized their skills. At the same time, military leaders expressed fears that MAVNI recruits posed a “risk to mission” and “may have a higher risk of connection to Foreign Intelligence Services” (Kurta and Lowery 2017). The heightened suspicion of MAVNI enlistees is analogous to the labor unions’ suspicion of the workers on temporary highly skilled visas. In fact, these are overlapping populations. Not only were some workers on these visas recruited into the MAVNI program, but in both cases the target of suspicion was Asian immigrants with high levels of education. While union leadership viewed these workers primarily as a threat to their existing base in the industries like education and healthcare, the military both framed them as valuable labor and source of useful diversity and held them in suspicion. This complexity is indicative of the military’s competing goals of securing exploitable military labor with specific skills and serving as a force of imperial aggression that relies on the demonization of racialized subjects and rivals.

For the military, immigrants are marked with a specter of foreignness. This suspicion leads to concerns about loyalty and assurances of the assimilationist potential of desirable immigrants. The military (not unlike unions) has endorsed calls for additional screening and scrutiny of immigrants.


### Immigrants as essential labor

This is a familiar trope often used by immigrant advocates to underscore the contributions of immigrants to U.S. society (Fujiwara 2005), but also used by restrictionists to warn how immigrants either take jobs from Americans or fail to work and tax the social safety net (Baker-Cristales 2009; Gleeson 2015). Unions focus on the aspects of immigrant labor that provide contributions to key union industries, and immigrants as a source of organizing energy. The military has focused more explicitly on the demographic reality that has challenged recruitment and retention efforts among the native-born, framing immigrants as an essential and high-quality source of labor.

## Conclusion


Our analysis of texts from the U.S. labor unions and the U.S. military have revealed three shared framings of immigrants in these institutions. Both institutions couch their positive support for immigration reform and immigrant contributions in terms of valuing certain immigrants as deserving and focusing on what they bring to each institution.  As such, immigrants are increasingly framed as an asset rather than a threat for each institution.  However, long-standing legacies of viewing immigrants as inherently suspect in both U.S. unions and the U.S. military remain apparent. In labor union texts, we see the undeserving immigrant excluded from the circle of solidarity, as well as a fear of specific immigrant populations as undermining the position of U.S. workers. In military texts, the same thing that makes immigrants into force multipliers in the military workplace makes their loyalty fundamentally suspect. Ultimately, these dualistic narratives reflect the ambivalence both institutions – and broader society - hold towards immigrants.  These two seemingly opposing characterizations co-exist serve to distinguish particular qualities and sub-populations of immigrants who are seen as more or less desirable.

Second, for both U.S. unions and the U.S. military, immigrants are seen as a source of collective labor strength.  They are in fact, essential labor, these institutions argue.  However, labor unions and the military in the United States both ascribe to a limited and narrow conception of immigrant utility and belonging that excludes many immigrant populations latently categorized as less deserving.  Arguments about immigrant contributions too quickly shade into suspicion of the very same useful immigrant workers.

Finally, immigrant-driven diversity holds instrumental value for both labor unions and the military, as it does for other institutions in the United States. There is institutional specificity, however, in how each institution frames immigrant diversity.  Immigrants generate institutional legitimacy by reflecting the diversity of the U.S. population. Labor unions express appreciation for the international connections to trades movements that immigrant diversity promises, and frame immigrant rights as part of the racial justice and DEI (diversity, equity, and inclusion) movement. Meanwhile, the military stresses immigrant cultural and language skills.  These assets, however, conflict with the military’s ambivalence around the loyalty of immigrants who to many are seen as perpetual foreigners worthy of suspicion.

All told, this paired institutional comparison between U.S. unions and the U.S. military makes a theoretical contribution to how political discourse on immigration is crafted in institutionally specific ways.  The similarities we find are by no means entirely congruent.  But the significant overlap we uncover is surprising given that these institutions have different relationships to immigrants.  Yet, both unions and the military draw on fundamental ideologies that can be discerned in broader U.S. society and political debate.  These ideologies reify a global capitalist society, glorify imperial pasts, and justify rights based on the economic value of beneficiaries.  Each of these ideologies are reflected in the discourse around immigration and immigrants in each institution.  In unpacking how unions and the military talk about immigrants’ contributions, we can learn a great deal about the immigrant qualities they reify as exemplary, making immigrants palatable for an otherwise hostile public.

This study does not engage the opposing positions over immigration that are taking place within labor unions and the military.  These debates are active and produce contradictions that are inherent to any institution. This study is also unable to fully and directly analyze institutional practices and how these may or may not derive from publicly stated narratives. Future research should take up these questions, including via interviews with institutional agents, as well as by investigating the roles of specific institutional entrepreneurs who drive policies and discourse (Hardy and Maguire 2008; Orton and Weick 1990) such as the late Richard Trumka, longtime president of AFL-CIO, or Margaret Stock, the U.S. Army officer who designed influential immigration policies in the U.S. military. Given the rich array of representations of both unions and the military in cultural products, an analysis of popular culture would complement the results presented here.

## Introduction


Nowadays, there are various approaches to literary text analysis, among which  stylistic analysis  attempts  to  develop  insights  into  the  practices  and  principles  of  literary  stylistics. Researchers conduct stylistic analysis because, in recent years, stylistics has become more wellknown for its effort to connect linguistics and literary criticism. The purpose of stylistic analysis is not only to demonstrate the linguistic characteristics of a piece of writing but also to explain the functional significance of such characteristics concerning the overall understanding of the piece of literary text. Stylistic analysis also seeks to uncover connections between the impacts of literary works and the linguistic characteristics considered significant in the areas where these influences are anticipated to appear.

Therefore, stylistic analysis is valuable for literature students because it enables them to explore both language and creative language use. Simpson (2004) stated that stylistic analysis enhances thinking ability about language because exploring language use provides considerable capacity for one's comprehension of literary works. Henceforth, researchers use stylistic analysis to  explain  the  relation  between  artistic  function  and  linguistic  features.  In  addition  to  the importance of stylistic analysis, the lack of sufficient stylistic analysis in poetry in general and in Dylan Thomas' poetry, in particular, has reinforced the idea of conducting a study in this field.

Born in 1914 in Swansea, Wales, Dylan Thomas, a prominent figure in 20th-century Welsh poetry, exhibited exceptional linguistic prowess from a young age, honed through his education at Swansea Grammar School. His early works established him as a poet known for his vivid imagery, complex wordplay, and innovative use of language. Thomas' linguistic mastery not only stemmed from his profound connection with Welsh poetic heritage but also demonstrated his capacity to transcend regional confines (Ackerman, 1996).

Studies conducted on Dylan Thomas typically rely on subjective interpretation, rather than on systematic approaches, although the majority of them were based on subjective interpretations. They lack  employing linguistic features and  explicit, detailed, and  comprehensive analysis to conduct an objective analysis. Despite the greatness of his poetry and its significant contribution to literary criticism, there remains a gap in understanding his poetry, as different linguistic choices made in his poetry can play an essential role in inferring particular meanings hidden in his poems. His  linguistic features are  greatly influenced and  shaped  by  his  religious and  Welsh  cultural backgrounds,  which  interact with  the  themes  of  his  poems.  Therefore,  one  can  observe  that researchers have not given sufficient attention to the stylistic analysis of Thomas' poems, missing the opportunity to examine these aspects and highlight the importance of such analysis.

This study aims to help literature students understand Thomas's writings by examining the stylistic features of his selected poem. This research not only enhances readers' understanding and appreciation of Thomas's works but also encourages other researchers to explore similar studies using diverse approaches and methods, leading to further in-depth investigations on this topic.

Thus, this research study will help readers gain insight into the stylistic choices made by the  poet.  Readers  will  gain  a  thorough  understanding  of  the  stylistic  devices,  themes,  and significance of the poems chosen.

The study is only limited to one of Dylan Thomas' poems, namely, Before I Knocked . To systematically examine his  linguistic nuances,  the study  depends on  stylistic analysis and  the theory of foregrounding supported by the Leech and Shorts checklist. Within the checklist, the study only focuses on foregrounding aspects, and figures of speech. Due to the word limit, the study excludes elements such as  lexical and  grammatical categories, as  well as  other features

## The Concept of Style


The definition of style is complex and controversial due to its various uses and different meanings. For instance, scholars define the notion of style as a variation in language usage. This definition is complicated to grasp because it is unclear what this stylistic variation is measured against. ## The Notion of Stylistics


Stylistics is assumed to have appeared as a discipline in the 1960s (Verdonk, 1993). It is essentially a formalist approach because it is closely related to New  Criticism and Formalism. Scholars believe that the  objective of  a  literary text is  to  concentrate on  the language.  Thus, stylistics is mainly concerned with examining written language (Spencer, 1964).

However,  this  concept  is  defined  based  on  different  fields  and  various  scholars' perspectives. As  an  example, Taylor (1980)  described stylistics as  the area  that examines the features of  language  structure from the  point  of  view  of  their  effectual contents,  that is,  the expression of feelings by users of language and the influence of language on feelings and emotions. On the other hand, Wales (2011) regards stylistics as akin to literary and practical criticism. In addition,  it  investigates literary texts.  Furthermore,  Widdowson  (1975)  is  the  first  writer  to consider stylistics as interdisciplinary between linguistics and literary criticism, indicating that learners either start with language or literature before moving through the medium of stylistics.

Stylistics, as  a  new  trend,  shares the  viewpoint  of  language-based scrutiny of  literary materials. In  this respect, Leech believed (1969), "Literature cannot be  examined in any depth apart from the language" (p. 1). Recently, stylistics has been defined as a way in which meaning is created through language in literature and other types of text. Stylists may use models, theories, and frameworks from linguistics as analytical tools to describe and explain how and why a text functions as it does and how we derive meaning from its words (Nørgaard et al., 2010).

The definitions of stylistics then focused on observing objectivity; for example, Turner (1973) defines stylistics as a method of studying the style with consideration of the form of the word, namely, a scientific or at least a methodological study. Accordingly, as mentioned earlier, the formalistic view of studying literary works investigates the formal properties of literary texts, such  as  the  existence of  repetition, rhythm,  parallelism, and  examples of  deviation  from the accepted linguistic norm. In this context, Chapman (1973) indicated that "the linguistic study of different styles is  called stylistics" (p.  11).  On  the other  hand,  Leech  (1969) highlighted that metaphors, antithesis, irony, rhythm, figurative vocabularies, and other basic vocabularies cannot be explained without resorting to notions of linguistics, and he (1969) furthermore depicts it "as a meeting ground of linguistic and literary study, stylistics being the field within which these basic questions lie" (pp. 1-2 Thus, stylistics is an approach to analyzing (literary) texts through linguistic description, encompassing both literature and linguistics. As a result, stylistics can sometimes look like either linguistics or literary criticism, depending on a reader's position and perspective (Short, 1996).

Generally,  the  reader's  experience  and  knowledge,  combined  with  linguistic features, indicate significant advancements and developments in stylistics. However, stylists barely rely on intuitive responses when interpreting a text; they are concerned with the "patterning of language in texts" and make no presuppositions regarding artistic value. Investigating language in a text reveals those  linguistic patterns on  which  an  intuitive awareness  of  artistic values  ultimately depends (Widdowson, 1975). That is why stylistic analysis is employed to help intuitive responses, especially when the reader, at the initial phase, has some intuitive interpretations of a literary work and later, through the use of language, investigates to support those intuitive responses.

## A Framework of Stylistic Analysis


Stylistics employs its method of analysis from a  linguistic perspective. In  the analysis process,  the  stylists  describe  linguistic elements  and  interpret  the  text.  Therefore,  stylistics combines elements from both linguistics and literary criticism

To investigate what a text means, it is usually best, to begin with established, agreed-upon interpretations of the text; despite all the differences in readers' experiences, there is a remarkable amount of agreement among readers on the meaning of a specific text (Short, 1996). Hence, the stylistic approach to text analysis may seem more objective than other branches of literary criticism because  of  the  scientific nature  of  linguistics as  compared  to  other  fields  in  the  humanities (Nørgaard et al., 2010). Despite this, it is proven that stylistics can provide valuable tools and methods for analyzing how meaning is created in texts through linguistic means.

The method of analyzing a work of literature has led critics to consider whether to start with a linguistic description or an intuitive approach. According to Leech (1985) and Short (1996), interpretation is performed from both perspectives. Nonetheless, they argue that it is not important from which perspective to begin an interpretation but rather the significant aspect is to perform the interpretation systematically to serve descriptive and explanatory purposes.

Short  (1996)  introduces  three  levels  of  text  analysis:  Description, Interpretation,  and Evaluation.  In  this  respect,  he  (1996)  demonstrated,  "If interpretation  is  logically  before understanding, it is  also  the case  that  what  I  have  called description (which in  turn  includes analysis) is logically before understanding" (p. 4). This means that the researcher can formulate text  understanding  and  appreciation levels through  the  performance of  the  description level. Stylistics deals with the relation of linguistic description to interpretation in an explicit manner. The comprehension of the linguistic form and meaning is implicit, but the discussion of literature, as critics do, is as explicit as possible.

On the other hand, when examining a literary text, the language and the literary function must receive equal attention. They are interdependent. A prominent feature in the text that appeals to first impressions may be literary or linguistic. If this observation is literary, stylists will seek linguistic evidence; if it is merely linguistic, they will attempt to suggest its potential literary effect (Verdonk, 2013). In this regard, one should begin with the literary effects of a poem and then attempt to see how particular linguistic features contribute to and help account for these effects. Hence, Within the framework of stylistic analysis, foregrounding appears as a critical concept, spotlighting deviations from linguistic conventions to generate prominence and enrich meaning. By investigating how  these stylistic devices work,  the study obtains detailed insights into the writer's aesthetic choices and  the text's cumulative effect. Samandarov, Ortiqov, and  Achilov (2022) elucidated foregrounding as a literary device employed by the author to attract attention to a specific part of a text or a literary work. Authors use some of the various literary devices to make some parts of their texts more prominent than others.  Poetry inherently contains various linguistic structures, and the functions of these structures may differ from what  a linguist might expect (Culler, 1975, as cited in Verdonk, 2013)

## An Overview of Before I Knocked


Thomas described Before I Knocked as a Jesus poem  It was written in September 1933 . and first published in 18 poems . As observed by Tindall (1962), 'the speaker is an undifferentiated, vital  liquid  before  it  has assumed  shape  as  sperm  cell;  yet  this  blind  mouth  foresees. Foreknowledge of life and death and man's condition are the themes of the poem' (p. 36). In other words, the liquid mouth identifies itself with Him because Christ is all men in one sense. According to Thomas' suggestion, the speaker of the poem is a mix of himself, everyman, and Christ in the themes of suffering, immortality/mortality, and  destiny. Through the stanzas of the  poem, the speaker recalls his acute suffering before and after birth and how his human form came into being. The speaker starts with a description of his existence before being conceived.

The other stanzas of the poem show how Christ endured suffering before his birth. He was a moving spirit with no idea of the world, at least not specific knowledge. In the final lines, the tension between various shapes of Christ is brought forward, in  which the  mortal Christ asks Christians to remember him and pity his immortal self. He also knew the future. In the poem, there are some allusions to the crucifixion. The poem ends with a four-line stanza directing those who worship him (Thomas, 2014, as edited by Goodby)

According to  Emery (1962),  there are generally two  types of  writers who  write about Christ. The ones who believe in the simultaneity of His manhood and Godhood distinguish Him from all other human beings and all mythical deities. Besides, some consider him as a man. Those who write about Christ either want to strengthen their readers' belief in His divinity or overturn this belief. It  is unclear which  of these motives encouraged Thomas.  The  poem depicts Jesus developing physically in the same way  as  every other man. However,  the emphasis is not  on physical development but on foreknowledge or fore-experience of life's impending suffering.

The poem comprises eight stanzas of a dramatic monologue, each containing six lines, known as sestets, except for the final stanza, which has four lines, known as a quatrain. The pattern alternates between nine- and eight-syllable lines. Metrically, the eight-syllable lines have iambic regular lines with an  occasional trochaic substitution, while the nine-syllable lines with many substitutions have an iambic rhythm. ABABAB is a half-full rhyme poem written by Thomas. The final stanza of the poem has the rhyme scheme ABAB.

Nothing will be planted. Nothing will be growing. There will be no plants in sight. It will be as desolate as Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, cities the LORD  destroyed in  fierce anger. (Wilson & Taylor, 2015, pp. 208-209)

The  imagery enriches the poem  depicting how  the  speaker addresses the  movements and  the moments before his birth. Thomas begins his poem with kinaesthetic and auditory imagery, like in "Before I knocked" and "With liquid hands tapped on the womb." In the same line, an image describes the wetness of 'hands,' highlighting the preconception stage. In the first line of the first stanza, with  the  use  of  euphemistic language,  Thomas indirectly refers to  sexual activity. To explain the speaker's suffering, the poem comprises an epithet and gustatory imagery in "salt adventure". Additionally, in stanza five, the poem  includes images that describe the speaker's internal feelings of thirst and hunger. The poem ends with the image of being "double-crossed." In this context, Tindal (1962, p. 38) described:

To doublecross means to deceive or betray. God deceived Mary and denied her pleasure by  ghostly  begetting.  Any  father  deceives  any  mother  by  engendering  death.  Two crossings of the maternal gate, one in and one out, two  knockings at the gate, and the double  crucifixion  of  birth  and  death,  of  man  and  poet,  are  also  present  in  this condensation. (p. 38)

With Tindall's interpretation, the final stanza is seen as an image of birth, death, and the dual nature of existence. According to Tindall, the phrase "doublecrossed" encompasses both the act of deceiving and betraying someone. Within the stanza's framework, it is plausible to interpret that the reference implies that Mary, the maternal figure of Jesus, may have been misled or let down by the divine act of conception attributed to the Holy Spirit. Likewise, in reference to Emery (1962), Mary "was cheated by suffering the pain" of birth "without the antecedent pleasure" (p. 207).  This  pertains  to  the  extraordinary  conception  of  Jesus  facilitated  by  the  Holy  Spirit.
