As noted earlier, the specificity of the Framework also facilitates behaviour prioritisation processes (Kneebone et al., 2021), and assists researchers, policy-makers and practitioners in correctly identifying the particular barriers and enablers of specific behaviours, rather than general barriers for vague 'types' of behaviours. The ability to accurate diagnose barriers and enablers is a necessary precondition for selecting or developing effective behaviour change interventions (Curtis et al., 2021).

In terms of future research, this Framework provides two immediate opportunities to grow the field's understanding of User behaviour in a circular economy. Firstly, the comprehensive set of behaviours contained in the framework can be integrated into behavioural surveys and observation, and used as a starting point for measuring current adoption levels of User circular behaviours, in order to understand the extent of the transition still required. Secondly, the framework can be used to accumulate and organise evidence of barriers and enablers of these behaviours, and the interventions that work to change them.

There are also opportunities to expand the coverage of the Framework. We note, for example, that our specification of the actor as a user of material products has constrained our focus to some extent. The focus on materials means this Framework currently excludes behaviours that seek to minimise use, and maximise value, of other resource inputs such as biological materials, water, energy and fuel. Our emphasis on 'User', even though extended to use of product and product services, obscures other types of behaviours unrelated to products, such as any 'civic' behaviours that may be required of 'citizens' in a circular economy. We note these additional types of behaviours as key avenues for future research and potential expansion / extrapolation of the current Framework.

## Strong interdependencies up- and downstream

Analysis of the inter-relationships between Users and up- and downstream actors revealed strong interdependencies in achieving the circular benefits of particular behaviours. While literature has noted the importance of supply and demand side changes in transitioning to a circular economy (see introduction), the discussion so far has remained relatively general. The Framework provides a level of granularity and clarity to these relationships that was previous lacking. In addition to highlighting when user behaviour can be enabled by up- or downstream activities, it also emphasises that User behaviour is critical to the success of many up- and downstream circular endeavour. These interdependencies are, however, preliminary, in that they did not receive the same level of scrutiny as the set of User behaviours. A key avenue for future research is therefore to validate and refine the connections presented here.

This explicit mapping of interdependencies is a novel and valuable contribution to existing knowledge of the circular economy, and can inform both future research and practice. By applying the Framework to specific business models, products or material streams, actors in research, policy and practice can trace the thread of behaviours and their dependencies through the circular economy in a much more lucid, and comparable way than before. For instance, researchers and implementers of emerging circular business models could use the Framework as a starting point for understanding the User behaviours they will need to achieve in order for their particular model to be successful and realise circular benefits. In addition, the Framework can be used to counter tendencies towards 'technological optimism' by supporting the critical evaluation of claims about likelihood of user uptake and acceptance of new business models or circular 'solutions. It does this through enabling measurement of current adoption levels and experienced barriers and facilitators of adoption, for example. At the same time, the Framework can also be used to prompt the identification of opportunities to improve existing offerings or develop new solutions that enable User circular behaviour.

Future research could also realise the interdisciplinary 'boundary object' potential of the Framework in a wide range of ways. One example is by utilising the User behaviour linkages as a departing point to increase connections between research focusing on consumers, and research focusing on producers/businesses. Importantly, understanding the interrelationships also supports 'sustainability policy as if people mattered' (Baum & Gross, 2017) - tracking the interdependencies and shared responsibilities and connections between powerful actors and publics. It should also be noted that the exercise to identify these relationships was preliminary in nature, and no similar, previous analysis could be identified to triangulate or validate the results. We therefore propose these outputs as a first iteration of a model of inter-relationships, and both hope for and look forward to future discussion about, contributions to, and iterations of this analysis by the field.

## Broader implications

## Language matters, and clarity is more important than consistency

As noted earlier different groups of stakeholders in different fields, positions and traditions use different language. The Australian stakeholders engaged in this process were no exception. A key finding from our research was that different understandings of language leads to confusion when stakeholders are not aware that others may use language differently. Overturning assumptions of the universality of terms, and recognising that the same words can hold different meanings for different people is a critical step in transdisciplinary collaboration. Once this understanding was reached amongst our stakeholders, it was interesting to note that clarity became prioritised, rather than consistency. The ensuring dialogue suggested that because language choices are driven by many factors including disciplinary background, intended audience and other needs, it is unrealistic to expect adoption of a single, consistent terminology for use in all spheres, particularly in the short-to-medium term.

In light of this, we acknowledge that there is likely language in this Framework that diverges or conflicts with language already in use in various academic fields. In addition, there are almost certainly new labels and terms that have not heretofore been commonly adopted in academic research. It is not our intention per se for the language in this framework to be adopted by all stakeholders, though we hope it may go some way to building a foundation for consistency. Instead, it is our aspiration for this and future iterations of the Framework to act as 'Rosetta stone' (Díaz et al., 2015) to enable those that currently use different terms, or use the same terms differently, to locate their concepts within the Framework in order to communicate with others with clarity.

## 'Circular' behaviours do not always support a circular economy

A key difference between this Framework and previous attempts is the explicit incorporation of the circular functions or outcomes of the included behaviours. Such an approach is valuable because many of these behaviours do not intrinsically contribute to achieving circular principles. In some cases, from a perspective of 'net circularity', these behaviours can actually engender negative environmental impacts (Camacho-Otero et al., 2020; Garcia et al., 2021; Maitre-Ekern & Dalhammar, 2019). For example, buying secondhand kitchen appliances reduces resource use if it displaces the purchase of new kitchen appliances. If, however, the behaviour is simply used to amass excess appliances, it is not promoting resource efficiency, but rather accumulation (Downes & Hatty, 2022). Similarly, donating unwanted clothing can extend the current life of clothing, but when it is undertaken to free up wardrobe space for new purchases, it can actually contribute to the damaging 'fast fashion' phenomenon (Williams, 2020). Camacho-Otero et al. (2020) describe this as the need for behaviours to have a 'sufficiency effect' in order to realise circular benefits. Including the circular function of each specified behaviour in the framework ensures that it is clear when, and how, the included behaviours can be considered circular.

Furthermore, the implied hierarchy of behaviours across the sequenced phases is useful for understanding whether certain behaviours are more or less 'circular' relative to others. However more work is needed to substantiate the proposed hierarchy and to illuminate under what conditions the circular benefits of the behaviours are realised. Locating behaviours in sequential, life cycle phases can similarly enable multi-criteria impact analysis which enables consideration of issues of 'additionality', spillover and moral budgeting.  In this way, the Framework also facilitates linking the 'social' and the 'technical' systems of circular economy through the lens of behaviour (Kaufman et al., 2021; Markard et al., 2020). A key future contribution would be rigorously analysing the 'material footprint' (Wiedmann et al., 2015) potential of different behaviours across the lifecycle, to provide more robust inputs to prioritisation exercises guiding development of interventions.

## Some circular behaviours are not part of the formal 'economy'

An interesting finding from the comparative analysis of the Framework against existing studies what that the three behaviours incorporated in our framework that were not covered by the existing seven models were all 'informal' behaviours; that is, they are not part of any systems of production or exchange that are central to the 'economy'.

We have made the point consistently that the terms we choose can constrain our thinking, and the choice of the term 'circular economy' is no different: the 'economy' aspect of circular economy may be limiting understandings of the behaviours and roles required (Hobson, 2021), just as our choice of the term 'user' did. Others have previously explored the distinction between 'circular economy' and 'circular society', and the impact the different terms / conceptions / discourses can have (Friant et al., 2020; Melles, 2021). We note that broadening the overarching framing concept to be more inclusive is likely to advance the value of this Framework even further.


## 5. Conclusion


Previous literature has clearly identified the need to more deeply consider the role of the consumer/user in a circular economy. An analysis of existing consumer-user research revealed that current effort is being undertaken without a clear and comprehensive understanding of the specific behaviours that will be required or desired of users in a circular economy.

A transdisciplinary, iterative process was undertaken with over 100 circular economy experts from across Australia's public, private, civil and research sectors to develop a comprehensive Framework of User Circular Behaviour. The Framework sets out 59 distinct user circular behaviours, clearly defined, and categorised according to circular function and user purpose. A comparison of the Framework against existing models of user behaviours reveals a new level of both breadth and depth now available to the field. Furthermore, the Framework provides a starting point for understanding the relationships between User behaviour and that of other actors, particularly the inter-dependency with up- and downstream activity. This analysis is critical to understanding the full range of behaviours needed across the value chain in order to successfully realise a transition to the circular economy. We recommend wide adoption of this framework in research and policy as a key advance in better integrating users, and the diverse actors enabling and constraining their options, as key actors in the transition to a circular economy. This includes further development, and we have set out some important avenues for refining and expanding the Framework.

## 1. Introduction


Why are adolescents drawn to certain occupations is a question that continuously attracts researchers and practitioners alike. It is of high importance because it not only addresses the reproduction  processes  of  social  inequality  but  the  chances  of  adolescents  to  aspire  an occupation  that  fits  their  vocational  interests.  Research  has  shown  that  a  successful  fit between vocational interests and matching occupations has a tremendous impact on people's lives. It increases  their  productivity,  job-satisfaction,  well-being,  job-performance,  and decreases their job turnover (Hoff, Perlus, & Rounds, 2019; Hoff, Song, Wee, Phane & Rounds, 2020;  Assouline  &  Meir  1987).  However,  even  if  such  a  fit  is  of  high  importance  for adolescents' future careers, not all will be able to achieve such a fit. The reason for this lies not alone in labor-market barriers but in the adolescents' vocational interests that are linked to occupations that do not match their gender or social class.

Gottfredson's (1981) theory on the circumscription of occupational aspirations, is based on the assumption that adolescents aspire to occupations that fit their self-concept. Her main argument is that adolescents' self-concepts circumscribe the available occupational choices and that  their  self-concept  is  based  on  their  gender,  social  class,  and  vocational  interests (Gottfredson,  1981).  I  follow  her  argument  that  depending  on  the  combination  of  the adolescents'  gender,  class,  and  vocational  interests,  there  might  be  situations  where  no occupation exists that simultaneously conforms to all three characteristics of the adolescents' self-concept. In these cases, the oldest element of the adolescents' self-concept will prevail (gender) whereas the youngest element will be abandoned (vocational interests).

Using data from the German Microcensus this study provides information about the gender composition, social class (socio-economic status and educational composition) of almost all

occupations in Germany. Exploiting the rich data of the German Microcensus I also identify the  primary  RIASEC  codes  for  each  occupation  even  though  the  German  Dictionary  of Occupational Titles (Kldb2010) does not directly provide any information on the RIASEC codes. The  primary  RIASEC  codes  are  based  on  Holland  (1997)  who  differentiated  six  primary vocational interests and six corresponding occupational environments ( ealistic,  nvestigative, r i a rtistic, s ocial, e nterprising, and c onventional) to identify people's vocational interests and to identify  fitting  occupations. 3 This  allows  me  to  investigate  Gottfredson's  (1981)  claim  that some vocational interests provide adolescents with a selection of occupations too limited to find a match with their self-concept. In combination with data from a study of adolescents in upper  secondary  schools  in  Germany  (ZuBAb),  I  determine  the  odds  of  a  fit  between adolescents' primary vocational interests and the occupations they aspire to with regard to the mismatch between their self-concept (gender, social class, and vocational interests) and the occupations gender and social class that are linked to their vocational interests. 4  I focus on adolescents who were still rather distanced from the realities of the labor market and who have  yet  to  be  confronted  with  the  need  to  compromise.  The  adolescents  were  also  old enough  to  have  progressed  through  all  developmental  stages  theorized  by  Gottfredson (1981).  This  allows  me  to  test  the  potential  impact  of  circumscription  processes  on  the adolescents' fit between their vocational interests and their occupational aspirations.

Using a series of logistic regressions, my analyses provide evidence that female adolescents with realistic and investigative interests do rarely aspire to occupations that fit their vocational interests,  because  realistic  and  investigative  occupations  are  male  dominated  and  hence,

incompatible  with  their  self-concept.  Social  class  is  often  maintained  through  academic education.  However,  my  analyses  provide  evidence  that  realistic  interests  are  linked  to occupations for which no tertiary degrees are provided in Germany. Hence, adolescents with realistic interests who also aspired to academic education forgo their vocational interests to follow their aspirations to higher education instead.

## 2. Key  theories addressing adolescents' vocational interests and  their fit with occupational aspirations

Matching occupational aspirations with the adolescents' vocational interests is all about trying to push square pegs into square holes and round pegs into round holes. Hollands (1997) theory on vocational interests and occupational environments states that people will thrive if they are  put  into  or  get  access  to  the  right  occupations  that  fit  their  vocational  interests  best. However, adolescents face barriers when they attempt to realize occupational aspirations that match their vocational interests. Theories like the career development theory (Super, 1990; Savickas, 1997), social cognitive career theory (Lent, Brown, & Hackett, 1994), the theory of circumscription and compromise (Gottfredson, 1981, 2002) or the living systems framework (Ford, 1987; Vondracek & Porfeli, 2008) saw the development of occupational aspirations as a dynamic  process  in  which  aspirations  are  adjusted  in  line  with  opportunities  and environmental limitations (Super, 1990; Nurmi, 2004). I will focus on Gottfredson's (1981) theory of circumscription and compromise, because she developed a theory that explains why some adolescents' do not aspire to occupations that fit their vocational interests before they even  meet  the  realities  of  the  labor  market.  Circumscription  processes,  which  will  be described in the next section, do not leave all adolescents with occupational alternatives that match their self-concept, because their vocational interests only match with occupations that are incompatible with the adolescents' gender or social class.


## 2.1. Gottfredson's theory on circumscription


Gottfredson's  (1981)  theory  assumed  that  occupational  choices  develop  through  various stages  in  which  children  and  adolescents  become  aware  of  themselves  and  aspire  to occupations that fit their self-concept. She distinguished between four main stages, in which the  self-concept  of  children  and  adolescents  develops  and  occupational  aspirations  are accordingly  circumscribed:  First,  fantasy  occupations  (fairies,  knights,  etc.)  are  rejected. Second,  they  become  aware  of  their  gender  and  gender  (in-)appropriate  occupations. Research  on  gender  status  believes  and  gender  stereotypes  support  Gottfredson  (1981), because gendered norms, social roles, and gendered socialization processes foster individual self-selection processes that result in the rejection of most gender non-conform occupations (Ridgeway 2009; Bian et al. 2017; Marini and Brinton, 1993; Buchmann and Kriesi 2012; Correl 2001; Eagly et al. 2000; Sinclair et al. 2019). Third, they become aware of their position in society,  and  the  existence  of  social  classes  and  occupations  that  correspond  with  them. Gottfredson (1981) assumed that social class should impact occupational aspirations, because social class corresponds with access to resources that adolescents will expect from their future occupations  too.  Hence,  adolescents  exclude  occupations  that  will  not  provide  the  classequivalent level of prestige, income or social standing. 5 Fourth, they explore their vocational interests  and  corresponding  occupations.  Vocational  interests  are  based  on  a  theory  by Holland  (1997),  which  captures  personalities  through  vocational  interests  that  match  the characteristics  and  affordances  of  specific  occupations  (Holland  and  Gottfredson  1976). Holland (1997) categorizes vocational interests and occupations as one of six types: realistic (R), investigative (I), artistic (A), social (S), enterprising (E), and conventional (C). Each person's

personality can be derived from rank-ordering the six types. The first three letters are usually referred to as the Holland code and the first letter is considered a person's or occupation's primary type (Holland, 1997). Holland also assumed that interests have varying degrees of similarity.  Using  a  hexagonal  model,  it  is  possible  to  identify  related  interests  as  well  as opposing interests. Based on this hexagonal interest-model by Holland (1997), Gottfredson (1981) assumed that individuals will exclude occupations that are dissimilar to their vocational interests. For example, if adolescents have artistic interests, they will eliminate occupations that are part of the conventional environment, because conventional environments require conformity whereas artistic interests are rooted in the opposite: creativity.

Gottfredson  (1981,  p.  556)  assumed  that  once  rejected,  an  occupation  will  not  be reconsidered,  except  in  unusual  circumstances  (e.g.  when  the  person  receives  intensive vocational counseling). The only occupations left as acceptable occupational alternatives are those  that  fit  the  adolescents  developing  self-concept.  When  asked  about  occupations adolescents aspire to, they will hence pick one occupation from the circumscribed selection of acceptable occupational alternatives.

Adolescents are aware that not all acceptable occupational alternatives are accessible to them. The accessibility of specific occupations might be restricted due to regional availability, assumed discrimination, and the necessary knowledge, training, and effort required to enter the occupation of interest (Hesketh, Durant, & Pryor,1990; Malin, & Jacob, 2019). Hence, the necessity of compromises arises. However, the compromised choices build on already preselected or circumscribed occupational alternatives and up to date we know very little about (the relevance of) circumscription.

A fit between adolescents' vocational interests and occupational aspirations might be unachievable not so much because of the harsh reality of the labor market (compromise) but

because no occupational alternatives exist that fit the adolescents' self-concept (circumscription). There might be situations where no occupation exists that simultaneously conforms to all three characteristics of the adolescents' self-concept (gender, class, and vocational interest). In these cases, the oldest and most established element of the adolescents' self-concept will prevail (gender) whereas the youngest and least established element should be abandoned (vocational interests) (Gottfredson 1981). An example: young adolescent women with realistic vocational interests can choose from a selection of realistic occupations, but realistic occupations are usually craft occupations, which are dominated by men. In theory, gender incompatible occupations should be eliminated from their range of acceptable occupational alternatives, leaving them with few or no alternatives that fit both, their gender and vocational interest.

H1: Adolescents should have low odds of aspiring to an occupation that has characteristics fitting  their  vocational interests (interest-aspiration fit) if their vocational interests provide them with a selection of occupations that are dominated by the opposing gender.

The same should apply for social class: Adolescents will most likely adopt the standards of success of their social class and might have a problem if their vocational interest are associated with occupations that do not match with their social class (e.g., Johnson 1995). However, occupational  aspirations  have  no  class-specific  upper  boundary  (Rodman  and  Voydanoff 1978).  Social  class  only  defines  lower  boundaries  of  occupational  choices  that  would  be considered to be not acceptable (Gottfredson 1981).

H2a:  Adolescents  should  have  low  odds  of  achieving  an  interest-aspiration  fit  if  their vocational interests are associated with occupations that are lower in social status than their social class.

Adolescents might be required to pursue academic credentials to reach the level of prestige, income or social standing that correspond with their social class. This link between education, occupations, and social class is generally recognized by the adolescents (Gottfredson 1981, p. 562; Blossfeld 2020). Hence, to maintain or improve once social class adolescents not only have to aspire to occupations that fit their (future) social class but they also have to aspire to academic education.

H2b: Adolescents who aspire to academic education should have low odds of achieving an interest-aspiration fit if their vocational interests are associated with occupations for which no academic education tracks exist.  6

If  adolescents'  vocational  interests  are  associated  with  occupations  that  match  with  their gender  and  social  class/educational  aspirations,  no  substantive  circumscription  processes should occur.

H3:  There should be no association between adolescents' gender or social class or educational aspirations and their interest-aspiration fit if their self-concept theoretically allows for a wide range of fitting occupational alternatives.


## 3. Method



## 3.1. Samples


Data were drawn from the 'Future and Career Plans before High School Graduation (ZuBAb)' study,  which  was  jointly  conducted  by  the  University  of  Cologne  and  by  the  Berlin  Social Science  Center  (WZB)  (Pietrzyk  et  al.,  2019,  Erdmann  et  al.,  2021).  The  study  selectively

targeted 42 academic-track secondary schools in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia that  were  predominantly  based  in  socioeconomically  disadvantaged  school  districts.  The paper and pencil classroom survey was conducted in February 2018 under the supervision of the Institute for Applied Social Sciences (Infas). Students in the sample were one and a half years away  from  graduating  with  the Abitur (comparable  to  qualifications like the baccalaureate or A-levels). The original sample consists of N = 1766 adolescents (57% female, mean age M = 17.81 years, SD = 0.83). In this study, I only included adolescents who provided complete  and  detailed  information  about  their  occupational  aspirations  and  parental occupations ( N = 972, 57% female, mean age M = 17.79 years, SD = 0.79).

Additional data were drawn from the German Microcensus for the year 2015, which provided information about occupations in Germany based on 292,190 employees between 20 and 60 years.  The  German  Microcensus  is  an  obligatory  one  per  cent  population  sample  of  the German  residential  population  using  a  single-stage  stratified  cluster  sampling  method.  I capitalized on the full one per cent population sample, which is available only through the Research Data Center of the Federal Statistical Office of Germany and the Statistical Offices of the German States. Table A2 in the supplementary material provides a detailed overview over the sample demographics of the adolescents and the occupations.


## 3.2. Measures



## 3.2.1. Vocational interests


To assess the adolescents' vocational interests, I used a derivation of the Revised General Interest Structure Test (GIST; Allgemeiner Interessen Strukturtest; Bergmann, & Eder, 2005). Using the GIST, Nagy et al. (2010) have shown that college-bound adolescents in Germany tend to structure their vocational interest profiles according to Holland's hexagonal RIASEC

model. The GIST is the standard instrument used in German-speaking countries and consists of a list of 60 items (for information on validity and reliability see Jörin, Stoll, Bergmann, & Eder, 2004). Following the German National Education Panel Study (NEPS), a shortened 18item version of the GIST for the high-school student sample was used (see Pietrzyk et al., 2019: Appendix: Scales Manual). Each item represents an occupational activity. Adolescents were asked to rate how interested they were on a 5-point Likert-scale ranging from 'not at all' to 'very much'. To confirm that the subscales of the shortened GIST conformed to the RIASEC model  I  used  an  exploratory  maximum  likelihood  factor  analysis  on  the  item  level.  The screeplot supports a six-factor solution, with all six factors being in line with the RIASEC model (see A3 in the supplementary material). The internal consistency was good for the realistic ( α =  0.74),  investigative  ( α =  0.73),  artistic  ( α =  0.68),  and  social  ( α =  0.78)  items  and  was acceptable for the enterprising ( α = 0.58), and conventional ( α = 0.59) items. The adolescents' item responses were averaged for each interest-domain.  7


## 3.2.2. Occupational aspirations


I  defined  occupational  aspirations  as  individuals'  goals  regarding  accessible  occupational future roles and activities. These aspirations were measured through the question 'Based on everything you currently know, what profession will you most likely have later on?', which required  the  adolescents  to  name  a  single  occupation.  The  open-ended  answer  to  the question was coded by Infas into the five-digit code of the German Dictionary of Occupational Titles  (KldB  2010,  5  digits;  Bundesagentur  für  Arbeit,  2011). 8 The  adolescents  named  168 distinct occupations they aspire to (15% of the adolescents did not answer the question and

4% of the adolescents gave to general an answer that could not be coded). The three most frequent  occupations  were  secondary  school  teachers  (8.4%),  law  enforcement  officers (4.8%), and physicians (specialization not specified; 3.8%).


## 3.2.3. The RIASEC codes for occupations in Germany


Unfortunately,  the  German  Dictionary  of  Occupational  Titles  (Kldb2010)  does  not  provide information on the RIASEC codes for its 1,286 occupational categories. However, there is a way to approximately identify the primary RIASEC codes for each occupation in Germany. To do so, I followed Holland's (1997) assertion that work environments can be commensurably described on the basis of the types of work-activities people typically do (see also: Spokane, & Cruza-Guet, 2005). I used the responses of the occupational incumbents to the question 'Which task do you primarily do in your job?' in the German Microcensus. Respondents had to  choose  one  category  of tasks  out  of  a  list  of  20  task  categories.  One  category  was,  for example, 'setting up, controlling, monitoring and maintaining machines, technical systems or devices'.  Another  category  included  'counseling,  advising,  informing'. Following  Holland's (1997)  description  of  each  RIASEC  domain,  I  assigned  each  task  category  to  one  RIASEC domain. For example: I assigned the  task  'advertising,  marketing,  public  relations'  to  the domain 'Enterprising' and the task 'educating, training, teaching' to the domain 'Social' (a documentation of all pairings between the main tasks performed in the occupations and the interest codes can be found in the supplementary material A1 and the RIASEC codes that I matched to the 5-digit codes of KldB2010 are available in Stuth (forthcoming). 9  I aggregated

the resulting individual-level information on the RIASEC-domains for each occupation (5-digit codes  of  the  KldB2010).  The  resulting  occupational-level  data  allowed  me  to  identify  the primary RIASEC domain for each occupation. In the majority of occupations, most incumbents identified the same main task they primarily do. The result is that there is very little main-task variation within the occupations (investigative occupations were the exception). Hence, it was not possible to identify the second-letter code or even the third-letter (Holland) code using this approach.

The  Research  Data  Center  of  the  Federal  Statistical  Office  of  Germany  and  the  Statistical Offices of the German States require that analyses with the Microcensus on the occupational level should only be done if the occupations contain at least 50 incumbents to ensure a low sampling error. Hence, only occupations with at least 50 or more incumbents were used to identify the first-letter RIASEC code (and other occupational characteristics). However, the loss of information was very small in comparison to the (potential) gain in data quality: Of the original Microcensus sample of 292,190 occupational incumbents, 96.38% incumbents (N = 281,632) from 554 occupations remained available for analysis (35% realistic occupations, 9%

investigative occupations, 3% artistic occupations, 23% social occupations, 14% enterprising occupations, and 16% conventional occupations).


## 3.2.4. The interest-aspiration fit


I matched the Microcensus-based first-letter interest codes to the occupations the students aspire  to  using  the  German  Dictionary  of  Occupational  Titles  (Kldb2010,  5digits).  The adolescents  aspired  to  168  unique  occupations. The  matching  between  the  Microcensus sample and the adolescent sample was successful for 93.1% of the adolescents with valid values  in  their  occupational-aspiration  variable.  The  dependent  variable  -  the  interestaspiration fit - was based on the exact match of the adolescents' first letter code of their vocational interests with the first letter code of the occupation they aspired to. The interestaspiration fit was coded one if a match was present (63 % of the adolescents) and was coded zero otherwise.


## 3.2.5. Adolescents' gender and social class


The gender of the adolescents is self-reported ( N = 972, 0 = men, 43%, 1 = women, 57%). I captured the adolescents' social class using two different approaches: First, their actual social class  is captured  by  the  international  socioeconomic  status  of  their  parents  (ISEI-08; Ganzeboom, De Graaf, & Treiman, 1992), which is derived from the parental occupations.  10 If  both parents worked, the highest status-score was used. Second, the maintenance of or aspiration  to  a  higher  social  class  is  captured  by  educational  aspiration.  I  captured  the educational aspirations the adolescents realistically aspire to using two questions: 1) What do you think: how likely are you to actually study in a university? 2) What do you think: how likely

is it that  you  will  actually  pursue  vocational  education  and  training?  The  respondents answered on a five-point scale (1 = very unlikely to 5 = very likely). These questions were based on  corresponding  instruments  in  the  Berliner-Studienberichtigten-Panel  (Best-Up),  NEPS (SC4), and BiKS 8-14 and refer to goals that respondents think they actually can achieve (Kurz, & Paulus, 2008, p. 5491; Stocké 2013, p. 269). I changed the scale for the vocational education and training item by multiplying it by minus one and summed up both variables ( N = 972, M = 1.4, SD =  2.4).  Positive  values  indicate  that  the  adolescents  aspired  to  tertiary  education. Values around zero indicate that the adolescents were undecided, because they gave similar ratings to both questions. Negative values indicated that the adolescents aspired to vocational education and training.

## 3.2.6. Controls

Occupational  aspirations  depend  on  adolescents'  school  achievement  (Furlong,  &  Biggart, 1999; Gottfredson, 1981, p. 558; Rojewski, & Kim, 2003; Shapka, Domene, & Keating, 2006). Therefore, I controlled for the school achievements of adolescents' using the average of their grades in math, German, biology, chemistry, physics, English, social science, and history. The average was based on grade points, which theoretically can range between 1 (failed to pass) and 15 (top student) ( M = 9.5, SD = 2).

Adolescents' vocational interests can vary in strength. Adolescents with low interests-levels might not have (yet) established a clear picture of their goals, interests, and talents (Holland, 1997, p. 5). Their information on their vocational interests and their occupational aspirations might thereby not be reliable. To control for differences in the level of adolescents' vocational interests,  I  measured  the  adolescents'  average  of  the  three  items  that  belonged  to  their primary first-letter interest domain ( M = 4.01, SD = 0.68). Such a measure is called interest

elevation and is associated with positive personality characteristics like openness, extraversion,  and  career  exploration  whereas  lower  elevations  are  associated  with  the opposite  (Fuller,  Holland,  and  Johnston  1999;  Tracey  et  al.,  2006;  Hirsche  &  Läge,  2007; Hirschi, 2009; Jaensch, Hirschi, and Spurk 2016).

Experiences of discrimination in the community of adolescents with migration background might  result  in  the  exclusion  of  occupations  from  the  range  of  acceptable  occupational alternatives  to  avoid  negative  (career)  experiences  in  their  later  working  life.  Additionally, Hirschi and Vondracek (2009) have pointed out that migrants might come from cultures where the correspondence between vocational interests and occupational aspirations was not as highly valued as in Germany. Both could result in an increased risk of an interest-aspiration mismatch. Hence, I controlled for the migration background of the adolescents using a dummy variable: Migration background was coded as one if the adolescents were not born in Germany or if at least one parent was born outside Germany (26.85% with migration background).


## 3.3. Analytical strategy


I used descriptive analyses, to identify primary vocational interests for which only few or no occupations  exist  that  simultaneously  conform  to  the  other  two  characteristics  of  the adolescents' self-concept (gender and social class). I tested whether the descriptive findings can help to explain the adolescents' success/failure to achieve an interest-aspiration fit, by calculating separate logistic regressions for each primary vocational interest. A good model fit and statistically significant independent variables should only be found for adolescents with primary vocational interests that theoretically should hinder their achievement of an interestaspiration fit, as identified in the descriptive analyses.

The  gender  model  (M1)  included  the  control  variables  and  the  independent  variable  of gender. Gender had a strong impact on the interest-aspiration fit of adolescents with realistic or investigative interests. Female adolescents had very low odds of achieving the fit compared to male adolescents ( OR realistic = .17, p realistic = .02; OR investigative = .27, p investigative = .004). These results lend support to hypothesis H1. Adolescents have low odds of an interest-aspiration fit if their vocational interests provide them only with a skewed selection of occupations that are dominated by the opposing gender. According to H3, similar associations between vocational interests and gender should not be noticeable for adolescents with social, enterprising, or conventional  interests, because  the  corresponding  occupations  provided  occupational alternatives for almost all gender-interests combinations. 11 The results in table 1 corroborated H3:  For  adolescents  with  social,  enterprising,  or  conventional  interests,  gender  had  no statistically significant impact on their interest-aspiration fit.

The social class (status) model (M2) included the controls and the parental ISEI-08 score. To ensure easily interpretable results, I centered the parental ISEI-08 score using the mean ISEI08 score of the occupational group that corresponded with the vocational interests of the adolescents. 12 Statistically significant and substantial effects of the parental ISEI-08 score were only found for adolescents with realistic interests ( OR realistic = .96, p realistic = .02): The higher the parents' ISEI-08 score the less likely the adolescents were to have an interest-aspiration fit.

These results lend support to hypothesis H2a: Realistic interests were associated with low status occupations and thereby decreased the odds of adolescents to achieve an interest-

aspiration  fit  if  their  parents'  social  status  was  higher.  Social  class  did  not  matter  for adolescents  with  other  vocational  interests.  This  is  in  line  with  H3,  because  the  other vocational  interests were  linked to  occupations with  a  broad  variety  of social  status  or  to occupations with very high status (investigative occupations).

The second model on social class (M3) included the controls and the aspiration to higher education  variable.  I  found  a  statistically  significant  and  substantial  negative  effect  of aspirations to enter higher education for adolescents with realistic and conventional interests ( OR realistic = .67, p realistic = .01; OR conventionalc = .67, p conventional = .000). The more adolescents with realistic or conventional interests aspired to enter tertiary education, the lower their odds of achieving an interest-aspiration fit were. In support of H2b, I found a strong and negative impact of aspirations to academic education on the interest-aspiration fit for adolescents with realistic interests, because the group of realistic occupations was incompatible with academic educational  aspirations.  It  was  a  rather  unexpected  finding  that  aspirations  to  academic education also had a negative impact on adolescents with conventional interests. Figure 2 provided  no  evidence  that  the  conventional  group  of  occupations  was  incompatible  with higher educational aspirations in a manner comparable to the realistic group of occupations.

The full model (M4) combines the control variables with all three independent variables at the same time. The impact of all three independent variables together remained substantially unchanged in comparison to the models M1-M3.


## 6. Discussion


The present study reports findings on the impact of circumscription processes on adolescents' interest-aspiration  fit  in  Germany.  I  focused  on  the  interest-aspiration  fit,  because  it  is important for adolescents' future well-being, job satisfaction, productivity, performance, and

thereby their career prospects. Based on Gottfredson's (1981) theory on circumscription, I provide new insights into conditions that prevent adolescents from achieving this fit.

Gottfredson's  (1981)  assumed  that  circumscription  processes  result  in  the  successive elimination of occupational alternatives based first on gender, second on social class, and third on vocational interests (e.g., Henderson, Hesketh, & Tuffin, 1988). The descriptive analyses provided the important finding that not all of the six RIASEC groups of occupations can provide adolescents with acceptable occupational alternatives that fit their interests and their gender and their social class. Realistic occupations in Germany are low in social class and heavily male dominated, whereas investigative occupations are male dominated too. Another important finding  is  that  gender  and  social  class  supersede  vocational  interests  and  confirm  the circumscription component of Gottfredson's (1981) theory of circumscription and compromise.

Circumscription  processes  will  result  in  gender-class-interest  combinations  for  female adolescents with realistic and investigative interests that will make an interest-aspiration fit highly improbable. Male dominated occupations were eliminated from female adolescents' selection of acceptable occupational alternatives. In the absence of occupations that are both realistic  or  investigative and gender-integrated or female, the adolescents had a very high probability to give up their realistic or investigative vocational interests and aspired to nonrealistic or non-investigative occupations instead.

Similar findings applied to adolescents' social class: Circumscription processes seem to have eliminated lower-class occupations from adolescents' selection of acceptable occupational alternatives. In the absence of occupations that are both realistic and are of the same social class or higher, the adolescents showed a high likelihood to give up their realistic vocational

interests  and  aspired  to  non-realistic  occupations  instead.  The  comparison  of  the  two measures of social class shows that socio-economic status of the parents, albeit statistically significant,  has  not  as  strong  an  impact  on  the  adolescents'  interest-aspiration  fit  as  their educational aspiration. The gap between adolescents' realistic interests and their educational aspirations  cannot  be  bridged,  because  very  few  university  courses  in  Germany  grant credentials for realistic occupations.

The  other  three  groups  of  RIASEC-occupations  (social,  enterprising,  conventional)  cover almost  all possible  gender-class-interest  combinations  and  should  thereby  not  cause circumscription-related  'blind  spots'  in  adolescents'  selection  of  acceptable  occupational alternatives.  The  analyses  confirmed  that  the  adolescents'  interest-aspiration  fit  was  not statistically significant associated with their gender or social class. However, there was one exception:  Adolescents  with  conventional  interests.  For  reasons  that  yet  have  to  be established,  their  aspiration  to  academic  education  also  had  a  negative  impact  on  their interest-aspiration fit.

The confirmation of Gottfredson's (1981) theory might be seen as surprising in the light of older  but  adverse  findings  that  have  been  reported  by  Hesketh,  Elmslie  &  Kaldor  (1990). However, Hesketh et al. (1999) analyzed the compromise component of Gottfredson's (1981) theory.  Their  results  provided  evidence  for  a  modified  account  of  Gottfredson's  (1981) compromise theory: Vocational interests are more present and important for the adolescents than their gender notions from the childhood, because they were established last (Hesketh, et  al.  1990).  The  present  results  give  reason  to  question  the  authors'  conclusion  that previously circumscribed occupations will be automatically reconsidered because vocational interests  are  more  important  for  compromises  than  gender  notions.  Whether  there  is  a

connection  or  not  between  processes  of  circumscription  and  compromise  has  yet  to  be established by other studies.

## Asadora as Female Entertainment Genre and Hometown Nostalgia


Although the first two decades of asadora productions appealed to a demographic somewhat younger than the current core audience, the majority of these fictionalized and romanticized stories were still aimed at a middle-aged female audience, especially housewives (Nihei 2020: 10). In more recent years, however, NHK also devises them to provide a source of pride for residents of the towns and prefectures from which the main figures emerged. Those with scenes set in these areas provide a welcome chance for local governments to capitalize on furusatō (hometown) nostalgia-based tourism (Respati 2022: 3-6). In the case of the upcoming Kasagi drama, the settings are rural Kagawa, the vibrant theater districts of pre-war Osaka and the world of immediate post-war Tokyo's entertainment districts. These locations and the role of asadora in both popularizing and at times distorting Japan's entertainment history, are part of the exploration of Kasagi's life that follows. Her personal story here will provide both Japanese and non-Japanese viewers of the drama with the background needed to assess the drama's veracity and its ability to convey the extraordinarily complex cultural, social, and sexual upheaval that her twenty-five-year entertainment career embodied.

As Scherer has noted, many asadora heroines are based on actual historical personalities. The actual life stories of these women, however, were in many cases unknown outside of a few historians or enthusiasts before their actual broadcast (2019: 105). In some cases, their relative historical anonymity can be attributed to the fact that, like many of their generation, their extraordinary efforts and activities were conducted, behind the scenes, in line with societal expectation of deference to husbands and sons. In other cases, the reason for their obscurity parallels those of long-ignored or underrated western women working in the arts in the 1930s and 1940s, such as American actress Hedy Lamar, screenwriter Frances Marion and R&B musician Sister Rosetta. The achievements of these and several other neglected western women pioneers, have only very recently been reassessed by American historians and documentary filmmakers and to a considerable degree, asadora can be seen as Japan's own version of the ongoing process of reassessing the contribution of unrecognized but extraordinary women to history.

Among the women with some connection to the world of art, fashion, and entertainment during the early to mid-Shōwa years that have been brought from obscurity to national attention through an asadora are singer Satō Chiyako ( Ichibanboshi, 1977); Asakusa actress Sawamura Sadako ( Otei-chan 1978); screenwriter Oishi Shizuka ( Odori , 2000); actresses Nakanishi Yuriko ( Teruteru Kazoku , 2003) and Naniwa Chieko ( Ochoyan 2021); dressmaker-designer Koshino Ayako ( Carnation , 2011) and entertainment company owner Yoshimoto Sei ( Warotenka , 2017) (NHK Archives n.d; Niehei et al 2020: 151-58). The somewhat formulaic manner in which the lives of these early Shōwa entertainment pioneers were portrayed in their respective asadora s can safely be relied on as a predictor of the ways in which the screenwriter and director will attempt to balance the fact and fiction surrounding Kasagi Shizuko's difficult but compelling life story. Unlike the earlier figures however, none of whom have any significant number of followers or academic biographers, Kasagi's life has long attracted interest from journalists and Shōwa entertainment fans and bloggers. As such, it seems highly likely that the inevitable licenses taken by the fictionalized Boogie Woogie will invite considerable comment and controversy on issues related to the veracity and accuracy with which certain key events in her life are portrayed. For this

reason, as well as to consolidate existing scholarship in English, that a detailed narrative of her life based on a wide range of Japanese primary and secondary sources is presented below, followed by a discussion of how the events described might feature in the asadora .

## From Orphan to Dance Troupe Entertainer: Exploring the Complexities of Kasagi Shizuko's Early Life and Career


Unlike many asador a heroines, Kasagi Shizuko enjoys some level of name recognition outside of the baby boom generation. This is largely due to NHK's musical 'Waga Uta Boogie Woogie' (1987) about the artist, which has been produced several times, as well as cover versions of 'Tokyo Boogie Woogie' by contemporary singers (Chidorin Diary 2022). Kasagi is also regularly mentioned in popular articles about post-war Japan and has a number of social media fans. Despite this, relatively little serious writing has been done in either Japanese or English on Kasagi's overall contribution to Japanese popular culture. Among the three scholars whose English language work informs this contribution, only Hosokawa (2006) deals at any length with her prewar career. However, while his work provides a detailed analysis of her vocal prowess, especially her scat singing innovations; her energetic dancing, and her ability to transform Hattori Ryōichi's melodies to capture the swinging sound of 1930s African American jazz, it does not deal much with her personal life and the ways in which this shaped her career. This is true too of popular music and post-war film scholars Bourdaghs (2012), Shamoon (2014) and Nagahara (2017), all of whom not surprisingly focus on her immediate post-war role as a symbol of the aspirations of ordinary Japanese during the Occupation. Bourdaghs' essay on her live performance gives attention to her 'celebration of the deliverance of female sexuality from wartime state regulation' and mentions in passing, her popularity with post-war panpan sex workers (35) while Shamoon emphasizes her 'exotic, Westernized, sexualized body and her successful 'imitation of American musical forms (118) and Nagahara her unambiguously American sound (2017: 153). In contrast with western scholarship, Kasagi's career has been examined by Japanese scholars largely in terms

of the inspirational impact of her most popular songs and movies as well as her influence on the career of Misora Hibari (Shimada 2010; Wajima 2020). Surprisingly, few western or Japanese academics, however, have fully explored Sakoguchi Sanae's 2010 biography. The only detailed study of her personal life and the many tragedies that she endured as a symbol of Shōwa history and post-war recovery itself, this work is an important secondary source for the narrative presented below.

Born Kamei Shizuko in August 1914 in rural Kagawa, Shikoku, Kasagi was the illegitimate daughter of the seventeen-year-old heir to a landowning family. Her complex life began with her adoption by a friend of her teenage mother in Osaka, a decision that was apparently the result of her own mother's inability to produce breastmilk. In 1931, while attending a memorial service for family members in Kagawa, the seventeen-year-old Kasagi overheard a secret conversation that partially uncovered the story of her adoption. In a highly traumatic moment, she met her mother, who did not acknowledge their relationship (BizConsul 2022). This harrowing and formative experience seems certain to be at the center of Boogie Woogie , given that maximizing family breakup-related pathos and sentimentality is a recurring trope in asadora . Four years before this traumatic experience, the thirteen-year-old Kasagi, an accomplished dancer from a young age, suffered rejection from the Takarazuka Opera based on her diminutive body size. Undeterred and with support from her adoptive family, she found her way to the Dotonbori Shōchikuza Theater, the home of the Shōchiku gakugeki-bu seito yōsei-sho (later Osaka Shōchiku Shōjo Kagekidan or OSSK) the more downscale south Osakan rival to the north-based elite girls dancing and entertainment troupe. In August 1928, under the stage name Mikasa Shizuko the fourteen-year-old was given the chance to appear on stage with the newly formed Tokyo branch of the dance troupe, Shochiku Shōjo Kagekidan (SSK). Here she met and made friends with the then thirteen-year-old Mizunoe Takiko, a new SSK recruit who went on to become perhaps the single most well-known female entertainer of 1930s Japan, and someone to whom Kasagi is often compared in terms of her role as a popular culture icon (Sakoguchi 2010: 23-26).

Although relatively little is known about Kasagi's early 1930s career, the late 1920s shift of OSSK from a focus on traditional Japanese dance to mostly tap dance, swing jazz, and chanson revues with a strong Parisian influence, seems to have suited her evolving vocal style and on-stage performance persona. In 1933 she was ranked among the top ten stars of OSSK and participated in the troupe's popular 'Autumn Dance.' A year later she recorded and performed the first of many songs composed by Hattori Ryōichi, "Koi no tōgemichi' (Step of Love) at the newly opened Daigeki (Osaka Grand Theater). Honing her craft, alongside future otokoyaku and onnayaku tap dancing stars Akizuki Emiko (1917-2002) and Ashihara Chizuko (1919-2009), her big break came in April 1938 when she was selected along with these two OSSK stars to join the Shōchiku Gakugekidan (SGD) a new and well-funded experimental male-female variety theater troupe under the musical direction of Kami Kyosuke (1902-1981), a conductor and jazz intellectual who had trained at the University of Southern California (Sakoguchi 2010: 27-8; Chiorin Diary 2022). The pioneering troupe, the only one of mixed gender in Japan, targeted a general audience for its combination of comic sketches, tap dance routines, and parodies of western movie songs. In this capacity, the multi-talented troupe, which included American nisei singers Miyagawa Harumi and

Betty Inada was seen by parent company Shōchiku as a vehicle to promote the company's plush new Imperial Theater and compete with rival Takarazuka's own new upscale theater as well as the growing movie audience at Toho's Nichigeki (Tsukahara 2006a; Hosokawa 2007:167-68; Kawatake n.d; Satō 2014).

During rehearsals, Kami became convinced that Akizuki's unmatched tap-dancing skills, under the direction of America-trained dancer Nakagawa Saburo, could be a key to the success of the troupe. By contrast, his newly appointed assistant, Columbia-affiliated Hattori Ryōichi, recently returned from Manchuria and having already failed with two of his jazz melodies performed by nisei singers Moriyama Hisashi and Riki Miyagawa, was on the lookout for something new. According to his account, Hattori was taken aback by the way in which the sickly-looking Kasagi transformed herself once on stage. Wearing high heels and 3-centimeter false eyelashes, the diminutive Kansai-accented singer showcased an energetic and untamed dancing style fused with skills honed in the tough world of Osaka's entertainment business. These marked her out as a potential vehicle for Hattori's interest in incorporating elements of the swing jazz style that had swept the United States two years earlier (Tsukahara 2006a; Tsukahara 2006b; Sakoguchi 2010: 30-31).

Late in 1938, Kami left SGD leaving Hattori with the final say in the artistic direction of the variety troupe. His favor created the conditions for Kasagi's emergence as one of the leading vocalists of pre-war Japan and the personification of so-called 'Hot Jazz.' Hattori, who also grew up in downtown Osaka, was particularly impressed by Kasagi's ability to project her powerful spontaneous vocals and enunciate vowels in a manner that echoed elements of the offbeat swinging style of African American jazz vocalist Maxine Sullivan and the comedic white jazz singer and actress Martha Raye (Hosokawa 2007: 159, 168). Both vocalists had broken through to a mass American audience in movie performances and by 1939 had become familiar and much admired by Japanese jazz aficionados and moviegoers. The critics among these enthusiasts showered Kasagi's first-ever scat-style performance of a new Hattori composition 'Rappa to Musume' (Trumpet and a Girl) with unrestrained praise for its embodiment of 'swing.' The song, featured in the SGD musical Green Shadow (July 1939), saw Kasagi acting as the daughter of a Black trumpeter and clearly was a homage to Marsha Raye's lightly corked character in the 1937 film 'Artists and Models' featuring Louis Armstrong. The success of the number and her compelling stage performances resulted in the entertainment magazine Star dubbing Kasagi the "Queen of Swing' and led to her being awarded an unusually high salary of two hundred yen. Of this, however, the singer kept only thirty yen for her spartan lifestyle, sending the rest to her parents and relatives, an example of filial devotion that seems tailor-made for the drama's screenplay (Tsukahara 2006b; Sakoguchi 2010: 32-34; Satō 2014; Shibuki 2022: 16-17).

The SGD performances led to a brief appearance in Makino Masahiro's 1938 comedy movie Yajikita tairiku dōchū (Yaji and Kita's Continental Road) which poked fun at a famous 1920s Kabuki comedy along with several other operettas and music shows. The most notable of these, 'Jazz Star' was directed by Hattori collaborator Omachi Tatsuo and saw Kasagi take center stage with the band arranged around her. Sensing the moment of her ascent to a unique status among contemporary singers, Hattori arranged an exclusive contract for Kasagi with Nippon Columbia,

and in late 1939 cut a recording of 'Rappa to Musume' along with the Columbia Jazz Orchestra featuring trumpeter Saito Hiroyoshi (Kawatake nd; Sakoguchi 2010: 33). Now recognized as a seminal musical recording in Japanese popular music history, the song has been much covered by contemporary artists. As such, this recording (and perhaps too, the follow-ups later in the year, 'Sentimental Dinah' 'St Louis Blues,' 'Penny Serenade' and 'Hot China'), could well be used as a key musical moment in the asadora . Hattori, meanwhile, increasingly aware of just how uniquely talented and charismatic Kasagi could be, made a risky commitment to her future career and development even as the political situation threatened to derail the trajectory of both of their careers (Hosokawa 2007: 169-70: Sakoguchi 2010: 32-33).

## Love and Acceptance in a Time of War: Yoshimoto Eisuke, Panpan Fandom and the Power of Single Motherhood


Although able to ignore the growing government clampdown on entertainment until mid-1940, the very fact that SDG was a mixed-gender troupe built on creative variations of American movie and musical culture ensured that the troupe in general, and Kasagi's energetic performance style in particular, came to the attention of authorities. In mid-1940, with SDG downsizing into a smaller theater, Kasagi found herself called into the local police station on a directive from military authorities. Here she was instructed to stay within ninety centimeters of the microphone and maintain an upright stance when performing (Sakoguchi 2010: 39-40). While not alone in being scrutinized by authorities, most of the other entertainers forced into making some changes in their stage personas were those using western names such as the crooner Dick Mine, The Milk Brothers, and nisei singer Betty Inada (Atkins 2001: 151). Within a year, however, several well-known cross-dressing otokoyaku stars of the racy girl's 'opera' troupe Shōchiku Shōjo Kagekidan (SKD) including Mizunoe Takiko and Kawaji Ryūko, were told to abandon their overtly male performing personas. In January 1941, with dance halls already closed and even coffee houses under scrutiny,

SDG disbanded. In response, Kasagi worked to set up her own small combo under trombonist Nakazawa Hisashi ('Kasagi Shizuko and Her Orchestra') and attempted to make a living performing Japanese folk or romantic pop songs in movie theaters or small venues, often in Osaka (Sakoguchi 2010: 40-42).

Unlike her slightly older contemporaries, music school graduates and chanson singers Awaya Noriko (1907-1999), Watanabe Hamako (1910-1999) and Futaba Akiko (1915-2011), Kasagi would find herself effectively downgraded by the Japan Music Culture Association ( Dai nippon ongaku bunka kyōkai ). Formed in 1941 under the influence of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, the committee consisted of composers and musicians charged with developing a national or light music ( keiongaku ) distinct from western genres or those designated as the enemy's cultural expression. This de-westernized, deracinated and melody-focused instrumental version of 'jazz' was utilized to support the war effort and to provide comfort for wounded soldiers (Atkins 2001: 129, 140-144). Ultimately, almost every pre-war entertainer, regardless of their actual feelings about this directive, participated in one form or another, with Hattori joining a who's who of actors, musicians, and comedians in the making of the music and song-based troop entertainment movie Ongaku Daishingun (Music March) in early 1943. The movie featured an early boogie-style song by Otani Rinko that the composer worked on while in Shanghai (Satō 2014; Satō 2021).

In 1942 Kasagi recorded a Hattori-Fujiura Ko composition 'Aire Kawaii' written in the socalled nanpō kayō (southern song) style that was considered acceptable by censors (Tsukahara 2006a: Satō 2014). The unreleased song, which contained elements of Cuban rhythms, proved to be her final recording of the war and in the following year the singer found herself stuck in yet another unmotivating tour of munitions factories. In June 1943, however, the twenty-eight-yearold's life was transformed by a chance meeting with Yoshimoto Eisuke, a nineteen-year Waseda University student and the oldest son of Yoshimoto Sei, the widowed wife of the founder of the Osaka-based Yoshimoto Kōgyō entertainment agency. Despite a nine-year-age gap, the unlikely pair fell in love and attempted to find some comfort in each other in the dark times of 1944-45. They faced strong opposition, however, from Eisuke's mother, the principal subject of 2017's asadora , Warotenka, and a major figure in the Kansai entertainment industry.

In August 1945, with both of their homes in Tokyo destroyed by firebombs, the couple were finally able to live together in a room found by Eisuke's uncle, Hayashi Hirotaka (the future president of Yoshimoto Kōgyō) in the same building as Hattori. Despite the extreme harshness of everyday life in 1945-46, the six months they lived together were perhaps the happiest time in Kasagi's life. Eisuke dropped out of Waseda University to work under Hayashi and helped Kasagi to reactivate her career under a new manager, Yamauchi Yoshi (Sakoguchi 2010: 49-51; Excite News 2018). Just three months into the U.S Occupation she appeared with Takarazuka actress Todoroki Yukiko and Hawaiian-born musician-actor Haida Katsuhiko in the first large-scale postwar musical event ('Highlight') at the Nichigeki theater (Sakoguchi 2010: 67; Bourdaghs 2012: 30-31; Sat 2014). Living freely and in the moment for perhaps the first time in her life, she found herself pregnant in October 1946. However, in another moment that seems sure to play a role in the TV drama, as they were contemplating marriage and Kasagi's retirement from show business,

the couple's happiness was abruptly cut short. Eisuke, suffering like many at the time from tuberculosis, was forced to leave Tokyo in early January to recuperate in his mother's house. With her pregnancy now visible, Kasagi announced to Hattori that her re-recordings of 'Sentimental Dinah' and 'Aire Kawaii' for Columbia and upcoming appearance as the star of his newly written musical operetta 'Jazz Carmen' in February 1947 would be her last. While perhaps not planning to fully retire, she made it clear that she would stop working at least until the birth of her child. While no photos of these legendary performances exist, Kasagi wore a skirt and shawl to hide her condition from the audience, a scene which is another obvious candidate for the asadora . Four months later and just weeks before the delivery of her daughter, her world collapsed on news of Eisuke's death (Sakoguchi 2010: 68-70: Satō 2014; Satō Tsuyoshi 2020).

Despite the tragic news, the birth of her daughter and the support of not only Hattori but Hayashi, who brought news of Eisuke's choice of names for his child before his death, proved to be a watershed moment in both her personal and public career. As an adoptee unacknowledged by her own mother, Kasagi informed her closest friends that she would raise her daughter (Eiko) as a single mother despite an offer of adoption from Eisuke's mother. This decision, symbolized by her frequent appearance on stage with her baby daughter, led to an outpouring of support from fans, including, many in the panpan sex worker community of Yūrakuchō (Ichikawa 2009: 58-59). These women were informally led by nineteen-year-old 'Rakucho no Otoki' a flamboyant panpan made famous by an NHK broadcast in April 1947 (Dower 2000: 123-24; Yabunirami Blog 2021) who was befriended by Kasagi. Many panpan it seems likely, saw commonalities in Kasagi's experience and resilience and would attend her performances, often, according to Hattori, bringing flowers to the stage and effectively acting as an informal fandom (Sakoguchi 2010: 94-98). Within a year of her tragic loss, Kasagi, who openly gave her support to sex worker rehabilitation centers, emerged as the voice of hope for not only these women of the night but for hundreds of thousands of war widows; abandoned and orphaned teenagers; elder sisters taking care of siblings and many others struggling to cope with a world of shortages, black markets, disease and daily humiliations (Kawaguchi 1996: 51). Her status with this demographic, especially the panpan, was in stark contrast to that of the more diva-like pre-war recording artists, most notably Awaya Noriko, Watanabe Hamako and Mizunoe Takiko all of whom indicated their unwillingness to be associated with any song or musical vehicle that acknowledged the plight of the panpan or that hinted of kasutori -inspired sexuality (Takai 2016: 18). Indeed Awaya, who had sung Hattori's songs before the war, pointedly turned down the song "Hoshi no Nagare ni" (In the Flow of the Stars), an orphaned woman's lament for being forced into prostitution that became a favorite of the panpan when recorded by Kikuchi Akiko. The movingly constructed lyrics by Shimizu Minoru were written after the poet read a letter in the Mainichi newspaper sent in by a young, orphaned woman left with no choice but to work on the streets. Sung in a style that echoed that of Marlene Dietrich's 'Lily Marlene,' the oft-covered song came to embody precisely the opposite sentiment of Kasagi's optimistic boogie-woogie songs (Nishiyama 2022; Ichikawa 2009: 62-63).

With strong support from the most disadvantaged sectors of immediate post-war urban Japan, Kasagi rebuilt her life and became the voice of Hattori's dream of a musical expression that could contribute to Japan's revival. This 'democratic' urge on the part of the artist to support the country's most vulnerable and outcast will likely provide NHK with an opportunity to showcase the idea that the immediate post-war years involved a rejection of the hierarchical, status-based society that is widely blamed for the rise of militarism. Meanwhile, now free from wartime restrictions and full of creative energy after a year in Shanghai and two years in which he composed numerous patriotic songs (Atkins 2001: 157), Hattori worked tirelessly to provide his muse with an outpouring of jazz-infused compositions that in combination with her vocal delivery, vibrant dance style, and modest but optimistic demeanor, perfectly matched the country's mood. Her performances and the reaction to them, especially by young women, also gave Kasagi the means with which to cope with her personal grief and achieve an unprecedented status as a single mother who embodied the post-war tenacity, resolution, and fortitude of women of her generation.


## Beyond Boogie Woogie: Kasagi as Occupied Japan Popular Culture Icon


The story behind Kasagi's 'Tokyo Boogie Woogie,' a song said to embody an optimistic brightness amid the ruins, has attained legendary status in Japanese popular culture. Most accounts detail Hattori's experimentation with rhythm after hearing the Andrews Sisters' 'Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy' while in Shanghai composing music as part of the war effort (Tsukahara 2006a). Others focus on how the rhythm came to him while riding a train in Tokyo and his dream of brightening not only Kasagi's mood but the gloominess of early Occupation Japan (Satō Tsuyoshi 2020; Sakoguchi 2010: 79). This was done by fashioning an optimistic new musical movement that was the anthesis of the dark blues songs of pre-war Japan, epitomized by his own 'Wakare no Blues' (Farewell Blues) a 1937 hit for Awaya Noriko. 'Tokyo Boogie Woogie' was recorded in late August 1947 with the Columbia Orchestra in front of a crowd of enthusiastic GIs who had been invited to the recording by the English-speaking lyricist Suzuki Masaru (Sakoguchi 2010: 8081). It was then performed by Kasagi in September at a concert at the Umeda Theater in Osaka and in the Nichigeki musical Odoru Manga Festival: Urashima Futari Ryugu-e Go . This was

followed by its use in the movie Haru no Kyōen (Spring Feast), (dir. Yamamoto Kajirō) featuring the popular Nichigeki Dancing Team at the end of the year (Satō 2014; Yabunirama 2021). The recording itself was released by Columbia in January 1948 and became a major hit following its adoption by NHK radio in March. Already seen by many as the voice of emotional resilience, perseverance, and hope in occupied Japan, Kasagi's status would only grow with the almost simultaneous appearance of her riveting and 'animal-like' performance of the earlier Hattori song 'Jungle Boogie' in Kurosawa Akira's Yoidore Tenshi (Drunken Angel), released in April 1948) (Tsukahara 2006a; Hosokawa 2007: 160; Shimada 2010: 14).

Kasagi's role in this Kurosawa movie classic has been the subject of both musicological and socio-cultural analysis by Bourdaghs, Shamoon, and Nagahara, all three of whom emphasize the physical liberation and female sexual desire aspects of her performance and persona (Bourdaghs 2012: 31-35; Shamoon 2014: 117-118; Nagahara 2017: 153-57). Bourdaghs also notes that Kasagi was not afraid to assert herself, going as far as to request that Hattori tone down the sexual innuendo of Kurosawa's original lyric for 'Janguru bugi' (Jungle Boogie). Both scholars give deserved attention to the way in which Yoidore Tenshi handles the complex, sensitive, and oftcensored topic of the panpan sex workers' dilemmas. This ultimately unavoidable subject, a byproduct of the massive scale and length of the military occupation, is also the indirect theme of November 1947's 'Sekohan Musume' (Secondhand Daughter). This Hattori song, with ingenious lyrics penned by Yuki Yujiro, sees the singer lament that her kimono, handbag, high heels, and even her lover are all secondhand castoffs obtained from the PX stores of GHQ and by implication acquired through a relationship with a GI (Tsukahara 2006a). The panpan theme is of course front and center in Shima Kōji's Ginza kankan musume (Ginza KanKan Girl) released in August 1949 with Kasagi singing and acting alongside the leading young actress of the era, Takamine Hideko (1924-2010). The two performers play the role of good-hearted impoverished orphans who, aspiring to be genuine artists, are persuaded by their humorous giant-like friend played by Kishii Akira (1910-1965) to earn money as cabaret singers, precisely the dubious environment of the panpan girls, gangsters and other members of the nighttime kasutori world of alcohol, crime, and sex. Show business legend has it that when asked by Kasagi and Takamine what the word 'Kankan,' an obvious replacement for panpan , actually meant, director Kōji claimed not to know. This anecdote matches Shamoon's reading of the song's 'light-hearted, innocent delivery' that when combined with Hattori's 'upbeat, cheery melody' acts to soften the 'references to prostitution in the lyrics' by Saeki Takao. By so doing, the film effectively tames 'the erotic aspects of kasutori culture' and leaves both Kasagi (and Takamine) untainted by hints of sexuality in their roles, despite Kasagi's known friendship with and sympathy for panpan (Shamoon 2014: 124-25).
