## Review of Literature


## Etymology of the Term Translanguaging


The etymology of the term translanguaging is derived from the Welsh word 'trawsieithu.' The term originated by  Williams and Whittal in 1996. Lewis, Jones, Baker,2012, p. 643) point out that translanguaging was first derived from the Welsh word 'Trawsiethu' in Welsh schools to explain  the  pedagogical  procedure  where  learners  systematically  make  a  transition  from  one language to another for  particular reasons,  for example reading in Second Language (L2) and discuss the text in First Language (L1), or listening to L1 and writing in L2 or another.


## Translanguaging as a Concept


Velasco and García (2014) noted that the term [translanguaging] emphasizes the susceptible and t significant actions through which bilinguals choose characteristics in their language repertory to convey  correctly.  From  this  standpoint,  the  language  practices  being  learned  by  emergent bilinguals  are  in  practical  interrelatedness  with  other  language  practices  and  form  an  integral system.

Therefore, translanguaging enables the learner to have input with a language and make an output with another language (Alzahrani, 2019). Anderson (2017) pointed out that: ''translanguaging, and 'translingualism,' shows the flexible use of several languages as a resource that exceeds traditional understandings of different languages''. Fittingly, these two terms highlight the softening of lines between named languages and are based on the concept that incipient bilinguals constantly use their thorough linguistic repertoires to make meaning (Pacheco, & Miller, 2016). Translanguaging defined by Garcia & Li (2014):'' is to educate all learners, regardless of their language practices, to maximize the meaning-making, creativity, and criticality of their educational experience' (pp. 370-371)

Sayer (2013) considered that translanguaging is better grasped as a descriptive name for bilingual practices  of  discourse  that  learners  and  teachers  use  for  both  educational  and  non-educational goals. The inclusion of translanguaging practices has been proposed to offer a scaffolding method for  instruction  (García  &  Sylvan, 2011). Canagarajah (2011) defined translanguaging  as'' the ability of multilingual speakers to shuttle between languages, treating the diverse languages  that  form  their  repertoire  as  an  integrated  system'  (p.  401.) This clarification not only alludes to switching between two languages but, it comprises the systematic employment of two languages in a particular language teaching activity.


## The Prominent Role of Translanguaging Practice in Second Language Learning


Translanguaging plays a crucial role in second language acquisition and helps language learners  improve  their  bi-lingual  personalities.  It  also  favors  teachers  in  several  ways,  e.g., translanguaging benefits teachers in enhancing students' knowledge and cognate awareness by employing  the  whole  repertoire  of  learners'  native  language.  Translanguaging  also  benefits learners by creating a secure and safe environment in which their identities are appreciated and valued (Cenoz, J., Leonet, O., & Gorter, 2021, Khan,  Nazir, & Khalid,2021).

## Methods


A  quantitative  research  method  was  adopted  by  the  two  researchers  to  investigate  the perception of students of drama on the use of translanguaging within English literature classrooms at King Khalid University.


## Participants


About twenty-five female students of English drama at the Department of English, Dhahran al-Janoub  female students campus   King  Khalid  University  during  the  summer  semester  2020 , joined this study at their discretion. These students were selected randomly. They were asked to answer a questionnaire of 13 items. The participants were bilingual as they spoke Arabic as the mother tonguage or first language (L1) and English as the second language (L2).


## Study Variables


The  independent  variable  included  in  this  study  was  practicing  translanguaging  within synchronous and non-synchronous lectures and in-person English drama classes. The dependent variable  included  in  this  study  consisted  of  the  perception  of  students  of  drama  on  the  use  of translanguaging within English literature classrooms.


## Research Instruments


To gather the data from the recent study, the two researchers used a questionnaire of 13 statements designed and prepared by them. Moreover, the questionnaire was composed of two sections: Section one dealt with perceptions of students of drama on the use of (L1) in an English literature classroom, and section two is devoted to perceptions of students of drama on the use of ( L2) in an English literature classroom. The questionnaire demanded the participants to manifest their agreement to each item in a four Likert-type questionnaire:  agree,  strongly, agree disagree, and strongly disagree.

To test the validity of the current questionnaire, the questionnaire was checked first by seven expert faculty members from King Khalid University and Jazan University. They were asked to review the instrument for content and face validity. To improve the validity of the instrument, the instrument was pilot tested with a group of 10 students of drama from the same university. The changes in the questionnaire were made by the two researchers based on the recommendations of five professors from the university.

## The Associative Diffusion Model


The associative diffusion model proposes that culture diffuses primarily as associations between (categories of) people, objects, genres, and events actors pick up from the world due to their everyday experiences (Goldberg & Stein, 2018). In other words, culture reflects people’s learned associations of what goes with what. Recent cultural analyses have conceived these networks of associations between cultural elements as cultural schemas governing individual choices, attitudes, and decision-making (Boutyline & Soter, 2021; Frye, 2017; Goldberg, 2011; Hunzaker & Valentino, 2019; Vaisey, 2009). To the extent that organizations determine and reify shared associations between cultural elements, organizations are essential causal agents in determining the “structure of culture” in society.

For instance, environmentally-conscious middle-class consumers associate themselves with such products as grass-fed beef (Weber et al., 2008), creating linkages between specific social positions, particular sociopolitical orientations, and patterns of culinary choice (Baumann et al., 2022). Such cultural associations are often facilitated by organizations working in multiple sectors (for-profit, non-profit, state) as sites of interaction where culture is created,  maintained, and matched. Cultural associations (between people, objects, products, and identities) are continuously updated as people observe new linkages between practices, kinds of people, and cultural objects in their daily lives. Social movements or other advocacy organizations dedicated to animal rights can work to shift the strength of existing associations, such as between Foie gras and fancy French cuisine, to ones more compatible with their goals, such as between Foie gras and animal cruelty (see DeSoucey, 2016). Culture-producing organizations draw on the pre-existing store of (already diffused) cultural associations to generate objects that themselves express, reify, and in some rare cases, transform those associations. In this respect, sector-specific organizational imperatives (e.g., toward profitability or classification) exert intense pressure on maintaining and matching the correlation between cultural items.

Why is this the case? First, categorical deviance is costly as it makes products illegible (Hannan, 2010). Categorically incoherent objects are those having partial memberships in distant slots in the classification structure, like a burger joint serving sushi. Because categorical deviance is generally—but not always (Silver et al., 2022)—penalized, there is an organizational incentive to sustain the current structure of cultural associations rather than to change it. Of curse, excepting social movement organizations engaged in cultural change (Armstrong & Bernstein, 2008). In this way, organizations become the primary agents policing categorically unruly objects (Rubio 2014). Organizations thus help reproduce existing associations while preventing the broader public from being exposed to novel or rule-breaking cultural associations (thus preventing their take-off and wider diffusion). Organizations tip the scale in favor of existing associations and only serve as the conduit for novel ones on rare occasions. Organizations are also the primary agents responsible for diffusing such associations because they monopolize institutionalized roles as rankers (Espeland & Sauder, 2007).

In what follows, we review evidence consistent with the idea that organizations are central players in creating, transforming, and maintaining pre-existing cultural associations in society.


## Organizations and Associational Creation



#### Unintended Associational Creation


It is essential to separate the overall effect organizations have on the structure of culture in society from whether these effects match those the organization set out to create. As a result, organizations often end up diffusing cultural associations entirely orthogonal and sometimes antithetical to those explicitly sought, resulting in the unintended creation of novel associations. McDonnell (2016) refers to this non-directed cultural associational drift as cultural entropy. While initiated by organizational attempts to create fixed cultural associations, entropic processes are aided by and channeled through people’s capacities to recontextualize cultural meanings carried by the symbols produced by the organization, leading to the creation of unexpected context-driven associations in concrete socio-material settings. In this way, organizations can have both intended (and more often than not) unintended effects on the structure of culture of society as a byproduct of their attempts to manipulate and generate cultural correlations.

Novel cultural associations—of both the intended and unintended kinds—can emerge due to dynamics occurring at the level of the entire organizational field. One such field-level dynamic that has received substantial empirical support is resource partitioning. Using the emergence of the microbrewery movement (and market segment) as their signal case study, Carroll and Swaminathan (2000) argue that markets go through two ideal-typical stages. First, there is an initial stage in which “generalist” producers rush to the market center where they can reach the majority of consumers producing relatively homogeneous products and taking advantage of economies of scale aided by the automated, technology-intensive (“industrial”) production processes. Large producers drive out small (“mom-and-pop shop”) ones during this stage. The American beer brewing industry went from having hundreds of independent producers in the early twentieth century with no one set of producers dominating the market to the top three breweries capturing the bulk of the market share by the mid-twentieth.

Counter-intuitively, as markets mature and become concentrated around a relatively small oligopoly of large producers, space opens up at the “edges” of the market. Here, relatively small “specialist” producers can cater to consumers with more differentiated tastes seeking novelty, diversity of consumption experiences, authentic production techniques, and a “craft” commitment to production (Ocejo, 2017). In this “partitioned” stage, the relationship between large generalists and small specialists is symbiotic, with specialists benefiting from the existence of large generalists hawking relatively homogeneous product offerings—in this case, the much-maligned “industrial American Lager” (Budweiser, Coors, Miller, and the like)—against which the new specialist producers were recreating craft production techniques to brew (then) novel beer styles like India Pale Ales, Red Ales, Porters, Saisons, and the like. Hence, the emergence of microbreweries in the contemporary American scene (now numbering the thousands).

Because partitioned markets have a more varied array of products, they also open up the potential for emerging cultural associations. Thus, as Darwin (2018) shows, when in the pre-partitioning American beer market dominated by the Industrial Lager, there was a simple association between “beer” and “gender”; beer was a “masculine” drink, and that was it. However, in the post-partitioning market featuring a large swath of “kinds” of beer produced by microbreweries, novel associations between beer and gender have emerged. Certain kinds of beer (light, fruity) are feminine, while others (hoppy, dark, strong) are “masculine.” These novel associations between gender and within-category product variants would not exist without the microbrewery movement. Importantly, these cultural associations are produced and reproduced by consumers and gender dynamics at the producer level, with microbreweries headed by women and men typecast into different types of beer.


#### Generating Novel Associations


In some cases, the organized production of culture generates novel associations between styles, products, and categories (sometimes bundled under the idea of “genre”) where there were none. Thus, genre emergence is a laboratory for creating novel associations in the structure of culture. For instance, musical genres are built from associations between the collective production context of particular music (regardless of underlying style) and specific genre labels (Lena, 2012). Some genres emerge within small, exclusive groups of avant-garde cultural creators. These producers mainly produce for themselves (they are their primary audience). Such genres thus retain the association with creativity and “independence” (e.g., from market forces) through most of their lifetimes (e.g., surf music, early twentieth-century jazz), even after they achieve a modicum (or sometimes great) levels of commercial success. Other genres emerge fully formed as creatures of large-scale, for-profit producers in “industry” (e.g., new wave, action movies). They are thus exempt from the associations that sometimes beset avant-garde genres yet carry their own. For instance, audiences do not expect authorial intention, creativity, or independence from market forces to be primary considerations in industry genres. Fans of such genres are comfortable with a level of repetition, “unoriginal” borrowing, and creative compromises that guarantee mass accessibility.

Other genres emerge in “scenes” featuring strong bonds (and sometimes creative co-production) between highly committed audiences and producers. Because audiences see producers as having chosen them (e.g., instead of a mass audience or even themselves as a primary audience), they tend to have a strong sense of ownership over the genre category. These audiences even associate their lifestyle (e.g., which may involve particular forms of attire, recreational drug use, and the like) with the genre’s specificity (e.g., grindcore, riot girl music, old-school rap, and early grunge music). On the rare occasion that scene genres achieve commercial success and producers move to the industry context of production, the original scene audience experiences this event as a dramatic betrayal of the scene’s core values. Thus, original scene audiences renounce producers who shifted to industry genres as traitors and sellouts while retaining allegiance to those less commercially successful producers that continue to display loyalty to the scene and authenticity in lifestyle self-presentation. This process reinforces cultural correlations people may have made between lifestyle markers and genres within the scene, even as they are weakened outside the scene, among producers who have moved who achieve widespread success.


## Organizations and Associational Rewiring


Creating associations between cultural objects is a primary concern of organizations, as the cultural understanding of what a product “is” and “where it goes” is a resource that needs active maintenance (Pfeffer & Salancik, 1979). Introducing a correlation where one does not exist is relatively easy compared to rewriting existing association structures. For example, as Mountain Dew was relatively unknown outside the American South, its association with “hillbillies” and moonshine was only regionally salient. When introduced outside the South via a television ad campaign featuring a young actor, Brad Pitt, the rest of the United States associated it with youthful nonchalance, adventure, and the cultural stereotype (itself a bundle of associations) of the “wild man” (Holt, 2004, p. 44ff). Today, one is much less likely to think of Appalachia and moonshine when exposed to Mountain Dew and more likely to link to “extreme sports,” computer gaming, or skateboarding among young, middle-class, white (and decidedly non-Southern) young men.

Organizational rewiring of known cultural associations relies heavily on linking a cultural product to alternative cultural associations. Grappa, a grape-based liquor, was associated with low-status and rural villages when a handful of Italian producers sought to transform it into a high-status product. Building new associations between grappa and particular types of people and categories were crucial to its subsequent status transformation. To pull this off, Italian grappa producers adopted cultural practices associated with foreign spirits by putting grappa in more elegant bottles, getting high-status restaurants to carry the product, increasing the price, and marketing using terroir characteristics. Rewiring consumers' cultural associations by repetitively conjoining grappa with these high-status cultural symbols and markers of authentic craft production increased grappa’s cultural status (Delmestri & Greenwood, 2016).

While organizations can innovate products from scratch, entirely new cultural objects are relatively rare, as most creativity is derivative of the recombination of prior cultural forms (Rao et al., 2003) However, organizational competition can still drive the process of associational diffusion, as there is an inherent tradeoff between categorical fidelity and demand for uniqueness (Goldberg et al., 2016). For instance, in French cuisine, chefs faced the categorical antagonism between haute and nouvelle cuisine. In contrast, a subset of chefs, insulated by their high status, gradually combined old and new styles. Bricolage by high-status chefs lowered the costs for subsequent transgressors, exacerbating fusion can categorical innovation over time (Rao et al., 2005). Competition dynamics, which incentivized fusion, gradually brought about stronger associations between previously segmented cultural genres, thus eroding previous categorical distinctions.

Implicit in our argument is that this organization-driven associational diffusion process is useful for understanding dynamics usually conceptualized as overly top-down (e.g., from larger cultural zeitgeist to individuals) or overly bottom-up (as the result of decentralized decision-making by multiple people) ways. A focus on organizations provides a more balanced and analytically robust approach. Take, for instance, the emergence of the “cultural omnivore” (Lizardo & Skiles, 2012; Peterson & Kern, 1996). This is a phenomenon whereby high-status actors distinguish themselves by a seeming unwillingness to exclude cultural forms (e.g., refusing to reject) instead of past practices where social status was demonstrated via cultural exclusion (Bryson, 1996; Lizardo & Skiles, 2016). While now there is a wide swath of literally hundreds of studies documenting correlations between markers of social position and cultural omnivorousness, there is very little work providing theoretically compelling explanations of the phenomenon's origins. Omnivorousness depends on the cultural classification of cultural objects (and producers) along lines associated with genre and lineage. It is clear that organizations are central to this society-level classification task. Therefore, a likely hypothesis is that omnivorousness emerges whenever arts organizations reshuffle the cultural deck, extending the category of “art” to include a wider variety of objects, performances, events, and experiences (Lena, 2021, p. 135ff), thus legitimating new categories, but more crucial for our argument creating associational linkages between folk and vernacular cultural products and those already invested with the imprimatur of “art.”


## Organizations and Associational Maintenance


Organizations reinforce and reproduce cultural associations as a routine byproduct of their operations. In organizations, the persistence of cultural associations is ensured by the imperatives of categorical fidelity, as audiences use established categorical expectations to interpret new products (Hannan et al., 2007; Rossman, 2012). The need for audience legibility stabilizes cultural forms and their association with other cultural forms. For example, producers and radio stations build their playlists around genre conformity to assess demand and mitigate the risk of people changing stations, thereby preventing the exposure of innovative associations between styles and producers (Rossman, 2012). Likewise, as a consumer, when quality is difficult to determine, consumers use adherence to cultural expectations as a proxy for quality, providing organizational incentives for the maintenance of existing cultural forms.

Organizations often disseminate existing cultural associations as critical nodes in the associational diffusion chain. Take, for instance, the set of associations between Blues music, smoke-filled bars in a slight state of disrepair, Black musicians down on their luck, and other markers of “authenticity” concerning this genre category. As Grazian (2005) shows, Chicago Blues clubs were the primary purveyors of these associations. Even clubs located in some of the city's most expensive (and whitest) neighborhoods felt the need to “decorate” the inside of the Blues clubs to convey a run down (but not exceedingly run down) appearance, served cheap beer and whiskey, and heavily police both what was played (relying heavily on “sets” of what they thought were the “classics”) and who played (making sure that bands on stage almost always contained majority Black musicians despite an overabundance of talented non-Black Blues musicians in the city). This spectacle is concocted by Blues clubs for the consumption of (majority white) tourist audiences, expecting to see the “real” Blues, and who, in consuming this product, get exposed to a set of linkages between people, events, and objects reinforcing pre-existing associations between whom, where, and how the Blues are played.

Organizations also perpetuate existing cultural boundaries by using institutionalized schemas to create new classification systems. For example, record labels’ classification concerns drove the introduction of “hillbilly” and “race records” to the American market in the early 20th century. Even though this nascent musical form was produced via inter-cultural exchange between black and white musicians, record distributors imposed American racial divisions onto the music. These genres would later transform into modern country and blues music (Roy, 2004). Given the social and cultural distances between Blacks and white Americans in the early 20th century, the counterfactual of presenting a single, racially unified genre risked cultural incoherence.

If existing cultural associations are challenged, organizations are forced to decide whether to change or defend existing cultural associations or accede to the change. For example, when turquoise jewelry spiked in popularity in the early 2000s, high-end jewelers were forced to decide whether to begin carrying turquoise (Podolny, 2010, pp. 12–13). However, this jewelry’s cultural association with roadside stands in the desert and vacation trinket shops made jewelers hesitant to adopt, lest their company become culturally associated with these otherwise distant cultural objects, ruining the prestige associated with their brands. Often organizations become the victims of unwelcome associative diffusion processes.


#### Associational Matching


Organizations can also reproduce existing cultural associations by serving as “sieves” at the point of recruitment, selecting particular people based on perceived matches or mismatches (respectively) with the existing organizational identity. This selection routine partially determines who gets to form long-standing relations at work. Moreover, organizations are particularly good at reinforcing existing cultural correlations by facilitating cultural matches via homophily preferences. We refer to this process as associational matching. Thus, homophily along multiple dimensions supports society-wide cultural associations. These cultural correlations, in turn, constitute society-wide perceptions linking certain professions or even positions within organizations (e.g., managerial posts) with Weberian “lifestyles.”

For instance, it has been shown that when organizational gatekeepers are assigned to hiring their junior co-workers, they show strong preferences for those who display similar hobbies and life stories as themselves and, by implication existing organizational incumbents (Rivera, 2012). This process is critical in the context of high-skill professional labor, which increasingly requires long hours at work, making other coworkers particularly salient in high-status professionals’ social networks. This tendency towards lifestyle homophily, above and beyond technical credentials and even the “pedigree” of the educational institution from which people receive their degree, reproduces cultural associations between organizational positions, kinds of organizations (e.g., law firms versus financial service organizations), and leisure activities outside of work (Rivera, 2016). In this way, selective recruitment processes, especially those housing high-status, high-paying occupations, reify the cultural associations that members of privileged positions make between their “fit” with specific organizations and extracurricular activities. For example, if people who ski and play squash are co-workers, the association between the two sports is strengthened. Likewise, if one person skis and the other watches wrestling, the association would also increase between these two objects if the organizational tie existed.

In creative industries, “omnivorous” taste (Peterson and Kern 1996) serves as a cultural matching criterion driving recruitment practices because it is associated with creativity and thinking outside the box. Selective recruitment practices thus reinforce the correlation between being an omnivore and having a strong fit with the “creative” side of organizations in advertising (Koppman, 2016). Likewise, the use of cultural references associated with men in company recruitment processes in the technology sector may limit women’s willingness to continue pursuing careers in this industry, serving as a mechanism of exclusion and cultural matching (Campero, 2020).

Organizational cultural matching reinforces long-standing cultural correlations via other processes beyond selective recruitment. Diversity in recruitment can inspire organizational backlash, leading to a transformation in cultural associations and practices. In examining the SNCC’s transition from participatory democracy to organizational hierarchy, Polletta (2005) finds that the change was motivated by the emergence of white activists enacting participatory democracy as a form of personal or moral fulfillment rather than as a tactic with which to achieve real-world transformation of white supremacist institutions. The association of the cultural practice with “people who aren’t us” was enough to justify adopting the opposite organizational practice by Black activists committed to more comprehensive social change. Direct democracy as a social movement practice became “white.” Organizations are sensitive to the network of associations and can rework their practices to properly align their cultural practices with their social location in the service of their larger objectives.

Key personnel in organizations also generate distinct associations between objects and types of people via active self-selection processes, actively developing associations between cultural products and people.  For instance, Childress and Nault (2019) show that in the case of trade fiction book publishing, the person-to-person link between prospective authors and editors is primarily mediated by the organization’s core product, namely, the book manuscript. Consequently, most editors have limited interpersonal contact with authors and evaluate their match mainly concerning the product. This context is characterized by the high levels of uncertainty characteristic of most culture production organizations (of the “all hits are flukes” variety), combined with extreme discretion and autonomy (Hirsch, 1972). However, in seeing themselves as “matching” the product via aesthetic judgment processes and imaginative identification with the fictional world developed by authors, editors reproduce existing associations between literary themes and types of authors. Accordingly, women editors are overwhelmingly more likely to work with authors who tell stories with women as main characters, and the same goes for white editors. In this way, by actively selecting certain thematic and narrative lines evident in the product while rejecting others as “not for them to evaluate,” editors indirectly play a role in what associations get diffused via the formal publication process and subsequent product dissemination. The result is that most of the stories told via high-status book fiction end up reflecting characters, themes, and settings that are socially close to the primarily homogeneous (e.g., white middle-class) life stations of book editors.


## Concluding Remarks


In a classic paper, Perrow (1991, p. 725) boldly argued that “organizations [are] the key phenomenon of our time, and thus politics, social class, economics, technology, religion, the family, and even social psychology take on the character of dependent variables.” Two things deserve notice here. First, as argued at the outset, the intellectual trend of late runs counter Perrow’s proposal; organizations and organizational structure are increasingly conceived mainly as dependent variables of institutional and cultural processes. But most importantly, even in making organizations as “independent variables” Perrow left culture out of the list of things that organizations are thought of as affecting. In this paper, we have sought to recapture the partial spirit of Perrow’s intervention—seeing organizations as causal actors shaping society—while focusing on the “structure of culture” as one of the main domains that are shaped and molded by organizations. We argued that people’s shared schemata as to “what goes with what,” are shaped by the routine action and output of organizations at multiple spatial and temporal scales.

We argued that organizations exert this pivotal effect on the structure of culture in various ways. First, organizations can create new correlations between cultural items where there were none initially; genre-emergence processes are a prototypical instance. Notably, organizations may, in trying to rewire cultural associations in one direction, end up rewiring them in another direction, as people downstream from the organization use agentic practices to subvert the organization’s original proposal. This associational diffusion process has been referred to as cultural entropy. Second, they can generate novel associations by “rewiring,” existing ones, transforming our perception of people, places, and products by linking them to novel categories. Here organizations must contend with an existing structure of cultural associations and engage in concerted cultural and institutional work to transform them.

Third, organizations shape the structure of culture by serving as powerful mechanisms for reinforcing and maintaining existing associations. In that respect, they are one of the primary ways in which cultural entropy is actually averted. Organizations can do this by reifying and locking in sets of associations that would otherwise drift in different directions (as in the case of Blues music), or by drawing on highly institutionalized schemas to separate cultural products into disjoint categories. Organizations can also defend challenges to the existing state of cultural affairs by actively resisting the emergence of novel associations. Finally, via routine processes of personnel recruitment and processing of cultural products, or organizations can both generate and maintain a given structure of cultural associations (e.g., between certain professions, tastes, and lifestyles, and even organizational practices and tactics). This associational matching process implicates organizations in reproducing and maintaining cultural associations at scale.

In this paper, we highlight the importance of organizations in structuring cultural correlation. However, we hope that such a perspective can inspire new research into the causal relationship between organizations and the structure of culture, manifested as shared cognitive associations as to what goes with what. Organizations are not merely important as actors with a larger scale or influence than individuals, but this scale makes their effects qualitatively distinct.

## Introduction


Along with the internationalization of higher education, English as Foreign Language(EFL) teachers  are  no  longer  viewed  as  technicians  who  only  acquire  language-teaching  tactics  in pedagogical methodology courses and then apply them in their classrooms (Freeman & Johnson, 1998; Beijaard et al., 2004). Instead, EFL teachers are recognized as active agents who should bring professional, sociocultural, and sociopolitical dimensions to classroom dynamics (Johnson & Golombek, 2011; Hamid & Nguyen, 2016). The shift from the cultivation of English skills to a more  sociocultural  perspective,  which  stresses  cross-cultural  communication  competence,  has placed teacher identity at the center of language teaching and learning (Miller, 2009).

Meanwhile, the development in constructivist education theory, the emphasis on the link between  language  skills,  cognition,  and  the  enhanced  accessibility  of  free  language  learning resources online have further shifted the outer environment for EFL teachers. Since the formation of professional identity is a reflective, interactive and ongoing dynamic process influenced by internal and external factors (Goodson & Cole,1984; Moore & Hofman,1988; Mishler, 2004), EFL teachers' identity formation is under the heavy influence of how the context conceptualizes who they are (Wright, 1987). The fast and significant shift in the external factors necessarily calls for the  adjustment  of  EFL  teacher's  internal  understanding  of  the  teacher's  role,  leading  to  more uncertainties,  pressure,  tension,  and  anxiety  among  the  teachers,  which  could  exert  a  negative impact on their identity formation and development in return, even causing severe mental health issues (Aslrasouli & Vahid, 2014). However, the emphasis of most studies on teacher identity was on the individual side rather than on the context. Moreover, we paid even less attention to the influence of the context on the individual (Nese & Aslan, 2016). Many previous identity studies have called  for  more  attention  to  the  impact  of  the  context  on  professional  identity  formation (Coldron & Smith, 1999; Goodson & Cole, 1984; Clandinin et. al., 1999). For example, Codron & Smith (1999) highlighted that policies that impose uniformity and conformity may threaten teachers'  active  and  dynamic  identity  formation.  Because  the  norms  and  values  embodied  in education  in  each  particular  society  contribute  to  the  structuring  of  attitudes,  perceptions,  and behaviours of teachers, thus it is necessary to study teacher identity formation within a particular social-cultural context.


## The Social-cultural Context in Chinese Universities


Against globalization in education, the drastic role shift and the diversified responsibilities have generated more pressure for Chinese EFL teachers, who are experiencing a rise in role anxiety considering  the  high  social  expectation  in  many  aspects.  The  explicit  external  reasons  are threefold.  First,  the  teaching  burden  of  EFL  teachers  in  China  is  increasing.  Because  English learning is compulsory for students of all majors in Chinese universities, EFL teachers have to teach larger classes for longer academic hours. The usual teaching time for EFL teachers in Chinese universities ranges from 350 academic hours to 450 hours. Due to enrollment expansion in recent years, the teaching workload is even heavier. Second, the increased pressure for academic research, mainly due to fierce competition in higher education on a global scale (Li, 2008); and third, the lack of professional-pedagogical training for many EFL teachers in Chinese universities. Apart from  the  above  three  external  reasons,  the  continuous  educational  reform  initiative  by  the educational policymakers rather than the front-line teaching faculty of universities also serves as a source for EFL teachers' role anxiety.

## The Study of EFL Teacher's Identity Through Teacher Metaphor


While the enhanced link between cognitive activities and language increased the complexity of  language  teaching,  it  also  makes  it  possible  to  study  teacher's  self-perception  by  analyzing classroom discourse, and one of the popular routes is through investigating teacher metaphors (Tait-McCutcheon & Drake, 2016; Lynch and Fisher-Ari, 2017; Craig, 2018; Kartal, 2020). Ever since the redefinition of metaphor as a cognitive tool, metaphor has been widely applied in the studies of teacher's identity. Saban (2006) identified metaphor as an archetype of professional identity, a medium of reflection, and a tool for evaluation. Originating in embodied philosophy, the generation of metaphor is rooted in daily practice and experience. Teacher metaphors can be interpreted as the concept reflecting certain features of the interactions between internal/external factors, which is an epitome of the dynamics of teacher identity formation and has the potential of shaping one's professional identity construction. Although many scholars have studied teacher identity  through  metaphors  in  different  educational  stages  in  western  countries  (Erickson  & Pinnegar, 2017; Martınez, Sauleda, & Huber, 2001), few studies have been carried out among teachers  of  Chinese  universities.  Besides,  even  fewer  studies  have  attempted  to  reveal  the contextual reasons for teacher's role anxiety by tapping into the perceptual discrepancy between teachers' internal self-identity and the pro-external identity rooted in the Chinese social-cultural context. Therefore, this  paper  aims  to  study  the  interactions  between  the  external  and  internal perceptions of EFL teacher's role in Chinese universities by comparing the main teacher metaphors adopted by the EFL teachers and the social narrative, aiming to better understand the reasons for the rise of role anxiety among Chinese EFL teachers.

Compared with previous studies on teacher identity, the methods adopted in this research are more comprehensive. In this paper, the conceptualization of teacher's role is perceived as a continuum, with one extreme as the completely individualized/internal perception of teachers' role, and the other extreme as the role defined solely by contextual/external factors. The assumption here is that teachers' images extracted from relevant research articles are closer to the external perception while the teacher's role summarized from anonymous questionnaires answered by EFL teachers themselves is closer to internal perception, as shown in the following Figure 1.

Following these two approaches, teacher metaphor is used as a window for studying the influential factors and their interplay in the EFL teachers' identity formation process. In this paper, metaphor-eliciting sentences were used to collect teacher metaphors from EFL teachers of Chinese universities;  and  teacher  metaphors  of  high  frequency  were  extracted  from  relevant  research articles using a corpus analysis tool, then the main themes of teacher metaphors collected from the two approaches were classified and compared according to a systemic categorization of metaphors from  four  perspectives:  Learner-oriented,  Social  Order,  Social  Reform,  Cultural  Transmission (Oxford et. al., 1998). Through the structural comparison between the two groups of metaphors, this paper attempts to demonstrate the consistencies and discrepancies between the internal and external perceptions of EFL teachers' roles, which may reveal the possible reasons for the role anxiety of Chinese EFL teachers and provide some implications for anxiety alleviation.


## Research Questions


The research seeks to find the reasons for the  rise of Chinese EFL teacher's anxiety by analyzing  the  interactions  between  the  social  conceptualization  of  teacher's  identity  and  EFL teacher's  self-positioning. Two groups of teacher metaphors  are used as the research material. Metaphors provided by  Chiese EFL teachers are collected to  represent  the  process-based  prointernal perception of teacher's role, and metapohrs found in published research articles in Chinese quality journals stand for the concept-based pro-external understanding of EFL teacher identity. Centring on the structural comparison of teacher metaphors between those given by EFL teachers and those extracted from research articles, the current research will mainly focus on the following research questions ：

- 1. What similarities and differences can be observed in metaphors given by Chinese EFL teachers  and  metaphors  found  in  research  articles  about  teacher  identity  published  in  Chinese educational journals?
- 2. What is the relationship between the differences in teacher's role perception revealed through comparative metaphor analysis and the rise of role anxiety among Chinese EFL teachers?
- 3. What's  the  relationship  between  the  high  concentration  on  certain  conceptual  teacher metaphors and Chinese EFL teachers' role anxiety?


## Methods



## Data collection


Teacher  metaphors  for  comparison  were  obtained  through  two  approaches.  Metaphors representing  the  pro-external  perception  of  EFL  teacher's  role  were  selected  in  high  quality Chinese educational journals. Altogether 40 articles are selected by searching keywords or phrases like 'teacher metaphor', 'teaching metaphor', and some common teaching/teacher metaphors like 'candle & teacher', 'engineer & teacher', and 'gardener & teacher' in an online journal database called Chinese National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI). The filtering parameter was limited to articles published after 2010 on topics relevant to university education or the identity of university teachers. And only articles published in high-quality journals included in Chinese Social Science Citation Index (CSSCI) were selected.

Then  all  40  research  articles  were  transferred  into  plain  texts  for  analysis,  and  teacher metaphors  of  high-frequency  were  extracted  with  the  help  of  Antconc  3.5.9.  Then  teacher metaphors were also gathered from EFL teachers through an anonymous online questionnaire. Participants of the survey were EFL teachers of a Sci-tech Chinese university. From Table 2. we can find that three teacher metaphors received more negative comments than positive ones in the research articles, they are 'silkworm', 'candle', and a 'bucket of water' . The first two teacher metaphors are rooted in the same well-known poem written by Li Shangyin, a poet from Tang Dynasty (618 BC - 907 BC) in ancient China. The original line of the poem is ' Silkworm keeps spinning until death, and the candle keeps burning until the last drop of the wax ', which was originally an ode to the loyalty between lovers. Later, the determination and willingness to sacrifice themselves for others were borrowed to depict the teacher's role in modern Chinese society. The  most  serious  criticism  of  these  two  teacher  metaphors  is  that  both  have  deprived teachers of their rights to pursue their best interests; sacrifice and altruism became mandatory rather than voluntary for the teacher under the scenario framed by these two metaphors. As to ' a bucket of water ' metaphor, it is derived from the conceptual metaphor KNOWLEDGE IS WATER, the narrative behind it is that to provide students with a cup of water , the teachers have to possess ' a bucket of water' . The ' bucket ' metaphor received more criticism in the research article because the educational theory suggested by the metaphor is seemingly limited to knowledge transmission. Under  the  influence  of  constructivist  educational  theory,  the  metaphor  is  disfavored  for  its underestimation of students' initiative and agency. Apart from these three negative metaphors, the other frequent metaphors extracted from the articles mainly received positive comments.

## The contrastive analysis of frequent teacher metaphors from articles and questionnaires


The five most commonly cited teacher metaphors in the research articles are 'gardener', friend', ' guide', 'facilitator', and 'parent' , the highlighted features of each metaphor can be seen in Table 2. To have a better understanding of the perceptual variance of the EFL teacher's identity, the distribution of these five metaphors in research articles is contrasted with their distribution in metaphors provided by the EFL teachers through the questionnaire. The results can be found in Figure 4.

Figure 4. shows that the most emphasized teacher metaphor in research articles is 'teacher as  a  gardener' ,  which  emphasizes  teacher's  care,  attention,  and  the  provision  of  customized teaching contents to the students. In contrast, the 'gardener ' metaphor accounts for less than 5% of metaphors given by EFL teachers. Meanwhile, what's in the leading position among metaphors collected from teachers is the 'guide' metaphor, which stresses students' agency and initiative in learning, limiting the teacher's responsibilities to guidance and navigation. It's interesting to note that when the external perception expects teachers to 'take a good care of the students' , teachers are expecting students to be more independent and take the initiative in learning, with teacher's job limited to navigation rather than 'sail the boat' for them.

Among the top 5 metaphors, 'friend' is the metaphor in which both sides share a more or less similar emphasis, indicating that free communication and a more equal status between teachers and  their  students  are  acknowledged  both  in  the  sociocultural  context  and  in  the  internal perception. As to 'parent' and 'facilitator' , the percentage of these two metaphors from articles is also much  higher  than  their  proportion  in  metaphors  from  questionnaires. As can be seen from Table 2. and Table 3, the 'facilitator' metaphor in research articles mostly adopts a panoramic view of EFL teacher's identity, emphasizing teacher's ability in facilitating between different roles; while to EFL teachers, the context for 'facilitator' is more specific, limited to how a teacher facilitates teaching activities in a classroom.


## Structural comparison of teacher metaphors


To have a comparative structural analysis of the metaphors concerning language teacher's roles, we use the categorization framework given by Oxford et. al. (1998) in their cross-cultural analysis of conceptual teacher metaphors. In this framework, teacher metaphors are classified into four  types:  Learner-centered,  cultural  transmission,  social  order,  and  social  responsibility. The Learner-centered perspective stresses the teacher's role in nurturing the personal growth of each student in the classroom; the cultural transmission perspective emphasizes the duty of transferring to students the cultural heritage of the society, and here for EFL teachers, cross-cultural knowledge is  also  attributed  to  this  category;  the  social  order  theme  puts  teachers  in  the  role  of  a  social engineer who taps into the potential of students to meet the needs of society; and the social reform perspective  highlights  a  less  hierarchical,  more  democratic  relationship  between  teachers  and students. The framework can provide us with a better understanding of the variance in the emphasis of the EFL teacher's role shown in Figure 4.

According to the characteristics of the four types of metaphors in the framework, we can classify the found metaphors of the two groups. Metaphors that highlight teachers' relations with the students were classified as the learner-centered type, and those stress teachers' knowledge and skills in teaching are classified as the cultural transmission type. Meanwhile, metaphors that pay attention to the relative status between teachers and students are classified as the social order type, while those lay emphasis on teachers' social responsibility is categorized as the social reform type of metaphor. It can be seen from Figure 5 that the proportion of metaphors in categories of learnercentred and social reform is similar among the two groups. The differences mainly lie in another two categories: cultural transmission and social order, of which the metaphors from EFL teachers placed more attention to the teacher's role as a cultural transmitter (16.65% vs 11.7%), while the

metaphors  from  research  articles  emphasised  EFL  teacher's  responsibility  in  social  building (22.2% vs 10.4). In other words, these metaphors from research articles attached more importance to the teacher's responsibility in cultivating the talents to the needs of society than the Chinese EFL teachers did.

Within the social order category, as displayed in the following Table 4, metaphors from our two sources differ in their interpretation of social order. Metaphors used in research articles stress EFL teachers' duty in social responsibility; specifically, teachers are expected to be conscientious and  mould  the  students  in  a  way  that  suits  the  demands  of  society  both  pragmatically  and spiritually. However, metaphors within the social order category given by EFL teachers are limited to teacher-student interactions within a classroom, including specific metaphors like 'doctor/patient',  'parents/child',  and  'sun/sunflower',  which  highlight  the  teacher's  capacity  in correcting, disciplining and influencing the students in teaching practice. By comparing the sample metaphors within the social order category from the two groups, we can observe that besides the overall proportional difference, they also differ in epistemological orientation. Metaphors from the research article such as 'engineer' and 'dream builder' were viewing or evaluating the teacher's role from a result-oriented perspective. Besides, articles' metaphors consider education results as 'products', and treat the quality of the 'products' as the determining factor for conceptualizing teacher identity. On the contrary, metaphors given by EFL teachers are process-oriented, which are closely associated with their daily teaching experience rather than the final goal of education.
