Apart  from  the  rather  significant  variance  in  metaphors  of  the  social  order  and  cultural transmission categories, the distribution of metaphors among the other two categories is roughly consistent, with metaphors from questionnaires given by EFL teachers taking up a slightly higher percentage  in  each  column.  Within  the  two  categories,  learner-centered  metaphors  are  the predominant metaphors from both groups. Closely related to collaborative learning and social constructivism theory (Vygotsky, 1978), learner-centredness was introduced into EFL teaching in China at the beginning of the 21st century (Feng, 2006; Zhang, 2008); and since then, learnercentred teaching has been actively advocated in EFL teaching of Chinese universities.

The fact that learner-centred metaphors have taken the dominant position in both groups indicates  the  common  strong  emphasis  on  students'  participation  in  EFL  teaching.  The  EFL teacher's  ability  in  motivating  students'  learning  agency  has  been  stressed  both  from  the  proexternal  perception  of  EFL  teacher's  role  and  from  the  pro-internal  conceptualization.  Two possible  reasons  are  contributing  to  the  consistent high  concentration  on  learner-centred metaphors. First is that the spread of new educational theory in China usually adopts a top-down approach, teachers receive new theories from the authorities in a very efficient way. Second, one of the main criticisms for Chinese EFL teaching and learning is student's lack of competence in using  English,  the  essence  of  learner-centred  educational  philosophy  seems  to  be  the  perfect 'medicine' by emphasizing 'learning by doing' in English learning.

However,  putting  aside  the  suitability  and  effectiveness  of  learner-centred  teaching,  the consistently high proportion of learner-centred metaphors from both groups also reveals issues in Chinese  EFL  teachers'  identity  formation.  Especially  when  it's  almost  impossible  to  reach  a unanimous interpretation of learner-centredness among various stakeholders including teachers, teacher educators, policymakers and academics (Bremner, 2021), the consistent over-emphasis on learner-centredness may also result in a rise in teacher's role anxiety. Dillabough (1999) pointed out that efforts to realize uniformity and conformity threaten teachers' active location. Teachers must find their way of identity formation and development, and the process usually is long and complex (Mawhiney & Xu, 1997), which is inevitable due to the individual characteristics  of teachers.  When  one  category  of  the  framework  is  consistently  over-emphasized,  the  features advocated by this category would naturally attract more attention and exert more influence on EFL teachers, resulting in less visibility of other essential components in teacher identity formation. For example,  cultural  transmission  is  the  predominant  task  of  teachers  in  the  traditional  Chinese sociocultural context; however, as can be seen from Figure 4, teacher metaphors attributed to this category account for less than 20%. We can sense from the criticism of the 'bucket' metaphor that as  long  as  teachers  don't  pay  special  attention  to  students'  engagement,  the  teacher's  role  in transmitting knowledge and cultural heritage is usually subjected to critical examination. Under

this  circumstance,  the  social  and  cultural  threshold  for  teachers  to  bring  public  attention  to  a different focus is higher, and even if another category is highlighted, it's usually shadowed by the central focus.

Teacher identity is never a definite result of a certain process, and anxiety cannot be simply understood as an obstacle in identity formation. The pressure and anxiety in this dynamic process are unavoidable and also necessary. However, the process would be hampered when its dynamics were challenged by the reduction of structural diversity. In other words, when the social narrative about teachers is narrowed down to more fixed or specified images, the flexible space left for EFL teachers to negotiate and mediate their role as a teacher would become limited too. The process is almost paradoxical in some way, as harmony and conflict are both needed to keep teacher identity formation  a  dynamic  process.  Harmony  between  the  internal  and  external  perception  of  the teacher's role is beneficial to the alleviation of the pressure and anxiety in the process; meanwhile, the  competition  between  various  sub-identities  is  the  main  source  of  vitality  for  the  teacher's personal growth. The balance between the degree of consistency and the amount of discrepancy between the internal and external perceptions of the EFL teacher's role is the key to maintaining a healthy and dynamic process for teacher identity formation and development.


## Conclusion


The paper has compared the teacher metaphors collected through anonymous questionnaires from EFL teachers in a Chinese Sci-tech university and those extracted from educational research articles published in quality academic journals (CSSCI) in China. Teacher metaphors from articles are seen as the reflection of a pro-external perception of the EFL teacher's role, while metaphors from questionnaires are considered as the demonstration of a pro-internal understanding of the EFL teacher's role. Through a structural comparison between the two groups of teacher metaphors, the  similarities  and  differences  in  metaphor  distribution  and  the  interpretation  of  specific metaphors within certain categories were presented. Moreover, possible reasons and effects of the consistency and discrepancy in EFL teacher's role perception were discussed, which can contribute to a deeper understanding of the role anxieties experienced by the EFL teachers in China.

From the comparison, the significant perceptive discrepancies in EFL teacher identity could be summarized into two main points. The results-oriented external perception of EFL teachers, which highlights teachers' responsibility in preparing suitable talents to meet the needs of society (Social Order), is contrasted with the process-oriented internal understanding of the EFL teacher's role,  which  lays  more  emphasis  on  the  teacher-student  relationship  in  the  teaching  process. Besides, the composition of teacher metaphors extracted from articles depicts a more generalized abstract image of EFL teachers, while the metaphors given by EFL teachers are more specific and diversified,  which  indicates  different  levels  of  generality  in  interpreting  EFL  teacher  identity between internal and external conceptualizations.

Apart from the discrepancies, the high concentration of learner-centred metaphors among the two groups encourages the teacher to rethink the assumptions they have about the teacher's identity,  reflect  on  the  identity  formation  process,  and  identify  the  contextual  influence  in  the process. The imbalanced distribution of teacher metaphors among the four categories may cause a rise in anxiety since it inevitably results in less visibility of other possible interpretations of the teacher's  role.  Besides,  the  high  proportion  of  learner-centred  metaphors  also  reflects  the efficiency  of  the  top-down  approach  in  introducing  and  implementing  a  certain  educational philosophy. But a unanimous efficient adoption of certain pedagogical approaches would naturally

require more self-adaption efforts from individual teachers. Especially considering the predominant role of the teacher as a cultural transmitter in the traditional sociocultural Chinese context, the shift to learner-centred teaching is rather dramatic; and the multiple interpretations of learner-centredness increase the complexity of the shift. Scaffolding is needed not just for students, but also for Chinese EFL teachers, especially when most of them lack teaching experience, and are  in  the  dynamic  process  of  identity  formation.  Therefore,  despite  the  seemingly  consistent results in all three categories between the two groups of metaphors, the imbalanced distribution of metaphors serves as the context for the rise of EFL teachers' role anxieties. The over-emphasis on learner-oriented teaching would undoubtedly facilitate EFL teachers' acceptance of this concept, but it reduces the visibility and restricts the independent development of other sub-identities at the same time. The diversity of EFL teachers' sub-identities could be compromised, increasing the chances of teachers' early attrition and burnout.

It  can  be  concluded  from  the  analysis  that  the  main  influencing  factors  of  Chinese  EFL teacher's rise in role anxiety include the discrepancies between EFL teacher's roles between the external and internal perceptions, and the imbalanced distribution of teacher metaphors among the four categories of the metaphor-categorization system, especially the consistent over-emphasis on being 'learner-centred in EFL teaching. The significance of this research is that by comparing the two groups of teacher metaphors both individually and structurally, the EFL teachers' awareness of their identity formation can be raised, and they are stimulated to give more thought to the reasons for  the  similarities  and  differences  between  their  understanding  of  the  teacher's  role  and  the external conceptualization of this role. The benefits of a clearer understanding of the process and the reasons would help them develop a critical evaluation of various descriptions of EFL teachers, be more objective when it comes to self-evaluation, and be more confident when encountering setbacks in their personal development.

One suggestion for the external stakeholders concerning the ease of EFL teachers' anxiety is to enhance the engagement of front-line EFL teachers of Chinese universities in the enactment of educational policies as well as the promotion of certain educational philosophies, in this way the role-model metaphors promoted by the context would fit better into teacher's specific teaching process, rather than relying too much on the "end-products" of education. Besides, the delegation of  more  rights  to  EFL  teachers  in  Chinese  universities  in  choosing  a  suitable  educational philosophy as well as pedagogical approaches stands a better chance of motivating teachers to be more creative  in  curriculum  design.  It's  also  recommended  that  educational  policymakers  and authorities could give EFL teachers an appropriate amount of time and space to reflect on their teaching independently, and delegate the power to choose the direction, approach and time for adjustment. Besides, a diversified understanding of the teacher's role should be encouraged; if each sub-identity enjoys the relatively same amount of attention rather than high concentration on one particular category, a more flexible context can be created, providing sustainable energy for continuous dynamic teacher identity development.

## Methods


This chapter explores how boundaries and moments of evaluation interact in a emerging research discipline. The aims are to specify an analytical perspective that can direct further inquiries and to provide a basis for future research by suggesting a focus on a particular construction of the object of analysis, a set of issues, and a group of interactions. As such, while it the discussion relies on empirical data, it does not attempt a systematic analysis or pretend to draw from an exhaustive dataset. This inquiry began with a seemingly straightforward empirical issue, necessary descriptive work in the service of a larger question: in the Swedish artistic research field as it stood in 2021, who were the 'peers' in peer review? Another framing of this question could use insider/outsider dichotomies, demarcation problems, or boundary work. What kinds of people counted as 'insiders' for the purposes of evaluation? Whose judgment counted when there were publications to be reviewed, applications to be evaluated, awards to be granted? This (probably inevitably) led to a more complicated set of questions, represented here as: in the Swedish artistic research field, when are insider/outsider dichotomies made meaningful? When are they minimized, pushed aside, or rejected?

I draw on a body of documentary evidence which initially focused on Swedish doctoral programs and national science council funding, but snowballed out from there as I followed references and citations wherever they led. The Swedish artistic research field is embedded in and interacts with others - Nordic, European, and global communities of artists, artistic researchers, university professors, curators, and art critics, to name just a few.  I concentrate on the Swedish field, including voices from those other contexts when they speak within it.

The  evidence considered here includes dissertations, written evaluations, funders' reports, publications from the past twenty years, and documentation from seminars, symposia, conferences, and exhibitions. Sometimes, data collection was systematic. For example, I noted the volumes shelved together as relevant to 'artistic research' at the library of one of the PhD-granting art schools and worked through the list one by one; I also collected evaluation reports for research funding applications, available through the Swedish principle of public access to official documents. Other data was collected ad hoc. For example, I followed references into particularistic rabbit holes, and I attended events as my interest, schedule, and budget allowed. The dataset follows artistic research as it interacts with Swedish and Nordic art worlds and, occasionally, with the general public through criticism published in print and online arts/culture magazines, newspaper, television, and radio reports, and documentation from public performances and exhibitions. I also draw on notes from my participation in public events. I have been an occasional participant in the field since at least 2013, when the term 'artistic research' first appeared in my notes. My role is as a researcher in another discipline with a theoretical and empirical focus on art, work, and value (e.g. Gerber 2017, Gerber 2019). I regularly attend events, sometimes speak at or teach in art and design schools, and co-supervise an artistic research PhD student. My notes record observations, quotes, interactions, and my impressions of exhibitions, performances, and audience reactions. These serve me now by illuminating the interplay of publications and inperson interactions as I develop a systematic investigation of the research field. As an exploratory study, the scope is limited. To preserve anonymity, minor details have been changed in reporting from my notes and materials that are not taken from the public record. All translations from Swedish to English, and any mistakes, are my own.


## Is it art?


In a widely-distributed yearbook on artistic research produced by the national research council, an artist sketched a vision of the future for her field with a focus on method. She was among the first in the Nordics to earn a practice-based PhD and is still influential, sitting on the editorial board of the leading peer-reviewed journal of artistic research and delivering keynotes. For her, the line between artistic practice and artistic research is rarely well-defined: 'Research is a normal part of artistic work in many areas of contemporary art (in the form of exploration, investigation, trial and error), but only rarely developed into a formal research inquiry.' According to this author, the reason art has not always developed into something recognized as 'artistic research' is clear: the purpose of the research is not usually 'knowledge as such' (Arlander 2014:30); 'the outcome being sought is not primarily to increase our knowledge and understanding, but to produce a new work' (Arlander 2014:33). The relation, then, between artistic practice and artistic research - whether or not the research involved is formalized as 'artistic research'  - is ideally a natural, productive, and generative one. And generally, among artists (both those who do and do not claim that their activities fall under the umbrella of 'artistic research') it is common to shrug and assert that research is only a label: 'Words like 'research' and 'investigation' have become a part of the rhetoric of art, along with 'radical' and 'critical'' (Petersson and Sandström 2015).

We usually see artistic research distinguished from artistic practice through its home in the academy or the label placed on its funding. There is a widespread view among artists that the main reason to enter a PhD program in artistic practice or apply for artistic research funding is the funding itself - or, in the terms that matter in this community, the time. They may underestimate how much the academy will resocialize them to new norms, but frequently artists compare PhD programs favorably to other funding sources, pointing to the stable and relatively high salaries and the distance from market forces that doctoral employment allows. A doctoral student told me, at a conference on artistic research, 'I enjoy the artistic research thing. I don't feel pressure to produce.' A visual artist who was among the first to complete a PhD in Sweden reflected on this issue ten years later in an art magazine: 'In the fine arts a number of interesting and time-intensive projects have been developed, in a way that would not have been possible through other contemporary art platforms' (Petersson and Sandström 2015). Another Swedish artist expressed a similar view: now head of a large Norwegian art school with a number of PhD candidates, they put the matter bluntly: 'many have found the PhD programme to be an excellent opportunity, offering three years' paid employment and time to focus on one's work.' (Breivik 2021). For those with experience in both artistic practice and artistic research, the relationships between the two are fairly easy, and the management of any purported boundary is highly pragmatic. Institutional links and funding are at the core of the definition for those actually engaged in practices that they call - and that others recognize as - artistic research. An MA student, debriefing with their supervisor after a conference on artistic research, perhaps said it best: 'When you're applying for money and things, then it's research. I get it.' Their supervisor nodded.

It is possible that specific features of the Swedish education system enable the smooth relationship between artistic practice and artistic research. Elsewhere, artistic research is often compelled to fit itself to the scientific research mold, but in Sweden this is not strictly necessary. As discussed above, the Swedish Higher Education Act introduced important changes in the 1990s by promoting 'artistic research' based on 'artistic grounds', entirely distinct from the 'scientific grounds' that underpin most other activities called, more simply, 'research' (SFS 1992:1434). In the law, 'artistic grounds' are not defined (and neither are

'scientific grounds'), and there have been limited efforts in practice to define such a basis for research. As in the sciences, research on artistic grounds has bumped along diverse lines of inquiry, with irregular and not always impactful inquiries into the philosophical plausibility of the enterprise.

For many reasons, the line between artistic practice and artistic research seems fuzzy at best to most practitioners. The artist quoted above leading the Norwegian academy rejected the notion of a strong dichotomy between artistic and academic research: 'The question of academicisation is up to those of us who work here. We have the opportunity to influence what the academy should be' (Breivik 2021). Those actually engaged in artistic research seem only sporadically concerned with the strictures and bureaucracy that we might imagine comes part and parcel with the academy. One artist, now head of artistic research for one of the large art schools, said in a panel discussion: 'When my doctoral cohort started, they asked us what artistic research could be. I kind of thought that the university should have had a clearer idea, but it gave us a lot of freedom' (Dziurlikowska et al. 2011). Among those active in the Swedish field, there seems to be limited appetite for a firm demarcation between artistic practice and artistic research.

But the analyst seeking strong statements distinguishing artistic practice from artistic research will find a wealth of such articulations, if they look long enough. We find one such statement in a leading Nordic art journal: 'Art as research […] is a combination of contradictory elements since practicing fine art is incompatible with adhering to an academic system of rules.' The author claims that artistic research 'is unfree art, conducted according to the terms of academic research. […] So-called 'artistic research' is undergoing a formalisation, disciplinisation, and academisation that renders it a mimetic and subservient replica of academic research' (Ericsson 2020). Another author, from the pages of that same journal: 'If it is determined by a grading committee, the art is no longer free; then it is something other than fine art in the historical sense. Artistic research, for example. […] If there are artistic researchers who can still distinguish between free and unfree art - and understand why that distinction matters - they haven't made themselves heard.' This author concluded his essay with a sneer at 'A new artistic ideal: the second-rater, perfectly adapted for an increasingly authoritarian age'  (Petersson 2020).  Having located symbolic boundaries between artistic practice and artistic research, the analyst also finds the valorization and devaluation that so often accompanies such boundary work. The boundary work seen here typically promotes a specific vision of autonomy, freedom, and purity that is held by these authors to be central to traditional fine arts practice and impossible in 'so-called 'artistic research''. But that same analyst, looking more closely, will notice something strange: only a small, highly vocal subset of those engaged with the artistic research field actually engage in this kind of boundary work on a regular basis. They also tend to be art historians and critics - not those actually active in the practice of artistic research, nor from artists who do not self-identify as researchers.

The boundary work of these historians and critics usually takes the form of forceful statements, as though the rightness of such views is self-evident. Very little of an art/research dichotomy can be seen amongst practitioners in the Swedish artistic research field - but that doesn't mean that the moral valence of the art/not-art binary has lost its power for those aiming to erect and protect the boundary. Art historians and critics claim that they are necessary participants in this burgeoning field, lest artists speak for themselves (which would, by definition, damage their freedom, autonomy, and purity - according to art historians and critics). But as they try valiantly to differentiate 'free' and 'unfree' art, the artistic research field has typically shrugged and gone about their work.

Those engaged in artistic research challenge the purity-and-danger framework (Douglas 2005) promoted by art historians and critics - but they do it gently, referring to their own experience whenevidence is required. An artist, head of an art school, writes in an art journal: 'The art academy, with its affiliations with the artistic tradition's understanding of freedom, as well as the academic tradition of open critical discussion and the development of free thought, provides opportunities for artistic practice, not limitations' (Arrhenius 2020). Another artist writes in an evening tabloid, 'There are benefits to artistic research, like the legal protections afforded researchers. It makes the academy an attractive place, with a sort of freedom that, in any case, is greater than that outside the university' (Frisk 2020b). An artist tells me, offhand, that she's excited to begin her new doctoral position because she will finally have access to a crucial archive that is restricted to credentialed researchers. Compare the casual tone of these remarks made by artistic researchers to the rigid pronouncements of onlookers; consider the role of boundary work in this context, and the roles of those who promote it.

It is the quiet but constant pushback of practitioners that suggests an uneven commitment to boundary work dichotomizing artistic practice and artistic research. I remember a conversation with a tenured professor active in artistic research who described being 'attacked' by a collaborator, a researcher from the sciences, in a public seminar. The scientist demanded to know where he stood on a particular, highly polarized framing of the distinctions between art and artistic research. He did not take a side; he did not, on later reflection, accept the premises of the question. But in the moment he recalled feeling stuck, feeling bullied. The two no longer speak. There is a value in drawing lines between dichotomized objects, not least in the clarity of mind it can offer. And in a public conversation between two actors - one committed to boundary work, the other open perhaps to the search for and cultivation of boundary objects - the former will appear momentarily to have the upper hand, with their articulate and logical arguments. But if we follow these two researchers out of the seminar room and into the future a different set of images comes into focus. A look at his CV ten years on shows that the scientist (whose engagement with artistic researchers looks in hindsight like a minor dalliance) walks away, never again to collaborate with members of far-afield disciplines, much less artistic researchers. The artistic researcher, still active in the field and now a well-cited, well-funded, and highly networked figure, shrugs and continues his work. If we look at the seminar - a moment of public performance - boundary work seems crucially important. But if we pay attention to the rest, we notice which researcher's approach and work has contributed to the artistic research field, and another view becomes possible.


## Is it research?


Within artistic research in Sweden, the boundary with artistic practice is fuzzy and pragmatic. That is not to say that there are no strong boundaries salient in the artistic research field in Sweden. The answer to the question 'is it art?' is waved off with a yes, obviously; it is the question 'is it research?' that requires real work in this field.

Artistic researchers regularly collaborate with researchers trained in scientific disciplines. Such projects are viewed positively, and artists point to the possibilities of cross-disciplinary work when they move into the artistic research field. Artistic researchers draw creatively on an idiosyncratic mix of scholarly and scientific research as they deem it useful, and rarely reject individual findings or theoretical tools when they are introduced to their arena. But they often draw a boundary between their activities and something like science-with-a-capital-s. This a science not in the English-language sense, but in the Germanic languages sense, where

vetenskap / wissenschaft means simply something like 'systematic, evidence-based inquiry'. In the Swedish context, disciplines whose English names indicate allegiance to the humanities and to alternative traditions of research and knowledge are instead termed 'sciences': art history is 'konstvetenskap', or art science; cultural studies is 'kulturvetenskap', or culture science. It is against that specific notion of science that those speaking for artistic research position the field against - a science that centers not a single 'scientific method' but systematic, evidence-based inquiry.

That version of science is loose and rangy given the wide array of disciplines it contains, but it is constant and powerful in the artistic research context. When an audience member at a symposium asks about the differences between scientific and artistic research, we hear the head of a large art school in Sweden, an artist and artistic researcher, answer confidently: 'It's not that we want to search for a truth, but something else.' Sometimes that 'something else' is positioned as explicitly anti-scientific, as when an artistic research PhD student told a tabloid newspaper that it might be best to 'think of artistic research as a fancy name for the mad scientist - a person who fulfils our need for the irrational' (Aagård 2009). Systematicity in method and argument are not necessarily seen as virtues, even in the doctoral thesis: a review of the first thesis in literary composition notes that the project's method can hardly be pinned down before describing it approvingly thus: 'It could be described using terms such as 'montage' and 'juxtaposition'. Instead of separating out and using hierarchically organised arguments, processing the research object (even if such operations can never be entirely avoided), different 'realisations' are placed next to each other to create resonance' (Olsson 2015:63). As discussed above, in this context there is a clear alternative to scientific research - 'artistic research' on 'artistic grounds'. And while a positive definition of artistic grounds has not yet coalesced in this field, its negative definition is clear: artistic research is not scientific research, and should not be produced or judged according to the standards of scientific inquiry.

It is in questions of method and a vernacular philosophy of science that the boundary work between art and science become clear: the first artist cited above, in that yearbook text on method in artistic research, wrote that artistic research (like artistic practice) is often iterative and experimental by nature, adding that artistic research 'produces experimental knowledge but not mathematical knowledge. Thus artistic research differs from empirical research, which tries to find general laws.' The author continually positions artistic research in line with artistic practice and against scientific research; we are reminded that artistic research does not, and should not, aim to find 'general laws' or 'knowledge as such' (Arlander 2014:28-34).

Many scientific ideals - distance from the research object, structured argument - are dismissed in favor of an expanded vision of knowledge production. The stuff of science is available to artistic researchers, but to play with or remix, catch-as-catch-can. My notes record an exchange between two well-known figures in the Swedish artistic research community on stage at a symposium sponsored by the national research council; they had originally met when the first told the second at his dissertation defense, 'actually, you are doing sociology.' After glossing over the details of what 'doing sociology' might have meant, claiming that 'to really get into it would be to go too deep into sociological method', the first artist acknowledged slyly that there might be some differences between artistic research, as exemplified by the second artist's work, and actual sociological research: 'As a professional sociologist Bourdieu would be more interested in truth, in what actually happened. Which might be a point of conflict with artistic research.' The second artist and the room chuckled, and moved on.

Occasionally this boundary work between artistic and scientific research involves strange assertions about how scientific disciplines work. For example, in another panel at that same symposium, the head of a Swedish art school complained, 'People in the artistic research field are asked to explain a lot. You don't ask a researcher from another field to explain what they do.' Recall also the artistic researcher outlining her vision for the field above who suggested that empirical research always aims to find general laws; these statements are obviously untrue, but they are often repeated, and for participants in this burgeoning field they appear to feel true. The signs of widespread resonance - the repetition of these tropes about scientific research, the knowing nods and chuckles of the audience - speak to the strength of the boundary between artistic and scientific research in this context, and to the commitment to boundary work against judgment on 'scientific grounds' that can be seen in the artistic research community.

As discussed above, two questions are typical of those encountering the concept of artistic research for the first time.And those two questions, which boil down to 'is it art?' and 'is it research?', prompt the analyst to clarify the relations between art, research, and artistic research. Given the status of artistic research as an academic discipline, and the importance of boundary work in the development of disciplines, we look for boundary work. We expect artistic researchers to claim that what they do is neither art nor (scientific) research, but something else, something more. In fact only one of these dichotomies appears to matter in the Swedish artistic research field. Practitioners engage in boundary work against the norms, standards, and values of scientific inquiry, but are relaxed about blurred boundaries between artistic practice and artistic research - this despite the significant efforts of outsiders to promote stark distinctions.


## Artistic research?


If the boundaries between artistic practice and artistic research are unclear, and if artistic research is not scientific research, how do we know it is research? As we have seen, discussions around knowledge production are typically negative within the field - artistic researchers are not looking for generalizations or laws, are not looking to uncover previously unknown facts. Specific arguments for the knowledges that can be gained through artistic research are many, but no single argument has yet won out and come to define the aim of artistic research. But one vision of a move beyond the particular is widespread. It is tied to the need to build a body of knowledge to ground the discipline, and the need to communicate, critique, and improve research in progress. This is where  'method' comes into its own.

For a scientifically-trained analyst, artistic researchers use the term 'method' so often, and in so many ways, that the mind boggles. Recall the author  above who approved so warmly of a PhD thesis whose methods he could not quite grasp. Another positive review of another PhD thesis reads, 'The text provides no thorough discussion of methodology, but it does open with a few pithy theories on methodological approaches' (Östersjö 2014:67). An overview of the Swedish field states simply, 'In artistic research there are no standard methods. We have a great acceptance for individual or genre specific methods and the evolution of methods over time during the process of work and research' (Lilja 2015:56).

The most common notion of artistic research methodology is that it should derive from artistic practices and might be little more than 'clarifying what one actually tends to do, in what order and in what way' (Arlander 2014:34). Presently, this leads to minimal standardization. An

artist speaking to students at an art academy's annual 'research week' says confidently that 'You don't start with method as an artist; you finish and then you can go back and say, what was my method?'. One report on a funded project explains that the researcher's method was 'reflective practice', defined as 'a focus on the dancer's practice and experience of the artistic process.' The report pointed to phenomenology, but without the buttresses of citation and argumentation that would be expected in disciplines like my own (Wikström 2014:106). Still, method - or the language of method, at least - is seen as the key to presenting artistic research and its results to others both inside and outside the field.

Amongst themselves and in conversation with artists, artistic researchers are typically satisfied with seemingly vague gestures towards method. The performativity associated with methodological rigor in other disciplines is openly discussed in this field: witness the author of a state-of-the-field report who writes that 'In this context, the terms 'method' and 'methodology' are used in their broadest sense, in that they have their own aesthetic and carry with them their own gestures, discourse and history in an art work, setting up a kind of 'methodological aesthetic' that is generic in the practice of research' (Dyrssen 2015:182). This vision of method and its uses will be uncomfortable for those trained in traditional empirical methods in scientific disciplines, and likely has more in common with recently articulated methods like speculative design and ethnography of the future (Watts 2019; Lindström and Ståhl 2020). But the link between something understood here as 'method' and the promise of artistic research in terms of knowledge production is clear: an artist active in the field writes, 'Artistic research is built on the idea that artistic methods can reveal knowledge which, if made visible, can contribute not only to the artistic field but can be useful for other fields as well' (Frisk 2020a).

A perspective centered on boundary work or competition might doubt that those aiming to develop this burgeoning research field could accept such ambiguity when status and resources are at stake. But if we conceptualize field formation as cooperative, we might see how the boundary objects framework explains the role that 'method' plays in the artistic research field, enabling coordination in a rangy, loose assemblage of diverse practitioners. Star and Griesemer's foundational text identified a few types of boundary objects they saw in action not an exhaustive list, but a productive one to think with (Star and Griesemer 1989). Their notion of 'ideal types' as boundary objects is valuable here; centering method as a boundary object gives us leverage on how symbolic boundaries are both constructed and avoided in artistic research. In Star and Griesemer's telling, the ideal type is 'abstracted from all domains, and may be fairly vague. However, it is adaptable to a local site precisely because it is fairly vague; it serves as a means of communicating and cooperating symbolically - a 'good enough' road map for all parties' (Star and Griesemer 1989:410). Sociologists have internalized a version of the ideal type, with a Weberian view on the utility and adaptability of concepts like 'democracy' (Weber 1949). While Star and Griesemer saw standardized methods as key to collaboration, it seems plausible that field-building might differ from collaborative scientific work. If  'method' is considered an ideal-type boundary object used by artistic researchers to relate both to artistic practices and to other researchers, its multiplex meanings begin to settle into patterns.

The expanded concept of method widespread in the artistic research field allows practitioners to communicate and find common ground with other researchers - both artistic researchers from disciplines far afield from one's own and with scientific researchers. A distinguished professor writes, 'In regular art production, we normally do not need to define our methods or express ourselves in relation to others. The need arises only in relation to an educational

situation or in research, or if we seek dialogue to develop our ways of working' (Lilja 2015:56). The language of methods also allows artistic researchers to differentiate 'artistic research' from the rest of their artistic practice. This differentiation is a kind of storytelling: a contextualization used to help one audience make a certain kind of sense of an artwork, one removed later for a different audience. This is one way that the fuzzy boundary between artistic practice and artistic research is managed in practice - particular practices, objects, and outcomes are narrated differently for art and research audiences, just as a CV is adjusted for prospective employers. But there are limits to the creative uses of  terminology. Method as an ideal type can be highly productive among artistic researchers and in relations with art worlds, but it is problematic in relations with scientific researchers and the academy.

Star and Griesemer's original article on boundary objects used language that I initially struggled with. They speak of marginality to refer both to people inhabiting multiple social worlds and to the boundary obects that bring them together. While I understood their oldfashioned use of the term in regards to people it was harder to accept in reference to boundary objects; the notion of the 'boundary' is also spatial (addressed in Star 2010). Drawing a venn diagram to conceptualize the role of boundary objects, perhaps one was required to draw them near edges. But  boundary objects seemed anything but marginal to the diverse groups who tried to work together - they were central to their activities in various ways. I have since realized the insight captured in that old-fashioned use of 'marginal': boundary objects cannot be made of stuff that strikes too deeply at the heart of one group but not the other, or they will be vulnerable to the kinds of boundary work that can threaten collaborative processes.

'Method' as an ideal-type boundary object works for artistic researchers in their relations to artists and other artistic researchers because it is somewhat marginal to their practice. But it is dangerous in the interface with scientific researchers, because for many of them 'method' is not at all marginal - it is central to the enterprise, and is a core mechanism of boundary work in everyday practice. It can be extraordinarily hard for scientists and those who are influenced by their epistemologies to accept method as an ideal type, as a boundary object. The adaptation of methods talk from the sciences is fraught, and vulnerable to attack when the ideal-typical 'method' in productive use in the artistic research field butts up against scientific methodologies. When those oriented to boundary work look carefully at method in artistic research, they don't always see something they recognize - and that can be upsetting. The productive misunderstandings that method as a boundary object can engender in diverse collaborations are fragile, temporary, and provisional.

A look back at the Swedish artistic research field over two decades shows that both the impulse to engage in boundary work and the effort involved in suspending such efforts enough to collaborate around boundary objects are unevenly distributed across the field. While generous relations to boundary objects like 'method' are ubiquitous among artists both those engaged in and distant from artistic research - relations between artistic researchers and scientific researchers are fragile because the scientifically trained are so strongly invested in their hard-won disciplinary expertise in things like 'methods,' 'research,' and 'knowledge.'


## Discussion: boundary objects, boundary work


This chapter began with an anecdote: that first public failure, a shock. Why did this first public failure happen now - especially if the artistic research field appears disinclined towards the kinds of closure, clear demarcations, and boundary work?

It is difficult to identify what was found lacking Szyber's work from reading the examination committee's written evaluation (which is publicly available). The language is harsh and certain but unspecific. For those familiar with Swedish artistic research one thing stands out: the evaluation cites Szyber's written text, specifying the pages with which it engages, but does not clearly discuss his submitted artworks in any detail in its arguments, though the evaluation is to be made on artistic grounds. The evaluation is often scholarly, solidifying the impression that Szyber's written work was treated as a text in the scientific research tradition rather than as an artwork in itself or a corollary to his other artworks. At one point the evaluators write that 'much to our regret, the candidate opted to omit some crucial debate and reference as well as statistical and/or qualitative evidence or analysis in the area of artistic, gender, postcolonial, feminist, media and performance studies'. To an outsider, it seems that the expectations of the examination committee were not only out of step with local norms; they were also incompatible with the standards of the supervisor and the other professors who enthusiastically recommended the project for the defense and who continue to stand by their judgment (Stockholms konstnärliga högskola 2020)

That disjuncture comes into focus if  boundary objects take priority in our analysis, if we assume that artistic research is typically and historically a collaborative problem to be solved - a project we undertake together - rather than an opportunity to draw lines, to erect a boundary around the field of legitimate artistic research. Looking back, Szyber's defense has the hallmarks of the Covid-pandemic artistic research defense. Despite the emphasis on art objects in the Swedish field, his examiners could not attend an exhibition or performance in person with others, instead working alone at home from video files on small screens. They did not experience the artworks as the artist intended, or observe audience interactions with the works. And despite ambivalence about the place of scholarly texts in the field, the written text appears to have constituted the majority of the work evaluated in Szyber's case. In that evaluation the oblique, indirect, and quiet references common in art objects are ignored, and specific references to the ways that art objects might have represented forms of inquiry, analysis, or conceptual development - or failed to do so - are largely absent.

A recurring theme of the boundary objects literature is the conviviality displayed in successful collaborations; comparative studies show the fragililty of boundary-object-enabled cooperation, and how easily boundary work can get in the way (e.g. Schindler 2019). Research on the architecture of evaluation has consistently shown that organizational constraints, whether well-motivated or adopted ad hoc, have enormous influence on outcomes (Langfeldt 2001; Rivera and Tilcsik 2019). Szyber's defense deviated from tradition in significant ways. Typically, examiners travel to and spend time together in the local context; they engage with artworks at exhibitions and performances, usually in the company of audiences, and they talk, walk, and dine with the local artistic research community. They have the time and tools to orient themselves to the local iteration of artistic research - the tools being the local working definitions of ideal types like 'methods'. None of that happened at Szyber's defense, and it seems unlikely that the unusual architecture of evaluation played no role in the outcome. Moments of failure in artistic research are important because they represent attempts to draw a symbolic boundary that links to specific social boundaries. In the case discussed here, an artistic researcher's PhD hung in the balance. That social boundary has inequalities attached and, of course, that's often the point of boundary work.

Conclusion

To understand the contemporary artistic research field in Sweden, one might imagine a set of overlapping spheres rather than a set of binary relations.  A category of 'research' touches both science and art, rather than naturally belonging exclusively to the sciences:

<!-- image -->

This allows one in turn to imagine a 'knowledge' produced through research activities that reaches more broadly than a category that centers propositional knowledge (Vaage 2019). It also clarifies how scientific practice - though we don't usually call it that - is not so different from artistic practice, either in its definition or its relation to the things recognized as research.

This exploratory chapter has shown how boundaries and moments of evaluation interact in an emerging research discipline. With an inquiry focused on the past twenty years of the Swedish artistic research field, I have demonstrated that insider/outsider dichotomies are sometimes made meaningful - as when artistic researchers draw clear boundaries between their activities and scientific research - and sometimes rejected, as when artistic researchers refuse others' attempts to distinguish between artistic practice and artistic research. The rejection of dichotomies, especially when confronted with those promoting such distinctions, requires tools and commitments - boundary objects like an expanded notion of 'method', and an orientation to generous relations. But boundary objects work best when their centrality or marginality to diverse groups' practices is roughly constant; when one group sees them as central to their identity while another is more ambivalent, relations between the two groups will be vulnerable to the kinds of boundary work that can threaten collaborative processes. Finally, in institutional contexts that minimize sociability or privilege public performance, those hoping to minimize the effects of boundary work can lose ground to those seeking to draw lines.

Collaborative work is hard, and requires coordination. The boundary objects literature shows us how, even without top-down coordination, diverse groups can work well together, given time, trust, and a common goal. In the development of the artistic research field in Sweden a fundamentally cooperative approach has reigned. Attempts to draw lines - between art and artistic research, between method and mess - have mostly been met with a shrug and redoubled efforts towards communication, collaboration, and community. But the boundary objects that have been relationally productive carry specific vulnerabilities. Even if the proponents of boundary work are few, they often have articulate logic and moral passion on their side; the hurried digital meetings that have replaced loitering engagements with local communities in recent years thanks to an ongoing pandemic likely raise up their voices at the expense of others. New fields of research, new kinds of knowledge, and innovation can come from the collaborative work made possible through generous relations to boundary objects but these need institutional support and an architecture to stabilize the field. Brief, high-stakes

meetings would be no one's choice if the goal is field-building; for boundary work, they can suffice.

## Introduction


During the past 75 years, under-five mortality rates have declined precipitously in low- and middle-income countries. This demographic shift is not only significant in signaling improvements in human health, but also because demographers have long theorized mortality decline is a catalyst for further social and demographic change (Chesnais 1992; Lloyd and Ivanov 1988; Mason 1997; Notestein 1945).

Despite demographers' theoretical interest in how lower under-five mortality conditions will affect individuals' perceptions, decisions, and behaviors, and ultimately influence subsequent macro-level population processes in low- and middle-income countries, we know little about how pervasive experiences of child mortality remain in these settings. Demographers tend to track child mortality conditions by calculating annualized death rates, paying little mind to how these annualized rates aggregate in the minds and lives of the surviving population. Seeking to remedy this empirical blind spot, recent research has studied mothers' cumulative burden of child mortality, demonstrating that under-five death remains a shockingly common maternal experience across the global south (Smith-Greenaway et al. 2021; Smith-Greenaway and Trinitapoli 2020). In many low- and middle-income countries, upwards of one-third to onehalf of mothers have ever experienced the death of a young child (Smith-Greenaway et al. 2021).

Although this research offers a first step towards understanding the pervasiveness of child mortality in contemporary global south populations, even amid historically low under-five mortality rates, it offers only an abbreviated view. Specifically, these estimates overlook the fact that many women enter motherhood having already intimately experienced under-five mortality in their immediate families in their role as siblings. Experiencing a sibling's premature death is known to influence women's behaviors and preferences even long after the death occurred

(Broussard and Weitzman 2020; Finnegan 2020; Pebley, Delgado, and Brinemann 1979; SmithGreenaway and Weitzman 2020). As such, studying the burden of sibling and offspring death will better clarify the diffuse nature by which recent cohorts of women in low- and middleincome countries continue to intimately experience the death of young children, and will more accurately clarify the potential for under-five mortality to affect the surviving population than solely considering one or the other.

Studying both sibling and offspring losses jointly can further clarify the extent to which these consequential experiences are intergenerationally correlated. The outsized burden of child loss borne by certain women in a single generation is well-established (Bocquier et al. 2021; Das Gupta 1990; van Dijk 2019; Sastry 1997), however, we know little about whether 'death clustering' extends vertically across kinship networks. Social science research demonstrates that many health (dis)advantages pass down from one generation to the next (Elo 2009), suggesting the same may be true of the premature death of young children in low- and middle-income countries. Of course, dramatic demographic and social change in these settings could protect women from experiencing the same reproductive adversities that their mothers experienced decades earlier. That is, secular declines in mortality and fertility could produce a generational chasm-rendering a mother's reproductive experience less predictive of her daughter's reproductive fate. Alternatively, this demographic change could simply reinforce existing health inequality (Stoebenau et al. 2021).

Considering how little we know about how contemporary low- and middle-income country populations experience under-five mortality, including the overall frequency and distribution of intimate losses, this study has two empirical goals. First, the study clarifies the prevalence of women in three birth cohorts (1960s, 1970s, and 1980s) in 50 low- and middle-

income countries that have intimately experienced under-five death, either via a sibling or offspring death, and identifies how this prevalence has-or has not-changed across these three birth cohorts. Second, the study assesses the extent of overlap in exposures to under-five sibling and offspring death and how it has (or has not) changed across birth cohorts. Together, the results clarify the potential for under-five mortality to have lingering consequences for population dynamics and health-despite overall declines in annualized under-five mortality rates.  Moreover, the findings demonstrate that repeated life course exposures are a fundamental feature of how disadvantaged women in contemporary low- and middle-income countries experience child mortality conditions, and that demographic change is not particularly disruptive to, but instead supportive of, generational continuity.


## Background



## The theoretical significance of tracking experiences of sibling and offspring loss


Child death is not only an extreme form of health disadvantage, but also as an experience that can leave an indelible mark on those who endure it. Thus, clarifying the prevalence of women in low- and middle-income countries who have been intimately exposed to under-five mortality, and how this is, or is not, changing over time, is theoretically relevant for at least two reasons.

First, exposure to under-five death in one's immediate family can be a source of poor mental health. In terms of one's own child's death, extensive research on low-mortality populations has outlined the consequential nature of a child's death for parents. Having one's own child die is a major source of stress, trauma, and grief with long-lasting implications for parents' health and wellbeing (Stroebe et al., 2007; Stroebe & Schut, 2005). Research shows that a child's death has significant and long-lived implications for parents' mental and physical

health, and even their own risk of mortality (Finnäs, Rostila, and Saarela 2018; Levav et al. 2000; Li et al. 2003, 2005; Rogers et al. 2008; Rostila, Mäki, and Martikainen 2018; Sanders 1980; Song et al. 2010; Stroebe and Schut 2005; Stroebe et al. 2007).

Correspondingly, an under-five child's death is a risk factor for parents' relationship dysfunction (Weitzman and Smith-Greenaway 2020), which can also have downstream consequences for surviving siblings' health and development, status attainment, and social mobility later in life (Goldberg 2013a, 2013b; Grant and Pike 2019). That is, couched in recognition that stress-inducing events can manifest in adversities that have intergenerational impacts, increasing research also demonstrates that a young sibling's death can have adverse consequences for individuals (Broussard and Weitzman 2020; Finnegan 2020; Fletcher et al. 2013a; Pebley et al. 1979). Together, the adverse consequences of bereavement for parents and siblings underscores the need to identify the total population burden of these experiences in lowand middle-income countries, and the extent to which they are changing over time.

Second, intimately experiencing a young child's death can shape people's outlook about the world-their sense of control and predictability, and the degree of uncertainty that occupies their minds and informs their decision-making. Exposure to premature death psychologically imprints people in a way that affects all sorts of behaviors from their risk taking and thinking about the future (Burke, Martens, and Faucher 2010; Pyszczynski, Greenberg, and Solomon 1999) to their fertility desires and preferences (Mathews and Sear 2008), and their overall approach to life (Nettle 2010). The psychological reach of intimate exposures to premature mortality in one's family further highlights the need to understand the totality of women's intimate exposures to child death in low- and middle-income settings-both in their natal and conjugal families. Attending to the population prevalence of adults who have intimately

experienced under-five death will clarify the potential for it to act as a continued source of population uncertainty, and driver of other demographic behaviors.


## Repeated mortality exposures: intergenerational clustering of under-five deaths?


The above literature implies that experiencing sibling or offspring mortality are consequential in their own right; it is possible, however, that experiencing under-five mortality in both one's natal and conjugal family is a fundamental feature of how disadvantaged women in contemporary low- and middle-income countries experience child mortality conditions. That is, studying both sibling and offspring loss may reveal the intergenerational clustering of these experiences; shared socioeconomic, behavioral, and health conditions could result in under-five deaths repeatedly scarring generations of the same family.

Beginning with the former, because socioeconomic disadvantage is tied to otherwise preventable deaths (Pamuk, Fuchs, and Lutz 2011), a woman's risk of experiencing offspring mortality may mirror that of her mother simply due to their similar positioning in the socioeconomic strata. Social scientists have long acknowledged that socioeconomic factors, like educational attainment, income, and occupation, are highly informed by those of one's parents (Carvalho 2012; Mare 2011a). Although this literature has focused almost exclusively on highincome populations, even in contexts of dramatic social and economic change, one's family background is highly indicative of one's position in the social strata (Carvalho 2012).

Intergenerational correlations in under-five deaths could also be borne out of the replication of life course patterns, and reproductive behaviors specifically, across generations. Reproductive outcomes, like a woman's age at first birth, marital context at the time of that birth, relationship stability, spacing of children, and total number of children correlate highly with those of her mother (Anderton et al. 1987; Axinn and Thornton 1992; Bates, Maselko, and

Schuler 2007; Booth and Kee 2009; Glick, Handy, and Sahn 2015; Kahn and Anderson 1992; Kumar, Bordone, and Muttarak 2016; Vidal et al. 2020; Wolfinger 2011). Given that each of these circumstances affects a child's likelihood of survival (DaVanzo et al. 2007, 2008; Pebley and Stupp 1987; Rutstein 2005), the replication of reproductive behaviors is another pathway by which a woman's experience as a parent, including the loss of an offspring, may come to mirror that of her mother.

As discussed above, a mother's bereavement, and a sibling's death, not only demarcates a family's disadvantage driven by other processes of inequality, but also reflects a vital conjuncture-a pivotal life course event that can subsequently influence the wellbeing of all family members going forward. In this way, having a bereaved mother, and experiencing a sibling death, could directly shape a woman's life course trajectory and ultimately elevate her own risk of bereavement when she herself becomes a mother. Exposure to stress-inducing events can manifest in adversities that have intergenerational impacts; as such, a child's premature death could come with long-term consequences for those-and the decedents of those-who endure it. In this way, child deaths may scar families, perpetuating health disadvantage among those impacted by the death, leaving subsequent generations themselves at risk of poor health and elevated risk of premature death (Umberson 2017).

One way this could occur is through the effect of death on a woman's parents. As described above, a child's death is a major source of stress, trauma, and grief with long-lasting implications for parents' health and wellbeing, as well as the stability and health of their marital relationship (Stroebe et al., 2007; Stroebe & Schut, 2005). Correspondingly, a child's death is a risk factor for family's subsequent wellbeing and stability (Weitzman and Smith-Greenaway 2020), which can ultimately have downstream consequences for surviving sibling's health and

development, status attainment, and social mobility later in life (Goldberg 2013a, 2013b; Grant and Pike 2019). Because a woman's adversities do not simply affect her own life chances but also those of her children (McEwen and McEwen 2017), adverse childhood events-in this case her loss of a sibling and her parents' loss of a child-may pattern her own children's chance of survival.

Beyond its consequences for her parents, losing a young sibling could also directly affect women's own wellbeing and outlook toward the future. As described above, what little we know about the implications of a sibling's death suggests that it can have significant, long-term consequences for individuals' subsequent socioeconomic achievements, risk-taking behaviors, and health and wellbeing (Fletcher et al. 2013b). Although some work emphasizes the surprising ways that sibling mortality can relate to having fewer children and safer childbearing behavior (Finnegan 2020; Kraehnert et al. 2019), other work outlines how sibling mortality can increase women's fertility intentions (Broussard and Weitzman 2020). It is thus possible that women desire more children and have them more quickly as a function of sibling bereavement, thereby elevating the risk of their child's death (Bocquier et al. 2021).

Overall, this work implies that women whose family history includes a sibling death may be more likely to experience the death of their own offspring. Yet, these family processes do not occur in isolation, but instead are intrinsically tied to the broader mortality and fertility landscape. Thus, in the next section, we describe how the immense social and demographic change in contemporary low- and middle-income countries in recent decades could reinforce-or disrupt-intergenerational linkages.

## Demographic and social change: subvert or support intergenerational clustering of underfive deaths?

The extent of intergenerational clustering of under-five deaths could change as a country undergoes the transition from high mortality and fertility to low levels of each. In terms of the former, mortality decline could weaken intergenerational clustering in child death, diminishing the predictive power of one's sibling death history for their own risk of offspring death. Asia, Latin America, and Africa have experienced sharp reductions in under-five mortality rates since the 1950s: under-five mortality rates were between four (Africa) and seven (Latin America and the Caribbean) times lower in 2015 than in 1950. These mortality improvements are, in large part, due to expanding infrastructural and service provisions (Headey and Palloni 2019; Joshi and Schultz 2013). Given evidence that mortality decline reduces inequality in the risk of under-five death (Sastry 2004), this diffuse social change could dramatically dampen the salience of one's mother's history for their own children's survival.

Sizeable fertility decline has accompanied these under-five mortality declines: the total fertility rate has fallen by nearly two children in Africa, and by approximately four children in Asia and Latin America. Some theoretical models emphasize how fertility decline disrupts intergenerational similarities, effectively working to equalize differences between families through the homogenization of family life towards smaller, more comparably resourced families (Beaujouan and Solaz 2019; Lachaud, LeGrand, and Kobiané 2017), further suggesting the weakening of intergenerational clustering of under-five mortality exposures.

On the other hand, recent demographic and social changes may have exacerbated, or at least left unbothered, between-family inequality, facilitating persistent or growing intergenerational correlations in under-five deaths. Countering the notion that demographic

change can act as a schism between generations-disrupting the longstanding reproduction of the social order-other work emphasizes the potential for demographic change to accentuate patterns of inequality, further amplifying the salience of one's family history to their future experiences (Thornton, Chang, and Sun 1984). Because better resourced families are among the first to enjoy lower mortality and to pursue lower fertility (Murphy 1999; Rotering 2017), mortality and fertility decline could work to concentrate disadvantage through a set of reinforcing demographic processes across generations (Stoebenau et al. 2021). Such a possibility is consistent with the fact that many low- and middle-income countries are increasingly some of the world's most unequal societies (Firebaugh 2009).


## Analytic Approach



## Data and sample


We make use of data from the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) Program, a long-running, international survey program that has collected mortality data from women ages 15-49 years-old in dozens of low- and middle-income countries. Critical to the current study, the DHS Program collects detailed birth histories from women, including for deceased offspring. The DHS Program also includes a sibling history module in many countries. The module is intended to track adult mortality conditions in countries that lack civil registration and vital statistics data (Feehan and Borges 2021; Masquelier 2013; Obermeyer et al. 2010). Together, the sibling and birth history data allow us to investigate women's under-five mortality exposures in both their natal and conjugal families.

An important feature of DHS Program data is that they are standardized across countries and rounds of data collection within each country, and thus facilitate a multi-country, multi-

cohort study design. In total, we make use of data for 50 countries in six geopolitical world regions. Within the 50 focal countries, we analyze data from 144 surveys, collected between 1992 and 2020, allowing us to track the level and distribution of under-five mortality exposure and how each have changed (or have not changed) over time.  Specifically, we create synthetic 2 cohorts using the repeated, cross-sectional data, categorizing women into one of three birth cohorts: 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s.  Figure 1 depicts the time over which the DHS Program 3 interviewed women, and thus they retrospectively reported on their exposure to sibling and offspring mortality, by cohort. The 1960s cohort completed interviews between 1992 and 2010 (at ages 32-49); the 1970s cohort completed interviews between 1992 and 2020 (at ages 22-49); and the 1980s cohort completed interviews between 1995 and 2020 (at ages 15-40 years old).

## Key measures


Under-five sibling and offspring death . Our key measures include independent indicators of whether women have ever experienced under-five sibling or offspring death (separately), as well as a combined indicator of whether they have experienced either. Beginning with the death of a sibling, the sibling module collects information on each of the respondent's siblings born to the same mother, including the sibling's birth year, vital status, and for deceased siblings, the year of death. With this information, we generated an indicator for woman's exposure to an under-five sibling's death (=1).  We also account for women's exposure to the death of one of their own 5 under-five-year-old children. We make use of information derived from a detailed birth history, including information on the mother's year of first birth, each offspring's birth year, vital status, and, for deceased offspring, year of death.

Some women in our data have not completed childbearing, creating censoring in our data. We do not account for this censoring in descriptive statistics; however, we do in the multivariable analyses of the intergenerational clustering of under-five death. Specifically, we model women's experience of under-five offspring loss as a time-varying outcome in a hazard framework, with the hazard beginning at the year of their first birth and person-years as the unit of analysis. Each person-year that a mother contributes is coded =0 if she has not yet experienced an under-five-year-old child die, and =1 in the year she first experienced a child die before the age of 5. Even though some women in our data experience multiple sibling and offspring deaths, we generate binary indicators of ever-exposure to both, and estimate single-event hazard models, meaning that a woman no longer contributes observations after she experiences her first underfive offspring death. For example, a 35-year-old woman who became a mother at age 20 and experienced an under-five offspring death at age 30 contributes 11 person-years before exiting (=1). Some women, of course, never experience an under-five offspring death; these women exit the hazard at their age at the time of the survey. For example, a 35-year-old woman who became a mother at age 20 and has never experienced a child's death is right censored and will contribute 16 person-years before exiting (=0).

Note that the retrospective nature of women's birth and sibling history data makes them prone to error. Women may forget or misremember the details of their own (Helleringer et al. 2020) or of their mothers' birth histories, or may not disclose all relevant events. This is a limitation shared by the vast literature using these data to study child mortality and to estimate adult mortality indirectly. Nonetheless, it is important to keep in mind when interpreting results.


## Methods


We begin by describing the prevalence of women who have experienced under-five death via the loss of a sibling and/or offspring in 50 countries across six world regions, and document how this prevalence is changing across cohorts. Next, we turn to assess whether women who experience sibling death are the same women who go on to experience offspring death.  To do so, we first 6 estimate the prevalence of women who experienced both under-five sibling mortality and offspring mortality, and how it has changed across cohorts. We then graph Kaplan-Meier curves to illustrate the extent to which this clustering is due to a disproportionate risk of offspring death among those who are sibling-bereaved. Specifically, we chart women's experience of offspring death over their reproductive years as a function of both their sibling-bereavement status and their birth cohort, offering further insights into how the intergenerational clustering of under-five deaths has changed.

Extending this bivariate analysis, we next estimate a series of multilevel discrete-time hazard models analyzing whether under-five sibling death is independently associated with women's subsequent risk of offspring death, net of covariates. Given regional differences in the timing and pace of fertility and mortality decline, we stratify these analyses by world region. To confirm that the patterns are comparable across diverse country-contexts, we estimate all models separately by country. In these models, person-years are the unit of observation, and the hazard

of child loss begins at the respondent's time of first birth. This strategy addresses the right censoring of our dependent variable (under-five offspring death) and the hierarchical structure of our data, where multiple mothers live in the same subnational region. ## Results



## Under-five mortality exposure: A multi-generation and cohort perspective


Figure 2 shows the exceedingly high prevalence of women across all countries and cohorts that have experienced an under-five death in their immediate natal or conjugal family-either through the loss of a sibling or their own child. Among women born in the 1960s, across all countries, on average, just over one-half of reproductive-age women had intimately experienced an under-five death in their natal or conjugal family, emphasizing the pervasive nature of under-

five death exposures. This percentage decreased only modestly to 37% of all women born in the 1980s in all countries despite precipitous declines in the under-five mortality rate, attesting to the lagged nature by which mortality improvements reflect in individuals' experiences.

## [Figure 2 about here]

There are notable world regional and country differences in women's exposure to underfive death in their families. Nearly 60% of women born in the 1960s in the Central, Western, and Eastern African countries studied experienced a sibling or offspring death, whereas closer to 40% of women experienced one in the Latin American, Asian, and Southern African countries analyzed. These geographic disparities persisted among the 1980s cohort, with about one-third of women having experienced under-five death in Latin American, Asian, and Southern African countries versus more than 40% of women in Central, Western, and Eastern African ones. Further, although country-level averages of women exposed to under-five death vary within regions, the percentage of women exposed to under-five mortality generally declined across cohorts, yet modestly so. On average, exposure to under-five death declined by only 16 percentage points. These modest reductions render clear that the burden of under-five death exposure is heavier than secular declines in annualized under-five mortality rates imply.

This comprehensive portrait of reproductive-age women's familial exposure to under-five death does not attend to the source of it. Figure 3 disaggregates exposure to under-five death through the loss of a sibling (left panel) versus offspring (right panel), by world region and cohort. Beginning with the left panel, the prevalence of women whose mothers endured the death of an under-five child, and thus lost a sibling, is incredibly high, especially in Latin American (31%), Central African (33%), Eastern African (33%) and Western African (30%) countries. Although the prevalence is high elsewhere, by comparison, fewer women experienced an under-

five sibling death in South and Southeast Asian (22%) and Southern African (23%) countries. Also of note is the remarkable stability in the high prevalence of sibling death; only in Latin America, Southern Africa, and Western Africa did the prevalence of women exposed to sibling mortality decline meaningfully among younger cohorts. In other world regions, where mortality and fertility declines are more recent, the burden of sibling death remained remarkably stable across the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s birth cohorts.
