## Won't they just use something else? The possibility of displacement


The issue of displacement was touched on earlier. Both theory and evidence indicate that, when crime is prevented, displacement often does not occur, or may occur to a limited extent. Nevertheless, we anticipate that displacement will be raised as a criticism of the present proposal. This section focuses on the possibility of a tactical switch to another sharp instrument or other weapon if pointed kitchen knives are controlled.

Much knife crime relates to knife carrying . We suggest the carrying of other weapons is less likely overall if pointed knives are removed from the equation. 'Status knife' is the term capturing that a key motivation for carrying some types of knife is the psychological reward from peers: the carrier may derive some kudos and be able to threaten others. Kitchen knives may have lower status than zombie knives, but for present purposes let us assume that being armed in any form brings status. Once pointed-end knives are removed, what other weapon might be a good substitute? Perhaps a chain of some sort could be carried as a weapon, except it is less readily available, harder to wield as a weapon, and less injurious on average. The status for chain-carrying is likely to be less than that of knife-carrying, which means the temptation to carry would also be reduced.  Most other objects are inferior both in terms of status and when used as weapons.

What about 'tinder-box' violence occurring in the home? If lethal kitchen knives are not available, what is the next-best alternative? Perhaps scissors or screwdrivers? Many scissors are already rounded rather than pointed. Further, the design of scissors makes them unwieldy for the purpose of stabbing. The default use of scissors involves the fingers being threaded through handles, which means using them to threaten or stab offers an uncomfortable grasp. To use the term favoured by designers such as Norman (2002), scissors do not readily afford the act of stabbing. Scissors are also less numerous than kitchen knives and less likely to be on open display compared to, say, a box set of knives. The reason that scissors do not already feature more prominently in the crime statistics for sharp instruments is that, for these reasons, they are a significantly inferior weapon.

Another contender is a screwdriver. However, there is a reason why screwdrivers account for only a small proportion of existing 'knife or sharp instrument' crimes: they are not as readily to hand as knives in a kitchen or other domestic setting, aside from perhaps a toolshed or garage. They are significantly inferior as 'status' weapons, arguably indicating the inability of the carrier to obtain a 'proper' status weapon, that is, a pointed knife.

Glass bottles are a potential alternative. However, most bottles and other domestic containers these days are manufactured from plastic, cardboard or aluminium. Available glass bottles are often unsuitable: they are the wrong size or too fragile, for instance. A perfume bottle makes a poor weapon. Beer for domestic consumption is often sold in cans, while some bottles are generally too large (750 ml and one litre bottles), and others too small (stubby 330ml bottles). The popularity of recycling means empties are routinely disposed of, reducing accessibility. Use of a bottle as a weapon not only requires availability but also requires a user to recognise and realise the potential, which cannot be assumed. Adopting a bottle as a weapon can shatter the bottle, which can injure the holder.

It is not obvious if other kitchen items will serve. Most require more effort or skill to utilise in a lethal fashion. Whisks and spatulas are mostly poor weapons. What about other household items? Perhaps a pencil could be a lethal stabbing weapon, but it is structurally weaker and likely to do far less damage than a pointed kitchen knife. Some garden tools - secateurs and such - are potentially dangerous but on average require significantly more time and effort to retrieve from the shed, garage or elsewhere, providing cooling-off and escape time, and they can be tricky to wield. Generally speaking, garden-tool weapons are a poor and unlikely substitute.

What about blunt objects and other potential weapons? Heavy ornaments or rocks from the garden are potential weapons but take time and effort to acquire and are wielded with difficulty. Books and remote controls may be available but are insufficiently dangerous for the most part. Most other items afford a low probability of weaponization, with consideration of many quickly lapsing into the absurd.

Put another way, the reason that the crime category used here is defined as 'knives and other sharp instruments' is because knives are significantly more dangerous than the closest substitute, and all alternatives are inferior - they do not afford threats or stabbing to the same extent - and are less readily available.

In discussing these alternatives, however, we should be clear that we are not claiming that no displacement will occur - and indeed this is not a requirement for success. It is true that a determined offender may be able to find an alternative weapon; however, only a minority of offenders are determined in this sense, and many more incidents are the result of impulsive decisions or the availability of a deadly weapon. It has repeatedly been shown that, in such circumstances, marginal increases in the difficulty of committing crime will deter some proportion of offenders, which in this case means fewer assaults. Furthermore, those assaults which do still occur, but with less lethal weapons, will result in less harmful outcomes, representing a secondary benefit. This is the key idea: reducing the availability and lethality of knives may not eradicate knife crime but it will prevent significant parts of it and make less harmful that which occurs.

This discussion is consistent with the existing theory and evidence relating to crime displacement. Displacement is generally scarce.  It may occur in some instances but usually in the context of a significant net reduction in crime. The clearest evidence for the fact that other items are inferior is the fact that they are not already the first choice. That is, lethal kitchen knives are the weapon of choice for homicide in England and Wales for a reason. We conclude that some small amount of displacement may occur but that for most part it will be conspicuous by its absence: look again at the vast difference in gun-related deaths in the UK and the US detailed earlier.


## The diffusion of benefits


A 'diffusion of benefits' effect is framed as the opposite of displacement (Guerette & Bowers 2009). Numerous evaluations have found that crime prevention effects extend beyond the initial scope, or that an anticipatory benefit is induced before a policy is implemented (Smith et al. 2022). We suggest that both types of diffusion may occur here. If customers and manufacturers anticipate legislative change, then behaviour relating to lethal knives may change in advance. Similarly, an impending ban on pointed knives may cause a broader effect upon violence and other types of crime. We would not only expect a reduction in homicides but also other knife-related crime types, proportional to the use of kitchen knives (which, in the context of bans on other lethal knives will be more effective overall). Previous research suggests that reducing crime opportunities reduces the involvement of young people in crime, which in turn reduces the size of cohorts progressing to habitual involvement in crime (Dixon and Farrell 2020): this type of broader beneficial effect may occur if the murder weapon of choice, and likely precipitator of much violent crime, is removed from the equation.

In this context, pointed knives cause avoidable injuries in domestic kitchens and the workplace. There were 43,000 knife-based reportable work place accidents in 2019 (British Safe Industry Federation 2021). Knife-related injuries account for over 10% of major injuries reported to the government's Health and Safety Executive (HSE) and 58% of all work-related accidents involving manual tools (British Safe Industry Federation 2021). We expect that a significant beneficial diffusionary aspect of safe knives would be a reduction, by potentially tens of thousands, in non-criminal injuries in workplaces,homes and elsewhere.


## Discussion of the study's contribution


Knife crime is a significant problem. It has been a dominant feature of news media and political discussions about crime in England and Wales in recent years, and knives are the most prevalent murder weapon. Existing efforts to reduce knife crime have met with limited success and have often focused on zombie knives, machetes and other status knives. In that context this study is ambitious in proposing a significant policy change and schedule to reduce knife crime. It details the mechanisms by which knife crime will be reduced with little or no displacement, and suggests other forms of crime and criminality, plus non-criminal injuries, will decline as a positive knock-on effect (a diffusion of preventive benefits). While the focus is England & Wales, there are significant implications for other countries which, depending on the nature of their knife crime problem, may wish to consider adopting this approach.

Central to the study is an original proposal. It is novel in the emphasis upon lethal knives in everyday life which contrasts with most media and policy debate centred on zombie and other 'status' knives or on gangs and young people. To do this, the study was underpinned by evidence of the dominant role of kitchen knives in homicide, in the context of extensive theory and evidence on the effectiveness of reducing crime opportunities. Few readers, we suggest, will have previously recognised the important crime prevention role of rounded-end dining room knives that they encounter every day.

The proposal outlined here will affect the lives of most householders and some businesses in England and Wales. Extensive justification such a policy change is required. But the study is rigorous in being evidence-based while informed by proven theory. Further, we detail the mechanisms by which the policy would work, explain why little or no displacement is expected and why, in contrast, a diffusion of benefits is likely. We also suggest a phased approach that allows time for the knife industry, markets and customers to adapt.


## CONCLUSION


Killer kitchen knives are the murder weapon of choice in England and Wales, and prevalent in knife crime in countries around the world. The sharp tip of kitchen knives is unnecessary for culinary purposes: it is possible to julienne a carrot, or even chop a butternut squash, without a lethal weapon. Safe kitchen knife designs already exist and are in production, and safe table knives are the default in dining rooms to the extent that we barely notice their crime prevention role. Extensive theory and evidence support the proposal, while fossil-fuel motor vehicles offer a high-profile precedent using a phased approach. The proposal will, we suggest, reduce knife-related homicide by half in England and Wales, reduce other crimes in proportion to the use of lethal kitchen knives, potentially reduce other crime types and criminality as a by-product, and prevent thousands of non-criminal knife-related injuries.

## Introduction


The notion of legitimacy in the monopoly of legitimate violence appears to be the keystone of the Weberian theory of state-building (R. Gordon 2009; E. Gordon 2014). On the one hand, the literature on legitimacy argues that for the state to maintain legitimacy, its stability must be based on the values of its citizens (Lipset ; Stillman). On the other hand, in the literature on post-conflict societies and state-building, the question remains as to what comes first. Schneckener (Schneckener) proposed a classification of state-building processes: liberalization, security, institutionalization, and the development of civil society. He argues that none of these approaches should take priority; rather, they should be addressed in concert. As models of violence use are enshrined as being paradoxically the central concept of state-building (Cohen, Brown, et Organski 1981), it seemed important to review the relevant literature to guide the theoretical development of this research in which the aim is to understand the transition from the legitimacy of the monopoly of the state to the legitimacy of the peripheries ; two interdependent concepts evolving in a spectrum of peripheral legitimacy between delegation and oligopoly. The research focuses on developing the challenges of a monopoly of legitimate violence in the context of a state-building process among non-state armed actors. Conventional wisdom portrays states without monopoly of violence as chaotic and anarchic (Arjona 2016). However, they are often orderly. The discussion of this research is based on a working definition of the oligopoly of violence as a tool to peripheral legitimacy that has evolved from the findings of several research inquiries. I define the peripheral legitimacy as a multilayered and parallel governance that is de facto imposed to a specific territory thanks to the recognition and legitimacy granted by a local population to a non-state actor who does not depend on central institutions to acquire this legitimacy (Giustozzi 2005; Diamond 1996; Boege et al. 2008b). I define the oligopoly of violence as a shifting pattern intended to delegate violence in a legitimate way granted by the state authority in a post-conflict society. In this case, the state authority recognizes parallel legitimacies and relies more or less long-term on the collaboration links to maintain a status quo between peripheral provider of violence and the state core (Kasfir, Frerks, et Terpstra 2018; Omeje 2010; A. Mehler, Lambach, Daniel, Smith-Höhn, Judy 2010; Davis 2009; Lambach 2007; Korf 2009). Theoretical development is ongoing within this conceptual field and a knowledge synthesis of the current literature and theoretical frameworks is needed to guide the theoretical deliberation and to develop the position in the debates and issues surrounding the concepts of monopoly and oligopoly of violence in state-building processes. The precise meaning of legitimacy and monopoly has varied with the context in which the term has been used in political science and international relations studies with numerous fundamental contributions from constructivist and critical research on the notion of the state outside the traditional western vision (Mohamedou 2020; Doyle et Dunning 2018; Acharya et Buzan 2017; Bagayoko, Hutchful, et Luckham 2016; Epstein 2014; Tickner 2013; Boege et al. 2008b; Bacon 2001; Linklater 1996). While this study recognizes the complexity of finding a universally acceptable and applicable definition of legitimacy of the use of violence, it was felt that a clearer understanding could be achieved by synthesizing the literature in political science and IR fields by broadening the conceptual and theoretical contribution of the evolution of state violence.

This article contributes to the debate by assuming that the study of state violence and its expansion or questioning must be emancipated from the context of civil war. The question of the Eurocentric approach was the basis of this study. After a short exposition and justification of the background that initiated this article, we discuss the methods chosen for this literature review. The results and the ensuing discussion are developed along two main lines: the questioning of the traditional scheme of the monopoly of legitimate violence [I] and the justification by the literature of in-depth research on the consequences of cooperation and regulation of extrastate violence [II] of which the oligopoly is a recurrent model.


### Background


The purpose of this study is to investigate the impact of the delegation of the monopoly of legitimate violence and how the resulting oligopoly jeopardizes or strengthens the state legitimacy. It adapts the dominant approaches to legitimacy and applies them to the unconventional context of post-conflict nonstate actors. These actors, subjects of the delegation of security, grow as autonomous militias or paramilitaries affiliated with political clans, depending on the official relations they maintain with client political parties and the support of local communities. This reflection on their involvement leads us to distinguish the sources of legitimacy of such groups.  We assume that the mechanisms of state-building are no longer focused on the universal application of Western causal knowledge through policy interventions but rather on the effects of specific local processes at work in societies themselves. The question of the sources of legitimacy arises when conceptualizing the use of legitimate forces. As Krause and Miliken suggested, the study of nonstate armed groups shall not be limited to civil war, but must be ‘expanded and expansive’ (Krause et Milliken) and must answer the need to broaden the scope of state legitimacy. This review asserts that, in certain contexts and to respond to the risk of post-conflict fragmentation, regimes voluntarily sacrifice their monopoly of legitimate violence by developing a controlled oligopoly. In so doing, it weakens its effective power and strengthens its symbolic power. This gives third-party political actors the possibility of imposing their own authority on a given territory as long as they share the same ideological agenda.


#### Rationale for this study


The growing interest in peripheral legitimacy issues through the complexity of current grey areas is noticeable in the international relations literature. Similarly, the debate on the role of the state is apparent not only in the Occidental case studies but increasingly in those that fall beyond the Eurocentric and Weberian perspectives. The traditional benchmark for assessing the control of a particular actor over a territory is its legitimacy (Hurd 1999; Clark 2003; R. Gordon 2009; Lake 2011). At the heart of all political crises is the question of who gets the right to rule. Barker defines political legitimacy as "the belief in the rightfulness of a state, in its authority to issue commands so that the commands are obeyed not simply out of fear or self-interest, but because they are believed to have moral authority, because subjects believe that they ought to obey" (Barker 1990). State-centricity and Eurocentrism are clearly illustrated here and although Baker argued this at a time when Fukuyama believed in the “end of history” and the dominance of the Western state model, an evolution in the perception of the state and the limits of its legitimacy has occurred with the emergence - but even more so with the gains in credibility - of state peripheral actors.

Beyond the Eurocentric academic world, the pyramidal perception of state authority rooted in national legitimacy is less evident. It is still a challenging task for researchers to emancipate from the Western-orientalist perception regarding the role of the state over regional and sub-state actors. However, it is precisely this lack of understanding of the inner dynamics that has shaped misunderstandings of the western state in numerous conflicts with substate actors. This review therefore intends to bring to the literature an additional bridge between different studies about the use of legitimate violence in order to understand the reality of intra-state dynamics exogenous to the Weberian model.


#### Method


To provide a structure that would reduce selection bias, a PRISMA-like research design was followed, as this method is relevant for any type of systematic review (Moher et al. 2009).

Although intrastate violence with its multilevel repercussions demonstrates the need for social perspectives, its complex nature, variations in its expression across locations and time point, and the range of evidence required for a sound evaluation of its effect across levels present special challenges for research. With these issues in mind, although aspects of the knowledge synthesis and review processes were used, a narrative format was chosen. To meet the inclusion criteria, the articles must be peer-reviewed and published in English or French. This selection addresses the research question of how the literature theoretically addresses the oligopoly of legitimate violence.

It should be kept in mind that the limitations of data sources may appear as a potential bias, and this synthesis must provide a general map to reach a consensus proposal. As such, Lawarée, Jacob, et Ouimet (2020) showed that the use of scoping review to limit bias was highly conclusive. Therefore this study is oriented as a meta-ethnographic synthesis, referred as a synthesis of interpretive research which relates qualitative studies (Noblit, Hare, et Hare 1988).

Databases such as Google Scholar and Web of Science were searched in 2022 using the term ‘oligopoly of violence, resulting in 143 and eight articles, respectively. To refine the search, an additional search was performed using the keywords ‘delegation’, ‘monopoly of violence‘,  and ’rebels’. In this step, 97 articles were excluded. The term ‘delegation’ was always combined with the term ‘rebels’ or ‘oligopoly’. They were searched at the level of the title and a brief view of the abstract (where the search terms are highlighted in their context), and then at the level of the abstract. Five articles were excluded from the remaining corpus because the theoretical framework classifies rebel groups as terrorist actors. They were not within the scope of this review, specifically to analyze the influence of non-state groups with delegated authority.

Peer-reviewed articles must be published between 2002 and 2022. The oligopoly and questioning of the monopoly of violence were central to the research. Finally, all articles should be oriented toward political science and/or international relations.

However, the selection of articles has remained open to relevant selection from the bibliographies of the cited sources as long as they fit the above-mentioned criteria. I was interested in exploring how the word oligopoly was used in IR literature. Full papers (n = 50) were selected by meeting these criteria and by excluding repeated articles.

Non-research-based studies were excluded, but informed the discussion on theoretical frameworks.


## Results and discussion


This review presents a conceptual proposal for the challenge of the monopoly of legitimate violence by the superposition of an oligopoly of legitimate violence carried out by peripheral actors. The initial observations are clear. On the first hand, the subject of challenging the monopoly of legitimate violence by an existing model is still hesitant in the literature. In addition to the small number of researchers from non-Eurocentric regions, the topic of oligopoly is considered at best a matter of curiosity, and at worst a misconception of post-conflict areas. On the other hand, among the selected literature, some studies refer to a certain discomfort in dealing with the legitimate use of violence by applying it to eurocentric and postcolonial perceptions.

The studies mobilized in this review provide a deeper understanding of the concept of monopoly suggested by an overly Eurocentric view. To suggest an alternative to the conceptions defined as Eurocentric or Western, in my usage here, I seek to overcome the Westphalian shell of the nation-state. The apparent omnipresence of the European perspective in international relations has been evident since critical and post-positivist literature committed themselves to arguing for the need for a new framework in conceptualizing the state (Blaydes 2017). Barkawi (Barkawi 2016, 2017; Barkawi et Laffey 2006) argues that international security studies should adapt to a new terminological decolonization of war, criticizing the Eurocentric view of the state, and the monopoly of violence allows for the development of local perspectives on legitimacy and the state. This article modestly follows the lead of Acharya and Buzan in their investigation of the so-called non-Western international relations (Acharya et Buzan 2017). Mohamedou expresses this uneasiness as the state is not yet the subject of a universal consensus, the debate on its nature and inherent features, such as the legitimacy of violence, can no longer ignore non-Western experiences and “transforming statehoods” (Mohamedou 2020) in the process of conceptual decolonization.

This uneasiness is especially apparent in studies based on case studies in MENA (Leonard 2013; A. Mehler, Lambach, Daniel, Smith-Höhn, Judy 2010; Omeje 2010). Hence, it was useful to include studies that do not explicitly mention oligopoly from an economic point of view, but rather refer, implicitly or explicitly, to a situation where the multiplication of poles of legitimacy and governance leads us to consider the need for a theoretical shift.

The expected results in the literature tend to both develop an economic approach to oligopoly following a pattern of supply and demand in the security market and to redefine the notion of legitimacy in a post-conflict society. We believe that these reflections tend to meet up on one point: the reexamination of what Rudolph von Jhering called the "monopoly of constraint" in 1877. None of the mobilized studies challenge Max Weber’s fundamental contributions related to a certain degree of state building and the monopolization of coercion. In their reassessment of Weberian theory, Lottholz et al. proposed a new conceptualization of state-making in the light of the interpretation of Charles Tilly, while assuming to preserve the primacy of Weberian thought in the conception of the European state (2016). However, this omniscient theory is eroded as we look at the patterns of sovereignty, where successful state formation depends on the forging of reciprocal connections between rulers and the ruled. Colliot (2003) pointed out that the modern state preserves subjective rights, but that the fundamental character of domination in a society, according to Weber, is that "its stability must be accepted over those over whom it is exercised". Two patterns emerged from this review, namely, a discussion around the issue of the monopoly of legitimate violence and a deeper insight into what the partial transfer of this Weberian function represents as an oligopoly.


### Extending the Pattern of Monopoly



#### Monopoly and territory


A monopoly implies disease empowerment. In the name of subjective rights, Hobbes' Leviathan fills the legal vacuum by becoming the only legitimate actor to use force. However, state law can mutate into extrastate law, especially in post-conflict societies. During the process of unification, even more so during the reconstruction of regalian institutions following a civil war, subjective law, and its means of coercion, which it is the State's responsibility to guarantee, are challenged. Colliot (Colliot-Thélène) argues that the legitimate monopoly of violence is the result of conflict between extra-state groups, with the right to monopoly going to the strongest group. Interventions outside of this group would not benefit from state legitimacy. To this theory, we add the framework of a post-conflict society.  The challenge of a Weberian monopolistic state framework is to fulfill its role in managing violence immediately after a civil war. The demand for security being too strong at the frontier of state legitimacy, alternative entrepreneurs of violence take possession of it, where the state does not provide security as a public good (Lambach). Lambach bounds a monopoly on the ability of a single actor to maintain a sizeable armed force at the national level. However, the line is thin when at least one rival to this monopoly appears, and the resulting conflict leads to the emergence of a duopoly of major actors of violence, resulting in a civil war. Therefore, the legitimacy of the monopoly of violence is intrinsically linked to the control of territory, where the allegiance of the population grants the security provider the supremacy of security control (Gawthorpe 2017). Davis (Davis) notes that the characteristics of territorial control and local allegiance are stumbling blocks to the legitimacy of the monopoly of violence. His analysis of "imagined communities" develops the construction of local belongings in which the monopolistic provider will try to inscribe himself. At the same time, the state will guarantee the protection of local markets, investors, and ‘local capitalists’ and set up a protection racket. In short, rebel organizations, perhaps best known for their violence, seek to provide basic goods and services and work to meet the needs of citizens in exchange for their perennial activity and their local safety (Loyle et al. 2021; Taylor et Botea 2008).


#### Monopoly and periphery


The monopolistic claims of a security provider do not imply a pre-existing institutional vacuum. Korf argues that intra-state conflict are not the results of anarchy “but a hybrid set of overlapping and contradictory sets of rules” (Korf 2009). The concept of overlapping is particularly relevant because it introduces the concept of multilayered governance, which has been discussed in the literature to develop the concept of oligopoly. The assumption of these “hybrid set of overlapping” governance challenges the Westphalian project of state sovereignty that possesses both the legal and practical monopoly of the use of force. The Treaty of Wespthalia consecrated the use of instruments of violence by the state within its territory. However, in his case study of Sudan, Omeje argues that this scheme, and even more so in its colonial export, did not take the peripheries into account (Omeje 2010). The contribution of Omeje's analysis of the weight of peripheries in the Sudanese case enables us to pinpoint the question of the monopoly of violence. According to Omeje, this fickle and unpredictable periphery challenges the provision of sustainable security and stability in Sudan. The latest concept joins concomitantly with what Krause et al. (2009) argue that only hybrid nonstate armed groups - exogenous to the Westphalian vision - can compete with the sovereign state in the legitimate use of violence through this hybrid set of overlapping rules. Krause notes that non-state-armed groups have been found to be relevant when they become capable of directly challenging the monopoly. However, they remain confined to the role of actors engaged as insurgents in the civil war context (Krause 2012). If the study of the peripheries is progressively gaining ground in the actualization of the legitimate monopoly of violence, it is because this Weberian concept is challenged by the weight of the peripheries, of minorities, and in the responsibility, they sometimes share alongside the state in the privatization of security functions, whether it be ethnic or paramilitary self-defence groups. In this challenge to monopoly, Wulf brings in the impact of globalization, which has challenged the porous postcolonial borders weakened by human migration and transnational criminal activity. In light of these increasingly prevalent factors, he argues that "the monopoly of force, based exclusively on the nation-state, seems anachronistic” (Wulf 2011). Ahram goes further in questioning the state's monopoly on violence in his comparative study of Southeast Asia and the Middle East. He asserts that globalization combined with decolonization processes has reinforced the competition between actors arising from the decentralization of conventional legal structures and those directly inherited from Western colonial models (Ahram 2011). In his study, he shows that the newly created young states were still able to benefit from the support of militias through a patron-client relationship in order to preserve their legitimacy in the peripheries. Thus, the state would attempt to preserve its monopoly by relying on its internal legitimacy in the territory under its control and on its margins, while preserving some of its traditional structures to assert its legitimacy among diverse regional populations.


#### Stakeholders of the monopoly


Krahmann (2013) examines the Montreux Document on Relevant International Legal Obligations and Good Practices for States Related to the Operations of Private Military and Security Companies during Armed Conflict, signed by 17 states in September 2008. In his study, he assesses how private militias reshape cards and influence the interpretation of the state-centric paradigm of the monopoly of violence. Moving from an ‘inherently governmental’, the legitimate use of force has evolved in its use by private contractors for national contracts. PMSCs do not fall under the legal prohibitions against mercenaries because they do not fit the definition entailed in the UN and Geneva conventions (Krahmann 2013) and leave room for such legal reinterpretation by international institutions but especially for states to take advantage of this legal limbo. Outside the context of state failure, the use of these militias challenges the common idea that states monopolize the use of force to consolidate state-building (Sabine C Carey, Mitchell, et Lowe 2013).

The question of legitimate monopoly of violence by a state entity is still subject to theoretical debate. The traditional Western image of the nation-state has been challenged by the empirical results of the dynamics between state institutions and peripheral governance. Privatization and delegation of security tools are common, not only in the context of fragile statehood. Indeed, without defining it as anachronistic, the monopoly of violence is a prey to the competition of security providers in a heterogeneous environment that is challenging state homogeneity.


### Cooperation and regulation: Heterogeneous oligopoly and cartel



Forms of oligopoly and their applications


Colliot (Colliot-Thélène) combines Weber's approach to the right to coercion with Charles Tilly's interpretation that war is waged by agents of the state. This function is assumed alongside the state by "communities of law, which derive their legitimacy from local populations. The monopoly granted for the use of violence can be visualized as being at the center of a nucleus that grows as populations make concessions to ensure their protection and whose membrane would represent the periphery. Within this periphery, the state could no longer "distribute the right" to use violence. In this hypothesis, the state would simply be one provider of violence among others. Colliot argues that if it remains a distributor of the right to violence and does not enjoy factual control over the monopoly, the state can control the oligopoly (Colliot-Thélène 2003). According to Lambach, delegation of the security function is explained by the context of competition between actors with limited influence.  The spaces of public security provision cross each other, and when two or more actors meet, the supply side of the security market is resolved by civil war or parties’ cooption (Lambach 2007). In a post-conflict society, "markets will be supplied by a small number of competitors without any single one of them being able to monopolize it completely” (A. Mehler, Lambach, Daniel, Smith-Höhn, Judy 2010). This context extends beyond the framework of Colliet’s oligopoly control. The concept of periphery appears more concretely in Mehler and Lambach's vision, in which the legitimacy of violence is not distributed according to the will of a preponderant actor - a cartel situation - but where it is appropriated, a homogeneous oligopoly. Only when the state - or any other actor - dominates the market will it avoid direct confrontation with other providers who defend their area of influence, even if this means colluding with the market leader. (A. Mehler et Bauer 2006). Cooperative oligopoly appears theoretically enviable after an internal conflict, but it is practically unstable because it implies that the state is both a neutral and a cooperative actor. Mehler and Tull (2005) present cooperative-neutral dominance with two factors: the absence of violence between the major providers and the "good faith" contact and coordination between all actors. However, in this context, each actor brings into play the legitimacy of the group acquired by the local population.

The case of Iraqi Kurdistan is a useful example as an application of oligopoly due to its status of  Iraqi semi-autonomous province. The multi-layered nature of security governance between the Peshmerga military corps emanating from the Iraqi Kurdish Ministry of Defence on the one hand, and the self-defence militias that have progressively grown up since the advent of the Islamic State on the other, is interesting. It demonstrates that this multipolarity of the legitimacy of the use of violence was not only necessary for the survival of the regional government, but also sought by the latter to compensate for the lack of legitimacy encountered by the Peshmerga among the local civilian population, mainly in the Kirkuk and Nineveh provinces (Nilsson 2016; Meier 2019) . In 2014, the collaboration of the Yezidi and Christian self-defence militias (HPE) with the Barzani clan in power cost them the popular support they had acquired during the defence of the Nineveh plain against the Islamic State. The Yezidi population has experienced the collaboration of the HPE with the pro-Barzani Peshmerga as a betrayal, denying them any legitimacy, which has gradually made them disappear. Popular support is an important element in maintaining oligopolistic dynamics, especially in the patron-client framework. Kalyvas' control-collaboration model (Kalyvas) explains that what accounts for civilian support of armed groups is that local populations are rational and self-interested actors. Malthaner (Malthaner) expands on this approach by assessing that popular support is not driven solely by a "collective reaction to grievances" or by a cost-benefit decision, but primarily by social and cultural attachments and deep-rooted traditional loyalty.

Gawthorpe (Gawthorpe) dismissed the idea that rational choice is prevalent in the legitimacy granted to actors. Rather, he argues that more local and traditional factors drive the dynamics of population self-identification with nonstate-armed actors.

Oligopoly assumes the status quo

Could the oligopoly of violence be the answer to the resulting instability in a post-conflict state? It is tempting to give the federal example as an answer to this case. However, the case of Iraqi federalism poses a conceptual problem, as Mako et Edgar (2021) point out, both in its sectarianized characteristic and in the democratisation process that resulted from its foreign occupation.  While a single security offer could not be assumed for the whole territory, Mehler (A. Mehler, Lambach, Daniel, Smith-Höhn, Judy) stated that despite some cooperation, rivalries persist in an environment that differs from the European rule of law. The competition between the monopolistic state core and the oligopolistic periphery "is based on a mixture of real repression and permanent readiness to negotiate" (A. Mehler 2004). The case studies selected for this review present an arranged oligopoly. In the typology presented by Mehler and inspired by economic models, the most dominant form is a territorial homogeneous oligopoly based on an arrangement or with a dominant leader, a cartel. As a result of internal conflict, imperfect competition between some providers generates heterogeneity, that is, different providers with different types of security offers, such as kin-based militias or private paramilitaries. As Davis (Davis) argues, some non-state armed groups exist only when they act on behalf of states. Delegation within a cartel is the most consistent form of controlled oligopoly in the recent literature (Thaler 2022; S. C. Carey, Mitchell, et Annual 2017). The persistence of oligopolies of violence can be explained by the fact that non-state-armed groups are the first and foremost pragmatic and rational actors whose objective is to maintain their foothold in a specific region. This practical approach forces them to cooperate in sharing jurisdictions between the core and the periphery (Marshall 2016). Within the periphery, these groups have informal ties with the provider and are counting on “informal indigenous societal institutions leading to the deviation of state institutions for the ideal type of  ‘proper’ state institutions” (Boege et al. 2008a). The introduction of traditional institutions in the relationship between the core and the periphery seems essential for the maintenance of a stable oligopoly.  Each actor preserves their local legitimacy by accepting these institutions. The transition from the rule of the state to the ‘rule of the intermediaries’ challenges the post-colonial eurocentric state model (Münch et Veit 2018). Hence, in a cooperative-neutral oligopoly, nonstate-armed groups act as regulatory intermediaries of violence. Cooperation can be mutually beneficial between dominant and delegated providers, as in the case studied by Arias and Barnes, where groups interact directly with the state, which in return guarantees freedom of movement within their respective communities (Arias et Barnes 2017). This case study highlights the existence of a model of peripheral governance in cooperation with the nucleus of the state and the existing interest of some states to delegate violence in an environment with limited state control.

Delegation and Privatization as a Controlled Oligopoly

The concept of delegation contradicts that of a looting peripheral warlord. Olson introduced a model of NSAG called ‘stationary bandit’ anchored in its territory (Olson 2002), whose delegated monopoly of violence is circumscribed only on its territory. Unlike ‘roving bandits’, they do not directly challenge the authority of the core state. Krause and Miliken (Krause et Milliken) acknowledged that there are many cases of NSAGs that do not pose a direct threat to the Weberian state because of the necessary collaboration maintained for the protection of local communities. In his study of the market for violence in postcolonial Sudan, Omeje (Omeje) noted that the non-Arab periphery, such as predominantly non-Muslim South Sudan, has always escaped the governance imposed by Arab elites in the state core. North Sudan's quest for a monopoly on violence has been unsuccessful since the country’s decolonization due to the heterogeneity of stakeholders seeking to maximize territorial and legitimacy gains. Here, we can deduce that the capacity for cooperation between providers is limited due to historical grievances between territories and the large heterogeneity of stakeholders. Sudan is a textbook case of the difficult integration of the monopoly of legitimate violence in the periphery and the acceptance of delegation and privatization. Berti argues that it is important to deem the notion of the non-state armed group as an actor opposed to the state, but as a de facto state collaborator in multilayered governance (Berti 2013). In fact, according to Zohar (E. Zohar), the analytical misconception is that the governance of non-state actors is rebellious, isolated, and a source of opposition to the state that generates terrorist elements.  According to these typologies, we can argue that the most advanced form of homogeneous oligopoly of violence is the privatization of forces from the periphery (S. C. Carey, Mitchell, et Annual 2017; Shultz, Farah, et Lochard 2004; Eran Zohar 2015). The state’s access to the periphery has led it to push back its prerogative to use violence and engage peripheral actors in the short-to medium-term (Ahram 2011). Therefore, it represents a rational choice for delegation in the short term, but it may ultimately undermine the legitimacy of employing such groups. Although the state is fragmenting its monopoly on violence and partially outsourcing government functions, Wulf assesses that privatization is a reaction to prevailing insecurity (Wulf 2011). Privatization is a formal response that strengthens the grip of the state core on the periphery. However, depending on the characteristics of the privatized group, patronage links can be volatile. Many typologies have outlined the characteristics of the relationship between a non-state-armed group and a patron state. Militias and paramilitaries will have different degrees of autonomy of movement and action and share different levels of responsibility in their operations on behalf of the patron state, both locally and regionally (Shultz, Farah, et Lochard 2004; E. Zohar 2016; S. C. Carey, Mitchell, et Annual 2017; Rauta 2020; Mampilly et Stewart 2021). The issue of government control over these private groups is fueled by numerous incentives to delegate to these groups. Indeed, Carey et al. (Sabine C. Carey, Colaresi, et Mitchell) point out that pro-government militias can operate where regular forces are subject to the international rules of war. In the Pro-government militias database, he deduces that state-sponsored militias are not part of the official institutions of the state, so they are better able to operate outside the territorial borders and areas of official governance (Sabine C Carey, Mitchell, et Lowe 2013). Although they can incorporate members of the regular forces, they organize and operate clandestinely, allowing the state to deny acting outside its jurisdiction and evade accountability for violence (Ahram 2014).  Delegation and its resulting privative form make the state evolve as a manager of violence by decentralizing its use (P.S. Staniland 2010). Aliyev notes that collaboration between state and state-parallel militias survives as long as the status quo is maintained. Their affiliations with the state make them agents of collaboration rather than "state-manipulated militias" because they maintain a degree of autonomy in their own political agenda (Aliyev 2016). Maintaining decentralized forces means that the state voluntarily subcontracts the control of territories that were previously controlled or planned to control. The stake - the control over the periphery - is perceived higher than the costs – the loss of the monopoly of violence to actors potentially more prone to ‘clothe [themself] in the garments of legitimacy’ (Gawthorpe 2017) and to gain local support and recognition among the population. Ek (Eck) argues that the delegation of repression to proxies confirms that delegation and a controlled oligopoly are rational decisions.

## Conclusion and implications for further research

By amassing 50 papers in peer-reviewed journals between 2002 and 2022, this meta-analysis provides a portrait on how the diversity of legitimacies for the use of violence within the Western and non-Western states is addressed. It exposes the limitations of the monopoly of violence when it moves beyond the Weberian and Eurocentric frameworks. It also exposes the difficulties of empirical conceptualizations of the cases studied in the context of the core state and periphery dynamics. It has been shown that monopoly suggests a distribution of coercion means. However, when the number of actors peripheral to the state is too large and state institutions are weakened, the monopoly disintegrates in favor of multiple legitimacies. This is how the multilayered governance framework becomes interesting for analyzing the legitimacy anchors of non-state actors. Staniland (P. Staniland) suggested that it would be useful for research to emancipate itself from the straitjacket of state-centric variables. The general assumptions about non-state-armed actors and the labels attached to them suffer from incompatibility with a rigid monopolistic vision. The general vision extracted from this study demonstrates that beyond the risks inherent to state-building in a post-conflict context, there is a need to broaden the scope of inquiry of who owns violence. This allows emancipation from the non-binary opposition of the state. However, the different forms of oligopoly and their granted legitimacy are still insufficient, given the binary vision of statehood. The effectiveness of the forms of oligopoly that could pave the way for state-building should be assessed by field studies of the peripheries. The monopoly of violence by Hobbes' Leviathan should be seen in many of the instances studied as an oligopoly controlled by Hydra.

In addition to questioning a single paradigm that allows the integration of a regionalist vision, the issue of the core-periphery hierarchy remains important. Delegation and rebel governance theories (Arjona 2016) are greatly enriched by the implementation of co-management principles in conflict resolution. Drawing on research on resource-sharing conflicts between communities and state institutions, the evaluation of conflict prevention between poles of legitimacy in the use of violence has not yet fully considered the idea of co-management of violence. According to De Pourcq, this is mainly because state agencies and peripheral local communities are generally considered homogeneous in the use of their resources (De Pourcq et al. 2015). Hence, similar to natural resource sharing issues, security is a hot topic in need of co-management between state agencies and local communities.

The process of state-building involves actors reliable to the viability of a sustainable state entity. The military is one, if not the primary, regal institution mobilized in the process of legitimizing the state and using legitimate violence. The Weberian perception has reinforced the vision of the nation-state in the Western and European world of the use of a unified armed force by legal state institutions. Outside the European world, the pyramidal perception of state authority rooted in national legitimacy is less evident. The COVID crisis has intensified the phenomenon of the loss of legitimacy of the state over its margins. The choice to switch to local actors is widespread due to the apparent incapacity of institutions to respond to the needs of peripheral populations (Buzan et Lawson 2015). Progressively, alternative authorities embodied by non-state armed actors in the case of Iraqi Kurdistan, are acquiring the legitimacy to provide human security to their population. By excluding this aspect would mean ignoring an empirical reality that needs to be understood without categorizing it with limited concepts. As the foundation of international relations, Western scholars should focus more on sovereignty as a multipolar concept, as uncomfortable as it seems, rather than strengthening postcolonial misconceptions (Lawson et Shilliam 2009).

This article sets the stage for future research to conceptualize the rapid evolution of the security sectors, which is the gradual acceptance of the multipolarity of violence by local populations through the prism of the oligopoly of the legitimacy of violence. In some areas, such as Iraqi Kurdistan and Syria, state institutions temporarily renounce the exclusivity of their coercive legitimacy (Leenders et Giustozzi 2019). However, it does not disappear but is either integrated into what Moghadam and Wyss define as a state sponsorship of proxies (Moghadam et Wyss 2020). Nonetheless, the concept of oligopoly captures more of a horizontal dynamic of legitimacies between state core and peripheries. In this case, the balance of state institutions depends on regional non-state armed actors, in a co-management of security within a multi-layered hybrid and form of governance.

## Introduction


Network science has many applications for archaeologists, and it can be particularly useful for breaking out of traditional spatial categories and examining data through new lenses (Feinman and Neitzel 2020; Holland-Lulewicz 2021). Multilayer network analysis combines multiple networks into one analytical framework (Kivel¨ et al. 2014). a Social systems are complex webs of interrelations. There is too much involved to model the material culture of even a technologically simple society, but certainly analyzing more than one type of material culture provides a more complete understanding of the social dynamics involved in the networks of interaction we wish to understand. Yet, there are few examples of multilayer networks in archaeology (e.g., Giomi 2022; Upton 2019) and none I am aware of that extend beyond ceramics.

Network studies are particularly prominent in the Southwest and there are examples of network studies that consider multiple types of material culture. To name just two: Mills and colleagues (2013a) used ceramics and obsidian to understand the transformation of large-scale social networks; Peeples (2018) used ceramics and architecture to understand identity and social change in the Cibola region. This paper is an applica-

tion of multilayer network analysis that seeks to further network research by examining multiple types of material culture in one framework. Given the frequent focus on single types of artifacts in network research, a primary question I seek to address is whether networks based on different types of material culture are positively correlated. This matters because archaeologists often make inferences based solely on ceramics or other types of material culture. Evidence regarding the ways material culture co-vary will help give better context to these studies. Furthermore, I also seek causal explanations for the co-variance, or lack thereof, for material culture in the case study I present here.

Tonto Basin holds great potential for archaeological research due to the large cultural resource management projects conducted in the region primarily in the 1980s1990s (Ahlstrom, Chenault, and Anderson 1991; Ciolek-Torrello, Shelley, and Benaron 1994; Doelle et al. 1992; Rice 1998), as well as the large number of syntheses and other studies focusing on the area (e.g., Clark and Vint 2004; Dean 2000; Elson, Gregory, and Stark 1995; Elson, Stark, and Gregory 2000; Hill et al. 2015; Huntley et al. 2016; Lange and Germick 1992; Lyons 2003; Lyons and Lindsay 2006; Lyons and Clark 2012; Neuzil 2008; Oliver 2001; Stark, Elson, and Clark 1998; Watts 2013). This analysis uses data from the Roosevelt Platform Mounds Study (RPMS), the largest of these projects (Rice 1998), to examine basic architectural data, typed ceramics, and data from a recent projectile point analysis (Bischoff 2022). There are two null hypotheses tested in this analysis: (1) that the data is spatially correlated-meaning that sites nearest to each other will be most alike-and (2) that the architecture, ceramics, and projectile points will all be positively correlated-meaning that similar types of architecture, ceramics, and projectile points will be found at the same sites. In reality, I expected significant variation between these types of material culture. As will be demonstrated, the results indicate a positive correlation between projectile point similarity and spatial distance. Additionally, ceramic and projectile point networks (hereafter point networks) exhibit significant differences. I posit that the differences in these networks are connected to the identities of the individuals creating the original social networks: particularly that of gender.


## Tonto Basin


Tonto Basin is in east-central Arizona and features Tonto Creek flowing from the Mogollon Rim into the Salt River (figure 1). Parts of the region have been intensively studied, while certain time periods and much of the uplands have been less intensively sampled (see Clark and Caseldine 2021, for a recent overview). The basin was conveniently located along regional travel routes, allowing major settlements-particularly those with platform mounds-to participate and benefit from this exchange (Caseldine 2022; Wood 2000, p. 129-133). The junction of the Salt River and Tonto Creek now forms Roosevelt Lake since the damming of the confluence of the Salt River and Tonto Creek. It was the expansion of the dam that precipitated the RPMS and its related projects in the late 1980s-1990s. Some important regional differences may have differentiated sites along the Salt River and Tonto Creek arms of Roosevelt Lake (Lyons 2013; Simon and Gosser 2001) based on non-local ceramics and obsidian. All of the artifacts/data from the RPMS project are hosted at the Center for Archaeology and Society at Arizona State University, and the data in this study come exclusively from this project.

Tonto Basin was occupied, although likely not continuously, from the Archaic
