## 1. Introduction


Humanity is increasingly challenged in its aspiration to meet the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including SDG 1 (ending poverty) and SDG 2 (zero hunger). Although some progress has been made since the inception of the SDGs in 2015, the international community was not on track to meet those goals (1), further aggravated by the COVID-19 pandemic. Specifically for agri-food systems, it is clear that the task ahead is daunting if we want to provide healthy, sufficient, socially acceptable and environmentally sustainable diets to a growing population expected to be around 10 billion people by 2050, living primarily in urban agglomerations. Staying within planetary boundaries is made even more difficult due to climate change. These multifaceted goals require a holistic approach (2).

Improving crops, livestock and related management practices are a recognized and important contribution to address these development challenges. Still, adapting and developing new varieties and related agricultural technologies is time consuming and requires longer term support to the agricultural research & development (R&D) pipeline. This also calls for partnerships and multi-stakeholder involvement -including private and public sector and national and international agricultural R&D.

Agricultural needs and opportunities are diverse with a lag between today's i nvestment decisions and impact on the ground. This calls for a robust understanding of the costs, benefits and potential tradeoffs, especially given the available funds are limited and choices have to be made.

The CGIAR is a major player in the international agricultural R&D domain in the Global South. It has released a new research strategy (3) towards its mission of ending hunger through science and innovation that advance transformation of food, land and water systems in a climate crisis. It sets out to deliver multiple benefits and transformative change across five SDG focused lenses or impact areas:

- 1. Climate adaptation & greenhouse gas reduction
- 2. Nutrition, health & food security
- 3. Poverty reduction, livelihoods & jobs
- 4. Gender equality, youth & social inclusion
- 5. Environmental health & biodiversity.

Crop improvement is one key intervention area in the CGIAR's research portfolio expected to variously contribute to theses impact areas.

The IMPACT model (International Model for Policy Analysis of Agricultural Commodities and Trade model) of the global agricultural economy (4) is frequently used for foresight analyses in international agricultural R&D (5,6). In recent years, a 2017 IMPACT simulation model-based exploratory study has also been variously used to explore breeding investment scenarios (7,8). While model-based foresight studies provide valuable quantitative insights, they are just one piece of the equation. Models are a simplified representation of reality and the assumptions used for the simplification are not always apparent to the users of the model results. As models tend to be complex, they are treated as a blackbox by most stakeholders. Moreover, parameters for complex models using large arrays of data depend critically on the reliability of that data. For instance, the IMPACT model (9) uses potentially outdated 2005 price data that was used to calibrate the model. Furthermore, there are questions about how well the models quantify price elasticities, particularly for crops that are little traded (e.g. yam) with potentially big implications for economic surplus. These caveats are recognized and documented but often ignored when the model results are used in isolation for decision-making processes (10).

As discussed in recent reviews (11 -13) there are different methodological approaches to doing foresight studies.  One way of addressing this is to take into consideration the level of uncertainty and complexity, ranging from facts (low uncertainty) through predictions, projections, exploration to  speculation (highest uncertainty) (11,14,15).  The IMPACT model results are explorations using an economic partial equilibrium model with some coupled biophysical models. The outcomes thereby are quite uncertain. There is some merit in revisiting the current situation as the starting point for future extrapolation in particular and foresight studies in general. Ideally, the current situation is the foundation and benchmark based on empirical evidence. This calls for a different approach and is the purpose of this paper. Our paper is a variant of the parity approach that is limited to gross production value, and adds indicators like shares of area or nutrient consumption. Still, empirical evidence can also be imperfect and data has varying levels of uncertainty, quality, comparability and completeness. For instance, despite the availability of some national level statistics, there is a lack of comprehensive and comparable data for all crops and all geographies. Using data-driven parsimonious approaches has benefits in overcoming some of the black-box approaches of partial and general equilibrium models, while masking others, notably equilibrium price relationships (10).

Our paper aims to develop a parsimonious approach to better understand the regional landscape and contributions of the various crops to end hunger in the Global South. It thereby sets out to build a foundational understanding of the current situation as a robust starting point for looking into the future. Our approach is based on making relevant existing datasets interoperable in order to create indicators that can be used for priority setting and for the identification of relevant market segments. The databased benchmark thereby serves as a starting point before engaging in predictions, projections and explorations on what the future holds in store.


## 2. Conceptual framework, data and indicators



## Conceptual framework


To understand the regional landscape and contributions of crops to end hunger in the Global South we can use different lenses. Traditionally international agricultural research has had a very strong focus on productivity enhancement (16,17). Two major considerations drove that focus. First, improved productivity is a mechanism to increase farmer income in resource poor rural areas. Second, improved productivity is a motor for increased production, necessary to keep the food availability in lock-step with population growth. These two considerations remain important, although with some adjustments.

While productivity growth remains fundamental, it is part of a broader set of considerations. Farmers do not produce crops as individual commodities, but use them as part of farming systems and livelihood strategies. Hence, a more holistic view then productivity growth is needed. We need to take into account not only the market value of the growth but also the role different crops play in farming systems and livelihood strategies. The choices of farmers within farming systems have repercussions on the environment in terms of resource use and environmental externalities.

Over the past decades, with mass starvation becoming rare (18), and hunger becoming less prominent, the focus has moved towards the need to have affordable and healthy diets to combat malnutrition and hidden hunger as well as addressing the rising obesity pandemic (Poole, Donovan and Erenstein, 2021). For productivity growth to farm income generation, the link between agricultural research outputs and farm level outcomes is relatively straight forward. In the case of improved food and nutrition to dietary change, the relationship is more indirect. Consumers, whether they are urban or rural, make their own decisions on what they eat based on a combination of dietary preferences, income, food prices and convenience, which includes access to food. An increase in staple food prices can lead to a decrease in non-staple demand by poor people due to the interplay between income and price elasticities of demand. Understanding the role of different food items within the food basket and their effect on nutrition is crucial for refining impact pathways.

The role crops play in farming systems, livelihood strategies and food baskets are primary drivers for CGIAR target beneficiaries and can help identify priorities and demarcate impact pathways. Two main relevant impact lenses are therefore rural livelihoods, and food and nutrition. The first has a primary focus on the production of important crops for the rural poor, including their roles in terms of land use and income. The second has a focus on consumption of key food items in terms of key nutrient groups. These nutrient groups include the traditional indicators of energy and total protein and we augment them with dietary fiber, selected minerals and vitamins. In addition, one would need to also incorporate

other considerations affecting both lenses, including climate change adaptation and mitigation, resource use efficiency, social inclusion and gender equity.


## Data and indicators


To operationalize our conceptual framework and the two lenses we identify key benchmark indicators. We require robust, comprehensive and comparable data across the Global South, and are thereby for now largely limited to global data sets based on census statistics or nationally representative indicators. This inherently limits the indicators that we can include. Fortunately, it is possible to generate a number of actual and proxy indicators related to both production as well as consumption. Still, this information is typically available at the country level and can be used only for high level prioritization. 1

Each of the two lenses can be supported by a number of such indicators. The indicators used here are based on what can be generated with comprehensive and comparable open access data sets covering the vast majority of the potential target areas of the CGIAR in the Global South. This implies that only globally representative datasets with a granularity of at least the national level can be used effectively (20 -24). More detailed explanation of the indicators, the underlying data sources (including any additional sources) and calculation methods can be found in the supplementary documentation.

Ideally, crop-based indicators linked to poverty, social inclusion and livelihoods are based on empirical data at low aggregation levels (including household and individual). While such empirical information is available through household surveys, they are typically not comprehensive nor comparable; nor available across all countries in the Global South; and can thus only serve the analysis in a stage further down the line. From comprehensive and comparable data sources, we can derive only second best indicators such as gross production value and cropped area at the aggregate country level. The gross production value indicator is the multiplication of production quantity and average producer (farm-gate) prices. It is a crude proxy of aggregate income and livelihood importance at best, albeit an indicator that can be calculated across geographies. Still, even here data availability and comparability can pose challenges to calibration, use and interpretation. For instance, volumes and prices of commodities across and within countries are often reported for their fresh and/or specific processed forms -but these may have varying underlying characteristics like water content as they do not necessarily refer to a standardized dry matter form, with roots and tubers being a case in point (25). The gross production value indicator also ignores production costs associated with both material inputs such as seed and fertilizer and factor inputs such as labor and capital. Labor requirements for crop production play an important role in livelihood strategies as many rural poor do not depend exclusively on agriculture for their income but have a mixed income portfolio that includes non-farm income. Cropped Area gives an indication of the rural livelihood strategies as it reveals the aerial extent crops are grown -with implications for relative agricultural resource use (particularly land); but also broader land use and environmental (dis)services. The information on cropped area and the data needed to calculate gross production value can be gleaned from the FAO statistics that are updated annually and also provide a historic overview.

The ideal food and nutrition-based indicators again require detailed information on consumption patterns at household and individual level. This data is not available as comprehensive and comparable data set, hence a second-best approach is used making use of average apparent consumption at the aggregate country level. The FAO food balance sheets provide this information but only in terms of average per capita calorie and protein intake. While this is important for quantitative malnutrition, additional information is needed for understanding potential issues of qualitative malnutrition or hidden hunger. Therefore, we combine the FAO food balance sheet data with information on the nutritional composition of different food items. Ideally, comprehensive national food composition tables should be used, but these are not available. Therefore, we opt to use the most comprehensive food composition database that we are aware of and apply this to all food items extracted from the food balance sheets. This allows us to identify average apparent intake of a vast array of nutritional components of diets. We opt to highlight only key intake indicators for: calorie, protein, dietary fiber, iron, zinc, calcium, vitamin A, folate and vitamin B-12 . The choice of vitamins and minerals is based identified major deficiencies (26 -29) contributing to malnutrition.

We calculate the indicators at the national level for all countries in the world, but report our findings here at aggregate levels relevant for the current debates for the Global South. Particularly, we distinguish between the Global South as a whole and the Low and Lower-Middle Income Countries in the Global South (i.e. excluding the Upper Middle-Income Countries such as China, the Southern Cone in South America and South Africa). The Low and Lower-Middle Income Countries subgroup comprise most of the prevailing poverty and reflect the priority countries for the CGIAR and international funder community. Still, it is recognized that poverty is heterogeneous, and all countries can still have important poverty pockets. Even the Low and Lower-Middle Income Countries are quite heterogeneous, and here we provide a subregional breakdown by two key subregions (SSA and S Asia) that brings to the fore some of the regional dimensions and how they influence our two impact lenses.

For the crop and related food item categories we use both broad categorizations (i.e. cereals; roots, tubers & bananas (RTB); legumes; other food & cash crops) as well more specific single CGIAR mandate crops (e.g. for cereals: rice, wheat, maize, millet, sorghum, and other cereals). The results of our calculations regarding crop production are summarized in Table 1 and for consumption in Table 2 (for energy and protein). In the supplementary documentation we provide crop disaggregated indicators, both for the production lens (Table A1-4) and the consumption lens (Table A6-8, for all consumption indicators).

We present the key indicators as relative shares in food production and food consumption. This allows to also generate a composite index. For the composite index we have used 10 indicators: 2 production indicators (area share; gross production value share) and 8 consumption indicators (shares in terms of energy, protein, fiber, Iron, Zinc, Calcium, Vitamin A/RAE, and Folate). We present a weighted score of these 10 indicators for different aggregation levels (Table 3). The indicators are thereby weighted by their relative importance (which is lens dependent). Here we assume equal weights for production (50%, with indicator weights (of total): area 20%; gross production value 30%) and consumption (50%, with indicator weights for energy 19%, protein 19%, fiber 2%, Iron 2%, Zinc 2%, Calcium 2%, Vitamin A/RAE 2%, and Folate 2%). The used weights are for illustration purposes but provide an approximation of their relative importance in each lens. Depending on the lens the weights can be adjusted. For comparison we have also included an unweighted score (i.e., all 10 indicators contribute equally with an implicit weight of 10%; but thereby giving an increased weight to consumption 80% vs production 20%).

In sum, our focus is on using empirical historic evidence and transparently imputed data based on combining information from open data sources. The novelty of our approach includes making different data sources interoperable which allows us to create new data sets and new aggregations.


## 3. Results



## Rural Livelihoods Lens (food production/supply)


The food crops can be broadly categorized by crop type: cereals; roots, tubers & bananas (RTB); legumes; and other crops. Cereals dominate the food crops in the Global South, with half the cropped area (Table 1).  Legume crops comprises 17% of the food crop area, with RTB 6% and other food crops 2 the remaining quarter (27%). The other food and cash crops comprise a diverse mix, including fruits & vegetables, sugar crops (e.g., sugarcane), other oil crops (e.g., oil palm, whereas soybean and groundnut have been included under legumes) and all other food and cash crops. Our focus here is on cereals, legumes and RTB -which comprise the more traditional staple food crops and have been the prime focus of the international agricultural research community and associated crop breeding, particularly the CGIAR.  Each crop type in turn is variously dominated by some main crops. For instance, rice, maize and wheat are leading cereals in the Global South, together comprising some 40% of the food crop area. The legume area is dominated by soybeans, other pulses (i.e., other than beans, peas, soybean, or groundnut) and beans. The RTB area is dominated by cassava, potatoes and other roots and tubers (i.e., other than cassava, potatoes and sweet potatoes, including e.g., yam).

Crop area is a key indicator for land use, rural livelihoods and associated impact areas (including scale and importance; environmental footprint). For income and rural poverty alleviation gross production value is arguable more important. Gross production value multiplies crop area by yield and product price. Both relative yield and product price thereby can have a marked influence on the relative importance of each crop. For the crop types, the gross production value however has less marked shifts than expected. RTB crops have comparable shares in area and value while other food and crops see a large increase in value relative to area, whereas cereals and legumes see similar decreases, whereas there are no shifts in the rankings of crop types per se. This suggests that some crops higher value is partly off-set by lower yields and vice versa. For instance, fruits and vegetable typically have higher value ( high value crops ), whereas cereals typically are lower value bulk crops but with potentially ' ' substantive grain yields. In the RTB and legume crops the production value does imply some ranking shifts within each group. For instance, in RTB cassava drops a few notches whereas potatoes, bananas & plantains and sweet potatoes rise to the fore. Similarly, groundnut rises in prominence among the legumes. Still, the plight of legumes as a group is noteworthy, their relative value insufficient to compensate for their relative low yields.

So far, the focus was on the Global South. Zooming in to the low and lower-middle income countries provides additional insights (Table 1), particularly as these countries are the poorer sub-set of the Global

South. Interestingly, there is no marked shift in the area shares for the aggregate crop types. However, within each crop type more marked shifts can be observed, including soybean dropping out of the top three legumes, potatoes out of the RTB top and fruits and vegetables dropping a notch (Table 1). This basically reflects the poorer status of the countries and increased focus on the traditional staple foods. The shifts are even more pronounced in terms of the value of production - traditional staple foods like cereals and RTB increasing their value share whereas the other crops drop numerous percentage points, reflecting their more luxurious nature.

Zooming in to the sub-regions within the low and lower-middle income countries provides further additional insights (Table 1). Here we present separately sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and South Asia. The two regions have contrasting rural livelihoods and food preferences. A marked contrast is the relative importance of RTB in SSA (18% of food crop area) compared to S Asia (2%). Cereals remain the dominant land use in each region, with the remainder split between the legumes and the other crops. Within each crop type there are also some marked differences. For instance, cereal land use in SSA is dominated by coarse grains (maize, sorghum, millet), whereas in S Asia fine grains (rice and wheat) prevail over maize; with fine grains also having a relatively higher value share. In SSA RTB is dominated by casava in terms of land use, but bananas and plantains in terms of value, whereas in S Asia potatoes prevail on both accounts. In terms of legumes, groundnuts are relatively important in SSA, whereas in S Asia other legumes prevail (e.g. lentil, pigeon pea, chickpea).


## Food and Nutrition Lens (food consumption/demand)


Human diets can be broadly categorized by food crop types and their associated products (cereals; roots, tubers & bananas (RTB); legumes; and other crops) and animal/fish-based food products. For simplicity we focus here on the energy and protein shares (Table 2).  Perhaps not surprisingly, cereals 3 provide half of the energy intake in human diets in the Global South. RTBs provide 7% of energy and legumes 5%, with animal/fish-based foods 13% and other crops the remaining quarter. Perhaps less known, cereals also provide 46% of protein intake in the Global South; followed by 32% for animal/fish based. Other crops and RTB provide markedly less protein than their energy shares, whereas legumes provide relatively more. The relative importance of specific crops within each type shifts somewhat between their energy and protein contribution. Within cereals though, rice, wheat and maize retain their dominance.

Zooming in to the low and lower-middle income countries and subregions (SSA and S Asia) again provides additional insights. Interestingly, the importance of cereals for energy provision increases further in the low and lower-middle income countries as a group (56%), albeit being somewhat lower in SSA (46%) and even higher in S Asia (59%). In contrast, RTBs are markedly more important as energy source in SSA (20%), and less so in S Asia. Given the increased poverty in low and lower-middle income countries, it is noteworthy that the protein share provided by cereals is even more marked: more than half in the group as a whole and similarly for SSA and S Asia. For legumes the role in energy share does not vary much, but its importance as protein source does increase, particularly for SSA and S Asia. The contribution of the animal/fish-based food products in the low and lower-middle income countries and

subregions is markedly lower than for the Global South as a whole. This reiterates the importance of traditional staple foods like cereals, RTB and legumes for both energy and protein intakes in the poorer countries and the relatively luxurious nature of animal/fish-based food products.


## Composite index


The weighted composite index brings together the foregoing two lenses and allows for a joint assessment of the foregoing two lenses by food crop types for the Global South and zooming into different country subsets (Table 3). For comparison purposes, we have also included the unweighted composite index for the Global South, which gives equal weight to all of the 10 underlying indicators and by implication a larger implicit weight to the Food and Nutrition Lens (80%, 8 indicators) compared to Rural Livelihoods Lens(20%, 2 indicators). The assumed weights provide a potentially more realistic weighting of the 10 indicators considering both lenses. Perhaps surprisingly, the weighting does not generate major shifts in the relative importance of the crop types or individual crops.

Zooming in to the low and lower-middle income countries and subregions (SSA and S Asia) reiterates some of the earlier insights, but with the advantage that the weighted index provides a single composite index highlighting the relative importance of the different food crop groups, including the continued dominance of cereals (with about half the index, and even 56% in S Asia with fine grains like rice and wheat being relatively important; and 43% in SSA with more importance for coarse grains like maize, and sorghum, as well as rice); the similarly important role of legumes in SSA and S Asia (14-15%); the relative importance of RTB in SSA (18%) and a similar role for other food crops in both regions (17-18%).


## 4. Discussion



## Current lenses and use


Due to data limitations regarding comprehensive global data sets on key desired indicators, we currently focus on two impact area lenses. The first lens zooms in on livelihoods of rural households through the proxies of gross production value and area under production. The gross production value is an imperfect proxy as it ignores the costs of production in terms of inputs and importantly the opportunity cost of labor. Increasingly rural households do not solely depend on agriculture for their livelihoods (30,31). The results indicate that the major mandate crops of CGIAR have important contribution to agriculture in terms of the areas covered and the gross production value. Particularly the staple cereals stand out, a prominence that persists across the subsets of countries by income level and/or geographic region, albeit with some variation in terms of the big three cereals, with particularly maize being more prevalent in SSA and rice and wheat in South Asia. The two regions also share a similar importance of legumes, albeit that RTB are markedly more prevalent on SSA.

The second lens zooms in on nutritional aspects of consumption and demand. While the approach quantifies a number of micro-nutrients beyond the traditional focus on calories and protein, the approach only captures the aggregate average consumption and disregards the distributional effects and hence the actual food baskets comprising the diets of the resource poor. Nevertheless, the results from the analysis indicate that key CGIAR mandate crops have a major contribution to both macronutrient and micro-nutrient availability in average diets. The food and nutrition contribution thereby follows the livelihoods lens, with a similar prominence of particularly the staple cereals and reiterating

the importance of legumes, and the importance of RTB in SSA diets. In some ways this supports the assertion that what you grow is what you eat, and that this largely persists at the regional and country level despite the increasing importance of imports for food security in some countries. Still, the importance of staple cereals beyond energy source is noteworthy across the Global South and particularly in the poorer low and low-middle income countries, including being the major source of protein and also contributing other micro-nutrients (also see Poole, Donovan and Erenstein, 2021).

The weighted composite index combines and in many ways aligns with the foregoing two lenses; with the advantage of having only one comprehensive indicator that allows for a joint assessment. Composite indices do have their limitations  - not least based on the underlying data and assumptions. However, conceptually they can also have limitations that the user should be aware of (e.g. see Chapter 7 of Alston et al. , 1995).

The choice of crops to present and the level of geographic aggregation strikes a balance between the interest in detail and need for a big picture. In the current presentation the choice was to present comparable data, for instance major food groups. For the geographic aggregation we focused on the key regional focus of the CGIAR, namely sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.

When analyzing agri-food systems, a focus on a single crop or food commodity can also be misleading. In production systems, crops are part of farming systems and the interaction between crops and production factors of land, labor and capital, implies that we should not view crops in isolation. From the perspective of consumption, we need to consider food baskets that contribute to diets. The empirical evidence on food baskets can be analyzed to what extent they are nutritious and sustainable. The empirical evidence shows the revealed preference and indicates that those food-baskets are actually affordable.

The benchmark indicators helps to understand the current, static situation. Looking at the historic pathways of the indicators from the past to the present can provide insights into the dynamics of the indicators relative to drivers of change. Projections of the future take into account scenario assumptions. These assumptions are related to prices, exogenous macro-economic parameters, plausible and probable changes in productivity, and the interactions between those assumptions.


## Towards additional lenses


There are additional lenses zooming in on other impact areas that are of interest but are more challenging due to data limitations. Poverty is a key lens. However, poverty metrics are typically limited to poverty head count and depth (see Table 4), sometimes disaggregated to rural and urban settings. Sub-national disaggregation is not available in a spatially and temporally comprehensive way. Poverty information is typically not linked to specific agri-food systems and certainly not to individual crops. Poverty is a sliding scale encompassing different dimensions including farm size, focus on subsistence or commercial production, and the role of agriculture in the overall livelihood strategy. These all have quite distinct poverty implications including to what extent consumption and production decisions are nonseparable.

A related lens that merits follow-up is gender and social inclusion.  Social inclusion, gender equity at a higher level of aggregation is often more difficult to link to specific components of agri-food systems,

hence a much stronger focus on these aspects within the context of the identified priority market segments.

The environmental lens which focuses on staying within planetary boundaries is also multi-faceted. A key focus in recent years has been on climate change adaptation in terms of breeding for heat and drought stress. This focus has been successful for some crop breeding programs. The importance of this focus is more difficult to quantify due to the lack of comprehensive data sets and well-defined metrics to capture climate change adaptation capacity across crops and agro-climatic environments. An additional dimension that will become increasingly important over time is the mitigation capacity of agriculture. With energy transition taking place in many parts of the world, especially in those countries with high energy consumption levels, one can expect that agriculture and land use will be the major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions. Greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture are not only linked to specific aggregate activities such as grazing beef cattle, or irrigated rice, but depend on specific management practices. The same holds true for use of scarce resources such as macro-nutrients and water. Finally there are negative externalities linked to specific management practices in terms of emission of pollutants from biocide use and effects on biodiversity.

A separate lens not covered directly by the CGIAR impact areas  is the issue of national food security. For governments this is a major theme that drives policy making and shapes the institutional and market environment of agri-food systems. The cost of food security is important,  including in terms of foreign exchange, i.e. the relationship between food imports and domestic production. The food security lens also  looks at different uses of crops for instance food or feed, or potentially for other uses such as biofuels. An additional aspect is linked to preferences. Where in global statistics commodities are grouped under a single heading, while there are clear preferences for specific types of commodity. There are areas that prefer long-grained rice, while other areas prefer short-grain types. White and yellow maize have distinct markets and uses, with white generally being preferred as food and yellow as feed.


## Towards market segmentation and investment cases


Understanding the present is a foundation for crop breeding programs in international agricultural R&D. Still, national crop aggregates only go so far for possible prioritization and the operationalization of market segments and associated investment cases. The CGIAR has in recent years started to move from generalized productivity improvement towards specific market segments for which product profiles guide the demand-driven breeding process (Ragot, Bonierbale and Weltzien, 2018; CGIAR Excellence in Breeding Platform). Market segments are the target geographies and beneficiaries of a breeding program, while the product profile is the set of traits that meet the demand of the target beneficiaries in the market segment. Market segments are generally based on descriptors that usually include some sort of regional focus, cropping system, farmer and consumer profile, and end use characteristics.

Identifying priority market segments hinges critically on well-established empirical evidence related to key indicators, including the impact lenses of interest. This calls for additional detailed data at lower levels of aggregation. Such further refinement often requires data that is not available as global comprehensive comparable data sets. Refined market segment descriptions based on more granular but idiosyncratic data may thus not be easily comparable across market segments. Still, these refined market segments may reveal important issues that are relevant for prioritization, that need to be

escalated to the broader level. Therefore, there is scope to further explore different levels of spatial aggregation and refine further based on the increasing data availability and quality. Still, in order to place market segments and product profiles into context, higher level of aggregation analysis can still provide the key information on what and where high level priorities are.

The key question is how these indicators and possible composite indices inform breeding programs in terms of market segments and product profiles. We can distinguish between three types of information. The first delineates broad market segments, in terms of production capacities and consumer demand. These broad market segments can be delineated using the type of metrics that are available in comprehensive global data sets. The second type of information provides a more granular description of market segments and sub-segments of broader segments. This more granular delineation typically requires different data than is available at global level.  The third set of data, also typically not easily available, are the metrics for defining product profiles.

Identification of market segments is important to develop the corresponding investment cases. For this one also needs to identify which organizations best address specific product profiles and market segments, potentially including international and national agricultural research and public and private sector breeding programs. This also calls for comparative advantage and market failure considerations and the corresponding implications for viable partnerships and investment cases using public funding. The investment cases would need to assess the value and cost of additional breeding investments over the current status and landscape. Crop breeding has a robust track record in relation to delivering genetic gains for yield and quality; but progress so far and prospects for further improvements vary by crop and market segment. The investment cases also need to pay particular attention to climate change resilience. This needs to go beyond the inherent crop resilience to climate change (e.g. sorghum is inherently more tolerant than maize to heat and drought stress) and take into account the targeted market segments and demand (e.g. maize is often preferred over sorghum for food and other uses across much of SSA, including already drought-prone areas). Indeed, the investment cases would need to particularly consider the scope to further enhance climate resilience through crop breeding (e.g. increased heat tolerance; drought tolerance), the recent and continued success of drought tolerant maize being a case in point.

In the end, identifying crucial information to create actionable information for the identification of market segments and product profiles requires a holistic approach and data from multiple sources. A better understanding of the current situation with backwards links to trend analysis and forward links to foresight analysis remains the much needed foundation.


## 5. Conclusions


The study shows the importance of being conscious of the impact lens of interest and the inherent data limitations. One may assume everyone agrees on the importance of achieving the SDG 1 (ending poverty) and SDG 2 (zero hunger). Most will also agree on the importance of agricultural development in achieving these SDGs. But objectively prioritizing which agricultural components would be the best to achieve either or both SDGs quickly runs into challenges. For one there are severe paucities in the data availability to both assess their relative potential contribution and track progress. Here we focused on key indicators that are available at the country level and that can be unambiguously linked to the

different crop types and specific crops. The available data allowed us to pursue two lenses: a Rural Livelihoods Lens (focused on food production/supply); a Food and Nutrition Lens (focused on food consumption/demand) and a composite index of the two. The results provide a big picture assessment of the relative contributions and allow for a zooming in and out to subsets of countries by income level and/or geographic region. The study thereby highlights the importance of data interoperability to create comprehensive actionable data sets.

The study used assigned weights to provide an approximation of reality through a composite index. One may argue over the exact weight for each indicator and the proposed actually allows one to select and refine weights to allow users to consider preferences. Still, it was interesting to note that based on the indicators included in the index, the relative rankings of crop types and crops was relatively robust -i.e. not being drastically influenced by applied weightings to lenses and underlying indicators. Nonetheless, one needs to remain transparent about the included indicators and applied weights to avoid potential manipulation. In any case, the sheer amount of data and combinations can easily lead to information overload and a semblance of accuracy. In much the same way, complex models remain a black box to most users and their quantitative outputs can be variously misinterpreted or misrepresented.  Indeed, models include many assumptions and implicit weights that have major impacts on the outputs but are not easily understood. The findings presented here are a simplification -but at least provide a reflection of the current situation that can be contrasted to current reality and serve as a parsimonious foundation for further extrapolation of scenarios into the future.

The current exercise remains an approximation of complex realities. The exercise could be strengthened by adding key lenses if we can resolve some of the missing data issues to come up with even better indicators. In many respects the current exercise is not a panacea for prioritization of crop breeding or agricultural research at large. We acknowledge the need to consider rural livelihoods and food baskets and not crop sil o's for production or consumption. Still, it provides a reality check and a foundation for further R&D. For one there is a need for further refinement for operationalization, including the inclusion of sub-national and additional data for more robust market segmentation. The results also say little about the comparative advantage of crop breeding vs other interventions; or of market failures and the comparative advantage of private sector vs public sector. Finally, the current exercise is inherently static and looks at the current situation, but thereby still serves as useful reality check and baseline for more dynamic/future oriented scenario analysis of further investments in international agricultural R&D and developing corresponding investment cases.

## 1 Introduction


Not only in the United States but also in other developed and developing countries, hostile attitudes based on partisanship can undermine the health and legitimacy of democracy (Michelitch 2015; Lauka, McCoy, and Firat 2018; Carlin and Love 2018). Party supporters tend to cooperate with in-group members based on in-group love and discriminate against opposing members due to out-group hate. The growing literature has investigated the role of partisan hostility in political (Bankert, 2021; Mayer, 2017) and apolitical settings (Michelitch, 2015; Iyengar and Westwood, 2015; Carlin and Love, 2018). In addition to economic discrimination and interparty distrust, one of the most terrible consequences of interparty hostility is political violence based on party identification. Actually, recent studies have found that strong partisanship is related to dehumanization and schadenfreude (Martherus et al., 2021; Kalmoe and Mason, 2019). Especially, Kalmoe and Mason (2019) reports that strong partisans in the United States hold schadenfreude against the opposing party, which implies that affective polarization may result in violent actions and justification of them among partisans. Actually, 40% of Republicans said that violence against government is sometimes justifiable, compared to 23% of Democrats (CNN 2022). While several studies have posited that affective polarization mainly takes the form of ingroup love rather than outgroup hate (Amira, Wright and Goya-Tocchetto, 2021; McConnell et al., 2018), we have not accumulated enough knowledge about how partisans respond to political violence based on partisanship. Especially, what is problematic is that most studies have relied on factional questions to understand partisan responses to violence. For example, while Kalmoe and Mason (2019) is a study that directly investigates partisan schadenfreude, they use an 'if' question'If you heard a politician had died of...' . However, it is not easy for voters to imagine how they feel if a politician dramatically dies. In other words, they face a problem of external validity. In sum, it is unclear how strong out-party hate is in real settings.

In a similar vein, scholars have found that violence against politicians increases the approval for the victim's party based on two psychological effects. The first is the rally-roundthe-flag effect. The rally effect increases the approval of the incumbent party through heightened threat and uncertainty. The second is the empathy effect. Since voters feel

empathy toward the targeted party, they hold positive attitudes toward the party after the event. These two effects lead us to draw different expectations. While the rally effect posits that support only for incumbent parties increases after the assassination, the empathy effect also leads to positive attitudes toward non-incumbent parties. In short, as Krakowski, Morales and Sandu (2020) note, predictions on the impact of nonincumbent assassinations on support for the targeted party are complicated. Actually, they argue that political violence against non-incumbent parties does not necessarily increase support for the party, contingent on responses from the party. Especially, if the party responds in an antagonistic way, the targeted party loses its popularity (Krakowski, Morales and Sandu, 2020).

To provide additional evidence to understand the effect of political violence on public opinion, I exploit a natural experimental design, in which the MP of the Labour Party, Jo Cox, in the United Kingdom was murdered. Using an unexpected event during survey design (Mu˜oz, Falc´-Gimeno and Hern´ndez, 2020), where BES Panel Study was conducted n o a during the event, this study found that immediately after the murder, feeling thermometer ratings among Conservatives toward the Labour Party. Contrary to the findings from Krakowski, Morales and Sandu (2020), this study finds that support for a non-incumbent party increases after the assassination only among partisans who have negative attitudes toward the party. Also, additional analyses provide little evidence of the rally-round-theflag effect of the assassination of the non-incumbent party politician. Finally, since I do not find strong evidence that favorability toward the Conservative party among Labour supporters, the improvement in affective polarization between the two parties largely results from heightened empathy among Conservatives. In sum, these results imply that the empathy effect is strong enough to improve interpartisan hostility.

This study contributes to the literature in two ways. First, I find that the empathy effect exists in a strong partisan context. Affective polarization in the United Kingdom is as strong as that in the U.S, or worse (Wagner, 2021). Especially, supporters of the Labour and Conservative parties, the two biggest parties in the U.K., hold negative attitudes toward each other (London School of Economics and Political Science, 2019). This study shows that, even in that situation, political violence causes partisans to become compassionate toward the opposing party.

Second, the results suggest that voters feel compassionate toward non-incumbent parties. I find that voters' positive feelings after political violence are through the feeling of compassion instead of the rally-round-the-flag effect. As Krakowski, Morales and Sandu (2020) note, predictions of the effect of political violence toward non-incumbent parties are not straightforward. While the rally effect is expected to work only when incumbent parties members are murdered, the empathy effect leads to the increase in favorability not only toward a governing party but also opposition parties.

In sum, this study provides the optimistic view of partisan conflict that, in face of the death of a real politician, partisans feel compassionate rather than schadenfreude toward the opposing party. In the British context where affective polarization is as strong as in the United States, political violence mitigates negative feelings toward the targeted party. Also, the present research shows a compassionate effect discussed in Dinas, Hartman and Van Spanje (2016) and Krakowski, Morales and Sandu (2020) on non-incumbent parties.


## 2 Theory


As pointed out by existing studies, affective polarization causes severe problems such as inter-party distrust (Carlin and Love, 2018), economic discrimination (Michelitch, 2015; McConnell et al., 2018), and reduced democratic accountability (Broockman, Kalla and Sean, N.d.).This kind of in-party bias is widespread across the globe (Carlin and Love, 2018; Westwood et al., 2018). Especially, one of the most extreme phenomena is partisan schadenfreude. Schadenfreude is defined as 'taking pleasure in another's misfortune' (Van Dijk et al., 2006). Also, studies in social psychology have suggested that we feel less empathy when an out-group member suffers (Cikara, Bruneau and Saxe, 2011). Such an emotional reaction is directly related to political violence. Kalmoe and Mason (2019) reports that strong partisans hold schadenfreude, which implies that affective polarization may result in violent actions among partisans. In reality, the 2021 United States Capitol attack can be one extreme consequence of the affectively polarized politics. This line of research posits that affective polarization is strongly related to schadenfreude, a lack of empathy, and political violence. Even in the absence of schadenfreude, social identity leads to empathy bias (St¨rmer et al., 2006). u In addition, based on the rally effect, Krakowski,

Morales and Sandu (2020) argue that non-incumbent parties do not necessarily benefit from political assassinations of their members. These studies lead us to suspect that partisans are apathetic about the death of an out-party politician and to establish a pessimistic hypothesis.

Shadenfreude Hypothesis: Feelings toward an out-party do not change when confronted with the death of an out-party politician.

On the contrary, according to some studies in social psychology, while individuals are willing to allocate more positive resources to ingroup members, such ingroup bias disappears when they are told to allocate costs, suggesting that they are reluctant to harm out-groups (Brewer, 1999; Mummendey et al., 1992). Also, Lelkes and his colleagues have found little evidence that affectively polarized partisans are more likely to intentionally harm out-partisans than those low in affective polarization (Lelkes and Westwood, 2017; Westwood, Peterson and Lelkes, 2019). Also, researchers have provided direct evidence that political assassinations lead to increased support for the targeted party (Dinas, Hartman and Van Spanje, 2016; Raviv et al., 1998). Based on theoretical predictions in Krakowski, Morales and Sandu (2020), the empathy effect leads to the prediction that even non-incumbent parties benefit support from violence against the party. The studies and ideas above help to induce an optimistic prediction below:

Empathy Hypothesis: Feelings toward an out-party improve when confronted with the death of an out-party politician.

In sum, previous studies have provided mixed evidence about whether in-party love leads to out-party derogation or 'the limits of partisan prejudice.' While an increasing number of studies have investigated whether and to what extent affective polarization is associated with schadenfreude and a lack of empathy, they use fictional questions as a way to measure empathy and schadenfreude. However, it is not easy for respondents to imagine how they feel when confronted with the misfortune of others. Thus, it is likely that people respond to bad events of others differently from what they did to such scenarios. Additionally, as Krakowski, Morales and Sandu (2020) maintain, predictions of citizens responses to the assassination of politicians in non-incumbent parties are complicated

because the rally-round-the-flag and empathy effects lead to different expectations. To explore how British citizens respond to the misery of a non-incumbent party, this study utilizes a natural experimental design, in which a UK politician, Jo Cox, was murdered in 2016.


## 3 Empirical Contexts


I assess the extent of interpartisan hostility in the United Kingdom. The UK is known for its weak two-party system, where either the Conservative party or the Labour party has controlled the prime ministership for long decades. While several studies have posited that partisanship among the British public exerts weak influences on political attitudes (Evans and Neundorf, 2020), some scholars have reported the strong influence of partisanship in the UK that cause partisan motivated reasoning (Bisgaard, 2015; Tilley and Hobolt, 2011). In addition, political contexts have changed. From the 1980s to the early 2000s, British elites had depolarized (Adams, Green and Milazzo, 2012). However, according to Cohen and Cohen (2021), While political elites in the UK had depolarized from the 1980s to the mid-2000s, they have been repolarizing since the late 2000s, and the public has been roughly following the trend. Also, comparing the extent of affective polarization across the globe, Wagner (2021) shows that the UK is slightly more affectively polarized than the United States. In sum, UK politics provide us with the best condition to test whether the death of an out-party politician invokes compassion or schadenfreude among partisans.

On 16th June 2016, Jo Cox, a member of the British Parliament who campaigned for remaining in the European Union, was murdered by a white supremacist. This event was so sensational that the news rapidly spread not only across the UK but also the world. The leaders of the two biggest parties responded compassionately. Jeremy Corbyn, a leader of the Labour party, said 'The whole of the Labour Party and Labour family-and indeed the whole country-will be in shock at the horrific murder of Jo Cox', and 'Jo was dedicated to getting us to live up to our promises to support the developing world and strengthen human rights' (Newsweek, 2016). David Cameron, the leader of the Conservative party, also said 'what we should do is recognise that her values - service, community, tolerance the values she lived by and worked by, those are the values that we need to redouble in our

national life in the months and years to come.' (Guardian, 2016). These comments from the leaders of the two biggest parties in the U.K. imply empathetic atmosphere after the incident. While some people were concerned that politicians would exploit the murder to advocate for 'Remain' in the following Brexit referendum (Dobreva, Grinnell and Innes, 2020), we did not observe a prominent political movement to use such political rhetoric among Labour politicians.

## 5 Results


Figure 2 shows the effect of Jo Cox's death on favorability toward the Labour Party. Row 1 in Figure 2 indicates the result with the full dataset. The first row suggests that British citizens did not increase the support for the Labour party after the event on the whole. In addition, when we turn our focus on non-Conservatives, we do not detect a statistically significant causal impact. However, when we narrow our focus to Conservative supporters, we find the increase in favorability toward the Labour party after the incident. The effect sizes are 0.33 in a model without control variables and 0.27 in a model with a full set of control variables 1 . Given Conservatives' negative attitudes toward the opposing, Labour, party, the effect size is substantively large. Actually, throughout the panel surveys, feeling thermometer ratings among Conservative supporters toward the Labour party are quite low. In Wave 7 of the panel surveys, Conservatives' favorability toward the Labour party

is 2.05. Therefore, the results lead us to conclude that the event significantly mitigated interpartisan hostility in the United Kingdom.

To make the results clearer, I plot feeling thermometer ratings toward the Labour party among Conservative supporters each day. Figure 3 shows a clear tendency that the event increased Conservatives' favorability toward the Labour party.

To verify the robustness of the results, I conducted the following robustness checks, which Mu˜ noz, Falc´-Gimeno and Hern´ndez (2020) recommended us to do. o a First, I plot the estimate by changing the bandwidth. ## 6 Alternative Mechanisms


While the results above show the strong and robust impact of the death of Jo Cox on hostile attitudes toward the Labour party among supporters of the Conservative party, they do not provide any empirical evidence that compassion among Conservative supporters reduced interparty antipathy among them. While the survey does not ask any questions about empathy and thus does not allow us to directly test the mechanism, we can test whether alternative mechanisms work. The first alternative mechanism through which the event decreased interparty hostility is that the terrorism heightened British national identity. Theories of the rally effect posit that support for the incumbent increases after dramatic crises such as terrorism. One of the theoretical mechanisms of the rally effect is heightened national identity (Kam and Ramos, 2008). Since external threats reinforce in-group attachment (Huddy, 2003), dramatic crises are likely to increase the support

## 7 Conclusion


In this paper, I investigate whether the death of the Labour party MP changed the hostile relationship with the Conservative party. One prediction from political and social psychology research is that they feel joy in an outgroup's misfortune and still hold strong hostile attitudes against it because of schadenfreude. The other prediction is that they feel compassionate toward the outgroup and reduce their hostility. While previous studies have measured the extent of schadenfreude produced by partisanship, they have not investigated it in real settings as they used hypothetical questions. In addition, predictions of how political violence against non-incumbent parties are unclear based on theories of the rally effect and empathy. Revealing a mechanism through which political violence mitigates interparty hostility is an important step to understanding how to reduce affective polarization.

In this study, exploiting a natural experimental setting, I first provide evidence that the death of an out-party politician reduced hostile attitudes based on partisan conflict. While we find little evidence that the death increased favorability toward the Labour party among British voters on the whole, it did among Conservative supporters. Based on this finding, we can conclude that political violence has a conflict-mitigating impact.

Conducting several robustness tests and checking the assumptions, I confirm that the results are robust, and the assumptions of UESD are not violated. Also, to test the validity of alternative mechanisms through which the event decreased partisan hostile attitudes among Conservative supporters. As I find little evidence that the event heightened British national identity, or reduced hostile attitudes among Labour supporters toward the Conservative party, I conclude that Conservative supporters hold decreased hostility after the event because they feel compassionate toward the Labour party. Also, while the regression analysis supported the hypothesis that the event also increased favorability among Labours toward the Conservative party, the findings are not robust across different bandwidths. As a whole, I argue that empathy for political opponents is a key factor in interparty cooperation.

This study contributes to the literature in three ways. First, while previous studies on affective polarization and partisan hostility have investigated the extent and causes of

partisan schadenfreude, they used 'what-if' questions. It is questionable whether these questions reflect partisans' responses to the death of a politician in reality because voters find it hard to imagine the death of an out-party politician. Since this study exploits the real event where an MP of the major party was murdered, the results can be seen as externally valid.

Second, contrary to some studies, this study provides an optimistic view of partisan hostility. Some of the previous studies on partisan hostility suggest that not a small part of partisans show the tendency of schadenfreude toward the out-party (Kalmoe and Mason, 2019), and they dehumanize out-partisans (Martherus et al., 2021) in the U.S. context. However, the results of the present research indicate that partisans feel compassionate toward the misfortune of the out-party and reduce their hostile attitudes toward it in the U.K. context where we observe as strong tendency of affective polarization as in the U.S. This implies that partisan hostility is not so deeply rooted that partisans treat their out-party in a dehumanizing way.

Finally, the results shown above provide us with a clue to understanding the effect of political violence on support for the targeted party. Given two different types of effects political violence has on party approval - the rally and empathy effects -, it is theoretically difficult to deduce predictions of how political violence changes favorability toward nonincumbent parties. Indeed, Krakowski, Morales and Sandu (2020) found the decreased support for a Polish opposition party after the murder of its member because of the negative campaigning after the incident. On the contrary, in the context of Jo Cox's murder, the Labour party did not necessarily respond in a hostile way. The leader of the party bemoaned the death and just gave her respectful words. The governing party behaved in a similar way. I found that, in such a situation, the empathy effect works and heightens favorability toward the victim's party even if the party is not governing. This leads to a further understanding of the impact of political assassination on citizens attitudes.

At the same time, we need to be aware of the limitations of this research. First, I do not provide direct evidence that partisans feel compassionate toward the opposing party while rejecting the alternative explanations. Therefore, there may be other potential causal paths through which the death of the MP decreased partisan hostility among Conservative

supporters. Second, we find it hard to investigate how long the effect lasts. Given that I use panel data, all participants interviewed after the event are classified as the treated. Thus, with the dataset, it is hard to know whether the effect is short- or long-term.

Despite the limitations, I provide externally valid evidence that partisans reduce their hostile attitudes toward an out-party when they are exposed to the misfortune of it. While a growing body of research has shown pessimistic results about affective polarization, it is still quite unclear how influential partisan conflict is on voters' attitudes. Further research is required to better understand the phenomenon of affective polarization around the globe.

## Introduction


The view of code-switching as a sign of competence or as a sign of incompetence has been a controversial topic for many researchers. As suggested by (Hymes, 1962, as cited in Kelekoula & Pjaileb, 2019), code-switching is described as a form of incompetence in one language. Hymes believes that bilingual speakers might switch from one language to another when they are unable to find alternative words or expressions. He says that it is 'used as a strategy of communication to compensate his lack of competence by using sometimes one language, sometimes the other to maximize the efficiency of the communications' (p. 200).

On  the  contrary,  Eldin  (2014)  highlighted  in  his  study  of  code-switching  of  Arabic language  speakers  that  'any  person  who  is  capable  of  switching  codes  must  be  a  competent bilingual'  (p.  79).  He  asserted  that  to  switch  codes,  linguistic  competence  should  always  be present. To code-switch effectively, bilinguals must possess a high level of understanding of the two cultures, as well as a deep understanding of the underlying structures and purposes of the two language systems (Hughes et al., 2006). He pointed out that code-switching reflects an intellectual advantage.

Investigating  the relationship between  code-switching  and  language  proficiency  is significant due to the increasing trend of switching between Arabic and English amongst Saudis in  their  daily  conversation.  Because  of  this  tendency  to  code-switching,  there  is  a  need  to understand this habit. Many studies have been conducted on the phenomenon of code-switching in Saudi Arabia. Most of these studies have examined the reasons for the code-switching of Saudi bilingual speakers and the frequency and types of code-switching. However, there is little research investigating the relationship between code-switching and the language proficiency of Saudis. In addition, no attention has been paid to whether Saudis view code-switching as a sign of language proficiency or as a symptom of language deficiency. Furthermore, to the best of my knowledge, no study has empirically investigated the relationship between code-switching and the level of language proficiency in the second language and how Saudis view code-switching in relation to language proficiency in a single study. Thus, this study aims to fill this gap in the literature.

This study aimed to better understanding the link between code-switching and language proficiency.  The  findings  of  this  study  would  be  of  great  value  for  the  development  of  codeswitching literature. Specifically, it had some pedagogical implications. Moreover, it would be significant for English language teaching (ELT) since code-switching has been discouraged in many ELT contexts because of the consideration of code-switching as a sign of limited language proficiency and the assumption that code-switching (CS) impedes fluency in the target language.

The study employed qualitative and quantitative method designs for data collection. The researcher used two main instruments: a questionnaire to obtain how Saudi female students at King Saud University (KSU) view the use of code-switching, as an indicator of language proficiency or as the lack thereof, and elicited production tasks with six female bilingual students in the English department at KSU.

## Literature Review



## Code-switching


The alternation between languages is a common phenomenon used among bilingual and multilingual to convey meaning. This phenomenon is known as code-switching (CS). The term CS has been defined by numerous linguists and researchers. CS is defined as "the alternation of two languages within a single discourse, sentence, or constituent." (Poplack, 1980, p. 583). Ja'afa and  Maarof  (2016)  also  define  CS  as  "a  communicative  phenomenon  of  constantly  switching between two languages in a bilingual's speech collection" (p. 212- 222).


## CS and Bilingual Proficiency


The view of CS as a sign of language proficiency or as a sign of language deficiency has always been controversial for many scholars. According to (Muthusamy 2009, as cited in Hadei et al., 2016, p. 125), when a particular word or expression is not available to a speaker, the speaker switches code. Salema (2010) studied CS between languages and stated that switching occurs for various  reasons,  including  a  change  in  conversation  topic  and  inadequate  vocabulary  in  one language. Another study was conducted by Cheng & Butler (1989) on "code-switching: a natural phenomenon vs. language deficiency" and showed that 100% of the participants agreed that codeswitching serves to compensate for a deficiency in language. In addition, although CS has been discouraged in English as a foreign language (EFL) classroom because of the consideration of code-switching as a sign of limited language proficiency, EFL teachers usually switch codes to express meanings precisely. Seventy percent of teachers code-switch from English to Spanish even though they viewed code-switching negatively (Pillips, 1975, as cited in Hughes et al., 2006). One of Hidalgo's studies (1988) findings is that using CS is perceived as a negative social trait. When bilinguals do not have equivalent words or phrases because of the inadequacy of their language abilities, they must switch to their first language to fill in the gap. "Code-switching serves as a "filler" to continue the flow of the communication process, but it is also an indicator of a weakness in the second language" (Hughes et al., 2006, p. 10). Similarly, Cook (2003) reported that when a speaker does not have the facility to express himself effectively, the speaker shifts to continue the flow  of  the  communication  process,  reflecting  the  speaker's  limited  language  proficiency.  In addition, the main reason for switching from one language to another is when a bilingual cannot express him/ herself in one language due to language deficiency (Crystal, 1987, as cited in Skiba, 1997, p. 1).

Contrary  to  the  negative  view  that  CS  is  due  to  a  lack  of  proficiency,  some  scholars indicated that code-switching requires language competence in both languages. Becker (1997), for instance,  asserted  that  CS  is  a  rule-governed  phenomenon  that  can  be  affected  by  linguistic,

CS can also be used as a strategy to extend bilinguals' competence. For instance, Arnfast and Jørgensen (2003) & Mirhasani and Jafarpour (2009) indicated that CS could be used as a communicative strategy that may lead to earlier language proficiency.  In addition, Nilop (2006) defined  CS  as  a  communicative  strategy  used  by  bilinguals,  and  he  viewed  CS  as  strategic competence.

Although CS has been extensively studied in Saudi Arabic, the studies that investigated CS in  relation  to  language  proficiency  are  limited.  For  instance,  Hamouda  and  Aljumah  (2020) investigated the perceptions of sixty-four Saudi EFL university students towards the reasons and functions of CS. They examined the attitudes toward CS and the uses of CS among Saudi students with various proficiency levels of English. They found a correlation between the level of language proficiency and the use of CS in EFL classes. Students with mid and low proficiency levels have positive attitudes toward the use of code-switching, whereas students with high proficiency levels have negative attitudes. It was also found that mid and low-proficient students used more CS than high-proficient students in EFL classes.  Hamouda and Aljumah's (2020) study is different from the present study in which it investigated the perceptions towards the reasons and the functions of CS in a classroom context, whereas the present study investigated how CS is viewed, a sign of language  proficiency  or  a  symptom  of  language  deficiency.  Moreover,  the  current  study investigated the relationship between language proficiency and frequency and types of CS.


## Bilingual Proficiency and Type of CS


Researchers  have  observed  that  language  proficiency  in  both  languages  is  one  of  the various factors affecting the type of CS. For example, Poplack (1980, p. 589) found that there is a correlation between the level of language proficiency and the type of CS employed by bilinguals. That is, bilinguals with high levels of language proficiency tend to use more intrasentential code switches (i.e., the occurrence of CS within a sentence). Similarly, Montes-Alcalá (2001) observed that bilinguals with the greatest degree of language proficiency in both languages tended to use more intrasentential code switches. In line with the previous two studies, Yow et al. (2018) found that proficient bilinguals tended to switch by intrasentential code-switches, whereas those who had low  levels  of  language  proficiency  tended  to  use  intersentential  code-switching  (i.e.,  the occurrence of CS after the sentence in one language has been completed or between speaker turns).

## Theoretical Frameworks


In relation to bilingualism and language competence, there are many theoretical models. First, according to Meuter & Allport's (1999) inhibitory control model, few CS are expected in bilingual  production  when speaking the weaker second language (L2) due to the effort that is needed to return to the dominant first language(L1). That means the cost of language-switching when bilinguals switch codes from the weaker L2 to the stronger L1. Second, in terms of using CS, bilinguals with a high level of language proficiency were expected to switch codes at a high rate due to their excellent knowledge of the grammatical rules of both languages (Poplack, 1980). In addition, Poplack (1980) indicated that bilinguals with high proficiency in both languages tend to be better at switching languages.

The present study is guided by the above-mentioned theoretical assumptions. The focus of this study is to investigate how CS is related to the language proficiency of adult bilinguals since most of the studies in the literature are related to bilingual children's CS. In specific, how Saudi female  university  students  from  two  different  levels  of  language  proficiency  switch  between English and Arabic.


## Research Methodology



## Participants


A total of 24 Saudi female university students at King Saud University participated in this study by filling in the questionnaire. The participants were students in the English department, which offers a master's degree program in the English language. They are highly educated. The participants  in  the  questionnaire  have  a  high  level  of  English  language  proficiency  as  they  all scored at least 6.5 in the IELTS exam as a requirement for the master's program. It was considered that the participants in the questionnaire have the high educational levels to investigate the effect of their high educational level on their attitudes toward CS.  In addition, six participants from two language proficiency levels, based on their IELTS scores, were asked to do a free speech task. Three were bachelor students in the English department at KSU, and the other three were master students in the same department. The information on the participants' level of language proficiency is significant as it is the only variable studied in performing the task.


## Research design


The study employed quantitative and qualitative method design of data collection. The researcher used a questionnaire and an elicited production task to collect data on whether using CS is a sign of competence or incompetence. The quantitative data from the questionnaire were analyzed using percentages to measure how Saudi female students at KSU view CS in terms of language proficiency.  Furthermore,  the  qualitative  data  from  the  elicited  production  task  were analyzed using content analysis to identify the frequency and type of CS in relation to participants' language proficiency.

The first research instrument was an online questionnaire, which SmartSurvey designed. In  the  first  open-ended  question,  the participants were asked whether they preferred to communicate with other bilinguals in English only or both Arabic and English. They were also requested to explain their preference. In the second open-ended question, the participants were asked whether their use of CS is related to their level of language proficiency. The two open-ended questions were used to identify the general preference and thoughts. The final data were analyzed using percentages. The results were then reported.

One of the techniques used to investigate CS is free speech in code-switch mode (Blot et al., 2003). The researcher conducted  the  free  speech  task  with  six  participants  to  gather  in-depth  information  about  the relationship between CS and language competence. The six participants participated voluntarily in this study. They were chosen based on their level of language proficiency. ## Conclusion


This  study  was  conducted  to  examine  the  relationship  between  code-switching  and language proficiency and determine how Saudi female students at KSU view code-switching in relation to language proficiency and deficiency. The findings revealed that although Saudi female students at KSU viewed the use of CS positively, they considered it as a symptom of language deficiency.  According  to  the  results  obtained,  the  type  of  CS  used  by  the  participants  was significantly related to their level of proficiency, whereas the frequency of CS was not. Besides this, the majority of the participants favored the use of CS while speaking with bilinguals. Thus, CS can be viewed as a tool that bilinguals prefer. Consequently, CS is not necessarily a sign of language incompetency.

The finding of the present study is significant in that it challenges the popular belief that CS is a signal of linguistic incompetency. Instead, it provides teachers and educators with some insights into the possibility that CS may be used by students as a favorable tool to meet their conversational goals as bilinguals. Thus, teachers and educators should not completely prohibit the  use  of  CS  in  EFL  classes,  and  they  also  should  not  judge  any  use  of  CS  as  a  sign  of unproficiency.

It  is  worth  pointing  out  that  to  generate  an  in-depth  understanding  of  the  relationship between code-switching and language proficiency, future studies should include participants with a low level of language proficiency. The absence of the low-level group might affect the result of the current study. The author used the free speech task to prove the finding of the questionnaire and  to  find  authentic  information.  However,  the  sample  of  the  task  consisted  of  only  six participants. With such a small size, it is difficult to find a significant relationship and generalize the findings. Furthermore, the limited time of the task might undermine the validity of the result. It would also be interesting for future research to examine this relationship among male subjects and compare the results with the result of the current study.
