## 1. Introduction


International  academic  literature  has  addressed  the  transformations  in  economic  and social systems caused by new revolutionary digital technologies (DAVIES et al. , 2017). Concepts such as "platform economy" (KENNEY; ZYSMAN, 2016), "platform society" (VAN DIJCK; POELL; WAAL, 2018), "platform capitalism" (SRNICEK, 2017) and "surveillance  capitalism"  (ZUBOFF,  2019),  although  presenting  different  nuances, highlight the role played by large private technology companies and call attention to the "revolution" (PARKER, GEOFFREY G.; ALSTYNE; CHOUDARY, 2016) caused by platforms.

Empirical  evidence  shows  that  platforms'  technological  architectures  and  governance choices are not neutral, affecting the functioning of both democracies and markets (VAN DIJCK;  POELL;  WAAL,  2018).  By  coordinating  and  managing  markets,  platform companies become a privileged point of friction, capable of appropriating part of the value transacted by these markets (TEECE, 2018). Therefore, having successful digital platform companies in a territory means that it will most likely become a gravitational point for capital accumulation. This relates to Arbache and Sousa's (2019) warning that participating in digital platforms as suppliers or consumers only confers first-degree gains while  controlling  digital platforms  provides  second-degree  gains.  This  ability  to appropriate value has led some of the main platform companies to develop their own corporate venture capital funds, also becoming dynamos of innovation and sources of economic dynamism.

Platform  companies  invest  a  good  part  of  their  budget  in  research  and  development activities  (R&D)  (DOLATA;  SCHRAPE,  2022)  at  a  time  when  many  industrial-age companies have moved towards financialization to the detriment of R&D investments (LAZONICK,  2007;  MAZZUCATO,  2016).  They  produce  new  technologies  and innovate due to their privileged positioning: by commanding the data flows that pass

through their platforms (VAN DIJCK, 2020), they have the technical and organizational apparatus  to be at the forefront of digital innovation  (NAMBISAN;  WRIGHT; FELDMAN, 2019). Platform companies generate new models of artificial intelligence (AI) since they have gigantic proprietary databases for their training. They also provide feedback to their business models on the insights generated by these same data, generating a virtuous growth cycle and worrying market domination (RIKAP; LUNDVALL, 2020, 2021). Moreover, finally, they are the ones moulding and transforming social behaviours (ZUBOFF, 2019).

That said, it is surprising that the literature that seeks to collect data on the population of platform  companies  in  a  given  region  is  scarce.  According  to  Riso  (2019),  the  only document that sought to geographically and sectorally map the distribution of the digital platform economy is Evans and Gawer (2016). The authors relied on expert advice and searches on the Quid web database to find the global population of digital platforms. However, they restricted their search to those firms whose market value is at least USD 1 billion. The authors identified 176 platform companies, of which 82 were in Asia and 64 in North America. Only 27 of them were based in Europe, two in South America (one in Brazil and one in Argentina) and one Africa-based platform (in South Africa). In terms of market value, the concentration remains, and it leans towards North America: 72% of the market value of the sample belonged to North American platforms, and 22% belonged to Asians.

Groen et  al. (2021)  recently  produced  a  census  of  digital  platforms  operating  in  the European Union. Focusing exclusively on platforms that intermediate some type of work, the authors identify 593 digital labour platforms. Also, with an exclusive focus on the European Union, Friederici, Reischauer and Lehdonvirta (2022) mapped four specific sectors: e-commerce, food delivery, health care, and social networking. Finally, Kässi; Lehdonvirta and Stephany (2021) mapped 351 online work platforms worldwide in an effort to calculate how many online workers there are in the platform economy.

The small number of platforms and the extreme geographic concentration identified by Evans and Gawer (2016) contrast with the statement proposed by Cusumano, Gawer and Yoffie  (2019)  that  the  2010-2020  decade  witnessed  a platformania ,  in  which  digital platforms multiplied to the point of becoming a standard organizational model (GAWER,

2021). Seeking to elucidate this apparent contradiction, Silva, Chiarini and Ribeiro (2022) carried out a new platform mapping at a global level. Using Natural Language Processing techniques, they identified over three thousand  digital platform companies worldwide leveraging data from Orbis database. Despite their contribution, they also recognized that, due to database limitations, they were not able to map smaller digital platform companies. As a consequence, geographic gaps remained, and the distribution of platform companies at a global level again showed a much greater representation of North America and Asia, especially the U.S. and China.

Given this literature gap, we continue with anecdotal evidence that there is consistent growth  in  the  platform  companies  in  the  Global  South,  such  as  Brazil,  but  without empirical and systematic verification of this phenomenon. Therefore, the question we address in this article is as follows: has Brazil joined the platformania decade (20102020)? In other words, has the Brazilian national private sector followed the global trend of developing digital platforms? If so, what are the main features of those digital platform companies in terms of size and sector? How are they distributed regionally in the country? How are they funded?

Building on Silva, Chiarini and Ribeiro's (2022) study, we replicate their methodology, however adopting a different database which covers early-stage startups: Crunchbase. Several  scholars  have  been  demonstrating  interest  in  assessing  the  potential  of  this database  for  economic  and  managerial  research  (BESTEN,  2020;  DALLE;  BESTEN; MENONI,  2017), for exploring innovative ecosystems (KEMENY;  NATHAN; ALMEER, 2017), and for mapping online work platforms (KÄSSI; LEHDONVIRTA; STEPHANY,  2021),  however,  its  full  potentiality  is  far  from  being  exhausted.  The novelty for Brazilian scholars is that it is the first time Crunchbase is used to investigate the digital platform economy phenomenon in the country.

In the next section, we make a quick incursion on the origins of digital platforms, and we suggest a lato and a stricto sensu concept of them. In section 3, we show the research methods that focus on the dataset used and how we identified what we called "digital platform companies". In section 4, we present the descriptive analysis and after, in section 5, we propose a discussion. Whenever possible, we cite digital platform firms to enrich the investigation; however, we do not dive into their characteristics, as it is not the scope

here  to  present  any  case  study  in  depth.  In  Annex  (Table  7),  we  provide  a  list  of  all Brazilian digital platform firms cited throughout the paper with links to their websites/apps.  Finally,  in  the  last  section,  we  propose  some  concluding  remarks  by affirming that the digital platform economy is challenging for researchers, policymakers and regulators.


## 2. Digital platforms



## 2.1. Digital platform origins


From a general or a lato sensu perspective, digital platforms are networks orchestrated by a controller that can be a private company or any other organisation, such as the State or even  academic  communities.  Understanding  digital  platforms  as  a  type  of  centrally managed network or as a point of friction in the network (COHEN, 2019) allows us to understand their evolution over time. After all, if the 1990s, the 'network society' was a central  discussion  (CASTELLS,  1996;  SANTOS,  1996);  two  decades  later,  there  are debates about the 'platform society' (VAN DIJCK; POELL; WAAL, 2018).

The network society concerns society's morphology, that is, the predominant form of social organisation that  occupies economic and cultural spaces. According to Castells (1996), social arrangements would take the form of networks for carrying out economic and cultural activities. However, in the 1990s, it was still unclear what specific form these networks would take. There was a certain glorification of the horizontality allowed by the networks.  However,  two  decades  later,  it  became  more  evident  to  researchers  that networks were being hierarchised (VAN DIJCK; POELL; WAAL, 2018) by orchestrators (PARKER, GEOFFREY G.; ALSTYNE; CHOUDARY, 2016) also called matchmakers (EVANS, DAVID S.; SCHMALENSEE, 2016) or digital platforms.

In this particular network form, at least two types of organisations differ in their position (centrality) and nature: controllers and participants. The former can be a private or public company (or a cooperative), and the latter can be other companies or people transacting goods or services (KENNEY; ZYSMAN, 2016). Its generic form (architecture) is that of a hub whose centre is stable and its periphery variable. Controllers are responsible for ordering and 'legislating' about the virtual environment provided by the platform. This

'legislation' occurs both explicitly through terms of service/use and implicitly through codes  unilaterally  defined  by  controllers.  Participants  join  the  platform  for  numerous reasons:  social,  financial  and/or  cultural.  However,  in  general,  their  participation  is restricted to the ways defined by the controller. In other words, the digital platform is a private network, with rules defined unilaterally (LEHDONVIRTA, 2022).

What would explain the  transition  from  the  network  society  to  the  platform  society? Although  the  literature  is  still  incipient  at  this  point,  there  are  two  ways  to  start  this exploration: economic and sociological. The economic explanation focuses on the ability to accumulate in a decentralised environment of digital abundance: the centralisation of control  over  the  network  makes  it  possible  to  configure  it  properly  for  commercial exploitation. In other words, the platforming of networks makes capitalism possible in the digital age. Mansell and Steinmueller (2020) mention how the abundance of networks on the Internet constituted an obstacle to capital accumulation and that the formation of silos, and walled networks, i.e., digital platforms, enabled this technological accommodation to the needs of the mode of production. In the 1990s, there were examples of how the media and online retail used platform models.

Besides, Lehdonvirta (2022) offers a convincing interpretation of the emergence of what he calls 'Cloud Empires' in a sociological interpretation, which considers the need for ordering institutions to provide trust and predictability in market interactions. According to  the  author,  the  anarchic  Internet  markets  in  the  late  1980s  and  early  1990s  were relatively horizontal and free but suffered from several difficulties. Especially when the number of users increased, the 'government' lack led to the deterioration of those markets due  to  fraud  and  inappropriate  behaviour  that  no  authority  controlled  or  enforced. Therefore, some entrepreneurs realised they could bring 'order' to online marketplaces and launched ventures like eBay and Amazon. The models worked well in creating online reputation management mechanisms and terms of service. By virtualising and ordering the  Internet,  they  allowed  value  transactions  and  the  growth  and  flourishing  of  these markets; on the other hand, what was a horizontal field became marked by oligopolies, the platform companies, which legislate without being elected on various aspects of new interactions and daily transactions.

In view of the narrated historical process, it is necessary to position the digital platforms analytically and conceptually. There is some confusion in the literature, which associates digital platforms with new technology. According to Silva, Bonacelli and Pacheco (2020), the digital economy, or the platform economy, is based on three technological pillars: big data, artificial intelligence and cloud computing. However, according to the authors, the platforms use these technologies, but they are not technology per se .

Given that digital platforms are not a single, specific technology, what would be the best way to conceptualise them? According to Perez (2002), technological revolutions unfold into techno-economic paradigms, which are generally good organisational and technological practices that spread throughout the socioeconomic  fabric. Digital platforms  can  be  understood,  under  this  lens,  as  an organisational  element or  even morphological  (CASTELLS,  1996,  2009),  fundamental  to  this  new  techno-economic paradigm.

This  conceptualisation  is  aligned  with  views  that  platforms  are  a  meta-organisational form  (GAWER,  2014),  a  new  standard  organisational  model  of  the  digital  economy (GAWER, 2021), an organisation providing new norms and institutions (LEHDONVIRTA, 2022), and a new organisational form of corporations (DOLATA; SCHRAPE, 2022; FRENKEN; FUENFSCHILLING, 2020). Kenney and Zysman (2020, p. 01) state that 'platforms are a new organisational form based on a relationship between the platform and the ecosystem of firms dependent on the platform and users who interact and transact through it.'

A  final  distinction  must  be  made  between  digital  platforms  and  digital  platform companies. Digital platforms are 'socio-technically structured social, market, consumption  or  service  spaces  in  which  social  actors  interact  based  on  detailed  and technically framed rules (…)' (DOLATA; SCHRAPE, 2022, p. 05). In the other hand, digital platform companies are traditional capitalistic organisations, 'not identical with their platforms but represent, rather, the organised places of strategic decision-making and the management of the platforms they own' (DOLATA; SCHRAPE, 2022, p. 10). In concrete terms, this means that Meta is a firm (a corporation) just like firms a hundred years ago. Organisational innovation is in the organisational structure the firm controls: a 'digital service space'. This organisational innovation is a strong candidate for an inter-

organisational model of the digital era: 'If the industrial revolution was organised around the factory, today's changes are organised around these digital platforms' (KENNEY; ZYSMAN, 2016, p. 62).

## 2.2.Digital platform functionalities and economic rationale

We presented a lato sensu definition of digital platforms in the previous section. Now we propose a more stricto sensu definition to guide our research effort. 'A platform is an entity  that  brings  together  economic  agents  and  actively  manages  network  effects between them' (BELLEFLAMME; PEITZ, 2021, p. 29). This interpretation highlights two essential characteristics. First, the purpose of connecting and enabling interactions and transactions between parties. Second, the network effects, which relate to the value of a network related to its size: 'the impact that an additional user of a product or service, or  an  additional  participant  to  some  interaction,  has  on  the  value  that  other  users  or participants attach to this product, service, or interaction.' (BELLEFLAMME; PEITZ, 2021). The network effects are important because they drive fundamental phenomena related to digital platforms, such as the attraction loops, the winner-takes-all dynamics and the growth strategies. Have these two characteristics in mind, as they will be essential to screen the Brazilian digital platform firms, as we shall discuss in the next section.

Before proceeding, it is necessary to call attention to how Belleflamme and Peitz (2021) refer to platforms: entities. However, they do not specify what kind of entities they are. There is a certain ontological confusion in distinguishing digital platforms as a virtual structure of inter-organizational governance and organizations per se . Digital platforms are, as we mentioned previously, a 'virtual structure' which can be controlled by (private) corporations,  States  or  academic  communities .  In  other  words,  it  is  necessary  to 1 distinguish between this inter-organizational structure and the organizations that control or participate in it (DOLATA; SCHRAPE, 2022). In our study, we considered companies that control digital platforms and named them 'platform companies'. Therefore, our unit

of analysis is the company. The common point between all these companies is that they are the controllers of a digital platform (but they can act in different other activities).


## 3. Research methods


## 3.1.The database

The data was sourced from Crunchbase , a commercial database of innovative companies 2 maintained  by  Crunchbase  Inc,  gathering  information  from  over  2  million  registered entities. It was created in 2007, and its scope has increased over the past years; however, its coverage is not clearly defined and may vary across countries  and sectors (DALLE; 3 BESTEN; MENONI, 2017). The information available on companies (entities) comprise their size, location (city and levels), primary role (firm, group, investor), status (active or closed), type (for-profit or non-profit), founding date, industry group , estimated revenue 4 range and brief description.

Crunchbase  gets  their  data  from  three  sources: i )  investor  network  (more  than  4,000 global  investment  firms  submit  monthly  portfolio  updates); ii ) active  community contributors (executives, entrepreneurs, and investors actively contributes to company profile pages, ensuring that the dataset is always growing and improving); and iii ) AI and

machine learning (algorithms that validate data accuracy, scan for anomalies, and alert Crunchbase data science team of conflicts in the data). With data in-house, Crunchbase data analysts provide manual data validation and curation, analyzing key interconnections in data to develop algorithms and provide valuable insights. In other words, Crunchbase is partially a crowd-sourced database, and it has mechanisms to verify the accuracy of data  by  applying  machine  learning  algorithms  to  endorse  data  accuracy,  examine inconsistencies  and  inform  their  data  scientists  of  eventual  discrepancies  (FERRATI; MUFFATTO, 2020).

## 4. The Brazilian digital platform economy



## 4.1. New and tiny


In Figure 1, we present the dispersion of the founding date of the companies of our set by year. The vast majority - 82% of digital platform firms - were founded from 2011 on, following  the  world  'platformization'  movement.  It  is  also  noticeable  the  number  of firms whose foundation dates back to the pre-Internet era; although not initially dedicated to digital services, these companies transformed their business models to include platform services at some point.

Incumbent  firms  were  founded  in  the  pre-Internet  phase  and  started  to  offer  digital services with the digital boom, and they can be found, for instance, in the real estate sector (such as Garcia Imóveis ), cooperatives (for example, Veiling ) or audiovisual sector (as Telecine ).

Despite  the  previous  examples,  today's  digital  platform  companies  in  Brazil  are  not simply a result of changing strategies of incumbent companies such as Garcia Imóveis , Veiling or Telecine . New businesses adopting digital platform models started to appear in the early 2010s, designed since the beginning to connect distinct groups and being able to create value by attracting new participants in the digital space. That was the case of the already born digital and 'platformed' Imóvelweb (founded 1999), VivaReal (founded in 2009), Loft (founded in 2018) and EmCasa (founded in 2018) , all from the real estate 7 sector. This gives an idea of the 'revolution' within the real estate service sector, where

incumbents had to change their business models while digital platform businesses were gaining market share.

## 5. Discussion


What  motivated  us  initially  was  to  verify  if  Brazil  followed  the  global  trend  of  the development of digital platforms by its companies. Our investigation and our data led us towards other related issues. One of them concerns the nature of this platforming process in  terms  of  markets:  would  the  Brazilian  platforming  process  follow  its  own  original trajectory, or would it have 'copied' the same markets that were platformed in the rest of the world? For instance, was Mundi.com (founded in 2008 and acquired by Kayak) the Brazilian version of the international platform Booking.com? Was 99Taxi (founded in

2012 and acquired by DiDi) the national version of the U.S. platform Uber? Many other examples exist (Table 6), and this possible 'tropicalization' of digital platforms deserves further investigation.

On the other hand, we also observe very unique Brazilian digital platform companies. Uboi , founded in 2016, is known as the 'Uber for cattle' and has over 3 thousand trucks registered in the app. It is controlled by JBS conglomerate and allows livestock farmers to access JBS' fleet and others registered in the app, offering real-time monitoring of the cattle transport. We also identified micro firms dealing with local challenges as Appgas - a platform connecting gas canister consumers and distributors, especially in locations not covered by natural gas pipeline systems - or Pleni 16 - an e-marketplace connecting distributors of bottled mineral water to consumers, relevant in regions where drinkable water  does  not  arrive  in  pipelines.  There  are  even  firms  like Goleiro  de  Aluguel connecting athletes to football teams and goalkeepers.

Besides,  we  found  a  large  number  of  marketplace  platforms  for  products  such  as i ) automobiles ( InstaCarro ); ii )  auto  parts  ( Origynal );  and  for  services  such  as iii )  ride-

hailing  ( 99Taxi ); iv )  delivery  via  motorcycles  ( Motoboy.app )  or  cars  ( Vuxx );  and v ) ancillary services for drivers (such as insurance or tow trucks CadeGuincho ). These examples demonstrate how the previous market characteristics remain and condition the platformization process.

Another  emerging  finding  from  our  data  is  digital  platform  companies  operating  in sustainability-related  markets.  We  highlight  here  some  that  connect  players  in  the renewable energy market, such as Lemon Energy and CleanClic; B2Blue.com , Descarte Legal and Agro2Business that have developed transactional systems for waste management and by-products commercialization, referring to the concept of industrial symbiosis (KROM; PISCICELLI; FRENKEN, 2022). This may indicate a potential for more platform companies to act towards sustainability and become important vectors of the twin transition (green and digital) 17 (FERREIRA et al. ,  2022; FOUQUET; HIPPE, 2022).  If  this  is  the  case,  this  'market'  of  sustainability-oriented  platform  companies deserves special attention and perhaps even public policies that promote its development and viability.

Moreover,  finally,  data  on  funding  (section  4.4.)  showed  the  participation  of  limited partners in the investment process, and most of the companies are still very small (preseed and seed). This seems to be a general characteristic of Brazilian Private Equity and Venture  Capital  market  structure  (CARVALHO;  GALLUCCI  NETTO;  SAMPAIO, 2014). Despite the restricted number of investors, once platform firms start to grow, either investment from abroad increases (secondary markets) or they are acquired/taken over by foreign platforms. This particularity deserves more investigation, specially to understand the international flows of investment in the platform economy worldwide and if special measures  should  be  taken  to  safeguard  market  and  national  interests  given  the  new dynamic of digital merges and acquisitions (GAUTIER; LAMESCH, 2021; PARKER, GEOFFREY; PETROPOULOS; VAN ALSTYNE, 2021).


## 6. Final considerations


It is worth mentioning again the unit of the analysis proposed in this paper: the digital platform firm. While a digital platform is an 'organized and more or less expansive social action  space  with  a  strong  technical  foundation  and  institutional  basis'  (DOLATA; SCHRAPE, 2022, p. 14), our unit of analysis is an organization that controls/owns a digital platform . Having that in mind, we proposed in this paper to verify if the Brazilian private sector has joined the platformania decade (2010-2020); and if so, which were the main characteristics regarding firms' size, sector, regional distribution and their source of funds.

The  identification  of  556  digital  platform  firms  based  in  Brazil,  of  which  82%  were founded  from  2011  on,  is  evidence  that  the  country  has  joined  the  international platformania trend, contrasting to studies that recurrently showed an empty map in the region regarding the existence of indigenous digital platform firms. As in Brazil and other Global South countries, there were only digital platforms controlled by big international techs. We do not deny their paramount presence in the national territory: in some sectors, foreign digital platform companies are dominant, as in ride-hailing (Uber); search engines (Google);  and  social  networks  (Meta),  demonstrating  a  very  serious  dependence  on international provision of digital services. However, we bring evidence that there is a nonneglectable domestic group gaining momentum: iFood, for example, controls today over 70%  of  market 18 and  there  are  other  domestic  digital  platform  firms  that  were  so successful that they ended up being purchased by international groups (as Akwan that developed a search engine platform and soon it was acquired by U.S. Google; or 99Taxi that got acquired by Chinese Didi).

Despite unicorns, like the just mentioned iFood, most of the Brazilian digital platforms are small in terms of revenue and employees; they are regionally concentrated; and they are immature in terms of funding.

Undoubtedly the industry group classification proposed by Crunchbase (as presented in section  4.2)  is  imprecise,  and  further  investigation  into  the  classification  on  Brazilian digital platforms is necessary. Moreover, screening Brazilian platform firms by function

(i.e., B2B, B2C, B2G), type (i.e., transactional, innovative, informational, hybrid), and market (i.e., ride-hailing, delivery, real estate, etc.) could bring an important contribution to understanding the Brazilian digital platform economy. The evidence presented seem to point to a specific form of insertion of Brazil in the global platform economy. They take on different types and specialize in specific niches, but in the end, they are variations of marketplaces that connect individuals or groups for transactions or interactions. These platforms generally have a lower market value than innovation platforms (CUSUMANO; GAWER; YOFFIE, 2019), have lower barriers to entry and lower development costs, as well as lower technological demands.

Further enquiry is also needed on data presented in section 4.3, which showed intense participation of São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro in the platformania. This has important implications  for  regional  development  in  the  country:  if  digital  platforms  are  the organizational element fundamental in the new techno-economic paradigm, as mentioned in section 2, and successful digital platform companies in a territory can be gravitational points  for  capital  accumulation,  the  value  appropriated  by  platform  controllers  are restricted to South and Southeast regions, which are already the most dynamic regions in terms of economic activity and in terms of higher income.

## 1 Introduction


With the rapid development of FinTech, digital credit service has deeply integrated with information technology, and the issuing of digital credit products through the Internet channel is gradually becoming the mainstream in our daily life (Chen et al., 2015; Francis et al., 2017). An example of a popular digital credit service in China is the consumer credit service provided jointly by Internet platforms and third-party financial institutions (Robinson et al., 2022). The Internet platforms, such as e-commerce platforms (e.g., Taobao), social media platforms (e.g., Sina microblog), and even search engines (e.g., Baidu), are providing digital credit services for their users.  It is only necessary for borrowers, who are also users of these platforms, to provide some personal information to apply for consumer credit services through these platforms without having to undergo a lengthy credit assessment. Providing digital credit services and issuing its products through the Internet channel has made them more convenient for Internet platforms,

third-party financial institutions, as well as borrowers (Francis et al., 2017). Particularly, it expands the range of applications for credit scoring, allowing for the identification of borrowers' credit risk with more useful information (Ariza-Garzon et al., 2021).

Credit scoring is a method of evaluating borrowers' credit risk quantitatively (Abdou & Pointon, 2011). Traditional approaches to determining borrowers' credit risk rely on their financial information and credit history information (AkkoGLYPH<141>, 2012; Hassan et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020), which we refer to as hard information 1 (Liang & He, 2020). One classic example is the FICO score, which combines the borrowers' repayment history with their credit report to evaluate their credit risk (Homonoff et al., 2021). In light of the deep integration of digital credit services with the Internet, scholars have found that the information borrowers leave on the Internet can be utilized to evaluate their credit risk, known as soft information 2 (Alves et al., 2016). For instance, borrowers' digital footprint s on the Internet, such as their browsing histories of web pages (Berg et al., 2020; Orlova, 2021), mobile phone usage histories (Bjšrkegren & Grissen, 2020; Ma et al., 2018; Pedro et al., 2015), and the e-mail usage histories (Djeundje et al., 2021), are collected and used to determine their credit risk. The credit risk evaluation incorporating borrowers' soft information breaks the limitations and broadens the application boundaries of credit scoring compared to conventional credit scoring based on hard information (Berg et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2021). However, further discussion is required regarding the reliability and accuracy of soft information used in credit risk evaluation.

Borrowers' hard and soft information can be considered as signals sent to lenders by which they evaluate borrowers' credit risk (Liang & He, 2020). Generally, information about borrowers' financial standing and credit history can directly reflect their repayment willingness and ability, which are highquality signals that can accurately identify borrowers' true credit quality (Barron & Staten, 2000; Spence, 1978). But due to the difficulties in collecting information and the delay in updating it, the information asymmetry may be exacerbated between borrowers and lenders (Dierkens, 1991; KorkeamŠki et al., 2014). Due to the growth of electronic credit services and their products, scholars believe that it is possible to reduce information asymmetry by utilizing borrowers' soft information from the Internet (Wang et al.,

2020). As the examples, scholars have found that borrowers' consumption behaviors on e -commerce platforms and social behaviors on social media platform may be indicative of their credit risk (Y. Li et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020). Compared with borrowers' financial standing and credit history information, borrowers' soft information provides a n additional amount of informational content that can be used in evaluating their credit risk, thereby reducing the degree of information asymmetry (Wang et al., 2020). In spite of this, borrowers' soft information still has some difficulties when it comes to evaluating their credit risk. First, soft information regarding borrowers does not directly reflect their willingness and ability to repay (Wang et al., 2020), which may result in an inaccurate portrayal of their credit quality, thereby reducing the efficiency of credit scoring. Furthermore, existing studies believe that the signal effect of the borrowers' soft information on their credit risk to be constant (Djeundje et al., 2021; Liang & He, 2020; Wang et al., 2020). However, the signal effect of the borrowers' soft information on their credit risk should vary depending on scenarios (Spence, 1978). The signal effect of borrowers' soft information on their credit risk may be exaggerated if it is ignored. As a result, further empirical analysis is needed regarding what soft information about borrowers accurately reflects their credit risk and what factors moderate the effect of such signals.

This paper applies signaling theory to examine whether the borrowers' credit risk is reflected by the ir platform behaviors and further explores the influence mechanisms between them. In our context, the borrowers are also the users of Internet platforms, which is different from peer-to-peer lending. Consequently, borrower would leave much information about their online behaviors on the platforms prior to applying for digital credit services. Thus, it provides a realistic basis for evaluating borrowers' credit risk based on their platform behaviors. Specifically, three research questions are addressed by collecting the digital credit application data from a traditional commercial bank and an Internet platform. Firstly, how borrowers' platform behaviors affect their credit risk. To answer this question, we quantify the borrowers' involvement intensity in terms of their average ratings of active days on the platform and employ a binary choice model to explore the relationship between borrowers' involvement intensity and their credit risk. The results indicate that borrowers' involvement intensity is a high quality signal that

negatively impacts their credit risk (Spence, 1978). Second, we discuss the reasons why borrowers' platform behaviors can be used to infer their credit risk. By conducting the mediating analysis, we quantify the value of borrowers to the platform, and find that the platform value of borrowers has a mediating effect on their involvement intensity and credit risk. In other words, platform lenders can infer borrowers' credit risk from their platform behaviors because they associate their platform behaviors with their value to the platform, and they believe that high value borrowers have lower credit risk. Third, what fa ctors moderate the effect of borrowers' platform behaviors on their credit risk. In signaling theory, the strength of signals depends on their ability to identify the true quality of its senders accurately and reliably (Spence, 1978). Depending on the circumstances, borrowers' involvement intensity may have a stronger or weaker signal effect. Our study examines whether the signal effect of borrowers' involvement intensity on their credit risk is stronger for borrowers (i) with higher stability of involvement intensity, (ii) with better credit history, and (iii) from regions with higher gross domestic product (GDP) per capita. The answers to these three questions provide insights into how borrowers' credit risk ca be derived from their platform behaviors. By exploring the relationship between borrowers' online behaviors and their credit risk, this study fills the research gap and provides additional empirical evidence for the existing literature.


## 2 Theoretical Background



## 2.1 Credit Scoring


Identify borrowers' credit risk is one of the key concerns of the credit industry (Ariza-Garzon et al., 2021; Crook et al., 2007). Numerous studies have been conducted on the models used in credit scoring to identify the credit risk of borrowers more efficiently. The existing studies on credit scoring models can be classified into two main categories. The first type is the predictive models, which are based on machine learning and deep learning, and are designed to identify whether the borrowers are eligible for credit application based on their historical information  (e.g., Bastani et al. (2019); Jiang et al. (2018); J. Y. Kim and S. B. Cho (2019)). Models such as support vector machines (Wang et al., 2018), tree-based models (Cai & Zhang, 2020), deep neural networks (Fu et al., 2019), and ensemble models (W. Li et al., 2020) are widely used to evaluate credit risk. Among them, scholars found that the ensemble models perform better

and are more adaptable in predicting borrowers' credit risk in most cases (Ariza-Garzon et al., 2021). Moreover, recent research has focused increasingly on how credit scoring improves the practical efficiency of its businesses (Ariza-Garzon et al., 2021). A key point is how economically significant the variables in credit scoring are. Considering this, the second category is the explanatory models that are based on econometric and statistical models, and study what, why and how variables impact borrowers ' credit risk (e.g., Ahelegbey et al. (2019); Chen et al. (2017); Ge et al. (2017)). It is clear from these studies that linear regression models and logistic regression models have been widely used (e.g., Canfield (2018)), and scholars and managers can identify the economic significance of these variables based on their coefficients in order to guide their management decisions.

Besides the models used in credit scoring, scholars have also explored which variables influence and reflect borrowers' credit risk, which can also be categorized into two groups. Firstly, borrowers' financial standing information, credit history information and transaction history information are used to evaluate their credit risk (Ji et al., 2019; A. Kim & S.-B. Cho, 2019; Xia et al., 2020). Known as hard information, these variables directly reflect the borrowers' willingness and ability to repay (Ariza-Garzon et al., 2021; Barron & Staten, 2000). A good example is the FICO score, which considers a variety of aspects of borrowers' credit history, such as their repayment records and transaction records (Adelino et al., 2016; Homonoff et al., 2021). Nevertheless, some scholars suggest that the application of hard information in credit scoring places too much weight on the borrowers' negative credit history, thereby limiting and adversely affecting their repayment behavior (Giannetti & Jentzsch, 2013). In addition, the delay in updating borrowers' hard information may lead to information asymmetry between borrowers and lenders, which reduces the effectiveness of credit risk evaluation (Xia et al., 2021). Therefore, the development of hard information used in credit scoring is facing challenges (Wang et al., 2020). Due to the limitations of hard information used in credit scoring, scholars have examined whether the variables related to soft information can be able to reflect borrowers' credit risk (e.g., X. Li et al. (2020); Wang et al. (2020); Wu et al. (2020)). These variables can potentially reflect the borrowers' ability and willingness to repay , such as borrowers' social behaviors on social media platforms (Y. Li et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2013) , borrowers'

consumption behavior on e-commerce platforms (Wang et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020) and the digital footprints borrowers left on the Internet (Berg et al., 2020; Orlova, 2021). Despite that the variables can be collected at a low cost and in large quantities, which mitigate some of the deficiencies of hard information, their theoretical foundations and validity for credit scoring remain open to doubt. Further empirical research is needed to determine which soft information variables are most appropriate for evaluating borrowers' credit risk. Moreover, it is also important to investigate the factors that influence the effect of soft information variables on credit risk assessment. We then employ signaling theory to explore the relationship between borrower's soft information variables and their credit risk.


## 2.2 Signaling Theory


An important issue in the evaluation of credit risk is information asymmetry (Burtch et al., 2014). Thus, borrowers have a better understanding of their true credit quality than lenders (e.g., traditional commercial banks, Internet platforms). Many studies and theories have been developed to alleviate the information asymmetry in credit evaluation, such signaling theory. According to Spence (1978), signaling theory focuses on how signals can be transmitted and screened in the case of information asymmetry so as to maximize potential trading gains and benefits. Generally, lenders evaluate the credit risk of borrowers by evaluating their financial standing and credit history (e.g., Abdou and Pointon (2011); Avery et al. (2004); Hassan et al. (2018); Zhang et al. (2020)), which can be viewed as signals sent by borrowers. As a result of such signals, lenders can more effectively evaluate borrowers' credit risk (Liang & He, 2020). However, identifying borrowers' credit quality using these signals has some drawbacks. For example, the updating of borrowers' credit history lags (Xia et al., 2021) and some individuals (such as young people) lack sufficient credit records (Wang et al., 2020). It is due to these issues that lenders are less efficient to evaluate borrowers' credit risk based on such signals. As digital credit services and their products have become increasingly prevalent, lenders are able to evaluate borrowers' credit risk from a more multidimensional perspective. A consensus exists that borrowers' soft information can alleviate the information asymmetry in the evaluation of their credit risk (Bachmann et al., 2011; Liang & He, 2020), since lenders can make full use of the additional information (Hu et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2021). In this

case, borrowers' soft information is the signal they send to lenders. It not only mitigates the deficiencies of hard information used in credit scoring, but also allows lenders to better identify the borrowers' credit risk (Hu et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2021).

Due to their difference in quality and cost, different types of signals have different effects (BliegeBird & Smith, 2005; Karasek III & Bryant, 2012). It has been suggested that costly signals are more helpful in mitigating information asymmetry (Aggarwal et al., 2012), because the informational value of the signal originates from the fact that the receivers believe it is more costly for low-quality signal senders to send high-quality signals (Spence, 1978). In the case of credit risk evaluation, borrowers are required to pay different cost when sending different quality signals. Borrowers  credit history is one ' example of such a signal, which has both high quality and high cost, since maintaining a good credit history requires a great deal of effort on the part of borrowers. Therefore, lenders can evaluate borrowers' credit risk effectively based on their credit history (Abdou & Pointon, 2011; Zhang et al., 2020). Currently, borrowers' soft information variables are also used to evaluate credit risk (e.g., Berg et al. (2020); Djeundje et al. (2021); Ma et al. (2018)). As opposed to hard information variables, these are more straightforward to collect, but they are not always reliable indicators of the borrowers' credit risk. To improve the efficiency of credit risk evaluation, it is particularly important to identify high-quality evaluation signals (Liang & He, 2020). Additionally, even the same type of signal may have different signal effects (Gulati & Higgins, 2003). A signal may have different effects depending on the sender (Cai et al., 2020), suggesting that the effects are closely tied to the characteristics of the sender. Besides, the effect of a signal is also influenced by other signals (Liang & He, 2020). As a result, it shows that the effect of a signals is not constant, which is susceptible to external influences.


## 3 Hypothesis Development


To develop our hypotheses, we employ signaling theory as the theoretical foundation (Spence, 1978). Signaling theory can be applied under two conditions. First, there is an information asymmetry between the sender and receiver of the signal. In our background, borrowers are more aware of their true credit quality than lenders are. Second, there is a potential interest conflict between the signal sender and

receiver. As a matter of fact, there is an inherent information asymmetry in the credit market, and borrowers can benefit from the information asymmetry by disguising themselves as good borrowers (Stiglitz & Weiss, 1981). By applying signaling theory, our study investigates the effect of borrowers' platform involvement intensity on their credit risk and identifies the factors that influence the signal effect of borrowers' involvement intensity. Based on our theoretical framework, the good borrowers could provide lenders with reliable information about their true credit quality by demonstrating their high level of platform involvement , since lenders attribute the borrowers' involvement intensity t o their value to the platform. Moreover, we believe that the impact of borrowers' involvement intensity on the reflection of their credit risk is not invariable, and it is influenced by other factors as well. We then examine how the stability of borrowers' involvement intensity, their credit history, and the economic environment in which they live impact the effect of borrowers' involvement intensity. Borrowers' platform involvement intensity reflects their dependence on the platform (Ray et al., 2014). In our context, we believe that the level of borrowers' involvement intensity can be a reliable signal

of reflection their credit risk. On the one hand, there are many functions integrated into the large ecommerce platforms in China that are relevant to the individual's daily life, and their large market share makes them oligopolistic platforms (Kwak et al., 2019). Increasing borrowers' involvement intensifies their dependence on platforms (Wan & Chen, 2019). If borrowers default, they must be forced to give up the services provided by the platform. In comparison to the borrowers with a lower involvement intensity, those with a higher involvement intensity have spent more time and effort in the previous use of the platform. In other words, the opportunity cost of default should be greater for borrowers with a higher involvement intensity. Moreover, it also suggests that borrowers with a higher level of involvement intensity are more likely to follow the platform's rules. As a result, the borrowers' high involvement intensity on the platform can serve as a high quality signal for lenders to determine the borrowers' true credit quality, as it takes borrowers longer and more effort for them to send the signal, which makes it difficult for the low credit quality borrowers to mimic and send the same signal. Accordingly, we propose our first hypothesis:

H1. The involvement intensity of borrowers on the platform has a negative impact on their credit risk.

In our opinion, platforms regard the borrowers' involvement intensity as an indicator of credit risk because these platforms associate borrowers' involvement intensity with their value to them. There is evidence that organizations attribute the value of their members to the level of their members' involvement intensity (Engen et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Sharma & Klein, 2020). The highly involved members are likely to be of high value to the organizations (Hollebeek et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2018), since they can bring greater benefits to them (Engen et al., 2021). It is important to note that Internet platforms are also a type of organization in our context, and borrowers are both users and members of the Internet platforms. In this regard, it is reasonable for the platforms to also consider borrowers with high involvement intensity as high-value users. Furthermore, high-value borrowers may have lower default risk due to the high cost of becoming a high-value borrower. In other words, borrowers with high values would incur greater opportunity costs if they defaulted. As a result, the platforms also

give priority to borrowers with high platform values when evaluating their credit risk (AkkoGLYPH<141>, 2012). Borrowers' platform value represents the credit risk that platform lenders attribute to the borrowers based on the extent to which they are involved with the platform. Following our discussion of the mediated effect of borrowers' platform value, we hypothesize that:

H2. The value of borrowers to the platform has a mediating effect between their involvement intensity and credit risk.

We then discuss the application boundaries of the main effect. In different conditions, the signal effect of borrowers' involvement intensity may be stronger or weaker, depending on whether signal receivers are able to accurately and confidently differentiate between low-quality signal senders and highquality signal senders based on the signals (Spence, 1978). As a result, the signal effect of borrowers' involvement intensity on their credit risk may be moderated by other variables, such as borrowers' personal characteristics and the environment in which they live.

The first moderator is the stability of borrowers' platform involvement intensity (involvement stability). Several previous studies have determined whether borrowers are likely to default by looking at the stability of their daily behaviors, such as their consumption patterns (Chen et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2018). These studies demonstrate that borrowers with stable behaviors are more reliable than those with erratic behaviors regarding credit quality (Tseng et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019). Consequently, borrowers' involvement stability can be viewed as an endorsement of their credit, which is an important consideration when evaluating their credit risks. It means that borrowers with a higher level of involvement stability are more likely to have stable demand for the platform. Since becoming stable users of the platform requires a certain amount of time and effort on the part of the borrowers, it is difficult for borrowers with lower levels of involvement stability to mimic and send the same signal (Spence, 1978). As a result, the higher level of involvement stability of borrowers makes the signal (borrowers' involvement intensity) stronger and enables lenders to distinguish between borrowers with poor credit and borrowers with excellent credit. Accordingly, we then propose the following hypothesis:

H 3. The signal effect of borrowers' invo lvement intensity on their credit risk is stronger for borrowers with higher level of involvement stability.

The second moderator is the borrowers' credit history. It is well known that borrowers with a good credit history are less likely to default (AkkoGLYPH<141>, 2012; Hassan et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). In China, borrowers' credit histories are recorded on their credit reports , and borrowers' credit history is a part of the social credit system. Credit history is important not only for credit applications but also other personal matters, such as the enjoyment of public rights (Lee, 2019). As a result, the borrowers' credit history is a strong signal of their future willingness to repay the credit (Spence, 1978), and lenders also take into account the their credit history when evaluating their credit risk. Without considering the borrowers' credit history, the signal effect of their involvement intensity on their credit risk may be overestimated. Therefore, good credit history can enhance the signaling value of the involvement intensity of borrowers. In other words, borrowers with poor credit history have a harder time mimicking and sending the same quality signals as borrowers with good credit history. Accordingly, we make the following hypothesis:

H4. The signal effect of borrowers' involvement intensity on their credit risk is larger for borrowers with better credit history.

Our third moderator is the per cap ita GDP at the borrowers' residence. A region's per capita GDP reflects the level of economic development in that region, where the residents generally earn higher wages. Therefore, borrowers from regions with a higher per capita GDP are likely to have a more remarkable ability to repay their credit in the future, and lenders are more likely to assume that borrowers from regions with high per capita GDP have a strong ability to repay. It is difficult for borrowers from regions with a lower per capita GDP to replicate and send the same signals. Thus, we propose our hypothesis as follows:

H5 The . signal effect of borrowers' involvement intensity on their credit risk is stronger for borrowers from the higher per capita GDP regions.


## 4 Data Description



## 4.1 Data Context


The data we obtained from a large e-commerce platform in China, which had partnered with many commercial banks to provide digital consumer credit services and develop digital consumer credit products. Over the period from August 2019 to December 2020, we collected the data on 595,477 borrowers who applied for consumer credit service through the e-commerce platform. Because of the large market share of the e-commerce platform in China, the borrowers on the platform can be well represented the borrowers in the overall consumer credit market. As it is common for borrowers to repay their consumer credit in installments, it should be used the last repayment to determine whether they are in default. To avoid the survival bias due to the short observation period, we focused on the borrowers who should have squared their installment consumer credit prior to February 2021 . In the case of borrowers 3 applying for consumer credit service through the platform, the platform evaluates their creditworthiness first based on their platform performance and credit history. Then the bank cooperating with the platform will conduct a second review of borrowers' credit quality based on the feedback provided by the platform. As a consequence, our dataset includes not only variables related to borrowers and their consumer credit applications, but also variables related to platform behavior and credit history for borrowers. We then provide the variable descriptions in the next section.

## 5.3.3 Replacement of Empirical Model Identification


As part of this section, we validate the robustness of our model with respect to model selection and estimation methods. A concern is that defaults are relatively rare in the general population (only about 1.2% of borrowers in our sample defaulted), and rare event bias may affect estimation results (Heinze, 2006; King & Zeng, 2001a). There are two ways in which we deal with rare event bias. To obtain biascorrected estimates, we first use the logistic regression model, but estimate the small sample bias caused by the rare events, and then correct the estimated coefficients of the original logistic regression model. This estimation method (relogit) can be completed by the Stata command provided by King and Zeng (2001a, 2001b). The column (1) of Table 6 reports the estimation results based on this estimation method. The coefficient of Involv\_ins is negative and statistically significant, which is consist with our

main model. Our second approach uses a complementary log-log model (clog-log) to handle the rare event bias by assuming the probability distribution of events occurring is left-skewed (Kitali et al., 2018; Penman & Johnson, 2009). If one represents a rare event occurring, and zero represents a rare event not occurring, the probability p of an event occurring tends to one faster than that tends to zero. This property corresponds exactly to the case of rare events occurring (Piegorsch, 1992). ## 5.4 Endogenous Check


In our context, the involvement intensity of a borrower may be endogenous, as it may be influenced by the borrower's credit performance. As a result, there may be a bidirectional causal relationship between a borrower's involvement intensity and its credit performance. To alleviate the endogenous concern, we exploit some more exogenous shocks from instrumental variables (IVs) to reduce the effects of endogeneity on the model (Wooldridge, 2002). The appropriate IVs should not only reflect the involvement intensity of borrowers, but also be unrelated to their potential credit risk. We use the average rating of the number of days a borrower visits the pages related to take-out ( Visit\_waimai\_days ) and group-buy ( Visit\_groupbuy\_days ) on the platform as IVs.

The good IVs should satisfy two conditions (Wooldridge, 2002).  Firstly, we should select IVs that are highly correlated with our independent variables. In our main model, we measure the independent variable Involv\_ins based on the average rating of the borrower's active days. It is a comprehensive measure since borrowers may visit the platform for the purposes of consumption or browsing information. Either of them reflects the borrower's involvement intensity. Regarding the first condition, our two IVs can serve the second purpose of reflecting a borrower's activity level on the platform. The selection of IVs is in accordance with previous research (Jabr & Zheng, 2014), which uses the individual's other activities as an instrument for the focal activity. Furthermore, the first condition can be tested statistically. In other words, if the IVs are weak (the IVs are not or weakly correlated with the independent variable), the estimation results using the weak IV are not the best linear unbiased estimators (Stock et al., 2002). We

address this concern by calculating the first-stage F statistics for our IVs (Stock et al., 2002). Test results reject the original hypothesis ( F >100), confirming that our IVs are not weak instruments and have high correlations with independent variable.

Second, the IVs should be unrelated to our dependent variable. Our IVs are a measurement of how active a borrower is on the platform, and they do not directly reflect the borrower's ability to repay. Thus, they should not directly affect a borrower's credit risk. According to signal theory (Spence, 1978), the signal receiver can receive different quality signals simultaneously, but only high-quality signal are capable of enabling the signal receiver to distinguish the actual state of the signal sender. Depending on our context, either the borrower's consumption habits or just browsing the information on the platform can be indicative of their involvement with the platform. However, the variables that can reflect the borrower's willingness and ability to repay (e.g., its consumption ability) are the high-quality signals that can be used by the platform to identify the borrower's actual credit quality. Unlike our independent variable Involv\_ins , which measures a borrower's ability to repay and be active, our IVs only reflect its active status, and they are not credible signals for a platform to identify a borrower's actual credit quality.  Due to the two basic functions of this e-commerce platform (takeout and group-buy), both borrowers with good credit and those with poor credit are likely to visit the web pages of them frequently. Therefore, it is more difficult and costly to evaluate a borrower's credit risk in this manner. As a result of the above discussion, our IVs should not have a direct impact on the credit performance of a borrower. In fact, the borrower's consumption ability may be more relevant with its credit risk, and we have already controlled for this in our study. As a further verification, we performed an overidentification test, and the result indicates that we have no reason to reject the original hypothesis ( p >0.1), namely that our IVs are more likely to be exogenous. Additionally, we conduct the Hausman test to examine whether the IV approach is more effective than ordinary least squares in our context. The result suggests that the IV approach is needed in our research ( p <0.01)
