## Discussion and Conclusion


This study aimed to investigate whether students with a cultural capital advantage also have a social network advantage with regard to their friends' school grades. Moreover, it sought to address whether social network mechanisms are related to the school grade gap between students with a different cultural capital endowment, potentially altering educational inequality. To this end, I used data from around 1400 adolescents in 18 German secondary schools and applied stochastic actororiented models (SAOM) as well as simulations.

SAOM results showed that-compared to students with less cultural capital-adolescents with more cultural capital tend to establish friendships with those who have better school grades. This seems to be especially the case for students at the lower end of the school grades spectrum. Here, cultural capital seems to compensate for bad school grades.

Concerning  the  school  grade  gap  between  students  with  different  cultural  capital  amounts, simulations reveal that network mechanisms can favour adolescents with less cultural capital: Peer influence can decrease the school gap in certain scenarios. Thus, in light of the SAOM results, the counterintuitive finding can be explained because adolescents with more cultural capital tend to have friends with better grades compared to their schoolmates , but their friends have slightly worse

grades compared  to  their  own  grades. Conversely, culturally-disadvantaged  students  do  have worse grades, but their friends have slightly better grades than themselves. This provides them with the chance to benefit from their friends. These selection patterns may be explained by the situation that culturally-advantaged students tend to be at the top of the school grade distribution and have, therefore, fewer chances to select similar or higher-achieving peers as friends. While I provide theoretical arguments for the underlying mechanisms, the current paper does not investigate how different homophiles (i.e. school grades or cultural) or meeting opportunities constitute the network advantage.

However, contrary to expectations, simulations show that more school grade or cultural capital homophily would not increase the school grade gap. This may be explained in two ways. Firstly, homophily, even in the scenarios at the extreme end, may still be too small to make a substantial difference.  Secondly,  while  students  with  more  cultural  capital  have  better  school  grades,  the association between these two indicators is still too weak to increase the school grade gap. Zhao and Garip (2021) show that only in cases where relevant indicators are 'consolidated' (Blau, 1977, 1994), an increase in homophily exacerbates intergroup inequality. They also report that a mere homophily increase without consolidated parameters does not impact intergroup inequality. Future research might address this by investigating networks in which these indicators are more or less consolidated to shed light on whether and why processes differ between schools (see also adams & Schaefer, 2016).

Taken together, the simulations suggest that social networks may reduce educational inequality under specific circumstances. However, even in the most extreme scenarios, the school grade gap between groups is still rather wide. Starting differences between adolescents with a different family backgrounds are and remain more important. In addition to these network effects, it has to be remembered that adolescents' family backgrounds already play a role in the school-choice (Jheng et  al.,  2022;  Kruse,  2019),  which  is  of  substantial  importance  for  individuals'  educational trajectories. Therefore, the findings of this paper have to be assessed in light of the bigger picture of educational (and social) stratification.

While this article produced novel insights, some limitations may serve as a starting point for future  research.  First  of  all,  the  analysis  sample  is  biased  towards  schools  with  a  higher socioeconomic  status.  Especially  lower-track schools  ( Hauptschulen) , which  tend  to  host socioeconomically disadvantaged and ethnic minority students, are under-represented. The reason for this is two-fold: The response rate of students in these schools was substantially lower than in

the other schools, leading to an exclusion from the analysis sample. In addition to that, these schools tend to be somewhat smaller and the overall amount of cultural capital is lower in these schools. This led to more issues with non-convergence in these schools. Future studies might address this issue by drawing on a sample with more lower-track schools to investigate whether the observed patterns can also be found there.

Secondly, I relied on adolescents' books at home and their theatre/opera/museum attendance to assess their cultural capital and inferred their habitus from these. Since research shows that habitus might act as a mediator between cultural capital and academic achievement, future research using a  more  precise  measurement to fill this  gap  is  needed  (Gaddis,  2013).  Moreover,  although  the indicator 'books at home' is a common indicator, it has come under scrutiny more recently (see, for example, Engzell, 2019; Sieben & Lechner, 2019). Using different cultural capital indicators may, therefore, prove to be a fruitful extension.

Thirdly, these results are based on simulations, it is not clear how this translates into the real world and it is unclear whether the other processes play out similarly if values were truly different.

Despite these limitations, this paper advances social network studies in empirical and conceptual ways. It is one of the few studies which investigates network mechanisms for different groups and, to my knowledge, the first study, which investigates behaviour outcomes as a result of network processes for different social groups. This approach leads to novel insights and may provide a foundation for future studies contributing to our understanding of group-specific network processes and their outcomes.

## INTRODUCTION


Understanding indicators of social vulnerability to the health impacts of climate change is increasingly recognized as essential to protecting population health (1). Through changes to the climate system and the failure to enact sufficient climate adaptations, anthropogenic climate change is having a detrimental impact upon human health to the extent that the recent 2022 Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate change report concludes  that  climate  change  is  affecting  all  monitored  dimensions  of  global  health  (2).  Yet, contrary to the notion that environmental risks like climate change represent a 'universalization of hazard' which  are  not  hierarchical  in  effect  but  'democratic',  affecting  all  irrespective  of  social  position  (3), research  is  finding  that  susceptibility  to  the  health  impacts  of  climate  change  reflects  broader  social structures and inequalities (4-9). For those exposed to climate-related hazards, vulnerability or potential to be harmed is greater when there are insufficient resources or adaptive capacity to minimalize the health impacts of climate change (6, 10). Indicators of vulnerability are needed for early community screening and rapid assessment that facilitate climate adaptation and health protection.

There are several pathways between climate change and human health (2). Direct effects on physical health have been documented including injury, cardiovascular, respiratory, and renal health conditions, and death, as well as poor mental health and wellbeing, from non-optimal temperature, shifting weather patterns, and climate-related disasters (11, 12). Indirect effects on health through climate change altering ecological and human systems that cascade to affect human health have also been described (13, 14). Changing climates and environmental conditions are more favorable to vector-borne and water-borne diseases (13), endanger crop yields and food security (14), put strain upon inadequately adapted healthcare systems (2), and increase societal conflicts (1), all of which constitute negative feedbacks that aggravate health losses.

To prevent these impacts, adaptations in response to climate change need to take social vulnerabilities into consideration. Vulnerability is one component of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)'s risk assessment model (hazard, exposure, and vulnerability) for understanding climate change impacts on ecological and social systems (1). The IPCC defines vulnerability as 'the propensity or predisposition to be adversely  affected'  and  'encompasses  a  variety  of  concepts  and  elements,  including  sensitivity  or susceptibility  to  harm  and  lack  of  capacity  to  cope  and  adapt'  when  exposed  to  hazards  (1).  Social vulnerability specifically encompasses all social practices, structures, and positions within sets of relations or hierarchies that render individuals, groups, or societies unable to respond or adapt to harms (6, 7, 15). This is often operationalized in terms of individual characteristics (including age, gender, ethnicity, income, wealth, and social status) and how these factors influence the set of resources and capacities available to individuals  and  social  groups  (5,  16).  Other  operationalizations  also  include  institutional  (including governance and service systems), structural (including sociodemographic and socioeconomic inequalities, power hierarchies, and discrimination),  and place-based (including urbanization, green space, and urban heat refuges)  features of social systems that afford or constrain adaptive capacity and therefore moderate susceptibility (1, 6, 7). Successive IPCC assessment reports have increasingly emphasized the importance of understanding and reducing social vulnerability to improve resilience to climate hazards, and the most recent assessment report noted that, at a urban and community level, a critical barrier to the implementation of  climate  adaptation  plans  includes  a  'limited  ability  to  identify  social  vulnerability  and  community strengths' (1).

This scoping review of the research literature concerning social indicators of vulnerability to the climate change impacts on health seeks to identify which indicators have been examined, and describes the key relationships between climate change, social vulnerability, and health. Research on social indicators went through a period of abeyance throughout much of the 1980s and 1990s, but since the early 2000s there has been  increased  calls  for  the  development  of  indicators  and  indexes  of  vulnerability  that  has  led  to  an exponential growth in indicator-based research this century (7). This review will 1) provide an overview of

the state of the empirical literature on social vulnerability to the health impact of climate change from 2012 to 2022,2) identify social indicators used for the analysis on the health impact of climate change and/or the development  of  social  vulnerability  indices,  and  3)  detect  areas  of  social  vulnerability  that  are  underresearched or under-theorized in current scholarly literature.


## METHODS



## Methodological overview


The scoping review process followed a predetermined protocol in accordance with the scoping review methodology  outlined  in  the  JBI  guide  and  was  checked  against  the  PRISMA  extension  for  Scoping Reviews framework (17, 18). The scoping review method is preferable to other review approaches because the aim of the review is to establish the scale of the literature on social vulnerability to the health impacts of climate change, which is not limited to a particular study design, and because climate change, social vulnerabilities, and health impacts are multidimensional concepts that are not easily reduced to a narrow set of preconceived variables. We applied the scoping review guidelines from the JBI (17), which integrates the original methodology proposed by Arksey and O'Malley (19) and the extension by Levac, Colquhoun, O'Brien (20). The five main steps of this method were followed: 1) formulation of research question, 2) collection of relevant studies from literature databases, 3) study selection or screening to identify papers that  fit  eligibility  criteria,  4)  data  charting  to  identify  the  frequency  of  topics  and  themes  within  the literature, and 5) collating, summarizing, and reporting of results (17, 19).


## Search strategy and selection criteria


The literature search was conducted on 7 th of May 2022 on four online databases: Web of Science, Scopus, CAB Direct, and PubMed. These databases were selected for their comprehensive archives of literature across social sciences, humanities, environmental sciences, and medical and health sciences to capture an overview of studies that investigate social vulnerability to the health effects of climate change. We used search  terms  consistently  for  each  database  that  combined  the  four  blocks  of  search  terms  including

vulnerability ('vulnerability', or 'sensitivity', or 'susceptibility'), climate change ("climate change", or "global warming", or "natural disaster", or "extreme weather", or 'weather extreme', or 'climate extreme', or 'extreme temperature'), health ('health', or 'mortality', or 'morbidity'), and indicators ('index', or 'indices', or 'indicator', or 'factor', or 'component').

Included studies were peer-reviewed articles published in English between 2012-2022 that studied factors (quantitative) or themes (qualitative) on social vulnerability to the health consequences of climate change. Articles selected for the review include quantitative and quantitative studies that examine the impact of climate change on human health and associated social vulnerabilities that heighten the risk of experiencing negative health effects. Excluded studies did not include one of the three components (i.e., climate change and related natural disasters as exposure, health outcomes, and social risk factors). Studies were excluded if they reference climate change and health without social vulnerability, examine social vulnerability to health conditions outside of the context of climate change, or include no health outcomes. Studies were excluded if they did not report original primary or secondary research such as reviews, commentaries, and other documents without an empirical component (either qualitative or quantitative). Studies were ineligible if not published in English during the above period. AL and MT independently examined the titles and abstracts of articles resulting from these searches, with any disagreements resolved by RB.  The full text review was conducted by AL and MT, with disagreements resolved by RB.


## Data Extraction and Charting


Data  charting  followed  the  establish  approach  for  scoping  reviews  (19,  20).  Data  was  extracted independently by two reviewers (AL and MT) with a standardized spreadsheet. Extraction focused on date of publication, setting in which the study was conducted, the sources of data, study design, the type of health  impacts  of  climate  change,  social  vulnerability  factors,  health  outcomes,  and  key  findings. Inconsistencies between the two sets of data extraction were discussed and resolved by all three reviewers.

Results  of  the  charting  process  are  reported  in  frequencies  tables  and  the  thematic  analysis  of  social vulnerability focuses on the prominent themes.


## RESULTS


Results of the database search returned 475 papers from Web of Science, 430 papers from Scopus, 486 papers from PubMed, and 382 papers from CAB Direct for a gross total of 1773 studies. Duplicates were removed in endnote (466) for a final corpus of 1307 studies for abstract and title screening process. The reviewers employing the inclusion and exclusion criteria excluded 957 papers in title and abstract screening due to full text being unavailable, non-English text, or missing component of climate change, health, or social indicators.  Full text screening was conducted on the remaining 330 papers and 125 did not meet the criteria for inclusion, leaving a final corpus of 205 papers for data extraction and charting (Figure 1).


## Age


Age is the most common indicator of social vulnerability within the literature (21-134), with 153 of 205 studies including age as a variable or theme. Extreme temperature and heatwaves are the most reported climate variable that correlate with poor health outcomes for elderly people (defined variously as those above 60, 65 or 75) (23, 30, 31, 34, 41, 50, 53-55, 60), while elderly are also found to be susceptible to cold snaps  (56)  and  other  climate  impacts  such  as  wildfire  (44)  and  floods  (42).  Mechanisms  for  this vulnerability are reduced thermoregulatory function with age, worsened perceptions of temperature and risk, lacked engagement in adequate adaptive behaviors, co-occurring chronic illness, limited mobility and

other socioeconomic risks such as living alone and lower socioeconomic status (28, 29, 38, 49, 51). Age has also been found to have a U-shaped relationship with the negative health effects of climate change, with younger age group (e.g., those under five years of age) and older age group (e.g., those over the age of 65) most commonly reported to be susceptible to the health effects of heatwaves and extreme temperatures (31, 32, 41, 53, 55, 60). Occasional studies found that other age groups (e.g., middle-aged) were susceptible to high temperatures and heatwaves depending on the setting (61, 80). Living alone and social isolation are compounding factors in many studies, increasing the vulnerability of older individuals and making them less climate resilient (46, 57).


## Sex/Gender


Sex/gender  is  used  as  an  indicator  of  social  vulnerability  across  multiple  settings,  though  relationship between  sex/gender  variables  and  susceptibility  is  contextual  and  differs  according  to  climate  change impact, health effect and setting (21, 26, 31, 34, 38-40, 43, 51, 53, 54, 60, 61, 63, 64, 66, 69, 71, 72, 76, 78, 79, 82-84, 89, 90, 94, 97, 99, 104, 106, 108, 114, 115, 119, 122, 124, 126, 128, 130-133, 135-157). Extreme temperatures are correlated with increased hypertension (135), ambulance dispatches (133), mortality (34) for men, though this gender health gap had narrowed over time (133). Alternatively, other studies have found women were more vulnerable to temperature variation (40, 141), heatwaves (54), cold spells (61) and that the proportion of female population was associated with higher volume of prescription usage for bronchodilator  prescriptions  (136).  There  is  no  clear  relationship  between  gender/sex  as  an  individual characteristic  and  social  vulnerability  to  the  climate  change  impacts  of  health,  and  the  association  of susceptibility and sex is highly contextual. Alternatively, variables that measure gender as a social structure such as proportion of population female and proportion of female headed household were used as indicators of vulnerability in several studies (70, 117, 158). These proportion-based indicators of vulnerability may capture dimensions of structural inequality similar to measures of gender inequality (148) in settings where female populations or households do not receive the resources needed for adaptation and health protection.


## Race, ethnicity, minority, and immigration


Multiple social vulnerability indices include race or ethnicity based indicators for social vulnerability which have been found to be good predictors of susceptibility to heat (21, 22, 26, 32, 37, 44, 46, 58, 72, 95, 98, 111, 116, 119, 158-164). This is attributed to the history of structural disadvantage and discrimination faced by minority communities (111, 112). Historical urban policies based on racial segregation continued to have an impact on the health and heat vulnerability of non-White populations due to the higher surface temperatures  in  areas  subject  to  'redlining'  (165).  Racial  inequality  is  compounded  by  the  associated economic and social deprivation. Urban areas with higher rates of people of colour were found to be highly correlated with higher incidences of poverty, low education attainment, and limited English proficiency, increasing the vulnerability of residents to heatwave related mortality (116). A few studies also included migration status (123, 148), country of birth (145, 158), and indigenous status (103, 132) as vulnerability factors.


## Economics and socioeconomics


There are several indicators that measure socioeconomic status at individual and area levels, including household income (28, 36, 50, 53, 70, 136, 148, 166-170), neighborhood deprivation (105, 137, 144), labor force participation (42, 48, 148), poverty (22, 24, 48, 58, 62, 70, 72, 73, 81, 85, 89, 90, 93, 95, 98, 100, 102, 111,  112,  116,  162,  171-173),  gross  domestic  product  (174-176),  income  inequality  (172,  176,  177), unemployment  (41,  49,  111),  emergency  fund  (42,  68),  asset  ownership  (67,  68),  welfare  payment recipience (57, 94), health insurance status (68, 104), and source of income (70, 140). The relationship between income or socioeconomic status, either on an individual or area-level scale, and susceptibility to the health impacts of climate change were consistently negatively related throughout the literature corpus. Higher  income  and  socioeconomic  levels  suggest  more  resources  for  resilience.  Compounding  the vulnerability of low income or socioeconomic individuals to extreme temperatures, studies find that lower income individuals spend more time outdoors during heatwaves (50) and are more likely to reside in urban areas that have higher temperatures (116).


## Education


Education is a commonly adopted indicator of social vulnerability (66 of 205 studies). Studies tend to find that lower educational attainment at an individual or area level is correlated with poorer health outcomes as the result of climate change impacts across all settings, in high, middle, and lower countries as well as urban and rural environments (43, 46, 72, 73, 89, 95, 114, 120, 178-180). Similar to socioeconomic status, the generally observed positive relationship between low educational attainment and climate-related health impacts is attributed to people with lower education having access to fewer resources and therefore less adaptive capacity (73, 179), though health related education interventions can reduce vulnerability (179). Findings are less consistent when considering the interaction of education with demographic variables such as sex (43, 181) or when other socioeconomic variables are also being controlled (182).


## Livelihood and occupation


Livelihood  strategies  are  frequently  included  as  a  main  driver  of  socioeconomic  vulnerability  for households supported by resource based livelihoods in developing countries such as Bangladesh (183), Uganda (184) and Ethiopia (158). These hazard-prone households are vulnerable due to their dependance on rain-fed agricultural livelihoods (184) and their existing livelihood status aggravate a vicious cycle of vulnerability (183).  Households  with  access  to  diverse  agricultural  activities  or  alternative  means  of livelihood,  measured  as  average  livelihood  diversification  index  (158),  crop  diversity  index  (70)  and livestock diversity index (70), are less vulnerable to extreme weather events. Across settings, occupational groups that require working outdoors, such as council workers, construction workers and farmers, were at risk during extreme heat (52, 59, 111, 185).


## Language, language proficiency, and literacy


Language barriers were identified as a source of social vulnerability to climate change, with 15 articles addressing linguistic isolation or lack of fluency in the primary local language (22, 72, 73, 85, 114, 116,

119, 145, 186) and 19 articles addressing illiteracy (28, 41, 47, 53, 59, 168, 171, 187, 188). Linguistic barriers thwart adaptive behaviors during extreme weather events as warnings are not fully understood (72, 73, 114, 116), with the vulnerability particularly higher in linguistically heterogenous areas (85). Multiple studies on populations in the United States found that a higher percentage of non-English speakers in an area have greater odds of heat wave related morbidity and mortality (145, 165, 189) and people with limited English language fluency reside in areas with the highest social vulnerability index scores (22). Illiteracy as social vulnerability indicator of health impacts to extreme weather events are often used in settings were education attainment is low (53, 94).


## Living and built environment.


Studies have identified lack of access to green or blue space (38, 39, 45, 48, 49, 58, 62, 67, 69, 95, 105, 112, 162, 188, 190, 191), building density and impervious surface (95, 105, 116, 145, 186, 192, 193), poor or polluted living environment (67, 68, 111, 118, 136), and the social distribution of access to public cooling facilities or urban heat refuges (52, 189, 194) as an social vulnerability factor that measures the aspect of living and built environment. Widely used indicators of green space include the normalized difference in vegetation index which measures that amount of vegetation vs non-vegetation surface coverage in an area (39, 105, 162, 188), distance to parks and other green space (69), the relative abundance of impervious surfaces (e.g. the normalized difference built-up index) as a proxy for the lack of green space (188), and the  percentage  of  non-green  space  (38).  Green  and  blue  space  is  associated  with  relatively  lower temperatures compared to urban spaces with little or no green space or no access to blue space (39, 49, 67, 112, 162). Modification or moderation of the heat effects of climate change via green and blue spaces and air conditioner ownership ameliorates the associated health impacts (39, 41, 119, 162, 191, 195), though the  evidence  on  increased  heat-related  health  effects  in  areas  that  lack  green  space  is  not  consistently reported across studies (38). The distribution of green and blue space and access to public cooling centers is  socioeconomically  and  racially  stratified.  Lack  of  green  and  blue  space  is  more  prevalent  in  socio-

economically disadvantaged areas (45, 105, 188), while public cooling space is positively correlated with black/African American populations in the United States (189).


## Urbanness and remoteness


The spatial distribution of human populations in urban, sub-urban, and rural areas increases vulnerability to the health impacts of climate change (16, 48, 49, 59, 62, 67, 70, 90, 91, 94, 96, 98, 105, 109, 116, 118, 144, 149, 162, 168, 172, 187, 193, 194). Urban and sub-urban areas have higher population densities (25, 41, 45, 48, 58, 62, 75, 98, 105, 109, 113, 119, 127, 151, 162, 171, 178, 196-201) and larger population sizes (98, 202, 203) that are associated with elevated exposure to extreme heat due to processes associated with urban  heat  island  effects  that  put  urban  populations  at  increased  risk  of  adverse  health  impacts,  while inequality within urban settings can further decrease adaptive capacity (48). On the other end, rural areas have  higher  vulnerability  at  equivalent  temperatures,  attributable  to  demographic  and  socioeconomic factors such as older age, lower education, less air conditioner use, agricultural occupations, and less access to health care services (150, 200). Though the heterogeneity in the health effects of extreme temperatures between urban and rural areas varies across settings (150).


## Governance and policy


Issues around governance as social indicators of vulnerability or adaptive capacity are less referenced in the corpus (119, 177, 204, 205). Researchers examining social factors that mediate or moderate the effect of climate-related disasters on health outcomes include the existence of emergency communication plans, medical and housing infrastructure, and greenhouse mitigation policy as important coping and preventive mechanisms  (119,  204).  In  a  more  direct  test  of  the  role  of  governance  and  institutional  quality  in determining  health  outcomes  from  climate-related  events,  the  worldwide  governance  indicators  and institution quality indicators (operationalized as an index of political stability, voice and accountability, absence of violence, government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law, and lack of corruption) were

used to operationalize the measure of government effectiveness that was found to be positively associated with lower mortality from climate-related disasters (177, 205).


## Household and household composition


Variables that measure aspects of household and household composition were used as indicators of social vulnerability  in  46  studies  in  the  corpus.  Living  alone  was  the  most  common  feature  of  household composition that studies have identified a source of vulnerability or susceptibility due to the lack of social connections or support that residing with others provide (28, 42, 46, 49, 57, 73, 85, 93, 95, 100, 112, 118, 165, 182, 194, 198, 206).  Other household composition factors that were indicative of vulnerability include household type (25, 42, 43, 75, 108, 111, 117, 118), marital status (26, 43, 96, 126, 184), family size (67, 69, 159, 207), female headed households (158, 173), family conflict (115, 184), and percentage of homes with orphans (70).


## Housing and housing affordances


Multiple dimensions of housing and housing affordances as a resource that is inequitably distributed in society were used as indicators of social vulnerability in the review (44 of 205 studies) (28, 35, 36, 38, 41, 42, 44, 46, 47, 58, 67, 75, 87, 89, 95, 100, 105, 112-114, 118, 119, 162, 176, 179, 182, 186, 188, 189, 195, 200, 201, 208-212). Social structures (i.e., tenure type, percentage of homeownership, and percentage of rental housing) (42, 44, 67, 75, 89, 105, 114, 119, 176, 182, 188, 201) and housing affordances (i.e., air conditioning ownership) (41, 58, 87, 100, 112, 119, 179, 189, 195) have been more often than covered, followed by building age (38, 47, 89, 95, 113, 118, 162), dwelling type (28, 35, 36, 46, 118, 186, 200, 212), dwelling size/overcrowding (22, 36, 42, 45, 75, 102, 123), building materials (95, 127, 166, 179, 192), and housing structural security (e.g., slum dwellers and informal settlement) (68, 213, 214). Housing adequacy in terms of housing affordability (110, 189), energy efficiency (113), dwelling conditions such as ventilation and roof construction (157), and homelessness (42) are less incorporated. While access to residential air

conditioning, unevenly distributed across populations (189), are adaptations that mitigate the impact of heatwaves and extreme temperatures within the home (28, 41), renting privately and overcrowding increase susceptibility and vulnerability to the detrimental health effects of climate change (44, 102, 212).


## Access to health care services


Access to health care service and facility was measured through proximity to health service (e.g., lack of health center, distance from health services, pharmaceutical access, average time taken for households to get to a nearby healthcare facility) (69, 70, 198, 215), density of health facilities (e.g., number of hospitals per  capita,  proportion  of  population  covered  by  primary  health  care)  (87,  89,  117),  density  of  health professionals  (e.g.,  number  of  medical  professionals)  (89),  and  health  expenditure  (e.g.,  mean  clinical expense, total health expenditure per capita) (81, 121). Most of the measures are recorded at the area level. Studies  consistently  found  access  to  health  services  and  medical  infrastructure  are  among  the  most influential indicators for sensitivity and adaptative capacity, especially for developing countries (69, 183), and limited access to or lower quality of health services is associated higher vulnerability (87, 89, 117, 151, 198). People with pre-existing illness such as cardiovascular and respiratory disease (47, 198), children (103, 105, 206), and the elderly (47, 55, 216) are particularly vulnerable due to additional medical needs and poor physical resistance to climate impact.


## Access to community infrastructure


There were multiple approaches to measuring access infrastructure, including access to clean water (e.g., distance to water resources, ground water availability) (51, 151, 168, 196, 217, 218), transportation (e.g., density  of  roads  and  railways,  distance  to  the  nearest  major  roadway)  (47,  105,  114,  119,  179,  193), sanitation facility (e.g., dwellings without bathing facilities, access to improved toilet infrastructure) (121, 123,  176,  196),  electricity  or  utility  (e.g.,  access  to  power)  (113,  151,  179,  188),  communication technologies (66, 151, 219), sewage facility (e.g., proportion of population with drainage connection) (66, 121, 168), and waste disposal (e.g., solid waste collection) (66, 121, 168). Adequate transportation is vital

for people to gather resources, seek safe shelters and access services to help them respond during disasters and aid in their recovery post disasters (220). Access to clean water and electricity alleviates heat stress by helping people overcome dehydration and providing access to the usage of fans and air conditioning during heat extremes (151). During climate or weather disasters, lack of access to public infrastructure can lead to people being stranded in the hazardous location and hamper the ability of public infrastructure to provide disaster relief (67).


## Health and health behavior


Chronic health conditions or pre-existing illness can cause adverse reactions to climate related stressors, leading to increased sensitivity to climate change. Pre-existing physical health (27, 36, 56, 70, 81, 89, 93, 100, 111, 112, 114, 185, 192, 194, 198, 215, 216, 221, 222) is more widely considered than pre-existing mental health (27, 36, 89, 114, 161, 194) in the corpus of studies. Some studies have adopted ecological study  designs  using  community-level  health  measures,  such  as  area  health  condition  prevalence,  area mortality and life expectancy (46, 92, 93, 100, 222). Persons with pre-existing medical conditions such as cardiovascular,  respiratory  and  endocrine  diseases  are  at  greater  risk  for  morbidity  or  mortality  when exposed  to  excessive  heat  and  cold  (216,  221).  Living  with  disability  considerably  reduces  adaptive capacity (35, 47, 55, 85, 111, 113, 114, 116, 148, 151, 159, 186). Cognitive impairment creates barriers to receive and comprehend warnings (114, 194, 220). As significant health risk factors, health related lifestyles and  behaviors  such  as  smoking,  drug  use,  coping  mechanisms  and  disaster  preparedness  such  as  food storage are also included in few studies (102, 106, 120). Compounding the vulnerability, people with preexisting  health  conditions  are  disproportionately  in  the  low  socioeconomic  group  with  poor  access  to infrastructure, contributing to increased vulnerability to the health impact of climate change (187).


## Social connection and isolation


The strength of social connection is identified as protective of health and wellbeing in the context of climate change, and social isolation as a source of vulnerability (27, 28, 42, 49, 52, 73, 75, 102, 108, 111, 114, 115,

119, 174, 179, 194, 223-225). Measures for social connection included social support, local connection, civic participation, social cohesion, and volunteering (27, 28, 70, 115, 174, 179, 224); and inversely, social isolation and living alone are measures of a lack of social connection (49, 73, 75, 111, 114, 119, 194, 225). Consistently throughout the literature, social connection is found to be a source of resilience as higher levels of social connection facilitate protection of vulnerable individuals and lack of social connection leaves atrisk individuals and communities without support or access to resources (42, 52, 70, 102). While race, unemployment, and poverty are vulnerability factors for post disaster vulnerability, social connection was a source of resilience and helped to ensure that isolated individuals were protected from climate impacts (102). Lack of volunteers during disasters, measured as percentage of households that volunteered during disasters, is found to increase vulnerability during flood events (70) which suggests the importance of social capital  to  reducing  sensitivity  to  disaster  events.  Similarly,  low  social  support,  operationalized  as  selfreported  number  of  close  friends  and  relatives,  increased  the  odds  of  depression  post  climate-related disasters (27).


## Social development


There are a limited number of studies that include indicators of general human development (148, 171, 172, 222,  226).  Human  development  indices  cover  many  dimensions  of  social  vulnerability  and  adaptive capacity identified in this review including education, health, and income per capita, and lower human development index scores were associated with higher health risks from extreme weather events (117, 172, 222,  226).  Gender  inequality  as  a  measure  of  socioeconomic  differences  is  another  indicator  of  social vulnerability that has been identified in both high-income and low-income settings (148, 171).


## Information and information seeking


Two studies identified Information seeking or awareness of information as a source of social vulnerability as a lack of information seeking behavior limits adaptive capacity and climate resilience (45, 70). High awareness of climatic threats assessed by the volume of google searches was correlated with higher adaptive

capacities to climate change impacts and lower socioeconomic disadvantage, suggesting that those most in need of increased information and awareness are not engaging information seeking behavior in proportion to their exposure and risk (45, 70).


## DISCUSSION


Research on indicators of social vulnerability to the health effects of climate change is a growing field which  has  bloomed  during  the  last  decades.  Indicators  of  social  vulnerability  to  climate  change  are described by researchers, policy makers, and the IPCC as crucial to address the challenge of the climate crisis, and the lack of means to gauge social vulnerability and adaptive capacity is viewed as a  significant impediment to the enactment of climate adaptation plans (1). Therefore, research into social vulnerability is needed to increase climate adaptation and resilience of communities and prevent further exacerbation of climate related adverse health effects and health inequality.

Synthesizing  a  large  corpus  of  205  studies,  our  review  assesses  the  current  state  of  research  on  social vulnerability to the health impacts of climate change and analyses a broad range of the social constructs that have been adopted in defining vulnerability. Along with the 121 social vulnerability factors identified, a  large  array  of  health  harms  and  losses  aggravated  by  climate  change  as  the  result  of  these  social vulnerabilities  are  discovered,  ranging  from  cardiovascular,  respiratory,  genitourinary,  endocrine,  and infectious  diseases,  hospital  admissions,  emergency  department  presentations,  and  medication  use,  to mortality  and  years  of  life  lost.  The  corpus  of  studies  provides  strong  evidence  on  the  role  of  social vulnerability and capacity in exacerbating or mitigating the negative impact of climate change on a large range of health outcomes, rendering some groups more susceptible to health harm than others.

Overall, results from the review show that inequality in social vulnerability, within and between countries, makes  significant  contribution  to  the  health  impact  of  climate  change.  The  health  impact  is  unevenly distributed across populations, with children, the elderly, people linguistically and socially isolated, people

with disability and chronic health conditions, people with limited access to or familiarity with services and infrastructure, people working in agriculture and outdoors, people in poor housing and built environment conditions, socioeconomically disadvantaged groups, and communities with low social development or not supported by quality institutions, climate policies, or robust governance  structures experiencing disproportionate health burdens from climate change.

Trends within the studies of social vulnerability factors highlight areas that have been well researched and areas that remain under-researched. Several gaps have been identified within the research on the social vulnerability to the health effects of climate change. First, except for China, a disproportionate amount of the global literature is focused on the Global North (North America, Europe, Japan, and Australia) which is more resourced to respond to climate change hazards. Climate justice and resilience requires that existing global health inequality is not intensified, and thus more research is needed into social vulnerability in the Global South to enable more adaptation to climate change in regions with less adaptive capacity.

Second, the most widely employed social vulnerability indicators are  demographic  and  socioeconomic status including age, sex, ethnicity, income, and education. A large proportion of the literature employs secondary administrative and hospital data that may not include data to operationalize other indicators. Other  dimensions  of  social  determinants  of  health,  such  as  the  role  of  housing,  access  to  community facilities beyond health services, and governance in supporting and sustaining health is relatively underresearched. Housing indicators are needed to capture the translation between outdoor and indoor climates, to predict more accurately the impact of temperature extremes on health, and to assess the social distribution of housing structures and their respective affordances. Indicators on access to community facilities allow the identification of protective and preventive resources needed at the local area level. Governance and policy are vulnerability factors that moderate other social risks factors require more attention to support the implementation  of  risk  reduction  strategies.  Broadening  the  range  of  social  indicators  of  vulnerability

included  enables  studies  to  capture  a  more  holistic  picture  of  capacities  and  resources  in  reducing vulnerability and facilitating adaptation in response to climate-related risks to health.

Third,  more  research  is  needed  that  incorporates  the  structural  and  institutional  dimensions  of  social vulnerability. Operationalizations of social vulnerability in this research area could draw upon the related concepts of structural vulnerability and structural violence (227, 228) to elaborate on the effect of social and political systems on harms by failing to provide health protection to vulnerable groups and redress the compounding effects of climate change and structural inequalities on marginalized communities. This will enable  researchers  to  conceptualize  and  explain  the  sociological  context  in  which  group  membership translates into social vulnerability.

Despite space for retheorization of social vulnerability to incorporate a relational or structural determination of vulnerabilities more comprehensively, data availability and existing data infrastructures may hinder these efforts. The majority of reviewed papers utilized secondary data, which indicate that lacuna in existing data infrastructures is an impediment in the development of indicators to measure and capture structural and institutional  contexts  that  increase  susceptibility  in  various  populations  and  settings.  On  the  positive methodological note, an increasingly number of studies have overcome static approaches to vulnerability and incorporated temporal scales.

This scoping review provides a broad overview of the state of research into social vulnerability to the health impacts of climate change. Social structures and practices exacerbate or mitigate the effects of shifting weather patterns on health, and understanding these social factors is necessary for developing adaptation strategies to mitigate climate related health harms. The review identified domains of social vulnerability research that  are  well  established  and robust  and  areas  that  remain  under-researched  and  require  more attention.  It  also  identified  the  need  for  more  research  on  social  vulnerability  beyond  individual  and demographic characteristics. Less in known about social vulnerability in the Global South and the critical

role of structural and institutional determinants of social vulnerability in preventing and reducing the health risks of climate change.

## 1. Introduction


Integration of immigrants has been high on the policy agenda in many countries, including Finland, for several years. Integration is often characterised as a continuous two-way process, which requires commitment and action from both the individuals that have migrated and the receiving society. We study the process from the perspective of labour market integration in different immigrant groups, while also examining the role of socio-cultural resources, proxied by partnership with a native-born Finn. Therefore, we combine two strands of literature: one on the economic integration of immigrants and the other on interethnic marriages.

The topic is increasingly relevant amid increasing immigration and the quest for economic and social sustainability in our welfare states. On the one hand, developed countries are in urgent need of a foreign labour force due to falling fertility, worsening dependency ratios and an ageing population demanding labour-intense care services (Rechel et al., 2013). On the other hand, research shows that immigrants are at a greater risk of unemployment, more likely to be overqualified for their jobs and over-represented  in  low-paying  jobs  and  in-work  poverty  as  compared  to  their  native-born counterparts  (e.g.,  Kaida,  2015;  Bárcena-Martín  and  Pérez-Moreno,  2017;  OECD,  2017a).  This creates tension in welfare states aiming at equality and fuels anti-immigrant sentiments.

Different reasons have been presented for the poor labour market outcomes of migrants: one of the most popular explanations focuses on low human capital on arrival (for a discussion, see Phythian et al., 2011), which is connected to the failure to recognise skills and education acquired in the country of origin, poor transferability of those skills to the new host country (Lancee and Bol, 2017), lower returns to work experience from another country and poor language skills (Kaida, 2013). Moreover, ethnic and racial discrimination, weaker social networks in the new country, or ethnic networks that lead new-comers to settle in certain neighbourhoods and low-wage jobs can be expected to negatively affect the socioeconomic outcomes of immigrants in the long run (Kalter and Kogan, 2014; Battisti et al., 2018).

In this study, we exploit the longitudinal format of Finnish register data to analyse development in earnings  and  employment  among  new  immigrants,  following  them  ten  years  after  their  entry  to Finland.  Such  focus  on  the  years  following  migration  is  key  to  understanding  the  process  of integration. Moreover, focusing specifically on a cohort of new immigrants enables us to provide information on the fragile - but also perhaps defining - period after immigration. We are able to contribute significantly to the literature on immigrants' labour market success by using rich register data on the total population in Finland, including detailed information not only on the immigrants but also their partners for each year during the 10-year follow-up.

Second, we focus specifically on the role of having a native-born partner and whether the role is different for different immigrant groups and genders. This analysis adds to the literature on interethnic marriages and their impact on economic integration. Research on the role of intermarriage in the European context has been particularly  scarce,  calling  for  more  detailed  studies  of  intermarriage patterns and immigrant integration in this context (Dribe and Lundh, 2008).

A gender perspective is important too, as labour market outcomes are known to vary significantly between men and women: employment rate disparities between native-born and foreign-born women five  years  after  arrival  in  Finland  has  been  found  to  be  40  percentage  points,  nearly  double  the employment rate gap found among men (OECD, 2018). In addition, many previous studies have mainly  concentrated  on  earnings  and  employment  outcomes  among  men  (with  the  exception  of Ballarino and Panichella, 2018), while there could be explanatory factors for income and employment - (interethnic) partnership status being one of them - that are unique to immigrant women (Read and Cohen, 2007).

In summary, as immigrants represent a growing share of the population in Finland, and also of the low-income  population,  it  is  important  to  examine  their  labour  market  trajectories  since  arrival. Finland is an interesting context for studying the economic integration of immigrants as the foreignborn population is still relatively small and immigration has only started to increase in the 2000s. Furthermore, Finland is characterised by a relatively high level of income equality, well-developed policies for migrant integration (Malmusi et al., 2010) and availability of comprehensive register data. This makes the case and lessons learnt from Finland internationally relevant.


## 2. Literature review and theoretical background



## 2 .1. The role of the first years following immigration and different starting points


There are many reasons to expect that the first years after entry to a new host country are significant for integration outcomes in the long run. The discrepancy between pre-migration high expectations and post-migration poor achievement is a known stressor for immigrants' mental health and wellbeing (Bhugra, 2004). This is also the period when many immigrants move back to their home country or elsewhere if their labour market success is modest at best (Van Hook and Zhang, 2011; Bijwaard and Wahba, 2014). In Finland, the first years after arrival are particularly crucial due to the early separation of integration pathways between the active and the inactive immigrants, i.e., those who are seeking work at the time of arrival versus those who are not, the former receiving integration support from employment services and the latter from the municipality (OECD, 2018). This early separation can  have  long-lasting  consequences,  making  it  difficult  for  those,  particularly  women,  who  are outside the labour force on arrival to find their way into employment.

Several  studies  show  that  time  spent  in  the  new  host  country  is  relevant  for  various  integration outcomes, while the process of integration  can  vary  across  different  factors,  like  an  immigrant's educational level (Villareal and Tamborini, 2018). In general, earnings and employment improve with time spent in the country, while the native-immigrant gap often remains (e.g., Sarvimäki, 2011 for Finland). Also, it has been noted that immigrants in the lowest income group, and with the worst integration outcomes, are the most likely to migrate back, which can affect results (Van Hook and Zhang, 2011; Bijwaard and Wahba, 2014).

Hypothesis  1:  We  expect  to  see  a  steady  increase  in  employment  and  earnings  over  time  in  all immigrant groups and for both genders, while the increase is likely to be steeper during the first years after immigration.

Distinct  patterns  of  integration  are  also  found  across  different  immigrant  groups,  with  the  most obstacles faced by persons from non-EU or non-Western countries of origin. Phythian et al. (2011) have argued that macro level features associated with an immigrant's country of origin are relevant -when we assess the economic integration of immigrants in their host country. These factors can relate to their social and human capital as well as prejudices they face in the host country. Villarreal and Tamborini (2018) found a racially differentiated pattern of earnings assimilation in the United States when analysing earnings trajectories for up to 20 years after arrival: white and Asian immigrants were more likely to reach the earnings level of native whites compared to black and Hispanic immigrants, while the latter caught up to the earnings level of natives of their own race and ethnicity.

Legal status upon arrival has been shown to affect long-term labour market outcomes (Kreisberg, 2019). Humanitarian migrants may be particularly exposed to precarious labour market positions, as involuntary migration often implies entry to the host society in a subordinate position, with little power to negotiate and increased vulnerability to discrimination and exploitation (Malmusi et al., 2010). Family migrants, the vast majority of whom are women and children, also face integration challenges and have less favourable outcomes than economic migrants (OECD, 2017b). Different reasons for entering the country and the legal status are likely to vary according to the country of origin. Therefore, we expect the country of origin to reflect some background characteristics affecting labour market integration that we are not able to measure in our data.

Hypothesis 2: Different starting levels, as well as development in earnings, are expected between different immigrant groups based on the country of origin. Immigrants from fragile and conflictaffected situations, and from regions that are perceived as culturally distant from Finns, such as Africa  and  the  Middle  East,  are  likely  to  experience  lower  earnings  levels  and  weaker  positive earnings  development  due  to  reasons  for  migration  (humanitarian  more  often  than  work)  and discriminatory attitudes of the host society.

In addition to the individual characteristics of immigrants and their households, we can also expect differences in economic outcomes across host countries according to the employment opportunities, extent of labour market regulation and integration policies. However, in a single-country study, it is impossible to investigate the role of these factors, while evidence from multiple contexts is important for a deeper understanding of integration in general.


## 2.2. The role of gender and interethnic partnerships


Noteworthy differences are known to exist between the employment rates of men and women, both in the general and in the immigrant populations. In Finland, the employment gap between immigrant and native women is particularly large among women with children (OECD, 2018). Even after five years  of  migration  to  Finland,  the  employment  rate  of  immigrant  women  with  children  is  47 percentage points lower compared to native-born women with children. Childcare choices explain this in part. In the Finnish context, there is strong policy support for both home care and childcare centres, and research shows that immigrant families take care of their children at home longer than native-born parents (Tervola, 2018). These highlight the importance of gender-sensitive analysis in integration research.

Gender segregation in the labour market is also worth noting. Despite the general view of Finland being gender-egalitarian, occupational segregation is particularly strong, and immigrants also face this  gender-segregation  in  the  labour  market  (Smyth  et  al.,  2008).  This  may  have  different consequences for men and women: it has been suggested that a higher level of Finnish language knowledge may be required especially in female-dominated fields (e.g., health care and childcare).

Hypothesis 3: The economic integration of immigrant women is likely to be slower compared to immigrant men, and the native-immigrant gap is likely to remain wider for women.

Hypothesis  4:  Poor  economic  performance  is  expected  to  be  especially  salient  among  those immigrant women that are more likely to arrive for humanitarian reasons or as family migrants, notably African and Middle Eastern women.

Intermarriage with the host country population is considered an integral part of immigrant societal integration. Intermarriage is not just a measure of social and economic integration, but also a factor that  potentially  influences  the  integration  process.  The  role  of  having  a  native-born  partner  can illustrate  mechanisms  behind  varying  integration  patterns,  signalling  both  social  and  cultural integration but also the probable reason for migration and legal status upon arrival. Cultural and social integration may facilitate economic integration and vice versa .

Existing  literature  identifies  various  ways  through  which  intermarriage  benefits  integration  by enhancing immigrant's country-specific social capital (Kanas et al., 2012; Medina and Valentova, 2022).  First,  native  partners  provide  immigrants  with  information  about  the  local  culture,  labour market opportunities  and  language.  Second,  native  partners  provide  immigrants  with  local  social networks, which may be useful for integration (Furtado and Theodoropoulos, 2010). It should be noted that co-ethnic social networks can also be beneficial for the new immigrant. Analysing bonding (co-ethnic)  and  bridging  (interethnic)  social  capital  separately,  Kanas  et  al.  (2012)  found  that,  in general, social contacts have a positive effect on both occupational status and income of immigrants in Germany, while interethnic contacts led to higher occupational status but not to higher income.

Despite a well-established nationwide system of public employment agencies in Finland, immigrants are shown to rely on predominantly ethnic networks throughout their employment histories (Ahmad, 2011). Social networks are known to help newly arrived immigrants in finding job opportunities; but in  the  long  run,  they  can  hinder  upward  mobility  (Battisti  et  al.,  2018).  The  examination  of international students' job search experiences in Finland has found that, even with a degree from a Finnish university, highly educated migrants' labour market integration is challenging without local networks (Alho, 2020).

Research from Sweden has found that immigrants married to natives are more likely to be employed and  have  higher  individual  and  household  incomes  (Dribe  and  Lundh,  2008).  At  the  same  time, income provided by a native-born partner could enable the foreign-born individual to stay home to care for children or to invest in human capital, as there is no immediate financial need for a secondearner  in  the  family.  Increase  in  the  partner's  earnings  could  be  related  to  a  decrease  in  the immigrant's earnings due to household-level decision making regarding labour market participation; this could be especially relevant for female immigrants with a native-born partner.

On the other hand, due to assortative mating, earning levels of partners can be expected to correlate. Chiswick and Houseworth (2011) have shown that interethnic marriages are more likely between individuals with similar educational levels. In addition, a native-born partner could be a sign of a longer-term commitment to stay in the host country and of a willingness to invest in host-countryspecific human  capital.  Interethnic partnerships can  reinforce expected  differences  between immigrant groups, as immigrants with a similar cultural background with the natives are more likely to  enter  interethnic  partnerships  (e.g.,  Hannemann  et  al.,  2018).  Earlier  research  also  shows  that interethnic marriages are more likely among highly educated and those with better language skills, i.e., immigrants that are likely to fare better in the host country labour market in the first place (van Tubergen and Maas, 2007).

In general, the impact of a native-born partner could vary, both according to gender and country of origin. The status exchange hypothesis postulates that there is an ethnic hierarchy in the marriage market based on cultural distance, for example (see Elwert, 2020). However, those with a low ethnic status can compensate with other desirable characteristics, such as higher socioeconomic status or younger age. Immigrant men and women are likely to compensate low ethnic status with different assets: men with higher education and women with younger age, and this is likely to lead to different outcomes in the labour market based on their partnership status.

Hypothesis 5: Based on the general idea of the role of social capital, we expect that immigrants with a partner have better labour market outcomes than those without a partner regardless of gender or country of origin (of the individual or the partner).

Hypothesis 6: Immigrant men with a native-born partner are expected to have higher earnings than those with a foreign-born partner. This pattern could be especially visible among immigrants from poorer non-EU countries due to differences in selection into interethnic partnership, as the status exchange hypothesis assumes.

Hypothesis 7: In contrast, immigrant women with a native-born partner are expected to have lower earnings than those with a foreign-born partner or without a partner when coming from poorer nonEU countries, as they are less likely to arrive for work-related reasons.


## 3. Integration policies, institutional context and immigration in Finland


Migration policy in Finland is based on Government objectives, the common migration and asylum policy of the European Union and various international agreements. The Migrant Integration Policy Index (MIPEX) measures policies to integrate migrants across a range of countries, including Finland.

The cross-country comparison of Malmusi (2015) grouped 14 European countries according to their integration policies and MIPEX index: Finland was included in the group scoring the highest points and characterised as 'multicultural'. At the same time, the racialised borders of 'Finnishness' are characterised to be exclusive and non-accommodating, underlining whiteness and 'Westernness' as fundamental for national identity, and thus restricting possibilities of integrating and feeling welcome in Finnish society (Rastas, 2005; Keskinen, 2014; Toivanen, 2014).

Immigration to Finland has been modest in size compared to its Nordic neighbours. Around 7 per cent of the overall population in the country (ca. 350 000 persons) are considered to be of foreign origin. The greatest share of migration to Finland is from other EU countries. In 2019, the registration of EU citizens comprised one-fourth of all new residence permits. Similarly, one-fourth consisted of third-country nationals arriving on the basis of family ties. Approximately one-fifth of the permits were  based  on  work,  and  15  per  cent  on  studying.  Ten  per  cent  were  granted  on  the  basis  of international protection or to resettled refugees (European Migration Network, 2019). The largest immigrant group in Finland is Russians, followed by Estonians, immigrants from the Middle East and immigrants from Asian countries other than China.

In our analysis, individuals are grouped into ten categories based on country of birth. When the size of the population is large enough, the unit of analysis is the country of origin (e.g., the case for Russia and the former USSR, Estonia, Somalia). When the size of the population does not allow countrylevel  analysis,  or  distinction  between  countries  is  otherwise  not  meaningful,  we  use  regional categories (e.g., Western countries, Middle East). The reasons for migration in these groups differ distinctly; for example, migrants from Russia have generally moved to Finland voluntarily, as much of this migration is explained by labour migration and personal relationships. In turn, migrants from Somalia began to arrive in Finland in the early 1990s, following a civil war, drought and the rapidly deteriorating overall situation in Somalia. As we focus on the immigrant cohort that arrived to Finland in 2004-2009, more recent events, such as the unprecedented number of asylum seekers arriving to Finland in 2015 or the arrival of refugees from Ukraine at the start of 2022, are outside the scope of our analysis and article.


## 4. Data, methods and research design



## 4.1. Data and variable definitions


Our empirical analyses are based on unique register-based data constructed in Statistics Finland and combining various administrative sources. It covers the full population of Finland and spans from 2004  to  2018.  The  data  consist  of  a  rich  set  of  individual  and  household-level  variables  on socioeconomic and demographic characteristics that we describe in more detail below. Individuals can be linked to their household members as well as married and cohabiting partners, and all the same individual-level information can be found for these linked partners as long as they are also living in Finland.

## Outcome variables

We  use  two  outcome  variables:  individual  earnings  and  being  employed.  Earnings  refer  to  an individual's wages and salaries from employment and self-employment. Earnings are measured on an annual basis and euros are deflated to 2019 level using the Household Index of Consumer Prices. Employment is a dummy variable indicating whether the main activity during the calendar year was employment. The main activity refers to the most common status during the calendar year. Outcome variables  are  available  for  each  year  of  the  10-year  follow-up  for  each  individual  in  the  analysis sample.

## Independent variables

We  focus  on  three  independent  variables  that  relate  to  our  hypotheses:  time  spent  in  Finland, partnership status and country of origin.

Time spent in Finland is identified based on the year of arrival. Time t-0 refers to the year of arrival and time t+9 refers to the last year of the observation period.

Besides time spent in the host country, other aspects of social and cultural integration can affect economic integration. We do not have information on language skills, etc., in the register data, but we have created a categorical variable on the person's partnership status upon arrival (measured at time t-0 and t+1 ): 1) no partner, 2) a Finnish-born partner or 3) a non-Finnish partner. This variable is used as a proxy to capture socio-cultural integration and social capital in Finland, for example, through better social networks. It also reflects a possible reason for migration.

Individuals  are  grouped  into  ten  categories  based  on  the  country  of  birth:  1)  native-born  Finns (including individuals born abroad to Finnish parents), 2) Western countries (incl. Western European countries, USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand), 3) Russia / former USSR, 4) Estonia, 5) other East European countries, 6) Somalia, 7) Middle East, 8) China, 9) other Asian countries and 10) other African countries. Second-generation immigrants, as well as immigrants from countries or regions not mentioned above, are excluded from the study due to the small number of cases in the workingage population. Our main interest is to look at the differences in the outcomes across these groups.

## Control variables

We control for the number of other working-age adults and the number of children in the household, living in one of the six largest cities in Finland (0 no, 1 yes), age and level of education (1 less than upper secondary education, 2 upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education, 3 tertiary education). The educational level of the partner and partner's earnings are also used in some models as control variables. All analyses are conducted separately for men and women.

It  should be noted that the information on education is not comprehensive, as degrees completed abroad are not automatically included in the Finnish registers. Therefore, the variable is not a perfect measure of the human capital of immigrants and may underestimate the true level of education among them. It has been noted elsewhere that the accuracy of measures of socioeconomic position, including education, vary greatly between ethnic groups (Fischbacher et al., 2014), and various challenges exist in the recognition and validation of education acquired particularly outside of the OECD countries (OECD, 2017b).


## 4.2. Analysis sample


We follow a cohort of new immigrants and limit the analysis sample to those foreign-born individuals who arrived in Finland between 2004 and 2009 (equalling to time t-0 ) and who were aged 20-45 at the time of arrival. We follow these individuals for ten years since their arrival in Finland. Those with gaps in the data (for example, moving in and out of the country multiple times in the follow-up period) are omitted from the analyses. As several studies (e.g., Van Hook and Zhang, 2011; Bijwaard and Wahba, 2014) have indicated that there is some selection in who remains in the new host country, we also compared this analysis sample to those new immigrants who left Finland during the follow-up period (see Table 2). We have normalised time so that t-0 is the arrival year, as this allows us to pool together immigrants who have arrived at different points between 2004 and 2009. In the regression analysis, we also control for the calendar year. Table 1 presents summary statistics regarding the study population.

## 5.2. Evidence from growth curve models


Figure 2 presents the main results of our growth curve models for employment separately for men and  women. This leads to the differences between groups growing smaller over time among men, while among women we do not observe this pattern. Third, among immigrant men, the positive employment trend seems to be stalling after the first four years in the country with the exception of Somalian and Middle Eastern men, while among immigrant women employment rates increase until the end of the observation period.

The trends regarding immigrant men's earnings in Figure 3 differ from employment in that earnings differences between groups grow wider over time and that earnings continue to rise throughout the observation period. The trend is similar among immigrant women, while the earnings differences do not change over time between groups when Somalian and Middle Eastern women are not considered. The results also support hypothesis 2 on the differences by country of origin, as we observe that immigrants from countries culturally further away from Finland and more affected  by  conflicts  are  starting  from  lower  initial  levels  and  also  seeing  poorer  earnings development over time. Next, we move on to see whether differences in labour market outcomes could be explained by initial levels of socio-cultural integration and, consequently, access to host-country-specific social capital. The role of partnership status upon arrival is examined in more detail with group-specific estimations. Figures 4 (men) and 5 (women) illustrate development in earnings among those with no partner upon arrival, with a Finnish-born partner and with a non-Finnish partner (based on Appendix Table A1). This evidence is interesting, as trends and levels in earnings vary according to partnership status and country of origin. First, we see that the role of partnership seems to be especially important among women, which we were not expecting. Second, compared to the overall trends in men's earnings (in Figure 3), we do not see widening disparities between groups when analysed separately by partnership status. Third, group differences are especially small when we look at immigrant women with a nativeborn partner.

As for our hypotheses, we cannot fully confirm our hypothesis on better outcomes for those with any partner as opposed to no partner (Hypothesis 5). For example, Middle Eastern men seem to fare better without  a  partner  than  with  a  non-Finnish  partner.  Perhaps  their  non-native  partners  are  not  a significant source of social capital that would help in the Finnish labour market. This is also the case among most immigrant women, as those without a partner upon arrival start from a higher earnings level than those with a partner. There is probably an important selection into these different groups by partnership status that partly explains these results, and this non-random selection into partnerships also  prevents  us  from  making  strong  causal  claims  about  the  effect  of  partnerships  on  economic integration.

Hypothesis 6 on the higher earnings among immigrant men when in a partnership with a native-born partner seems to be supported by evidence especially when we look at Somalian and Middle Eastern men. This pattern is even stronger among women and against our hypothesis 7 on worse outcomes of women in a partnership with native-born men when coming from poorer non-EU countries. It should be noted that in some immigrant groups, such as Somalis, there are very few individuals in the sample that  are  in  a  partnership  with  a  native-born  Finn  upon  arrival  in  Finland.  We  also  see  a  stronger earnings development among other Eastern European women when in a partnership with a nativeborn man. The long observation period allows us to see that, while women in a partnership start from a lower initial level, they do more catching up over time with a steeper earnings curve.

As for the characteristics of the partner, Appendix Table A2 shows that a partner's higher education and earnings are positively associated with immigrants' earnings, both when having a native-born partner and when having a non-native partner. The association is especially strong among immigrant men,  perhaps  indicating  a  non-random  selection  into  partnerships  with  highly  educated  Finnish women. While a partner's high education plays a role for earnings in both types of partnerships, it should  be  noted  that  immigrants  are  much  more  likely  to  end  up  in  a  partnership  with  a  highly educated person when in a partnership with a native-born Finn (Appendix Table A3).
