## 3.2. Measurements


Table 2.1. lists the variables used for testing the hypotheses. The sociodemographic group consisted of AGE, GENDER, EDUCATION, ANNUAL INCOME, and RACE. AGE was the age of the respondents in years (continuous). GENDER refers to the respondent's gender (1 = male and 0 = female). EDUCATION is the respondent's level of education, originally with six categories. EDUCATION and several other variables were recoded to combine their cells when greater than 20 percent of expected cell values were less than 5 (collapsing cells ensures an adequate number of distinct observations per cell and accurate p values). EDUCATION was recoded to a dummy variable (1 = 'at least a 4-year college graduate education' and 0 = 'all others'). 'All others' included 'Less than high school', 'high school (or equivalent) graduate', 'some college or post-high school trade school', and 'other.' ANNUAL INCOME refers to annual household income, which originally had seven different categories (1= less than $15,000, 2= $15,000 but less than $25,000, 3 = $25,000 but less than $50,000, 4 = $50,000 but less than $75,000, 5 = $75,000 but less than $100,000, 6 = $100,000 but less than $150,000, 7 = $150,000 or more, 8 = Refused, and 9 = Don't know) but was recoded into three categories (1= 'Less than $50,000'; 2= '$50,000-$100,000'; and 3 = 'More than $100,000'). Responses such as 'refused' and 'don't know' were removed from the analysis. RACE was the respondent's self-reported race/ethnicity with five different categories (1= African American; 2= Caucasian; 3= Asian; 4= Hispanic/Latino; and 5 = Native American).

OWNER measured whether the respondent owned forest land or not. Respondents were asked if they owned forest and how many acres did they own. A dummy variable was created from this response (1= 'forest owners' and 0 = 'non-forest owners').

To measure knowledge regarding longleaf pine and prescribed fire, questions were asked about how familiar were respondents with longleaf pine and prescribed fire. LLP KNOWLEDGE and PF KNOWLEDGE indicated landowners' and non-landowner's knowledge regarding longleaf pine and knowledge regarding prescribed fire, respectively. Separate binary response survey questions asked whether respondents were aware about longleaf pine and prescribed fire or not. Both variables were measured as binary (1 = 'yes' and 0 = 'no'). When required, survey interviewers provided a definition of longleaf pine and prescribed fire.

To measure ownership objectives, a question was posed with eight items for landowners to indicate their priority objectives. Items included: (1) land investment (to sell all or part of my forest land at a profit), (2) hunting opportunities, (3) camping, hiking, or other recreation, (4) growing trees for sale, (5) income from a recreation lease (e.g., hunting), (6) produce pine straw, (7) enjoyment of owning forest land, and (8) as an asset to pass on to my heirs. These items were measured with a 5-point Likert type scale (1 = very important; 2 = somewhat important; 3 = neither important nor unimportant; 4 = somewhat unimportant; and 5 = very unimportant). To determine which items would raise the interest in longleaf pine reestablishment, I ran bivariate correlation and among the eight items, PINE STRAW, RECREATION, ENJOYMENT, and INHERITANCE (described in Table 2.1.) were associated. I chose these four variables for regression analysis. Responses such as 'very important' and 'somewhat important' were categorized into 'important' category and recoded '1'. Similarly, responses such as 'neither important nor unimportant', 'somewhat unimportant', and 'very unimportant' were categorized into 'not important' category and recoded as '0'. Responses such as 'Don't know' was removed from analysis.

Place attachment has been measured using a variety of approaches and scales (see Stedman 2003). In this study, a place attachment scale incorporated functional attachment and emotional attachment measures of landowners' and non-landowners' level of attachment to the Gulf Coast as a special place (Williams and Vaske 2003). Ten item Likert scales (1= strongly agree; 2= somewhat agree; 3= neither agree nor disagree; 4= somewhat disagree; and 5=strongly disagree) were used to ask 'To what extent do you (1) Agree or (2) Disagree with the following statements, with a follow-up probe of (3) Strongly Agree (4) Strongly Disagree (9) (VOL) Don't know/no opinion. Items included six emotional attachment measures and four functional attachment measures:

- ( 1)  I feel strong, positive feelings for the Gulf Coast (emotional attachment)
- (2)  I identify strongly with the Gulf Coast (emotional attachment)
- (3)  I feel Gulf Coast is a part of me (emotional attachment)
- (4)  I feel I can really be myself in the Gulf Coast (emotional attachment)
- (5)  I get more satisfaction out of visiting Gulf Coast than any other natural area  (functional attachment)
- (6)  The Gulf Coast is my favorite place to be (functional attachment)
- (7)  The Gulf Coast is the best place for what I like to do (functional attachment)
- (8)  I feel happiest when I am at Gulf Coast (emotional attachment)
- (9)  I wouldn't substitute any other area for doing the types of things I do at Gulf Coast (functional attachment)
- (10) I really miss Gulf Coast when I'm away too long (emotional attachment)

From the original Likert scale responses, I computed the new variable by taking the average of these ten items for each respondent to create the PLACE ATTACHMENT score. Responses such as 'don't know' were removed from analysis.

LLP INTEREST represented landowners' and non-landowners' interest in longleaf pine reestablishment. The survey question asked respondents to indicate to what extent they were interested in longleaf pine restoration. Response was measured as a categorical variable: (1) not at all; (2) not much; (3) some; and (4) a lot. Responses were recoded into a binary variable (1 = 'yes' and 0 = 'no') where responses 'not at all' and 'not much' were combined into 'no' and responses 'some' and 'a lot' were combined to 'yes'.

Reasons for not implementing prescribed fire included liability concerns, capacity (i.e., lack of technical knowledge/ technical assistance/ equipment), limited parcel size, cost (expenses related to labor and equipment), smoke issues, and preference for herbicides and/or mechanical treatments. Survey questions asked how important these factors were in decisions NOT to implement a prescribed fire. Responses were measured as 5-point Likert scales (1 = very important; 2 = somewhat important; 3 = neither important nor unimportant; 4 = somewhat unimportant; and 5 = very unimportant). I computed a new variable, REASONS, by taking the average of the seven items for each respondent. 'Don't know' responses were removed from analysis. Similarly, COLLABORATION measured landowners' interest in participating in a local landowner organization that facilitates the appropriate use of prescribed fire on the organization's members' land. Such an activity would create economies of scale and knowledge exchange that may surpass the reasons landowners have for not applying prescribed fire. Responses were measured as a 5-point Likert type scale (1 = very unlikely; 2 = somewhat likely; 3 = neither likely nor unlikely; 4 = somewhat likely; and 5 = very likely). These responses were recoded into a binary response. 'Somewhat likely' and 'very likely' were recoded to 'likely', coded as '1', and all other response were categorized as 'Unlikely' and recoded as '0'. 'Don't know' responses were removed from the analysis.


## 3.3. Data analysis


Hypotheses 1 and 2 considered the full set of respondents: landowners and non- landowners. Hypothesis 3 considered only landowners. A Chi-square test was used to test the first hypothesis i.e., to determine if there were significant associations between pairs of categorical variable. Chisquare tests provided a picture of the association between two variables. If the proportion of individuals in the different columns varied significantly, the two variables were dependent (i.e., there is contingency). If there was no contingency, the two variables were considered independent. To explore other two hypotheses i.e., effect of place attachment on interest in longleaf pine and effect of place attachment and interest in longleaf pine on intent to apply prescribed fire, a binomial logistic regression model based on Figure 2.1. was used. This model was used to predict the probability that an observation fell into one of the two categories of a dichotomous dependent variable based on one or more independent variables that was either continuous or categorical. A positive coefficient for an independent variable indicated a positive effect upon the probability of occurrence of the dependent variable while a negative coefficient indicated the independent variable had a negative effect upon the probability of the dependent variable. Data were analyzed through descriptive as well as statistical comparison method to search for differences. For analysis, all statistical procedures were carried out in IBM SPSS 22 (Statistical Package for Social Scientists) with statistical significance at the p < 0.05 level.

## 4.3. Interest in longleaf pine and prescribed fire (Hypothesis 1, landowners and nonlandowners)


Forty-one percent of respondents, landowners and non-landowners alike, were aware of differences between longleaf pine and other pine species, while 59 percent reported little to no knowledge about longleaf pine (Figure 2.4.). Fifty-five percent of all respondents knew that longleaf pine was once the dominant forest ecosystem in the Southern United States. Eighty-two percent reported that, when restored to full ecological function, longleaf pine ecosystems provide habitat for numerous plant and animal species. Respondents were relatively evenly distributed (47.4 percent) regarding knowledge about the need of fire for longleaf pine restoration, while 32 percent reported there had been extensive efforts to increase longleaf pine acreage. Eighty-one percent of the net sample reported had an interest in reestablishing longleaf pine ecosystems (Figure 2.5.).

In short, 81 percent of the respondents had an interest in reestablishing the longleaf pine ecosystem and three different variables were significantly associated with interest in longleaf reestablishment. Landowners and non-landowners were interested in longleaf pine restoration. A Chi-square test revealed associations between GENDER, OWNER, and LLP KNOWLEDGE variables with an interest in longleaf pine reestablishment (Table 2.5.). These variables were GENDER (χ 2 = 7.948, p = 0.005), RACE (χ 2 = 11.099, p = 0.000), OWNER (χ 2 = 6.356, p = 0.012), and LLP KNOWLEDGE (χ 2  = 18.537, p = 0.000) which were significantly associated with interest in longleaf pine reestablishment.

More than half (58%) of the 2,700 respondents were familiar with the term prescribed fire, while 72 percent of participants were aware of the benefits of prescribed fire. Ninety-two percent agreed prescribed fire removes accumulated material on the ground to prevent wildfire. Similarly, 93 percent of respondents agreed prescribed fire improves conditions for longleaf pine establishment, and 89 percent agreed that prescribed fire maintains a natural balance in the ecosystem. Fifty-four percent of landowners reported they would be concerned about a prescribed fire in or near their property. Most of the respondents (42%) would trust statecertified prescribed burn managers to implement a prescribed fire, followed by uncertified public foresters (35%) and then wildlife biologists (31%) who would conduct the burn as part of the government sponsored wildfire fuel reduction. Only 22 percent of the respondents knew about prescribed fire regulations. Nine percent of 821 landowners reported they had ever conducted a prescribed fire on their property, while nine percent of landowners said they had purchased insurance to conduct a prescribed fire. Nearly half (49%) of the landowners would consider conducting a prescribed fire on their property in future.

Landowners rated seven factors which they regarded as reasons for not implementing prescribed fire (Figure 2.6). Sixty-seven percent of participating landowners reported potential liability as the primary reason. Sixty-two percent reported capacity as the other important reason followed by limited parcel size (54%) and cost related issues (52%). Concern about smoke was recognized as another reason by 51 percent of landowners.

## 4.4. Effect of place attachment on interest in longleaf pine (Hypothesis 2, landowners and non-landowners)

I expected place attachment to have a significant effect on landowners' and non- landowners' interest in longleaf pine restoration. A logistic regression model explained 10 percent of the variation in responses (Table 2.6.). As age of the respondent increased, interest in longleaf pine diminished by two percent (p=0.005). Respondents with higher levels of knowledge regarding longleaf pine and its benefits were more than six times more interested in longleaf pine restoration than their counterparts (p=0.000). Similarly, respondents with higher levels of knowledge regarding prescribed fire and its benefits were more than three times more interested in longleaf pine reestablishment than those with lower levels of knowledge (p=0.011). Landowners owning land to pass on to their heirs were more than twice as interested in restoration programs compared with landowners with other management objectives (p=0.022). Similarly, landowners owning land for enjoyment were more than three times interested in restoring longleaf pine than other management objectives (p=0.001). Finally, as the place attachment score decreased, interest in longleaf pine restoration decreased by 20 percent (p=0.026). In other words, as the level of attachment increased, interest in longleaf pine reestablishment increased as well. Variables such as 'GENDER', 'EDUCATION', 'ANNUAL INCOME', 'PINE STRAW', and 'RECREATION' were not found to be statistically significant in the analysis.


## 4.5. Effect of place attachment and interest in longleaf pine on intent to apply prescribed fire (Hypothesis 3, landowners)


A logistic regression model added the variables above, including interest in restoration, to predict intent to apply prescribed fire. REASONS for not applying prescribed fire and COLLABORATION were also added to the model which explained 46.1 percent of variation ion responses (Table 2.7.). As age increased, younger landowners were nearly two times more interested in applying prescribed fire than older landowners (p=0.025). Landowners with increasing knowledge regarding longleaf pine were nearly four times more interested in applying prescribed fire on their land than their counterparts (p=0.007). Similarly, landowners with knowledge regarding prescribed fire and its benefits were more than three times more interested in applying prescribed fire than those without knowledge about prescribed fire (p=0.018).

In addition, as the REASONS score increased, landowners were less likely to apply prescribed fire. Landowners were 36 percent less likely than those landowners who think various limiting factors were not the reason to apply prescribed fire on their property (p=0.028). Landowners who were interested in restoration of longleaf pine were nearly twice as likely as landowners who were not interested in restoration of longleaf pine to use prescribed fire on their property (p=0.033). Landowners who were interested in participating (COLLABORATION) with other landowners for appropriate use of fire were nearly three times interested in applying prescribed fire (p=0.000) in comparison to the landowners who were not interested in COLLABORATION. Variables such as 'PLACE ATTACHMENT', 'GENDER', 'EDUCATION', and 'ANNUAL INCOME' were not found statistically significant in the analysis.


## 5. Discussion


This study explored how place attachment and the Theory of Planned Behavior influenced the general public's and landowners' interest in longleaf pine restoration and landowners' intent to apply prescribed fire on their property. Similar explanatory approaches have been employed to understand other forestry behaviors with family forest owners (e.g., Brough et al. 2013; Karppinen 2005; Thompson and Hansen 2013).

Among Gulf Coast residents, the results suggest that respondents were interested in reestablishing longleaf pine - as explained by age, knowledge in longleaf pine and prescribed fire, some landowner objectives, and place attachment. As well, Johnson and Franklin (2000) suggested much of the interest in longleaf restoration has been the result of an increasing interest in ecological values of longleaf forests. In addition, this growing interest may be explained by the perception that some of the unique characteristics of longleaf are superior to other southern pines. While this would be related to subjective attitudes, a stand of longleaf pine does produce a greater percentage of high-valued poles than other southern pine species (Williston and Screptis 1975). These high valued poles have a potential financial advantage for landowners and industry because poles may be twice as valuable as sawtimber.

In terms of demographic characteristics, age was negatively significant in both regression models. Younger respondents were more interested in longleaf pine restorationwere more likely to apply prescribed fire than older respondents. This finding is similar to other studies that have found a negative association between age and acceptance of forest management practices (Joshi and Arano 2009; Loyland et al. 1995; Kuuluvainen et al. 1996; Zhang and Flick 2001). One explanation for this is that older landowners are interested in leaving the forest land for future generation resulting in minimal or no restoration efforts during the lifetime of the older landowner. Another possible reason for lack of interest might be that they want to use forest land for recreation and enjoyment rather than for restoration, which require active management and investment.

Results from this research are consistent with studies which have documented that knowledge regarding longleaf pine and prescribed fire is important for ecological restoration (Kreuter et al. 2008; Morton et al. 2010; Piatek et al. 2010). These studies suggest that educational efforts increasing knowledge significantly raise interest and support for restoration programs. Increased levels of knowledge contribute to understanding of the benefits of the species and the practices, including risks and benefits, required in restoration efforts.

Findings illustrate how the relationships people have with a particular place influence environmental attitudes and interest in restoring native habitats. Similar to other studies applying place attachment to natural resource management, this study supports the notion that place attachment is an important indicator of intention and support for restoration (Alam 2011; Stedman 2003; Williams and Vaske 2003). This study indicated that individuals who were strongly attached to the Gulf Coast exhibit high interest in conservation and restoration of longleaf pine. This might be because individuals holding a high level of place attachment wish to maintain the original settings of the place as they prefer those settings, which may be historical, actual or imaginary. Although this analysis did not specify the most important place attachment measure, in general, the attachments that individuals have to a place is important for public acceptance of restoration efforts (Stedman 2003).

Ownership objectives also influenced interest in longleaf pine restoration. Landowners who owned their land for enjoyment were interested in restoring longleaf pine forest. As shown in Butler et al. (2004), enjoyment is one of the most important landownership objectives among private landowners. If landowners place high importance in this objective, they seem more interested in environmental conservation, preservation, and restoration. Similarly, landowners who were planning to pass their forest lands to their heirs were more interested in longleaf pine restoration. This result is similar to Butler (2008), who illustrated forest owners wish to pass their land to family heirs illustrating a tremendous opportunity for management horizons that span generations. Although goals of forest industry are designed primarily for long-term profit, this does not suggest that such NIPF landowners do not manage forests for secondary, nontimber benefits, in addition to timber. As a matter of both good business sense and environmental concerns, NIPF landowners could support the management practices that ensure sustainability of multiple resource values. These findings were consistent with my initial expectations; however, education level, gender, and annual household income were not significant predictors of interest in the prescribed fire despite these variables being significant in other studies (Amacher et al. 2003; Butler 2008; Joshi and Arano 2009).

While the TPB model guided prediction of intentions of implementing prescribed fire, the inclusion of additional factors enriches the TPB framework of beliefs, attitudes, and intentions. Intent towards applying prescribed fire was influenced by interest in collaboration with various organizations, a result that is consistent with previous studies (Kobziar et al. 2015; Kreuter et al.

2008). This research suggests collaboration with peers will influence perceptions regarding prescribed fire use. Collaboration works toward educating the public, local communities, and decision-makers about the benefits of prescribed fire use, and enhances communication between local officials, fire-managers, and landowners (McCaffrey and Olsen 2012). Collaborative programs can provide informational materials and non-monetary (or monetary in some instances) incentives for landowners. Such programs would also promote peer-to-peer sharing of experiences. Although uncommon, prescribed fire groups found in some states and county forestry associations are examples of such local collaborative activities.

Implementation of prescribed fire is challenging. This research identified 'liability', 'capacity', 'cost-related issues' and 'smoke issues' as the major reasons for not using prescribed fire in the study region. Previous literature has documented liability as the major reason (Kreuter et al. 2008; Kobziar et al. 2015; and Morton et al. 2010). This previous research has shown high levels of concern among NIPF landowners and agencies regarding lawsuits from an escaped fire or smoke issue. Although there is some degree of prescribed fire liability protection, these protections are not comprehensive. As well, most NIPF landowners probably are not aware of the legal considerations of prescribed fire. Results highlighting capacity as an important reason were similar to a lack of technical knowledge as reported by Harr et al. (2014) and 'need for assistance' as reported by Jarret et al. (2009) and Kreuter et al. (2008). Demand for prescribed fire is increasing while the capacity to use prescribed fire is not (Melvin 2012). This is because the supply of technical service providers and burn practitioners is insufficient across the region. In some cases, capacity may be the most important issue to address in promoting prescribed fire. In addition to liability and capacity, NIPF landowners also considered the cost of prescribed fire treatment to be a critical reason for not burning. This finding, was consistent with results from Fischer (2011) and Kobziar et al. (2015) which found management costs related to applying prescribed fire at a regular interval were higher that what landowners preferred, which was exacerbated by long investment horizons needed to recover costs. Cost is a major reason because prescribed fire implementation varies widely due to terrain and weather, with application not always feasible. A lack of agency and nonprofit funding for prescribed fire programs also presents challenge to incentivize landowners. In short, NIPF landowners' cost-benefit analysis often does not lead to motivations to apply prescribed fire.

The survey also reported concerns about smoke, similar to one results by Blanchard and Ryan (2007) and Morton et al. (2010). Smoke concerns are linked to the regulations regarding airquality (Achtemeier et al. 1998). Smoke issues and management have been considered the major reason in other studies (Blanchard and Ryan 2007; Morton et al. 2010); yet, this study revealed smoke issues as only the fourth most important reason. This might be because when respondents have a better understanding about the benefits of prescribed fire, people are more acceptable of smoke as a risk. Smoke and its effects on air quality can lead to public health concerns, limitations of acceptable to burn days, and negative press. Properly trained personnel and proper assistance are required for maintaining and implementing prescribed fire and for balancing out the benefits and potential costs of prescribed fire.


## 6. Conclusions and Recommendations


This study verified the applicability of using the TPB to analyze landowners' intentions and behaviors towards ecological restoration using prescribed fire. The chi-square and binomial logistic regression results showed that TPB was theoretically appropriate. Results support the hypothesis of a causal chain between the variables of the TPB model. Results are consistent with my initial expectations regarding the growing interest in longleaf pine restoration among landowners and also general public (as stated in hypothesis 1); hence, the null hypothesis is rejected. According to the results, interest towards longleaf pine reestablishment would be positively influenced by demographic characteristics, knowledge regarding longleaf pine and prescribed fire, place attachment, and ownership objectives (as stated in hypothesis 2); hence, the null hypothesis can be rejected. Findings from this study also suggest intent towards prescribed fire would be positively influenced by socio-demographic characteristics, along with knowledge regarding longleaf pine and prescribed fire, landowners' level of attachment to place, some perceived reasons for not implementing prescribed fire, interest in longleaf pine restoration, and collaboration with other landowners for using prescribed fire (as stated in hypothesis 3). These findings were partially consistent with my initial expectations. Therefore, the null hypothesis was not rejected because using landowners' intention to reflect their forthcoming behavior was acceptable.

Future research should consider additional factors such as past experience, trust in prescribed burners, and environmental concerns, which could influence interest in implementing prescribed fire. Previous experience with prescribed fire may be associated with less concern about smoke. Trust is those implementing a prescribed fire practice reflects landowners' views on professional knowledge and experience. Environmental concerns may affect willingness to implement prescribed fire if landowners are concerned about air pollution, landscape damage, or promoting 'natural' landscapes.

This study suggests educational efforts to enhance literacy about longleaf and prescribed fire should be customized for various demographic target groups. Based on the idea that people have emotional attachments to special places, demonstration sites should be promoted, e.g., state parks, wildlife management areas, natural areas, and other public lands to showcase habitat restoration efforts. This research helps to identify key messages, such as longleaf pine restoration is an important part of Gulf Coast identity, to develop and distribute to the public to expand understanding of the historical role of fire in Gulf Coast landscapes and the role that prescribed fire can play today. Collaboration and peer-to-peer learning (or landowners helping other landowners) and partnering with land management agencies may provide additional motivations for extending the longleaf range. While not ideal due to its unsustainable nature, cost-share assistance may incentivize some landowners by offsetting the costs of implementing prescribed fire. Similarly, increasing the amount of funding available through state, federal, and nongovernmental grant programs may resonate with some landowners, especially if their primary objectives are not economic-based. To decrease the risk of liability, prescribed burn association can ensure members have proper training and equipment, or provide contracting of professionals within economies of scale. Capacity issues can be addressed through increasing training/certification of private landowners, many of whom could eventually implement prescribed fire in their own. Results from this study are indicative of the need for more efforts to enhance general awareness and knowledge of longleaf pine and prescribed fire among public and landowners for expansion of the use of prescribed fire for longleaf pine restoration.

## Introduction


Diabetes is a chronic health condition that affects approximately 10.5% of the United States population [1]. People with diabetes are typically advised to engage in several self-management behaviors in order to improve their health outcomes. According to the Association of Diabetes Care & Education Specialists [2], ADCES7 Self-Care Behaviors TM diabetes self-management behaviors include: regular monitoring, medication adherence, nutrition, physical activity, problem-solving, reducing risks, and healthy coping. When the COVID-19 pandemic began its trajectory across the United States in early 2020, several states saw surges in COVID-19 cases in April [3], leading to government or self-imposed social distancing practices, even in states that were less affected at the time [4]. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to significant unemployment and increased work-from-home practices. To help control the spread of the virus, social distancing practices have been widely implemented, and the pandemic has disrupted the lives of many people, including children [5].

People with diabetes face the additional burden of having to maintain, re-establish, and/or re-invent self-management behaviors during the pandemic. The range of self-management behaviors that are expected from people with diabetes include eating

1

healthily (e.g., controlling carbohydrate intake), engaging in regular physical activity (e.g., 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity physical activity), taking medications as prescribed, monitoring blood glucose, and managing stress and mental well-being. While the need to perform self-management has not changed because of the pandemic, the barriers to performing them are arguably higher, and the resources needed to overcome them are in many cases in more limited supply. As described in an article in The Lancet [6], the combination of COVID-19 and non-communicable diseases (including diabetes) has created a perfect storm of two syndemics. Van der Ploeg and Bull [7] further emphasize how COVID-19 has worsened access to healthy foods and opportunities for engaging physical activity in most countries. The Atlantic, an American general editorial magazine, has published a series of news articles that reflect on how the pandemic is re-shaping society in the United States, and it specifically discusses how grocery shopping [8] and exercising [9] in the United States may be experiencing significant and permanent shifts.

In the context of these new and unsettling changes to lifestyle, how are diabetics controlling their self-management? Between May and June 2020, we interviewed 21 people living with type 2 diabetes in the United States. The objective of the interviews was to capture how people with type 2 diabetes make decisions regarding self-management behaviors (with a particular emphasis on healthy eating and exercise), and how the COVID-19 pandemic may have impacted their behaviors. Our research is intended to highlight the challenges with self-management behaviors that our participants attributed to the current pandemic-and, as we saw a distinct lack of support in the face of these challenges, we also highlight the types of interventions that could address them. In this article, we describe the challenges that patients reported with respect to maintaining physical activity and healthy eating behaviors during the pandemic. Additionally, we apply the Behavior Change Wheel (BCW) framework [10] to suggest relevant categories of behavioral interventions and policy options to support self-management behaviors during the pandemic. In this way, we outline a potential method for identifying, analyzing, and addressing potential issues to diabetes self-management in the face of a large-scale external disruption to day-to-day life.


## Related Literature


In the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, the focus of the medical community centered around controlling the spread of the virus and the treatment of patients with COVID-19. In this article, we apply the Behavior Change Wheel (BCW) framework of Michie, Van Stralen, & West [10] to identify appropriate behavioral and policy interventions for supporting behavior change during the pandemic. This framework was developed by [10], and is based on a systematic literature review of scholarly articles containing frameworks of behaviour change interventions. The BCW is a consolidation of 19 frameworks that were identified in the systematic review into a single, comprehensive framework. At the core of the BCW is the COM-B model, which recognizes that a target behavior (B) can be driven by an individual's capabilities (C), opportunities (O), and motivations (M). The individual's capabilities, opportunities and motivations are collectively referred to as 'sources of behavior'. Capability can be a physical capability or a psychological capability; opportunity can be afforded by their physical environment or social environment; and motivation can be either automatic or emotion-based, or reflective and goal-directed.

The BCW links the three sources of behavior to nine behavior change intervention functions: (a) education, (b) persuasion, (c) incentivization, d) coercion, (e) training, (f) enablement, (g) modelling, (h) environmental restructuring, and (i) restrictions. Notably, only a subset of the nine intervention functions may apply to a given source of behavior. Additionally, the BCW links each intervention function to a subset of seven policy categories: (a) communication/marketing, (b) guidelines, (c) fiscal, (d) regulation, (e) legislation, (f) environmental/social planning, and g) service provision. The reader is referred to [10] for further details on the BCW. In this article, we leverage this framework to connect the sources of behaviors described by our study participants to relevant intervention functions and policies.

## Materials and methods



## Sample


21 individuals (12 women) with type 2 diabetes aged 28-81 years (mean age: 52.7 years, s.d.: 18.1 years) were recruited into the study. All participants self-reported meeting the following eligibility criteria: they were over 21 years old, had been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes by a qualified medical professional within the past 5 years, were currently a resident of the United States, were regularly engaged in their own meal planning and preparation, and had not participated in a focus group or in-person market research study within the past 6 months. Participants were additionally screened for basic fluency in English.


## Recruitment


Participants were recruited through Schlesinger Group, a marketing research company. A pre-screening step identified a pool of potentially eligible participants, who were then further screened for eligibility. Consent forms were emailed to all eligible participants, who signed and returned the forms to Schlesinger Group. Participants who completed the informed consent process were scheduled by Schlesinger Group to attend a 90-minute virtual interview session with the research team. All interviews took place within the months of May and June 2020, and all participants were paid $ 125 as compensation for their time. Our study protocol was approved by an Institutional Review Board.


## Interviews


Our interview guide included topics related to a participant's understanding of their diabetes, their diabetes treatment plan, the services and support they receive from clinicians for managing their diabetes, how they make decisions about self-management behaviors, and how those behaviors may have been affected by the pandemic. With respect to self-management, we inquired about the full range of behaviors, but our emphasis was on nutrition and physical activity related behaviors. Interviews took approximately 60-90 minutes to complete. Table A1 displays primary questions from the interview guide and is included as an additional file. All interviews were conducted by a lead interviewer who conducted a semi-structured interview based on the interview guide. On any given interview, the role of lead interviewer was held by one of three researchers for the duration of the interview. The Cisco Webex ™ web conferencing software was used to conduct and record the interviews. Participants connected to the web meeting on their computers so that relevant content (e.g., definitions of rating scales and sample menus) could be displayed on their screens. We did not utilize the video feature of the web conferencing platform. Audio recordings of the interviews were transcribed verbatim and anonymized using a professional transcription service contracted by Schlesinger Group.


## Analysis


Deductive thematic analysis [29] was used to analyze the transcripts. All passages containing mentions of self-management behaviors that were explicitly described as having changed or remained unchanged as a result of the pandemic, were extracted from the transcript. At least two out of the four researchers reviewing the passages were assigned to the same interview transcript. Within each extracted passage, we identified all mentions of self-management behaviors and coded according to whether the behavior had changed or was maintained after the start of the pandemic. ## Part I - Sources of behavior for disease self-management during the pandemic



## Nutrition


There were four types of nutrition-related self-management behaviors that our participants reported being affected by the pandemic. These behaviors include: (1) purchasing foods consistent with a diabetic-friendly diet, (2) preparing healthy recipes at home, (3) (re-)balancing their nutritional intake, and (4) limiting unhealthy snacking.

Since restaurant closures and work-from-home practices have made it necessary and/or more practical to prepare most meals at home, the opportunity to purchase diabetic-friendly foods from the grocery store now plays a more important role in determining overall nutritional intake. Although grocery stores remained open in the United States, most of the participants we interviewed were motivated to limit their exposure to the virus by reducing the number of visits they made to the grocery store, which meant that they needed to be able to afford purchasing more food at once, and know how to keep them fresh for longer periods of time. For a similar reason, many of our participants also reported making greater use of grocery shopping services 1 . When using a shopping service, participants had to be able and willing to pay the fees associated with the service, and to cook using ingredients that may be different from what they had expected. They may also benefit from knowing how to research the nutritional content of items online before adding them, sight unseen, to their virtual shopping carts. As one participant puts it:

## Discussion


The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant disruption to the daily lives of people around the world. For people with diabetes, self-management behaviors are an essential component of treating and preventing the progression of the disease, and they need support in adapting their prior behaviors to accommodate the 'new normal' and to develop greater resiliency to recurring disruptions. Our guided interviews with diabetics on their experiences with self-management during the first wave of the pandemic in the United States revealed pandemic-induced challenges in maintaining self-management behaviors. We also discovered a lack of support in helping diabetic self-management during the pandemic, and in our analysis, we applied the BCW framework to link sources of behavior to behavioral and policy interventions, with an emphasis on those that were of increased relevance and importance to diabetics during the pandemic.

Our participants did not report seeking out pandemic-specific self-management support from available literature, clinicians, or family and friends. We decided to assess the publicly available guidance published by pertinent and accredited websites (as described in the 'Related Literature'), and found that much of the information needed to educate diabetics during the pandemic is distributed across multiple websites, some of which are not written specifically for people with diabetes. In most cases, any COVID-19 specific education for people with diabetes was focused on the risks associated with being infected by the virus, how to prevent infection, and what to do if an infection was suspected. The reported challenges, however, call for a more comprehensive and tailored set of educational and informational resources, one that goes beyond merely encouraging people with diabetes to maintain self-management behaviors, to accommodate the unique circumstances created by the confluence of COVID-19 and diabetes.

In this article, we have not reported on aspects of self-management outside of nutrition and physical activity. However, the experiences that our participants shared regarding either in-person or virtual visits with their physicians during the pandemic were rarely related to managing their lifestyle changes. Instead, visits were used to discuss and/or obtain lab work, or sometimes to deal with changes in medication. The illustrative interventions that we have included in our results are therefore more likely to be implemented through trusted internet sources, social networks, social services, and other health professionals (e.g., diabetes educators, registered dietitians, certified personal trainers, clinical social workers, etc.).

Our study was limited to 21 people with diabetes, who were within five years of being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, and who self-reported being highly engaged in making decisions regarding how their food is prepared. Therefore, the experiences of our participants cannot be generalized. For instance, diabetics who are more experienced with managing their condition may have responded differently (perhaps better) to the disruptions. Similarly, diabetics who played a less active role in planning and preparing their own meals could have responded differently (perhaps worse) to the disruptions.

Given the widely-accepted health benefits of adhering to recommended lifestyle behaviors for diabetes management, along with the substantial limitations in lifestyle options due to the pandemic, people with diabetes face considerable challenges in (re-)establishing healthy behaviors. Our research adopts a principled method for identifying appropriate behavior change interventions based on the Behavior Change Wheel and the actual experiences reported by people with diabetes during the pandemic. ## Introduction


This  study  examines  high-achieving  students  in  Norwegian  lower  secondary  schools  who follow accelerated learning trajectories in mathematics, so-called fast-tracks . These fast-tracks 1 allow advanced students to take classes and exams in single subjects at a higher grade level

than  their  current  grade  level.  We  examine  the  differences  between  regular  and  fast-track students' academic achievements in mathematics. We do so to address whether and how fast tracks improve these high-performing students' learning and performance. These questions are essential because higher-performing students' accelerated learning provides a unique window into student learning more generally.

Mathematics has a unique position in education and is considered one of the essential school subjects. Mathematical thinking is an integral part at the core of several fields of study (e.g., natural science and engineering), and essential to many other educational fields (e.g., medicine, nursing, social science). International organizations like OECD and IEA regard the population's mathematical competence as decisive for economic growth and conducts periodic tests like TIMMS, PISA, and PIAAC to monitor such skills. It is also the subject in which Norwegian pupils most commonly accelerate their learning by following the fast track (NOU 2016: 14).

The  political  motivation  for  introducing  the  opportunity  to  accelerate  the  teaching  was  to improve the learning for pupils with high learning potential. Learning is, however, inherently difficult to measure. Just observing whether or not the students following the accelerated track get better grades is insufficient. Accelerated students may get better grades for at least three reasons:  One  explanation  is  that  fast-tracks improve  students'  learning . Fast-tracks  may improve learning because of a better-matched skill level and peer-influences (Betts 2011). It may also be because teachers treat these students differently. In psychology and pedagogy, researchers have been concerned about self-fulfilling prophecies (Merton 1948) due to teachers' expectations; if teachers expect that students are talented and treat them accordingly, they will perform better (Rosenthal & Jacobsen 1968; Bandura 1977). Students may learn more through getting  more  challenges  that  motivate  them  and  improve  their  knowledge  (Bandura  1977, Dweck 2006, Yeager et al. 2019, Duflo, Dupas et al. 2011, Card and Giuliano 2016). They may also  learn  more  because  they  get  more  inspired  by  attending  classes  with  peers  on  similar achievement levels and motivations or similar personality traits (Antonioni and Park 2001). Finally, their learning pace may increase if they, to a lesser degree, will be disrupted by less motivated students (Bonesrønning 2008).

The second explanation of a possible difference in grades may be that these students would have performed the same without participating in the fast tracks. The self-selection of  these students into accelerated tracks is voluntary and anything but random. The students need to perform well in  the  subject  and  be  willing  to  leave  their  regular  classes  for  lectures  in  the accelerated subject. The students that make this choice then are probably both high performers

and quite ambitious. Therefore, the self-selection is likely to be shaped by individual and family characteristics,  such  as  students'  cultural  dispositions  (Bourdieu  1986),  genetic  dispositions (Neisser et al. 1996; Heath et al. 1986), but also their rational choices (Boudon 1974, Lucas 2001, Raftery and Hout 1993, Breen and Goldthorpe 1997). Such self-selection into the fast tracks represents a considerable challenge to making appropriate causal inferences about fasttracks' effectiveness.

The third explanation is that students who attend these fast tracks do not learn more but still get better grades because the teachers label them as more talented than other students. Labeling of fast-track  students  could  be  considered  a form  of  teacher  bias in  the  expectations  of  how students will perform. If the teachers view themselves as being quite good in mathematics, better grades among the accelerated students may also be the result of examiners' tendency to reward students they think to resemble themselves ('the like me effect'), which Fleming (1999) considers being the chief source to biased marking.

Our study differentiates between these three explanations using rich Norwegian administrative register data. First, to rule out the self-selection effect, we examine the association between fast tracks  and  school  marks  in  mathematics,  adjusted  for  background  characteristics  and  prior performance.  To  identify  the  fast-track  students,  we  exploit  a  small-scale  school  reform  in which the Norwegian government opened for optional accelerated learning for gifted students. Only a fraction  of  the  schools  has  chosen  to  implement  fast  tracks.  We,  therefore,  employ school-level  fixed  effects  regressions  to  account  for  possible  selection  effects  based  on socioeconomic compositions on schools, schools' self-selection  to  fast-track  programs,  and more  general  influences  of  teachers  and  peers.  Second,  to  assess  whether  the  remaining association  between  fast  track  attendance  and  performance  is  due  to  improved  learning  or teacher bias, we compare marks set by the students' regular teachers with the marks the students receive on written exams from random and anonymous external teachers.

Contrary to the students' teachers, these examiners have no prior knowledge of whether the students attend fast tracks or not. Discrepancies between these two types of grades could shed light on possible teacher bias processes at work for fast-track students. This research design does not only allow us to disentangle the impact of fast-tracks on learning; it enables us to examine whether teachers evaluate fast-track students differently.

Causal answers to questions about student learning already  exist. Some studies address the effectiveness of fast tracks directly (Betts 2011). But less is known about the role played by

teacher  bias.  Our  study  adds  especially  to  this  critical  blind  spot  in  the  literature  using  the particular case of fast tracks. In particular, we contribute by bringing in new perspectives on teacher bias based on social stratification research. Reviewing 30 years of research, Jussim and Harber (2005) find that teachers' expectations have small (if any) and time-limited effects on student  intelligence  and  achievements.  Contrary  to  the  theory  of  self-fulling  prophecies, sociologists have been concerned more about teachers' gatekeeping role: teachers favor students with middle-class backgrounds, who signal specific high-brow characteristics (Bourdieu 1986). Attending fast tracks could be such a signal. In addition to possible self-fulfilling prophecies, teachers' expectations and differential treatment may affect students' future educational careers through their grading practices. This way, teacher bias may contribute to the reproduction of social  inequality  in  two  ways,  although  research  provides  mixed  evidence  (Quazad  2008; Quazad and Page 2013; Andersen and Hansen 2009; Jæger and Møllegaard; Fleming 1999). However, in the egalitarian Norwegian context (see below), teachers might also try to even out existing differences, especially for 'deserving' disadvantaged students who seem motivated and hard-working, signaled through their attendance in fast-tracks. This way, teachers might try to compensate student disadvantage in the same way parents do when they invest in their children's human capital in a compensatory fashion by investing more in the less endowed child (Bernardi 2014; Bernardi & Cebolla-Boado 2014; Grätz and Wiborg 2020).


## Fast-tracking in Norway


In  Norway,  accelerated  learning  opportunities  for  a  sub-group  of  high-performing  students represent something new and a break with long-standing norms about schooling. These school norms are deep-seated in norms of egalitarian values that characterize Scandinavian societies (Hjellbrekke,  Jarness  &  Korsnes,  2015),  where  equality  is  often  understood  as  sameness (Gullestad, 1992). This egalitarian sameness is also an essential aspect of the unitary school system. All pupils within a geographical area (with different abilities, class backgrounds, etc.) attend  the  same  municipal  school  (Imsen  &  Volckmar,  2014).  All  students  are  included  in mixed (i.e.,  heterogeneous,  comprehensive, and  non-grouped) schools and classes.  Usually, there  is  no  organizational  differentiation  based  on  pupils'  abilities.  These  norms  are  also incorporated  in  the  law.  The  Education  Act  §  8-2  states  that  "pupils  shall  not  normally  be organized according to the level of ability, gender or ethnic affiliation." This means that students will  receive  a  mainly  uniform  teaching  environment,  only  differentiated  through  internal pedagogy within the same school classes. This study, thus, is set in a comparatively egalitarian climate, where a particular concern for "gifted" students is generally not encouraged.

In recent years, however, international tests have revealed a mediocre performance with few students at the highest levels in Norway (OECD, 2016), fuelling concern for the most "gifted" students (NOU 2016: 14; Kjærnsli & Jensen, 2016; Smedsrud 2018). To address this concern, Norwegian  politicians  have  pushed  for  greater  use  of  accelerated  learning  programs.  The growth and proliferation of these programs in the lower and upper secondary schools have significantly increased since the government wrote a white paper in 2008 encouraging their use (St.meld. nr. 44 (2008-2009), 2008). The special status of students fast-tracking is expressed in the Education Act, §1-15, which permits deviations from the uniform educational track. The fast-tracking program is meant to increase flexibility for the individual to tailor their educational track to their intellectual capacity and learning speed. The program should encourage and make room for academically strong students to develop their skills within subject areas they excel in. However, the fast-tracks are entirely optional and voluntarily on two levels. Schools choose whether they want to offer fast-tracks for their students. And students can opt for these fasttracks if they want more challenges. Currently, fast-tracking is mainly available for math and English.

The program for accelerated learning is at least partly, at odds with the egalitarian tradition in Norwegian  schools  with  its'  caring  for  the  'brightest'  students.  While  fast-track  students receive and might benefit from accelerated learning, other students could perceive them as overachievers and different, thus making fast-track participation a potential social cost. How the Norwegian  mathematics  teachers  respond  to  such  an  'elitist'  (by  Norwegian  standards) initiative will be discussed in the theoretical part below and examined in our empirical analyses.


## Why should fast-tracks matter for student learning?


Fast tracks may improve learning for various reasons (Betts 2011). Fast-track classes target high-performing students and could be considered a form of adapted education. The adapted education of fast tracks improves learning by matching high achieving motivated students with a curriculum and a learning speed corresponding to their ability and prior knowledge (Duflo, Dupas et al. 2011, Card and Giuliano 2016). Thus, fast-track programs are designed to create encouraging learning environments.

Encouraging environments of fast tracks may increase the students' belief in their own ability to  produce the desired result, something social cognitive psychologists label 'self-efficacy' (Bandura 1977). Students' self-efficacy improves their learning because it affects what they do (mastery),  the  efforts  they  put  into  it  (motivation),  and  how  they  feel  while  doing  it

(psychological states).  In more recent learning theories, self-efficacy plays a central  role in students'  mindsets  that  promote  learning  (Dweck  2006).  Students  can  believe  that  their intelligence and learning abilities are unchangeable and fixed. A fixed mindset leads students to have lower learning curves than if they believe their learning potential can change, increase, and grow with training. In contrast, a growth mindset leads students to have higher learning outputs when challenged, experiencing increasingly difficult tasks, which again reinforces and boosts their self-efficacy. A growth mindset is more focused on the larger learning goals and processes  rather  than  the  immediate  outcomes.  A  fixed  mindset  can  be  altered  to  a  growth mindset,  as  demonstrated  by  intervention  studies  (Yeager  et  al.  2019;  Yeager  et  al.  2016; Burnette et al. 2012; Bettinger et al. 2018). If encouraging and adapted environments of the fast tracks  alter  students'  mindsets,  these  environments  can  change  students'  beliefs  about  their ability to learn, for example, through repeated experiences of mastery, which again would lead to  improved  learning.  Teachers  are  integral  parts  of  such  an  environment,  and  teachers' expectations  of  high  student  performance  of  fast  track  students  may  lead  to  self-fulfilling prophecies (Merton 1948).

Fast track peers also contribute to an encouraging learning environment. Grouping similar high achievers  in  fast-tracks,  like  it's  done  in  Norway,  will  make  the  learning  environment  and experience more homogenous. Such more homogenous (and high-performing) environments may foster positive peer effects from other high-achieving students, increasing the students' level of self-efficacy, self-esteem, confidence, motivation, and ambition. Students might benefit from these environments even with fixed mindsets, as similar personality traits in the peer group also increase learning (Antonioni and Park 2001). At the same time, the homogenous fast-track environment with motivated students may also reduce the negative influence of less motivated peers and disruptions during class (Bonesrønning 2008).

All of these factors give us reasons to expect fast tracks to improve student learning. But a range of possible factors could confound the association between fast-track and performance since students  self-select  into  fast-tracked  programs.  Only  already  high-performing  students  can participate in the fast tracks. Therefore, fast-track students might perform better than others because they were high-performing students at the outset, not because they learn faster and better in fast-track classes. Fast-track students are also likely to differ from other students on family background characteristics and gender, factors often associated with educational choice

and performance. 2 And fast track students may differ from others on mindsets. Choosing a fast track is consistent with the self-development goal of the growth mindset. Given the focus on learning in mathematics, we hypothesize that:

H1:  Fast-track  programs  in  mathematics  improve  students'  school  marks,  controlling  for potential confounding background characteristics and prior achievements.


## What happens if teachers think fast-track students are more talented than others?


Attending fast tracks could work as a signal that affects how teachers perceive the students. While attending fast-tracks  is  a  rather  specific  signal,  and  its  interpretation  could  generally relate  to  how  teachers  evaluate  students.  For  example,  fast-track  students  might  get  better school  marks  because  teachers  perceive,  label,  and  treat  them  as  more  talented  than  other students.  Research  has  approached  the  labeling  process  from  two  different  angles  -  with different implications for learning.

Teachers might expect high student performance of fast-track students, which again could lead to  self-fulfilling  prophecies  (Merton  1948).  A  seminal  psychological  study  relying  on  a randomized control experiment showed that if teachers expect that students are talented and treat them accordingly, they will become even more talented (Rosenthal and Jacobsen 1968). That teachers expect more would be particularly relevant for fast-track students since teachers base  their  expectations  predominantly  on  the  demonstrated  student  performance  (Andersen 2018; (I. G. Andersen, 2018; Driessen et al., 2008; Jussim et al., 1996; Jussim & Harber, 2005a). However, later evidence for self-fulfilling prophecies is more mixed (Friedrich et al., 2015). Jussim and Harber (2005) reviewed nearly 35 years of research and concluded that: teacher expectations affect students' underlying ability, but the effects are much smaller than initially estimated. Self-fulfilling prophecies generally apply to young school children, and effects only occur early in the school year (Jussim & Harber, 2005b). Still, self-fulfilling prophecy theories could also connect to the concept of the growth mindset discussed above. Teachers and schools shape students' beliefs in their abilities to learn, making students develop a growth mindset, which would lead the students to perform better. So, if teachers affect student learning because they expect more of fast-track students and treat them accordingly, we expect something similar

as  in  the  first  hypothesis  (H1):  That  attending  fast  tracks  would  actually  increase  students' learning because teachers affect the students' beliefs about their ability to learn.

Teachers' evaluations have been approached somewhat differently by sociologists. Sociologists have been concerned with how teachers' grading favors students from the middle class, who signal high-brow characteristics, such as embodied skills, tastes, knowledge, and personality, i.e.,  cultural capital. Bourdieu's influential social reproduction theory is particularly relevant (Bourdieu, 1984; Bourdieu & Passeron, 1977). The main concern is that the school system, through  teachers'  evaluations,  rewards  high-brow  status  signals.  These  signals  are  not necessarily attached to the students' actual academic performance but instead ascribed to their social origins (Bourdieu, 1996, p. 22). This ascription represents teacher bias if the teachers' perceptions and expectations differ from the students' actual performance.

This form of teacher bias has received mixed empirical support in Scandinavian countries. In Norway,  Andersen  and  Hansen  (2012)  found  that  examinators  disproportionally  rewarded students  with  high  socioeonomic  backgrounds  with  better  marks  on  oral  relative  to  written exams. Because of the students' superior and self-confident oral performance - signaling high academic potentials, the teachers gave better marks on oral exams to students with high-class than low-class backgrounds. Consistently, based on experimental data from the U.S., Norway, and the Netherlands, Geven et al. (2021) found that teachers had higher expectations of students' academic potential if the students had high socioeconomic backgrounds. However, other studies provide weak evidence of teacher bias among U.S. and Danish students (Breinholt & Jæger 2020, Møllegard & Jæger 2017). Rather than functioning as a mere signal of high academic potential, students' cultural capital from high socioeconomic backgrounds seems to enhance performance. But if fast tracks influence the teachers' expectations and beliefs about student performance, we might expect the following:

H2: School class teachers give fast-track students higher marks than what the students receive by random, anonymous examinators on exams.

Attending fast tracks programs could affect teachers' evaluations of the students -independently,  on  top  of  other  student  characteristics.  This  could  make  an  advantage  to accumulate for fast-track students with high socioeconomic backgrounds. In a sense, attending fast-tracks  would  be  especially  beneficial  for  those  with  high  socioeconomic  backgrounds, giving them a double advantage. If so, we expect that:

H3: Already advantaged students who attend fast tracks get a double advantage - there is an even  greater  discrepancy  between  teachers'  school  marks  and  marks  on  written  exams  if students attend fast- tracks and have high socioeconomic background.

But attending fast tracks could also make teachers attempt to reduce assumed negative impacts of other student characteristics and be biased in the opposite direction, particularly perhaps in the egalitarian Norwegian context. Teachers might act in the same way parents do, trying to mitigate and compensate initial disadvantage by investing more in less endowed children (Erola and  Kilpi-Jakonen  2017,  Bernardi  2014,  Bernardi  &  Cebolla-Boado  2014).  Parents  have rational incentives to use their resources to prevent downward mobility (Breen and Goldthorpe 1997)  and  maintain  an  advantage  for  their  children  (Lucas  2001).  However,  teachers  are probably  not  motivated  by  the  same  principles  assumed  in  these  rational  choice  theories. Instead, especially in the Norwegian context, teachers may be motivated by egalitarian values and norms. Teachers may wish to even out initial differences if they think that some students are 'deserving.' Just attending a fast track could suggest that a student is genuinely interested in math, being a hard-working and highly motivated student -despite having low socioeconomic family background. Teachers could then reward these disadvantaged students extra by giving them higher grades than the actual level of performance, and thus higher than marks  on  written  exams.  Also,  other  student  characteristics  could  be  perceived  as  being disadvantageous.  For  example,  prevailing  views  in  STEM  subjects  like  mathematics  and science, often depict that girls have lower self-confidence and aspirations shaped by gendered roles, identities, cultural-beliefs, and stereotypes (e.g. Archer et al. 2013). Having an immigrant background could be yet another student characteristic associated with disadvantage. If teachers compensate  what  they  perceive  as  deserving  hard-working  and  motivated  disadvantaged students by giving them higher marks, because they attend the fast-tracks, we expect that:

H4: Teachers compensate disadvantaged fast track students - compared to students with high socioeconomic backgrounds, there is a greater discrepancy between school marks and written exams among assumed disadvantaged fast track students, i.e., low socioeconomic backgrounds, girls, immigrant backgrounds


## Analytical strategy


To shed light on whether fast tracks improve learning and whether teachers give higher grades than the students' actual performance, we rely on two different analytical approaches. First, we

rely on a standard control variable strategy to rule out some of the main confounding factors behind the selection process to fast tracks. Second, we compare students' school marks set by regular  school  class  teachers  with  marks  on  written  exams  set  by  random  and  anonymous external teachers.

The  first  strategy  addresses  the  extent  to  which  students  improve  their  learning  when participating in the fast tracks. The strategy assesses two different levels of the selection process due to the nature of the school reform. The selection process is likely to occur both on the school-level and individual-level. One potential self-selection issue on the school-level is that the  school  reform  only  encouraged  schools  to  use  fast-tracks  (St.meld.  nr.  44,  2008-2009). Schools may choose whether to implement fast-tracks or not. Some schools have embraced the fast-tracks, most did not.

To account for possible selection bias on the individual level, we start using standard control variable  methods.  We  incrementally  include  likely  observable  culprit  confounders,  such  as gender, ethnicity, and highest parental education reflecting family background. We also account for  prior  demonstrated academic performance achieved on national mathematics tests in 8 th grade. Although significant individual-level differences may be measured easily, students may also differ in dimensions that are harder to measure, such as motivation, ambition, and learning potential  and  ability.  This  means  that  we  do  not  estimate  causal  effects,  but  we  rule  out important factors that influence the data generating process. This strategy addresses the first hypothesis (H1).

Our second analytical approach is much simpler but allows for more robust causal inferences. It addresses the possible teacher bias processes in the evaluations of student performance. We use individual-level fixed effects where school marks and marks on the exams are nested within each individual. This differencing strategy controls for all stable individual-level characteristics, also those that are unmeasurable. By including a dummy variable for teachers' marks in this model, we can compare marks set by regular school class teachers at the end of the school term with the marks the students receive on written exams. School class teachers monitor  student  performance  over  the  more  extended  periods  but  can  be  influenced  by subjective  judgments  and  prejudice.  The  exams,  however,  are  graded  by  random  and anonymous  external  teachers.  These  teachers  have  no  prior  knowledge  of  the  students themselves,  their  performance,  or  whether  they  attended  fast  tracks  or  not.  Discrepancies between these two types of grades could shed light on possible teacher bias processes at work for fast-track students. Furthermore, we include interactions between the dummy variable and

fast tracks to estimate how much more or less the discrepancy is for fast track students. This test assesses the second hypothesis. We also run separate analyses for regular and fast-track students, to assess three-way interactions with other stable aspects such as gender, immigrant background,  and  parental  education.  This  last  strategy  considers  the  third  and  fourth hypotheses: whether disadvantaged students get compensated or advantaged students get an additional advantage if they attend fast-track programs.


## Data and variables


To  study  fast-tracking  in  mathematics,  we  use  rich  Norwegian  administrative  register  data covering  all  lower  secondary  students  (10 th grade)  attending  a  school  offering  a  fast-track program for at least one year from 2010 to 2014. This period covers 301,689 students, and only a  tiny  fraction  of  1,884  students  attend  fast-track  in  mathematics.  The  first  set  of  analysis includes  all  the  students  (see  Table  1),  although  the  analytical  selection  is  listwise  deleted (N=277,921). The second set of analysis includes only those who have taken a written exam. Each  year  about  1/3    of  the  students  are  randomly  chosen  for  written  examinations  in mathematics. Additionally, to avoid ceiling effects in the individual-level fixed effects analyses, we also exclude students with top-scores both at the exam and the teachers' grade (See Table 2) . The second analytical selection includes N=99,657 students, where 515 of these attend fast 3 tracks.

Explanatory variable: Whether students participate in accelerated fast tracks in mathematics

We operationalize fast track students as those who participate in particular mathematics classes on an upper-secondary level at least one year before leaving lower-level secondary schools. As the primary explanatory variable, we include a dummy variable that indicates whether a student attends fast tracks in mathematics or not.


## Potential confounders


In the first set of analyses we control for likely confounders. Several confounding variables affect the self-selection process into the fast-track programs. One of the most critical variables that  drive  the  selection  to  fast-tracks  is  prior  achievements  in  math.  We  include  a  national standardized mathematics test for all 8 th -grade students. As with the written exams, these tests are less prone to teachers' beliefs about the students. In contrast to exams, these tests are often graded by teachers at the same schools as the students, but the tests are also more standardized than exams. We also include measures of social origin, gender, and immigrant background. Social  origin  is  measured  in  terms  of  parents'  highest  achieved  educational  degree.  For immigrant  background,  we  distinguish  between  descendants  and  immigrants  and  between western and nonwestern origins. The models include the school fixed effects to net out possible selection effects to particular schools with different student and teacher populations.

## Dependent variables: Teachers' marks and written exams in mathematics


Our  two  main  dependent  variables  are  10 th grade  school  mathematics  marks  and  grades achieved on exams. Teachers' school marks are based on student performance during the entire year and capture students' long-run performance. But teachers also get to know their students: they know them more personally, their backgrounds and gender. And beliefs about students' characteristics might affect the teachers' evaluations (Geven et al. 2021, Andersen and Hansen

2011). In contrast, beliefs about student characteristics cannot affect achievements on written exams. Written exams are blinded in the sense that students and examinators are anonymous to each  other.  And  examinators  come  from  schools  other  than  those  the  students  attend.  This means that marks on written exams more neutrally reflect the actual achievements. However, the discrepancy between the two types of marks seems limited, as the two grades are highly correlated, r=0.86 (Table S5). Exams have two important limitations worth mentioning. Only 1/3 of the students are drawn each year randomly to take exams. And exams do not capture the students' long-run performances. While these issues affect the efficiency of estimates, none of them are important for the consistency of the estimates. We believe that considering teachers' marks and written exams together will capture a more complete picture of the learning process.

A central advantage of using marks in the 10 th grade is that they include all students before they proceed  to  upper-secondary.  After  lower  secondary  school,  the  students  choose  either  an academic or vocational track in upper secondary schools. These tracks have different grading practices making it more difficult to compare school marks.


## Fast-tracked math students outperform regular students


Regular students are outperformed by fast-track students. Fast track students have higher school marks than regular students (Table 1); set by the teacher (5.6 vs. 3.6); on written exams (5.2 vs. 3.1); and national tests (1.4 vs. 0 z-scores). The distributions are broader for regular students, as indicated by the standard deviations of the point estimates. These differences in averages and shapes are undoubtedly evident in plots of the distributions (Figure 1). While the distributions of  regular  students  (green  bars)  are  wide  and  normally  distributed  around  the  population averages, the distributions  of  fast  track  students  (red  bars)  are  left-skewed  and  compressed distribution towards top achievements. The range of the distributions also differs. Almost none of the fast track students receive school marks in math lower than 3 points in 10 th -grade. And very few of them score lower than -1 standard deviations on the 8 th -grade national tests  in mathematics. Regular students, however, range from 1 to 6 on the school marks in 10 th -grade and -2,8 to 2,5 on the 8 th -grade tests. Clearly, fast-track students outperform regular students in math both in the 8 th and 10 th grades.

## Do fast tracks improve math performances?


Judging by the descriptive statistics alone, we cannot be sure whether fast-tracks improve math performances or not. The descriptive results indicate that fast-tracked students already perform better in math than regular students in the 8 th grade. And the students seem to be self-selected on parental education. Nearly 80 percent of the fast track students have parents with universitylevel education; only 48,5 percent of the regular students do (Table 1). Surprisingly, the fasttrack students do not differ from regular students when it comes to the share of boys and girls. Except  for  students  with  nonwestern  descent,  the  same  goes  for  students'  immigrant backgrounds: fast track and regular students have fairly similar proportions.

Another potential obstacle to judging whether fast tracks improve math performances is that the schools themselves play a role, for example, through influences of peers and teachers or school  policy  and  practices.  Thus,  we  are  likely  to  omit  many  relevant  school-level characteristics that are hard to measure and account for the fast-track math selection process.
