## Discussion and conclusions


This study has examined whether and how so-called fast-tracks improve students' learning and performance  in  Norwegian  lower  secondary  schools.  Our  results  establish  that  fast-track students  outperform  regular  students  in  mathematics.  To  understand  why  these  differences might  occur,  research  offers  three  possible  explanations:  (1)  the  fast-tracks  improve  the students' learning, (2) the students are selected and self-selected - on prior performance and background characteristics - and therefore, they actually do not learn more by attending the fast tracks, or (3) they do not learn more, but still get better grades because the teachers perceive or label them as more talented than other students.

The two first explanations, emphasizing learning and selection, both play vital roles in our results. Students who attend fast-tracks seem to improve their learning in mathematics . Fast 6 track students receive 2 grade points higher on their math marks (exams and teacher grades) than regular students. However, more than half of these differences are driven by self-selection based  on  the  students'  background  characteristics  and  prior  achievements  in  the  8th-grade

national math tests. Not surprisingly, prior achievements contribute most to this reduction. Our design does not rule out the possibility of omitting other relevant unobserved characteristics (such as motivation, talent, effort, personality). But we believe that prior math achievements should  be  a  significant  selection  factor  for  the  fast-track  programs.  It  seems  reasonable  to assume that prior math achievements (and background characteristics)  work as a combined proxy for both skills and unobserved characteristics improving performance in mathematics. After accounting for such significant determinants to the fast tracks, our results still suggest that fast-track students benefit from attending the fast-tracks: the fast-track students receive nearly 0,8 grade points higher math marks than regular students.

As we have discussed above, there could be several reasons why fast tracks programs improve learning. That fast-tracks stimulate an encouraging learning environment could be especially important.  Encouraging  environments  may  facilitate  learning  because  they  match  the  skills level of the curriculum to the learning pace of students (Duflo, Dupas et al. 2011, Card and Giuliano, 2016). Also, influences from like-minded, highly motivated peers could play a role (Antonioni and Park 2001) and the absence of less motivated students (Bonesrønning 2008). But these programs might also affect psychological dispositions that promote learning more generally.  These  programs  may  boost  the  students'  motivation  and  feeling  of  mastery,  and consequently,  improving  the  students'  self-perception  and  confidence,  i.e.,  self-efficacy (Bandura 1977), and their mindsets about learning (Dweck 2006, Yeager et al. 2019; Yeager et al. 2016; Burnette et al. 2012, Bettinger et al. 2018). These explanations all help us understand why attending a fast track improve learning. But they do not necessarily emphasize the role of teachers.

Teachers  are  important  because  they  play  an  essential  role  in  these  encouraging  learning environments. Teachers might have different expectations of regular and fast-track students, which may lead these students to improve learning more than regular students. Such improved learning could lead to self-fulfilling prophecies (Merton 1948). Evidence of such self-fulfilling prophecies is mixed regarding how significant these effects are (Rosenthal and Jacobsen 1968; Jussim and Harber 2005; Friedrich et al. 2015). Teachers may also improve student learning by altering the students' self-efficacy (Bandura 1977) and mindsets about learning (Dweck 2006, Yeager et al. 2019; Yeager et al. 2016; Burnette et al. 2012, Bettinger et al. 2018).

The teachers' role is also emphasized by the third explanation but in a different way. Students might not necessarily learn more by attending fast-tracks. They could also get better marks because the teachers perceive them as more talented than other students and give them better

grades (Fleming 2009). Such labelling and differential treatment is a concern addressed by our second set of analyses. We analyzed differences between the 10 th grade marks given by the teachers and the marks on written exams assessed by anonymous examinators. Our models come close to identify the teacher bias. The fixed-effects models are robust against omitted variable bias because they control for any (stable) unobserved individual-level factors (such as dispositions of genetic or social origin). Most students get better grades from their teachers than from examinators. Our results show that the bias varies across gender and parental education: disadvantaged fast-track students get even higher grades from their teachers than anonymous examinators  when  attending  fast-track  mathematics.  Fast-track  students  with  low  social backgrounds  benefit  greater  from  bias  than  those  with  high  social  backgrounds.  And  fasttracked girls benefit more than boys. Teacher bias of fast-track students seems to be restricted to  those  who  teachers  may  perceive  as  disadvantaged  students.  However,  the  additional advantage does not extend to immigrant backgrounds.

These  findings  on  teacher  bias  support  our  deduced  prediction  that  Norwegian  teachers compensate disadvantaged fast track students - compared to students with high socioeconomic backgrounds,  there  is  a  greater  discrepancy  between  school  marks  and  written  exams. Consequently, these findings are consistent with our explanation that teachers' are trying to reduce  initial  disadvantage  in  the  same  way  parents  do,  as  shown  by  social  stratification researchers (Bernardi 2014, Bernardi & Cebolla-Boado 2014). In contrast to parents, however, teachers may not be motivated by promoting advantage, but more in egalitarianism and work ethics.  A  teacher  may  believe  that  a  fast-track  student  is  more  deserving  -  because  their attendance  signal  that  they  are  genuinely  interested  in  math,  hard-working,  and  highly motivated. So, if teachers reward these disadvantaged students extra - by giving them higher grades than the actual level of performance, this would explain the observed pattern of more significant bias for initially disadvantaged fast-track students. Such a tendency may be more marked in an egalitarian context such as in the Norwegian case.

In conclusion, our study has several important implications for both research and educational policy.  The  fast-track  programs  seem  to  work.  Fast-track  students  get  better  grades  in mathematics. It's not just because they are better at math in the first place - before they attend the fast-track programs. They learn too. At the same time, students are treated favorably by their teachers if they are girls, or if they have a low social background. It seems like teachers reward disadvantaged fast-track students they perceive as hard-working and motivated. So, our study speaks to psychological research on individual development and learning. But it also has

implications for social inequality. Fast-track students are recruited disproportionally from high social backgrounds, and the improved learning will possibly accumulate educational advantage across  generations.  But  it's  not  that  simple  either.  Teachers  seem  to  counteract  initial disadvantages  by  giving  better  grades  to  disadvantaged  fast-track  students.  In  a  sense,  the teachers function as levelers: equalizing outcomes for those students they feel deserving.

## Introduction


Research in  intergenerational  mobility  points  to  a  puzzling  paradox:  Countries'  ranking  in terms of their level of mobility depends on the way mobility is measured (Breen and Jonsson 2005;  Blanden  2013).  Perhaps  most  prominently,  the  United  States  is  characterized  by  a relatively  high  level  of  occupational  mobility,  at  par  with  the  levels  reported  for  the Scandinavian countries, but a very low level of economic mobility. While research suggests that there is ample room for the two types of mobility to differ (Björklund and Jännti 2000; Blanden, Gregg, and Macmillan 2013; Breen, Mood, and Jonsson 2016), the existing literature mainly focuses on the relationship between canonical types of mobility (e.g., intergenerational associations in income, class, or education), thus relying on a relatively stylized framework for analyzing the many and potentially differing family background factors that affect labor market success (Björklund and Jäntti 2020; Thaning 2021).

In this paper, we examine the extent to which occupational and economic attainment originate in the same underlying characteristics that make up a person's family background. We extend previous research using sibling correlations to gauge the overall impact of family background and local community by considering how sibling correlations in different labor market outcomes overlap. We analyze brother data from Denmark and the United States and quantify the degree to which the unmeasured family background factors that affect attained occupational status also affect attained income in the two countries. This 'overlap' in family background  factors  is  a  direct  measure  of  whether  attainment  in  different  labor  market outcomes are rooted in the same underlying family characteristics, and can be considered an overall  measure of the extent  to  which  intergenerational  mobility  in  different  labor market domains overlap. Denmark and the United States constitute an ideal comparison because they represent two countries that likely follow the mobility paradox pattern: While the two countries

have similar levels of occupational mobility, Denmark is characterized by a much higher level of income mobility.

Our  estimated  brother  correlations  confirm  this  pattern,  showing  that  while  the correlation in occupational status is identical in the two countries (35 percent), the correlation in wages is much larger in the United States than in Denmark (50 compared to 30 percent). However, despite these significant differences, we find that the overlap in unmeasured family factors that affect the two outcomes is substantial, amounting to around 70 percent, and is virtually identical in the two countries. This finding suggests that attainment in the two labor market outcomes to a very considerable extent are rooted in the same family characteristics. Further analyses show that, although conventional family background covariates explain about half of the family variance components in each outcome, they explain only about one-fifth of the  overlap  in  these  components  in  each  country.  These  surprising  findings  point  to  that brothers being similar in attainment across different labor market domains results from largely unknown family characteristics.


## Background


Stratification scholars consider sibling correlations an omnibus measure of the total impact of family  background  on  a  given  life  outcome  of  interest.  Sibling  correlations  express  in percentages how much of the total variance in an outcome can be attributed to 'what siblings share,' i.e., their shared genetic make-up, common rearing environment, mutual interactions, and  local  community  (Solon  1999;  Sieben  and  de  Graaf  2001).  Sibling  correlations  thus provide a much more comprehensive picture of how life chances depend on family background than more conventional mobility metrics focusing on the transmission of specific resources such as occupational status (Treiman and Terrell 1975), social class (Erikson and Goldthorpe 1992),  income  (Solon  1992),  or  education  (Pfeffer  2008).  Indeed,  estimated  levels  of

intergenerational mobility may differ across resources, even in contradictory ways, because these  resources  are  not  perfectly  exchangeable  (Björklund  and  Jännti  2000;  Jæger  2007; Blanden 2008, 2011; Blanden, Gregg, and Macmillan 2013; Breen, Mood, and Jonsson 2016; Mood 2017; Thaning 2021; Hällsten and Thaning 2022).

The lack of exchangeability may also affect country comparisons of overall levels of mobility as some countries may be highly mobile in some resources but not in others (Breen and  Jonsson  2005).  One  prominent  example-sometimes  referred  to  as  the  'mobility paradox'-is the comparison of liberal welfare state countries such as the United States with universal welfare state countries in Scandinavia (Breen, Mood, and Jonsson 2016). Mobility in income, for example, is much lower in liberal welfare countries (Black and Deveraux 2011; Corak 2013), whereas mobility in occupation or education is virtually similar and comparably high in international comparison (Erikson and Goldthorpe 1992; Hout and Dohan 1996; Beller and Hout 2006; Pfeffer 2008; Blanden 2008).

However, this literature mainly studies canonical forms of mobility (i.e., in income or occupation),  thus  neglecting  the  many  other  ways  in  which  family  background,  broadly considered, affects life outcomes across different domains. A growing literature attempts to resolve this issue by including multiple parental characteristics to get a more comprehensive picture of how different aspects of family background affect different outcomes (e.g., Bukodi and Goldthorpe 2013; Gugushvili, Bukodi, and Goldthorpe 2017; Sullivan et al. 2018; Thaning and Hällsten 2022).  For example, Thaning (2021) examines how parental income, occupation, 1 and education accounts for sibling similarities within and between three outcomes (income,

occupation, and education). He finds that parent-to-child transmission rates are larger in same parent-child resources, pointing to the salience of within-resource transmission.

Another  literature  examines  the  extent  to  which  sibling  similarities,  i.e.,  the  total influence of family background and local community on a given outcome, can be accounted for  by  parental  characteristics  (Mazumder  2008;  Björklund,  Lindahl,  and  Lindquist  2010; Andrade 2016; see also, Sieben and de Graaf 2001). For example, Björklund, Lindahl, and Lindquist (2010) find that about one-third of the sibling correlation in labor market income in Sweden  can  be  explained  by  conventionally  used  socioeconomic  characteristics  such  as parental income, occupation, and education. In their six-country comparative study, Sieben and de Graaf (2001) similarly report that parental education and occupation account only for a moderate portion of the sibling correlation in occupational status. Considered together, these studies  suggest  that  conventional  family  background  variables  cannot  fully  explain  why siblings are more similar in key labor market outcomes than two randomly selected individuals (for a similar finding, see Thaning 2021). 2

Notwithstanding the key insights offered by these studies, previous research has not directly  considered  the  extent  to  which  sibling  similarities  in  one  outcome  overlap  with similarities in other outcomes. This paucity is surprising given that such overlap speaks directly to whether unmeasured family background (and local community) characteristics that affect for example income are similar to or distinct from the unmeasured characteristics that affect occupational  status  (or  any  other  outcome  of  interest).  Indeed,  we  consider  empirically establishing this overlap fundamental to quantifying the shared family origins of attainment across different domains. The overlap approach provides a general framework for studying the

overall influences of family background on different life outcomes. Whereas existing research examines  outcomes  separately,  the  overlap  approach  allows  for  an  assessment  of  which observed family factors make up the common (over outcomes) and unique (to outcomes) family background influence on different outcomes. 3

We propose  measuring  the  overlap  directly  using  a  'seemingly  unrelated'  variance components  model  in  which  between-family  and  within-family  errors  correlate  across outcomes. 4 This correlation in 'family unobservables' is a direct measure of the overlap, and we propose using the squared correlation as measure of the overlap expressed in percentages. Moreover, following the approach in Mazumder (2008) and Björklund, Lindahl, and Lindquist (2010), we add conventional family background covariates to the income and occupational status equations. This analytical approach  allows  us to study not only how  family characteristics explain sibling similarities in each outcome but also their overlap. We detail this approach in the data and methods section.

We apply our overlap approach to data on brothers from the United States and Denmark. These two countries constitute an ideal comparison, because they-on the one hand-represent different  welfare state  regimes  with  very  different  levels  of  redistribution  and  provision  of public services (Esping-Andersen 1990; Heckman and Landersø 2022) and-on the otherfollow a contradictory pattern in which income mobility differs but occupational mobility does not. For income mobility, research clearly points to the United States being characterized by low  mobility  and  Denmark  by  high  mobility  (Björklund  et  al.  2002;  Jännti  et  al.  2006;

Schnitzlein  2014;  Landersø  and  Heckman  2017;  Mitnik,  Helsø,  and  Bryant  2022).  For example, Schnitzlein (2014) reports a brother correlation in permanent earnings of 45 and 20 percent for the United States and Denmark, respectively, implying that Denmark is more than twice as mobile by this measure. 5

For occupational mobility, research shows that the United States is a relatively fluid country (Erikson and Goldthorpe 1992; Björklund and Jännti 2000; Beller and Hout 2006; Blanden 2008; Hertel and Groh-Samberg 2019), while the evidence for Denmark is scarce. Hertel  and  Groh-Samberg (2019) place Denmark as a relatively fluid country with fluidity levels not far from those reported for the other Nordic countries and the United States and the United Kingdom. Findings from comparisons of the United States to other Nordic countries generally  support  this  pattern  of  similarity  in  occupational  mobility  (e.g.,  Erikson  and Goldthorpe 1992; Beller and Hout 2006). 6 Furthermore, Karlson and Birkelund (2022) find that the brother correlation in occupational status for Danish men born in 1965-1971 is 35 percent,  a  percentage  similar  to  that  reported  for  the  United  States  by  Hauser  and  Mossel (1985), Hauser and Sewell (1986), Jencks et al. (1979), Hauser et al. (1999), or Conley and Glauber (2005). It is also very close to the 37 percent average over five countries reported in Sieben and de Graaf (2001). 7

In sum, we expect the brother correlations in occupational status and income to follow the  'paradoxical'  pattern  that  Denmark  and  the  United  States  are  similar  in  terms  of

occupational mobility but different in terms of income mobility. However, we have no a priori expectations about whether the overlap in family unobservables in the two outcomes are similar or different between the two countries. Indeed, even if family background has a larger impact on income in the United States than in Denmark, we cannot predict from the previous literature how  large  is  the  overlap  in  family  unobservables  and  whether  it  differs  between  the  two countries.  We  provide  empirical  evidence  to  shed  light  on  this  question,  and  we  explore whether conventional family background variables account for the overlap in each country.


## Data and Methods


We analyze sibling data from the United States and Denmark. For the United States, we rely on the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (NLSY79), which follows a sample of 1421-year-olds in 1979 (i.e., born 1957-1964) through today (Bureau of Labor Statistics 2019). Because  the  NLSY79  samples  households,  we  can  identify  brothers  living  in  the  same household at the time of the interview. The survey contains information on the occupational and economic attainment of brothers, and also comprises information on parents' attainment and other aspects of the family of origin. Of the 6,403 male respondents in the original sample, 2,016 are brothers distributed on 913 families. As a result of missing values on key variables, our analytical sample comprises 2,616 males of which 1,835 are singletons and the remaining 781 brothers are distributed on 363 families. 8

For  Denmark,  we  analyze  Danish  administrative  registers,  which  is  a  collection  of annually updated databases containing information on the entire Danish population. We restrict our sample to all males born 1960-1965, and identify brothers born within that period.  Similar 9

to  the  NLSY79,  the  administrative  registers  contain  very  rich,  repeated  information  on occupational and economic attainment and characteristics of the family of origin. Our final sample comprises 175,252 males, of which 43,717 are brothers distributed on 21,156 families.

We measure occupational attainment in terms of occupational status. For the United States, we use Duncan's socioeconomic index (SEI) using the scoring of occupations provided in Attachment 3 of the NLSY79 documentation (Bureau of Labor Statistics 2019). 10 To average out measurement error, we measure occupational status as an average of five reports from ages 35/36  through  41/42.  For  Denmark,  we  recode  a  person's  ISCO  code  at  age  40  into  the International  Socioeconomic  Index  (ISEI)  using  the  scoring  in  Ganzeboom,  de  Graaf,  and Treiman (1992).

We measure income in terms of permanent log hourly wages. For the United States, we follow Mazumder (2008) and take an average of total hourly wages over five reports from ages 36/37 through 44/45. For Denmark, we take an average of annual total hourly wages from ages 36 through 44. 11 We measure all income variables in 2017 USD and, following Mazumder (2008), we omit those with average hourly wages lower than 1.7 USD and higher than 338 USD (the equivalent of 0.5 USD and 100 USD in 1970 dollars).

We include three 'conventional' family background variables: total net family income, parental highest grade completed, and parental highest occupational status. 12 Although we have done our best to harmonize these family background variables across the two countries, the Danish registers only start recording income from 1980, education from 1981, and occupational

status from 1991. For this reason, we cannot measure parental attainment at around ages 1516 for the Danish cohorts we analyze here. For example, for a man born in 1961, we only observe his parents' occupation from when he turns 30, i.e., when his parents are likely to be in their mid- or late 50s. Similarly, we can only observe the parents' income from around the time he turns 20. These differences reduce the comparability with the United States for which most parental characteristics are measured between child ages 13 and 24.

## Results


Table 1 reports the results from the gross seemingly unrelated variance components model in Eq. ## Discussion


This paper is the first to study the overlap in brother correlations in two widely analyzed labor market outcomes: income and occupational status. Even though brother correlations--the most comprehensive measure of the total impact of family background on attainment--have been analyzed extensively in previous research, their overlap has never been empirically established. Providing estimates of the overlap is nonetheless important if we are to understand the extent to which success across different labor market outcomes are rooted in the same or different family characteristics. Such estimates will also be informative about the extent to which we should consider family background influences as operating in the same or in different ways on key life outcomes.

We propose  using  a  multilevel  seemingly  unrelated  variance  components  model  to estimate the overlap, and we apply the model to harmonized data from the United States and Denmark for cohorts born in the late 1950s and early 1960s. In line with the existing literature, we find that brother correlations in income are much larger in the United States (~ 50 percent) than  in  Denmark  (~  30  percent),  whereas  correlations  in  occupational  status  are  virtually identical (~ 35 percent). However, the overlap in the unmeasured family-specific factors that affect wages and income is very large, around 70 percent, and is virtually identical in the two countries. This finding suggests that, to a very considerable extent, it is the same unmeasured characteristics of one's family background that affect occupational and economic attainment. Despite this substantial overlap, however, we also find that only a minor portion (around 1617  percent)  of  the  overlap  can  be  accounted  for  by  conventional  family  background

characteristics, including parental income, occupation, and education. This finding holds for both countries.

Our finding that only a minor portion of the overlap can be explained by conventional family background characteristics begets the question what other family factors may explain this overlap. For the United States, we provide an auxiliary analyses in which we control for a range of other family factors such as family status, race, and cultural capital. However, these covariates do not explain any significant, additional portion of the overlap over and above that explained  by  the  conventional  family  background  variables.  What  then  may  explain  the overlap? In their study of what explain sibling correlations in income, Björklund, Lindahl, and Lindquist (2010) include measures of what can broadly be considered parenting styles. They find that including these family-level measures explain a substantial, additional portion of the family-level variance. Although we do not have such rich data at our disposal for this study, their findings suggest that the significant, residual overlap in unmeasured family factors may originate in aspects of the home environment that are uncorrelated with parental socioeconomic resources but which otherwise explain why siblings tend to more similar than two randomly selected individuals in a range of key life outcomes. These mechanisms are likely related to skill and preference formation, and future research could therefore fruitfully attempt to unpack these effects with appropriate data.

Other parental characteristics that we cannot include in this study but which might be important  are  parental  wealth  and  social  networks.  Studies  shows  that  wealth  constitute  a crucial dimension of stratification over and above that caused by income and can act as a tool for families to maintain their social positions across generations (Pfeffer and Hällsten 2012; Hällsten and Pfeffer 2017; Hällsten and Thaning 2022; Hansen and Toft 2021). Parents may also draw on their social networks to provide advantages for their children in terms of getting

access to lucrative jobs (Erikson and Jonsson 1998). To the extent that parental wealth and social  networks  provide  advantages  to  children  independently  of  the  conventional  family background characteristics that we control for in this study, they will likely explain some of the remaining overlap in the family unobservables. Determining the extent to which this is the case will be important to settle in future research on this topic.

Our  findings also indirectly speak  to the literature examining  the  overlap in intergenerational  mobility  in  different  domains  or  the  exchangeability  of  resources  in intergenerational transmission (e.g., Breen, Mood, and Jonsson 2016; Thaning 2021). Given the nature of sibling correlations (Solon 1999), estimates of intergenerational associations from this literature will be contained in the overlap estimates we report. From this perspective, our approach could be considered a common  baseline for studies examining resource exchangeability  and/or  overlap  in  levels  of  mobility  across  different  domains,  and  future research might therefore benefit from applying our approach for better understanding crossnational variation in the transmission of resources across generations.

## Introduction


Anthropological and archaeological investigations of violence focused on evolutionary origins (e.g., Knauft et al. 1991; Manson et al. 1991; Trudeau et al. 1981) before turning toward ecological explanations (e.g., Bishop and Lytwyn 2007; Carneiro 1970; Haas 1990; LeBlanc 1999). This ecological interest centered a large body of research that includes subsistence stress and competition (e.g., Billman 2008; Gat 2006; Guilaine and Zammit 2005; Heider 1970; Lambert 2002) and either increasing population density or the decreased carrying capacity of the land (e.g., Chagnon 1990; Haas 1990; Lambert 2002). One important realization that emerged from these research lines, though, is the slim likelihood that any single process led to an outbreak of violence. Many scholars now recognize that a holistic approach (i.e., Keeley 1996) that emphasizes the unique historical processes present in each region (for example Thorpe 2005) is a more reasonable tactic for examining the causes and consequences of violence in the past.

Other researchers have focused on causes of violence that are not prompted by biological or evolutionary motives unknown to the human actor. These include various forms of social regulation and control (Bourdieu 2004, Foucault 2004; Gibson 1990), including witchcraft (Darling 1998; Turner and Turner 1999; Walker 2008; Whiteley 2008); intergroup or intervillage conflict (Wilcox and Haas 1994; Wilcox et al. 2001); social conscription (Carneiro 1961;

These hypotheses generally result from a reductionist and environmentally deterministic view of the causes of conflict (see Keeley 1996; LeBlanc 1999), one that relies on common sense ideas of competition rather than cooperation driving how communities react to crises. Southwestern populations have survived many debilitating droughts without killing their neighbors (e.g., Borck et al. 2015).

Other approaches could be used, such as From Everywhere to Everywhere (White and Barber 2012) cost path modeling using all sites in both the starting points and ending points. However, this has been done for this specific region focusing only on the starting and end points (Safi 2014) and the resulting optimal path corridors through the Gallina region parallel those here (see also Borck 2012).

I employed a modified version of the least-cost path analysis tool in ArcGIS to model the possible migration routes. A least-cost analysis finds the cheapest path from one location to another. A typical least-cost path analysis starts with a slope surface, generally derived from a digital elevation model (DEM). The slope is used to create a resistance surface (Conolly and Lake 2006). From this resistance surface, an accumulated cost surface is created (Xu and Lathrop Jr 1995). The least-cost path is then calculated as traveling backwards from the destination to the source using the accumulated cost surface. The proposed route is then the 'cheapest' course

In addition, standard least-cost path analyses treat slope in an isotropic manner and assign similar values regardless of whether the movement is uphill, downhill, or perpendicular to the direction of the slope, which can decrease their value for modeling human movement decisions.

One of the main limitations in a standard least-cost path analysis is the failure to integrate time into the model (or any other cost variable that is important to us humans) as well as the inability for standard (isotropic) least-cost path analyses to differentially value upslope or downslope movement. To overcome these issues, I used Tobler's hiking function (1993:3), which is inherently anisotropic and differentially evaluates the cost of uphill versus downhill movement (see Kantner 2012 for a discussion of problems with using isotropic measures). The hiking function was implemented in ArcGIS using a vertical factor table to determine modifiers for each positive and negative slope degree. When applied, this function produces the minimum time path, based on off-path human walking velocity.

Migrants were leaving the Four Corners region (Cordell 1995; Kohler et al. 2010; Lekson and Cameron 1995; Lipe 1995; Ortman 2012; Varien 2002) for destinations throughout the greater Southwest, including, but not limited to, the Rio Grande Corridor (Cordell 1979; Duwe 2020; Lipe 2010; Ortman 2012). This eventual depopulation of the Four Corners region by Ancestral Pueblo groups resulted from multiple processes interacting in a complex web of social, demographic, and environmental factors. People were leaving a social situation with increasing levels of violence (Kohler et al. 2009; Kuckelman and Martin 2007; Kuckelman et al. 2000; Lightfoot and Kuckelman 2001) where deteriorating environmental conditions were negatively affecting food supplies (Van West and Dean 2000) for points farther south and east where better conditions existed. This seems to be a situation that could engender violence, and in at least 12 cases, it appears to have done just that.

Of the Gallina sites associated with route four, which has source points mostly in the western and southwestern portion of the Four Corners, most post-date A.D. 1250. Three have cutting dates to this period and the rest were argued to be inhabited post-A.D. 1250 by the investigators who excavated the sites. Of the four sites present along route three from Bluff, one has no dates and three are dated to the early A.D. 1200s. Since the sites with evidence of violence on route four mostly date to the latter half of the thirteenth century and the sites on route three mostly date to the earlier half of the thirteenth century, it is possible that these sites with evidence of violence that are associated with these two potential migration routes are displaying a bimodal pattern of movement and violence through this region, with earlier movement on the

For violence that results in the death of up to 17 members of a village to occur, relatively large numbers of people would have to be traveling through the Gallina region. It would not be possible for an individual household to attack a community and kill this many people. We know archaeologically that in a few cases, at least (Hibben 1939), the Gallina were fighting back. This indicates, at minimum, movement of migrants in numbers above the household level. This is unsurprising given recent analyses of oral traditions that indicate that migration commonly occurred beyond the household level (see Bernardini 2005). Ethnographic research indicates that migration occasionally involved acts of violence (Dongoske et al. 1997:603-604; Ellis 1988; Haas and Creamer 1997:249-250; Lekson and Cameron 1995:194). With hundreds and perhaps thousands of migrants leaving the Mesa Verde area-the population just immediately prior to depopulation is estimated at just under 20,000 people in just the Village Ecodynamics Project's study area (Varien 2010:Table 1.1)-the probability of interaction between migrants and Gallina would have been very high.

One critique against the violence in the Gallina region resulting, potentially, from raids that has been discussed ad hoc among Gallina researchers is that, if this conflict was a prehistoric case of raiding, possibly for food supplies en route to a Rio Chama or Rio Grande destination, why did so many sites with evidence of violence in the Gallina region contain so much maize? Part of this might be answered by the very behavior of raiding for a relatively fast-moving group of migrants. No more food than could easily be carried would be removed from these structures.

## Conclusions


The pattern of violence that emerges in the Gallina highlands is far too complex for a single explanatory model. At least some internecine conflict between Gallina communities may have occurred, as seen at Rattlesnake Ridge. Conflict with external agents materialized along at least two corridors through the Gallina heartland that look to be potential migration routes to the Lower Rio Chama and Northern Middle Rio Grande from the Mesa Verde, Aztec, Salmon, Sand Canyon, and Bluff regions. This modeling strongly suggests that while there is no singular source of violence in the Gallina region, the majority appears to be linked with potential corridors of movement originating outside of the region and ending in the northern Rio Grande and Rio Chama valleys.

Around A.D. 1300, the Gallina left their highland environments. In the Southwest, migration is a common coping strategy when social and/or environmental conditions become too inhospitable. The Gallina, a cultural moment emerging from a social movement that used isolation and material change to create an egalitarian system that contested the rise and spread of hierarchy in the religious and political worlds originating in Chaco and Mesa Verde societies (Borck 2018; Borck and Simpson 2017), were facing an increasingly failing isolationist strategy. They migrated, data suggests both freely (i.e., Beal 1987; Borck 2017; O'Donnell and Ragsdale 2017; O'Donnell and Schillaci 2021; Sando 1982), and as captives (Bishop and Knüsel 2005, Turner et al. 1993) to other regions. A new social identity was negotiated in these regions, one that did not necessitate a separation from other groups. The direction, or directions, of this movement is still unknown (cf. Wiseman 2007), although it is probable, based on evidence from this analysis, and as Beal (1987) originally argued, that there are at least some descendants of the Gallina in the Lower Rio Chama, as well as in the Northern Middle Rio Grande area (O'Donnell and Ragsdale 2017; O'Donnell and Schillaci 2021) and that other material culture elements point to (Borck 2018; Borck and Simpson 2017).

In the Gallina region, we have a migration narrative, but it is not migration as it is traditionally observed and investigated. It is not migration from either the end or the beginning. It is a chronicle of movement itself, migration seen from the middle, evidence of humanity in motion.
