## Introduction


Processes of discrimination and exclusion have been part and parcel of debates concerning the coronavirus disease-2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. In 2020, the World Health Organization highlighted fear, stigma, and misinformation as bigger threats to human lives than the COVID-19 outbreak (World Health Organisation 2020). Discrimination, through the process of ‘othering’ groups of people, has also been observed during previous outbreaks of infectious diseases (McCauley, Minsky, and Viswanath 2013; Yadav and Rawal 2015), emphasising the need for pandemic responses to ensure the safety of all members in society without perpetuating harmful stereotypes (White 2020). Marginalised groups, including refugees, migrants, and racially minoritised communities (Marchi et al. 2022; Strassle et al. 2022), are more vulnerable to negative treatment and blame during a contagion such as the COVID-19 pandemic, with adverse physical and psychological consequences (Yuan et al. 2022).

One way in which discrimination is enacted is through stigma. Link and Phelan conceptualise stigma with five elements, starting with an individual or group being identified as “different” based on factors such as sexuality, skin colour or health status (Link and Phelan 2006). Individuals or groups are then stereotyped and separated based on this characteristic, labelled as “undesirable”. Consequently, they are subjected to discrimination and loss of social standing. The final element of stigma pertains to disempowerment, where stigmatised people may attempt to reverse the stigma but are unable to or actively prevented from doing so.

Stigma and discrimination can have serious health consequences in a disaster, emergency, or pandemic. For instance, when racial and ethnic discrimination occurs in healthcare settings, it has been linked with delays in healthcare utilisation (e.g., filling prescriptions) (Alcalá and Cook 2018), influenza vaccine refusal (Bleser, Miranda, and Jean-Jacques 2016), and lower perceived quality of medical care, including insufficient time with a physician and low involvement in shared decision-making (Benjamins and Middleton 2019). Racial and ethnic discrimination during the COVID-19 pandemic has been specifically linked to the refusal of COVID-19 vaccines, partly due to this discrimination leading to low trust in the health system (Paul, Fancourt, and Razai 2022). Various forms of stigma relating to COVID-19 have also been shown to lead to higher levels of poverty and unemployment (Ransing et al. 2020). Thus, in many ways, the COVID-19 pandemic has amplified the existing fractures in society by widening social inequality (Scambler 2020), thereby making research into understanding stigma and discrimination more timely now than ever.

Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, a wide range of platforms for discrimination and amplification of difference emerged among affected communities. For example, several studies have highlighted the harmful impacts of discrimination on individuals and communities based on race and ethnicity. When cases of COVID-19 first started to be recorded in the City of Wuhan, China, there were reports of Asian people experiencing racism, including being banned from restaurants in Hong Kong and China (Chung and Li 2020; He et al. 2020). Furthermore, Asian people wearing facemasks at the beginning of the pandemic were treated with fear and disrespect and even physically attacked in public in the US (Choi 2021). Asian and Asian American people living in the US said they had been treated with suspicion in public and been the target of racist jokes, verbal assault, and physical threats (Lee and Waters 2020). In UK-based qualitative research, racially minoritised young people expressed that they felt blamed in government messaging for rising COVID-19 cases and poorer COVID-19 outcomes in racial and ethnic minority groups (Burgess et al. 2022).

Age has been another focal point of discrimination during the COVID-19 pandemic, often intersecting with health status. For example, in the UK, the government encouraged all people aged 70 and over to remain at home as much as possible during the early stages of the pandemic to protect their health, leading to concerns that this group would experience increased social isolation and discrimination (Scott 2020). Similar concerns of age discrimination were also observed internationally. For instance, in a nationally representative study of “older” adults (aged 50+) in Israel, participants who believed older adults were perceived as a burden during the COVID-19 outbreak had higher anxiety about dying and reported more age-based discrimination (Cohn-Schwartz and Ayalon 2021). In addition, evidence suggests that COVID-19-related discrimination (i.e., negative treatment based on presumed vulnerability to or infection with COVID-19 due to age) was associated with poorer mental health during the pandemic (Miconi et al. 2021). However, it is not simply older age that has been associated with discrimination. Researchers in the same study found that younger adults (ages 18-39) were more than twice as likely to have experienced COVID-19-related discrimination than older adults (Miconi et al. 2021). This effect was heightened by the messages suggesting that young people were responsible for spreading the virus (Idoiaga Mondragon et al. 2022).

The COVID-19 pandemic has additionally highlighted gender inequality. In response to school closures and lack of childcare availability in the UK during the lockdown periods, qualitative research participants said they felt that progress towards equality had diminished in response to pandemic-related changes (Dawes et al. 2021). Several studies have illustrated how men were more frequently featured in international news media reporting as experts while women’s names and voices were noticeably absent (Howell 2020). In articles reporting information about COVID-19, mentions from “experts” were more likely to be men than women (Jones 2020). Crucially, these gendered impacts were not felt equally across groups, with evidence illuminating how race and social class compounded the effects of the pandemic. For example, a US study reported that Black and Hispanic women were more likely to experience unemployment during and after the pandemic than White women (Gezici and Ozay 2020). Consequently, there have been calls for more focus on intersectionality in work on discrimination and social inequality (Seng et al. 2012).

### Study rationale

Although necessary for quantifying the frequency and other epidemiologic features of discrimination during the pandemic, the scope of findings from previous quantitative data are limited to the questions asked. As a result, many previous studies have focused on an overall ‘experience of discrimination’ rather than providing examples of specific types of experiences that could be considered discrimination. This could lead to under-reporting, as individuals do not always recognise certain events as discriminatory. One way to address this limitation is by asking more detailed questions about various types of discrimination and the assumed reasons for these experiences. Granular data from the pandemic, such as where, when, and amongst whom health discrimination occurs are not currently known. Research on what other types of discrimination may have appeared during the pandemic is also lacking. Forms of discrimination that were previously less prominent may have become more common during the COVID-19 pandemic. For example, health discrimination, or discrimination due to others’ perceptions of one’s health status or vulnerability to the disease, has been reported (Hahm et al. 2021). Therefore, there is a need for mixed methods approaches whereby data can be collected by different means, inductive and deductive, and triangulated to complement and build on each other and enrich our understanding of complex social phenomena.

Consequently, this study sought to build on prior reports of discrimination during the pandemic and utilise quantitative data to shed light on the various manifestations of discrimination during the first eight months of the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, the study used qualitative methods to help identify potentially under-acknowledged characteristics that were the targets of discrimination during the pandemic to help inform future public health awareness campaigns.

### Aims

The first aim of this study was to quantitatively describe factors associated with participant responses to questions on experiences of discrimination due to age, racial/ethnic identity, gender, or ‘other’ characteristics, where the discrimination occurred during the first four months of the pandemic (collected July 2020) and over the next year (collected July 2021). We explored this within seven response options (including an ‘other’ option). The second aim was to explore participants’ qualitative accounts of stigma and discrimination during the first year of the pandemic by analysing free-text data when they responded to questions on factors that affected their mental health and wellbeing.


## Methods



### Study Design


We used an explanatory sequential mixed methods study design whereby we administered a quantitative questionnaire followed by qualitative free-text questions. Qualitative data were collected at a separate timepoint after the initial survey to help explain the results in further detail (Creswell et al. 2003). Quantitative data analysis took place first and served as a framework to guide the direction of the subsequent qualitative data analysis. The University College London Ethics committee reviewed and approved the research (Project ID:14895/005).


### Study Sample


We used data from the COVID-19 Social Study, a panel study of the psychological and social experiences of over 70,000 adults (aged 18+) in the UK during the COVID-19 pandemic. The study commenced on 21 March 2020 and involved online weekly surveys (to August 2020) and then four-weekly data collection through April 2022. Sampling methods were not random, and it is therefore not representative of the general UK population. Participants were recruited using three primary approaches. First, convenience sampling was used, including promoting the study through existing networks and mailing lists (such as large databases of adults who had previously consented to be involved in health research across the UK), print, and digital media coverage. Second, more targeted recruitment was undertaken, focusing on (i) individuals from a low-income background, (ii) individuals with no or few educational qualifications, and (iii) individuals who were unemployed. Third, the study was promoted via partnerships with third-sector organisations supporting vulnerable groups, including adults with pre-existing mental health conditions, older adults, carers, and people experiencing domestic violence or abuse. More information can be found in the study User Guide (https://osf.io/jm8ra/).

Two samples were used in the present study. See Figure S1 for a visual representation of sample selection for both the quantitative and mixed methods samples. First, to quantitatively describe participant experiences of discrimination during the first four months of the pandemic (collected July 2020) and over the next year (collected July 2021) and factors associated with experiencing discrimination, participants were included if they provided data for the quantitative discrimination module at both time points. Furthermore, they provided data on demographic variables needed to construct statistical weights (gender, age, ethnicity, country, and education) and on other socio-demographic variables, leaving a sample size of 15,154 participants. Proportions of missing data for participants who were excluded are in Supplemental Table S1. Excluded participants were more likely to be younger, from an ethnic minority group, come from households with slightly higher incomes, were less likely to have physical or mental health conditions, and reported slightly higher proportions of discrimination experiences (Supplemental Table S2).

Second, for the mixed methods analyses, participants were included if they provided data on the July 2020 discrimination module, had experienced at least one instance of discrimination since the start of the pandemic and had also provided free-text data (which was optional and collected 14 October to 26 November 2020), leaving a final sample for the mixed methods analyses of 1,121. The proportion of males, older adults, people from White ethnic groups with higher household incomes, and people who did not have a mental health condition were higher in the excluded versus included sample.

Compared to the mixed methods sample, individuals who had reported in July 2020 that they had experienced at least one form of discrimination since the start of the pandemic did not differ meaningfully in any demographics or experiences of discrimination observed (Supplemental Table S3).


### Measures


### Quantitative data

#### Discrimination experiences

Discrimination experiences were measured quantitatively from an adapted version of the Everyday Discrimination Scale (EDS) (Williams et al. 1997). The scale was first administered in July 2020 and asked about discrimination experienced since the start of the first lockdown. The second administration occurred a year later, in July 2021, and asked about discrimination experienced over the past year. The EDS was designed to measure routine and relatively subtle experiences of unfair treatment in everyday situations. The widely used scale has shown good internal reliability (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.87) and expected associations with internalising and externalising symptoms. We used three items from the short version of the EDS (being threatened or harassed; being treated as if you are dishonest; people acting as if they were afraid of you) and added four questions from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA). In addition, we made subtle changes to some of the phrasings of the ELSA questions to account for the unique social situation of COVID-19. For example, due to lockdowns affecting the in-person use of services, the item “received poorer service in restaurants or stores” was changed to “received poorer service than other people (e.g., for deliveries or in stores)”, and an item about receiving “poorer service than others from doctors or in hospitals” was added. Participants who reported each experience were asked to give one of four possible reasons (i.e., gender, race/ethnicity, age, or another reason) for the discrimination and were allowed to select more than one reason. See Table S4 for a full listing of items.

#### Exposure variables

Six socio-demographic characteristics were collected when participants first signed up to take part in the study. A binary gender (male vs female) variable was included. The survey offered participants an “Other/prefer not to say” option; however, as we could not construct statistical weights for these participants, they were excluded from the main quantitative sample for analysis. Tables S2 and S3 show unweighted proportions of those who chose this option and were excluded, and the two included samples. Nonetheless, we conducted unweighted sensitivity analyses that did include these and other participants who were excluded (see below). Age (18-29, 30-45, 46-59, and 60+), ethnicity (White ethnic background vs ethnic minority groups [Asian/Asian British - Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Other, Black/Black British - Caribbean, African, other, Mixed race - White and Black/Black British, Mixed race – Other, White - British, Irish, Other, Chinese/Chinese British, Middle Eastern/Middle Eastern British - Arab, Turkish, Other, Other ethnic group]), household income (> £30,000 per year vs < £30,000 per year) and education (up to GCSE/O Levels, A-Levels or vocational training, and degree or higher) were also included.

Finally, two binary variables constructed from participant responses at baseline were included to indicate the presence of a) a clinically diagnosed physical health condition (i.e., high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease, lung disease (e.g., asthma or COPD), cancer, another clinically-diagnosed chronic physical health condition, another disability that “affects my ability to leave the house,” or any other disability); and b) a clinically diagnosed mental health condition (depression, anxiety, or another clinically diagnosed mental health condition).


### Analysis


Quantitative data were analysed as follows. First, proportions of different discrimination types, causes, and causes within types reported in July 2020 and July 2021 are presented. Next, two multivariate logistic regression models were conducted, which included all predictor variables entered simultaneously; one with having reported any discrimination in July 2020 as the outcome variable and the second with a report of any discrimination in July 2021 as the outcome. Finally, to increase the representativeness of sample demographics to those of the general UK population, a multivariate reweighting method was used to create sample weights to the proportions of gender, age, ethnicity, country, and education in the UK population obtained from the Office for National Statistics (Office for National Statistics 2020). Because complete self-report data on these five demographic variables was required to make the sample weights, the quantitative analyses were conducted only on the subsample of participants without missing data on these variables, which ranged from 0.77% for ethnicity to 25.92% on income (N=15,154). To examine the impact on findings this exclusion may have had, we also report quantitative results from a sensitivity analysis, including people for whom we were unable to calculate statistical weights.

### Qualitative data

Between 14 October and 26 November 2020, UCL COVID-19 Social Study (CSS) participants were given the option to respond to any of eight free-text questions as part of a one-off free-text module administered as part of the survey. The questions were developed by DF, AM and AB and predominantly enquired about factors contributing to participants’ mental health and wellbeing during the pandemic. Topics included: the impact of changes brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic, causes of changes in mental health and wellbeing during the pandemic, and personal attributes or circumstances that influenced participants’ experiences during the COVID-19 pandemic (see Table S5 for a full list of questions and the average number of characters in response to each question). After participants completed their answers, free-text data were cleaned and imported into Microsoft Excel for analysis.


### Quantitative Results


In the quantitative sample, before weights were applied, most participants were female, of older age (60+), from a White ethnic background, and had obtained at least a university degree (Supplemental Table S2). However, after weighting, the proportions of socio-demographics in the sample better reflected those of the general UK population (Table 1).

In July 2020, one in five reported at least one instance of discrimination over the first four months of the pandemic (19.8%). By July 2021, the proportion who said they had been discriminated against in the past year was 28.4% (Table 2). The most common type of discrimination at both time points was being treated with less courtesy or respect than others (9.9% in July 2020; 18.1% in July 2021). In addition, proportions experiencing threats or harassment (3.6% in July 2020 vs 7.7% in July 2021), poorer service than others from doctors or in hospitals (3.3% in July 2020 vs 7.7% in July 2021), and other types of discrimination (4.0% in July 2020 vs 7.0% in July 2021) were also higher in 2021 compared to 2020. However, this was likely due to differences in time frames for which participants reported experiencing the discrimination (i.e., the first four months of the pandemic in July 2020 vs the past year in July 2021).

Participants were allowed to select more than one personal characteristic for the discrimination. Discrimination for another reason was the most often reported personal characteristic attributed to the discrimination (15.1% in July 2020; 20.9% in July 2021) (Table 2). These proportions were followed by age (5.1% in July 2020 vs 8.4% in July 2021), gender (2.1% in July 2020 vs 5.6% in July 2021), and race/ethnicity (1.5% in July 2020 vs 2.1% in July 2021). Within types of discrimination, the most common characteristic attributed was due to another reason. For example, at both time points, just over 80% of people who experienced other people acting as if they were afraid of them said it was due to another reason, whilst age (13.4%) and gender (9.8%) were the most common characteristics attributable to this type of discrimination in July 2020 and 2021, respectively.

In multivariate logistic regression models examing factors associated with discrimination (Supplemental Table S6), at both time points, participants who reported at least one instance of discrimination were more likely to be under the age of 60, with progressively larger odds with decreasing age (e.g., ages 46-59: odds ratio [OR] = 1.59; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.37 to 1.84; ages 30-45: OR = 2.10; 95% CI = 1.74 to 2.54; ages 18-29: OR = 2.55; 95% CI = 1.84 to 3.55 for discrimination experienced in 2020; Figure 1). People from ethnic minority groups, those who had obtained at least a university degree (relative to people with education up to GCSE levels), people with lower household incomes, and those with a long-term physical or mental health condition were all more likely to have been discriminated against at both time points. In July 2021, women were more likely to have experienced discrimination than men (OR = 1.38; 95% CI = 1.23 to 1.54), but not in July 2020 (OR = 1.01; 95% CI = 0.89 to 1.14; Figure 2).

Sensitivity analysis

In order to include participants who had selected ‘other/prefer not to say’ in response to the gender question and participants who were missing data on other variables, we conducted (unweighted) analyses that included the quantitative sample in addition to participants who had been excluded. Proportions experiencing each type of discrimination were largely similar to those in the weighted sample (Supplemental Table S7). However, amongst participants who had reported ‘other/prefer not to say’ in response to the gender question, proportions experiencing discrimination were much higher than those of the total sample (Supplemental Table S8). Substantive results for the logistic regressions examining factors associated with having experienced discrimination were the same as in the main analyses (Supplemental Table S9). However, adding the ‘other/prefer not to say’ category to the gender variable resulted in over 3.5 times the likelihood (OR = 3.64; 95% CI = 2.16 to 6.13) of being discriminated against in 2020 but not in 2021.


### Qualitative Results


The qualitative analysis identified 135 descriptions of personal characteristics linked with stigma or discrimination among 92 participants.  61 participants qualitatively described experiencing one form of stigma or discrimination, 21 described two forms, and 10 described three or more (92 individual participants and 8% of the total sample). Experiences of discrimination were attributed mainly to having a health condition or disability, age, or based on pandemic-related changes that perpetuated existing discrimination (see Table 3). Discrimination due to gender, age, and ethnicity or race was mentioned by 33 participants; however, the qualitative results also elucidated some of the “other” reasons for discrimination that people had selected in the quantitative survey. Specifically, 58 participants described some “other” form of stigma or discrimination due to factors including their health or disability status, having tested positive for COVID-19, social class, personal finances, or occupation.

### 1. Gender Inequality

Five participants said that their sex or gender had influenced the outcome of their pandemic-related experiences, often related to the division of labour within the home and at work, causing feelings of being “overwhelmed.” Some felt that progress that had previously been made towards gender equality had been undone due to the pandemic: “I firmly believe that gender equality has reversed during this time.” Some felt left behind and “just more invisible than I ever was.”

### 2. Age Discrimination

Twenty-four participants described experiences of age-related discrimination during the pandemic. A frequently reported view was that government actions and policies in response to the pandemic were discriminatory. When social distancing restrictions were introduced, people over 70 were categorised as extremely clinically vulnerable. Some were displeased that they were classified as “vulnerable” by government and healthcare services due to their age. Descriptions of the impact of this label varied, with some feeling “invisible” or “old and hopeless for the first time.” However, other participants over 60 rejected being labelled as “vulnerable” and did not identify with the label or wish to be associated with this word. In some cases, this had an impact on mental health and wellbeing.

Several participants worried that this categorisation would have secondary implications on their ability (or their elderly partner’s ability) to find work after the pandemic because they might be viewed as “less able,” “weak,” or “expendable.” These concerns were described by middle-aged people in low-wage positions or experiencing ill health. The introduction of “support schemes” that were perceived as being focused on younger people left some in their 40s and older age groups feeling forgotten about. Furlough and other pandemic support schemes were seen to have been “geared towards young people, families, renters.” Two participants pointed to an assumption from the government and members of the public that being of a certain age meant people would be financially stable, not “financially vulnerable”; consequently, the future felt uncertain and “bleak.”

### 3. Racial discrimination

Four participants discussed changes in racial discrimination during the pandemic. Two participants said their race or ethnicity had influenced their experiences during the pandemic, including feelings of being “less safe” and “at risk”. Conversely, two participants said they “experience[d] far far less racism than before” during periods of lockdown due to less frequent face-to-face encounters with other people: “I have far more peace because I am not experiencing as much racism- I have not felt this comfortable or free since I was 4.”

### 4. Health Status or Disability

Forty participants said they experienced stigma or discrimination during the pandemic due to health status or disability. As with participants in older age groups, some participants with disabilities felt "frustrated” with the implications of the “clinically extremely vulnerable” label. Some said that workplaces, businesses, or organisations did not make necessary adjustments for their inclusion when social distancing or remote working changes were implemented.

Participants who were shielding or living with disabilities often described experiences of mistreatment from others during the pandemic because of their health condition, resulting in feeling “alienated,” “disrespected,” or “disposable and unimportant.” For those who were exempt from mask-wearing during pandemic restrictions because of “hidden disabilities” such as asthma or PTSD, the imagined or real-life “negative reactions” of others were a considerable source of fear and stress when out in public. In addition, some participants said that being in public as a disabled person during the pandemic could draw new forms of “negative” attention from neighbours or strangers. For instance, one participant described a situation where they were confronted by a member of the public for being outside during lockdown, where the assumption was that “as a wheelchair user”, being outside “wasn’t exercise” (one of the only permitted reasons for being outside at that point in the lockdown).

Access to “prompt medical care” and essentials was harder for some participants with disabilities, as “provisions” had not been made for their needs with the introduction of pandemic-related changes. For instance, many relied on frontline key workers for their access to essentials; however, social distancing policies that drivers were required to follow during deliveries left some disabled people feeling humiliated, stranded, and “diminished as a person.” In some cases, benefits renewals required a face-to-face assessment from either the Department of Work and Pensions, GP, or a consultant. However, this was often not possible or caused considerable distress for those with chronic illness or who were shielding.

### 5. Contracting COVID-19

A subgroup of participants discussed views held by themselves or others that there wasstigma associated with contracting the COVID-19 virus. As a result, some people felt ostracised by their neighbours and “fearful of each other” during the lockdown. In addition, participants already facing discrimination before the pandemic said that stigma around having COVID-19 created an additional challenge for them to cope with. For instance, having COVID-19 on top of a pre-existing health condition was described as “making things worse.”

### 6.  Occupation

A small group of participants mentioned occupation as a source of discrimination. Pandemic-related policies imposed by the government and other organisations were often seen as “too harsh” for certain professions (such as hospitality and teaching) compared with other industries. Some people felt that a consequence of their jobs being less prioritised than others meant that they were more exposed to the virus because their “health was disregarded” by those making decisions for people in frontline professions.

7. Social class.

Divisions between different “social classes” were felt by six participants, particularly for those experiencing financial hardship or immigration precarity. Others thought they had received unfair treatment from the government due to rules favouring “the elite” and “privileged.”

### Discussion

We describe different types of discrimination across different settings, attributable to four characteristics (gender, race/ethnicity, age, or another reason) from the start of the pandemic through the first 16 months. A number of socio-demographic factors were associated with having been discriminated against at both time points, including gender, age, ethnicity, education, household income, and physical and mental health conditions. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design comprised of survey and free-text data from 1,121 adults in the UK, we identified seven topics related to discrimination concerning participants’ experiences over the first eight months of the COVID-19 pandemic (gender inequality, racial discrimination, ageism, health and disability discrimination, stigma from contracting COVID-19, and discrimination relating to occupation and social class). 31% of participants reporting discrimination in the qualitative group described multiple characteristics that they felt discriminated against which highlights the need for an intersectional lens when seeking to challenge instances of discrimination and social inequality.

In the quantitative analyses, women were more likely than men to have been discriminated against, but only in 2021. This may have been due to a cumulative or longer term impact of pandemic conditions on women. International evidence has highlighted the disproportionate impact of the pandemic on women for varying reasons, including the closure of schools leading to increased pressure from childcare and sector closures where women’s employment tends to be highest, including healthcare and education (Brodeur et al. 2021). Women working in healthcare were more likely than men to report increased stress (Lorello et al. 2021), depression and burnout linked to increased family and work pressures during the pandemic (Sriharan et al. 2020; Torrente et al. 2021). Based on our qualitative findings, women were more likely to report the effects of discrimination in terms of their roles in the workplace and as parents, suggesting these areas as the focus of future interventions. In order to minimise the social and economic cost of lockdowns, interventions should be targeted to alleviate the impacts on women and all people from ethnic minority groups, who were also more likely to have been discriminated against at both time points. Interventions could include clear communication in public messaging about the availability of support to offset the adverse effects of the pandemic (Le and Nguyen 2021). Ignoring these ramifications can deepen racial and gender inequality (Le and Nguyen 2021).

Our quantitative findings suggest that younger people were more likely to be subject to discrimination than older adults, with this pattern being exacerbated from 2020 to 2021. This could have been due to perceptions of younger adults being less likely to comply with COVID-19 rules and guidelines, which was evident in media (Grover 2021) and research reports (Wright, Steptoe, and Fancourt 2022). We also found that people with physical and mental health conditions were more likely to have reported discrimination at both time points. In the UK, certain demographic groups (e.g., those over 70 and those with a chronic condition) were deemed more clinically vulnerable to severe outcomes from COVID-19. They were advised to shield and were given priority for vaccinations once they became available. They were also eligible for some sources of support (e.g., delivery of groceries, medications, or other items) not available to the rest of the population. Individuals in clinically vulnerable categories may have felt they had to justify why they received these supports, particularly if the reason for being classified as clinically vulnerable was not immediately apparent to others. Some thought this targeting could lead to increased social isolation and discrimination (Scott 2020), and our qualitative findings suggest that some people felt unfairly labelled and mistreated by others. In countries such as the US, the portrayal of clinically vulnerable people was perceived to reinforce negative stereotypes, and extreme care is recommended in the development of public health messaging to avoid this (Lytle et al. 2022).

In our quantitative analyses, people from ethnic minority groups were more likely to have been discriminated against, although this effect was slightly more pronounced during the first wave of the pandemic compared to the year that followed. This echoes findings from other research conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic. For example, in a subsample of adults from ethnic minority groups from the UCL COVID-19 Social Study, 40% had experienced some form of discrimination over the first four months of the pandemic, and this, in turn, increased the likelihood of COVID-19 vaccine refusal. This association was mediated by distrust of the health service to handle the pandemic (Paul et al. 2022). In addition, 7% had experienced discrimination in a medical setting due to their race or ethnicity over the first four months of the pandemic (Paul et al. 2022). In a US study, nearly 1 in 10 (9%) of respondents reported mistreatment by a doctor or nurse due to race at the end of December 2020 (Savoia et al. 2021). Small studies of ethnic minority adults suggest that not feeling listened to by medical professionals may be a pervasive experience of discrimination in medical settings (Hausmann et al. 2010; López-Cevallos and Harvey 2019). People from ethnic and racial minority groups were widely cited in public health messaging from the government and in news media as being at higher risk for contracting and becoming seriously ill from the virus. In addition, UK government messaging was developed explicitly for increasing COVID-19 vaccine uptake in people from minority ethnic groups, some of whom have had lower COVID-19 vaccine uptake than others (Office for National Statistics 2022). This could have led to additional perceptions of blame amongst ethnic minority groups.

In addition to gender, age, and race/ethnicity, we examined participants’ reports of “other” forms of stigma and discrimination during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. Discrimination due to another characteristic not listed was the most commonly cited in our quantitative analyses at both time points. Our qualitative findings identified manifestations of health stigma described in the sociological literature long before the COVID-19 pandemic. For instance, the view that individuals might be “tainted” from having a positive COVID-19 diagnosis bears a resemblance to Goffman’s work on “spoiled” identities (Goffman 1986). Historically featured in research into lived experience of chronic illness, epilepsy and HIV, a stigmatised individual may be excluded from society based on having been seen to possess undesirable characteristics (Scambler 2009), leaving them feeling discredited from the treatment of others. We found examples of this being manifested to an extent within local communities as people felt afraid of one another and consequently more isolated. We also found evidence of internalised or felt stigma (Scambler 2004); whereby people with health conditions unable to wear Personal Protective Equipment experienced mental health consequences from fearing the perceived negative actions and judgements of others in public.

A group of participants said they felt that public health messaging contained biased assumptions based on having a disability and having a physical health condition was also associated with increased odds of having experienced discrimination in the quantitative analyses. Biased health messaging has been observed by others during the pandemic, including people identifying as obese or overweight witnessing stigmatising language that affected their mental health and self-esteem (Stewart and Ogden, 2022). Young minoritized people in the UK also articulated feelings of poor representation within media, which resulted in feelings of blame, and disconnect from wider society (Burgess et al., 2022). Policy responses and public health messaging must be developed in tandem with structures that avoid adverse impacts on health (Devakumar et al. 2020). Stigma reduction strategies exist at the micro-, meso-, and macro levels and include using language in public health messaging that is accessible to a wide range of literacy and disability needs, and even better if the targeted groups participate in the co-production of such messages (Gronholm et al. 2021). Mass media interventions aimed at the general public that challenge myths and stereotypes are also recommended (Devakumar et al. 2020) alongside participatory engagement for reducing stigma and prejudice (Burgess et al. 2021).

### Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, the sample was not representative of the general adult UK population, so the findings cannot be generalised, nor can we provide figures of prevalence for the new forms of stigma and discrimination identified in the results. The sample comprised predominantly White, female, university-educated adults; therefore, it is likely that findings are biased towards the experiences of people in these groups. However, the sample size was large, there was good heterogeneity across different population groups, and all our statistical analyses were weighted to align with population proportions. Additionally, it is a strength that there were no differences between participants who said they had experienced discrimination in July 2020 and those who did not provide free-text data compared to those that did. We also had a relatively large sample size compared to many qualitative studies, allowing more representation of detailed perspectives from under-represented groups. Secondly, the free-text module in the survey was developed specifically for use in the UCL Covid-19 Social Study in the context of an ongoing pandemic with inherent limitations. It was not a formal or standardised assessment measure. It is also possible that participants did not perceive experiences as discrimination or that all instances of stigma and discrimination were identified during the coding process. The question wording was broad, with several examples of characteristics linked with discrimination; however, there was no comprehensive list of examples of discrimination. While we prompted on several topics that ended up being the most popular to report on, it is possible that people did not self-identify discrimination, meaning the topics presented here are likely not exhaustive.

Nonetheless, our mixed methods approach provided more opportunity to identify types of and reasons for discrimination, helping to mitigate this issue. Thirdly, the time span for the quantitative discrimination questions varied across the two time points. In July 2020, participants reported on discrimination they had experienced since the pandemic had started (3-4 months), whilst in July 2021, they reported on discrimination over the past year. Comparisons in the proportions reporting discrimination at these two time periods should therefore be interpreted with caution. Fourth, use of the terminology relating to gender and sex was at times erroneously used interchangeably throughout the survey and consequently, our analyses may have missed important nuances pertaining to sex and gender identity characteristics. Further work is needed to help understand and elucidate the impact of sex and gender identity with regards to experiences of discrimination during the COVID-19 pandemic.

In addition, due to the small number of participants within specific ethnic minority groups in our sample, ethnic minority groups were examined as a whole in our analyses. This approach prevented us from accounting for the variation in the current and historical experiences of discrimination across these diverse groups. Finally, while a strength of the research is we were able to learn more about the multiple forms of discrimination that individuals are subjected to, often simultaneously, further work is needed on the intersectional nature of stigma and discrimination and the health consequences of this for people living in a pandemic.
