## Study 2b: Replicating Affective Outcomes


Due to our results and theorizing in Study 2a, we aimed  to  replicate  our  prior  results.  Therefore,  we conducted an additional experimental online survey study to examine the effect of dispositional FOMO susceptibility on affect based on Instagram content in a  between-participants design. This replication was essential to provide further evidence for the relevance of the DFS scale and the need to examine FOMO and its personality-based antecedents more granularly.


## Method


This preregistered study (www.bit.ly/3dpAr7h) aimed at reducing the initial pool of items to create the first draft of the DFS scale (OSF: www.bit.ly/3vaxD70).  We  recruited  participants  in an  online  survey  for  exploratory  factor  analysis (EFA)  in  October  2019  from  the  general U.S. population using the Dynata sampling service (Sample A, N = 731). We compensated participants according to their panel membership and the Dynata compensation scheme and asked them to respond to all  79  items  of  the  reviewed  item  pool.  However, after completing the data collection for Sample A, we inspected  the  item  pool  of  79  items  again  and excluded  five  items  that  reflected  romantic  regrets (e.g.,  "You  wonder  if  you  maybe  have  missed  the opportunity to be with your soul mate"). We submitted data for 74 items to parallel analysis (Horn, 1965) to determine the number of factors to extract in consequent  EFA  using  unrotated  Eigenvalues  and 5,000  bootstrapping  intervals.  After  selecting  the number of factors to extract (Ford et al., 1986; Kline, 2013),  we  submitted  data  to  EFA  using  maximum likelihood estimation and Promax rotation (Churchill,  1979).  We  excluded  items  with  crossloadings or factor loadings < .50.


## Procedure


We recruited participants (Sample C, N = 90) from a  public  university  student  pool  in  March 2021  for this  preregistered study  (www.bit.ly/3sJku1g; OSF: www.bit.ly/3v9Fz8t).  We  screened  participants  for having an active Instagram account and compensated them  with  course  credit.  They  answered  the  DFS scale and completed the Positive and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS, Watson et al., 1988). We asked them to imagine a short scenario in which they evaluated twelve mock-up Instagram posts in blockrandomized order. We determined a priori that 100 participants  should  suffice  based  on  the  withinparticipants design.


## Results



## Manipulation-Check


Participants  were  significantly  more  likely  to experience  FOMO  when  seeing  social  posts  vs. branded  products  posts  ( Msocial =  5.37, Mbranded  = 2.02, t (359) = 22.3, p < .001, d = 1.18) and vs. control posts  ( Mcontrol =  1.61 ,  t (359)  =  23.3, p <  .001, d = 1.23). Participants were  slightly more  likely to experience FOMO when seeing branded products vs. control posts ( (359) = 4.8, t p < .001, d = 0.25).


## Multilevel Regression Analysis


We submitted standardized dependent and grandmean-centered  independent  variables  to  the  same series of multilevel regression models as in Study 2a. Our findings (upper section of Table 8) confirmed the findings  in  Study  2a.  Social  content  induced  lower positive ( b = -0.26, 95% CI [-0.50; -0.02], p = .037) and higher negative affect ( b = 0.48, 95% CI [0.26; 0.71], p <  .001) with increasing scores on the DFS scale as compared to control content. These findings were the same across all individual FOMO components  except  for  experiential  envy.  Though there  was  a  negative  association  between  positive affect and experiential envy for social content compared  to  control  content,  this  effect  was  not statistically significant.


## Word Fragmentation Task Results


Supplemental  to  our  preregistered  analyses,  we conducted eight linear regression analyses. Findings for implicit affectivity mirrored results from explicit affectivity  analyses.  Our  results  (lower  section  of Table  8)  indicated  that participants who  scored higher  on  the  DFS  scale  identified  more  negative words  in  the  social  condition  than  in  the  control condition ( b = 0.33, 95% CI [0.02; 0.63], p = .037). Though this effect was similar across all DFS subscales the main driver of negative affect was experiential envy ( b = 0.43, 95% CI [0.13; 0.72], p = .005). When comparing effect sizes for the interaction term across multilevel models, experiential envy (b = 0.43, p = .005) showed a more potent standardized effect than social disconnectedness  (b  =  0.22, p =  .109)  or  regret anticipation (b = 0.23, p = .081).

These  findings  aligned  and  partially  replicated Study 2a. The relationship between individuals' DFS and FOMO-related  affect  is based on people's susceptibility  to  the  three  FOMO  components.  As suggested  previously,  we  showed  that  Instagram content might threaten users' subjective well -being depending on their dispositional FOMO susceptibility  (Barry  &  Wong,  2020).  We  consider our  predictive  validity  testing  for  the  DFS  scale successful.


## General Discussion


The  findings  from  explicit  (self-reported)  and implicit (word fragmentation task) affect assessment align with each other and partially replicated Study 2a. The relationship between individuals' tendency to experience FOMO and FOMO-related affect is based on  complex  cognitive  experiences.  In  general,  our findings speak to the negative affective nature of the FOMO experience in the context of social media. We show that social media content may threaten users' subjective  well-being  depending  on  their  cognitive disposition  for  FOMO,  which  has  been  suggested previously (Barry & Wong, 2020). We consider these negative emotions not necessarily adverse effects, as some  research  found  that  consumers  emotionally bond with brands they encounter under fear (Dunn & Hoegg,  2014).  However,  since  fear  appeals  may interfere  with  message  processing  (Rhodes,  2017), marketers must be careful when  using FOMO appeals.

Our  findings  have  two  important  implications. First,  they  speak  to  the  predictive  validity  of  our developed measurement instrument because increases in DFS  scores were associated with negative affect when social information was received via  social  media.  Second,  the  main  driver  for  the (implicit) affective outcomes was experiential envy and  the  other  cognitive  components  to  a  lesser degree.  We  show  that  a  detailed  and  fine-grained view  of  FOMO  as  a  multidimensional  concept  is essential.


## Limitations and Future Research


This  present  research  does  come  with  several limitations. First, concerning the scale development process, we were limited to items based on qualitative research,  including  interviewees  from [omitted  for blind review). Future  work  should conduct cross-cultural research to validate the DFS

scale within different cultural environments. Because these constructs should reflect relatively stable individual  differences,  we  invite  future  research  to establish the temporal validity of the developed scale (DeVellis, 2017).

Additionally, although we offer a more sophisticated explication of the FOMO concept as a trait than  other  research,  we  only  provide  weak evidence for the DFS sub-scales potentially differing roles. Therefore, future research should design studies specifically to explore the various predispositions comprising FOMO as antecedents for when  one  is  to  experience  FOMO.  Though  we provide  the  much-needed  measurement  instrument that allows for a context-independent and multifaceted exploration of FOMO in the future, it was  out  of  the  scope  of  this  current  research  to robustly  test  these  mechanisms  in  detail.  Research should design studies to establish boundary conditions.


## Conclusion


In  summary,  we  developed  a  scale  representing individuals' p ersonality-based cognitive predisposition for FOMO independent of the context of this research. We  examined the impact of Instagram content on emotional outcomes dependent on  individuals' dispositional  FOMO  susceptibility scores. Thus, we offer an evolved explication of the FOMO phenomenon. Comprised of social disconnectedness, regret anticipation, and experiential envy, the dispositional FOMO susceptibility  as  a  personality  trait  might  be  an essential  driver  of  affectivity.  By  identifying  the dispositions  leading  to  negative-affective  FOMO experiences, we offer a novel perspective on FOMO that  may  help  investigate  protective  behaviors  for people who  suffer from FOMO  in  the  future. Offering  a  multidimensional,  context-independent personality  trait  measure  allows  future  research  to detangle the different drivers of FOMO in a diverse set of contexts. Thus, we invite scholars to conduct fine-grained explorations of the phenomenon to aid its conceptual evolution.

## 1 Introduction


Meritocracy is an ideal that aspires to the distribution of resources in a society according to personal effort and talent (Young, 2006). This ideal is widely found in modern societies, where it is raised as a legitimate way to progress individually based on personal achievements, and therefore contrasts with the use of family privileges and personal contacts to get ahead (Hadjar, 2008). While obtaining rewards through effort and talent seems to be a credible representation of justice through equity, the implementation of meritocratic systems is far from being unproblematic. On the one hand, it has been argued that meritocracy allows the

legitimization of inequalities by attributing success to personal achievement, thus underestimating the conditions of origin or the 'starting point' (Bay-Cheng, 2015; Hadjar, 2008). This implies great psychological and social pressure on young people, who regardless of the inequalities of their contexts, grow up surrounded by meritocratic discourses that constantly contrast with reality (Allen, 2016). On the other hand, the emphasis on individual capacities would lead to making people responsible for their situation and therefore less supportive of social policies that compensate for disadvantages: 'For why do the successful owe anything to the less advantaged members of society?' (Sandel, 2021, p. 292). In this way, the belief in meritocracy can diminish concern for the common good and solidarity.

Recently, interest in the study of meritocracy in the social sciences has increased. From the field of sociology, a research agenda has been developed that highlights the subjective aspects of meritocracy (Castillo et al., 2019 ; Mijs, 2018; Mijs & Hoy, 2020), where a central distinction is the one between meritocratic perceptions (how meritocratic society is) and meritocratic preferences (how meritocratic society should be) (Castillo et al., 2019; Reynolds & Xian, 2014). Until now, research in this area has focused on the adult population, neglecting the role that different socialization agents could have in the formation of perceptions, attitudes and beliefs during the school-age period (Gidengil et al., 2016; Torney-Purta, 2002).

In this paper, our objective is to study the extent to which parental and school socialization is associated with meritocratic perceptions of secondary school students. Based on research about justice preceptions in schools and family political socialization, we seek to answer two main questions: Is there an association between the meritocratic perceptions of parents with those of their offsprings? To what extent is school experience in terms of distributive justice (in relation to grades) linked to the meritocratic perceptions of students?

Through our first question, we focus on the extent to which the meritocratic perceptions of parents are associated with those of their children. For this, we rely on studies on the intergenerational reproduction of political attitudes (Astill et al., 2002; Miranda, 2018), through which the transmission of opinions and intentions of political participation (Boonen et al., 2013; Quintelier, 2015), political beliefs about democracy (Greenstein, 2016) and political orientations (Jennings et al., 2009) have been approached. However, these investigations generally do not incorporate aspects related to distributive justice, which can be fundamental if we consider that people's ideas about inequality and the distribution of resources can generate political apathy (Easterbrook, 2021), as well as to tolerance towards authoritarian ideas (Azevedo et al., 2019; Madeira et al., 2019).

The second topic of interest in this work is the role of the school in the meritocratic perceptions of students. In this regard, the literature on justice in schools has succeeded in highlighting the importance of distributive experiences in shaping the world view of young people. Works such as Resh and Sabbagh (2014, 2017) have shown that the sense of justice that students have regarding the distribution of grades has an impact on their democratic attitudes and behaviors, as well as on institutional and social trust (Resh, 2018). This evidence calls for a deeper understanding of the effect of the sense of justice on other aspects of young people's worldview, such as perceptions of meritocracy.


## 2 Conceptual and empirical background



## 2.1 Perception of meritocracy


Much of the research on meritocratic perceptions has focused on the extent to which objective conditions of social inequality affect the way people perceive the distribution of goods and rewards. In general, these investigations show that subjects have biased estimates of both the levels of inequality and the actual functioning of meritocracy (Gimpelson & Treisman, 2018). However, McCall et al. (2017) shows that exposing US citizens to the real levels of inequality encourages them to believe less in opportunities to get ahead based on their own effort. In the same vein, Mijs & Hoy (2020) points out that exposing Indonesian, Australian and Mexican citizens to real levels of inequality and social mobility diminishes their perception of meritocracy. These distorted perceptions of inequality and meritocracy also vary consistently according to socioeconomic level, as socioeconomically advantaged people tend to perceive higher levels of meritocracy than people at the lower end of the socioeconomic scale (Reynolds & Xian, 2014).

Adherence to meritocratic beliefs is often interpreted from a rational interest perspective, considering that those with greater economic resources and status have better reasons to perceive and prefer meritocracy (Kunovich & Slomczynski, 2007). In addition, it has been shown that these differences in perception according to socioeconomic level are affected by the level of economic inequality in society, which is addressed by different theories. On the one hand, the theory of conflict assumes that higher levels of inequality generate less perception of meritocracy and less tolerance of inequality, while there is greater dissent on these issues between different social strata (Newman et al., 2015). On the other hand, the theory of relative power (Solt et al., 2016) maintains that greater economic inequality brings with it a greater concentration of wealth and power, which has the consequence that the visions of the most advantaged groups permeate the visions of those most disadvantaged, in which case with greater inequality there is also greater consensus among social

groups on the perception of meritocracy.

Another characteristic of the relevant socioeconomic status in the study of meritocratic perceptions and preferences has been the possession of educational credentials that give way to higher-skilled occupations in the labor market (Goldthorpe, 2003). Two hypotheses have been used to explain the relationship between meritocratic beliefs and years of education. On the one hand, there is the reproductionist approach (Bernstein, 1988; Bourdieu et al., 1998), from which it is argued that the role of the school contributes to reinforcing the meritocratic principles of individuals; therefore, greater educational achievement translates into greater attachment to meritocracy as a distributive principle (Lampert, 2013; Reynolds & Xian, 2014; Xian & Reynolds, 2017). On the other hand, there is the hypothesis of instruction , which maintains that more educated individuals have greater critical capacity regarding the role that structural and individual factors play in the acquisition of rewards in society, which translates into a weakening around the meritocratic ideal (Castillo et al., 2019; Duru-Bellat & Tenret, 2012).


## 2.2 Meritocracy in the school-age period


Research on meritocracy in younger populations has been scarcely addressed, but it is possible to find some studies on attitudes towards inequality and justice that can be linked to this topic. In terms of attitudes towards inequality, research shows that children are able to form notions about justice and inequality at a very young age (Imhoff & Brussino, 2015). Although younger children have trouble understanding the terms 'rich' and 'poor' (Danziger, 1957), between the ages of 3 and 6, this distinction can be grasped. However, it is not until children are around 10 years of age that they can explain the differences (Sigelman, 2013). At this age, children tend to greatly highlight individual meritocratic attributions as causes of inequality (Sigelman, 2012), while presenting incipient explanations based on inequality of opportunity, especially as a consequence of discrimination (Imhoff & Brussino, 2015). Nonetheless, some authors point out that the multifaceted attributions of inequality can be found at younger ages. For example, a study with children aged 5 to 8 found that at this stage children were able to explain poverty from factors such as individual effort and situational elements, alluding to wage inequalities and discrimination (Mistry et al., 2016). According to these authors, the results are consistent with the theory of cognitive development (Leahy, 1981) and social constructionism (Emler & Dickinson, 1985), which suggest greater cognitive development will allow a more complete understanding of inequality.

In addition to children's understanding and explanations of inequality, there are some in-depth studies on the use of distributive justice criteria by children. Along these lines, Kanngiesser & Warneken (2012) point

out that despite their egotistical tendencies, children between 3 and 5 years of age are already able to use meritocratic criteria to distribute resources, considering the efforts invested by other children even when this could affect their own interest. In sum, children at an early age are able to understand concepts related to inequality and can use different distribution criteria to explain these differences or allocate resources.

In relation to studies on meritocracy in the adolescent population, Hjort (2014) has found evidence of a widespread adherence to the discourses of individualism and meritocracy by young people in the city of Oslo. However, although young people point to merit as central, this does not prevent them from recognizing differences in starting points related to the transmission of family resources. Along these lines, the work of Irwin (2009) has demonstrated the importance that young people place on individual factors to 'get ahead,' although they also suggest the importance of emotional support that can be provided by the family. Additionally, research on high school youth in the United States suggests that adolescents' visions of rewards for effort find greater support in second-generation migrant students who hold higher expectations of upward social mobility (Peguero & Bondy, 2015, p. 33). Finally, Sun & Wang (2010) have studied whether there is a value gap between the younger and older generations in China, finding that younger people tend to be more individualistic in their ways of life. These studies show that, from an early age, children and young people form judgments and opinions about inequality, which probably also apply to their views on meritocracy.


## 2.3 The present study: The socialization of meritocracy by the family and the school


The family is a first agent of socialization that provides values, expectations and rules (Martinez & Cumsille, 2015). Although an adult-centered bias in studies of political socialization studies has been criticized for focusing on the study of value transfer (Andersson, 2015), there is strong evidence to suggest the importance of family socialization, in which parental beliefs influence children's beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors (Bandura et al., 2001; Olivos, 2021; Wigfield et al., 2006). Moreover, parents raise their children based on class cultures, transmitting stratified beliefs and attitudes (Calarco, 2014). Consistently, it has been shown that parents transmit civic attitudes, intentions of participation, and political positions to their children, among other characteristics (Muddiman et al., 2019; Nesbit, 2013). Along these lines, the evidence around the socialization of different subjective characteristics allows us to assume that intergenerational transmission would also be expressed around meritocratic perceptions, in such a way that

parents and their children.

A second relevant agent of socialization is school. Beyond its educational role, the school contributes to shaping the behavior and worldviews of young students (Nishiyama, 2019). In this context, the students' experience of justice or fairness plays a fundamental role (Resh, 2018; Resh & Sabbagh, 2014) as it encourages the inference of ideas regarding inequality (Mijs, 2018). Among the different types of justice in the school experience (Resh & Sabbagh, 2016), the role that the feeling of fairness plays in student grades stands out. Grades reflect students' experiences of fairness or unfairness, affecting both self-image formation, classroom hierarchy building, and their worldview on various topics (Jasso & Resh, 2002). Studies in this area have shown that the sense of justice in grades promotes liberal-democratic orientations (Resh & Sabbagh, 2014), builds trust in institutions (Resh, 2018), and contributes to stronger student support for the meritocratic assignment of grades (Resh, 2009). In view of the above, this research proposes that the sense of justice in terms of student grading also encourages a greater perception of meritocracy on the part of the students, which is consistent with the evidence indicated by Olivos (2021). Based on this, our second hypotehsis is the following:

Hypothesis 2: Students with a greater sense of fairness in their grades will perceive greater meritocracy.

Family and school socialization of meritocratic perception occur together and probably affect each other. Therefore, we propose that the association of the meritocratic perception of parents with that of their children will be enhanced if the student feels that their grades are fair. Conversely, even if the student is socialized into meritocratic beliefs, if students experience injustice in their grades the effect of parental beliefs will be weaker. Therefore, we propose

Hypothesis 3: The relationship between meritocratic perception of parents and children (H1) will be more positive for those who experience a greater sense of justice in school (H2).

Evidence around meritocratic beliefs highlights the role that factors associated with social standing play. Reynolds & Xian (2014) points out that people with higher social status in the United States have a higher perception of meritocracy than those with lower social status. In the same vein, Kunovich & Slomczynski (2007) provide evidence consistent with a rational interest approach such that the higher the income and education of subjects, the greater the preference for meritocratic payment they will have. Despite their

differences, the results of Solt et al. (2016) and Newman et al. (2015) provide empirical support for the positive relationship between income and meritocratic beliefs. Based on this evidence, it is possible to argue that parents with a higher socioeconomic level will manifest a higher level of meritocratic beliefs. In the same vein, we propose that students from schools with a higher socioeconomic level will tend to perceive greater meritocracy.

## 3 Methodology



## 3.1 Data


The data come from the School Citizenship Panel Survey (PACES), a study on family political socialization that was carried out by applying a survey to second-year high school students (approximately 16 years of

age at first application), their parents or guardians, and their teachers during 2019-2021. In this article we use the first segment of the panel available at the time of this research, so this can be considered a cross-sectional study The sample is representative of high school students (grade 10) who attend schools in Chile in the Santiago Metropolitan area and in Antofagasta, Calama, Talca, Curicó and Linares. In total, 64 schools were randomly selected, and in each educational establishment, a complete course of second year high school students, their parents or guardians, and their history, social sciences and/or citizen training teachers were surveyed. Specifically, we collected data from 1635 students, 744 parents or guardians and 103 teachers. The data of this first segment of the panel were collected between August and December 2019.

The sampling framework used for the selection of the schools was built from the 2019 Directory of Schools of the Ministry of Education, considering all the schools in the sectors indicated above. The selection was random and systematic, considering locality, type of administrative unit (public, subsidized or private) and type of education (scientific humanist, professional technicial or mixed). The survey for students and teaches was conducted at schools, whereas for the parents or guardians it was self-administered in their homes.


## 3.2 Variables


The individual level variables of this study are presented in Table 1. Meritocratic perception is operationalized with questions that have been used in other research, in particular those that analyze data from the module of social inequality of the International Social Survey Program (ISSP) (Reynolds & Xian, 2014). In this article, the meritocratic perception of students was measured based on two indicators related to the role of effort and hard work to succeed in life. Both indicators correspond to Likert scales of four categories, measuring degree of importance and degree of agreement, respectively.

Table 1. Individual level variables

Individual-level independent variables were divided according to whether they corresponded to parents or students. In the case of parents, there are two relevant variables: perception of meritocracy and socioeconomic status. For the perception of meritocracy, parents or guardians were asked the same question as the

students. To simplify the modeling in the parent/guardian variable, we proceeded to group the categories' 'Very important', 'Important' and 'Somewhat important' for the variable of Importance of hard work. Likewise, for the statement that in Chile those who make more effort get ahead, we grouped category 'Agree' with the category 'Strongly Agree,' and 'Disagree' with 'Strongly disagree.'

In the case of socio-economic status, household income and the educational level of the parents or guardians were used as indicators. Quintiles were constructed from the original indicator of 11 income levels declared by the parents. In the case of the educational level of the parents or guardians, a dummy variable was created where 1 is 'Parents have a university degree' and 0 the rest of the lower educational levels.

The variable of justice in grading is key to our study since it represents distributive justice within the school experience. Two ways of measuring the sense of justice or fairness in grading were used: direct and indirect. The direct form corresponds to a question about whether the grades obtained were deserved, while the indirect is a numerical indicator based on the justice evaluation formula proposed by Jasso (1980), and which in this case uses questions about grades (Resh, 2018; Resh & Sabbagh, 2014, 2017). This formula corresponds to the ratio between the reward obtained and the fair reward, to which a logarithmic term is applied under the principle that under-rewarding is felt more intensely than over-rewarding. Therefore, in the case of absolute justice (grade obtained=grade deserved) the value of the term will be zero (Log 1=0), less than zero in the case of justice for under-reward, and greater than zero in the case of justice for overreward. Following the applications made to the educational field by Resh & Sabbagh (2014), the grades reported by the students were used as the reward that is distributed in the school. ## 5 Conclusions


This article addresses the socialization of meritocratic perceptions in students in the second year of high school. The central hypothesis revolved around two agents of socialization: the family and the school. In addition, we investigated whether the relationship between socioeconomic level and meritocratic perceptions was replicated in the young population, for which we used two indicators of meritocratic perception: the importance of effort to get ahead, and the the perception of whether those of working hard can get ahead. Despite the similarity between the two indicators, for what follows it is important to remember that the correlation between the two is moderate; therefore, they are not apparently measuring exactly the same aspect of the perception of meritocracy. In this way, it would be different to believe that meritocracy is important than to note that it actually occurs in terms of rewarding efforts. This point is relevant to be able to later develop some of the differences that we observed in the analysis of the results.

According to our analysis, there is partial evidence supporting the assumption that the meritocratic perceptions of parents manage to be passed on to their children. This association appears when meritocratic perception refers to the importance of effort to get ahead, but not when it is asked if those who work hard do indeed get ahead. In relation to the role of the school, we see an inverse situation: the experience of justice in grading is not associated with the importance of effort, but rather with the second indicator of whether efforts are rewarded. This association makes sense when considering school as a concrete space where rewards are expressed through grades, and our results show that those who feel unjustly rewarded in school actually perceive less meritocracy.

The dissimilar nature of the indicators used to operationalize the perception of meritocracy also has implications when analyzing the interactions between family and school. In the case of the importance of effort, we note that the positive bond between parents and children in perception of meritocracy may diminish in case of feeling unjustly rewarded with school grades. Instead, when asked about the agreement that effort is rewarded, those who feel justly rewarded in school are able to counteract negative meritocratic perceptions of their parents. Therefore, with the information we have so far, we do not necessarily see that the school or the parents are the main socializing agent of perceptions of meritocracy. Nevertheless, we have evidence to suggest that there are different associations depending on the specific aspect of the perception of meritocracy observed: the family would be more relevant in relation to the importance of effort, while the school in relation to the perception that efforts are justly rewarded.

The results of this research allow us to propose some possible future developments in this topic. The study of inequalities from an attitudinal perspective has consistently shown how inequalities can be legitimized by individuals (Castillo, 2011). Individuals who perceive that society functions according to meritocratic criteria tend to give less support to social policies (Sandel, 2021) and, ultimately, to care less about the common good and solidarity. If this problem is taken to the level of intergenerational transmission, then it could be argued that the legitimization of inequality begins to form early in adolescence: if young people form their meritocratic perceptions from the family and school sphere, then it can be assumed that the legitimization of inequality is a continuous and early reproduction process. From this perspective, focusing on how school-age children experience justice in school could shape the formation of citizens with a greater interest in the common good.

Although there is evidence in this research on the relevance of family and school elements in the socialization of meritocratic perception, there are a number of limitations to be taken into account in future research. First, the perception of meritocracy is only one aspect of research on meritocracy, which in turn is a spe-

cific element of the larger family of studies of subjective inequality. Future research should include tools to better cover the concept of meritocracy, considering not only perceptions but also preferences as well as aspects considered non-meritocratic, such as the use of family contacts and privileges. Secondly, this agenda should be linked in the future with other aspects of subjective inequality, such as redistributive preferences, as well as with the more traditional agenda of citizen formation that covers issues of participation, coexistence and democratic attitudes. Finally, the transversal nature of the data used has limitations to affirm the directionality of the relationships, therefore future studies could consider longitudinal data as well as survey experiments that can advance arguments of causality.

## 2 Institutional Advancement and Collective Action 74


- The topic of campaign fundraising in Congress is traditionally discussed as a collective active 75
- problem for political parties. It is argued that being the majority party in Congress affords 76
- many important benefits to members. Majority party members can more easily accomplish 77
- their legislative goals and deliver benefits to constituents (Cox and McCubbins 1993), but 78
- in order to obtain majority status members need to get elected, something that requires a 79
- lot of money. Not all members, however, can raise money equally as well. Senior members 80
- of Congress and congressional leaders all raise money much more easily because of their 81
- influence in the chamber, established track records, and likelihood of being reelected (Bonica 82
- 2014; Fouirnaies and Hall 2018; Grier and Munger 1986; Snyder 1992). Conversely, more 83
- junior members and challengers are a risk to donors because they are unlikely to win and 84
- because their legislative behavior is less predictable. Thus, in order to realize the benefits 85
- of being in the majority party, members should be willing to redistribute campaign funds 86
- in such a was as to maximize the chances of each member winning their election. This 87
- redistribution is not so easily realized, however, because members have a strong incentive 88
- to tend to their own election needs. Individually, members want to raise as much money as 89
- possible to get (re)elected and amass a war chest to discourage potential challengers in the 90
- future (Ansolabehere and Snyder 2000). 91
- To overcome this collective action problem, party leaders offer their members with selective 92
- benefits for contributing funds to their party's campaign arm that can be redistributed to 93
- members in need. For example, members who make large contributions to their party's 94
- congressional campaign committees and party's candidates have been given leadership posi95

- 2007), committee chairmanships (Kistner Forthcoming), and even more favorable treatment 97 of legislation (Hasecke and Mycoff 2007). 98
- Although fundraising ability and a willingness to contribute to the party are important 99 to party leaders, they are not the only qualities that leaders want. Party leadership also 100 incentivizes qualities like loyalty and policy expertise. Loyalty is important to increase 101 party voting on role calls and has traditionally been incentivized by giving committee chair 102 positions to members who consistently vote with their party (Cox and McCubbins 2005). 103 Incentivizing policy expertise helps produce more effective policies and is incentivized by 104 rewarding members with specific committee assignments (Krehbiel 1992). Similarly, seniority 105 is encouraged by giving members with the most seniority leadership positions. While these 106 have historically been important qualities, there is growing evidence that party leaders care 107 more about fundraising ability than anything else. 108

As competition for majority status in Congress has increased over the last couple decades, 109 party leaders started shifting their priorities towards raising more money to support their 110 members' campaigns. In recent years, fundraising has become so crucial to party leaders that 111 members are expected to spend around 30 hours a week on the phone at Republican and 112 Democratic call centers raising money (O'Donnell 2016). Congressman David Jolly (R-FL) 113 was so frustrated with this pressure that he introduced the Stop Act, an amendment to the 114 Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 to 'prohibit an individual holding federal office from 115 soliciting funds directly from any person: (1) for or on behalf of any political committee, or (2) 116 for or on the behalf of any person for use for federal election activity', in the 114th Congress 117 (Stop Act 2016). As a result of Congressman Jolly's vocal opposition to these fundraising 118 practices, the NRCC pledged not to help him with his reelection which he ultimately lost. 119

The increased importance on caucus fundraising eventually manifested itself with formal 120 programs requiring members to pay dues for their committee and leadership positions. These 121 programs attach fundraising targets for all party members that are scaled up depending 122 on the committees that members are assigned to and the leadership positions that they 123

In addition, seats on the prestigious Ways and Means, Appropriations, Energy and 126 Commerce, and Financial Services committees all have higher fundraising targets than other 127 non-exclusive committees. 1 The fundraising targets for Republicans follow a similar pattern. 128 These schedules clearly show that both parties expect more senior members and members 129 with influential positions to raise more money than junior members without positions of 130 influence. 131

It is clear that party leaders in Congress want to raise money for their party, but do they 142 reward their members' fundraising efforts or do they exploit them? Researchers investigating 143 caucus fundraising have typically assumed the former. I argue party leaders exploit their member's fundraising abilities in a way that maximizes 153 their party's fundraising potential and that leaders favor fundraising ability over competency 154 when making decisions about congressional organization. If leaders are concerned with raising 155 money to help maintain a majority status in Congress, then they should consider putting 156 their party's best fundraisers into positions that would maximize their party's campaign 157 contributions. One area where strategically positioning members in Congress would make a 158 big difference is with committee assignments. Committees are increasingly becoming 167 less important in the policy formation process as party leaders exert more control over the 168 process and increasingly rely on special rules to get legislation passed. ## 3 Empirical Implications 177


My argument that party leaders position their party's members in a way to maximize 178 campaign contributions, and that they prioritize fundraising ability over competency, has 179 several testable predictions. First, if fundraising ability has replaced the desire for policy 180 competency, then members should be assigned to committees independent of their legislative 181 capacity. Instead, members placed on the most lucrative committees should be selected 182 for these seats on the basis of how much money they contribute to their party and party's 183 candidates. This leads to my first hypothesis: 184

Hypothesis 1: Contributions from members to their parties and parties' candidates have 185 a larger effect on getting assigned to a lucrative committee than member competency and 186 seniority. 187

Previous research and changes in the congressional landscape over the last couple decades 188

led some support for Hypothesis 1. First, congressional scholars have noted the declining 189 importance of committees in the policy-making process (e.g. Lewallen 2020). Overtime, party 190 leaders have exercised more authority over the actions of Congress by controlling the agenda 191 (Cox and McCubbins 2005), using legislative task forces (Oleszek 1999), using special rules, 192 and other means to bypass normal committee procedures (Sinclair 2017). When party leaders 193 have ways to accomplish their legislative objectives outside of the committee system, then 194 the competency of individual committee members is much less important. Second, recent 195 work by Adler and Cayton (2020) finds that party leaders are much more likely to place 196 electorally vulnerable freshmen on prestigious committees in order to help them fundraise 197 for their next election. Since freshman are typically not the most capable legislators, this 198 indicates that leaders are willing to risk incompetency on the most important committees in 199 order to increase the chances of maintaining majority control. 200

Second, since I argue that party leaders aim to maximize their party's campaign contri201 butions, then assignments to the most lucrative committees should be given to members 202 who raise the most money for their party and party's candidates. Moreover, if party leaders 203 operate with the goal of maximizing fundraising, then members who raise the most money 204 for their party should receive assignments to lucrative committees independent of what 205 committees they request to serve on. ## 4 Data and Methods 229


To distinguish between members being rewarded with the committee assignments that they 230 want for their campaign contributions and members being assigned committees despite their 231 preferences, I use the most comprehensive data available on member committee requests 232 (Frisch and Kelly 2006b). These data provide the committee request preferences for members 233 between the 102nd and 110th Congress and are arguably the most accurate measure of a 234 member's revealed committee assignment preferences. These data allow me to correct for 235 member committee request preferences when using party contributions to estimate assignments 236 to lucrative committees. 237

What counts as a lucrative committee? In the past, political scientists have used many 238 different classification schemes to categorize committees, but the focus is usually on identifying 239 prestige, policy, constituent, and service committees. Deering and Smith (1997), for example, 240

classify the prestige committees as Appropriations, Budget, Rules, and Ways and Means, but 241 Cox and McCubbins (1993) only consider Ways and Means, Appropriations, and Rules as 242 prestige committees. In his study investigating the effects of caucus fundraising on committee 243 transfers, E. S. Heberlig (2003) adds Energy and Commerce for Democrats starting in the 244 104th Congress to Cox and McCubbins' list of prestige committees. In contrast to these 245 authors, I use the list of prestige, or exclusive, committees defined by Judy Schneider who is 246 a 40 year veteran of the Congressional Research Service and regularly instructs members on 247 the workings of Congress (Gangitano 2018). 248

According to Judy Schneider's review of Democratic and Republican rules, the prestige 249 committees are Appropriations, Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce (starting in the 250 104th Congress for Democrats), Financial Services (starting in the 109th Congress for 251 Democrats) and Rules. This list of committees is also consistent with the most lucrative 252 committees. In their article investigating the importance of campaign contributions in the 253 committee assignment process, Adler and Cayton (2020) calculate the fundraising value of 254 House committees by estimating how a member's fundraising totals change after gaining 255 or losing a seat on each committee. According to their model, the top five most lucrative 256 committees are Way and Means, Appropriations, Rules, Energy and Commerce, and Financial 257 Services. Thus, these are the committees that I define as lucrative. 258

For Hypotheses 1 and 2, I use the committee assignment data and list of lucrative 259 committees to create an indicator variable that measures whether a member was assigned 260 to a lucrative committee. Using this variable as my outcome, I test Hypotheses 1 and 2 261 with a Bayesian multilevel logistic regression where party contributions is my predictor of 262 interest. I also include several control variables. I include indicators for the type of committee 263 requested (either lucrative or policy with constituent as the reference group) in order to 264 account for which committee type a member wanted to serve on. This allows me to narrow in 265 on whether a member was assigned to a lucrative committee that they wanted or not, which 266 is something that previous studies have not taken into account. I include member seniority 267

because seniority has traditionally been one of the most important factors in determining 268 committee assignments (Cann 2008a; Katz and Sala 1996; Kellermann and Shepsle 2009; 269 Shepsle 1978) and more senior members are typically better at fundraising and thus more 270 likely to contribute to their party and party's candidates. I include an indicator for whether 271 or not a member is a member of the majority party for a given Congress. The majority party 272 gets more committee seats and may be better situated to get their members on important 273 committees. Also, interest groups tend to favor majority party members because they have 274 more influence over the legislative agenda meaning that majority members receive more in 275 campaign contributions. I also include a member's legislative effectiveness score (LES) lagged 276 by one congressional session, because party leaders may want more productive members to 277 sit on lucrative committees and more effective members may also attract more campaign 278 contributions. Seniority, majority status, and legislator effectiveness data all come from 279 Volden and Wiseman (2014). Finally, I include each member's margin of victory in the last 280 election. The committee assignment literature has argued, with mixed empirical evidence, 281 that more vulnerable members may be given better committee assignments to improve their 282 reelection prospects (Clapp 1964; Frisch and Kelly 2006a; Masters 1961). Members with 283 a large margin of victory may also have more money on hand to give to their party and 284 party's candidates. The margin of victory is computed with data from the MIT Election 285 Data + Science Lab. Finally, because the outcome variable is binary, I center all predictor 286 variables and divide by two standard deviations. This helps with interpreting the coefficients 287 by placing them on the same scale as the outcomes (Gelman, Hill, and Vehtari 2020), and 288 enables comparisons of the size of each coefficient. Standardizing in this way changes the 289 interpretation of each predictor to be a 1-unit change corresponding to a change from 1 290 standard deviation below the mean to 1 standard deviation above the mean. 291

In addition to these controls, I also include intercepts (random effects) for states, Congress, 292 and members. However, instead of estimating the state and Congress effects as independent 293 of one another, I nest them to allow for correlation between them. This is theoretically 294

justified because the steering committees responsible for making committee assignments 295 consider the geographical representation of members when making assignments, which varies 296 from Congress to Congress. Said differently, the effect of which state you represent with 297 your committee assignment is not constant over time. Thus, treating time effects as constant 298 across states yields an unrealistic model. Nesting these intercepts allows them to vary across 299 states and across time within states. I do, however, assume that the effects of each member 300 are constant across both time and space and therefore estimate the member intercepts as 301 independent of the nested state and Congress intercepts. 302

To test Hypothesis 3, I use the committee request data from Frisch and Kelly (2006b) and 303 assignment data from Stewart and Woon (2017) along with the list of lucrative committees 304 from Adler and Cayton (2020) to create 4 categories of members: members who requested 305 a lucrative committee but did not receive one, members who did not request a lucrative 306 committee but received one, members who did not request a lucrative committee and did 307 not receive one, and members who requested a lucrative committee and received one. Thus, 308 this variable classifies members according to their ultimate committee assignments as well 309 as their committee requests to help measure whether members are being rewarded for their 310 contributions with the committees that they want or being assigned to committees because 311 of their contributions. To model these lucrative assignment categories and test Hypothesis 3, 312 I use a Bayesian multinomial logistic regression where, like before, I include nested random 313 effects for states and Congress along with crossed, or unnested, random effects for members. 314 In this model, party contributions is my predictor of interest and I include controls for 315 member seniority, being a member of the majority party, a member's legislator effectiveness 316 score (lagged by one congressional session), and a member's margin of victory in the last 317 election. 318

Although the coefficient estimates are positive in both models, some readers more familiar 399 with the frequentist approach to statistics may question the statistical significance of the 400 effect of party contributions for the 'No Request-Assigned' category in the Republican model 401 because the 90 and 95 percent highest density intervals cross 0. There is an important caveat 402 to make about this observation, however. Unlike frequentist methods, Bayesian methods allow 403 for a probabilistic interpretation of uncertainty intervals. So, for example, a 90 percent highest 404 density interval shows the range of values for a particular estimate that have a 90 percent 405 probability of containing the true value. This has the advantage of eliminating the need 406 for arbitrary cut-off points (like 95 percent) that are typically employed in null hypothesis 407 significance testing. Instead researchers can make inferences about the direct probability of a 408 coefficient estimate. The dots above the interval help with making this inference. To help 409 with understanding the probability of coefficient estimates, Kay et al. (2016) and Fernandes et 410 al. (2018) suggest using what they call quantile dotplots. These dotplots divide the posterior 411 estimates into an arbitrary number of bins of approximately equally likely points. So, Figure 412 4 shows 50 equally likely estimates to summarize the marginal posterior distributions for 413 each coefficient. Counting the dots to the right of the 0 mark for the 'No Request-Assigned' 414 category shows that the probability of a positive effect for this estimate is about 88 percent. 415

Although this misses the conventional cut-off of 95 percent, an 88 percent probability is still 416 reasonably good evidence of an effect, and under the frequentist framework we would need to 417 conduct a null hypothesis significance test to determine if this probability level is significantly 418 different from the 90 or 95 percent cut-off. Still, it is clear that the probability that party 419 contributions have a positive effect on getting a lucrative committee assignment when it was 420 not requested is stronger for Democrats than it is Republicans. 421


## 6 Conclusion 422


Fundraising is an increasingly important aspect of congressional campaigns and one that is 423 fueled by the strategies that party leaders have developed to pressure their members into 424 raising money, but are member's fundraising efforts rewarded or exploited? Are they more 425 or less important than legislative competency and seniority? This article leverages novel 426 data on committee requests to show that when making assignments to the committees that 427 matter most for fundraising, party leaders exploit strong fundraisers by assigning them to 428 these committees despite their preferences and that fundraising ability plays a larger role in 429 predicting lucrative committee assignments than legislative ability and seniority. 430

This article contributes to the existing literature on caucus fundraising by demonstrating 431 that member are not always rewarded with the committees that they want for making large 432 contributions to their parties and parties' candidates (E. S. Heberlig 2003; E. Heberlig, 433 Hetherington, and Larson 2006; E. S. Heberlig and Larson 2007). This finding also speaks to 434 what we know about the committee assignment process. Previous research has argued that 435 committee assignments are made with an end towards accommodating member preferences 436 (e.g. Shepsle 1978), improving legislative success (e.g. Cox and McCubbins 1993), or to 437 maximize issue expertise (e.g. Krehbiel 1992), but the results shown in this article provide 438 reason to rethink these theories. With the decrease importance of committees in the legislative 439 process and the increasing importance of fundraising, committee assignments might have 440

become yet another tool for maintaining majority control by improving fundraising. 441

If it is true that committees and legislative competency are being overshadowed by 442 fundraising prowess, and that committee assignments are made on this basis, then the role 443 of money in the legislative process may be more pervasive than previously thought. The 444 distributional, partisan, and informational theories' arguments with respect to the committee 445 assignment process all assume that committee assignments are made to increase legislative 446 efficiency, albeit in different ways. However, if seats on the most important committees are 447 being given to each party's best fundraisers, then it becomes unclear whose interests are 448 really being represented in committee. 449

## Surface texture analysis 293

Confocal  microscopy  applied  to  archaeological  artifacts  is  able  to  distinguish  wear 294 signatures of natural and anthropogenic agents (Evans & Donahue, 2008; Galland et al., 2019; 295 Ibáñez et al., 2016; Rosso et al., 2017). Archaeological lustrous and non-lustrous gravels from 296 Landry and lustrous gravels from Fourneau du Diable, Casserole, Pech de la Boissière, Laugerie 297 Haute, from natural deposits and gravels experimentally polished (Table 3) were analysed with 298 a Sensofar S-Neox confocal microscope equipped with a long-working-distance 50x objective 299 (numerical aperture = 0.45), allowing a spatial sampling of 0.26µm. We measured on opposite 300 aspects of each gravel two areas of 351x264µm with a vertical repeatability of 3 nm and 42° of 301 maximum acquisition slope. Measures were taken on areas free of micro-concretions. The data 302 obtained  were  processed  by  the  SensoMAP  Premium  7.4  software.  Post-acquisition  data 303 treatment followed a procedure similar to that described by Martisius and colleagues (Martisius 304 et al., 2018). Using built-in operators, this included levelling the surface with the least squares 305 method, removing isolated outliers and noise, filling in non-measured points by interpolating 306 from neighbours, and removing the surface form using a polynomial of third order. 307

A Gaussian filter of 80µm was applied as a cut-off to remove waviness from roughness, 308 which appeared to separate roughness values of glossy from non-glossy gravels better than the 309 25µm filter.  Three  ISO  25178  parameters  were  calculated  (Table  4):  the  root  mean  square 310 height (Sq , the degree of bias of the shape of the roughness (Ssk), and the developed surface ) 311 ratio  (Sdr). ## Discussion


Polished pebbles have been found repeatedly at archaeological, including ancient, sites 529 (Boivin et al., 2007; Moncel et al., 2012). Few are the cases, however, in which complementary 530 analyses were conducted to eliminate the possibility of a natural origin of the polish or that, the 531 case of Landry, provide contextual information to assess their nature. A remarkable exception 532 are the polished pebbles found at the Jiahu site, Henan Province, China (Zhang et al., 1999). At 533 this  site,  the  skeleton  of  a  male  individual  with  the  skull  missing,  dated  to  c.  9,000  BP,  is 534 associated with two seven-hole bone flutes and a turtle shell with polished pebbles inside. The 535 latter is interpreted as a musical instrument to produce a rhythmic sound. 536

The geoarchaeological study of the Landry site indicates that the spatial distribution of 537 archaeological  remains  has  not  been  marginally  affected  by  post-depositional  disturbances 538 (Brenet et al., 2018). Landry is currently the only site for which unequivocal information is 539 available on the stratigraphic and the spatial provenance of the lustrous gravels, their spatial 540 relationship  to  the  other  archaeological  remains,  and  their  cultural  affiliation.  The  lustrous 541 gravels are clearly associated with the other archaeological remains and dispersed within the 542 archaeological  layer,  which  make  their  attribution  to  the  Solutrean  undisputable.  They  are 543 highly concentrated in an area interpreted as reflecting domestic activities connected to the use 544 of  metamorphic  rocks.  This  area  has  also  yielded  few  incised  dolerite  blocks  and  pebbles 545 (Brenet et al., 2018). For the archaeological sites excavated earlier, only the cultural and, in few 546

cases, the stratigraphic provenance are known. Theoretically, the best available information on 547 the  gravel  cultural  attribution  come  from  Fourneau  du  Diable  (D.  Peyrony,  1922)  where 548 Peyrony is formal in attributing them to both the Gravettian and the Solutrean. The 136 gravels 549 arranged one next to the other to form a rectangle (Fig 4) were apparently found in Gravettian 550 layers, the others in layers attributed to the Upper Solutrean. Although left a drawing of this 551 chest piece, it is difficult at present, in absence of additional information, to assess the reality 552 of this  surprising findings. At  Laugerie Haute the gravels were also apparently retrieved in 553 Upper Solutrean layers; at Pech de la Boissière and Casserole, they were recovered in Solutrean 554 layers. Our spatial analysis has demonstrated that the distribution of lustrous gravels at Landry 555 is not random nor uniform. They are concentrated in an area corresponding to a portion of the 556 zone with the highest density of the other archaeological remains. On the contrary, the non557 lustrous gravels are evenly distributed on the excavated area. Unlike the lustrous gravels, all 558 made of  white  quartz,  they  are  more  variable  in  size,  morphology  and  color.  This  finding 559 contradicts the hypothesis that the distribution of the lustrous gravels is the result of a natural 560 process and argues in favor of humans being the main or the exclusive accumulation factor. 561 Apparently Landry visitors selected small, round, white gravels and left or disposed them inside 562 their main activity area. Although the lack of direct comparative samples makes it difficult to 563 establish what criteria guided the choice of the gravels at the other archaeological sites, their 564 comparatively  low  dimensional  variability  and  roundness  suggest  these  were  certainly  key 565 selection criteria. It can be therefore reasonably inferred that humans were the major gravel 566 accumulation factor at the other sites as well. 567

At all the analyzed sites, what makes the gravels peculiar is also their shiny appearance. 568 Since the mode of formation of the sedimentary layers is not different at Landry between the 569 concentrations and the areas outside them, there is no reason for thinking that the site formation 570 processes could have affected the gravels inside and outside the concentrations in a different 571 way and create a gloss only on the former. No evidence of chemical alteration or a similar gloss 572 is observer on the remainder of the archaeological remains found inside the concentrations of 573 artifacts(Brenet et al., 2014; Mesa, 2016). In addition, experimental polishing of quartz gravels 574 from the Landry sieving rules out the possibility that the action of silt may produce the gloss 575 observed  on  the  gravels  found  in  the  archaeological  concentrations.  The  hypothesis  of 576 gastroliths originating from animal carcasses can also be discarded since the lustrous gravels 577 differ in size, morphology and surface condition from such gravels (Tryon, 2010; Wings, 2004). 578 This supports the hypothesis that differences in the appearance of gravels found inside and 579

outside the concentrations are due to human agency. Roughness analysis has identified three 580 significantly  different  types  of  surfaces:  rough,  typical  of  gravels  collected  in  natural 581 accumulations and in the Landry sieving; glossy, only found on archaeological gravels from 582 sites excavated in the past; moderately glossy, characteristic of the Landry gravels associated 583 with concentrations of cultural remains. Experimental tumbling of Landry gravels collected 584 outside the archaeological concentrations has produced a shine absent in natural accumulations 585 and similar to that of  gravels  found  at  archaeological  sites  excavated  in  the  past  and  some 586 lustrous gravels from Landry. 587

In summary, the roughness analysis of natural, experimental and archaeological gravels, 588 supports  the  hypothesis  that  after  being  selected  by  their  size  and  shape,  they  have  been 589 subjected  to  a  human  action  that  has  strongly  polished  them.  The  wear  could  have  been 590 produced deliberately or be the unintended consequence of their use or transport. These three 591 possibilities are not mutually exclusive. The differences in roughness observed between the 592 lustrous gravels from Landry and other archaeological sites may be due to: the fact that only 593 the most lustrous gravels were collected in early excavations; the fact that at Landry non- or 594 low-gloss  gravels  were  naturally  present  in  archaeological  concentrations,  which  created  a 595 sample  that  included  both  lustered  and  non-lustered  gravels;  the  fact  that  the  activity  that 596 lustered the gravels at Landry was not as extensive as at other sites; or the fact that due to their 597 mineralogical composition, the Landry gravels could not reach the degree of lustering observed 598 at other sites, where the gravels are composed of other rocks, while being subjected to the same 599 modifications. Selective collection of gravels from older excavations is possible, but two of the 600 collections examined were from recent excavations in which the sediment was systematically 601 sieved  with  water.  The  degree  of  luster  of  the  gravels  from  these  sites  is  not  substantially 602 different  from  that  observed  in  the  ancient  collections,  which  contradicts  the  hypothesis  of 603 selective gathering. The possibility that the rock of which they are composed may determine 604 the  lower  luster  of  the  Landry  gravels  seems  partly  contradicted  by  the  fact  that  the 605 experimentally tumbled gravels, composed of quartz, attained a degree of luster similar to that 606 observed on the lustered gravels from other archaeological sites. Although it is difficult to rule 607 out  the  possibility  that  some  of  the  discarded  factors  may  be  a  contributing  factor  to  the 608 differences in luster between Landry and the other sites, the most likely hypothesis appears to 609 be that the luster on the Landry gravels is either the result of the same action to which the 610 gravels from the other sites were subjected, but for a shorter period of time, or the result of a 611 slightly different action. The fact that experimental tumbling of gravels produced wear that was 612

comparable to that of archaeological gravels suggests that prolonged contact with a soft material 613 such as hide was the cause of the luster. The experimental results also indicate that variations 614 in  the  treatment  of  soft  materials  in  contact  with  the  gravels  may  be  responsible  for  the 615 differences in roughness observed between sites. The long duration of the experiment necessary 616 to produce the luster seems to contradict the hypothesis that sporadic contact with soft material 617 or human skin, for example when handling the gravels, can produce such a developed luster. 618 These results do not allow us to identify with certainty the action to which the gravels were 619 subjected to acquire the luster and it is possible that this action tells us little about the function 620 for which the gravels were intended. The luster may, for example, be the result of repeated 621 transport of the gravel from one site to another in leather containers, but this does not tell us the 622 function for which the gravel was intended once the Solutreans arrived on site, as this function 623 may have produced little or no luster. In reverse, the luster could be the direct consequence of 624 the function of the gravel. In this case it could have been produced deliberately by tumbling the 625 gravel into a leather bag to then exploit its lustrous appearance, for example in an adornment 626 device as suggested by Peyrony, or unintentionally, for example by tumbling the gravel into a 627 leather  container  to  produce  a  rhythmic  sound.  These  last  two  cases  do  not  eliminate  the 628 possibility that the transport of gravels from one site to another may also have contributed to 629 the production of the luster. The likely multi-causal nature of the luster and its variation between 630 sites, as well as the potential equifinality of different process, which could produce the same 631 luster, reduces the likelihood that further experimentation will be able to identify precisely the 632 action  that  produced  the  luster,  let  alone  the  function  of  the  gravels.  One  cannot  rule  out, 633 however, the possibility that future experiments will identify more precisely the material to 634 which the archaeological gravels have been in contact during their social life. 635

It is worthwhile for this reason to turn to the ethnographic and archaeological record. The 636 former may inform us on the uses of gravels in different traditional human cultures. The latter 637 may identify cases in which contextual information would allow us to understand the function 638 that gravels had in past populations. Both records open the possibility of analyzing in the future, 639 with the same methodologies applied in our study, ethnographic and archaeological gravels and 640 compare the results of these analyses with ours. 641

Our  ethnographic  survey  shows  that  the  most  common  functions  for  small  pebbles  are 642 magico-religious ritual uses, and as game pieces. Worldwide, pebbles are used as talismans, 643 amulets,  and  charms  (Bunzel,  1932;  Fortune,  1934;  Róheim,  1945)  (see  SM  Table  1  for 644 examples), appear in divination or sorcery kits (Karsten, 1935; Little, 1951), and often embody 645

spirits and ancestors (Lehtisalo & Schütze, 1924; Olson et al., 2001; Preuss & Furst, 1996). 646 When used in games, pebbles are most often in multiples and handled frequently, including by 647 children  (Anderson,  1983;  Junod,  1927;  Opler,  1966;  Taylor,  1962).  The  use  of  gravels  in 648 musical  instruments  mimics  experimental  tumbling  and  can  obviously  produce  the  same 649 effects: in our survey we noted drum/rattle containers made from dried fruit (Larken, 1926), 650 cocoons (Kaufmann & Neuse, 1910), animal shells (Birket-Smith & De Laguna, 1938), birch 651 bark (Skinner, 1911), as well as hides and gourds (Gayton, 1948). Further uses include tools or 652 weapons, elements in medicinal treatments, ornaments, and in counting (see SM Table 6 for 653 examples). All these functions involve the transport of gravels, which can produce their gradual 654 polishing.  A  use  for  games  or  shamanism/divination  also  implies  a  more  or  less  prolonged 655 handling,  which  can  contribute  to  their  polishing-possibly,  in  the  case  of  games,  from 656 hide/leather surfaces on which pieces are scattered. Some of these functions (games, music, 657 medicine, and counting) are more consistent with the use of many gravels than others (weapons, 658 tools and 'other' uses are often single items), but ritual uses can involve single or multiple 659 stones with equal likelihood (Table 6). 660

While many of the ethnographically attested functions imply a choice of gravels on the basis 661 of size, shape, weight and raw material criteria, exact remarks on size were uncommon in the 662 sources.  Anthropologists occasionally  noted qualitative features such as  color or shape e.g. 663 'marble-like stones'  (Westermann, 1912), 'preferably those of a black color'  (Teit, 1956). 664 However, these remarks were too infrequent (only 12/152 cases) to support generalizations 665 regarding specific functions for the archaeological gravels studied in our work. It is however 666 possible that the smaller and rounder gravels from the Landry and Casserole sites had another 667 function than the larger gravels of the Fourneau du Diable, Laugerie Haute and Pech de la 668 Boissière.  However, this is  only  partially  consistent  with  the  result  of  the  textural  analysis, 669 which  rather  highlights  a  difference  between  Landry  and  the  other  sites.  By  ethnographic 670 analogy, ritual and gaming uses are most likely, with the uniformity of the gravels indicating a 671 deliberate aesthetic preference. Although our cross-cultural survey indicates the use of gravels 672 in counting systems is relatively uncommon (in our sample, 3 of 128 uses or 2.5%), their use 673 for other functions (games, ornaments, divination etc.) certainly implies their approximate and, 674 especially in the case of games, possibly precise quantification. In both cases, the creation of a 675 cultural innovation involving the use of small, visually homologous objects may have played 676 an adjunct role in the complexification of modalities for precise quantification (verbal, finger 677

- counting, notational) or may have been a reflection of contemporary or prior advances in these 678

fields (Bender & Beller, 2018; d'Errico et al., 2017; Núñez, 2021). 679

## Conclusion 680

The results of our study indicate that there are means to distinguish objects modified by 681 natural processes from artifacts minimally modified by humans. Use-wear analysis has been 682 widely applied to prehistoric artefacts to identify their function. However, this approach has 683 been  implemented  on  artefacts  recognized  as  the  outcome  of  human  agency.  In  our  case, 684 instead,  we  have  faced  the  challenge  of  identifying  such  agency  exclusively  from  surface 685 modification. The chosen means to pursue this endeavor involved evaluation of contextual data, 686 creation  of  natural  and  experimental  frames  of  reference,  and  characterization  of  natural, 687 experimental and archaeological material using adapted analytical tools. These analyses leave 688 no  doubt:    the  lustrous  gravels  discovered  in  several  Gravettian  and  Solutrean  sites  in 689 southwestern France were lost or abandoned in these sites after having been selected on the 690 basis of size and shape criteria and having been involved in one or more specific activities that 691 produced  their  lustrous  appearance.  These  gravels  were  not  discovered  in  older  Gravettian 692 layers during the numerous excavations conducted in the region despite the fact that many of 693 these excavations were conducted in recent times, with modern excavation techniques and by 694 archaeologists  aware  of  the  possibility  of  discovering  glossy  gravels  in  Upper  Palaeolithic 695 archaeological layers. This leads us to conclude that the activity in which the gravels were 696 involved, which is impossible to identify precisely but could involve a long-time use or curation 697 in a leather bag, reflect a cultural innovation that developed during the Gravettian period and 698 continued into the Solutrean period at the least. 699

## 1. Introduction


In many places, groundwater resources support the livelihoods of the communities and sustain human health. The availability of groundwater is influenced both by natural  factors  such  as  spatial  distribution  of  rainfall  patterns  across  and  the heterogeneous geology, soil, and topographical characteristics (Prajapati et. al., 2021). Precipitation  helps  in  recharging  groundwater  through  seepages  into  the  ground. However, in the urban areas, when an intense rainfall occurs within a short interval, it fails to seep into underground natural reservoirs due to impervious built-up areas. The rainwater does not reach the aquifers, nor it gets out as baseflow, but it directly flows to streams and rivers as a surface run-off, and eventually drains into the sea and becomes non-fresh water. Through this process, local water source is depleted both by anthropogenic causes and natural processes. Local groundwater levels plummet and then slowly rise up creating a sine-wave form of the water table over time based on the use and recharge of water. Since underground water is usually isolated in constricted spaces when it is pumped out especially in the summer season from locations using high pressures, soils, and rock materials crumble under the surface because they move to fill the gaps created by the removal of water. As groundwater becomes the primary source of water supply for various uses during the lean wet seasons, especially, when rainfall is nominal (Belhassan, 2011), excess of groundwater pumping in the densely populated areas such as in the Kathmandu Valley often leads to land subsidence (Bhattarai et al., 2017) if the underground water stock is not immediately replenished.

Water table can go down due to anthropogenic and natural processes. Pumping out of water for household or other uses is one of the anthropogenic causes that depletes groundwater stored /or floating on top of underground lakes and rivers. Evapotranspiration is not natural causes of groundwater depletion. Naturally, deeprooted  trees  take  water  out  and  it  evaporates  into  the  atmosphere  through evapotranspiration. Also, when plants use underground water during the photosynthetic processes, the water table goes down. Groundwater is also influenced by  climatic  factors  because,  during  rains  and  intense  precipitation  within  a  short interval increases the surface runoff rate resulting in floods, especially in urban areas. At high surface temperatures, groundwater is also lost at a rapid rate due to a high degree of evapotranspiration in presence of deep-rooted broad-leaved trees (Ghiat et. al., 2021), and surface evaporation occurs due to irradiance and high temperature (Buitink  et.  al.,  2020).  Large  leaf  surfaces  in  windy  and  warm  environmental conditions, evaporate more water than tiny needle surface leaves, such as in coniferous trees. For this reason, broad-leaved plants are planted to drain groundwater in many parts of the world. For example, in the Netherlands, Eastern Cottonwood (Populus deltoides) plants are cultivated to drain water while reclaiming sea surfaces (Jacobs et. al., 2014).

<!-- image -->

Groundwaters are found both in confined and unconfined aquifers which represent a dynamic balance between groundwater storage, recharge, and discharge (Prajapati et al., 2021; Conlon et al., 2005). Confined aquifers are common in urban environments and in areas such as those made from rocks and compact clay where the water level is saturated  because  impermeable  materials  are  present  above  and  below  the  water surface, such as in the Great Artesian Basin of Australia (National Water Commission, 2013). When such water resources are drilled, water rushes out easily because of the pressure created by the underground water (USGS, 2022; Sanders, and Thompson, 2020).  Confined  aquifers  recharge  quickly  when  there  are  surface  fissures  and earthquake  cracks  that  help  the  percolation  of  rainwater  or  surface  recharging. Funneling rainwater from the roof and other clean surfaces into wells helps to easily recharge confined aquifers. Ponds, lagoons, and other landfills are frequently used to recharge confined aquifers. In many places, mechanical gushing is used to recharge groundwaters through deep well injection. Deep well injection is a type of reverse pumping out of water using external energy. This practice can be applicable to areas like the Kathmandu Valley where built-up surfaces such as paved roads, sidewalks, and building roofs have converted natural ground into impervious surfaces causing increased surface runoff, especially during intense rainfall events. Injecting water into underground  aquifers  requires  careful  monitoring  because  of  the  possibility  of pumping in polluted water to the underground aquifers.

Natural recharge of ground water in highly built up areas is limited unless there are interferences by human beings. The g r o u n d w a t e r recharge can be naturally and passively achieved through retention ponds or recharging ponds (Figure 1).

In urban centers like the Kathmandu Valley, the water injection process (sometimes also called reverse boring) has become necessary as high water usage activities often drain water from the confined aquifers. In many cities, such as Phoenix, Arizona, USA,  stringent  rules  are  in  place  to  regulate  the  recharging  of  aquifers  to  avoid contamination while recharging ground water (Silber-Coats and Eden, 2017).
