## 1.1. A minor 'cultural shift' in political and legal sciences


The 'cultural turn' initiated in the humanities and social sciences in the early 1970s was an intellectual movement that was significant not only because of its scope but also because of its broadly interdisciplinary nature. At that time, sociologists, historians and geographers followed a movement initiated by authors such as Clifford Geertz (1970) to question,   in   a   unified   movement   and   in   their   respective   fields   of   research,   the predominance   of   functionalist,   mechanical   or   organicist   approaches   to   social phenomena, in which the complexity of social life is always reduced to relations of cause and effect (Bonnell et al., 1999, pp. 1-5). The question of the meaning of action was then brought to the forefront in the idea that 'to be intelligible, the practices and ideals of other peoples must be placed in their context, understood as positional values in the field of their cultural relations, rather than judged according to our moral and intellectual criteria' (Sahlins, 2007, p. 26).

For their part, the political and legal sciences remained relatively unaffected by this intellectual movement (Suny, 2002, p. 1489). The attention of political scientists was at that time entirely focused on the development of rational choice theory (Smith, 1996). Juridical   scientists,   on   the   other   hand,   remained   generally   attached   to   a   positivist conception   of   scientific   work,   demonstrating   an   evolutionary   use   of   history   and concerned   with   formulating   normative   recommendations   for   political   authorities (Gordon, 1996). Despite the lack of interest in comprehensive approaches in these two disciplines,   comprehensive   approaches   have   nevertheless   had   some   success.   In particular, comprehensive approaches established the idea that people's rationality is always guided by the way they understand the world, their own place in it and the

meaning of their actions (Bates et al., 1998; Lockhart, 1999). They also challenged classical cultural units such as the nation, the state, and social classes, and in so doing have created new objects of research (Steinmerz, 1999).

Within legislative studies more specifically, a field of research in which political and legal sciences tend to share a monopoly, the observation is even more severe. Indeed, its resistance  to   disciplinary   innovations   seems   to   be   one   of   its   characteristic   features (Geddes and Rhodes, 2018). In particular, it is notable that few political scientists followed the pioneering work of Richard Fenno (Fenno 1978, 1990), even though the results of his research were very successful and widely used. It is only since the 2000s that   comprehensive   analyses   were   developed   around   targeted   issues   such   as parliamentary discourse analysis (e.g. Bayley, 2004) or performance in politics (e.g. Rai and Johnson, 2004).

Paradoxically, it is outside the political and legal sciences that Richard Fenno's ideas received the most attention. His proposals in favour of the contextualised study of parliamentary activities interested anthropologists, especially in the particular context of France in the 1990s, when several of them turned to the study of Western societies and their   institutions   (Abélès,   1997).   Here   the   comprehensive   study   of   the   properly linguistic, ritual and symbolic dimensions of political life in the centres of democratic power was truly born (e.g. Abélès, 2001; Bellier and Wilson 2001; Crewe, 2005 and, by extension, the sub-field of the 'anthropology of parliaments' (Crewe, 2021) within legislative studies.


## 1.2. The presupposition that all parliamentary systems share a common foundation


However, the influence of the theory of rational choice among political scientists and the positivist dogma of juridical scientists are not sufficient to fully explain the hermeticism of   legislative   studies   to   comprehensive   approaches,   and   more   broadly   to   the consideration   of   cultural   factors   in   the   analysis   of   parliamentary   systems.   Two complementary causes help to explain this situation.  The methodological difficulty of studying   parliamentary   institutions,   particularly   through   fieldwork   and   in-depth interviews, must also be taken into account. Access to the sites of political activities, the availability   of   elected   representatives,   the   management   of   confidentiality,   and   the freedom of analysis generate a source of problems that are as thorny as they are endless. Engaging in comprehensive research in this type of field thus requires an investment of time and energy which is all the more prohibitive as the result is uncertain. This helps to explain why researchers prefer to concentrate on studying the production of documents by assemblies or the sociography of their members, even if these data do not offer the same analytical depth (Crewe, 2021, p. 206).

The third cause is more profound and has to do with the existence of a singular presupposition at the foundation of legislative studies. By this I mean the shared idea that   the   unity,   homogeneity   and   universality   of   the   parliamentarism   - as   a   social phenomenon - do not require any demonstration, which correlates with the idea that

their plurality is only superficial, in the sense that they differ from one another only at the fringes in the mode of variation around a single theme. This  presupposition of a common foundation thus leads to the study of the diversity of parliaments with the implicit aim of assessing the flexibility and scope of already known traditions (often French or British) across historical, political and social contexts (Ihalainen et al ., 2016, pp. 5-6). From this point of view, therefore, the possible coexistence of fundamentally different parliamentary ontologies is never considered, since all parliaments are seen as belonging to the same cultural and historical filiation.

Two main expressions of this presupposition can be found in the literature. For some authors, the universal presence of parliaments in the world's democracies makes this uniqueness a self-evident assumption, so that it is never really made explicit. Typically, research that seeks to assess the effectiveness of parliamentary work (e.g. Arter, 2006), to promote good practice (e.g. Beetham, 2006), to develop an encyclopaedic knowledge of it (e.g. Norton, 1998), to describe its transformative dynamics (e.g. Copeland and Patterson, 1994) is of this kind. However, what is seen here as a factual universality is in reality the consequence of a tautological reasoning, since only political systems with a parliament, or at least a deliberative institution, are considered. In this logic, indeed, contexts without standard-compliant assemblies tend to be ignored, so that the idea of that all parliamentary systems share a common foundation is an illusion produced by a selection   bias,   caused   by   a   differentiated   treatment   of   the   political   contexts   under consideration (Przeworski, 2000, pp. 8-10).

For other authors, this presupposition is not unthought of, but results from an explicit methodological gesture intended to support a typological project. Here, the diversity of parliamentary systems is initially recognised as a reality to be problematised, but then tends to be reduced to common properties (e.g. Mezey, 2008; Deschouwer and Despaw, 2014) to the  detriment   of   studying   their   specific   properties.   This   is   the   case,   for example, of the research by the juridical scientist Christophe de Nantois (2010) on the role of MP in France, Germany and the United Kingdom. In this study, the author presents the variability of the roles of 'MP' in these three contexts due to their cultural and historical roots, but he explains that he does not take this into account in the name of 'common theoretical foundations' (p. 7), preferring to postulate the existence of a 'typical   MP'  (p.   14).   This   abstract   figure   allows   him   to   assess   the   strengths   and weaknesses of the three ways of being an MP and finally to formulate proposals 'to improve the functioning of the [French] National Assembly' (p. 579). In this case, the weak point of the reasoning is the tendency to give a universal scope to concepts that are politically and culturally situated - typically within Western parliamentary traditions which generates a deeply ethnocentric  knowledge.  The  idea   that   all   parliamentary systems share a common foundation is then no longer the consequence of a selection bias of the case studies, but results from an abusive homogenisation carried out during the analysis.


## 1.3. The limits of the idea of the common foundation: the case of the 'MP' category


It is true that neighbouring parliamentary systems may show strong similarities, due to shared or partly shared histories and cultures. It is also true that certain parliamentary traditions, because of their precedence, may to some extent have played a structuring role in the formalisation of many parliaments that have emerged more recently in the world (Ihalainen et   al. ,   2016,   p.   6).   However,   are   these   similarities   and   influences necessarily a sign of a common foundation shared by all parliamentary systems in the world,   beyond   history   and   time?   Indeed,   they   could   also   be   the   result   of   other phenomena, such as those linked to the dynamics of colonisation or to the networks of influence   developed   by   certain   parliamentary   administrations.   Similarly,   should legislative terminologies always be considered equivalent on the basis that they are similar in different contexts? Nor is there any indication that discourses and procedures are underpinned by values, representations and norms that can be compared without being seriously questioned.

This problem is particularly evident in the case of the notion of 'MP'. Several authors have already highlighted the fact that this notion has a flexible meaning (e.g. Rozenberg and Vigour, 2018) in the eyes of the individuals elected to this role themselves, and thus designates very broad practices. It can be added that the meaning of the term 'MP' is also attached to local perceptions of what political representation should be, to the expected behaviours of those who carry the voice of the collective, to the socio-political histories in which parliamentary work is embedded, and to the legal idiosyncrasies of each context. There are no strict criteria for defining what is or is not a 'MP', even within a single parliamentary system. Even the most open definitions, for example, taking as sole criterion victory in a legislative election (which excludes appointed members, such as the British Lords) or the right to sit in a law-making assembly (which excludes   members   of   deliberative   assemblies   only),   do   not   capture   the   whole phenomenon.   Yet   the   term   'MP'   (or   its   equivalents)   remains   a   label   that   is conventionally used to refer to actors in parliamentary representative mandates.

However, the universal use of this label is not neutral; on the contrary, it has serious implications, on two levels. Firstly, at a descriptive level, the floating meaning of this notion makes it uncertain whether its use by the populations studied corresponds to the use of the researchers who study them, or to the uses that are made by the audiences to whom the researchers are speaking. Consequently, the more culturally distant the case studies are from the audiences they address, the more likely it is that the generic use of the   term   'MP'   will   generate   misunderstandings   and   distortions   of   the   phenomena described. Secondly, on an analytical level, the use of a single term tends to simplify a social phenomenon that is complex, by preventing the plurality of its expressions from being considered. This tends to favour the study of consensual and dominant forms of political   representation,   with   the   additional   risk   that   their   scientific   recognition reinforces them even more, to the detriment of its alternative or innovative forms.

Finally, it is notable that this singular conception of the notion of 'MP' is already challenged in the literature. In Bangladesh, for example, Ahmed (2019) reports that 'there is no formal set of requirements or official explanations about what roles MPs play while carrying out their duties' (p. 6), so that each elected member of parliament is forced to continually negotiate his or her role with citizens. The author invites us to rethink the contours of political representation. On the other hand, Gabrehiwot (2020) explains   that   for   the   Kunama   people   in   Ethiopia,   the   adoption   of   representative democracy and the election of MPs allowed the community to gain political recognition within the national state, but also challenged the traditional power exercised by the council   of   elders.   This   means   that,   in   contrast   to   the   Western   conception   of parliamentary   representation,   'the   Kunama   see   the   representatives   as   a   sign   of belonginess in the state but not as people who listen to them and address their issues on a regular basis. The values and mission of the general public are defined, drawn and redrawn, by elders who are more charmismatic than elected representatives' (p. 191).


## 2. Vernacular categories and analytical categories


In his famous book Anthropology, politics and the state: democracy and violence in South Asia (2007), the anthropologist Jonathan Spencer wonders whether he should consider   that   Sri   Lanka's   history,   culture   and   sociology   significantly   shape   its institutions into a local variant of democracy, or whether he should relate the processes and dynamics he observed to the more universal logics of representative politics. If he finally comes to the decision that this country shows too many 'small peculiarities' and strong similarities with ideas and institutions of 'a lot of other places' (p. 92-95), it is crucial here to see that, in Spencer's mind, the possibility of dealing with a singular democratic system lasted all the time of his reflection and was only settled at its end. Similarly, I defend that our first assumption as researchers should be that each context we are interested in may have its own conception of what parliamentary representation is and, by extension, to take seriously the idea that a notion such as 'MP' can be associated with very different roles, until proven otherwise.

So,   the   inclination   to   presuppose   the   existence   of   a   common   background   to   all parliamentary systems is an analytical dead end. To overcome it, it is firstly worthwhile for researchers to critically examine the terminology currently used to describe the parliamentary fact in order, as I will now explain, not to be trapped by the mechanics of local or global ideologies that they often fail to perceive. It also seems necessary to consider that, until proven otherwise, each context has its own conception of what parliamentary representation is and, by extension, to take seriously the idea that a notion such as 'MP' can designate very different conceptions of political representation. Here are   important   prerequisites   for   developing   a   fully   comprehensive   approach   to   the ordinary life of these institutions, i.e. to introduce cultural aspects into their analyses.


## 2.1. Deliberative assemblies, beyond the state and democracy


The project of developing a comprehensive approach of parliamentary systems is part of a broader programme, that of denaturalizing the concept of democracy (Paley, 2002). Indeed, parliamentarianism itself is part of the wider reality of deliberation, which must be seen as a 'total social fact' (Mauss, 1934), i.e. consubstantial to social life. Indeed, 'assembling to deliberate on common affairs' (Détienne, 2003, pp. 13-24) is an act that lies at the heart of politics, which responds mainly to two human needs: firstly, to develop a collective awareness of one's community and, secondly, to take charge of its future. In this perspective, spontaneous street assemblies, village assemblies or town councils (Richards and Kuper, 1971), supra-national assemblies and executive councils share with parliaments a common purpose and respond to a common need.

Deliberative assemblies are not, of course, the only tool available to populations to think of themselves as a political community and to act as such, especially in the context of states   where  the  forms  of political  representation  are plural.  Moreover, deliberative assemblies are themselves of several kinds, since they often coexist, supporting or competing with each other, within these same states. However, parliaments - i. e. the specific   form   that   deliberative   assemblies   takes   when   their   power   to   act   are institutionalised at the top of a state - frequently have a special place in today's societies. They all tend to embody the political sovereignty of peoples and nations, and to be recognised as such not only by the state authorities but above all by the populations, even if the place given to this voice, its effective power and the representations of 'collective action' may vary significantly according to the context.

This perspective leads to two important shifts for legislative studies. First, it is important to consider that deliberative assemblies are primary over states, and not vice versa. This means that while states can dictate the way deliberative assemblies function, for example by imposing the rule of majority rule (Graeber, 2007), this does not prevent them from existing and surviving when states evolve or disappear. Secondly, and by extension, it is important   to   consider   deliberative   assemblies   to   be   primary   to   the   democracies, understood as a mode of government of states apparatus. Deliberative assemblies can indeed find a place in republican, monarchical or authoritarian regimes, as well as in societies existing on the fringes of the state or within spontaneous protest movements.

Framing the problem in this way allows us to introduce two dimensions into our understanding   of   parliamentary   systems   that   are   little   explored   today:   those   of   its diversity but also of its dynamism. In the literature, deliberative assemblies tend to be a characteristic of democratic regimes, i.e. associated with a mode of government that is sometimes refused to the people and sometimes imposed by them during favourable historical   circumstances.   Conversely,   by   considering   parliamentary   systems   more broadly as one manifestation among others of deliberative assemblies, we are allowed to think of what is a mode of political action inalienable to each society, which it performs collectively on a day-to-day basis, in the light of its constraints, aspirations and values, by drawing positive or negative inspiration from the way it is implemented elsewhere.


## 2.2. Reflective work and study of the categories of practical meaning


Questioning the relationship between democracy and parliamentarianism is worthwhile in   order   to   highlight   that   this   connection   is   a   social   construction,   produced   and maintained largely by the institutions of democratic regimes themselves. More precisely, if this connection appears to us as obvious, it is because of a set of discourses thought and carried by the democratic states institutions and of a certain number of international organisations (such as the UN, e.g. Newman and Rich, 2004), but also of activities and objects specifically dedicated to materialise and make this connection perceptible (such as museum or exhibition, e. g. Bennett, 1988). It is therefore important to see that categories of thought, such as that of 'MP', are neither external nor independent of parliamentary   systems,   and   are   therefore   not   neutral   means   that   citizens,   elected officials, jurists and scientists can use to designate, describe and think objectively about parliamentary life. They are in themselves produced by social institutions which, in a given context, generate classifications, categories and ways of thinking (Douglas, 1986). Their use is closely linked to the social orders from which they emanate, shaping the perception, understanding and expectations of each individual.

Thus, when researchers carelessly borrow categories such as 'MP' to describe and analyse the realities they observe, they not only contribute to the global legitimisation of their own society's political order, but also to the extent to which their own categories of thought are naturalised and made invisible by giving them the seal of scientificity. The trap here is the well-known one of ethnocentrism, which lies in the propensity of any society to universalise its  own system of thought (Lévi-Strauss, 1966) and of any institution to impose a vision of the world that is favourable to it (Douglas, 1986). The risk is then to feed neo-colonial logics based on the idea that Europe is the historical seat of democracy (Graeber, 2007), which would give it legitimacy to impose its views on the way states are governed (Comaroff and Comaroff, 1997).

To counter such a drift, anthropologists early on proposed that neutralising the natural inclination of any researcher to impose his or her own concepts, terminology, norms and values on the phenomena he or she observes outside his or her own country was a necessity   (Bohannan,   1957).   Although   awareness   of   these   issues   within   legislative studies is more recent, two essential propositions have already been formulated: on the one hand, the importance of taking 'seriously the way in which political actors interpret the world around them' and, on the other, the need 'to 'decentre' the interpretations and concepts used by political actors' (Geddes and Rhodes, 2018, p. 8).

The first proposal here is methodological and concerns the requirement of 'reflexive work' in the study of parliamentary systems (Crewe, 2021, pp. 11-14). We should indeed admit that our definition of this object is not universal, and therefore accept to transform our own understanding of the phenomenon. By extension, we should also question the 'comparative approach' itself in the framework of legislative studies, i.e. the way in which this type of research tends to be elaborated, since the presupposition of

a common foundation shared by parliamentary systems testifies to a biased perception of the latters.

The second proposal by Geddes and Rhodes is in line with the proposals of authors for whom 'to understand the working of the concept of a society is to understand its institutions' (Gellner, 1959, p. 18). The challenge here is to pay attention to peoples' practical categories, and thus to take into account the fact that identical terminologies can conceal very different procedures and patterns of activity, even when parliamentary systems are culturally and politically close (Rozenberg et al. , 2011). It seems clear that 'the   possibilities   for   transfer   in   parliamentary   language,   as   foreign   models   and references have usually been adopted selectively and even tendentiously in order to serve particular purposes in domestic circumstances' (Ihalainen et al. , 2016, p. 6).


## 2.3. Inductive reasoning and ideal-typical methodology


Should we then refuse at all costs to use the term 'MP' ourselves in our research? Should we instead create a new analytical category, independent of existing vernacular terminologies? These questions take us directly back to the controversy between Paul Bohannan and Max Gluckman at the turn of the 1950s and 1960s 1 . For a brief reminder, the former criticised the latter for using British legal terminology to describe the legal practices of the Barotse people, generating what he considered to be a distorted and ethnocentric   knowledge   of   the   indigenous   system.   Gluckman,   on   the   other   hand, defended himself by arguing that the approximation to British concepts is more likely to help the Western reader understand a legal system significantly different from his own. The fact that neither side emerged victorious from this debate should certainly prompt us to seek a middle ground (Donovan, 2007, pp. 167-168).

However, the debate is framed in slightly different terms here. Indeed, within legislative studies,   people   and   scientists   share   the   same   terminology,   those   of   the   Western democratic tradition. Or, to put it another way, given that parliamentarianism was the focus of an early process of globalisation, its terminology tends to have a universal character, even if this is not the case for the associated categories of thought. In our case, the question that occupies Bohannan and Gluckman is thus displaced in favour of another: which analytical categories should we mobilise if all those based on universal terminology are to be set aside?

To answer this question, the work of Bernard Manin (2010) offers an inspiring example. After studying numerous parliamentary regimes in history, he identifies four 'principles of representative government' and then develops three ideal types of political regimes based   on   these   principles:   'parliamentarism',   'party   democracy'   and   'public democracy'. The originality of this work lies in the fact that the analysis is based on analytical categories that are tailor-made for the needs of the research, and that are not produced ex nihilo but through inductive reasoning. Indeed, the author here employs neither the categories of thought promoted by the institutions themselves, nor categories

that he himself would have imagined before the analysis. Halfway between the two approaches, the author shaped his operational categories as he conducted his research, creating   order   and   meaning   from   the   study   of   contextualised   data.   While   Manin's conclusions tend, like many others, to universalise the Western parliamentary tradition, he nevertheless develops a methodologically-convincing empirical approach.

Here we recognise the strong influence of Max Weber's proposals in favour of reasoning by 'ideal-type' (Weber, 1949). There is indeed a solid path to follow for researchers who wish both to have conceptual tools independent of the phenomena they are studying and to develop a comprehensive approach. As a reminder, reasoning by ideal-type consists of developing a model for analysis, which is not intended to describe the reality that has been observed, but to highlight it and make comparison possible (Weber, 1949, p. 90). In this, it also offers a useful safeguard against our tendency to universalise beyond measure and our natural propensity to ethnocentrism, by making explicit the specific issues and delimitations of our research.


## 3. Deconstructing the notion of 'MP' in the French case


I will now close this reflection by taking the example of my own research in order to show, on the one hand, how the presupposition of what should be MPs can pose a problem and, on the other hand, to present how reasoning by ideal-type makes it possible to circumvent this obstacle.

My research project aimed to understand the extent to which the conditions of existence of   the   French   parliamentary   institution   have   been   transformed   by   the   long-term evolution of communication technologies (Chibois, 2019). In particular, my ambition was to focuse on the reconstructions generated by the emergence of digital technologies in the ordinary organisation of centres of state power. To this end, between 2007 and 2017, I undertook a long-term ethnographic investigation of French parliamentary life, between the Palais Bourbon, which hosts legislative activities in Paris, and various constituencies. One of my objectives was to look at the concrete ways in which MPs' mandates are organised, in order to shed light on how these elected representatives manage their material, technical and human resources on a day-to-day basis in carrying out their duties. For this purpose, I met with 22 different parliamentary teams (out of the 577 in the Assembly), to whom I was able to ask specific questions about the tools and collective work procedures used internally.


## 3.1. Three ways of distributing activities within the parliamentary teams


However, I was not prepared for the variety of ways in which parliamentary teams are organised, which are not often addressed in conventional approaches to parliamentary work. I therefore sought firstly to understand how the ways in which MPs view their role influence the ways in which they organise the work of their team, and secondly to make fine comparisons. For this purpose, I classified the parliamentary teams I had met by taking the type of relationship between MPs and their staff as a criterion. Three profiles

thus emerged, which I specified by taking up the entrepreneurial metaphor that several authors have already used to deal with the management by MPs of their resources (Loomis, 1979; Salisbury and Shepsle, 1981).

Following Weberian principles of ideal-typical reasoning, I do not claim that these are directly faithful to reality, their characteristics have indeed been slightly exaggerated both to erase their most contextual specificities and to clarify what distinguishes them mutually. Together, they delimit an abstract framework within which all the operating modes of French parliamentary teams can theoretically be described. It should also be noted that these three profiles are not intended to essentialise the organisation of a given parliamentary team, as the ways in which MPs manage their resources may vary during their term of office, depending on the political situation, the legislative files or the skills of the members of their team.

The first profile is the 'MP as a boss'. Here, the elected representative tends to carry out his or her mandate by carrying out the maximum number of tasks alone, as if he or she were the sole repository of the know-how and address book of his or her mandate. The division of work between him and his collaborators is indexed to a hierarchy of the value of the tasks to be accomplished, from the most noble (for example: giving a speech, answering an interview) to the most thankless (for example: answering mail, feeding the website,   managing   the   agenda).   Of   course,   the   value   of   a   given   task   can   vary considerably from one elected official to another (depending on his or her partisan anchorage, political trajectory, the political power at his or her disposal), but this does not alter the general logic of their distribution. Here, collaborators are above all seen as 'unskilled workers' whose vocation is to remain invisible, indispensable for taking care of what the elected official cannot or does not wish to do himself.

In contrast to this profile, some elected representatives choose to function 'as a team', encouraging their collaborators to invest as much as possible in the management of the mandate in the same way as they do. To do this, elected representatives tends to minimise their own roles, keeping for themselves only the roles that are legally attached to their person and the role of arbitrating differences within the team. In this case, staff members are both colleagues and avatars of the elected representative and can take on the role of the latter in certain circumstances (e.g. meeting constituents, giving a speech, drafting an amendment). The primary objective of such an organisation is to increase efficiency, both by valuing and involving staff more and by better coping with dispersion and workload. Some of its supporters also use it to defend a more inclusive and less elitist conception of democracy. It is true that this type of profile remains proportionally rare, even if it is tending to spread.

As a counterpoint to these first two profiles, 'outsourced MPs' are distinguished by their low personal investment in the activities of the mandate and by the fact that they delegate these activities essentially to their collaborators, and even asking other MPs to vote for them via proxy when possible. In this case, the main challenge for the team is to make up for the absence of the elected representative as much as possible, which means

that the mandate is mainly focused on the constituency. Elected representatives who adopt such an organisation often did not run in the legislative elections because of a national political ambition but to consolidate their local power (e.g. to join the group or party that holds a majority in parliament, to prevent the seat from being occupied by an opponent or to consolidate a network of territorial influence). This profile corresponds to a way of holding office that has been widespread in France since the end of the 19th century,   but   is   less   and   less   accepted   today   and   now   tends   to   be   opposed   by   the parliamentary institution itself 2 .


## 3.2. Shifting the definition of 'MP'


Describing parliamentary activity on the basis of these three modes of organisation has the main advantage of injecting plurality and complexity into the way of thinking about the role of MP, which already allows for several conceptual shifts. In particular, we realise that the idea according to which parliamentary activities are the result of the action of elected representatives, as required by law and common sense, corresponds to only a part of the observed reality (the 'MP as a boss' profile). And yet, for this normative conception to be fully valid, we must not only turn a blind eye to the many menial tasks that staff members perform, but we must also consider these tasks to be unnecessary. In other words, this way of describing parliamentary activity makes it clear that the use of the standard descriptive category of 'MP' leads to making certain actors and activities invisible, and thus to removing some of the conditions of possibility of the parliamentary mandate from the scope of analysis.

Thus,   these   three   profiles   highlight   a   counter-intuitive   reality:   conducting   a parliamentary term of office is in the French context an eminently collective activity. Although this fact has already been highlighted in various ways, notably within the sociology of political collaborators (e.g. Busby and Belkacem, 2013; Winzen, 2011), to my knowledge no author has drawn general conclusions on the 'mythical' character (Barthes, 1972) of parliamentary work. The fact that a large part of parliamentary work, and in particular some of its most political activities, is carried out by non-elected staff calls into question the commonly accepted definition of what MPs are and raises many questions. What are the characteristic activities of this role? What distinguishes their role from that of collaborators? How can we identify in a given situation who is acting as collaborator or MP? Can we think of the collective formed by a MP and his/her collaborators as a full-fledged actor, and if so, what term could we use to describe this?

Today, there is a general tendency in the literature of French legislative studies to consider that the political role of parliamentary collaborators is negligible overall, which leads to the view that the profile of the 'MP as a boss' is an obvious yardstick. To justify this position, one could argue that since alternative organisational modes are not morally and legally legitimate, they are marginal in practice and therefore also negligible in the

analysis. There are two strong objections to this argument. Firstly, this moral and legal legitimacy imposing the profile 'MP as a boss' is contextual. It did not exist in the past in France 3  and it does not necessarily exist elsewhere. If this profile is indeed the one most in line with the democratic ideal in a given socio-political context, it would be a mistake to take this reality as a universal truth. Secondly, no longitudinal study can establish that a more legitimate practice necessarily leads to a more common practice in a strict causal relationship. The 'MP as a boss' organisational profile could also exist only as an ideal model towards which elected representatives try to move without necessarily succeeding, or as a conformist public discourse detached from the actual realities of the collective organisation that have been adopted.

The highlighting of these three profiles of MPs finally leads me to argue that in France, it is not elected representatives who take charge of the parliamentary term of office but the sum of the individuals who make up their team, including the MPs themselves 4 . In doing so, I propose to redefine the contours of the analytical category of MP in order to consider   it   in   a   collective   perspective,   with   the   aim   of   creating   a   break   with   the spontaneous, ideological   and   hegemonic   knowledge   that   we   have   of   parliamentary systems. By extension, I also try to break with a monolithic view of legislative activities which, because it is necessarily situated in space and time, is partial and therefore biased. By extension, my ambition is to open the way to a multiple and complex way of thinking that goes beyond the single localised case of French parliamentarianism. In this sense, my approach is part of the 'implicit comparative method' (Glazer and Strauss, 1999, p. 148) in the sense that, although it focuses on a single context 'it employs concepts that make it possible to derive generalizations that can be tested elsewhere' (Rose, 1991, p. 454).


## 4. Conclusion


I explained in this article that it is misleading to rely on vernacular categories emanating from Western democratic ideology to describe and analyse parliamentary systems. I then argued that it is important for researchers to use them with care, first by resituating them in their context of use, and then by trying to develop new ones on the basis of empirical observations. This approach meets both an ethical and epistemological requirement, which   makes   it   possible   to   break   with   a   prescriptive   mode   of   knowledge   of parliamentary systems and to engage in a comprehensive analysis, which is still not very widespread in political and legal sciences. Taking the example of the concept of 'MP' in the French case thus allowed me to show how it was possible to renew the scientific discourse on ordinary parliamentary activities.

This article is part of a broader reflection on the way in which anthropology could contribute   to   renewing   the   study   of   representative   democracies   in   the   world.   This reflection aims to take the opposite view of the analyses, which are widely dominant

today,   that   interpret   the   multiple   tensions   that   the   institutions   of   democracy   are experiencing   as   an   erosion   of   the   democratic   ideal.   Another   hypothesis   could   be formulated,   however,   that   of   a   transformation   of   the   democratic   project   and   its implementation, which would originate not so much from the rise of alternative political ideals but rather from the demands of collectives for a better representation of their interests   within   the   institutional   functioning.   In   this   more   'global'   hypothesis (Appadurai, 1996), it is crucial to study carefully how parliamentarianism is envisaged in local contexts, taking seriously the idea that it may be subject to representations and values that differ significantly from those in force in the Western tradition.

## 1 Introduction


With the United States now at the center of the secularization debate, the U.S. General Social Survey (GSS) has become the de facto arbiter of the ongoing discussion about the future of religion (Schnabel and Bock 2018; Voas and Chaves 2018; Schnabel and Bock 2017). The U.S. was long seen as a counterexample to the secularization thesis, but with the rapid rise of religious 'nones' (Hout and Fischer 2002; Hout and Fischer 2014) and declining on average religiosity, some scholars now claim the U.S. fits the secularization thesis (e.g., Voas and Chaves 2016). Recent debate has focused on divergent patterns among types of religion in the U.S., with research showing that intense religion (e.g., strong affiliation, very frequent religious practice, biblical literalism, and evangelicalism) - arguably the most socially impactful type of religion - persists as a strong, stable, and seemingly ever-present minority of American religion while only moderate religion is on the decline (Schnabel and Bock 2017). This study provides an update to the U.S. secularization debate by examining data from the 2021 GSS. The data suggest an unprecedented change in religion. However, this change could be the result of period effects during a unique span of time, the COVID-19 pandemic, or mode effects resulting from the typically face-to-face survey being fielded online due to the pandemic. If a mode effect, this apparent change could be a canary in the coal mine for the representativeness and comparability of surveys, highlighting foundational issues in the trend toward online surveys.


## 1.1 Religious Change, Secularization, and the COVID-19 Pandemic


Secularization and class conflict were the foundational predictions of 19th century social science. Comte, Marx, Freud, Durkheim, Weber, and other early theorists marked religion as part of premodern culture and predicted it would decline into obscurity within, at most, a few generations as society modernized. Their conjecture laid the foundation for the long-standing dominant theory for interpreting religious change: secularization

theory, which predicted a rapid decline into general irrelevance driven by modernization (Bruce 2011).

But the rapid decline into irrelevance and obscurity did not materialize. Religion remained relevant in people's lives and world affairs. Most of the world was still religious and some even began arguing for a radicalization if not resurgence of religion in the last half of the 20th century. Other work similarly showed persistent if not rising levels on at least some measures like belief in an afterlife and more general stability than decline (Greeley and Hout 1999; Hout and Greeley 1998; Hout and Greeley 1990; Hout and Greeley 1987). With secularization theory challenged by reality, even some of its core proponents reversed their earlier perspective, with Peter Berger (1999), for example, arguing for desecularization rather than secularization.

The vitality of religion in the United States was a central part of arguments against secularization theory, with some scholars even arguing that the United States had become more religious over time (Finke and Stark 2005). Although America was long seen as exceptionally religious, perhaps the most dramatic story in American religion over the past few decades is the decline of religious preference (Hout and Fischer 2002; Hout and Fischer 2014). Some scholars have come to see disaffiliation as a sign of secularization, suggesting that the United States is not an exception to the secularization thesis and reinvigorating claims for secularization (Voas and Chaves 2016).

However, those who want to see disaffiliation as the late arrival of secularization as modernization theory meant it must answer three important questions. First, why did it take so long to happen so fast? Second, why do we not see similarly rapid declines on measures of religion besides affiliation? Third, why do we only see a decline in moderate religion while intense religion persists? As several studies show, there is only a decline in the middle categories of more liminal religiosity while the most extreme levels persist unabated (Hout and Fischer 2002; Hout and Fischer 2014; Schnabel and Bock 2017; Schnabel and Bock 2018; Hout 2017b; Hout 2017a). Perhaps societal disruptions are necessary to prompt more rapid religious decline and otherwise change is slow. Could something like a global pandemic finally provide the impetus necessary for people to

become less religious more quickly and for intense religion to finally abate in the United States?

Although something disruptive such as a pandemic could prompt faster social change, we do not have a strong basis for assuming that all disruptions will affect trends in religious change or that all religious change is downward. In fact, some research suggests that when faced with uncertainty and hardship, people turn to religion; adversity of various kinds seems to yield greater religious commitment or at least greater religious coping (Hastings and Roeser 2020; Berkessel et al. 2021; Du Bois 1903; Schnabel 2021). For example, Bentzen (2019) suggests that natural disasters increase religiosity by promoting greater religious coping. Similarly, Storm (2017) suggests that economic insecurity predicts greater religiosity over time cross-nationally.

Other work on natural disasters and life stressors, however, suggests that they have the potential to both make people more religious or less religious (Hussain, Weisaeth, and Heir 2011; Vargas 2012). But the direct evidence we have to date on what we might expect during the COVID-19 pandemic suggests that this time of crisis prompted people to use religion to cope (Schnabel and Schieman 2022) and some even argue that 'religiosity has risen globally due to the pandemic' because people are turning to it to deal with adversity (Bentzen 2021).


## 1.2 Survey Mode Effects and Data Collection During a Pandemic


The 2021 GSS was unique in multiple ways as illustrated in Table 1 (Davern et al. 2021). Most notably, the data were collected during a global pandemic. The pandemic could create period effects, which we might expect to amplify religiosity if people turn to religion in adversity (Bentzen 2019; Thunstr¨m and Noy 2019; Berkessel et al. 2021; o Bentzen 2021). Alternatively, if there was sufficient political backlash against Trump, Christian nationalism, and any perceived mishandling of the pandemic, it is possible that some people might have jumped ship (Hout and Fischer 2014; Bock 2021) similar to drops in some religion measures following prominent televangelist sex and financial scandals in

1987 and 1988 (Smith 1992). Or maybe this was just finally the type of disruptive catalyst needed to bring about secularization theory's long-prophesied rapid religious decline.

## [Table 1]

The pandemic could also create survey mode effects. Typically, the GSS is fielded by trained interviewers contacting people in-person and conducting face-to-face interviews, which leads to relatively high response rates and to high-quality data, even from those with limited literacy. Lockdowns and common sense precluded in-person interviewing through most of 2020, so the GSS switched modes, adopting a mail-to-web survey that was conducted from December 2020 to May 2021 with a much lower response rate. The web self-administered questionnaire (SAQ) required higher literacy (General Social Survey 2021). With interviewers, the usual GSS allowed volunteered responses. For example, when asked by an interviewer if they are a 'strong' or 'not strong' adherent to their religion, many people voluntarily provide the answer 'somewhat strong.' The SAQ either offers a response or does not, respondents cannot create their own response category. Several items of interest to religion researchers typically feature volunteered responses. The SAQ offered several of these in two forms - with and without the responses typically recorded by interviewers if 'volunteered.' We will compare the forms to evaluate the impact of changing mode on trends in religiosity, but first we consider previous literature on survey effects and especially mode effects.

Survey researchers have delved into response bias in regard to religion for years. Much of that research focused on a tendency for religious people to overestimate how frequently they attend religious services - with some arguing that people face social pressure to report more religiosity when talking to interviewers and others suggesting that people have a tendency to report their desired amount of attendance due to their religious commitments and identities rather than potentially lower actual levels (Brenner 2011; Brenner 2014; Hout and Greeley 1998; Presser and Stinson 1998). More recently, however, some work has also begun to suggest that survey bias can also lead to broader misestimation and for populations to appear less religious, rather than more religious, than they are. It is well known that opt-in online samples underestimate some forms of social engage-

ment, especially on factors such as religion. For example, mTurk samples are known to be particularly secular (Lewis et al. 2015; Burnham, Le, and Piedmont 2018; Baker, Hill, and Porter 2017). But could there be similar issues with who agrees and who declines to participate in population-based surveys, especially as they move online and have lower response rates? Alternatively, is it possible that religious people are actually more likely to opt into surveys - perhaps due to general dutifulness, conscientiousness, age, gender, or other factors associated with survey response rates - and the decline would have been even more rapid without their greater likelihood to agree to participate when asked?

Beyond religion, methods research has considered general mode effects for online surveys. In 2010, a task force created by the American Association for Public Opinion Research (AAPOR) noted that online surveys, especially opt-in panels, have significant coverage error and concluded that nonprobability online panels should not be used to estimate population values (Reg et al. 2010). These experts concluded that nonprobability online panels are more useful, however, for examining relationships between variables or experimental effects. While online panels are better suited for multivariable analysis than estimating population parameters, research suggests that care should still be taken and that the accuracy of data varies by platform (e.g., Qualtrics is more accurate than MTurk) (Zack, Kennedy, and Long 2019; Simmons and Bobo 2015).

Some online panels, however, are probability-based rather than non-probability, which removes much of the error that enters due to the opt-in nature of some online panels. Tom Smith (2003), long-time director of the General Social Survey, conducted an experiment to compare the most promising online survey approach, pre-recruited panels of the general population, with the General Social Survey. Fielding the same items on both the Knowledge Networks panel and the GSS, he found that while many comparisons showed similar results, there were also a number of notable differences.

In Smith's experiment, the online panel yielded more 'don't knows,' especially for some items, because of the nature of the difference between oral ask-and-answer questions and read-and-click questions. The online panel also tended to yield more extreme responses on agree/disagree scales. While there was often general similarity on individual

items, on some there were systematic differences. For example, when talking to an interviewer more people support government spending on cities, drug rehabilitation, racial minorities, and welfare than when filling out the survey online, which Smith suggested might be in part social desirability bias. Among items not about spending, Smith noted the one large difference was on school prayer, with people saying they are more likely to support the ban on school prayer in the online sample than in the in-person interviews, which Smith suggested could be in part a function of the question being something of a double negative (people are asked if they support the decision to ban school prayer, and GSS pretests indicate that there is a tendency for people to confuse approving of the ban with approving of school prayer). Overall, the report highlighted factors related to how the survey was fielded (the online platform requires adjustments), with less attention to potential difference in who participates (which is important in light of the generally lower response rates on online surveys and how that could produce nonresponse bias even in probability-based online surveys).

Smith and Kim (2015) later reviewed data collection modes as a whole with a focus on computerization (both online surveys and computer-assisted technology in other survey delivery formats). He concluded that survey modes can produce different outcomes, with mode effects being a key factor to consider in a total survey error framework. He concluded with a cautionary message about the importance of collection method and the need to be particularly careful with newer methods as all methods have a learning curve for establishing best practices and determining the accuracy limits of various approaches.

Certainly, the costs of in-person surveys motivate an interest in moving to web options. Some major data collection efforts have moved partially or fully online, with most organizations making such a switch having reports that typically seem to justify the move, suggesting that online and in-person surveys yield generally equivalent results. For example, the American National Elections Study (ANES) put out a report suggesting that their online data were equivalent to their in-person data (Guggenheim 2019). Other researchers, however, have conducted research suggesting that online methods were not as accurate as the in-person ANES (Malhotra and Krosnick 2007; Simmons and Bobo

2015). Notably, the GSS's own report about the online methodology necessitated by the pandemic differs from the optimism put forth in other institutional reports justifying mode switches, suggesting great caution when using the 2021 data because of the mode switch and the likelihood that it could affect some results in potentially substantial ways (General Social Survey 2021).


## 2 Results



## 2.1 Sudden Secularization in the 2021 GSS?


Figure 1 presents intense religion over time, demonstrating what looks like a dramatic decline in the 2021 GSS. In fact, it appears to fall off a cliff. There had already been what appeared to be a very slight decline on some measures in 2018 (perhaps the result of political backlash against Trumpism - or, as we will discuss later, a lower response rate), but the change from 2018 to 2021 is an unprecedented decline and apparent rapid secularization, especially on the non-practice measures. Frequent prayer held steady and the decline in frequent attendance was within the realm of typical year-to-year fluctuation (though with some downward tendency). But strong affiliation and biblical literalism dropped lower than ever measured in the GSS and evangelical affiliation declined to levels not seen in four decades. As a result, frequent prayer, which at some points was only about half as common as strong affiliation, appears to have overtaken both strong affiliation and literalism for the first time ever. Period effects and rapid change in intense religion are not unheard of, but in the past such period effects resulted in increases of intense religion - such as during the Reagan years - rather than the decrease we see in 2021. Figure 1 presents trends with the special 2021 survey weights that do help to slightly increase intense religion, but not by much. For example, instead of 24% literalism with the weights, it would be even lower at 21% without them.

## 2.2 Do Mode Effects Explain 'Secularization' Patterns?


Although period effects are possible, survey mode effects are another possibility. As already noted, the 2021 GSS was unique not only in when it was fielded but also how it was fielded. The pandemic changed how respondents were invited to participate, how interviews were carried out, and other factors including how to translate a face-to-face interview protocol into an online instrument that could affect these data.

The 2021 cross-sectional GSS provides some measures that allow for consideration of mode effects. For example, while the vast majority of surveys were fielded on the web, some were fielded by phone. Across measures, surveys completed over the phone demonstrate substantially higher levels of intense religion than those fielded via the web as shown in Figure 2. The differences were especially large on measures such as the idea that the success of the United States is a part of God's plan, an indicator of Christian nationalism (Whitehead and Perry 2020) that 43% of those who took the survey on the phone agreed with but which only 25% who took the survey via the web agreed with. Table 2 demonstrates the impact of including previously volunteered responses, such as people saying 'somewhat strong' when asked if they were a 'strong' or 'not strong' adherent to their religious group, on the proportion of people classified as intensely religious. For example, whether 'somewhat strong' is provided as an option determines whether 24% or 31% of people would be classified as intensely religious on strength of affiliation.

While some information can be gleaned from within the cross-sectional survey itself about the possible importance of mode effects, what we really need is information on nonresponders to differentiate between factors such as social desirability bias and nonresponse bias. Typically, it is not possible to compare those who completed a survey and those who were invited but did not complete it. Panel data can help, making it possible to use earlier data to compare those who complete later waves and those who do not. But typical panel attrition is different from this mode change where a previously face-to-face

survey with a high response rate shifts to a push-to-web approach with a much lower response rate. Even if panel data with the same mode switch did exist, the pandemic is a unique time period. In a perfect data world, we would have high-quality data that made the same mode switch during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The GSS anticipated this issue and included reinterviews with past respondents in their accommodation to the pandemic. Between August 24 and September 26, 2020, NORC re-contacted a sample of respondents from the 2016 GSS and all respondents from the 2018 GSS by mail, using a push-to-web sampling approach identical to the one they used for the 2021 GSS cross-section. These are much less select samples than most as the 2016 GSS had a response rate of 61% and 2018 had a response rate of 60%. As such, we can then compare those who completed a push-to-web survey to those who declined to do so - and even other groups, including those not selected for a follow-up invitation, those who were selected but died before they could be reinterviewed, and even those who became ineligible through such things as incapacitation or moving out of the country - and arguably generalize to nonresponse in the 2021 GSS cross-section for which respondents were invited in an equivalent way only three months later.

Substantial nonresponse bias leads to the underestimation of intense religion. As shown in Table 3, those who declined the follow-up are much more intensely religious than are those who completed the follow-up interview. In other words, comparing a similar mode switch among people who previously participated in person shows that the mode switch introduces substantial nonresponse bias. For example, 36% of those who participated in the 2016 face-to-face GSS but did not accept the invitation to participate in the push-to-web follow-up are biblical literalists. But only 25% of those who completed the follow-up were biblical literalists in 2016. By 2020, 25% of those who completed the follow-up were biblical literalists, suggesting that among those who completed the followup, biblical literalism (and all other measures of intense religion) did not change. If we were to compare the full sample in 2016 to the full sample in 2020 it would look as though intense religion had declined similarly to the cross-sectional data, but that pattern is a function of nonresponse bias in the follow-up survey. Similar to how there was less decline

on the practice measures in the 2021 cross-sectional GSS, there was less non-response bias on the practice measures in the GSS panel.

## 2.3 Who Opts Out of Web Surveys?


Why are some people, disproportionately the intensely religious, selecting out of web surveys? One possibility is partisanship. With religion and politics correlated, perhaps people with certain political views are more opposed to or simply less interested in participating in scientific research (Hout and Fischer 2002; Hout and Fischer 2014). In light of recent research suggesting that partisanship predicts nonresponse, this could be a particularly relevant factor (Clinton, Lapinski, and Trussler 2022). But Table 3 shows that those who did not participate in the follow up are only very slightly more likely to be Republican (and we might have expected at least as much if not more of a partisan difference based on the larger gap in intense religion alone). This suggests the possibility that the research finding a relatively small partisan gap in non-response may be explained by intense religion. Another possibility is age. Maybe older people are more intensely religious and were less likely to participate in an online survey. But, in fact, it is younger people who were a bit less likely to participate in a push-to-web follow-up survey.

Although women tend to be more religious, men tend to be more religiously dogmatic, and there are known gender differences in survey response (Schnabel 2018). But despite women being more likely to respond to surveys generally, there are not gender differences in who agrees to make the shift to an online survey from an in-person survey.

A further possibility is opposition to science. Many intensely religious Americans have come to see religion and science in conflict with one another and perhaps for this reason they simply do not want to participate in scientific research (Ecklund 2021; Noy and O'Brien 2016; O'Brien and Noy 2015). Table 3 shows that there is not a difference in opposing research. Those who did not complete the follow up are more likely to distrust science, but as we will show those sentiments parallel general distrust and are not unique to science.

If partisanship, age, gender, and opposition to science are not key determinants of who declines to participate, thereby leading to the underestimation of intense religion, what are the key factors? As also shown in Table 3, non-responders in push-to-web surveys can be characterized with five terms that distinguish them from responders, all of which are interrelated with both intense religion and skepticism about, lack of confidence in, and less integration with formal institutions besides religion (e.g., those fielding surveys): non-responders are more disillusioned, distrusting, disinformed, disadvantaged, and disconnected. In terms of disillusionment, they are more likely to think that most politicians and government administrators are corrupt and that they have no say in politics. They are more often bored with nothing to do, less likely to vote, expect the worst, think they wouldn't be able to get out of a jam, less likely to be always happy, and less likely to keep their homes clean. In terms of disadvantage, they are more likely to be working class, minorities, renters, in poor health, low income, and to have less control over their work schedules.

This group of non-respondents are also generally distrusting, strongly oppose wiretapping of phones, think GMOs and nuclear power are very dangerous, think people are out to take advantage to them, and less likely to have provided consent to have their interviews recorded. Notably, they are over twice as likely to live in the West South Cen-

tral region that encompasses Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Texas, where general distrust is highest. Their general distrust parallels their distrust of science, which they do not seem to distrust more than they distrust other formal institutions. The exception to their distrust is religion, which they are more likely to have confidence in than those who completed the follow-up interview. Perhaps this is not surprising: whereas religion was once a key part of civic society and still is in some ways, the type of intense religion found among this distrusting, disadvantaged, and disillusioned subset of Americans is purposefully more sectarian and deinstitutionalized.

People who do not participate in online, written surveys but had participated in an in-person oral survey are more disinformed in several ways. Their vocabulary knowledge and understanding of survey questions are more limited. They are not necessarily more opposed to science, but they are less likely to understand it: they are more likely to provide incorrect information when asked scientific questions, regardless of whether the question is about a politicized issue or not. They are less likely to have completed high school math and science courses and are more likely to never read a newspaper. Difficulty or disinterest regarding the written format of online surveys seems to be a key factor; those who completed the follow up but did so over the phone rather than online are also more disinformed.

Survey nonresponders are disconnected from other people, from civic society, and from the internet. They are lonelier and less likely to be married. Their cultural interests lean more toward farming than integration with high culture and they are less likely to have gone to an art exhibit or science museum in the last year (likely correlated with disadvantage). They are also less likely to live in safe neighborhoods that facilitate connection. They are much less likely to use LinkedIn but are about just as likely to use Facebook - a problematic source of disinformation in 2016 (Jamieson 2018) and presumably 2020 - and use the internet less overall.

The factors we identified as important to nonresponse are interrelated with intense religion and help provide context for the nonresponse gap in intense religion. As shown in Figure 4, after accounting for these factors in regression models there is no longer a

difference in intense religion by whether people agree to participate in an online survey. In other words, if they were not more likely to be disillusioned, distrusting, disinformed, disadvantaged, and disconnected, intensely religious people appear as though they would be just as likely to participate in online surveys. And we would not expect to see the rapid secularization apparent on non-practice measures in the 2021 cross-sectional GSS data. This suggests that poststratification adjustments for these factors may yield better estimates than adjusting only for a few demographic factors.

In short, people who did not participate when invited to take part in a push-to-web survey are not simply partisan, opposed to science, or older. Instead, they face a harder time in life, are not thriving, find written material and survey questions more challenging, and are not particularly engaged in civic society apart from religion. Religion provides disheartened, disillusioned, and disengaged people an alternative form of community and institutional involvement, but they are more involved in the fundamentalist and sectarian forms of religion that are fairly disconnected from other forms of civic society - and may even prompt further distrust of secular society and its institutions, such as universities and research centers conducting surveys.

Because intensely religious people are less likely to participate in surveys with a pushto-web design, the 2021 GSS creates an illusion of secularization. The GSS panel is the ideal comparison for the GSS cross-section because it provides a direct comparison of a GSS in-person face-to-face approach compared to a push-to-web approach. If anything, the difference between those who were reinterviewed and those who were selected for reinterview in the panel but were not reinterviewed is likely a conservative estimate of the differences between those who do and do not participate in push-to-web online surveys. The 2020 panel was sampled from people who had already participated once, removing the people least likely to participate in the first place and leaving those who had established some trust in the organization (and we already saw trust is a key issue in nonresponse).


## 3 Discussion


Mode effects, survey response rates, and nonresponse bias can have drastic implications for our estimation of social phenomena like intense religion. Satisfied, trusting, informed, advantaged, and connected people are more likely to participate in online surveys. Intensely religious people are less likely to agree to take surveys and are more likely to drop out of panels. When they do take surveys, they are less likely to do them online. Therefore, online surveys with substantial nonresponse likely grossly underestimate intense religion, which can help explain why religiosity sometimes looks lower in datasets other than the GSS. And, though raw tabulations from the 2021 GSS indicate otherwise, panel results show that intense religion persisted through the early months of the pandemic (and some indicators rose). It is possible that even changes in earlier years of the GSS cross-section are at least in part a function of changes in response rates over time in a changing social and political climate. For example, there was a large drop from 2014 to 2016 (69% response rate to 61%) and then a further, though smaller, drop in 2018.

The collection of the 2021 GSS provides unique insight into religion and mode effects, allowing us to see how measurements of religion can be biased in online surveys even when population-based sampling methods are used: religion is more persistent than it appears, intensely religious people are less likely to agree to participate in surveys, and data collection efforts like the typical in-person GSS are invaluable for accurately estimating religion and other ideological factors in the United States associated with the likelihood of participating in surveys.

As the 2021 GSS methodological primer itself notes, 'any changes in public opinion seen in the 2021 GSS data could be due to either changes in actual opinion and/or methodological shifts to adapt to COVID-19.' Notably, the GSS is not the only gold standard data collection effort affected by pandemic disruption; reports are emerging that the U.S. Census, the only dataset used more than the GSS in the social sciences and which does not include religion measures, disproportionately undercounted racial and ethnic minorities in 2020 (U.S. Census Bureau 2022). We caution that when users employ 2021 GSS data to examine trends over time, they carefully consider if changes

in the GSS methodology may be impacting the analysis (General Social Survey 2021). As we have shown, methodological changes clearly impact analyses involving religion as well as other factors associated with the characteristics we identified as integral to who declines to participate in surveys: disillusionment, distrust, disinformation, disadvantage, and disconnection. For example, an unprecedented decline in happiness was noted by NORC (2020), demonstrating the lowest levels of happiness ever recorded in the GSS. But the reality is likely worse. Happier people are more likely to participate in pushto-web surveys: we showed that 34% of people who completed the 2020 panel follow up reported 'all or most of the time' when asked how happy they were in the past week in 2016 whereas only 20% of those who declined the follow-up reported the same. Therefore, the reported decline in happiness is among a group of people biased to be happy. We agree completely on the need for care and would go one step further and say that absent sufficient care - and it is unclear exactly what would be needed for sufficient care, especially when evaluating trends in religion - it would probably be better to exclude the 2021 GSS wave when focusing on change over time.

The results clearly highlight the importance of ongoing efforts like the GSS that seek to collect high-quality data in person. They also demonstrate that the GSS should continue to be funded for in-person data collection. Although more costly than web surveys, the in-person GSS is an invaluable resource providing more accurate information than other surveys. Just as the GSS was right to resist the common shift to phone surveys in the past (Ellis and Krosnick 1999), it has been right to resist the shift to the web even as other surveys are increasingly moving there (e.g., the ANES collects the majority of their responses on the web rather than in person) (Guggenheim 2019). That is not to say that web surveys cannot be valuable, especially for survey experiments concerned more with effects than overall levels and with treatments that cannot be replicated in person. But as the gold standard in social research generally and social change specifically, the GSS should continue collecting data in person (and continue to be funded to do so as it is a unique and irreplaceable tool in the social sciences).

Beyond the General Social Survey itself, this study indicates that the trend toward

relying on online surveys with lower response rates more generally may lead to the continual exclusion of certain segments of the population in social research. Here, we have focused on the exclusion of the intensely religious, resulting in an illusion of secularization. Future studies of religious change in the U.S. will likely show similar patterns if mode effects are not properly accounted for. But systematic non-response bias in surveys affects more than just religion and will likely lead to the misestimation of other social phenomena as well, particularly inequality, well-being, trust, knowledge, and connectedness along with the vast range of processes and characteristics related to these factors. Although in-person surveys with high response rates might be the ideal-case solution, given the reality of data collection costs, many surveys will be fielded online. A common method used to address issues with nonresponse is the creation of postratifiaction weights that account for demographic factors. If wanting to actually adjust for nonresponse, rather than just matching Census benchmarks for a few demographics, survey researchers should consider taking into account the factors, such as those we identified like trust and happiness, that predict whether people participate in surveys. Of course, making such an adjustment requires that the gold-standard GSS continue in-person data collection to provide baseline levels.
