## 1. Introduction


The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted economies and societies worldwide. One of the most critical ways in which COVID-19 has affected the economic activity and security of individuals has been through the impact of measures affecting the workplace: the International Labour Organization (2020) estimates that, as of April2020, m ore than 80% of the world's workforce was affected by full or partial lockdown measures. Many governments have recommended or even mandated remote work, thereby making the feasibility of adapting work arrangements to home settings a critical element in ensuring business and employment continuity during the COVID-19 pandemic (International Labour Organization, 2020).

Our article aims to study the antecedents of working from home (WFH) as a consequence of COVID-19 in a revealing societal case. We focus on Uruguay, a small Latin American economy with a relatively strong welfare state and a large public presence in the economy. Uruguay is a predominantly urban (95%) country, with one of the smallest Latin American territories and economies, dwarfed by its giant neighbors Argentina and Brazil (United Nations, 2019). Nonetheless, Uruguay occupies an enviable position among South American nations in terms of low levels of income inequality and poverty and high levels of political stability, as well as relatively effective digital inclusion policies (Nathan, Pardo, & Cabella, 2016; Robinson et al. 2020). Uruguay decreed a national health emergency on March, 13 th of 2020 (Decree N°93/2020), immediately after the first couple of COVID-19 cases were detected (International Monetary Fund, 2020). This swift governmental response, critical to mitigating the spread of COVID-19, has had several expected negative consequences for the workforce, with more than 250,000 individuals, out of 1.6 million active workers, apply for COVID-19-related partial or full unemployment benefits (Presidency of the Republic of Uruguay, 2020). As for the Decree N°93/2020, the government also called upon all public and private companies to develop teleworking strategies wherever possible. This mandate for public companies and recommendation for private ones became the first legal instance in which telework was directly addressed by Uruguayan governmental authorities, as no previous legislation for the practice had existed in the country. Based on national data from the Uruguayan Work Monitor of Equipos Consultores, a social research company in the country, we will assess a) the odds of working for companies that developed policies to enable WFH as a consequence of COVID-19, and b) the odds of WFH as a consequence of COVID-19. Building on the existing literature on teleworking, we will consider both organizational and individual level determinants of WFH in order to examine telework during the COVID-19 pandemic. Delving into the phenomenon of telework, particularly within the national and temporal settings in which our study takes place, can shed new light on its enablers and determinants, and fill existing gaps by bridging the potential-to-telework literature, more direct telework a ssessments, and parts of the digital inequalities' literature.


## 2. Literature Review



## 2.1. Origins and Definitions


The origin of the term telecommuting can be traced to a period almost half a century before the current pandemic, during the 1970 's oil crisis . It was initially presented as a solution to traffic congestion due to commuting a way of reducing the consumption of fossil fuels. Information and

Technologies (IT) companies also explored the idea in the 1970s. The attention paid to telework also increased as women entered the workforce in large numbers, adding to the number of commuters on the roads (Allen et al., 2015).

Despite the long history of teleworking, there is still no clear consensus on what exactly constitutes teleworking. For example, compared to other languages where there is an precise term suitable to define the phenomenon (i.e. 'teletrabajo' in Spanish), in English speaking countries, several terms exist to refer to the same phenomenon: telework, telecommuting, WFH, distance or remote work, ICT-mobile work, and virtual teams, just to name a few (Allen et al., 2015; Bick et al., 2020; Eurofound & ILO, 2017).  Building on seminal works and most extended legal definitions relating to the subject (i.e. Allen et al., 2015; Eurofound & ILO, 2017; Messenger, 2019; OIT, 2016), we summarize some key common elements of telework:

- i) it is a practice or form of labor arrangement adopted by a company either partially or in its entirety
- ii) it is embedded in a contract or employment arrangement (formal or informal)
- iii) it involves carrying out tasks that, while possible to be carried out within the employer's premises, are carried out elsewhere; and
- iv) these tasks are carried out through information and communication technologies (ICT).

The consensus ends here as, for example, the extent of the 'elsewhere' , and the minimum threshold for a work arrangement to be considered telework are contested (Eurofound & ILO, 2017; Messenger, 2019). Among several typologies that combine place and daily duration of working time, Eurofound and ILO's (2017) is one of the most useful. They classify telework into three groups: regular homebased teleworkers; occasional teleworkers or ICT-mobile workers with mid-to-low mobility and frequency of work outside the employer's premis es; and extremely mobile ones with high frequency of working in various places. Our study will be focused more specifically on what Buck et al. (2020) refers as pandemic-caused WFH. These are teleworkers who adopted this work arrangement only as a consequence of the COVID-19 pandemic; probably full-time teleworkers but just for the duration of Uruguayan lockdowns.


## 2.2. Minimal Conditions for Teleworking From Home in the 21st Century


Some of the critical factors necessary for teleworking from home are ICT's mediation of tasks that can be conducted remotely, as well as work roles which allow for reasonable levels of autonomy in the job or tasks (Allen et al., 2015). Equitable access to digital technologies, particularly the internet, requires hardware and connectivity as well as software and process implementation, all key barriers to teleworking in small and medium enterprises (Greer and Payne, 2014). Furthermore, both management and workers need to have a certain level of digital skills to sustain an adequate level of usage of specialized ICT, something which is severely unequally distributed in populations across the globe (ITU, 2018).

Not all jobs or occupations are suitable for telework. Physically portable tasks and/or ones that can be performed online are more easily adaptable to telework; this can be described as different occupations' 'ability to WFH' in Bick et al. (2020) terms. Numerous scholars have adapted occupational descriptions from the Occupational Information Network (O*NET) to administrative or official statistics data in order to estimate the ability to WFH in different occupations and national contexts. In Uruguay, where this study takes place, at least three other recent studies employed this method: de los Santos and Fynn (2020) and Guntín (2020). Although this method is useful and ability

to WFH is critical, we propose that, organizational and managerial determinants are similarly relevant for WFH before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic.


## 2.3. Worker-level Determinants of Work from Home


Research suggests that WFH has substantive costs and drawbacks, and that positive expectations with regards to telework do not necessarily translate into positive outcomes for all individuals alike. Temporal sovereignty appears to be the first and clearest advantage for teleworkers, according to current research. Theoretically, telework allows for a better balance of work and private life by easing the management of care and household tasks, saving commute time, and bypassing the limitations of traditional working arrangements (Allen et al., 2015; Eurofound & ILO, 2017; Messenger, 2019). Nonetheless, empirical findings signal that this is not always the case, as without clear regulations telework can increase the number of working hours compared to in-office workers, to the point of making the work-life balance even more difficult (Cléach, & Metzger, 2004). Partial and home-based teleworkers, compared to full-time and mobile ones, reap the most benefits from temporal flexibility (Allen et al., 2015; Eurofound & ILO, 2017).

Furthermore, teleworkers often outsource care while at home in order to carry out their jobs (Greer & Payne, 2014). This is a key arena where gender differences, which severely condition the division of the childcare burden, are expected to affect the teleworking experiences of male and female workers unequally (Alon, Doepke, Olmstead-Rumsey & Tertilt, 2020). With the closures of schools and daycares, the balance of private and working life became even more complex and unequal for parenting female teleworkers (Alon et al., 2020).

Mobility-related issues such as commute time, and the health-related benefits of avoiding long trips and traffic jams are some of the clearer advantages of teleworking from home (Allen et al., 2015; Eurofound & ILO, 2017; Messenger, 2019). Moreover, as mobility-based inequalities condition the access to in-office job opportunities, telework is expected to be even more appealing to workers living outside of large urban areas or working hubs (Hernández, Hansza and Massobrio, 2020)

The familiarity, skills, and attitudes of individuals towards the integration of technology in the workplace could also be linked to their likelihood of teleworking, as they would also be an indicator of their level of support towards other technological innovations. Younger workers and those with tertiary education have more positive attitudes towards technological innovations, even after controlling for job's characteristics (Dodel & Mesch, 2020).


## 2.4. Organizational-level Determinants and Deterrents of Telework from Home


Whereas  ability  to  WFH  approaches  focus  on  the  characteristics  of  individual s' jobs  and occupations  as  the  key  determinants,  there  is  consensus  in  the  literature  that  organizational-level characteristics can severely hamper telework, even when individual abilities to WFH optimal.

For example, Bi ck et al. (2020)'s study on changes in commuting related to COVID -19 among US workers provides strong evidence for this claim. They found that, prior to the pandemic, a large majority of on-site workers who switched to WFH after the pandemic attributed their on-site work in the past to their employers' preferences rather than their own desires .

In  this  sense,  supervisors  and  managers  -  especially  middle  management  -  are  the  main opponents of WFH within companies (Allen et al., 2015; Messenger, 2019).  Research has uncovered differences in management styles, cultures, and control preferences behind these barriers. For example, managers who exhibited  more  positive  attitude  towards  worker  autonomy  and  more  flexible  work

dynamics, such as abandoning the direct supervision of employees in favor of more indirect and goalsoriented approaches, were more inclined to enable WFH (Tapasco & Giraldo, 2020; Peters & Batenburg, 2015; Pyoria, 2011). As these organizational and managerial configurations tend to be more prevalent in sectors of the economy such as technology industry, education, and scientific and professional services, during WFH adoption before and, particularly, during the COVID-19 pandemic was comparatively higher in these sectors (Bick et al., 2020).

Furthermore, certain organizational capabilities related to WFH depend on the development of ICT infrastructure, cyber-safety measures, and digital skills (Pyoria, 2011; Tapasco & Giraldo, 2020) are also unequally distributed, favoring the same sectors of economy designated previously (i.e. see INE & DINATEL, 2015 for Uruguay), as well as being lees prevalent in small and micro enterprises, particularly in Latin America (Plottier, Stumpo & Rovira, 2013).

Lastly,  the  key  organizational-level  advantage  of  WFH  during  the  COVID-19  pandemic  is  its centrality for business continuity (Bick et al., 2020; WHO, 2020). As Bick et al. (2020), the increases in cost of on-site work due to health risks related to COVID19 predict this kind of employers' behavior; something which already occurred during previous large-scale health crises or natural disasters such as the 2009 'a swine flu pandemic (Messenger, 2019). That said, business continuity is not something usually considered by small companies in countries where such crises rarely occur. Fabeil, Pazim, and Langgat (2020), for example, argue that most decisions taken by small companies during COVID-19, even the ones related to WFH, were mainly ad-hoc and survival responses.


## 2.5. National-level Determinants and Deterrents of Telework from Home


The COVID-19 pandemic has made visible various national-level determinants of telework, mainly investments in ICT goods and services, and telework-related frameworks and regulations. Two types of national scale investments are critical. First, public and private investments in internet connectivity are necessary to enable digital services to be delivered to households during lockdowns (Robinson et al., 2020). Second, investments in the digital services necessary to undertake emergency public services - such as education, health and governmental interactions - are also critical for some economic sectors during the pandemic (Robinson et al., 2020).

Uruguay is probably an outlier among developing economies in terms of physical and digital infrastructure.  Most basic services are provided by the public sector. Moreover, recent public administrations have invested strongly in technological infrastructure, affordable fiber-optic enabled connectivity across the country, the development of digital government services, and the distribution of technological devices and services free of charge to all students and teachers in the public education sector (Robinson et al., 2020).


## 2.6. Telework in the Context of the COVID-19 Pandemic


The COVID-19 pandemic has brought about an increased interest in telework and WFH research, but aside from some excellent comparative surveys in the European Union, pre-COVID-19 teleworking data collection was uneven and presented problems of cross-national comparison (Eurofound & ILO, 2017; Messenger, 2019). Therefore, two different approaches to measuring telework in the context of COVID-19 prevail: the ability to WFH method, based on secondary data, and telework-specific surveys. Regarding the former, most of these studies appear to be associated with the evaluation of the economic impacts of social distancing measures adopted to stop the spread of COVID-19. For example, Dingel and Neiman (2020), using the O * NET to classify occupations,

classified the occupations in the US in terms of the ir 'teleworkability' and found that 37% of jobs could be plausibly done at home. These are jobs which are generally better paid than those requiring commuting, (Bick et al., 2020) . The application of Dingel and Neiman (2020)'s classification criteria t o 85 other countries reveals that low-income economies have a lower proportion of jobs that can be done from home. For example, de los Santos and Fynn (2020) and Guntin (2020) all apply a similar approach to Uruguay Their figures range from 47% of the employees with ability to WFH to 23%.

The second strategy, based on primary data, can draw on both company and individual worker-level data (Allen et al., 2015). For our purposes we will discuss only the latter, as the data collection strategy utilized was substantially more prevalent prior to COVID-19.  Incidentally, before the pandemic, regular teleworking was of low prevalence across the world, except for a few Nordic nations. On the other hand, teleworking seemed to be growing steadily in all countries (Allen et al., 2015; Messenger, 2019). Even considering the problems and differences in measurement, developed economies consistently reported higher levels of telework before the pandemic, doubling or tripling Latin American countries (Messenger, 2019; Eurofound & ILO, 2017).

In Uruguay in 2019 only six percent of surveyed internet users had teleworked in the prior three months, more than twice as many as had done so in 2010 (AGESIC 2020). Even so, data shows that teleworking was not a widespread practice in the country before March 2020. Both the ability to WFH and the direct inquiry approaches arrive at similar findings with regards to the unequal opportunity structure for WFH.

Finally, the national context and historical circumstances in which our data collection occurs makes the study very relevant to timely questions regarding the future of telework.  More than a year ahead of the beginning of the global pandemic, several studies of WFH as a consequence of COVID19 now exist. The largest and most accurate example was carried out by Eurofound in the framework of its Living, Working and COVID-19 (2020) survey on European residents. The survey showed that, on average, 37% of workers in the European Union member states began to telework after the onset of the pandemic. The levels of telework were related to the prevalence of various services and sectors in the national economies, the ones taking part in the knowledge economy. Divergences in WFH correlate with the nations' disparities in terms socioeconomic development . Bick et al. (2020) conducted a similar study for US workers, focusing on WFH before and after the COVID-19 outbreak. They found that WFH increased sharply and persistently after the outbreak, particularly in occupations with greater ability to WFH. The share of WFH only arrangements in their sample was 8% before the pandemic (February 2020), and rose up to 31% by May 2020. Barrero, Bloom & Davis (2021) conducted several online surveys assessing potential impacts of WFH in the US. They found substantial support for an increase in WFH arrangements after the pandemic ends, projecting that full WFH workdays will quadruple compared to pre-COVID-19 levels.

In Uruguay, the National Statistical Office (INE in Spanish) added a short teleworking question to the official household survey (INE, 2020). INE estimated that the percentage of workers who declared WFH regularly during the COVID-19 pandemic (19%) quadrupled previous figures (5%). These surveys are consistent with past findings as well as with private sector assessments such as the 'Work Monitor' survey (Bericat & Acosta, 2020), on which we will base the following analysis.

In sum, the context of our study, namely Uruguay, is a developing economy with relatively low levels of pre-COVID-19 WFH. In addition, teleworking is particularly concentrated among particular social groups and occupations in Uruguay, as compared to European countries and the US . Because of the social distancing measures and regulations that came into effect following COVID-19, WFH became more of a necessity than a choice for most, but not the only alternative nor the option

by default. The government increased the coverage and reduced the requirements for partial or full unemployment benefits, as well as creating specific COVID-19-related ones. In addition, whereas WFH was encouraged, the central government did not mandate it (Presidency of the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, 2020).

Our work will advance WFH/telework research by integrating these two levels into a more comprehensive framework by studying: a) the presence of company policies to enable telework from home as a consequence of COVID-19, and b) teleworking from home as a consequence of COVID-19. ## 3. Method



## 3.1. Data


Our analyses are based on data from the Work Monitor, an ongoing study conducted by the social research organization Equipos Consultores in Uruguay. The Work Monitor survey has been carried out bimonthly since 2014 covering people over 18 years old who reside in the country and own a cell phone. In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic the Work Monitor 's wave, conducted on the weekend of the 21 st and 22 nd of March, changed its collection and sampling strategies due to the social distancing limitations in place that reduced the company's call -center capabilities. The COVID19 wave consisted of a web survey based on a non-probability sample using advertisements on the social networks Facebook and Instagram for its distribution. Sample size was of 1110 cases and respondents were Uruguayan residents over the age of 18. Our study, however, is based on a subsample of employed individuals, which amounted to 847 cases. Data was weighted by age, sex, region, educational level and activity condition based on the Continuous Household Survey of the INE. The questionnaire gathered information on respondents' socioeconomic position, job placement, job satisfaction and links, along with a set of practices that sought to measure changes in work organization, incidence of telework due to COVID-19, workers' perceptions of the impact of the pandemic on work, and emotional well-being, among others.


## 3.2. Measures


## Dependent variables

COVID-19-related teleworking policies. Employed individuals were asked if the company for which they worked the most hours had taken a series of measures for at least some of their workers as a consequence of COVID-19. Our first dependent variable referred to 'The possibility to work from home through telework'. Responses were recoded as follows: 1 for 'yes', and 0 for 'no' and 'does not apply'.

Working from home as a consequence of COVID-19. Employed individuals were asked if they were 'currently working from home remotely, or teleworking'. Response categories consisted of 'yes, as a

consequence of COVID19', 'yes, I was teleworking before COVID -19 (and not as a consequence of the pandemic)' and 'no'. We recoded the question into a dichotom ous variable wher e 'teleworking as a consequence of COVID19' was coded as 1, and everything else as 0.

## Controls

- - Sociodemographic controls. Age was specified as a continuous variable, whereas sex was recoded as a binary variable where 'male' was coded as 1. The geographical place of residence was recoded as 1 for individuals living in Montevideo, the nation's capital, which has close to half of the country's population, and 0 for individuals residing in all other localities.

## 3.4. Analytical Strategy


To test our hypotheses, we fitted multiple logistic regressions. This technique was selected primarily due to the nature of the dependent variables. Contrary to school-based studies, workrelated surveys such as ours targeting  individuals seldom collect organizational data from organizations as part of an additional level besides individual responses, and they are therefore inadequate for generating multilevel units. Given the lack of multilevel data, we were forced to leave aside multilevel models (Cameron & Trivedi, 2009). For respondents employed by an organization, our study uses respondent-reported information about the employer to test organizational-level hypotheses. Consequently, the analysis deals with determinants which correspond to different levels of aggregation without adequate data for hierarchical modeling, nor information to control for the potential scenario were multiple employees work in the same organization. Whereas this is clearly a limitation, this is not unprecedented in the literature of WFH studies (i.e. see Bick et al., 2020) and there are some techniques to correct the potential biases arising from it. As recommended by other quantitative researchers, we corrected our regressions estimates  using clustered standard errors, which the literature indicates as the adequate correction when observations may be randomly sampled but the explanatory or treatment variable (COVID-19 related teleworking policies in this case) is measured at a higher level than the outcome variables (Nichols & Schaffer, 2007; McKenzie, 2017) . 1

Finally, as H7 involves assessing potential indirect effects of sector of activity mediated by COVID19 related teleworking policies, we conducted mediation analysis for logistic models. As diverse techniques often yield differing results (Grotta & Bellocco, 2013), three different methods to compute the mediation will be used to assess the existence of indirect effects: STATA's user -written commands 1) khb based on Breen, Karlson & Holm, 2018 and Kohler et al 2011; 2)ldecomp based on Buis, 2010; and 3) med4way based on Bellavia & Valeri (2018). Results will be considered valid only when at least two procedures signal statistically significant indirect effects, counting as  partial or full mediations (Rucker et al., 2011).

## 5. Discussion


Our article studies shifts in working practices ensuing from  COVID-19 measures. In developing economies, the advent of COVID-19 lockdowns and social distancing measures forced some companies to allow some of their workers to WFH to ensure business continuity. We find, that in a distinctively revealing national setting, namely an unequal but politically stable country with a centralized government, one of the strongest welfare states in Latin America, and almost non-existent WFH before the pandemic, differences in telework are associated with a combination of sectoral, organizational, and individual-level factors.

Moreover, as the adoption of WFH during the COVID-19 pandemic was largely unplanned and abrupt, it has highlighted both pre-pandemic differences across organizations in terms of preparedness, technological investment, and management practices, as well as differences across individuals in terms of their capacity to telework. Adoption patterns might have been different, had WFH been gradually diffused over time outside of an emergency situation.

We fitted several multivariate regression models predicting a) the odds of working for organizations that developed COVID-19-related teleworking policies for at least some of their workers, b) the odds of WFH as a consequence of COVID-19. One of the key findings of our study is that the employers' commitment to take measures to enable teleworking is the strongest predictor, at any level, of the likelihood of individuals to telework during this national emergency. Conventional wisdom holds that the main determinants of teleworking during the pandemic stem almost exclusively from the nature of jobs themselves. This article expands the traditional understanding of telework determinants by showing that individual-level attributes of workers as well as organizational and managerial features of the employer are joint contributors to the likelihood that a given worker adopts teleworking during the pandemic.

Nonetheless, according to the responses of individual workers, not all businesses had the same incentives or capacities to take such actions. Differences in company size and sector of economic activity also matter. Preparedness to enact WFH in the short-term and having higher shares of employees with ability to WFH, appear to both be critical factors enabling or impeding the swift implementation of teleworking-related policies within organizations. Working in certain sectors had a twofold effect on both the chances of developing policies, and on teleworking per se. Whereas in some cases the effect on the sector of activity over the chances to WFH was direct, in others they were mediated by the development of telework policies. This pattern appears with regard to the professional, scientific and technical activities sector, and the communication, transportation and storage sector.  This pattern could indicate that organizational and managerial choices in these sectors play particularly strong roles in determining telework arrangements.

Our findings also provide evidence of the role that governments and state investments can play to encourage telework, or at least to further the conditions that favor a smoother transition from in-office work to WFH during national emergencies. In the context of a small, statist, and politically centralized economy like the Uruguayan economy, most public services are provided by government monopolies. Moreover, due to Uruguay's welfare -state tradition, the government had made significant nationwide investments aimed at modernizing and democratizing government through the

use of ICT, as well as the integration of ICTs across all levels of the educational system. The chances of working for a company that had developed teleworking policies as a consequence of COVID-19 almost doubled for public servants, even after controlling by sector of activity and size of the company. The executive branch's order to telework in the public administration appears to have been successful, at least in the beginnings of the pandemic (Presidency of the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, 2020).

Regarding individual factors, neither gender nor proximity to the capital city had a statistically significant effect on pandemic-related telework. Nevertheless, we think neither factor should be discarded as a potential teleworking antecedent. For example, gender-based teleworking disparities are intrinsically linked to childcare and other domestic economic inequalities (Eurofound & ILO, 2017), a disparity that the COVID-19 pandemic severely intensified (Alon et al., 2020). On the other hand, the geographical distance-to-job measure available was very basic and did not reflect distance-to-work inequalities within the capital, which have already been discussed in the literature on Montevideo (see Hernandez et al., 2020).

On the other hand, age was a statistically significant predictor of WFH, as younger generations, ceteris paribus, are more likely to be teleworking in the wake of COVID-19. We argue that this is a consequence of cohort-based digital inequalities. In other words, younger workers tend to be more familiar with technological innovations and perceive such advancements to have had a positive impact in their job life compared to older workers (Dodel & Mesch, 2020). Improvements in individual and household-level digital inequality measures are required to further advance this line of research, proven to be critical in both telework and potential-to-telework literature.

Human capital was by far the strongest individual-level predictor of WFH due to COVID-19, which is in line with all existing ability to WFH and telework literature (i.e. Allen et al., 2020; Bick et al., 2020; Guntin, 2020). Nonetheless, our findings provide a more nuanced understanding of how educational attainment as operationalized by tertiary education versus lower educational attainment, interacts with organizational-level determinants.

All else equal, higher levels of human capital have a statistically significant effect on teleworking only when COVID-19-related teleworking policies are in place. Working for companies that developed COVID-19-related teleworking policies proved to be a statistically significant predictor, with or without high levels of human capital. Nonetheless, its effect on WFH was substantially stronger when individuals had tertiary education. These results are in line with Buck et al. (2020)'s finding that the ma jority of US workers' changes in commuting practices during the pandemic were caused by the temporary lifting of prior commuting mandates relating to daily on-site working, not just their personal preferences.

We argue that, as a whole, these findings inform the risks of assessing telework exclusively based on individual-level determinants of the ability to WFH. It also highlights the risks of overlooking the interactions of organizational and individual determinants. Organizational support is critical for the existence of WFH arrangements and can be considered a quasi-necessary condition for effective telework to occur, even when occupational attributes such as familiarity with ICT and ability to WFH are favorable to telework.


## 5.1. Limitations and Future Research


Whereas survey-based estimates of telework incidence often coincide with official statistics as in this case, our study utilizes a survey based on non-random sampling. Our study also had the constraint common to most population surveys set outside the work environment: organizationallevel data was provided by workers, partially reducing its quality, and hindering the creation of

multilevel models, which are the ideal techniques to analyze this type of phenomenon. National statistics offices could provide this type of information to further advance the assessment of aggregate-level determinants and the proportion of explained variance accounted for by each level.

Lastly, we should insist on distinguishing the WFH during the COVID-19 pandemic from WFH in a post-COVID-19 world. In the first place, several workers and employers are expected to have had their first teleworking experiences during the pandemic under extraordinary circumstances. They had little choice but to work from home, despite their lack of experience and the potential for disruption because of forced homeschooling of children and the suspension of childcare services outside the home. (Bericat & Acosta, 2020). These are not ideal conditions for WFH. It is hoped that post-COVID19 telework can unfold under more auspicious circumstances. Further research should focus on differentiating the sources and consequences of emergency versus regular telework, as well identifying the disparities which companies and individuals continue to face vis-a-vis WFH.  In line with Barrero et al. (2021), we expect that partial-time WFH or hybrid arrangements will grow in prevalence as the frequency and intensity of WFH has a great impact on the well-being of workers and their satisfaction with telework as a whole (Allen et al., 2015; Eurofound & ILO, 2017).

## Introduction


In January 2021, nearly one year following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a mandate requiring all people in the United States to wear face masks on all 'conveyances into and within the United States' (CDC 2021). Acting on scientific evidence suggesting that mask wearing can help curb the spread of COVID-19 (e.g., Cofas et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; see also: Jefferson et al., 2008) -- and in response to several high-profile altercations between transit passengers and employees over mask-wearing policies (Schaper 2021) --  newly-inaugurated President Biden issued an executive order urging the CDC to take action to slow the spread of COVID-19.

The CDC's ability to issue this mandate was made possible by powers enumerated to the Department of Health and Human Services (of which the CDC is a subsidiary) under the Public Health Service Act of 1944. These powers include not only the ability to declare a public health emergency in the face of threats from infectious disease, but to take 'such action as may be appropriate to respond to the public health emergency' (42 USC 247d), and to 'prevent the spread of communicable diseases' (42 USC 264a). Actions the CDC could take to accomplish these goals included, per the statute, 'inspection, fumigation, disinfection, sanitation, pest extermination and destruction of contaminated animals and articles'  (see also: HHS 2021).

In the months that followed the mask mandate, however, the CDC's powers to regulate health behavior on public transit drew significant legal scrutiny. At the heart of these legal challenges were questions about whether the CDC's powers under the Public Health Services Act included the aforementioned actions like fumigation, disinfection and sanitation, or were limited to those actions. In Spring 2022, a US District Court judge in Tampa, Florida decided in favor of the latter. The judge reasoned that while the CDC is empowered to take action to disinfect and sanitize, she argued that this authority ought to only apply to physical surfaces; i.e., that preventing the spread of pathogens through physical touch fell under the CDC's purview, while respiration did not (Kamarck 2021).

The Biden administration's decision to appeal the Tampa Court's ruling could have dramatic consequences for the CDC's regulatory authority. If the case appears before the Supreme Court, a ruling in favor of the Tampa decision could severely restrict the CDC's ability to issue regulations that address the spread of communicable disease beyond physical surfaces. The fate of CDC's regulatory authority is, as of this writing, unclear. However, amending the 1944 Public Health Service Act to clarify that the CDC does indeed have broad regulatory authority could help to circumvent these legal challenges.

Codifying CDC regulatory authority, of course, is theoretically more likely if lawmakers feel they have an electoral incentive to take action on this issue and maintain and/or bolster the CDC's powers (Mayhew 1974; Stimson MacKuen, & Erikson 1995; Lax & Phillips 2012; Wlezien & Soroka 2016). Correspondingly, we aim to better understand: (a) the degree to which the public is broadly supportive of CDC regulatory authority, (b) whether some Americans are more supportive of this authority than others, and (c) the conditions under which Americans skeptical of CDC regulatory authority might be convinced to abandon their previously-held beliefs.

We theorize that while most Americans support the CDC's regulatory powers, opposition is likely elevated among self-identified ideological conservatives. We believe this for two reasons. First, conservatives are more likely than liberals to harbor anti-expert attitudes (Oliver & Rahn 2016; Motta 2018; Merkley 2020), and - to the somewhat-limited extent that ideological preferences are grounded in policy preferences (Converse 1964)  - to favor a small role for the federal government in American political life (Ellis & Stimson 2012; Kinder & Kalmoe 2018), including on health-related issues, e.g., Aitleiva & Park 2019). Second, as we review in detail shortly, we suspect that conservatives are more receptive to elite political messaging that takes aim at undermining CDC authority. Correspondingly, we also ask whether efforts to remind Americans - particularly those on the ideological right - of the agency's central role in keeping Americans safe from infectious disease might boost support for the CDC's regulatory role. This may be especially effective messaging for conservatives, as self-identified conservatives tend to be more sensitive to pathogen-related threats (O'Shea et al., 2022).

Consistent with our expectations, we find that while most Americans support the CDC's regulatory authority, self-identified conservatives are significantly less likely to do so. However, in a survey experiment where we manipulate the presence (vs. absence) of information from the CDC's website outlining the agency's role in responding to the COVID-19 pandemic, we find that self-identified conservatives are significantly more likely to favor increasing CDC regulatory authority when reminded of the agency's central role in addressing pathogen threats. Additionally, we replicate both results when swapping ideological preferences for partisan identification, and provide evidence that all observational results hold in nationally representative survey data.  We conclude by discussing the implications of this research for health communicators and policy practitioners facing escalating political and legal attacks.


## A Review of the CDC's Regulatory Power


The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) serves as a national public health leader and is responsible for 'developing and applying disease prevention and control, environmental health, and health promotion and … education activities … to improve the health of the people of the United States' (CDC 2022a). As an operating division of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the CDC plays a primary role in disease prevention in the United States and is at the forefront of international efforts to combat disease (CDC 2022b). Statutorily, much of the CDC's regulatory power in the area of infectious disease comes from Section 361 of the Public Health Services Act which was passed in 1944. The Act stipulates that the Secretary of HHS -- who delegates authority to the CDC -- is responsible for regulations 'necessary to prevent the foreign and interstate spread of communicable diseases' (Shen 2021).

Critically, there is considerable legal tension over the scope of this power. One concern is the extent to which the enforcement of Section 361 may be in conflict with state police powers under the 10th amendment (McCusky 2016; Nolan and Lewis 2018). Control over infectious disease is nowhere enumerated as a federal power under the constitution and, as such, could be construed as as falling under states' right to provide for the health and safety of their citizens (McCusky 2016; Nolan and Lewis 2018). Additionally, tensions have mounted throughout the COVID-19 pandemic over whether Section

361 should be interpreted broadly or narrowly. While a narrow interpretation would argue that only quarantines should fall under the CDC's purview as necessary to prevent the spread of disease, the CDC under the Biden administration has taken a broader view - using the statute to justify CDC rules about masking and moratoriums on housing evictions (Shen 2021).

These rising tensions have been exacerbated by the politicization of public health over the course of the pandemic, internal strife at the CDC, and the politicization of attitudes toward scientific experts in the United States (Motta 2018; Bandler 2020; Sharfstein 2021). Combined, these forces have sown discord in public faith in the CDC, necessitating research on public attitudes towards the CDC and strategies to improve public confidence in the institution.


## The Theory


In general, Americans tend to place at least some amount of trust in federal public health authorities, including the CDC (Kowitt et al., 2017; Duffin 2021). However, while most Americans see some role for the CDC and other federal health agencies in responding to public health emergencies, observational survey research also documents an ideological asymmetry in support of the CDC.

For example, a YouGov poll conducted at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic in July 2020 found that whereas 44% of self-identified liberals place a 'a lot of trust' in the CDC, just 15% of conservatives feel the same way (Jaimungal 2020). These asymmetries are not limited to the COVID-19 era, as they mirror results from academic research documenting sharp ideological divides in CDC trust (e.g., Hamilton & Stafford 2020), and trust in the scientific community more generally (e.g., Gauchat 2012), prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. They also mirror the the results of other YouGov Surveys (e.g., Orth 2022), academic studies (e.g., Hamilton & Safford 2021), and public opinion research (e.g., APPC 2022) documenting sharp partisan asymmetries (which tend to be highly correlated with ideological preferences; see Bafumi & Shapiro 2009; Ellis & Stimson 2012; and Kinder & Kalmoe 2018) in public trust in the CDC.

What is less clear, however, are the reasons why self-identified conservatives express greater levels of distrust in the CDC than self-identified liberals.

There are several reasons why we might expect distrust in the CDC to be elevated on the ideological right. For example, self-identified conservatives are more likely than liberals to distrust scientific experts (Oliver & Rahn 2016; Motta 2018; Merkley 2020), which has been shown to be correlated with opposition to evidence-based policy-relevant views regarding vaccination (Callaghan et al., 2021; Motta 2021; Motta et al., 2021; Farhart et al., 2021), prosocial behaviors aimed at stopping the spread of infectious disease (Motta & Goren 2021; see also Merkley  & Loewen 2021), and a wide range of other topics (Motta 2018; Merkley 2020; Callaghan & Motta 2020). As the CDC is comprised of individuals with educational/vocational training in medicine, epidemiology, and public health (among other specialties), insights from work assessing conservative distrust of scientific expertise could be vital to explaining a lack of faith in the CDC on the ideological right.

Moreover, self-identified conservatives tend to be more likely to favor a limited role for the federal government across a variety of policy domains (Ellis & Stimson 2012; Kinder & Kalmoe 2018). This includes the role that the federal government plays in overseeing public health (Aitleiva & Park 2019). Preferences for limited federal government intervention in matters related to public health and wellbeing might help to further explain the partisan asymmetries in CDC attitudes documented above.

We suspect, however, that accounting for conservatives' anti-expert and limited government preferences does not offer a full explanation of the ideological differences in support for the CDC. Instead, we contend that the contemporary political context - specifically, anti-CDC communication from high-profile Republican elites during the COVID-19 pandemic - might also play a crucial role in shaping conservatives' CDC attitudes.

Consider, for example, the Trump administration's relationship with the federal health bureaucracy. Federal investigations made public in Spring 2021 revealed that former Trump administration officials took action to, as Representative Clyburn (D-SC) put it, engage in a 'persistent pattern of political interference in the nation's public health response to the coronavirus pandemic.' (Mendez 2021) These more-covert actions mirror the Trump administration's antagonistic rhetoric and policy action (Dyer 2020; NEJM 2020).

For instance, Trump appointed Scott Atlas as a special medical advisor to the president, who advocated for making no effort to contain the spread of COVID-19; at odds with CDC policy recommendations (Romo 2020). Trump also placed his former campaign staffer Michael Caputo -- who advanced 'deep state' conspiracy theories regarding the motivations of government scientists -- as the top spokesperson at the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC (Huang 2020).

Former President Trump himself often made claims that undermined the authority of federal health officials. In addition to clashing with government scientists about the utility of unproven and potentially-dangerous treatments for COVID-19 (Mahase 2020; Madanay, McDevitt, & Ubel 2022), the president amplified calls for removing former NIAID director -- and, arguably, the public face of the government's COVID-19 response -- Anthony Fauci from his post (Behrmann & Santucci 2020). Former President Trump also pressured former CDC director Robert Redfield to 'clarify' (i.e., modify) statements he made regarding the severity of the COVID-19 pandemic to more-closely align with the former president's comparatively lower levels of concern (Smith 2020). The former president's comments and actions mirror his longstanding opposition to scientific consensus, and penchant for promulgating scientific misinformation, on issues related to climate change, vaccine safety, and more (Motta 2018; Yamey & Gonsalves 2020; Thorp 2020; Broniatowski et al., 2020).

As the standard bearer of the Republican Party, and one of the most identifiable figures in American politics, it may be the case that the former President's words play a unique role in promoting the prevalence of anti-CDC among other GOP elites (Dress 2022), but distrust of the CDC on the ideological right throughout the mass public.

Throughout and following his time in the White House, conservatives tended to place high levels of trust in the former President (Dugan 2018; Enders & Uscinski 2021; Bowman 2021). Consistent with insights from the study of source credibility (e.g., Berinsky 2017; Benegal & Scruggs 2018; Sylvester et al., 2022), it may be the case that conservatives hold negative attitudes toward the CDC not only because they distrust scientific experts and prefer a smaller role for the federal government, but because they accept the former president's anti-CDC rhetoric and policy action.

Of course, we recognize that negative views toward the CDC are not unique to the ideological right. Self-identified liberals may, for example, take issue with recent CDC actions,  such as the loosening of recommendations regarding mask wearing and social distancing in schools and other public spaces (Stone & Huang 2022) in late Summer 2022. Because liberals have tended to express greater concern about the pandemic's public health risks  and have been more willing to adhere to CDC-recommended social distancing and mask wearing guidelines (Gadarian et al., 2020; Rulsch et al., 2021), some may have perceived these actions as not going 'far enough' to stave off the COVID-19 pandemic. Still, we think that while liberals may disagree with individual decisions that the CDC might make, their comparatively higher levels of trust in scientific authorities should lead them to draw a more-nuanced distinction between opposition to specific CDC policies and views toward the institution itself.

Bearing these points in mind, we hypothesize that:

H1: Self-identified conservatives should be significantly more likely than self-identified liberals to express opposition to the CDC's regulatory powers, holding constant anti-expert attitudes and support for limited government.

Next, we recognize that an emerging body of research characterizes conservatives as significantly more 'pathogen sensitive' than liberals (e.g., O'Shea et al., 2022). This means that when the threats of infectious disease are made salient, conservatives (vs. liberals) should be more likely to use this information to inform their political and policy related judgments (see: Schaller & Park 2011; Arøe et al., 2020). In application to CDC attitudes, this raises (we think) a fascinating possibility.

On the one hand, because conservatives tend to be more pathogen sensitive, highlighting the central role that the CDC plays in curbing infectious disease threats may be particularly effective at increasing trust in the CDC on the ideological right. On the other hand, however,  it could be the case that even the CDC's ability to respond to infectious disease is not sufficient to overcome the influence of anti-expert attitudes, limited government preferences, and political contextual considerations in shaping CDC opinion.

Correspondingly, we ask:

RQ1: When presented with information highlighting the role that CDC regulatory powers play in responding to infectious disease threats, will ideological conservatives become more likely, less likely, or neither more nor less likely to hold positive views toward the CDC compared to those conservatives who were not exposed to this information?


## Data & Methods


Analytic Strategy. We test these expectations via two sets of analyses. First, we test Hypothesis 1 by constructing a multivariate ordered logistic regression model that regresses an ordinal indicator of respondents' CDC attitudes (see: Measures) on ideological conservatism, limited government attitudes, anti-expert views, and several demographic controls. If we detect an effect of ideological conservatism that holds independently of these other factors, we believe this provides evidence in favor of Hypothesis 1. Note that we avoid the possibility of experimental contamination effects (which we describe shortly) by restricting models to include individuals not shown experimental treatment materials highlighting the many roles that the CDC plays in responding to public health crises.

Second, we assess the effects of providing conservatives with information about the role that the CDC plays in responding to pathogen threats by randomly assigning half of our survey respondents to read a short passage containing this information prior to answering questions about their attitudes toward the CDC. Additional information about our experimental design can be found below (see: Figure 1).

Correspondingly, we construct a multivariate ordered logistic regression model that regresses an ordinal measure of CDC attitudes on Americans' ideological preferences, a binary indicator of whether or not respondents were exposed to read this 'treatment' information, and the interaction of the two. If we find that self-identified conservatives are significantly more likely to hold positive views toward the CDC when exposed to the treatment materials, we will have reason to suspect that highlighting the CDC's central role in responding to infectious disease concerns can improve trust in the CDC on the ideological right.

Note that these models do not include additional control variables (unlike those described above). This analytical choice is consistent with best practices in the literature; offering a parsimonious modeling approach, contingent on successful randomization across potential treatment effect confounds (e.g., Mutz 2011). Correspondingly, we note that, per randomization checks available in the Supplementary Materials, experimental treatment assignment was distributed equally across all covariates presented in Table 1. Thus, we opted not to include potentially-extraneous terms in the model used to estimate experimental treatment effects.

Data. Data for this study come from a demographically representative sample of 5,483 US adults conducted via Lucid Theorem from June 24-28 2022. Lucid used quota sampling procedures to selectively invite individuals from its large online opt-in panel to participate in this study by targeting demographic representativeness on the basis of respondents' age, race/ethnicity, educational attainment, household income, and partisan identification. A full comparison of our sample's demographic makeup to nationally representative benchmarks from the US Census is available in the

Supplementary Materials. As we show in the Supplementary Materials, our data closely mirror these demographic benchmarks.

Before discussing the operationalization of our primary outcome and independent variables, two points about the use of online, opt-in survey data bear mentioning.

First, we recognize that demographic representativeness on observable factors is no guarantee that the results derived from online opt-in panel surveys match those derived from formally-representative probability data. Nevertheless, we believe that the use of Lucid data is appropriate for studying the dynamics of trust in the CDC for at least three reasons:

- 1. Data from Lucid have been shown to not only closely resemble demographic benchmarks derived from probability surveys of the American public, but across a wide range of political attitudes; including political ideology, which we study in the present research (Coppock & McClellan 2019).
- 2. Relatedly, Lucid data have been employed widely in both the observational (e.g., Callaghan et al., 2021; Motta 2021a; Kreps et al., 2022) and experimental (e.g., Motta 2021b; Kreps & Kriner 2021; Sylvester et al., 2022) study of health policy and politics, and have been shown to produce estimates of policy-relevant health attitudes (e.g., vaccine hesitancy) that mirror results derived from nationally representative data from the American National Election Study (Motta 2021).
- 3. Third, as this study contains an experimental component, we note that Lucid studies have been shown to replicate well-studied experimental effects, both prior to and throughout the COVID-19 pandemic (Coppock & McClellan 2019; Peyton et al., 2021).

Taken together, we think that points #1 and #2 demonstrate strong evidence in favor of the idea that the political and health-related attitudes we measure via Lucid's online opt-in panel data are likely similar to those that we would otherwise observe in formally representative data. Moreover, as our study includes a survey experimental component, we think that point #3 provides additional assurance that the results we observe should be likely to replicate in formally representative studies. Collectively,  this research provides additional assurance that the political dynamics we hope to study in this piece are likely to mirror the results we might otherwise obtain in formally-representative surveys.

We also recognize that several survey methodological studies (e.g., Ternovski & Orr 2022) have raised concerns about respondent attentiveness on the Lucid platform. Low engagement can introduce random, or - more problematically - systematic error into the results obtained from survey research (Krosnick 1991).

Correspondingly, we exclude inattentive respondents from our analyses by: (a) limiting analysis to only those respondents who correctly answered a simple attention check (note that full question wording is available in the Supplementary Materials), and (b) excluding from analysis those who may have 'rushed' through the survey by completing it in less than one third of the anticipated completion time (i.e., 5 minutes, for a 15 minute survey).

Importantly, given the central explanatory role of political ideology in this study, some might ask whether or not conservatives were more likely to be excluded from analysis due to low engagement with the survey (e.g., non-compliance with a survey pertaining to science and medicine; avoiding engaging with stimulus materials pertaining to the CDC). This would pose a potential problem for interpreting the results of our experimental study, as treatment effects we might observe on the ideological right would be limited to a subset of particularly-attentive conservative respondents.

In analyses presented in the Supplemental Materials, we detect ideological asymmetries in exclusion from analysis, but not on the ideological right . Instead, we find that self-identified liberals were somewhat more likely to be excluded from analysis than conservatives (on a seven-point ideological scale scored to range from 0-1 [see: Measures]; M incuded = 0.50 , M excluded = 0.37, ∆ ~ 0.12, p < 0.01). We also note that respondents were more likely to be classified as inattentive if they self-identified as men (vs. women), self-identified as Black (non-Hispanic) or Hispanic, had lower incomes, and/or were younger. Please refer to Table SX for additional information.

Measures. The primary outcome variable in this study is a measure of the extent to which Americans favor expanding, contracting, or making no changes to the role that the CDC plays in 'responding to public health crises.' Respondents could indicate that the CDC's role should be increased (decreased) either greatly or somewhat, or indicate that its role should be 'kept about the same' on a standard five-point Likert scale. Full question wording information is available in Figure 1.

Additionally, prior to answering this question, we randomly assigned half of respondents to read a short passage summarizing the role that the CDC plays in responding to public health crises. Specifically, after presenting all respondents with information about the political and legal challenges to CDC authority taking place in Spring 2022, half of respondents were the shown the following text; which we adapted from CDC-provided information about its role in responding to the COVID-19 pandemic (see: https://www.cdc.gov/budget/documents/covid-19/CDC-247-Response-to-COVID-19-fact-sheet.pdf).

This information is provided in full in Figure 1. An indicator of whether or not respondents were exposed to the additional information about the role that the CDC plays in responding to health crises serves as the primary explanatory variable in the experimental portion of our analyses.


## Experimental Results


Having documented that ideological conservatism is strongly associated with negative views toward the CDC, we conclude our analyses by considering whether providing information about the role the CDC plays in responding to public health threats increases support for the agency on the ideological right.

Table 2 presents the results of the interactive models described above. We present this information in two ways. Column 1 presents linear treatment effects derived from a model that treats conservatism as a single indicator of ideological self-identity. Recognizing that treatment effects may be heterogeneous with respect to the strength of Americans' ideological attachments, Column 2 allows for non-linear treatment effects by interacting each point on the seven point scale with treatment group assignment (omitting the strongest self-identified liberals as an analytical reference category). For ease of graphical interpretation, we calculate interactive effects with the untransformed (i.e., ranging from 1-7, rather than 0-1) measure of political ideology.

In Column 1, we detect a negative (B = - 0.07) and statistically significant (p = 0.03) interactive effect of treatment group assignment across levels of political ideology. Column 2, however, offers important contextualization to this point. There, we detect statistically significant treatment effects at just one level of the seven-point ideology measure; i.e., for strong conservatives (B = - 0.62, p = 0.01). This implies that the effect of our treatment may be limited to the approximately 10% of our sample who identify as 'extreme conservatives.'

Collectively, the results presented in Table 2 offer strong, preliminary evidence that exposure to information about how the CDC's regulatory powers enable the agency to respond to infectious disease threats is capable of improving support in the CDC on the ideological right; particularly among the strongest self-identified conservatives.

## Robustness Checks


Although Americans' partisan identities and ideological preferences are strongly correlated with one another (Bafumi & Shapiro 2009), we nevertheless recognize that these are conceptually distinct constructs. As some may be curious to know whether or not partisan identity exhibits a different pattern of effects from those documented with political ideology throughout this piece, we replicate all analyses presented thus far by swapping the self-reported ideology measure for a measure of partisan identification.

In analyses presented in the Supplemental Materials, we find that self-identification with the Republican Party is, much like conservative ideological preferences, significantly associated with decreased support for the CDC (B = 0.31, p < 0.05). We also find that both the linear and non-linear estimation of our experimental treatment effects hold when swapping ideology for partisanship. Specifically, our experimental treatment effects are again associated with more-positive feelings toward the CDC for Republicans (B = -0.05, p < 0.05); especially those who strongly identify with the Republican Party (B = -0.47, p < 0.05). These results suggest that our results are not sensitive to using ideological conservatism as a measure of political attitudes, and likely extend to right-leaning preferences more generally.

Additionally, we recognize that some readers may express concern about the use of online opt-in survey data to draw conclusions about the role that political ideology plays in motivating negative views toward the CDC. Although our data closely approximate Census benchmarks on several observable demographics, it may nevertheless be the case that self-identified conservatives in our sample differ from conservatives in the population in ways that we do not observe.

Consequently, we replicate several key findings presented in this manuscript using nationally representative data from the American National Election Study. Although the ANES did not include experimental treatments analogous to our own, it nevertheless contains measures of (a) attitudes toward the CDC -- specifically, a 100 point feeling thermometer capturing the extent to which respondents feel positively (100), negatively (0), or neutral (50) toward the CDC -- and (b) all covariates included in Table 1. Additional information about these data and measures can be found in the Supplementary Materials.

There, we again find that -- even after accounting for the effects of anti-intellectual attitude endorsement (B = -11.43, p < 0.05) and feelings toward the size and scope of government (B = -16.21, p < 0.05)  -- ideological conservatism is associated with approximately a three degree decrease (B = -2.51, p < 0.05) in positive feelings toward the CDC.  These results suggest that the effects of political ideology documented throughout this piece are unlikely to result from differences between our online opt-in sample and more-representative surveys of the general public.


## Conclusion


Given the heightened salience of the CDC and its role in curbing the spread of COVID-19 during the pandemic, we expected that most Americans would be supportive of the CDC's regulatory powers. We found this to be the case. However, we also expected ideological conservatives to be more opposed to CDC regulatory authority in light of prominent Republican rhetoric criticizing the CDC (H1). Our results support this expectation: self-identified conservatives are significantly more likely to oppose CDC regulatory powers, even when accounting for the influence of anti-expert attitudes and support for limited government.

Importantly, though, we found that opposition to CDC authority on the ideological right can be reduced by providing Americans with information about the CDC's role in combating COVID-19 during the pandemic; i.e., by, at least in theory, making an effort to capitalize on conservatives' tendencies to be more sensitive to pathogen-related threats, and reminding them that the CDC has power to address these threats. More specifically, we find that support for CDC regulatory powers increased among the strongest conservatives who were randomly exposed to this information in the context of a survey experiment  - meaning that the treatment was effective among those most likely to be unsupportive of the CDC.

Our work has important implications for the federal government's ability to respond to ongoing and future communicable disease threats.. To increase support for the CDC and the important role that it plays in combating disease, promotion strategies should be targeted towards conservative Americans who are the most likely to hold low levels of support in the institution. Critically, our experimental findings suggest that simply highlighting the actual work that the CDC does could be an effective strategy for increasing CDC support, especially among strong conservatives. Investing resources in this kind of promotion campaign could prove critical to reducing politicization of the CDC.

That said, our study is not without limitations. First, as we noted above, our sample relies on an online opt-in panel for recruitment. We take several measures to address this issue, including excluding from analysis  'low quality' survey responses and replicating all observational analyses in nationally representative data. Still, we recognize this remains a potential limitation of our work. Second, we employ just one messaging strategy aimed to change attitudes toward the CDC. We recognize that other approaches to increasing support for the CDC  may yield different results, or they may be comparatively more effective among other groups beyond strong conservatives. We urge future research to expand upon the messaging strategy employed here.

Finally, and perhaps most importantly, we note that data limitations prevent us from assessing two of the theoretical mechanisms proposed in this piece; i.e., the extent to which elite GOP rhetoric might motivate conservatives opposition to CDC authority, and the effects of pathogen sensitivity on receptivity to our experimental treatments. While we believe that these theoretical mechanisms are well-justified, and while our analyses provide evidence consistent with each of these expectations, we do not test them outright. We look forward to future research that makes an effort to further unpack the psychological mechanisms underlying the effects documented throughout this piece.

Despite these limitations, we nevertheless think that this study advances our understanding of public attitudes towards the CDC. We show that independent of attitudes towards the size of government or attitudes towards expertise, conservatives hold lower levels of support for the institution. Importantly however, by highlighting the important work that the CDC does to combat disease, we may be able to mitigate negative attitudes towards the CDC, especially among strong conservatives.

## THE PERFECT LOLITA: SHŌJO AESTHETICS AND AFFECT


Lolita is a way of living. I think it is a life, someone's way of living, a principle of thinking. To put loving kawaii things at the forefront, to live under a selfcreated rule to which one applies the things that one finds kawaii. I think that is what would be called in Japan a Lolita. (Chisato 2010)

In this quote by Tokyo-based Chisato, it is apparent that Lolita is about more than just clothes. Interviewees see it as a way of life, a philosophy or a feeling close to the heart with an emphasis on understanding and advancing a personally defined concept of beauty that includes  a  sense  of  kawaii  deviating  from  mainstream  tastes.  Lolita  combines  an appreciation of kawaii with shōjo sensibility. Shōjo is 'not so much a literal description of any individual girl's consciousness' as a 'cultural logic' accessible to writers and artists and the people who enjoy these works (Mackie 2010: 199). Since its beginnings in the Meiji era, shōjo has provided a repository of images, tropes, feelings and motifs accessible to generations of girls and women. It provides a valuable resource and common language for certain kinds of expression in literature and art that convey senses of liminality and distance  from  the  conventional  gender  lines  of  Japanese  society  in  covert  feminist resistance (Dollase 2003: 740).

In examining the aesthetics, ideas and objects that inform the concept of 'girl' in North America, Swindle argues that:

Many of the objects of girl culture are not products at all, but aesthetics (pink, polka dots and poodles), relationships (girlfriends and crushes), movements (dancing and hopscotch), rhetorical modes (gossip and diary writing) and affects (most notably, happiness). (2011: 30)

Objects create collectives of feeling, sensing and experiencing, bringing people together

through shared affect. Aside from understanding girl as a discursive subject, a gender and an age position that moves in linear fashion towards the position of woman, girl as an affect comprises an embodied knowledge and experience that can be revisited and recalled. It may both circulate unconsciously and be self-consciously employed to engage in feeling girl (Swindle 2011: 19).

Some Lolitas describe Lolita clothing as being fuwafuwa, expressing something fluffy and bouncy, like the visual movement and tactile feeling of a bell-shaped Lolita skirt with a full petticoat underneath as it sways with each step. Other words are sometimes paired with fuwafuwa, such as hirahira (flutter), a notion that is also important in describing shōjo feeling in Honda Masuko's influential essay about shōjo aesthetics ([1982] 2010). Hirahira is found in the movement of objects like ribbons and frills that 'flutter in the breeze as symbols  of  girlhood'  (Masuko  [1982]  2010:  20).  Hirahira  imagery  transcends materialistic  realities  and  crosses  'sensual  boundaries',  blurring  the  border  between  the ordinary and the imagined (Masuko [1982] 2010: 35).

Both words invoke a sense of movement, and Honda describes shōjo as 'rejecting the intervention of everyday logic' in its alogical and unworldly nature as it sways and drifts ([1982] 2010: 36). The construction of girl and shōjo is ongoing and incomplete in the sense of Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming-'.

Girls do not belong to an age group, sex, order, or kingdom: they slip in everywhere, between orders, acts, ages, sexes; they produce n molecular sexes on the line of flight  in  relation  to  the  dualism  machines  they  cross  right  through.  (1987:  277, original emphasis)

Becoming-girl  is  movement  that  constantly  traverses  borderlines  of  childhood  and adulthood,  innocence  and  disenchantment,  naivety  and  wisdom.  Becoming-girl  has  a liminal status that allows a girl the ability to break off from established molar identities and to travel in the in-between yet also makes her a subject for concern and control. She may be  perceived  as  dangerous,  deadly  and  delinquent  or,  even  worse,  frivolous  and unimportant. However, there are also people who borrow the mask of the girl or shōjo so that they too can try to move like she does.
