## Introduction


Learning a foreign language in a classroom setting occurs through a communication/interaction process between non-native speakers and the teacher who teaches them a foreign language. During this  communication  process,  the  learners  may  reach  different  proficiency  levels  of  the  Target Language (TL). To solve the potential problem of a low level of English language proficiency, teachers may code-switch to the learners' native language to help them understand the meaning and structures of the target language to save time and lead to more effective learning (Cook, 2001).

This shift is called Code-Switching (CS); it alternates between the native and target languages. As Maftoon and Amjadiparvar (2018) indicate, this alternation is considered predetermined result of mastering different language varieties and has always been seen in multilingual communities. However, whether or not the students' native language should be used to teach a foreign language has been controversial for several years.

Some applied linguists advocate the use of Target-Language-only (TL-only) instruction in EFL classrooms.  Inspired  by  Krashen's  (1982)  comprehensible  input  hypothesis  that  calls  for  the exposure of EFL learners to comprehensible TL input, linguists consider this strategy optimal for ensuring the EFL/ESL learners' acquisition of the foreign/second language (Hall & Cook, 2012). They emphasise that it offers more exposure to the target language, primarily when the TL is taught in the First Language (L1) contexts and facilitates learning for beginners. However, the TL-only instruction ignores the scientific fact that a previously learned language is present in the learners' minds, even when the focus is on the TL (Kroll, Dussias, Bogulski, & Valdes-Kroff, 2012).

Researchers who have advocated alternating use of the first and target languages indicate that the teachers perform various useful functions in the classroom that facilitate language learning (e.g. Collier & Thomas, 2017). Language instructors who favour bilingual instruction through CS believe it is a valuable and effective tool that fosters beginner-level learning. For example, some researchers argued in favour of CS over monolingual instruction for the sake of course-content clarity, indicating that students are more attentive and less confused when teachers instruct them through CS (e.g. Al-Enezi, 2018).  Others have developed instructional approaches in this regard, such as translanguaging, multilingual teaching, and plurilingual education (e.g. Piccardo, 2013).

Reading comprehension plays a critical role in the acquisition and learning of any foreign language, and it is considered the scaffolding for the remaining language skills. It helps language learners  to  construct,  contextualise,  and  comprehend  any  received  information  in  the  target language.  EFL  teachers  tend  to  employ  different  instructional  strategies  to  teach  reading  and facilitate reading comprehension in language classrooms. One of the critical factors that directly affect reading comprehension is the number of known words in a reading text. When all the words in a text are unknown to the reader, comprehension cannot take place. In the case of EFL learners, the  CS  strategy  discussed  above  might  be  useful  in  this  regard,  especially  for  beginners.  EFL learning is also affected by emotional factors (Mehmood, 2018; Rahim & Chun, 2017). This study examines how female EFL college reading comprehension beginners perceive the effects of CS versus TL-only instruction on their learning and affective sustenance in the classroom. It also aims

at examining their preferences for CS or TL-only instruction used by their teachers and the reasons behind their preferences.


## Literature Review


Researchers are increasingly interested in understanding the perceptions of teachers and learners regarding CS versus TL-only instruction. For the Saudi K-12 stage, Al-Nofaie's (2010) study showed the positive attitudes of both teachers and students toward using Arabic, students' L1, as a  clarification  tool  in  English  classes.  Although  the  teachers  preferred  using  the  native language for specific functions, they were reluctant to use it or allow students to use it. Also, AlShammari (2011) examined the purpose of L1 use at two technical colleges in Saudi Arabia. It also examined Saudi teachers' and students' attitudes toward the L1 role in the EFL classroom. The results showed that L1 is used for clarification purposes. The study concluded that L1 judicious use  in  EFL  classrooms  is  beneficial  for  language  learning  processes,  increasing  learners' comprehension  of  new  vocabulary  and  complex  concepts.  Gulzar  and  Al-Asmari  (2014) investigated students' and teachers' awareness of CS dynamics at Saudi Taif University English Language Center. They found that although both Saudi EFL teachers and students share similar, relatively positive attitudes toward the use of CS, they have different views on the effectiveness of different functions of CS. Furthermore, they also have considerable differences in their awareness of CS and the idiosyncratic customs of CS in Saudi EFL university classrooms.

Additionally, Al-Mohaimeed  and  Almurshed  (2018)  investigated  Saudi  EFL  female preparatory-year college students' attitudes and perceptions toward L1 use in English classrooms. The results show that while beginner students hold positive perceptions of CS in English classes, advanced  students  have  a  negative  attitude  toward  it.  Al-Enezi  (2018)  also  examined  Saudi Arabian medical students' attitudes toward CS to Arabic in their classrooms. The results of the study revealed positive attitudes toward CS over TL-only instruction. Although most of them are aware  of  the  benefits  of  using  TL-Only  instruction,  they  viewed  CS  as  more  preferred  for understanding  the  course  content.  Moreover,  they  contended  the  idea  that  CS  might  lead  to confusion in the classroom and showed increased respect for teachers who use CS. The study called EFL teaching and learning leaders to incorporate CS positives in EFL classrooms.

One year later, Mahdi and Al-Malki (2019) examined Saudi EFL learners' attitudes toward using  in  EFL  classrooms.  They  also  explored  CS  functions  for  teachers.  The  results  showed negative perceptions about CS. However, the results revealed that the teachers used CS to aid lowlevel learners and streamline various language activities. Maguddayao and Rosario (2019) also examined the views of 41 students and five teachers on CS in ESL classrooms in the Philippines. The  results  revealed  that  teachers  preferred  it  since  it  helps  them  in  classroom  management, curriculum access, and building interpersonal relations with the students. The students also had positive attitudes toward CS, considering it an effective teaching strategy to simplify complex concepts and enhance interaction. Moreover, Narayan (2019) examined the role of CS to L1(Fiji Hindi) in Fijian ESL classes and whether it enhances classroom interaction. The results revealed that  CS  is  a  promising  strategy  for  language  learning.  The  study  called  for  enlightening  ESL teachers about the benefits of CS.

Aoyama (2020) recently investigated Japanese high school students' use of CS to L1 during their  communicative ESL activities and their attitudes toward such use. He used a survey and

classroom  observation.  The  results  revealed  that  all  the  participants  partially  used  CS  during communicative activities. The results also showed they used it for five speech functions (adding information,  providing  feedback,  asking  for  help,  giving  equivalences,  and  explaining  using metalanguage). The study called EFL Japanese high school teachers to benefit from CS in their classrooms to accompany communicative teaching strategies. More recently, Tubayqi and Al Tale' (2021) examined the attitudes of Saudi female EFL beginners at Jazan University and their two teachers toward CS to Arabic in EFL grammar classes and the reasons for using and avoiding CS. The study also presented some of the CS functions in EFL grammar classes. The study revealed that despite having positive attitudes toward MT in EFL classes, students and teachers are also aware of the  adverse  effects  of  its  overuse.  In  addition,  the  results  revealed  that  teachers  and students use MT to perform a variety of tasks in the classroom that facilitate teaching and learning.


## Rationale and Research Questions


As seen in the literature above, although several studies have explored the attitudes and perceptions  of  learners  about  CS  in  Arab  and  non-Arab  EFL  classes,  most  of  them  have concentrated on the attitudes of teachers and students toward CS and its functions. This study adds to the previous literature by deeply investigating the impact of both CS versus TL-only instruction on female   reading comprehension beginners' learning and affective sustenance in the classroom. It compares their perceptions of the impact of CS versus TL-only instruction on their learning and affective sustenance in the classroom, attempting to present useful insights about the impact of CS versus  TL-only  instruction  on  learning  and  psychological  states  of  reading  comprehension beginners.

Thus,  based  on  the  concepts  of  CS  and  TL-only  instruction,  the  researchers'  teaching experiences, and the related literature, this study addresses Saudi EFL learners' perceptions of the impact of CS versus TL-only instruction on their learning of reading and their affective sustenance in the classroom.

The specific research questions are as follows:

- 1 What are the perceptions of female Saudi EFL reading comprehension beginners at King Khalid University about the impact of CS versus TL-only instruction on their learning and their affective sustenance in their reading comprehension course?
- 2 What are the differences between beginners' perceptions of CS versus TL-only instruction in their learning and affective sustenance in their reading comprehension course?
- 3 What are the beginners' preferences of CS versus TL-only instruction in their reading classes and why?


## Method


This study adopts a mixed-method research design to give an in-depth report of the participants' perceptions of CS versus TL-only instruction as teaching strategies and their effect on learning and affective sustenance in the classroom.

## Participants


The context of this study was a female Saudi university campus during the first semester of 2019-2020. Data were collected from 52 female Saudi EFL Level One reading comprehension students. Access to male students was not possible since they were taught by male teachers on a separate campus because of cultural constraints. The participants (aged between 18 and 20) were students in the English department, which offers a bachelor's degree in the English Language. They constitute a convenient sample since they were taught by one of the researchers during that semester. They were studying listening, speaking, reading comprehension, and writing English language skills. The researchers chose this specific level because they were novices at studying reading comprehension Level One. The prescribed book was the Well Read 1 Student Book: Skills and Strategies for Reading Student Guide series (Pasternak & Wrangell, 2007). Some of their teachers were bilingual, and others were native speakers of English who did not speak Arabic.

As shown in Table four above, most of the students (eight per cent) favoured being taught through CS, while only a few (20 per cent) felt they needed to be taught only in the target language. Those interviewees who preferred CS think that it is a helpful strategy since they are beginners and do not have adequate language competency to comprehend the target language easily. They added that a reading comprehension course needs the teacher's CS since it depends on comprehension. As beginners, it takes time to comprehend any received information in the target language, especially unfamiliar words. One of the interviewed students had studied the same course before with a teacher who did not code-switch. She reported that it was easier for her to understand the course with code-switching.

The few interviewees (20 per cent) who reported that they prefer TL-only instruction think that it is essential to be taught only in the target language as language learners. When the teacher speaks only in the TL, they think that she will give the learners an excellent opportunity to listen to and learn the TL and provide learners with the necessity of learning the language. They added that using TL will help them learn it faster and start thinking in that language. The interviewees added that it is their responsibility as language learners to translate and learn the TL. They believe that the  teacher  should  use  only  the  TL  in  the  classroom,  considering  her  to  be  a  source  for  that language.


## Discussion


Regarding the first part of the first research question about the perceptions of the participants about  the  impact  of  CS  versus  TL-only  instruction  on  their  learning,  the  results  revealed  that generally, most participants believe that CS in class makes it easy for them to understand the course and learn difficult concepts and new vocabulary. These findings support Al-Shammari's (2011) conclusion that college beginners see CS as helpful in understanding new vocabulary and difficult concepts. They are similar to the previous studies that consider CS a beneficial tool in accelerating learners' language learning process, particularly for beginners, to whom most of the skills are new (Aoyama;2020;  Maguddayao  &  Rosario,  2019;  Mahdi  &  Al-Malki,  2019;  Narayan,  2019; Modupeola, 2013).

As for the second part of the first research question about the perceptions of the participants about the impact of CS versus TL-only instruction on their affective sustenance in their reading comprehension course, most respondents see CS as a strategy that gives them more confidence and  support  in  EFL  language  classrooms.  CS  helps  them  enjoy  the  lecture  and  makes  them satisfied, comfortable, less stressed, and feel less lost during the lecture. This finding supports Aoyama's  claim  (2020),  which  was  in  favor  of  CS  to  support  the  adoption  of  varying communicative  teaching  strategies.  As  a  result,  students  can  have  ample  opportunities  to  be engaged with communicative activities and produce the target language confidently.

Regarding the third research question about the beginners' preferences of CS versus TL-only instruction in their reading classes the reasons for their preferences, most participants prefer their teacher's CS over TL-only instruction to teach them reading skills. They reported that they are beginners and need the input to be more comprehensible to them. This finding goes with those findings  of  previous  literature  reporting  positive  attitudes  toward  CS  to  the  learners'  native language in EFL classrooms (Tubayqi & Al Tale, 2021;  Maguddayao & Rosario, 2019). This reasoning supports Krashen's (1982) comprehensible input hypothesis, in which he states that the TL input should be only one level above the learners' current level (+1) to be comprehensible to them. They also think that CS makes their language learning process more accessible with fewer psychological barriers, supporting Meyer's (2008) conclusion that 'the primary role of the students' L1 in the language classroom is lowering affective filters' (p. 147). It is natural and rational that using  the  mother  tongue  in  a  new  learning  environment  gives  positive  affective  support  to beginners.


## Conclusion


As seen in the above sections, EFL reading comprehension beginners' perceptions of CS as a  teaching  strategy  is  immensely  positive  compared  with  their  perceptions  of  the  TL-only instruction, which is highly negative. These findings indicate their need, as beginners, for a CS strategy  to  give  them  affective  support  in  the  classroom  and  help  them  understand  the  target language's new vocabulary and difficult concepts. Such findings will contribute to the field of English Language Teaching (ELT) and be of use for language institutions decision makers who may consider adopting new regulations and policies in favour of CS as a clarification tool for language instruction.


## Implications, Limitations, and Recommendations


The  findings  of  the study  have  practical implications for teaching  EFL/ESL  reading comprehension. Based on these results, EFL teachers might code-switch to EFL beginners' native language to create a more encouraging learning environment and make the input that students receive  more  understandable  so  that  they  can  internalize  it  quickly.  However,  teachers  should remind the beginner students that this strategy is just to help them understand the new vocabulary and difficult concepts. They must concentrate on the target language, using the teachers' CS only to understand the target language. This study also recommends that EFL teachers be aware of their students' perceptions of CS and code-switch when appropriate.     The present study has some limitations that  should  be  addressed  in  future  research.  First,  the  study  was  conducted  on  two beginner classes of a reading comprehension course. To support or reject the study's findings, researchers  can  further  investigate  the  students'  perceptions  of  CS  versus  TL-only  as  an

## 1.1 Code-switching


According to Grosjean (2013, cited in Alkhresheh, 2015, p. 2), 'code-switching is the alternate use of two or more languages in the same utterance, and this can be in a form of a single word, or a phrase, or a sentence/s'. Also, Habtoor and Almutlagah (2018) stated that CS can occur even in language varieties. Additionally, Wardhaugh (2006, p. 101) mentioned that Gal (1988) defined CS as 'a conversational strategy used to establish, cross or destroy group boundaries; to create, evoke or change interpersonal relations with their rights and obligations. Code-switching occurs in conditions of change, where group boundaries are diffuse, norms and standards of evaluation vary, and where speakers'.

CS is identified among other language communication phenomena such as code mixing, borrowing, diglossia, etc. According to Wardhaugh (2006) CS and code mixing refer to the same linguistic phenomenon. He stated that 'code-switching (also called code-mixing) can occur in conversation between speakers' turns or within a single speaker's turn'. Wardhaugh (2006, p. 89) defined diglossia as 'a diglossic situation exists in a society when it has two distinct codes which show clear functional separation; that is, one code is employed in one set of circumstances and the other in an entirely different set'. Borrowing, on the other hand, refers to the process of morphological or phonological integration while CS is not based on the integration process of the words or clause from one language to another (Jalil, 2009) . 1

## Chapter 3: Methodology


This chapter presents the methodology that was adopted to achieve the goals of this current study. It provides a description of the participants, a review of how this study was piloted, and ways of data collection and analysis.


## 3.1 Study design and methods


This study was based on both quantitative and qualitative methods. I followed both Habtoor and Almutlagah (2018) and Novianti (2013)'s studies; Habtoor and Almutlagah (2018) investigated the occurrence of intra-sentential CS among Saudi females on Twitter using a quantitative approach, thus; my study investigated the occurrence of Arabic-English CS among KKU students on Twitter by utilizing a quantitative approach. Also, depending on a study conducted by Novianti (2013) on the reasons and types of CS on Twitter using a qualitative approach, my study looked for the types of CS appeared in chosen tweets on KKU students' Twitter accounts and examined the reasons of why KKU students used CS while communicating on Twitter by using a qualitative approach whereas the frequency and the percentage of each CS type and reason were conducted quantitatively.


## 3.2 Participants


The participants were 20 students who studied at KKU. Their ages were between 18 and 24. They were specialized in various fields: medicine, dentistry, nursing, and

media. All of them were able to communicate in English. English language is used as the main teaching language of these fields at KKU. The participants had Twitter accounts. Through KKU hashtags on Twitter, some of the participants' accounts were found and others were found through friend lists of these accounts. The accounts were chosen based on the following criteria:

- a. The account should be public in order to facilitate reaching tweets and contacting with the user.
- b. The user tweeted in both Arabic and English languages to ensure that the user was bilingual.
- c. The user should have an active Twitter account by looking at the time of tweeting and replying to other Twitter accounts (Alaslaa, 2018).
- d. The user should have at least one thousand tweets on his/her Twitter account in order to guarantee that the account is active on Twitter (Alaslaa, 2018).
- e. The user's account should indicate that the user was a KKU student and that appeared through involved KKU hashtags in the user's profile and tweets.
- f. The user's profile should show some personal information about the user, such as gender, college, major, and level (Alaslaa, 2018).

By applying the above six criteria to select the Twitter accounts of the participants, I chose 20 KKU students' Twitter accounts. The users are different in age, gender, major and level of education . Before collecting data, I obtained the permission of the 2 subjects via the direct message service on Twitter. The subjects participated voluntarily in this project.


## 3.3 Data collection


In order to collect the data for this study, there were two techniques that were utilized. First, in order to investigate the first and second research questions, the primary data was conducted from tweets of 20 KKU students' Twitter accounts. The researcher took 15 tweets from each Tweeter account that were tweeted during a year ago (from March 2018 to March 2019). The tweets were collected by using i-phone, particularly by taking screenshots of 15 tweets for each participant's Twitter account (Habtoor & Almutlagah, 2018) (see Appendix 1 for a sample of screenshots). The total number was 300 tweets from all Tweeter accounts of the participants. The screenshots of the tweets were saved on the phone to keep the data from deletion (Habtoor & Almutlagah, 2018). Second, in order to investigate the third question of this study, the secondary data of this study was conducted using an online questionnaire. The online questionnaire contained two parts. The first part was an open question and asked the respondents personal information about their names, username, major, level, and college. The second part was a question in the form of multiple choices (see Appendix 2 for the questionnaire). The respondents had the opportunity to choose more than one choice. The online questionnaire was sent to respondents via the direct message service on Twitter. This study was piloted before the main study was carried out; the results of the pilot study are examined in the next section.

## 4.2 Discussion


The findings gained from the quantitative and qualitative analyses of this current study are discussed in this section. Many Arabic-English CS tweets had been identified on Twitter accounts of KKU students. Depending on the results, the occurrence of the CS phenomenon between Arabic and English languages was proved on KKU students' Twitter accounts at more than half of the total conducted tweets. This result was expected as KKU students participated in this study are bilingual and the main teaching language of their majors, such as medicine, dentistry, nursing, and media, is English language. Thus, the first hypothesis, which states that the students at KKU CS between Arabic and English on Twitter, was supported by this result. Also, it was noticed that Arabic language was dominant and English elements were inserted in the CS tweets.

On the other hand, the most frequent type of CS used by KKU students on Twitter was intra-sentential CS. This was compatible with the findings of Habtoor and Almutlagah's study (2018). Then, the second frequent type of CS was inter-sentential CS, and the least frequent type of CS appeared in the tweets was tag switching. Therefore, the second hypothesis, which is the most frequent types of CS that occur among KKU students in their tweets are intra-sentential, inter-sentential, and then tag switching, was also approved by this finding. These findings were compatible to the results of the pilot study, too. In addition, these findings agreed with the studies of Novianti (2016), Al Heeti and Al Abdely (2016), Skujins (2017), and Yaseen and Hoon (2017) which proved that the types of CS occurred in the same order of the frequency of the CS types of this current study. This may be attributed to the insertion of a word from one language to the other and it was easier than creating a completed

sentence in two languages. On the contrary, the study of Sihombing and Meisuri (2014) provided a different order of the frequency of the CS types from this study. Regarding the grammatical types, Sihombing and Meisuri's study (2014) found the most frequent type was inter-sentential CS, then tag switching, and finally intrasentential CS. It also provided the dominance of the contextual types of CS. It showed that the metaphorical CS was dominant and then followed by situational CS.

Moreover, according to KKU students' responses to the questionnaire, the most frequent reason that motivated KKU students to CS between Arabic and English languages were the necessity of talking about a particular topic. Actually, KKU students posted their CS tweets in identified issues. For instance, they used CS in most tweets related to their studying and majors as medicine, dentistry, nursing, and media, tweets expressing their feelings, and some tweets in fashion. This may justify that the CS reason for talking about a particular topic was admitted by the majority of KKU students. Then, the reasons for the need to soften or strengthen request or command was the second frequent CS reason. KKU students might CS their language by using some expressions from another language to be more friendly and polite, such as using the word please in Arabic tweets. After that, the frequent use of the necessity of real lexical needs was attributed to the use of English language as a mean of teaching in such majors at KKU. They tweeted in Arabic and inserted some English words and expressions that related to their fields and cannot easily find compatible words to those expressions in Arabic language. Also, the necessity of repetition used for clarification was admitted as a frequent CS reason by KKU students for communicating effectively and accurately on Twitter as their most followers were Arabs. The reasons for quoting somebody else, intention of clarifying the speech content for interlocutor, excluding other people when a comment is intended for only

a limited audience, being emphatic about something, and interjection were the least frequent reasons for CS used by few KKU students. On the other hand, the reason for expressing group identity was never elected by KKU students as a motivated reason to CS their language on Twitter because they might reject other identities. They were not aware enough of the concept of identity.

## Chapter 5: Conclusion


This chapter ends this study by providing a conclusion and recommendations.


## 5.1 Conclusions


It cannot be ignored the significant role of social media in the world, especially in the Arab world. Understanding how Arabs utilize their language on these media to communicate with each other is a critical subject matter. It may help us to recognize many issues related to Arabic societies and language. However, CS is one of the apparent linguistic and sociolinguistic phenomena that are found among Arabs in a variety of social media networks. The use of CS on Twitter is not enough examined by bilingual Arabic speakers especially bilingual students of Arab universities. This understanding serves as the justification for conducting this study. The main aim of this study was investigated the occurrence of the CS phenomenon between ArabicEnglish among KKU students on Twitter. Also, it examined and identified the frequent types and reasons for CS found in selected KKU students' tweets. The data was 300 tweets collected from Twitter accounts of 20 KKU students and their responses to the online questionnaire. Then, the quantitative and qualitative analysis of the data was utilized to achieve the aims of the study. This study proved the occurrence of CS among KKU students on Twitter. In addition, the most frequent type of CS found in the selected tweets of KKU students was intra-sentential CS. Also, regarding the questionnaire, the most frequent CS reasons for KKU students

were the need to talk about a particular topic and the need to soften and strengthen request or command.


## 5.2 Recommendations


The findings of this current study are significant because it might enrich this field among Arab university. The current study investigated CS on Twitter among KKU students from a linguistic perspective. So, it is suggested to study CS among KKU students in the real context from a sociolinguistic perspective and cover a large sample. Also, it will be significant to study the relation between the teaching languages of different majors to the occurrence of CS. In addition, the researcher recommends studying CS on social media from linguistic and sociolinguistic perspectives among Saudi university students and comparing the findings as CS carries critical linguistic and social implications that will help to develop the higher education in universities generally as well to improve our understanding of Saudi university students.

## 'LOVING NATION' (AIGUO): SENTIMENTALISM AND PATRIOTISM


China  had  been  contending  with  aggravating  foreign  threats  and  national  crises  since  the  late nineteenth  century,  especially  after  the  first  Sino-Japanese  War  (1894-95),  when  Chinese intellectuals realized that print media could be an effective way to stimulate nationalist feelings. In an advertisement promoting New Fiction ( Xin xiaoshuo ), a leading literary journal founded by Liang Qichao in Japan in 1902, Liang listed the 'story of sentiment' (xieqing xiaoshuo) as one of the 'new fiction' genres aimed at 'evoking citizens' political thoughts and inspiring their patriotic spirit'  (Liang  [1902]  1997:  41-45).  A  Reformist  writer  even  argued  that  a  'story  of  romantic sentiment' should 'use strong emotions between lovers as a metaphor for one's heroic spirit in order to arouse readers' patriotic  mind' (Bo [1907] 1997: 229). Liang and  his  contemporaries viewed fiction as an integral part of the construction of a new national identity and the shaping of modern Chinese citizens, legitimizing the mingling of political consciousness of the nation and personal emotions in the late Qing 'new fiction'.

One of the earliest examples of such politically engaged 'story of sentiment' appeared in New Fiction in 1903, in a short story entitled 'Mr. Tang' (Tang Sheng), written by Pingdeng Ge, the pen name of Di Baoxian (1872-1939). Based on a news story published in a San Francisco Chinese-language newspaper, it tells a poignant story of Mr Tang, the son of a Cantonese merchant who grew up in San Francisco, and his beautiful American girlfriend named Yiniang, the daughter of a wealthy Chicago businessman. When China capitulated to foreign forces during the Boxer Rebellion of 1900 and was derided by American media, Tang feels so humiliated that he breaks up with Yiniang. Forced by her  father to marry  the son of a rich American  merchant, the girl commits suicide, leaving two suicide notes in which she expresses her loyalty to her beloved and bequeaths everything that she owns to Mr Tang (Di 1903). Although labelled a 'story of sentiment', 'Mr. Tang' is, ironically, a story intentionally downplaying romantic feelings while celebrating the triumph of patriotism over love. The hero's retreat from his interracial relationship is justified by his national pride and insistence on preserving his Chineseness. Modern readers may find little romance in this story as it vividly illustrates the moralization and nationalization of qing (emotion or sentiment) in late Qing fiction, endorsing Liang Qichao's idea of 'the subordination of citizen to state in a relationship that ensured the survival of the state' (Fitzgerald 1996: 88). Relating a

transnational romance between 'one from the old imperial nation' and 'one from the new world', the  narrator  nonetheless  posed  a  conflict  between  patriotic  sentiments  against  romantic  love. Meanwhile,  in  linking  Tang's  emotional crisis  to  military  failures  of  China,  Di  saw  the  social function of  love  stories  in  inspiring  people's  patriotic  passion  for  national  salvation.  Although there  seemed  to  be  a  lack  of  a  psychological  explanation  of  how  romantic  feelings  may  be sublimated into heroic spirits, stories of sentiment such as 'Mr. Tang' situated individual emotions within a broader political and social context, inextricably connecting one's private plight to public traumas, and romantic sentiments to nationalistic consciousness.

A nationalist narrative in the guise of a romance, 'Mr. Tang' is a confluence of the motif of dying for love-a dominating theme of Mandarin Ducks and Butterflies (yuanyang hudie pai, Butterfly  hereafter)  'sentimental  fiction'  (aiqing  xiaoshuo), 2 and  the  plotline  of  patriotism triumphing over love, both of which were developed further in 'patriotic stories' (aiguo xiaoshuo). As popular  fiction  genres,  'sentimental  fiction'  and  'patriotic  stories'  emerged  in  the  1910s  to espouse the new ways of expressing individual emotional life and nationalist concerns. With the commercial success of Xu Zhenya's (1889-1937) best-selling novel Jade Pear Spirit ( Yu li hun ), which  initiated  a  trend  of  Butterfly  'sentimental  fiction'  in  Shanghai  popular  media, 3 the intersection between patriotism and romantic love was dramatized acutely by the development of the  themes  of  'dying  for  the  country'  and  'dying  for  love'.  Applying  the  'sentimental-erotic tradition of Chinese literature' (Hsia [1982] 2004: 271) in a modern setting, Jade Pear Spirit relates an  agonizing  story  of  Platonic  love  between  He  Mengxia,  a  talented  yet  ill-fated  young schoolteacher, and a chaste, graceful widow named Bai Liniang. Tortured by their forbidden and hopeless love, the couple suffers excruciating pain and agony of both mind and body. Soon after Liniang dies for love, Mengxia participates in the Chinese Revolution of 1911, sacrificing his life in the battle of Wuhan. The narrator reminds readers that Mengxia is not only a frustrated lover but  also  a  'patriotic  young  man'  and  'an  unknown  hero  in  the  revolutionary  army'  who demonstrates that 'dying in the revolutionary war is dying for love' (Xu  [1913] 1991: 586-87). As Haiyan Lee points out, Jade Pear Spirit was 'the first modern articulation of the relationship between romantic love and heroism' (Lee 2007: 83). Envisioning war heroism and patriotism as a solution to personal crisis, the novel transformed a desperate lover into a national hero. Unlike the nationalism in 'Mr. Tang', which was affirmed through renunciation of love, in Jade Pear Spirit we see the exaltation of private feelings as an essential driving force for nation-building and as laying a foundation for the protagonist's patriotic duties and heroic deeds, signifying the narrative strategy of popular fiction that amalgamated sentimentalism with nationalism to foster a popular sense of nationhood. Such a sense of nationhood was widely and enthusiastically promoted by popular media as a common sense of patriotic citizens in the newly founded Republic of China.

'Mr. Tang' and Jade Pear Spirit were instrumental in introducing the dialectic between romantic  love  and  patriotic  sentiment  into  modern  popular  fiction.  'Mr.  Tang'  positioned  this melodramatic tension in a global context in an attempt to correlate polity with sentimentality in a gendered nationalist narrative, a point to which I will return later. By contrast, Jade Pear Spirit tactfully transfigured a frustrated love affair into revolutionary passion on the battlefield, and thus posited the psychological linkage between romantic and nationalistic sentiments. Soon thereafter a wave of 'patriotic fiction' emerged, coinciding with the rise of 'sentimental fiction' in popular literary  journals  in  the  mid-1910s. Although  the  earliest  story  to  be  labelled  'patriotic  story' appeared in Women's World ( Nüzi shijie ) in 1904,  most patriotic stories were published in popular 4 fiction magazines between 1915 and 1916, when anti-Japanese sentiment reached its height. The blooming patriotic fiction in popular press was evidently a response to the vehement nationalist

feelings triggered by Yuan Shikai's (1859-1916) acceptance of Japan's Twenty-One Demands and the  establishment  of  the  May  Ninth  National  Humiliation  Day  (wujiu  guochi)  in  1915.  On  25 February 1915, soon after Japan delivered the Twenty-One Demands to China, 'Free Talk', the literary supplement of Shenbao , launched the 'Patriotic Serial' (Aiguo congtan) column, originally aimed at publishing translated Euro-American patriotic stories but later including Chinese stories. The column was edited by Zhou Shoujuan (1895-1968), one of the most prolific and influential Butterfly  writers of  sentimental  fiction  of  his  time.  Entitling  these  stories  'For the  Sake of the Nation' (Wei zuguo gu), Zhou condemned the 'powerful neighboring country', and expressed his hope that 'knowing how westerners love their nations, we Chinese can follow their examples and catch up with them' (Zhou 1915a). The 'Patriotic Serial' column ran for three and half months, during  which  time  over  100  patriotic  stories,  both  translated  and  original,  were  published  by numerous Butterfly writers. Many of these stories were later collected and reprinted in a book entitled A Brief History of Patriotic Heroes  Aiguo yingxiong xiaoshi ( ). Published in 1917, it was promoted as one of the volumes in the 'One Thousand Literary Classics' book series by Shanghai Jiaotong Library.

A  number  of  translated  patriotic  stories  were  published  in  popular  fiction  magazines, seeking to imbue Chinese readers with a national spirit and direct the public imagination towards a national ascendancy. A major formulaic plot in these stories was the tension between private feeling and patriotic sentiment, or between 'dying for love' and 'dying for the country', a theme introduced in Jade Pear Spirit . One can readily discern such a dramatic conflict from story titles such as 'Loving Husband and Loving Country' (Aifu yu aiguo), 'Lover or Motherland' (Qingren yu zuguo yu) and 'Loving Wife and Loving Country' (Aiqi yu aiguo), all published in 1915 in The Saturday weekly.  The first two stories, translated by Zhou Shoujuan, shared a similar plot pattern. 5 The  heroine  from  England  faces  an  anguishing  dilemma  between  the  love  of  her  nation  and affection for her beloved, as unfortunately she and her lover belong to two combatant nations. The patriotic heroine eventually gives priority to her national loyalty. Since her patriotic action puts her lover's life at risk, she fulfils her love by committing suicide, thereby conjoining the ideals of 'dying for the country' with 'dying for love' (Zhou 1915b, 1915c). Recently, some scholars have suggested that these stories were likely Zhou's pseudo-translation, a cultural practice employed by Zhou Shoujuan that coalesced the imagination of the nation, the reconstruction of the exotic West, romanticism, aestheticized violence and ethical ideals (Pan 2011; Chen 2015). The ideal of love and patriotism was incorporated into Zhou's creation of a tragic female character who chooses patriotic sentiment over romantic feelings, and ultimately sacrifices her life for love.

Zhou Shoujuan was a major figure in contemporary literature promoting 'patriotic fiction' and popularizing this model of tragic love  versus patriotism through various cultural products, ranging from editing patriotic columns in newspapers to translating and writing patriotic fiction. The translated stories may have given an impetus to Zhou's writing of the short story 'Till We Meet Again' (Xing zai xiangjian), published in 1914 in The Saturday , which uses a similar structure of sentimentality. A British man in Shanghai named Fu Limen, a passionate lover who represents the  ideal  of  romantic  love  and  individual  freedom,  falls  in  love  at  first  sight  with  a  beautiful Chinese girl named Hua Guifang, who studies western letters in a missionary school, speaks fluent English and pursues freedom of love. As the story progresses, Fu is identified by Hua's uncle as the foreigner who shot Hua's father many years earlier during the Boxer Uprising in Beijing. Hua suddenly faces the difficult choice between love and vengeance. Like her western counterparts, and also as a Chinese citizen and a filial daughter, Hua decides to sacrifice her romantic love in favour of her filial and national duties. Before poisoning Fu, Hua assures her beloved that she will

love him forever and 'accompany him to the end of the world' (Zhou 1914). As I discussed earlier, 'Mr. Tang' introduced the subject of nationalism in interracial romance in a modern context by associating love with China's failure to resist western colonial encroachments. 'Mr. Tang' was not so much a love story as a patriotic story, wherein the romantic love and the heroine's 'dying for love' are completely overshadowed by the hero's nationalistic sentiment. In 'Till We Meet Again', however, we see that the development of the romantic relationship is situated firmly at the centre of the narrative, dramatizing the fatal encounter between love and moral/national obligations, all while adding to the story its distinctly tragic dimension. Zhou situates the transnational romance both against and within the context of foreign assault on China, underscoring the dilemma of love and patriotism.

As John Fitzgerald argues, the rise of patriotism in China was closely associated with the 'discovery of the personal self and of the heroic nation' in modern romantic fiction, in which 'the nation  was  put  forward  as  an  object  not  just  of  loyalty  but  of  affection'  (1996:  92-95).  The formulaic figure of the 'patriotic lover', notably in Xu Zhenya and Zhou Shoujuan's sentimental stories, was an imaginative synthesis of modern national martyrdom with romantic love, conflating the  two  seemingly  contradictory  notions  of  love.  On  a  popular  level,  this  model  of  'romantic patriotism' that mixed idealized romances, sometimes in exotic foreign settings, and patriotism in the  modern  national  discourse,  had  considerable  commercial  appeal  to  Chinese  readers.  The antithesis between the individual and nation evoked what Toming Jun Liu has called 'sentimental nationalism', a kind of nationalism shaped by a nation's culture, history, memory and past traumas (2001). Having their characters dying both for country and love, Butterfly writers illustrated the symbiotic  emotional  connections  between  sentimentalism  and  nationalism,  and  thereby  both justified and elevated sentimentality as a means of arousing public nationalistic feelings.


## 'SUBJUGATED  NATION'  (WANGGUO):  NATIONAL  IDENTITY,  GENDER  AND NATIONAL IMAGINARY


This  sentimental  nationalism  was  mediated  by  authors'  individual  and  collective  feelings  of national  humiliation,  which  shaped  their  perception  and  imagination  of  the  dynamic  interplay between individual and national identities. A particularly keen example of such interplay is found in the work of Di Baoxian. Setting the transnational romance against the backdrop of the invasion of Beijing, 'Mr. Tang' captured how a historical incident impacted on private life. An enthusiastic advocator of the reform movement led by Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, Di fled to Japan after the failure of the reform in 1898. When he returned to Beijing in the winter of 1900, Di witnessed the turbulence and chaos during Beijing's occupation by the western powers. At the end of 'Mr. Tang', Di quoted a lengthy commentary from an article by his friend Taiping Ke, a pen name of Ou Jujia (1865-1913), in which Ou denounces the manner of xenophilia (meiwai) prevalent among both the government and the public. Using the example of an extinct native Hawaiian tribe that fell into decline as a result of interracial marriage between native Hawaiian women and Caucasian men, Ou warns that China would be in a great danger, facing potentially extinction 'if the racial division was not enforced' (Di 1903). Similar comments can be found in Di Baoxian's essays that were serialized in Shibao , one of the most influential Shanghai-based newspapers founded by Di in  1904,  in  which  Di  provided  a  detailed  account of  the  appalling  atrocities  committed  by  the western powers, excoriated the xenocentrism and submission of officials and scholars in Beijing as shameless 'people who submitted to foreign invaders' (shunmin) and lamented the destruction of Chinese culture: 'There is no greater sorrow than a dead heart, and there is no greater pain than the humiliation of national subjugation' (Di [1914] 1984: 1-5).

With this perspective, we gain a richer understanding of  'Mr. Tang' and Di  Baoxian's rendering of  Chinese  identity  and  the  western  'other'  in  the  story.  The  American  girl  Yiniang represents private romantic love, eulogizing the power of love to transcend race and nation. She even assures her Chinese lover that she already considers herself Chinese, for the reason that both her heart and her body have belonged to a Chinese man. It is Tang's rejection of her love that leads to the tragedy; however, the hero is venerated for his patriotism and 'righteousness of saving the nation and preserving the race' (baoguo cunzhong). While Yiniang is a woman of feeling, Mr Tang is portrayed as a man of integrity and a true patriot, whose rejection of a marriage proposal from a wealthy American woman is evidence of his national allegiance and identity. Tang is filled with righteous  indignation  against  western  colonist  exploitation  in  China  and  racial  prejudice  in American news media, which leads to his decision to sever his emotional bonds with her and her family, even after she expresses her willingness to give up her 5American identity. In this sense 'Mr. Tang' may be read as a political allegory of China's colonized situation in expressing the author's inveterate anxiety about maintaining his cultural and national identity in times of national turmoil. Tang symbolizes the struggle of China for national self-determination, which, as implied by the story, requires the subordination of private emotions to patriotic concerns. To Di Baoxian, himself  an  eyewitness  of  China's  national  tragedy,  preserving  a  racial,  cultural  and  national identity was  a firm gesture of resistance to western  encroachment.  Therefore,  only by differentiating self and other, and building a modern self, could China resist foreign aggression and  achieve  national  salvation.  A  masculine  national  identity  thus  becomes  reinforced  and integrated into the imaginary national and racial identity. The shift of Tang's attitude towards a foreign woman from initial attraction to eventual repudiation was symbolic of Chinese writers' ambiguous attitude towards western modernity, perpetuating a gendered narrative of race, nation and politics.

As  Jing  Tsu  argues  convincingly  in  her  study  of  Chinese  nationalistic  discourse, victimization and humiliation, a shared cultural experience in early twentieth-century China, were important components of modern nationalism, particularly in constructing and articulating national and racial identities (Tsu 2005). The collective feelings of national shame were also embedded in Zhou Shoujuan's stories, and became a driving force for imagining a national identity through the rendering  of  the  western  'other'.  Hua  Guifang  in  'Till  We  Meet Again',  whose  surname  is  an eloquent reminder of her Chinese nationality (Hua means 'China'), is also a survivor of the Boxer Rebellion  of  1900.  When  persuading  Hua  to  kill  her  British  lover,  Hua's  uncle  revives  the traumatic memories of the death of her father and reiterates the moral causes of this vengeance: 'You must fulfill your filial obligation!' 'You are Chinese, and you must obey the orders of your elder!' It is worth noting that Zhou Shoujuan's father also died during the national calamity of 1900.  Zhou  later  wrote  about  'family  suffering  and  national  trouble'  (jiayou  guohen),  as experienced  by  Zhou  as  a  six-year-old  boy,  and  recounted  vividly  his  father's  concerns  of  a beleaguered nation and its times of trouble (Zhou [1917] 2015). In 'Till We Meet Again', the reader comprehends  how  Zhou  responded  to  the  trauma  of  national  humiliation  by  imagining  the antithesis  of  his  character's  individual  romantic  identity  (as  a  devoted  lover)  and  collective identities (as a filial child and Chinese citizen), and by reaffirming the latter.

The anxiety regarding national and racial extinction, a collective response to a series of national traumas generated by the colonial powers in recent Chinese history, was epitomized by the  imagination  of  'national  subjugation'  (wangguo)  in  popular  fiction.  In  Zhou  Shoujuan's patriotic stories, the traumatic experience became a source for imagining the sufferings and grief of 'slaves in subjugated nations' (wangguo nu). Zhou's very first short story 'Sorrow of a Falling

Flower' (Luo hua yuan), published in The Women's Times in 1911, manifested his first attempt to utilize this trope of wangguo. It tells the story of Miss Huang, a young woman studying in England, where she is treated with disdain and cursed as a 'slave of a subjugated country' and as belonging to  'the  most  despicable  race  in  the  world'. After  she  marries  an  Englishman,  she  finds  herself completely  isolated  and  living  in  ignominy,  and  ultimately,  she  cannot  endure  the  shame  and commits suicide.  An atmosphere of pervasive anxiety and agony was developed  in the story's psychic connection of Huang's sentimental self-image and the imaginary subjugation of China. Huang's  anguish  and  sense  of  inferiority  are  derived  from  the  shame  of  being  a  citizen  of  a conquered nation, although in reality China was not fully subjugated. Nevertheless, just like Mr Tang, Miss Huang's national identity is never imperiled: she insists that she is from China when she  is  mistaken  as  Japanese  by  foreigners.  In  her  suicide  note,  she  even  swears:  'Alive,  I  am Chinese; Dead, I am a ghost of Chinese' (Zhou 1911).

In his study of Shanghai modernist culture, Leo Ou-fan Lee observes that Shanghai writers' 'sense  of  Chinese  identity  was  never  in  question  in  spite  of  the  Western  colonial  presence  in Shanghai' (Lee 1999: 312). Indeed, from 'Mr. Tang' to Zhou Shoujuan's portrayal of interracial romance, we see that the protagonists' moral identity and integrity is not challenged as no matter how humiliated  they  feel,  they  never  feel  guilty  or  uncertain  about  their  national  and  cultural identity. In 'Mr. Tang', the American girl loses her national identity when she falls in love, because, in her view, loving a man is equal to loving his nation and culture. To the Chinese man, Mr Tang, however, his Chinese identity is uncompromising, endowing him with a strong sense of belonging and personal identification with his country. Similarly, in Zhou Shoujuan's 'Sorrow of a Falling Flower' and 'Till We Meet Again', the heroines' Chineseness is an important component of their modern identity. The western male 'other' in Zhou's sentimental stories, unlike the female 'other' in Di Baoxian's 'Mr. Tang', who is represented in a less confrontational manner, poses a potent threat  to  Confucian  social  ethics  and  national  sovereignty.  In  both  stories,  the  handsome  and amorous Englishmen fall in love with Chinese beauties and conquer their souls and bodies. Yet the female protagonists eventually awaken to fulfil their national responsibility by separating from their western lovers through revenge or suicide. In these stories treating the topic of transnational romance,  both  individual  and  national  subjectivity  are  testified  and  authenticated  through  the interface between the national self and the western 'other', whether female or male.

In the beginning of 'Sorrow of a Falling Flower', Zhou writes: 'With the blood and tears over falling flowers, I cry for my homeland that will be the second Korea'. Before Miss Huang hangs herself, she cries out:

My Chinese compatriots, listen to me: If you indulge in a dream life of the past, the day will come when you won't be able to be a slave even if you want to. The tragedy of the Jews and Poland mirrors the future of our nation (Zhou 1911).

China's defeat by western powers and Japan inspired a trend of historical fiction set in conquered nations in reaction to the institutionalization of shame and the rising public feelings of humiliation. As Rebecca Karl argues, Chinese intellectuals employed the slavery and wangguo tropes at the turn of the twentieth century to link metaphorically China's problem to modern colonization and imperialism, and to define the Chinese nation in a larger global space (Karl 2002a, 2002b). Korea, historically  a  tributary  state  of  China,  but  under  the  Japanese  occupation  since  1910,  drew particular public attention. Often told in a melancholy and mournful tone, sentimental stories about Korea's demise stimulated a strong sense of  humiliation among  Chinese readers, appealing to

readers through the interweaving of innermost despair and national anxiety. While intellectuals focused on the analysis of Korea's domestic crisis and Korea-Japan relations, popular writers were more preoccupied by individual tribulations as innocent people became forced to face catastrophic social and political upheavals.

'The Spirit of a Beauty' (Meiren hun) by Li Dingyi (1892-1964), a renowned Butterfly writer of sentimental fiction, represents an example of this trope of Korea. A rendition of historical facts,  nationalist  sentiment  and  sentimental  narrative,  'The  Spirit  of  a  Beauty'  manifests  how wangguo narrative accompanied the trend of sentimental fiction, and yet brought into focus the impact of national tragedy on personal life. In contrast to the uncomplimentary image of Queen Min  of  Korea  (1851-95)  in  Liang  Qichao's  political  essays  on  the  demise  of  Korea,  who  is depicted as an ambitious woman who 'usurped the political power of the state' (Liang [1910] 1999: 2193), Li describes her as a 'beautiful, intellectual, and resolute' woman who 'saw the decline of the  nation  and  aspired  to  renew  it'.  As  suggested  by  its  subtitle  'A Tragic  History  of  National Subjugation' (Wangguo canshi), the story was published  in New Journal of Fiction ,  a  popular fiction  magazine  edited  by  Li  Dingyi,  as  one  in  a  series  of  stories  about  the  loss  of  nations throughout the world. The  first  part of  the  story  focuses  on  Queen  Min's  cruel  murder  by  the Japanese,  and  the  subsequent  social  upheaval  and  suffering  of  ordinary  people.  Queen  Min  is portrayed simultaneously as a victim of military failure and foreign aggression, and as a talented, elegant, yet ill-fated, melancholy lady, a typical female protagonist in Butterfly sentimental fiction. Set in Korea's colonial period, it adopted the theme of victimization and national shame integral to the wangguo narrative of this period, reflecting Liang Qichao's vision of Korea as a warning to the Chinese government and people. It also calls special attention to individual suffering following national distress, a recurrent theme explored in Zhou Shoujuan's sentimental patriotic stories.

The second part of the story is narrated from the perspective of Miss Shen, a loyal maid of Queen Min and an eyewitness to the national tragedy. The author maintains a narrative focus on the political turmoil that Miss Shen experiences, and her sorrow, longing and spiritual encounter of Queen Min's soul after she returns to the palace. The reunion of Queen Min's spirit and her maid may remind Chinese readers of the poem 'The Song of Everlasting Sorrow' (Chang hen ge) by the famous Tang poet Bai Juyi (772-846), which recounts the tragic love story of Tang Emperor Xuanzong and his favourite consort, Yang Guifei. In fact, in his introductory comment, the author mentions 'Tianbao Palace lady' (Tianbao is a reign period of Emperor Xuanzong) to imply the analogy of the collapse of the Tang empire and Korea's  fall (Li 1915). Queen Min, 'the  most beautiful woman in the world', as depicted poetically in Li Dingyi's story, is reminiscent of Yang Guifei, one of the 'Four Beauties' in Chinese popular culture, on both emotional and aesthetical levels, suggesting China's emotional identification with Korea by virtue of being victimized by Japan's  aggressions.  Korea thus  became  an  object  of  reader  sympathy,  carrying  a  particularly sentimental charge to Chinese writers. It was on such grounds of national sympathy that Korea's past was projected onto the public perception of a future China. Korea was conceived of by popular writers as a shadow and a mirror of China and as a nationless 'other' in expressing their anxiety about losing China's identity.

Like Miss Huang in Zhou Shoujuan's story, Queen Min is emblematic of a nationalistic sense  of  humiliation.  Such  a  passionate  sympathy  towards  the  innocent  victims  of  national subjugation  was placed at the centre of the popular wangguo rhetoric.  In Chinese nationalistic discourses, women became the embodiment of victimhood, and thereby were often identified with the weakness of the nation.  The image of delicate and melancholic women of subjugated nations 6 simultaneously perpetuated the 'popularity of the image of victimized women' in modern Chinese

literature (Ko 1995: 4) and yet, as I argue, also formed the very core of the sentimental mode of patriotic  fiction,  whose  main  purpose  was  to  arouse  readers'  compassion  for  both  vulnerable women and the nations with which these women were identified. For example, Zhou Shoujuan began  his  story  of  'Sorrow of  a  Falling  Flower'  with  a  question  to  evoke  readers'  empathetic reaction to Miss Huang's tragedy:

Alas! How can I bear to write such a heartbreaking story to make my readers cry? When I was writing this story, I felt as though a knife has been plunged into my heart, and I couldn't help but weep with my tears streaming down my brush. But I must write this story to share with both male and female readers of the world (Zhou 1911).

By inviting readers to share in the tears for the protagonist, that is, a displaced woman suffering from China's weakness and inferior position in foreign countries, yet also willing to die to preserve her  national  dignity  and  identity,  Zhou  emphasized the  emotional  connection  of  readers  to the subject, and  thereby attempted  to  forge  a  link between  national  identity  and individual sentimentality in the reader.

Paul Cohen argues that during the late Qing and the early years of the republic 'a vast guochi (national humiliation) literature' emerged to awaken the Chinese public to its national crisis, and to 'rework the past' to suit 'the needs and aspirations of the present' (2003: 148-66). Indeed, popular  media  joined  in  this  process  of  promoting  the  remembrance  of  national  humiliation through the imagination, exaggeration and fabrication of a subjugated nation so as to evoke popular nationalism  among  Chinese  readers.  A  set  of  advertisements  for  Nanyang  Brother's  Tobacco Company Limited (Nanyang xiongdi yancao gufen youxian gongsi, Nanyang Company hereafter) published  in Shenbao in  1920  serves  as  a  uniquely  fascinating  instance  of  how  the  wangguo imagination, sentimentalism and commercial interests converged to shape a common understanding  of  a  modern  nation  and  its  citizens.  In  one  of  the  advertisements,  a  short  story entitled 'The Sorrow of a Subjugated Nation' (Wangguo hen) by Huizhan is juxtaposed with the advertising lines to promote the new brand of 'Patriotic cigarette', together with the picture of a packet  of  cigarettes,  with  the  two  Chinese  characters  composing  the  word  'patriotic'  placed prominently at the centre of the image (Figure 1). To the right of the image of 'Patriotic cigarette' is a poignant story that features a sorrowful Korean sing-song girl named Qiaozhu, who lives in exile and travels around China performing shows to express her agony at Korea's national demise. Comparing the patriotic Korean woman with Wang Zhaojun, the classical Chinese beauty whom Qiaozhu  plays  onstage, the  author  laments  the  miserable  destruction  of  Qiaozhu's  nation,  and reminds  readers  that  a  nation's  wealth  and  power  relies  on  its  commerce.  'War  of  commerce (shangzhan) is the most important matter in the contemporary world, as commercial prosperity is like a great wall to defend the nation', admonishes the author in the comments (Huizhan 1920). To the  left  of  the  image  of  the  cigarette  packet  is  advertising  copy  that  emphasizes  the  national characteristics  of  the  China-made  cigarette:  '[…]  in  nationalistic  spirit,  using  Chinese  capital, adopting Chinese materials, and hiring Chinese employees'. The advertisement attempts to link everyday  consumption  activities  with  anti-foreign  nationalism,  in  this  case  by  identifying  the smoking of Patriotic cigarettes as a gesture of patriotism. It advocates that an important part of citizens'  responsibilities  is  to  consume  'national  products'  (guohuo),  explicitly  connecting  the conception of a republican nation with the consumption of domestically produced goods.

Although  the  idea  of  'war  of  commerce'  can  be  traced  back  to  the  Self-Strengthening Movement in the late Qing (Yeh 2007: 17-23), what makes Nanyang Company's advertisements fascinating  is  that,  in  attracting  the  middle-  and  upper-middle-class  consumers  and  readers  in Shanghai    (Tsai  2010:  18-21), 7 they  ingeniously  and  discreetly  employed  their  story-telling strategy to stir up  both nationalistic pride and a  sense of  humiliation to promote their  national products. The image of the lonely and mournful Korean girl was reminiscent of Wang Zhaojun, who was also forced to depart her homeland when the Han Dynasty was suffering decline, together with the  long  and  rich  sentimental  literary  tradition  centring  on  the Wang  Zhaojun  legend.  Of particular interest here is the effect of such advertisements that appealed to the reading public of both  the  newspaper Shenbao and  of  sentimental  fiction  by  their  interweaving  of  nationalistic ideology  with  individual  emotional  reaction  and  everyday  commercial  practice.  In  this  case, Chinese nationalism was built upon patriotic feelings aroused by the sentimental wangguo story, a confirmation of the national identity by comparing China and Korea's history, and a sense of pride of consuming national products.


## CONCLUSION


If,  as  Anderson  suggests,  nation  is  an  'imagined  community',  and  nationalism  is  a  'cultural artefact', then patriotism can also be viewed as a cultural production that needs to be constructed through memory, imagination and reinterpretation. Patriotic stories illustrate how the nation was 'imagined, modeled, adapted, and transformed' (Anderson 1991: 141) in popular print media. As I have attempted to show, transcending time and geographic boundary, Butterfly patriotic fiction showcased a hybrid mode of nationalistic narrative conjoining sentimentalism, patriotism and an increasing fancy of the 'other'. From 'Mr. Tang' to sentimental fiction such as Jade Pear Spirit , 'Sorrow of  a  Falling  Flower'  and  'The  Spirit  of  a  Beauty'  by  major  Butterfly  writers,  we  see different representations of nationalism between late Qing ideologically driven 'new fiction' and Republican sentimental patriotism. The anxiety of national and racial preservation in late Qing gave  way  to  a  new  preoccupation  with  national  identity  through  the  discovery  of  female emotionality  interwoven  with  the  narrative  of  national  traumas  in  popular  fiction.  Popular nationalism  thus  placed  special  emphasis  on  the  emotional  and  empirical,  rather  than  rational construction of the imaginary community of nation. This popular national imaginary was further complicated by a gendered sentimental narrative and a literary response to national humiliation in China's recent history. In this process, the western and Korean 'others' contributed to the exotic,

historical  and  global  settings  in  patriotic  stories,  which  ultimately  helped  affirm  an  imaginary Chinese  modern  identity.  By  shifting  the  narrative  focus  to  feminine  sentimentality,  popular patriotic  stories  illuminated  a  sentimental  nationalist  discourse  best  manifested  in  women's emotionality that signifies the continuum of private romantic feelings and patriotic sentiments. The coalescence  of  the  contested  notions  of  love  -  romantic  love  and  'love  of  one's  country'  highlighted the emotional bonding between the individual and the nation.

Furthermore, we shall also remember that these patriotic stories were published in popular fiction  magazines  and  newspaper  literary  supplements  targeted  at  a  growing  group  of  urban middle-class readers in China. The writing/translation, publishing and reprinting of patriotic stories was a market strategy spurred on by both the heated nationalistic sentiment responding to Chinese national humiliation and a pursuit of commercial interests. Central to popular nationalism is a kind of national imaginary fostered, bolstered and in some sense invented by popular print media. The trope of  Korea,  for  instance,  has  become  part of  the  cultural  product of  patriotism,  by  linking personal  tragedy  with national subjugation,  and  by  kindling  an  amalgamated  feeling  of sentimentalism and nationalism in the reader to promote national products. It was no coincidence that 'sentimental fiction' and 'patriotic stories' emerged concomitantly to endorse a new type of patriotism as a central virtue of modern citizens in the thriving fiction market. Popular writers on the one hand rediscovered the patriotic spirit of the past, while on the other constructed a new national identity through a nationalistic narrative drawing heavily on indigenous cultural tradition and western sources. Patriotic fiction, as both literary texts and cultural artefacts, became a potent force  in articulating the  imagination of  a new China, evoking national feelings, memories, and sentimentality, and illuminating the nature of the relationship between popular literature and the nation state.

## Introduction


Since the 1958 revolution that saw the defeat of its colonial oppressors, Iraq has continued to struggle to find its own cultural identity. In response to colonization, the Iraqi poet, Badr Shaker al-Sayyāb (1926-1964), a key founder of the Arabic Free Verse Movement, wrote the poem, 'The Blind  Prostitute.'  This  paper  argues  that  an  important  effect  of  the  ongoing  interference  and manipulation of Iraq's national and economic interests by Western hegemonic forces has been the development  of  a  form  of  Iraqi  Arabic  free  verse  poetry  that  both  reveals  and  critiques  a problematic Du Boisian double consciousness as an expression of Iraqi identity. Through the lens of decolonization read as a form of neo-colonization, as well as its idiosyncratic use of the Arabic language, al-Sayyāb's poem, The Blind Prostitute , expresses a form of Iraqi double consciousness in ways that critique the tenuous bridges between the lingering invisibility of colonial powers and the  neocolonial  nation  of  Iraq.   The  poem  further  reveals  that  this  emergence  of  Iraqi  double consciousness as national identity is deeply embedded within the effects of global capitalism that continue to subordinate the Iraqi nation and oppress the people of Iraq. To these conditions of double consciousness and continuing oppression, al-Sayyāb's poem not only brings awareness but ultimately also works to incite resistance.

As part of the poem's historical background, al-Sayyāb's poetry was influenced by the political and economic ramifications of the first and second Anglo-Iraqi treaties, written in 1922 and 1930, that removed Iraq from the British mandate (Jackson, 2006). Even after Iraq signed the second Anglo-Iraqi Treaty of Alliance and Mutual Support in 1930, Britain nevertheless remained the  primary  power  that  controlled  Iraq's  external  and  militaristic  affairs  (Jackson,  2006).  In particular, al-Sayyāb was writing during the rule of the monarchical state that came after the end of the Ottoman Empire, which had been precipitated by the First World War. Thereafter, Britain retained control of Iraq, as the League of Nations had given Britain a mandate over Iraq in 1920.

The Iraqi people soon realized that Britain was keen to retain its influence in Iraq to exploit local oil resources while excluding Iraqi citizens from actively participating in the rule of their own country. This, coupled with the League of Nations mandate and the appointment of Faysal ibn Al-Husayn made Iraqi citizens feel as if they had been subjected to alien rule on two fronts (Saeed & O'Sullivan, 2006).

In 1936, Iraq became the first Arab nation to experience a coup d'état, known as the Bakr Sidqi coup (Scott, 1995). Ultimately, however, the coup led to increased Western influence in Iraq as well as the reassertion of neo-colonial rule. During the Second World War, instability in Iraq meant that America was also forced to intervene in Iraqi affairs, despite its wish to stay out of that arena (Thorpe, 1971). This ongoing foreign influence and resentment over British exploitation of Iraqi oil resources eventually culminated in the 1958 revolution, in which the Iraqi monarchy was overthrown and replaced with a republic (Saeed & O'Sullivan, 2006). This brief historical review of  the  waxing  and  waning  of  British  and  American  influence  over  Iraq  in  the  mid-and  latetwentieth century and the resulting nationalist movements in reaction to foreign dominance over Iraqi  affairs  provides  background  for  the  expression  of  strong  nationalistic  sentiments  and  the desire to experience true Iraqi independence found in al-Sayyāb's poetry.
