Wherever one walks in Japan, one has the chance to encounter advertisements of idols promoting  the  latest  products.  Likewise  on  television,  be  it  in  commercials,  variety shows, game shows, etc., one is regularly greeted by cute smiling girls. Idols are even featured  in  manga  magazines  (Young  Animal)  and  in  gravure  magazines  (Entame). Considering this widespread presence across multiple fields in Japanese society, one would almost forget that these idols are, first and foremost, singers and dancers.

The fact that idols are so omnipresent and idol-groups endlessly proliferate has not escaped the attention of scholars around the world. Exploring this aidoru genshō (Idol  phenomenon), scholars underline three  important facets that characterize these energetically dancing and singing girls.

The  first  characteristic  concerns  the  fact  that  idols  are,  in  essence,  images. Galbraith (2012: 186) convincingly argues that idols 'occupy the same conceptual space' as  anime,  manga  and  videogame  characters.  The  signifier  imēji  kyarakutā  (image character), which is also used to denote idols in marketing campaigns, further highlights the image-essence of the idol.

The second characteristic scholars have sufficiently explored concerns the role of the jimusho, i.e. the performer management companies that dominate and structure the  Japanese  entertainment  industry.  The  jimusho  are  responsible  for  training  the female subjects who come to embody the idol-image they have carefully produced for them. That the jimusho, acting as mothers, raise 'them in singing, dancing and other skills,  [schedule]  […]  daily  activities,  [book]  […]  television  appearances  […]  and [coordinate] […] live performances', implies that the idol-images are products of their jimusho and that the female subjects have very little creative input in the process of embodying  their  idol-image  (Condry  2006;  Marx  2012:  38).   A  final  characteristic 2 concerns the fact that the female subjects who are chosen by the jimusho are usually not extraordinarily talented in singing, dancing and/or acting - their 'talent' generally

2

ranges  between  'fairly  untalented'  and  'having  talent  just  above  average'.  Both  the signifier hijitsuryoku (non-ability), which emerged in the mid-80s to denote what fans desired in an idol, and the signifier tōshindai (life-sized) underline that the idol-image finds its support in the female subject's absence of extraordinary talent (Aoyagi 2005; Galbraith 2012).

While  these  elements  (image,  being  produced  and  life-sized)  already  give important indications to understand the Japanese  idol, this article aims to provide a deeper understanding of these life-sized manufactured idol-images. In the first part of this  article,  the  imaginary,  the  symbolic  and  the  real  dimensions  of  the  idol  will  be successively  explored.  By  approaching  these  dimensions  from  the  viewpoint  of  the idol-image's most ardent fans, i.e. the male idol-otaku, I will be able to highlight how the idol-otaku enters into relation with an idol-image and how this relation should be characterized. In the second part, a deeper examination of the specificity of this relation will  be  provided.  This  will  allow  us  to  show  how  the  idol-otaku  keeps  consuming, which function the idol-image has for the otaku, and how the otaku can satisfy himself. Finally,  I  will  question  if  the  relation  between  the  otaku  and  the  idol-image  can  be understood as a love relationship.


## CAPTURING THE DESIRE OF THE OTAKU: THE AIMED-FOR-OBJECT A


The first thing I need to clarify is how a particular idol-image can become desirable for the  idol-otaku.  How is  the  idol-otaku  able  to  encounter  an  idol-image  he  can  desire among  the  endless  proliferation  of  idol-images  in  Japanese  society,  among  a  near endless supply of idol-images aiming to become desired by him?

That  not  every  idol-image  can  become  desirable  for  an  otaku-subject  or,  as Galbraith  (2012:  188)  formulates  it,  that  it  has  become  'increasingly  difficult  [for producers] to predict consumer tastes', underlines the fact that whenever an otaku is

faced with an idol-image his subjectivity is in play. Whether an idol-image is raised to the status of oshimen, i.e. one's favourite idol-image from a certain idol-group, or one enters into a relation of gachi-koi (serious love) depends solely on the particularity of the  otaku  as  such.  While  an  otaku  can  have  more  than  one  oshimen,  the  gachi-koi relation  entails  the  otaku's  loyal  dedication  to  only  one  idol-image  while  having virtually no interest in other idol-images or subjects of the other sex.

The possibility for an idol-image to capture the desire of the otaku has to be situated in the otaku's meeting with the idol as image. In this meeting the otaku-subject does not meet the idol-image in its entirety, but encounters a partial aspect, a difficult to concretize 'something' of the body-image. That diffuse 'something' that the otaku encounters in the idol's body-image as embodied by a particular female subject, that aspect that glistens in the eye of the otaku, is nothing other than the hidden presence of the agalmatic object (Miller 2004). In order to highlight that this encountered object is an experience residing on the side of the otaku as a subject and not anything that the idol-image  as  such  possesses,  I  need  to  introduce  the  difference  that  Miller  makes between object a as object-cause of desire and object a as the aimed-for-object (Miller 2004). While the object a that causes the otaku's desire resides on the side of the subject, the otaku's perception of a glistening object a in  the body-image gives his desire its aim. The latter object, while possessing the important function to lure the desire of the otaku, is nothing other than a deceptive semblance (Miller 2004).

That the jimusho, the performer management companies, have a persevering aspiration of ensnaring the male gaze of the otaku and his desire is illustrated by the endless  exhibition  of  the  idol-body-images  embodied  by  these  female  subjects  in  a societal space.  While this aspiration  is already  hinted at by the diffused presence of idol-images  at  different  levels  of  Japanese  society  as  such,  one  can  find  the  best illustration of it in Promotional Videos (PVs) and Music Videos (MVs). These videos,

besides aiming to promote new-to-be-released singles, also showcase the idol-images as such. Especially, the close-up sections that exhibit a particular idol-body-image as she makes eye contact with the spectator aim to force a luring encounter with the aimedfor-object that can capture his desire and thus instigate his consumption. This seducing feature  of  these  videos  is  clearly  illustrated  by  the  PV's  of  Tsuribit  (2015)  and S/mileage (2014).


## IMPLICATIONS FOR CONSUMPTION: SUBJECTIFIED COMMODITIES


The aspect of meeting the aimed-for-object in the body-image of the female subject who embodies the idol-image has far-reaching implications on how idol-image related commodities should be understood. While it makes sense from the perspective of the entertainment industry to conceptualize the idol-image as a commodity in itself or as image-commodity as Lukács (2010) puts it, this conceptualization appears insufficient when approached  from  the  perspective  of  the  subjectivity  of  the  male  otaku.  Since commodities, as carriers of idol-images, only gain subjective value by the object a the otaku-subject  perceives  in  the  idol-image,  I  propose  to  use  the  more  appropriate signifier  'subjectified  commodities'.  With  this  signifier,  I  aim  to  underline  that  the 'external'  idol-image  can  only  become  a  catalyst  for  consumption  by  becoming  an 'internal'  presence  for  the  otaku.  In  other  words,  the  idol-image  that  adorns  the commodities is desired and consumed precisely because this idol-image, by becoming an internal presence in the desiring economy of the subject, loses its externality. The consumption  of  commodities  of  his  desired  idol-image  is  therefore  driven  by  the internal presence of that external idol-image. The perceived possession of object a in the body-image of the idol makes the externality of her image and the commodities her image adorns continuous with her internality.

But  what  is  the  function  of  the  otaku`s  consumption  of  the  subjectified commodities of either his oshimen or the idol-image implicated in a relation of gachikoi? In my view, the otaku's consumption allows him to construct the narrative that structures his desired idol-image.

## THE IDOL-IMAGE AS A GRAND-NARRATIVE OF LACK

Donna koto mo futari de issho ni norikoe te ikitainda

Dare ni mo mane dekinai SUTOORI

Itsu made mo anata dake no tame ni

Utaitsudzukete iku kara ne yakusoku.

(Kashiwagi 2013: Type-A track 3) 3

By introducing the narrative dimension or the symbolic dimension of the idol-image, I want to emphasize that the idol-image can only produce signification for the otaku as a narrative.  In  order  to  explain  how  the  consumption  of  (subjectified)  commodities enables  the  otaku-subject  to  construct  his  desired  idol-image's  narrative,  i.e.  the network of signifiers that give meaning to her presence in the Japanese societal space, it's fruitful  to  introduce  Eiji  Otsuka's  theory  of  Monogatari  Shohiron  (narrative consumption theory).

Using  the  example  of  bikkuriman  chocolates,  Otsuka  (2010)  convincingly argues that the main object of consuming these chocolates was to obtain the grandnarrative, rather than the chocolate or the individual stickers. Only by way of gathering stickers,  i.e.  'the  differential  and  fragmented  'small  narrative'  commodity  form[s]', children were able to gain hold of the grand-narrative (Otsuka 2010: 109). In a similar way, I argue that the narrative of the idol-image constitutes such kind of grand-narrative, a  narrative  grounded  by  her  own  name  and/or  nickname  that  is  only  accessible  by consuming  the  (subjectified)  commodities,  the  small-narratives  of  that  idol-image. 4

Nevertheless, contrary to Otsuka's theory, the grand-narrative of the idol-image is not a given before consumption, but something that is to be consumed in its process of becoming, a metonymic consumption of small narratives writing the grand-narrative up until the final small-narrative. The myriad of small narratives are, in other words, the very coordinates by which the consuming otaku is able to construct the grand-narrative of his desired idol-image.

The coming-into-being of her grand-narrative, which highlights the temporal aspect of the idol-image's grand-narrative, coincides with the process of becoming that marks the idol-image as such. The grand-narrative tells, in its process of being written by  the  proliferation  of  small-narratives,  a  narrative  of  becoming.  This  narrative  of becoming can only function because it circles around lack.

The lack that underpins the idol-image's grand-narrative of becoming can be situated at two different levels. The first lack, a structural lack, is found at the level of the temporal frame of the grand-narrative. The grand-narrative is ever framed by the transient period between 'not being a child anymore' and 'having become a woman' and is thus characterized by a lack of mature womanhood or by an infinite girlhood. This lack is usually emphasized by visual references (e.g. school uniforms, junior or high school settings for PV or MV's, etc.) to the junior and senior high school period, which spans from 12 to 18 years old. In some cases, this school-period is explicitly referred to in the idol-band's name, as Shiritsu Ebisu Chugaku (Ebisu Private Junior High  School),  Sakura  Gakuin  (Cherry  Blossom  Academy),  Flap  Girls  School  and Aoyama Saint Hachamecha High School illustrate. In other cases, such as Yumemiru Adolescence and groups with 'girls' in their name, the lack of womanhood is explicitly mentioned.

It might come as a surprise that many female subjects embodying an idol-image have enjoyed their seijin-shiki (coming of age ceremony at the age of 20), but this only

reveals  that the  evoking  of  this  transient  period, this  girlhood  -  with  or  without the backdrop of the high school years - is far more important than the actual age of the female subject or the actual school year she is in.  The idol-image's girlhood, her lack5 of-surplus, forms the structural fantasmatic backdrop of her entire grand-narrative.

Within the grand-narrative of the idol-image, as marked by an infinite girlhood, another lack is ever in play. This lack, which gives direction to the idol-image's grandnarrative,  is  evoked  by  the  dreams  (of  becoming  an  actress,  of  becoming  better  at dancing among others) that a given idol-image expresses. Even though these dreams and  the  lack  they  denote  may  shift  as  the  idol-image's  grand-narrative  unfolds,  the presence of a lack the idol wants to resolve is never annulled.

The  fact  that  the  idol-image  wants  to  realize  certain  dreams  structures  the interaction between the otaku and his desired idol-image around the notion of ganbaru (to  support).  Every  interaction  between  the  otaku  and  his  desired  idol-image  is,  in essence, an interaction of ganbaru. It is only because his desired idol-image is lacking with respect to a certain ideal-image she wants to realize, that the support of the otakusubject becomes meaningful. It is, in other words, her energetic intention to realize that ideal-image  that  resonates  with  the  otaku-subject  and  gives  rise  to  his  supportive consumption. That the easiest way for the idol-otaku to support his desired idol-image is by consuming her small-narratives that trace out her grand-narrative of lack, should not surprise anyone.

## ACCESSING HER GRAND-NARRATIVE BY CONSUMING SMALLNARRATIVES

Having revealed the lack expressed at the level of dreams and the lack of womanhood that  imprisons  her  in  an  infinite  girlhood,  both of  which  serve  to  structure the  idolimage's grand-narrative, I can now turn our attention to the small-narratives by which

the  idol-otaku can express his  support and construct the grand-narrative of lack that structures his desired idol-image.

I  propose  to  classify  the  abundance  of  small-narratives  into  three  different categories. The first category, the small-image-narratives, is mainly preoccupied with the exhibition of the idol-body-image. This category includes shashin-shū (photobooks),  gravure, photographs that are either signed, kissed (by way of lipstick) 6 or sprayed  by  her  perfume, ishou kadou  (costume  cards),   Instagram  profiles, 7 commercials  and  promotional  campaigns.  The  small-image/signifier-narratives,  the second category, emphasize signifiers and image in an equal manner and include imeiji bideo (image video), 8 concerts, PVs, MVs, akushukai (hand-shake events), Showroom, 9   and  television  appearances.  In  the  third  category,  the  small-signifiernarratives  emphasize  the  idol-image's  narrative  dimension.  These  small-narratives include  CD's,  twitter-profiles,  Line  and  Ameba-blogs,  magazine  interviews  and messages on official Facebook pages.

The reason why such a classification is important is to reveal that the categories where the idol-body-image is on the fore enable the otaku-subject to keep encountering the  aimed-for-object  of  his  desire,  while  the  categories  where  signifiers  are  on  the foreground  introduce the  idol-otaku to the  lacks  that  mark  his  desired  idol-image's grand-narrative.

Lastly,  it  is  important  to  note  that  the  consumption  of  small-narratives  as subjectified commodities means that the idol-image's grand-narrative of lack can only be read as a subjectified grand-narrative of lack. The idol-otaku is, in other words, only able  to  read  his  desired  idol-image's  grand-narrative  of  lack  by  inserting  -  via  the consumption of images and signifiers - his own position of support within this grandnarrative of lack. This supportive position, a position inaugurated by the capturing of the otaku's desire and supported by the dreams the desired idol-image has, is thus not

only  the  fundamental  dimension  that  marks  the  idol-otaku's  interaction  with  his oshimen or the idol-image subjected to his gachi-koi, but also the way he marks the grand-narrative of his desired idol-image with his subjectivity.


## THE BODILY SUPPORT OF THE GRAND-NARRATIVE OF LACK


Karada dake ga otona ni natta you na

Kimetsuke de mikudasu to naki miru yo

Mou sukoshi surya makka na kuchibeni de

Anta no kokoro wo zenbu sometageru

Makenai yo.

(Juice=Juice 2016: track 2) 10

Even  though  idol-images  only  receive  signification  when  their  subjectified  smallnarratives  are  consumed,  the  idol-images  and  their  grand-narratives  cannot  function without a material bodily support. An idol-image needs, in other words, a real body (and a real voice) to animate and vitalize the double lack that marks its grand-narrative.

While I already touched upon this bodily support in our explanation of how the desire of the otaku is ensnared by the idol-body-image, the role the body plays can only be grasped by contrasting it with the bodily supported idol-image with Hatsune Miku, world's first true virtual idol-image.

In the case of Hatsune Miku, her 'body' as well as her 'voice' are non-material commodities. Programmes like MikuMikuDance and MikuMikuMoving enables the idol-otaku  to  animate  the  virtual  body  of  Miku  and  by  using  Yamaha's  vocaloid software technology 11 the otaku is given the tools to make Hatsune Miku sing whatever lyrics he can come up with. As there is no bodily support whatsoever, since Hatsune Miku is nothing but digital data, the male otaku is given the responsibility to vitalize the  virtual  idol-image  with  his  subjectivity,  i.e.  his  signifiers  and  his  fantasies.  The

contrast  between  this  and  the  commodification  of  the  body  and  the  voice  and  the grounding of the idol image in a living speaking/singing body enables us to unearth three additional characteristics of the non-virtual idol-image.

The first characteristic  is spatial  in  nature and concerns the seemingly trivial fact that the bodily support gives the idol-image an 'independent' spatial presence in the social space. In other words, the idol-image moves and dances and speaks and sings of her own  accord.  This is easily experienced  at handshake  events  and live performances.  And  even  in  the  fixation  of  the  idol-image  as  a  surface-reality  (for instance, in gravure, MV/PV's, photobooks and image-videos) her spatial existence is ever implied. Thus, while the idol is an image with a narrative, she is, due to this bodily support,  more  than  just  a  'reality'  confined  to  the  two-dimensional  surfaces  of  the Japanese societal space.

Secondly, the presence of  bodily support installs a temporal dimension. The temporal presence of a particular bodily support inaugurates the barebones structure of the idol-image's grand-narrative of lack, a grand-narrative starting with her promotion/selection and ending with her sotsugyō (graduation), i.e. her graduation from girlhood. 12 The 'heavy rotation' of bodily supports, the ebb and flow of bodily supports, furthermore  implies  that,  while  the  idol-image  needs  to  be  animated  by  a  body,  its grand-narrative of lack functions irrespective of the body that brings this narrative to life.

The last characteristic concerns the lack present in the bodily support as such, a bodily  lack  supporting  the  evocation  of  the  lack  of  womanhood  as  well  as  the  lack expressed  through  the  dreams  signifying  the  idol-image.  As  the  age  when  female subjects  become  a  support  for  the  idol-image  is  generally  young,  their  bodies corroborate the lack of womanhood endlessly evoked in the small-narratives. Of course, as the female subject ages - as she passes the adolescence, her body grows towards

adulthood as well. The otaku-subject is thus given, in accordance with his position of support, the chance to experience the bodily 'growth' of his oshimen or the idol-image subjected to his gachi-koi. Nevertheless, a lack of well-pronounced secondary sexual characteristics is not a fundamental condition for the idol-image's grand-narrative of lack  to be  able  to  function. As  the  gravure  spreads  of  Asakawa  Nana  (from SUPER ☆ GiRLS) and Nemoto Nagi (from Niji no Conquistador) for example illustrate, having well-pronounced bodily aspects, i.e. a notable cup size, is not problematic in any way. The interplay between this bodily surplus and the lack-of-surplus inherent to the  schoolgirl  position  can,  in  fact,  even  enhance  the  potency  of  the  idol-image  to capture the otaku's desire.

The bodily lack is also made present by the imperfection that marks the singing and dancing performances of idol-images. This lack of having extra-ordinary talent, designated by the signifier life-sized in our introduction, generally finds its echo in the dreams idol-images have, her dreams of becoming a better dancer, a better singer, etc. 13 Because of its link to the idol-image's dreams, this lack never fails to empower the interactions  of  support  between  the  idol-otaku  and  his  desired  idol-image.  That  the bodily lack corroborates the lack brought to the fore in many small-narratives, gives the support  of  the  idol-otaku,  a  support  underpinned  by  his  desire,  a  dimension  of necessity. 14 It  is  only  through  his  supportive consumption, which coincides with  his subjectification of his desired idol-image's grand-narrative, that the idol-otaku is able to take part in (and supposedly enable) the idol-image's process of 'growing to be less lack -ing', i.e. the seicho o miru (to see growth) (Galbraith 2012: 196).


## KAWAII AND ITS RELATION TO THE LACK OF WOMANHOOD AND THE AIMED-FOR-OBJECT


Having explained the importance of the aimed-for-object in capturing the otaku's desire and the importance of lack, bodily as well as at the level of the small-narratives, in sustaining  the  supportive  position  of  the  otaku,  I  can  now  further  explore  the particularities surrounding the relation of the otaku to his oshimen or the idol-image subjected to his gachi-koi.

First of  all,  there  is  a  need  to  clarify  the  link  between  kawaii  (cute)  and the double lack that structures the grand-narrative of the idol-image as well as its relation to the beautification of the aimed-for-object perceived by the otaku in his desired idolimage.

The notion of kawaii, a polysemic signifier used to denote all sorts of images (persons, animals  or  objects)  as cute, is generally  used  to  aesthetically uplift imperfection  and  incompleteness.  The  centrality  of  lack  in  the  kawaii  discourse  is evident in the modern origins of this discourse, i.e. 'the cute handwriting craze' that started in 1974 and became a nationwide phenomenon by 1978 (Kinsella 1995: 222). Burikko-ji (fake child writing) and the kawaii fashion it engendered constituted a form of rebellion against traditional Japanese social values or, in our words, an appropriation of lack with respect to the traditional expectations structuring Japanese society. Kawaii thus implicitly damned adulthood.

It  is  not  difficult  to  see  that  the  lack  of  womanhood that  structures the  idolimage's  grand  narrative  is  important  for  framing  her  as  kawaii.  The  idol-image, suspended  from  womanhood  and  the  implicit  and  explicit  societal  expectations  of sekinin (responsibility) that marks such womanhood, is kept in a continual state of pure and  innocent  girlhood.  The  kawaii  nature  of  the  idol-image's  girlhood  is  mainly

corroborated through gestures, comportments, speech and the way she has been clothed, e.g. with certain types of costumes, make-up and hairstyles.

The fact that almost any aspect of the idol-image can evoke kawaii-ness implies that kawaii has to be understood as an aesthetic discourse within the Japanese Other, the Other being 'the locus of the treasure trove of signifiers' as well as the 'complex network of rules and other kinds of presuppositions' that one accepts and relies on to ground one's reality (Lacan [1966] 2005: 682; Žižek 2007: 8). In other words, kawaii is a discourse of the Other, an Other 'supported' by all the individuals subjected to the very signifiers, rules, and discourses this Other consists of. This aspect enables us to understand why this aesthetic discourse, as enclosed in the Japanese Other, functions like 'the desire of the Other' with respect to 'the desire of man', of the otaku (Lacan [1973] 2004: 235). As the otaku, like any other individual, comes-into-being  in the Japanese  Other  by  becoming  subjected  by  the  signifiers  of  the  Other,  his  desire  is mediated by this Other he derives his symbolic existence from. But the kawaii discourse can only influence the desire of the otaku by structuring the intermediary element: the fantasy of the otaku.

As the fantasy provides the subject with 'the coordinates of his desire, specifies its […] [aimed-for-object], and allocates him the position he assumes in it' (Žižek 1991: 6), it is not that difficult to understand why the aimed-for-object of the otaku is always marked  by  kawaii  aesthetics.  It  is  because  the  very  possibility  of  encountering  the aimed-for-object  in  the  body-image  of  the  idol-image  is  in  function  of  the  otaku's fantasy .

14 That the aimed-for-object is marked by kawaii aesthetics is illustrated by the way the otaku uses the signifier kawaii. While this signifier is used to deem all kinds of appearances, comportments and statements of one's oshimen or the idol-image subject to his gachi-koi as 'sweet' and 'cute' - elements pointing to her lack, the otaku's use of this signifier comes down to an attempt to qualify the aimed-for-object a ,  the  'zeropoint of desire', that the otaku encountered and keeps encountering in the body-image of  his  desired  idol  (Lacan  [2004]  2014:  241-42). 15 The  otaku's  use  of  kawaii  as  a signifier thus implies a corroboration of his desire for his oshimen or the gachi-koi -image as such.

## REN'AI  KINSHI:  THE  DESIRE  TO  DESIRE  AND  THE  DESIRE  FOR RECOGNITION

Even though I have explained the supportive relation between the otaku and the idolimage as instigated by his desire, a desire directed towards the perceived kawaii aimedfor-object, I have not touched upon the fundamental question of what the otaku actually desires.

It is the rule of ren'ai kinshi, a rule mediating the relation between the otaku and the desired idol-image, that gives us the first indication of what the otaku's desire aims for. This rule, a common rule in the Japanese entertainment industry, forbids female subjects who embody the idol-image to be publicly involved in romantic relationships with fans or other men. Could one, based on this rule, assume that the idol-otaku desires a romantic relationship with his oshimen or the idol-image subjected to his gachi-koi? Is the desire, a desire directed at the aimed-for-object, a desire to have a relationship with the idol-image as a whole?

The answer is surprisingly no. As most idol-otaku's fully realize that their idolimage, while having a bodily support, is but a fictional performance, the ren'ai kishi should  be  viewed  as  a  translation  of  an  inherent  impossibility  that  structures  the supporting interaction between the otaku and his desired idol-image (Okudara 2016). This impossibility is underlined by the consequences of transgressing the rule of ren'ai kinshi. Such a transgressing, denoted by the signifier tsunagaru (to be connected to),

annuls the distance the rule installs between the otaku and the idol-image. The annulling of  this  distance,  through  establishing  a  relationship  with  one's  desired  idol-image, forces the female subject who up until that point embodied the desired idol-image to manifest  herself  as  a  subject.  Such  a  forced  appearance  destroys  by  definition  the necessary fictionality of this image.

The  impossibility  of  transforming  the  supportive  relation  of  desire  into  a romantic relationship with one's desired idol-image, in fact, supports the otaku in a desire not to realize their desire. Their desire is, in essence, not a desire for a relationship. Instead, the  otaku-subject  unconsciously  realizes  'the  essential  dimension  of  desire' which is 'the desire of desire' (Lacan [1986] 1992: 14). The otaku needs the distance corroborated by ren'ai kinshi in order to keep his desire in a state of desiring.

Nevertheless, the distance safeguarded by ren-ai kinshi also supports another (more imaginary) desire, a desire underpinned by the unconscious desire to desire. This desire concerns the 'desire of recognition' or, in better words, the desire to have one desire recognized (Kojève [1947] 1980: 7). The importance of this desire is revealed by the  signifier  resu  (response).  Resu  is  used  to  designate  those  moments  at  live performances  where  one's  oshimen  or  the  idol-image  subjected  to  one's  gachi-koi makes some form of eye-contact with the otaku. This kind of eye-contact, which of course elicits some pleasure, has no other effect than validating the otaku's desire and the relation of support he installed. The importance of having one's desire validated is also underlined by the signifier ninchi (acknowledgement). This signifier is used when the  desired  idol-image  remembers the otaku's  face  and  name. The derived  signifier blog/twitter ninchi, which concerns the recognition of one's blog or twitter by the idolimage - a recognition that provides possible conversation topics at handshake events further pleasures the otaku's desire to have one's desire recognized, while engendering feelings of closeness.

The importance of such recognition of one's desire is most clearly illustrated by the unusual but tragic stabbing-incident (Stabbed idol 2016). When Tomohiro Iwazaki, who wanted to know why Mayu Tomita, his desired idol as image, returned his gift, attacked  the  girl  embodying  the  idol-image  he  desired  with  a  knife,  he  did  not experience her refusal of his gift and her 'unsatisfactory' explanation as a refusal to satisfy his desire but as a refusal to recognize and legitimate his desire.

Now, the relation between ren'ai kinchi and the otaku's desire can  be better understood. This rule safeguards the distance between the otaku and the desired idolimage, so that the otaku's desire to desire can subsist and the otaku can extract some pleasure by seeing his desire recognized. Desire needs this obstacle of distance in order to  remain  desiring  (Hoornaert  2018).  But  this  continuous  desiring  state,  as  already touched upon earlier, also needs the support of the otaku's fantasy, which is formed by his birth in the Japanese Other (Lacan [1973] 2004). The question now becomes: what kind of fantasy sustains the otaku's desire?

The fantasy that supports the otaku's desire and enables him to locate his aimed-forobject of desire  is nothing other than the otaku's private fantasy of writing a sexual relationship. As there is no harmonious, natural relation between the sexes - 'the sexual relation  does  not  exist'  as  Lacan  pronounced,  such  private  fantasy  gives  out  the

particular coordinates by which a sexual relationship might be written (Lacan [1991] 2007: 134).

That the otaku's fantasy of a writable sexual relationship is able to sustain his desire for a certain idol-image is caused by the very dynamic his supportive position of consuming puts in motion. By consuming her signifiers, the signifiers expressed in her small-image/signifier-narratives, e.g. PVs and image-video's, and the small-signifiernarratives, e.g. songs, the otaku is not only able to appropriate the grand-narrative of lack of his desired idol-image, but also to revel in the fantasies she endlessly produces. These fantasies exploit her lack of romance (as ensured by ren-ai kinshi) in order to evoke a supposedly writable sexual relation with her. 17

These small-narratives, which are always fantasmatic in nature, call the singular fantasy of the otaku into play. The signifiers expressed in the consumed and subjectified commodities reflect the otaku's own desire as well as evoke what is/should be desirable as such. The fantasmatic commodities (of a writable sexual relationship) are thus not scenarios that fulfil the otaku's desire, but scenarios that 'realizes, stages, […] [his] desire as such' (Zizek 1991:  6). That  the otaku's fantasy, ever in perpetual communication with the  fantasmatic  small-narratives, succeeds  in sustaining (rather than fulfilling) the otaku's desire indicates that his fantasmatic consumption of smallnarratives or small-fantasies has a specific function for the otaku.

The small-fantasies that exploit a certain lack marking his desired idol-image provide  the  possibility  for  the  desiring  otaku  to  temporally  efface  his  own  lack  as subject.  By  consuming  the  signifiers,  especially  those  expressed  through  speech,  in songs  and  image-videos,  the  otaku  is  able  to  situate  himself  as  the  answer  to  the question, [w]hat does my oshimen or the idol-image subjected to my gachi koi desire?. In other words, the supportive consumption of the otaku gives him the ability to meet himself as possessing the phallus, i.e. that imaginary object which would make a sexual

relationship with her possible. It is important to underline that the phallus is a veiled and enigmatic signifier without a signified (Lacan [1966] 2005). Even if the otaku's supportive consumption of the idol-image's lack at the level of romance enables him to temporally position himself as possessing the phallic complement, this phallic element has no substance. It is the very veil that hides the phallus as lack that allows the otaku to temporally  fantasize  himself  as  having  the  enigmatic  element that the  idol-image desires in his possession.

The endless offering of her lack at the level of romance by which the male otaku can temporally feel himself as possessing her phallic complement underlines why the idol-image has to have a 'zettai-teki na sonzai' (absolute existence) (Sasakibara 2004: 50 [O.T]). The  idol-image allows the otaku to substantiate  his  value as  man. Or as Tsunku formulates it, the function of the girl marked by lack is to enable the otaku to believe  'that  [he]  can  […]  take  care  of  her'  (2000:  99  [O.T]).  Needless  to  say,  the possibility  of  fantasmatically  experiencing  himself  as  the  phallic  complement  that would negate his desired idol's lack at the level of romance provides some pleasure for the consuming otaku.

But even though this fantasmatic consumption, just like the recognition of his desire, allows the idol-otaku to gain some pleasure, the satisfaction the otaku derives from his supportive consuming interaction with his oshimen or the idol-image subjected to his gachi-koi is situated at a different level: the level of the drive.


## SATISFYING THE SCOPIC DRIVE: KAWAII EROTICA


The possibility for the otaku to satisfy his drive is closely related to how the otaku's fantasy, which allows the otaku to find what his desire aims at, and ren'ai kinshi, which safeguards  the  desiring  state  of  desire,  sustains  the  supportive  consumption  of subjective commodities. It is, in other words, due to the establishment of the kawaii

aimed-for-object that the possibility of satisfying the drive by way of consumption is opened up. But in order to satisfy the drive, the otaku does not consume his desired idol-image  at  the  level  of  the  small-fantasies  she  produces,  but  at  the  level  of  the proliferation of objectifying images of her body, i.e. her small image-narratives like her photobooks and small image/signifier-narratives like her image-videos, PVs and MVs. The drive that the otaku is able to satisfy is thus first and foremost his scopic drive.

In order to explain how the consumption of idol-body-images can satisfy the otaku's scopic drive, it is necessary to refer to Lacan's schema of the partial drive (see Figure 1; Lacan [1973] 2004). The a in the schema, the object of the drive, is nothing other than the kawaii aimed-for-object, the object-cause of desire as situated by the otaku in the body-image of the idol. It is this aimed-for-object that the otaku keeps on seeing by consuming the body-images of his oshimen or the idol-image subjected to his kachi-goi.

The thrust of the drive arises from the eye as a rim-like structure only to return, after tracing a circuit around the kawaii aimed-for-object or, as Miller (1997) calls it, the hetero-object, to its source. It is only by starting from and returning to the eye of the otaku that the visual consumption of body-images becomes auto-erotic. The goal of the  drive  is  not  to  attain  this  kawaii  aimed-for-object,  but  to  repeat,  by  supportive consumption, this circuit and attain the satisfaction that the circling as such generates. In other words, the temporary scopic satisfaction that such circling enables motivates the otaku to keep consuming the image-based small-narratives of his desired idol-image.

This satisfying circling  around  the object a reveals  that the  kawaii-aesthetic, beyond  its  use-value  as  the  aimed-for-object,  also  functions  as  erotica.  The  otaku's scopic satisfaction, as generated by a consummative looking that eroticizes the body-

image of  his  desired  idol-image,  is  intimately  linked  with  the  kawaii  aesthetics  that mark the representation of the idol-image.

Of course, the possibility for the otaku to visually enjoy his desired idol-image is  supported  by  the  way  in  which  the  body-image  of  the  idol  is  presented  in  her photobooks,  image-videos,  etc.  Kawaii  aesthetics  are  generally  applied  in  order  to highlight the tension between the idol-image's body-image, which is often marked by a bodily surplus, and her (fictional) lack of knowing her own sexuality. In this case, it is  the  visual  evocation  of  her  innocence  as  linked  to  being  not-yet-a-woman  that  is offered to the otaku's circling scopic drive. In other instances, it is a playful interplay between her body-image, as framed by kawaii aesthetics, and the subtle hinting towards her  consciousness  of  being  a  sexualized  being  that  is  donated  to  the  otaku's  autoerotism.  Both the  exploitation  of  her  girly  innocence  and  the teasing  of  her  nascent sexual  consciousness  as  woman  underline  that  the  idol-image  is,  by  the  jimusho, manufactured as a commodity to be eroticized, as a commodity that the body of the otaku can use to satisfy itself. 18

Having introduced the dimension of drive satisfaction, a differentiation between the otaku with oshimen and the otaku that subjects an idol-image to his gachi-koi can finally be made. While the desire to desire leads to fantasmatic consumption and scopic consumption for both types of idol-otaku, the emphasis in their supportive position with respect to the desired idol-image is different. The otaku organizing multiple oshimen around him, creates, following the erratic nature of desire, a harem of idol-images that he consumes, first and foremost, at the level of the fantasy, at the level where he can fantasize himself as her complement. The ease by which this otaku is able to change his oshimen - the changing of one's oshimen is called oshihen - further underlines that his fantasmatic consumption follows the irregularity of desire. The second type of otaku fixates  his  supportive  consumption  on one  idol-image.  While  his  desire  is  kept  in  a

desiring state, his supposed love for his desired idol-image halts the metonymic nature of  desire  and  allows  him,  first  and  foremost,  to  satisfy  his  scopic  drive  by  visually enjoying the proliferation of her body-images.

Given our exploration of the dimensions of desire, fantasy and the drive in the otaku's interaction  with  his  desired  idol-image,  can  the  otaku's  supportive  consumption  by characterized as 'love'?

If  love  is  conceptualized as a 'subject-to-subject relationship' as 'based on a certain relationship between two unconscious knowledges', then the relation between the otaku and his desired idol-image can't be qualified as a relation of love because the otaku never, in his supportive consumption, meets the female subject behind his idolimage  (Lacan  [1975]  1998:  144).  The  space  where  idol-images  function  is  a  space where female subjects are lacking. It is, as Lamarre states, 'a world […] without actual women' (2006: 241). But it is precisely because female subjects as such are lacking that the idol-image as produced by the jimusho can be so successful. It is only because the otaku at no point in his consumption whatsoever meets a female subject that his desire to desire can be exploited.

This evading of women as subjects constitutes a crafty manipulation of the way non-otaku male subjects commonly engage with the female subjects they desire. While

the non-otaku subject eventually has to deal with the woman as a subject, the otaku only ever meets his desired idol as an image and as a narrative. In fact, he can only show his desire and find recognition for his desire by consuming her small-narratives and inscribing himself in her grand-narrative of 'growing-to-be-less lacking'.

The very impossibility of meeting the female subject, as safeguarded by ren-ai kinshi, allows the otaku to employ his desired idol-image for his own pleasure and own satisfaction. The otaku gains pleasure by consuming the signifier-based narratives of his desired idol-image as fantasies of a sexual relationship that could be written and finds auto-erotic satisfaction by consuming her image-based narratives at the level of his scopic drive.

While the interaction between the otaku and his desired idol-image resembles the  structure  of  courtly  love  -  the  otaku  desiring  the  idol-image  and  the  sexual relationship  that  could  be  written  with  her  from  a  distance  -  the  otaku-subject's consumption of the commodities of the desired idol-image reveals that this supportive interaction is, when all is said and done, beyond any true love whatsoever.

## Introduction


The emerging health measures of coronavirus (Covid-19) have demanded adaptations in almost all aspects of life, including social and educational domains. Full and partial lockdowns worldwide have imposed restrictions  on  individuals  and  institutions.  Closures  of  schools  and  universities forced the shift to online learning.  In Jordan, and according to the enforcement of the Jordan National Defense Law No. 13 of 1992 (Ministry, 2021), fully online classes have started in March 2020 till the end of August 2021. Starting from the academic year 2021/2022, a hybrid education system at schools and universities took place under the government's recovery plan. The design incorporates in-person, blended, and online classes depending on the development of the measures due to the vaccination rates and the constant mutation of the virus.

Although online instructions started earlier in Jordan during the 2000s by individual institutions and scholars (Badran, 2014), most students and instructors have never experienced formal online instructions. Moodle platform is the Learning Management System (LMS) used by most Jordanian universities (Wimpenny, Adefila, & DeWinter, 2018; Al-Shboul & Alsmadi, 2014).  At an earlier stage, the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research tolerated a '25% cap for online content'  (Wimpenny,  Adefila,  &  DeWinter,  2018,  p.  28).    Following  the  aftermath  of  the pandemic, 'online learning is no longer an option but a necessity' (Al-Salman & Haider, 2021, p. 296). Thus, the ministry has issued regulations for officially merging electronic instructions in higher education institutions, valid on the 30th of June 2021 (Education, 2022).

To understand how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students received online learning to enhance its points of strength and address its challenges, the researchers applied TAM constructs and  two  external  variables.  They  were  the  characteristics  of  the  online  learning  system  and experience in online learning. The Technology Acceptance Model ( TAM) constructs, introduced by Davis (1989), stemmed from the Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA). TRA states that people's perceptions  identify  their  attitudes  toward  an  object,  which  determines  their  intentions  to  act accordingly, and they will finally decide on their actual behavior (Agudo-Peregrina, HernándezGarcía,  &  Pascual-Miguel,  2014).    Davis  regarded  that  the  use  of  a  particular  system  was  a behavior that could be explained by TRA, and the user's attitudes towards that system were 'a major determinant of whether the user will use or reject the system' (Granic & Marangunic, 2019, p. 2574).

As  for  the  external  variables,  experience  in  online  learning  was  cited  as  among  the  most commonly used external factors (Abdullah & Ward, 2016). The researchers assumed that the EFL learners'  previous  experience  in  online  learning  had  a  positive  impact  on  their  attitudes  and behavioral intentions to use online learning. Researchers who used online learning experience as an external variable found that 'the greater the online learning experiences of users, the stronger their intention to use an online learning community' (Liu, Chen, Sun, Wible, & Kuo, 2010, p. 608).  Furthermore, the characteristics of online learning as an Information System (IS) are defined in this research by the features this system offers to assist the online user of the learning system (Hassanzadeh, Kanaani, & Elahi, 2012).


## Rationale and Significance of the Study


This  study  attempts  to  understand  how students perceive online learning and their attitudes towards using it after Covid-19 to help teachers and officials at the universities to improve and develop online learning to achieve the best of students' interests.  This study is believed to be the first on EFL students using TAM in Jordan.

Thus, in the context of EFL online learning, it was hypothesized that:

- H1: Online learning system characteristics significantly affected PU of online learning.
- H2: Online learning system characteristics significantly affected PEOU of online learning.
- H3: Online learning system characteristics significantly affected attitudes towards using online learning.
- H4: Online learning system characteristics significantly affected the BIs of online learning.
- H5: PEOU significantly affected PU of online learning.
- H6: PEOU of online learning significantly affected attitudes toward using online learning.
- H7: PU of online learning significantly affected attitudes towards using online learning.
- H8: PU significantly affected BIs to use online learning.
- H9: Attitudes towards online learning significantly affected BIs to use online learning.
- H10: The positive effect of proposed determinants on attitudes and BIs was more robust for EFL students who studied online for four semesters or more than EFL students who studied less than four semesters.

For this research, besides the primary constructs of TAM, online learning system characteristics and online experience, which the researchers argue to influence the EFL learners' acceptance of using  technology  in  an  online  learning  setting,  were  used.  In  the  following  section,  empirical literature concerning the constructs of the learners' acceptance of and their attitudes towards the online learning systems will be examined.


## Literature Review


Technology  Acceptance  Model  is  introduced  by  Davis  (1989)  to  anticipate  the  user's acceptance of a new technology before launching it. It suggests that the use of the new technology is predicted by the behavioral intentions of the user.  It is based on two primary constructs, i.e., perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) of that technology. Davis (1989) defines PU as the degree to which users believe that using a particular system would enhance their performance, and PEOU as the degree to which users believe that using a specific system would be free of effort. That is to say, if the new technology is easy to use, this means it is usefully perceived, and users' attitudes and behavioral intentions are positive concerning it.

In  their  research,  Pituch  and  Lee  (2006)  studied  the  effect  of  the  online  learning  system characteristics on the learners' acceptance of technology. The findings revealed a strong impact of online  learning  system  characteristics  on  the  students'  acceptance  of  using  online  learning. Previous  research  has  also  shown  that  online  learning  system  characteristics  have  positively affected PU of online learning (Hsieh, Huang, & Wu, 2016). Moreover, in their research, Alharbi and Drew (2014) and Salloum, Alhamad, Al-Emran, Abdel Monem, & Shaalan (2019) found a positive  correlation  between  system  characteristics  and  PU  of  the  online  learning  systems. Likewise, it had been determined that the online learning system characteristics positively affected

As  stated  by  Pituch  and  Lee  (2006),  if  the  online  learning  system positively affected PU and PEOU of online learning, it meant that this system was user-friendly. Therefore, the learners' attitudes towards online learning would be enhanced completely. Kanwal and Rehman (2017), who examined the effect of online learning system characteristics on the students'  attitudes  towards  using  online  learning,  reported  a  positive  relationship  between  the online learning system characteristics and the students' attitudes toward using it.

Kanwal and Rehman (2017) stated a significant correlation between the online learning system characteristics and the learners' BIs to use it. Pituch and Lee (2006) pointed out that if the online learning  system  characteristics  have  positively  impacted  the  learners'  attitudes  toward  it,  the learners would have apparent behavioral intentions to use it.

Research that examined the potential relation between PEOU and PU  in the domain of online learning has shown that PEOU of online learning positively affected the learners' PU of online learning (Almarabeh, 2014; Al-Okaily, Alqudah, Matar, Lutfi, & Taamneh, 2020; Farahat, 2012; Hsieh, Huang, & Wu, 2016; Jiang et al., 2021).  While previous research has shown a significant relationship between learners' PEOU of online learning and their attitudes towards using online learning (Almarabeh, 2014; Farahat, 2012; Jiang et al., 2021), learners' PEOU of using online learning  in  the  study  of  Natasia,  Wiranti,  &  Parastika,  (2022)  did  not  significantly  affect  the learners' attitudes towards using online learning system.

Regarding PU as a TAM construct that significantly affected the learners' attitudes towards using online learning, previous research acknowledged that PU has positively affected learners' attitudes towards using online learning systems  (Almarabeh, 2014; Farahat, 2012; Jiang et al., 2021; Natasia et al., 2022). As stated in the literature, several research articles have shown that PU had  a  positive  impact  on  the  learners'  BIs  using  online  learning  systems  (Almarabeh,  2014; Farahat, 2012; Haleman & Yamat, 2021; Jiang et al., 2021; Natasia et al., 2022; Salloum et al., 2019).

Some  researchers  indicated  that  the  students  with  positive  attitudes  toward  online  learning systems had greater BIs toward them (Almarabeh, 2014; Farahat, 2012; Haleman & Yamat, 2021; Natasia et al., 2022). On the contrary, others claimed that learners' attitudes toward online learning systems had an insignificant effect on the learners' BIs toward them because the online learning systems were the only choice they had during the lockdown in the era of covid-19 (Jiang et al., 2021; Teo, Wong, & Chai, 2008).

Experience, as one of the common external constructs used in the TAM in an online learning setting in literature, had been generally viewed as an important one to be examined for its possible effect on the learners' attitudes toward using online learning systems besides their intentions to use it. Some research articles revealed that both the learners' attitudes towards using an online learning system and their BIs to use it were positively affected to different degrees by the online learning experience (Abramson, Dawson, & Stevens, 2015; Jiang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2010), whereas other related research revealed that online learning experience had no significant effect

on the learners' attitudes towards using online learning system and their BIs to use it (Hrtoňová, Kohout, Rohlíková, & Zounek, 2014; Mailizar, Burg, & Maulina, 2021).

The previous research showed similarities and differences in terms of the positive effect of the core constructs of the TAM and the proposed external ones in the learners' acceptance of using online learning (Almarabeh, 2014; Al-Okaily et al., 2020; Farahat, 2012; Hrtoňová et al., 2014; Hsieh, Huang, & Wu, 2016; Jiang et al., 2021; Mailizar et al., 2021). This research combined the core constructs of the TAM (PEOU and PU of using online learning), which were believed to have an effect on the learners' acceptance of technology, with the external constructs (online learning system  characteristics  and  experience  of  online  learning)  to  examine  their  impact  on  the undergraduate EFL Jordanian students' attitudes towards accepting the use of online learning. However,  the  researchers  found  that  no  previous  research  was  conducted  to  examine  the undergraduate EFL learners' attitudes towards accepting online learning systems using TAM and the  two  proposed  external  constructs  (online  learning  system  characteristics  and  experience  of online learning) at the national and local levels.


## Methods


This is quantitative research. The researchers used an online Likert-scale questionnaire targeting FEL students. The study investigated the factors that predict EFL students' attitudes toward using online learning during covid-19 by applying TAM constructs to design the questionnaire. The questionnaire items were adopted from the previous literature (see Table one). It contained six sections (demographic information, PU, PEOU, BIs, attitudes, and characteristics of online learning systems). Participants were asked to choose their answers for the demographic part. Five-point Likert scale was used in sections two to six (strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, and strongly agree). The ethical considerations were met despite the low-risk nature of the research. They included voluntary participation, anonymity, and confidentiality.

Preliminary data computation was conducted using SPSS 26 (Pallant, 2020). Meanwhile, the measurement model and structural model were assessed using Smart PLS 3.3. Smart PLS is a Structural  Equation  Modeling  (SEM)  method  that  has  received  much  significance  in  recent decades, and its popularity has grown for testing concepts and theories. The success of SEM is justified by its ability to evaluate measurement models that include latent variables and, at the same time, test relationships among the latent variables (Babin et al., 2008; Hair, Hult, Ringle, & Sarstedt, 2021), making this approach helpful for this study.


## Research Procedures


The distribution  of  the  online  questionnaire  was  done  through  Microsoft  Forms.  The questionnaire link was sent to the targeted students with a cover letter explaining the study's goals and instructions to fill out the questionnaire. Several reminders were sent to students to increase the  responding  ratio.  After  two  months  (November  and  December  2021),  data  collection  was stopped as no more responses were received, and the sampling approach was based on simple random methods. The targeted population comprised 602 EFL students who are studying for their B.A. degree in the English Language and Literature Department at Al-Balqa Applied University, making the required sample 234. The sample size was determined by statistical tables proposed by (Bougie & Sekaran, 2019) for the sample size needed at a confidence of 95% and a 5.0% margin of error.

Further, as this study used the SEM approach for statistical analysis, SEM-AMOS was not seen as suitable for this study because the goodness of fit indices in AMOS is sensitive to sample size. Fitness indices in AMOS require using a ratio of 1:10 per parameter (Bentler & Chou, 1987). Since the instrument has 25 parameters, this requires a sample comprising 250 responses. However, the exact sample size in this study included 177 responses. Therefore, Smart PLS was seen as more suitable since Smart PLS discards data distribution assumptions, and it is ideal for small samples (Hair et al., 2021). In total, 187 complete responses were received. However, ten responses were dropped due to patterns in assessments. The exact sample size that was deemed for further analysis comprised 177 answers.

## Measurement Model Testing

## Discussion


This study investigated factors that predict EFL students' attitudes toward online learning in the COVID-19 era.  TAM was successfully employed to capture the factors that explain students' attitudes. To do so, the quantitative approach guided this study to gather students' perceptions while using an online questionnaire. Scales were adopted from previous studies. The instrument was validated and exhibited satisfactory statistical reliability and validity.

Starting  with  descriptive  analysis,  critical  implications  can  be  concluded.  Although  online learning  systems  became  the  primary  means  to  interact  with  students  and  thus  required  such systems to be thoroughly and professionally tailored to provide education of high quality, students' perceptions of benefits that should be provided by systems were of moderate levels. This entailed that these systems were still subject to improvement and enhancement that should be considered by these systems developers.

Through path estimates supported by bootstrapping results, most hypotheses were supported except for the association between PEOU and attitudes. Findings of Alharbi and Drew (2014), Hsieh et al. (2016),  Pituch and Lee (2006), and Salloum et al. (2019) all supported the positive effect of online learning system characteristics on PU of online learning. Pituch and Lee (2006) and Salloum et al. (2019) also found a positive impact of online learning system characteristics on the PEOU of online learning. Positive effects of online learning system characteristics on both attitudes and BIs of EFL learners were also depicted in studies by Kanwal and Rehman (2017) and Pituch and Lee (2006). Like online learning system characteristics, the positive effects of PU of online learning on attitudes and BIs of EFL learners were also supported by most of the studies (Almarabeh, 2014; Farahat, 2012; Haleman & Yamat, 2021; Jiang et al., 2021; Natasia et al., 2022; Salloum et al., 2019;).

In contrast,  PEOU  and  attitudes  toward  EFL  learners'  use  of  online  learning  received contradictory views. While most of the studies supported the positive effects of PEOU on PU of online learning (Almarabeh, 2014; Al-Okaily et al., 2020; Farahat, 2012; Hsieh et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2021), some studies were inconsistent about the relationship between PEOU and attitudes towards online learning. Natasia et al. (2022) findings were conformed with our results that PEOU did not positively affect EFL learners' attitudes toward using online learning. On the contrary, Almarabeh (2014), Farahat (2012), and Jiang et al. (2021) findings revealed positive effects of PEOU  on  learners'  attitudes.  The  association  between  PEOU  and  attitudes  was  seen  as insignificant. This entailed a critical implication that should be considered.  The ease of using online learning systems couldn not foster or shape the students' attitudes. This took us to the earlier point that the ease of use of online learning is still a subject for improvement to promote its role in becoming a significant predictor of attitudes.

Likewise,  the  findings  related  to  attitudes  and  BIs  towards  using  online  learning  were  also discordant. While studies by Almarabeh  (2014), Farahat (2012)2, Haleman and Yamat (2021), and Natasia et al. (2022) supported our findings that attitudes towards online learning significantly affected their behavioral BIs, findings of other studies like Jiang et al. (2021) and Teo et al., (2008) found  that  EFL  learners  attitudes  towards  online  learning  had  an  unimportant  effect  on  their behavioral intentions to use online learning. Finally, our findings proved that the experience in online learning did not have a positive impact on EFL learners' attitudes and BIs to use it.  We argued that the insignificant effect of previous online learning experience on students' attitudes toward  using  online  learning  might  be  because  dealing  with  technology  and  its  tools  was considered a normal part of the students' daily life with different degrees. It could also be attributed to  the  sudden,  supposedly  temporary,  and  abrupt  shift  to  online  learning  because  of  Covid-19 lockdown  measures.    Studies  by  Hrtoňová  et  al.  (2014)  and  Mailizar  et  al.  (2021)  showed concordance with these findings, while studies by Abramson et al. (2015) and Jiang et al. (2021) revealed a positive effect of experience on attitudes and BIs to use online learning.

Path  estimates  for  all  proposed  associations  that  reported  significant  positive  influences  to support the idea that these factors as predictors for attitudes and BIs provided a promising scenario if online learning systems are maintained effectively. Students' attitudes will be in favor of these systems. Accordingly, their future intention to use these systems can be granted.


## Conclusion


The aim of this research is to understand how EFL students receive online learning to enhance its  points  of  strength  and  address  its  challenges.  As  a  result,  the  researchers  applied  TAM  to investigate  students'  attitudes  towards  using  the  online  learning  system.  The  most  significant findings of this study revealed that characteristics of the online learning system positively affect the EFL learners' PEOU, PU, and attitudes towards online learning systems. Additionally, our findings revealed that the online learning system characteristics positively impact the learners' BIs of the online learning system.   Furthermore, PEOU has a positive impact on PU of online learning system and the attitudes toward using it. The PU of online learning has significantly affected the attitudes and the BIs to use it. This study has asserted the essential role the online learning system characteristics ought to play in affecting the learners' attitudes towards the online learning system.

## Practical Implications


The outcomes of this research have some practical implications for the successful adoption of online  learning  in  teaching  English  as  a  foreign  language.  Taking  into  consideration  that  the research results might be shared with other tertiary students, online officials in the higher education institutions  in  Jordan  ought  to  make  use  of  the  positive  impact  of  online  learning  system characteristics on students' attitudes and behavioral intentions towards the adoption of the online learning system. This positive impact could be enhanced by getting programmed and continuous feedback  from  the  students.  Accordingly,  the  flexibility  and  constant  improvement  of  online learning system tools empower students learning styles to keep them up-to-date with technological innovation and ultimately produce an autonomous and long-life learner.

The online learning system could be considered an employability skill because EFL learners, especially  the  future  teachers  of  them,  need  not  to  stop  developing  their  language  and communication skills. Secondly, and despite the insignificant impact of online experience on EFL students, attention should be paid to the students' psychological aspect towards online learning since  it  is  unquestionably  linked  to  Covid-19  pandemic  measures,  which  gave  it  a  sense  of  a temporary nature. Education administration and instructors might gradually use all the opportunities to merge online learning as part of the students' lifestyle.

## 1 Introduction



## 1.1 Biodiversity conservation and knowledge exchange


Biodiversity  loss  is  one  of  the  most  pressing  issues  of  our  time  due  to  its  vast  scale  and  significant detrimental impacts on people and nature (Cardinale et al., 2012, IPBES, 2019, Roe, 2019). However, only developing  knowledge  about  how  to  conserve  biodiversity  is  not  enough  as  effective  biodiversity conservation  practice  relies  on  both  the  development  and  dissemination  of  salient  (i.e.,  relevant  and timely)  and  credible  knowledge  (Cook  et  al.,  2013)  and  on  its  deployment  to  improve  conservation practices. Knowledge exchange is central to these processes.

Knowledge exchange is a broad concept that can be defined as 'a process of generating, sharing and/or using knowledge through various methods appropriate to the context, purpose, and participants involved' (Fazey et al., 2012). When both academics and practitioners engage effectively in knowledge exchange, it can  bolster  the  usefulness  of  research  for  purposes  beyond  academia  (Ray,  1999,  Van  de  Ven,  2017). However,  inadequate  academic-practitioner  knowledge  exchange  persists  for  work  on  biodiversity conservation (Whitten et al., 2001, Gossa et al., 2014, Knight et al., 2008, Lemieux et al., 2021, Toomey et al., 2017). This is problematic because it can lead to less effective conservation practice (Kark et al., 2015, Taff et al., 2015, Rose, 2015). Thus, knowledge exchange between academics and practitioners working on biodiversity conservation has been identified as a key area for further research (Fazey et al., 2014, Fazey et al., 2012, Nguyen et al., 2017).

Inadequate academic-practitioner knowledge exchange in biodiversity conservation has been attributed to several interconnected challenges (Linklater, 2003, Arlettaz et al., 2010, Roche et al., 2021, Knight et al., 2008, Sutherland et al., 2004, Moshier et al., 2019, Cook et al., 2013, Redford and Taber, 2000). One of the main challenges is  inadequate  communication, which can occur in the early stages of the research or project design process and can lead to stakeholders pursuing research questions with limited applicability to  practice  and  policy  or  unsound  project  goals  (Linklater,  2003,  Arlettaz  et  al.,  2010).  Inadequate communication can also occur in the later stages of a project, for example when academics or practitioners do not share data or when findings are published in peer-reviewed journals that are inaccessible or not easily understandable for certain practitioners (Roche et al., 2021, Knight et al., 2008). A related challenge is that academics and practitioners in biodiversity conservation tend to exchange knowledge through close social connections and therefore do not make full use of the networks of relevant and available personnel and organisations (Sutherland et al., 2004, Moshier et al., 2019). Additionally, although academics and practitioners working on biodiversity conservation often have overlapping goals, they usually differ in their aims  and  worldviews:  the  main  driver  of  academics  is  to  publish  in  peer-reviewed  journals  whereas practitioners require pragmatic fundable solutions for conservation problems. Such differences can lead to conflicts around project design, communications, and willingness to share knowledge; for instance, when academics focus on academic rigour to the extent that findings become less salient to practitioners or practitioners refuse to share evidence going against their worldviews (Cook et al., 2013). These challenges are  often  underpinned  by  the  insufficient  resources  that  are  budgeted  by  funding  bodies  to  promote collaboration (Moshier et al., 2019, Redford and Taber, 2000). In all, these interconnected challenges can hamper academic-practitioner knowledge exchange and so undermine conservation effectiveness.


## 1.2 Illegal wildlife trade and knowledge exchange


Illegal  wildlife  trade  (IWT),  which  encompasses  all  unlawful  activities  associated  with  the  commercial exploitation of, and trade in, wildlife specimens, is a major driver of biodiversity loss (Sas-Rolfes et al., 2019, Hughes,  2021). For example, it is widely acknowledged that behaviour change interventions that meet particular design benchmarks are more likely to be successful; yet, whilst the number of demand reduction campaigns for illegal wildlife

Therefore, the goal of this paper is two-fold: (1) to gain a deeper understanding of the main challenges to academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT to produce a structured and overarching outline of them,  and  (2)  based  on  these  insights,  to  propose  measures  for  improving  academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT.


## 2 Methods



## 2.1 Data collection


We conducted three workshops to explore the challenges to knowledge exchange between academics and practitioners working on IWT. The first stage of choosing participants involved identifying organisations with established and substantial portfolios of international work on IWT issues. Individuals within these organisations who worked on IWT issues were then identified and contacted. In terms of the personal characteristics of participants, we particularly aimed to have a balanced gender ratio and mix of junior and senior academics and practitioners.

Each workshop lasted between four and five hours. The first workshop was held in October 2018, in Oxford, and had seven participants from three British academic institutions. The second workshop was held in November  2018,  in  Cambridge,  and  had  nine  participants  from  eight  different  non-governmental organisations (NGOs). This workshop was complemented by an interview, in November 2018, with a senior conservation practitioner who worked for a conservation NGO headquartered in London but had been unable to attend the workshop. The third workshop was carried out in July 2019, in London, and was attended by four academics and four practitioners from eight different institutions. This research was approved by the Saïd Business School Departmental Research Ethics Committee, University of Oxford (SSH SBS C1A 18 067).

## 3 Results


Our three workshops involved a total of 10 academics from five universities in the United Kingdom and 15 practitioners from nine organisations that have offices in the United Kingdom but work internationally on IWT issues. Our one interview was with a senior conservation practitioner whose NGO was headquartered in London. In terms of our participants, our practitioner sample was predominantly female but balanced in terms of career stage, while our academic sample was gender balanced but primarily early career.

The main challenges to academic-practitioner knowledge exchange for work on IWT identified in this study pertain to the general differences in the aims and worldviews of academics and practitioners; various manifestations of inadequate communication; and the presence of large, diverse, and dynamic networks of personnel and organisations working on IWT. These challenges are reportedly accentuated by people working  in  the  field  having  insufficient  time  to  foster  collaborative  relationships  and  are  largely underpinned by the nature of existing funding systems.


## 3.1 Aims and worldviews


General differences in the aims and worldviews of academics and practitioners were identified as a main challenge to academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT. According to our study, academics are largely driven by the need for peer-reviewed publications and, in comparison to practitioners, tend to advocate  for  a  stronger  evidence  base  in  project  design.  Practitioners,  on  the  other  hand,  were characterised as tending to be more action-focused and inclined to act quickly rather than allowing time for further research, even in contexts where the most effective intervention is uncertain. Our participants emphasised that the divisions related to these differences in the aims and worldviews of academics and practitioners are most acute when the expectations of what a collaboration entails, its main goals, and the responsibilities of the different parties are not clearly outlined at an early stage.

General differences in academic and practitioner perceptions of how research priorities should be chosen and how findings should be used were identified as key challenges to knowledge exchange for work on IWT. Regarding the selection of research priorities, our study suggests that academics tend to select topics due to academic curiosity or to conservation needs identified by evidence. However, the same topics may not be prioritised by practitioners or of relevance to them, as they may not appeal to the stakeholders that practitioner  rely  on  for  funding.  For  example,  academics  working  on  non-charismatic  species  that  are affected by IWT find collaborating with practitioners more difficult as these species are not prioritised, reportedly as they are less marketable to non-specialist audiences or funding bodies. Regarding the use of research evidence, some of our participants from academia reported that practitioners may choose to ignore it to go ahead with actions regardless of whether there is evidence of effectiveness or even when there is evidence that the approach being taken does not deliver the desired benefits. Our participants reported that this is often the result of competition and external pressures in the non-profit sector (e.g., funder requirements; pressures of public perceptions), and, in some cases, because of entrenched beliefs and the culture of an organisation. This is frustrating for the academics who produce the relevant evidence and might discourage individuals who have directly experienced or heard about them from collaborating.

## 3.2 Communication


Poor communication was identified as a main challenge to meaningful knowledge exchange for work on IWT, and one that can manifest in various forms. A major manifestation is that the main output of academic knowledge on IWT is papers in peer-reviewed journals, which are often inaccessible for practitioners due to paywalls. Our participants reported that this issue is particularly acute for practitioners from smaller organisations  that  cannot  devote  their  (limited)  resources  to  access  papers  from  certain  journals. Furthermore, the knowledge on IWT that is published in academics papers might be communicated in ways that might not be easily understandable nor useable, such as some practitioners who may lack the specific technical  expertise.  Our  participants  identified  this  issue  as  being  particularly  acute  in  the  context  of knowledge exchange on IWT. This is because the field requires interdisciplinary approaches in order to achieve positive impacts and, therefore, practitioners are likely to need to interpret and use knowledge from  disciplines  with  which  they  are  less  familiar.  Another  manifestation  of  poor  communication  was inadequate  academic-practitioner  communication  in  the  early  stages  of research on  IWT.  Such communication between academics and key stakeholders, including practitioners, can be inadequate in both quality and quantity and, as a result, can lead to academics carrying out research on IWT that does not address the needs of practitioners and so has minimal potential for real-world impact.
