## 3.3 Size, diversity, and dynamism of academic and practitioner communities


Certain features of the academic and practitioner communities working on IWT contribute to the challenge of effective knowledge exchange. Most relevantly, our academic and practitioner participants both stated that the size and diversity of the networks of personnel and organisations working on IWT can make it difficult to identify the most appropriate people or organisations with whom to exchange knowledge. The diversity of the relevant communities presents the further challenge of both academics and practitioners needing to engage with people with different areas of expertise, which can hinder the flow of knowledge. In fact, our participants reported that the diversity of academic and practitioner communities is particularly acute for knowledge exchange on IWT because successfully countering IWT usually demands tools and techniques  from  multiple  disciplines.  Moreover,  it  was  acknowledged  in  both  the  academic  and practitioner workshops that the global prevalence of IWT means that academics and practitioners working on IWT issues might operate under a diverse array of cultural and political conditions, which can constitute a further challenge to knowledge exchange.

Additionally, knowledge exchange on IWT can be disrupted by the high turnover rates of personnel in some institutions. As happens in other areas of conservation, these high turnover rates, particularly in non-profit and government bodies, can disrupt existing academic-practitioner relationships for knowledge exchange on IWT. Thus, academics and practitioners face the challenge of simultaneously preserving knowledge from old relationships, maintaining current relationships, and regularly cultivating new relationships. However, disruptions from the high turnover rates in certain institutions can dissuade academics and practitioners from putting effort into establishing, developing, and maintaining relationships, and so from collaborating.


## 3.4 Available time


Accentuating each of the aforementioned challenges (3.1, 3.2, 3.3) is the insufficient time that academics and practitioners who work on IWT have available to develop and maintain relationships for knowledge exchange. Both our academic and practitioner participants stressed that it is a time-consuming exercise, and that people who work on IWT already tend to feel overstretched. Our practitioner participants, in particular, reported that collaboration, including knowledge exchange, is often perceived as an additional burden rather than an integral part of their work and as an endeavour that can take time away from more impactful activities. Both our academic and practitioner participants stated that this challenge of lack of time is largely underpinned by the funding for work on IWT, as the relevant funding does not usually cover the time to develop and maintain relationships, nor the time to translate and communicate findings to audiences beyond the main target group(s). Yet, it was also reported that lack of time is sometimes used as an excuse to avoid unwanted collaborations.


## 3.5 Funding


A fundamental challenge to academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT, that was stressed by our practitioners and especially academic participants, relates to the funding for work on IWT issues. Our study identified three ways in which existing funding makes effective knowledge exchange challenging. First, funding cycles for work on IWT tend to be short term, focused on novelty, and come with restrictions (e.g., requiring focus on certain themes or taxa, limited to no staff time). These traits hinder the development and maintenance of long-term relationships. This is problematic in the context of work on IWT as certain indicators of impact (such as trends in the populations of traded species) can take a long time to respond to any interventions and impacts can be hard to disentangle from other influencing factors over those

## 4.1 Contextualising the challenges


Our study identifies and describes five main challenges to academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT: (1) differences in the aims and worldviews of academics and practitioners; (2) poor communication; (3) the presence of large, diverse, and dynamic networks of personnel and organisations working on IWT; (4) insufficient time; and, underpinning these challenges, (5) the nature of the existing funding landscape. Our identification and description of these main challenges to academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT enriches the existing literature because it plainly sets out the challenges whose mediation in current or future work could lead to widespread improvements in academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT and, in turn, the effectiveness of strategies to counter IWT.

Notably, the challenges that we identified for academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT largely align with the challenges faced by academics and practitioners working in biodiversity conservation more generally (Pullin et al., 2004, Roche et al., 2021, Knight et al., 2008, Linklater, 2003, Arlettaz et al., 2010, Keene and Pullin, 2011, Moshier et al., 2019, Cook et al., 2013, Toomey et al., 2017, Sutherland et al., 2004). They also largely align with the challenges to academic-practitioner knowledge exchange that have been identified by previous studies on IWT; for instance, the challenges related to poor academic-practitioner communication (Thomas-Walters et al., 2020, Moshier et al., 2019), the differing aims and worldviews of academics and practitioners (Arias et al., 2021, Greenfield and Verissimo, 2018), engagement with close social connections rather than people or organisations in the wider networks (Moshier et al., 2019), and the limited funding for work on IWT (Moshier et al., 2019). Ultimately, the similarities between our findings and the findings of relevant past studies support the validity of the main challenges that we identified to academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT. Moreover, the presence of these similarities means that previously recommended measures for improving knowledge exchange might be useful for improving academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT (see 4.2).

## 4.2 Potential approaches to addressing the challenges


Our structured and overarching outline of the challenges to academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT shows that the challenges to knowledge exchange on IWT are similar to the challenges to knowledge exchange on other biodiversity conservation issues and beyond. The presence of these general similarities could mean that some of the commonly recommended measures for improving knowledge exchange could be applicable to IWT (see 4.2.1, 4.2.2).


## 4.2.1 Research agreements, diverse outputs, and boundary individuals or organisations


Aligning the aims of academics and practitioners and improving aspects of communication could markedly bolster academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT. For instance, we found that practitioners who work on IWT perceive some research to have limited relevance to countering IWT and that the lack of clear expectations at the start of collaborations can lead to conflicts between partners. Such challenges have been identified for work on other biodiversity conservation issues (Caudron et al., 2012) and in the context of work on IWT issues (Cugniere et al., 2019, Costa, 2020). A useful, and previously advocated, strategy for countering such challenges is the use of formal a priori research agreements when drafting proposals and designing projects (De Pelecijn and Feys, 2021). These can help collaborating personnel and organisations have more realistic expectations for the work, for instance, by stating planned research topics, methods, and outputs, and thus clarifying the relevance of the work and reducing the likelihood of conflicts during or after it (De Pelecijn and Feys, 2021). Furthermore, research agreements have proven useful for guiding collaborative work on biodiversity conservation (Kaiser-Bunbury et al., 2015, Laird and Noejovich, 2002, Preece et al., 2021, Johnson et al., 2021). Therefore, the more consistent use of robust and open research agreements for academic-practitioner work on IWT could well result in sounder collaborations and the increased likelihood of knowledge exchange. Importantly, it could help to increase the perceived relevance of  IWT  research  to  practitioners,  preserve  the  perceived  independence  of  academics  working  with practitioners on IWT, and bolster the trust between academics and practitioners working on IWT.

Our workshops also highlighted the challenge of academic findings on IWT being inaccessible or unusable by practitioners if they are communicated via publications in academic journals. One previously advocated form of communication of academic findings that could counter this barrier and appeal to both academics and practitioners is preprints (Christie et al., 2021). Preprints are complete manuscripts that are made available  without  formal  review,  often  before  submission  to  academic  journals  and  without  hindering future submissions. In this way, preprints speed up practitioners' access to evidence to inform actions as well as providing academics with a public record of their work to mediate concerns about being scooped. The  capacity  of  preprints  to  speed  up  the  communication  of  findings  could  be  especially  useful  for informing  interventions  to  counter  IWT  given  the  rapidly  changing  IWT  landscape.  Also,  preprints  are inherently open access and thus available to practitioners who may be unable to obtain articles in closed access journals. Yet, there are challenges to knowledge exchange via preprints. These include ensuring that preprints are discoverable by relevant practitioners and that the knowledge within them is understandable to non-expert audiences and sufficiently robust. The absence of peer review can also compromise trust in the quality of the research being reported. Indeed, there have been examples of preprints influencing IWT policy despite concerns being raised about the quality of the research that they report (e.g., Hsiang and Sekar, 2016).

Other potentially useful formats for communicating knowledge on IWT could include infographics, training 429 courses, reports, policy briefs, dialogues, toolkits, and side events at key stakeholder meetings (such as 430 CITES conferences of the parties). Such outputs have already been used in the context of IWT, for instance, 431

the Behaviour Change for Conservation Online course and toolkit produced by TRAFFIC, the Tools and 432 Guidance documents produced by the Oxford Martin Programme on Wildlife Trade (Arias et al., 2020, 433 Olmedo et al., 2019, Wright, 2019), and the Wildlife and Forest Crime Analytic Toolkit produced by the 434 United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC, 2012). Importantly, such outputs could aid academic435 practitioner knowledge exchange by providing knowledge on IWT in more accessible and useable formats. 436 Nevertheless, there are difficulties with communicating knowledge on IWT through such outputs, including 437 the need for additional training, and the fact that producing and disseminating such outputs can be time 438 consuming but not necessarily seen nor supported as part of the job. 439

Another strategy to counter the challenges posed by the differing aims of academics and practitioners and the poor communication, as well as the difficulties associated with the large size, diversity, and dynamism of  the  networks  working  on  IWT,  could  be  to  increase  or  improve  the  use  of  boundary  individuals  or organisations. For instance, the  Baltic  Eye  Project  at  Stockholm  University,  which  includes  researchers  from  various  fields,  science communicators,  journalists,  and  policy  analysts,  has  established  and  supported  engagement  between academics and key stakeholders from beyond academia and, in so doing, has successfully bolstered the use of robust evidence in practices and policies related to Baltic Sea management (Cvitanovic et al., 2018). Boundary individuals or organisations that facilitate academic-practitioner knowledge exchange can also be based beyond universities, such as the Regional Ecology Program of the United States Forest Service, which  specialises  in  the  facilitation  of  knowledge  transfer,  especially  between  academics  and  key practitioners (Safford et al., 2017). Given the proven capacity of boundary individuals and organisations to facilitate  academic-practitioner engagement, and therefore their potential to counter a number of the challenges that were identified in this study, further research into their current use and potential further value in the context of academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT could be useful. Nevertheless, a fundamental barrier to any increases or improvements in the use of boundary individuals or organisations for academic-practitioner engagement on IWT issues would be if and how they would be incorporated into the already stretched funding landscape.


## 4.2.2 Changes to funding


Our findings stress that existing funding for work on IWT presents a fundamental challenge to academicpractitioner knowledge exchange because it budgets insufficient resources, including time, for it. Reports of this challenge to knowledge exchange in other areas has spurred recommendations for funders to more effectively expect and support knowledge exchange activities and solutions to communications challenges (Shanley and Lopez, 2009, Lacey et al., 2015, Cvitanovic et al., 2015a, Cvitanovic et al., 2015b). In line with such recommendations, amending the nature and magnitude of funding for IWT work to provide more time, resources, and expectations for knowledge exchange could have a beneficial impact on the quality of knowledge exchange by helping to address some of the main challenges. More specifically, funders could request collaborative proposals to integrate knowledge exchange at the root of the projects as well as support  the  routine  use  of  boundary  individuals  or  organisations  to  facilitate  effective  academicpractitioner  engagement (see 4.2.1). Requiring funding recipients to lay out a full  and  costed  plan  for knowledge  exchange  (including  stakeholder  maps,  research  agreements,  measures  of  success  and evaluation of outcomes) would help, as would providing longer-term, more strategically targeted, funding that encouraged the appropriate use of evidence in designing, implementing, monitoring and evaluating IWT interventions. Indeed, requirements along these lines have already been adopted by some funding bodies for IWT, such as the Species Conservation Catalyst Fund of the United States Fish and Wildlife Program (https://www.fws.gov/service/species-conservation-catalyst-fund). Adding conditionality to funding based on clear policies on the use and availability of data generated from the funded work (with due regard to ethics and the sensitivity of some datasets) would promote learning and communication within the sector.

Future research could also examine the challenges that were identified in this study in greater detail. For example, we found that lack of time, resources, and expectations for academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT are key challenges that largely stem from the funding for work on IWT. Furthermore,  the  workshops  for  this  study  predominantly  focussed  on  the  challenges  to  knowledge exchange  on  IWT,  rather  than  on  potential  approaches  for  its  improvement. Finally, it is important to note that whilst the main challenges identified in this study may well be experienced by many academics and practitioners working on IWT, they could manifest in various ways and change over time, and, so, might need to be examined with focussed research and countered with context-specific strategies.


## 5 Conclusion


Academics and practitioners engaging in academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT experience several interconnected challenges (i.e., inadequate communication; large, diverse, and dynamic networks; different aims and worldviews; insufficient time; limitations of funding). Furthermore, facets of the main challenges can be especially acute in the context of IWT versus other conservation issues; namely, the large size and diversity of the academic and practitioner networks, the particularly partisan perspectives of some of the organisations, and the difficulties due to the illegality of IWT. Key stakeholders, especially academics and practitioners, could benefit from an awareness of the potential challenges identified and outlined in our study before engaging in knowledge exchange on IWT.

Consideration of the challenges we identified alongside recommendations from the wider literature flags several potential measures to improve academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT, like the more routine use of boundary individuals or organisations, research agreements, and a diverse set of formats for communicating findings. To this end, the results of this study will also be available via a preprint and an accompanying infographic that will be circulated amongst relevant stakeholders. Increased support and explicit expectations from funding bodies for academic-practitioner knowledge exchange on IWT could also drive pervasive improvements. If key stakeholders, especially end users of knowledge to counter IWT, demand  more  robust  or  nuanced  recommendations  for  improving  academic-practitioner  knowledge exchange on IWT than the recommendations from this study, then analogous future research could yield them by using larger and more diverse sets of academics and practitioners and more nuanced methods (e.g., scenario interviews or scenario planning).

## WEBTOONS


Webtoons, which are commonly referred to as webcomics in the English language, have been a staple of online Korean popular culture for over a decade, having first appeared in the early 2000s as personal blog or online journal entries that the artists would draw in short comic strip format;  as such, the earliest webtoons were those of graphic designers and illustrators who were well versed in using computer software for drawing, rather than manhwa artists who primarily utilized  pen  and  paper  (Han  et  al.  2015:  19).  However,  with  the  increase  in  artists  drawing comics online, and with the sponsorship of major websites (the most prominent being the web portals Naver and Daum) providing channels for these artists to regularly serialize their material, webtoons have since expanded their media presence in South Korean culture. With diversified content, ease of access, and greater profitability, webtoons have gained an increased share of the

comics market (Han et al. 2015: 19), which has also led to originally print-based manhwa artists to  reinvent  themselves  as  webtoon  artists.  With  the  increased  popularity  and  prominence  of webtoons, there has also been some academic scholarship paying attention to the subject, though still very little in the English language. 2

I would emphasize here that webtoons cannot be as easily defined as 'manhwa published online', in that manhwa also exists online through illegal scans, e-book forms, etc. That is, scanned pages of  page-format  comics  that  have  been  uploaded  online  does  not  fall  into  the  category  of webtoons.  Rather,  'webtoons'  are  manhwa  specifically  created  in  and/or  for  an  electronic, Internet  context,  and  as  such  are  inherently  defined  by  that  context.  Because  webtoons  artists overwhelmingly  use  computers  and  software  to  draw,  many  webtoons  typically  feature  clean lines and opaque colour fills, which show none of the 'flaws' of physical media; yet there is a persistent  minority  of  artists  who  prefer  a  more  'realistic'  style,  and  use  physical  media  (pen, crayon,  watercolour  paint,  etc.) or particular software  to recreate the effect (Figure  1).
