## THEORETICAL FRAMEWORKS


I found in approaching this material that Huhtamo's (2004)work on media archaeology and Francesco Casetti's  frameworks  in The Lumière Galaxy: Seven Key Words for the Cinema to Come (2015)  were  particularly  helpful.  In  understanding  the  shift  from  a  physically  rooted, materially  contingent  mode  of  media  consumption  to  a  mode  that  is  'liberated'  from  these conditions, it is useful to think of Huhtamo's approach in his work on 'screenology', where he argues that 'the meaning of screens…cannot be fully grasped without exploring their antecedents and  (re-)placing  these  within  the  contexts  of  their  own  times'  (Huhtamo  2004:  64)    While Huhtamo's own work focuses on the changing cultural significance and presence of a material media object (the screen), I feel strongly that his approach is useful to keep in mind in terms of understanding 'patterns and schemata that have appeared in earlier contexts', and to avoid the 'disregard  for the past' that Erkki  Huhtamo  and  Jussi  Parikka  warned  against  in  their introduction to Media Archaeology: Approaches, Applications and Implications (2011).

From Casetti's work, I borrow the concepts of remediation and relocation to structure and organize  my  own  observations.  In The  Lumière  Galaxy ,  Casetti  foregrounds  the  differences between  remediation  and  relocation  by  first  laying  out  the  see-sawing  balance  between 'machine-based' and 'experience-based' film theories throughout the twentieth century. He notes that these two threads have swung in and out of favour in different decades, with 'the first three decades  of  the  twentieth  century  consistently  [developing]  this  experiential  approach',  after which  'the  machine  took  the  upper  hand',  before  giving  way  once  more  to  the  'experiential approach' with André Bazin and Edgar Morin (Casetti 2015: 37).

This  contrast  between  machine  and  experience-focused  theories  leads  directly  to  Casetti's conceptualization of the difference between remediation and relocation. For remediation, Casetti refers back to the work of Bolter and Grusin, where they define the term as 'the process through which one medium is itself incorporated or represented in another medium'; Casetti notes that the term is invoked particularly with regards to electronic media and dematerialization: 'either a reabsorption of the old medium in the new one or a remodeling of the old medium by the new one'. Remediation, by Casetti's understanding, focuses on the presence or absence of device and its configuration; the examples he gives here are the family photo album that is digitized into an electronic file, and films that have been made into video games (2015: 40-41).

He contrasts this approach - a focus on materiality/device - with relocation ,  which he views as focusing more on experience, and the specific practices that are attached to the act of consuming media.

A given medium is defined by a specific type of watching, listening, attention, and sensibility. Therefore, it is not the permanence of its physical aspect, but the permanence of its way of seeing, hearing, and sensing, that ensures its continuity. A medium survives as long as the form of experience that characterizes it survives. (Casetti 2015: 42)

I believe it is important to keep both of these concepts in mind in approaching webtoons, as  the  shift  from  print  manhwa  to  webtoons  clearly  calls  for  both  methods.  The  changes  that occurred in the material conditions of production, distribution, and consumption of webtoons in  a  nutshell,  the  shift  from  paper  book  to  cell  phone  screen  -  has  clearly  reconfigured  the medium while absorbing elements of the old medium, but at the same time I also would like to shed light on shifts that have taken place on the experiential level. These experiential changes are not  merely  to  do  with  the  cultural  practices  attached  to  manhwa  reading,  but  also  have implications  in  socio-economic  dimensions:  while  certain  traits  of  manhwa  practice  remain, social connotations have clearly changed.


## REMEDIATION: MATERIAL RESOURCES AND NARRATIVE TECHNIQUES


So what are the key differences that have emerged between manhwa and webtoons? In this first section, I examine content-based changes, and in the second section, I will examine spacefocused changes. Content changes primarily stem from the differences in material, mechanical resources between the two forms, and therefore can be viewed principally from a remediation point  of  view.  These  differences  in  material  conditions  have  directly  shaped  certain  major features that set webtoons distinctly apart from manhwa, which may give rise to the question of how and why we juxtapose these two media forms as related in a kind of genealogy.

Casetti, in exploring the various ways that cinema 'emerges' from various different situations, emphasizes that audiences must be able to recognize, or associate, a media form as one that has come before it. That is, in order to discuss the 'cinema beyond', one must be able to identify a moving image work being screened in an art gallery as the same type or category of medium as

films  being  played  in  theatres  (Casetti  2015:  45-46).  While  Casetti  concedes  that  the  act  of recognition is, on some levels, a mental decision, there are key characteristics shared by manhwa and webtoons that make it easier for readers to connect them in a kind of genealogy.

Scott McCloud, in his theoretical comic book, explores various essential elements of comics to  come  up  with  a  clear  definition.  Beginning  with  comics  artist  Will  Eisner's  definition, 'sequential  art',  McCloud  goes  on  to  point  out  that  comics  have  a  curious,  sibling-like relationship  to  cinema,  in  that  comics  are  a  composition  of  spatially  sequenced  images,  while films  are  a composition of temporally sequenced ones. 'However', he writes, 'you might say that before it's projected, film is just a very…very slow comic!' (McCloud 1993: 6-8). McCloud ultimately  completes  his  definition  as  'juxtaposed  pictorial  and  other  images  in  deliberate sequence, intended to convey information and/or to produce an aesthetic response in the viewer', which  I  find  to  be  a  clear  and  valid  classification  that  include  both  manhwa  and  webtoons (McCloud 1993: 9).

Beginning with McCloud's definition as a starting point, we can then go on to understand how webtoons diverge from the well-established traditions and conventions of comics that have been  put  in  place  by  manga  and  manhwa  for  many  decades.  While  this  is  far  from  a comprehensive, thorough review of all manhwa and all webtoons, and therefore I cannot make conclusive statements about the differences between the two forms, I can generally identify three major stylistic and content-based changes: layout, colour and movement.

The  two-page  layout  system  -  primarily  comprised  of  panels,  characters,  and  script  -  of manhwa and manga has long been a subject of extensive theorization and analysis, particularly in Japan.  Fusanosuke  Natsume,  a  prominent  manga  theorist,  writes  that  'manga  has  formed  a unique code of gaze movement… The sometimes efficient, sometimes ambivalent moves of the reader's gaze are determined by the 'reading' direction…linking and structuring visual elements like  script  and  images  (and  sometimes blank spaces)'. The two-page layout is encoded with a specific trajectory along with the reader's eye travels, the 'panels and pages [becoming] a system that consolidates the movement of the gaze' (Natsume 2010: 46). As such, the various panels, speech bubbles, and other elements form specific relations and dynamics with each other on the page according to the page's composition. These characteristics are also common denominators that connect manga and manhwa to the American comic and the European bande dessinée.

It is interesting to note that this layout theorization, which I feel is applicable to both manga and manhwa, also dwells a good deal on the relationship between manga and cinema, in terms of how  manga  has  borrowed  and  appropriated  various  cinematographic  elements  in  developing narrative techniques. Deborah Shamoon (2011: 22), in her examination of the genre of gekiga (dramatic, adult-oriented manga), points out that editing and framing techniques for continuity, such  as  the  close-up  and  the  shot-reverse-shot,  have  been  directly  taken  from  cinema  and  are now  used  widely  across  manga.  Continuity  editing  techniques  in  mainstream  cinema  have become a 'key site' from which manga panels learn to execute smooth or striking transitions.

With the transferral to a digital, web-page context, however, this complex dynamic of panels on  a  two-page  layout  is  completely  broken.  First,  webtoons  almost  all  adopt  a  downwardscrolling format, not unlike a very long comic strip, and therefore the eye no longer travels both vertically and horizontally. While some webtoons do maintain panels, and indeed may compose page-like layouts in the style of print manhwa, a large portion of webtoons do away with panels completely,  with  the  entire  white  expanse  of  the  screen  available  as  potential  page  space. Drawings are  no  longer  encased,  either  within  lines  or  within  physical  page  margins,  but  are rather placed freely down the webpage in a long scrolling strip. In the cases where panels are still used, it is often the case that they are no longer arranged tightly in conjunction with each other, and instead descend somewhat detached from one another, floating in a stretch of white.

Another clear divergence from manhwa that can be found in webtoons is the proliferation of colour. While colour may perhaps seem like too obvious a component in illustration, I emphasize it here because in the context of manhwa and manga, it is a privileged element. It is important to note  that,  on  an  economic  level,  it  would  be  exceptionally  laborious  and  costly  to  produce coloured print manhwa; each series of manhwa and manga are usually the work of one or a few artists per series (in contrast with animation, which employs a large number of animators to work on a single project), and illustrating with coloured pen or any other coloured media is a longer and more expensive process than merely drawing with pen. Moreover, colour drawings require higher  quality  paper  and  ink  for  printing,  driving  up  the  production  cost.  Therefore,  coloured illustrations  are  treated  in  the  context  of  manga/manhwa  as special items: they  are most often used for physical book or magazine covers, sometimes included in special issues, sold separately as posters, or included in other merchandise. However, illustration and graphic software has done away with many of the restraints of producing coloured work, and the online platform provides

an easier and less costly mode of dissemination, which means that most webtoons are splashed with colour.

Perhaps  the  most  interesting  innovation  to  emerge  from  the  remediation  of  manhwa  into webtoons is the introduction of increasingly 'cinematic' factors into the work, an element that is a little more difficult to pin down as it is one that has been experimented with year to year. This brings  us  back  to  the  earlier,  important  point  that  manga  has  long  been  heavily  influenced  by film  and  cinematographic  techniques,  in  particular  continuity  editing.  When  considering  the jump  of  the  gaze  from  panel  to  panel  (in  particular  with  action  sequences,  where  each  panel portrays  a  different  movement),  I  would  suggest  that  there  often  is  an  impulse  towards movement inherent within them. Even with individual panels that are merely images in stasis, there are techniques such as the orientation of the onomatopoeia or the use of dramatic lines and panel shapes that argue for static images as being capable of conveying dynamic movement.

I  would argue that this impulse towards dynamism finds at least some degree of release or manifestation in the various opportunities afforded by webtoons through their online platform, though I am cautious in arguing for anything revolutionary at this point in time. In recent years, webtoon artists have been increasingly experimenting with the incorporation of movement into their work, most commonly with movement that is triggered by the downward scroll. That is, a variety  of  works  feature  a  kind  of  partial  animation  that  is  activated  as  the  reader  reaches different points along the webtoons strip; currently, this effect is predominantly used in horror webtoons, a popular staple in the summer in South Korea.

Animation  and  manhwa  are  two  fairly  different  modes  of  production  that  need  vastly different resources and manpower; print manhwa artists would never be able to adapt their works to  animated  formats  on  their  own.  However,  this  new  generation  of  comic  artists  working  in webtoons include not just those who have migrated from pen-and-paper, but also those who have entered  the  field  from  game  design,  graphic  design  and  web  design.  Borrowing  the  new technologies  at  their  disposal,  these  artists  have  been  at  the  forefront  of  experimentation  with movement.  However,  as  Scott  McCloud  commented  in  a  2011  blog  posting  about  the  first webtoon to try partial animation, this particular method (which works in conjunction with the webtoons  reader's  own  scrolling  movement)  does  not  escape  the  bounds  of  comics  as  fully formed  animation  does.  'This  is one  of those interesting cases where  the  insertion of motion…doesn't  automatically  tear  at  the  fabric  of  the  medium',  he  wrote.  'It  still  feels  like

comics,  because  that  static  juxtaposition  is  maintained'  (McCloud  2011).  That  is,  the  partial movement still remains within a certain static context, and maintains continuity with the images that come before and after it.

The  most  interesting  and  unusual  example  of  movement  incorporation  in  webtoons  that  I have  found  so  far  has  been  in  'Constanze  Iyagi',  a  bold  and  innovative  narrative  work  that examines the aftermath of sexual assault. 'Constanze Iyagi' is most notable in that it is - to my knowledge - the only webtoon that inserts a fully formed animated short film into its diegesis, embedding  it  in  the  webtoon  strip  as  'security  camera  footage'  that  the  webtoon's  narrator watches in the story (Kim 2011). The webtoon artist, an industrial design major, had originally begun her career as an animator, and submitted her short film to a Korean film festival as well as publishing it as part of her webtoon  (Korean Manhwa Contents Agency [KOMACON] 2012). 3 While  I  can  find  no  other  webtoon  artists  who  have  followed  her  lead  -  understandably  so, considering the labour-intensive process of animating even a short film - her work nevertheless effectively showcases the potential for utilizing both moving and static images in webtoons.


## RELOCATION: THE SPATIAL EXPERIENCE OF MANHWA AND WEBTOONS


So far I have briefly introduced some of the 'content'-based differences that have emerged with  the  shift  from  print  manhwa  to  online  webtoons.  I  must  also  point  out  here  that  these changes are not radical shifts that have sprung as manhwa organically migrated to webtoons, but rather  have  a  great  deal  to  do  with  how  webtoons  came  to  be.  As  the  earliest  webtoons  were works that initially began as posts on personal blogs or websites in a journal/diary like form, they were consequently very  informal  in  their  style  (Han  et  al.  2015:  17)  The  creators  did  not  put panels  and  dividing  lines  in  their  work  in  part  because  the  comics  were  mostly  free-floating musings,  rather  than  concrete  narratives;  it  is  only  later  that  webtoons  also  began  to  feature action narratives, romance and other genres that exist in manhwa and manga, and thus re-import various stylistic conventions from print manhwa into webtoons. 4

As mentioned before, relocation is very much to do with the experience of the medium, and this experience is defined by the physical or technological space; with changes to that space, it is a matter of course that the experience is also changed. Therefore, in approaching manhwa and webtoons  from  a  relocation  point  of  view,  my  queries  become  crystallized  into  a  contrast  of 'where does manhwa happen?' versus 'where do webtoons happen?'The question is a slippery

one, in that it forces me to make certain statements about the practice of consuming manhwa and webtoons that may be far too generalizing and broad. Yet, perhaps by framing this issue of space as a matter of associations that have been formed in the cultural imaginary (as opposed to the intricate  varieties  of  practices  of  consumption  that  exist  in  lived  reality),  I  can  still  make  an argument  for  the  relation  between  the  space  of  manhwa/webtoon  consumption  and  its  social standing.  In  approaching  the  question  from  this  angle,  it  would  be  helpful  to  borrow  from Thomas LaMarre's The Anime Machine: A Media Theory of Animation (2009), where he writes about the manga reading experience:

One of the prototypical manga experiences is that of picking up at a kiosk one of  the  thick  inexpensive  weekly  volumes  that  are  full  of  new  installments  of  a number  of  continuing  series,  and  reading  it  on  the  commuter  train.  Some commentators even claim that the length of episodes in weeklies roughly matches the time between train stations. This is apocryphal, no doubt. Yet the appeal of the idea reinforces a sense of connection between manga and commuting, and other popular venues for reading manga include manga coffee shops (usually located near train stations), convenience stores en route, and more recently…used book stores. (2009: Kindle Loc. 137)

Much in the same way as LaMarre writes here, the 'prototypical' manhwa experience in South Korea  can  be  said  to  be  that  of  renting  and  reading  at  manga  rental  stores  or  cafes.  While  I cannot  assert  that  everyone  read  manhwa  in  rental  stores  or  manhwa  cafes,  the  cultural association between the medium and the space is fairly strong; moreover, these manhwa rental stores are a very distinct physical space that came with a specific experience.

Manhwa stores were arguably quite shabby urban spaces, often not well-ventilated, smelling of cigarette smoke and stale instant food. This was not an atmospheric leisure space, like as a picturesque coffee shop or bar, but rather an individualized leisure space, in that the grubby and unpleasant  environmental  features  did  not  matter  so  much  because  the  main  objective  in  a manhwa  cafe  was  to  become  absorbed  in  volumes  of  manhwa  for  a  period  of  time,  before emerging into the real world. (Often, the 'emerging' was literal, in that these rental stores and cafes  were  usually  situated  underground.)  In  these  subterranean  spaces,  one  would  often  see

teenage students dropping by after school, salarymen on their lunch break - generally people in search of a low-cost mode of leisurely escape.

Like the PC cafes or karaoke bars that still populate the urban landscapes of many East Asian cities, the manhwa cafe is/was a space of temporary distraction and of renting ,  where manhwa readers could borrow the book for a small fraction of its sales price. Manhwa, through this rental practice, became a media product that was to be rented and quickly consumed, not owned. The dinginess  of  the  space  also  meant  that  the  experience  of  consuming  manga  was  shaped  and coloured  by  it,  despite  the  'immersion'  into  the  comics  that  would  occur:  just  as  a  pinball machine  or  jukebox  may  conjure  up  the  smells  and  sounds  of  an  old-fashioned  pub,  print manhwa  may  conjure  up  the  memories  of  a  local  manhwa  café,  with  its  worn  couches  and littered ashtrays.

Through webtoons, however, comics have become divorced from this physical space and its characteristics; readers no longer have to go to a specific location to rent or buy comics, but can instead quickly turn to their laptops or cell phones. The act of reading webtoons is an uprooted, mobile  one,  ironically  more  akin  to  LaMarre's  account  of  reading  manga  on  the  morning commute rather than the trip to a local rental café. It has also interestingly become arguably less individualized as a reading experience than that of the manhwa cafe (where one could hunker down in peace with a stack of manhwa volumes), in that at the end of each serialized episode, the reader can also view the artists' and readers' comments below. The community of readership is made both more mediated and more directly connected.

I  would  like  to  extend  my  argument  about  the  space  of  cultural  practice  here  to  say  that, potentially, what the image of the manhwa rental cafe represents is not merely the shabbiness of this space, but also the social standing of comics in general. It would be difficult to give a proper history of manhwa and its marginalization in the late twentieth century in this short article, and further research - both economic and ethnographic - would be necessary to make more decisive statements on this topic, but I suggest that, in becoming detached from this underground space of escapism and rental practice, Korean comics have elevated themselves in the cultural hierarchy, gaining increased respect and legitimacy.

Though  this  may  be  a  crude  attempt  to  substantiate  my  claims,  a  simple  economic comparison could at least give a snapshot of how comic artists and the estimation of the value of their  work  has  improved  from  the  1990s  to  the  2000s.  An  informal  survey  and  analysis

undertaken  by  the  Korean  Manhwa  Contents  Agency  (KOMACON)  calculated  that,  for  an experienced manhwa artist serializing a manhwa in the 1990s, income would likely have been under $2000 in US currency at the time (Park 2010). In 2015, a larger survey conducted by the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA) of average monthly salaries provided by major web portals  (the  primary  site  of  publication  for  webtoons)  estimated  that  'mid-level  artists'  were being  paid  at  minimum  $2400,  while  'major  artists'  were  offered  figures  between  $4200  and $5000 a month (Han et al. 2015: 74). These figures also see a massive increase when including all income sources outside of publication; Lezhin comics, the only major webtoon provider (so far) that has instituted a paywall system that requires all readers to pay to read,  announced that 5 one of their artists, Neonbi, reported an average $23,000 in monthly income for the 2013-2014 fiscal year (Lezhin Comics 2014).

While this is a very limited, general snapshot, and there is clearly a confluence of factors that have contributed to the socio-economic rise of comic artists in Korea, what I'm trying to convey is that with the change of space of medium consumption, what has also occurred is a change in the social standing of the medium. No longer seen merely as a difficult occupation that produces works usually consumed in dingy spaces, comics are now increasingly viewed as a potentially very  lucrative,  even  stable  career,  and  moreover  as  important  source  materials  for  film  and television adaptations.


## CONCLUSION


It is tempting, when faced with a seemingly new medium that has grown so quickly in stature and presence, to make large, bold claims about its significance and 'revolutionary' potential. I have attempted to give credit to the innovations that webtoons have brought to a medium that has long  been  characterized  by  its  rigid  structure  and  immobility.  It  is  clear  that,  with  the  new opportunities afforded by a digital, online environment, webtoons are testing and stretching the definition of comics - a shift that I do not think is unique to, but definitely prominent in, South Korea. At the same time, I have also made a conscious effort to recognize the significance of this 'newness' in the context of pre-existing practices of production and consumption. It would be a major  mistake  to  turn  a  blind  eye  to  the  fact  that  key  elements  of  paper  comic  practice  have carried over to webtoon practice, just as watching DVDs at home still inspire people to recreate 'film theater' conditions (Casetti 2015: 50).

In a mobile phone or a computer, the webtoon stands side-by-side with the newspaper app, the  YouTube  app,  the  music-playing  app.  There  is  no  longer  an  inherent  connotation  of shabbiness or dilapidation attached to the consumption of comics. At the same time, the way in which webtoons are used as convenient ways to pass the time has not changed from manhwa, though  the  time  frame  may  have  shrunk:  as  short,  consumable  strips  of  sequenced  images,  a webtoon episode is ideal for a short bus or subway commute. As Casetti writes, 'a given medium is  defined  by  the  situation  in  which  it  operates'  (2015:  42).  Manhwa,  in  its  remediation  and relocation  into  webtoons,  has  become  transformed  and  redefined  in  a  plethora  of  ways: appearance, narrative style, modes of practice, and spaces of consumption. Yet both institutionally and popularly, webtoons are recognized as manhwa, or at least as its contemporary manifestation, and that implicit genealogy is what has brought about the rise of the medium's social  'class'  as  a  cultural  product,  and  the  changes  in  the  livelihood  of  South  Korean  comic artists.

## INTRODUCTION


A great storyteller will always be rooted in the people.

(Benjamin 1955: 100)

The storyteller is the figure in which the righteous man encounters himself. (Benjamin 1955: 107)

During ethnographic fieldwork focused on the market and temple fairs of Jinhua municipality in Zhejiang province (see Cooper 2012), I became aware of the local popular cultural performance genre known as Jinhua daoqing ( 道情 ), one of the 'five great folk arts of Zhejiang'. Daoqing is a

narrative singing genre, one of the so called shuo-chang (speak-sing) genres, with great historical depth  and  geographical  breadth,  although  it  has  not  attracted  much  attention  in  western scholarship, and faces an uncertain fate in the present.

Daoqing was performed traditionally  by  blind  male  practitioners  (with  yugu  drum  and clappers)  on  urban  streets  and  in  teahouses,  in  village  squares  and  at  temple  fairs,  weaving together traditional  folk tales and stories, with commentary on more recent and local events. It was occasionally taken up as a diversion by young scholars who had failed the imperial exams, and  was  hugely  popular  in  the  Jinhua  region  during  the  late  Qing  and  early  decades  of  the twentieth century. Daoqing performers also played a role in encouraging resistance against the Japanese invasion in the 1930s and 1940s, and the genre survived into the Communist period but was  suppressed,  along  with  other  folk  arts,  during  the  Cultural  Revolution.  It  experienced  a vigorous if brief revival during the 'spring wind', which ensued in the folk arts with the advent of  economic  reform  in  the  late  1970s  and  early  1980s,  and  to  some  extent  has  become institutionalized/folklorified as a semiprofessional stage art. But the genre faces new challenges in the world of expanding and globalizing media, and may not survive another generation.

While there are still a handful of daoqing artists performing in their traditional venues on street  corners  at  temple  fairs  and  in  teahouses  in  Jinhua,  it  was  never  my  privilege  to  have witnessed one of these performances in situ in the course of my work. What I have learned about the genre is mainly derived from written sources, and the scholarly work and personal generosity of  Mr  Zhang  Zhulin,  a  tireless  promoter,  performer  and  composer  of  daoqing,  as  well  as  a prolific folklore scholar, to whom I express my heartfelt thanks.

In this article, I present  an introduction  to  the  genre,  its  distinctive performance characteristics  and  its  historical  narrative,  stretching  from  its  supposed  origins  with  Daoist Immortal  Zhang  Guolao,  through  the  Republican  (1911-49),  and  into  the  Communist  period (1949-present), paying particular attention to its evolution since arriving in Jinhua during the late Ming dynasty (1368-1644 AD). I conclude by placing daoqing performers alongside the musings of Walter  Benjamin  (1955)  about  storytellers  as  communicators  in  an 'artisan mode  of production',  increasingly  eclipsed  and  superseded,  nay,  overwhelmed  by  new  forms  of  media and multimedia. 1


## JINHUA DAOQING


Daoqing is a solo performance genre that includes sung portions interspersed with spoken parts (shuo-chang).  The  sung  portions  are  set  in  pentatonic  scales,  with  text  arranged  in  seven character lines. A daoqing singer is capable of singing across the spectrum of traditional operatic voice roles, both male and female (Zhang 2003: 40). Thus it is said: 'One man [performs] one opera, perform the literary, perform the martial, all myself' (Zhang 1990: 181).

Spoken  parts  include  interludes  of  narration,  asides  and  dialogue,  expressive  of  the various personalities and emotions of the characters in the story, their happiness, anger, sorrow and joy. The accompanying instrumentation is quite simple - a three-segment long bamboo tube (yugu or qingtong - daoqing tube) with an oiled pigskin attached at one end, which gives off a 'peng peng' sound when beaten, and a set of two-inch-wide foot-long bamboo clappers/castanets which produce a 'ji ta' sound (Mao 1996: 92).

But the range of sounds the performer is able to create, with just the drum and clapper and his own voice, is quite astounding: the sounds of natural phenomena, wind, rain, thunder and lightning, the roar of the sea, the echoes of the mountain, etc. (Mao 1996: 93; Wu 1987: 521; Shi

1997), as well as the sounds of animals, chickens, dogs, tigers, etc., 'making children cry and old women moan' (Zhang 2003: 36).

Folk  myths  and  stories  make  up  much  of  the  content,  so  daoqing  is  also  known  as 'Singing Stories' (chang gushi), but local news or anecdotes also constitute a significant part of an artist's repertoire, so daoqing was often called 'Singing the News' (chang xinwen). A kind of minstrelsy, daoqing can thus be seen as an 'artisanal' form of communication as well as having an entertainment function.

Artists would often 'buy' stories from Yamen  personnel who had inside information on 2 criminal or civil proceedings in the region, in transactions known as Mai Kougong (a Kougong is a statement or confession made by an accused under examination). The artist would invite his inside  man  out  to  a  meal  to  talk  about  the  latest  case  or  cases,  and  subsequently  edit  the information  into  a  daoqing  narrative  (Zhang  2003:  37). Titles  of  daoqing  composed  with  such information are usually marked by the character ji 记 (meaning 'record of'), like 'Record of the Silver  Pouch'/'Yindai  ji',  'Record  of  the  Silver  Token'/'Yinpai  ji',  'Record  of  the  [Buddhist] Nun'/'Nigu ji', 'Record of the Red Snake'/'Hongshe ji', etc.

The daoqing repertoire is divided into tantou or duanpian (meaning 'short pieces'), and zhengben (meaning middle and long pieces; literally 'main text'). Tantou, which are generally performed before the zhengben to attract and warm up the crowd, are of two types: one type has no  story,  no  spoken  parts,  and  these  are  sung  as  folk  songs  might  be  -  e.g.  'Flowers  of  the Twelve  Months'/'Shi'eryue  huaming',  'Twenty  Four  Solar  Calendrical  Terms'/'Ershisi  jieqi', 'Thirty Six Docks'/'Sanshiliu matou', etc. The other type of tantou is narrative in form, generally brief stories that make people laugh, poking fun at the foolish, praising the wise, often laced with vulgarity and profanity.

Zhengben  are  often  called  'Singing  the  Operatic  Libretto'  (changxiwen),  and  are generally  divided  into  several  installments.  Daoqing  was  a  fixture  of  entertainment  at  the teahouses of the Republican and early Communist periods, and performances like 'Strong Young Man'/'Zhuangding  ji',  'Meeting  of  the  Dragon  Duo'/'Shuanglonghui'  and  'Meeting  of  the Heroes at Wudang'/'Wudang yingxionghui', might be strung out over more than ten evenings, encouraging patronage among customers not wanting to miss a single installment (Mao 1996: 92, 94). The longest zhengben, like '[Qing dynasty emperor] Qianlong tours Jiangnan [the southern region]', can last several tens of hours (Zhang 2003: 40).

As in other popular cultural performance genres, themes are generally didactic, encouraging  people  to  cleave  to  the  righteous  path,  castigating  deception  and  treachery, criticizing  the  unprincipled  pursuit  of  wealth,  rewarding  loyalty  and  filial  piety,  praising righteous  officials,  etc.  The  items  of  the  traditional  repertoire  with  their  emotionally  moving plots  are  especially  enjoyed  by  the  elderly.  Into  the  early  Communist  period,  during  bright moonlit  summer  evenings,  men  and  women,  old  and  young  might  sit  at  the  village  entrance under a great camphor tree, in a pavilion, or threshing ground, or open space, in crowds as large as several hundred straining to hear the performance deep into the night. Others might gather in the teahouses of the town to hear daoqing performed, or be entertained by daoqing performers on the streets during temple fairs (Mao 1996: 94). 'When the yugu sounds, the audience is full; No matter the season, the singing goes on' (Wu 1987: 521).

Daoqing has its roots in the lower rungs of society. Its performers were most often blind men, who performed on an itinerant basis all over Jinhua (Wu 1987: 520). Their social standing was quite low, and under the circumstances of the old society they had few alternatives to earn a living, although some were lucky enough to find stable employment in urban teahouses, or to be

invited to perform on occasion in the homes of the wealthy. But generally, their experience was of a cold, unforgiving world (Zhang 2003: 37), given expression in the following ballad: 'The blind  do  not  cultivate  the  soil,  /  Their  heaven  and  earth  are  planted  in  their  three-sectioned bamboo tube. / Everyone listens to the flavorful daoqing, / Pity the blind man's stomach is (still) empty' (Mao 1996: 93).

Thus  even  though  the  various  song  styles  of  daoqing  differ  in  dialect  from  Jinhua,  to Dongyang,  to  Pujiang,  to  Wuyi,  to  Yiwu  (see  Appendix  2),  they  are  all  marked  by  a  sad, mournful, sorrowful musical style (Zhang 2003: 37, 41-42).

Daoqing is said to have originated with Zhang Guolao, one of the Eight Daoist Immortals, who, having gone down to earth to set people back on the path of righteousness (the Dao), was lacking musical accompaniment. The old man of the south pole provided him with the trunk of an  'Immortals'  bamboo,  from  which  Zhang  Guolao  took three  sections  and  fashioned  a  yugu drum to accompany him in singing daoqing. Ever since, Zhang Guolao has been depicted with his  yugu  slung  over  his  shoulder,  seated  backwards  on  his  mule.  Later  generations  of  daoqing singers  celebrate  him  as  their  patron/founder  and  each  year  on  his  supposed  birthday,  the  first day of the sixth lunar month, they come together to pay respects to their master  (Zhang 2003: 232, 167).

Historically,  as  opposed to  mythologically,  it  is  fairly  commonly  agreed  in  the  sources that  daoqing  originated  in  the  repertoire  of  Jiuzhen,  Chengtian,  and  other  Daoist  songs  of  the Tang dynasty  (618-906  AD).  Indeed  Tang  Emperor  Xuanzong  (known  posthumously  as  Tang Minghuang), who ruled from 713-756 AD, was said to have  been something of an aficionado, and is also worshiped by daoqing performers as a founding ancestor along with Zhang Guolao (Zhang 2003: 233; Mao 1996: 93; Wu 1987: 520).

However,  Chen  (1986:  51-52)  has  offered  a  revisionist  view,  arguing  that  modern 'daoqing' has little to do with the Daoist songs of the Tang; that the melodies, songs and stories originate in local rural airs, ballads and events much less remote in time. And while Chen's view has yet to be widely accepted, it is agreed by most authorities that  daoqing, although Daoist in origin, did indeed absorb local folk influences as it evolved into a form of accompaniment to the preaching of the Dao among the people (Zhang 2003: 233; Wu 1987: 520). In the course of that evolution, the yugu drum and jianban clappers were said to have been added as accompaniment during  the  southern  Song  dynasty  (1127-1280  AD),  when  literary  references  to  daoqing  also appear. But due to the fact that in the old society there were very few daoqing performers who were literate, and most of them were blind, the repertoire of daoqing was generally passed down from master to apprentice by word of mouth, with no written texts left behind (Zhang 2003: 3637; Mao 1996: 93; Wu 1987: 520-21).

During the Ming (1368-1644 AD) and Qing (1644-1911 AD) dynasties, daoqing spread more broadly nationwide, and the content also expanded, continuing to combine with and absorb local stories and themes from local events and folk ballads, and leaving its Daoist content (if ever there was any) behind (Mao 1996: 93). While no one knows for certain exactly when  daoqing entered the Jinhua region, extant  daoqing pieces  set in Jinhua's various counties can  be dated from their content to the end of the Ming dynasty, which suggests that daoqing was circulating in Jinhua from at least the early Qing (Zhang 2003: 233).

In one story, which may be apocryphal, daoqing's arrival in Jinhua occurred as a result of events  which  transpired  at  the  Ming  court  (Zhang  2003:  234).  An  official,  native  to  eastern Jinhua, surnamed Zhu, was convicted of treachery, stripped of his position, and thrown in jail. Upon hearing the news, his son, Zhu Fengyi travelled to the capital to help his father, but arrived

too late. His father had already been convicted and imprisoned, and Fengyi had no money to get back to Jinhua. Just at this time, daoqing performer Fang Qing was gaining fame in the capital, and daoqing was all the rage. After watching him perform, Fengyi fashioned a yugu and clappers for  himself,  and  crafted  the  tale  of  his  father's  misfortune  into  a  daoqing  narrative,  which  he 'sold'  on the  streets  until  he  had  enough  money  to  return  to  Jinhua,  bringing  the  art  with  him (Zhang 2003: 234).

In  any  event, there  seems  little  question  that  by  the  late  Ming,  daoqing  was  a  national phenomenon.  Down  to  the  present,  daoqing  artists  have  a  saying  to  express  its  circulation nationwide:  'Liang  jin,  shiba  liang'/'two  Chinese  pounds,  18  ounces',  a  pun  on  two  capitals (Nanjing and Beijing) and eighteen provinces - 'Liang jing, shiba sheng', which is to say that daoqing could be heard in every corner of the nation (Zhang 2003: 233).During the reign of the Qing  dynasty  emperor  Qianlong,  composing  and  performing  daoqing  became  a  diversion  for young scholars who had failed the imperial exams to while away their idle hours, but even wellknown Qing literati, Zheng Banqiao, Xu Dachun and Jin Nong were known to have composed short daoqing pieces (Li 1982: 54; Zhang 2003: 36-37, 41).

The Yiwu branch of daoqing is said to have had its beginnings in the nineteenth century with a Mr Yan Song, and there is a tablet with his image in the Yangji theatre near Yiwu's west gate  where  the  Yiwu  Folk  Artists  Association  convened  its  first  meeting  in  1951  and  was subsequently  headquartered.  Yan  was  a  former  court  official  of  the  nineteenth  century,  who, having  lost  his  official  position  in  a  scandal,  founded  the  theatre  to  support  the  elderly  and orphaned of his native Yiwu (Yangji means support and assist). He edited many of his past deeds and misdeeds into daoqing narratives, and performed them both in the theatre and on the street outside the theatre for passers-by (Zhang 2003: 233).

But daoqing also seems to have arrived in Yiwu via at least one other independent route. According to an investigation carried out by the Cultural Bureau of Panzhai Township in Pujiang County,  Dongyang's  Zhao  Huniang,  known  as  the  'wet  nurse'  (lao  mama)  of  daoqing,  had  a hand in the process. Born in 1863, she learned the art of daoqing (from whom it is not clear), and while  performing  in  Pujiang  took  on  apprentice  Mao  Jinxiu  from  Yiwu,  who  is  said  to  have brought the art to his hometown for the first time (Zhang 2003: 40).

In Yiwu, blind male daoqing artists often combined their performances with blind female huagu (flower drum) artists, and historically the genres were known as  'husband and wife folk arts' (fuqi quyi). 'Men sing daoqing, women sing huagu', or 'husband sings daoqing, wife sings huagu'. The repertoire is the same, the accoutrements of performance differ (Zhang 2003: 4041).

Like daoqing, huagu is classified in the folk art category of  shuo-chang, and is usually performed while seated, generally sung, but interspersed with spoken parts. In huagu performance, the left hand holds a small cymbal and a  'yaogu' drum; the right hand holds the cymbal hammer and the drum stick. The drum and cymbal keep the rhythm, and accompany the speech-song. Like daoqing, the singing style is slow and mournful, with the sung text in seven character lines. Its melodies are said to be gentler and softer than daoqing, its content including family-themed operettas, love stories, as well as local anecdotes and news (Wu 1987: 520).

At  the  end  of  the  Qing  dynasty,  huagu,  like  daoqing,  was  circulating  in  the  Jinhua counties of Yiwu, Dongyang and Pan An, although its practitioners were fewer in number than their male daoqing counterparts. In Republican times, Zhang (2003: 48) estimates the number of huagu performers in Yiwu and Dongyang to have been about thirty or forty. 3

By the end of the Qing dynasty (early twentieth century), daoqing was quite common in Jinhua cities, towns and villages (Zhang 2003: 37), and during the Republican period, daoqing was second only to local Wuju opera as the most important form of entertainment in Jinhua. The teahouse trade created a great demand. Artists took the important and not so important news of the  time  and  edited  it  into  daoqing  pieces  (Zhang  2003:  37).  During  the  early  Republic,  Luo Zhanglun was known in city and town as one of daoqing's premier performers (Wu 1987: 521; Mao 1996: 94).

During  the  anti-Japanese  war,  many  daoqing  artists  created  pieces  that  reflected  the resistance to Japanese occupation, among whom Ma Lieshang was especially noteworthy (Zhang 2003: 38). Ma began his career at the age of 8 singing the daoqing 'Tai Er zhuang dajie'/'Great victory  [over  the  Japanese]  at  Tai  Er  Village'.  At  10  he  performed  the  anti-Japanese  daoqing 'Wozi ji'/'Tale of the Wozi (the Japanese)', and  has been editing and performing  daoqing  for more than sixty years in the service of popular struggles and resistance. In 1982, Ma contributed to  the  post-Cultural  Revolution  revival  of  daoqing,  when  at  the  request  of  fellow  artist  Wu Rongchun, he collaborated with Zhao Shouxing in the creation of 26 new  daoqing pieces, and began a training class to teach daoqing, giving new life to the art. It is said of Ma that he was the 'first  master  who  opened  the  road'  for  sighted  artists;  he  was  a  performer,  composer  and promoter  of  daoqing  (Zhang  2003:  245);  and  in  1993  he  was  designated  Zhejiang  Provincial Level Folk Artist (Zhang 2003: 42-43).

In  the  last  years  of  the  Republic  (late  1940s) there  were  some  200  daoqing  performers still active in Jinhua's various counties, 100 of whom were concentrated in the various villages and towns of Yiwu county, and most of whom were blind or partially blind (Zhang 2003: 38; Chen 2005: 24; Wu 1987: 521). In their repertoires were more than 300 traditional zhengben and 100 tantou that survived into the communist period (Zhang 2003: 37), and there have been some fifty  additions  to the  repertoire  of  assorted  length  since  (Zhang  2003:  40).  Some  twenty  or  so repertoire items still extant memorialize events that actually happened in and around Yiwu (e.g. 'Shuangdao ji'/'Double  Knives',  'Huoxiao  xiangshanshi'/'Fire  Consumes  Xiangshan  Temple', 'Yingdeng  ji'/'Greet  the  Lanterns',  'Siniu  ji'/'Four  Cows',  'Jiesan  ji'/'Borrowed  Umbrella', 'Zaozhu ji'/'Chase the Pig', 'Maimi ji'/'Buy Grain', 'Erduo ji'/'Ear' and 'Tuoxie ji'/'Sandals') (Mao 1996: 94; and see Appendix 1).

The official master narrative of the development of daoqing has daoqing artists throwing themselves  enthusiastically  into  the  great  wave  of  the  revolution  in  the  early  years  of  the People's  Republic,  composing  and  performing  daoqing  narratives  and  songs  for  the  antiAmerican struggle during the Korean War, for land reform, for the campaign to crush counterrevolutionaries, etc., and there is plenty of evidence to justify that narrative (Zhang 2003: 42).

But  it  is  also  fair  to  say  that  when  the  Yiwu  people's  government  approved  the establishment of the Yiwu Folk Artists Association in August 1951, it was seeking not only to put the blind artists to work in a propaganda role, but was also duly concerned for the welfare of these folk to whom no one paid much attention; that they also have the opportunity to walk the road of civic engagement in the new society. The Folk Arts Association appears to have  been organized  by eight  folk  art  performers  on  their  own  initiative,  from  the  bottom  up  as  it  were, among whom was Ye Yingmei, a blind daoqing performer from Fotang town about whom we have more to say below. Forty-one practitioners of daoqing and huagu among other folk artists attended  the  first  meeting  held  at  the  old  Yangji  theatre,  which  also  became  the  association's headquarters (Wu 1987: 521).

Relevant offices in the cultural field helped the artists transcribe, record and organize the traditional  repertoire,  as  well  as  to  compose  and  edit  new  stories,  and  to  participate  in  the propaganda efforts of the new government (Mao 1996: 94). Among the accomplishments of the association was carrying out a registration of all folk art practitioners in the county in 1956 (Wu 1987: 521), and winning government wages for Yiwu's blind performers in 1959 (Zhang 2003: 40). In 1965 there were 65 registered member practitioners of various popular performance arts (Wu 1987: 521).


## YE YINGMEI (1925-1964)


Ye Yingmei was a native of Wuqiye village located on a branch tributary of the Yiwu River in Fotang township. Born blind, he lost both his parents early in life, and at the age of 13/14 was already begging for a meagre living on the streets of Fotang. At the age of 16, he returned to his home village, and to reduce the burden on his uncle with whom he resided, he took up the yugu drum and clappers of the daoqing profession, and began going from village to village  'selling' songs (Zhang and Fu 1998; Mao 1996: 95; Zhang 2003: 237).

In  1949,  when  the  Communist  forces  proved  victorious  in  the  civil  war,  Ye  took  the creation  of  a  new  society  seriously  and  'fanshen'-ed  (turned  over),  becoming  a  leader  in  the organization of folk performers. In the early years of the People's Republic of China (PRC), he embraced the idea that art should serve the people, going out to perform at workplaces, fields and markets, leaving his footprints throughout Yiwu (Fotang Township Government 2005: 89). He sang out, comparing the old society with the new, using his daoqing genre to sing the praises of socialism, and the new society (Zhang 2003: 237; Zhang and Fu 1998). During land reform he sang: 'The landlord eats and plays, the peasants are his horses to ride, / Hungry all year round, this society is unjust' (Zhang and Fu 1998; Mao 1996: 95).

In 1953, during the movement to cooperativize land in the rural areas, there was a severe drought in Yiwu. Ye was out performing in the mountain villages and chanced upon a group of rural folk going up the mountain to pray to the Dragon King for rain. When he heard what they were up to, he blocked the way, and composed a tantou (short piece) on the spot:

You can't believe in the Dragon King, don't spread superstition. To fight the drought we must rely on everyone's cooperation, If we unify in our struggle, a bountiful harvest will be guaranteed; If you want water, dig a well, human ability beats heavenly power; Superstition has hurt people over thousands of years; Smart people should not be fooled. (Zhang 2003: 237; Mao 1996: 95; Zhang and Fu 1998)

Beginning in 1954, Ye Yingmei was successively selected as representative to the first, second, third, fourth and fifth annual Yiwu County People's Congress. In 1958, he was elected chairman of  the  Yiwu  County  Folk  Arts  Association  (Quyi  Xiehui)  he  helped  to  found,  while  also participating in the formation of the Zhejiang Provincial Folk Artists Association which elected him vice chairman. In the same year, he was admitted to membership in the communist party, and  was  invited  to  Beijing  to  participate  in  the  'First  National  Folk  Arts  Festival'  (Fotang Township Government 2005: 89; Mao 1996: 95).

He took the stage in Beijing's Chang An Opera Theater with his  yugu and clappers and sang his own composition, 'Yu Xiaoyu', celebrating the career of a woman of that name from Yiwu's Huaqi township, Binshitou village, who lost a son in the Korean War, but unfazed, went

on to make great contributions to the construction of socialism. In later years, she served as the party branch secretary at the Ershisan Li feather products factory of Yiwu, where she expanded the  labour  force  from  ten  workers  to  over  500,  and  enterprise  production  value  to  ¥400,000 (Zhang  and  Fu  1998;  Mao  1996:  95).  At  the  end  of  Ye's  performance,  there  was  continuous applause, and three curtain calls; the crowd refused to quiet down.

In 1963, Ye was named a national 'red flag' worker in the rural propaganda effort. At the awards ceremony, a banner declared: 'In the north there is Han Qixiang, in the south there is Ye Yingmei.' 4 In 1963, Ye went to Beijing again, this time as chair of the National Conference of Outstanding  Workers  in  Education,  and  at  the  banquet  of  leaders  sat  with  Zhou  Enlai,  who served him his food. Ye was quoted as saying: 'Even in my dreams, I never thought such a day would happen, I must keep on singing…' Unfortunately, Ye Yingmei would not have a chance to  sing  much  longer,  passing  away  in  the  following  year  of  kidney  disease  at  the  age  of  39 (Zhang and Fu 1998; Fotang Township Government 2005: 89).


## SUPPRESSION AND REVIVAL


With the onset of the Cultural Revolution, some folk artists organized their own  'Mao Zedong Thought  Frontline  Struggle  Teams'  (Wu  1987:  521),  but  their  efforts  on  behalf  of  the revolutionary masses were ultimately unappreciated. Folk arts practitioners and their organizations were attacked as 'rotten'. Performances from the traditional repertoire, associated with the 'Four Olds' (old ideas, old habits, old customs, old culture) were prohibited, and many artists were forced to confess to 'spreading feudal, capitalist, revisionist propaganda'. Many who had  sincerely  lent  their  efforts  to  propagandizing  on  behalf  of  the  new  society  were  forced  to endure public criticism and humiliation, and had their equipment confiscated and destroyed. The Yiwu  Folk  Arts  Association  was  disbanded  altogether,  and  38  of  its  members  on  state  salary were taken off the state payroll and transferred to the countryside (Wu 1987: 521).

To support themselves during this period, artists held 'underground performances' where they  could,  performing  behind  closed  doors  and  windows  and  in  back  rooms.  Others  simply dropped their paraphernalia and changed  from singing  daoqing to telling  stories. Even though daoqing performances were prohibited, it is claimed that  daoqing and other shuo-chang genres continued  to  be  performed  privately  throughout  the  Cultural  Revolution  without  interruption (Wu 1987: 521; Zhang 2003: 38; Mao 1996: 96).

In  any  event,  once  the  'gang  of  four'  (whom  Mao  had  tapped  as  leaders  during  the Cultural Revolution) were repudiated, and reform and openness adopted by the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee of the communist party in 1978-79, a 'Spring Wind' in the arts ensued, and the folk arts in Jinhua experienced a renaissance. Various performance arts: daoqing, huagu,  xiaoluo  shu  (small  cymbal  narrative),  kuaiban  (clapper  narrative),  xiangsheng  (comic dialogue), shuogushi (storytelling), all came back to life (Chen 2005: 24). In June of 1980, the Yiwu Folk Arts Association revived, housed in the Yiwu Cultural Center, and beginning in 1984 it has sponsored a folk arts performance festival every year (Zhang 2003: 40).

A 'heat wave of daoqing' commenced in the late 1970s and 1980s in which the number of sighted performers expanded, and a new level of creativity in the art was attained (Zhang 2003: 38; Mao 1996: 96; Zhang 1990: 184). That new level was represented by practitioners like Ma Lieshang whose 26 new daoqing pieces were composed at this time, but also by performers like Ms  Zou  Aiqin  who  is  credited  with  creating  'new  method  daoqing'.  Stepping  into  a  role traditionally the domain of blind men, she introduced Jinhua folk songs and music from the local Wuju opera genre into daoqing performance, and adapted the content to make it more compatible

with  the  new  times  and  the  contemporary  lifestyle.  In  1981  she  performed  in  Beijing  at  the National  Rural  Cultural  Congress  of  Progressive  Workers,  performing  Zhang  Zhulin's  newly composed  'He  xinfang'/'Congratulate  the  Newlyweds'  and  'Zhicong'/'Control  the  Insects'  to great acclaim. She became known as the 'King's Choice' of daoqing (Zhang 2003: 39).

Daoqing artist Ye Yingsheng  is another practitioner credited with carrying  forward the tradition  of  his  similarly  named  predecessor  Ye  Yingmei,  composing  many  new  pieces  that reflected  the  great  changes  in  Yiwu  society  since  the  implementation  of  economic  reforms. Starting at the age of 12, he performed in rural markets, by the side of paddy fields, in distant villages, teahouses and temple fairs, with his yugu and bamboo clappers. Later he served as vice chair of the Jinhua Municipal Folk Art Association and director of the Zhejiang Provincial Folk Art Association.

In 1985, he was invited to Beijing to perform his daoqing piece, 'Remembering Wuhan', written  for  the  70 th anniversary  of  the  deceased  Wu  Han's  birth,  in  the  Peoples'  Political Consultative  Conference  Hall.  It  was  of  course  Mao's  criticism  of  Wu  Han's  play  'Hairui Dismissed  from  Office'  that  launched  the  Cultural  Revolution,  and  led  to  Wu's  disgrace  and relegation  to  the  category  of  counter-revolutionary.  Ye's  performance  brought  Wu  Han's younger sister, as well as many others in the audience, to tears (Mao 1996: 96).

Among  folk  artists,  Ye  Yingsheng  was  known  as  the  'revolutionary  mounted  cavalry leader'  ('Wulan  Muqi')  (Zhang  2003:  41),  and  in  2003,  was  awarded  the  title  Artist  of Excellence by the Zhejiang Provincial Folk Art Association (Chen 2005: 24). 5


## CONTEMPORARY CHALLENGES


Despite the post-Cultural Revolution revival of daoqing and other popular cultural performance arts, new challenges lie ahead for their reproduction and continuity. 'There's no hiding the facts' (Wu  1987:  521).  Following  the  nation's  economic  development,  and  the  expansion  and improvement  in  the  cultural  life  of  ordinary  folk,  the  proliferation  of  movies,  TV,  CDs  and DVDs,  and  magazines,  and  various  'modern'  forms  of  media  and  entertainment,  domestic  as well as from Hong Kong and Taiwan, daoqing has been eclipsed and superseded. Its role as a source of news and information is insignificant in the present day, its appeal to youth minimal, its  audience  much reduced. Many blind performers have sought less anachronistic occupations (Wu 1987: 521), and the genre now faces a crisis to which  local cultural offices have tried to respond (Mao 1996: 97).

In  an  effort  to  stem the  brain  drain  away  from  daoqing,  the  Cultural  Affairs  Bureau  of Jinhua city has held daoqing training classes, in which many younger people have participated, and in which women have been the majority, with performers like Zou Aiqin as their role model. These youngsters have continued to move away from the sad and mournful tones and rhythms of the traditional genre (Li 1982: 55), to a more upbeat, more optimistic, more contemporary tone, with  more  complex  musical  accompaniment  and  instrumentation  (Zhang  1990:  184).  Their efforts have yielded some results in revitalizing the genre and encouraging new developments.

If the  genre  does  survive  another  generation,  it  will  no  doubt  be  as  a  gentrified, folklorified genre, far removed from the blind beggars for whom it served as means of livelihood in the old society.

Walter Benjamin's characterization of storytelling might well be applied to daoqing: an 'artisan  form  of  communication',  cradled  in  a  web  'woven  thousands  of  years  ago  in  the ambience of the oldest forms of craftsmanship', but a web that is 'becoming unraveled at all its ends' (1955: 90-91).

As  the  artisan  mode  of  production  in  China  continues  to  unravel,  with  unprecedented speed in the context of economic reform, everywhere replaced by the industrial and digital, so this artisan form  of  communication  has  been  eclipsed  and  superseded  by  contemporary multimedia, online chat, etc.

Still, the daoqing genre clings to existence in the hands of those like Zhang Zhulin who continues to compose, perform and promote the art. In Jinhua villages, if there is someone failing in  their  responsibilities  to  the  elderly,  or  someone  with  a  gambling  problem,  or  otherwise inappropriate or anti-social behavior, they say: 'We'll get Zhang Xiaogui [little devil Zhang, i.e. Zhang Zhulin] to write you up in a daoqing, then where will you show your face?' (Zhang 2003: 249).

## A POSTCOLONIAL LANDSCAPE


On a small  hill  beside  the  Wushantou  Reservoir  rests  a  bronze  statue of  a  lone  Japanese  man sitting on the ground in common work clothes with his head resting in his hand (see Figure 1). This casual pose of the statue is said to be an appearance commonly witnessed by others while the  engineer  supervised  a  massive  construction  project.  With  the  small  gravestone  erected  for him  and  his  wife  behind  the  statue,  the  area  constructs  a  site  of  memory,  'where  memory crystallizes and secretes itself' (Nora 1989: 7). The reservoir attracts visitors throughout the year, and  a  grand  service  is  held  annually  on  8  May,  the  day  of  his  death,  to  commemorate  the engineer who, at the time, designed the largest reservoir in Asia (Furukawa 2009: 104).

Wushantou is  located in Tainan, a southern region of Taiwan  just below the Tropic of Cancer. The man is Hatta Yoichi ( 八田與一 1886-1942), perhaps the most celebrated Japanese on the island. Taiwan, an island nation with a population of 23 million, had been ruled by Japan for  half  a  century  (1895-1945)  and  the  memories  of  the  colonial  past  are  contested  and  are divided largely by ethnic fault lines. The Mainlanders or waishengren who fled to Taiwan with the Chinese  Nationalist  Party  (or  Kuomintang,  hereafter  KMT)  ensuing  the loss to the Communists in the civil war in 1949 generally retain a negative view of Taiwan's colonial past.

They fought eight years of war with the Japanese, and commonly viewed the Taiwanese to be 'enslaved'  by  Japanese  thought  and  culture  (Huang  2006;  He  2007).  The  native  Taiwanese  or benshengren, which consists of the majority Hoklo, Hakka and a dozen indigenous tribes, share a different view of the island's colonial past. They reject the 'enslaved' argument, and in the face of  the  corruption,  incompetence  of  and  the  democide  by  the  Chinese  authorities,  they  have produced a discourse that praises the modernization bestowed by the Japanese. Historically, the KMT  government  had  basically  negated  the  Japanese  past.  It  was  not  until  the  political liberalization  in  the  1990s  that  the  official  discourse  on  the  Japanese  past  was  challenged, reviewed and revised.

In present-day Taiwan, Hatta is a deity. To his worshippers, he is a miracle-maker who turned dry  land  into  a  massive  granary.  The  commemoration service,  held  since  1947   by  the 1 local residents, had traditionally been a low-profile affair. Yet in recent years, it has turned into a high-profile  national  and  international  event, thanks  to the  power of  popular  culture  and  mass media. President Ma Ying-jeou (Ma Yingjiu) attended the service in 2009 and again in 2011 for the  opening  of  the  memorial  park,  accompanied  by  other  cabinet  members.  Dignitaries  from Japan,  including  former  prime  minister  Mori  Yoshiro,  joined  the  opening  ceremony.  The Ministry of Transportation spent a total of 120  million NT dollars (4.2 million US dollars) to repair  and  rebuild  the  residence  of  the  late  Japanese  engineer  that  had  been  lying  in  ruins  for several  decades  (Yang  2011).  Celebrating  the  occasion,  the  road  in  front  of  the  park  was renamed  'Hatta  Road'. 2 What  is  noteworthy  is  that  Hatta,  as  a  widely  known  figure,  is  a relatively new discovery and modern invention. The man, who was virtually unknown until the late 1980s, 3 even in his  hometown of Kanazawa, is a social phenomenon: his products include historical and cultural exhibitions, books, comics, an animated movie, a TV drama, musicals, a Taiwanese glove puppet show (budaixi) and songs. This article explores the manifold interests that made Hatta a modern myth. It deals with the Japanese engineer not so much as a historic figure  but  as  a  cultural  production.  After  a  brief  introduction  about  Hatta  and  his  construction work, this article investigates the representation of the late Japanese engineer in the present-day popular  culture  of  Taiwan  and  Japan.  In  this  regard,  two  video  productions  are  analysed:  Jp. Pattenrai!! Minami no Shima no Mizu Monogatari / Hatta Has Come!! Tales of Water from a Southern Island and Ch. Shuishi Jia'nan / Water Colour Jia'nan .  The former is an anime film directed by Ishiguro Noboru for Mushi Productions, a major Japanese animation studio. It was

released  in  2008  in  Japan  and  a  year  later  in  Taiwan  with  Chinese  subtitles.  Hitoto  Yō  -  a Japanese singer who, appropriately, has a Taiwanese father and a  Japanese mother - sings the movie's theme song and plays the voice actress for Toyoki, Hatta's wife. Shuishi Jia'nan is  a Taiwanese TV drama directed by Li Yue-feng that was broadcast in 2009. The series lasted for twenty  weeks. Like  other  popular  soap  operas  in  Taiwan,  the  whole  production  uses  taiyu  or minnanhua, a spoken vernacular of the majority Hoklo people.

Although popular culture does not best or alone  in  itself represent 'historical  truth',  its influence  is  hard  to  ignore  in  the  age  of  globalizing  media  capitalism.  Our  conceptions  of  the past are greatly shaped by the images projected to us through media, be it manga, TV drama or film. They form our 'imaginative landscape of the past' (Morris-Suzuki 2005: 17). At the same time,  as  Morris-Suzuki  (2005)  acutely  points  out,  due  to  the  economic  rules  of  the  market, cultural  producers,  such  as  novelists,  publishers  and  film-makers,  are  constrained  by  the preconceptions of what consumers want, as they wish to sell their products as widely as possible. Thus, representation of the past is an outcome of an ongoing interplay between the producers and consumers. Although this article examines cultural productions and consumptions separately, I do not subscribe to the conceptual binary. Instead, I agree with the notion of a 'circuit of culture', an ongoing dialogue between the producers and consumers for meaning-making (du Gay 1997: 10). Popular culture is perceived in this piece as an arena in which different actors compete for cultural meaning;  consumers  of  cultural  productions  are  not  'passive  dupes'  but  'active participants  in  the  creation  of  meaning'  (Harrington  and  Bielby  2001:  4).  As  analysed  in  the following pages,  Hatta Yoichi, a formerly  neglected colonial engineer, is given new  meanings through the numerous productions and consumptions by different political and civic groups in both Taiwan and Japan.

Lastly, cultural productions and consumptions construct identities. What is at stake in the cultural  representation  of  Hatta  Yoichi,  I  argue,  is  the  issue  of  national  identity.  On  an  island nation that strives to reconstruct its own national  identity, 4 popular culture is a continuation of politics  by  other  means.  Or  as  Tim  Edensor  (2002)  argues,  it  is  the  quotidian  practices  of everyday  life  through  which  a  national  identity  is  constituted  and  reproduced,  contested  and reaffirmed. Countless cultural forms and practices provide 'an epistemological and ontological basis which foregrounds the nation as a hegemonic, common-sense entity' (Edensor 2002: 20). Representation  of  Hatta  concerns  Taiwan  and  the  construction  of  a  Taiwanese/Taiwaneseness

since memories of the island's Japanese past are not shared by the post-war Chinese regime. In other  words,  colonial  memories  and  legacies  are  appropriated  and  utilized  in  constructing  a postcolonial  identity  (Amae  2011;  Kushner  2007).  Beneath  the  innocent-looking  images  of popular culture thus lies a subtle, yet fierce, battle for influence to define what Taiwan is and is not.


## HISTORICAL HATTA YOICHI


Hatta  Yoichi  was  born  in  1886  as  the  fifth  son  of  a  wealthy  farming  family  in  Kanazawa,  a community in northern Japan. Hatta studied civil engineering at the prestigious Tokyo Imperial University  and,  upon  graduation  in  1910,  became  an  engineer  in  the  Office  of  the  GovernorGeneral of Taiwan. After successfully constructing the Taoyuan Canal in northern Taiwan, the door  was  opened  for  him  to  tackle  larger  and  more  complicated  projects:  the  Wushantou Reservoir and the accompanying Jia'nan Canal. The purpose of the construction was to irrigate an area in the plain of southern Taiwan that equals the size of the island of Oahu to increase rice and other agricultural production. The project contained three parts: (1) to build an embankment to block the streams; (2) to dig a tunnel through the mountain to draw water from the bigger river on  the  other  side;  and  (3)  to  build  canals  to  deliver  water  to  the  fields  on  the  plains.  The construction begun in 1920 and was completed in 1930. The total cost of the construction project amounted to roughly half of the colonial government's annual expenditure of 1927 (Saito 2009: 55). The construction completely changed the landscape; the hills were submerged under water. A bird's-eye view of the reservoir resembles the shape of a coral (see Figure 2). The small canals run through the vast plains like capillaries connecting a vein and an artery.

The  project  was  full  of  challenges  from  the  onset.  Hatta  had  to  convince  sceptical bureaucrats who feared the project's unprecedented scale, as well as local farmers who insisted on  traditional  ways.  Nature  was  not  on  his  side,  either.  Malaria  and  other  deadly  diseases threatened  the  lives  of  workers  and  their  families  at  the  construction  sites.  In  1922,  a  gas explosion in the tunnel claimed 50 lives (Eda 1930: 39). The 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake and the resulting recovery plan for earthquake-damaged Tokyo, the heart of the Empire, significantly slowed the progress of the project in its imperial periphery. Yet against all odds, Hatta prevailed, finishing the project in ten years, thanks in part to his clever use of the most sophisticated civil engineering skills and modern machinery. He adopted a semi-hydraulic method of construction,

which  uses  gravel,  clay  and  sand  instead  of  concrete,  thereby  providing  both  strength  and structural longevity. The technique also provides protection from earthquakes. Prior to its use in this  reservoir,  this  method  had  never  been  used  in  such  a  large-scale  project.  In  addition,  he purchased state-of-the-art machinery - particularly steam shovels and air dump cars - from the United States. The completion of the project increased the rice field area 30-fold, rice production six-fold  and  sugarcane  production  two-fold  (Eda  1930:  198).  It  ensured  Hatta  a  place  in  the 5 history of Taiwanese engineering.

Hatta's  talent  was  sought  in  regions  beyond  Taiwan.  In  1935,  he  was  summoned  by  the Governor of Fujian Province who sought his expertise to solve the food shortage problem in the region.  In  1939,  Hatta  received  the  highest  honour  given  to  an  engineer  of  the  GovernorGeneral's  Office  in  Taiwan  (Saito  2009:  179). 6 As  Japan's  borders  changed  during  the  war, Hatta's role also expanded. Hatta travelled to Hainan Island in 1940 and Korea, Manchuria and China  in  1941  to  observe  and  advise  on  the  hydraulic  engineering  projects  in  the  respective regions. In 1942, Hatta was chosen by the Imperial Army to be part of an industrial development mission  to  the  Philippines  to  conduct  a  land  survey.  The  ship,  which  was  carrying  1000 engineers  and  military  personnel,  was  sunk  in  the  East  China  Sea  by  an  American  torpedo. Casualties numbered 817, including Hatta (Nihon Yūsen Kabushiki Gaisha 1956: 342). He was

56 years of age. Prior to this  journey, Hatta visited his alma mater in Tokyo, where he gave a speech  titled  'Future  Prospects  of  Civic  Engineering  in  the  Greater  East  Asia  Co-Prosperity Sphere'. Hatta's subordinate, who survived the attack at sea, recalls the late engineer sharing his vision of using Lake Toba in Sumatra to produce electricity with others during the final journey (Saito 2009: 226).

On the personal side, Hatta married a young woman named Toyoki from his hometown in 1917, at the age of 31. Toyoki was only 16 years old at the time of their wedding. The couple had eight children - two boys and six girls. Shortly after Japan's surrender in 1945, Toyoki threw herself into the spillway of the reservoir her husband had designed.

## REPRESENTATIONS OF HATTA YOICHI


Nearly  half  a  century  after  his  death,  Hatta  was  'resurrected'  and  given  new  meaning  in  the realm of popular culture. This section investigates the cultural representations of Hatta, with a special focus on  the cultural appropriation. As  mentioned  at  the  beginning,  two  visual productions, Pattenrai and Shuise Jia'nan ,  are chosen as main illustrations. My research shows that the 'resurrected Hatta'  is  more than a competent engineer. First, he is a moral figure who fights the injustice of racial discrimination, preaches  the virtues of racial equality and exemplifies the ideal social harmony. Second, he and his wife are good and caring friends of the Taiwanese  people.  Third,  the  couple  represents  the  Nihon  seishin / Ch.  Riben  jingshen or

Japanese spirit,  a  moral  code  especially  admired  by  the  older  Japanese-speaking  generation  in Taiwan, a generation that directly experienced Japanese rule. While not entirely without basis, many  stories  are  exaggerated,  arranged  and  romanticized.  Also,  the  whole  colonial/imperial context is  conveniently  downplayed,  if  not obliterated,  in  such  representations  (Tainaka  2007; Weng 2010).


## Preacher of ethnic/racial harmony


Racial  discrimination  was  pervasive  and  institutionalized  under  Japanese  rule.  Schools  were segregated. Taiwanese workers were shut out from most government jobs and received different salaries from their Japanese counterparts. The racial composition of the island during the colonial period  was  not  entirely  dichotomous,  however.  There  were,  for  instance,  other  colonized members of the Japanese Empire, such as Ryukyuans (Okinawans) and Koreans. Although never considered  equal  to  'Japanese'  (naichijin),  they  enjoyed  higher  social  status  than  'Taiwanese' (hont ō jin). In addition, there were indigenous tribes (Takasago zoku) who were segregated in the mountain areas and were ruled differently  from the rest of the  island's  inhabitants. They were positioned on the lowest rung of the Japanese racial hierarchy. Since the 1920s, efforts had been made by the government to eliminate racial discrimination under the new policy of assimilation. Japanese became the only official  language  in public spaces, adoption of Japanese  names and interracial marriage were legalized and encouraged, while worship of the Japanese Shinto gods became compulsory in the 1930s (Komagome 2000). Though perceived racial differences  and discrimination  never  fully  disappeared,  the  war  effort  and  experience  seem  to  have  allowed different  races  and  ethnicities  in  the  Empire  to  be  commonly  imagined  as  'the  Emperor's children'. Yet, it was not in the living but through the death or marching toward the common fate of dying for the Emperor that made them become Japanese (Ching 2001: 94).

Racial harmony and reconciliation is the main theme of the movie Pattenrai .  The story revolves around two male figures: Susumu, a son of a Japanese engineer who works for Hatta, and  Eitetsu,  a  son  of  a  local  farmer,  who  opposes  Hatta's  project.  The  two,  in  conflict  at  the beginning, gradually become friends. Throughout the production, Hatta and the other engineers repeat  the  mantra,  'It  does  not  matter  whether  you  are  a  Japanese  or  Taiwanese'.  In Shuise Jia'nan ,  a  Taiwanese  production,  the  theme  of  racial  harmony  is  embodied  by  Hatta  and  his three  subordinates:  Abe  (Japanese);  A-shan  (Taiwanese  Hoklo)  and  Aiueo  (indigenous  Siraya

tribe). 7 Hatta  plays  the  role  of  mediating  the  conflicts  among  the three.  In the twelfth  episode, Hatta  surprises  everyone  by  announcing  that  in  Wushantou,  unlike  other  parts  of  the  island, Japanese, Taiwanese and Siraya indigenous people would study together in the same school. He says, 'Taiwanese, Japanese and Siraya, we are all equal.' In another key moment of the drama, he  tells  his  wife  that  'there  is  no  difference  between  Taiwanese  and  Japanese.  We  are  all humans'.

The theme of racial harmony is culturally appropriated, as well as accentuated, through the appearance of the third Other. In Pattenrai , it is an Okinawan girl named Miyo who befriends Susumu and Eitetsu. The image of Miyo on a wooden cart, pushed by the two boys in Pattenrai is  both  classic  and  symbolic  (see  Figure  6).  It  reminds  critical  viewers  of  a  Manchukuo-like minzoku ky wa or 'concord of the races'. In ō Shuise Jia'nan , the third Other is played by Aiueo, a  Siraya.  The  presence  of  a  Siraya  in Shuise  Jia'nan is understandable,  as  the  tribe  had historically resided in the region in which the reservoir was built. However, it is not historically accurate.  By  the  time  of  the  construction  in  1920,  members  of  the  tribe  had  been  already sinicized  and  thus  not  so  detectable.  Their  presence  in  the  Taiwanese  drama  is  nothing  but  a reflection  of multiculturalism  in  present-day  Taiwan  and  is  thus  an  outcome  of  cultural appropriation.
