## AUDIENCE ANALYSIS


The study uses Japanese, Korean and Taiwanese university undergraduate and postgraduate students familiar with Japanese popular culture. As Livingstone notes: 'Young people are a distinctive and significant cultural grouping in their own right - a sizeable market segment, a subculture even, and which often 'lead the way' in the use of new media' (Livingstone 2002: 3). The intent, rather than focusing on Hana yori dango , is to ascertain their knowledge and views about representations of Japan.

The  analysis  is  based  on  qualitative  methods,  'a  field  of  enquiry  in  its  own  right' (Denzin and Lincoln 2005: 2). This approach is used to collect, collate and analyse data to provide  information  from  which  conclusions  can  be  drawn.  The  research  is  two-fold  and comprises  the  completion  of  questionnaires  by  the  participants  with  ensuing  focus  group interviews.  I  do  not  consider  it  necessary  to  have  a  preconceived  hypothesis,  although  the study  is  cognizant  of  the  research  questions  informing  the  focus  group  component  of  the study. Focus group findings were then compared to answers from the survey results in order to  draw  conclusions.  As  Lunt  and  Livingstone  point  out,  'the  method  of  focus  group interviews involves collecting a group or, more often, a series of groups of people together to discuss an issue in the presence of a moderator'; a focus group is effective for 'speeding up sampling for one-to-one interviews' (Lunt and Livingstone 1996: 4). My research intent was directed to gain knowledge from a compound methodology.

The study searches for the emotional experience of the fans, without which fan cultures would not exist (Hills 2002). The research methodology in respect of focus groups is guided by Sternberg (2005). The focus group interviews were structured with reference to the nine steps proposed by Vaughn, Schumm and Sinagub (1996), namely:

-  Delineate the general purpose
-  Designate a moderator
-  Refine the research goals
-  Select the participants
-  Determine the number of focus group interviews
-  Arrange for the focus group facility
-  Develop an interview guide
-  Conduct the focus group interview
-  Analyse the focus group data

The analysis advances the idea that pan-Asian exports of TV, drama and anime have allowed Japan's image to become 'attractive', echoing the notion of 'cool' soft power and, in effect, constituting a shift away from the negative image of an aggressor nation. In taking advantage of East Asian cultural proximity, Japanese pop culture has become a resource for interaction that can be shared among people from this region (Nakano 2008).

For the audience research, I enlisted participants from two cohorts: the first, university students  from  Korea,  Taiwan  and  Japan  studying  in  Australia;  and  the  second,  university students  domiciled  in  Korea,  Taiwan  and  Japan.  With  this  selection,  my  intention  was  to determine the views of each cohort whilst I also searched for possible influences on the views of Cohort 1, because of studying in Australia, compared with the views of Cohort 2.

The two tools used for audience analysis were a survey questionnaire and focus group interviews  conducted  shortly  after  completion  of  the  questionnaires.  The  fieldwork  in Australia  preceded  the  overseas  data  collection.  All  participants  remained  anonymous.  All students have a common interest in Japan and Japanese culture; thus, they are only partially representative of the overall composition of their respective societies.


## FINDINGS FROM FOREGROUNDING, TEXTUAL AND AUDIENCE ANALYSES


The Japanese TV drama closely follows the plot of the manga. The manga are construed as significantly  influenced  by  aspirations  derived  from  the  heady  days  of  Japan's  bubble economy,  as  well  as  by  the  dreams  of  the  audience  about  the  acquisition  of  expensive consumer  items.  Japanese  culture  places  a  high  societal  value  on  a  so-called  high  status lifestyle. The achievement in life of the individual and their family is measured in terms of income and lifestyle. High personal  income and  the ownership of expensive  items accords with high standards and status (Miura 2005). The Japanese Hana yori dango TV drama plays out  in  such  an  environment.  Lifestyle  considerations  extend  to  overseas  education  for children  of  wealthy  families;  this,  however,  is  not  shared  in  the  Taiwanese  or  Korean productions.

The Taiwanese production retains the overall structure and skeleton of the storyline of the original manga  The original manga is set in a high school environment, whereas for the . Taiwanese version, the age group is older and in a university setting. This change came about because of sensitivities  in  Taiwan  about the  association  of  a  love  story  with  a  high  school setting (Chen, 29 November 2011, interview). Interestingly, one of the defining characteristics of the Japanese production is its setting in an exaggerated, upper-class fantasy environment,  including  well-known  and  iconic  local  and  international  locations.  In  the Taiwanese  version,  the  setting  is  closer  to  a  normal  urban  landscape.  In  this  sense,  the Taiwanese TV drama appears to displace the main message in the Japanese version, which is the aspiration, in material terms, for a better life. The iconic luxury elements of the story are missing, in turn discarding the fantasy element of the original manga. The repositioning of the drama  from  a  fantasy  to  a  completely  different  and  more  mundane,  or  realistic, perspective is a somewhat surprising contrast to the initiating text and is counterintuitive to my preconceptions. I did expect the owner of  the copyright to keep this aspect of the text closer  to  the  originating  text.  In  the  case  of  the  Korean  production,  the  scriptwriter,  Yoon Ji-Ryun, is attuned to the planned audience needs. It is possible that this is also the case with the  Taiwanese  production,  but  I  was  not  able  to  arrange  an  interview  with  the  Taiwanese scriptwriter to confirm this. I refer to Tania Lim's research of Meteor Garden to compensate for this shortfall in my study (Lim 2005).

Lim's case study of Meteor Garden is  primarily  focused on production and financing. However,  she  notes  that  magazine  interviews  and  newspaper  sources  indicate  that  the television dramas Hana yori dango and Meteor Garden portray contemporary social issues and provide an avenue for young viewers to express themselves in terms of friendship, love and family conflict. She also draws on an interview with the Taiwanese producer Angie Chai, who says that Meteor Garden creates a new mode of expressing real-life, youth-centric issues in  similar  terms,  with  the  addition  of  rivalry  and  failure.  These  points  are  significant  in  an appreciation of the essence of the Hana yori dango manga and its subsequent remakes across cultures.

As can be anticipated, the pace of the TV drama develops more quickly in comparison to the  manga, which  comprises  29  volumes.  Recognition  of  differences  in  the  Japanese  and Taiwanese  societies  are  evident  in  the  remaking  process  as  Japanese  cultural  settings  and expressions  are  replaced.  For  example,  an  authentic  Japanese  dango  (sticky  rice  sweet dumpling) shop is replaced by a cake shop. The bullying scenes, construed as bad by social norms, are more overt in the Taiwanese TV drama than depictions  in the Japanese  manga, and  the  body  language  and  expressions  more  severe.  However,  with  the  counterpoise  of  a greater focus on the love story, construed as good, in the Taiwanese version, there was almost a replication of yin and yang; the bad counterbalanced by the good to achieve a more neutral message.

The Korean drama is close to the original  manga and places an emphasis on the  love story,  relationships,  fashion  and  parties.  Settings  are  extraordinarily  luxurious.  The  music foregrounds and romanticizes the scenes: in the Japanese TV drama production, one feature is a  solo  violin  but the  Korean  version  features  a  violin,  guitar,  piano,  harp,  an orchestra  and love songs. The emphasis on bullying, as in the Taiwanese production, is more overt than the original  manga.  Japanese  cultural  implications  and  expressions  are  discarded,  illustrated  in the comparisons in Tables 2 and 4. Localization, as with the Taiwanese version, is clearly in evidence throughout the production. Shōjo, the main female character, is portrayed as more strong-willed and assertive than her Japanese counterpart. Overall, producers changed many Japanese  cultural  elements  to  Korean  elements;  for  example,  the  Japanese  tea  ceremony house is replaced by a Korean pottery shop.

Hana yori dango certainly adds to fan culture in East Asia, and its acceptance, even with substantial  repositioning  in  some  cases,  illustrates  elements  of  commonality  of  values.  I would argue that not only the story but also other factors represent 'Japaneseness', even when processed through multiple remakes, and this is attractive to youth across Asia. The essence of this attraction is the Japanese imagination. It is this that makes the superficially impossible possible  and  realizes  those  dreams  that  are  often  buried  in  the  human  psyche,  converting them  to  conscious  realities.  The  international  appeal  of  Japanese  manga and  its  remaking perhaps confirms this opinion. Boentaram (2002) remarks: 'Japanese manga has always been popular for its romantic plots, which have the right mixture of humour, fantasy and tragedy.'

In the focus group interviews, which further explored issues arising from the questionnaires, it was apparent that the participants from Korea, in both Australia and Korea, and,  similarly,  the  Taiwanese  in  Australia  and  Taiwan,  want to  know  more  about  Japanese culture  and  are  very interested in what  was  happening  among  Japanese  youth.  In  a supplementary interview that I conducted with Jeffrey Lai, President of the Taiwanese Youth Society  of  Australia,  the  interviewee  observes  that  Taiwan  has  adapted  Japanese  popular culture  (Lai,  4  June  2009,  interview).  Moreover,  the  Korean  group  confirms  that  young Koreans, particularly in high school, copy Japanese culture, whether it is good or bad, such as ijime / bullying. This may reflect the influence of Japanese culture on the youth of East Asia through media products. The Korean government mediates this issue by suppressing violence portrayed  in  Japanese  TV  dramas.  This  watering  down  of  content  does  not  have  the  total support of Korean participants.

This  study  finds  that  the  opinions  of  the  participants  in  Australia  were  remarkably similar to the opinions of participants in their respective countries. This supports the idea of 'coevalness'  (Iwabuchi 2002: 122; Chua 2004: 203), that people  in these countries share a sense of modernity, which is linked to 'cultural proximity'. With TV dramas, remade from Hana yori dango , there is a positive commonality of interest in storylines and actors among all students interviewed. Some viewers see predictability of outcome as a negative. Koreans like  Japanese  humour,  which  they  think  is  not  so  evident  in  Korean  drama  productions. Emotional involvement by females, confirmed by my audience research, is commonplace in Japan and Korea; however, the Taiwanese appear to be more circumspect.

Fandom is strongly evident in all groups. Viewers of television drama eagerly await the next  episode,  and  they  sustain  a  common  interest  in  peer  conversation.  The  Koreans particularly  like  the  freshness  of  Japanese  TV  dramas,  the  fewer  episodes  and  the  faster moving  stories.  The  influence  of  popular  culture  on  participants  is  more  significant  and evenly  distributed  across  ethnicity.  This,  in  part,  confirms  the  point  made  by  Chua:  'This empirically  highly  visible  cultural  traffic  allows  for  the  discursive  construction  of  an  East Asian popular culture' (Chua 2004: 202).

Advertising  influences  the  viewing  habits  of  the  Japanese,  Taiwanese  and  Korean participants, usually via the Internet. For one Korean participant, blogs are a prime source of information. There was a consensus with the respondents on cultural proximity, arguably a commonality of cultural aspects in everyday life. The change in government policy in Korea is seen as beneficial in regard to pop cultural products (Yasumoto 2009). The Koreans see it as a positive for cultural exchange and as confirmation of illegal and unauthorized access to Japanese media products. Later in the interview process, one of the Taiwanese respondents volunteers the view that Korean dramas popular in Taiwan are placed in a later time slot to protect Taiwanese dramas. This can be an adverse decision from a regional perspective, given the progressive elimination of restriction on media culture flowing in and out of Korea. As one Korean respondent comments, 'Leave politics to the politicians.' The Japanese textbook issue  has  fuelled anti-Japanese  sentiments (Ducke 2002) and concerns a number of Korean and Taiwanese respondents, pointing to the need for Japan to review this matter for the sake of regional harmony. The word 'forgiveness' was even used.


## CONCLUSION


This article has drawn attention to the intrinsic value of the core narrative of the manga Hana yori dango . This value is confirmed by the successful regional and progressively international transfer of cultural content through the process of remaking it. The manga was remade into television serial dramas in Taiwan, Korea, Japan and elsewhere, receiving very high audience numbers and becoming, at a point in time, the top show of its genre in many countries in the region.  Foregrounding  analysis confirms that variations  in  content  are  minimal  and  remain close to the original manga. There are many shared elements across the selected remakes of the manga, and the retention of these particular thematic elements of the storyline across the range  of  TV  drama  presentations  reflects  cultural  proximity.  The  textual  analysis  confirms that  the  productions  have  moved  closer  to  local  values.  Cultural  expressions  are  country specific, and societal positioning and lifestyles similarly so.

The  results  of  the  respondent  cohorts  are  not  necessarily  representative  of  the  overall composition of Taiwanese, Korean and Japanese societies. Youth acceptance of East Asian pop  culture,  remade  across  cultures,  brings  a  new  awakening  in  Japan.  Japanese  popular culture  has  and  continues  to  make  a  significant  contribution  to  regional  harmony  and understanding.  It  is  progressively  eroding  historical  regional antipathy  towards  Japan. Impressions of Japan by the  Korean and Taiwanese respondents included such concepts as cute culture, pop  culture, technology, electronic products, beauty, cultural traditions, politeness  and  respect  for  seniors  from  junior  societal  positions.  They  perceive  Japanese people  as  strong,  enthusiastic  and  confident.  There  is  a  common  opinion  that  Asian  pop culture had piqued global interest. The responses suggest that the youth of three cultures are willing and open to embrace change and to move on from historical prejudices.

The respondents within my audience analysis are young and educated members of their respective societies. Their views may well prove to be influential in reshaping the future for upcoming generations. I acknowledge that in both Japan and Korea there are anti-Korean and anti-Japanese activists and that the future will bring forward the reinforcement or dilution of these sentiments, which are prospectively destructive to regional harmony. The focus groups and  surveys  have  found  that  there  is  still  some  residual  stigmatism  against  Japan  for  its colonial history, more so in Korea than in Taiwan, but that media trade is having a positive effect  in  bringing  historical  stereotypes  into  a  modern  and  more  forgiving  context.  The combination of replies to questionnaires, allied with subsequent focus group interviews, is a valuable method to use in researching the influence of Japanese original and remade media in East  Asia.  The  questionnaires  elicited  individual  views,  and  the  focus  group  interviews

allowed for free-flowing discussions, which, while confirming the survey findings, drew out insights for me in the content of the discussions and also in non-verbal communication (Hall 1990).

There is a caveat in respect of my research findings. In respect of audiences, gender was not the criteria for the selection of participants, but the overall segmentation turned out to be 4:1,  with  more  females  than  males.  The  prime  gender  imbalance  is  due  to  39  female participants from Kobe Shinwa University in Japan. There is also another prospective bias in that the majority of participants, if  not of Japanese origin, were studying Japanese language and/or  culture.  The  male  participants,  more  so  than  the  females,  in  the  research  are  more conservative in their views on the social value of media interchange with regional cultures. Notwithstanding the gender differences, the overall positive feedback on representations of Japan in Taiwan and Korea far outweighed the negative ones. Stereotypes of past Japanese military  excesses  remained  an  issue  with  males,  whereas  female  participants,  while  not disregarding  history,  put  past  Japanese  militarism  and  all  that  is  good  about  contemporary Japan into a holistic context. It would seem, then, that Japanese popular culture is positively influencing females, more so than males. I argue that the female demographic will be more influential  in  reshaping  Asia  in  the  future  as  they  exhibit  a  more  embracing  and  forgiving regional view. They have a strong desire to move forward into the future rather than dwelling in the past, which is particularly important for Japan. The Japanese need to re-evaluate their East Asian  neighbours,  as my  audience  survey showed  that  a minority of Japanese participants considered Japan culturally superior to Taiwan and Korea.

The  main  finding  of  the  study  is  the  similarity  of  critical  comments  from  across  the ethnic spectrum of Taiwanese, Korean and Japanese participants within and outside Australia. The  findings  confirm  Livingstone's  view (2002) that audiences are  not trivial  and  passive. Shared  cultural  elements  far  outweigh  contrasting  ones  while  exhibiting  no  diminution  of national  identity.  There  is  a  commonality  of  enthusiasm  for  Japanese  original  and  remade television serial drama and cultural interchange, particularly with female participants. Hana yori  dango has  added to its  fan  culture  in  East Asia  and  has  been  enjoyed  across  cultures, illustrating a commonality of regional core values. This has enhanced regional harmony.

## BACKGROUND



## Addressing arguments against counting stillbirth in demographic measures of mortality


This section describes and critically analyzes five common arguments that pervade current thinking about why it is difficult or does not make sense to include stillbirth as a more mainstream form of mortality within demography.  These arguments are: (1) stillbirth is too difficult to measure; (2) focusing on neonatal/infant mortality tells us enough about health and

wellbeing; (3) stillbirths are already included in the perinatal mortality rate, which has existed for a long time; (4) stillbirth is more an outcome of fertility since it is similar to other kinds of pregnancy losses; and (5) stillborn babies cannot be counted as deaths because they never entered the population.


## Argument 1: Stillbirth is too difficult to measure


Stillbirth measurement remains a challenge in much of the world. This is particularly true in LMICs where vital registration systems are often underdeveloped (UN IGME 2020), and where even the births and deaths of living children and adults are not consistently recorded (Mikkelson et al 2015).  In fact, a 2010 estimate found that only 2% of the world's stillbirths were counted through vital registration (Lawn et al 2010).  Stillbirth may be additionally difficult to measure because discussing stillbirth can be emotionally sensitive or taboo (Roberts et al 2012, Haws et al 2010). Some argue that these measurement issues make any conclusions about stillbirth too unreliable.

Limitations in data quality also exist for other types of mortality, like maternal mortality (AbouZahr 2011) and adult mortality (Clark 2019). Rather than turning away from complicated but consequential data quality concerns, demographers have recognized that data limitations are not a reason to ignore mortality outcomes that are critical to accurately understanding the health challenges that the world faces. Instead, they have innovated solutions for learning about a range of mortality outcomes while recognizing data imperfections that require further work. These approaches include developing modeling frameworks, measuring mortality in surveillance sites or surveys, and improving routine measurement by strengthening vital registration.

Similarly, challenges in measuring stillbirth must not preclude its study or efforts to improve its measurement. Traditional demographic analyses of mortality simply ignore the occurrence of stillbirth and its meaning for our understanding of health. But there is enormous value in measuring and describing real-world phenomena with uncertainty, rather than simplistically assuming that the phenomenon is unimportant because it is difficult to measure (Manski 2009, Woods 2009, Nobles & Hamoudi 2019). Although there is growing interest in stillbirth and its measurement (Froen 2016), the field of demography has yet to fully begin grappling with the implications of widening definitions of mortality to include stillbirths.

Argument 2: A focus on neonatal/infant mortality tells us enough about health and wellbeing

Since both stillbirth and neonatal mortality are indicators of health and wellbeing, some argue that including stillbirth will not provide a radically different picture of population health. Given stillbirth measurement challenges, focusing attention on counting stillbirths better may not be useful when it is much simpler to collect data on neonatal mortality.

While stillbirth rates and neonatal mortality rates may be predictive of a similar state of health, early life mortality in most of the world is steadily becoming more and more concentrated in the earliest days and hours of life. As this trend continues, what happens at the moment of birth, being able to distinguish more closely a stillbirth from a live birth, and measuring stillbirth will become increasingly consequential.

Additionally, demographers have shown the value of improving data collection and measurement for many indicators that are correlated with one another, knowing that each indicator can give slightly more nuanced information. Some examples include measures of wealth and income, or child death and adult death, or life expectancy and healthy life expectancy. While related, they are not exactly the same. If the goal is a greater understanding of the details of the health of populations, measuring and tracking stillbirth alongside other forms of child mortality is crucial.

More importantly, there is no way to know for certain how adding stillbirth to our current measures of mortality will change our understanding of child health until better data on stillbirth are available. Guillot et al (2022) show that the age patterns of under-5 mortality differ across places. We do not understand these patterns for stillbirth in part because the arbitrary importance given to the line of live birth supports the prominence of traditional child mortality. This leads to the neglect of stillbirth and of the close connection between maternal, neonatal, and fetal health (Woods 2009). The focus in demographic study on one form of mortality (i.e. after live birth) rather than on overall mortality (i.e. both stillbirth and child death) increases measurement error and creates perverse incentives that may lead to more misclassification than if stillbirth were measured and understood as important in its own right, and in a more rigorous way.


## Argument 3: Stillbirth is already included in the perinatal rate


Improvements in health have led to a concentration of early-life mortality in the first 30 days of life (neonatal mortality), and within that, in the first 7 days of life (early neonatal

mortality). In recognition of the fact that early neonatal mortality and fetal loss in late pregnancy are closely related, a measure known as perinatal mortality was created in 1948, encompassing deaths that occur from 22 weeks of gestation to seven days after birth (WHO 2006).  It is used as an indicator of maternal care, nutrition, and of the quality of obstetric and pediatric care. It also simplifies questions of whether a baby showed signs of life at birth. Some argue that since the perinatal rate includes information about stillbirth, separate study of stillbirth is not required. But despite its existence for over 70 years, the perinatal mortality rate has not gained relevance in the demographic study of mortality in the way that child mortality, infant mortality, neonatal mortality, and early neonatal mortality have.

Importantly, the idea of perinatal mortality obscures the unique challenge of stillbirth and the preventability of many stillbirths. For example, while efforts exist to classify stillbirths within perinatal deaths (WHO 2016), the poor recording of perinatal deaths persists. In addition, studies of interventions relevant to stillbirth prevention often only report perinatal deaths, despite having data on stillbirths (Froen 2011, Ota et al 2020). With such neglect of stillbirth, perinatal mortality's grouping of late pregnancy losses together with early neonatal mortality may mean that efforts at bringing down perinatal mortality focus more on addressing early neonatal mortality rather than stillbirth. The factors that influence stillbirth and early neonatal mortality are similar, but they are not all the same (Bhutta et al 2011): reducing stillbirth more heavily requires investing in mothers and their health throughout pregnancy and delivery (Ahmed et al 2018, Taylor et al 2020). In contrast, environmental factors after birth can also play a role in early neonatal mortality. Investing only in interventions that address early neonatal mortality will not automatically bring stillbirth rates down (Froen 2011, Kelley & Rubens 2010).


## Argument 4: Stillbirth is more an outcome of fertility than mortality


Despite being the death of a viable baby, stillbirth is often still seen as a loss of a pregnancy rather than a loss of a child. Before the creation of the perinatal mortality statistic, stillbirths were understood as being similar to other kinds of fetal losses, like miscarriage and abortion (Armstrong 1986).  In many ways, this idea persists.  For example, rather than consistently being described only as deaths or non-live births alongside the perinatal mortality rate, stillbirths are also often described as adverse pregnancy losses or fetal losses.  Some Demographic and Health Survey reports discuss stillbirth only in chapters on fertility, or in

chapters on fertility earlier and more extensively than in chapters on mortality (DHS Reports). In addition, arguments endure that say that because of the close alignment of stillbirth with abortion, counting stillbirths as deaths go too far down a morally slippery slope that undermines women's reproductive freedom (Kelley 2011, Phillips & Millum 2015, Cacciatore & Bushfield 2008). This grouping with pregnancy loss leads some to argue that stillbirth is not actually a mortality event at all.

The alignment with pregnancy loss also means that stillbirth is often not given importance because it is seen as a women's issue, and women's wellbeing is often a low priority, particularly in contexts with widespread gender inequality. In many cases, stillbirth is not seen as a real loss, with grief hastily brushed away (Roberts et al 2012, Lovell 1983): for example, a common myth persists that women who are accustomed to high early-life mortality feel the emotional cost of losing a pregnancy less than women in high-income countries (Kelley 2011). This devaluation of the experience of stillbirth causes legal and political indifference (Lens 2018, Lovell 1983, Cacciatore & Bushfield 2008). And the stigma sometimes associated with stillbirth pushes women to underreport stillbirth even when they do experience it (Haws et al 2010).

Lastly, there is a long history within demography, even in studies focused on fertility, of dismissing the importance of pregnancy loss. For example, important population health surveys in use today, like the Demographic and Health Surveys purposely decided to exclude detailed questions on pregnancy loss (including stillbirth) because they do not lead to more accurate accounting of fertility (Casterline 1989).  Despite ample evidence of social patterning of stillbirth (Froen 2011, Zeitlin et al 2016, Carvalho et al 2018, Adeyinka et al 2019, Altijani et al 2018), canonical demography literature on fertility assumes that stillbirth, like miscarriage, is biologically determined and has little variation across populations (Bongaarts & Casterline 2018). This leads to the belief that these losses are of little demographic significance because they cannot be impacted by prenatal health interventions (Bongaarts 1978).  It is worth questioning this legacy.


## Argument 5: Stillbirths have not yet entered the population


An important assumption in population theory is that entry into the population must be defined in some way, and drawing the line at live birth is the easiest way. If a baby is not born, they do not die. Thus some argue that it is unnecessary to consider stillbirths because stillbirths

do not contribute to the traditional balancing equation and other widely used population measures.

This argument is rooted in a lack of recognition of stillbirth as a form of mortality.  One reason for this may be that there has yet to be broader recognition of stillbirth as a preventable problem of society, rather than an unalterable problem of biology. As the WHO notes, stillbirths, and even perinatal deaths, are seen today in many societies as natural occurrences, and births are often counted only after a child has survived some initial period (WHO 2006).  Even among health professionals working in maternal and child health, many incorrectly believe that most stillbirths are not preventable, even though only approximately 5% of stillbirths are attributed to unpreventable congenital anomalies (Froen 2011). There are low expectations of preventability because much is unknown about the exact causes of remaining stillbirths. Many thus believe that stillbirth prevention should not be prioritized as highly as the prevention of maternal and infant deaths (Froen 2011). This fatalism, however, is paradoxical because stillbirths in high-income countries are defined as losses at 20, 22, or 24 weeks of gestation, rather than the WHO's 28week definition for LMICs. Additionally, stillborn babies in high-income countries are often issued death certificates (Hure et al 2015), a clear recognition of the fact that these babies could, in fact, have lived.

Armstrong (1986) and Preston & Haines (2014) describe how historically, this apathy and perception of inevitability was also true of infant and child mortality in the 19th century. Only after there was broader social awareness of these deaths did infant and child mortality come to be seen as a public responsibility worth counting and measuring. Armstrong (1986) describes how as infants began to be recognized as viable, and infant mortality seen as preventable, the infant began to be conceptualized as a social object and a humanized individual, as an analytically separate entity rather than just an appendage of the mother. This, in turn, 'enabled a more sophisticated view of mortality to be introduced.'  He goes on to note that perceptions matter for what is counted as mortality and what is not: the infant's medical and social existence only came about after an analytic framework imposed the importance of the first year of life upon all deaths.

In the same way that infants came to be seen as viable beings, worthy of being counted as an important and distinct part of the population, so stillbirths can be too.  Indeed, as Phillips & Millum (2015) posit, no one would argue that a society in which many babies are stillborn is as

healthy as one in which those babies went on to live healthy lives. And yet, this is what traditional mortality statistics indicate.  Expanding the balancing equation and updating mortality statistics will not be easy and will have many imperfections to begin, but it is a worthwhile endeavor to more accurately understand the health and wellbeing of individuals and societies.

Finally, it is important to consider the ethical considerations that such an exercise would entail (Kelley & Rubens 2010). In particular, incorporating stillbirths into the balancing equation and counting stillbirths as deaths grants the significance of life to the stillborn baby. On the surface, this may seem to have implications for ongoing controversy around abortion. However, there are two reasons that updating demographic measures to define entry into a population beginning at 28 weeks of gestation rather than at the moment of birth need not become entangled with abortion in order to address important issues of mortality and population health. First, the stillbirths in this analysis are those that occur at late-term in pregnancy, and are definitionally called stillbirths because of their viability (UN-IGME 2020, Dong & Sun 2016, Connolly et al 2020). These stillbirths have little to do with arguments about when life begins because they are biologically indistinguishable from newborn babies. In fact, most high-income countries use much earlier gestational cut-offs to define viability and stillbirth than the 28-week cut-off used by the WHO and in this analysis. Second, because these are losses that occur late in pregnancy, they are likely pregnancies that are wanted. Leaving stillbirths uncounted in population health statistics of mortality is dismissive of the traumatic experience of loss. Counting stillbirths as mortality events does not lend support to those who oppose a woman's choice to have an abortion, or impinge on women's reproductive rights because both access to abortion and counting stillbirths well are moves towards reproductive justice with a focus on women's wellbeing.


## Stillbirth in the demography literature


Most early demographic studies do not analyze stillbirths on their own, but rather consider the occurrence of pregnancy loss generally. Inspired by Bourgeois-Pichat's idea that infant deaths were either caused endogenously, through congenital abnormalities or the birthing process, or exogenously, through postnatal environmental factors (Woods 2009), several studies taking place at the community level or in places with high-quality data have used demographic life table methods to examine the probabilities of various pregnancy outcomes throughout the

course of a pregnancy (Stevenson & Warnock 1959, Bakketeig et al 1978, French & Bierman 1962, Shapiro et al 1962, Taylor 1964). These exercises have sought to understand how the environment in-utero relates to the occurrence of disorders in childhood.

Other studies consider pregnancy losses only as they pertain to women's overall fertility. For example, Sheps (1964) models the effect of fetal wastage on fertility rates as women face varying periods of infecundability in the face of different types of pregnancy losses. Bongaarts (1975) also only mentions stillbirths as they pertain to the calculation of fecundability. Casterline (1989) describes that fetal deaths were of interest because they were seen as 'a source of lost fertility exposure time.' However, stillbirths and other late fetal losses were not considered worthy of detailed study because they were believed to constitute only a small fraction of spontaneous pregnancy losses (Casterline 1989).

Because vital registration systems in many countries are underdeveloped, sample surveys are often used to understand population health trends. However, sample surveys like the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) have been inconsistent in recording stillbirth (Bradley et al 2015, MacQuarrie et al 2018, Akuze et al 2020, Akuze et al 2021). In a recent study looking across DHS surveys between 2005 and 2015, Christou et al (2017) found that many different methods are used to collect data on pregnancy loss.  Some do not allow for the calculation of rates of stillbirth at all, many lump all types of terminations (abortions/miscarriages/stillbirth) all together, and in most cases, fetal loss data cannot be linked to health seeking activity or health consequences. Other studies have documented social taboos that impact the reporting of stillbirth in sample surveys (Haws et al 2010).

A recent trend in demography examines stillbirth in the context of definitional challenges, and biases in survey estimates of early life mortality. Anderson and Silver (1986) describe how definitional ambiguities in registering live versus stillbirths produced drastic changes in infant mortality in the Soviet Union. Gourbin and Masuy-Stroobant (1995) find wide variation in classification regimes and registration practices of live births and stillbirths across Europe. In a comparison of full birth history data with Health and Demographic Surveillance System (HDSS) data in Guinea-Bissau, Helleringer et al. (2020) find that that stillbirths were often misclassified as neonatal deaths, inflating the neonatal mortality rate. Similarly, Liu et al. (2016) compare a full birth history with verbal/social autopsy survey in Malawi and find that one-fifth of reported neonatal deaths were stillbirths. In contrast, Gonzalez and Gilleskie (2017)

find evidence of infant deaths being misclassified as stillbirths, artificially lowering the infant mortality rate in Cuba. They suggest including stillbirths in current measures of infant mortality to combat incentives for misclassification. Nobles and Hamoudi (2019) demonstrate the significant bias that can result from not accounting for prenatal selection in studies of the fetal origins of later life health. While these articles demonstrate how the line of live birth is not necessarily as straightforward as demographic theory assumes, none focus on stillbirth as an important demographic category.

I expand this literature by creating measures of 'stillbirth-adjusted' child mortality, and demonstrating their use with data from present-day low- and middle-income countries (LMIC), where stillbirth is most common and where data quality is often poor. These new measures are useful to overcome misclassification challenges that distort our understanding of progress on child mortality globally, to bring attention to the important phenomenon of stillbirth, and to expand demographic conceptions of mortality. In his historical study of fetal death, population geographer Robert Woods (2009) sought to bring a new focus to stillbirths and posited that 'when the distinction between fetal death and infant death is blurred it will be difficult to ascertain the true level of mortality.' I build from this observation to show the importance of understanding stillbirth and child mortality, both separately and together.  To demonstrate one possible path forward for demographic study to reach a more complete description of the health of societies, I now turn to a more focused analysis that takes seriously the idea that stillbirths are deaths that can and should be counted in traditional demographic measures of mortality.


## METHODS



## Data


USAID's Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) collects data on health and population using standardized questions across 92 countries. This analysis uses data from the most recent DHS survey from each country in which a reproductive calendar data was collected for all women in the sample, from 2005 onwards. Data from a total of 42 countries are included (see Table 2).

DHS surveys include a birth history, which includes information on every birth in a woman's reproductive history. For children who died after birth, the DHS also collects data on

the number of days, months, or years they lived. Most DHS surveys do not count the number or type of pregnancy losses that each woman ever had. However, pregnancy losses are captured for the five years prior to the survey in the reproductive calendar, separately from data on live births.

The DHS reproductive calendar is a month-by-month history of key reproductive events for each female respondent.  Depending on interview date, the reproductive calendar records whether a woman was pregnant, gave birth, or had a pregnancy termination for every month in the five to seven years prior to the start of the survey. As shown in Figure 1, pregnancies in the calendar are marked with a 'P', births are marked with a 'B', and terminations are marked with a 'T' (numbers refer to contraceptive measures).  The calendar is read from right to left in terms of chronological time, so the right end of the calendar variable is the furthest back in time, and events closer to the date of the interview are on the left end.  While one cannot tell whether any given T indicates a miscarriage, abortion, or stillbirth, it is possible to separate out stillbirths: if there are terminations ('T') with 6 or more 'P''s in front of them, they can be identified as stillbirths (i.e. 'TPPPPPP').  Miscarriages and abortions are, however, indistinguishable from one another.

## A note on modeled approaches to stillbirth and child mortality estimation


Stillbirth and other child mortality rates across LMICs are often based on detailed modeling exercises that combine various sources of data and make predictions based on related covariates, rather than relying solely on measured data. The purpose of these modeled estimates is to overcome known data quality problems and, particularly in the case of stillbirth, its underreporting in vital registration systems and surveys (Cousens et al 2011, Christou, Dibley & Rayenes-Greenow 2017). Most recently, the United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME) released updated global stillbirth estimates in 2020 (UN IGME 2020).

This paper's main exercise of calculating 'stillbirth-adjusted' rates of neonatal and infant mortality can be done using modeled data just as with survey data. There is large uncertainty in all stillbirth estimates. More work is needed both to improve stillbirth data quality and to understand underreporting more deeply. In the interest of transparency, this analysis uses DHS survey data on stillbirth and child mortality. For further discussion and analysis comparing DHS and UN IGME stillbirth rates, and results showing 'stillbirth-adjusted' neonatal and infant mortality rates using UN IGME data, see the Appendix.

## Comparison of stillbirth rates with rates of early neonatal mortality


A common way to assess the quality of stillbirth data in the DHS is to compare rates of stillbirth to rates of early neonatal mortality (WHO 2006, Bradley, Winfrey & Croft 2015). Using a mortality indicator that is less prone to error to understand the patterns of a separate mortality indicator that is known to be inaccurate in some way (Guillot et al 2012) is a useful way to identify biases in the weaker indicator.

The use of the early neonatal mortality rate (ENMR) as a comparator is justified for two reasons: first, almost one third of neonatal deaths happen on the first day of life (Blencowe et al 2016) and many of the same factors that cause stillbirths cause early neonatal deaths, verifying the close relationship between early neonatal mortality and stillbirth.  Since early neonatal deaths and stillbirths are believed to be nearly equivalent in number (Hart 1998, WHO 2006, Bradley, Winfrey & Croft 2015, UN-IGME 2020), a comparison of the two rates can demonstrate the extent of underreporting within stillbirth estimates. Second, much attention has been paid to child mortality (Guillot et al 2012, Silva 2012, Pedersen & Liu 2012, Lawn et al 2010) with global organizations setting specific targets for countries to meet. Measures of early neonatal mortality are thus far more developed and of higher quality than those of stillbirth, and as a result, suffer from less underreporting (Hill & Choi 2006).

Looking across high and low contemporary mortality regimes, and using a historical review of ratios of stillbirth to early neonatal mortality in countries with developed vital registration systems, the WHO (2006) suggests using 1.2 as the ratio to translate between the two rates. They found ratios higher than 1.2 in rich country contexts with better data and greater technology available for newborn survival, and ratios lower than 1.2 in higher mortality countries with worse data (WHO 2006). Because epidemiologically stillbirths likely exceed neonatal deaths, the ratios that fall below 1.2 are conservatively assumed to be the result of underreporting (WHO 2006). Though further work to understand the nuances within the

relationship between stillbirth and early neonatal mortality is warranted, this 1.2 ratio has been used by many researchers as a method to assess the quality of stillbirth data (Cousens et al 2011, Bradley, Winfrey & Croft 2015, Lawn et al 2010). Countries with ratios further below the 1.2 mark are considered to have poorer measurement of stillbirth (Bradley, Winfrey & Croft 2015).

For all countries in the dataset, Figure 2 graphs the relationship between the ratio of the stillbirth rate to the ENMR, and the actual ENMR, over the period of the past five years using DHS data. Each circle represents one country. The dotted line shows the level of the 1.2 stillbirth to ENMR ratio. The downward sloping trend line shows that places with worse early neonatal mortality, and thus presumably higher rates of stillbirth, have poorer measurement of stillbirth than places with better early life health.  This suggests that undermeasurement is not uniform across places, and that undermeasurement may be far greater in the places that need the most improvement.

It is worth noting that most countries do not reach the 1.2 ratio. Most do not even come within 0.5 of the 1.2 ratio.  This is not surprising given that the reproductive calendar's main purpose is to track contraceptive use, not pregnancy loss.  These low ratios likely reflect underreporting of stillbirth (Cousens et al 2011, Bradley, Winfrey & Croft 2015). Further research on current SB:ENMR ratios, and more nuanced understandings of the reasons for underreporting would be fruitful.

## Stillbirth as a component of child mortality


If stillbirth is undermeasured in the places where it is likely happening the most, what does this mean for our understanding of child mortality and wellbeing in individual countries and globally?  Answering this question requires taking seriously the idea that stillbirth should be considered and included as a type of mortality.  This makes sense for two reasons. First, stillbirths are those fetuses that have gestated to a time past the line of viability, meaning that these are recognized as babies who can survive outside the mother's womb.  Second, stillbirths are often separated into antepartum stillbirths, which occur before the onset of labor, and intrapartum stillbirths, which begin after the onset of labor. Globally, it is estimated that 42% of

all stillbirths are intrapartum (UN-IGME 2020). These are understood to be preventable through access to high-quality labor care and improved obstetric practices Additionally, many of the remaining antepartum stillbirths, particularly in high-risk countries, can also be prevented through closer attention to the mother's health (i.e. improved nutrition and risk-factor monitoring), improved antenatal care, and fetal growth monitoring (UN-IGME 2020).

Figures 3, 4, and 5 demonstrate the amount of mortality that is missed by not including stillbirth in traditional demographic rates of child mortality. This is important for two reasons. First, these updated measures show a more accurate and complete picture of population health and wellbeing in these countries. This is a crucial but overlooked issue in population policy.

The second reason that these new measures matter is because of the number of lives that newly become perceptible as worth investing in through health and population policy.  For example, the 'traditional' neonatal mortality rate in India is 29.9 per 1000 live births, which is equivalent to the deaths of approximately 721,000 babies per year. The 'stillbirth-adjusted' neonatal mortality rate in India is 41.3 per 1000 pregnancies of seven or more months of gestation, which is equivalent to the deaths of approximately 1.01 million babies per year.  In India alone, this is a difference of almost 300,000 babies each year that policymakers are insufficiently considering when trying to make improvements to population health.


## DISCUSSION


This analysis demonstrates that without accounting for stillbirth, existing measures of child health do not adequately capture the burden of mortality that individuals and societies face. In particular, estimates in this paper suggest that traditional measures may be missing large fractions of infant and neonatal mortality. Their focus only on the outcomes of live births additionally contributes to the neglect of stillbirth and our understanding of it. However, these are conservative estimates and it is likely that the problem is far larger than existing data allow us to see.  The aim of this article is to call attention to stillbirth itself, and to its measurement, as incorporating these losses into our understanding of child mortality will lead to a richer and more nuanced understanding of the health challenges that children in the world face.

The implications of this analysis for public health are clear. A majority of neonatal deaths occur very close to the time of birth, and at least some of the factors that cause stillbirth overlap with those that cause early neonatal death. Not counting stillbirth well means that a large portion of what would be considered mortality is being undermeasured. For decades, demographers have continuously improved upon the methods used to count childhood deaths (Guillot et al 2012, Silva 2012, Pedersen & Liu 2012, Lawn et al 2010, Rajaratnam et al 2010, Alkema et al 2014), to track these losses and ultimately to prevent them from happening. A lack of attention to

stillbirth likely contributes to biases in the measurement of child mortality, and tardy progress on reducing its burden.

While the focus of this paper has been on stillbirth as a facet of child mortality, this does not diminish the importance of how a greater understanding of stillbirth would additionally contribute to improving maternal health (Pattinson et al 2011). This is because stillbirths are often caused by conditions that are known to be dangerous to women's health (Kelley 2011). The impact of stillbirth on both the physical and mental health of mothers is enormous. It is also likely undermeasured, given the poor measurement of stillbirth itself.

This analysis also has implications for population theory, and underlying assumptions in demographic measurement. The clarity and simplicity of using live birth for purposes of defining entry into a population for demographic accounting are beyond doubt. Indeed, including stillbirth in our understanding of mortality will require a shift in decisions about who gets counted in a population.  However, most stillbirths in the world are unambiguously viable and can reasonably be thought of as babies rather than fetuses. Thus a researcher of bioethics whose work focuses on stillbirth (Kelley 2011) asks,

In most countries a baby who is born alive, breathes a few breaths but dies a few hours later is counted as a neonatal death, a life lost. However, thirdtrimester or intrapartum stillbirths are not typically classified as deaths. If the 35-week-old stillborn baby and the 35-week-old neonate who dies of respiratory failure 24 hours after delivery are developmentally indistinguishable, why the paradox in our mortality statistics?

The purpose of demographic measures such as infant and neonatal mortality is not only to understand whether someone lives or dies, but also to know how well they are born, how well they live, and how well they die.  Improving our measurement of stillbirth would enable the use of measures like the 'stillbirth-adjusted' NMR and the 'stillbirth-adjusted' IMR alongside traditional measures of NMR and IMR, giving us the ability to measure mortality in early life in a more complete way, and allowing for a more comprehensive assessment of the health of societies.

Many questions remain in terms of stillbirth measurement and classification, that make the estimates in this analysis conservative.  For example, definitional ambiguities highlight more sharply the scale of the problem of stillbirth undermeasurement. The WHO's 28-week

definitional threshold for stillbirths used in this analysis is based on when a fetus can survive outside of the womb.  As technology develops, this line of viability inches ever earlier in pregnancy.  Many developed countries have earlier cutoffs, such as 20 weeks in Australia and the United States, and 24 weeks in the United Kingdom (Froen 2011).  Thus, many losses that are counted in high-income countries may remain uncounted in LMICs. If LMICs had earlier cutoffs, many of the rates presented here and in the UN-IGME estimates would be higher (Temmerman & Lawn 2018).  Additionally, the DHS data used here to calculate 'stillbirthadjusted' infant mortality and 'stillbirth-adjusted' neonatal mortality are not explicitly focused on collecting information on stillbirth. Thus there is much room for improvement in measuring stillbirth, potentially through direct survey reporting.  And last, the WHO's recommended ratio of 1.2 for comparing stillbirth rates to rates of early neonatal mortality is a lower bound, even though they suggest that ratios may be higher in many high-risk places.

While historically stillbirth measurement has been considered too complex to contemplate seriously, not being able to measure something does not mean that demographers should not think carefully about its meaning and consequences (Woods 2009). Most of these losses are preventable, and the need for better quality data on stillbirth is urgent.  There are several fruitful avenues for future research.  First, more work is needed to understand the reasons behind such widescale underreporting of stillbirth in different contexts, in addition to social stigma and social, legal, and political indifference that has been documented (Haws et al 2010, Roberts et al 2012, Lens 2018, Lovell 1983, Cacciatore 2008).  The DHS has recently shifted to a full pregnancy history, which should be able to capture more stillbirths (Akuze et al 2021), but previous studies suggest that this may not fully resolve issues of underreporting (Bradley, Winfrey & Croft 2015).

In addition, it is important to begin moving away from thinking about stillbirth primarily as an outcome of pregnancy, or as it effects women's future fertility, as has historically been the case (Casterline 1989).  Stillbirth is an important form of mortality in itself that deserves attention. One way to do this may be quantifying stillbirth as mortality from the perspective of the women who experience it (Smith-Greenaway & Trinatopoli 2020), to shed light on the effects of these losses on women's physical and emotional health (Heazell et al 2016, Winkvist, Rasmussen & Habicht 1992).  This may make it clearer that stillbirth is not just an issue of the health of children, but also about the wellbeing of women.

Many puzzles also remain in terms of the details of measurement.  For example, the 1.2 stillbirth to early neonatal mortality rate ratio was derived from populations in 2006. It is possible that the ratio is different today in the LMICs where DHS surveys are currently undertaken.  Further work is needed to understand variation in the relationship between rates. As progress on addressing early neonatal mortality continues, this ratio may be even higher today if stillbirth reduction does not keep up, possibly suggesting even greater levels of 'stillbirthadjusted' NMR and IMR than shown in this analysis.  Another measurement issue is one of misclassification of stillbirths and early neonatal deaths in cases when signs of life at birth are unclear. Depending on definitions of stillbirth, cultural norms, and health provider incentives, it may be more likely in some countries for early neonatal deaths to be classified as stillbirths, while in other countries, it may be more likely for stillbirths to be classified as early neonatal deaths (Helleringer et al 2020).  Research on classification and its impact on measures of stillbirth will be useful.  Lastly, there are important issues of selection into live birth that remain to be explored, that may shed light on which populations and subgroups are most likely to experience the burden of stillbirth, and additionally help us reach a more accurate understanding of which children are most likely to survive (Nobles & Hamoudi 2019).

Most global health assessments of child health report only on measures such as the neonatal mortality rate and the infant mortality rate to compare progress on health worldwide. This analysis is an attempt to look across the line of the moment of birth, in recognition of the fact that 'to understand the death or disease of the newborn infant it is necessary to take into account the circumstances through which the infant's organism has passed before birth…' (Hart 1998).  This means fully recognizing that improvements in early life mortality must focus attention on the mother's wellbeing and antenatal factors, in addition to the birthing process and postnatal factors, as they all have an important impact on child health.  Paying greater attention to stillbirth and its measurement will help us more accurately assess health and wellbeing at the population level. Better measurement will ultimately feed into a better understanding of stillbirth, which can help ensure that the babies who are born are born healthier.


## Strengths and limitations of model-based and survey-based stillbirth estimates


Of the many challenges of measuring stillbirth, its underreporting has been explored most extensively.  Currently, there are two main ways of assessing stillbirth prevalence across countries: through survey estimates, and through modeled estimates.  Both approaches have strengths and limitations, as described below. Their existence demonstrates that measurement of stillbirth, while imperfect and difficult, can in fact be done, and that there is much room for improvement.

Modeled stillbirth estimates. To overcome weaknesses in vital registration system and survey data, specifically with regard to underreporting, official UN and WHO estimates are often based on detailed models that try to compute stillbirth estimates to understand country-level and global burdens of stillbirth.

Most recently, a 2020 joint UN and IGME Report presents estimates of stillbirths globally for 195 countries (UN-IGME 2020). However, because of data availability and quality concerns, many estimates had to be extrapolated from data from three to ten years earlier. Estimates for 62 countries, which account for 30 percent of all stillbirths, were derived with no empirical stillbirth data at all. For these countries, estimates were based on covariates associated with stillbirth rates, including the fraction of women who attended at least four antenatal care visits, the fraction of live births that were low birthweight, c-section rate, average years of schooling for females, neonatal mortality rate, and gross national income based on purchasing power parity.  Unfortunately, data on these covariates is sometimes also not of high quality. Issues in terms of how various countries define a stillbirth add additional bias to their estimates.

Though the methods to ascertain these estimates appear sophisticated and careful in considering various data sources and their accuracy, and are designed to provide estimates when actual data are lacking, modeled estimates based on smoothing techniques can be highly uncertain (UN IGME 2020) and potentially biased (WHO 2006). Modeled estimates also use time series trends in calculating estimates. While this is a useful check for accuracy, older data also may be flawed, inhibiting us from seeing longstanding errors that persist (WHO 2006). These limitations highlight the need for improved measurement and timely data collection at both the country and sub-national levels.

Stillbirth estimates in survey data . Because vital registration systems across countries differ greatly in terms of definitions of stillbirth, reporting systems, sources of information, and levels of accuracy and completeness (WHO 2006), international surveys with standardized data collection practices are often used to assess comparative prevalence.  The household survey that is most widely used today to estimate rates of stillbirth is USAID's Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), which collects data on health and population using standardized questions across 92 countries.

Existing research has documented substantial variation in capturing stillbirth prevalence using the DHS: in particular, studies have documented downward bias in its measurement of stillbirth and its very limited ability to link stillbirth with risk factors (Cousens et al 2011, Christou, Dibley & Rayenes-Greenow 2017). One reason for these problems is that the DHS has not, until very recently, asked questions specifically about pregnancy loss. Instead, most recent DHS datasets utilize a live birth history in conjunction with a reproductive calendar. This allows for the identification of stillbirths within a woman's reproductive history within the five years prior to the survey, using a consistent method across countries. Unfortunately, this data is not linked to any details about the specific pregnancies in which the stillbirth took place.

In response to calls for better quality data, starting in its latest questionnaire update in 2020, the DHS shifted from a birth history focused only on live births to a full pregnancy history that records the outcome of each pregnancy (Akuze et al 2021, DHS Model Questionnaire 2020). Some studies suggest that pregnancy histories are better able to capture stillbirths (Akuze et al 2020), while others suggest that even pregnancy histories substantially underestimate stillbirth prevalence (Bradley, Winfrey & Croft 2015).  There are not yet enough DHS data available to assess how much of an improvement the new questionnaire will bring.

Despite these obvious limitations, survey data have the advantage of being transparent. They are collected as directly reported by respondents. In fact, though it is far from an ideal way of collecting data on stillbirth, the ancillary method of utilizing the reproductive calendar to identify stillbirths (described in detail in the Data section) may serve as an accuracy check: because women report their monthly reproductive status, and are not only answering a yes or no question about whether they experienced stillbirth or not, the reproductive calendar may catch stillbirths that might otherwise have been omitted.

## 1 Introduction


The coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, which started in early 2020, had already resulted in more than 100 million confirmed cases and two million deaths worldwide by the end of 2020. Large-scale social anti-contagion policies, such as the lockdown of cities, temporary closure of businesses, and prohibition of group gatherings, have been employed throughout the world to contain the spread of infection (Hsiang et al., 2020; Flaxman et al., 2020), through the reduction of people's movements and contact (Zhang et al., 2020). These anti-contagion policies inevitably have been accompanied by a deep recession in the world economy (OECD, 2020). This short-run trade-off between health and wealth (Glover et al., 2020) polarized society into two: those who wish to control the spread of the virus and those who emphasize the economic down-side (Allcott et al., 2020). In the longer run, however, anti-contagion policies could benefit both health and the economy (Jordà et al., 2020). At the same time, governments have introduced several economic policies to soften the economic damage of anti-contagion policies, such as massive injections of money into lending markets and the provision of direct subsidies to households and firms. To make the correct decisions under crisis, governments need to understand the short-run economic and epidemiological trade-off as well as the potential long-run benefits of anti-contagion and economic policies.

In this study, we perform a causal inference on the short-run effects of anti-contagion policies on the economy, the impacts of subsidies to firms to ease the economic damage, as well as the potential medium-run economic benefits of the anti-contagion policies. This study focuses on small businesses, which are most vulnerable to the economic crisis. We study this issue in the context of Japan, where the number of new infections surged from March to April 2020, followed by the declaration of emergency state, which led to the local governments' request for firms to suspend business temporarily and for individuals to stay at home. At the same time, the Japanese government introduced a series of new subsidy schemes to rescue small businesses. The Japanese case is unique in that the attempt to contain infections is closely tied to a longer-term economic goal, namely, the possibility of hosting the Tokyo Olympic Games. Thus, Japan's short-run stringent anti-contagion policies could lead to a longer-run economic goal, thereby providing an ideal case for evaluating the short-run tension between epidemiological and economic goals as well as the longer-run complementarity between these two goals.

First, we investigate how the emergency declaration and the business suspension request hurt the performance of small businesses. For identification of the causal effects, we use two alternative strategies: 1)

using the variation in local governments' suspension requests across areas and industries over time and 2) randomizing the survey dates to be either just before or after the partial lifting of the emergency declaration to examine the impacts of this information on expected performance. Second, we study whether the subsidy schemes are expected to help small businesses to survive and whether they changed their on-going decisions, such as those on investment and employment. We exploit a discontinuity in eligibility cutoff of each subsidy scheme to estimate the impacts using the regression discontinuity design. Finally, we quantify the mediumrun economic impacts of successfully controlling SARS-Cov-2 infection, particularly, how much business performance would improve if the infections were contained quickly and if the situation could stabilize enough for Japan to host the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. In doing so, we use the variation in managers' beliefs about the timing of infection containment and quarterly sales in a difference-in-difference framework. As such, we contribute to the policy debate by uncovering part of the short-run and the medium-run effects of the Japanese version of anti-contagion and economic policies to tackle the COVID-19 crisis.

## 3 Causal Impacts of Anti-Contagion and Economic Policies



## 3.1 How Did the Emergency Declaration and Business Suspension Requests Affect Businesses?


Our evidence based on the Difference-in-Difference estimation shows that the emergency declaration and the requests to suspend business lowered realized and expected firm sales in the short run while it reduced the number of new infections.

In Japan, on April 7, the government declared the state of emergency until May 6 in 7 prefectures (Tokyo, Kanagawa, Saitama, Chiba, Osaka, Hyogo, and Fukuoka). Under the emergency state, local municipalities requested business suspension at targeted industries and called for staying at home to citizens. It is noteworthy that these policies only took the form of 'requests' that were not legally enforced, implying that the Japanese policies were milder than countries which implemented lock-down of cities. On April 16, the government expanded coverage of the emergency declaration to all prefectures in Japan. On May 4, the government extended the emergency declaration to May 31, indicating that it could be lifted earlier depending on the situations. On May 13, the government indicated that the emergency declaration in 39 among 47 prefectures was expected to be lifted, and this decision was formalized on May 14. At the same time, the government announced guidelines for lifting the emergency declaration for the remaining areas, specified based on the number of new infections, tightness of medical capacity, improvement of preparedness of testing conditions. The declaration was lifted on May 25 in all remaining areas. See the Appendix A.4 for more details.

Using the variation in business suspension requests across industries and prefectures, we examine how much of the sales decline from March to April is the direct effect of the business suspension request and the indirect effect through the spontaneous change in people's behaviors. We restrict the samples to the business-to-consumer (B-to-C) service industries in this chapter, because the business suspension requests were limited to these industries.

## 3.2 Can Subsidies Soften the Economic Damage of Anti-Contagion Policies?


We next identify the effects of two subsidy schemes: the business continuation subsidy and short-time work compensation, exploiting Regression Discontinuity Design.

The business continuation subsidy grants up to JPY 1 million ( GLYPH<25> USD 10,000) to the self-employed and JPY 2 million ( GLYPH<25> USD 20,000) to small corporations, with limitations for the amount of the sales decline from the last year. The eligibility criteria are as follows: 1) at least one month of year-to-year sales in 2020 declined more than 50%; 2) the firm has continued business operations since before 2019; and 3) its capital is below JPY 1 billion or it employs fewer than 2,000 employees in the case of corporations. The sales decline must be proven based on the sales ledger, which is the basis for the tax on profits. Therefore, it is highly costly for a firm to misreport numbers. The application process is simple: the eligible firm only needs to access the specific website and submit the form, the copy of its sales ledger, and its identity certificate. The transfer is usually made within 2 weeks of the application directly to the firm's bank account. The subsidy scheme was announced on April 8 and applications opened on May 1. By the end of June, more than 2 million applicants had applied for and received subsidies totaling JPY 3 trillion, which is equivalent to about 3% of the total national budget in Japan in 2019. According to our survey data, the subjective probability of receiving this subsidy by the end of June 2020 was 37% on average.

The short-time work compensation reimbursed part of the payment of the leave allowance up to JPY 8,330 per day per employee. 2 This compensation was established in 1975 in response to exogenous and temporary recessions, such as oil shocks, under the premise that retaining the workforce was more efficient than reducing and reemploying workers for a temporary shock. Under normal economic conditions, to receive the subsidy, the firm has to show that it has maintained employment either by giving leave, training, or reallocating the workplace during a recession. To be eligible for short-time work compensation, firms had to show that their year-on-year monthly sales had dropped below -10% for 3 consecutive months, in principle. In March 2020, the sales decline criterion was relaxed to a 10% decline in a single month, as for the COVID-19-induced sales decline. On April 1, in response to the growing COVID-19 shocks, the sales decline criterion was further relaxed to a 5% decline in a single month in 2020. The application process was slightly complicated. The manager first has to agree to the leave plan with the relevant labor union. The firm then has to grant leave to employees, and only after paying the leave allowance, it can apply to the local

labor office for the subsidy. The average subjective probability of receiving the subsidy by the end of June 2020 was 18% in our data.

To estimate the impact of these subsidies, we adopt a regression discontinuity design using the cutoff in the eligibility criteria. To be eligible for the business continuation subsidy, sales in at least one month should declined more than 50% relative to the same month of the previous year. Therefore, we can consider a fuzzy regression discontinuity design for identifying the local average treatment effect of the perceived probability of receiving the business continuation subsidy. We use the minimum of year-on-year monthly sales during January-April 2020 as the running variable with the cutoff point at the value of -50%. The treatment variable is the subjective probability of receiving the business continuation subsidy from the central government by the end of June 2020. In Figure 1, we checked that the baseline employment, capital, and sales as of 2019 were all continuous at the threshold.

Table 6 panel (a) shows the estimation results. The bias is corrected and the standard errors are robust to heteroskedasticity according to Calonico et al. (2014). The results suggest that a manager's prospect for survival until the end of 2020 improves by 19.8 percentage points if the manager's prospect of receiving the subsidy increases from 0 to 100%. This is a large effect given that the average subjective probability of continuing business until the end of 2020 is 82%, while the subsidy did not affect the firm's quarterly investment and employment plans. As shown in Table 7, we also find that the exogenously increased perceived probability of receiving the business continuation subsidy decreases temporary business suspension, establishment or section closure, and the adoption of working from home. This may be because the business continuation subsidy enabled firms with liquidity to keep operating business amid the COVID19 crisis. On the contrary, the effects on the adoption of new information technology, expansion of online sales, selection of suppliers, and introduction of new product and service are insignificant. The message from these results is that the subsidy enabled small business managers to maintain the current business, but it was not large enough to change employment or to initiate new business.

One possible concern for this analysis is the manipulation of the reported sales or the actual sales by the managers. In the current context, the manipulation of the reported sales would be limited. First, it is hard for the managers to misreport the sales to the government because they have to show their sales lodger, which is the basis for the tax calculation. Second, the managers have no incentive to misreport to us. Thus, the only way for them to manipulate the number is to actually delay the receipt of payment. However, the manipulation of the actual sales would be also limited. First, there was little time to plan this, because the

announcement of the policy was at the end of March and we use data up to April. Second, delaying the receipt of cash should have been costly especially during the emergency state. As a robustness check, we also focused on the sample of business-to-consumer service sector, where the receipt of the money is likely to be when the transaction took place. Even though the statistical significance was lost, the sign and the magnitude of the effect of continuation subsidy was the same.

We similarly employ a regression discontinuity design to identify the effects of short-time work compensation. In this analysis, we focus on samples with at least one employee at the end of 2019, because only firms with employees can benefit from the subsidy. We use the April sales decline as the running variable with the cutoff point at the value of -5%. The treatment variable is the subjective probability of receiving the short-time work compensation from the central government by the end of June 2020. As shown in panel (b) of Table 6, we find no statistically significant effects on the firm's business performance. As shown in Table 8, we did not find any statistically significant effects on their behaviors. Even though the policy goal of this subsidy was to maintain employment, the effect on employment growth was not statistically significant, either.

The difference between the effect of the business continuation subsidy and short-time work compensation may be partly due to the lack of power. If we focus on the same sample, firms with positive employment at the end of 2019, the effect of business continuation subsidy becomes statistically insignificant, though the estimate is almost unchanged. Another reason may be that this subsidy was not attractive enough for small business managers targeted in this survey compared to the business continuation subsidy, for several reasons: there is additional paper work for the application and it is necessary to give leave to employees to receive the subsidy and to reimburse the leave allowance.
