## Conclusion


In this chapter, we examined family SES inequalities in non-cognitive skills among young Korean adolescents. Using nationally representative data for 6 th  graders and 9 th  graders between 2004 and 2014 and school-fixed effects models, we showed how internal motivation, self-esteem, sociability, perseverance, and the composite score from those four indicators differ across students with varying family SES. Additionally, we examined how family SES gaps vary by grade and test score, as well as across the quantiles of noncognitive skills.

Our analyses uncover several significant new pieces of evidence regarding educational inequality. To begin, we find robust family SES inequalities across all non-cognitive outcomes regardless of model or sample specification. However, we find no discernible systematic trends in the decade following 2004. In terms of the role of academic performance, we find that academic performance partially but considerably explains family SES differences in non-cognitive outcomes. More than half of total family SES gaps persist among students with identical test scores. Additionally, we find evidence that academic performance significantly moderates family SES inequality in non-cognitive skills. Family SES gaps are greatest at the lowest scores and at the highest scores, implying that both compensatory and reinforcing family advantages are at play. For 9 th  graders, we find strong

evidence that the correlation between non-cognitive skills and academic performance is unequally distributed across family SES groups and increases over time. Finally, we find that family SES disparities are greatest at the top of the non-cognitive score distribution, which is largely explained by the advantage of the top quartile SES families.

Perhaps, it is no surprise that family SES inequalities exist in non-cognitive skills. However, our analyses reveal several important findings that add new dimensions to our understanding of educational inequality.  First, the relationship between family SES and non-cognitive skills is not linear, and many nonlinear patterns are driven by families in the top SES quartile. Non-cognitive skill differences from the bottom SES quartile group, particularly internal motivation and perseverance, are greater for the top SES quartile group than for other lower SES quartile groups, indicating that the top SES group is distinct from other SES groups (Table 3). This is true not only on an average basis, but also for various quantiles (Table 4 and Figure 5). The relationship between non-cognitive skills and academic performance is significantly stronger for the top SES group than for the other three SES groups (Figure 4). It is only the top family SES group that is capable of successfully compensating for academic failure and enhancing academic strength through the use of their SES advantages (Figure 3). The top SES students are also the only group that demonstrates a significant increase in their family SES advantage at higher quantiles of non-cognitive skills (Table 4 and Figure 5).

All of these findings suggest that the non-cognitive inequality may exist primarily between wealthiest students and their less well-off or poorer peers, and that the inequality may be qualitative rather than quantitative. Moreover, they show unequivocally that non-

cognitive inequality among young Korean adolescents should be characterized as exclusive benefits for wealthy families rather than as disadvantages for students from poor families. We believe that this result elucidates a critical aspect of child development and education in early 21 st  century Korea.

Second, 6 th  graders and 9 th  graders differ remarkably in several critical aspects of non- cognitive inequalities. In general, family SES gaps are greater in 6 th  grade than in 9 th  grade. The advantage of the top family SES group in acquiring the top level of non-cognitive skills is also more salient for 6 th  graders than for 9 th  graders. Academic performance, on the other hand, matters more for 9 th  graders as a factor that mediates and moderates family SES gaps in non-cognitive skills, than for 6th graders. If we assume that the 6 th  graders and the 9 th graders in the AQS represent two distinct school stages of young adolescents, the differences between two grade samples suggest an important pattern of child development in Korea: Early adolescence does not accumulate (dis)advantages in non-cognitive skills. However, non-cognitive skills become more tightly linked to academic performance, and this increased coupling is particularly strong for students from wealthy families. What does this life course pattern suggest? As competitions for colleges admissions become more severe, academic performance may take precedence over everything else, including noncognitive skills, particularly those that are not directly related to academic activities. In addition, certain non-cognitive skills may be deliberately and strategically promoted as long as they benefit academic performance.

Lastly, the trends we identified in this study have significant implications for the current direction of school education and child development in Korea. We reported that family SES

disparities in non-cognitive skills did not increase (or decrease) in a systematic manner between the 2000s and the 2010s. Additionally, we documented an increasing degree of coupling between non-cognitive skills and academic performance in 9 th  grade. This finding implies that, at least with regard to non-cognitive skills, a looming concern is not about growing inequality per se , but about the possibility that educational diversity will erode. What parents and schools value in terms of child development and education can never be unidimensional. While academic performance is always a primary goal, but educational institutions also pursue other equally critical goals, such as vocational preparation, the cultivation of democratic citizenship, and the provision of healthy environments (Van de Werfhorst and Mijs 2010) . Non-cognitive skills are critical for achieving these nonacademic goals and should be valued and evaluated by parents and schools. Unfortunately, Korean education has already earned a reputation for emphasizing academic success excessively, promoting criticisms that it does not adequately nurture and evaluate noncognitive traits. Our result, however, suggests that the problem is escalating; non-cognitive skills are becoming more tightly coupled with on academic performance, losing their autonomous dimension in education. As a result, Korean education may be failing  to embrace the diversity of values it is expected to seek and promote.

## 1 INTRODUCTION


As a response to growing rates of COVID-19 infection, on March 16th 2020, the UK Prime Minister advised everyone in the UK against 'non-essential' travel and contact with others, as well as to work from home if possible and avoid visiting social venues. A few days later, all cafes, pubs, restaurants, theatres would close, and on March 26th full 'Lockdown Regulations' came into effect for the first time, effecting a dramatic change in people's daily lives. The aim of this study is to describe the changes in behaviour that followed through the COVID-19 pandemic period, with a special focus on those changes that persisted following the announcement of 'Freedom day' on 19th July 2021.

For most people, the COVID-19 pandemic turned everyday life upside down. Most noticeably, we spent more time at home, which led to other important changes - not only in terms of the activities we did, but also in when we did them. In many cases, the magnitude of these changes, occurring over a period of under two years, exceeds those observed over decades of historical change in time use behaviour [1]. However, relatively little research has analysed changes in our main daily activities across all the main key phases of pandemic restrictions. Even less has been based on real-time time use diary data, the recognised 'gold standard' for the collection of information on the use of time [2]. For obvious reasons, the focus of many data collection efforts and associated research during the pandemic was on the changes that occurred during periods of lockdown. Other time use diary-based studies have documented how, during UK lockdowns, people spent less time commuting and doing paid work, and more time sleeping and on housework and leisure - with a shift towards leisure at home to replace the reduction of leisure out of home [3; 4; 5]. These studies, however, did not enable the tracking of changes across all the key phases of pandemic restrictions, with the capacity to compare them directly both to a baseline wave, and to a wave conducted following the ending of almost all restrictions.

This documentation of what changed in our daily behaviour across the course of the pandemic is important in itself, not least because the pandemic is a global event that has been part of our lives now for over two years. However, it is also of key scientific and policy interest to examine which of the changes associated with the pandemic period as a whole are likely to persist. For much of the population the pandemic produced very particular life circumstances that either forced people, or gave them the opportunity, to try out new behaviours (such as exercising more, spending more time with children, and more time working from home). In this paper we address the question; how many of these new behaviours survived the lifting of most official regulations on the UK government-designated 'freedom day' of 21st July 2021?

The opportunity to compare behavioural responses to all main phases of pandemic restrictions, using time use diary data, with both a pre-pandemic survey and a post 'freedom day' survey collected using identical methodology is, to our knowledge, unique to the dataset that we analyse: the Centre for Time Use Research UK Time Use Survey 6-Wave Sequence across the COVID19 Pandemic [6]. Crucially, the final wave of this survey, conducted a month after the lifting of most restrictions, allows us to consider to what extent some of the new ways of doing things that developed during periods of restrictions may survive in the aftermath of the current pandemic. Using instantaneous subjective enjoyment information collected from the same diary data, we consider whether these surviving behaviours are associated with higher levels of enjoyment, which might both explain their persistence following 'freedom day' and lend support to the argument that they may be with us to stay.

Which of these new behaviours will 'stick' is not only an interesting question from a social science point of view, it is also one critical to many areas of policy, for example, in relation to teleworking, sleep, physical exercise, and travel behaviour. Some of the trends we document, such

as exercising more or changes in sleeping patterns, have potentially significant implications for our health. Others, such as teleworking, carry important policy implications for both transportation and urban policies. Several point to a potential reduction in the risk associated with future infectious respiratory diseases through a decline in activities done outside the home and in confined spaces in proximity to non-household members. This paper contributes to filling these gaps in the literature using a rich representative dataset collected across the key moments of pandemic restrictions in the UK to provide a comprehensive overview of behavioural changes and their persistence across a broad range of activities.


## 2 REVIEW OF TIME USE DATA AND LITERATURE


The outbreak of COVID-19 and its consequences generated a huge amount of literature across most academic fields, and behavioural change in relation to time use is no exception. However, rather little has been written based on representative time use diary evidence - which is the most reliable way of measuring how we use our time [2]. This is because there was a relative paucity of time diary evidence collected in real time across the pandemic, as most representative time use diary surveys take time to put into the field. This paper contributes to filling this gap in the literature by analysing an online time use diary survey collected in real time using the same market research panel and collection instrument in 2016, and then across 5 successive waves of the UK COVID-19 pandemic [6; 7].

Each wave of the survey, collected via an online diary (the 'Click and Drag Diary Instrument', or CaDDI for short), was designed to take place at a key moment of the pandemic restrictions the first, collected pre-pandemic in 2016, acts as a baseline. During the pandemic this was followed by three surveys coinciding with the three nation-wide lockdowns, interspersed with another wave during the summer of 2020 between lockdowns one and two, and a final wave in the summer of 2021 after almost all legal restrictions had been lifted. Each survey provides a representative snapshot of the behaviour of the UK population at that time; including their activities, their location, their social interactions, and their wellbeing. The CaDDI survey dataset has previously been used to evaluate the risk of exposure to infection by combining diary information on activity, location, and co-presence to estimate the infection risks associated with daily behaviours across the pandemic for different subgroups of the population [7; 8]. The current study is the first to use all six waves of the data to investigate broad changes in the UK population's use of time across the pandemic, and their persistence following 'freedom day'.

There were other time use diary data collected during the pandemic in the UK. The UK Office of National Statistics (ONS) collected online time use diaries based on a random probability panel of respondents to an existing social science dataset [4; 9]. Data was collected at four points in time, but publications to date relate only to the first three waves - during the first nation-wide lockdown, during the relaxation period between the first and second national lockdowns, and during the early period of relaxation following the third lockdown [4]. While the associated reports [4; 5; 10] provide some interesting comparative information, the sequence of surveys across the pandemic is less complete than that of the CaDDI surveys, missing both the second and third national lockdowns, and a baseline comparator wave collected using the same methodology. In addition, the last wave for which there are published reports available took place over 3 months before the lifting of most restrictions on 'freedom day'.

Also of relevance is the dataset collected by Lee and Tipoe [3], who deployed online time use diaries for a demographically diverse sample in the UK collected at two points: during the first and third lockdowns. The most interesting feature of this dataset is that it was longitudinal, and thus the authors can and do explore within-individual variability. The main weakness in relation

to the CaDDI data is that no data was collected other than for two periods of lockdown, while the 'pre-pandemic' comparison was based on respondents being asked to recall what their days were like in February 2020, 3 months before the data was collected, raising concerns in relation to both recall and normative bias. Findings from both the above surveys are referred to in our discussion of results below.

Outside of the UK, the most complete time use diary data collected during pandemic times is the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) [11]. The ATUS normally collects time use diaries all year round, and in 2020 they collected diaries as usual, other than for the period March-May. The data for 2020 are already available and the data from 2021 is promised soon. The ATUS is of exceptional quality and should prove a useful comparative resource for studying the effects of the pandemic on daily behaviour in the USA. Other time use diary data collection efforts of note during the pandemic outside the UK have taken place in Austria [12], Turkey [13], and a small non-representative (online self-selected) sample in Belgium [14].

In much of the research on the effects of the pandemic associated with the above time-use diary surveys, the focus has been on the impact that lockdowns had on the division of unpaid labour between men and women. All agree that men increased their share of unpaid work somewhat, reducing the unpaid work gap between men and women. The gender gap in housework and childcare during lockdowns has also been one of the most popular topics in the social science literature on the pandemic that is not based on time-use diary surveys. Most have reached similar conclusions, based on data for the UK [15; 16; 17], the US [18], and Australia [19; 20]. Less optimistic conclusions have been drawn using data from Hungay [21], Singapore [22], and in a multi-country meta-analysis study (in which there was, however, no comparison made with the pre-pandemic gender division of domestic labour [23]). Indeed, few analyses have been able to address changes in the full range of main activities across all the main phases of pandemic restrictions and beyond.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows: the next sections present the dataset and our methodological strategy. We then present results for general changes in time use patterns in the major activity categories of paid work, sleep, physical activity, travel, eating/drinking, housework, childcare, shopping and leisure. We show trends across the five pandemic periods in relation to the 2016 baseline data, and discuss to what extent the changes associated with lockdown conditions persisted into the final wave conducted following the lifting of most restrictions in July 2021. We conclude our analyses by investigating the subjective wellbeing (instantaneous enjoyment) associated with those activities that persisted beyond the lifting of restrictions.


## 3 DATA AND METHODS


The data were collected via a low-respondent-burden (12 to 15 min on average per day), online time-use diary instrument (the CaDDI) suitable for rapid deployment in real time in situations such as the COVID-19 pandemic, and described in detail elsewhere [6; 7]. Figure 1 shows an example of a completed diary day from the instrument. Respondents were volunteers from the Dynata market research panel, recruited separately for each wave and accepted up to the point that socio-demographic quota limits were reached. Quotas were set to represent the UK population in 2016 according to sex, age group, region and social grade. Each respondent completed diaries for between 1 and 3 days, yielding a total across the six waves of the survey of close to 7000 diary days. Table 1 of Appendix A of the Supplementary Materials shows how these diary days are distributed by wave.

The CaDDI dataset allows us to explore changes in time use during all the key phases of pandemic restrictions in the UK. Figure 2 summarises the dates of these phases and the restrictions in place at the time, in relation to the dates of the CaDDI survey waves.

The paper is organised in sections according to the different main activities analysed (see Table 2 of Appendix A for the detailed list of activities making up these main activities). The figures we include show time (mean minutes per day) spent on the activity, and, where relevant, participation rates and the time spent on the activity only by participants. For some activities, the timing of the activity across the day is also shown. We disaggregated all results by sex, age group, employment situation, type of day and parental status subgroups, but we only discuss subgroup results when different patterns were identified. To ensure that the changes we show are behavioural changes and not due to changes in the sociodemographic structure of the population or day-of-week collection effects, we ran OLS regression analyses to calculate predicted means and participation rates when controlling for sex, age-group, employment status, parental status and type of day (weekday or weekend). As expected, and with the exception of employment status, there were few sociodemographic changes over the relatively short period covered by the pandemic, so results based on predicted means coincide well with those based on raw means. Most of the figures and associated text show predicted means/participation odds and their associated confidence intervals and P-values.

For most analyses we include the entire sample, with two exceptions. When analysing paid work we use only individuals defining themselves as 'in work' (employed or self-employed), since the interest is in patterns of paid work among those in work. In that section we additionally control for occupational group in the regression analyses.Throughout the rest of the paper we use 'the employed' as short-hand for this group of employed and self-employed workers. The other exception is childcare, where we analyse only parents (fathers and mothers). Weights were used to ensure that the sample resembles the UK population in 2016 in terms of sex and age, and to ensure a balanced distribution of days of the week; information on the exact calculation of weights is found in the supplementary files accompanying the six-wave CaDDI data, which is available from the UK Data Archive, Study number 8741. For these analyses, we also calculated additional weights for the 'normal' waves of the survey (i.e. the pre-pandemic wave in 2016 and that in August 2021 following the lifting of restrictions). These correct for imbalances in the proportion of diaries collected on days reported by respondents as 'atypical', particularly holidays (higher in the August 6th wave than in the 1st wave, where data was collected at three points across the year to correct for seasonal effects).

The full results can be found in the appendices of the Supplementary Materials. Appendix B contains tables showing mean minutes per day (+ standard errors) across subgroups for each activity. Appendix C shows participation rates across subgroups and activities. Appendix D shows results of the regression analyses used to produce the predicted means, confidence intervals and P-values.

## 4 RESULTS



## 4.1 Paid work


As is already well documented, there was a significant reduction in employment rates during the pandemic as employees were laid off or furloughed, which contributed to considerable reductions in the overall average time spent in paid work at the population level. Our focus here, however, is on paid work times among the employed (including the comparison between those who remained working in the workplace and new teleworkers).

Figure 3a shows that the greatest change compared to the pre-pandemic period was a substantial reduction in overall paid work time for those still employed during the first national lockdown, with a decrease of 75 minutes from the pre-pandemic period ( P < . 001). The decrease applied across key subgroups of the employed population (men, women, parents and non-parents - not shown). This pattern resonates with findings from the previously-referred to UK longitudinal time use diary dataset, and from the longitudinal (although not time-use-diary based) COVID-19 Survey in Five National Longitudinal Cohort Studies [25]), in both of which a substantial reduction in paid work among the employed during lockdown was also found [3] [26]. However, by the final CaDDI survey wave in August 2021, time spent in paid work among the employed had returned to 2016 levels. This was true, again, for men, women, parents and non-parents.

What is also noticeable about Figure 3a is the big change in the location of work following the first lockdown (refer to the stacked components of the bars). Pre-pandemic, in 2016, most work happened in workplaces outside the home; approximately 80% working in the workplace, and just 20% in the home. However, this figure changed radically with the first lockdown, when the majority of paid work (for those who remained employed) transferred to the home. After first lockdown ended, time spent working away from home rose again, although by August 2021 the proportion remained at 50-50 - still far off the 80-20 split of the pre-pandemic period. The ONS also report this shift of paid work to the home during first lockdown, with a partial return shown in their final wave in March 2021 [4; 5].

One of the advantages of time use diary data is that it is also possible to investigate the diurnal rhythms and patterns of activities. Figure 3b shows changes in relation to participation in paid work across the day for the pre-pandemic, first and third lockdowns, and post 'freedom day' waves of the survey. Again, there was a change evident during first lockdown, when there was a

statistically significant reduction in paid work time done during the mornings (-43 minutes/day of paid work done by 1pm; P < . 001). By August 2021, however, the timing of paid work across the day had reverted to its pre-pandemic pattern (no statistically significant difference), so the change during first lockdown can probably be attributed to the suddenness and exceptional shock of that event. There was also no change observed between the pre-pandemic and 'post'-pandemic waves in either mean start or end times of paid work. There was, however, a difference in the prevalence of late work, measured by the proportion of diaries containing paid work recorded after 7 pm, which increased substantially with the first lockdown, ( P < . 001, see Figure 3c). This rise in the odds of working late was also identified in the other two time use diary datasets that collected data during the first lockdown in the UK [3; 27]. However, the odds of working late subsequently declined again, and by August 2021 they were only slightly higher than in pre-pandemic times, showing an average increase of 5.7 percentage points ( P = 036). We also examined whether more flexible patterns of . home working had led to a shift of paid work to the weekend. That also does not seem to be the case; even though during lockdown periods the odds of working on weekends declined somewhat, by the summer of 2021 the probability of doing paid work at weekends was equal to what it had been before the outbreak of the pandemic (not shown).

If there has been an important change in the location of paid work, but not in the amount or timing of that work, this suggests that, overall, teleworking has not led to a significant change in the amount or pattern of paid work being done. In the CaDDI data it is possible to distinguish those who were working in a workplace outside the home in 2016, but who were currently working from home ('new teleworkers') from those who were working in the workplace before and during the pandemic waves ('continuing commuters'). In fact, when we compare the predicted mean time spent in paid work by new teleworkers and those still commuting to workplaces across all waves, new teleworkers did 24 minutes/day more of paid work ( P = 012) than their counterparts who remained . working from the workplace (Figure 3d). There was a difference in the same direction recorded for the August 2021 wave (i.e. new teleworkers did more paid work than continuing commuters), but due to small sample numbers this difference was outside the boundary of statistical significance (20 mins/day, P = 381 - not shown). .


## 4.2 Sleep


Our data allows the examination not only average durations of sleep, but also daily sleeping patterns, both of which are well recognized to have important implications for health [28; 29]. Mean sleep duration for the adult population in the UK from the CaDDI data was approximately 8 hours and 30 minutes in 2016, before the pandemic started (see Figure 4a; refer to the 'daily average' line). This coincides exactly with the estimate from the last nationally-representative UK time use diary survey in 2014/15 [30]. It increased by 14 minutes with the first national lockdown ( P = 032), and . stayed at around that level until the third lockdown (January 2021), when it rose again to 9 hours per night, before returning to a level close to that of the first lockdown at the final wave in August 2021. At that point, mean sleep duration was still 11 minutes higher than in 2016, although this difference was just outside the boundaries of statistical significance ( P = 087). . An increase in sleep duration during the pandemic is consistent with the findings reported from the (fewer) ONS waves of data [4; 5; 10]. The decrease in time spent sleeping between the final (third) lockdown and the sixth, 'post'-pandemic, wave may be thought to have been related to a gradual return to pre-pandemic working rhythms over that period, involving more time spent commuting to workplaces again, and related earlier rising. However, it is worth highlighting that among the employed there was a clear and statistically significant increase in sleep duration of 22 minutes/night (P = .009) between the 2016 level and August 2021 (not shown). We also find an important difference

between men and women (Figure 4b). While for men there was a return to the 2016 average by the final wave (August 2021), this was not the case for women, whose average durations remained much higher, meaning that their average sleep duration had increased by 25 minutes compared to pre-pandemic times (significant at P = 003). .

In sum, the most important point in relation to pandemic effects on sleep durations is the upwards trend that began with the first lockdown. Figure 4c shows that, using a standard measure of sleep deprivation defined as diaries containing less than 7 hours of sleep time, the impact of the pandemic cut sleep deprivation almost in half, from 14 percent pre-pandemic to around 8 percent during the third lockdown ( P < . 001), before returning again to 2016 levels in August 2021.

The weekday-weekend gap in mean minutes of sleep also reduced in size, . both overall, but particularly during first lockdown, suggesting a reduction in 'social jetlag'. This measure of conflict between the internal clock and socially determined schedules is often proxied by sleep inequality between weekdays and weekend, and has been found to have very negative effects for health [29; 32]. While there was a 50-minute difference in predicted sleep duration between weekends and weekdays in 2016, that gap went down to just above 10 minutes during the first lockdown, and by the summer of 2021 it was still only 19 minutes ( P < . 001). The evidence on daily sleep rhythms is consistent, with a 30-minute backwards shift in sleep onset (going to sleep) between the first and last survey waves (Figure 4d). This backward shift applied both to weekdays and weekends (in pre-pandemic times, median time for going to bed was 23:00, compared to 22:30 by the summer of 2021). There was a corresponding forward shift in offset (waking up) evident particularly on weekends, where average waking time was approximately 30 minutes later (not shown).


## 4.3 Physical activity


Physical activity is another area that is strongly linked to health. Understanding changes across the pandemic is therefore important, especially when the protective measures taken during lockdowns, such as the closure of gyms and reduced outdoor socialising could have had the effect of making the population more sedentary. Here we analyse change in four categories of daily activities,

Physical activity as measured by all four of these activity categories rose with the pandemic, both in terms of increased participation, as well as increased time spent in these activities by participants. Of the four activities identified, this increase was primarily driven by increases in walking (see Figure 5a).

In 2016, before the pandemic started, the UK population spent approximately 40 minutes per day engaged in these four activities, while in August 2021 this had gone up to almost 60 minutes ( P < . 001). During first lockdown physical activity went up by 20 minutes ( P < . 001), and that increase was driven almost entirely by purposeful exercise. After first lockdown it declined somewhat but never returned to pre-pandemic levels. By the summer of 2021, following 'freedom day', levels of physical activity were still 17 minutes higher than in 2016. However, unlike during first lockdown, close to 40% of that increase came from active forms of travel (walking, jogging and cycling; up 6 minutes/day from the third lockdown, P = 014). The ONS data, too, shows an . increase in time devoted to exercise across the pandemic [5; 10].

Even more encouraging in terms of population health, this increase in physical activity derived at least partly from an increase in participation (Figure 5b). The greatest increase in participation happened with the first lockdown and, although it subsequently declined, it did not return to prepandemic levels. By the summer of 2021 participation in physical activity overall (blue line) had risen 5.5 percentage points from the pre-pandemic wave ( P = 014). Again, this trend was driven . by an increase in participation in exercise (yellow line) (there was no such increase in participation in active travel).

The increase in physical activity we identify happens for men and women alike, although the trend was somewhat more pronounced for men (not shown). There were also some differences across employment status. For the employed the increase derived from an increase in exercise that happened initially during first lockdown and persisted to the summer of 2021. This may be related to teleworking. Certainly, working from home permits taking more breaks, and it seems that participating in more exercise was one of those things that people did while working from home. In the diurnal rhythm analysis shown in Figure 5c note how the increase in exercise peaked during morning and afternoon (paid work) times; this effect is even more pronounced for those in paid employment only (not shown).


## 4.4 Travel


The reduction in travel time during the lockdown and the pandemic in general is one of the most well-documented time use facts to emerge from the pandemic literature. It shows up in research using time use diary evidence, as in [3; 4; 33], as well as in non-diary evidence [34]. The pandemic not only led to shorter travel times due to the imposition of furlough, teleworking and social distancing rules affecting social leisure, but also produced a substantial shift to safer (and more physically active) forms of travel (see section 4.3 above). In the CaDDI data, travel time in general observes a drawn-out u-shaped evolution across the waves of the survey (see Figure 6a). As expected, it declined substantially with the first national lockdown (-36 minutes/day, P < . 001), then recovered a little, but remained low through to the third lockdown. However, by the final wave of the survey, travel time had recovered substantially, to just 9 minutes lower than in 2016 ( P = 011). .

Because we have information not only on travel times but on travel mode, we are able to compare use of motorised transport with more physically active travel (refer to stacked bars of Figure 6a). Note that in the first, pre-pandemic, wave, walking and cycling as a mode of transport constituted just 27% of all travel, whereas by the final wave they made up 41% of the total.

## 4.8 Shopping; home and away


The main story in relation to shopping across the pandemic was change in the mode of shopping from visits to the shops to online shopping. Online shopping increased compared to conventional shopping from the first lockdown onwards. In 2016, 36% of all shopping time happened online, but with the first lockdown that figure increased to 62% (Figure 10a). By the summer of 2021 the proportion of shopping time done online remained as high as 51%. On the other hand, total shopping time (adding together visits to the shops and online shopping) stayed stable across the pandemic; it was only significantly lower during the first lockdown, when it declined by more than a third compared to the 2016 pre-pandemic survey wave ( P < . 001), perhaps before people made adjustments to online shopping. The size and statistical significance of these changes in conventional shopping time can be appreciated in Figure 10b, which compares shopping time in 2016 with both the first lockdown and August 2021. ## 5 DISCUSSION: THE ENJOYMENT OF 'STICKY' ACTIVITIES


At the start of the COVID-19 pandemic some activities were abruptly forbidden, and some others seemed just too risky to undertake. As a result, people experienced substantive changes in their daily routines in less than two years, while under normal circumstances, large-scale, populationwide, changes in time use behaviour tend to be slow [1; 2]. The restrictions and policy recommendations that were introduced to avoid infection limited our freedom in many ways, but they also presented an opportunity to do different things or do things differently. So that, when 'freedom day' came and people were allowed to resume their lives more or less normally, some things changed back, and some things didn't. We postulate that one key to which changes 'stuck', and which didn't, lies in the subjective enjoyment of the alternatives involved. Ceteris paribus, if a particular change in the way you normally do something brings you more enjoyment, you would choose to stick to it, whereas if it doesn't, you go back to the way things were before. The CaDDI diary contains an enjoyment field for just such a purpose, allowing us to assess the instantaneous enjoyment of the different episodes of time experienced throughout respondents' diary days. These estimates of the enjoyment of activities derived from CaDDI dataset correspond closely to the estimates from comparable time use surveys that have collected enjoyment data (see [38]).

Figures 12a-g compare the reported enjoyment levels of the competing alternatives for the

different activities. We find that, in almost all cases, the 'enjoyment explanation' is consistent with which activities persisted after the end of restrictions. For instance, exercise and leisure done outside the home are both found to be significantly more enjoyable than home-based leisure (Fig 12a). The imposition of lockdowns led to a reduction of leisure time spent outside the home (section 4.9), which was replaced by use of mass media, other home leisure and, to a lesser extent, by exercise (section 4.3). When lockdowns were over in August 2021, home leisure time declined to its previous level, while leisure done out of the home increased again (although still not reaching its 2016 level). Doing exercise, however, which rose significantly from the first lockdown, 'stuck', and remained at a higher level. We also described the substantial shift towards more physically active modes of travel (see section 4.4). At the time, this shift was probably the result of seeking safer travel modes, but the greater enjoyment they brought compared to travelling in a vehicle has doubtless a lot to do with why, to some extent, they 'stuck' following the end of restrictions. In support of this, cycling is by far the most enjoyed of the possible travel modes, but even walking is more enjoyable than any form of vehicle travel (Fig 12b). A similar situation occurs with online shopping, which is rated more enjoyable than conventional shopping (Fig 12c). The fact that online shopping remained higher than pre-pandemic times by the summer of 2021 (section 4.8) suggests that it may have conquered territory for good, and will remain one of those activities that is never likely to return to pre-pandemic levels.

Teleworking (section 4.1) is also likely to be (one of) the most important legacies of the pandemic, and, once again, reported levels of enjoyment provide a clue as to why, as well as providing one of our more surprising results. Although average enjoyment levels summed across all waves were higher when working from home than in the workplace (Figure 12d), disaggregating this result by sex shows that teleworking was in fact only statistically significantly more enjoyable for women (for men there was no significant difference in average enjoyment between the two options - see Figure 12e). So the various reasons that might make working from home more enjoyable (including avoiding the costs and hassle of commuting, working in more comfortable surroundings, and the ability to manage work and family life more flexibly) seem to have influence only for women. On the other hand, when those who became teleworkers during the pandemic ('new teleworkers') were asked in the questionnaire accompanying the online diary survey about their satisfaction with their new work arrangements, both women and men in this situation declared very high levels of satisfaction. In August 2021, 84% of male and 79% of female new teleworkers declared that they were 'satisfied' or 'very satisfied' with their new work arrangement (this percentage may be compared with the national UKTUS data from 2014/15, in which only 74% of all paid employees reported positive levels of satisfaction).

Last, but not least, another major change brought about by the pandemic that seemed to survive the ending of restrictions is the large increase in the proportion of leisure time that fathers spent in the company of their children (section 4.7). Figures 12f-g compare enjoyment of different leisure activities done with and without the copresence of children. For fathers it is clear that some leisure activities were more enjoyable done with children than without them (while others were about the same). This may help explain why fathers spent an increasing amount of leisure time with their children across the pandemic. In the case of mothers, in contrast, it seems as if the presence of children on the whole made their leisure activities less enjoyable. This issue requires more investigation and is beyond the scope of this paper, but one possible explanation may be to do with diminishing marginal returns to activities [38]. As indicated in section 4.7, the increase in the time fathers spent with their children came mainly from an increase in participation, that is, more fathers started to spend (some) time with their children. In the case of mothers, where participation levels were already high, it was more a matter of spending more time with their children, perhaps crossing the threshold over which they experienced diminishing marginal returns

## 6 CONCLUSIONS


The first lockdown was, with almost no exception, the moment of the pandemic during which the most dramatic changes in time use took place. Overall time spent in paid work fell by 75 minutes, travel time was cut in half, and leisure done outside of the home almost disappeared from the record, being replaced by leisure done at home. Total shopping time declined by more than a third (although online shopping stayed unchanged). Conversely, time spent sleeping rose by almost one quarter of an hour, and housework time increased by a similar amount. Meanwhile, levels of physical activity increased by a full 50%.

By the summer of 2021 some activities had completely returned to their 2016 levels, but others had not. Sleep durations were still 22 minutes higher among the employed and 25 minutes higher for women. Although daily mean time in childcare recorded as a primary or secondary activity remained the same as in 2016, time spent recorded as co-present with children doing other activities had risen by an hour and a half. While the total amount of leisure time did not change over the course of the surveys, parents were spending more of that leisure time together with their children (up by 50 minutes). Time spent in physical activity was also significantly higher than prepandemic, and contributing to this trend was an increase in participation - with all the advantages for population health that entails. The increase in physical activity was partly driven by an increase in purposeful exercise, but also contributing was a shift towards more active forms of travel. Online shopping time represented, by the summer of 2021, over 50% of total shopping time (compared to 36% in 2016). Housework at the population level basically remained unchanged between 2016 and the summer of 2021, but that apparent stability hides a very large increase in housework time for those identifying as homemakers (up by over one and a half hours). This is associated (unsurprisingly, given that housework is one of the least enjoyed of activities) with much lower reported levels of life satisfaction for homemakers in August 2021.

Which of the above changes are going to stay with us is hard to predict. One month following the relaxation of restrictions may be too early to assess the permanence of these changes. However, to date it is the best time use estimate that we have. One possible clue to what may 'stick' lies in the enjoyment of alternative, competing, activities. Our analyses suggest that, when the new alternative dictated by the pandemic was less enjoyable than the pre-pandemic option (for example, TV-watching or other in-home leisure time compared to leisure out of home), things returned moreor-less to 'normal' as soon as people were free to do so. However, when the new option was more enjoyable (the increase in exercise, the shift towards physically active travel modes, the expansion of online shopping, the growth in working from home - for women -, and, in the case of fathers, an increase in participation in leisure spent with children), the new activity 'stuck'.

To an audience not familiar with time use studies, the size of the pandemic-related changes described in this paper may seem rather small, for example, the 10-minute increase in exercise, or the 124-minute increase in the amount of time per day that fathers spend co-present with their children. To get an idea of their importance, we should compare them with long-term historical changes in time use behaviour. For instance, take exercise. Over the waves of our data, this increased by 50% between 2016 and August 2021 (21 minutes/day to 31 minutes/day). However, there was no change experienced in overall time spent in exercise at the population level over the last 20 years in either the UK or the US (countries for which we have reliable data over that period), which remained at around 20 mins/day. Something similar happens with the time fathers spent in the company of their children. During the pandemic, fathers increased the time spent with their children by over two hours per day. In the UK, in the fifteen years between 2000 and 2014/15 (the dates of the two last major UK time use surveys), that time increased by approximately 30 minutes, while in the US there was no change at all. These comparisons indicate the magnitude

and potential importance of some of the 'step-changes' in these activities that have taken place in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

In relation to policy, the overall increase in physical activity that we have identified is clearly good news for population health. Although studies based on activity tracking tend to show reduced sample mobility (measured by the number of steps) during lockdowns [40; 41], this is likely to be at least partly due to the fact that the opportunity for all activities outside the home that people normally engaged was severely restricted (for example, commuting, shopping, out-of-home leisure and sports). Interestingly, such studies also show very substantive differences in mobility - measured by the number of steps - across countries, depending on the type of lockdown imposed. For example, one study finds that in the UK the number of steps only declined by 8%, while in Spain it declined by 41% [40]. During the first lockdown in Spain, leaving the home to do exercise was not allowed, while in the UK it was. In combination with our findings, this has important policy implications. In places where exercising out of home was permitted, it seems likely that people used that as an excuse or reason to get out. Therefore, permitting leaving the home in order to exercise led people to exercise more - including those who were already exercising regularly, but also those new to exercise. And these changes 'stuck'. The switch to more active forms of transport is also of relevance, not only from the perspective of population health, but also from an environmental perspective, as it reduces dependency on motorized means of transportation (private cars and public transport). The increase in sleep durations among some groups resonates with earlier research on sleep in the UK since the early 1970s [42]. From a health policy perspective this is also encouraging, since there is growing body of epidemiological literature showing that insufficient sleep and the disruption of circadian rhythms are associated with several health problems, such as obesity [43] or type 2 diabetes [28].

The substantial movement towards working from home (which still accounted for 50% of all paid work time by the summer of 2021) has generated much policy debate, and some political controversy. This trend represents a major change in where the UK works, and yet, perhaps surprisingly, little seems to have changed in terms either in the total amount of time spent on paid work, or in the times of the day during which we do it. Average start and end times for paid work remained practically unchanged, and, overall, we were not more likely to work late in the evenings or on weekends than in pre-pandemic times. These results may serve to allay the fears of those who, on the one hand, believed that working from home would lead to significant skiving, and, on the other, those who feared that the result would be to 'turn the home into the office', effectively ending the separation between family and paid work time.

In addition to these changes, our results point to a forward-looking consideration for health policy in relation to infectious disease preparedness. Several of the alternative ways of doing things that we have identified as being both more enjoyable and having 'stuck' following the end of restrictions are also associated with a lower risk of exposure to infectious respiratory disease through being in confined spaces with strangers. This is the case for working from home instead of at a workplace, for physically active travel as opposed to the use of public transport, and for online shopping as opposed to going to the shops. The promotion and facilitation of these behaviours, at least in terms of providing greater flexibility for their increased take-up at times of crisis, may therefore assist in buffering the population against the spread of future infectious respiratory diseases.

Despite these relatively positive conclusions for certain areas of policy relating to population health and wellbeing, it would be difficult to argue that, overall, the impact of the pandemic on individual lives has been anything but negative, across multiple dimensions. The effects on individual subjective wellbeing of this global calamity are already well documented. How then can we explain the apparent paradox that such an incontestably negative event might have nevertheless

increased the potential for enjoyment of the population's daily lives by leading (or forcing) us to do things that we might not otherwise have done? And doing them, found that we enjoyed them more than how we have previously done things, giving us the incentive to keep them up? This glimmer of a silver lining will, of course, only continue to manifest itself if policy can be tailored to support the more enjoyable alternatives, which in many cases might also have health and environmental benefits, - i.e. government and employer commitments in support of teleworking where it is desired by employees; support for flexible working arrangements permitting a continued reduction in 'social jetlag'; and continuing commitment to the provision of facilities related to active travel and exercising.

## REFERENCES

## 1 Introduction


Economic, social and public health institutions rely on mortality forecasts to estimate, among other things, health care and disability costs, plan social security policies or estimate pension costs in an aging population. This entails a demand for robust and coherent forecasts for general mortality, but also for some components of mortality, such as causes of death. Oeppen (2008) listed two main advantages to disaggregating mortality forecast: 1) the risks are known for diverse factors, such as age, sex, cause of death etc. and 2) spending (on capital investment, preventive measures or palliative care) could be more efficient if the forecasts were known for diverse mortality components. Further, forecasts by cause of death can be very important when pricing life insurance products and can allow for a better specification of the morbidity process (Caselli, 1996).

Different approaches have been suggested to forecast mortality by cause of death. A common approach is to forecast age-specific death rates for each cause independently and then sum them to obtain an all-causes mortality forecast (Caselli and Vallin, 1996; Di Cesare and Murphy, 2009; Wilmoth, 1995). The Lee and Carter (1992) model has been used to forecast causes-of-death mortality independently, but also age-period-cohort models and Bayesian models (Di Cesare and Murphy, 2009; Foreman et al., 2017; Wilmoth, 1995). The use of expert and public health opinions to forecast disease-specific mortality and its impact on overall mortality has also been used (Canudas-Romo et al., 2016).

Forecasts by cause of death remain, however, less common, as they can be subject to many limitations. Di Cesare and Murphy (2009) found that commonly used forecasting models perform differently for different causes of death and that no model is the 'best' for all causes. Such forecasts also tend to produce more pessimistic forecasts compared to an all-causes forecast (Wilmoth, 1995) and, sometimes, unrealistic trends (Caselli and Vallin, 1996). Forecasts by cause of death are confronted with different methodological problems and have often failed to provide coherent forecasts between components (Caselli and Vallin, 1996; Wilmoth, 1995).

An important issue with mortality forecast by cause of death is that cause-specific trajectories are considered independent, but are in reality interconnected (Oeppen, 2008). Causes-specific mortality is traditionally analysed with a multiple-decrement life table. The main assumption behind multiple-decrement life tables is that cause-specific death rates are independent. How-

ever, cause-specific survival probabilities in the life table are not independent, as the proportion of individuals dying from one cause is affected by the mortality from other causes. This relates to competing risks issue between causes. Kjærgaard et al. (2019) state that 'Independent modelling and forecasting of cause-specific mortality is not only unattractive because it ignores dependence patterns amount the causes, but also because forecasts often fail to be coherent in the sense that cause-specific deaths must sum to the total number of deaths, which could lead to implausible results' (Kjærgaard et al., 2019, p.1352). Oeppen (2008) proposed an elegant solution to this problem. He suggested abandoning the conventional way to forecast death rates and use Compositional Data Analysis (CoDA), pioneered by Aitchison (1986), in a forecasting context. CoDA is a methodology developed to deal with compositional data, defined as positive values representing parts of a whole that sum to a constant (e.g. proportions).

Oeppen (2008) used the multiple-decrement life table deaths to forecast mortality by age and cause simultaneously. By treating life table deaths as compositional data and using a CoDA framework, the deaths are constrained to vary between 0 and the life table radix (e.g. 1 or 100,000), conditioning the relationship between components. Deaths are thus directly dependent on each other on the aggregate level, such that the decrease in deaths from one cause will lead to an increase in deaths from at least one other cause. The main advantage of this method is that it addresses the coherence problem between trends of components by using constrained variables which cannot vary independently, which is manifest in the variance-covariance structure of the components (Bergeron-Boucher et al., 2017; Kjærgaard et al., 2019; Oeppen, 2008).

The use of CoDa to forecast mortality has gained some attention in the recent years and has shown many advantages, including its consideration of a dependence structure between components. Oeppen (2008) also showed that the CoDA approach does not systematically lead to a more pessimistic forecast than an all-causes forecast. Bergeron-Boucher et al. (2017) have used a CoDA approach to forecast mortality by age in a multi-population context, showing that this approach leads to less bias forecast than the Lee-Carter approach, for all-causes mortality forecasts. Kjærgaard et al. (2019) suggested two new CoDA forecasting models, which improved the forecast accuracy of the Oeppen (2008) model.

Another important issue with forecasts by cause is that they can be inconsistent with allcauses forecasts. This issue relates to how changes in mortality by age and cause interact. Deaths have been simultaneously shifted towards older ages and more diverse causes of death

over time (Bergeron-Boucher et al., 2020). Hence, the question is how the different methods model this shift, which varies with the level of disaggregation and the number of categories. So how can we model and forecast the relation between age and cause in a coherent manner? Both Oeppen (2008) and Kjærgaard et al. (2019) used multiple-decrement life table to forecast the age-and-cause-of-death distribution. So, deaths can be shifted from one age-cause category to another. However, some authors have forecast age-specific causes-of-death distributions using CoDA techniques and linked it to an all-causes forecast by age (Piveteau and Tomas, 2018). The latter approach assumes dependence between causes within a given age-group but independence between causes-of-death distribution between age groups. Such a simplification could be corrected by using coherent forecast models, generally used for multi-population forecasts. Coherent models have been previously used to forecast mortality by cause to consider inter-cause coherences (Kjærgaard et al., 2019; Lyu et al., 2020).

Based on the existing literature we find that some questions still remain unanswered. How the age and cause dimensions interact when forecasting has been overlooked. Should they be forecast simultaneously or separately? How do different approaches affect the forecast? To our knowledge, no study has evaluated how forecasting mortality by age and cause simultaneously or as two separate steps can affect the forecasts. To answer these questions, this study evaluates different CoDA approaches to forecast by age and cause of death and suggests new ones.


## 2 Data


Death counts by cause of death were extracted from the WHO mortality database (WHO, 2021). Multiple-decrement life tables were constructed combining information from the Human Mortality Database (HMD) life tables (HMD, 2021) and the WHO causes of death distributions. The mortality of both females and males was forecast.

The WHO data are provided for the ages 0 to 4 by single-year of age and then by 5-year age groups until age 95+. As most deaths today occur above age 85 in low-mortality countries, we ungrouped the data to include data up to age 110+, using the Penalized Composite Link Model (PCLM) (Rizzi et al., 2015) to avoid an artificial compression in the open age-group when forecasting (Bergeron-Boucher et al., 2017). The PCLM also smooths the younger age groups, avoiding random fluctuations due to low death count. We kept the 5-year age grouping.

We selected seven countries with long time-series, i.e. at least 20 years of causes-of-death data classified under ICD-10: Australia (1998-2018), Denmark (1994-2018), Germany (1998- 2017), Japan (1995-2018), Netherlands (1996-2018), Sweden (1997-2018) and Switzerland (1995- 2018).

Causes of death were grouped into eight broad groups: Infectious and parasitic diseases; neoplasms; mental and behavioural disorders and diseases of the nervous system; diseases of the circulatory system; diseases of the respiratory system; diseases of the digestive system; external causes and others (Table 1). This grouping has three advantages: Large groups are less affected by natural fluctuations, they are the main causes of death in most of the selected countries, and they are in line with previous forecast studies.

## 3.4 Forecasting κ t

The parameters κ t in independent models and K t in coherent models are forecast with the ARIMA model with first-order differentiation having the best AIC value, using the auto.arima function in the R package forecast (Hyndman et al., 2020). As shown in Section 4.1, κ t is often, but not always, linear. In the coherent models, κ t in the deviation factor is forecast with a stationary ARMA model.

A linear forecast can lead to one cause with faster increase to dominate the forecast. We thus also use a Holt linear damped trend (labelled HD) when forecasting the CDD, so that the

causes of death distribution eventually levels off. The latter model is used to limit the transfer of deaths towards one cause. The HD forecast is used in step 2 of approach A2 and step 1 of approach A3.


## 3.5 Forecast evaluation


To evaluate the forecast accuracy, we used an out-of-sample approach based on six different forecast horizons. Mortality of the last 5 to 10 years observed was forecast, based on data outside the forecast window. For example, we forecast mortality in Japan starting from year 2009 to 2014 (jump-off year) with the last year of the forecast being 2018. This means that for the first forecast, mortality was forecast from 2009 to 2018, based on data from 1995 to 2008. For the last forecast, mortality was forecast from 2014 to 2018, based on data from 1995 to 2013. We apply this rolling window approch to avoid the evaluation to be dependant on specific years and forecast horizons. Due to differences in years with available data by country, the years of evaluation and fitting period vary across countries.

The model accurary is assessed based on the age-and-causes-of-death distribution. We used the Aitchison distance to evaluate the accuracy of the forecasts of these distributions. In addition, the models were evaluated based on their accuracy in predicting life expectancy at birth, using the mean absolute error.

In total, 11 models and variants are compared. Differences in accuracy might sometimes be small between some models. We used a model confidence set (MCS) procedure, suggested by Hansen et al. (2011), to test if the difference in a loss function (Aitchison distance or mean absolute error) is significant. Based on the out-of-sample performance of the models, the MCS procedure constructs a set of preferred models, called superior set models (SSM), comprising models with predictive abilities that are not significantly different from one another, based on t-statistics, for a 95% confidence level (Bernardi and Catania, 2015; Hansen et al., 2011).
