To simplify the analysis, we only model and forecast trends for Sweden and Spain, as they have among the biggest sample sizes of the six options reducing uncertainty.

The fitting period is 2004 to 2019. We would need the survey data of 2021 to fit the MSLT model for 2020, which was not available at the time the study was done. We could use 2020 to fit the Sullivan approach. But, for a matter of comparison with the MSLT model, we used the same fitting period with both models. In addition, there was a decline in life expectancy in 2020 due to the pandemic (Aburto et al., 2022). Modelling and forecasting during pandemic require additional assumptions - e.g. how long will Covid affect mortality? or how does Covid affect health in the short and long run?

As ∑ X x =1 ∑ S s =1 d s tx = 1, this indicator is a composition. Compositional data are vectors of relative information constrained to sum to a constant, e.g. proportions or percentages. ## 3.3 Confidence and prediction intervals


We assumed that the mortality estimates are accurate. Confidence intervals around estimates of life expectancy are generally small (Villavicencio et al., 2021), especially when they are based on death registries and population-wide estimation. The uncertainty in the forecast comes from

- (1) the estimation of the number of years lived with and without disability and (2) extrapolating the trends with equations (4) and (6).

We calculated confidence intervals around the estimate of healthy life expectancy using bootstrapping. We resampled with replacement n times the distribution of health-state by age and year from the SILC survey. Life expectancy and healthy life expectancy are then calculated for each simulation. The 95% confidence intervals are estimated from the 2.5% and 97.5% percentiles of the n simulations.

For each simulation previously described, a new time index is found and extrapolated using the selected time series model. For each κ t estimate, prediction intervals are calculated using simulations with resampled errors (bootstrap) m times. The 95% predictions intervals are estimated from the 2.5% and 97.5% percentiles of the n × m simulations.

For the multistate approach, mortality is forecast separately. We also include uncertainty from this forecast using bootstrapping.

## 4.2 CoDAM parameters and forecast


Figure 4 shows the parameters of the CoDAM model for Swedish and Spanish females. The parameters have a similar interpretation to that of the CoDAS model. The parameter κ t is a time-index indicating how the the transition matrix has been changing over time. For Spanish females, the index increased over time. The β j parameter indicates the state to which individuals have been transiting over time, in relative terms. When κ t is increasing, the shift occurs from states with negative values towards states with positive values. In Spain, individuals transit increasingly towards mild limitations and no limitations and less and less towards severe limitations, suggesting a dynamic equilibrium scenario. For Sweden, individuals transfer increasingly towards no limitation and less and less towards the other states, suggesting a compression of morbidity. The parameter γ x i ∗ indicates how fast each age and origin state has been experiencing the common transfer process towards state j defined by κ β t j . For example, Spanish females aged 50 with an origin state without limitations transited less and less towards severely limited over time and more and more towards mildly limited or remained without limitations. A similar process was observed for individuals of the same age with an origin state with mild limitations, but to a lesser extent. On the other hand, Spanish females aged 80+ with severe limitations increasingly remained as severely limited over time.

## 5 Discussion


We introduced two forecast models based on the two most common procedures to estimate healthy life expectancy: Sullivan and MSLT. One of the main advantages of the proposed models is that coherence between health state and mortality is accounted for. Both introduced forecast models show that mortality and health can be forecast simultaneously and coherently. In addition, the CoDAM model can include all possible transitions. Other methods based on the MSLT do not allow for recovery, i.e. transition from poor health to good health (Majer et al., 2013). No such assumption is needed with the CoDAM model, while still keeping the model relatively simple.

These models are the first step towards simple and coherent forecasts of the number of years lived with and without limitations. There is space for improvement in the models. For example, the model could be adjusted to include smoking related mortality or some other covariates; and impose age and state weights. The CoDAM model assumes coherence across age and state of origin. But, if a different process occurs across age or state of origin, the model can be applied to each age or origin independently. Similar methods can be used to model and forecast an array of the transition probabilities by year, state of destination and age, for each state of origin ( q i t,j,x ); or by year, state of destination and state of origin, for each age ( q x t,j,i ). The former assumes some coherence in the change in the transition rates between ages, while the latter assumes coherence between states of origin. This approach would increase the complexity of the method, but might provide more accurate estimation. Similarly, a separate time trend could be estimated for each age or each state for the CoDAS model (see Kjærgaard et al. (2019)). It was outside the scope of the study to test all possible variants and extensions of the models.

The data on health states is taken from surveys with usually small sample sizes. There is then more uncertainty around the estimates and forecasts of healthy life expectancy, compared with that of the total life expectancy. This limitation applies also to EU-SILC. Furthermore, the scope of EU-SILC is to collect information on families' economic conditions. Health data collection is only a minor part of the survey, making the quality of such information more questionable (Sajani et al., 2014).

To test the accuracy of the models, we did an out-of-sample test over a short forecast horizon of 5 years. The time series available on health state are generally short. In our case, we had 16 years of observation. As the general rule of thumb is to have as long of a fitting period as the forecast horizon, we could not test the model for a long forecast horizon. not be recommended to forecast healthy life expectancy far into the future. Studies have shown that the longer the fitting period, the more robust and accurate the forecast (Bergeron-Boucher et al., 2020; Janssen and Kunst, 2007).

There are differences in the estimation and forecast of healthy life expectancy whether we used the Sullivan-CoDAS or the MSLT-CoDAM models. The MSLT model is generally seen as the best one in estimating the number of years lived in good or poor health, as it can model the shift from one health-state to another over time, while the Sullivan method only accounts for the health prevalence at a given time. However, the MSLT model is more data demanding and the limitation of the Sullivan method is not critical in situations where changes in population health are smooth and relatively regular over the longer term. This makes the Sullivan method acceptable for monitoring such trends in health expectancies (Mathers and Robine, 1997; Murakami et al., 2018). Our results are in line with this argument. We found that the differences between models are not always significant. In fact, the differences were not significant in most cases. Both the Sullivan and MSLT models showed similar trends over time (observed and forecast): they both show a compression of morbidity in Sweden and a dynamic equilibrium in Spain. We were unable to determine which forecast model, the CoDAS or CoDAM, was the most accurate in forecasting the different health indicators. Comparing more countries and using different fitting periods and forecast horizons might help assessing in more detail the accuracy of the forecast. But, more data is required. Based on our results, we can draw similar conclusions using both models. If longitudinal data is not available to calculate the MSLT estimates, the Sullivan and CoDAS are a reasonable alternative from which we can expect similar trends and general conclusions. But we cannot conclude whether these results are generalizable to other countries or time-periods.

Our results fuel the debate on expansion or compression of morbidity. For Sweden we observe a reduction of the number of years lived with mild and severe limitations. This trend, arguing in favour of compression of morbidity, has been observed by other researchers considering individuals at age 65 (Lagergren et al., 2017) but not when analyzing oldest-old only (Sundberg et al., 2016). In general, results vary substantially when considering different age-groups, surveys and health indicators, even within the same country (Jagger and Kingston, 2020). For Spain, our results support the dynamic equilibrium theory, as opposed to the expansion scenario discussed by other scholars for relatively recent years (Sol´-Aur´ 2014). e o This difference might be explained by both the indicator used for measuring disability-free life expectancy and the analysis of different level of severity of the limitations. In fact, our results suggest a (relative) increase in the number of years lived with mild limitations that would be included in the number of years spent with disability if we did not consider the severity of the limitations.

Only a few models were developed to forecast healthy life expectancy. The introduced models are then a welcome addition to the literature. Unlike previously developed models, the suggested approach can forecast simultaneously health and mortality in a coherent manner, while accounting for changes in prevalence and transition probabilities over time. These models solved some of the problems encountered when forecasting HLE and can be further developed.

## INTRODUCTION


There is growing evidence that direct interactions with the police can shape both situationspecific and global perceptions of procedural justice and legitimacy (Mazerolle, Antrobus, et al., 2013; Mazerolle, Bennett, et al., 2013; Reisig et al., 2018). At the same time, exposure to policing through media and other sources shows that negative events can also influence public trust  in  police  and  legitimacy  (Choi,  2021;  Graziano,  2019;  Intravia  et  al.,  2018;  Nägel  & Lutter, 2021; Reny & Newman, 2021). In a nationally representative sample of people aged 16 and over in the United States, 24% reported having reported having had personal contact with the police in the past 12 months (Harrell & Davis, 2020). Given that the majority do not have personal contact with the police, these other 'experiences' should also play a role in conveying information about the police and shaping citizens' attitudes. Individuals are therefore likely receiving numerous different signals about police performance through multiple channels in daily life. Evaluating how and when these different experiences influence attitudes is important to understanding the role of the police in shaping public attitudes in the short- and long term over the life course (Fine et al., 2022; McLean et al., 2019).

However,  survey  research  typically  measures  contact  and  experiences  with  police cross-sectionally and retrospectively (e.g., in the past 6 months to 2 years, Jackson et al., 2010; Kääriäinen, 2008). These measures also tend to be unidimensional, that is, they aim to measure one type of contact with the police, most often personal or vicarious interactions with a police officer (Augustyn, 2016). For example, the European Social Survey asks whether respondents have been approached, stopped, or contacted by police in the last 2 years (Jackson et al., 2010). While others have employed survey items with a greater variety of types of contact such as voluntary/involuntary or violent contact (Piccirillo et al., 2021), these retrospective measures are still limited in capturing the variety of experiences that may occur in daily life, and can be affected by recall biases wherein respondents forget incidents or characteristics of incidents, report  incidents  outside  the  timeline  boundaries,  or  misinterpret  the  scope  of  the  question (Lynch & Addington, 2010).

The current study explores the application of smartphone-based experience sampling techniques to measure experiences close to the moment that they occur. The term 'experiences' is used here to refer to a broad variety of encounters, either personally or vicariously through family, friends, media, or observations. We take this broader approach in order to explore the different ways in which people may encounter the police in day-to-day life. Similar to time use surveys,  experience  sampling  techniques  prompt  respondents  to  complete  short  surveys  on

experiences and attitudes, allowing for more accurate self-reported measurement of activities in context (Beal, 2015; Shiffman et al., 2008; van Berkel et al., 2018). The use of experience sampling techniques is growing in social science, and to some extent in criminological research (Borah  et  al.,  2021;  Del  Toro  et  al.,  2019;  Engström  &  Kronkvist,  2021),  however  the application of these techniques is still new to policing research. The current study uses results from a pilot study to explore the feasibility of using experience sampling techniques to measure daily experiences with the police and their relationship with perceptions of police.


## Experience sampling in criminology


Experience  sampling,  also  known  as  ecological  momentary  assessment,  aims  to  collect information  about  events,  attitudes,  and  behaviors  within  one's  natural  environment  (Beal, 2015; Borah et al., 2021; Shiffman et al., 2008). This 'momentary' approach can overcome limitations of retrospective self-reported surveys because it arguably improves validity and reduces  the  potential  for  recall  biases  (Beal,  2015;  Csikszentmihalyi  &  Larson,  2014;  van Berkel et al., 2018). Retrospective measures of any phenomena that occur in daily life, such as media consumption, experiences of strain, or feelings of safety, cannot adequately capture the situational characteristics and momentary thoughts and feelings experienced in relation to the event (Schwarz, 2011). There is evidence to suggest that retrospectively measured experiences do  not  correspond  well  to  momentary  assessments,  as,  on  the  one  hand,  momentary assessments can capture phenomena that are underreported on retrospective reports (Gratch et al., 2021), while on the other hand, retrospective assessments can overestimate the frequency or  severity  of  events  (Naab  et  al.,  2019;  Schuler  et  al.,  2021).  In  addition,  retrospective assessments rely on the skill and memory of the participant to accurately recall the incident, the nature of the incident, and how he or she felt about that incident in that moment (Kronkvist & Engström, 2020). In relation to experiences with the police, individuals must remember the encounter, the reason for the encounter, and how they felt the police treated them at the time. Often  these  retrospective  assessments  are  more  likely  to  reflect  the  respondent's  personal beliefs  rather  than  the  actual  experience  (Schwarz,  2011).  Taken  together,  retrospective measures  of  experiences  with  the  police  are  limited  in  adequately  capturing  the  dynamic, situational  processes,  evaluations,  and  emotions  that  are  relevant  to  understanding  how experiences shape attitudes and behaviors (Kronkvist & Engström, 2020). Since these are the precise processes that are of interest to the study of police interactions, procedural justice, and legitimacy, it is important to explore alternative methodological techniques that can measure experiences and attitudes in daily life.

Experience  sampling  typically  uses  short,  repeated  questionnaires  that  respondents complete  using  an  app  via  their  own  smartphone  (Shiffman  et  al.,  2008).  The  design  and measurement of experiences can vary, with some studies prompting respondents to complete one or more surveys each day, and others allowing respondents to report experiences as they occur. In psychology, experience sampling techniques are increasingly attractive in capturing short-term changes in behaviors, as well as more immediate emotional and cognitive processes (Burr et al., 2021; Hofmann et al., 2014; Myin-Germeys et al., 2018). Reviews of experience sampling using smartphones have shown that this approach is feasible, with relatively high response rates and valid measurements (Beal, 2015; Gabriel et al., 2019; Shiffman et al., 2008; van Berkel et al., 2018). One review reported an average response rate of 69.6% among a sample  of  42  papers  that  reported  response  rates  (van  Berkel  et  al.,  2018).  Nevertheless, participant  recruitment,  burden,  and  retention  are  key  challenges  to  implementing  and collecting experience sampling data (Eisele et al., 2022; Gabriel et al., 2019; van Berkel & Kostakos, 2021). Although smartphones permeate society, requiring a smartphone and app can be significant burdens for some participants that may affect selection into this type of study (Dejonckheere & Erbas, 2021; Hofmann & Patel, 2015). In addition, repeat surveys may lead to  respondent  fatigue  and/or  careless  responding  (Eisele  et  al.,  2022).  Researchers  try  to minimize these issues by providing intrinsic motivations (e.g. contribute to knowledge) and extrinsic  (e.g.  monetary  compensation)  incentives  to  participate  (van  Berkel  &  Kostakos, 2021). A review of compensation in surveys suggests that compensation based on responses is one of the more effective tools to ensuring retention (van Berkel et al., 2018).

While the use of experience sampling techniques is growing in other fields (Wrzus & Neubauer, 2022), its use in criminology, and particularly policing studies, is still relatively rare (Borah et al., 2021; Del Toro et al., 2019; Goldner et al., 2011; Kronkvist & Engström, 2020; Solymosi et al., 2021). Research on aggression using experience sampling techniques show that perceived rejection and anger were associated with momentary aggression (Borah et al., 2021; Colasante et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2022). Solymosi et al. ( 2015) explored the use of experience  sampling  to  measure  fear  of  crime  based  on  geographical  locations  in  order  to describe how fear varied within and across physical environments. Similarly, Engström and Kronkvist  (2021)  found  that  features  of  the  immediate  environment  were  associated  with experiencing fear of crime in daily life.

To our knowledge, the only study has used experience sampling to measure contact with  police  and  its  impact  on  momentary  outcomes  among  a  sample  of  adolescents  in  the United States (Del Toro et al., 2019). Two waves of data collection took place in 2019 and

2020, which amounted to 35 days total. Each day, students were asked whether they had been stopped by the police or not, and to rate to what extent the police were intrusive during this stop.  Students  were  also  asked  about  their  feelings  of  disengagement  with  school  and psychological  distress.  A  total  of  387  students  participated,  wherein  51%  (n=197)  did  not complete at least 14 diaries. Across the study time period (35 days), 9% of students reported being stopped at least once, with 66 police stops reported overall. Using hybrid (betweenwithin) regression models, the authors found that police stops were associated with greater psychological stress and school disengagement the next day. These results suggest that there were  a  non-negligible  amount  of  interactions  in  a  small  window  of  time,  and  that  these interactions can shape individual attitudes and well-being even in the short term.


## The relationship between experiences and attitudes towards the police


A substantial body of research suggests that direct and vicarious interactions with the police can influence how individuals perceive and interact with the police (Alberton & Gorey, 2018; Lee et al., 2019; Mazerolle, Bennett, et al., 2013; Walters & Bolger, 2019). Procedural justice theory proposes that individuals develop attitudes towards the police based on how police treat individuals as well as the outcome of the encounter (Tyler & Huo, 2002). More specifically, procedural justice is based on the quality of treatment, determined by the extent to which an officer treats people with dignity and respect and acts with trustworthy motives, and the quality of decision-making, determined by officer neutrality and opportunities for voice (Solomon, 2019). Each interaction or experience has the potential to be a 'teachable moment' in which individuals  receive  signals  about  police  behavior  and  performance,  and  update  their  views accordingly (Tyler et al., 2014). Throughout the life course, fair and respectful experiences with the police are expected to shape more global perceptions of procedural justice, trust, and legitimacy (McLean et al., 2019).

While there is empirical evidence supporting the association between experiences and attitudes, reviews have pointed out that the majority of research tends to be cross-sectional (Donner et al., 2015; Walters & Bolger, 2019; Worden & McLean, 2017). These studies also tend to focus on personal contact with the police, whereas research on media effects suggests that  these  'indirect'  experiences  can  also  shape  individual  feelings  of  trust  and  legitimacy (Graziano, 2019; Graziano et al., 2010). In particular, research on vicarious exposure to media about  police  violence  and  misconduct  shows  that  these  experiences  can  clearly  serve  as 'teachable moments' that can influence public perceptions of trust in police (Kochel, 2019; Nägel & Nivette, 2022; Nix & Pickett, 2017; Pryce & Gainey, 2022; Reny & Newman, 2021).

In addition, there is some question as to what extent effects of experiences on attitudes are 'asymmetrical,'  that  is,  whether  negative  experiences  have  a  stronger  effect  compared  to positive experiences (Skogan, 2006). While there is some evidence to support asymmetry in the  effects  of  both  personal  and  media  experiences  (Choi,  2021;  Li  et  al.,  2016;  Solomon, 2019), the strength and consistency of asymmetry is mixed (Bradford et al., 2009; Maguire et al., 2017).


## The context and current study


In  the  Netherlands,  local  police  ('basis  teams')  are  organized  under  a  centralized  national police organization, the Dutch National Police. Confidence in the Dutch police is relatively high:  according  to  the  World  Values  Survey,  72.4%  of  people  in  2022  reported  that  they personally have confidence in the police (i.e., responded with 'a great deal' or 'quite a lot' instead of  'Not very much', or 'None at all' when being asked about their confidence in the Dutch  police. This  level  of  confidence  is  relatively  in  line  with  other  Northern  European countries.  The contexts in which individuals may encounter police in the Netherlands may 1 vary across geographical space, as many smaller police stations have been closed in recent years, meaning rural residents may be less likely to encounter police in daily life (Schaap, 2018). The Dutch police offer a number of ways in which to report a crime, including through the internet or social media. According to Schaap (2018), police encourage citizens to first use the internet to report crimes, meaning that personal interactions are less prioritized and less likely to occur among the general public. In addition, the Dutch police rely on a combination of traffic stops, cameras, and 'speed trajectory controls' to enforce traffic laws.  In the 2010s, 2 the priorities shifted from enforcing traffic rules to the detection and interception of criminal behavior  in  traffic,  meaning  that  traffic  and  safety  enforcement  was  substantially  reduced (Goldenbeld et al., 2019). As a result, while 'random' traffic stops still may occur, interactions with police among the general public in this context are less likely compared to countries with higher police traffic enforcement such as the United States (Pierson et al., 2020). Overall, we can expect that the number of personal interactions reported will be low, and that respondents will more likely report 'vicarious' experiences via media and other sources. Although personal

interactions may be infrequent, it is still important to measure and understand to what extent individuals encounter police in different ways in daily life.

The current  study  aims  to  explore  the  application  of  experience  sampling  to  police procedural justice research using data from a pilot study of daily experiences with the police among young people in the Netherlands. Specifically, this paper has three goals: the first goal is to describe and evaluate the feasibility of using experience sampling techniques to measure daily  experiences  and  attitudes.  Here  we  will  describe  the  implementation,  as  well  as characteristics associated with participation and attrition during the study. Second, this paper will describe the experiences measured and explore the variation in attitudes during the study period. Finally, we will provide a preliminary analysis exploring the relationship between the quality of treatment observed in experiences and attitudes towards the police. Given the nature of the pilot convenience sample, we do not aim to draw generalizations from the analyses. Instead,  we  present  the  pilot  data  and  analyses  as  a  starting  point  for  discussion  of  the measurement of experiences and attitudes in policing research, and to what extent experience sampling  techniques  may  complement  and  address  some  of  the  limitations  of  existing approaches.


## METHODS


Data for the current study were collected between April and May 2022 from young people (aged  18-30)  living  in  the  Netherlands.  The  survey  instruments  were  developed  and implemented by the authors using YourResearch, which is a research platform that recruits and carries  out  a  range  of  clinical,  tracking,  and  diary  studies.  Potential  participants  from  the YourResearch panel were sent an invitation to participate with a link to the study website, which  provided  further  information  about  the  study,  compensation,  and  informed  consent. Participants provided digital consent prior to enrolling in the study and completing the baseline survey.

The study consisted of two parts. First, participants completed a baseline questionnaire (~25-30 minutes) which measured demographic characteristics, social attitudes, and previous experiences with the police. The second part consisted of short (~5 minute) daily surveys on well-being,  attitudes  towards  the  police,  and  experiences  they  have  had  since  the  previous (daily) survey. Participants could list up to five experiences with different authorities, including

the police, BOAs,  courts, the municipality, or 'other'. If respondents reported an experience 3 with an authority, they were prompted with follow-up questions about the type of experience, perceptions of authority behavior during the experience, emotional reactions to the experience, and overall satisfaction with the authority. The daily questionnaires began the day following the completion of the baseline questionnaire, and lasted for 21 days. Respondents had 24 hours (i.e.,  from  midnight  to  midnight)  on  the  day  to  complete  the  questionnaire,  and  were  not allowed to retrospectively complete daily questionnaires so as to ensure that responses were captured as close as possible to the time that the event occurred (see Appendix A for a list of all item wordings). Participants were compensated €10 (~10 USD) in gift card vouchers for completing the baseline questionnaire and €30 in vouchers for completing at least 80% of the daily questionnaires. All questions were fielded in Dutch. The study received ethical approval from  the  Ethics  Committee  of  the  Faculty  of  Social  and  Behavioural  Science  at  Utrecht University.

The target sample size for the pilot study was around 150 participants. In the three days that registration was open, 322 people registered for the study. Of the 322 registrations, 209 participants at least partially completed the baseline questionnaire and 206 fully completed the questionnaire.  Out  of  the  209  participants  who  fully  or  partially  completed  the  baseline questionnaire, 6% did not complete any daily questionnaires, 27% completed 10 or fewer daily questionnaires, 37% completed 15-20 daily questionnaires, and 29% completed all the daily questionnaires.  Overall,  a  total  of  3042  daily  questionnaires  have  been  completed  out  of  a possible 4389 (69%), which is in line with the average response rate from previous reviews of experience sampling studies (van Berkel et al., 2018).


## Measures


This section is divided into two parts. The first part provides information on the measures used to evaluate the characteristics of participation and attrition within the study. The second part provides information on the measures used to explore the association between experiences and attitudes over the study period.


## Characteristics of participation and attrition


Participation and attrition are assessed in two ways. Participation refers to the completion of a daily survey, and is measured using a binary indicator as to whether the participant completed

a daily survey or not (1=missing survey). In this case, missing daily surveys are nested within individuals. Attrition refers to what extent a participant completes none, occasional, or (almost) all required daily surveys over the study period. We define three categories of attrition and compliance, whereby participants who completed none or less than 20% of the daily surveys are considered 'low' or 'non-compliers' and participants who completed at least 20% or more daily surveys are considered 'compliers'. The  remaining  participants are considered 'occasional' compliers. We use the threshold of 20% to define compliers because this was the stated condition for full payment (i.e., 80% or more completed daily surveys). We are not able to evaluate characteristics of individuals who registered for the study, but did not complete the baseline survey, as information provided on registration was minimal.

We include several socio-demographic characteristics to assess the characteristics of participation and attrition. Since young people were recruited for the study, age ranges from 18 to 30. A respondent's gender is measured using a binary indicator (0=male, 1=female). 4 Respondents were asked to report their highest level of completed education, and the responses were  recoded  to  reflect  (1)  lower  secondary  education,  (2)  middle  (i.e.,  upper  secondary education),  and  (3)  high  (i.e.,  higher  education).  Finally,  we  include  a  variable  reflecting whether or not the respondent has a migrant background. Respondents who reported that they or at least one of their parents were born outside the Netherlands were coded as (1) 'migrant background', whereas all others were coded as (0) 'no migrant background'.

In  addition,  we  include  four  variables  that  capture  global  perceptions  of  police (procedural  justice,  distributive  justice,  effectiveness)  and  engagement  with  police  media. These characteristics can help us evaluate to what extent prior beliefs and engagement might potentially  shape  motivation  and  influence  participation  itself. Procedural  justice was measured using four items drawn from the European Social Survey (Jackson et al., 2010) and Murphy et al. (2010). Respondents are asked to what extent they agree on a 4-point Likert-type scale (1=not at all often, 4=very often) with statements such as 'The police generally treat people in the Netherlands with respect.' The scale is reliable with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.81.

Distributive justice was measured using three items that capture public perceptions as to whether the police provide services and treat individuals equally. The items were drawn from Murphy et al. (2010), and include statements such as 'Police treat everyone equally' and 'Police provide better service to the rich than to the average citizen.' Respondents' agreement

was  measured  using  a  4-point  Likert-type  scale  ranging  from  (1)  'strongly  agree'  to  (4) 'strongly disagree' (Cronbach's alpha=0.79).

Police effectiveness was measured using three items drawn from Murphy et al. (2010) that ask to what extent respondents feel that the police are doing a good job at solving crime, preventing crime, and keeping order. Responses range from (1) 'very good' to (5) 'very bad'. The items were reverse-coded so that higher values reflect more positive perceptions of police effectiveness. The scale was less reliable compared to others, but still relatively acceptable (Cronbach's alpha=0.65).

Finally, we measured whether or not the respondent was currently following a social media account from the police (1=yes).


## Measures of daily attitudes and experiences



## Daily attitudes


Respondents were asked each day to rate on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 10 (completely) to what extent they agree with several statements about the police. These statements were selected to  reflect  different  elements  of  police  performance  and  legitimacy,  including  procedural fairness, distributive justice, effectiveness, and legality (Jackson et al., 2010; Tankebe, 2013). This included whether the respondent trusts the police, and whether they feel that the police treat people fairly, do their job well, provide the same quality service to all citizens, and behave according to the law. In the current study, we focus particularly on measures of trust in police and procedural fairness for simplicity. In addition, these outcomes reflect two relevant 'global' attitudes  that  are  often  of  interest  in  policing  research.  Although  single-item  measures  are limited in demonstrating internal reliability, studies have shown that single-item measures can perform as well as multiple-item measures in terms of predictive reliability (i.e., how well it predicts a future state) in intensive longitudinal studies (Song et al., 2022).


## Daily experiences


The primary variable used to explain within-person variation in attitudes is the respondent's rating of their daily experience(s) with the police. When respondents reported that they have had at least one experience with the police, they were asked follow-up questions rating the experience according to fair treatment, respectful treatment, and fair outcome (see Appendix A). Specifically, respondents were asked to what extent they agree on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 'strongly disagree' to 5 'strongly agree' with the statement that the police were fair,

respectful,  to  what  extent  the  outcome  was  fair,  and  their  overall  rating  of  the  experience. Respondents could also respond that they 'do not know enough to say' for the fair, respectful and outcome ratings, but did not have this option for the overall rating. Since respondents were able to report multiple experiences, the rating was averaged over all reported experiences with the police for a particular rating and day (excluding the 'don't know' category). In order to ensure  that  scaling  was  consistent  and  interpretable  across  days  and  respondents,  we  then recoded the ratings to reflect a nominal scale categorizing daily experiences where (0) reflects no experience that day, (1) reflects a negative rating of an experience (e.g. unfair, disrespectful, negative), (2) reflects a neutral rating (e.g., neither agree nor disagree, neither negative nor positive), and (3) reflects a positive rating (e.g., fair, respectful, positive). This means that we examine the effect of both having an experience and the quality of the experience on attitudes compared to respondents who did not have any experiences that day. We exclude the 'don't know' category in the variable. In the main analyses, we present the results for fair ratings, however results for respectful, outcome, and overall ratings for Models 1-6 are presented in Appendix D.


## Analytical plan


Given  that  the  current  study  is  a  pilot,  we  take  an  exploratory  approach  to  answering  our research questions. First, in order to assess patterns of participation and attrition, we examine to  what  extent  socio-demographic  characteristics  and  prior  attitudes  towards  the  police  are associated daily participation (completion of a daily survey), and whether the participant was a low, occasional, or high complier during the survey period. To assess daily participation, we used multilevel logistic regression models in which missing daily surveys (level 1) were nested in individuals (level 2). We then evaluated to what extent background characteristics (measured at level 2) were associated with the likelihood of missing a daily survey on a given day. Because we are only interested in associations, we estimate the relationship between each characteristic and participation separately. To assess characteristics associated with attrition, we used oneway  Analyses  of  Variance  (ANOVAs)  and X 2 tests  to  estimate  whether  the  means  or proportions  of  background  characteristics  differed  across  groups  (low/none,  occasional, compliers).

Second, in order to assess the prevalence and patterns of everyday contact, we provide a  summary  of  the  different  types  of  experiences  overall,  how  many  occurred  per  day  on average, and how participants rated various experiences. Here we also explored to what extent daily attitudes varied between and within individuals during the study period. Specifically, we

employed 'empty' multilevel linear models to estimate the intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC] for both trust and procedural fairness outcomes. The ICC provides an estimate of the variance that is attributable to between-individual differences compared to within-individual differences over the 21-day study period.

Finally, in order to evaluate to what extent the quality of contact is associated with attitudes, we use fixed effects linear regression models with person fixed effects. Fixed effects models  can  account  for  potential  time-invariant  factors  that  may  confound  the  association between explanatory and outcome variables. A fixed effects approach models the effects of within-individual deviations of an explanatory variable on within-individual deviations in the outcome (Long, 2021). All models also estimated standard errors clustered by individual and day. All analyses are conducted with panelr (Long, 2020) in R (R Core Team, 2021). In order to evaluate the robustness of results, we estimate three models and specifications. First, we run a basic fixed effects model estimating the relationship between experiences and daily attitudes. Second, we estimate a model that is limited to only participants who completed at least 7 daily surveys. Third, we estimate a model including a lagged ( -1) experience variable. For all models t we use all completed daily surveys and listwise deletion for any missing values in the observed variables, resulting in an unbalanced panel containing a maximum of 2789 observations nested in 188 participants.

## Explaining perceptions of police legitimacy


Table 5 reports the results for the fixed effects model specifications. The results suggest that experiences  rated  unfairly  are  associated  with  more  negative  perceptions  of  trust  and procedural fairness compared to those who had reported no experience at that point in time (e.g.,  Model 1, b=-0.26, 95%CI=-0.44, -0.08, p<.01). Fair experiences are not significantly associated with attitudes (e.g., Model 1, b =0.04, 95%CI=-0.04, 0.12, p >.05). In order to assess whether  the  effects  for  negative  and  positive  were  significantly  different,  we  estimated  an additional model with fair experiences as the reference category. The results show that unfair experiences  were  associated  with  significantly  lower  trust  ( b =-0.30,  95%CI=-0.49,  -0.11, p <.01)  and  procedural  fairness  ( b =-0.34,  95%CI=-0.52,  -0.15, p <.01)  at  that  point  in  time compared to fair experiences. Full results are available in Appendix C (Table C2). Models 3 and 4 use only those who have completed at least 7 surveys. The results are similar for trust,

but drop to non-significance for procedural fairness. Models 5 and 6 estimates to what extent previous experiences are associated with later attitudes using a lagged explanatory variable. The results suggest that experiences have a rather contemporaneous or momentary effect, as lagged  unfair  experiences  are  not  associated  with  later  attitudes  (e.g.,  Model  5, b =-0.03, 95%CI=-0.22, 0.16, p >.05).  Generally,  the  sizes  of  the  within-individual  effects  are  small. Based on Models 1 and 2, the proportion of within-individual variance explained was 1%.

## Additional models

We ran additional models estimating the association between other specific ratings (respectful treatment,  fair  outcome,  overall  positive/negative)  and  perceptions  of  trust  and  procedural fairness  (all  tables  and  results  are  presented  in  Appendix  D).  The  findings  for  respectful treatment  are  relatively  similar  to  the  results  for  fair  treatment,  however  unfair  treatment remains significant for trust and procedural fairness among those who completed at least 7 surveys (Table D1). Perceived outcome (un)fairness is not related to either trust or fairness in any model (Table D2). Generally negative overall ratings were associated with significantly less  procedural  fairness  across  most  model  specifications  (Table  D3).  Interestingly,  lagged negatively rated experiences were associated with higher procedural fairness during the next survey moment (Model 6, b=0.28, 95%CI=0.11, 0.44, p<.01). However, this result may be spurious and requires further investigation in future studies.

## DISCUSSION


The current study aimed to explore new ways of measuring experiences with the police, and in evaluate to what extent these experiences influence attitudes in the short term. Most research on  contact  with  the  police  focuses  primarily  on  personal  contact,  while  measuring  these experiences in a retrospective manner that may be prone to bias (Lynch & Addington, 2010). This study pilots the use of experience sampling techniques to capture different types of daily experiences and momentary feelings about police performance and behavior. We find that the number and type of experiences can vary substantially across individuals and time, and that overall experiences with the police are prevalent in everyday life. The overall response rate is average compared to other experience sampling studies (69%), and the proportion of compliers in the  sample  was  relatively  high  (63.64%).  Individuals  who  reported  more  negative perceptions of procedural justice were more likely to miss surveys and complete less than 20% of  daily  surveys.  In  addition,  unfair  experiences  were  associated  with  lower  trust  and procedural fairness at that point in time, but this was sensitive to model specification. While these effects are small and short-lived, they nevertheless suggest that daily experiences with the police can shape attitudes within a relatively short window of time. These findings have implications for how we measure interactions with police and their effects on attitudes towards the police. Specifically, we highlight four main implications for the use of experience sampling and the study of police-citizen interactions.

First, our descriptive analyses show that most of our respondents had 'experiences' with the police through media and observation of police 'on the job'. The number of personal experiences was fairly low (n=27, 4%), but that is likely not unusual in the Dutch context where personal interactions with citizens are given relatively lower priority. To compare, a study of police  contact  among  urban  youth  in  the  United  States  suggested  that  19%  of  the  sample reported ever being personally stopped by the police (Geller, 2021). What this suggests is that individuals in some contexts are more likely to get their information about police treatment and behavior in daily life from media sources compared to personal encounters. If citizens in some contexts  indeed  will  experience  little  to  no  direct  contact  with  the  police  in  their  lifetime, considerations  about  procedural  justice  in  direct  encounters  could  have  been  overstated  in previous research as implied by Weitzer (2002). Our descriptive results thus emphasize the need to think outside the box of procedural justice in direct encounters and to consider other forms of exposure to police behavior. While research on the role of media in shaping attitudes

is well-developed, this research tends to be largely cross-sectional and conducted separately from studies examining personal interactions (Choi, 2021; Graziano et al., 2010). Research on the influence of media on political and legal attitudes suggests that individual exposure to news is in part driven by prior beliefs (Moule Jr et al., 2019), and that accessing news via social media  can  lead  to  the  consumption  of  more  polarized  information  (Wojcieszak,  2021; Wojcieszak et al., 2021). Given self-selection into consuming certain types of media and news stories, experiences via media likely work to reinforce prior beliefs about the police over time. For individuals who consume more polarized information about police (positive or negative), this information is not only likely to shape attitudes directly, but influence how individuals interpret personal experiences as well. More research is needed to measure what types of media are being consumed, and evaluate to what extent media and personal experiences interact to influence attitudes towards the police in the short- and long-term.

Likewise,  exposure  to  police  'on  the  job'  can  vary  substantially  in  how  it  shapes attitudes.  While  personal  interactions  may  be  infrequent,  too  much  police  presence  may contribute to feelings of 'overpolicing,' or the disproportionate targeting and harassment of certain neighborhoods and populations (Boehme et al., 2022). Alternatively, too little police presence may send signals that the police are ineffective and not 'doing their job' to protect citizens and control crime in the neighborhood. Although observing the police on the job in the current study was often not informative (i.e., they did not know enough to rate the experience), they nevertheless make up a large proportion of daily experiences. In addition, a substantial amount of these observations were informative enough for the participant to rate as fair (53%). In some studies, witnessing an encounter is included as a form of vicarious contact, and the majority in these samples only experience this type of exposure to the police (Jackson et al., 2020). This suggests that observing police on the street 'doing their job' provides an important source of information about police behavior in addition to personal and media experiences.

Second, our results suggest that, even among a relatively small and limited sample, respondents reported a variety of different experiences over the time period. However, not all experiences were equally informative in the sense that the respondent could make judgements about the treatment and outcome. In particular, judgements about the fairness of the outcome were most often rated as 'don't know.' It is important to recognize that signals are not always clear, and that information conveyed through various experiences is imperfect. The 'outcome' of a particular interaction may be delayed or unknown, meaning that measures of distributive justice may be more challenging to identify and judge for respondents. These issues may result in measurement error, and may also explain why judgements about procedural fairness can

influence perceptions of outcome fairness (McLean, 2020). In other words, it is possible that the respondents do not know enough to make a clear judgement about the outcome, and so infer fairness based on what they know about treatment. Taken together, our results suggest that not all experiences convey the same information, and that individual judgements about different elements of a single experience may be difficult to distinguish in practice.

Third, although the effects are small, we found asymmetrical effects of experiences on perceptions of trust and procedural fairness. This finding was replicated when assessing other specific  and  more  general  ratings  (i.e.,  respectful  treatment  and  overall  positive/negative perception). This finding is in line with research showing that negative experiences have a more substantial impact on attitudes compared to positive experiences (Choi, 2021; Maguire et al., 2017; Skogan, 2006; Thompson & Pickett, 2021). In the Netherlands, trust in the police is relatively  high  on  average,  which  is  also  reflected  in  the  high  average  levels  of  police legitimacy in this study. A negative experience in this context may therefore have a greater likelihood of influencing perceptions compared to positive experiences. This may also be due to ceiling effects given that levels of trust were already fairly high, limiting the absolute range in which respondents can report higher agreement (similarly, see White et al., (2018) on 'floor' effects of vicarious experiences in Baltimore). Alternatively, respondents who identify more strongly with society may place greater emphasis on treatment, meaning a negative interaction may  be  more  impactful  among  this  sample  compared  to,  for  example,  ethnic  minorities (Murphy  &  Cherney,  2011;  Slocum  &  Wiley,  2018).  Given  that  the  current  sample  is predominantly majority Dutch, this may explain the asymmetry found in treatment effects.

However, it is important to note that these associations are 'momentary,' as lagged experiences were not significantly associated with attitudes. While existing research suggests that there is a strong, possibly causal, association between direct and vicarious experiences and attitudes (Mazerolle, Antrobus, et al., 2013; Nägel & Nivette, 2022; Sahin et al., 2017), there is  relatively  less  research  on  how  long  these  effects  last.  Studies  that  have  evaluated  the 'indirect'  effects  of  exposure  to  police  violence  (e.g.,  the  death  of  George  Floyd,  police violence in France) on public attitudes have found that the impact of these major events is relatively  short-lived,  disappearing  over  a  few  days  or  weeks  while  being  somewhat  more persistent for ethnic minorities (Nägel & Lutter, 2021; Reny & Newman, 2021). More minor experiences may have even more 'fleeting' effects on attitudes, however it is not clear to what extent these experiences (big and small) may more gradually and cumulatively shape attitudes over time. More research is needed to measure and evaluate the interactive and cumulative effects of different experiences on attitudes in the short- and long-term.

Finally, our analyses of participation and attrition showed that individuals who have more negative perceptions of police, measured by global police procedural justice, are more likely to miss a survey on a given day and overall complete few or no daily surveys. This has implications  for  recruitment  of  participants  within  experience  sampling  studies,  and  more broadly surveys on police contact and attitudes. Non-random attrition in longitudinal studies is not unknown to criminology (Brame et al., 2010), and has the potential to substantially bias coefficients (Mitchell et al., 2022). An evaluation of participation and attrition in experience sampling measuring fear of crime found that the most dedicated participants tended to be those who were most interested in the studied outcome (Kronkvist & Engström, 2020). Our results seem to be in line with this conclusion as well, as individuals who thought more positively about the police were the most compliant during the study period. Nevertheless, the proportion of compliers in the current study (63.64%) was higher than the fear of crime study (13.6% for daily assessment), which may be explained by the apparent lack of compensation in the latter case. Compensation is an important technique to maintain participation, but other techniques such as gamification, reminders, and feedback on compliance can work to minimize attrition as well (Dejonckheere & Erbas, 2021; Kronkvist & Engström, 2020; van Berkel & Kostakos, 2021; Wrzus & Neubauer, 2022). Future studies aiming to implement experience sampling techniques must therefore consider ways to increase and maintain participation among broader populations, as well as account for potential biases due to (often inevitable) attrition.


## Limitations


The current study was a pilot that aimed to explore the use of experience sampling in measuring everyday experiences with the police. It is important to stress that this pilot was conducted using a non-probability convenience sample, and so is not generalizable to broader populations. Since respondents were recruited through the research platform, it is likely that the sample systematically differs from the general population. Most notably, the sample is more highly educated, with a low proportion of respondents reporting a migration background. The current study therefore does not adequately capture different types of experiences occurring among migrant populations in the Netherlands.

Furthermore, this pilot was conducted in the relatively 'high trust' and 'low contact' context of the Netherlands. It is possible that the number of personal experiences are lower compared to other contexts where there are more opportunities to come in contact with the police,  such  as  the  United  States  (Pierson  et  al.,  2020).  However,  we  stress  that  our  study demonstrates, in line with previous research (Geller, 2021), that personal contacts are far from

the only source of information and potential 'teachable moments' about police that people encounter  in  daily  life.  It  is  important  to  repeat  this  study  across  a  variety  of  societal  and institutional  contexts  that  capture  different  overall  levels  of  trust  and  potential  for  police interactions.

In order to reduce the burden on participants, measurements were restricted to single items, meaning that attitudinal outcomes may not adequately reflect more nuanced dimensions of trust and procedural justice. Future research using experience sampling techniques should evaluate  ideal  short-form  measures  of  relevant  constructs  in  order  to  balance  burden  with reliable measurement (see for example, Murray et al. 2022 on a short-form aggression scale).

The  current  study  also  focused  relatively  narrowly  on  the  role  of  experiences  in explaining within-individual variation in attitudes. The proportion of variance explained by experiences was very small, suggesting that there are likely other daily factors that can help explain  attitudes  in  the  short  term.  Future  research  should  examine  other  within-individual factors that may shape attitudes, such as fear of crime or victimization. Likewise, it is important to  assess  to  what  extent  situational  characteristics  or  emotional  affect  may  moderate  the relationship between experiences and attitudes (Barkworth & Murphy, 2015).

Nevertheless, these pilot results raise questions about how we measure experiences with the police, and to what extent different experiences have short- or long-term effects on attitudes towards the police. Respondents reported a wide range of different experiences in a relatively short period of time, albeit some were more informative about police behavior than others. If the public experiences a diverse array of experiences in daily life as suggested in the current  study,  which  of  these  experiences  would  they  be  likely  to  report  in  a  retrospective measure of police contact? Are some more likely to remember and report positive or negative experiences  than  others?  These  questions  also  have  important  implications  for  the  idea  of 'teachable moments' and their impact on attitudes and behaviors. Given the array of moments, it  is  necessary  to  better  understand  which  are  'teachable'  and  which  are  not.  Experience sampling  techniques  can  help  us  capture  these  short-term  processes  in  order  to  better understand when and how experiences are likely to shape perceptions of police.

## 1. Introduction


School achievement is socially stratified (in the following referred to as the SES-achievement gap ) in all countries but there is substantial variation in the degree of stratification. In PISA 2018 social origin of children explains on average 14% of the variance in achievement in OECD countries. However, in some countries, social origin explains less than 8%, but in others almost 24% (OECD, 2019b: Table II.B1.2.4).

An important reason for these country differences might be differences in education systems, particularly whether and how students are assigned to different schools or courses. The earlier children are tracked to different schools (' between-school tracking' ) the larger the SES gaps in achievement (OECD, 2020: 81f.; van de Werfhorst and Mijs, 2010). Whereas most countries have abolished or delayed between-school tracking in lower secondary education sorting was not fully abolished. Instead of sorting students into different schools, they are sorted into more or less advanced courses (' course-by-course tracking ') within schools now (Lucas, 1999). In contrast to  between-school tracking, there is  no  conclusive association between  course-bycourse tracking and SES-achievement gaps on the country level in OECD countries (OECD, 2020:  82f.). Both  types of differentiation result in  more homogeneous learning groups.  As student's achievement as well as track or course selection, above and beyond  achievement, depend on social origin (Jackson, 2013) differentiation does not only lead to more homogeneous groups concerning skills but also concerning social background (Bol et al., 2014).

Even without between-school tracking, residential segregation and school choice often result in the uneven distribution of students from different SES across schools. In turn, large variations in  the  social  composition  across  schools  is  associated  with  more  social  stratification of achievements (e.g., OECD,  2019a: 67). While segregation by student achievement and social school composition are highly correlated, social school composition seems to increase SES-

achievement gaps net of segregation by achievement and vice versa (e.g., Holzberger et al., 2020;  van  Ewijk  and  Sleegers,  2010).  Therefore,  part  of  country  differences  in  SESachievement  gaps  may  be  attributable  to  country  differences  in  the  variance  of  social composition of schools.

While several cross-country studies indicate that tracking  (Chmielewski, 2014;  Le  Donné, 2014) and social school composition (Holzberger et al., 2020; van Ewijk and Sleegers, 2010) are associated with larger SES-achievement gaps, these studies have a  central shortcoming: they consider cross-sectional data. Thus, the larger SES-achievement gaps in countries with early tracking may have already emerged before tracking takes place. A few studies have tried to overcome this problem by  comparing SES-achievement gaps  in primary school to  SESachievement gaps  in  secondary  school  and  found  that  SES-achievement gaps  grew  more strongly in countries with early tracking. These studies did not evaluate longitudinal data of the same students but relied on the assumption that the studies that took place in primary school with one sample of students are comparable to the studies that took place in secondary school with a different sample of students (Dämmrich and Triventi, 2018; Waldinger, 2007).

The fact that low and high SES students attend different schools, either because of betweenschool tracking or other reasons, could be the main reason for SES-achievement gaps. However, previous research has only evaluated how much of the total variation in achievement can be attributed  to  differences  between  or  within  schools,  i.e.,  the  intra-class  correlation  of achievement at the school level (Marks, 2006; Bol et al., 2014) and did not consider how this contributes to SES-achievement gaps. More interesting for research on social stratification in education  is  how  much  of  the  SES-achievement gap  can  be  attributed to  between-school differences.

In our contribution, we want to overcome these shortcomings and shed new light on the role of both between-school tracking and course-by-course tracking and social school composition by

examining SES gaps in students' mathematics achievement at  the  end  of  lower  secondary school based on longitudinal microdata.

We  consider  three  prototypes  whether  and  how  tracking  takes  place  in  lower  secondary education in large high-income countries: no or hardly any tracking (France), early tracking (Germany), and course-by-course tracking (England and US).

Besides describing the SES-achievement gaps at the end of lower secondary school, we aim to answer five research questions:

- 1)  Conditional  on  achievement  at  the  start  of  lower  secondary  school,  how  much  does achievement differ by parental education at the end of lower secondary school?

To what extent can these achievement differences be attributed:

- 2) to (any) differences between schools,
- 3) to schools' social composition,
- 4) to tracking?
- 5)  To  what  extent  do  these  contributions  differ  by  country  and  depend  on  the  specific institutional context?


## 2. Theoretical Considerations and Literature Review



## 2.1 Framework


For theorizing how tracking and the schools' social composition contribute to SES-achievement gaps, it is helpful to conceptualize the school or course / track and the social composition of the school  as  mediating  processes  between  SES  and  children's  achievement  (see  Figure  1). Achievement growth  and,  more  specifically, changes  in  the  SES-achievement gap  during secondary school can be partially attributed to socially stratified track (path b in Figure 1) and

course attendance (path c ), partially to schools' social composition (path a ), and partially to other mechanisms (path d, e.g., the difference in the usage of private tutoring or parental support with schoolwork). In turn, attending upper school tracks (path  ), advanced courses (path f g ), or schools with a higher share of high-SES students (path e ) may affect achievement.

All else being equal (i.e., d being the same in all countries), the growth in the SES-achievement gap should be largest in countries, in which the sum of the indirect effects via between-school tracking  (path b ×  path f ),  course-by-course  tracking  (path c ×  path g ),  and  the  social composition of the schools (path a × path e ) is the largest.

Tracking and social school composition are intertwined, as between school-tracking increases the  uneven  distribution  of  social  school  composition  and  parents  might  respond  to  a comprehensive school system with more residential segregation and school choice. In addition, some explanations why  tracking and social  school composition should have any  impact on achievement development strongly overlap.

## 2.2 Tracking


Several studies showed  that there are larger SES-achievement gaps  in countries with  more rigorous between-school tracking (Brunello and Checchi, 2007; van de Werfhorst and Mijs, 2010). Likewise, several studies found that rigorous course-by-course tracking is associated with larger SES-achievements gaps (Gamoran, 2010; Domina et al., 2019).

So, for which tracking regime can we expect larger SES-achievement gaps? This depends on two factors, as shown in Figure 1:

- 1. The degree to which school/course attendance is socially stratified (paths b and c in Figure 1), and

- 2. The impact of attending higher school tracks/advanced courses on achievement gains (paths   and f g in Figure 1).

Concerning the first factor, existing research unambiguously shows that high SES children are more likely to attend higher tracks and are more likely to attend advanced courses (Crosnoe and Schneider, 2010). The increased likelihood of high SES children attending higher tracks can be partially attributed to their higher achievement before tracking. However, high SES children are also more likely to attend higher tracks, net of their earlier achievement (Jackson, 2013).

Several arguments suggest that track attendance is more strongly socially stratified in countries with between-school tracking than in countries with course-by-course tracking. First, attending higher between-school tracks is more obviously a necessity for enrolling in tertiary education later on than attending advanced courses. Few students who plan to enroll in university want to take the detour of attending a vocational school track. Second, track changes are more common between courses than between schools (Chmielewski, 2014; Chmielewski, 2017), creating more opportunities for students who started in lower tracks to move up and for students faring badly to move down  in a  course-by-course tracking system. However,  it may also be  difficult to change to an advanced course if there are prerequisite contents that are only taught in advanced classes (Frank et al., 2008).

The few existing studies support the hypothesis that between-school tracking is more strongly socially  stratified  than course-by-course  tracking  (Dupriez,  Dumay  and  Vause,  2008; Chmielewski, 2014; Schnabel et al., 2002).

Likewise,  concerning  the  second  factor,  existing  research  largely  supports  the  claim  that children in higher tracks have larger achievement gains than children on lower tracks (Traini, Kleinert and Bittmann, 2021; Triventi, Barone and Facchini, 2021), and children who attend advanced courses have larger achievement gains than children who attend remedial courses

(Domina, 2014). Potential reasons for this are the more challenging curricula, more qualified or motivated teachers, higher teachers' expectations, more favorable learning environments, more resources, students profiting from their peers, and  stigma attached to attending lower tracks (Gamoran, 2010; Maaz et al., 2008).

Whether  between-school  tracking  or  course-by-course  tracking  has  larger  impacts  on achievement  gains  is  less  clear.  Between-school  tracking  may  have  a  larger  impact  on achievement growth because children who attend high-track schools are surrounded by students with similar skills, motivation, and expectations all the time (Dollmann and Rudolphi, 2020), while students in advanced courses only have such conditions when they are in the advanced course, but not in other courses. Moreover, between-school tracking seems to have a larger impact on educational aspirations than course-by-course tracking (Buchmann and Park, 2009; Chmielewski, 2017). In  turn, the low educational aspirations of students in lower betweenschool tracks may reduce their motivation to learn.

Yet,  there are also arguments why  course-by-course tracking may  have a  larger impact on achievement. Course-by-course tracking will result in more homogenous courses concerning skills in the specific subject than between-school tracking because between-school tracking depends  on  the  combination of  prior school performance in  several subjects. Furthermore, course-by-course tracking  seems  to  have  a  larger  impact  on  academic  self-concepts than between-school tracking (Chmielewski, Dumont and Trautwein, 2013; Dupriez, Dumay and Vause, 2008) potentially because students compare themselves to students in the same school and not to students in other schools.

Most existing studies indicate that between-school tracking has a similar impact on achievement gains as course-by-course tracking (Dupriez, Dumay and Vause, 2008; Huang, 2009).  1

Taken together, if course-by-course tracking has  a  similar impact on  achievement gains as between-school tracking (g = f) but between-school tracks are more strongly socially stratified than course-by-course tracks (b >  c), then, ceteris paribus, SES-achievement gaps should be larger in countries with between-school tracking ( b × f > c × g ).


## 2.3 Differences in Schools' Social Composition


Even in countries with a comprehensive school system, other processes might be at work that lead  to  different  social  compositions  across  schools,  like  school  choice  and  residential segregation. Consequently, despite a comprehensive school system, schools might not prove to be heterogeneous regarding social origin and, in turn, also ability or achievement. Hence, in comprehensive systems with late or no external tracking, there could be differential learning gains over time due to schools' social composition.

Research found that a large share of low-SES students in a school are associated with lower achievement (Holzberger et al., 2020; van Ewijk  and Sleegers, 2010). This  association can partially be attributed to other factors that affect both the social composition and achievement gaps such as the academic or ethnic composition of schools. 2  Effect sizes get smaller when taking these factors into account but a substantial association between social composition and achievement remains (Sciffer, Perry and McConney, 2020).

How much school's social composition contributes to growing SES-achievement gaps depends on two factors:

- 1. The degree to which schools differ in their social composition (path a in Figure 1), and
- 2. The impact of school's social composition on achievement (path e in Figure 1).

Concerning the first factor, between-school differences in the social composition will be more pronounced when there is strong residential segregation, when  between-tracking takes place, and  when  there is  a  free school  choice for  families and  access to  schools depends  on  the

resources of families (for example, ability to cover tuition fees, information about school quality or application processes).

The  social composition of  schools may  affect students learning  (path e )  both  directly and indirectly (Dumay and Dupriez, 2008; Rumberger and Palardy, 2005). On the one hand, how much students learn will be directly affected by the composition of their peers. A high share of high SES students could lead to a 'culture of success' (Jencks and Mayer, 1990) where students internalize their  peers' high  motivation and  high  educational aspirations. Students  will  be rewarded by the acceptance of their peers if they conform to this behavior but will be punished if they deviate from their peers' high educational norms. Moreover, students benefit from their peers'  resources  (Crosnoe,  2009).  Conversely,  in  schools  where  students  do  not  value education, students may be punished by their peers for having high aspirations and putting effort into learning (Agirdag, van Houtte and van Avermaet, 2012).

On the other hand, how much students learn might be affected indirectly by  schools' social composition. Schools'  resources may depend  on  the  composition of  the  students' body  or schools may adjust their organization to the composition of their students. Teachers may avoid the trouble of teaching in schools with  a high  share of low  SES  students. Thus,  the mostqualified teachers may end up in schools with a high share of high SES students. Lastly, teachers may adjust the coverage of their curriculum, their motivation, and their expectations for their students to the composition of the class. In turn, these adaption processes may affect learning progress (Rumberger and Palardy, 2005; Dumay and Dupriez, 2008).

Based  on  these  considerations we  expect  larger  effects  of  schools'  social  composition in countries where funding depends more strongly on the resources of the neighborhood and/or parents, and where schools are more autonomous (i.e., for hiring teachers and the choice of curricula and methods).

Overall,  social  composition  of  schools  will  contribute  most  to  SES-achievement  gaps  in contexts with a large variation in the social composition of schools and high impact of schools' social composition on achievement.


## 3. Country Contexts


In  the four considered countries, there are remarkable differences in the organization of the education systems at the secondary level.

In most German states, students are tracked after 4 years of schooling, when students are about 10 years old. The academic school track ( Gymnasium ) prepares students for universities. The lower ( Hauptschule ) and the middle school track ( Realschule ) are offered in different school types  across  states  and  prepare  students  for  vocational  training.  Moreover,  there  are comprehensive schools (e.g., Gesamtschule ) in some regions. In recent decades it has become easier to switch school types but  mobility between tracks is still relatively low  (Blossfeld, 2018).

In the other countries, there is no external tracking before the age of 15 (France), 16 (England), or none (United States), with the exception of small numbers of grammar schools (England) and  elite high schools (United  States). Instead,  in  England  and  the United  States, the  vast majority  of  students  are  tracked  into  courses  of  varying  difficulty  and  can  therefore  be characterized as 'á la carte integration' tracking regimes (Dupriez, Dumay and Vause, 2008). In  England, where math is concerned, preparation for exit exams of varying difficulty takes place in different classes from around age 14, although many schools will stream from age 11. In the United States, there are also different levels of math classes: honors for more talented students, basic, or remedial for students performing below grade level (see Table 1).

The French school system can be characterized as an 'integrated' tracking regime. There are comprehensive secondary schools and only a very mild form of tracking concerning language

classes. Once  students have passed an  entrance test, they may  enter an advanced  language learning track (classes européennes), international sections, or music sections from around age 11  for with  possible entrances and  exits  hereafter. In  some  cases,  this also  leads  to  more homogeneous classes in terms of achievement in other subjects for timetabling reasons. We define this as a form of tracking up (Bertaux, 2008). However, less than 10% of students were tracked up in 2011 (DEPP, 2011). Students with learning difficulties may also be put in smaller classes  with  individualized support  (classes  Segpa).  Schools  can  suggest  these  classes  to families at any point at the end of primary or during lower secondary school (ages 11-14). However, as for classes européennes, Segpa's have theoretically the same curriculum leading to the same final exam in the same schools. We define these as tracking down (Herbaut et al., 2019).

Moreover, there is some variation how students are allocated to tracks. In England and most schools in the United States, students are allocated to tracks based on students' performance and  teachers'  recommendations.  In France  students  are  tracked-up  based  on  parents' preferences and tracked-down based on learning difficulties, but in accordance with parents. In most states in Germany parents make the decision.

Results of PISA  2018 show that schools with a large share of low SES students have fewer qualified teachers and are more likely to lack educational materials than schools with many high SES students in Germany, the United States, and England. In contrast, in France, there are no  or  only  small  associations  between  schools'  social  composition  and  staff  shortage, qualification of teachers, and availability of educational materials (OECD, 2020).
