## 4. Hypotheses


Based on our theoretical model and the different institutional contexts in the four countries, we derive the following hypotheses:

- 1. Differences by  parental education at the end of lower secondary school are partially mediated by achievement at the beginning of lower secondary school but substantial differences in achievement progress by parental education remain.
- 2. The  differences  in  achievement  progress  by  parental  education  can  be  partially attributed to  any  differences between  schools.  Schools  will  contribute most  to  the remaining differences in Germany and the United States because differences between schools are larger here than in the other two countries.
- 3. The  differences  in  achievement  progress  by  parental  education  can  be  partially attributed to schools' social composition. Schools' social composition will contribute least  to  the  remaining differences in  France,  as  school  resources are  less  strongly correlated with schools' social composition than in other countries.
- 4. The  differences  in  achievement  progress  by  parental  education  can  be  partially attributed  to  tracking  (both  between-school  and  course-by-course).  Tracking  will contribute most to SES-achievement gaps in Germany and least in France.


## 5. Methods and Data



## 5.1 Data


We use recent longitudinal microdata for France, Germany, the United States, and England to answer  our  research  questions.  The  most  important  characteristics  of  these  datasets  are presented in Table 2. 3

For France, we use the data of the DEPP panel ( La Direction de l'évaluation, de la prospective et de la performance ; DEPP, 2011). The DEPP panel randomly sampled 1/22 of children born

in  1996  from  the  national administrative student register. Students  and  their parents  were surveyed for the first time in 2007 when children attended Grade 6 and at the end of secondary school in 2011 (or 2012 for repeaters). Some administrative information was collected annually in between. In the first wave, 34,986 students belonging to 6,857 schools were surveyed.

For Germany, we use data from the National Educational Panel Study (NEPS), Starting Cohort 3 (Blossfeld and Roßbach, 2019; NEPS Network, 2021). The target population was all students who attended the 5 th grade in a school in Germany in fall of 2010. In the first wave,  5,788 students from 291 schools participated. Students were surveyed annually in the following years.

For the United States, we use the data of the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study 1998 (ECLSK;  Tourangeau et  al., 2009).  The  ECLS-K  sampled  a  nationally representative cohort  of children who attended kindergarten in fall of 1998 and spring of 1999. In the first wave, 21,260 children participated. The following surveys took place in 2000 (1 st grade), 2002 (3 rd grade), 2004 (5 th grade), and 2007 (8 th grade).

For  England,  we  use  the  data  of  the  Millennium Cohort  Study  (MCS,  University College London,  UCL  Institute  of  Education,  Centre  for Longitudinal Studies  and  Department for Education, 2022). The MCS is a large-scale longitudinal study representative of children born in 2000-2001 and living in the UK at an age of nine months. In the first wave, 18,552 families participated. The further surveys took place when children were 3, 5, 7, 11, 14, and 17 years old.

## 5.2 Variables


## Outcome

The  outcome  of  interest in  our  study  is  students' math  achievement at  the  end  of  lower secondary  school.  For  France,  Germany,  and  the  United  States,  math  achievement  was measured as  the student's test scores in standardized math tests. For  England, there are no standardized math test scores, and we use math grades in the GCSE instead. Therefore, students in England are one to two years older than students in the other countries. The grades of students depend on their course level: students on the lower track can get grades between 1 (lowest) and 5; students on the higher track can get grades between 3 and  9 (highest). For France, some students can sit the test two years in a row, for example, if they repeat a class. In that case, we use the first year's result, to have results from the same year for everyone. To make achievement gaps comparable, we standardize test scores to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one in all countries.

## SES

We use the highest parental educational qualification to measure parental SES as it is more strongly associated with children's achievement than other dimensions of parental SES  like their occupational class or their income (e.g., Bukodi, Goldthorpe and Zhao, 2021). Moreover, it  should  be  more  stable over  time. For  all  four  countries, we  categorize parents' highest education  into  three  categories: high,  middle,  and  low.  The  highest  educational  category contains those parents who  have at least a bachelor's degree. The lowest educational group contains parents with no qualification beyond the socially expected minimum (at least a grade C qualification at the end of compulsory schooling in England; Baccalauréat general in France, graduation from the lower  school track with  a  vocational degree in  Germany;  high  school diploma in the United States). The medium education group contains all parents that do not fall into the high or low education category (Bradbury et al., 2015).

All descriptive statistics are presented in Table 3. In the United States sample, 36% of parents have high education, compared to 31% in Germany, 29% in England, and 19% in France (see Table 3). Moreover, the share of parents that are classified as having low education is much larger in  France (52%) and England  (45%) than  in the United States (29%), and Germany (16%).

## Early Achievement

Like  for  math  achievement  at  the  end  of  secondary  school,  we  use  students'  scores  in standardized tests at the end of primary school or beginning of secondary school to measure earlier achievement. We consider both test scores in math and reading to reduce the impact of measurement error. Early test performance tests took place in the 5 th grade in Germany and the United States, at the end of the 6 th grade in France, and when children were 11 years old (Grade 6) in England. We standardize test scores to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one.

## Tracking

Between-school tracking in secondary school only takes place on a large scale in Germany, where  we  distinguish  between  children  on  the  upper  track  ( Gymnasium ),  comprehensive schools, and other tracks (mostly Hauptschule and Realschule ).  A small fraction of secondary school  students  also  attends  academically selective  public  schools  in  England  (grammar schools, attended by 5% of students) and the United States (elite high schools, attended by 1% of students), although elite high schools tend to serve students in the upper secondary grades only, beyond the observation period in this study. Availability of grammar schools in England is geographically driven for local historical reasons (Long, Foster and Roberts, 2017). In our analysis,  we  use  a  dummy  variable  indicating  whether  students  attend  a  grammar  or  a comprehensive school. However, their low prevalence limits their contribution to inequalities in the national distribution (see Table 3).

For course-by-course tracking, we distinguish between advanced courses, general courses, and remedial courses in math in the United States. For France, we distinguish between children that attend the normal classes, children that attend advanced language classes ( classes européennes ), and remedial classes ( classes Segpa ).  Information on course-by-course tracking is not available for England and for Germany, where course-by-course tracking takes place in comprehensive schools.

## Social Composition of the School

For England, we  use the rounded (to the nearest 10) proportion of students eligible for free school  meals  as  provided  in  the  administrative data.  For  France,  we  measure  the  social composition of the school by the teacher-reported proportion of students whose parents are blue-collar workers or not working. Likewise, for Germany, we use the proportion of students from a  low social status as  reported by the school's headmaster. For the United States, we

measure the social composition by the proportion of students eligible for free or price-reduced lunch as reported by school administrators.

## Controls

We consider several factors that may confound the association between parental education and children's achievement. We include the immigration status (at least one parent born in a foreign country), the family structure (two biological or adoptive parents vs. single parents vs. one biological parent with a new  partner vs.  other compositions), child's gender, child's age in months (mean-centered for  each  country),  the  number  of  siblings  in  the  households,  and whether the family lives in a rural or urban area.

## 6. Results



## 6.1 SES-gaps in Achievement Progress


In all four countries, the difference between high and low SES students in math achievement at the end of lower secondary school is substantial (see M1 in Table 4). We find the largest gap between children with high and low parental education in Germany (0.96 SD; 95%-CI: 0.781.14) followed by the United States (0.92 SD; 95%-CI: 0.79-1.06). The SES-achievement gaps are smaller in France (0.82 SD; 95%-CI: 0.79-0.86) and England (0.78 SD; 95%-CI: 0.71-0.85). For Germany, England, and the United States, this country ranking aligns with previous results. For France, we find less inequalities than found by PISA (OECD 2019b: Tables II.B1.2.3 and II.B1.2.4), which may be explained by the fact that SES-achievement gaps in PISA do not adjust for demographic characteristics.

Next, we additionally control for children's achievement at the beginning of secondary school to identify SES gaps in achievement progress (M2 in Table 4). We find substantial SES gaps in achievement  progress  during  lower  secondary  school  in  all  four  countries,  supporting hypothesis 1. This means, that differences in achievement are not simply carried forward during lower secondary education, although previous achievement is an important predictor for later ones  (see  full regression results in  the  supplementary materials E).  We  find a  statistically significantly larger SES gap in achievement progress in Germany (0.35 SD; 95%-CI: 0.24-0.46) and England (0.35 SD; 95%-CI: 0.30-0.40) than France (0.20 SD; 95%-CI: 0.17-0.22) and in

the United States (0.16 SD; 95%-CI:  0.07-0.24). Information on  the exact p-values of each country contrast is provided in the supplementary materials D.


## 6.2 The Role of Schools in SES Gaps in Achievement Progress


In the next step, we want to know whether the SES gap in achievement progress during lower secondary school can be attributed to differences between schools. Therefore, we add school fixed effects in M3. This allows us to decompose the SES gap in achievement progress into a part that can be attributed to SES gaps within schools and a remaining part that can be attributed to high and low SES students attending different schools. To ease interpretation, we also present the results in Figure 2. Remember, estimations for England are not possible due to the sampling design.

When applying school-fixed effects, we find similar SES gaps in achievement progress across countries: there is an SES gap in achievement progress of 0.15 SD in Germany (95%-CI: 0.030.27), 0.16 SD in France (95%-CI: 0.13-0.18), and 0.10 SD in the United States within schools (95%-CI: 0.01-0.19, M3 in Table 4 and 'Within schools' in Figure 2). These small country differences are not statistically significant (all p>0.20).

Instead, the country difference in the SES gap in achievement progress can be attributed to high and low SES students attending different schools (see 'Between schools' in Figure 2). The SES gap in achievement progress that can be attributed to between-school differences is statistically significantly larger in Germany (0.20 SD, 95%-CI: 0.12-0.27) than in the United States (0.06 SD, 95%-CI: -0.03-0.14) and France (0.04 SD, 95%-CI: 0.02-0.06), which partially supports our hypotheses 2. In relative terms, between school differences account for about 56% of the SES gap in achievement progress in Germany, compared to 36% in the United States and 20% in France.


## 6.3 Mediation Through Schools' SES Composition


One of the reasons for the between-school SES gap in achievement progress could be the social composition of schools. Indeed, when adding the schools' social composition in M4, the SES gap in achievement progress shrinks in all four countries (compared to M2) but only to a minor extent. In absolute terms, the contribution of the social composition is similar across countries: 0.03 SD in England (95%-CI: 0.02-0.05), 0.03 SD in France (95%-CI: 0.02-0.04), 0.03 SD in the United States (95%-CI: 0.01-0.06), and 0.02 SD in Germany (95%-CI: -0.01-0.05, see 'Via soc. comp.' in Figure 2). In relative terms, the contribution is larger in the US (20%) and France (14%), than in England (9%) and Germany (6%) because the achievement progress gaps in England and Germany are larger.


## 6.4 Mediation Through Track or Course-by-Course Attendance


In contrast to social composition, tracking seems to be crucial for SES gaps in  achievement progress in Germany, as predicted in hypothesis 4. Tracking also contributes to SES gaps in achievement progress in England, France, and the United States but to a lesser extent (see M5 in  Table  4  and  'Via  Tracking'  in  Figure  2).  Tracking accounts  for  0.10  SD  of  the  SESachievement gap in Germany (95%-CI: 0.04-0.15; 28% of the gap in M2) but much less in the other countries: only 0.02 SD in the United States (95%-CI: 0.00-0.03; 10% of the gap in M2), 0.01 SD in England (95%-CI: 0.00-0.02; 3% of the gap in M2), and 0.01 SD in France (95%CI: 0.00-0.01; 3% of the gap in M2). Thus, the SES gap that can be attributed to tracking is statistically significantly larger in Germany than in the other three countries (all p<0.01). Note, for  England  we  only  have  information on  whether  children attend  a  comprehensive or  a grammar school but not which course level they attend, and therefore, will underestimate the importance of tracking for SES achievement gaps in England.

Tracking seems to be one of the main reasons why we  see larger SES gaps in achievement progress in Germany than in France and the United States. Once we control for tracking, the

difference in the SES-gaps in achievement progress between Germany and the other countries is not statistically significant anymore (all p>0.10; see 'Not via tracking' in Figure 2).

As  between  school  tracking  results  in  social  segregation,  we  consider  both,  the  social composition of  schools  and  tracking simultaneously (see  M6  in  Table  4).  Both  indicators account for 0.10 SD of the SES gap in achievement progress in Germany (95%-CI: 0.04-0.15), for 0.05 SD in the United States (95%-CI: 0.02-0.08), for 0.04 SD in England (95%-CI: 0.020.05),  and  for 0.04  SD  in  France (95%-CI:  0.03-0.04, see  'Via  seg  +  track' in  Figure 2). However, in relative terms, tracking and the social composition of schools together account for a similar share of the SES gaps in achievement progress in France (19%), Germany (28%), and the United States (31%). It is, however, lower in England (10%), likely because we cannot measure course-by-course tracking in England.

## 6.5 Robustness Checks


We  conducted  four  robustness checks:  1)  Repeating  the  analysis  for  reading  achievement (Figure 3 and supplementary materials F), 2) Using years of education instead of educational groups (supplementary  materials  G), 3) Additionally  controlling  for grade repetition (supplemental material H), and 4) specifying non-linear effects of the social composition of schools (supplemental material I).

Overall, our substantial results do not change in any of the robustness checks. When considering reading achievement, the social composition of schools becomes more important in Germany and less important in England. Furthermore, we find slightly smaller SES gaps in achievement progress in France when also considering grade repetition.


## 7. Conclusion and Discussion


We make five contributions to the research on the effects of the institutional setting on SESachievement gaps by using longitudinal microdata from England, France, Germany, and the United States, which represent different tracking regimes in lower secondary school.

First, we  find  the  largest SES-achievement gaps  at  the  end  of  lower  secondary  school  in Germany, followed by the United States. Gaps in England and France are smaller. Conditional on prior achievement, we again find the larger SES gaps in Germany (the country with betweenschool  tracking) and  smaller SES  gaps  in  France  (the  country  with  the  most  'integrated' tracking regime). However, the United States appears more like France in showing a relatively small SES gap during lower secondary school. Its larger gap at the end of secondary school overall reflects larger and/or more persistent pre-existing differences at the end  of primary school. Conversely, England exhibits a large gap in progress during secondary school, similar in magnitude to that seen in Germany, but this is offset by less, or more transient, inequality at the end of primary school.

Second, for three of the four countries, we evaluate whether these SES gaps in achievement progress during lower secondary school can  be  attributed to  differences between or  within schools. We find that between one fifth (France) and a half (Germany) of the changes in the SES-achievement  gap  during  secondary  school  can  be  attributed  to  differences  between schools. With one-third, the United States is in between. In contrast, SES gaps in achievement progress  within  schools  are  similar  in  all  three  countries,  suggesting  that  cross-country differences are largely driven by the allocation of students to schools and differences in school characteristics and resources in the broadest sense.

Third, we find that the social composition of schools contributes rather little to SES gaps in all countries. However, in Germany, the social composition of a school is largely a consequence

of the attended track. In  contrast, in France, the United States, and England, the correlation between the attended track and the social composition of the school is much weaker.

Fourth, we evaluate whether country differences in the development of the SES-achievement gap during secondary school can be attributed to the different ability tracking regimes. We find that a substantial share of the growth of the SES-achievement gap can be attributed to betweenschool  tracking  in  Germany,  while  the  contribution  of  within-school  tracking  to  SESachievement gaps is small to negligible in France and the United States. These results seem to indicate that between school tracking increases SES-achievement gaps even when evaluating the achievement of the same students longitudinally instead of comparing them to students in other datasets (Dämmrich and Triventi, 2018; Waldinger, 2007). Moreover, our results suggest that between-school tracking is more consequential for SES-achievement gaps than course-bycourse tracking with longitudinal micro-data while existing studies have evaluated this with cross-sectional data (Chmielewski, 2014; Schnabel et al., 2002; Dupriez, Dumay and Vause, 2008). However, this finding relies mostly on the comparison between Germany and the United States, and not on England where course-by-course tracking is of similar importance as in the United States.

Overall, we  can conclude that progress during secondary school differs by  SES in different educational systems  but  there  is  also  substantial country  variation. Social  composition of schools seems to play a similar, minor but still non-trivial role in the slower progress of low SES students in secondary school in all countries. However, external tracking seems to magnify SES gaps in achievement progress.

Some limitations must be considered for the interpretation of our findings. Although we tried to  harmonize measures in  the  different countries as  much  as  possible,  there remain  some differences such as indicators of school composition. The measure of the social composition in Germany  is  more  subjective  than  in  the  other  countries,  which  could  be  an  alternative

explanation for its smaller effect in Germany. For England, we have no information about the course the child attended, meaning the contribution of tracking to SES-achievement gaps will be underestimated. Further, as we rely on z-standardized achievement values, we cannot be sure that SES gaps increase in absolute terms. To overcome these limitations, large-scale assessment studies with standardized achievement measures and course attainment, such as PISA, should adopt a panel design, covering primary and secondary school. Moreover, the results found for the four  countries in  this study  cannot be  assumed to generalize to  all countries. The  way children are sorted into tracks, the resources and curriculum associated with different tracks, and the wider economic and social environment could all moderate the effects of tracking.

The analysis relies on the assumption that there are no country level confounders such as time of  instruction  or  shadow  education,  which  affect  the  attended  track/course,  the  social composition of schools, and achievement progress in lower secondary schools. Note that many of these potential confounders will be captured by the early achievement measures. It would require a different research design to make causal claims about the contribution of tracking and the social composition of schools. Tracking reforms could be framed as a natural experiment but they are often implemented at the same time as other aspects of educational systems like increasing the years of mandatory school (Meghir and Palme, 2005), which may also affect SES achievement gaps. In addition, only countries with such reforms in the last decades could be considered.

Importantly, our study focuses on lower secondary education only and does not consider the consequences of tracking in upper secondary school. Formal tracking is much more common in upper secondary school and also takes place in France. Therefore, tracking regulation and may contribute more to  inequalities emerging in upper  secondary  school (Schindler et al., 2023).  However,  particularly in  Germany  and  England,  many  students  leave  the  general

education system after lower secondary school and tracking effects on achievement can only be evaluated for the selective group of remaining students.

Despite these limitations, our study provides new insights that can be obtained from neither comparative, but cross-sectional data nor from non-harmonized comparisons of longitudinal data. For instance, Triventi et al. (2020) claim that 'advantage finds its way' in countries with very  different  secondary  school  systems.  They  focus  on  the  complex  interplay  between achievement,  transitions  and  (final)  attainment  across  countries.  Our results  focus  on achievement development only, which may be an important determinant of final attainment across countries; nevertheless, our results are consistent with their broader claims. The extent of the educational advantages that high SES families secure for their children depends on the institutional  contexts.  Countries  with  early  between-school  tracking  make  it  easier  for advantaged  families to  secure  advantages  in  achievement  development for  their  children. Without  early  between-school  tracking,  high  SES  families  find  other  ways  to  secure achievement  advantages  for  their  children,  for  instance  through  residential  segregation, enrollment in private schools, or attendance in special and more selective classes. Yet, these seem to result in less pronounced advantages in achievement. It remains that the strategies of advantaged  families may  have  consequences  for  disadvantaged  families who  have  fewer facilities to choose and influence their children's educational path.

## BACKGROUND AND EXPECTATIONS



## Politics, Religion, and 'Rights' in the United States


Research on how Americans evaluate 'rights' often shows that persons who are more politically and theologically conservative are likelier to favor more circumscribed definitions of 'rights' while prioritizing rights that maximize the liberty of the in-group, including the liberty

of the in-group to defend itself from cultural, economic, or political threats (see review in Davis and Perry 2021). As political theorist Corey Robin (2016:8) explains, this tendency is fundamental to the conflict between conservatism and liberalism.

Though it is often claimed that the left stands for equality while the right stands for freedom, this notion misstates the disagreement between right and left. Historically, the conservative has favored liberty for the higher orders and constraint for the lower orders. What the conservative sees and dislikes in equality, in other words, is not a threat to freedom but its extension. For in that extension, he sees the loss of his own freedom.

Political conservatism, in part, can thus be understood as a movement to maximize in-group liberty and control threats to that liberty. So too conservative religion often functions as broad marker of ethno-cultural identity, justifier of the social status quo, and foundation for beliefs about cultural or moral 'purity' (Adler et al. 2021; Rawls 1972). It is consequently a key mechanism for constraining outsiders' within-group privileges. Unsurprisingly then, Schwadel and Garneau (2019) find evidence that affiliation with evangelical denominations, and a literalist interpretation of the Bible is associated with lesser willingness to allow full freedom of speech to marginalized out-groups. Similarly, Eisenstein and colleagues (2017) demonstrate that, while evangelical Protestants have increased in political tolerance toward stigmatized groups since the 1980s, they remain consistently less willing to extend free speech than are mainline Protestant or Catholic respondents.

Far from simply acting as a marker of which rights Americans are more inclined to restrict , however, sociologists and political scientists have demonstrated that religion also helps us understand which rights Americans support . Gun ownership (Mencken and Froese 2019; Stroope and Tom 2017; Yamane 2016), expansive police powers and desires for more stringent social control (Thompson and Froese 2016; see also Baker and Booth 2016), and support for broadly defined 'freedoms' associated with conservative or libertarian ideologies (Braunstein

and Taylor 2017; Marti 2020) are all frequently couched within a religious framework in political and social discourse. Lewis (2017) describes the recent decades as a 'rights turn' among conservative religious groups who now articulate their political agenda to preserve their cultural influence while marginalizing others in terms of 'religious liberty' or 'religious freedom' (see also Mayrl 2018; Mayrl and Venny 2021). Furthermore, Braunstein and Taylor's (2017) research indicates that religio-political appeals undergird claims that some conscribed set of rights are god ordained even among the irreligious, suggesting that rhetorical strategies sacralizing some freedoms over others may be more important for understanding American political beliefs than religious belonging or practice per se. Such studies highlight the need for research outlining the sustained and transformative role of religious influences in American civic life (Adler et al. 2021; Delehanty et al. 2019; Stewart et al. 2018; Williams and Fuist 2013).


## Christian Nationalism, Civic Belonging, and Rights


Burgeoning research on 'Christian nationalism' characterizes the ideology as 'reactionary' and 'ultra-conservative' in its willingness to endorse authoritarian means of social control to the point of encroaching on others' rights, while prioritizing the total freedom of the in-group, in particular white, native-born, conservative Christian men. Predictably, white Christian nationalism is associated with approval for rights that are culturally and historically connected with the project of whiteness including protection of gun rights (Du Mez 2020; Marti 2020; Whitehead et al. 2018) and voting for candidates whom they feel are committed to 'religious freedom' (Perry, Schnabel, et al. 2022).

Importantly, these studies highlight the role of perceived cultural threats as a fundamental organizing force driving Christian nationalism's association with protecting rights which have historically facilitated and legitimated white Americans' privileged position within society.

Indeed, those rights which are more intimately tied to whiteness are often more fully integrated into what Gorski and Perry (2022) call white Christian nationalism's 'deep story' of America. This deep story, steeped in the language of abstract liberalism and personal liberty, further resulted in support for more libertarian responses to the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020 (Adler et al. 2021; Corcoran et al. 2021; Perry et al. 2021). Taken together, this research demonstrates white Christian nationalism's association with support for expansive understandings of rights typically reserved for whites, as well as a suspicion of and resistance to efforts which may cause imposition.

At the same time, however, white Christian nationalism is strongly associated with efforts to constrain the liberties of perceived outsiders. In as much as Christian nationalism serves to construct and reinforce group-boundaries delineating the 'real Americans,' from those for whom the deep story suggests the United States was not intended. Prior research demonstrates that Christian nationalism predicts greater opposition to same-sex marriage, and reigning in access to abortion services for women (Whitehead and Perry 2015, 2020). Similarly, Cravens (2022) finds that Californians who report higher levels of Christian nationalist beliefs are less supportive of political leaders who identify as LGBT+, arguing that adherence to this ideology supports hetero and cisnormative conceptions of who is fit for leadership positions in America. Supporting this connection between beliefs that America is a 'Christian nation,' and adherence to more stringent sexual norms, Perry and Whitehead (2022) show that Christian nationalists are significantly more inclined to support bans on pornography across multiple sources of data.

Beyond influencing attitudes towards sexual morality, Christian nationalism's commitment to social order often inclines adherents to express more authoritarian and racialized views of civic belonging and rights. Civic engagement, particularly voting rights, has become

increasingly framed as a 'privilege' among republican voters and political representatives (Gomez and Doherty 2021). Supporting this understanding are beliefs that voting in the United States is 'too easy,' and that this allows for 'rampant voter fraud' which are significantly more common among Americans who subscribe to Christian nationalism compared to other cross sections of the population (Perry, Whitehead, et al 2022). This suggests that commitment to social order encapsulated in Christian nationalist mythos implicitly views broader access to civic influence as a threat. Specifically, Christian nationalists strategically reserve support for the rights and privileges of society for those who are cultural and political allies, while working to restrict and control the rights of outsiders. Among historically marginalized groups Christian nationalism's commitment to social order writ large is associated with preferences more constrained speech for all groups but implicit understanding of this order being built upon racialized hierarchies prioritizes the rights of racists and militarists over communists, atheists, and homosexuals (Davis and Perry 2021; see also Dahab and Omori 2019). Other research finds that these elements of Christian nationalism are reflected in how Americans evaluate racialized federal spending (Davis 2019) and the use of authoritarian means of social control to control problem populations (Davis 2018; Perry et al. 2019).

Emergent research in Christian nationalism has also suggested that it intersects with other social identities, specifically race and gender, in ways that attenuate its relationships with social or political attitudes. Some of these findings are particularly relevant to our discussion of Christian nationalism and 'rights.' In an analysis of American attitudes towards Covid-19 restrictions, for example, Perry and colleagues (2021) report significantly stronger resistance to precautionary measures among Christian nationalist men than women. They also find evidence that resistance to these measures along the lines of Christian nationalism are stronger among

white respondents than Black respondents. And Gorski and Perry (2022) show that Christian nationalism's association with beliefs in more libertarian, 'laissez faire' economic policies are similarly racialized.  Taken together, evidence suggests that the understanding of America's 1 'Christian heritage,' and desires for religiously informed governance in American society are couched in implicit racialized and gendered understanding of who America's intended inheritors are-namely, white, conservative men. White-male privilege, then, can be understood as a sometimes necessary but insufficient catalyst for the reactionary aspects of Christian nationalism which provides the conditions necessary to interpret 'Christian' and 'American' to mean 'only people like me.'


## Expectations


Given Christian nationalism's association with more authoritarian and anti-democratic desires for social control over 'outsiders' (especially those commonly framed as cultural or political adversaries) and evidence linking it to stronger disdain for restrictions on in-group liberties, we expect Christian nationalism to be significantly tied to respondents' support, or lack thereof, for various civil rights.

Specifically, we expect that adults who more strongly adhere to Christian nationalist ideology will be less likely to support rights associated with liberal democracy including the

freedom of the press-whom Trump framed as the 'true enemy of the people' (Wagner 2018)and protections for free speech. We would also expect this aspect of Christian nationalism to manifest itself in disregard for rights which might protect denigrated minority populations (e.g., those suspected of criminal activity) and thus stifle efforts to maintain social order and hierarchy. Such rights include the right to a speedy and fair trial and protections against unlawful search and seizure. And because voting represents a pathway by which citizens can peaceably overthrow those in power, we also anticipate Christian nationalism would be negatively associated with defining voting as a 'right' as opposed to a 'privilege' that those in power can curtail or revoke.

At the same time, we expect Christian nationalism to bolster support for civil liberties traditionally associated with more conservative, authoritarian, and racially-coded worldviews such as religious liberty, gun rights, and states' rights.

Finally, given previous findings outlining the racialized and gendered effects of Christian nationalism, as well as the racial histories of civil liberties in the United States, we investigate whether race or gender attenuate Christian nationalism's association with respondents' support for certain civil liberties.


## METHODS



## Data


Data for this study come from the Public Discourse and Ethics Survey (hereafter PDES) (Author DATE). There are eight waves of the PDES. For our analysis, we use data from two PDES waves: Wave 1, collected in August 2019 (for most controls) and Wave 8, collected in August 2021 (for Christian nationalism and views about rights). Survey waves were designed by the authors and the survey instrument was fielded by YouGov, an international research data and

analytics company. YouGov recruits a panel of respondents through websites and banner ads. 2 These respondents are not paid directly but are entered into lotteries for monetary prizes. In order to draw a nationally representative sample, YouGov employs a method called 'matching.' Drawing a random sample from the American Community Survey, YouGov then matches a respondent in the opt-in panel who is the closest to the Census respondent based on key sociodemographic factors. Because of the specific recruitment and sampling design used by YouGov, the company does not publish traditional response rates. However, YouGov develops sampling weights to ensure the survey sample aligns with nationally representative norms for age, gender, race, education, and census region. Results from the PDES Wave 1 compare favorably with results from the 2018 General Social Survey on demographic factors such as age, gender, race, marital status, region, educational attainment, and evangelical affiliation (see Appendix Table A1). The resulting original survey sample included 2,519 Americans that were matched and weighted. Sample attrition between Waves 1 and 8 over two years and a very modest amount of missing data leaves our final analytic sample with 1,139 cases in full models. For descriptive statistics of all variables in the models, see Table 1.

## Outcomes: Americans' Views on Rights


The outcomes for this study come from two measures used in Wave 8 of the PDES. For the first, we provided Americans with a list of 7 rights outlined in the Bill of Rights. These are: (1) freedom of speech, (2) freedom of the press, (3) freedom of religion, (4) the right to a speedy and fair trial, (5) the right to keep and bear arms, (6) rights not outlined as going to the federal

government go to the states, and (7) no unlawful searches or seizures. We then asked Americans to indicate which right they thought was 'the most important right.' For our multivariate analyses, we created 7 dummy-coded variables in which each right = 1 and all others = 0. We then estimate binary logistic regression models estimating Christian nationalism's association with the likelihood that Americans believe \_\_\_\_\_ is the most important right vs. all the others.

Because initial bivariate analyses indicated these outcomes fell predictably along patterned lines, we also created another binary outcome separating respondents who prioritized rights that were consistently selected by ideological and partisan conservatives and those who chose rights that were not. Specifically, respondents who indicated the 'most important right' was freedom of religion, the right to keep and bear arms, or states' rights were coded 1, while all others who selected freedom of speech, freedom of the press, right to a speedy and fair trial, or no unlawful searches or seizures were coded 0.

For the last outcome, we use a single question from Wave 8 of the PDES in which we ask Americans simply whether they believe voting is a 'privilege' or a 'right.' We code responses such that those who believe voting is a right = 1, privilege = 0. We estimate binary logistic regression models to estimate Christian nationalism's association with viewing voting as a right (something that shall not be infringed) rather than a privilege (something that can be limited or taken away entirely).


## Christian Nationalism


While 'Christian nationalism' has been measured in various ways (e.g., Al-Kire et al. 2021, 2022; Corcoran et al. 2021; McDaniel et al. 2011), the Christian nationalism scale used by Whitehead and Perry (2020) has become the standard across disciplines like sociology, social

psychology, and political science (Al-Kire et al. 2021, 2022; Davis 2018; Armaly et al. 2022). We use a slightly extended version adopted by Gorski and Perry (2022).

The Whitehead and Perry (2020) scale includes six level-of-agreement questions with the statements: 'The federal government should advocate Christian values,' 'The federal government should declare the United States a Christian nation,' 'The federal government should enforce strict separation of church and state (reverse coded),' The federal government should allow religious symbols in public spaces,' 'The federal government should allow prayer in public schools,' and 'The success of the United States is part of God's plan.' Gorski and Perry's (2022) scale adds an additional statement: 'I consider founding documents like the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution to be divinely inspired.' Responses range from 0 = Strongly disagree to 4 = Strongly agree. Following previous research, we combine these measures into an additive scale ranging from 0 to 28, with higher scores indicating greater adherence to Christian nationalism (Cronbach's alpha = .91). The Christian nationalism measures used in these analyses appear on Wave 8 of the PDES. The average score is 13.1 (SD = 8) indicating most Americans hold views on Christian nationalism slightly below the median.


## Control Variables


In light of previous research on Americans' views of rights, we expect our outcomes to be highly correlated with political and religious characteristics. All controls come from Wave 1 of the PDES. For party identification, we use binary indicator variables for Republican (reference), Democrat, Independent, and Other/Not sure. For conservative political ideology we use dummy variables with the Very liberal (reference), Liberal, Moderate, Conservative, Very Conservative, and Not Sure Politically.  Religion controls include religious tradition and 3

frequency of service attendance. Affiliation with a religious tradition is measured with six categories: Evangelical Protestant (reference), Liberal Protestant, Catholic, Other Christian, Other Religion, and Seculars (including atheists, agnostics, and the unaffiliated).  Religious 4 service attendance is measured from 1 = never to 6 = several times a week.

Sociodemographic controls from Wave 1 include variables for race, gender, family income, and region as well as a range for age and educational attainment.  These categories are shown as binary indicators for race (white = reference, Black, Hispanic, Other race), gender (male = 1), household income (less than $30,000 per year = reference, $30,000-59,999, $60,00099,999, $100,000-199,999, $200,000 or more, did not report income), and region (Southern residence = 1). Age is measured in years from 20 to 82. And educational attainment ranges from 1 to 6 representing having completed less than a high school diploma to a postdoctoral degree.


## RESULTS


Table 1 presents descriptive statistics for all variables along with zero-order correlations between variables and Christian nationalism. Bivariate findings affirm that prioritizing particular rights falls consistently along predictable lines. Americans who score higher on Christian nationalism are more likely to believe that gun rights (r = .29, p < .001), religion (r = .25, p < .001), or states' rights (r = .11; p < .001) are the 'most important right,' while selecting freedom of the press (r = -.28, p < .001), free speech (r = -.16, p < .001), right to a speedy and fair trial (r = -.9, p < .01), or protection from unlawful searches and seizures (r = -.16, p < .001) are negatively associated with Christian nationalism. Unsurprisingly, Christian nationalism is

positively associated with selecting 'conservative rights' (gun rights, religion, and states' rights) as the most important (r = .46, p < .001). Christian nationalism is also negatively associated with believing that voting is a right rather than privilege (r = -.30, p < .001). Given that these patterns are so intuitively associated with partisanship, ideology, and racial identity, we turn to multivariate analyses.

Table 2 presents standardized coefficients from binary logistic regression models predicting Americans would select each particular right as the 'most important right' rather than the others. As in the bivariate associations, Christian nationalism is significantly associated with each right in the expected directions, except for freedom of speech. Indicators of political ideology or partisanship were also not associated with selecting freedom of speech. These patterns may be due to the fact that a plurality of Americans chose this right and thus it is prioritized across partisan and ideological camps. Regarding both freedom of the press or a right to a speedy and fair trial, however, Christian nationalism is negatively associated and is the strongest predictor in these models. In other models, Christian nationalism is among the leading predictors, often just behind factors like conservative political ideology. Associations all follow the directions observed at the bivariate level.

Figure 1 illustrates the preponderance of choosing each particular right by showing the distribution of predicted probabilities across quartiles of Christian nationalism (Whitehead and Perry 2020).  While the plurality of Americans in first three quartiles of Christian nationalism all 5 select 'freedom of speech' as the most important right, the plurality of those in the upper quartile of Christian nationalism (roughly 34%) say that gun rights is the most important rights, with

roughly the same percentage choosing freedom of press (28%) or freedom of religion (27%). The figure also clearly shows that as Americans increase in their adherence to Christian nationalist ideology, they are more likely to prioritize gun rights, freedom of religion, and states' rights, and deprioritize free speech, freedom of the press, right to a speedy and fair trial, and protection from unlawful searches and seizures.

## DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS


Americans often express profound disagreement as to what sorts of opportunities and resources constitutes 'rights' and which rights are more important than others. Building on research suggesting Christian nationalist ideology exhibits authoritarian and anti-democratic tendencies that emphasize in-group liberty and out-group control, we anticipated that (especially white, male) Christian nationalism would prioritize rights that maximize the liberty of dominant majorities while deprioritizing rights that grant protections and subversive liberties to those outside of power. Our findings largely confirm our hypotheses, with one key exception. Christian nationalism was among the strongest predictors that Americans would prioritize 'conservative rights' (freedom of religion, gun rights, states' rights) either separately or together, while deprioritizing rights like freedom of the press, right to speedy and fair trial, and protection from unlawful searches or seizures. Descriptively, Christian nationalism was also clearly associated with declining emphasis on freedom of speech. Lastly Christian nationalism was also the strongest predictor Americans view voting as a 'privilege' rather than a 'right.' Contradicting our expectation, however, race and gender did not significantly moderate these associations,

suggesting Christian nationalism inclines Americans generally toward more authoritarian, and anti-democratic views on 'rights.'

Our findings extend research on Americans' understandings of 'rights' as well as Christian nationalism research in several important ways. First and foremost, the data clearly and consistently indicate that Americans' divergent views on whether to prioritize certain rights over others, or even to define certain civic activities as 'rights,' are not solely determined by partisanship or political ideology, but also by beliefs that center 'Christianity' within America's deep story and future. Indeed, Christian nationalism was often a stronger predictor than party identification and often on par with political ideology in its influence. In terms of religious factors shaping Americans' views about civil rights, Christian nationalism was almost always more substantively important than religious tradition and most often contributed more substantively than religious service attendance. Why is this the case? As work on 'public religious expression' has argued, Christian nationalism represents a fundamentally different religious dynamic than personal religious identity or religiosity that is ultimately related to broader social order and power (Delehanty et al. 2019; Perry and Whitehead 2022; Stewart et al. 2018). Indeed, as Whitehead and Perry (2020) have shown in their analyses, we also found that indicators of personal religiosity exhibit opposite directional associations to Christian nationalism when both are included in the model. This suggests that while religious commitment is often associated with conservative or reactionary political views, it is likely Christian nationalist ideology that accounts for that association. Once we hold that influence constant, our results indicate that religious commitment can exhibit a more liberalizing tendency.

Why does Christian nationalism relate to 'rights' in a way that partisanship or political ideology does not? Even more than partisanship, which can encompass a variety of political

philosophies, Christian nationalism is fundamentally about American cultural membership and who rightfully deserves access to citizenship and civic participation. To those Americans who subscribe to Christian nationalism, 'rights' are intended to protect 'our' liberties, not those of deviants, usurpers, outsiders, or those who are 'unworthy' (Perry, Whitehead, et al. 2022). Yet Christian nationalism is also clearly different from 'conservative' political ideology in that both remain powerfully significant predictors of emphasizing various rights. Though Christian nationalism is certainly a form of conservatism, it is possible that Christian nationalism captures a more explicit, reactionary 'us vs. them' dynamic in American politics compared to the singleitem measure of political ideology on its own. 6

An issue that requires discussion is why the associations were generally consistent across racial identity and gender. In contrast with numerous other studies (e.g., Armaly et al. 2022; Gorski and Perry 2022; Perry, Cobb, et al. 2022; Perry and Whitehead 2019), black and white Americans did not diverge sharply in their patterns of association between Christian nationalism and political attitudes. And only Hispanics showed minor slope differences from whites. Meanwhile, the associations for men and women were largely the same except that Christian nationalist men were slightly more likely to prioritize 'conservative' rights than their women counterparts. Though enough research has shown that Christian nationalism's influence is often racialized and gendered, it is also common that various outcomes in such studies did not necessarily yield the same patterns. In this case, it may simply be that Christian nationalism's influence on how Americans prioritize and deprioritize various 'rights' is more uniform in its

tendency to elevate the rights that bolster in-group liberty and deprioritize 'subversive' protections and rights. To our knowledge, research looking at Christian nationalism and the rights of gender or sexual minorities has never found a moderating effect of race or gender, and thus, we may simply be witnessing a similar pattern here (Whitehead and Perry 2015, 2019, 2020).

Some data limitations should be acknowledged in order to chart a path for future research. First, the key variables come from Wave 8 of the PDES, making the analysis crosssectional. As such we are unable to establish temporal precedent and strong causal claims must be made with caution. It is conceivable that Americans who hold certain views on fundamental rights are more inclined to favor political theologies like Christian nationalism that justify their prioritization (e.g., religious liberty). Though we would argue that our assumed causal ordering (Christian nationalism influencing the prioritization of certain rights over others) is more plausible and has more precedent in research, we acknowledge the possibility of bidirectional relationships. Future studies would ideally make use of temporal and experimental methods to order to establish causal direction more definitively. Also, future studies could inquire about other 'rights' issues that currently divide Americans, such as abortion rights, health care, welfare, privacy, and education. Though we have focused on more fundamental rights (voting, free speech, and religious liberty), many other opportunities and 'entitlements' would be worth examining.

Our findings have particular relevance amidst the current political discussions about gun rights following numerous mass shootings, transgender rights, what seems to be the imminent fall of Roe, and increasing voter restrictions throughout the country. We have shown that Christian nationalist ideology seems to incline Americans toward authoritarian and anti-

democratic views of 'rights' that prioritize in-group liberty, such as freedom of religion (ours, not theirs, see Perry, Schnabel, et al. 2022), gun rights, and states' rights. It also tends to deprioritize the rights and protections that either facilitate criticism of government leaders (free speech, free press, and voting rights) or limit the governments' ability to suppress problem populations (right to speedy and fair trial, protection from unlawful searches and seizures). Given these patterns, we would expect Christian nationalism's role in contemporary debates over abortion, guns, and voter access to favor the liberty of historical majority groups (whites, conservative Christians, cisgender persons, and men) and to limit the rights of racial, religious, sexual, and gender minorities.

## 1 Introduction


US higher education is distinctive in its emphasis on student choice, autonomy, and mobility despite frequently failing to meet such a promise through the many examples of educational inequality and stratification [1]. For example, the course selection decisions made by first year college students are stratified by social class [2]. One of the most frequently discussed sites of these ideas and arguments is college admissions, particularly through the well understood correlations between household income and test scores [3]. This line of research, along with the Covid-19 pandemic, have coalesced to push many universities' decisions to drop standardized testing from first year admissions.

Anew wave of research in and around college admissions has leveraged computational methods to analyze how other elements in college applications are similarly correlated with other information about the applicant. These include examples of how admissions essays are strong predictors of gender, income, and SAT scores [4, 5]. Other studies have considered letters of recommendation [6, 7] and which high schools are targeted by universities for recruitment [8]. However, this growing literature along with the now classic approaches to analyzing variation and stratification in application materials have rarely considered an important feature of US higher education: transfer admissions.

In the US, transferring is the process where students from community colleges or bachelors degree granting institutions apply to college or university to complete their undergraduate education. These institutions are stratified by the types of degrees they are able to award as well as through their selectivity (community colleges have open admissions, four year schools do not) and economic opportunities (bachelors degrees often lead to higher paying jobs and are a prerequisite into high paying professional degree programs). Recent research has found that educational outcomes (ie. graduation rates after transferring) are stratified by the direction of the transfer [9]. The 'direction' refers to the academic pathway of the applicant: 'lateral' for students transferring from a four year institution to another four year institution; 'vertical' for students transferring from community college to a four year university; and 'reverse' for students transferring from four year institutions to community college (the aforementioned study compared lateral and reverse transfers). Studies have examined how coursework, gender, remedial classes, and other student characteristics lead to successful vertical transfer [10]. But fewer studies have examined how, like first year application materials, dimensions of stratification can be connected to variation in transfer application materials.

Despite receiving less attention in academia and popular discourse, the transfer system is quite popular (nearly 40% of all undergraduates transfer schools at least once) and emblematic of the ideals in US higher education of giving students flexibility and 'second chances' [11]. Enrolling in community colleges to eventually transfer is also popular in Latinx 1 communities.

Latinx students are the largest ethnic group enrolled in California community colleges: 46% of Latinx students graduating from the highest performing high schools in the state still end up going to community college first [12]. But because community colleges also have to serve a wider variety of students along with their mission of helping students transfer out, their experiences are much different from students already enrolled in four year schools. Analyzing application data, such as admissions essays, could provide unique snapshots into these differences as articulated by the students themselves and how they vary by academic pathway. Doing so with computational methods would also expand the burgeoning literature of computation and systems of evaluation. It could also push current notions of fairness and bias in data science, which often focuses on race and gender [13], to consider how institutional experiences and pathways are also fateful in analysis and practice.

In this paper, we apply computational and human reading of text to measure variation in transfer admissions essays based on the institutional stratification of the applicants. Generally, students at community colleges have access to very different educational resources and experiences than students enrolled in four year schools, and these differences likely go beyond traditional outcome metrics. Our work therefore highlights another way stratification can shape educational mechanisms but also how these differences can be measured in text and how the transfer application itself could help reduce these differences. Our analysis focuses on three elements that are stratified in many social contexts: linguistic, cultural, and narrative capital. These constructs have been used in the theoretical and empirical development of the sociology of evaluation [14] and culture. We consider both the stratified academic pathway of the applicants (lateral and vertical) and the essay prompt students responded to. We find that the essays are fairly distinctive based on the applicant's educational pathway, though these differences are also sensitive to the language of the essay prompt they were given. Outside the research context, systems of evaluation might consider these results before or after adopting technology related to evaluation. See Figure 1 for a conceptual diagram of the paper.


## 2 Admissions Essays and Beyond: Computational Methods and Systems of Evaluation


Previous work studying admissions essays has been mostly descriptive and correlational. For example, studies using both computational and qualitative methods have found that applicant gender, income, college GPA, and thematic choices have all been found to be correlated with admissions essays [4, 5, 15, 16]. Another study found that word vectors trained on essays written by applicants in the highest income quartile performed better on the Google Analogy Test Set and various word similarity tests than essays written by the two lowest income quartiles [17]. The computational studies have been consistent in their results: applicants characteristics and information are predictable from essays.

Our study uses this stratification as a lens to examine variation in transfer application materials, namely the essays.

Other studies have analyzed essays using other methods. A study of admissions essays submitted to selective universities in the UK found narrative and orthographic patterning based on the type of school attended by the applicants, such as students from elite backgrounds name-dropping their elite networks and connections [18]. Findings from a study of diversity statements submitted to the University of Michigan found that students from similar class backgrounds would write about similar topics, regardless of race [19], and the information dashboards used in holistic review were found to improve equity in admissions outcomes for students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds [20]. These studies match the results of the computational analyses to a degree but not entirely due to the unique affordances of qualitatively oriented methods. We took these as cues to complement our computational analyses with qualitative coding.


## 3 Data Science and Institutional Stratification


Some of the guiding principles of the new wave of data science for education research are the abilities to ask 'old questions with new methods and data' but also 'new questions with old data' [21-23]. Computational sociology has adopted similar positions by seizing opportunities to analyze new sources of data to study social interactions and processes [24]. However, most of the 'new types' of data are often unstructured, non-numerical data (eg. text, visual, audio) that have long been analyzed using qualitative methods. Sociologist Laura Nelson has taken this insight and presented frameworks to combine computational and human reading of text to both deepen analysis towards a framework of 'computational grounded theory' [25] and to generate points of reference and comparison [26]. Given the relative paucity of information

## Transfer Essays

about transfer application materials and how they might be stratified, we follow Nelson's frameworks towards methodological plurality to generate deeper, multiplex insights into a key social process.

Though research into transfer application materials is relatively sparse, social scientists in the US have generated insights into the transfer process from other perspectives. For example, a national study found that students were less likely to transfer laterally if they were more socially integrated into their school [27]. Sociologists have also observed stratification in the community college system and constituent transfer processes [28]. In an even broader sense, other scholars have pointed out that there is stark stratification across all institutions of higher education, including graduate school [29, 30]. Our study applies the 'new ways' and 'new data' frameworks described above to examine how applicants are stratified by the type of institutions they attend at the moment of application to reframe the transfer application itself as an outcome of different types of acculturation and socialization.

Prior research on transfer and institutional stratification in higher education has shown in various ways that students combine their own sociocultural capital [31] with those acquired and accumulated at their respective institutions. If we accept the premise that lateral applicants have a distinguishable forms of sociocultural capital as at least partly evidenced by their ability to enroll in a four year school from high school, we might also expect that these differences not only change but also become more pronounced given their experiences in colleges relative to the experiences of students in community college. Likewise, students attending community colleges are also experiencing an accumulation of different types of sociocultural capital. In our study, we look specifically at how this manifests through differences in essay content and style, the culture of how closely students follow prompts, and narrative patterns. Understanding stratification in what many might assume is an 'equalizing' force is important not just to scholarship but also practice.


## 4 Framework


Measuring institutional stratification and variation in transfer application materials could be done in many ways, but here we apply concepts from Bourdieusian sociocultural capital [31]. Specifically, we consider linguistic, cultural, and narrative capital with respect to academic pathway (lateral or vertical). Other computational analyses of text data have adapted similar theoretical constructs and measured macro level factors [32, 33]. We also consider how specific essay prompts might activate different types of capital that either exacerbate or reduce variation [34]. We hypothesize that since transfer applicants are stratified by the types of schools they attend, the content of their essays likewise vary with respect to their academic pathway and in response to specific essay prompts. There are many different perspectives from which to measure this variation, but we adapt sociocultural frameworks and theories in our analysis.


## 4.1 Linguistic Capital


Bourdieu described linguistic capital as the knowledge and capacity to use linguistic forms and styles in a given social context [35]. Though Basil Bernstein used different terminology, he also noted how linguistic features varied and that schools tended to prefer the language practices of students from higher social classes [36]. While their focus was on spoken language, we use computational methods to test these theories with textual data. In our study, we measure the strength of the relationship between academic pathway and transfer essays based on word choice patterns and writing style to observe how institutional stratification relates to linguistic variation. Given our use of the same methods, we can also compare these results with the aforementioned research on first year college admissions essays which found strong correlation between essay content and style, income, and SAT scores.


## 4.2 Cultural Capital


Cultural capital, perhaps the most well known of Bourdieu's theories of capital, is defined as the cultural practices, knowledge, and performances that are enacted in social situations [31]. We pair this concept with Durkheim's theories of rules and education, specifically that schools teach and reinforce rules and approaches to life that students carry in and out of school [37], and examine cultural practices around how closely transfer applicants follow the wording of the essay prompts. Put differently, do lateral and vertical applicants follow the 'rules' of the essay prompt in the same way? Computers can be used to identify markers of cultural capital, such as references to specific named entities in text, something we take advantage of here.


## 4.3 Narrative Capital


Although narrative capital is similar in spirit to other forms of Bourdieusian capital, [38] describes it as the raw narrative materials that go into storytelling and self presentation. It therefore relies much on mastery of both language and culture [38]. Computational methods could be good at identifying and modeling narrative capital, but there also is no reported description of the narrative tropes and themes which comprise the genre of 'transfer admissions essay' comparable to something well known like Hollywood movie narrative arcs [39]. To capture narrative capital, we therefore qualitatively code and analyze the essays. Doing so could inform future work on personal statements beyond numerical measures.

As a first pass, we analyzed the essays using commonly used, relatively simple metrics. These included Simpson's diversity index, a statistic sometimes used to measure lexical diversity in text [40]; the Flesch-Kincaid grade level

The lexical diversity index was the same for both groups up to the fourth decimal (0.012). ## 6 Methods


We use outputs from the computational models as independent variables to analyze using various statistical techniques. We then complement these analyses with inductive qualitative coding to compare the human and machine reading and provide deeper insight into the specific tropes and themes transfer applicants deploy in their essays. Each of the methods correspond to specific theories of sociocultural capital and their stratification among transfer applicants by their academic background. The results of the paper are also organized this way and are presented as study one, two, and three. We hope the three sets of findings can become reference points for future studies of transfer admissions in the US.


## 6.1 Study One: Essay Content and Style


First, to capture linguistic stratification we use correlated topic modeling (CTM) [42] and the LIWC software package [43] to model variation in essay content and style, following [4]. We use CTM to model thematic patterns with the STM package in R; when the primary STM function of this specific package is used without covariates, the code defaults to a fast implementation of CTM [44]. Prior to generating the model, we removed stopwords (using the SMART list of English stopwords [45]), stemmed the words (using the Snowball stemmer [46]), removed numbers and punctuation, and lowercased all letters. After removing these, we only included the 10,000 most frequent terms to account for rare and infrequent words. These are common textual preprocessing techniques that can potentially improve the quality of the topic model and downstream analysis [47], though this is not guaranteed to always be the case [48]. These procedures were also used in the aforementioned study of essay content and style [4]. We use the ldatuning package in R [49] to determine the number of topics (see Figures SM1 through SM3 in the supplementary materials). To model writing style and other patterns, we use LIWC (specifically LIWC-15). We exclude the LIWC feature of 'Word Count' due to the change in essay

formats between the years. Combined, these methods can show how linguistic capital varies among transfer applicants based on their educational histories.

Differences in the prevalence of topics and LIWC features were analyzed by educational pathway using a traditional comparative approach with t-tests along with a supervised learning framework to predict whether applicants are applying from community college or bachelor's granting institutions based on their essays. To account for the data imbalances, we use Welch's t-test and two different but complementary methods within the supervised learning framework. The first is the InterModel Vigorish (IMV), a new technique to analyze the outcomes of predictive models (specifically logistic regression) that works by comparing the predictive accuracy of a given model with another model that only predicts the mode outcome [50]. The results from this method could be compared to the common vigorish (percentage of winnings deducted from players) of 1% in blackjack which, on average, becomes 0.0099 cents per dollar for the casino.

Along with the IMV, we use undersampling and report prediction accuracies over several thousand trials. The first step in undersampling is to make the two groups (lateral and vertical) the same size. We follow standard procedures by generating a random sample of observations from the larger group that is the same size as the smaller group. Then, we use 10 fold cross validation to predict if essays were written by lateral applicants or vertical applicants. This procedure was repeated thousands of times. Repeated undersampling allows for a robust analysis where 1) classification accuracy can be compared with random guessing (expected accuracy of 50%) and 2) create points of comparison for how well text classifiers can predict academic pathways of applicants solely based on their essays and their respective prompts. We use logistic regression as our classifier based on how well it worked in a similar study [5]. These different approaches would show how specific thematic and stylistic features of writing vary for individual variables (eg. specific topics) but also in the aggregate among transfer applicants.


## 6.2 Study Two: Named Entity Recognition


Next, we perform an observational experiment to measure how the essays changed (or did not change) with the new prompt as a way to describe cultural stratification in transfer admissions essays. Specifically, we use named entity recognition (NER) to measure the effect that the new essay prompt had on students naming specific organizations, people, businesses, places, and other entities. The older prompt solicited students to describe the specific examples of how they participated in various organizations related to their field of interest, but the newer prompt was less specific. This study will examine if transfer applicants responded to the prompt by bringing up named entities even though the new prompt did not explicitly solicit them as before. The specific 'culture' being measured here is not the types of named entities (eg. businesses vs. non-profits) but rather the culture of essay prompt interpretation. Since

the new prompt did not specifically solicit named entities like it did the year prior, are students making fewer references to them?

The emerging causal inference with NLP literature has so far focused on word embedding [51] and topic modeling [52] methods. We extend this rapidly growing literature in our use of a finer grained method, NER, and in our more sociological context (as opposed to political science or traditional computer science). The first step was to use NER on the essays and tag every instance of a named entity being mentioned. To do this, we used the SpaCy package [53] in Python. SpaCy's NER tags many different types of entities, including times and numbers, but we limited the tagging to people, organizations, and concepts. To verify the tags, we took random samples of essays and checked that all of the tags were referencing named entities and reflected entities the students were associating with their intended majors in various ways.

After tagging the essays with NER, we counted the number of words and number of characters that the applicants used in the named entities for a given essay. These were used to create the outcome of interest: the percentages of the essays (based on words and characters) that were used on named entities. Our percentage approach was chosen to reflect the different word limits applicants had on their essays from year to year (478 words on average vs. 312 words on average). Focusing on word and character based percentages helps serve as robustness check (eg. if some NER tags have very few words or many characters). Once the NER percentages per essay were calculated, we use propensity score weighting to make statistical adjustments to the data and control for any selection biases. See Table 3 for a full list of the variables used for weighting. The propensity score weighting was calculated with the average treatment effect (ATE) as the estimand [54] with the 2016-2017 essay prompt as the treatment.

While it is possible that some students in our data applied in 2015-2016 and 2016-2017, it is an unlikely scenario because transfer applicants to the UC must have already completed a significant amount of coursework (equivalent to an associates degree) and would be unable to complete additional units. It is also not likely that applicants in 2015-2016 were even aware that a new

essay prompt was going to be used in 2016-2017. Combined, we assume the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA) was not violated [55], giving us additional confidence in the data and findings. Note that we do not include reported household incomes in our analysis. We did this because approximately 20% of all transfer applicants report a household income either below $ 10,000 or no income at all. Among students reported an income of at least $ 10,000, there was also a weak correlation with the essays ( R 2 = ∼ 0 05). . This is likely due to many community college students working at least part time and reporting that income rather than the income of their entire household.


## 6.3 Study Three: Inductive Qualitative Coding


Finally, we model narrative stratification with qualitative inductive coding. This approach complements the previous analyses because it provides a perspective on the essays that would be difficult to capture with purely computational methods [26]. For this analysis, we coded a stratified random sample of essays submitted by transfer applicants intending to major in computer science and sociology for each year. Computer science and sociology were selected because they are very different disciplines and students presumably have different experiences leading up to declaring each as a major; they are also both popular majors and attract a wide variety of students. We ended up coding a total 198 essays divided roughly equally into fourths by intended major and application year.

First, we developed a qualitative codebook through an iterative process to identify the narrative themes and arcs described by the students in their essays. Once the codebook was finalized, we handcoded each of the essays to census. More information about the codebook is available in Table SM5 in the supplementary materials. We then report the codes that lateral and vertical applicants used the most differently over the two years. These were the codes that one group used more or less and the other group did the opposite. For example, we would highlight a code that lateral applicants used more in the second year but vertical applicants used less. We further filter the results by focusing on codes where the differences in code frequency for one group is at least three times the difference for another group. Using the previous example, this means we would present a code used by lateral applicants more in the second year only if the increase was at least three times larger than the decrease among the vertical applicants. These are the codes that get at the strongest narrative responses to the essay prompts for each group and intended major.

## 7.1 Study One: Variation in Essay Content and Style


Three CTM models were generated: one for the 2015-2016 transfer essays; one for the 2016-2017 transfer essays; and one for all of the transfer essays. The outputs from the ldatuning package indicated that 30 topics for the individual
